# 00 — Hello, Dojo

Welcome. This course teaches you SQL by making you write it — every line,
yourself, against a real PostgreSQL database with millions of rows in it.
Nothing here autocompletes, autocorrects, or writes queries for you. You type
SQL into a file, you run a command, and an automated gate tells you whether
your answer is right — and if it isn't, it shows you evidence: the rows it
expected, the rows you produced, and what to reconsider.

This first lesson has one job: prove your toolchain works and teach you the
gameplay loop you'll repeat 47 more times.

## The loop

Every lesson lives in a directory like this one. Inside you'll find:

- `README.md` — the lesson. Read it top to bottom.
- `ex1/`, `ex2/`, ... — one directory per exercise. You edit
  `exN/solution.sql` and nothing else.
- `test_lesson.py` — the gate. You never edit it, but you should read it;
  it's quoted at the bottom of every README so you always know exactly what
  is being checked.

The commands you'll live in:

```
uv run dojo test 00_hello_dojo        # grade this lesson
uv run dojo test 00_hello_dojo ex2    # grade just one exercise
uv run dojo hint 00_hello_dojo ex2    # stuck? reveal the next hint tier
uv run dojo status                    # the big progress dashboard
uv run dojo next                      # what should I work on?
```

Every graded run happens against a **fresh clone** of a template database.
You cannot break anything. Drop a table, fill it with garbage — the next run
gets a pristine copy.

## The database

The dataset is a small e-commerce shop: 50,000 customers, 10,000 products,
500,000 orders, a million order line-items, a million product reviews, three
million clickstream events, and a 500-person staff table. Read
[docs/dataset.md](../../docs/dataset.md) now — five minutes there saves you
an hour of guessing later. Exact numbers live in
[docs/dataset_facts.md](../../docs/dataset_facts.md), regenerated from the
real data every time you seed.

## Exercise 1 — run a query someone else wrote

Just this once, the answer is given to you. Copy the query below into
`ex1/solution.sql`, replacing the `SELECT 1;` placeholder:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM customers;
```

Then run:

```
uv run dojo test 00_hello_dojo ex1
```

Before you paste it in, run the gate once with the file as shipped. Watch it
fail. That failure output — expected rows vs. your rows — is the shape of
every failure you'll see in this course. Get comfortable reading it.

## Exercise 2 — your first solo query

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. The shop wants to see **everything about product
4242**: every column of the `products` table, for the single row whose `id`
is 4242.

You haven't been taught `WHERE` yet — that's lesson 02 — but you need one
tiny preview of it here: appending `WHERE id = 4242` to a `SELECT` keeps only
the rows where the `id` column equals 4242. To select every column, SQL has
the shorthand `*`.

Required output: all six columns of `products` (`id`, `name`, `category`,
`price`, `description`, `attributes`), one row. Ordering doesn't matter (one
row can't be out of order).

```
uv run dojo test 00_hello_dojo ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — the same trick, a different table

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Return **everything about customer 4242**:
every column of the `customers` table, for the single row whose `id` is
4242.

Same two ideas as ex2 — `*` for all columns, `WHERE id = ...` for one row —
applied to a table with a different shape. Five columns come back this time
(`id`, `name`, `email`, `country`, `created_at`), not six. Predict the
column *count* before you run it; being surprised by the shape of your own
result is the habit this course is trying to break.

Run: `uv run dojo test 00_hello_dojo ex3`

## Exercise 4 — ask for less

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Product 4242 again — but this time return only
two columns, `name` and `price`, in that order.

`*` is convenient and almost always wrong outside a scratch console: it
couples whatever reads your query to columns it never asked for, and it
quietly changes shape the day someone adds a column. Naming your columns is
the default habit; lesson 01 is entirely about it.

One row, two columns.

Run: `uv run dojo test 00_hello_dojo ex4`

# Reading - 00_hello_dojo

The loop you just ran — write, grade, read the evidence — is the whole
course. This page is the other half of every lesson: the *why* behind the
problems you just solved. It is meant to be read **after** you attempt a
problem, whether the gate went green or red. Failing first and reading
second is not a consolation prize; it is the version of studying that
actually sticks.

## Notes

**Why a real database and not a toy one.** Almost every SQL tutorial runs
against a dozen rows, where every query is instant and every mistake is
invisible. This course runs against 500,000 orders and 3,000,000 events on
purpose. At that size, a missing `WHERE` takes noticeably longer, a missing
index is something you can *feel*, and the difference between a good query
and a bad one stops being an aesthetic opinion. Part 5 depends on this
entirely — you cannot learn to read a query plan on data that fits in a
cache line.

**Why every run gets a fresh clone.** PostgreSQL can create a database
`TEMPLATE another_database`, which copies the files on disk rather than
replaying the data. That is how `dojo test` hands each exercise a private,
pristine copy of a multi-gigabyte database in a second or two. The practical
consequence for you: there is no state to corrupt and no reason to be
careful. Drop a table. Delete every row. `UPDATE` without a `WHERE`. The
next run does not know or care — and deliberately breaking things is one of
the fastest ways to learn what a constraint or a transaction is actually for.

**Why the gate is quoted in every README.** Being graded by a program you
cannot read is how people learn to game a test instead of learning the
subject. Every lesson prints its own grader at the bottom, verbatim. When
you are stuck, reading the gate is legitimate and often the fastest route to
understanding what the question is really asking — is order being compared?
is the plan being inspected? is it timing me?

**A note on determinism.** The dataset is generated from a fixed random seed
with fixed timestamps and no `now()` anywhere. Customer 4242 has the same six
orders on your laptop as on anyone else's. That is what lets the lessons cite
exact numbers, and it is why `docs/dataset_facts.md` is worth a bookmark.

## ex1 — running someone else's query

The instruction to run the gate *before* pasting the answer is the real
exercise. A test suite you have only ever seen pass teaches you nothing; the
failure output is the interface you will actually use for the next fifty
lessons. Read it once, deliberately: it shows the rows the reference query
produced, the rows yours produced, and a one-line diagnosis of the
difference. Every failure in this course is written to teach rather than to
scold, and the ones in Part 5 will show you an entire query plan.

## ex2 — your first solo query

Two ideas arrive at once. `*` means "every column of the row", and it is a
convenience for humans at a console, not a thing to ship. `WHERE id = 4242`
is a *filter*: it is evaluated once per row, and keeps the row only when the
result is true. Filtering is conceptually independent of which columns you
select — SQL lets you describe *what* you want without describing *how* to
find it, and the planner decides the how. That separation is the whole
premise of the language.

## ex3 — the same shape, a different table

Transfer is the point. The query differs from ex2 in exactly two tokens, and
the result differs in shape because `customers` has five columns and
`products` has six. If you predicted "six columns" out of habit, notice
that: most SQL bugs in production are a correct query pointed at the wrong
assumption about the data.

## ex4 — asking for less

`SELECT *` in application code is the most common smell in SQL review. It
drags columns across the network that nobody reads (`products.description`
is a paragraph of marketing text), it makes the result shape depend on
unrelated schema changes, and — the part that bites in Part 5 — it makes an
*index-only scan* impossible, because the index cannot possibly contain
every column. Lesson 34 will make that concrete. For now: name your columns.

## Further reading

- [The SQL Language — a first query](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-select.html) — the official five-minute version of what you just did.
- [`SELECT` reference page](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — dense, and the single most useful page in the docs. Skim it now; you will return to it for the rest of your career.
- [`CREATE DATABASE ... TEMPLATE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/manage-ag-templatedbs.html) — how `dojo test` gives you a pristine multi-gigabyte database per run.
- [Don't Do This](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) — the PostgreSQL wiki's list of things that look reasonable and are not. Worth ten minutes now and another ten after Part 4.

## The gate

This is the entire test file for this lesson. Every lesson README shows you
its gate like this — the grader is never a mystery:

```python
"""Gates for 00_hello_dojo. Quoted verbatim in README.md."""
from dojo import grader
from dojo.lesson import Lesson

L = Lesson(__file__)


def test_ex1(shared_lesson_db):
    ex = L.exercise("ex1")
    expected = ex.fetch(shared_lesson_db, ex.expected_sql)
    actual = ex.fetch(shared_lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_rows_equal(actual, expected)


def test_ex2(shared_lesson_db):
    ex = L.exercise("ex2")
    expected = ex.fetch(shared_lesson_db, ex.expected_sql)
    actual = ex.fetch(shared_lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_rows_equal(actual, expected)


def test_ex3(shared_lesson_db):
    ex = L.exercise("ex3")
    expected = ex.fetch(shared_lesson_db, ex.expected_sql)
    actual = ex.fetch(shared_lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_rows_equal(actual, expected)


def test_ex4(shared_lesson_db):
    ex = L.exercise("ex4")
    expected = ex.fetch(shared_lesson_db, ex.expected_sql)
    actual = ex.fetch(shared_lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_rows_equal(actual, expected)
```

In plain English: each test loads your `solution.sql`, runs it against a
fresh clone, runs the reference query in `expected.sql` against the same
clone, and asserts your rows equal the expected rows.

## The teaching point

Real database work has this same loop: write a query, run it, compare what
came back against what you *believed* should come back. The discipline of
predicting the output before you run — and treating a mismatch as
information, not annoyance — is the core skill. The dojo just makes the loop
honest by automating the comparison.

Next: **01_select_basics**, where you start writing real SELECTs.

<!-- spaced-retrieval:v1 -->
## Ten-pass spaced repetition

Use this ladder after completing **00 — Hello, Dojo**. Each pass changes the retrieval
task so repetition strengthens recall instead of becoming answer recognition.
Do the named exercise from a blank starting point whenever practical, and only
open its hints after recording your first attempt.

| Pass | When | Practice target | Retrieval task |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | now | `ex1` | Close the notes and state the central rule in one precise sentence. |
| 2 | 3 days | `ex2` | Rebuild the smallest valid example from memory, then explain each part. |
| 3 | 7 days | `ex3` | Predict the result or behavior before running anything; reconcile surprises. |
| 4 | 21 days | `ex4` | Solve from a blank file and name the first tempting mistake you avoided. |
| 5 | 60 days | `ex1` | Contrast this technique with its nearest alternative and choose between them. |
| 6 | 120 days | `ex2` | Add one realistic constraint and adapt the solution without consulting notes. |
| 7 | 240 days | `ex3` | Debug a deliberately broken version; explain the evidence before the repair. |
| 8 | 1 year | `ex4` | Teach the idea aloud in two minutes, including one boundary case. |
| 9 | 18 months | `ex1` | Transfer the pattern to a new domain and verify the result with the gate. |
| 10 | 3 years | `ex2` | Complete a cold, timed solution and write the rule you want to retain long-term. |

A failed pass is useful evidence: return to pass 1 after three days. A clean
pass advances to the next interval. After pass 10, revisit the skill every
three years or whenever real work exposes a weak edge case.

# Reading - 00_hello_dojo

The loop you just ran — write, grade, read the evidence — is the whole
course. This page is the other half of every lesson: the *why* behind the
problems you just solved. It is meant to be read **after** you attempt a
problem, whether the gate went green or red. Failing first and reading
second is not a consolation prize; it is the version of studying that
actually sticks.

## Notes

**Why a real database and not a toy one.** Almost every SQL tutorial runs
against a dozen rows, where every query is instant and every mistake is
invisible. This course runs against 500,000 orders and 3,000,000 events on
purpose. At that size, a missing `WHERE` takes noticeably longer, a missing
index is something you can *feel*, and the difference between a good query
and a bad one stops being an aesthetic opinion. Part 5 depends on this
entirely — you cannot learn to read a query plan on data that fits in a
cache line.

**Why every run gets a fresh clone.** PostgreSQL can create a database
`TEMPLATE another_database`, which copies the files on disk rather than
replaying the data. That is how `dojo test` hands each exercise a private,
pristine copy of a multi-gigabyte database in a second or two. The practical
consequence for you: there is no state to corrupt and no reason to be
careful. Drop a table. Delete every row. `UPDATE` without a `WHERE`. The
next run does not know or care — and deliberately breaking things is one of
the fastest ways to learn what a constraint or a transaction is actually for.

**Why the gate is quoted in every README.** Being graded by a program you
cannot read is how people learn to game a test instead of learning the
subject. Every lesson prints its own grader at the bottom, verbatim. When
you are stuck, reading the gate is legitimate and often the fastest route to
understanding what the question is really asking — is order being compared?
is the plan being inspected? is it timing me?

**A note on determinism.** The dataset is generated from a fixed random seed
with fixed timestamps and no `now()` anywhere. Customer 4242 has the same six
orders on your laptop as on anyone else's. That is what lets the lessons cite
exact numbers, and it is why `docs/dataset_facts.md` is worth a bookmark.

## ex1 — running someone else's query

The instruction to run the gate *before* pasting the answer is the real
exercise. A test suite you have only ever seen pass teaches you nothing; the
failure output is the interface you will actually use for the next fifty
lessons. Read it once, deliberately: it shows the rows the reference query
produced, the rows yours produced, and a one-line diagnosis of the
difference. Every failure in this course is written to teach rather than to
scold, and the ones in Part 5 will show you an entire query plan.

## ex2 — your first solo query

Two ideas arrive at once. `*` means "every column of the row", and it is a
convenience for humans at a console, not a thing to ship. `WHERE id = 4242`
is a *filter*: it is evaluated once per row, and keeps the row only when the
result is true. Filtering is conceptually independent of which columns you
select — SQL lets you describe *what* you want without describing *how* to
find it, and the planner decides the how. That separation is the whole
premise of the language.

## ex3 — the same shape, a different table

Transfer is the point. The query differs from ex2 in exactly two tokens, and
the result differs in shape because `customers` has five columns and
`products` has six. If you predicted "six columns" out of habit, notice
that: most SQL bugs in production are a correct query pointed at the wrong
assumption about the data.

## ex4 — asking for less

`SELECT *` in application code is the most common smell in SQL review. It
drags columns across the network that nobody reads (`products.description`
is a paragraph of marketing text), it makes the result shape depend on
unrelated schema changes, and — the part that bites in Part 5 — it makes an
*index-only scan* impossible, because the index cannot possibly contain
every column. Lesson 34 will make that concrete. For now: name your columns.

## Further reading

- [The SQL Language — a first query](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-select.html) — the official five-minute version of what you just did.
- [`SELECT` reference page](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — dense, and the single most useful page in the docs. Skim it now; you will return to it for the rest of your career.
- [`CREATE DATABASE ... TEMPLATE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/manage-ag-templatedbs.html) — how `dojo test` gives you a pristine multi-gigabyte database per run.
- [Don't Do This](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) — the PostgreSQL wiki's list of things that look reasonable and are not. Worth ten minutes now and another ten after Part 4.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — run a query someone else wrote

Just this once, the answer is given to you. Copy the query below into
`ex1/solution.sql`, replacing the `SELECT 1;` placeholder:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM customers;
```

Then run:

```
uv run dojo test 00_hello_dojo ex1
```

Before you paste it in, run the gate once with the file as shipped. Watch it
fail. That failure output — expected rows vs. your rows — is the shape of
every failure you'll see in this course. Get comfortable reading it.

## Hint 1
The README literally contains the query. Copy it — including the semicolon —
into `ex1/solution.sql`, replacing the `SELECT 1;` line. Keep the comment
line at the top if you like; SQL ignores lines starting with `--`.

## Hint 2
Your file should contain exactly one statement:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM customers;
```

If the gate still fails, check you edited `ex1/solution.sql` (not `ex2/`),
and that you saved the file.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — your first solo query

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. The shop wants to see **everything about product
4242**: every column of the `products` table, for the single row whose `id`
is 4242.

You haven't been taught `WHERE` yet — that's lesson 02 — but you need one
tiny preview of it here: appending `WHERE id = 4242` to a `SELECT` keeps only
the rows where the `id` column equals 4242. To select every column, SQL has
the shorthand `*`.

Required output: all six columns of `products` (`id`, `name`, `category`,
`price`, `description`, `attributes`), one row. Ordering doesn't matter (one
row can't be out of order).

```
uv run dojo test 00_hello_dojo ex2
```

lessons.briefing:
# 01 — SELECT basics

The `products` table holds 10,000 rows, and each row has six columns. Almost
no real question needs all six. "What do we sell and for how much?" needs
two. The first skill in SQL is not fetching data — it's fetching *only* the
data you asked about. That's what the SELECT list (the part between `SELECT`
and `FROM`) does.

## Concept

A query has a shape:

```sql
SELECT column_a, column_b    -- which columns, in which order
FROM some_table;             -- from which table
```

Three refinements this lesson adds:

- **Aliases** rename a column on the way out: `SELECT price AS usd FROM
  products` returns a column called `usd`. You can also compute new columns:
  `SELECT price * 2 AS double_price ...` — arithmetic on a column happens
  per-row.
- **DISTINCT** collapses duplicate rows *of the whole selected row*:
  `SELECT DISTINCT country FROM customers` gives each country once.
- **LIMIT n** truncates the result after n rows. Without an ORDER BY (lesson
  03) *which* n rows you get is not guaranteed — remember that.

Paste this in `dojo lab 01_select_basics` and play:

```sql
SELECT name AS product, price, price * 0.5 AS half_price
FROM products
LIMIT 5;
```

Column order in the output follows your SELECT list, left to right. The gate
checks it, because readers of your query results care about it.

## Exercise 1 — just two columns

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Return **every product's `name` and `price`** — two
columns, in that order, all 10,000 rows. Row order doesn't matter.

Run: `uv run dojo test 01_select_basics ex1`

## Exercise 2 — a computed, aliased column

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Finance wants a tax-inclusive price list: for every
product return three columns, in this order:

1. `name`
2. `price`
3. `price * 1.2`, aliased **`price_with_tax`**

Row order doesn't matter. (The gate compares values, not the alias name —
but write the alias anyway; queries are read by humans.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 01_select_basics ex2`

## Exercise 3 — DISTINCT

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Marketing asks: **which countries do our customers
come from?** Return one column, `country`, each country exactly once. Row
order doesn't matter.

Run: `uv run dojo test 01_select_basics ex3`

## Exercise 4 — DISTINCT on a big table

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Support asks: **which customers have ever placed
an order?** Return one column, `customer_id`, from `orders`, each id
exactly once. Row order doesn't matter.

There are 500,000 orders and far fewer distinct customers among them, so
this is the first query where `DISTINCT` has to do real work — PostgreSQL
must either sort or hash 500,000 values to find the unique ones. Note the
row count it returns and compare it with the 50,000 customers in the
`customers` table; the gap is a real business fact, and lesson 09 will teach
you the join that names those missing customers.

Run: `uv run dojo test 01_select_basics ex4`

## Exercise 5 — DISTINCT over three million rows

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. The analytics team wants to know **what kinds of
events the storefront emits**. Return one column, `event_type`, from
`events`, each value exactly once. Row order doesn't matter.

`events` has 3,000,000 rows and exactly five distinct event types, so this
query throws away 99.9998% of what it reads. Time it in the lab
(`\timing on` in psql). It is the clearest demonstration in the course so
far that *what you ask for* and *what the database must touch to answer* are
two different things — the idea Part 5 is built on.

Run: `uv run dojo test 01_select_basics ex5`

## Exercise 6 — two computed columns at once

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Wholesale wants a bulk price sheet. For every
product return four columns, in this order:

1. `name`
2. `category`
3. `price`
4. `price * 3`, aliased **`bulk_price`**

All 10,000 rows, any row order. Nothing new here — this is a rep. Getting
the SELECT list right without thinking about it is the point of a rep.

Run: `uv run dojo test 01_select_basics ex6`

## Challenge — DISTINCT over a pair (optional, harder)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Merchandising wants every distinct
**(category, color)** combination we sell. Category is a normal column, but
color lives *inside* the `attributes` JSONB column. You haven't met JSONB
yet (that's lesson 19) — here's the one operator you need: `attributes ->>
'color'` extracts the `color` field as text.

Return two columns: `category`, then the color (alias it `color`). Each
combination once. Row order doesn't matter.

Run: `uv run dojo test 01_select_basics challenge`

## Spaced review

`review1/` is a variant that `dojo review` will bring back days from now:
return each distinct order `status` from the `orders` table — one column,
each status once. Same skill, different table.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 01_select_basics

The SELECT list looks like the easy part of SQL and is where a surprising
share of production problems begin: rows nobody reads, shapes nobody
expected, and duplicates nobody asked about.

## Notes

**A query is a description, not a procedure.** `SELECT name, price FROM
products` does not say "open the table, walk it, copy two fields". It says
"the set of (name, price) pairs drawn from products". PostgreSQL's planner is
free to get there by any route it likes — a sequential scan, an index-only
scan, several worker processes in parallel. This is why the same SQL gets
dramatically faster when you add an index in Part 5 without a character of
the query changing.

**`DISTINCT` is about the whole row, not the first column.** This is the one
genuine trap in this lesson. `SELECT DISTINCT country FROM customers`
returns 12 rows. `SELECT DISTINCT country, name FROM customers` returns
almost 50,000 — adding a nearly-unique column to the list destroys the
deduplication, because two rows are duplicates only when *every* selected
value matches. People reach for `DISTINCT` to "fix" a query that returns
unexpected duplicates, add the column they actually needed, and quietly get
the duplicates back.

**`DISTINCT` is never free.** To know that a value is unique, PostgreSQL has
to compare it against everything else — by sorting the whole input, or by
building a hash table of every value it has seen. On the 3,000,000-row
`events` table that is real work for a five-row answer. `DISTINCT` sprinkled
on a query to make a symptom disappear is one of the most common causes of
slow reports, and the usual honest fix is a join written correctly (Part 1)
or a `GROUP BY` that says what you mean (lesson 07).

**Aliases rename, they do not compute.** `AS` attaches a label to the
expression next to it, for the benefit of whoever reads the output. The
gates in this course compare *values*, not labels, so a missing alias never
fails a test — write them anyway. An unaliased `price * 1.2` comes back to
the caller as a column named `?column?`, which is PostgreSQL politely telling
you the query was written for a machine and not a person.

**`LIMIT` without `ORDER BY` is a bug in waiting.** `LIMIT 5` means "stop
after five rows", and *which* five depends on the plan the planner chose
today. It is stable enough in development to look correct and unstable
enough in production to file a ticket about. Lesson 03 fixes this properly.

## ex1 — just two columns

The whole exercise is the discipline of naming what you want. Worth
knowing what you avoided: `products.description` is a paragraph of text per
row, so `SELECT *` here would move roughly an order of magnitude more data
across the wire for a result nobody would use.

## ex2 — a computed, aliased column

`price * 1.2` is evaluated once per row, and its type follows from its
inputs: `numeric * numeric` stays `numeric`, which is why the money stays
exact. Had `price` been `float`, this multiplication would introduce binary
rounding error — the reason `products.price` is `numeric(10,2)` and not
`double precision`. Lesson 24 revisits that choice properly.

## ex3 — DISTINCT

Twelve rows out of fifty thousand. Notice that the answer is a property of
the *data*, not the schema: nothing declares that there are twelve countries,
and a query that assumes there are will break the day a thirteenth appears.

## ex4 — DISTINCT on a big table

The interesting number is the one that is missing. 500,000 orders belong to
about 45,000 distinct customers, and the `customers` table has 50,000 rows —
so roughly 5,000 customers have never ordered anything. Getting from "the
count doesn't match" to "here are their names" is exactly what a `LEFT JOIN`
does, and it is lesson 09.

## ex5 — DISTINCT over three million rows

Five rows out of three million. Every one of those three million rows was
read, hashed, and discarded. Nothing you can write in the SELECT list avoids
that; the only thing that would is a different physical structure, which is
the entire subject of Part 5. Keep the timing you observed here in mind — you
will make queries like this one dramatically faster later.

## ex6 — two computed columns at once

A rep, deliberately. Fluency with the SELECT list — column order, commas,
aliases, expressions mixed with plain columns — is the thing you want to
stop spending attention on, because every remaining lesson assumes it.

One detail worth pausing on: `price * 3` returns `numeric`, the same type as
`price`, so the bulk price is exact to the cent. Multiply by `1.15` instead
and PostgreSQL still keeps it exact, because the literal `1.15` is parsed as
`numeric` rather than as a float. That is a deliberate choice by the
language, and it is the opposite of what most programming languages do with
a bare decimal literal.

## challenge — DISTINCT over a pair

Two lessons collide early. `attributes ->> 'color'` reaches into a JSONB
document and pulls out a value *as text* (lesson 19 covers `->` vs `->>`
properly). More importantly, this is the whole-row rule from the notes,
working *for* you rather than against you: you want combinations, so a pair
in the SELECT list is exactly right.

## review1 — distinct statuses

Four rows. A column with four possible values in half a million rows is a
*low-cardinality* column, and that fact will matter twice more: lesson 07
groups by it, and lesson 39 shows that indexing it naively is usually
pointless.

## Further reading

- [Select Lists](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-select-lists.html) — column labels, `*`, and what `AS` actually binds to.
- [`DISTINCT`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-select.html) — the "Table Expressions" chapter's section on removing duplicate rows; note `DISTINCT ON` waiting at the bottom (lesson 49).
- [Numeric Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-numeric.html) — why money is `numeric` and never `float`. Read the "Arbitrary Precision Numbers" section.
- [Don't Do This — `SELECT *`](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) — short, opinionated, and correct.

# Reading - 01_select_basics

The SELECT list looks like the easy part of SQL and is where a surprising
share of production problems begin: rows nobody reads, shapes nobody
expected, and duplicates nobody asked about.

## Notes

**A query is a description, not a procedure.** `SELECT name, price FROM
products` does not say "open the table, walk it, copy two fields". It says
"the set of (name, price) pairs drawn from products". PostgreSQL's planner is
free to get there by any route it likes — a sequential scan, an index-only
scan, several worker processes in parallel. This is why the same SQL gets
dramatically faster when you add an index in Part 5 without a character of
the query changing.

**`DISTINCT` is about the whole row, not the first column.** This is the one
genuine trap in this lesson. `SELECT DISTINCT country FROM customers`
returns 12 rows. `SELECT DISTINCT country, name FROM customers` returns
almost 50,000 — adding a nearly-unique column to the list destroys the
deduplication, because two rows are duplicates only when *every* selected
value matches. People reach for `DISTINCT` to "fix" a query that returns
unexpected duplicates, add the column they actually needed, and quietly get
the duplicates back.

**`DISTINCT` is never free.** To know that a value is unique, PostgreSQL has
to compare it against everything else — by sorting the whole input, or by
building a hash table of every value it has seen. On the 3,000,000-row
`events` table that is real work for a five-row answer. `DISTINCT` sprinkled
on a query to make a symptom disappear is one of the most common causes of
slow reports, and the usual honest fix is a join written correctly (Part 1)
or a `GROUP BY` that says what you mean (lesson 07).

**Aliases rename, they do not compute.** `AS` attaches a label to the
expression next to it, for the benefit of whoever reads the output. The
gates in this course compare *values*, not labels, so a missing alias never
fails a test — write them anyway. An unaliased `price * 1.2` comes back to
the caller as a column named `?column?`, which is PostgreSQL politely telling
you the query was written for a machine and not a person.

**`LIMIT` without `ORDER BY` is a bug in waiting.** `LIMIT 5` means "stop
after five rows", and *which* five depends on the plan the planner chose
today. It is stable enough in development to look correct and unstable
enough in production to file a ticket about. Lesson 03 fixes this properly.

## ex1 — just two columns

The whole exercise is the discipline of naming what you want. Worth
knowing what you avoided: `products.description` is a paragraph of text per
row, so `SELECT *` here would move roughly an order of magnitude more data
across the wire for a result nobody would use.

## ex2 — a computed, aliased column

`price * 1.2` is evaluated once per row, and its type follows from its
inputs: `numeric * numeric` stays `numeric`, which is why the money stays
exact. Had `price` been `float`, this multiplication would introduce binary
rounding error — the reason `products.price` is `numeric(10,2)` and not
`double precision`. Lesson 24 revisits that choice properly.

## ex3 — DISTINCT

Twelve rows out of fifty thousand. Notice that the answer is a property of
the *data*, not the schema: nothing declares that there are twelve countries,
and a query that assumes there are will break the day a thirteenth appears.

## ex4 — DISTINCT on a big table

The interesting number is the one that is missing. 500,000 orders belong to
about 45,000 distinct customers, and the `customers` table has 50,000 rows —
so roughly 5,000 customers have never ordered anything. Getting from "the
count doesn't match" to "here are their names" is exactly what a `LEFT JOIN`
does, and it is lesson 09.

## ex5 — DISTINCT over three million rows

Five rows out of three million. Every one of those three million rows was
read, hashed, and discarded. Nothing you can write in the SELECT list avoids
that; the only thing that would is a different physical structure, which is
the entire subject of Part 5. Keep the timing you observed here in mind — you
will make queries like this one dramatically faster later.

## ex6 — two computed columns at once

A rep, deliberately. Fluency with the SELECT list — column order, commas,
aliases, expressions mixed with plain columns — is the thing you want to
stop spending attention on, because every remaining lesson assumes it.

One detail worth pausing on: `price * 3` returns `numeric`, the same type as
`price`, so the bulk price is exact to the cent. Multiply by `1.15` instead
and PostgreSQL still keeps it exact, because the literal `1.15` is parsed as
`numeric` rather than as a float. That is a deliberate choice by the
language, and it is the opposite of what most programming languages do with
a bare decimal literal.

## challenge — DISTINCT over a pair

Two lessons collide early. `attributes ->> 'color'` reaches into a JSONB
document and pulls out a value *as text* (lesson 19 covers `->` vs `->>`
properly). More importantly, this is the whole-row rule from the notes,
working *for* you rather than against you: you want combinations, so a pair
in the SELECT list is exactly right.

## review1 — distinct statuses

Four rows. A column with four possible values in half a million rows is a
*low-cardinality* column, and that fact will matter twice more: lesson 07
groups by it, and lesson 39 shows that indexing it naively is usually
pointless.

## Further reading

- [Select Lists](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-select-lists.html) — column labels, `*`, and what `AS` actually binds to.
- [`DISTINCT`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-select.html) — the "Table Expressions" chapter's section on removing duplicate rows; note `DISTINCT ON` waiting at the bottom (lesson 49).
- [Numeric Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-numeric.html) — why money is `numeric` and never `float`. Read the "Arbitrary Precision Numbers" section.
- [Don't Do This — `SELECT *`](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) — short, opinionated, and correct.

## Challenge — DISTINCT over a pair (optional, harder)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Merchandising wants every distinct

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — DISTINCT on a big table

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Support asks: **which customers have ever placed
an order?** Return one column, `customer_id`, from `orders`, each id
exactly once. Row order doesn't matter.

There are 500,000 orders and far fewer distinct customers among them, so
this is the first query where `DISTINCT` has to do real work — PostgreSQL
must either sort or hash 500,000 values to find the unique ones. Note the
row count it returns and compare it with the 50,000 customers in the
`customers` table; the gap is a real business fact, and lesson 09 will teach
you the join that names those missing customers.

Run: `uv run dojo test 01_select_basics ex4`

## Exercise 5 — DISTINCT over three million rows

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. The analytics team wants to know **what kinds of
events the storefront emits**. Return one column, `event_type`, from
`events`, each value exactly once. Row order doesn't matter.

`events` has 3,000,000 rows and exactly five distinct event types, so this
query throws away 99.9998% of what it reads. Time it in the lab
(`\timing on` in psql). It is the clearest demonstration in the course so
far that *what you ask for* and *what the database must touch to answer* are
two different things — the idea Part 5 is built on.

lessons.summary: orders has 500,000 rows. Every query you wrote in lesson 01 returned all the rows of its table, because you had no way to say which ones you wanted. WHERE is that way. It sits after FROM, holds a condition, and keeps only the rows for which the condition is true.
lessons.briefing:
# 02 — WHERE: filtering rows

`orders` has 500,000 rows. Every query you wrote in lesson 01 returned *all*
the rows of its table, because you had no way to say which ones you wanted.
`WHERE` is that way. It sits after `FROM`, holds a condition, and keeps only
the rows for which the condition is true.

## Concept

```sql
SELECT id, total
FROM orders
WHERE total > 1900;
```

Conditions compose. The operators you need this lesson:

- Comparisons: `=`, `<>` (not equal), `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`
- Combining: `AND`, `OR`, `NOT` — **and `AND` binds tighter than `OR`**.
  `a OR b AND c` means `a OR (b AND c)`. When mixing them, always write the
  parentheses you mean. This is the single most common WHERE bug in the
  wild.
- `IN (v1, v2, ...)` — equal to any of the listed values.
- `BETWEEN x AND y` — inclusive on both ends.
- `LIKE` / `ILIKE` — pattern matching; `%` matches any run of characters,
  `_` exactly one. `ILIKE` ignores case; `LIKE` doesn't.

Try in `dojo lab 02_where_filtering`:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND total BETWEEN 100 AND 110;
SELECT count(*) FROM customers WHERE name ILIKE 'mar%';
```

## Exercise 1 — a simple comparison

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. The finance team wants the big-ticket orders:
**every order with `total` greater than 1900**. Return three columns in this
order: `id`, `customer_id`, `total`. Row order doesn't matter.

Run: `uv run dojo test 02_where_filtering ex1`

## Exercise 2 — AND, OR, and the parentheses you mean

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Fraud review wants **paid orders with an extreme
total**: status is `'paid'`, and the total is *either* under 20 *or* over
1980. Return `id`, `status`, `total`. Row order doesn't matter.

Write it with explicit parentheses. If you get twice as many rows as you
expected, you've just met the precedence bug from the concept section —
that's the lesson working as intended.

Run: `uv run dojo test 02_where_filtering ex2`

## Exercise 3 — pattern matching

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Return every customer whose **name contains the
letters `son`, matched case-insensitively** (Anderson, Sonia, Jackson...).
Columns: `id`, `name`. Row order doesn't matter.

Run: `uv run dojo test 02_where_filtering ex3`

## Exercise 4 — IN and BETWEEN together

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The gift-guide editor wants **mid-priced toys and
garden products**: every product whose `category` is either `'toys'` or
`'garden'`, and whose `price` is between 100 and 150 **inclusive**.

Columns, in order: `id`, `name`, `category`, `price`. Row order doesn't
matter.

Write the category test with `IN` and the price test with `BETWEEN` — both
are shorthand you will read in other people's SQL constantly, and both are
worth being able to write without hesitating.

Run: `uv run dojo test 02_where_filtering ex4`

## Exercise 5 — negation done right

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Accounting is chasing tiny orders that were never
cancelled: every order whose `status` is **not** `'cancelled'` and whose
`total` is **under 10**.

Columns: `id`, `status`, `total`. Row order doesn't matter.

Write the negation with `<>` (or `NOT`, or `NOT IN` — all three work here).
Look at the statuses that come back and satisfy yourself that all three
survivors are present. This query is safe today for a reason you cannot yet
see: `orders.status` is `NOT NULL`. Lesson 05 shows you the same query on a
nullable column, where it silently loses rows.

Run: `uv run dojo test 02_where_filtering ex5`

## Exercise 6 — case matters (until it doesn't)

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Marketing wants a shortlist: customers in the
**US, GB, or DE** whose `name` begins with a capital **A**, matched
**case-sensitively**.

Columns: `id`, `name`, `country`. Row order doesn't matter.

Use `LIKE` (not `ILIKE`) so the capital letter is enforced, and `IN` for the
country list. Run the same query with `ILIKE` in the lab afterwards and note
whether the row count changes — on this dataset it should not, and knowing
*why* your two queries agree is worth more than the row count itself.

Run: `uv run dojo test 02_where_filtering ex6`

## Challenge — fix the precedence bug (optional)

A colleague wrote this query, meaning to get *pending or paid* orders over
1000, and swears SQL is broken because cheap pending orders keep appearing:

```sql
SELECT id, status, total
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'pending' OR status = 'paid' AND total > 1000;
```

Edit `challenge/solution.sql` with the **fixed** query: orders whose status
is `'pending'` or `'paid'`, **and** whose total exceeds 1000. Same three
columns. Row order doesn't matter. (Two fixes work: parentheses, or `IN`.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 02_where_filtering challenge`

inclusive** — columns `id`, `name`, `price`, any row order.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 02_where_filtering

`WHERE` is where SQL stops being a data dump and starts being a question.
It is also, measured in production incidents, the most dangerous clause in
the language — not because it is hard, but because a wrong `WHERE` returns
a confident, plausible, wrong answer.

## Notes

**A `WHERE` clause is a per-row predicate.** Conceptually PostgreSQL walks
the rows, evaluates your condition against each one, and keeps the row when
the answer is *true*. Two things follow. First, "true" is doing real work in
that sentence — SQL has three truth values (lesson 05), and a row whose
condition is *unknown* is discarded exactly like a false one, silently.
Second, the walk is conceptual: the planner may use an index to skip most
rows entirely, which is why the same `WHERE` can take 300 ms or 0.3 ms
depending on Part 5.

**`AND` binds tighter than `OR`.** `a OR b AND c` parses as `a OR (b AND c)`.
This is standard, it matches arithmetic (`AND` is the `*`, `OR` is the `+`),
and it is responsible for an enormous number of real bugs, because the wrong
reading is usually *more* rows rather than an error. The habit that
eliminates the whole class: parenthesize every clause that mixes `AND` with
`OR`, even when you are sure. Your reviewer cannot tell "I meant this" from
"I forgot" without the parentheses.

**`BETWEEN` is inclusive on both ends.** `price BETWEEN 100 AND 150` is
`price >= 100 AND price <= 150`. That is fine for integers and prices, and
it is a bug waiting to happen for timestamps: `created_at BETWEEN
'2023-01-01' AND '2023-01-31'` excludes almost all of January 31st, because
the bare date means midnight. The rule professionals use for time ranges is
half-open — `>= start AND < next_start` — and lesson 18 returns to it.

**`LIKE` is not a search engine.** `%` matches any run of characters, `_`
matches exactly one, `ILIKE` is the case-insensitive version, and a leading
`%` means PostgreSQL cannot use an ordinary B-tree index at all — a
`LIKE '%son%'` on a large table is a guaranteed full scan. When you need
real text search, you need `tsvector` and a GIN index, which is lesson 41.
Knowing which of the two you are reaching for is the skill.

**`IN` is `OR` in a smaller box.** `status IN ('paid','shipped')` is exactly
`status = 'paid' OR status = 'shipped'`, with the parenthesization already
correct — which is a quiet argument for preferring it. `IN` also accepts a
subquery (lesson 13), and there its NULL behaviour becomes genuinely
dangerous (lesson 05).

## ex1 — a simple comparison

The first query in this course that reads a large table to return a small
answer. Roughly 25,000 of 500,000 orders survive the filter; the other
475,000 are read and discarded. That ratio — *selectivity* — is the single
number the planner cares most about, and lesson 36 is about how it estimates
it before running anything.

## ex2 — AND, OR, and the parentheses you mean

The precedence trap, deliberately walked into. If you got roughly 83,000
extra rows, you wrote `status = 'paid' AND total < 20 OR total > 1980`, which
PostgreSQL read as `(paid AND cheap) OR (expensive, any status)`. Nothing
warned you, because the query was perfectly valid — it just answered a
different question. This is the shape of most `WHERE` bugs: not an error, a
different question.

## ex3 — pattern matching

`ILIKE '%son%'` reads every one of the 50,000 names. There is no index in the
world that makes a leading-`%` pattern cheap without changing the data
structure — that is what trigram and full-text indexes are for (lesson 41).
Note also that case-insensitivity is not free or universal: `ILIKE` uses the
database's collation rules, and "case" is a much harder question in Turkish
or Greek than the ASCII intuition suggests.

## ex4 — IN and BETWEEN together

Two shorthands in one predicate. Worth noticing: this query has two
independent filters, and the planner will apply whichever it estimates is
cheaper first. When you get to Part 5 and start building composite indexes,
the *order* of the columns in the index will be decided by exactly this kind
of reasoning (lesson 32).

## ex5 — negation done right

Negation is where three-valued logic ambushes people, and this exercise is
deliberately safe: `orders.status` is declared `NOT NULL`, so `<> 'cancelled'`
really does mean "one of the other three". Change one thing — make the column
nullable — and the same query starts dropping every row with a NULL status
without a word of complaint. That is lesson 05, and this exercise is the
before picture.

## ex6 — case matters (until it doesn't)

`LIKE 'A%'` and `ILIKE 'a%'` return the same rows here only because the
generated names are all capitalised. Real customer data is not: people type
their names in lower case, in caps, with leading spaces. Filtering on
user-entered text with `LIKE` and hoping is a recipe for a support ticket;
normalising the data (or indexing `lower(name)` — lesson 40) is the fix.

## challenge — fix the precedence bug

`WHERE status IN ('pending','paid') AND total > 1000` and `WHERE (status =
'pending' OR status = 'paid') AND total > 1000` are the same query. Prefer
the first: it makes the intent obvious and it removes the parenthesis you
could have got wrong. The general lesson is that the best fix for a
precedence bug is usually a rewrite that has no precedence to get wrong.

## review1 — a range inside a category

Two conditions, one of them a `BETWEEN`. When this comes back in three
days, check yourself on the inclusivity of both endpoints before you run it.

The useful habit to rehearse here is prediction: say the row count you
expect out loud, then run it. Being wrong is the information. A filter that
returns ten times what you expected is usually a precedence bug; one that
returns zero is usually a NULL or a typo in a string literal; one that
returns *nearly* the whole table is usually a condition that is true for
almost every row and therefore was not the question anyone meant to ask.

## Further reading

- [Comparison Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html) — `BETWEEN`, `IN`, `IS DISTINCT FROM`, and the truth tables that make lesson 05 make sense.
- [Pattern Matching](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-matching.html) — `LIKE`, `SIMILAR TO`, and POSIX regexes; note which of them an index can help with.
- [The `WHERE` Clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — where filtering sits in the logical order of a query's evaluation.
- [Use The Index, Luke — The Where Clause](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause) — the same clause seen from the index's point of view. You will re-read this in Part 5; skimming it now makes Part 5 easier.

# 02 — WHERE: filtering rows

`orders` has 500,000 rows. Every query you wrote in lesson 01 returned *all*
the rows of its table, because you had no way to say which ones you wanted.
`WHERE` is that way. It sits after `FROM`, holds a condition, and keeps only
the rows for which the condition is true.

## Concept

```sql
SELECT id, total
FROM orders
WHERE total > 1900;
```

Conditions compose. The operators you need this lesson:

- Comparisons: `=`, `<>` (not equal), `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`
- Combining: `AND`, `OR`, `NOT` — **and `AND` binds tighter than `OR`**.
  `a OR b AND c` means `a OR (b AND c)`. When mixing them, always write the
  parentheses you mean. This is the single most common WHERE bug in the
  wild.
- `IN (v1, v2, ...)` — equal to any of the listed values.
- `BETWEEN x AND y` — inclusive on both ends.
- `LIKE` / `ILIKE` — pattern matching; `%` matches any run of characters,
  `_` exactly one. `ILIKE` ignores case; `LIKE` doesn't.

Try in `dojo lab 02_where_filtering`:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND total BETWEEN 100 AND 110;
SELECT count(*) FROM customers WHERE name ILIKE 'mar%';
```

## Exercise 1 — a simple comparison

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. The finance team wants the big-ticket orders:
**every order with `total` greater than 1900**. Return three columns in this
order: `id`, `customer_id`, `total`. Row order doesn't matter.

Run: `uv run dojo test 02_where_filtering ex1`

## Exercise 2 — AND, OR, and the parentheses you mean

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Fraud review wants **paid orders with an extreme
total**: status is `'paid'`, and the total is *either* under 20 *or* over
1980. Return `id`, `status`, `total`. Row order doesn't matter.

Write it with explicit parentheses. If you get twice as many rows as you
expected, you've just met the precedence bug from the concept section —
that's the lesson working as intended.

Run: `uv run dojo test 02_where_filtering ex2`

## Exercise 3 — pattern matching

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Return every customer whose **name contains the
letters `son`, matched case-insensitively** (Anderson, Sonia, Jackson...).
Columns: `id`, `name`. Row order doesn't matter.

Run: `uv run dojo test 02_where_filtering ex3`

## Exercise 4 — IN and BETWEEN together

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The gift-guide editor wants **mid-priced toys and
garden products**: every product whose `category` is either `'toys'` or
`'garden'`, and whose `price` is between 100 and 150 **inclusive**.

Columns, in order: `id`, `name`, `category`, `price`. Row order doesn't
matter.

Write the category test with `IN` and the price test with `BETWEEN` — both
are shorthand you will read in other people's SQL constantly, and both are
worth being able to write without hesitating.

Run: `uv run dojo test 02_where_filtering ex4`

## Exercise 5 — negation done right

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Accounting is chasing tiny orders that were never
cancelled: every order whose `status` is **not** `'cancelled'` and whose
`total` is **under 10**.

Columns: `id`, `status`, `total`. Row order doesn't matter.

Write the negation with `<>` (or `NOT`, or `NOT IN` — all three work here).
Look at the statuses that come back and satisfy yourself that all three
survivors are present. This query is safe today for a reason you cannot yet
see: `orders.status` is `NOT NULL`. Lesson 05 shows you the same query on a
nullable column, where it silently loses rows.

Run: `uv run dojo test 02_where_filtering ex5`

## Exercise 6 — case matters (until it doesn't)

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Marketing wants a shortlist: customers in the
**US, GB, or DE** whose `name` begins with a capital **A**, matched
**case-sensitively**.

Columns: `id`, `name`, `country`. Row order doesn't matter.

Use `LIKE` (not `ILIKE`) so the capital letter is enforced, and `IN` for the
country list. Run the same query with `ILIKE` in the lab afterwards and note
whether the row count changes — on this dataset it should not, and knowing
*why* your two queries agree is worth more than the row count itself.

Run: `uv run dojo test 02_where_filtering ex6`

## Challenge — fix the precedence bug (optional)

A colleague wrote this query, meaning to get *pending or paid* orders over
1000, and swears SQL is broken because cheap pending orders keep appearing:

```sql
SELECT id, status, total
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'pending' OR status = 'paid' AND total > 1000;
```

Edit `challenge/solution.sql` with the **fixed** query: orders whose status
is `'pending'` or `'paid'`, **and** whose total exceeds 1000. Same three
columns. Row order doesn't matter. (Two fixes work: parentheses, or `IN`.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 02_where_filtering challenge`

## Spaced review

`review1/`: all products in category `'toys'` priced **between 10 and 20
inclusive** — columns `id`, `name`, `price`, any row order.

## The teaching point

Production incident reports are full of WHERE clauses that were *almost*

# Reading - 02_where_filtering

`WHERE` is where SQL stops being a data dump and starts being a question.
It is also, measured in production incidents, the most dangerous clause in
the language — not because it is hard, but because a wrong `WHERE` returns
a confident, plausible, wrong answer.

## Notes

**A `WHERE` clause is a per-row predicate.** Conceptually PostgreSQL walks
the rows, evaluates your condition against each one, and keeps the row when
the answer is *true*. Two things follow. First, "true" is doing real work in
that sentence — SQL has three truth values (lesson 05), and a row whose
condition is *unknown* is discarded exactly like a false one, silently.
Second, the walk is conceptual: the planner may use an index to skip most
rows entirely, which is why the same `WHERE` can take 300 ms or 0.3 ms
depending on Part 5.

**`AND` binds tighter than `OR`.** `a OR b AND c` parses as `a OR (b AND c)`.
This is standard, it matches arithmetic (`AND` is the `*`, `OR` is the `+`),
and it is responsible for an enormous number of real bugs, because the wrong
reading is usually *more* rows rather than an error. The habit that
eliminates the whole class: parenthesize every clause that mixes `AND` with
`OR`, even when you are sure. Your reviewer cannot tell "I meant this" from
"I forgot" without the parentheses.

**`BETWEEN` is inclusive on both ends.** `price BETWEEN 100 AND 150` is
`price >= 100 AND price <= 150`. That is fine for integers and prices, and
it is a bug waiting to happen for timestamps: `created_at BETWEEN
'2023-01-01' AND '2023-01-31'` excludes almost all of January 31st, because
the bare date means midnight. The rule professionals use for time ranges is
half-open — `>= start AND < next_start` — and lesson 18 returns to it.

**`LIKE` is not a search engine.** `%` matches any run of characters, `_`
matches exactly one, `ILIKE` is the case-insensitive version, and a leading
`%` means PostgreSQL cannot use an ordinary B-tree index at all — a
`LIKE '%son%'` on a large table is a guaranteed full scan. When you need
real text search, you need `tsvector` and a GIN index, which is lesson 41.
Knowing which of the two you are reaching for is the skill.

**`IN` is `OR` in a smaller box.** `status IN ('paid','shipped')` is exactly
`status = 'paid' OR status = 'shipped'`, with the parenthesization already
correct — which is a quiet argument for preferring it. `IN` also accepts a
subquery (lesson 13), and there its NULL behaviour becomes genuinely
dangerous (lesson 05).

## ex1 — a simple comparison

The first query in this course that reads a large table to return a small
answer. Roughly 25,000 of 500,000 orders survive the filter; the other
475,000 are read and discarded. That ratio — *selectivity* — is the single
number the planner cares most about, and lesson 36 is about how it estimates
it before running anything.

## ex2 — AND, OR, and the parentheses you mean

The precedence trap, deliberately walked into. If you got roughly 83,000
extra rows, you wrote `status = 'paid' AND total < 20 OR total > 1980`, which
PostgreSQL read as `(paid AND cheap) OR (expensive, any status)`. Nothing
warned you, because the query was perfectly valid — it just answered a
different question. This is the shape of most `WHERE` bugs: not an error, a
different question.

## ex3 — pattern matching

`ILIKE '%son%'` reads every one of the 50,000 names. There is no index in the
world that makes a leading-`%` pattern cheap without changing the data
structure — that is what trigram and full-text indexes are for (lesson 41).
Note also that case-insensitivity is not free or universal: `ILIKE` uses the
database's collation rules, and "case" is a much harder question in Turkish
or Greek than the ASCII intuition suggests.

## ex4 — IN and BETWEEN together

Two shorthands in one predicate. Worth noticing: this query has two
independent filters, and the planner will apply whichever it estimates is
cheaper first. When you get to Part 5 and start building composite indexes,
the *order* of the columns in the index will be decided by exactly this kind
of reasoning (lesson 32).

## ex5 — negation done right

Negation is where three-valued logic ambushes people, and this exercise is
deliberately safe: `orders.status` is declared `NOT NULL`, so `<> 'cancelled'`
really does mean "one of the other three". Change one thing — make the column
nullable — and the same query starts dropping every row with a NULL status
without a word of complaint. That is lesson 05, and this exercise is the
before picture.

## ex6 — case matters (until it doesn't)

`LIKE 'A%'` and `ILIKE 'a%'` return the same rows here only because the
generated names are all capitalised. Real customer data is not: people type
their names in lower case, in caps, with leading spaces. Filtering on
user-entered text with `LIKE` and hoping is a recipe for a support ticket;
normalising the data (or indexing `lower(name)` — lesson 40) is the fix.

## challenge — fix the precedence bug

`WHERE status IN ('pending','paid') AND total > 1000` and `WHERE (status =
'pending' OR status = 'paid') AND total > 1000` are the same query. Prefer
the first: it makes the intent obvious and it removes the parenthesis you
could have got wrong. The general lesson is that the best fix for a
precedence bug is usually a rewrite that has no precedence to get wrong.

## review1 — a range inside a category

Two conditions, one of them a `BETWEEN`. When this comes back in three
days, check yourself on the inclusivity of both endpoints before you run it.

The useful habit to rehearse here is prediction: say the row count you
expect out loud, then run it. Being wrong is the information. A filter that
returns ten times what you expected is usually a precedence bug; one that
returns zero is usually a NULL or a typo in a string literal; one that
returns *nearly* the whole table is usually a condition that is true for
almost every row and therefore was not the question anyone meant to ask.

## Further reading

- [Comparison Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html) — `BETWEEN`, `IN`, `IS DISTINCT FROM`, and the truth tables that make lesson 05 make sense.
- [Pattern Matching](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-matching.html) — `LIKE`, `SIMILAR TO`, and POSIX regexes; note which of them an index can help with.
- [The `WHERE` Clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — where filtering sits in the logical order of a query's evaluation.
- [Use The Index, Luke — The Where Clause](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause) — the same clause seen from the index's point of view. You will re-read this in Part 5; skimming it now makes Part 5 easier.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — fix the precedence bug (optional)

A colleague wrote this query, meaning to get *pending or paid* orders over
1000, and swears SQL is broken because cheap pending orders keep appearing:

```sql
SELECT id, status, total
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'pending' OR status = 'paid' AND total > 1000;
```

Edit `challenge/solution.sql` with the **fixed** query: orders whose status
is `'pending'` or `'paid'`, **and** whose total exceeds 1000. Same three
columns. Row order doesn't matter. (Two fixes work: parentheses, or `IN`.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 02_where_filtering challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The bug: `AND` binds tighter than `OR`, so the query means
`pending OR (paid AND total > 1000)` — every pending order sneaks in, cheap
or not. Your fix must make the `total > 1000` apply to both statuses.

## Hint 2
Either wrap the OR: `WHERE (status = 'pending' OR status = 'paid') AND
total > 1000`, or collapse it: `WHERE status IN ('pending', 'paid') AND
total > 1000`. Pick one and write the full query.

## Hint 1
The bug: `AND` binds tighter than `OR`, so the query means
`pending OR (paid AND total > 1000)` — every pending order sneaks in, cheap
or not. Your fix must make the `total > 1000` apply to both statuses.

## Hint 2
Either wrap the OR: `WHERE (status = 'pending' OR status = 'paid') AND
total > 1000`, or collapse it: `WHERE status IN ('pending', 'paid') AND
total > 1000`. Pick one and write the full query.

SELECT id, status, total
FROM orders
WHERE status IN ('pending', 'paid')
  AND total > 1000;

WHERE (status = 'pending' OR status = 'paid') AND total > 1000;

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Three conditions: one on `status`, two on `total` joined by OR. The OR pair
must be wrapped in parentheses so the AND applies to both branches.

## Hint 2
```sql
WHERE status = 'paid' AND (total < ... OR total > ...)
```

Without the parentheses, `AND` grabs only the first comparison and every
order over 1980 leaks in regardless of status.

## Hint 3
Fill in 20 and 1980. Text values like `'paid'` take single quotes; numbers
don't.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Three conditions: one on `status`, two on `total` joined by OR. The OR pair
must be wrapped in parentheses so the AND applies to both branches.

## Hint 2
```sql
WHERE status = 'paid' AND (total < ... OR total > ...)
```

Without the parentheses, `AND` grabs only the first comparison and every
order over 1980 leaks in regardless of status.

## Hint 3
Fill in 20 and 1980. Text values like `'paid'` take single quotes; numbers
don't.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT id, status, total
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
  AND (total < 20 OR total > 1980);
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, status, total FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid' AND (total < 20 OR total > 1980);

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — negation done right

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Accounting is chasing tiny orders that were never
cancelled: every order whose `status` is **not** `'cancelled'` and whose
`total` is **under 10**.

Columns: `id`, `status`, `total`. Row order doesn't matter.

Write the negation with `<>` (or `NOT`, or `NOT IN` — all three work here).
Look at the statuses that come back and satisfy yourself that all three
survivors are present. This query is safe today for a reason you cannot yet
see: `orders.status` is `NOT NULL`. Lesson 05 shows you the same query on a
nullable column, where it silently loses rows.

Run: `uv run dojo test 02_where_filtering ex5`

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — case matters (until it doesn't)

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Marketing wants a shortlist: customers in the
**US, GB, or DE** whose `name` begins with a capital **A**, matched
**case-sensitively**.

Columns: `id`, `name`, `country`. Row order doesn't matter.

Use `LIKE` (not `ILIKE`) so the capital letter is enforced, and `IN` for the
country list. Run the same query with `ILIKE` in the lab afterwards and note
whether the row count changes — on this dataset it should not, and knowing
*why* your two queries agree is worth more than the row count itself.

lessons.briefing:
# 03 — ORDER BY, LIMIT, OFFSET

"Give me the ten most expensive products" is two operations, not one: sort
10,000 rows by price, then keep the first ten. Until now your result rows
came back in whatever order PostgreSQL found convenient — and that order is
**not guaranteed and not stable**. The moment anyone says "top", "latest",
"first", or "page 2", you need `ORDER BY`.

## Concept

```sql
SELECT id, name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY price DESC, id ASC
LIMIT 10;
```

- `ORDER BY` takes a comma-separated list of sort keys. Each key sorts
  ascending (`ASC`, the default) or descending (`DESC`). Later keys break
  ties in earlier keys.
- **Always give the gate a deterministic order.** If two products share a
  price, "order by price" alone leaves their relative order to chance. Every
  ordered exercise in this course names a tie-breaker (usually `id`) —
  include it.
- `NULLS FIRST` / `NULLS LAST` control where NULLs sort. By default NULLs
  come last when ascending, first when descending. (`staff.manager_id` is
  the NULL column you'll meet properly in lesson 05.)
- `LIMIT n` keeps the first n rows *of the sorted result*. `OFFSET m` skips
  m rows first — that's how naive pagination works, and why deep pages get
  slow: OFFSET 100000 still sorts and walks the first 100,000 rows to throw
  them away.

This lesson's gates check row order (`ordered=True`) — the first time the
gate cares not just *which* rows, but *in what sequence*.

## Exercise 1 — top N

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. **The 10 most expensive products.** Columns, in
order: `id`, `name`, `price`. Sort by `price` descending; break price ties
by `id` ascending. Exactly 10 rows.

Run: `uv run dojo test 03_order_limit ex1`

## Exercise 2 — multi-key sort

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. HR wants a salary review sheet: the **top 20 staff
rows** sorted by `department` ascending, then `salary` descending within
each department, then `id` ascending as the final tie-break. Columns:
`name`, `department`, `salary`.

Run: `uv run dojo test 03_order_limit ex2`

## Exercise 3 — pagination with OFFSET

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. The admin UI shows customers **newest first**, 10
per page. Produce **page 3** — that is, skip the first 20, return the next
10. Sort by `created_at` descending, tie-break `id` descending. Columns:
`id`, `name`, `created_at`.

Run: `uv run dojo test 03_order_limit ex3`

## Exercise 4 — where do NULLs sort?

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The org-chart tool renders the reporting tree from
the top down, so it wants the row with **no manager first**. Return the
**first 10** staff rows sorted by `manager_id` **ascending with NULLs
first**, breaking ties by `id` ascending.

Columns: `id`, `name`, `manager_id`. Exactly 10 rows, and the order is
graded.

By default an ascending sort puts NULLs *last* in PostgreSQL. You have to
say `NULLS FIRST` to get the CEO to the top — and other databases pick the
opposite default, which is why portable SQL says it explicitly.

Run: `uv run dojo test 03_order_limit ex4`

## Exercise 5 — top N over half a million rows

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Finance wants the **15 largest orders ever
placed**. Columns, in order: `id`, `customer_id`, `total`. Sort by `total`
descending, break ties by `id` ascending. Exactly 15 rows, order graded.

Exercise 1 sorted 10,000 products; this sorts 500,000 orders to return 15
rows. Run `dojo plan 03_order_limit ex5` afterwards and look for the word
`Sort` — you are watching PostgreSQL sort half a million rows to answer a
question about fifteen of them. Lesson 35 removes that sort entirely with an
index, and this is the query you will compare against.

Run: `uv run dojo test 03_order_limit ex5`

## Exercise 6 — a deep page

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. The product catalogue lists items **cheapest
first**, 10 per page. Produce **page 51** — skip the first 500 rows and
return the next 10.

Sort by `price` ascending, tie-break `id` ascending. Columns: `id`, `name`,
`price`. Exactly 10 rows, order graded.

Exercise 3 asked for page 3. This one asks for page 51, and the query is
identical except for one number — which is precisely the problem with
`OFFSET`. To hand you rows 501–510, PostgreSQL sorts the catalogue and then
walks past the first 500 results and throws them away. Page 5,000 would
throw away 50,000. The reading explains what real systems do instead.

Run: `uv run dojo test 03_order_limit ex6`

## Challenge — top 5 per category, no window functions (optional, hard)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. **The 5 most expensive products in *each* of
the 6 categories** — 30 rows. Columns: `category`, `name`, `price`. Order
the whole result by `category` ascending, then `price` descending, then `id`
ascending.

This is genuinely hard with what you know so far — `LIMIT` applies to the
whole result, not per group. The intended tool is a *correlated subquery*
(lesson 13 material, previewed here): for each product, ask "is this
product's id among the top 5 ids of its own category?". The hints walk you
through the shape. In lesson 15 you'll solve this in three lines with a
window function and feel great about it.

Run: `uv run dojo test 03_order_limit challenge`

## Spaced review

`review1/`: the **5 cheapest products in category `'food'`** — columns
`id`, `name`, `price`, ordered by `price` ascending then `id` ascending.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 03_order_limit

Sorting is the first operation in this course with a *cost model* worth
carrying in your head, and pagination is the first place where a query that
is correct on page one becomes a production incident on page one thousand.

## Notes

**There is no default order, and there never was.** A table is a set of
rows; the order you see without `ORDER BY` is an artefact of how PostgreSQL
happened to read them — insertion order in a fresh table, something else
after an `UPDATE` moves a row, something else again when the planner uses an
index or splits the scan across parallel workers. The failure mode is
cruel: it looks stable for months and then changes when the data grows past
a threshold. If an order is visible to a human, it belongs in the SQL.

**Ties must be broken explicitly.** `ORDER BY price DESC` over 10,000
products with duplicate prices leaves the tied rows in an arbitrary
sequence, and "arbitrary" is allowed to differ between two runs of the same
query. Every ordered exercise in this course names a tie-breaker — usually
`id`, because it is unique — and that habit is what makes an ordering
*total* rather than merely *partial*. It is also what makes pagination
coherent: without a total order, "the next ten rows" is not a well-defined
concept.

**`ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` is not a sort followed by a truncation.**
PostgreSQL recognises the combination and switches to a *top-N heapsort*,
keeping only the best n rows it has seen in memory rather than sorting the
whole input. You can see it in `EXPLAIN` as `Sort Method: top-N heapsort`.
It is a large constant-factor win — but it is still O(rows), because every
row must be looked at to know it is not in the top fifteen. The only way to
avoid touching every row is an index whose order already matches your
`ORDER BY`, which is lesson 35.

**`OFFSET` does not skip work, it discards it.** `OFFSET 500 LIMIT 10`
produces 510 rows internally and throws 500 away. The cost grows linearly
with the page number, so deep pagination gets slower the further a user
scrolls, and — worse — it is *incorrect* under concurrent writes: if a row
is inserted before page 2 is requested, one row shifts across the boundary
and the user sees a duplicate or misses an item entirely. The professional
alternative is **keyset pagination** (also called seek, or cursor
pagination): remember the sort key of the last row you showed and ask for
`WHERE (price, id) > (last_price, last_id) ORDER BY price, id LIMIT 10`.
It is constant-time per page, it is stable under concurrent inserts, and
with the right index it is one of the fastest things a database can do.
Markus Winand's page on this is in the links below and is worth reading
twice.

**`NULLS FIRST` / `NULLS LAST` is a real decision.** PostgreSQL's default is
NULLs last when ascending, first when descending — consistent with treating
NULL as larger than everything. Other engines differ. Writing it explicitly
costs two words and removes a portability question and a code-review
question at once.

## ex1 — top N

10,000 rows sorted to produce 10. Look at the plan: `Limit` above `Sort`
above `Seq Scan`, and the sort reporting `top-N heapsort`. That shape — the
whole table read, most of it discarded — is the baseline that Part 5 exists
to improve on.

## ex2 — multi-key sort

Three sort keys, each breaking ties in the one before. This is also the
first exercise where the *order* of the keys is the whole answer: sorting by
salary then department produces a completely different report from
department then salary. When a stakeholder says "sorted by department and
salary", they have not told you which is primary, and asking is not pedantry.

## ex3 — pagination with OFFSET

Page 3 of a customer list, newest first. Note the descending tie-break on
`id`: with `created_at DESC` and two customers created in the same second,
`id DESC` keeps them in a stable, meaningful order. Choosing a tie-breaker
that *agrees* with the primary key's direction is a small thing that makes
paginated output feel coherent to a user.

## ex4 — where do NULLs sort?

One NULL in five hundred rows, and it changes the first line of the report.
The deeper point: NULL is not "smaller" or "larger" than a number — SQL has
to be *told* where to put it, because the question is not answerable by
comparison. That is the same fact that makes `NULL = NULL` unknown, and
lesson 05 is entirely about it.

## ex5 — top N over half a million rows

Same query shape as ex1, fifty times the data. The plan is identical; only
the row counts change. Keep the timing in mind — in lesson 35 you will add
one index and watch the `Sort` node disappear from this plan, because a
B-tree is already sorted and PostgreSQL can simply read the first fifteen
entries in order.

## ex6 — a deep page

The point of this exercise is that it is *identical* to ex3 apart from one
number, and yet a report that scrolls deep enough will eventually time out.
Try `OFFSET 9990 LIMIT 10` in the lab and watch the timing move. Then read
the keyset-pagination link below; the rewrite is not hard, and it is what
you should reach for whenever a page number can grow without bound.

## challenge — top 5 per category without window functions

Genuinely hard, and deliberately so. `LIMIT` applies to the whole result, so
"per group" needs something that evaluates *per row* — a correlated subquery
that asks, for each product, how many products in the same category are more
expensive. It is O(n²)-ish and it is what people wrote before 2003. In
lesson 15 you will replace the whole thing with `row_number() OVER
(PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC)` and in lesson 48 with a
`LATERAL` join. Solving it the hard way first is what makes those two
lessons land.

## review1 — the five cheapest in a category

A filter, a sort, and a limit — the three clauses of this lesson and the
last, composed. Predict the tie-break behaviour before you run it.

Worth noticing when it returns: the five cheapest products in a category is
a *top-N within a group* question restricted to one group. Ask it for all
six categories at once and you have the challenge, which needs a correlated
subquery today and a window function in lesson 15. Recognising that two
questions are the same question with a different `WHERE` is most of what
makes SQL feel small rather than endless.

## Further reading

- [Sorting Rows](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-order.html) — `ASC`/`DESC`, `NULLS FIRST`/`LAST`, and what `ORDER BY` can reference.
- [`LIMIT` and `OFFSET`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-limit.html) — including the docs' own warning about inconsistent results without `ORDER BY`.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Paging Through Results](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/partial-results/fetch-next-page) — the definitive explanation of why `OFFSET` is the wrong tool and what keyset pagination looks like.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Top-N Queries](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/partial-results/top-n-queries) — how an index turns `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` into a few page reads. Preview of lesson 35.

appears. The rule in real systems is: **if order reaches a user, it's in the
SQL** — never rely on accidental order, and always break ties
deterministically.
