# Reading - 03_order_limit

Sorting is the first operation in this course with a *cost model* worth
carrying in your head, and pagination is the first place where a query that
is correct on page one becomes a production incident on page one thousand.

## Notes

**There is no default order, and there never was.** A table is a set of
rows; the order you see without `ORDER BY` is an artefact of how PostgreSQL
happened to read them — insertion order in a fresh table, something else
after an `UPDATE` moves a row, something else again when the planner uses an
index or splits the scan across parallel workers. The failure mode is
cruel: it looks stable for months and then changes when the data grows past
a threshold. If an order is visible to a human, it belongs in the SQL.

**Ties must be broken explicitly.** `ORDER BY price DESC` over 10,000
products with duplicate prices leaves the tied rows in an arbitrary
sequence, and "arbitrary" is allowed to differ between two runs of the same
query. Every ordered exercise in this course names a tie-breaker — usually
`id`, because it is unique — and that habit is what makes an ordering
*total* rather than merely *partial*. It is also what makes pagination
coherent: without a total order, "the next ten rows" is not a well-defined
concept.

**`ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` is not a sort followed by a truncation.**
PostgreSQL recognises the combination and switches to a *top-N heapsort*,
keeping only the best n rows it has seen in memory rather than sorting the
whole input. You can see it in `EXPLAIN` as `Sort Method: top-N heapsort`.
It is a large constant-factor win — but it is still O(rows), because every
row must be looked at to know it is not in the top fifteen. The only way to
avoid touching every row is an index whose order already matches your
`ORDER BY`, which is lesson 35.

**`OFFSET` does not skip work, it discards it.** `OFFSET 500 LIMIT 10`
produces 510 rows internally and throws 500 away. The cost grows linearly
with the page number, so deep pagination gets slower the further a user
scrolls, and — worse — it is *incorrect* under concurrent writes: if a row
is inserted before page 2 is requested, one row shifts across the boundary
and the user sees a duplicate or misses an item entirely. The professional
alternative is **keyset pagination** (also called seek, or cursor
pagination): remember the sort key of the last row you showed and ask for
`WHERE (price, id) > (last_price, last_id) ORDER BY price, id LIMIT 10`.
It is constant-time per page, it is stable under concurrent inserts, and
with the right index it is one of the fastest things a database can do.
Markus Winand's page on this is in the links below and is worth reading
twice.

**`NULLS FIRST` / `NULLS LAST` is a real decision.** PostgreSQL's default is
NULLs last when ascending, first when descending — consistent with treating
NULL as larger than everything. Other engines differ. Writing it explicitly
costs two words and removes a portability question and a code-review
question at once.

## ex1 — top N

10,000 rows sorted to produce 10. Look at the plan: `Limit` above `Sort`
above `Seq Scan`, and the sort reporting `top-N heapsort`. That shape — the
whole table read, most of it discarded — is the baseline that Part 5 exists
to improve on.

## ex2 — multi-key sort

Three sort keys, each breaking ties in the one before. This is also the
first exercise where the *order* of the keys is the whole answer: sorting by
salary then department produces a completely different report from
department then salary. When a stakeholder says "sorted by department and
salary", they have not told you which is primary, and asking is not pedantry.

## ex3 — pagination with OFFSET

Page 3 of a customer list, newest first. Note the descending tie-break on
`id`: with `created_at DESC` and two customers created in the same second,
`id DESC` keeps them in a stable, meaningful order. Choosing a tie-breaker
that *agrees* with the primary key's direction is a small thing that makes
paginated output feel coherent to a user.

## ex4 — where do NULLs sort?

One NULL in five hundred rows, and it changes the first line of the report.
The deeper point: NULL is not "smaller" or "larger" than a number — SQL has
to be *told* where to put it, because the question is not answerable by
comparison. That is the same fact that makes `NULL = NULL` unknown, and
lesson 05 is entirely about it.

## ex5 — top N over half a million rows

Same query shape as ex1, fifty times the data. The plan is identical; only
the row counts change. Keep the timing in mind — in lesson 35 you will add
one index and watch the `Sort` node disappear from this plan, because a
B-tree is already sorted and PostgreSQL can simply read the first fifteen
entries in order.

## ex6 — a deep page

The point of this exercise is that it is *identical* to ex3 apart from one
number, and yet a report that scrolls deep enough will eventually time out.
Try `OFFSET 9990 LIMIT 10` in the lab and watch the timing move. Then read
the keyset-pagination link below; the rewrite is not hard, and it is what
you should reach for whenever a page number can grow without bound.

## challenge — top 5 per category without window functions

Genuinely hard, and deliberately so. `LIMIT` applies to the whole result, so
"per group" needs something that evaluates *per row* — a correlated subquery
that asks, for each product, how many products in the same category are more
expensive. It is O(n²)-ish and it is what people wrote before 2003. In
lesson 15 you will replace the whole thing with `row_number() OVER
(PARTITION BY category ORDER BY price DESC)` and in lesson 48 with a
`LATERAL` join. Solving it the hard way first is what makes those two
lessons land.

## review1 — the five cheapest in a category

A filter, a sort, and a limit — the three clauses of this lesson and the
last, composed. Predict the tie-break behaviour before you run it.

Worth noticing when it returns: the five cheapest products in a category is
a *top-N within a group* question restricted to one group. Ask it for all
six categories at once and you have the challenge, which needs a correlated
subquery today and a window function in lesson 15. Recognising that two
questions are the same question with a different `WHERE` is most of what
makes SQL feel small rather than endless.

## Further reading

- [Sorting Rows](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-order.html) — `ASC`/`DESC`, `NULLS FIRST`/`LAST`, and what `ORDER BY` can reference.
- [`LIMIT` and `OFFSET`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-limit.html) — including the docs' own warning about inconsistent results without `ORDER BY`.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Paging Through Results](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/partial-results/fetch-next-page) — the definitive explanation of why `OFFSET` is the wrong tool and what keyset pagination looks like.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Top-N Queries](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/partial-results/top-n-queries) — how an index turns `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` into a few page reads. Preview of lesson 35.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — top 5 per category, no window functions (optional, hard)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. **The 5 most expensive products in *each* of
the 6 categories** — 30 rows. Columns: `category`, `name`, `price`. Order
the whole result by `category` ascending, then `price` descending, then `id`
ascending.

This is genuinely hard with what you know so far — `LIMIT` applies to the
whole result, not per group. The intended tool is a *correlated subquery*
(lesson 13 material, previewed here): for each product, ask "is this
product's id among the top 5 ids of its own category?". The hints walk you
through the shape. In lesson 15 you'll solve this in three lines with a
window function and feel great about it.

Run: `uv run dojo test 03_order_limit challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Per-category top-5 means each product row must be tested against *its own
category's* leaderboard. A subquery in the WHERE clause can see the current
outer row — that's called a correlated subquery. Ask: "is my id in the top-5
ids of my category?"

## Hint 2
The shape:

```sql
SELECT category, name, price
FROM products p
WHERE p.id IN (
    SELECT p2.id
    FROM products p2
    WHERE p2.category = p.category
    ORDER BY p2.price DESC, p2.id ASC
    LIMIT 5
)
ORDER BY ...;
```

The inner query re-ranks the *current row's* category each time.

## Hint 3
The only piece missing above is the outer ORDER BY — the prompt specifies
`category ASC, price DESC, id ASC`. Assemble and run it. (Yes, it's slow —
10,000 correlated sorts. Lesson 15 fixes the elegance, Part 5 the speed.)

```sql
SELECT id, name, price
FROM products
```

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — where do NULLs sort?

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The org-chart tool renders the reporting tree from
the top down, so it wants the row with **no manager first**. Return the
**first 10** staff rows sorted by `manager_id` **ascending with NULLs
first**, breaking ties by `id` ascending.

Columns: `id`, `name`, `manager_id`. Exactly 10 rows, and the order is
graded.

By default an ascending sort puts NULLs *last* in PostgreSQL. You have to
say `NULLS FIRST` to get the CEO to the top — and other databases pick the
opposite default, which is why portable SQL says it explicitly.

Run: `uv run dojo test 03_order_limit ex4`

placed**. Columns, in order: `id`, `customer_id`, `total`. Sort by `total`

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — a deep page

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. The product catalogue lists items **cheapest
first**, 10 per page. Produce **page 51** — skip the first 500 rows and
return the next 10.

Sort by `price` ascending, tie-break `id` ascending. Columns: `id`, `name`,
`price`. Exactly 10 rows, order graded.

Exercise 3 asked for page 3. This one asks for page 51, and the query is
identical except for one number — which is precisely the problem with
`OFFSET`. To hand you rows 501–510, PostgreSQL sorts the catalogue and then
walks past the first 500 results and throws them away. Page 5,000 would
throw away 50,000. The reading explains what real systems do instead.

Run: `uv run dojo test 03_order_limit ex6`

lessons.briefing:
# 04 — Expressions and functions

You already computed one column (`price * 1.2` in lesson 01). This lesson
makes that a habit: arithmetic, text functions, `COALESCE` for filling
NULLs, and `CASE` — SQL's per-row if/else. These appear in virtually every
production query; reports are mostly *expressions over columns*, not raw
columns.

## Concept

Per-row functions you'll use constantly:

```sql
SELECT
  round(price * 1.2, 2)              AS with_tax,      -- 2 decimal places
  round(salary, -3)                  AS to_thousands,  -- negative = left of the point
  upper(name)                        AS shouting,
  left(name, 8)                      AS clipped,
  name || ' (' || category || ')'    AS label,         -- || concatenates text
  concat(name, ' / ', category)      AS label2,        -- concat() too
  coalesce(manager_id, 0)            AS mgr_or_zero,   -- first non-NULL argument
  substring(email FROM 1 FOR 6)      AS prefix
FROM ...;
```

And the workhorse, `CASE`:

```sql
CASE
  WHEN price < 50  THEN 'budget'
  WHEN price < 200 THEN 'mid'
  ELSE 'premium'
END AS tier
```

`CASE` evaluates top-to-bottom and stops at the first true `WHEN` — so the
second branch already knows `price >= 50`. Without an `ELSE`, non-matching
rows get NULL.

One trap worth meeting early: `||` with a number needs a cast, because
PostgreSQL won't guess. `'x' || 5` fails; `'x' || 5::text` works. `::type`
is the cast syntax you'll see everywhere.

## Exercise 1 — price tiers with CASE

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Merchandising tiers every product: `'budget'`
under 50, `'mid'` from 50 up to but not including 200, `'premium'` at 200

# Reading - 04_expressions_functions

A production report is mostly *expressions over columns*, not columns. The
decision this lesson is really teaching is **where** a derived value should
be computed — and the answer is "in the query" far more often than people
who are comfortable in Python assume.

## Notes

**Expressions are evaluated per row, and their types are inferred.**
`price * 1.2` on a `numeric(10,2)` column produces `numeric` and stays
exact; the same expression on a `double precision` column produces binary
floating-point error. PostgreSQL will not warn you, because both are legal.
Types are the quiet half of every expression you write.

**`CASE` is an expression, not a statement.** It evaluates to a value, so it
can go anywhere a value can: the SELECT list, a `WHERE` clause, an
`ORDER BY`, inside an aggregate (lesson 17 builds pivots this way), even
inside a `GROUP BY`. Branches are tested top to bottom and evaluation stops
at the first true `WHEN`, which is why the ladder in ex1 does not need
`price >= 50 AND price < 200` in its second branch. Omitting `ELSE` does not
raise an error — it produces NULL, which is a very common source of
mysterious NULLs downstream.

**`coalesce` is not a NULL-fixer, it is a display decision.** Replacing a
missing manager with `0` is correct for a CSV export and wrong for an
average: `avg(coalesce(salary, 0))` quietly counts unknown salaries as zero
and drags the mean down, whereas `avg(salary)` — which skips NULLs — answers
the question people actually asked. Reach for `coalesce` at the edge of the
system, where a human or a file format needs a value; leave the NULLs intact
while you are still computing. Related: `nullif(a, b)` is the inverse, and
`nullif(divisor, 0)` is the standard way to make a division return NULL
instead of raising a division-by-zero error.

**Casting is explicit on purpose.** `'x' || 5` is an error because
PostgreSQL will not guess whether you meant text concatenation or something
else. `::text` (or the standard `CAST(5 AS text)`) says what you meant. The
same strictness is why `'2023-01-01'::date` and `'{"a":1}'::jsonb` work — a
cast is how a literal string becomes a typed value.

**Expressions and indexes.** A filter written as `WHERE lower(name) = 'ana'`
cannot use an ordinary index on `name`, because the index stores `name`, not
`lower(name)`. PostgreSQL can index the *expression* instead — `CREATE INDEX
ON customers (lower(name))` — and lesson 40 is entirely about it. Keep that
in your pocket: a computed column is not automatically slow, but it is
automatically un-indexed until you say otherwise.

## ex1 — price tiers with CASE

The classic ladder. Worth noticing that the boundary conditions are stated
in the prompt as "under 50" and "from 50 up to but not including 200" —
half-open intervals, exactly as `<` and `<` in the ladder produce. Whenever
a stakeholder describes buckets in prose, pin down the endpoints before you
write the `CASE`; off-by-one bucket boundaries are one of the most common
silent reporting bugs.

## ex2 — building display text

`round(salary, -3)` is the surprise. A negative scale rounds to the *left*
of the decimal point — to the nearest thousand here. It is a genuinely
useful trick for banding numbers in reports, and it is far less error-prone
than a `CASE` ladder with eight branches.

## ex3 — filling a hole with COALESCE

One row in five hundred. That is the ratio that makes NULL dangerous: a
transformation can look perfect across your entire test output and still be
wrong on the row that matters. Lesson 05 turns this from a display concern
into a logic concern.

## ex4 — building an SKU

`||` refusing to concatenate an integer is the language being pedantic in
your favour. In a weakly-typed language, `'BOO-' + 4242` might produce
`'BOO-4242'` or `4242` or an exception depending on the day; SQL makes you
say which one you meant. Note also that this SKU is a *derived* value — it
is not stored, it cannot drift out of sync with the category, and every
consumer that runs this query agrees on its definition. That is the argument
for computing in SQL, and lesson 27 (views) is how you stop repeating it.

## challenge — a nested label

Function composition plus the cast. If you fought with the em dash, that is
a real-world detail too: string literals are bytes with an encoding, and
`' — $'` only round-trips because the database, the client and the terminal
agree on UTF-8.

## review1 — a discounted price

`round(price * 0.9, 2)`. Two things to check yourself on when this returns:
that you rounded *after* multiplying, and that the result is still `numeric`
rather than a float. Money that has been through a `double precision` at any
point in its life is money you cannot reconcile.

## Further reading

- [Conditional Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-conditional.html) — `CASE`, `COALESCE`, `NULLIF`, `GREATEST`, `LEAST`. Short page, high value.
- [String Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-string.html) — `left`, `substring`, `concat`, `format`, and the difference between `||` and `concat()` when an argument is NULL.
- [Mathematical Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-math.html) — including `round`'s two-argument form and what a negative scale does.
- [Type Conversion](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/typeconv.html) — the rules PostgreSQL uses when it *can* infer a cast, and why it refuses to for `||`.

# 04 — Expressions and functions

You already computed one column (`price * 1.2` in lesson 01). This lesson
makes that a habit: arithmetic, text functions, `COALESCE` for filling
NULLs, and `CASE` — SQL's per-row if/else. These appear in virtually every
production query; reports are mostly *expressions over columns*, not raw
columns.

## Concept

Per-row functions you'll use constantly:

```sql
SELECT
  round(price * 1.2, 2)              AS with_tax,      -- 2 decimal places
  round(salary, -3)                  AS to_thousands,  -- negative = left of the point
  upper(name)                        AS shouting,
  left(name, 8)                      AS clipped,
  name || ' (' || category || ')'    AS label,         -- || concatenates text
  concat(name, ' / ', category)      AS label2,        -- concat() too
  coalesce(manager_id, 0)            AS mgr_or_zero,   -- first non-NULL argument
  substring(email FROM 1 FOR 6)      AS prefix
FROM ...;
```

And the workhorse, `CASE`:

```sql
CASE
  WHEN price < 50  THEN 'budget'
  WHEN price < 200 THEN 'mid'
  ELSE 'premium'
END AS tier
```

`CASE` evaluates top-to-bottom and stops at the first true `WHEN` — so the
second branch already knows `price >= 50`. Without an `ELSE`, non-matching
rows get NULL.

One trap worth meeting early: `||` with a number needs a cast, because
PostgreSQL won't guess. `'x' || 5` fails; `'x' || 5::text` works. `::type`
is the cast syntax you'll see everywhere.

Expressions belong in SQL more often than in application code: computing a

"push it into the query" (or a view — lesson 27).

# Reading - 04_expressions_functions

A production report is mostly *expressions over columns*, not columns. The
decision this lesson is really teaching is **where** a derived value should
be computed — and the answer is "in the query" far more often than people
who are comfortable in Python assume.

## Notes

**Expressions are evaluated per row, and their types are inferred.**
`price * 1.2` on a `numeric(10,2)` column produces `numeric` and stays
exact; the same expression on a `double precision` column produces binary
floating-point error. PostgreSQL will not warn you, because both are legal.
Types are the quiet half of every expression you write.

**`CASE` is an expression, not a statement.** It evaluates to a value, so it
can go anywhere a value can: the SELECT list, a `WHERE` clause, an
`ORDER BY`, inside an aggregate (lesson 17 builds pivots this way), even
inside a `GROUP BY`. Branches are tested top to bottom and evaluation stops
at the first true `WHEN`, which is why the ladder in ex1 does not need
`price >= 50 AND price < 200` in its second branch. Omitting `ELSE` does not
raise an error — it produces NULL, which is a very common source of
mysterious NULLs downstream.

**`coalesce` is not a NULL-fixer, it is a display decision.** Replacing a
missing manager with `0` is correct for a CSV export and wrong for an
average: `avg(coalesce(salary, 0))` quietly counts unknown salaries as zero
and drags the mean down, whereas `avg(salary)` — which skips NULLs — answers
the question people actually asked. Reach for `coalesce` at the edge of the
system, where a human or a file format needs a value; leave the NULLs intact
while you are still computing. Related: `nullif(a, b)` is the inverse, and
`nullif(divisor, 0)` is the standard way to make a division return NULL
instead of raising a division-by-zero error.

**Casting is explicit on purpose.** `'x' || 5` is an error because
PostgreSQL will not guess whether you meant text concatenation or something
else. `::text` (or the standard `CAST(5 AS text)`) says what you meant. The
same strictness is why `'2023-01-01'::date` and `'{"a":1}'::jsonb` work — a
cast is how a literal string becomes a typed value.

**Expressions and indexes.** A filter written as `WHERE lower(name) = 'ana'`
cannot use an ordinary index on `name`, because the index stores `name`, not
`lower(name)`. PostgreSQL can index the *expression* instead — `CREATE INDEX
ON customers (lower(name))` — and lesson 40 is entirely about it. Keep that
in your pocket: a computed column is not automatically slow, but it is
automatically un-indexed until you say otherwise.

## ex1 — price tiers with CASE

The classic ladder. Worth noticing that the boundary conditions are stated
in the prompt as "under 50" and "from 50 up to but not including 200" —
half-open intervals, exactly as `<` and `<` in the ladder produce. Whenever
a stakeholder describes buckets in prose, pin down the endpoints before you
write the `CASE`; off-by-one bucket boundaries are one of the most common
silent reporting bugs.

## ex2 — building display text

`round(salary, -3)` is the surprise. A negative scale rounds to the *left*
of the decimal point — to the nearest thousand here. It is a genuinely
useful trick for banding numbers in reports, and it is far less error-prone
than a `CASE` ladder with eight branches.

## ex3 — filling a hole with COALESCE

One row in five hundred. That is the ratio that makes NULL dangerous: a
transformation can look perfect across your entire test output and still be
wrong on the row that matters. Lesson 05 turns this from a display concern
into a logic concern.

## ex4 — building an SKU

`||` refusing to concatenate an integer is the language being pedantic in
your favour. In a weakly-typed language, `'BOO-' + 4242` might produce
`'BOO-4242'` or `4242` or an exception depending on the day; SQL makes you
say which one you meant. Note also that this SKU is a *derived* value — it
is not stored, it cannot drift out of sync with the category, and every
consumer that runs this query agrees on its definition. That is the argument
for computing in SQL, and lesson 27 (views) is how you stop repeating it.

## challenge — a nested label

Function composition plus the cast. If you fought with the em dash, that is
a real-world detail too: string literals are bytes with an encoding, and
`' — $'` only round-trips because the database, the client and the terminal
agree on UTF-8.

## review1 — a discounted price

`round(price * 0.9, 2)`. Two things to check yourself on when this returns:
that you rounded *after* multiplying, and that the result is still `numeric`
rather than a float. Money that has been through a `double precision` at any
point in its life is money you cannot reconcile.

## Further reading

- [Conditional Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-conditional.html) — `CASE`, `COALESCE`, `NULLIF`, `GREATEST`, `LEAST`. Short page, high value.
- [String Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-string.html) — `left`, `substring`, `concat`, `format`, and the difference between `||` and `concat()` when an argument is NULL.
- [Mathematical Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-math.html) — including `round`'s two-argument form and what a negative scale does.
- [Type Conversion](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/typeconv.html) — the rules PostgreSQL uses when it *can* infer a cast, and why it refuses to for `||`.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — a nested label (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. The mobile app shows compact product cards:
one column, `card`, for every product, formatted as the first 12 characters
of the upper-cased name, then `' — $'`, then the price. Example:

```
AERO WIDGET  — $137.53
```

Exactly: `left(upper(name), 12) || ' — $' || price`. The catch: `price` is
numeric, and `||` needs text — you'll have to cast. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 04_expressions_functions challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Work inside-out: `upper(name)`, then `left(..., 12)`, then concatenate the
literal `' — $'`, then the price. The only failure you should hit is the
type error — read it; it names the two types it can't concatenate.

## Hint 2
The cast: `price::text`. Full expression:

```sql
left(upper(name), 12) || ' — $' || price::text AS card
```

One column, FROM products. (The dash is an em dash — copy it from the
README, or from this hint.)

## Exercise 3 — filling a hole with COALESCE

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. The org-chart export cannot cope with a missing
manager, so it wants a `0` where there is no one. For every staff member
return three columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, and `manager_id` with
NULL replaced by `0`, aliased **`manager_or_zero`**.

All 500 rows, any order. Exactly one of them exercises the `coalesce` —
find it in the output and you have found the CEO.

`coalesce(a, b)` returns `a` unless `a` is NULL, in which case it returns
`b`. It takes any number of arguments and returns the first non-NULL one.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — building an SKU (and meeting the cast)

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The warehouse needs a printable SKU for every
product: the **first three letters of the category, upper-cased**, then a
hyphen, then the product's `id`. For product 4242 in `books` that is
`BOO-4242`.

Two columns, in this order: `id`, and the SKU aliased **`sku`**. All 10,000
rows, any order.

Three functions compose here — `left(text, n)`, `upper(text)`, and `||` for
concatenation — plus the trap from the concept section: `id` is an integer
and `||` will not silently stringify it for you. Cast it with `id::text`.

lessons.briefing:
# 05 — NULL: three-valued logic

Exactly one row in this whole database has a NULL in it on purpose: the
CEO's `manager_id` in `staff`. One NULL is all it takes. NULL is not zero,
not empty string, not "unknown value that acts like a value" — it's SQL's
marker for *absent*, and every comparison with it returns neither true nor
false but **unknown**. WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is *true*,
so unknown rows silently vanish. That rule, applied consistently, produces
some famously surprising behavior — today you meet it in a controlled
environment instead of a 2 a.m. incident.

## Concept

```sql
NULL = NULL      -- unknown, not true!
NULL <> 5        -- unknown
NOT (unknown)    -- still unknown
```

- To test for NULL: `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`. Never `= NULL`.
- `IS DISTINCT FROM` is `<>` that treats NULL as a comparable value:
  `NULL IS DISTINCT FROM 5` is true, `NULL IS DISTINCT FROM NULL` is false.
  Use it when NULLs must count as "different" (or "same") instead of
  "unknown".
- Aggregates skip NULLs (`count(manager_id)` counts only non-NULL — lesson
  06 makes this precise).
- **The `NOT IN` trap**, this lesson's boss fight: if the list inside
  `NOT IN (...)` contains even one NULL, the whole condition can never be
  true for any row, and you get **zero rows** with no error and no warning.
  Why: `x NOT IN (a, b, NULL)` means `x <> a AND x <> b AND x <> NULL`, and
  that last comparison is unknown, which poisons the AND.

One preview: `NOT IN` can take a subquery — `id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id
FROM staff)` means "id is not in that column's values". Subqueries proper
are lesson 13; you only need this one-line form today.

## Exercise 1 — find the CEO

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Return the one staff member with no manager.
Columns: `id`, `name`. One row.

Run: `uv run dojo test 05_null_logic ex1`

## Exercise 2 — the NOT IN trap

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. HR wants every **individual contributor** — staff
who manage nobody, i.e. whose `id` never appears in the `manager_id`
column. Columns: `id`, `name`. Any order. (Most of the company qualifies.)

The "obvious" query is:

```sql
SELECT id, name FROM staff
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM staff);
```

Run it in the lab. **Zero rows.** The CEO's NULL `manager_id` is in that
list, and one NULL poisons `NOT IN` completely. Your job: make it work —
filter the NULL out *inside* the list (`WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL`).
(Lesson 13 will show you `NOT EXISTS`, which shrugs NULLs off entirely.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 05_null_logic ex2`

## Exercise 3 — NULL is contagious

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Payroll wants a manager *code* rather than an id:
for every staff member return `id`, `name`, and `manager_id + 1000` aliased
**`mgr_code`**.

All 500 rows, any order.

Nothing filters here, so every row survives — but look at the CEO's row in
the output. `NULL + 1000` is not `1000`; it is NULL. **Any** arithmetic,
concatenation, or function applied to NULL propagates the NULL outward,
because the answer to "what is the unknown value plus a thousand?" is still
unknown. This is the same rule as `NULL = NULL`, applied to arithmetic
instead of comparison, and it is why a single missing value can turn an
entire computed column into NULLs.

Run: `uv run dojo test 05_null_logic ex3`

## Exercise 4 — when NOT IN is safe

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Merchandising is auditing the launch window: which
products **never appeared on any line of the first 1,000 orders** (that is,
`order_items` rows whose `order_id` is 1000 or less)? Columns: `id`,
`name`. Any order.

Use `NOT IN` with a subquery this time:

```sql
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_items WHERE order_id <= 1000)
```

In exercise 2 that shape returned zero rows and lied to you. Here it works
perfectly — and the difference is not luck. Before you run it, look up
`order_items.product_id` in [docs/dataset.md](../../docs/dataset.md) and
work out *why* this one is safe. If you can state the rule out loud, this
lesson has done its job.

(The `order_id <= 1000` narrowing is not cosmetic. Drop it and the same
query has to check 10,000 products against a million values and takes
minutes — `NOT IN` over a large subquery is a performance trap as well as a
NULL trap. The reading explains both.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 05_null_logic ex4`

## Challenge — IS DISTINCT FROM (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Return every staff member whose
`manager_id` **IS DISTINCT FROM 1** — i.e. everyone who does *not* report
directly to the CEO (id 1), **including the CEO herself**, whose NULL would
be dropped by a plain `<> 1`. Columns: `id`, `name`. Any order.

Try it with `<> 1` first in the lab and count the rows — you'll be exactly
one short. That missing row is the entire point of `IS DISTINCT FROM`.

Run: `uv run dojo test 05_null_logic challenge`

## Spaced review

`review1/`: every **finance** staff member who *has* a manager — columns
`id`, `name`, any order. (Two conditions; one of them is a NULL test.)

# Reading - 05_null_logic

SQL's logic has three values, not two, and every surprising NULL story is a
consequence of that one fact. This is the lesson that separates people who
have been bitten from people who are about to be.

## Notes

**NULL is not a value; it is the absence of one.** That is why it has no
equality: asking whether one unknown equals another unknown cannot be
answered `true` or `false`, so SQL answers `unknown`. Every comparison
operator behaves this way, including `<>`, `<`, and `>`.

**`WHERE` keeps rows where the condition is `true` — and only `true`.**
`unknown` is discarded exactly like `false`, silently and without a warning.
This single rule generates almost all NULL bugs, because the query does not
fail; it returns a smaller, plausible answer.

**`NOT` cannot rescue you.** `NOT unknown` is `unknown`. So `WHERE NOT
(status = 'x')` drops NULL-status rows just as surely as `WHERE status = 'x'`
does — the same row is missing from *both* halves of what looks like a
complete partition. If you have ever had two reports that were each correct
and did not add up to the total, this was probably why.

**The `NOT IN` trap.** `x NOT IN (a, b, NULL)` expands to `x <> a AND x <> b
AND x <> NULL`. That last conjunct is `unknown`, and `true AND unknown` is
`unknown`, so the whole predicate can never be `true` — the query returns
**zero rows**, always, no matter the data. Note the asymmetry: `IN` with a
NULL is merely unhelpful (it can still return `true` on a real match), while
`NOT IN` with a NULL is catastrophic. This is why experienced reviewers stop
at every `NOT IN (SELECT ...)` and ask one question: *can that column be
NULL?* If it is declared `NOT NULL`, the shape is safe forever, and the
declaration is the proof. If it is nullable, use `NOT EXISTS` (lesson 13),
which compares row-by-row and is completely immune, or filter the NULLs out
inside the subquery.

**The tools for working with NULL deliberately:**

- `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` — the only correct way to *test* for absence.
- `IS DISTINCT FROM` / `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` — comparison that treats NULL
  as an ordinary comparable value. `NULL IS DISTINCT FROM 5` is `true`;
  `NULL IS NOT DISTINCT FROM NULL` is `true`. Reach for these whenever
  "different" should include "one side is missing".
- `coalesce` — substitute a value at the edge of the system (lesson 04).
- Aggregates skip NULLs, which is usually what you want and occasionally a
  trap: `avg` over a column that is 90% NULL is the average of the other
  10%, reported without comment (lesson 06).
- `UNIQUE` constraints treat NULLs as distinct from each other, so a
  nullable unique column accepts unlimited NULL rows (lesson 25).

**Why NULL exists at all.** Because "we do not know this customer's phone
number" is genuinely different from "their phone number is the empty
string", and a database that cannot express the difference forces every
application to invent a magic sentinel — `-1`, `''`, `'1900-01-01'` — which
is worse in every way. NULL is the right idea with famously sharp edges. The
design response is not to ban it but to *declare* `NOT NULL` wherever
absence is meaningless, which turns whole categories of this lesson's bugs
into schema errors. Lesson 25 makes that concrete.

## ex1 — find the CEO

`WHERE manager_id IS NULL`. Try `= NULL` in the lab first: no error, no
warning, zero rows. PostgreSQL parses it, evaluates it to `unknown` for every
row, and returns an empty set with a straight face.

Some databases have historically offered a setting that makes `= NULL`
behave like `IS NULL` for compatibility with old client code. PostgreSQL
does not, and that is a feature: a query that means two different things
depending on a server setting is a query nobody can review. `IS NULL` is
four characters longer and unambiguous everywhere.

## ex2 — the NOT IN trap

The boss fight, and the reason it is memorable is that the failure is
*total* rather than partial. Zero rows out of five hundred. Partial failures
you argue with; total failures you investigate. Note what the fix does not
require: no change to the outer query, no `NOT EXISTS`, just
`WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL` inside the list, removing the poison at the
source.

## ex3 — NULL is contagious

Propagation through arithmetic. The same rule covers `||` (which is why
`concat()` exists — it treats NULL as an empty string instead), `upper()`,
`round()`, and essentially every scalar function. When a computed column
comes back full of unexpected NULLs, the bug is almost always one nullable
input several expressions upstream.

## ex4 — when NOT IN is safe

The point of this exercise is the *reasoning*, not the rows.
`order_items.product_id` is declared `NOT NULL` and enforced by a foreign
key, so the subquery cannot produce a NULL, so `NOT IN` cannot be poisoned —
and no future data can change that without a schema migration. This is what
constraints buy you: not just data hygiene, but the ability to prove a query
is correct. When the column is *not* declared `NOT NULL`, you have no such
proof, and `NOT EXISTS` is the right reflex.

There is a second reason to distrust `NOT IN (subquery)`, and the
`order_id <= 1000` narrowing is hiding it from you. Remove it and the query
takes *minutes* on this dataset. PostgreSQL would like to answer `NOT IN` by
hashing the subquery's results, but the hashed strategy is only valid when
NULLs are provably absent and the values fit in `work_mem` — miss either
condition and it falls back to re-scanning the subquery per outer row, which
is 10,000 × 1,000,000 comparisons. `NOT EXISTS` and the `LEFT JOIN ... IS
NULL` anti-join (lesson 09 ex2 asks this exact question that way) both plan
as a proper hashed anti-join and finish in milliseconds. So the reviewer's
rule has two halves: `NOT IN (subquery)` is a correctness hazard on nullable
columns *and* a performance hazard on large ones. The idiom that is never
either is `NOT EXISTS`.

## challenge — IS DISTINCT FROM

`<> 1` returns 499 rows minus the CEO — 498. `IS DISTINCT FROM 1` returns
499. One row, and it is the row a human would obviously expect to be there.
`IS DISTINCT FROM` is the operator to reach for whenever you are comparing
two things that might each be missing — change-detection queries ("has this
column changed since yesterday?") are the canonical case, and they are
subtly broken with `<>` on every nullable column.

## review1 — finance staff with a manager

Two conditions, one of them a NULL test. When this comes back in three days,
notice that "has a manager" cannot be written as `manager_id <> NULL`, and
that nothing in the SQL will remind you.

There is a quieter point in this one. Filtering to `finance` *and* "has a
manager" happens to be redundant on this data — every finance employee has a
manager, since the only manager-less row is the CEO. A redundant condition
is harmless today and load-bearing tomorrow, when someone promotes a finance
director to report to nobody. Writing the condition you mean, rather than
the condition the current data makes sufficient, is what keeps a query
correct as the data changes.

## Further reading

- [Comparison Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html) — the truth tables, `IS DISTINCT FROM`, and `IS NULL`. The authoritative source for everything above.
- [`NOT IN` and NULL](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) — the subquery expressions page; read the `NOT IN` paragraph slowly, twice.
- [Don't Do This — NULL handling](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) — including why a nullable column with a magic sentinel is worse than a NULL.
- [`NOT NULL` constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-constraints.html) — the schema-level answer to this entire lesson. Preview of lesson 25.

# Reading - 05_null_logic

SQL's logic has three values, not two, and every surprising NULL story is a
consequence of that one fact. This is the lesson that separates people who
have been bitten from people who are about to be.

## Notes

**NULL is not a value; it is the absence of one.** That is why it has no
equality: asking whether one unknown equals another unknown cannot be
answered `true` or `false`, so SQL answers `unknown`. Every comparison
operator behaves this way, including `<>`, `<`, and `>`.

**`WHERE` keeps rows where the condition is `true` — and only `true`.**
`unknown` is discarded exactly like `false`, silently and without a warning.
This single rule generates almost all NULL bugs, because the query does not
fail; it returns a smaller, plausible answer.

**`NOT` cannot rescue you.** `NOT unknown` is `unknown`. So `WHERE NOT
(status = 'x')` drops NULL-status rows just as surely as `WHERE status = 'x'`
does — the same row is missing from *both* halves of what looks like a
complete partition. If you have ever had two reports that were each correct
and did not add up to the total, this was probably why.

**The `NOT IN` trap.** `x NOT IN (a, b, NULL)` expands to `x <> a AND x <> b
AND x <> NULL`. That last conjunct is `unknown`, and `true AND unknown` is
`unknown`, so the whole predicate can never be `true` — the query returns
**zero rows**, always, no matter the data. Note the asymmetry: `IN` with a
NULL is merely unhelpful (it can still return `true` on a real match), while
`NOT IN` with a NULL is catastrophic. This is why experienced reviewers stop
at every `NOT IN (SELECT ...)` and ask one question: *can that column be
NULL?* If it is declared `NOT NULL`, the shape is safe forever, and the
declaration is the proof. If it is nullable, use `NOT EXISTS` (lesson 13),
which compares row-by-row and is completely immune, or filter the NULLs out
inside the subquery.

**The tools for working with NULL deliberately:**

- `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` — the only correct way to *test* for absence.
- `IS DISTINCT FROM` / `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` — comparison that treats NULL
  as an ordinary comparable value. `NULL IS DISTINCT FROM 5` is `true`;
  `NULL IS NOT DISTINCT FROM NULL` is `true`. Reach for these whenever
  "different" should include "one side is missing".
- `coalesce` — substitute a value at the edge of the system (lesson 04).
- Aggregates skip NULLs, which is usually what you want and occasionally a
  trap: `avg` over a column that is 90% NULL is the average of the other
  10%, reported without comment (lesson 06).
- `UNIQUE` constraints treat NULLs as distinct from each other, so a
  nullable unique column accepts unlimited NULL rows (lesson 25).

**Why NULL exists at all.** Because "we do not know this customer's phone
number" is genuinely different from "their phone number is the empty
string", and a database that cannot express the difference forces every
application to invent a magic sentinel — `-1`, `''`, `'1900-01-01'` — which
is worse in every way. NULL is the right idea with famously sharp edges. The
design response is not to ban it but to *declare* `NOT NULL` wherever
absence is meaningless, which turns whole categories of this lesson's bugs
into schema errors. Lesson 25 makes that concrete.

## ex1 — find the CEO

`WHERE manager_id IS NULL`. Try `= NULL` in the lab first: no error, no
warning, zero rows. PostgreSQL parses it, evaluates it to `unknown` for every
row, and returns an empty set with a straight face.

Some databases have historically offered a setting that makes `= NULL`
behave like `IS NULL` for compatibility with old client code. PostgreSQL
does not, and that is a feature: a query that means two different things
depending on a server setting is a query nobody can review. `IS NULL` is
four characters longer and unambiguous everywhere.

## ex2 — the NOT IN trap

The boss fight, and the reason it is memorable is that the failure is
*total* rather than partial. Zero rows out of five hundred. Partial failures
you argue with; total failures you investigate. Note what the fix does not
require: no change to the outer query, no `NOT EXISTS`, just
`WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL` inside the list, removing the poison at the
source.

## ex3 — NULL is contagious

Propagation through arithmetic. The same rule covers `||` (which is why
`concat()` exists — it treats NULL as an empty string instead), `upper()`,
`round()`, and essentially every scalar function. When a computed column
comes back full of unexpected NULLs, the bug is almost always one nullable
input several expressions upstream.

## ex4 — when NOT IN is safe

The point of this exercise is the *reasoning*, not the rows.
`order_items.product_id` is declared `NOT NULL` and enforced by a foreign
key, so the subquery cannot produce a NULL, so `NOT IN` cannot be poisoned —
and no future data can change that without a schema migration. This is what
constraints buy you: not just data hygiene, but the ability to prove a query
is correct. When the column is *not* declared `NOT NULL`, you have no such
proof, and `NOT EXISTS` is the right reflex.

There is a second reason to distrust `NOT IN (subquery)`, and the
`order_id <= 1000` narrowing is hiding it from you. Remove it and the query
takes *minutes* on this dataset. PostgreSQL would like to answer `NOT IN` by
hashing the subquery's results, but the hashed strategy is only valid when
NULLs are provably absent and the values fit in `work_mem` — miss either
condition and it falls back to re-scanning the subquery per outer row, which
is 10,000 × 1,000,000 comparisons. `NOT EXISTS` and the `LEFT JOIN ... IS
NULL` anti-join (lesson 09 ex2 asks this exact question that way) both plan
as a proper hashed anti-join and finish in milliseconds. So the reviewer's
rule has two halves: `NOT IN (subquery)` is a correctness hazard on nullable
columns *and* a performance hazard on large ones. The idiom that is never
either is `NOT EXISTS`.

## challenge — IS DISTINCT FROM

`<> 1` returns 499 rows minus the CEO — 498. `IS DISTINCT FROM 1` returns
499. One row, and it is the row a human would obviously expect to be there.
`IS DISTINCT FROM` is the operator to reach for whenever you are comparing
two things that might each be missing — change-detection queries ("has this
column changed since yesterday?") are the canonical case, and they are
subtly broken with `<>` on every nullable column.

## review1 — finance staff with a manager

Two conditions, one of them a NULL test. When this comes back in three days,
notice that "has a manager" cannot be written as `manager_id <> NULL`, and
that nothing in the SQL will remind you.

There is a quieter point in this one. Filtering to `finance` *and* "has a
manager" happens to be redundant on this data — every finance employee has a
manager, since the only manager-less row is the CEO. A redundant condition
is harmless today and load-bearing tomorrow, when someone promotes a finance
director to report to nobody. Writing the condition you mean, rather than
the condition the current data makes sufficient, is what keeps a query
correct as the data changes.

## Further reading

- [Comparison Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html) — the truth tables, `IS DISTINCT FROM`, and `IS NULL`. The authoritative source for everything above.
- [`NOT IN` and NULL](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) — the subquery expressions page; read the `NOT IN` paragraph slowly, twice.
- [Don't Do This — NULL handling](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) — including why a nullable column with a magic sentinel is worse than a NULL.
- [`NOT NULL` constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-constraints.html) — the schema-level answer to this entire lesson. Preview of lesson 25.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — IS DISTINCT FROM (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Return every staff member whose
`manager_id` **IS DISTINCT FROM 1** — i.e. everyone who does *not* report
directly to the CEO (id 1), **including the CEO herself**, whose NULL would
be dropped by a plain `<> 1`. Columns: `id`, `name`. Any order.

Try it with `<> 1` first in the lab and count the rows — you'll be exactly
one short. That missing row is the entire point of `IS DISTINCT FROM`.

Run: `uv run dojo test 05_null_logic challenge`

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — the NOT IN trap

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. HR wants every **individual contributor** — staff
who manage nobody, i.e. whose `id` never appears in the `manager_id`
column. Columns: `id`, `name`. Any order. (Most of the company qualifies.)

The "obvious" query is:

```sql
SELECT id, name FROM staff
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM staff);
```

Run it in the lab. **Zero rows.** The CEO's NULL `manager_id` is in that
list, and one NULL poisons `NOT IN` completely. Your job: make it work —
filter the NULL out *inside* the list (`WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL`).
(Lesson 13 will show you `NOT EXISTS`, which shrugs NULLs off entirely.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 05_null_logic ex2`

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — NULL is contagious

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Payroll wants a manager *code* rather than an id:
for every staff member return `id`, `name`, and `manager_id + 1000` aliased
**`mgr_code`**.

All 500 rows, any order.

Nothing filters here, so every row survives — but look at the CEO's row in
the output. `NULL + 1000` is not `1000`; it is NULL. **Any** arithmetic,
concatenation, or function applied to NULL propagates the NULL outward,
because the answer to "what is the unknown value plus a thousand?" is still
unknown. This is the same rule as `NULL = NULL`, applied to arithmetic
instead of comparison, and it is why a single missing value can turn an
entire computed column into NULLs.

Run: `uv run dojo test 05_null_logic ex3`

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — when NOT IN is safe

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Merchandising is auditing the launch window: which
products **never appeared on any line of the first 1,000 orders** (that is,
`order_items` rows whose `order_id` is 1000 or less)? Columns: `id`,
`name`. Any order.

Use `NOT IN` with a subquery this time:

```sql
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_items WHERE order_id <= 1000)
```

In exercise 2 that shape returned zero rows and lied to you. Here it works
perfectly — and the difference is not luck. Before you run it, look up
`order_items.product_id` in [docs/dataset.md](../../docs/dataset.md) and
work out *why* this one is safe. If you can state the rule out loud, this
lesson has done its job.

(The `order_id <= 1000` narrowing is not cosmetic. Drop it and the same
query has to check 10,000 products against a million values and takes
minutes — `NOT IN` over a large subquery is a performance trap as well as a
NULL trap. The reading explains both.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 05_null_logic ex4`

lessons.summary: Every query so far returned one row per table row. But most business questions are about many rows at once: how many orders? what's the average total? what's our worst rating? lessons.briefing:
# 06 — Aggregates

Every query so far returned one row per table row. But most business
questions are about *many* rows at once: how many orders? what's the
average total? what's our worst rating? Aggregate functions collapse a
whole set of rows into a single value — and with `FILTER`, several
differently-scoped answers can share one pass over the table.

## Concept

```sql
SELECT count(*), sum(total), round(avg(total), 2), min(total), max(total)
FROM orders;
```

- `count(*)` counts **rows**. `count(some_column)` counts rows where that
  column is **not NULL** — on `staff`, `count(*)` is 500 but
  `count(manager_id)` is 499, because the CEO's is NULL (lesson 05 pays
  off already). This distinction is a classic interview question and a
  classic production bug.
- `sum`/`avg`/`min`/`max` also skip NULLs.
- `avg` on our `numeric` columns returns long decimals — `round(avg(x), 2)`
  keeps reports readable.
- `FILTER (WHERE ...)` scopes one aggregate without a second query:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')      AS paid,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled
FROM orders;
```

One pass over 500,000 rows, two answers. (You may have seen the
`sum(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` idiom — FILTER is the modern,
readable form; lesson 17 uses both.)

With no `GROUP BY` (next lesson), an aggregate query returns **exactly one
row**, even over an empty table (`count` gives 0, the others NULL).

## Exercise 1 — the orders dashboard row

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. One row, five columns, in this order: the number
of orders, the smallest `total`, the largest `total`, the average `total`
rounded to 2 decimals, and the sum of all totals. From `orders`.

(Sanity anchor from `dataset_facts.md`: the average is 1004.58.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 06_aggregates ex1`

## Exercise 2 — status counts with FILTER

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. One row, four columns, in this order: how many
orders are `paid`, `pending`, `shipped`, `cancelled`. Use one query with
four filtered counts — not four queries.

Run: `uv run dojo test 06_aggregates ex2`

## Exercise 3 — count(*) is not count(column)

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. HR wants a one-row summary of the company. Five
columns, in this order:

1. the number of staff rows
2. the number of staff who **have** a manager
3. the average `salary`, rounded to 2 decimals
4. the highest `salary`
5. the earliest `hired_on` date

From `staff`. One row.

Columns 1 and 2 differ by exactly one, and the difference is the entire
point: `count(*)` counts **rows**, `count(manager_id)` counts **non-NULL
values of that column**. Both are spelled `count`. Neither warns you which
one you meant.

Run: `uv run dojo test 06_aggregates ex3`

## Exercise 4 — counting distinct things

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The weekly ops report needs three numbers about
`orders`, in this order:

1. how many orders there are
2. how many **distinct customers** placed them
3. how many **distinct statuses** appear

One row, three columns.

`count(DISTINCT col)` deduplicates before counting. It is the honest way to
answer "how many customers?" from a table of orders — and it is much more
expensive than `count(*)`, because PostgreSQL must remember every value it
has seen. You wrote the same question as `SELECT DISTINCT customer_id` back
in lesson 01; this collapses it to a single number.

Run: `uv run dojo test 06_aggregates ex4`

## Challenge — the all-hands KPI row (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Leadership wants one row with four numbers
pulled from *different tables*: total customers, total orders, revenue
from `paid` orders (sum of their totals), and the average review rating
rounded to 2 decimals.

You can't FROM four tables at once for this — the trick is *scalar
subqueries*, each one a parenthesized single-value query in the SELECT
list (a preview of lesson 13):

```sql
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM customers) AS customers, ...
```

Run: `uv run dojo test 06_aggregates challenge`

rounded to 2 decimals, and the total number of reviews.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 06_aggregates

An aggregate is a *fold*: it consumes a set of rows and produces one value.
Everything surprising about aggregates follows from two details — what they
do with NULL, and the fact that the fold happens after `WHERE` and before
`SELECT`.

## Notes

**`count(*)` and `count(col)` are different functions wearing the same
name.** `count(*)` asks "how many rows are in this group?" and never
inspects a value. `count(col)` asks "how many rows have a non-NULL `col`?"
and is really a filter and a count in one. On `staff` they differ by one
because of a single CEO; on a real table with a 40%-nullable column they
differ enormously, and the report says neither which one it used nor why the
numbers do not tie out.

**Every other aggregate skips NULLs too.** `sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`
silently ignore them. This is usually right — the average of the salaries we
know is a more honest number than treating unknown as zero — but it means
`avg(x)` is the average over a denominator you did not specify and cannot
see. When it matters, say it: `avg(x)` versus `sum(x) / count(*)` versus
`avg(coalesce(x, 0))` are three different questions with three different
answers.

**Aggregates over zero rows.** `count` returns `0`. Everything else returns
`NULL`, not zero. So `sum(total)` over a `WHERE` clause that matched nothing
gives NULL, and a downstream `NULL * 1.2` gives NULL, and a dashboard shows
a blank instead of a zero. `coalesce(sum(total), 0)` is the standard fix,
and it is one of the few places where wrapping an aggregate in `coalesce` is
unambiguously right.

**`FILTER` scopes one aggregate without a second pass.**

```sql
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')      AS paid,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled
FROM orders;
```

One scan of 500,000 rows, two independent answers. The older idiom is
`sum(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`, which works identically
and reads worse; `FILTER` is standard SQL (since 2003) and PostgreSQL has
supported it since 9.4. Lesson 17 builds whole pivot tables out of this one
construct. Note the trap in the old idiom: `count(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 END)`
works only because the missing `ELSE` yields NULL and `count` skips NULLs —
write `ELSE 0` there and you count every row.

**`count(DISTINCT x)` is a different cost class.** `count(*)` can be
answered by incrementing a counter. `count(DISTINCT x)` requires remembering
every distinct value seen — a sort or a hash table proportional to the
cardinality. On high-cardinality columns over millions of rows this is
frequently the slowest part of a report, and it is the reason approximate
distinct counts (HyperLogLog, available in PostgreSQL through extensions)
exist at all.

**Where aggregation sits in a query.** Logically: `FROM` builds the row set,
`WHERE` filters rows, then aggregation folds them, then `HAVING` filters the
*groups*, then `SELECT` computes output, then `ORDER BY` sorts. That order
explains two rules that otherwise look arbitrary — you cannot use an
aggregate in `WHERE` (it has not happened yet), and you cannot use a SELECT
alias in `WHERE` (it does not exist yet). Lesson 07 makes the whole ladder
explicit.

## ex1 — the orders dashboard row

Five folds over the same 500,000 rows, computed in one pass. Check the
average against `docs/dataset_facts.md` — 1004.58. Anchoring an aggregate to
a known number is a habit worth keeping: it catches a wrong `WHERE` far
faster than reading the query again.

## ex2 — status counts with FILTER

Four scoped counts, one scan. The alternative — four separate queries — is
four scans of half a million rows, and the four answers can disagree with
each other if the data changes between them. Consistency, not just speed, is
an argument for doing it in one statement.

## ex3 — count(\*) is not count(column)

500 versus 499. Now imagine the column is `shipped_at` and the report is
titled "orders this month": `count(shipped_at)` quietly excludes every
unshipped order, the number looks reasonable, and nobody notices for a
quarter. The discipline is to ask, of every aggregate in a review, *what
does this do with NULLs?* — and if the answer is not instant, lesson 05 is
the reread.

## ex4 — counting distinct things

44,997 distinct customers behind 500,000 orders. Two things worth taking
away: the ratio (about eleven orders per buying customer) is a real business
metric that fell out of a `count(DISTINCT)`, and this query is
*significantly* more expensive than ex1 despite returning fewer numbers.
Cheap-looking SQL is not the same as cheap SQL.

## challenge — the all-hands KPI row

Four numbers from four tables in one row, via scalar subqueries. A scalar
subquery is a query in parentheses that returns exactly one row and one
column, and it can appear anywhere a value can. It is the right tool
precisely when the four numbers have *no join key* in common — you are not
relating them, just placing them side by side. Try to do it with joins and
you will produce a cross product or a wrong denominator; lesson 13 covers
the general case.

## review1 — average rating and review count

Two folds over a million rows. The average is 3.00 by construction — a
uniform distribution across the five ratings. When a real-world average
lands exactly on the midpoint, be suspicious: it usually means the data is
synthetic, or the column is not measuring what you think.

## Further reading

- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) — the complete list, including `bool_and`, `string_agg`, `array_agg`, and the ordered-set aggregates like `percentile_cont`.
- [Aggregate Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html) — the syntax page: where `DISTINCT`, `ORDER BY` and `FILTER` may appear inside an aggregate call.
- [`FILTER`](https://modern-sql.com/feature/filter) — Markus Winand on why `FILTER` replaced `sum(CASE ...)`, with the portability notes.
- [Query Evaluation Order](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the logical order of `FROM`/`WHERE`/`GROUP BY`/`HAVING`, which explains why aggregates cannot appear in `WHERE`.

# 06 — Aggregates

Every query so far returned one row per table row. But most business
questions are about *many* rows at once: how many orders? what's the
average total? what's our worst rating? Aggregate functions collapse a
whole set of rows into a single value — and with `FILTER`, several
differently-scoped answers can share one pass over the table.

## Concept

```sql
SELECT count(*), sum(total), round(avg(total), 2), min(total), max(total)
FROM orders;
```

- `count(*)` counts **rows**. `count(some_column)` counts rows where that
  column is **not NULL** — on `staff`, `count(*)` is 500 but
  `count(manager_id)` is 499, because the CEO's is NULL (lesson 05 pays
  off already). This distinction is a classic interview question and a
  classic production bug.
- `sum`/`avg`/`min`/`max` also skip NULLs.
- `avg` on our `numeric` columns returns long decimals — `round(avg(x), 2)`
  keeps reports readable.
- `FILTER (WHERE ...)` scopes one aggregate without a second query:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')      AS paid,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled
FROM orders;
```

One pass over 500,000 rows, two answers. (You may have seen the
`sum(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` idiom — FILTER is the modern,
readable form; lesson 17 uses both.)

With no `GROUP BY` (next lesson), an aggregate query returns **exactly one
row**, even over an empty table (`count` gives 0, the others NULL).

## Exercise 1 — the orders dashboard row

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. One row, five columns, in this order: the number
of orders, the smallest `total`, the largest `total`, the average `total`
rounded to 2 decimals, and the sum of all totals. From `orders`.

(Sanity anchor from `dataset_facts.md`: the average is 1004.58.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 06_aggregates ex1`

## Exercise 2 — status counts with FILTER

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. One row, four columns, in this order: how many
orders are `paid`, `pending`, `shipped`, `cancelled`. Use one query with
four filtered counts — not four queries.

Run: `uv run dojo test 06_aggregates ex2`

## Exercise 3 — count(*) is not count(column)

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. HR wants a one-row summary of the company. Five
columns, in this order:

1. the number of staff rows
2. the number of staff who **have** a manager
3. the average `salary`, rounded to 2 decimals
4. the highest `salary`
5. the earliest `hired_on` date

From `staff`. One row.

Columns 1 and 2 differ by exactly one, and the difference is the entire
point: `count(*)` counts **rows**, `count(manager_id)` counts **non-NULL
values of that column**. Both are spelled `count`. Neither warns you which
one you meant.

Run: `uv run dojo test 06_aggregates ex3`

## Exercise 4 — counting distinct things

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The weekly ops report needs three numbers about
`orders`, in this order:

1. how many orders there are
2. how many **distinct customers** placed them
3. how many **distinct statuses** appear

One row, three columns.

`count(DISTINCT col)` deduplicates before counting. It is the honest way to
answer "how many customers?" from a table of orders — and it is much more
expensive than `count(*)`, because PostgreSQL must remember every value it
has seen. You wrote the same question as `SELECT DISTINCT customer_id` back
in lesson 01; this collapses it to a single number.

Run: `uv run dojo test 06_aggregates ex4`

## Challenge — the all-hands KPI row (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Leadership wants one row with four numbers
pulled from *different tables*: total customers, total orders, revenue
from `paid` orders (sum of their totals), and the average review rating
rounded to 2 decimals.

You can't FROM four tables at once for this — the trick is *scalar
subqueries*, each one a parenthesized single-value query in the SELECT
list (a preview of lesson 13):

```sql
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM customers) AS customers, ...
```

Run: `uv run dojo test 06_aggregates challenge`

## Spaced review

`review1/`: one row, two columns from `reviews`: the average `rating`
rounded to 2 decimals, and the total number of reviews.

## The teaching point

`count(*)` vs `count(col)` has caused real revenue misreports: counting
`shipped_at` instead of rows silently drops unshipped orders from an "all
orders" metric. When you review aggregate SQL, ask about every aggregate:
*what does this do with NULLs?* If you can't answer instantly, lesson 05
is the reread.

# Reading - 06_aggregates

An aggregate is a *fold*: it consumes a set of rows and produces one value.
Everything surprising about aggregates follows from two details — what they
do with NULL, and the fact that the fold happens after `WHERE` and before
`SELECT`.

## Notes

**`count(*)` and `count(col)` are different functions wearing the same
name.** `count(*)` asks "how many rows are in this group?" and never
inspects a value. `count(col)` asks "how many rows have a non-NULL `col`?"
and is really a filter and a count in one. On `staff` they differ by one
because of a single CEO; on a real table with a 40%-nullable column they
differ enormously, and the report says neither which one it used nor why the
numbers do not tie out.

**Every other aggregate skips NULLs too.** `sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`
silently ignore them. This is usually right — the average of the salaries we
know is a more honest number than treating unknown as zero — but it means
`avg(x)` is the average over a denominator you did not specify and cannot
see. When it matters, say it: `avg(x)` versus `sum(x) / count(*)` versus
`avg(coalesce(x, 0))` are three different questions with three different
answers.

**Aggregates over zero rows.** `count` returns `0`. Everything else returns
`NULL`, not zero. So `sum(total)` over a `WHERE` clause that matched nothing
gives NULL, and a downstream `NULL * 1.2` gives NULL, and a dashboard shows
a blank instead of a zero. `coalesce(sum(total), 0)` is the standard fix,
and it is one of the few places where wrapping an aggregate in `coalesce` is
unambiguously right.

**`FILTER` scopes one aggregate without a second pass.**

```sql
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid')      AS paid,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled
FROM orders;
```

One scan of 500,000 rows, two independent answers. The older idiom is
`sum(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`, which works identically
and reads worse; `FILTER` is standard SQL (since 2003) and PostgreSQL has
supported it since 9.4. Lesson 17 builds whole pivot tables out of this one
construct. Note the trap in the old idiom: `count(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 END)`
works only because the missing `ELSE` yields NULL and `count` skips NULLs —
write `ELSE 0` there and you count every row.

**`count(DISTINCT x)` is a different cost class.** `count(*)` can be
answered by incrementing a counter. `count(DISTINCT x)` requires remembering
every distinct value seen — a sort or a hash table proportional to the
cardinality. On high-cardinality columns over millions of rows this is
frequently the slowest part of a report, and it is the reason approximate
distinct counts (HyperLogLog, available in PostgreSQL through extensions)
exist at all.

**Where aggregation sits in a query.** Logically: `FROM` builds the row set,
`WHERE` filters rows, then aggregation folds them, then `HAVING` filters the
*groups*, then `SELECT` computes output, then `ORDER BY` sorts. That order
explains two rules that otherwise look arbitrary — you cannot use an
aggregate in `WHERE` (it has not happened yet), and you cannot use a SELECT
alias in `WHERE` (it does not exist yet). Lesson 07 makes the whole ladder
explicit.

## ex1 — the orders dashboard row

Five folds over the same 500,000 rows, computed in one pass. Check the
average against `docs/dataset_facts.md` — 1004.58. Anchoring an aggregate to
a known number is a habit worth keeping: it catches a wrong `WHERE` far
faster than reading the query again.

## ex2 — status counts with FILTER

Four scoped counts, one scan. The alternative — four separate queries — is
four scans of half a million rows, and the four answers can disagree with
each other if the data changes between them. Consistency, not just speed, is
an argument for doing it in one statement.

## ex3 — count(\*) is not count(column)

500 versus 499. Now imagine the column is `shipped_at` and the report is
titled "orders this month": `count(shipped_at)` quietly excludes every
unshipped order, the number looks reasonable, and nobody notices for a
quarter. The discipline is to ask, of every aggregate in a review, *what
does this do with NULLs?* — and if the answer is not instant, lesson 05 is
the reread.

## ex4 — counting distinct things

44,997 distinct customers behind 500,000 orders. Two things worth taking
away: the ratio (about eleven orders per buying customer) is a real business
metric that fell out of a `count(DISTINCT)`, and this query is
*significantly* more expensive than ex1 despite returning fewer numbers.
Cheap-looking SQL is not the same as cheap SQL.

## challenge — the all-hands KPI row

Four numbers from four tables in one row, via scalar subqueries. A scalar
subquery is a query in parentheses that returns exactly one row and one
column, and it can appear anywhere a value can. It is the right tool
precisely when the four numbers have *no join key* in common — you are not
relating them, just placing them side by side. Try to do it with joins and
you will produce a cross product or a wrong denominator; lesson 13 covers
the general case.

## review1 — average rating and review count

Two folds over a million rows. The average is 3.00 by construction — a
uniform distribution across the five ratings. When a real-world average
lands exactly on the midpoint, be suspicious: it usually means the data is
synthetic, or the column is not measuring what you think.

## Further reading

- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) — the complete list, including `bool_and`, `string_agg`, `array_agg`, and the ordered-set aggregates like `percentile_cont`.
- [Aggregate Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html) — the syntax page: where `DISTINCT`, `ORDER BY` and `FILTER` may appear inside an aggregate call.
- [`FILTER`](https://modern-sql.com/feature/filter) — Markus Winand on why `FILTER` replaced `sum(CASE ...)`, with the portability notes.
- [Query Evaluation Order](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the logical order of `FROM`/`WHERE`/`GROUP BY`/`HAVING`, which explains why aggregates cannot appear in `WHERE`.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — the all-hands KPI row (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Leadership wants one row with four numbers
pulled from *different tables*: total customers, total orders, revenue
from `paid` orders (sum of their totals), and the average review rating
rounded to 2 decimals.

You can't FROM four tables at once for this — the trick is *scalar
subqueries*, each one a parenthesized single-value query in the SELECT
list (a preview of lesson 13):

```sql
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM customers) AS customers, ...
```

Run: `uv run dojo test 06_aggregates challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Each of the four values is a complete one-value query wrapped in
parentheses, sitting in the SELECT list. There is no FROM clause at the
outer level at all.

## Hint 2
```sql
SELECT
  (SELECT count(*) FROM customers),
  (SELECT count(*) FROM orders),
  (SELECT sum(total) FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid'),
  (SELECT ... FROM reviews);
```

The last one is the rounded average rating from ex-review territory.

## Hint 3
The fourth subquery is `(SELECT round(avg(rating), 2) FROM reviews)`.
Assemble all four.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Each of the four values is a complete one-value query wrapped in
parentheses, sitting in the SELECT list. There is no FROM clause at the
outer level at all.

## Hint 2
```sql
SELECT
  (SELECT count(*) FROM customers),
  (SELECT count(*) FROM orders),
  (SELECT sum(total) FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid'),
  (SELECT ... FROM reviews);
```

The last one is the rounded average rating from ex-review territory.

## Hint 3
The fourth subquery is `(SELECT round(avg(rating), 2) FROM reviews)`.
Assemble all four.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM customers)                        AS customers,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM orders)                           AS orders,
       (SELECT sum(total) FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid')   AS paid_revenue,
       (SELECT round(avg(rating), 2) FROM reviews)             AS avg_rating;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM customers),
       (SELECT count(*) FROM orders),
       (SELECT sum(total) FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid'),
       (SELECT round(avg(rating), 2) FROM reviews);

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — count(*) is not count(column)

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. HR wants a one-row summary of the company. Five
columns, in this order:

1. the number of staff rows
2. the number of staff who **have** a manager
3. the average `salary`, rounded to 2 decimals
4. the highest `salary`
5. the earliest `hired_on` date

From `staff`. One row.

Columns 1 and 2 differ by exactly one, and the difference is the entire
point: `count(*)` counts **rows**, `count(manager_id)` counts **non-NULL
values of that column**. Both are spelled `count`. Neither warns you which
one you meant.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — counting distinct things

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The weekly ops report needs three numbers about
`orders`, in this order:

1. how many orders there are
2. how many **distinct customers** placed them
3. how many **distinct statuses** appear

One row, three columns.

`count(DISTINCT col)` deduplicates before counting. It is the honest way to
answer "how many customers?" from a table of orders — and it is much more
expensive than `count(*)`, because PostgreSQL must remember every value it
has seen. You wrote the same question as `SELECT DISTINCT customer_id` back
in lesson 01; this collapses it to a single number.

Run: `uv run dojo test 06_aggregates ex4`

lessons.briefing:
# 07 — GROUP BY and HAVING

Lesson 06 collapsed 500,000 orders into one row. Business questions are
usually one step subtler: one number **per something** — revenue per
status, orders per customer, products per category. `GROUP BY` partitions
rows into groups and runs your aggregates once per group.

## Concept

```sql
SELECT status, count(*), sum(total)
FROM orders
GROUP BY status;
```

Four groups in, four rows out (per `dataset_facts.md`: paid is by far the
biggest at ~250k orders — the seed weights it 3-in-6).

**The grouping rule** — internalize this and half your future error
messages disappear: *every column in the SELECT list must either appear in
GROUP BY or sit inside an aggregate.* Postgres enforces it because a group
of many rows has no single value for an ungrouped column. If you see
`column "x" must appear in the GROUP BY clause...`, that's this rule.

Filtering happens at two distinct moments:

- `WHERE` filters **rows, before grouping** — cheap, do it here when you can.
- `HAVING` filters **groups, after aggregation** — the only place that can
  see `count(*)`.

```sql
SELECT customer_id, count(*)
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
```
