# Reading - 07_group_by_having

`GROUP BY` is the clause that turns a table into a report. It is also where
SQL's evaluation order stops being an academic diagram and starts producing
error messages you have to understand to get past.

## Notes

**The grouping rule, and why it exists.** Every column in the SELECT list
must either appear in `GROUP BY` or sit inside an aggregate. This is not
pedantry: after grouping, a row *is* a group of many original rows, and an
ungrouped column has many values there. There is no sensible answer to
"which name?" so PostgreSQL refuses to invent one. (MySQL historically did
invent one, silently, which produced a decade of wrong reports. Standard SQL
and PostgreSQL make it an error.)

There is one principled exception: if you group by a table's primary key,
PostgreSQL knows every other column of that table is functionally dependent
on it and lets you select them ungrouped. `GROUP BY c.id` therefore permits
`c.name` in the SELECT list — legal, useful, and it surprises people.

**`WHERE` before, `HAVING` after.** The logical order is `FROM` → `WHERE` →
`GROUP BY` → aggregates → `HAVING` → `SELECT` → `ORDER BY` → `LIMIT`. So:

- `WHERE` cannot see aggregates (they have not been computed).
- `HAVING` can, and is the only place a `count(*) > 20` filter can go.
- `SELECT` aliases are invented after `WHERE` and `HAVING`, which is why you
  cannot filter on an alias — but `ORDER BY` and `GROUP BY`, which come
  later or are special-cased, *can* see them in PostgreSQL.

**The performance version of the same rule.** A condition that filters *rows*
belongs in `WHERE`, always. Writing `GROUP BY customer_id HAVING status =
'paid'` is not just stylistically wrong — it is illegal here, and where a
variant of it is legal it means aggregating the whole table and discarding
most of the work afterwards. In Part 5 you will read plans where this is
visible as the row count flowing between nodes: the earlier a filter appears
in the plan, the less work everything above it does.

**Grouping by an expression.** `GROUP BY date_trunc('month', created_at)`
groups by a computed value, and the same expression must appear in the
SELECT list for you to see it. This is how every "per month" report in
existence is built. Two practical notes: PostgreSQL lets you write `GROUP BY
1` (the first SELECT-list item) or `GROUP BY tier` (an output alias) as
shorthands — convenient, and the ordinal form is genuinely error-prone when
someone reorders the SELECT list later. And a `GROUP BY` on an expression
cannot use an ordinary index on the underlying column, which is what
expression indexes (lesson 40) are for.

**Groups you cannot see.** `GROUP BY` produces one row per group *that has
at least one row*. A month with no orders does not appear as zero — it
simply does not appear, and a chart drawn from that result silently skips
it. The fix is to generate the full set of periods (`generate_series`) and
`LEFT JOIN` the aggregate onto it, which is a lesson 09 + lesson 18 combination.

**How PostgreSQL actually groups.** Two strategies: `HashAggregate` builds a
hash table keyed by the grouping columns, and `GroupAggregate` requires the
input sorted by the grouping key and walks it. The planner picks based on
estimated group count and `work_mem`. You will see both node types in Part
5, and a `GroupAggregate` fed by an already-sorted index scan is one of the
cheapest shapes in the system.

## ex1 — revenue per status

Four groups, half a million rows. Compare the `paid` row against
`docs/dataset_facts.md` (250,472 orders) — the habit of tying an aggregate
back to a known count is what catches a mis-typed `WHERE` in ten seconds
instead of a week.

There is also a free consistency check available here: the four counts must
sum to 500,000. Whenever a `GROUP BY` partitions a table with no `WHERE`
clause, the group counts have to add up to the row count, and when they do
not it is because a grouping key was NULL and you did not expect it. Adding
up the parts is the cheapest audit in reporting.

## ex2 — the heavy buyers

`HAVING count(*) > 20` is the exercise, and it is worth noticing that this
is not expressible any other way in a single query without a subquery. The
average customer here has about eleven orders, so >20 is a genuine outlier
segment — the shape of nearly every "power user" query you will ever write.

## ex3 — filter the rows, then group them

The `WHERE`/`HAVING` decision made concrete. Try moving `price > 100` into
`HAVING` in the lab: PostgreSQL rejects it, because `price` is neither
grouped nor aggregated. That error message is the grouping rule protecting
you. (`HAVING avg(price) > 100` *is* legal and asks a completely different
question — the average of the group, not the price of a product.)

## ex4 — grouping by an expression

Two grouping keys, one of them computed. Two things to take from it: the
same expression appears in the SELECT list and the `GROUP BY` (or the alias
does), and the result is a small cross-tab that is *tall* — one row per
combination. Lesson 17 turns a result of exactly this shape sideways into
columns, which is what a human actually wants to look at. Lesson 50 shows
how to get subtotals per category and a grand total in the same pass.

## challenge — monthly revenue

`date_trunc('month', created_at)` maps every timestamp in a month to the
month's first instant, so grouping by it groups by month. Thirteen rows,
because the data spans 2022-11-14 to 2023-11-14 — two partial months at the
ends. Partial periods at the boundaries of a time series are a permanent
feature of real reporting, and reports that do not label them mislead people
who read the first and last bars of the chart.

## review1 — products per category

The simplest possible `GROUP BY`, brought back deliberately. When it
reappears, write it without looking, then check the six category counts
against `docs/dataset_facts.md`.

Two questions to ask yourself while it runs. Do the six counts sum to
10,000? And would a seventh category with zero products appear in this
result? (No — `GROUP BY` invents nothing, so a category with no rows simply
does not exist as far as this query is concerned. That is the gap you have
to fill with a lookup table and a `LEFT JOIN` when the categories are a
fixed list that must always be shown.)

## Further reading

- [`GROUP BY` and `HAVING`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the "Table Expressions" chapter, sections 7.2.3 and 7.2.4. Read the functional-dependency paragraph about grouping by a primary key.
- [`SELECT` — the `GROUP BY` clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — including `GROUP BY` ordinals, output aliases, and a first look at `GROUPING SETS` (lesson 50).
- [`date_trunc` and date/time functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) — the toolkit behind every per-period report. Preview of lesson 18.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Grouping](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/sorting-grouping) — how an index can turn a hash aggregate into a pipelined group aggregate, and why that matters for `LIMIT`.

# 07 — GROUP BY and HAVING

Lesson 06 collapsed 500,000 orders into one row. Business questions are
usually one step subtler: one number **per something** — revenue per
status, orders per customer, products per category. `GROUP BY` partitions
rows into groups and runs your aggregates once per group.

## Concept

```sql
SELECT status, count(*), sum(total)
FROM orders
GROUP BY status;
```

Four groups in, four rows out (per `dataset_facts.md`: paid is by far the
biggest at ~250k orders — the seed weights it 3-in-6).

**The grouping rule** — internalize this and half your future error
messages disappear: *every column in the SELECT list must either appear in
GROUP BY or sit inside an aggregate.* Postgres enforces it because a group
of many rows has no single value for an ungrouped column. If you see
`column "x" must appear in the GROUP BY clause...`, that's this rule.

Filtering happens at two distinct moments:

- `WHERE` filters **rows, before grouping** — cheap, do it here when you can.
- `HAVING` filters **groups, after aggregation** — the only place that can
  see `count(*)`.

```sql
SELECT customer_id, count(*)
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING count(*) > 20;
```

You can also group by an expression (`GROUP BY date_trunc('month',
created_at)`) — the challenge does exactly that.

# Reading - 07_group_by_having

`GROUP BY` is the clause that turns a table into a report. It is also where
SQL's evaluation order stops being an academic diagram and starts producing
error messages you have to understand to get past.

## Notes

**The grouping rule, and why it exists.** Every column in the SELECT list
must either appear in `GROUP BY` or sit inside an aggregate. This is not
pedantry: after grouping, a row *is* a group of many original rows, and an
ungrouped column has many values there. There is no sensible answer to
"which name?" so PostgreSQL refuses to invent one. (MySQL historically did
invent one, silently, which produced a decade of wrong reports. Standard SQL
and PostgreSQL make it an error.)

There is one principled exception: if you group by a table's primary key,
PostgreSQL knows every other column of that table is functionally dependent
on it and lets you select them ungrouped. `GROUP BY c.id` therefore permits
`c.name` in the SELECT list — legal, useful, and it surprises people.

**`WHERE` before, `HAVING` after.** The logical order is `FROM` → `WHERE` →
`GROUP BY` → aggregates → `HAVING` → `SELECT` → `ORDER BY` → `LIMIT`. So:

- `WHERE` cannot see aggregates (they have not been computed).
- `HAVING` can, and is the only place a `count(*) > 20` filter can go.
- `SELECT` aliases are invented after `WHERE` and `HAVING`, which is why you
  cannot filter on an alias — but `ORDER BY` and `GROUP BY`, which come
  later or are special-cased, *can* see them in PostgreSQL.

**The performance version of the same rule.** A condition that filters *rows*
belongs in `WHERE`, always. Writing `GROUP BY customer_id HAVING status =
'paid'` is not just stylistically wrong — it is illegal here, and where a
variant of it is legal it means aggregating the whole table and discarding
most of the work afterwards. In Part 5 you will read plans where this is
visible as the row count flowing between nodes: the earlier a filter appears
in the plan, the less work everything above it does.

**Grouping by an expression.** `GROUP BY date_trunc('month', created_at)`
groups by a computed value, and the same expression must appear in the
SELECT list for you to see it. This is how every "per month" report in
existence is built. Two practical notes: PostgreSQL lets you write `GROUP BY
1` (the first SELECT-list item) or `GROUP BY tier` (an output alias) as
shorthands — convenient, and the ordinal form is genuinely error-prone when
someone reorders the SELECT list later. And a `GROUP BY` on an expression
cannot use an ordinary index on the underlying column, which is what
expression indexes (lesson 40) are for.

**Groups you cannot see.** `GROUP BY` produces one row per group *that has
at least one row*. A month with no orders does not appear as zero — it
simply does not appear, and a chart drawn from that result silently skips
it. The fix is to generate the full set of periods (`generate_series`) and
`LEFT JOIN` the aggregate onto it, which is a lesson 09 + lesson 18 combination.

**How PostgreSQL actually groups.** Two strategies: `HashAggregate` builds a
hash table keyed by the grouping columns, and `GroupAggregate` requires the
input sorted by the grouping key and walks it. The planner picks based on
estimated group count and `work_mem`. You will see both node types in Part
5, and a `GroupAggregate` fed by an already-sorted index scan is one of the
cheapest shapes in the system.

## ex1 — revenue per status

Four groups, half a million rows. Compare the `paid` row against
`docs/dataset_facts.md` (250,472 orders) — the habit of tying an aggregate
back to a known count is what catches a mis-typed `WHERE` in ten seconds
instead of a week.

There is also a free consistency check available here: the four counts must
sum to 500,000. Whenever a `GROUP BY` partitions a table with no `WHERE`
clause, the group counts have to add up to the row count, and when they do
not it is because a grouping key was NULL and you did not expect it. Adding
up the parts is the cheapest audit in reporting.

## ex2 — the heavy buyers

`HAVING count(*) > 20` is the exercise, and it is worth noticing that this
is not expressible any other way in a single query without a subquery. The
average customer here has about eleven orders, so >20 is a genuine outlier
segment — the shape of nearly every "power user" query you will ever write.

## ex3 — filter the rows, then group them

The `WHERE`/`HAVING` decision made concrete. Try moving `price > 100` into
`HAVING` in the lab: PostgreSQL rejects it, because `price` is neither
grouped nor aggregated. That error message is the grouping rule protecting
you. (`HAVING avg(price) > 100` *is* legal and asks a completely different
question — the average of the group, not the price of a product.)

## ex4 — grouping by an expression

Two grouping keys, one of them computed. Two things to take from it: the
same expression appears in the SELECT list and the `GROUP BY` (or the alias
does), and the result is a small cross-tab that is *tall* — one row per
combination. Lesson 17 turns a result of exactly this shape sideways into
columns, which is what a human actually wants to look at. Lesson 50 shows
how to get subtotals per category and a grand total in the same pass.

## challenge — monthly revenue

`date_trunc('month', created_at)` maps every timestamp in a month to the
month's first instant, so grouping by it groups by month. Thirteen rows,
because the data spans 2022-11-14 to 2023-11-14 — two partial months at the
ends. Partial periods at the boundaries of a time series are a permanent
feature of real reporting, and reports that do not label them mislead people
who read the first and last bars of the chart.

## review1 — products per category

The simplest possible `GROUP BY`, brought back deliberately. When it
reappears, write it without looking, then check the six category counts
against `docs/dataset_facts.md`.

Two questions to ask yourself while it runs. Do the six counts sum to
10,000? And would a seventh category with zero products appear in this
result? (No — `GROUP BY` invents nothing, so a category with no rows simply
does not exist as far as this query is concerned. That is the gap you have
to fill with a lookup table and a `LEFT JOIN` when the categories are a
fixed list that must always be shown.)

## Further reading

- [`GROUP BY` and `HAVING`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the "Table Expressions" chapter, sections 7.2.3 and 7.2.4. Read the functional-dependency paragraph about grouping by a primary key.
- [`SELECT` — the `GROUP BY` clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — including `GROUP BY` ordinals, output aliases, and a first look at `GROUPING SETS` (lesson 50).
- [`date_trunc` and date/time functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) — the toolkit behind every per-period report. Preview of lesson 18.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Grouping](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/sorting-grouping) — how an index can turn a hash aggregate into a pipelined group aggregate, and why that matters for `LIMIT`.

## Hint 1
The group key is an expression, not a column: truncate `created_at` to the
month. The same expression appears in the SELECT list and the GROUP BY.

```sql
SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month, sum(total) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY date_trunc('month', created_at)
ORDER BY month;
```

(You may write `GROUP BY 1` or repeat the expression — both work; ORDER BY
can use the alias.)

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The group key is an expression, not a column: truncate `created_at` to the
month. The same expression appears in the SELECT list and the GROUP BY.

## Hint 2
```sql
SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month, sum(total) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY date_trunc('month', created_at)
ORDER BY month;
```

(You may write `GROUP BY 1` or repeat the expression — both work; ORDER BY
can use the alias.)

references.solution.sql:
SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month,
       sum(total) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY date_trunc('month', created_at)
ORDER BY month;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at), sum(total)
FROM orders GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — filter the rows, then group them

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Merchandising wants a summary of the **premium end
of the catalogue only**: considering just the products priced **above
100**, return per `category` the category name, how many such products
there are, and their average price rounded to 2 decimals.

Three columns in that order, six rows, any order.

The price filter is about individual products, so it belongs in `WHERE` —
before grouping, where it throws rows away cheaply. Put it in `HAVING`
instead and PostgreSQL will refuse (`price` is not grouped), which is the
error message doing you a favour.

Run: `uv run dojo test 07_group_by_having ex3`

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — grouping by an expression

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Combine lesson 04's `CASE` with this lesson's
`GROUP BY`. For every combination of **category** and **price tier**,
return the category, the tier, and how many products fall in it.

The tiers are the same three as lesson 04: `'budget'` under 50, `'mid'`
from 50 up to but not including 200, `'premium'` at 200 and above.

Three columns in this order: `category`, the tier aliased **`tier`**,
`count(*)`. Any row order. (Six categories times three tiers — expect 18
rows.)

You can group by the expression itself, or — a PostgreSQL convenience — by
the output alias `tier`. Both work; the first is portable, the second is
readable.

Run: `uv run dojo test 07_group_by_having ex4`

lessons.briefing:
# 08 — INNER JOIN

`orders` knows a `customer_id`; it does not know the customer's name. The
name lives 500,000 row-lookups away in `customers`. A relational database
is *designed* around this separation — each fact stored once — and `JOIN`
is how you reassemble facts at query time. This is the single most
important lesson in Part 1.

## Concept

```sql
SELECT o.id, c.name, o.total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.total > 1990;
```

Read it as: for each row of `orders`, find the `customers` rows where the
ON condition holds, and emit one combined row per match. Details that
matter:

- `o` and `c` are **table aliases**. With two tables in play, every column
  reference should be qualified — `id` alone is now ambiguous and Postgres
  will say so.
- `JOIN` means `INNER JOIN`: rows with **no match are dropped**. An order
  whose customer vanished (impossible here, thanks to the FK) would
  silently disappear. Lesson 09 is about *keeping* such rows.
- The **ON clause is the join key**; the WHERE clause is your filter.
  Mixing them up works for INNER joins but becomes a real bug with OUTER
  ones — build the right habit now.
- Joins chain: orders → order_items → products walks two relationships in
  one query.
- Join then group: after joining line-items to products you can `GROUP BY
  p.category` and sum revenue — join and aggregation compose freely.

A wrong-ON join doesn't error — it either loses rows or multiplies them
(the dreaded accidental cross join: 500,000 × 50,000 rows). If a join
returns a suspicious row count, the ON clause is the first suspect.

## Exercise 1 — orders with names

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. The 2,569 orders with `total > 1990`, each with
its customer's name. Columns in order: `id` (the order's), `name`,
`total`. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 08_inner_joins ex1`

## Exercise 2 — a receipt, three tables

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Print the line items of **order 123**: for each
item, the product's `name`, the item's `quantity`, and the item's `price`.
Route: `orders` → `order_items` (on order id) → `products` (on product
id). Three columns, three rows, any order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 08_inner_joins ex2`

## Exercise 3 — revenue per category

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Which product categories make the money? Join
`order_items` to `products` and return each `category` with its revenue —
the sum of `quantity * price` (the *item's* price: it's the historical
snapshot; product prices can change). Two columns, six rows, any order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 08_inner_joins ex3`

## Exercise 4 — reputation per category

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Which categories do customers actually *like*?
Join `reviews` to `products` and return, per category, the category name,
the average `rating` rounded to 2 decimals, and the number of reviews.

Three columns in that order, six rows, any order.

Same shape as exercise 3 — join, then group by a column of the *other*
table — on a different pair of tables. The join key is
`reviews.product_id = products.id`; get into the habit of writing the ON
clause before anything else in the query.

Run: `uv run dojo test 08_inner_joins ex4`

## Exercise 5 — filtering across the join

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. The returns team is auditing **bulk purchases of
expensive electronics**: every order line whose product is in the
`electronics` category, where the line's `quantity` is exactly 5 **and**
the line's `price` is above 480.

Columns, in this order: the line's `id`, the product's `name`, the line's
`quantity`, the line's `price`. Any row order.

Two of those conditions are about `order_items` and one is about
`products`, but all three go in the `WHERE` clause — for an **inner** join
it makes no difference where a filter lives. Remember that sentence,
because lesson 09 is about the case where it stops being true.

Run: `uv run dojo test 08_inner_joins ex5`

## Exercise 6 — revenue by country

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. The board wants revenue by market. Join `orders`
to `customers` and return, per `country`, the country code and the sum of
the orders' `total`.

Two columns in that order, twelve rows, any order.

Half a million orders joined to fifty thousand customers and folded into
twelve numbers. Run `dojo plan 08_inner_joins ex6` when it passes and look
at what PostgreSQL chose: almost certainly a **Hash Join** — it builds a
hash table of the smaller table (`customers`) and streams the larger one
past it. Lesson 37 explains when it picks that over the alternatives.

Run: `uv run dojo test 08_inner_joins ex6`

## Challenge — the five-table drill-down (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Customer service pulled up **customer
4242** and wants their purchase history with product reputation attached:
for every (order, product) pair this customer ever bought, return the
order `id`, the product `name`, the total units of that product in that
order (`sum(quantity)` — a product *can* appear on two lines of one
order), and the product's average review rating rounded to 1 decimal.

Tables: `customers`, `orders`, `order_items`, `products`, `reviews`.
Group by order id and product name. Columns: `order_id`, `product`,
`units`, `avg_rating`. Any order. (12 rows.)

Grain warning, and why this works: joining `reviews` multiplies each item
row by that product's ~100 reviews — but `avg(r.rating)` inside a group
that spans exactly one product still averages that product's reviews.
`sum(quantity)` would be inflated 100× though! The fix: `sum(DISTINCT
oi.id)`-style tricks are fragile; the honest fix is aggregating quantity
*before* the review join (subqueries, lesson 13) — here, since each
(order, product) group has one line item in practice for this customer,
`min(oi.quantity)`-style dodges also work. Simplest correct trick that
passes: use `avg(oi.quantity)::int` — every duplicated row carries the
same quantity, and the average of n copies of q is q. The hints walk
through it; the teaching point is *noticing* the grain problem at all.

Run: `uv run dojo test 08_inner_joins challenge`

## Spaced review

`review1/`: every order over 1950 placed by a customer in `'PH'`:
columns `name`, `id` (order), `total`, any order.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 08_inner_joins

A relational database stores each fact once and reassembles facts on demand.
`JOIN` is the reassembly. Everything else in Part 1 was preparation for this
lesson, and every difficult query in Parts 2 and 5 is a join wearing a
costume.

## Notes

**A join is a filtered cross product, conceptually.** Take every pairing of
a left row with a right row, keep the pairs where the `ON` condition is
true. No database actually does that — it uses a nested loop, a hash table,
or a merge of two sorted streams (lesson 37) — but the mental model is
exactly right for reasoning about *results*. It also explains the classic
disaster: omit the `ON` condition and you get all 500,000 × 50,000 pairs,
which is not an error, just twenty-five billion rows.

**Cardinality — "the grain" — is the question to ask first.** Before you
write a join, know whether the relationship is one-to-one, one-to-many, or
many-to-many, because it determines the number of rows that come out.
Joining `orders` to `customers` is many-to-one: the row count stays 500,000.
Joining `orders` to `order_items` is one-to-many: the row count *doubles* to
a million, and every `orders` column is now duplicated across its lines.
That duplication is harmless until you aggregate — and then
`sum(o.total)` counts each order once per line item and your revenue figure
is wrong by exactly the average basket size. Production dashboards have
shipped numbers inflated 100× for precisely this reason. The fix is to
aggregate before joining (a subquery or CTE — lessons 13 and 14) or to
aggregate something that is not duplicated.

**`ON` versus `WHERE`.** For an inner join they are interchangeable — the
planner may even move conditions between them. Build the habit anyway:
`ON` expresses *how the tables relate*, `WHERE` expresses *which rows you
want*. Lesson 09 is where the distinction stops being stylistic and starts
changing the answer.

**Qualify every column.** With two tables in scope, a bare `id` is
ambiguous, and PostgreSQL will tell you so. With three, an unqualified
column that happens to be unique today becomes an error the day someone adds
a column with that name elsewhere. Alias every table, qualify every column;
it costs two characters and makes the query readable by someone who does not
know the schema.

**`USING` and `NATURAL JOIN`.** `JOIN order_items USING (order_id)` is a
shorthand when both columns have the same name, and it merges them into one
output column. `NATURAL JOIN` guesses the join key from *every* commonly
named column — including `id` and `created_at`, which is why it is a
footgun and why you will not see it in this course. Explicit `ON` clauses
never surprise anyone.

**Joins compose freely with everything else.** Join then filter, join then
group, join three tables then group by a column of the second — the query is
built by composing clauses whose meanings do not change. That
compositionality is the actual reason SQL survived fifty years.

## ex1 — orders with names

The canonical many-to-one join. 2,569 rows out of 500,000, each carrying a
name that lives in another table. Note that the result count equals the
number of matching *orders* — because every order has exactly one customer,
guaranteed by the foreign key.

## ex2 — a receipt, three tables

Joins chain: `orders` → `order_items` → `products`. Read the FROM clause as
a path through the schema diagram in [docs/dataset.md](../../docs/dataset.md).
Once you see joins as walking edges of a graph, five-table queries stop
being intimidating.

Notice that `orders` contributes no columns to the output — it is there
purely to be filtered on. That is completely normal and worth being
comfortable with: a table can appear in a join because it holds the
condition, because it holds the output, or because it is a bridge between
two tables that do not reference each other directly. `order_items` here is
all three at once.

## ex3 — revenue per category

Join then group, and the first place the *grain* matters in your favour:
`sum(quantity * price)` uses the line item's own price — the historical
snapshot — not the product's current price. Using `p.price` here would
silently rewrite history every time someone edited the catalogue. Storing
the price at order time is a deliberate schema decision, and lesson 26 comes
back to why.

## ex4 — reputation per category

The same shape as ex3 on a different pair of tables. Reps like this are what
make the pattern automatic: identify the two tables, write the ON, decide
the grouping column, choose the aggregates. Note the averages come out near
3.00 in every category — uniform synthetic data — which is a good reminder
that a join and a group can be perfectly correct and still tell you nothing
interesting.

## ex5 — filtering across the join

Three filters spanning two tables, all in `WHERE`. This is the exercise to
remember when lesson 09 tells you that moving one of them into `ON` changes
the answer. For an inner join, `ON` and `WHERE` are algebraically the same;
for an outer join they are not, and the difference has cost people months of
wrong dashboards.

## ex6 — revenue by country

The plan is the interesting part. Half a million rows meet fifty thousand,
and PostgreSQL builds a hash table on the smaller side — you can see it in
`dojo plan` as `Hash Join` with a `Hash` node under it. Lesson 37 covers why
it chose that over a nested loop (no index on `orders.customer_id`, and it
needs every row anyway) and what would change its mind.

## challenge — the five-table drill-down

The grain problem, weaponised. Joining `reviews` multiplies every order line
by roughly a hundred, so `sum(quantity)` is inflated a hundredfold while
`avg(rating)` is unaffected — because averaging a hundred copies of the same
set of ratings gives the same answer. The `avg(oi.quantity)::int` dodge works
for the same reason, and it is a dodge: the honest fix is to aggregate the
line items before joining the reviews. The point of the exercise is not the
trick, it is *noticing that there is a problem to solve*.

## review1 — big orders from one country

A two-table join with filters on both sides. When it returns, ask yourself
the grain question out loud before you look at the row count.

The answer, for this one: `orders` to `customers` is many-to-one, so the
result has exactly one row per qualifying order and no order is duplicated.
That is the property that would make `sum(o.total)` safe here — and the
property that evaporates the moment somebody adds a join to `order_items`
"just to get the product names". Every added join is a fresh cardinality
question.

## Further reading

- [Joined Tables](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the definitive description of `INNER`/`LEFT`/`RIGHT`/`FULL`, `ON`, `USING`, and `NATURAL`.
- [`SELECT` — FROM clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — table aliases and how they scope column references.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Joins](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/join) — nested loops, hash joins and sort-merge joins explained from the index outward. This is the best single preparation for lesson 37.
- [Don't Do This — `NATURAL JOIN`](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) — why guessing the join key is a bad idea in a schema that will change.

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Which product categories make the money? Join
`order_items` to `products` and return each `category` with its revenue —
the sum of `quantity * price` (the *item's* price: it's the historical
snapshot; product prices can change). Two columns, six rows, any order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 08_inner_joins ex3`

## Exercise 4 — reputation per category

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Which categories do customers actually *like*?
Join `reviews` to `products` and return, per category, the category name,
the average `rating` rounded to 2 decimals, and the number of reviews.

Three columns in that order, six rows, any order.

Same shape as exercise 3 — join, then group by a column of the *other*
table — on a different pair of tables. The join key is
`reviews.product_id = products.id`; get into the habit of writing the ON
clause before anything else in the query.

Run: `uv run dojo test 08_inner_joins ex4`

## Exercise 5 — filtering across the join

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. The returns team is auditing **bulk purchases of
expensive electronics**: every order line whose product is in the
`electronics` category, where the line's `quantity` is exactly 5 **and**
the line's `price` is above 480.

Columns, in this order: the line's `id`, the product's `name`, the line's
`quantity`, the line's `price`. Any row order.

Two of those conditions are about `order_items` and one is about
`products`, but all three go in the `WHERE` clause — for an **inner** join
it makes no difference where a filter lives. Remember that sentence,
because lesson 09 is about the case where it stops being true.

Run: `uv run dojo test 08_inner_joins ex5`

## Exercise 6 — revenue by country

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. The board wants revenue by market. Join `orders`
to `customers` and return, per `country`, the country code and the sum of
the orders' `total`.

Two columns in that order, twelve rows, any order.

Half a million orders joined to fifty thousand customers and folded into
twelve numbers. Run `dojo plan 08_inner_joins ex6` when it passes and look
at what PostgreSQL chose: almost certainly a **Hash Join** — it builds a
hash table of the smaller table (`customers`) and streams the larger one
past it. Lesson 37 explains when it picks that over the alternatives.

Run: `uv run dojo test 08_inner_joins ex6`

## Challenge — the five-table drill-down (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Customer service pulled up **customer
4242** and wants their purchase history with product reputation attached:
for every (order, product) pair this customer ever bought, return the
order `id`, the product `name`, the total units of that product in that
order (`sum(quantity)` — a product *can* appear on two lines of one
order), and the product's average review rating rounded to 1 decimal.

Tables: `customers`, `orders`, `order_items`, `products`, `reviews`.
Group by order id and product name. Columns: `order_id`, `product`,
`units`, `avg_rating`. Any order. (12 rows.)

Grain warning, and why this works: joining `reviews` multiplies each item
row by that product's ~100 reviews — but `avg(r.rating)` inside a group
that spans exactly one product still averages that product's reviews.
`sum(quantity)` would be inflated 100× though! The fix: `sum(DISTINCT
oi.id)`-style tricks are fragile; the honest fix is aggregating quantity
*before* the review join (subqueries, lesson 13) — here, since each
(order, product) group has one line item in practice for this customer,
`min(oi.quantity)`-style dodges also work. Simplest correct trick that
passes: use `avg(oi.quantity)::int` — every duplicated row carries the
same quantity, and the average of n copies of q is q. The hints walk
through it; the teaching point is *noticing* the grain problem at all.

Run: `uv run dojo test 08_inner_joins challenge`

`review1/`: every order over 1950 placed by a customer in `'PH'`:
columns `name`, `id` (order), `total`, any order.

## The teaching point

In code review, the first question about any JOIN is "what's the
cardinality?" — one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many? The challenge just
showed you why: aggregates over a fanned-out join silently inflate.
Production dashboards have shipped 100× revenue numbers for exactly this
reason. Know the grain of every joined row set before you aggregate it.

# Reading - 08_inner_joins

A relational database stores each fact once and reassembles facts on demand.
`JOIN` is the reassembly. Everything else in Part 1 was preparation for this
lesson, and every difficult query in Parts 2 and 5 is a join wearing a
costume.

## Notes

**A join is a filtered cross product, conceptually.** Take every pairing of
a left row with a right row, keep the pairs where the `ON` condition is
true. No database actually does that — it uses a nested loop, a hash table,
or a merge of two sorted streams (lesson 37) — but the mental model is
exactly right for reasoning about *results*. It also explains the classic
disaster: omit the `ON` condition and you get all 500,000 × 50,000 pairs,
which is not an error, just twenty-five billion rows.

**Cardinality — "the grain" — is the question to ask first.** Before you
write a join, know whether the relationship is one-to-one, one-to-many, or
many-to-many, because it determines the number of rows that come out.
Joining `orders` to `customers` is many-to-one: the row count stays 500,000.
Joining `orders` to `order_items` is one-to-many: the row count *doubles* to
a million, and every `orders` column is now duplicated across its lines.
That duplication is harmless until you aggregate — and then
`sum(o.total)` counts each order once per line item and your revenue figure
is wrong by exactly the average basket size. Production dashboards have
shipped numbers inflated 100× for precisely this reason. The fix is to
aggregate before joining (a subquery or CTE — lessons 13 and 14) or to
aggregate something that is not duplicated.

**`ON` versus `WHERE`.** For an inner join they are interchangeable — the
planner may even move conditions between them. Build the habit anyway:
`ON` expresses *how the tables relate*, `WHERE` expresses *which rows you
want*. Lesson 09 is where the distinction stops being stylistic and starts
changing the answer.

**Qualify every column.** With two tables in scope, a bare `id` is
ambiguous, and PostgreSQL will tell you so. With three, an unqualified
column that happens to be unique today becomes an error the day someone adds
a column with that name elsewhere. Alias every table, qualify every column;
it costs two characters and makes the query readable by someone who does not
know the schema.

**`USING` and `NATURAL JOIN`.** `JOIN order_items USING (order_id)` is a
shorthand when both columns have the same name, and it merges them into one
output column. `NATURAL JOIN` guesses the join key from *every* commonly
named column — including `id` and `created_at`, which is why it is a
footgun and why you will not see it in this course. Explicit `ON` clauses
never surprise anyone.

**Joins compose freely with everything else.** Join then filter, join then
group, join three tables then group by a column of the second — the query is
built by composing clauses whose meanings do not change. That
compositionality is the actual reason SQL survived fifty years.

## ex1 — orders with names

The canonical many-to-one join. 2,569 rows out of 500,000, each carrying a
name that lives in another table. Note that the result count equals the
number of matching *orders* — because every order has exactly one customer,
guaranteed by the foreign key.

## ex2 — a receipt, three tables

Joins chain: `orders` → `order_items` → `products`. Read the FROM clause as
a path through the schema diagram in [docs/dataset.md](../../docs/dataset.md).
Once you see joins as walking edges of a graph, five-table queries stop
being intimidating.

Notice that `orders` contributes no columns to the output — it is there
purely to be filtered on. That is completely normal and worth being
comfortable with: a table can appear in a join because it holds the
condition, because it holds the output, or because it is a bridge between
two tables that do not reference each other directly. `order_items` here is
all three at once.

## ex3 — revenue per category

Join then group, and the first place the *grain* matters in your favour:
`sum(quantity * price)` uses the line item's own price — the historical
snapshot — not the product's current price. Using `p.price` here would
silently rewrite history every time someone edited the catalogue. Storing
the price at order time is a deliberate schema decision, and lesson 26 comes
back to why.

## ex4 — reputation per category

The same shape as ex3 on a different pair of tables. Reps like this are what
make the pattern automatic: identify the two tables, write the ON, decide
the grouping column, choose the aggregates. Note the averages come out near
3.00 in every category — uniform synthetic data — which is a good reminder
that a join and a group can be perfectly correct and still tell you nothing
interesting.

## ex5 — filtering across the join

Three filters spanning two tables, all in `WHERE`. This is the exercise to
remember when lesson 09 tells you that moving one of them into `ON` changes
the answer. For an inner join, `ON` and `WHERE` are algebraically the same;
for an outer join they are not, and the difference has cost people months of
wrong dashboards.

## ex6 — revenue by country

The plan is the interesting part. Half a million rows meet fifty thousand,
and PostgreSQL builds a hash table on the smaller side — you can see it in
`dojo plan` as `Hash Join` with a `Hash` node under it. Lesson 37 covers why
it chose that over a nested loop (no index on `orders.customer_id`, and it
needs every row anyway) and what would change its mind.

## challenge — the five-table drill-down

The grain problem, weaponised. Joining `reviews` multiplies every order line
by roughly a hundred, so `sum(quantity)` is inflated a hundredfold while
`avg(rating)` is unaffected — because averaging a hundred copies of the same
set of ratings gives the same answer. The `avg(oi.quantity)::int` dodge works
for the same reason, and it is a dodge: the honest fix is to aggregate the
line items before joining the reviews. The point of the exercise is not the
trick, it is *noticing that there is a problem to solve*.

## review1 — big orders from one country

A two-table join with filters on both sides. When it returns, ask yourself
the grain question out loud before you look at the row count.

The answer, for this one: `orders` to `customers` is many-to-one, so the
result has exactly one row per qualifying order and no order is duplicated.
That is the property that would make `sum(o.total)` safe here — and the
property that evaporates the moment somebody adds a join to `order_items`
"just to get the product names". Every added join is a fresh cardinality
question.

## Further reading

- [Joined Tables](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the definitive description of `INNER`/`LEFT`/`RIGHT`/`FULL`, `ON`, `USING`, and `NATURAL`.
- [`SELECT` — FROM clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — table aliases and how they scope column references.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Joins](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/join) — nested loops, hash joins and sort-merge joins explained from the index outward. This is the best single preparation for lesson 37.
- [Don't Do This — `NATURAL JOIN`](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) — why guessing the join key is a bad idea in a schema that will change.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — the five-table drill-down (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Customer service pulled up **customer
4242** and wants their purchase history with product reputation attached:
for every (order, product) pair this customer ever bought, return the
order `id`, the product `name`, the total units of that product in that
order (`sum(quantity)` — a product *can* appear on two lines of one
order), and the product's average review rating rounded to 1 decimal.

Tables: `customers`, `orders`, `order_items`, `products`, `reviews`.
Group by order id and product name. Columns: `order_id`, `product`,
`units`, `avg_rating`. Any order. (12 rows.)

Grain warning, and why this works: joining `reviews` multiplies each item
row by that product's ~100 reviews — but `avg(r.rating)` inside a group
that spans exactly one product still averages that product's reviews.
`sum(quantity)` would be inflated 100× though! The fix: `sum(DISTINCT
oi.id)`-style tricks are fragile; the honest fix is aggregating quantity
*before* the review join (subqueries, lesson 13) — here, since each
(order, product) group has one line item in practice for this customer,
`min(oi.quantity)`-style dodges also work. Simplest correct trick that
passes: use `avg(oi.quantity)::int` — every duplicated row carries the
same quantity, and the average of n copies of q is q. The hints walk
through it; the teaching point is *noticing* the grain problem at all.

Run: `uv run dojo test 08_inner_joins challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Build it in two stages in the lab. Stage 1: the four-table join (customer
4242 → orders → items → products) grouped by (order id, product name) with
`sum(quantity)` — verify 12 rows and sane units. Stage 2: add the reviews
join and watch `sum(quantity)` explode. That explosion is the lesson.

## Hint 2
After the reviews join, each group holds ~100 copies of the same line
item. `avg(r.rating)` is immune (it averages the reviews). For units, use
`round(avg(oi.quantity))::int` — n copies of the same q average back to q.

## Hint 3
```sql
SELECT o.id, p.name, round(avg(oi.quantity))::int AS units,
       round(avg(r.rating), 1) AS avg_rating
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o       ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p     ON p.id = oi.product_id
JOIN reviews r      ON r.product_id = p.id
WHERE c.id = 4242
GROUP BY o.id, p.name;
```

Understand why avg-of-duplicates works before you paste this.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Build it in two stages in the lab. Stage 1: the four-table join (customer
4242 → orders → items → products) grouped by (order id, product name) with
`sum(quantity)` — verify 12 rows and sane units. Stage 2: add the reviews
join and watch `sum(quantity)` explode. That explosion is the lesson.

## Hint 2
After the reviews join, each group holds ~100 copies of the same line
item. `avg(r.rating)` is immune (it averages the reviews). For units, use
`round(avg(oi.quantity))::int` — n copies of the same q average back to q.

## Hint 3
```sql
SELECT o.id, p.name, round(avg(oi.quantity))::int AS units,
       round(avg(r.rating), 1) AS avg_rating
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o       ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p     ON p.id = oi.product_id
JOIN reviews r      ON r.product_id = p.id
WHERE c.id = 4242
GROUP BY o.id, p.name;
```

Understand why avg-of-duplicates works before you paste this.

SELECT o.id AS order_id,

       round(avg(r.rating), 1) AS avg_rating
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o       ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p     ON p.id = oi.product_id
JOIN reviews r      ON r.product_id = p.id
WHERE c.id = 4242
GROUP BY o.id, p.name;

## Hint 1
Two hops: order_items rows for order 123, then each item's product. You
can start FROM orders and join twice, or start FROM order_items — both
pass; the expected rows are the same.

```sql
SELECT p.name, oi.quantity, oi.price
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p     ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.id = 123;
```

Trace each ON clause: which column of which table matches which?

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — filtering across the join

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. The returns team is auditing **bulk purchases of
expensive electronics**: every order line whose product is in the
`electronics` category, where the line's `quantity` is exactly 5 **and**
the line's `price` is above 480.

Columns, in this order: the line's `id`, the product's `name`, the line's
`quantity`, the line's `price`. Any row order.

Two of those conditions are about `order_items` and one is about
`products`, but all three go in the `WHERE` clause — for an **inner** join
it makes no difference where a filter lives. Remember that sentence,
because lesson 09 is about the case where it stops being true.

Run: `uv run dojo test 08_inner_joins ex5`

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — revenue by country

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. The board wants revenue by market. Join `orders`
to `customers` and return, per `country`, the country code and the sum of
the orders' `total`.

Two columns in that order, twelve rows, any order.

Half a million orders joined to fifty thousand customers and folded into
twelve numbers. Run `dojo plan 08_inner_joins ex6` when it passes and look
at what PostgreSQL chose: almost certainly a **Hash Join** — it builds a
hash table of the smaller table (`customers`) and streams the larger one
past it. Lesson 37 explains when it picks that over the alternatives.

Run: `uv run dojo test 08_inner_joins ex6`

lessons.briefing:
# 09 — OUTER JOINs and the anti-join

5,003 of our 50,000 customers have **never placed an order**. Ask lesson
08's INNER JOIN to list customers with their orders and those 5,003 simply
don't appear — an inner join drops non-matching rows without comment. But
"who has never bought anything?" is one of the most valuable questions in
the building. Answering it requires a join that *keeps* the lonely rows.

## Concept

```sql
SELECT c.id, c.name, o.id AS order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;
```

- `LEFT JOIN` keeps **every** row of the left table. Where no right-side
  match exists, the right-side columns come back as **NULL** — the
  NULL-extension. (`RIGHT JOIN` is the mirror; `FULL JOIN` keeps
  non-matchers from *both* sides.)
- **The anti-join pattern**, built from that NULL:

```sql
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;          -- only the customers with no match at all
```

  Test the *right table's key column* for NULL — it's never NULL in a real
  match, so NULL there means "no match existed".

- **ON vs WHERE, the distinction that finally bites.** With INNER joins,
  a filter works the same in either place. With a LEFT join:
  - a right-table condition **in ON** filters *which rows count as
    matches* — left rows keep appearing, possibly NULL-extended;
  - the same condition **in WHERE** runs *after* NULL-extension, and since
    `NULL > 1900` is unknown, it silently deletes every non-matching left
    row — your LEFT JOIN just became an expensive INNER JOIN. If you've
    ever seen a LEFT JOIN "not work", this was it.

## Exercise 1 — who never bought anything?

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. All 5,003 customers with zero orders. Columns:
`id`, `name`. Any order. Use the LEFT-JOIN anti-join pattern (the gate
only checks rows, but you're here to practice the pattern).

Run: `uv run dojo test 09_outer_joins ex1`

## Exercise 2 — dead stock

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. The 300 products that have never appeared on any
order line. Columns: `id`, `name`. Any order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 09_outer_joins ex2`

## Exercise 3 — counting things that might not exist

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. The catalogue team wants a review-coverage report
for **toys**: every product in category `'toys'`, with the number of
reviews it has — and products with **no** reviews must appear with a count
of **0**, not vanish.

Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, and the review count aliased
**`reviews`**. Any row order.

Two details decide whether this is right. The join must be a `LEFT JOIN`
from `products`, so unreviewed products survive. And the count must be
`count(r.id)`, not `count(*)` — a NULL-extended row is still a row, so
`count(*)` would report **1** for a product with no reviews at all. Lesson
06's `count(*)` versus `count(column)` distinction, finally showing its
teeth.

Run: `uv run dojo test 09_outer_joins ex3`

## Exercise 4 — a filter that belongs in ON

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Now the same report, but only **5-star** reviews
count: every product in category `'garden'`, with the number of reviews it
has **whose rating is 5** — and again, products with none must appear with
`0`.

Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, and the count aliased
**`five_star`**. Any row order.

This is the lesson's whole point in one query. `r.rating = 5` is a
condition on the **right** table of a `LEFT JOIN`, so it must go in the
`ON` clause, where it decides *what counts as a match*. Put it in `WHERE`
and it runs after NULL-extension: `NULL = 5` is unknown, every unmatched
product is deleted, and your LEFT JOIN has silently become an INNER JOIN.
Write it both ways in the lab and compare the row counts before you submit.

Run: `uv run dojo test 09_outer_joins ex4`

## Challenge — ON vs WHERE, felt in your hands (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Sales wants **all 2,924 Mexican (`'MX'`)
customers**, and *for those who have any*, their orders over 1900 —
customers without such an order still listed, with NULLs. Columns:
`c.id`, `c.name`, the order `id`, the order `total`. Any order.

The country filter goes in WHERE (it's about the left table). The
total-filter goes **in the ON clause** — move it to WHERE and watch 90% of
the customers vanish. Try both in the lab; count the rows.

Run: `uv run dojo test 09_outer_joins challenge`

## Spaced review

`review1/`: Japanese (`'JP'`) customers with zero orders — columns `id`,
`name`, any order.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 09_outer_joins

An inner join answers "which rows go together?". An outer join answers the
much more valuable question "which rows *don't*?" — and the entire
difficulty of outer joins comes from the NULLs it invents to say so.

## Notes

**`LEFT JOIN` keeps every left row and manufactures NULLs.** Where no right
row matches, PostgreSQL emits the left row once with every right-side column
set to NULL. Those NULLs are not in the data; the join created them. Once
you internalise "the NULL means *no match existed*", the rest of this lesson
is mechanical.

**The anti-join idiom.** `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL` returns
exactly the left rows with no match, because a genuine match can never have
a NULL key. Test the right table's **key** column — a nullable data column
would be NULL for real matches too, and the query would be wrong in a way
that looks right. `NOT EXISTS` (lesson 13) expresses the same idea more
directly and is usually clearer; both plan well in PostgreSQL, which
recognises the pattern and executes it as a genuine anti-join.

**`ON` versus `WHERE` — the distinction that finally bites.** The logical
order is: build the joined rows using `ON`, NULL-extend the unmatched left
rows, *then* apply `WHERE`. So:

- A right-table condition in **`ON`** decides which right rows count as
  matches. Unmatched left rows still appear, NULL-extended.
- The same condition in **`WHERE`** runs after NULL-extension. Since
  `NULL = 5` is unknown and `WHERE` keeps only `true`, every NULL-extended
  row is deleted — and your `LEFT JOIN` has become an `INNER JOIN` with extra
  steps.

This is the single most common outer-join bug in the wild, and it is
invisible: no error, no warning, just a report whose "customers with no
orders" line has been empty for six months. When reviewing a `LEFT JOIN`,
read the `WHERE` clause hunting for right-table columns. Each one is a bug
until proven otherwise — the exception being a deliberate `IS NULL` test,
which is the anti-join.

**`count(*)` versus `count(col)` over an outer join.** A NULL-extended row
is still a row, so `count(*)` returns 1 for a group with no matches at all.
`count(right.id)` returns 0, because `count(column)` skips NULLs. This is
lesson 06's distinction and it is not a corner case — "how many of X does
each Y have, including the zeroes" is one of the most common reports there
is, and getting 1 instead of 0 is a bug nobody spots in a spreadsheet.
The same applies to `sum`: `sum(right.amount)` over no matches is NULL, not
0, so wrap it — `coalesce(sum(r.amount), 0)`.

**`RIGHT` and `FULL`.** `RIGHT JOIN` is `LEFT JOIN` with the tables written
in the other order; most teams standardise on `LEFT` so the preserved side
is always the one you read first. `FULL JOIN` keeps unmatched rows from both
sides and is the tool for reconciliation — comparing two systems' records
and listing what each one has that the other does not.

**Outer joins constrain the planner.** An inner join can be reordered
freely; `A LEFT JOIN B` cannot always be. That is why a chain of left joins
sometimes plans worse than the equivalent inner joins, and why replacing an
unnecessary `LEFT JOIN` with an `INNER JOIN` occasionally produces a
dramatic speedup. Something to remember in Part 5.

## ex1 — who never bought anything?

5,003 customers out of 50,000 — ten percent of the customer base, completely
invisible to every inner-join report. The commercial value of an outer join
is concentrated in questions like this one: churn, dead stock, unconverted
signups, orphaned records. They are all the same query.

## ex2 — dead stock

300 products that have never been ordered. Same pattern, other direction.
Worth noticing that the anti-join answers the question *exactly* — no
approximation, no "probably" — which is why it is the standard tool for
reconciliation jobs.

Three percent of the catalogue has never sold a single unit. In a real shop
that number drives decisions — delisting, repricing, a merchandising review —
and it is completely invisible to every report built on inner joins, because
the rows simply are not there to be counted. The most valuable thing an
outer join produces is often a row that does not exist anywhere else.

## ex3 — counting things that might not exist

The `count(r.id)` trap, live. Write it with `count(*)` in the lab and look
for products reporting exactly 1: those are the ones with zero reviews. The
bug produces plausible numbers, which is the worst kind.

Also note where the category filter went. `p.category` is a **left**-table
column, so `WHERE` is correct and moving it into `ON` would be wrong in the
other direction — it would keep every product in the database and simply
stop matching reviews for the ones outside `toys`.

## ex4 — a filter that belongs in ON

The reason the lesson exists. Two queries, one word moved, wildly different
answers:

```sql
LEFT JOIN reviews r ON r.product_id = p.id AND r.rating = 5   -- ~1,635 rows
LEFT JOIN reviews r ON r.product_id = p.id WHERE r.rating = 5 -- only reviewed ones
```

The second one is not "a bit different" — it has silently answered a
different question, and the missing rows are precisely the ones the report
was commissioned to find.

## challenge — ON vs WHERE, felt in your hands

The same distinction on the customer side, with a left-table filter
(`country`) and a right-table filter (`total`) in the same query — one in
`WHERE`, one in `ON`. Being able to say, for each condition, *which table it
constrains and therefore where it goes* is the skill. Everything else about
outer joins follows from it.

## review1 — Japanese customers with zero orders

The anti-join with an extra left-table filter. When it returns, write it
once more as `NOT EXISTS` for comparison — by then lesson 13 will have
introduced it.

Check one thing while you are there: the country filter is on `customers`,
the left table, so it belongs in `WHERE` and the anti-join still works. Had
the filter been on `orders` — "Japanese customers with no orders *over
1900*" — it would have had to move into the `ON` clause, and the query would
mean something quite different. Left-table filter, right-table filter: the
question to ask of every condition in an outer join.

## Further reading

- [Joined Tables — outer joins](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the formal description of `LEFT`/`RIGHT`/`FULL` and the exact point at which NULL-extension happens relative to `WHERE`.
- [Subquery Expressions — `EXISTS`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) — the other idiomatic anti-join, and why it shrugs off NULLs. Preview of lesson 13.
- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) — re-read the `count` entry with outer joins in mind: `count(*)` versus `count(expression)` is the whole of ex3.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Joins](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/join) — why an outer join restricts join-order freedom, and what that costs.

# Reading - 09_outer_joins

An inner join answers "which rows go together?". An outer join answers the
much more valuable question "which rows *don't*?" — and the entire
difficulty of outer joins comes from the NULLs it invents to say so.

## Notes

**`LEFT JOIN` keeps every left row and manufactures NULLs.** Where no right
row matches, PostgreSQL emits the left row once with every right-side column
set to NULL. Those NULLs are not in the data; the join created them. Once
you internalise "the NULL means *no match existed*", the rest of this lesson
is mechanical.

**The anti-join idiom.** `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL` returns
exactly the left rows with no match, because a genuine match can never have
a NULL key. Test the right table's **key** column — a nullable data column
would be NULL for real matches too, and the query would be wrong in a way
that looks right. `NOT EXISTS` (lesson 13) expresses the same idea more
directly and is usually clearer; both plan well in PostgreSQL, which
recognises the pattern and executes it as a genuine anti-join.

**`ON` versus `WHERE` — the distinction that finally bites.** The logical
order is: build the joined rows using `ON`, NULL-extend the unmatched left
rows, *then* apply `WHERE`. So:

- A right-table condition in **`ON`** decides which right rows count as
  matches. Unmatched left rows still appear, NULL-extended.
- The same condition in **`WHERE`** runs after NULL-extension. Since
  `NULL = 5` is unknown and `WHERE` keeps only `true`, every NULL-extended
  row is deleted — and your `LEFT JOIN` has become an `INNER JOIN` with extra
  steps.

This is the single most common outer-join bug in the wild, and it is
invisible: no error, no warning, just a report whose "customers with no
orders" line has been empty for six months. When reviewing a `LEFT JOIN`,
read the `WHERE` clause hunting for right-table columns. Each one is a bug
until proven otherwise — the exception being a deliberate `IS NULL` test,
which is the anti-join.

**`count(*)` versus `count(col)` over an outer join.** A NULL-extended row
is still a row, so `count(*)` returns 1 for a group with no matches at all.
`count(right.id)` returns 0, because `count(column)` skips NULLs. This is
lesson 06's distinction and it is not a corner case — "how many of X does
each Y have, including the zeroes" is one of the most common reports there
is, and getting 1 instead of 0 is a bug nobody spots in a spreadsheet.
The same applies to `sum`: `sum(right.amount)` over no matches is NULL, not
0, so wrap it — `coalesce(sum(r.amount), 0)`.

**`RIGHT` and `FULL`.** `RIGHT JOIN` is `LEFT JOIN` with the tables written
in the other order; most teams standardise on `LEFT` so the preserved side
is always the one you read first. `FULL JOIN` keeps unmatched rows from both
sides and is the tool for reconciliation — comparing two systems' records
and listing what each one has that the other does not.

**Outer joins constrain the planner.** An inner join can be reordered
freely; `A LEFT JOIN B` cannot always be. That is why a chain of left joins
sometimes plans worse than the equivalent inner joins, and why replacing an
unnecessary `LEFT JOIN` with an `INNER JOIN` occasionally produces a
dramatic speedup. Something to remember in Part 5.

## ex1 — who never bought anything?

5,003 customers out of 50,000 — ten percent of the customer base, completely
invisible to every inner-join report. The commercial value of an outer join
is concentrated in questions like this one: churn, dead stock, unconverted
signups, orphaned records. They are all the same query.

## ex2 — dead stock

300 products that have never been ordered. Same pattern, other direction.
Worth noticing that the anti-join answers the question *exactly* — no
approximation, no "probably" — which is why it is the standard tool for
reconciliation jobs.

Three percent of the catalogue has never sold a single unit. In a real shop
that number drives decisions — delisting, repricing, a merchandising review —
and it is completely invisible to every report built on inner joins, because
the rows simply are not there to be counted. The most valuable thing an
outer join produces is often a row that does not exist anywhere else.

## ex3 — counting things that might not exist

The `count(r.id)` trap, live. Write it with `count(*)` in the lab and look
for products reporting exactly 1: those are the ones with zero reviews. The
bug produces plausible numbers, which is the worst kind.

Also note where the category filter went. `p.category` is a **left**-table
column, so `WHERE` is correct and moving it into `ON` would be wrong in the
other direction — it would keep every product in the database and simply
stop matching reviews for the ones outside `toys`.

## ex4 — a filter that belongs in ON

The reason the lesson exists. Two queries, one word moved, wildly different
answers:

```sql
LEFT JOIN reviews r ON r.product_id = p.id AND r.rating = 5   -- ~1,635 rows
LEFT JOIN reviews r ON r.product_id = p.id WHERE r.rating = 5 -- only reviewed ones
```

The second one is not "a bit different" — it has silently answered a
different question, and the missing rows are precisely the ones the report
was commissioned to find.

## challenge — ON vs WHERE, felt in your hands

The same distinction on the customer side, with a left-table filter
(`country`) and a right-table filter (`total`) in the same query — one in
`WHERE`, one in `ON`. Being able to say, for each condition, *which table it
constrains and therefore where it goes* is the skill. Everything else about
outer joins follows from it.

## review1 — Japanese customers with zero orders

The anti-join with an extra left-table filter. When it returns, write it
once more as `NOT EXISTS` for comparison — by then lesson 13 will have
introduced it.

Check one thing while you are there: the country filter is on `customers`,
the left table, so it belongs in `WHERE` and the anti-join still works. Had
the filter been on `orders` — "Japanese customers with no orders *over
1900*" — it would have had to move into the `ON` clause, and the query would
mean something quite different. Left-table filter, right-table filter: the
question to ask of every condition in an outer join.

## Further reading

- [Joined Tables — outer joins](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the formal description of `LEFT`/`RIGHT`/`FULL` and the exact point at which NULL-extension happens relative to `WHERE`.
- [Subquery Expressions — `EXISTS`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) — the other idiomatic anti-join, and why it shrugs off NULLs. Preview of lesson 13.
- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) — re-read the `count` entry with outer joins in mind: `count(*)` versus `count(expression)` is the whole of ex3.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Joins](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/join) — why an outer join restricts join-order freedom, and what that costs.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — ON vs WHERE, felt in your hands (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Sales wants **all 2,924 Mexican (`'MX'`)
customers**, and *for those who have any*, their orders over 1900 —
customers without such an order still listed, with NULLs. Columns:
`c.id`, `c.name`, the order `id`, the order `total`. Any order.

The country filter goes in WHERE (it's about the left table). The
total-filter goes **in the ON clause** — move it to WHERE and watch 90% of
the customers vanish. Try both in the lab; count the rows.

Run: `uv run dojo test 09_outer_joins challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two conditions, two homes: `c.country = 'MX'` is about the left table →
WHERE. `o.total > 1900` decides *what counts as a match* → into the ON,
ANDed with the join key.

## Hint 2
```sql
SELECT c.id, c.name, o.id, o.total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.total > 1900
WHERE c.country = 'MX';
```

Before submitting, move the total-filter to WHERE in the lab and compare
row counts — that's the entire lesson in one experiment.

## Exercise 1 — who never bought anything?

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. All 5,003 customers with zero orders. Columns:
`id`, `name`. Any order. Use the LEFT-JOIN anti-join pattern (the gate
only checks rows, but you're here to practice the pattern).

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
LEFT JOIN customers to orders, then keep only the rows where the
NULL-extension happened. Which column do you test? A right-table column
that can never be NULL in a genuine match — its key.

## Hint 2
```sql
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;
```

Make sure you understand why testing `o.customer_id` would also work here,
but testing, say, a nullable right column would not.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
LEFT JOIN customers to orders, then keep only the rows where the
NULL-extension happened. Which column do you test? A right-table column
that can never be NULL in a genuine match — its key.

## Hint 2
```sql
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;
```

Make sure you understand why testing `o.customer_id` would also work here,
but testing, say, a nullable right column would not.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — counting things that might not exist

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. The catalogue team wants a review-coverage report
for **toys**: every product in category `'toys'`, with the number of
reviews it has — and products with **no** reviews must appear with a count
of **0**, not vanish.

Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, and the review count aliased
**`reviews`**. Any row order.

Two details decide whether this is right. The join must be a `LEFT JOIN`
from `products`, so unreviewed products survive. And the count must be
`count(r.id)`, not `count(*)` — a NULL-extended row is still a row, so
`count(*)` would report **1** for a product with no reviews at all. Lesson
06's `count(*)` versus `count(column)` distinction, finally showing its
teeth.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — a filter that belongs in ON

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Now the same report, but only **5-star** reviews
count: every product in category `'garden'`, with the number of reviews it
has **whose rating is 5** — and again, products with none must appear with
`0`.

Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, and the count aliased
**`five_star`**. Any row order.

This is the lesson's whole point in one query. `r.rating = 5` is a
condition on the **right** table of a `LEFT JOIN`, so it must go in the
`ON` clause, where it decides *what counts as a match*. Put it in `WHERE`
and it runs after NULL-extension: `NULL = 5` is unknown, every unmatched
product is deleted, and your LEFT JOIN has silently become an INNER JOIN.
Write it both ways in the lab and compare the row counts before you submit.

Run: `uv run dojo test 09_outer_joins ex4`

The ON clause can hold more than the join key: `ON r.product_id = p.id
AND r.rating = 5`. The category filter stays in WHERE.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT p.id, p.name, count(r.id) AS five_star
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN reviews r ON r.product_id = p.id AND r.rating = 5
WHERE p.category = 'garden'
GROUP BY p.id;

lessons.briefing:
# 10 — Self-joins and hierarchies

`staff.manager_id` points back into `staff` itself: employee 87's manager
is just another row of the same table. Org charts, category trees,
thread replies, "people also bought" — self-referencing tables are
everywhere, and querying them means joining a table **to itself**. There
is no new syntax; there is a new mental move: *the same table, worn as two
different hats, distinguished purely by alias*.

## Concept

```sql
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM staff e
JOIN staff m ON m.id = e.manager_id;
```

`e` and `m` are both `staff`. The alias is doing all the work — `e` plays
"employee", `m` plays "manager". Two things to notice:

- With an INNER join, the CEO (NULL `manager_id`, lesson 05) drops out:
  NULL matches nothing. 500 staff, 499 pairs. If the report must include
  her, that's a LEFT JOIN (lesson 09 — see how these stack?).
- Nothing stops you comparing the two hats: `e.salary > m.salary` is a
  perfectly good join-or-filter condition. Self-joins are how you ask
  *relative* questions inside one table.

**The pairs trick.** "All pairs of same-department colleagues" naively
gives you each pair twice (A,B and B,A) plus self-pairs (A,A). The idiom:

```sql
ON a.department = b.department AND a.id < b.id
```

`<` kills self-pairs *and* keeps exactly one of each mirror-pair. Remember
this; it shows up in dedup interviews constantly.

## Exercise 1 — who reports to whom

# Reading - 10_self_joins_hierarchies

A self-join is not a special feature. It is the ordinary join, applied to a
table that happens to appear twice in the same `FROM` clause — and the only
new idea is that an alias creates an *independent* view of the same rows.

## Notes

**Aliases are the whole mechanism.** `FROM staff e JOIN staff m` puts two
independent copies of `staff` in scope. PostgreSQL does not care that they
are the same physical table; it scans it twice (or scans once and uses an
index for the second, which is why lesson 31's first index makes self-joins
dramatically faster). Once you stop reading `staff e` as "the staff table"
and start reading it as "a row playing the employee role", every hierarchy
query gets easier.

**Self-joins answer *relative* questions.** `e.salary > m.salary`,
`a.created_at < b.created_at`, `a.id < b.id` — comparing two rows of the
same table is impossible with a `WHERE` clause alone, because `WHERE` sees
one row at a time. This is the fundamental limitation that self-joins work
around, and it is also the limitation that **window functions** (lesson 15)
address far more elegantly. "Compare each row to its neighbours" is a
self-join in Part 1 and a `lag()` in Part 2, and the window-function version
is usually both shorter and faster.

**The pairs idiom.** To enumerate unordered pairs from one table, join it to
itself with a strict inequality on the key:

```sql
FROM staff a JOIN staff b ON a.department = b.department AND a.id < b.id
```

`a.id < b.id` does two jobs at once: it kills self-pairs (a row cannot be
less than itself) and it keeps exactly one of each mirror image. With `<>`
instead you get every pair twice. This is the standard answer to a whole
family of dedup and "find duplicate records" interview questions, and it is
worth being able to write from memory.

**Watch the cardinality.** A self-join on a *non-unique* key is a many-to-many
join, and it squares the group size: 61 finance staff produce 1,830 pairs;
a 5,000-person department would produce 12.5 million. Self-joins on
low-cardinality columns are one of the classic ways to accidentally generate
a billion rows from a small table.

**Where self-joins run out.** They handle a *fixed* number of levels. Two
levels up needs two joins; "the whole chain to the CEO" needs as many joins
as the tree is deep, which you cannot write when the depth is data-dependent.
That is a genuine expressiveness limit, not a stylistic one, and recursive
CTEs (lesson 14) are the answer. Recognising which of the two a question
needs — fixed depth or arbitrary depth — is a real senior-engineer tell.

**Adjacency list versus the alternatives.** `manager_id` pointing at the
same table is the *adjacency list* model: trivial to update, cheap to query
one level, expensive to query transitively. The alternatives trade the other
way — materialised path (store `'/1/7/42/'` and use `LIKE '/1/7/%'`),
nested sets (store left/right bounds, O(1) subtree queries, painful
inserts), and closure tables (a row per ancestor-descendant pair). PostgreSQL
users mostly stay with the adjacency list plus a recursive CTE, because
`WITH RECURSIVE` is fast enough and nothing else has to be maintained.

## ex1 — who reports to whom

499 rows from 500 staff, and the missing row is the CEO. This is lesson 09's
point arriving without being announced: an inner join silently dropped the
row that had no match. Almost every "why is the total one short?" bug is
this.

## ex2 — finance pairs

1,830 pairs from 61 people — n(n-1)/2, the handshake number. Try the query
with `a.id <> b.id` and count: 3,660, exactly double. Then try it with no
condition beyond the department and count 3,721, which includes the 61
self-pairs. Seeing all three numbers once makes the idiom permanent.

## ex3 — the org chart with nobody missing

The fix for ex1, and the reason to reach for `LEFT JOIN` as a *default* when
the left side is the population you are reporting on. Note that the NULL in
the output is doing real work: it says "this person has no manager", which
is a fact, not a gap in the data.

## ex4 — two levels up

Three aliases, two joins, one fixed depth. The exercise is really an
argument: count how many joins you would need for "everyone in the CEO's
reporting tree" and notice that the answer depends on data you do not have
at write time. Lesson 14 replaces this entire pattern with six lines that
work at any depth.

## challenge — paid more than the boss

The join condition and the filter are doing different jobs: `m.id =
e.manager_id` relates the rows, `e.salary > m.salary` selects among the
related pairs. Both are comparisons between two rows of the same table,
which is exactly what `WHERE` alone cannot do. Nineteen rows, and the reason
there are any is that the generator overlaps the salary bands between levels
on purpose — as real companies do, which is why this report exists.

## review1 — the teammates of employee 42

One hat holds employee 42, the other holds everyone sharing their
`manager_id`, and the `WHERE` excludes 42 from their own team list. No
subquery needed. When this comes back, write it without looking at ex1
first.

The detail worth re-deriving is why `a.id <> b.id` is right here while
`a.id < b.id` was right in ex2. In ex2 you wanted each *pair* once, so the
strict inequality removed the mirror image. Here you have a fixed anchor row
and want everyone else, so the mirror image never arises and you only need
to exclude the self-match. Same shape, different question, different
operator — and getting it backwards silently halves your answer.

## Further reading

- [Joined Tables and table aliases](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the section on `FROM` items and aliases, which is what makes a self-join legal at all.
- [`WITH` Queries — recursive](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) — where fixed-depth self-joins stop and lesson 14 begins. Read the org-chart example.
- [Window Functions Tutorial](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) — the other escape from "compare a row to its neighbours". Preview of lesson 15.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Joins](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/join) — why a self-join on an unindexed column is quadratic, and what an index on `manager_id` would change.
