# 10 — Self-joins and hierarchies

`staff.manager_id` points back into `staff` itself: employee 87's manager
is just another row of the same table. Org charts, category trees,
thread replies, "people also bought" — self-referencing tables are
everywhere, and querying them means joining a table **to itself**. There
is no new syntax; there is a new mental move: *the same table, worn as two
different hats, distinguished purely by alias*.

## Concept

```sql
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM staff e
JOIN staff m ON m.id = e.manager_id;
```

`e` and `m` are both `staff`. The alias is doing all the work — `e` plays
"employee", `m` plays "manager". Two things to notice:

- With an INNER join, the CEO (NULL `manager_id`, lesson 05) drops out:
  NULL matches nothing. 500 staff, 499 pairs. If the report must include
  her, that's a LEFT JOIN (lesson 09 — see how these stack?).
- Nothing stops you comparing the two hats: `e.salary > m.salary` is a
  perfectly good join-or-filter condition. Self-joins are how you ask
  *relative* questions inside one table.

**The pairs trick.** "All pairs of same-department colleagues" naively
gives you each pair twice (A,B and B,A) plus self-pairs (A,A). The idiom:

```sql
ON a.department = b.department AND a.id < b.id
```

`<` kills self-pairs *and* keeps exactly one of each mirror-pair. Remember
this; it shows up in dedup interviews constantly.

# Reading - 10_self_joins_hierarchies

A self-join is not a special feature. It is the ordinary join, applied to a
table that happens to appear twice in the same `FROM` clause — and the only
new idea is that an alias creates an *independent* view of the same rows.

## Notes

**Aliases are the whole mechanism.** `FROM staff e JOIN staff m` puts two
independent copies of `staff` in scope. PostgreSQL does not care that they
are the same physical table; it scans it twice (or scans once and uses an
index for the second, which is why lesson 31's first index makes self-joins
dramatically faster). Once you stop reading `staff e` as "the staff table"
and start reading it as "a row playing the employee role", every hierarchy
query gets easier.

**Self-joins answer *relative* questions.** `e.salary > m.salary`,
`a.created_at < b.created_at`, `a.id < b.id` — comparing two rows of the
same table is impossible with a `WHERE` clause alone, because `WHERE` sees
one row at a time. This is the fundamental limitation that self-joins work
around, and it is also the limitation that **window functions** (lesson 15)
address far more elegantly. "Compare each row to its neighbours" is a
self-join in Part 1 and a `lag()` in Part 2, and the window-function version
is usually both shorter and faster.

**The pairs idiom.** To enumerate unordered pairs from one table, join it to
itself with a strict inequality on the key:

```sql
FROM staff a JOIN staff b ON a.department = b.department AND a.id < b.id
```

`a.id < b.id` does two jobs at once: it kills self-pairs (a row cannot be
less than itself) and it keeps exactly one of each mirror image. With `<>`
instead you get every pair twice. This is the standard answer to a whole
family of dedup and "find duplicate records" interview questions, and it is
worth being able to write from memory.

**Watch the cardinality.** A self-join on a *non-unique* key is a many-to-many
join, and it squares the group size: 61 finance staff produce 1,830 pairs;
a 5,000-person department would produce 12.5 million. Self-joins on
low-cardinality columns are one of the classic ways to accidentally generate
a billion rows from a small table.

**Where self-joins run out.** They handle a *fixed* number of levels. Two
levels up needs two joins; "the whole chain to the CEO" needs as many joins
as the tree is deep, which you cannot write when the depth is data-dependent.
That is a genuine expressiveness limit, not a stylistic one, and recursive
CTEs (lesson 14) are the answer. Recognising which of the two a question
needs — fixed depth or arbitrary depth — is a real senior-engineer tell.

**Adjacency list versus the alternatives.** `manager_id` pointing at the
same table is the *adjacency list* model: trivial to update, cheap to query
one level, expensive to query transitively. The alternatives trade the other
way — materialised path (store `'/1/7/42/'` and use `LIKE '/1/7/%'`),
nested sets (store left/right bounds, O(1) subtree queries, painful
inserts), and closure tables (a row per ancestor-descendant pair). PostgreSQL
users mostly stay with the adjacency list plus a recursive CTE, because
`WITH RECURSIVE` is fast enough and nothing else has to be maintained.

## ex1 — who reports to whom

499 rows from 500 staff, and the missing row is the CEO. This is lesson 09's
point arriving without being announced: an inner join silently dropped the
row that had no match. Almost every "why is the total one short?" bug is
this.

## ex2 — finance pairs

1,830 pairs from 61 people — n(n-1)/2, the handshake number. Try the query
with `a.id <> b.id` and count: 3,660, exactly double. Then try it with no
condition beyond the department and count 3,721, which includes the 61
self-pairs. Seeing all three numbers once makes the idiom permanent.

## ex3 — the org chart with nobody missing

The fix for ex1, and the reason to reach for `LEFT JOIN` as a *default* when
the left side is the population you are reporting on. Note that the NULL in
the output is doing real work: it says "this person has no manager", which
is a fact, not a gap in the data.

## ex4 — two levels up

Three aliases, two joins, one fixed depth. The exercise is really an
argument: count how many joins you would need for "everyone in the CEO's
reporting tree" and notice that the answer depends on data you do not have
at write time. Lesson 14 replaces this entire pattern with six lines that
work at any depth.

## challenge — paid more than the boss

The join condition and the filter are doing different jobs: `m.id =
e.manager_id` relates the rows, `e.salary > m.salary` selects among the
related pairs. Both are comparisons between two rows of the same table,
which is exactly what `WHERE` alone cannot do. Nineteen rows, and the reason
there are any is that the generator overlaps the salary bands between levels
on purpose — as real companies do, which is why this report exists.

## review1 — the teammates of employee 42

One hat holds employee 42, the other holds everyone sharing their
`manager_id`, and the `WHERE` excludes 42 from their own team list. No
subquery needed. When this comes back, write it without looking at ex1
first.

The detail worth re-deriving is why `a.id <> b.id` is right here while
`a.id < b.id` was right in ex2. In ex2 you wanted each *pair* once, so the
strict inequality removed the mirror image. Here you have a fixed anchor row
and want everyone else, so the mirror image never arises and you only need
to exclude the self-match. Same shape, different question, different
operator — and getting it backwards silently halves your answer.

## Further reading

- [Joined Tables and table aliases](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the section on `FROM` items and aliases, which is what makes a self-join legal at all.
- [`WITH` Queries — recursive](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) — where fixed-depth self-joins stop and lesson 14 begins. Read the org-chart example.
- [Window Functions Tutorial](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) — the other escape from "compare a row to its neighbours". Preview of lesson 15.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Joins](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/join) — why a self-join on an unindexed column is quadratic, and what an index on `manager_id` would change.

## Hint 1
Exercise 1's join, plus one comparison between the two hats — as a WHERE

`WHERE e.salary > m.salary` on top of the ex1 skeleton; SELECT

references.solution.sql:
SELECT e.id, e.name, e.salary, m.salary AS manager_salary
FROM staff e
JOIN staff m ON m.id = e.manager_id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — two levels up

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The skip-level meeting tool needs three names per
row: an employee, their manager, and their **manager's manager**.

Columns, in this order: `employee`, `manager`, `grandmanager` — all three
being names. Only rows where all three exist (a plain inner join at both
steps). Any row order.

The same table now wears three hats. Notice what this costs: one more
level of hierarchy means one more join, written by hand, and a query that
only works for *exactly* that depth. "Everyone under the VP of Sales,
however deep" cannot be written this way at all — which is precisely the
argument for the recursive CTE waiting in lesson 14.

lessons.title: 11 — Set operations
lessons.summary: Joins combine tables sideways — matching rows, widening them. Set operations combine result sets vertically: two queries, same column shape, stacked. "Customers who are big spenders or live in Brazil." "US customers who have never ordered." When the question contains or / and-also / but-not between two lists, think set ops.
lessons.briefing:
# 11 — Set operations

Joins combine tables *sideways* — matching rows, widening them. Set
operations combine result sets *vertically*: two queries, same column
shape, stacked. "Customers who are big spenders **or** live in Brazil."
"US customers **who have never ordered**." When the question contains
or / and-also / but-not between two *lists*, think set ops.

## Concept

```sql
SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE total > 1990
UNION
SELECT id FROM customers WHERE country = 'BR';
```

- `UNION` merges and **deduplicates**. `UNION ALL` merges and keeps
  duplicates — it's also faster, because dedup costs a sort or hash of
  the whole result. If duplicates are impossible or harmless, reach for
  `UNION ALL` by default.
- `INTERSECT` keeps rows present in **both** results. `EXCEPT` keeps rows
  of the first result **not present** in the second. Both dedup like UNION.
- **Column compatibility**: both sides must produce the same number of
  columns with compatible types. The *names* come from the first query;
  Postgres doesn't care if the second query calls it something else.
- Set ops treat two NULLs as equal for dedup purposes — one of the few
  places SQL does that (compare lesson 05's `IS DISTINCT FROM`).

## Exercise 1 — either list

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. One deduplicated column `customer_id`: every
customer who placed an order with `total > 1990`, **plus** every customer
from `'BR'`. Any order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 11_set_operations ex1`

## Exercise 2 — in one list, not the other

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Every `'US'` customer id that has **never**
appeared as an `orders.customer_id`. One column, any order. Yes, this is
lesson 09's anti-join wearing set-op clothes — with EXCEPT it's two lines.
(Bonus thought, not graded: why is EXCEPT immune to lesson 05's NOT IN
NULL trap? Because EXCEPT compares NULLs as equal instead of unknown.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 11_set_operations ex2`

## Exercise 3 — in both lists

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Marketing wants the overlap between two segments:
customers who are **in the US** *and* have placed **at least one order
over 1900**.

One deduplicated column, `id`, any order.

`INTERSECT` keeps the rows that appear in both results. Note that you could
also write this as a join — and for two lists of ids, `INTERSECT` says
exactly what you mean with no join key to get wrong, no risk of the
many-to-many fan-out that would duplicate a customer with three big orders,
and automatic deduplication. Try the join version in the lab and count the
rows before you dedupe; the difference is the argument for the set
operator.

Run: `uv run dojo test 11_set_operations ex3`

## Exercise 4 — UNION ALL, and the duplicates it keeps

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Build a raw contact list for two campaigns,
**keeping every duplicate**: every `customer_id` from orders with `total >
1995`, stacked with `UNION ALL` onto every `id` from customers in
`'AU'`.

One column, any order, duplicates preserved.

Then run the same query with plain `UNION` in the lab and compare the row
counts. Two effects are mixed into that difference: a customer with three
enormous orders appears three times in the first half alone, and an
Australian customer with a big order appears in both halves. `UNION` erases
both — sometimes that is the fix and sometimes it is the bug, and only you
know which.

Run: `uv run dojo test 11_set_operations ex4`

## Challenge — symmetric difference (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Marketing has two segments: **A** =
customers with at least one order over 1980; **B** = customers in `'AU'`.
They want everyone in **exactly one** of the two segments — A-not-B plus
B-not-A. One column `id`, any order. There's no SYMMETRIC EXCEPT
operator; compose it from two EXCEPTs and a UNION (parentheses around
each half keep the precedence honest).

Run: `uv run dojo test 11_set_operations challenge`

## Spaced review

`review1/`: the holiday gift guide — one result with two columns `label`,
`name`: the literal text `'gift'` with every toys-category product under
20, stacked (UNION ALL) with the literal `'snack'` and every food product
under 10. Any order. (Literals in a SELECT list produce the same value
for every row — that's how you tag which half a row came from.)
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 11_set_operations

Joins combine tables sideways; set operations stack result sets vertically.
The distinction sounds cosmetic and is not: set operations compare *whole
rows* by value, which gives them NULL semantics, deduplication behaviour and
performance characteristics that no join has.

## Notes

**The four operators.** `UNION` (in either), `UNION ALL` (in either,
duplicates kept), `INTERSECT` (in both), `EXCEPT` (in the first and not the
second). Everything except `UNION ALL` deduplicates its result, and
deduplication is not free — it costs a sort or a hash over the entire
combined output.

**`UNION ALL` should be your default.** Write `UNION` only when you actually
need the dedup. The reasoning is symmetrical: `UNION` on provably disjoint
sets pays for a sort that removes nothing, and `UNION` on sets that *do*
overlap silently deletes rows a report may have been commissioned to show.
"Which dedup behaviour does this query need, and which did it get?" is a
question worth asking of every `UNION` you review.

**Column compatibility is positional, not by name.** Both sides must produce
the same number of columns with compatible types, matched left to right. The
output column names come from the **first** query and the others are
ignored — which means a `UNION` between two queries whose columns are in
different orders is not an error, it is a data-corruption bug that type
compatibility happily allows (`id, total` versus `total, id` on two numeric
columns will run). Always read a set operation column by column.

**Set operations treat NULLs as equal.** This is one of the very few places
in SQL where `NULL = NULL` behaves as true: two rows containing NULL in the
same position are duplicates for `UNION`, and `EXCEPT` will remove a
NULL-containing row using another NULL-containing row. This is why `EXCEPT`
is immune to lesson 05's `NOT IN` trap while looking superficially similar,
and it is a genuinely useful property for reconciliation queries.

**Precedence.** `INTERSECT` binds tighter than `UNION` and `EXCEPT`, and
`UNION`/`EXCEPT` are left-associative — so `A UNION B EXCEPT C` means
`(A UNION B) EXCEPT C`. As with `AND`/`OR` in lesson 02, the right response
is not to memorise the table but to parenthesise anything mixed.

**`ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` apply to the whole thing.** They are written once,
after the last query, and they sort the combined result. To sort or limit
one branch, wrap that branch in parentheses — `(SELECT ... ORDER BY x LIMIT
5) UNION ALL (SELECT ...)`.

**When to prefer a set operation over a join.** When both sides are lists of
the same kind of thing and you want "or", "and also", or "but not" between
the *lists*. The set operator cannot fan out — a join between customers and
orders duplicates a customer once per matching order, and every "why does
this customer appear four times?" bug is that fan-out. The set operator also
has no join key to get wrong. Conversely, when you need columns from both
sides in the same row, only a join will do.

**Performance note.** `EXCEPT` and `INTERSECT` both materialise and sort or
hash both inputs. `NOT EXISTS` / `EXISTS` (lesson 13) can often stop early
and are usually the faster idiom when one side is huge and you only need a
membership test. The set operators win on clarity when both sides are
already small, filtered lists.

## ex1 — either list

A `UNION` between two genuinely overlapping sets: a Brazilian customer with
a 1,995-real order is in both halves and appears once. That is the dedup
earning its cost.

Note what the two branches have in common and what they do not. Both produce
a single integer column that means "a customer id" — that shared *meaning*
is what makes the union sensible. Nothing in SQL checks it: the same query
would happily union customer ids with product ids, because both are `int`.
Type compatibility is the only guard rail, and it is a low one.

## ex2 — in one list, not the other

The anti-join from lesson 09 in two lines. Worth holding all three idioms
side by side, because you will meet all three in other people's code:
`LEFT JOIN ... WHERE key IS NULL`, `NOT EXISTS (...)`, and `EXCEPT`. They
answer the same question; they differ in NULL safety (`NOT IN` is the only
broken one), in whether they can return columns from the right side (only
the join can), and in how they plan.

## ex3 — in both lists

`INTERSECT` where a join would fan out. This is the cleanest demonstration
in the lesson of why set operators exist: the join version needs a `DISTINCT`
bolted on to be correct, and a `DISTINCT` bolted onto a join is usually a
sign that the query is answering a set question with the wrong tool.

## ex4 — UNION ALL, and the duplicates it keeps

Two different sources of duplication in one query — within a branch, and
across branches — and `UNION` erases both indiscriminately. The lesson is
that `UNION`'s dedup is not a "cleanup"; it is a semantic decision about
what a row *means*. If a row means "one order over 1,995", deduplicating
destroys information. If it means "one customer to email", deduplicating is
the point.

## challenge — symmetric difference

There is no `SYMMETRIC EXCEPT`, so you compose it: `(A EXCEPT B) UNION (B
EXCEPT A)`. Parenthesise both halves — this is exactly the precedence
situation from the notes, and without the parentheses the left-associative
reading gives you a different (and wrong) answer.

## review1 — the gift guide

Literals in a SELECT list produce the same value on every row, which is how
you tag which branch a row came from. This little trick is the foundation of
a surprising amount of real reporting SQL — it is how you build a union of
heterogeneous sources that a downstream consumer can still tell apart, and
it is what `GROUPING SETS` (lesson 50) automates.

## Further reading

- [Combining Queries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-union.html) — `UNION`, `INTERSECT`, `EXCEPT`, their `ALL` variants, and the precedence rules.
- [`SELECT` — the `UNION`/`INTERSECT`/`EXCEPT` clauses](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — the reference-page detail on column matching and where `ORDER BY` may appear.
- [Subquery Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) — `EXISTS`, `IN`, `ANY`/`ALL`: the other way to express membership, with different NULL and performance behaviour. Preview of lesson 13.
- [Sorting Rows](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-order.html) — why `ORDER BY` after a set operation sorts the whole result and how to sort one branch.

# 11 — Set operations

Joins combine tables *sideways* — matching rows, widening them. Set
operations combine result sets *vertically*: two queries, same column
shape, stacked. "Customers who are big spenders **or** live in Brazil."
"US customers **who have never ordered**." When the question contains
or / and-also / but-not between two *lists*, think set ops.

## Concept

```sql
SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE total > 1990
UNION
SELECT id FROM customers WHERE country = 'BR';
```

- `UNION` merges and **deduplicates**. `UNION ALL` merges and keeps
  duplicates — it's also faster, because dedup costs a sort or hash of
  the whole result. If duplicates are impossible or harmless, reach for
  `UNION ALL` by default.
- `INTERSECT` keeps rows present in **both** results. `EXCEPT` keeps rows
  of the first result **not present** in the second. Both dedup like UNION.
- **Column compatibility**: both sides must produce the same number of
  columns with compatible types. The *names* come from the first query;
  Postgres doesn't care if the second query calls it something else.
- Set ops treat two NULLs as equal for dedup purposes — one of the few
  places SQL does that (compare lesson 05's `IS DISTINCT FROM`).

## Exercise 1 — either list

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. One deduplicated column `customer_id`: every
customer who placed an order with `total > 1990`, **plus** every customer
from `'BR'`. Any order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 11_set_operations ex1`

## Exercise 2 — in one list, not the other

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Every `'US'` customer id that has **never**
appeared as an `orders.customer_id`. One column, any order. Yes, this is
lesson 09's anti-join wearing set-op clothes — with EXCEPT it's two lines.
(Bonus thought, not graded: why is EXCEPT immune to lesson 05's NOT IN
NULL trap? Because EXCEPT compares NULLs as equal instead of unknown.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 11_set_operations ex2`

## Exercise 3 — in both lists

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Marketing wants the overlap between two segments:
customers who are **in the US** *and* have placed **at least one order
over 1900**.

One deduplicated column, `id`, any order.

`INTERSECT` keeps the rows that appear in both results. Note that you could
also write this as a join — and for two lists of ids, `INTERSECT` says
exactly what you mean with no join key to get wrong, no risk of the
many-to-many fan-out that would duplicate a customer with three big orders,
and automatic deduplication. Try the join version in the lab and count the
rows before you dedupe; the difference is the argument for the set
operator.

Run: `uv run dojo test 11_set_operations ex3`

## Exercise 4 — UNION ALL, and the duplicates it keeps

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Build a raw contact list for two campaigns,
**keeping every duplicate**: every `customer_id` from orders with `total >
1995`, stacked with `UNION ALL` onto every `id` from customers in
`'AU'`.

One column, any order, duplicates preserved.

Then run the same query with plain `UNION` in the lab and compare the row
counts. Two effects are mixed into that difference: a customer with three
enormous orders appears three times in the first half alone, and an
Australian customer with a big order appears in both halves. `UNION` erases
both — sometimes that is the fix and sometimes it is the bug, and only you
know which.

Run: `uv run dojo test 11_set_operations ex4`

## Challenge — symmetric difference (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Marketing has two segments: **A** =
customers with at least one order over 1980; **B** = customers in `'AU'`.
They want everyone in **exactly one** of the two segments — A-not-B plus
B-not-A. One column `id`, any order. There's no SYMMETRIC EXCEPT
operator; compose it from two EXCEPTs and a UNION (parentheses around
each half keep the precedence honest).

Run: `uv run dojo test 11_set_operations challenge`

## Spaced review

`review1/`: the holiday gift guide — one result with two columns `label`,
`name`: the literal text `'gift'` with every toys-category product under
20, stacked (UNION ALL) with the literal `'snack'` and every food product
under 10. Any order. (Literals in a SELECT list produce the same value
for every row — that's how you tag which half a row came from.)

## The teaching point

UNION vs UNION ALL is a real performance lever: deduplicating a
10-million-row union costs a sort/hash you may not need, and reviewers
who spot a UNION between provably-disjoint sets will ask for ALL. The
reverse bug is subtler — UNION silently *hiding* duplicates a report was
supposed to show. In every code review: which dedup behavior does this
query need, and which did it get?

# Reading - 11_set_operations

Joins combine tables sideways; set operations stack result sets vertically.
The distinction sounds cosmetic and is not: set operations compare *whole
rows* by value, which gives them NULL semantics, deduplication behaviour and
performance characteristics that no join has.

## Notes

**The four operators.** `UNION` (in either), `UNION ALL` (in either,
duplicates kept), `INTERSECT` (in both), `EXCEPT` (in the first and not the
second). Everything except `UNION ALL` deduplicates its result, and
deduplication is not free — it costs a sort or a hash over the entire
combined output.

**`UNION ALL` should be your default.** Write `UNION` only when you actually
need the dedup. The reasoning is symmetrical: `UNION` on provably disjoint
sets pays for a sort that removes nothing, and `UNION` on sets that *do*
overlap silently deletes rows a report may have been commissioned to show.
"Which dedup behaviour does this query need, and which did it get?" is a
question worth asking of every `UNION` you review.

**Column compatibility is positional, not by name.** Both sides must produce
the same number of columns with compatible types, matched left to right. The
output column names come from the **first** query and the others are
ignored — which means a `UNION` between two queries whose columns are in
different orders is not an error, it is a data-corruption bug that type
compatibility happily allows (`id, total` versus `total, id` on two numeric
columns will run). Always read a set operation column by column.

**Set operations treat NULLs as equal.** This is one of the very few places
in SQL where `NULL = NULL` behaves as true: two rows containing NULL in the
same position are duplicates for `UNION`, and `EXCEPT` will remove a
NULL-containing row using another NULL-containing row. This is why `EXCEPT`
is immune to lesson 05's `NOT IN` trap while looking superficially similar,
and it is a genuinely useful property for reconciliation queries.

**Precedence.** `INTERSECT` binds tighter than `UNION` and `EXCEPT`, and
`UNION`/`EXCEPT` are left-associative — so `A UNION B EXCEPT C` means
`(A UNION B) EXCEPT C`. As with `AND`/`OR` in lesson 02, the right response
is not to memorise the table but to parenthesise anything mixed.

**`ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` apply to the whole thing.** They are written once,
after the last query, and they sort the combined result. To sort or limit
one branch, wrap that branch in parentheses — `(SELECT ... ORDER BY x LIMIT
5) UNION ALL (SELECT ...)`.

**When to prefer a set operation over a join.** When both sides are lists of
the same kind of thing and you want "or", "and also", or "but not" between
the *lists*. The set operator cannot fan out — a join between customers and
orders duplicates a customer once per matching order, and every "why does
this customer appear four times?" bug is that fan-out. The set operator also
has no join key to get wrong. Conversely, when you need columns from both
sides in the same row, only a join will do.

**Performance note.** `EXCEPT` and `INTERSECT` both materialise and sort or
hash both inputs. `NOT EXISTS` / `EXISTS` (lesson 13) can often stop early
and are usually the faster idiom when one side is huge and you only need a
membership test. The set operators win on clarity when both sides are
already small, filtered lists.

## ex1 — either list

A `UNION` between two genuinely overlapping sets: a Brazilian customer with
a 1,995-real order is in both halves and appears once. That is the dedup
earning its cost.

Note what the two branches have in common and what they do not. Both produce
a single integer column that means "a customer id" — that shared *meaning*
is what makes the union sensible. Nothing in SQL checks it: the same query
would happily union customer ids with product ids, because both are `int`.
Type compatibility is the only guard rail, and it is a low one.

## ex2 — in one list, not the other

The anti-join from lesson 09 in two lines. Worth holding all three idioms
side by side, because you will meet all three in other people's code:
`LEFT JOIN ... WHERE key IS NULL`, `NOT EXISTS (...)`, and `EXCEPT`. They
answer the same question; they differ in NULL safety (`NOT IN` is the only
broken one), in whether they can return columns from the right side (only
the join can), and in how they plan.

## ex3 — in both lists

`INTERSECT` where a join would fan out. This is the cleanest demonstration
in the lesson of why set operators exist: the join version needs a `DISTINCT`
bolted on to be correct, and a `DISTINCT` bolted onto a join is usually a
sign that the query is answering a set question with the wrong tool.

## ex4 — UNION ALL, and the duplicates it keeps

Two different sources of duplication in one query — within a branch, and
across branches — and `UNION` erases both indiscriminately. The lesson is
that `UNION`'s dedup is not a "cleanup"; it is a semantic decision about
what a row *means*. If a row means "one order over 1,995", deduplicating
destroys information. If it means "one customer to email", deduplicating is
the point.

## challenge — symmetric difference

There is no `SYMMETRIC EXCEPT`, so you compose it: `(A EXCEPT B) UNION (B
EXCEPT A)`. Parenthesise both halves — this is exactly the precedence
situation from the notes, and without the parentheses the left-associative
reading gives you a different (and wrong) answer.

## review1 — the gift guide

Literals in a SELECT list produce the same value on every row, which is how
you tag which branch a row came from. This little trick is the foundation of
a surprising amount of real reporting SQL — it is how you build a union of
heterogeneous sources that a downstream consumer can still tell apart, and
it is what `GROUPING SETS` (lesson 50) automates.

## Further reading

- [Combining Queries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-union.html) — `UNION`, `INTERSECT`, `EXCEPT`, their `ALL` variants, and the precedence rules.
- [`SELECT` — the `UNION`/`INTERSECT`/`EXCEPT` clauses](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — the reference-page detail on column matching and where `ORDER BY` may appear.
- [Subquery Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) — `EXISTS`, `IN`, `ANY`/`ALL`: the other way to express membership, with different NULL and performance behaviour. Preview of lesson 13.
- [Sorting Rows](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-order.html) — why `ORDER BY` after a set operation sorts the whole result and how to sort one branch.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — symmetric difference (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Marketing has two segments: **A** =
customers with at least one order over 1980; **B** = customers in `'AU'`.
They want everyone in **exactly one** of the two segments — A-not-B plus
B-not-A. One column `id`, any order. There's no SYMMETRIC EXCEPT
operator; compose it from two EXCEPTs and a UNION (parentheses around
each half keep the precedence honest).

Run: `uv run dojo test 11_set_operations challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Write segment A and segment B as standalone queries first (A needs
DISTINCT or just relies on EXCEPT/UNION dedup). Then: (A EXCEPT B) UNION
(B EXCEPT A), with parentheses around each half.

## Hint 2
```sql
(SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE total > 1980
 EXCEPT
 SELECT id FROM customers WHERE country = 'AU')
UNION
(SELECT id FROM customers WHERE country = 'AU'
 EXCEPT
 SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE total > 1980);
```

Trace one customer who is in both segments and confirm they fall out.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — in both lists

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Marketing wants the overlap between two segments:
customers who are **in the US** *and* have placed **at least one order
over 1900**.

One deduplicated column, `id`, any order.

`INTERSECT` keeps the rows that appear in both results. Note that you could
also write this as a join — and for two lists of ids, `INTERSECT` says
exactly what you mean with no join key to get wrong, no risk of the
many-to-many fan-out that would duplicate a customer with three big orders,
and automatic deduplication. Try the join version in the lab and count the
rows before you dedupe; the difference is the argument for the set
operator.

Run: `uv run dojo test 11_set_operations ex3`

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — UNION ALL, and the duplicates it keeps

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Build a raw contact list for two campaigns,
**keeping every duplicate**: every `customer_id` from orders with `total >
1995`, stacked with `UNION ALL` onto every `id` from customers in
`'AU'`.

One column, any order, duplicates preserved.

Then run the same query with plain `UNION` in the lab and compare the row
counts. Two effects are mixed into that difference: a customer with three
enormous orders appears three times in the first half alone, and an
Australian customer with a big order appears in both halves. `UNION` erases
both — sometimes that is the fix and sometimes it is the bug, and only you
know which.

Run: `uv run dojo test 11_set_operations ex4`

exercises.prompt:
## Spaced review

`review1/`: the holiday gift guide — one result with two columns `label`,
`name`: the literal text `'gift'` with every toys-category product under
20, stacked (UNION ALL) with the literal `'snack'` and every food product
under 10. Any order. (Literals in a SELECT list produce the same value
for every row — that's how you tag which half a row came from.)
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Each half is a two-column SELECT whose first column is a quoted literal
(`'gift'` / `'snack'`). Stack with UNION ALL — duplicates are impossible
here anyway, so skip the dedup cost.

## Hint 2
```sql
SELECT 'gift' AS label, name FROM products
WHERE category = 'toys' AND price < 20
UNION ALL
SELECT 'snack', name FROM products
WHERE category = 'food' AND price < 10;
```

# 12 — Fundamentals capstone: the quarterly review

No new SQL in this lesson. Instead: three requests written the way they
actually arrive — as stakeholder asks, not query specs. Your job includes
the *translation*: choosing the joins, the grouping, the filters, the
ordering. That translation is the actual job; the SQL is the easy part by
now.

The company's fiscal quarter in question is **Q3 2023: July 1 through
September 30, 2023** (i.e. `created_at >= '2023-07-01' AND created_at <
'2023-10-01'` — half-open ranges avoid the "was September 30 23:59:59
included?" argument forever; make them a habit).

## Exercise 1 — "How did Q3 go, by status?"

> *From: CFO. "One table: for each order status in Q3, how many orders and
> how much money. Alphabetical by status so I can find things."*

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Columns in order: `status`, `orders` (count),
`revenue` (sum of `total`). Filter to Q3 2023 as defined above. **Ordered
by status ascending.**

Run: `uv run dojo test 12_fundamentals_capstone ex1`

## Exercise 2 — "Who are our whales?"

> *From: VP Sales. "Top ten customers by lifetime real revenue — count
> paid and shipped orders only, cancelled and pending are vapor. Names,
> please, and their totals."*

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Columns in order: `id` (customer), `name`,
`spend` (sum of qualifying order totals). Sort by `spend` descending,
tie-break `id` ascending, 10 rows.

Run: `uv run dojo test 12_fundamentals_capstone ex2`

## Exercise 3 — "What actually sells?"

> *From: Merchandising. "Category league table, real revenue only —
> paid or shipped orders. For each category: how many units moved and the
> line-item revenue. Don't care about the order of rows."*

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Columns in order: `category`, `units` (sum of
quantities), `revenue` (sum of `quantity * price` from the line items).
Filter orders to status paid or shipped. Any row order. (Three tables:
`orders`, `order_items`, `products`.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 12_fundamentals_capstone ex3`

## Exercise 4 — "Did our Q3 signups convert?"

> *From: Growth. "We spent a lot acquiring people in Q3. How many of them
> never actually bought anything? Give me the list, I want to email them."*

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Customers whose **`created_at` falls in Q3 2023**
(same half-open range as above) and who have **never** placed an order at
all — not "no orders in Q3", none ever. Read that sentence twice; it is the
kind of distinction the requester did not realise they were making.

Columns: `id`, `name`. Any row order.

Two lessons compose: a date range on `customers`, and an anti-join to
`orders`. Any of the three anti-join idioms is fine.

Run: `uv run dojo test 12_fundamentals_capstone ex4`

## Exercise 5 — "Show me the trend, not the total"

> *From: CFO, again. "The quarterly number is fine but I can't see the
> shape. Give me paid revenue by month for calendar 2023, in order, with
> the order counts next to it."*

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. For **paid** orders created in calendar year 2023
(`>= '2023-01-01'` and `< '2024-01-01'`), one row per calendar month.

Columns in this order: `month` (the month truncated with
`date_trunc('month', created_at)`), `orders` (count), `revenue` (sum of
`total`). **Ordered by month ascending.**

Expect 11 rows, not 12 — the data stops on 2023-11-14. A trend report that
silently ends early is a reporting bug you should be able to *see* coming;
this is what a partial period looks like.

Run: `uv run dojo test 12_fundamentals_capstone ex5`

## Exercise 6 — "What were our five best sellers in Q3?"

> *From: Merchandising. "Top five products by units sold last quarter —
> real orders only, same definition as before. Name and category."*

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Across `orders` → `order_items` → `products`, for
orders whose `status` is `'paid'` or `'shipped'` **and** whose `created_at`
falls in Q3 2023, return the five products with the most units sold.

Columns in this order: `id` (the product's), `name`, `category`, `units`
(sum of `quantity`). **Ordered by `units` descending, tie-broken by `id`
ascending, exactly 5 rows.**

"Same definition as before" is the requester assuming you remember what
they meant by *real orders* in exercise 2 and 3. They will not always be
this consistent — write the definition down where the query can be read.

Run: `uv run dojo test 12_fundamentals_capstone ex6`

## Spaced review

`review1/`: revenue per customer country for **paid** orders in Q3 2023 —
columns `country`, `revenue`, any order. (Joins `customers` to `orders`;
12 rows.)

# Reading - 12_fundamentals_capstone

Part 1 is over. The SQL in this capstone is nothing you have not already
written; what is new is that nobody told you which tables to use. That
translation step — from a sentence a human said to a query with a defensible
definition in it — is the actual job.

## Notes

**Every one of these requests contained a hidden definition.** "Real
revenue" meant paid and shipped, and the requester did not think that needed
saying. "Never bought anything" could mean *never*, or *not in the period* —
two different queries, both defensible, one of them wrong for this request.
"Last quarter" means one thing on July 1st and another on October 1st. The
single most valuable question a data person asks is **"what exactly
counts?"**, and it is asked before writing SQL, not after the number is
questioned.

**Half-open ranges, permanently.** `created_at >= '2023-07-01' AND
created_at < '2023-10-01'` is correct; `BETWEEN '2023-07-01' AND
'2023-09-30'` silently excludes almost all of September 30th, because a bare
date is midnight. Half-open ranges also compose without gaps or overlaps —
consecutive quarters tile the timeline exactly — which is why every date
filter in this course is written that way. Lesson 18 makes the timezone
version of this argument.

**Aggregates over joins need the grain checked, every time.** In ex6 the
join to `order_items` multiplies each order by its line count, which is
exactly what you want because you are summing line quantities. Sum
`o.total` over that same join and you would count each order once per line
and report revenue inflated by the average basket size. The rule from lesson
08 in one sentence: *know how many rows one input row became before you
aggregate*.

**Report the denominator.** A "top five products" list is meaningless
without the population it was drawn from, and a churn list is meaningless
without the cohort size. When you hand a stakeholder a list, hand them the
count it came out of too. This is not politeness — it is the cheapest
possible defence against a filter bug, for you and for them.

**Partial periods are permanent.** The data ends on 2023-11-14, so November
is a partial month and the trend line drops. Real data does this constantly:
the current month is always partial, and a chart that does not say so
produces a "why is revenue collapsing?" meeting every month. Label them or
exclude them, but never ship them unmarked.

**A note on naming.** `sum(total) AS revenue` is a claim. Somebody will read
that column name and act on it without reading the `WHERE` clause. If the
definition is contested — and revenue always is — encode it in the name
(`paid_revenue`), or put it in a view (lesson 27) where the definition lives
in exactly one place and everyone who disagrees has one thing to argue with.

## ex1 — "How did Q3 go, by status?"

A filter, a group, an order. The interesting part is the shape of the
answer: four rows including `cancelled`, which is revenue that did not
happen. Leaving cancelled orders in a "revenue by status" table is right —
the reader can see what they are excluding. Silently dropping them is what
produces two reports that disagree.

## ex2 — "Who are our whales?"

A join, a filtered aggregate, a top-N. Note the tie-break on `id`: without
it, two customers with identical lifetime spend swap places between runs and
someone eventually notices. Every ordered report needs a total order
(lesson 03).

"Lifetime" is the other buried definition here. It means *all* qualifying
orders regardless of date — so no date filter — which is a decision the
request made in a single word. Had they said "top customers this year" the
same query with one extra condition answers a different business question,
and the two lists will not have the same people on them.

## ex3 — "What actually sells?"

Three tables, and the revenue definition uses the line item's own price
rather than the product's current price. That is the historical snapshot
decision from lesson 08 — using `p.price` here would silently rewrite last
quarter's revenue every time someone edited the catalogue.

## ex4 — "Did our Q3 signups convert?"

The ambiguity exercise. "Never bought anything" is unqualified in the
request and qualified in the prompt, and the two readings produce different
lists. In real life you go and ask. When you cannot ask, you write down
which reading you used, next to the number.

## ex5 — "Show me the trend, not the total"

`date_trunc` plus `GROUP BY` plus `ORDER BY` — and eleven rows where a
reader expects twelve. Notice also that this query cannot show a month with
*zero* paid orders: `GROUP BY` produces rows only for groups that exist, so
an empty month vanishes rather than appearing as zero. Fixing that needs
`generate_series` and a `LEFT JOIN` (lessons 18 and 09 combined), and it is
one of the most common real reporting requirements there is.

## ex6 — "What were our five best sellers in Q3?"

The full Part 1 stack in one query: three-table join, two filters, group,
aggregate, order, limit — plus the functional-dependency shortcut of
grouping by `p.id` alone and still selecting `p.name` and `p.category`,
which PostgreSQL allows because `p.id` is the primary key.

## review1 — revenue per country

The same shape as ex1 with the grouping key on the other side of a join.
When this comes back, check that you filtered orders and grouped customers,
not the reverse.

Twelve rows, one per country — which means every country had at least one
paid Q3 order. If one had not, it would be missing from the result entirely
rather than showing zero, and a bar chart drawn from this would quietly have
eleven bars. By now that should be a reflex: `GROUP BY` reports the groups
that exist, never the groups that should.

## Further reading

- [Date/Time Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) — `date_trunc`, intervals, and the comparison rules that make half-open ranges work. Preview of lesson 18.
- [`generate_series`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-srf.html) — how to produce the periods that `GROUP BY` cannot invent, so an empty month shows as zero.
- [Query Evaluation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — worth one more read now that you have used every clause in it.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Top-N Queries](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/partial-results/top-n-queries) — what ex6's `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 5` costs today, and what Part 5 will do about it.

# Reading - 12_fundamentals_capstone

Part 1 is over. The SQL in this capstone is nothing you have not already
written; what is new is that nobody told you which tables to use. That
translation step — from a sentence a human said to a query with a defensible
definition in it — is the actual job.

## Notes

**Every one of these requests contained a hidden definition.** "Real
revenue" meant paid and shipped, and the requester did not think that needed
saying. "Never bought anything" could mean *never*, or *not in the period* —
two different queries, both defensible, one of them wrong for this request.
"Last quarter" means one thing on July 1st and another on October 1st. The
single most valuable question a data person asks is **"what exactly
counts?"**, and it is asked before writing SQL, not after the number is
questioned.

**Half-open ranges, permanently.** `created_at >= '2023-07-01' AND
created_at < '2023-10-01'` is correct; `BETWEEN '2023-07-01' AND
'2023-09-30'` silently excludes almost all of September 30th, because a bare
date is midnight. Half-open ranges also compose without gaps or overlaps —
consecutive quarters tile the timeline exactly — which is why every date
filter in this course is written that way. Lesson 18 makes the timezone
version of this argument.

**Aggregates over joins need the grain checked, every time.** In ex6 the
join to `order_items` multiplies each order by its line count, which is
exactly what you want because you are summing line quantities. Sum
`o.total` over that same join and you would count each order once per line
and report revenue inflated by the average basket size. The rule from lesson
08 in one sentence: *know how many rows one input row became before you
aggregate*.

**Report the denominator.** A "top five products" list is meaningless
without the population it was drawn from, and a churn list is meaningless
without the cohort size. When you hand a stakeholder a list, hand them the
count it came out of too. This is not politeness — it is the cheapest
possible defence against a filter bug, for you and for them.

**Partial periods are permanent.** The data ends on 2023-11-14, so November
is a partial month and the trend line drops. Real data does this constantly:
the current month is always partial, and a chart that does not say so
produces a "why is revenue collapsing?" meeting every month. Label them or
exclude them, but never ship them unmarked.

**A note on naming.** `sum(total) AS revenue` is a claim. Somebody will read
that column name and act on it without reading the `WHERE` clause. If the
definition is contested — and revenue always is — encode it in the name
(`paid_revenue`), or put it in a view (lesson 27) where the definition lives
in exactly one place and everyone who disagrees has one thing to argue with.

## ex1 — "How did Q3 go, by status?"

A filter, a group, an order. The interesting part is the shape of the
answer: four rows including `cancelled`, which is revenue that did not
happen. Leaving cancelled orders in a "revenue by status" table is right —
the reader can see what they are excluding. Silently dropping them is what
produces two reports that disagree.

## ex2 — "Who are our whales?"

A join, a filtered aggregate, a top-N. Note the tie-break on `id`: without
it, two customers with identical lifetime spend swap places between runs and
someone eventually notices. Every ordered report needs a total order
(lesson 03).

"Lifetime" is the other buried definition here. It means *all* qualifying
orders regardless of date — so no date filter — which is a decision the
request made in a single word. Had they said "top customers this year" the
same query with one extra condition answers a different business question,
and the two lists will not have the same people on them.

## ex3 — "What actually sells?"

Three tables, and the revenue definition uses the line item's own price
rather than the product's current price. That is the historical snapshot
decision from lesson 08 — using `p.price` here would silently rewrite last
quarter's revenue every time someone edited the catalogue.

## ex4 — "Did our Q3 signups convert?"

The ambiguity exercise. "Never bought anything" is unqualified in the
request and qualified in the prompt, and the two readings produce different
lists. In real life you go and ask. When you cannot ask, you write down
which reading you used, next to the number.

## ex5 — "Show me the trend, not the total"

`date_trunc` plus `GROUP BY` plus `ORDER BY` — and eleven rows where a
reader expects twelve. Notice also that this query cannot show a month with
*zero* paid orders: `GROUP BY` produces rows only for groups that exist, so
an empty month vanishes rather than appearing as zero. Fixing that needs
`generate_series` and a `LEFT JOIN` (lessons 18 and 09 combined), and it is
one of the most common real reporting requirements there is.

## ex6 — "What were our five best sellers in Q3?"

The full Part 1 stack in one query: three-table join, two filters, group,
aggregate, order, limit — plus the functional-dependency shortcut of
grouping by `p.id` alone and still selecting `p.name` and `p.category`,
which PostgreSQL allows because `p.id` is the primary key.

## review1 — revenue per country

The same shape as ex1 with the grouping key on the other side of a join.
When this comes back, check that you filtered orders and grouped customers,
not the reverse.

Twelve rows, one per country — which means every country had at least one
paid Q3 order. If one had not, it would be missing from the result entirely
rather than showing zero, and a bar chart drawn from this would quietly have
eleven bars. By now that should be a reflex: `GROUP BY` reports the groups
that exist, never the groups that should.

## Further reading

- [Date/Time Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) — `date_trunc`, intervals, and the comparison rules that make half-open ranges work. Preview of lesson 18.
- [`generate_series`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-srf.html) — how to produce the periods that `GROUP BY` cannot invent, so an empty month shows as zero.
- [Query Evaluation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — worth one more read now that you have used every clause in it.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Top-N Queries](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/partial-results/top-n-queries) — what ex6's `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 5` costs today, and what Part 5 will do about it.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Join orders to customers, keep status IN ('paid','shipped'), group by
customer id and name, order by the sum descending with the id tie-break,
LIMIT 10. (Grouping by both id and name is legal and standard — the id
already determines the name.)

## Hint 2
```sql
SELECT c.id, c.name, sum(o.total) AS spend
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status IN ('paid', 'shipped')
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY spend DESC, c.id
LIMIT 10;
```

## Hint 1
Join orders to customers, keep status IN ('paid','shipped'), group by
customer id and name, order by the sum descending with the id tie-break,
LIMIT 10. (Grouping by both id and name is legal and standard — the id
already determines the name.)

## Hint 2
```sql
SELECT c.id, c.name, sum(o.total) AS spend
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status IN ('paid', 'shipped')
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY spend DESC, c.id
LIMIT 10;
```

ORDER BY spend DESC, c.id
LIMIT 10;

## Hint 1
The signup-date filter is about `customers`; the "never ordered" part
is an anti-join to `orders`. Both conditions are on the left table's
population, so a LEFT JOIN with `o.id IS NULL` works.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE c.created_at >= '2023-07-01'
  AND c.created_at <  '2023-10-01'
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.created_at >= '2023-07-01'
  AND c.created_at <  '2023-10-01'
  AND o.id IS NULL;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — "Show me the trend, not the total"

> *From: CFO, again. "The quarterly number is fine but I can't see the
> shape. Give me paid revenue by month for calendar 2023, in order, with
> the order counts next to it."*

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. For **paid** orders created in calendar year 2023
(`>= '2023-01-01'` and `< '2024-01-01'`), one row per calendar month.

Columns in this order: `month` (the month truncated with
`date_trunc('month', created_at)`), `orders` (count), `revenue` (sum of
`total`). **Ordered by month ascending.**

Expect 11 rows, not 12 — the data stops on 2023-11-14. A trend report that
silently ends early is a reporting bug you should be able to *see* coming;
this is what a partial period looks like.

Run: `uv run dojo test 12_fundamentals_capstone ex5`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Group by the same `date_trunc(...)` expression you select. PostgreSQL
also accepts `GROUP BY 1` (the first SELECT-list item) and
`GROUP BY month` (the output alias).

## Hint 2
`SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month, count(*), sum(total) FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' AND created_at >= '2023-01-01' AND created_at < '2024-01-01' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;`

lessons.briefing:
# 13 — Subqueries

You've already smuggled two subqueries past customs: lesson 05's `NOT IN
(SELECT manager_id ...)` and lesson 06's scalar KPIs. Part 2 starts by
making them official. A subquery is a complete query used as a *value*, a
*list*, or a *test* inside another query — and choosing which of the three
you're writing is most of the skill.

## Concept

**Scalar** — returns one value; usable anywhere a value goes:

```sql
SELECT id, name, price
FROM products
WHERE price > (SELECT avg(price) FROM products);
```

**List** — returns one column; feeds `IN` / `NOT IN`:

```sql
WHERE id IN (SELECT order_id FROM order_items WHERE quantity = 5)
```

**Correlated** — mentions the outer row, so it conceptually re-runs per
row (you met one in lesson 03's challenge):

```sql
WHERE o.created_at = (SELECT max(o2.created_at)
                      FROM orders o2
                      WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id)
```

**EXISTS / NOT EXISTS** — the test form: "does at least one such row
exist?" It returns true/false, never NULL, and doesn't care what you
SELECT inside (the conventional `SELECT 1` signals "presence only"):

```sql
SELECT c.id FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);
```

This is the third anti-join you've met (lesson 09's LEFT-JOIN-IS-NULL,
lesson 11's EXCEPT) — and the one to reach for by default: unlike
`NOT IN` it is **immune to lesson 05's NULL trap**, because each row's
test is a plain exists-check, not a comparison with a possibly-NULL list
element.

## Exercise 1 — above-average products (scalar)

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Every product priced strictly above the average
product price. Columns: `id`, `name`, `price`. Any order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 13_subqueries ex1`

## Exercise 2 — orders containing a luxury item (list)

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Every order that includes at least one product
priced over 490. Columns: `id`, `total`. Any order. Use `IN` with a
subquery that joins `order_items` to `products`. (No DISTINCT needed —
`IN` never duplicates outer rows, which is itself worth remembering: a
plain JOIN here *would* duplicate orders containing two luxury items.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 13_subqueries ex2`

## Exercise 3 — NOT EXISTS anti-join

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Spanish (`'ES'`) customers who have never placed
an order. Columns: `id`, `name`. Any order. Use `NOT EXISTS` this time —
same rows as lesson 09's pattern, sturdier idiom.

Run: `uv run dojo test 13_subqueries ex3`

## Exercise 4 — EXISTS, the positive form

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Support wants to call the French customers who
have had an order **cancelled**: every customer in `'FR'` for whom at
least one `orders` row exists with status `'cancelled'`.

Columns: `id`, `name`. Any order.

Exercise 3 used `NOT EXISTS`; this is the same construct without the
negation. Two things to notice. `EXISTS` stops at the first matching row —
it is a *test*, not a count, so the database can abandon the search
immediately. And it never duplicates the outer row: a customer with nine
cancelled orders appears exactly once, where a join would list them nine
times and force you to bolt on a `DISTINCT`.

Run: `uv run dojo test 13_subqueries ex4`

## Exercise 5 — a subquery in the SELECT list

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. The account-management dashboard shows the first
twenty customers with their order counts. For every customer with `id <=
20`, return `id`, `name`, and their number of orders aliased **`orders`** —
computed with a **correlated scalar subquery** in the SELECT list, not a
join.

Three columns, twenty rows, any order.

A scalar subquery in the SELECT list runs conceptually once per outer row
and must return exactly one row and one column — return two rows and
PostgreSQL raises an error at runtime, which is a real hazard of the form.
Its virtue is that it cannot change the outer row count: twenty customers
in, twenty rows out, guaranteed, with no grain question to answer.

Run: `uv run dojo test 13_subqueries ex5`

## Exercise 6 — a subquery in FROM (the derived table)

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Finance wants the customers whose **real
lifetime revenue** (orders with status `'paid'` or `'shipped'`) exceeds
**20,000**.

Columns: `customer_id`, `revenue`. Any order.

You cannot filter on `sum(total) > 20000` in `WHERE` — the sum does not
exist yet — and `HAVING` would work, but this exercise wants the fourth
kind of subquery: one in the **`FROM`** clause. Aggregate in a parenthesised
query, give it an alias, and treat the result as a table you can filter:

```sql
FROM (SELECT ... GROUP BY ...) AS per_customer
WHERE revenue > 20000
```

A derived table must have an alias — PostgreSQL insists. This is exactly
what a CTE (lesson 14) does with a nicer name, and being able to read both
matters because you will meet both.

Run: `uv run dojo test 13_subqueries ex6`

## Challenge — latest order per customer (correlated)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. For customers with `id <= 10`, their most
recent order: `customer_id`, order `id`, `created_at`. Any order. The
correlated pattern from the concept section is the intended tool: an
order qualifies if its `created_at` equals the max for *that customer*.
(Customers 1–10 all have orders, and no customer has two orders on the
same timestamp — the seed guarantees both.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 13_subqueries challenge`

## Spaced review

`review1/`: staff earning strictly more than **their own department's**
average salary — columns `id`, `name`, any order. (Correlated scalar:
the inner query averages the *outer row's* department.)
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 13_subqueries

A subquery is a query used as a value, a list, a table, or a test. Choosing
which of the four you are writing is most of the skill — and the choice is
about *stating intent*, because PostgreSQL's planner will rewrite most of
them into the same handful of physical operations anyway.

## Notes

**The four shapes.**

- **Scalar** — returns one row, one column. Usable anywhere a value is:
  `WHERE price > (SELECT avg(price) FROM products)`, or in the SELECT list.
  If it returns more than one row at runtime, the query *errors* — which
  makes it fragile if the data can change shape.
- **List** — returns one column, feeding `IN` / `NOT IN` / `ANY` / `ALL`.
- **Table (derived table)** — returns rows and columns, sits in `FROM`, and
  must be aliased. This is a CTE without the name.
- **Test** — `EXISTS` / `NOT EXISTS`, returning a boolean and nothing else.

**Correlated versus uncorrelated.** An uncorrelated subquery does not
mention the outer query and can be evaluated once. A correlated one refers
to a column of the outer row, so *conceptually* it re-runs per row. The word
"conceptually" is load-bearing: PostgreSQL usually rewrites correlated
`EXISTS` and `IN` into semi-joins and hash joins, so the quadratic mental
model is not the physical reality. Trust the `EXPLAIN`, not the intuition —
Part 5 will show you the rewrite happening.

**`EXISTS` is the anti-join to reach for.** You now know three:

| idiom | NULL-safe? | can return right-side columns? |
|---|---|---|
| `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE r.key IS NULL` | yes | yes |
| `EXCEPT` | yes (NULLs compare equal) | no |
| `NOT EXISTS` | yes | no |
| `NOT IN (subquery)` | **no** | no |

`NOT IN` is the only broken one, and lesson 05 explains why. `NOT EXISTS`
is the default because it says what it means, it short-circuits, and no
future nullable column can break it.

**`EXISTS` never fans out.** This is its other quiet virtue. A join to a
one-to-many table duplicates the outer row per match, which is why so much
real-world SQL has a `DISTINCT` bolted onto it. `EXISTS` asks a yes/no
question and returns the outer row once. When you see `SELECT DISTINCT`
sitting on top of a join whose right-hand columns are never selected, the
query wanted `EXISTS`.

**`IN` versus `EXISTS` versus `= ANY`.** `x IN (subquery)` and `x = ANY
(subquery)` are the same thing. `EXISTS` is more general because the
correlation condition can be anything — an inequality, several columns, a
range overlap — not just equality on one column.

**Scalar subqueries in the SELECT list are convenient and dangerous.** Three
of them means three correlated lookups per row; on a large outer set that is
a real cost, and the equivalent `LEFT JOIN ... GROUP BY` or a window function
(lesson 15) is usually faster. Their advantage is that they cannot change
the outer row count, which makes them safe when you are nervous about grain.

**Where a subquery may not go.** You cannot use a bare aggregate in `WHERE`,
and you cannot reference a SELECT-list alias there either — both because of
the evaluation order from lesson 07. The derived table exists precisely to
give you a place to stand: compute in an inner query, filter in the outer
one.

## ex1 — above-average products (scalar)

`(SELECT avg(price) FROM products)` is uncorrelated, so it is computed once
and compared against every row. Notice the shape of the answer: fewer than
half the products are above average, because the price distribution is not
symmetric. "Above average" is a phrase stakeholders use loosely and it very
rarely means "the median".

## ex2 — orders containing a luxury item (list)

The `IN` form avoids a fan-out that a join would create: an order with three
products over 490 appears once here and three times with a naive join. The
prompt calls this out and it is worth internalising — most `SELECT DISTINCT`
in the wild is compensating for a join that should have been an `IN` or an
`EXISTS`.

## ex3 — NOT EXISTS anti-join

Same rows as lesson 09's `LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL`, sturdier idiom. Run both
through `dojo plan` when you reach Part 5: PostgreSQL executes both as an
anti-join, so the choice really is about the reader, not the machine.

Sturdier in a specific sense worth naming. The `LEFT JOIN` version breaks if
somebody later tests the wrong column for NULL — a nullable data column
instead of the key — and the `NOT IN` version breaks if the inner column
ever becomes nullable. `NOT EXISTS` has no column to get wrong and no NULL
to be poisoned by. Idioms that cannot be subtly mis-edited are worth
preferring even when all three work today.

## ex4 — EXISTS, the positive form

Short-circuiting and no fan-out, in one query. The `SELECT 1` convention is
worth explaining once: `EXISTS` discards the subquery's output entirely, so
`SELECT 1`, `SELECT *`, and `SELECT 1/0` are all equivalent — the last one
genuinely does not raise, because the expression is never evaluated. Writing
`SELECT 1` signals to a human reader that presence is all you want.

## ex5 — a subquery in the SELECT list

Twenty correlated counts. The form's guarantee — the outer row count cannot
change — is the reason people reach for it, and its cost is the reason
people regret it at scale. When you find yourself writing three of these in
one SELECT list, that is a `LEFT JOIN ... GROUP BY` trying to be born, or a
window function (lesson 15) that would compute all three in one pass.

## ex6 — a subquery in FROM (the derived table)

The shape that unlocks "filter on an aggregate you just computed". Note that
`HAVING sum(total) > 20000` answers this exercise too, in fewer lines — the
derived table earns its keep when the outer query needs to do more than
filter (join the result to something, window over it, aggregate it again).
Lesson 14 gives this exact construct a name and turns nesting into a
readable pipeline.

## challenge — latest order per customer (correlated)

The correlated `max()` pattern, and it is worth knowing that this is the
*old* way. It re-derives the maximum per customer, and it breaks subtly when
two orders share a timestamp (you get both). Lesson 15 does it with
`row_number()` and one pass; lesson 49 does it with `DISTINCT ON` in three
lines. Writing it the hard way first is what makes those land.

## review1 — above your department's average

A correlated scalar in `WHERE`: the inner `avg` depends on the outer row's
department. This is the canonical "compare a row to its group" question, and
it is exactly what `avg(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department)` does in one
pass in lesson 15. Two lessons from now you will be able to see why the
window version is both clearer and cheaper.

## Further reading

- [Subquery Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) — `EXISTS`, `IN`, `NOT IN`, `ANY`/`SOME`, `ALL`, and the row-constructor forms. The NULL notes here are the whole of lesson 05 restated.
- [Table Expressions — subqueries in FROM](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — derived tables, why they need an alias, and how `LATERAL` lifts the restriction on referring to earlier FROM items (lesson 48).
- [Scalar Subqueries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html) — the one-row-one-column rule and where such a subquery may appear.
- [`WITH` Queries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) — the same power with names attached, plus the inlining rules that matter for performance. Lesson 14.

# 13 — Subqueries

You've already smuggled two subqueries past customs: lesson 05's `NOT IN
(SELECT manager_id ...)` and lesson 06's scalar KPIs. Part 2 starts by
making them official. A subquery is a complete query used as a *value*, a
*list*, or a *test* inside another query — and choosing which of the three
you're writing is most of the skill.

## Concept

**Scalar** — returns one value; usable anywhere a value goes:

```sql
SELECT id, name, price
FROM products
WHERE price > (SELECT avg(price) FROM products);
```

**List** — returns one column; feeds `IN` / `NOT IN`:

```sql
WHERE id IN (SELECT order_id FROM order_items WHERE quantity = 5)
```

**Correlated** — mentions the outer row, so it conceptually re-runs per
row (you met one in lesson 03's challenge):

```sql
WHERE o.created_at = (SELECT max(o2.created_at)
                      FROM orders o2
                      WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id)
```

**EXISTS / NOT EXISTS** — the test form: "does at least one such row
exist?" It returns true/false, never NULL, and doesn't care what you
SELECT inside (the conventional `SELECT 1` signals "presence only"):

```sql
SELECT c.id FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);
```

This is the third anti-join you've met (lesson 09's LEFT-JOIN-IS-NULL,
lesson 11's EXCEPT) — and the one to reach for by default: unlike
`NOT IN` it is **immune to lesson 05's NULL trap**, because each row's
test is a plain exists-check, not a comparison with a possibly-NULL list
element.

## Exercise 1 — above-average products (scalar)

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Every product priced strictly above the average
product price. Columns: `id`, `name`, `price`. Any order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 13_subqueries ex1`

## Exercise 2 — orders containing a luxury item (list)

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Every order that includes at least one product
priced over 490. Columns: `id`, `total`. Any order. Use `IN` with a
subquery that joins `order_items` to `products`. (No DISTINCT needed —
`IN` never duplicates outer rows, which is itself worth remembering: a
plain JOIN here *would* duplicate orders containing two luxury items.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 13_subqueries ex2`

## Exercise 3 — NOT EXISTS anti-join

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Spanish (`'ES'`) customers who have never placed
an order. Columns: `id`, `name`. Any order. Use `NOT EXISTS` this time —
same rows as lesson 09's pattern, sturdier idiom.

Run: `uv run dojo test 13_subqueries ex3`

## Exercise 4 — EXISTS, the positive form

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Support wants to call the French customers who
have had an order **cancelled**: every customer in `'FR'` for whom at
least one `orders` row exists with status `'cancelled'`.

Columns: `id`, `name`. Any order.

Exercise 3 used `NOT EXISTS`; this is the same construct without the
negation. Two things to notice. `EXISTS` stops at the first matching row —
it is a *test*, not a count, so the database can abandon the search
immediately. And it never duplicates the outer row: a customer with nine
cancelled orders appears exactly once, where a join would list them nine
times and force you to bolt on a `DISTINCT`.

Run: `uv run dojo test 13_subqueries ex4`

## Exercise 5 — a subquery in the SELECT list

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. The account-management dashboard shows the first
twenty customers with their order counts. For every customer with `id <=
20`, return `id`, `name`, and their number of orders aliased **`orders`** —
computed with a **correlated scalar subquery** in the SELECT list, not a
join.

Three columns, twenty rows, any order.

A scalar subquery in the SELECT list runs conceptually once per outer row
and must return exactly one row and one column — return two rows and
PostgreSQL raises an error at runtime, which is a real hazard of the form.
Its virtue is that it cannot change the outer row count: twenty customers
in, twenty rows out, guaranteed, with no grain question to answer.

Run: `uv run dojo test 13_subqueries ex5`

## Exercise 6 — a subquery in FROM (the derived table)

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Finance wants the customers whose **real
lifetime revenue** (orders with status `'paid'` or `'shipped'`) exceeds
**20,000**.

Columns: `customer_id`, `revenue`. Any order.

You cannot filter on `sum(total) > 20000` in `WHERE` — the sum does not
exist yet — and `HAVING` would work, but this exercise wants the fourth
kind of subquery: one in the **`FROM`** clause. Aggregate in a parenthesised
query, give it an alias, and treat the result as a table you can filter:

```sql
FROM (SELECT ... GROUP BY ...) AS per_customer
WHERE revenue > 20000
```

A derived table must have an alias — PostgreSQL insists. This is exactly
what a CTE (lesson 14) does with a nicer name, and being able to read both
matters because you will meet both.

Run: `uv run dojo test 13_subqueries ex6`

## Challenge — latest order per customer (correlated)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. For customers with `id <= 10`, their most
recent order: `customer_id`, order `id`, `created_at`. Any order. The
correlated pattern from the concept section is the intended tool: an
order qualifies if its `created_at` equals the max for *that customer*.
(Customers 1–10 all have orders, and no customer has two orders on the
same timestamp — the seed guarantees both.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 13_subqueries challenge`

## Spaced review

`review1/`: staff earning strictly more than **their own department's**
average salary — columns `id`, `name`, any order. (Correlated scalar:
the inner query averages the *outer row's* department.)

## The teaching point

Subquery-vs-join is rarely about performance — PostgreSQL's planner
rewrites most IN/EXISTS forms into joins internally (you'll watch it do
so in Part 5's plans). It's about *stating intent*: EXISTS says "I'm
testing presence", IN says "membership in this list", a scalar comparison
says "against this one number". Write the form that reads as the
question; let the planner pick the algorithm.
