# Reading - 13_subqueries

A subquery is a query used as a value, a list, a table, or a test. Choosing
which of the four you are writing is most of the skill — and the choice is
about *stating intent*, because PostgreSQL's planner will rewrite most of
them into the same handful of physical operations anyway.

## Notes

**The four shapes.**

- **Scalar** — returns one row, one column. Usable anywhere a value is:
  `WHERE price > (SELECT avg(price) FROM products)`, or in the SELECT list.
  If it returns more than one row at runtime, the query *errors* — which
  makes it fragile if the data can change shape.
- **List** — returns one column, feeding `IN` / `NOT IN` / `ANY` / `ALL`.
- **Table (derived table)** — returns rows and columns, sits in `FROM`, and
  must be aliased. This is a CTE without the name.
- **Test** — `EXISTS` / `NOT EXISTS`, returning a boolean and nothing else.

**Correlated versus uncorrelated.** An uncorrelated subquery does not
mention the outer query and can be evaluated once. A correlated one refers
to a column of the outer row, so *conceptually* it re-runs per row. The word
"conceptually" is load-bearing: PostgreSQL usually rewrites correlated
`EXISTS` and `IN` into semi-joins and hash joins, so the quadratic mental
model is not the physical reality. Trust the `EXPLAIN`, not the intuition —
Part 5 will show you the rewrite happening.

**`EXISTS` is the anti-join to reach for.** You now know three:

| idiom | NULL-safe? | can return right-side columns? |
|---|---|---|
| `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE r.key IS NULL` | yes | yes |
| `EXCEPT` | yes (NULLs compare equal) | no |
| `NOT EXISTS` | yes | no |
| `NOT IN (subquery)` | **no** | no |

`NOT IN` is the only broken one, and lesson 05 explains why. `NOT EXISTS`
is the default because it says what it means, it short-circuits, and no
future nullable column can break it.

**`EXISTS` never fans out.** This is its other quiet virtue. A join to a
one-to-many table duplicates the outer row per match, which is why so much
real-world SQL has a `DISTINCT` bolted onto it. `EXISTS` asks a yes/no
question and returns the outer row once. When you see `SELECT DISTINCT`
sitting on top of a join whose right-hand columns are never selected, the
query wanted `EXISTS`.

**`IN` versus `EXISTS` versus `= ANY`.** `x IN (subquery)` and `x = ANY
(subquery)` are the same thing. `EXISTS` is more general because the
correlation condition can be anything — an inequality, several columns, a
range overlap — not just equality on one column.

**Scalar subqueries in the SELECT list are convenient and dangerous.** Three
of them means three correlated lookups per row; on a large outer set that is
a real cost, and the equivalent `LEFT JOIN ... GROUP BY` or a window function
(lesson 15) is usually faster. Their advantage is that they cannot change
the outer row count, which makes them safe when you are nervous about grain.

**Where a subquery may not go.** You cannot use a bare aggregate in `WHERE`,
and you cannot reference a SELECT-list alias there either — both because of
the evaluation order from lesson 07. The derived table exists precisely to
give you a place to stand: compute in an inner query, filter in the outer
one.

## ex1 — above-average products (scalar)

`(SELECT avg(price) FROM products)` is uncorrelated, so it is computed once
and compared against every row. Notice the shape of the answer: fewer than
half the products are above average, because the price distribution is not
symmetric. "Above average" is a phrase stakeholders use loosely and it very
rarely means "the median".

## ex2 — orders containing a luxury item (list)

The `IN` form avoids a fan-out that a join would create: an order with three
products over 490 appears once here and three times with a naive join. The
prompt calls this out and it is worth internalising — most `SELECT DISTINCT`
in the wild is compensating for a join that should have been an `IN` or an
`EXISTS`.

## ex3 — NOT EXISTS anti-join

Same rows as lesson 09's `LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL`, sturdier idiom. Run both
through `dojo plan` when you reach Part 5: PostgreSQL executes both as an
anti-join, so the choice really is about the reader, not the machine.

Sturdier in a specific sense worth naming. The `LEFT JOIN` version breaks if
somebody later tests the wrong column for NULL — a nullable data column
instead of the key — and the `NOT IN` version breaks if the inner column
ever becomes nullable. `NOT EXISTS` has no column to get wrong and no NULL
to be poisoned by. Idioms that cannot be subtly mis-edited are worth
preferring even when all three work today.

## ex4 — EXISTS, the positive form

Short-circuiting and no fan-out, in one query. The `SELECT 1` convention is
worth explaining once: `EXISTS` discards the subquery's output entirely, so
`SELECT 1`, `SELECT *`, and `SELECT 1/0` are all equivalent — the last one
genuinely does not raise, because the expression is never evaluated. Writing
`SELECT 1` signals to a human reader that presence is all you want.

## ex5 — a subquery in the SELECT list

Twenty correlated counts. The form's guarantee — the outer row count cannot
change — is the reason people reach for it, and its cost is the reason
people regret it at scale. When you find yourself writing three of these in
one SELECT list, that is a `LEFT JOIN ... GROUP BY` trying to be born, or a
window function (lesson 15) that would compute all three in one pass.

## ex6 — a subquery in FROM (the derived table)

The shape that unlocks "filter on an aggregate you just computed". Note that
`HAVING sum(total) > 20000` answers this exercise too, in fewer lines — the
derived table earns its keep when the outer query needs to do more than
filter (join the result to something, window over it, aggregate it again).
Lesson 14 gives this exact construct a name and turns nesting into a
readable pipeline.

## challenge — latest order per customer (correlated)

The correlated `max()` pattern, and it is worth knowing that this is the
*old* way. It re-derives the maximum per customer, and it breaks subtly when
two orders share a timestamp (you get both). Lesson 15 does it with
`row_number()` and one pass; lesson 49 does it with `DISTINCT ON` in three
lines. Writing it the hard way first is what makes those land.

## review1 — above your department's average

A correlated scalar in `WHERE`: the inner `avg` depends on the outer row's
department. This is the canonical "compare a row to its group" question, and
it is exactly what `avg(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department)` does in one
pass in lesson 15. Two lessons from now you will be able to see why the
window version is both clearer and cheaper.

## Further reading

- [Subquery Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) — `EXISTS`, `IN`, `NOT IN`, `ANY`/`SOME`, `ALL`, and the row-constructor forms. The NULL notes here are the whole of lesson 05 restated.
- [Table Expressions — subqueries in FROM](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — derived tables, why they need an alias, and how `LATERAL` lifts the restriction on referring to earlier FROM items (lesson 48).
- [Scalar Subqueries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html) — the one-row-one-column rule and where such a subquery may appear.
- [`WITH` Queries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) — the same power with names attached, plus the inlining rules that matter for performance. Lesson 14.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — latest order per customer (correlated)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. For customers with `id <= 10`, their most
recent order: `customer_id`, order `id`, `created_at`. Any order. The
correlated pattern from the concept section is the intended tool: an
order qualifies if its `created_at` equals the max for *that customer*.
(Customers 1–10 all have orders, and no customer has two orders on the
same timestamp — the seed guarantees both.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 13_subqueries challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Outer: orders, filtered to customer_id <= 10. Condition: this order's
created_at equals the maximum created_at *among this customer's orders* —
the inner query must reference the outer order's customer_id.

## Hint 2
```sql
SELECT o.customer_id, o.id, o.created_at
FROM orders o
WHERE o.customer_id <= 10
  AND o.created_at = (SELECT max(o2.created_at)
                      FROM orders o2
                      WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id);
```

Lesson 15 solves this family with `row_number()` — compare once you get
there.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — EXISTS, the positive form

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Support wants to call the French customers who
have had an order **cancelled**: every customer in `'FR'` for whom at
least one `orders` row exists with status `'cancelled'`.

Columns: `id`, `name`. Any order.

Exercise 3 used `NOT EXISTS`; this is the same construct without the
negation. Two things to notice. `EXISTS` stops at the first matching row —
it is a *test*, not a count, so the database can abandon the search
immediately. And it never duplicates the outer row: a customer with nine
cancelled orders appears exactly once, where a join would list them nine
times and force you to bolt on a `DISTINCT`.

Run: `uv run dojo test 13_subqueries ex4`

The subquery is correlated: it mentions `c.id` from the outer row. What

SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE c.country = 'FR'
  AND EXISTS (
        SELECT 1
        FROM orders o
        WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
          AND o.status = 'cancelled');

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — a subquery in the SELECT list

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. The account-management dashboard shows the first
twenty customers with their order counts. For every customer with `id <=
20`, return `id`, `name`, and their number of orders aliased **`orders`** —
computed with a **correlated scalar subquery** in the SELECT list, not a
join.

Three columns, twenty rows, any order.

A scalar subquery in the SELECT list runs conceptually once per outer row
and must return exactly one row and one column — return two rows and
PostgreSQL raises an error at runtime, which is a real hazard of the form.
Its virtue is that it cannot change the outer row count: twenty customers
in, twenty rows out, guaranteed, with no grain question to answer.

Run: `uv run dojo test 13_subqueries ex5`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
A parenthesised `SELECT count(*) ...` can sit in the SELECT list like
any other expression, and it may refer to `c.id` from the outer row.

## Hint 2
`SELECT c.id, c.name, (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) AS orders FROM customers c WHERE c.id <= 20;`

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — a subquery in FROM (the derived table)

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Finance wants the customers whose **real
lifetime revenue** (orders with status `'paid'` or `'shipped'`) exceeds
**20,000**.

Columns: `customer_id`, `revenue`. Any order.

You cannot filter on `sum(total) > 20000` in `WHERE` — the sum does not
exist yet — and `HAVING` would work, but this exercise wants the fourth
kind of subquery: one in the **`FROM`** clause. Aggregate in a parenthesised
query, give it an alias, and treat the result as a table you can filter:

```sql
FROM (SELECT ... GROUP BY ...) AS per_customer
WHERE revenue > 20000
```

A derived table must have an alias — PostgreSQL insists. This is exactly
what a CTE (lesson 14) does with a nicer name, and being able to read both
matters because you will meet both.

lessons.briefing:
# 14 — CTEs: WITH, chains, and recursion

Lesson 13's subqueries nest inward — by the third level of parentheses,
nobody can read them. A **Common Table Expression** turns nesting into a
pipeline: name an intermediate result, then build on the name.

## Concept

```sql
WITH heavy_buyers AS (
    SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS n
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
    HAVING count(*) > 20
)
SELECT c.name, hb.n
FROM heavy_buyers hb
JOIN customers c ON c.id = hb.customer_id;
```

- CTEs **chain**: `WITH a AS (...), b AS (SELECT ... FROM a), c AS
  (SELECT ... FROM b)` — each step reads like a paragraph. This is how
  analysts actually write 100-line reports.
- A CTE can be referenced twice — handy when a result is both displayed
  and aggregated against.
- Since PostgreSQL 12, plain CTEs are usually inlined into the main query
  by the planner — write them for **readability**, not as an optimization
  fence (add `AS MATERIALIZED` in the rare case you need one; Part 5
  territory).

**Recursion.** The form that does something joins genuinely can't:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
    SELECT id, name, 1 AS depth          -- base case: the CEO
    FROM staff WHERE manager_id IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT s.id, s.name, org.depth + 1   -- step: everyone managed by
    FROM staff s                         --       someone already in org
    JOIN org ON s.manager_id = org.id
)
SELECT * FROM org;
```

Postgres runs the base case, then re-runs the step against the *newest*
rows until a step adds nothing. Lesson 10's self-join reached one level;
this walks all four levels of our org chart — or forty, without changing
a character.

## Exercise 1 — name the intermediate step

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. The heavy-buyers report, finished: customers
with more than 20 orders, with names attached. Columns: `id`, `name`,
`n` (their order count). Any order. Use a CTE for the aggregation, then
join customers to it. (250 rows.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 14_ctes ex1`

## Exercise 2 — a chained pipeline

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Which categories out-earn the average category?
Step 1 (CTE): revenue per category from `order_items` × `products` (sum
of `quantity * price`). Step 2: keep the categories whose revenue exceeds
the average of those six revenues. Columns: `category`, `revenue`. Any
order. (A second CTE or a scalar subquery over the first both work.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 14_ctes ex2`

## Exercise 3 — the whole org chart

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Every staff member with their depth in the org
tree: CEO = 1, her direct reports = 2, and so on. Columns: `id`, `name`,
`depth`. All 500 rows, any order. The concept section gives you the
skeleton — type it, don't paste it, and make sure you can say *why* the
UNION ALL step terminates.

Run: `uv run dojo test 14_ctes ex3`

## Exercise 4 — two CTEs, joined

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The market overview: for each customer
`country`, how many customers we have there and how much those customers
have spent in total (all orders, any status).

Columns, in this order: `country`, `customers` (count), `revenue` (sum of
order totals). Twelve rows, any order.

Build it as two named steps and join them: one CTE counting customers per
country, another summing revenue per country, then a join on `country`.

You could do this in one query with a single join and two aggregates — try
it, and check the customer count carefully. Joining `customers` to `orders`
first duplicates each customer once per order, so `count(*)` counts orders
and `count(DISTINCT c.id)` becomes necessary. Aggregating each side
*separately* and joining the small results afterwards sidesteps the grain
problem entirely, and that is a pattern worth having in your hands.

Run: `uv run dojo test 14_ctes ex4`

## Exercise 5 — recursion without a hierarchy

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Produce the integers **1 through 12**, one per
row, in a single column named `n`, using `WITH RECURSIVE` — no table
involved at all.

Twelve rows, any order.

Recursion is not only for trees. The base case is `SELECT 1`, the step adds
one to what it has, and the `WHERE n < 12` inside the recursive branch is
the **termination condition** — remove it and PostgreSQL will happily count
forever. (Ctrl-C is your friend; the lab is a throwaway clone.)

Being able to generate a series matters more than it looks: it is how you
produce the months a `GROUP BY` cannot invent, so a report can show a zero
instead of a missing bar. PostgreSQL also ships `generate_series(1, 12)`,
which is what you would actually use — but writing the recursion once
teaches you what it does.

Run: `uv run dojo test 14_ctes ex5`

## Exercise 6 — one person's whole subtree

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Employee **2** is being promoted, and HR needs
everyone in their reporting tree — direct reports, their reports, all the
way down — plus employee 2 themself.

Columns: `id`, `name`, `depth` (employee 2 is depth 1, their direct
reports 2, and so on). Any row order.

Exercise 3 started the recursion at the CEO (`manager_id IS NULL`). The
only change here is the base case: start at one specific row. That is the
whole trick to subtree queries, and it is why the adjacency-list model plus
a recursive CTE is enough for almost every hierarchy problem you will
meet.

Run: `uv run dojo test 14_ctes ex6`

## Challenge — the management chain (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Walk **upward**: for employee 442, produce
their management chain from the employee themself up to the CEO.
Columns: `pos` (1 = employee 442, 2 = their manager, ...), `id`, `name`.
**Ordered by `pos` ascending.** The base case is employee 442; the step
joins on *the current row's manager_id* — recursion upward instead of
downward.

Run: `uv run dojo test 14_ctes challenge`

## Spaced review

`review1/`: with a CTE named however you like: pending-order revenue per
customer country. Columns: `country`, `revenue` (sum of totals of
`'pending'` orders). Any order.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 14_ctes

A CTE does two unrelated things that happen to share a keyword: it gives a
subquery a name, and — with `RECURSIVE` — it expresses iteration, which no
amount of joining can. The first changes how your SQL reads; the second
changes what SQL can say.

## Notes

**`WITH` turns nesting into a pipeline.** Three levels of parentheses is
where a subquery stops being readable. `WITH a AS (...), b AS (SELECT ...
FROM a), c AS (SELECT ... FROM b) SELECT ... FROM c` reads top to bottom
like a paragraph, and — crucially — it is *debuggable*: run the `WITH`
prefix with `SELECT * FROM a` at the end and you can inspect any
intermediate step. Debugging a report CTE by CTE until the numbers stop
making sense is the single most useful technique in analytics work.

**Name each step after its business meaning.** `qualified_orders`,
`first_purchases`, `monthly_revenue`. A reviewer who can read the CTE names
and follow the argument will actually review the query; one who meets `t1`,
`t2`, `t3` will rubber-stamp it.

**CTEs are inlined since PostgreSQL 12 — mostly.** Before 12, a CTE was an
*optimisation fence*: always materialised, never pushed into. Since 12, a
CTE that is referenced exactly once and is not recursive and has no side
effects gets folded into the main query like any subquery, so you pay
nothing for readability. When you want the old behaviour — because the CTE
is expensive and referenced three times, or because you are deliberately
stopping the planner from pushing a filter down — say `AS MATERIALIZED`.
`AS NOT MATERIALIZED` forces the other way. Knowing that this knob exists is
Part 5 material; reaching for it before you have read a plan is premature.

**Recursion: how it actually runs.** `WITH RECURSIVE name AS (base UNION ALL
step)` evaluates the base term once into a working table, then repeatedly
runs the step against *only the rows produced by the previous iteration*,
appending results, until an iteration produces nothing. Three consequences:

- The termination condition is that the step eventually returns zero rows.
  A cycle in the data — employee A manages B manages A — means it never
  does, and the query runs until it exhausts disk. Guard real hierarchies by
  carrying an array of visited ids and adding `WHERE NOT s.id = ANY(path)`,
  or by capping `depth`.
- `UNION` instead of `UNION ALL` deduplicates each round, which is slower
  but does terminate on cyclic graphs.
- The reference to the CTE inside the step may appear exactly once, and not
  in a subquery or an outer join's nullable side. These are real
  restrictions and PostgreSQL will tell you about them.

**Recursion is not just for trees.** Generating a series, walking a linked
list, running a fixed-point computation, splitting a string into rows — all
the same shape. Anything where "the next state depends on the previous
state" is recursive-CTE territory. For plain integer or timestamp series,
`generate_series()` is the practical tool and is far faster.

**Where CTEs stop.** A CTE cannot see the *current row* of an enclosing
query — it is evaluated as a standalone relation. When you need "for each
row of A, run this query against B", that is a `LATERAL` join (lesson 48) or
a correlated subquery, not a CTE.

## ex1 — name the intermediate step

Aggregate first, join second. Notice the row count is unchanged from lesson
07's version of the same question — the CTE bought readability, not
different results. That is the point: `WITH` is a refactoring tool.

It also buys testability. Replace the final `SELECT` with `SELECT * FROM
heavy_buyers` and you can inspect the intermediate result on its own, which
is not possible with the same logic buried in a subquery three levels deep.
When a report disagrees with someone's spreadsheet, running it CTE by CTE
until the numbers diverge is how you find out who is right.

## ex2 — a chained pipeline

The first genuinely two-stage query in the course: compute revenue per
category, then compare each against the average *of those six numbers*. The
subtle bit is that the average is over categories, not over line items — six
values averaged, not a million. Getting that wrong produces a plausible
number that answers a different question, and it is exactly the kind of
error naming your steps makes visible.

## ex3 — the whole org chart

Type it rather than pasting it, and make sure you can say why it stops: the
step joins `staff` to the rows added in the previous round, and once the
deepest level has been reached no staff row has a `manager_id` in that set,
so the round returns nothing. Four levels here; the same six lines handle
forty.

## ex4 — two CTEs, joined

Aggregate each side separately, then join the small results. This is the
standard cure for the fan-out problem from lesson 08: instead of joining
first and then trying to un-duplicate with `count(DISTINCT ...)`, you never
create the duplicates. It is also usually *faster*, because both aggregates
run over their own table and the join happens on twelve rows instead of half
a million.

## ex5 — recursion without a hierarchy

The minimal recursive CTE, with nothing to distract from the mechanism.
Worth doing once and then never again in production — `generate_series(1,
12)` is the real answer, and the reason to know it is that "the months that
should exist" is the missing half of every `GROUP BY` time series (lesson
07's notes, lesson 12's ex5).

## ex6 — one person's whole subtree

Same six lines, different base case. Once you see that the base case
*selects the roots you care about* and the step *walks one edge*, the whole
family of hierarchy questions collapses into one template: subtree of X,
ancestors of X (join the other way — the challenge), all leaves, depth of
each node, path to root.

## challenge — the management chain

Recursion upward. The step joins `staff s ON s.id = chain.manager_id` rather
than `s.manager_id = chain.id`, which is the entire difference between
"everyone below me" and "everyone above me". Carrying `pos` through the
recursion gives you an ordering the outer query can sort by — recursion
produces rows in an unspecified order, so if you need a sequence, compute it
in the CTE.

## review1 — pending revenue per country

A one-CTE warm-up. When it comes back, name the CTE something a stakeholder
would recognise and notice how much the query improves for free.

Two checks while it runs. Twelve rows, one per country — and would a country
whose customers have placed no pending orders appear at all? No: the CTE
filters to pending orders before the join, so a country with none vanishes
rather than showing zero. Whether that is right depends on whether the
reader is comparing countries. That question — "does a missing row mean
zero, or does it mean nothing happened?" — never stops being worth asking.

## Further reading

- [`WITH` Queries (CTEs)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) — the definitive page. Read the recursive section, the cycle-detection example, and the `MATERIALIZED` notes.
- [`SELECT` — `WITH` clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — the restrictions on where the recursive self-reference may appear.
- [Set Returning Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-srf.html) — `generate_series` for numbers and timestamps: the practical alternative to ex5, and the tool for filling gaps in a time series.
- [`SEARCH` and `CYCLE` clauses](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) — PostgreSQL 14+ syntax that makes depth-first ordering and cycle detection declarative instead of hand-rolled.

# Reading - 14_ctes

A CTE does two unrelated things that happen to share a keyword: it gives a
subquery a name, and — with `RECURSIVE` — it expresses iteration, which no
amount of joining can. The first changes how your SQL reads; the second
changes what SQL can say.

## Notes

**`WITH` turns nesting into a pipeline.** Three levels of parentheses is
where a subquery stops being readable. `WITH a AS (...), b AS (SELECT ...
FROM a), c AS (SELECT ... FROM b) SELECT ... FROM c` reads top to bottom
like a paragraph, and — crucially — it is *debuggable*: run the `WITH`
prefix with `SELECT * FROM a` at the end and you can inspect any
intermediate step. Debugging a report CTE by CTE until the numbers stop
making sense is the single most useful technique in analytics work.

**Name each step after its business meaning.** `qualified_orders`,
`first_purchases`, `monthly_revenue`. A reviewer who can read the CTE names
and follow the argument will actually review the query; one who meets `t1`,
`t2`, `t3` will rubber-stamp it.

**CTEs are inlined since PostgreSQL 12 — mostly.** Before 12, a CTE was an
*optimisation fence*: always materialised, never pushed into. Since 12, a
CTE that is referenced exactly once and is not recursive and has no side
effects gets folded into the main query like any subquery, so you pay
nothing for readability. When you want the old behaviour — because the CTE
is expensive and referenced three times, or because you are deliberately
stopping the planner from pushing a filter down — say `AS MATERIALIZED`.
`AS NOT MATERIALIZED` forces the other way. Knowing that this knob exists is
Part 5 material; reaching for it before you have read a plan is premature.

**Recursion: how it actually runs.** `WITH RECURSIVE name AS (base UNION ALL
step)` evaluates the base term once into a working table, then repeatedly
runs the step against *only the rows produced by the previous iteration*,
appending results, until an iteration produces nothing. Three consequences:

- The termination condition is that the step eventually returns zero rows.
  A cycle in the data — employee A manages B manages A — means it never
  does, and the query runs until it exhausts disk. Guard real hierarchies by
  carrying an array of visited ids and adding `WHERE NOT s.id = ANY(path)`,
  or by capping `depth`.
- `UNION` instead of `UNION ALL` deduplicates each round, which is slower
  but does terminate on cyclic graphs.
- The reference to the CTE inside the step may appear exactly once, and not
  in a subquery or an outer join's nullable side. These are real
  restrictions and PostgreSQL will tell you about them.

**Recursion is not just for trees.** Generating a series, walking a linked
list, running a fixed-point computation, splitting a string into rows — all
the same shape. Anything where "the next state depends on the previous
state" is recursive-CTE territory. For plain integer or timestamp series,
`generate_series()` is the practical tool and is far faster.

**Where CTEs stop.** A CTE cannot see the *current row* of an enclosing
query — it is evaluated as a standalone relation. When you need "for each
row of A, run this query against B", that is a `LATERAL` join (lesson 48) or
a correlated subquery, not a CTE.

## ex1 — name the intermediate step

Aggregate first, join second. Notice the row count is unchanged from lesson
07's version of the same question — the CTE bought readability, not
different results. That is the point: `WITH` is a refactoring tool.

It also buys testability. Replace the final `SELECT` with `SELECT * FROM
heavy_buyers` and you can inspect the intermediate result on its own, which
is not possible with the same logic buried in a subquery three levels deep.
When a report disagrees with someone's spreadsheet, running it CTE by CTE
until the numbers diverge is how you find out who is right.

## ex2 — a chained pipeline

The first genuinely two-stage query in the course: compute revenue per
category, then compare each against the average *of those six numbers*. The
subtle bit is that the average is over categories, not over line items — six
values averaged, not a million. Getting that wrong produces a plausible
number that answers a different question, and it is exactly the kind of
error naming your steps makes visible.

## ex3 — the whole org chart

Type it rather than pasting it, and make sure you can say why it stops: the
step joins `staff` to the rows added in the previous round, and once the
deepest level has been reached no staff row has a `manager_id` in that set,
so the round returns nothing. Four levels here; the same six lines handle
forty.

## ex4 — two CTEs, joined

Aggregate each side separately, then join the small results. This is the
standard cure for the fan-out problem from lesson 08: instead of joining
first and then trying to un-duplicate with `count(DISTINCT ...)`, you never
create the duplicates. It is also usually *faster*, because both aggregates
run over their own table and the join happens on twelve rows instead of half
a million.

## ex5 — recursion without a hierarchy

The minimal recursive CTE, with nothing to distract from the mechanism.
Worth doing once and then never again in production — `generate_series(1,
12)` is the real answer, and the reason to know it is that "the months that
should exist" is the missing half of every `GROUP BY` time series (lesson
07's notes, lesson 12's ex5).

## ex6 — one person's whole subtree

Same six lines, different base case. Once you see that the base case
*selects the roots you care about* and the step *walks one edge*, the whole
family of hierarchy questions collapses into one template: subtree of X,
ancestors of X (join the other way — the challenge), all leaves, depth of
each node, path to root.

## challenge — the management chain

Recursion upward. The step joins `staff s ON s.id = chain.manager_id` rather
than `s.manager_id = chain.id`, which is the entire difference between
"everyone below me" and "everyone above me". Carrying `pos` through the
recursion gives you an ordering the outer query can sort by — recursion
produces rows in an unspecified order, so if you need a sequence, compute it
in the CTE.

## review1 — pending revenue per country

A one-CTE warm-up. When it comes back, name the CTE something a stakeholder
would recognise and notice how much the query improves for free.

Two checks while it runs. Twelve rows, one per country — and would a country
whose customers have placed no pending orders appear at all? No: the CTE
filters to pending orders before the join, so a country with none vanishes
rather than showing zero. Whether that is right depends on whether the
reader is comparing countries. That question — "does a missing row mean
zero, or does it mean nothing happened?" — never stops being worth asking.

## Further reading

- [`WITH` Queries (CTEs)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) — the definitive page. Read the recursive section, the cycle-detection example, and the `MATERIALIZED` notes.
- [`SELECT` — `WITH` clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — the restrictions on where the recursive self-reference may appear.
- [Set Returning Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-srf.html) — `generate_series` for numbers and timestamps: the practical alternative to ex5, and the tool for filling gaps in a time series.
- [`SEARCH` and `CYCLE` clauses](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) — PostgreSQL 14+ syntax that makes depth-first ordering and cycle detection declarative instead of hand-rolled.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — the management chain (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Walk **upward**: for employee 442, produce
their management chain from the employee themself up to the CEO.
Columns: `pos` (1 = employee 442, 2 = their manager, ...), `id`, `name`.
**Ordered by `pos` ascending.** The base case is employee 442; the step
joins on *the current row's manager_id* — recursion upward instead of
downward.

Run: `uv run dojo test 14_ctes challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Reverse the join direction: base case is `WHERE id = 442` with pos 1; the
step finds the row whose `id` equals the *current* row's `manager_id`,
pos + 1. Each step yields exactly one row until the CEO's NULL ends it.

## Hint 2
```sql
WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
    SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS pos
    FROM staff WHERE id = 442
    UNION ALL
    SELECT s.id, s.name, s.manager_id, chain.pos + 1
    FROM staff s
    JOIN chain ON s.id = chain.manager_id
)
SELECT pos, id, name FROM chain ORDER BY pos;
```

Note the CTE carries `manager_id` along even though the output doesn't —
the recursion needs it.

Lesson 07 ex2 built the aggregation. Wrap it in `WITH <name> AS (...)`,
then write a plain join between `customers` and the name.

## Hint 2
```sql
WITH heavy AS (
    SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS n
    FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING count(*) > 20
)
SELECT c.id, c.name, heavy.n
FROM heavy JOIN customers c ON c.id = heavy.customer_id;
```

WITH heavy AS (
    SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS n
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
    HAVING count(*) > 20
)

FROM heavy
JOIN customers c ON c.id = heavy.customer_id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name, t.n FROM customers c
JOIN (SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS n FROM orders
      GROUP BY customer_id HAVING count(*) > 20) t
  ON t.customer_id = c.id;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — a chained pipeline

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Which categories out-earn the average category?
Step 1 (CTE): revenue per category from `order_items` × `products` (sum
of `quantity * price`). Step 2: keep the categories whose revenue exceeds
the average of those six revenues. Columns: `category`, `revenue`. Any
order. (A second CTE or a scalar subquery over the first both work.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 14_ctes ex2`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
CTE: lesson 08 ex3's category revenue. Main query: `WHERE revenue >
(scalar subquery averaging the CTE)`. The CTE gets read twice — that's
allowed and normal.

## Hint 2
```sql
WITH cat_rev AS (
    SELECT p.category, sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) AS revenue
    FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
    GROUP BY p.category
)
SELECT category, revenue
FROM cat_rev
WHERE revenue > (SELECT avg(revenue) FROM cat_rev);
```

references.solution.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
    SELECT id, name, 1 AS depth
    FROM staff
    WHERE manager_id IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT s.id, s.name, org.depth + 1
    FROM staff s
    JOIN org ON s.manager_id = org.id
)
SELECT id, name, depth
FROM org;

WITH RECURSIVE org AS (

)

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — two CTEs, joined

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The market overview: for each customer
`country`, how many customers we have there and how much those customers
have spent in total (all orders, any status).

Columns, in this order: `country`, `customers` (count), `revenue` (sum of
order totals). Twelve rows, any order.

Build it as two named steps and join them: one CTE counting customers per
country, another summing revenue per country, then a join on `country`.

You could do this in one query with a single join and two aggregates — try
it, and check the customer count carefully. Joining `customers` to `orders`
first duplicates each customer once per order, so `count(*)` counts orders
and `count(DISTINCT c.id)` becomes necessary. Aggregating each side
*separately* and joining the small results afterwards sidesteps the grain
problem entirely, and that is a pattern worth having in your hands.

Run: `uv run dojo test 14_ctes ex4`

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
`WITH a AS (...), b AS (...) SELECT ... FROM a JOIN b ON ...` - the
comma separates CTEs, and only the final SELECT is the query.

## Hint 2
First CTE: `SELECT country, count(*) FROM customers GROUP BY country`.
Second: join orders to customers and `GROUP BY c.country`. Then join the
two on `country`.

references.solution.sql:
WITH customers_per_country AS (
    SELECT country, count(*) AS customers
    FROM customers
    GROUP BY country
), revenue_per_country AS (
    SELECT c.country, sum(o.total) AS revenue
    FROM orders o
    JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
    GROUP BY c.country
)
SELECT cpc.country, cpc.customers, rpc.revenue
FROM customers_per_country cpc
JOIN revenue_per_country rpc ON rpc.country = cpc.country;
references.expected.sql:
WITH cust AS (
    SELECT country, count(*) AS customers
    FROM customers
    GROUP BY country
), rev AS (
    SELECT c.country, sum(o.total) AS revenue
    FROM orders o
    JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
    GROUP BY c.country
)
SELECT cust.country, cust.customers, rev.revenue
FROM cust
JOIN rev ON rev.country = cust.country;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — recursion without a hierarchy

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Produce the integers **1 through 12**, one per
row, in a single column named `n`, using `WITH RECURSIVE` — no table
involved at all.

Twelve rows, any order.

Recursion is not only for trees. The base case is `SELECT 1`, the step adds
one to what it has, and the `WHERE n < 12` inside the recursive branch is
the **termination condition** — remove it and PostgreSQL will happily count
forever. (Ctrl-C is your friend; the lab is a throwaway clone.)

Being able to generate a series matters more than it looks: it is how you
produce the months a `GROUP BY` cannot invent, so a report can show a zero
instead of a missing bar. PostgreSQL also ships `generate_series(1, 12)`,
which is what you would actually use — but writing the recursion once
teaches you what it does.

Run: `uv run dojo test 14_ctes ex5`

## Exercise 6 — one person's whole subtree

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Employee **2** is being promoted, and HR needs
everyone in their reporting tree — direct reports, their reports, all the
way down — plus employee 2 themself.

Columns: `id`, `name`, `depth` (employee 2 is depth 1, their direct
reports 2, and so on). Any row order.

Exercise 3 started the recursion at the CEO (`manager_id IS NULL`). The
only change here is the base case: start at one specific row. That is the
whole trick to subtree queries, and it is why the adjacency-list model plus
a recursive CTE is enough for almost every hierarchy problem you will
meet.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Exercise 3's query with a different base case: `WHERE id = 2` instead
of `WHERE manager_id IS NULL`.

## Hint 2
The recursive step is unchanged: `JOIN subtree ON s.manager_id = subtree.id`,
with `subtree.depth + 1`.

references.solution.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE subtree AS (
    SELECT id, name, 1 AS depth
    FROM staff
    WHERE id = 2
    UNION ALL
    SELECT s.id, s.name, subtree.depth + 1
    FROM staff s
    JOIN subtree ON s.manager_id = subtree.id
)
SELECT id, name, depth
FROM subtree;
references.expected.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE subtree AS (
    SELECT id, name, 1 AS depth
    FROM staff
    WHERE id = 2
    UNION ALL
    SELECT s.id, s.name, subtree.depth + 1
    FROM staff s
    JOIN subtree ON s.manager_id = subtree.id
)
SELECT id, name, depth FROM subtree;

exercises.prompt:
## Spaced review

`review1/`: with a CTE named however you like: pending-order revenue per
customer country. Columns: `country`, `revenue` (sum of totals of
`'pending'` orders). Any order.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
CTE: pending orders (or go straight to the join — but practice the WITH).
Main: join to customers, group by country, sum totals.

## Hint 2
```sql
WITH pending AS (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending')
SELECT c.country, sum(p.total) AS revenue
FROM pending p JOIN customers c ON c.id = p.customer_id
GROUP BY c.country;
```

lessons.briefing:
# 15 — Window functions I: numbering and ranking

GROUP BY answers "one row per group". But half of real reporting wants
**every row kept, with group context attached**: each product *and* its
category's average; each order *and* its rank among that customer's
orders. Collapsing loses the rows; correlated subqueries (lesson 13) keep
them but re-run per row and read like riddles. Window functions are the
purpose-built tool: per-row results computed *over a window* of related
rows.

## Concept

```sql
SELECT name, salary,
       row_number() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS rn,
       rank()       OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)     AS rnk,
       dense_rank() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)     AS drnk
FROM staff;
```

- `OVER (...)` marks a window function. Empty `OVER ()` means "the window
  is the whole result".
- `PARTITION BY x` splits the window into per-group sub-windows — GROUP
  BY's sibling that *doesn't collapse rows*:

```sql
avg(price) OVER (PARTITION BY category)   -- each row sees its category avg
```

- The numbering trio: `row_number()` — unique 1,2,3 (needs a tie-break in
  its ORDER BY to be deterministic!); `rank()` — ties share a number,
  then gaps (1,1,3); `dense_rank()` — ties share, no gaps (1,1,2).
- **Windows are evaluated after WHERE** — so you can't filter on one
  directly. The idiom: compute in a CTE (hello, lesson 14), filter
  outside:

```sql
WITH ranked AS (SELECT ..., row_number() OVER (...) AS rn FROM ...)
SELECT ... FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 5;
```

That idiom is *the* top-N-per-group solution — the thing lesson 03's
challenge made you sweat for.

## Exercise 1 — the salary leaderboard

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. All 500 staff: `name`, `salary`, and `rn` =
their company-wide salary position (1 = highest paid; equal salaries
broken by `id` ascending). **Ordered by `rn`.**

Run: `uv run dojo test 15_window_functions_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2 — each product against its category

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Every product: `id`, `name`, `price`, and
`category_avg` — the average price of its category, rounded to 2
decimals. Any order. One window function, no join, no GROUP BY: that's
the point.

Run: `uv run dojo test 15_window_functions_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3 — top-5 per category, the right way

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Lesson 03's challenge, revisited on your terms:
the 5 most expensive products per category. Columns: `category`, `name`,
`price`. **Ordered by `category` ASC, then `price` DESC, then `id` ASC.**
Use `row_number()` partitioned by category (ordered by price DESC, id) in
a CTE, filter `rn <= 5` outside. Feel how much better this is.

Run: `uv run dojo test 15_window_functions_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4 — rank versus dense_rank, side by side

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Put the three numbering functions' difference in
front of your eyes. For all 500 staff return `name`, `salary`, `rnk`
(`rank()` over salary descending) and `drnk` (`dense_rank()` over the same
order). **Ordered by `salary` descending, then `id` ascending.**

Four columns, 500 rows, order graded.

Scroll to the first tie in the output. `rank()` gives both tied rows the
same number and then *skips* — 1, 1, 3. `dense_rank()` gives them the same
number and carries on — 1, 1, 2. Neither is more correct; they answer
different questions ("what position did they finish?" versus "how many
distinct salary levels are above them?"), and picking the wrong one puts a
visibly wrong number on a leaderboard.

Run: `uv run dojo test 15_window_functions_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5 — how far from the category average?

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Merchandising wants every product scored against
its own category: `id`, `name`, `category`, and **`vs_category`** — the
product's price minus its category's average price, rounded to 2 decimals.
Negative means cheaper than its category's average.

Four columns, all 10,000 rows, any order.

Exercise 2 attached the category average; this subtracts it, which is the
form a human can actually read. One window function does it with no join,
no `GROUP BY`, and no subquery — compare that against lesson 13's review
exercise, which asked the same *kind* of question with a correlated scalar
subquery and re-derived the average once per row.

Run: `uv run dojo test 15_window_functions_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6 — the latest row per group

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. For every customer with `id <= 50`, their **most
recent order**. Columns: `customer_id`, `id` (the order's), `created_at`.
Any row order.

This is lesson 13's correlated-`max()` challenge rewritten as the ranked-CTE
idiom: `row_number()` partitioned by customer, ordered by `created_at`
descending (tie-break `id` descending), filtered to `rn = 1` outside the
CTE.

The idiom generalises to almost every "latest / best / first per group"
question there is — latest event per device, best offer per product, first
touch per campaign. Learn the shape, not the example. Note also what the
tie-break buys you: the correlated-`max()` version returns *both* rows when
two orders share a timestamp, while `row_number()` picks exactly one, every
time.

Run: `uv run dojo test 15_window_functions_1 ex6`

## Challenge — departmental podium (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. The top 3 salaries **per department** —
but using `rank()`, so that if two people tie for 3rd, both appear.
Columns: `department`, `name`, `salary`. Any order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 15_window_functions_1 challenge`

## Spaced review

`review1/`: "page 2" of the product catalog priced high-to-low: rows 11
through 20 by (`price` DESC, `id` ASC). Columns: `id`, `name`, `price`,
**ordered** the same way. Do it with `row_number()` in a CTE — same rows
OFFSET would give, but the pattern extends to per-group pagination, which
OFFSET can't do.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 15_window_functions_1

`GROUP BY` collapses rows to answer questions about groups. Window functions
answer questions about groups **without collapsing anything** — each row
keeps its identity and gains context. Half of real reporting needs exactly
that, and before SQL:2003 there was no good way to express it.

## Notes

**The mental model.** For each row, a window function looks at a *window* of
related rows and computes a value. `OVER ()` makes the window the entire
result set. `OVER (PARTITION BY category)` makes it the rows sharing that
row's category. `OVER (ORDER BY x)` adds a direction and, for aggregates,
turns the window into "everything up to here" (lesson 16). The row itself is
always in its own window.

**`PARTITION BY` is `GROUP BY` that does not collapse.** That single sentence
covers most of the lesson. `avg(price) OVER (PARTITION BY category)` gives
every product its category's average, on the same row, with no join and no
subquery — which is the same answer lesson 13's correlated subquery
produced by re-running an aggregate once per row.

**Where windows sit in the evaluation order.** After `FROM`, `WHERE`,
`GROUP BY` and `HAVING`; before `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT`. Two consequences you
will hit immediately:

- You cannot filter on a window function in `WHERE` — it has not been
  computed. Compute it in a CTE or derived table and filter outside. That
  restriction *is* the top-N-per-group idiom.
- The window sees the rows that survived `WHERE`. Filtering before ranking
  changes the ranks, which is usually what you want and occasionally a bug —
  "rank among all staff" and "rank among the staff shown" are different
  reports.

**The numbering trio.**

| function | ties | gaps | use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `row_number()` | broken arbitrarily | n/a | pick exactly one row per group |
| `rank()` | share a number | yes (1,1,3) | competition placing |
| `dense_rank()` | share a number | no (1,1,2) | "how many levels above me" |

`row_number()` without a deterministic `ORDER BY` inside the `OVER` is
non-deterministic: two rows with equal sort keys can swap between runs. Add
a unique tie-break — usually the primary key — every single time.

**The ranked-CTE idiom.** Number the rows, filter outside:

```sql
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT ..., row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY k DESC, id) AS rn
    FROM t
)
SELECT ... FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 5;
```

This is the answer to top-N-per-group, latest-per-key, best-per-category —
an enormous family of real questions, and a standard interview filter
because it cleanly separates people who reach for `OFFSET` in a loop, people
who write a correlated subquery, and people who window. PostgreSQL also
offers `DISTINCT ON` for the special case of N = 1 (lesson 49), and
`LATERAL` for the case where you need N rows *and* the per-group query is
expensive (lesson 48).

**A performance note.** A window function requires its input sorted by
`PARTITION BY` then `ORDER BY`. PostgreSQL will add a `Sort` node, or skip it
if an index already provides that order — which is exactly the situation
lesson 35 engineers deliberately. Windowing three million raw rows when
thirty-one aggregated rows would do is a real and common production smell:
aggregate first in a CTE, window over the small result.

**`WINDOW` clause.** When several functions share a window, name it once:
`... rank() OVER w, dense_rank() OVER w ... WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY salary
DESC)`. It reads better and guarantees the definitions cannot drift apart.

## ex1 — the salary leaderboard

`row_number()` with an explicit tie-break, and the outer `ORDER BY` matching
it. Two different `ORDER BY` clauses in one query doing two different jobs —
one defines the numbering, one defines the output order — is worth sitting
with for a moment. They are frequently the same and are not required to be.

## ex2 — each product against its category

One window function; no join, no `GROUP BY`, no subquery. Compare this
against what lesson 13 would need: a correlated scalar subquery re-computing
a category average for every one of 10,000 rows. Same answer, very different
query, and the window version sorts once.

## ex3 — top-5 per category, the right way

Lesson 03's challenge, which took a correlated subquery and a paragraph of
apology, is now four lines. This is the moment the course pays back the
earlier struggle — and the reason the earlier struggle was worth having, is
that you now know *what* is being replaced.

## ex4 — rank versus dense_rank, side by side

The difference, visible in one result set. The practical consequence is a
question to ask whenever someone asks for "rank": if two people tie for
third, should the next person be fourth or third? Stakeholders have an
opinion and have never articulated it.

## ex5 — how far from the category average?

The window function used as an ordinary expression, inside arithmetic,
inside `round()`. That composability is the thing to take away: a window
function is a value like any other, and the only special rule is *where* it
may appear in the query.

## ex6 — the latest row per group

The idiom in its most common form. Worth noting what the tie-break does
here beyond determinism: with `row_number()` you get exactly one row per
customer guaranteed, whereas `rank() ... WHERE rnk = 1` would return two
rows for a customer with two orders at the same instant. Which one you want
is a real decision — "the latest order" usually means exactly one.

## challenge — departmental podium

`rank()` rather than `row_number()`, so a tie for third place shows both
people. The exercise exists to make you choose the numbering function on
purpose rather than by habit.

The consequence is that the result no longer has a fixed row count: with
`row_number()` you get exactly three rows per department, with `rank()` you
get three *or more*. Downstream code that assumed "three per group" — a
fixed-height chart, a template with three slots, a test asserting fifteen
rows — breaks on the day of the first tie. Choosing `rank()` is a decision
about the report's contract, not just about fairness.

## review1 — page 2 by row_number

The same rows `OFFSET 10 LIMIT 10` would give, computed a different way.
The reason to know the window version: `OFFSET` cannot paginate *per group*.
"Rows 11-20 of each category" is trivial with `row_number()` and impossible
with `OFFSET`.

The two versions are not equivalent in cost, though, and not in the
window's favour. `ORDER BY price DESC, id LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10` can stop after
twenty rows if an index supplies the order; the `row_number()` version must
number every one of the 10,000 products before it can discard 9,990 of them.
Use the window when you need per-group paging or the rank itself as a value —
not as a general replacement for `LIMIT`.

## Further reading

- [Window Functions Tutorial](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) — the gentlest correct introduction, with the evaluation-order rules that explain why you cannot filter in `WHERE`.
- [Window Function Calls](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html) — the syntax: `PARTITION BY`, `ORDER BY`, frames, and the `WINDOW` clause.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) — the built-in list: `row_number`, `rank`, `dense_rank`, `ntile`, `lag`, `lead`, `first_value`, `nth_value`.
- [`SELECT` — `DISTINCT ON`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — PostgreSQL's shortcut for the N = 1 case of ex6. Lesson 49 makes it a whole topic.

# Reading - 15_window_functions_1

`GROUP BY` collapses rows to answer questions about groups. Window functions
answer questions about groups **without collapsing anything** — each row
keeps its identity and gains context. Half of real reporting needs exactly
that, and before SQL:2003 there was no good way to express it.

## Notes

**The mental model.** For each row, a window function looks at a *window* of
related rows and computes a value. `OVER ()` makes the window the entire
result set. `OVER (PARTITION BY category)` makes it the rows sharing that
row's category. `OVER (ORDER BY x)` adds a direction and, for aggregates,
turns the window into "everything up to here" (lesson 16). The row itself is
always in its own window.

**`PARTITION BY` is `GROUP BY` that does not collapse.** That single sentence
covers most of the lesson. `avg(price) OVER (PARTITION BY category)` gives
every product its category's average, on the same row, with no join and no
subquery — which is the same answer lesson 13's correlated subquery
produced by re-running an aggregate once per row.

**Where windows sit in the evaluation order.** After `FROM`, `WHERE`,
`GROUP BY` and `HAVING`; before `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT`. Two consequences you
will hit immediately:

- You cannot filter on a window function in `WHERE` — it has not been
  computed. Compute it in a CTE or derived table and filter outside. That
  restriction *is* the top-N-per-group idiom.
- The window sees the rows that survived `WHERE`. Filtering before ranking
  changes the ranks, which is usually what you want and occasionally a bug —
  "rank among all staff" and "rank among the staff shown" are different
  reports.

**The numbering trio.**

| function | ties | gaps | use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `row_number()` | broken arbitrarily | n/a | pick exactly one row per group |
| `rank()` | share a number | yes (1,1,3) | competition placing |
| `dense_rank()` | share a number | no (1,1,2) | "how many levels above me" |

`row_number()` without a deterministic `ORDER BY` inside the `OVER` is
non-deterministic: two rows with equal sort keys can swap between runs. Add
a unique tie-break — usually the primary key — every single time.

**The ranked-CTE idiom.** Number the rows, filter outside:

```sql
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT ..., row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY k DESC, id) AS rn
    FROM t
)
SELECT ... FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 5;
```

This is the answer to top-N-per-group, latest-per-key, best-per-category —
an enormous family of real questions, and a standard interview filter
because it cleanly separates people who reach for `OFFSET` in a loop, people
who write a correlated subquery, and people who window. PostgreSQL also
offers `DISTINCT ON` for the special case of N = 1 (lesson 49), and
`LATERAL` for the case where you need N rows *and* the per-group query is
expensive (lesson 48).

**A performance note.** A window function requires its input sorted by
`PARTITION BY` then `ORDER BY`. PostgreSQL will add a `Sort` node, or skip it
if an index already provides that order — which is exactly the situation
lesson 35 engineers deliberately. Windowing three million raw rows when
thirty-one aggregated rows would do is a real and common production smell:
aggregate first in a CTE, window over the small result.

**`WINDOW` clause.** When several functions share a window, name it once:
`... rank() OVER w, dense_rank() OVER w ... WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY salary
DESC)`. It reads better and guarantees the definitions cannot drift apart.

## ex1 — the salary leaderboard

`row_number()` with an explicit tie-break, and the outer `ORDER BY` matching
it. Two different `ORDER BY` clauses in one query doing two different jobs —
one defines the numbering, one defines the output order — is worth sitting
with for a moment. They are frequently the same and are not required to be.

## ex2 — each product against its category

One window function; no join, no `GROUP BY`, no subquery. Compare this
against what lesson 13 would need: a correlated scalar subquery re-computing
a category average for every one of 10,000 rows. Same answer, very different
query, and the window version sorts once.

## ex3 — top-5 per category, the right way

Lesson 03's challenge, which took a correlated subquery and a paragraph of
apology, is now four lines. This is the moment the course pays back the
earlier struggle — and the reason the earlier struggle was worth having, is
that you now know *what* is being replaced.

## ex4 — rank versus dense_rank, side by side

The difference, visible in one result set. The practical consequence is a
question to ask whenever someone asks for "rank": if two people tie for
third, should the next person be fourth or third? Stakeholders have an
opinion and have never articulated it.

## ex5 — how far from the category average?

The window function used as an ordinary expression, inside arithmetic,
inside `round()`. That composability is the thing to take away: a window
function is a value like any other, and the only special rule is *where* it
may appear in the query.

## ex6 — the latest row per group

The idiom in its most common form. Worth noting what the tie-break does
here beyond determinism: with `row_number()` you get exactly one row per
customer guaranteed, whereas `rank() ... WHERE rnk = 1` would return two
rows for a customer with two orders at the same instant. Which one you want
is a real decision — "the latest order" usually means exactly one.

## challenge — departmental podium

`rank()` rather than `row_number()`, so a tie for third place shows both
people. The exercise exists to make you choose the numbering function on
purpose rather than by habit.

The consequence is that the result no longer has a fixed row count: with
`row_number()` you get exactly three rows per department, with `rank()` you
get three *or more*. Downstream code that assumed "three per group" — a
fixed-height chart, a template with three slots, a test asserting fifteen
rows — breaks on the day of the first tie. Choosing `rank()` is a decision
about the report's contract, not just about fairness.

## review1 — page 2 by row_number

The same rows `OFFSET 10 LIMIT 10` would give, computed a different way.
The reason to know the window version: `OFFSET` cannot paginate *per group*.
"Rows 11-20 of each category" is trivial with `row_number()` and impossible
with `OFFSET`.

The two versions are not equivalent in cost, though, and not in the
window's favour. `ORDER BY price DESC, id LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10` can stop after
twenty rows if an index supplies the order; the `row_number()` version must
number every one of the 10,000 products before it can discard 9,990 of them.
Use the window when you need per-group paging or the rank itself as a value —
not as a general replacement for `LIMIT`.

## Further reading

- [Window Functions Tutorial](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) — the gentlest correct introduction, with the evaluation-order rules that explain why you cannot filter in `WHERE`.
- [Window Function Calls](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html) — the syntax: `PARTITION BY`, `ORDER BY`, frames, and the `WINDOW` clause.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) — the built-in list: `row_number`, `rank`, `dense_rank`, `ntile`, `lag`, `lead`, `first_value`, `nth_value`.
- [`SELECT` — `DISTINCT ON`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — PostgreSQL's shortcut for the N = 1 case of ex6. Lesson 49 makes it a whole topic.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — rank versus dense_rank, side by side

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Put the three numbering functions' difference in
front of your eyes. For all 500 staff return `name`, `salary`, `rnk`
(`rank()` over salary descending) and `drnk` (`dense_rank()` over the same
order). **Ordered by `salary` descending, then `id` ascending.**

Four columns, 500 rows, order graded.

Scroll to the first tie in the output. `rank()` gives both tied rows the
same number and then *skips* — 1, 1, 3. `dense_rank()` gives them the same
number and carries on — 1, 1, 2. Neither is more correct; they answer
different questions ("what position did they finish?" versus "how many
distinct salary levels are above them?"), and picking the wrong one puts a
visibly wrong number on a leaderboard.

ORDER BY salary DESC, id;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — how far from the category average?

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Merchandising wants every product scored against
its own category: `id`, `name`, `category`, and **`vs_category`** — the
product's price minus its category's average price, rounded to 2 decimals.
Negative means cheaper than its category's average.

Four columns, all 10,000 rows, any order.

Exercise 2 attached the category average; this subtracts it, which is the
form a human can actually read. One window function does it with no join,
no `GROUP BY`, and no subquery — compare that against lesson 13's review
exercise, which asked the same *kind* of question with a correlated scalar
subquery and re-derived the average once per row.

Run: `uv run dojo test 15_window_functions_1 ex5`

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — the latest row per group

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. For every customer with `id <= 50`, their **most
recent order**. Columns: `customer_id`, `id` (the order's), `created_at`.
Any row order.

This is lesson 13's correlated-`max()` challenge rewritten as the ranked-CTE
idiom: `row_number()` partitioned by customer, ordered by `created_at`
descending (tie-break `id` descending), filtered to `rn = 1` outside the
CTE.

The idiom generalises to almost every "latest / best / first per group"
question there is — latest event per device, best offer per product, first
touch per campaign. Learn the shape, not the example. Note also what the
tie-break buys you: the correlated-`max()` version returns *both* rows when
two orders share a timestamp, while `row_number()` picks exactly one, every
time.

Run: `uv run dojo test 15_window_functions_1 ex6`

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Windows are computed after WHERE but before the outer query can filter
on them - so number the rows in a CTE and filter `rn = 1` outside.

## Hint 2
`row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC) AS rn`, then `WHERE rn = 1`.

references.solution.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT customer_id,
           id,
           created_at,
           row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                              ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC) AS rn
    FROM orders
    WHERE customer_id <= 50
)
SELECT customer_id, id, created_at
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1;
references.expected.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT customer_id, id, created_at,
           row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                              ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC) AS rn
    FROM orders
    WHERE customer_id <= 50
)
SELECT customer_id, id, created_at
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1;

exercises.title: Review1
exercises.prompt:
## Spaced review

`review1/`: "page 2" of the product catalog priced high-to-low: rows 11
through 20 by (`price` DESC, `id` ASC). Columns: `id`, `name`, `price`,
**ordered** the same way. Do it with `row_number()` in a CTE — same rows
OFFSET would give, but the pattern extends to per-group pagination, which
OFFSET can't do.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Number every product by (price DESC, id), keep 11–20, order by the same
key. `WHERE rn BETWEEN 11 AND 20` reads nicely.

## Hint 2
```sql
WITH numbered AS (
    SELECT id, name, price,
           row_number() OVER (ORDER BY price DESC, id) AS rn
    FROM products
)
SELECT id, name, price FROM numbered
WHERE rn BETWEEN 11 AND 20
ORDER BY price DESC, id;
```

lessons.briefing:
# 16 — Window functions II: frames, LAG, running totals

Lesson 15's windows looked at *whole* partitions. Add `ORDER BY` inside
the OVER and the window gains a direction — and suddenly you can express
"so far" (running totals), "compared to yesterday" (LAG), and "average of
the last 7 rows" (frames). This is the grammar of every time-series
report you will ever build.

## Concept

```sql
sum(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day)                       -- running total
lag(revenue)  OVER (ORDER BY month)                    -- previous row's value
lead(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)                    -- next row's value
avg(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day
                   ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING
                        AND CURRENT ROW)               -- 7-row moving average
ntile(4)     OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)               -- quartile buckets
```

- With ORDER BY inside OVER, an aggregate's **frame** defaults to "start
  of partition through current row" — which is precisely a running total.
- `ROWS BETWEEN ... AND ...` sets the frame explicitly. `ROWS` counts
  physical rows; there's also `RANGE` (peers by value) — subtly different
  with ties; when in doubt, say ROWS and mean it.
- `lag(col)` / `lead(col)` return NULL at the edges — remember lesson 05:
  arithmetic with that NULL yields NULL, which is usually the *correct*
  display for "no previous month".
- `ntile(n)` deals rows into n near-equal buckets in frame order.

These all compose with lesson 14's CTEs: aggregate first (per day, per
month), *then* window over the small result. Windowing 3 million raw rows
when 31 daily rows suffice is a real production performance smell.

All of this lesson's exercises work on **October 2023** daily revenue or
the monthly series — small, checkable numbers.

## Exercise 1 — running total

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Daily revenue for October 2023 with a running
month-to-date column. CTE: one row per day (`date_trunc('day',
created_at)`), revenue = sum of totals, for `created_at >= '2023-10-01'
AND < '2023-11-01'`. Main: `day`, `revenue`, `running` = running sum in
day order. **Ordered by `day`.** (31 rows.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 16_window_functions_2 ex1`

## Exercise 2 — month-over-month with LAG

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. The 13-month revenue series (all orders, grouped
by `date_trunc('month', created_at)`), each month with the previous
month's revenue beside it and the difference. Columns: `month`,
`revenue`, `prev` (LAG, NULL for the first month), `delta` (revenue −
prev, NULL for the first month). **Ordered by `month`.**

Run: `uv run dojo test 16_window_functions_2 ex2`

## Exercise 3 — 7-day moving average

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. October 2023 daily revenue again, now with
`ma7` — the average of the current day and the 6 preceding days, rounded
to 2 decimals (early days average over however many rows exist).
Columns: `day`, `revenue`, `ma7`. **Ordered by `day`.**

Run: `uv run dojo test 16_window_functions_2 ex3`

## Exercise 4 — a running total per partition

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. October 2023 again, now split by status. In a
CTE, produce one row per (`day`, `status`) with that day's revenue for
that status. Then add **`running`** — the month-to-date total *within each
status*.

Columns, in this order: `day`, `status`, `revenue`, `running`. **Ordered by
`status` ascending, then `day` ascending.** (31 days x 4 statuses = 124
rows.)

One phrase in the `OVER` clause does all the work: `PARTITION BY status
ORDER BY day`. The partition restarts the accumulation for each status, so
November's `cancelled` running total never inherits `paid`'s. Getting a
running total to reset per group is a question that comes up constantly and
has exactly this one-word answer.

Run: `uv run dojo test 16_window_functions_2 ex4`

## Exercise 5 — looking forward with LEAD

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. The 13-month revenue series (all orders, grouped
by `date_trunc('month', created_at)`), each month with the **next**
month's revenue beside it.

Columns, in this order: `month`, `revenue`, `next_month` (NULL for the
final month). **Ordered by `month` ascending.**

`lead()` is `lag()` pointing the other way, and the NULL lands at the *end*
of the series instead of the beginning. Both take an optional offset —
`lag(revenue, 12)` is the year-ago comparison every finance report wants —
and an optional default: `lag(revenue, 1, 0)` substitutes zero instead of
NULL at the edge, which is occasionally right and usually a lie.

Run: `uv run dojo test 16_window_functions_2 ex5`

## Exercise 6 — the best day so far

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. October 2023 daily revenue one last time, with
**`best_so_far`** — the highest single-day revenue seen up to and including
that day.

Columns, in this order: `day`, `revenue`, `best_so_far`. **Ordered by
`day` ascending.** (31 rows.)

`sum()` over an ordered window gives a running total; `max()` over the same
window gives a running maximum. Every aggregate you know works this way —
`min`, `avg`, `count`, `bool_or` — and the default frame ("from the start
of the partition to the current row") is what makes them all cumulative.
Once that clicks, "highest water mark to date", "worst drawdown so far" and
"has this ever happened yet" all stop being special cases.

Run: `uv run dojo test 16_window_functions_2 ex6`

## Challenge — growth percentage, one query (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. The classic board-deck column: monthly
revenue with **growth_pct** = 100 × (revenue − previous) / previous,
rounded to 1 decimal, NULL for the first month. Columns: `month`,
`revenue`, `growth_pct`. **Ordered by `month`.** One LAG can feed two
expressions — or window once in a CTE and compute outside.

Run: `uv run dojo test 16_window_functions_2 challenge`

## Spaced review

`review1/`: salary quartiles: every staff member with `quartile` =
`ntile(4)` over (`salary` DESC, `id`). Columns: `name`, `salary`,
`quartile`. **Ordered by `salary` DESC, `id`.**
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 16_window_functions_2

Adding `ORDER BY` inside `OVER` gives a window a direction, and direction is
what turns an aggregate into a *sequence* operator. Running totals,
period-over-period comparisons and moving averages are all the same
construct with different knobs — and together they are the grammar of every
time-series report you will ever write.

## Notes

**The frame is the real subject of this lesson.** A window function operates
on a *frame* within the partition. Without `ORDER BY` inside `OVER`, the
frame is the whole partition — that is why lesson 15's `avg(price) OVER
(PARTITION BY category)` gave every row the same value. **With** `ORDER BY`,
the default frame becomes `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT
ROW`: everything from the start of the partition up to here. That default is
precisely a running total, which is why `sum(x) OVER (ORDER BY d)` does what
you want without a frame clause.

**`ROWS` versus `RANGE`, and why it matters.** `ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND
CURRENT ROW` counts *physical rows*. `RANGE` counts *peers* — rows with the
same value in the `ORDER BY` — so with ties, `RANGE` includes all of them
and `ROWS` does not. The default frame uses `RANGE`, which means a running
total over a column with duplicate sort keys jumps by the whole tie group at
once rather than one row at a time. That is usually correct for a running
total by date and almost never what someone hand-rolling a moving average
expects. When you write a frame explicitly, say `ROWS` and mean it.
(PostgreSQL 11+ also has `GROUPS`, which counts tie-groups.)

**Moving averages have an edge problem.** `ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND
CURRENT ROW` on day 3 averages three rows, not seven, because only three
exist. That is what the function is defined to do, and it means the first
six points of any 7-day moving average are computed over a different
denominator. Charts that do not drop or mark those points show a spurious
ramp at the start of every series.

**`lag` and `lead` return NULL at the edges — on purpose.** There is no
previous month before the first month, and NULL is the honest answer.
Arithmetic then propagates it (lesson 05), so `revenue - lag(revenue)` is
NULL for the first row, which is exactly the right thing to display. Both
functions take an offset and a default: `lag(revenue, 12)` for year-over-
year, `lag(revenue, 1, 0)` to substitute zero. Use the default argument
sparingly — a zero at the edge of a growth calculation produces an infinite
percentage or a nonsense one.

**Divide-by-zero in growth calculations.** `100 * (revenue - prev) / prev`
raises an error when `prev` is zero and returns NULL when `prev` is NULL.
`nullif(prev, 0)` converts the first case into the second, which is the
standard defensive idiom for every percentage-change column.

**Aggregate first, then window.** All of this composes with lesson 14's
CTEs, and the order matters for performance: aggregate three million rows
into thirty-one daily rows, *then* window over thirty-one. Windowing the raw
rows would force a sort of the whole table for the same answer. This is one
of the most common performance smells in analytics SQL.

**What this replaces.** Before window functions were widely available,
running totals were written as self-joins with `t2.day <= t1.day` — which is
quadratic — or accumulated in application code, where they break the moment
someone paginates. When you see a Python loop adding up query results, you
are usually looking at a window function that escaped. Push it down: the
database sorts once, scans once, and the number is correct on every page.

## ex1 — running total

The default frame doing its job. Check the last row against the month's
total from a separate `sum()` — a running total whose final value does not
equal the plain aggregate means the frame or the partition is wrong.

Note the two-stage shape, which every exercise in this lesson repeats:
aggregate half a million orders down to 31 daily rows in a CTE, then window
over 31 rows. Windowing the raw orders would give the same answer and force
PostgreSQL to sort the whole table. Aggregate first, window second — it is
the single most useful performance habit in analytics SQL.

## ex2 — month-over-month with LAG

Thirteen rows, and the first `prev` is NULL. The `delta` column is NULL
there too, by propagation, which is the correct display for "no previous
month" — resist the urge to `coalesce` it to zero, which would claim growth
of exactly the first month's revenue.

## ex3 — 7-day moving average

The first explicit frame. Look at days 1 through 6 in the output: those
averages are over 1 to 6 rows respectively, not 7. Whether to show, drop or
flag them is a reporting decision, and it should be a conscious one.

## ex4 — a running total per partition

`PARTITION BY status ORDER BY day` — the partition resets the accumulation,
the order drives it. This is the point at which the two clauses inside
`OVER` become clearly independent in your head: one chooses *which rows*,
the other chooses *in what sequence*.

## ex5 — looking forward with LEAD

`lead` is `lag` with the sign flipped and the NULL at the other end. Useful
beyond reporting: `lead(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY
created_at)` gives you each event's successor, and subtracting yields the
gap between consecutive events per customer — the foundation of sessionising
a clickstream, funnel analysis, and churn windows.

## ex6 — the best day so far

`max()` over the running frame. The generalisation is the useful part: every
aggregate becomes cumulative under the default ordered frame. `count(*)
OVER (ORDER BY day)` is a row number; `bool_or(revenue > 100000) OVER (ORDER
BY day)` is "has a record day happened yet"; `avg(x) OVER (ORDER BY d)` is
the cumulative mean.

## challenge — growth percentage, one query

The board-deck column, and the two traps are both edge cases: NULL for the
first month (correct), and division by zero if any month had zero revenue
(use `nullif(prev, 0)`). One `lag` can feed both the subtraction and the
division, or you can window once in a CTE and compute outside — the second
reads better and is easier to check.

## review1 — salary quartiles

`ntile(4)` deals rows into four near-equal buckets in frame order. "Near
equal" is the detail: when the row count is not divisible by the bucket
count, the earlier buckets get the extra rows. `ntile` also does not care
about ties — two people on identical salaries can land in different
quartiles, which is a genuine surprise on a compensation report and an
argument for `percent_rank()` or `cume_dist()` when the boundary matters.

## Further reading

- [Window Function Calls — frames](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html) — `ROWS`/`RANGE`/`GROUPS`, the default frame, and the exclusion clauses. The most important page in this lesson.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) — `lag`, `lead`, `first_value`, `last_value`, `nth_value`, `ntile`, `percent_rank`, `cume_dist`.
- [Window Functions Tutorial](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) — worth a second read now that frames make sense.
- [Date/Time Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) — `date_trunc` and interval arithmetic, which every one of these exercises leans on. Lesson 18 next.
