# Reading - 16_window_functions_2

Adding `ORDER BY` inside `OVER` gives a window a direction, and direction is
what turns an aggregate into a *sequence* operator. Running totals,
period-over-period comparisons and moving averages are all the same
construct with different knobs — and together they are the grammar of every
time-series report you will ever write.

## Notes

**The frame is the real subject of this lesson.** A window function operates
on a *frame* within the partition. Without `ORDER BY` inside `OVER`, the
frame is the whole partition — that is why lesson 15's `avg(price) OVER
(PARTITION BY category)` gave every row the same value. **With** `ORDER BY`,
the default frame becomes `RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT
ROW`: everything from the start of the partition up to here. That default is
precisely a running total, which is why `sum(x) OVER (ORDER BY d)` does what
you want without a frame clause.

**`ROWS` versus `RANGE`, and why it matters.** `ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND
CURRENT ROW` counts *physical rows*. `RANGE` counts *peers* — rows with the
same value in the `ORDER BY` — so with ties, `RANGE` includes all of them
and `ROWS` does not. The default frame uses `RANGE`, which means a running
total over a column with duplicate sort keys jumps by the whole tie group at
once rather than one row at a time. That is usually correct for a running
total by date and almost never what someone hand-rolling a moving average
expects. When you write a frame explicitly, say `ROWS` and mean it.
(PostgreSQL 11+ also has `GROUPS`, which counts tie-groups.)

**Moving averages have an edge problem.** `ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND
CURRENT ROW` on day 3 averages three rows, not seven, because only three
exist. That is what the function is defined to do, and it means the first
six points of any 7-day moving average are computed over a different
denominator. Charts that do not drop or mark those points show a spurious
ramp at the start of every series.

**`lag` and `lead` return NULL at the edges — on purpose.** There is no
previous month before the first month, and NULL is the honest answer.
Arithmetic then propagates it (lesson 05), so `revenue - lag(revenue)` is
NULL for the first row, which is exactly the right thing to display. Both
functions take an offset and a default: `lag(revenue, 12)` for year-over-
year, `lag(revenue, 1, 0)` to substitute zero. Use the default argument
sparingly — a zero at the edge of a growth calculation produces an infinite
percentage or a nonsense one.

**Divide-by-zero in growth calculations.** `100 * (revenue - prev) / prev`
raises an error when `prev` is zero and returns NULL when `prev` is NULL.
`nullif(prev, 0)` converts the first case into the second, which is the
standard defensive idiom for every percentage-change column.

**Aggregate first, then window.** All of this composes with lesson 14's
CTEs, and the order matters for performance: aggregate three million rows
into thirty-one daily rows, *then* window over thirty-one. Windowing the raw
rows would force a sort of the whole table for the same answer. This is one
of the most common performance smells in analytics SQL.

**What this replaces.** Before window functions were widely available,
running totals were written as self-joins with `t2.day <= t1.day` — which is
quadratic — or accumulated in application code, where they break the moment
someone paginates. When you see a Python loop adding up query results, you
are usually looking at a window function that escaped. Push it down: the
database sorts once, scans once, and the number is correct on every page.

## ex1 — running total

The default frame doing its job. Check the last row against the month's
total from a separate `sum()` — a running total whose final value does not
equal the plain aggregate means the frame or the partition is wrong.

Note the two-stage shape, which every exercise in this lesson repeats:
aggregate half a million orders down to 31 daily rows in a CTE, then window
over 31 rows. Windowing the raw orders would give the same answer and force
PostgreSQL to sort the whole table. Aggregate first, window second — it is
the single most useful performance habit in analytics SQL.

## ex2 — month-over-month with LAG

Thirteen rows, and the first `prev` is NULL. The `delta` column is NULL
there too, by propagation, which is the correct display for "no previous
month" — resist the urge to `coalesce` it to zero, which would claim growth
of exactly the first month's revenue.

## ex3 — 7-day moving average

The first explicit frame. Look at days 1 through 6 in the output: those
averages are over 1 to 6 rows respectively, not 7. Whether to show, drop or
flag them is a reporting decision, and it should be a conscious one.

## ex4 — a running total per partition

`PARTITION BY status ORDER BY day` — the partition resets the accumulation,
the order drives it. This is the point at which the two clauses inside
`OVER` become clearly independent in your head: one chooses *which rows*,
the other chooses *in what sequence*.

## ex5 — looking forward with LEAD

`lead` is `lag` with the sign flipped and the NULL at the other end. Useful
beyond reporting: `lead(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY
created_at)` gives you each event's successor, and subtracting yields the
gap between consecutive events per customer — the foundation of sessionising
a clickstream, funnel analysis, and churn windows.

## ex6 — the best day so far

`max()` over the running frame. The generalisation is the useful part: every
aggregate becomes cumulative under the default ordered frame. `count(*)
OVER (ORDER BY day)` is a row number; `bool_or(revenue > 100000) OVER (ORDER
BY day)` is "has a record day happened yet"; `avg(x) OVER (ORDER BY d)` is
the cumulative mean.

## challenge — growth percentage, one query

The board-deck column, and the two traps are both edge cases: NULL for the
first month (correct), and division by zero if any month had zero revenue
(use `nullif(prev, 0)`). One `lag` can feed both the subtraction and the
division, or you can window once in a CTE and compute outside — the second
reads better and is easier to check.

## review1 — salary quartiles

`ntile(4)` deals rows into four near-equal buckets in frame order. "Near
equal" is the detail: when the row count is not divisible by the bucket
count, the earlier buckets get the extra rows. `ntile` also does not care
about ties — two people on identical salaries can land in different
quartiles, which is a genuine surprise on a compensation report and an
argument for `percent_rank()` or `cume_dist()` when the boundary matters.

## Further reading

- [Window Function Calls — frames](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html) — `ROWS`/`RANGE`/`GROUPS`, the default frame, and the exclusion clauses. The most important page in this lesson.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) — `lag`, `lead`, `first_value`, `last_value`, `nth_value`, `ntile`, `percent_rank`, `cume_dist`.
- [Window Functions Tutorial](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) — worth a second read now that frames make sense.
- [Date/Time Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) — `date_trunc` and interval arithmetic, which every one of these exercises leans on. Lesson 18 next.

## Challenge — growth percentage, one query (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. The classic board-deck column: monthly
revenue with **growth_pct** = 100 × (revenue − previous) / previous,
rounded to 1 decimal, NULL for the first month. Columns: `month`,
`revenue`, `growth_pct`. **Ordered by `month`.** One LAG can feed two
expressions — or window once in a CTE and compute outside.

Run: `uv run dojo test 16_window_functions_2 challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
`lag(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)` appears twice in the formula
(subtraction and division) — either repeat it, or compute `prev` in a
second CTE layer and do plain arithmetic outside.

## Hint 2
```sql
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month, sum(total) AS revenue
    FROM orders GROUP BY 1
), with_prev AS (
    SELECT month, revenue,
           lag(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev
    FROM monthly
)
SELECT month, revenue,
       round(100 * (revenue - prev) / prev, 1) AS growth_pct
FROM with_prev
ORDER BY month;
```

Why no divide-by-zero guard? Every month has revenue here — but notice
the first month: NULL/NULL arithmetic just yields NULL, exactly right.

## Hint 1
Two layers: a CTE grouping October's orders into (day, revenue), then a
window `sum(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day)` on top. The default frame does
the "so far" for you.

## Hint 2
```sql
WITH daily AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at) AS day, sum(total) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE created_at >= '2023-10-01' AND created_at < '2023-11-01'
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT day, revenue,
       sum(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS running
FROM daily
ORDER BY day;
```

## Hint 1
CTE: the 13-row monthly series (lesson 07's challenge). Then `lag(revenue)
OVER (ORDER BY month)` gives `prev`; `revenue - lag(...)` gives `delta` —
NULL propagates through the subtraction on row one, which is what the
prompt wants.

```sql
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month, sum(total) AS revenue
    FROM orders GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month, revenue,
       lag(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)           AS prev,
       revenue - lag(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS delta
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;
```

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — a running total per partition

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. October 2023 again, now split by status. In a
CTE, produce one row per (`day`, `status`) with that day's revenue for
that status. Then add **`running`** — the month-to-date total *within each
status*.

Columns, in this order: `day`, `status`, `revenue`, `running`. **Ordered by
`status` ascending, then `day` ascending.** (31 days x 4 statuses = 124
rows.)

One phrase in the `OVER` clause does all the work: `PARTITION BY status
ORDER BY day`. The partition restarts the accumulation for each status, so
November's `cancelled` running total never inherits `paid`'s. Getting a
running total to reset per group is a question that comes up constantly and
has exactly this one-word answer.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The CTE groups by two keys this time. The window adds
`PARTITION BY status` to exercise 1's running total.

## Hint 2
`sum(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY status ORDER BY day) AS running`, then
`ORDER BY status, day` on the outside.

references.solution.sql:
WITH daily AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at) AS day,
           status,
           sum(total) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE created_at >= '2023-10-01'
      AND created_at <  '2023-11-01'
    GROUP BY 1, 2
)
SELECT day,
       status,
       revenue,
       sum(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY status ORDER BY day) AS running
FROM daily
ORDER BY status, day;
references.expected.sql:

    GROUP BY 1, 2
)
SELECT day, status, revenue,
       sum(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY status ORDER BY day) AS running
FROM daily
ORDER BY status, day;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — looking forward with LEAD

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. The 13-month revenue series (all orders, grouped
by `date_trunc('month', created_at)`), each month with the **next**
month's revenue beside it.

Columns, in this order: `month`, `revenue`, `next_month` (NULL for the
final month). **Ordered by `month` ascending.**

`lead()` is `lag()` pointing the other way, and the NULL lands at the *end*
of the series instead of the beginning. Both take an optional offset —
`lag(revenue, 12)` is the year-ago comparison every finance report wants —
and an optional default: `lag(revenue, 1, 0)` substitutes zero instead of
NULL at the edge, which is occasionally right and usually a lie.

Run: `uv run dojo test 16_window_functions_2 ex5`

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — the best day so far

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. October 2023 daily revenue one last time, with
**`best_so_far`** — the highest single-day revenue seen up to and including
that day.

Columns, in this order: `day`, `revenue`, `best_so_far`. **Ordered by
`day` ascending.** (31 rows.)

`sum()` over an ordered window gives a running total; `max()` over the same
window gives a running maximum. Every aggregate you know works this way —
`min`, `avg`, `count`, `bool_or` — and the default frame ("from the start
of the partition to the current row") is what makes them all cumulative.
Once that clicks, "highest water mark to date", "worst drawdown so far" and
"has this ever happened yet" all stop being special cases.

references.solution.sql:
WITH daily AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at) AS day,
           sum(total) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE created_at >= '2023-10-01'
      AND created_at <  '2023-11-01'
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT day,
       revenue,
       max(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS best_so_far
FROM daily
ORDER BY day;

WITH daily AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at) AS day, sum(total) AS revenue

    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT day, revenue,
       max(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS best_so_far
FROM daily
ORDER BY day;

lessons.briefing:
# 17 — Conditional aggregation and pivots

"One row per category, one **column** per status." The data lives in long
form — (category, status, revenue) triples — but the CFO's spreadsheet
brain wants a grid. Rotating rows into columns is called **pivoting**, and
in SQL it's nothing more than conditional aggregation: one aggregate per
desired column, each scoped to its slice.

## Concept

Two equivalent idioms:

```sql
-- FILTER (modern, readable — you met it in lesson 06)
sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'paid')    AS paid,

-- CASE inside the aggregate (older; you'll see it in every legacy codebase)
sum(CASE WHEN o.status = 'paid'
         THEN oi.quantity * oi.price ELSE 0 END)                AS paid,
```

One subtle difference: with no matching rows, FILTER yields **NULL**, the
CASE...ELSE 0 form yields **0**. Neither is "right" — but your report
should choose deliberately (`coalesce(..., 0)` converts).

The reverse — columns back into rows — is **unpivoting**. The neat
PostgreSQL idiom is a LATERAL join against a little inline table of
(label, value) pairs:

```sql
SELECT w.category, v.status, v.revenue
FROM wide w
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (VALUES ('pending', w.pending),
                           ('paid',    w.paid)) AS v(status, revenue);
```

`LATERAL` lets the VALUES list mention the current row of `w` — each wide
row explodes into one row per pair. (LATERAL is also worth knowing on its
own; it's "a subquery that can see the row to its left".)

## Exercise 1 — the revenue grid

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. One row per product `category`; columns:
`category`, then line-item revenue (`sum(quantity * price)`) for each
order status: `pending`, `paid`, `shipped`, `cancelled` — four FILTERed
aggregates over an `orders` × `order_items` × `products` join. Any row
order. (6 rows × 5 columns.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 17_conditional_pivots ex1`

## Exercise 2 — signups by year, the CASE way

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. One row per `country`: `country`, `y2022`
(customers created in 2022), `y2023` (created in 2023). Use the
`count`/`sum`-with-CASE idiom for at least one of them — you need to be
able to *read* it in legacy code, so write it once. Counts, not NULLs:
a country with no 2022 signups must show 0. Any order. (12 rows;
signups span 2021–2023, so the two columns don't sum to the total.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 17_conditional_pivots ex2`

## Exercise 3 — salary bands per department

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. HR wants a compensation grid: one row per
`department`, with a **count** of staff in each of three salary bands.

Columns, in this order: `department`, `under_60k` (salary below 60,000),
`mid` (60,000 up to but not including 100,000), `over_100k` (100,000 and
above). Five rows, any order.

Note what changes when the aggregate is `count` rather than `sum`: an empty
band shows **0**, not NULL, because `count` over zero rows is defined as
zero while every other aggregate returns NULL. That asymmetry is the reason
a `sum(...) FILTER (...)` pivot usually needs a `coalesce` and a
`count(*) FILTER (...)` pivot never does.

Run: `uv run dojo test 17_conditional_pivots ex3`

## Exercise 4 — each group's share of the whole

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The order-status breakdown with percentages: one
row per `status`, with the order count and that status's **share of all
orders** as a percentage rounded to 1 decimal.

Columns, in this order: `status`, `orders` (count), `pct`. Four rows, any
order. The four percentages should add to 100.

The denominator is the trick. You need the grand total *while* grouping,
and the tool is a window function layered on top of an aggregate:

```sql
round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 1) AS pct
```

`sum(count(*)) OVER ()` reads strangely and is exactly right: aggregation
happens first, producing four rows, and the window then sums across those
four. Windows are evaluated *after* grouping, so a window function may take
an aggregate as its argument — but not the other way round.

Run: `uv run dojo test 17_conditional_pivots ex4`

## Challenge — unpivot it back (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Take ex1's wide grid (rebuild it in a CTE)
and unpivot to long form: `category`, `status`, `revenue` — 24 rows (6
categories × 4 statuses), using the LATERAL VALUES idiom. Any order.
Statuses spelled exactly `pending`, `paid`, `shipped`, `cancelled`.

Run: `uv run dojo test 17_conditional_pivots challenge`

## Spaced review

`review1/`: one row, four columns: the **average** order total per status
(`pending`, `paid`, `shipped`, `cancelled`), each rounded to 2 decimals,
via FILTER.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 17_conditional_pivots

A pivot is not a feature. It is `GROUP BY` plus one aggregate per output
column, each scoped to its own slice — which is why PostgreSQL never needed
a `PIVOT` keyword and why you can build far stranger grids than a `PIVOT`
keyword would allow.

## Notes

**Conditional aggregation is the whole idea.** "One row per category, one
column per status" means: group by category, and for each status write an
aggregate that only sees that status's rows. `FILTER (WHERE ...)` scopes an
aggregate; the older `sum(CASE WHEN ... THEN x ELSE 0 END)` does the same
thing less readably. Both make exactly one pass over the data.

**`FILTER` and `CASE` differ on the empty case.** With no matching rows,
`sum(x) FILTER (WHERE ...)` is **NULL** and `sum(CASE WHEN ... THEN x ELSE 0
END)` is **0** — because the second form contributed a real zero for every
non-matching row. Neither is right; a report should choose deliberately.
`coalesce(sum(x) FILTER (...), 0)` gets the zero without abandoning `FILTER`.
`count` is the exception that catches people: it returns 0 over zero rows,
so a count-based pivot never needs the `coalesce`.

**The old `CASE` idiom has a trap.** `count(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 END)`
works, because the missing `ELSE` yields NULL and `count` skips NULLs. Add
`ELSE 0` "for tidiness" and it counts every row in the group, because 0 is
not NULL. This bug is in production somewhere near you.

**Windows layer on top of aggregates.** `sum(count(*)) OVER ()` is legal and
useful: grouping happens first, then the window sees the grouped rows. That
one line gives you every "percentage of total", "share of parent", and
"rank among groups" column without a second query or a self-join. The
reverse — an aggregate over a window function — is not allowed, because the
window has not been computed yet. The evaluation order from lesson 07 is
doing all the explaining here.

**Unpivoting: columns back into rows.** The PostgreSQL idiom is a `LATERAL`
join against an inline `VALUES` list, which can mention the current row:

```sql
FROM wide w
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (VALUES ('paid', w.paid), ('pending', w.pending))
           AS v(status, revenue)
```

Each wide row explodes into one row per pair. `unnest(ARRAY[...])` does the
same job for a single column. Lesson 48 makes `LATERAL` a topic in its own
right.

**When *not* to pivot in SQL.** When the column set is dynamic. "One column
per month, forever" means a schema change every month, or generated SQL, or
the `crosstab()` function from the `tablefunc` extension — which needs the
column list up front anyway. The rule that production reporting stacks
converge on: **SQL emits long form; the presentation layer rotates.** Long
form has a stable schema, tests cleanly, and every BI tool, spreadsheet and
dataframe library can pivot it in one line. Pivot in SQL when the columns
are a small, closed set — four order statuses, three salary bands — and the
result is a final artefact rather than an input to something else.

## ex1 — the revenue grid

Four filtered aggregates over a three-table join, and the join's grain is
what makes it correct: `sum(quantity * price)` over line items, not over
orders. Also worth checking: do the four columns sum to the category's total
revenue? They must, because the four statuses partition the orders.

## ex2 — signups by year, the CASE way

Written the old way on purpose, because you will read it in legacy code far
more often than you write it. Note the prompt's requirement that a country
with no 2022 signups shows 0 — that is the `ELSE 0` question, and with
`count` it resolves itself.

## ex3 — salary bands per department

Three counts, three half-open bands. The bands come from lesson 04 and the
`FILTER` from lesson 06; nothing here is new, which is the point of a pivot —
it is composition, not a feature. Check that each row's three numbers sum to
that department's headcount.

## ex4 — each group's share of the whole

`sum(count(*)) OVER ()` is the line worth memorising. It appears in every
"share of total" column ever written, and the `100.0` rather than `100` is
the second detail: integer division would truncate the ratio to zero before
`round` ever saw it. Cast or use a numeric literal whenever you divide.

## challenge — unpivot it back

`LATERAL` earns its introduction here: the `VALUES` list refers to `w.paid`
and `w.pending` from the row on its left, which an ordinary subquery in
`FROM` cannot do. Round-tripping a grid back to long form is a genuinely
useful skill when someone hands you a wide spreadsheet and the rest of your
pipeline expects tidy data.

## review1 — average order total per status

Four `avg(...) FILTER (...)` aggregates on one row. Two things to predict
before running: whether any status could produce NULL here (no — all four
statuses have orders), and whether the four averages average to the overall
average (no — that would require equal group sizes, and `paid` is half the
table).

## Further reading

- [Aggregate Expressions — `FILTER`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html) — the syntax and where `FILTER` may appear.
- [`FILTER` versus `CASE`](https://modern-sql.com/feature/filter) — Markus Winand on the empty-set difference and portability.
- [`tablefunc` / `crosstab()`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tablefunc.html) — PostgreSQL's actual pivot function, and why its fixed column list is a real constraint.
- [Table Expressions — `LATERAL`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the unpivot idiom's engine. Lesson 48.

## Ten-pass spaced repetition

Use this ladder after completing **17 — Conditional aggregation and pivots**. Each pass changes the retrieval
task so repetition strengthens recall instead of becoming answer recognition.
Do the named exercise from a blank starting point whenever practical, and only
open its hints after recording your first attempt.

| Pass | When | Practice target | Retrieval task |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | now | `challenge` | Close the notes and state the central rule in one precise sentence. |
| 2 | 3 days | `ex1` | Rebuild the smallest valid example from memory, then explain each part. |
| 3 | 7 days | `ex2` | Predict the result or behavior before running anything; reconcile surprises. |
| 4 | 21 days | `ex3` | Solve from a blank file and name the first tempting mistake you avoided. |
| 5 | 60 days | `ex4` | Contrast this technique with its nearest alternative and choose between them. |
| 6 | 120 days | `review1` | Add one realistic constraint and adapt the solution without consulting notes. |
| 7 | 240 days | `challenge` | Debug a deliberately broken version; explain the evidence before the repair. |
| 8 | 1 year | `ex1` | Teach the idea aloud in two minutes, including one boundary case. |

# Reading - 17_conditional_pivots

A pivot is not a feature. It is `GROUP BY` plus one aggregate per output
column, each scoped to its own slice — which is why PostgreSQL never needed
a `PIVOT` keyword and why you can build far stranger grids than a `PIVOT`
keyword would allow.

## Notes

**Conditional aggregation is the whole idea.** "One row per category, one
column per status" means: group by category, and for each status write an
aggregate that only sees that status's rows. `FILTER (WHERE ...)` scopes an
aggregate; the older `sum(CASE WHEN ... THEN x ELSE 0 END)` does the same
thing less readably. Both make exactly one pass over the data.

**`FILTER` and `CASE` differ on the empty case.** With no matching rows,
`sum(x) FILTER (WHERE ...)` is **NULL** and `sum(CASE WHEN ... THEN x ELSE 0
END)` is **0** — because the second form contributed a real zero for every
non-matching row. Neither is right; a report should choose deliberately.
`coalesce(sum(x) FILTER (...), 0)` gets the zero without abandoning `FILTER`.
`count` is the exception that catches people: it returns 0 over zero rows,
so a count-based pivot never needs the `coalesce`.

**The old `CASE` idiom has a trap.** `count(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 END)`
works, because the missing `ELSE` yields NULL and `count` skips NULLs. Add
`ELSE 0` "for tidiness" and it counts every row in the group, because 0 is
not NULL. This bug is in production somewhere near you.

**Windows layer on top of aggregates.** `sum(count(*)) OVER ()` is legal and
useful: grouping happens first, then the window sees the grouped rows. That
one line gives you every "percentage of total", "share of parent", and
"rank among groups" column without a second query or a self-join. The
reverse — an aggregate over a window function — is not allowed, because the
window has not been computed yet. The evaluation order from lesson 07 is
doing all the explaining here.

**Unpivoting: columns back into rows.** The PostgreSQL idiom is a `LATERAL`
join against an inline `VALUES` list, which can mention the current row:

```sql
FROM wide w
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (VALUES ('paid', w.paid), ('pending', w.pending))
           AS v(status, revenue)
```

Each wide row explodes into one row per pair. `unnest(ARRAY[...])` does the
same job for a single column. Lesson 48 makes `LATERAL` a topic in its own
right.

**When *not* to pivot in SQL.** When the column set is dynamic. "One column
per month, forever" means a schema change every month, or generated SQL, or
the `crosstab()` function from the `tablefunc` extension — which needs the
column list up front anyway. The rule that production reporting stacks
converge on: **SQL emits long form; the presentation layer rotates.** Long
form has a stable schema, tests cleanly, and every BI tool, spreadsheet and
dataframe library can pivot it in one line. Pivot in SQL when the columns
are a small, closed set — four order statuses, three salary bands — and the
result is a final artefact rather than an input to something else.

## ex1 — the revenue grid

Four filtered aggregates over a three-table join, and the join's grain is
what makes it correct: `sum(quantity * price)` over line items, not over
orders. Also worth checking: do the four columns sum to the category's total
revenue? They must, because the four statuses partition the orders.

## ex2 — signups by year, the CASE way

Written the old way on purpose, because you will read it in legacy code far
more often than you write it. Note the prompt's requirement that a country
with no 2022 signups shows 0 — that is the `ELSE 0` question, and with
`count` it resolves itself.

## ex3 — salary bands per department

Three counts, three half-open bands. The bands come from lesson 04 and the
`FILTER` from lesson 06; nothing here is new, which is the point of a pivot —
it is composition, not a feature. Check that each row's three numbers sum to
that department's headcount.

## ex4 — each group's share of the whole

`sum(count(*)) OVER ()` is the line worth memorising. It appears in every
"share of total" column ever written, and the `100.0` rather than `100` is
the second detail: integer division would truncate the ratio to zero before
`round` ever saw it. Cast or use a numeric literal whenever you divide.

## challenge — unpivot it back

`LATERAL` earns its introduction here: the `VALUES` list refers to `w.paid`
and `w.pending` from the row on its left, which an ordinary subquery in
`FROM` cannot do. Round-tripping a grid back to long form is a genuinely
useful skill when someone hands you a wide spreadsheet and the rest of your
pipeline expects tidy data.

## review1 — average order total per status

Four `avg(...) FILTER (...)` aggregates on one row. Two things to predict
before running: whether any status could produce NULL here (no — all four
statuses have orders), and whether the four averages average to the overall
average (no — that would require equal group sizes, and `paid` is half the
table).

## Further reading

- [Aggregate Expressions — `FILTER`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html) — the syntax and where `FILTER` may appear.
- [`FILTER` versus `CASE`](https://modern-sql.com/feature/filter) — Markus Winand on the empty-set difference and portability.
- [`tablefunc` / `crosstab()`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tablefunc.html) — PostgreSQL's actual pivot function, and why its fixed column list is a real constraint.
- [Table Expressions — `LATERAL`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the unpivot idiom's engine. Lesson 48.

## Hint 1
CTE = your ex1 query verbatim. Then CROSS JOIN LATERAL a VALUES list of

## Hint 2
```sql
WITH wide AS ( <your ex1 query, minus the semicolon> )
SELECT w.category, v.status, v.revenue
FROM wide w
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (VALUES
```

references.solution.sql:
WITH wide AS (
    SELECT p.category,
           sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'pending')   AS pending,
           sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'paid')      AS paid,
           sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'shipped')   AS shipped,
           sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled
    FROM orders o
    JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
    JOIN products p     ON p.id = oi.product_id
    GROUP BY p.category
)
SELECT w.category, v.status, v.revenue
FROM wide w
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (VALUES
    ('pending',   w.pending),
    ('paid',      w.paid),
    ('shipped',   w.shipped),
    ('cancelled', w.cancelled)
) AS v(status, revenue);
references.expected.sql:
SELECT p.category, o.status, sum(oi.quantity * oi.price)
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
GROUP BY p.category, o.status;

## Hint 1
Start from lesson 12 ex3's three-table join. Replace the single revenue
column with four copies of the same sum, each wearing a different
`FILTER (WHERE o.status = '...')`.

## Hint 2
```sql
SELECT p.category,
       sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'pending')   AS pending,
       sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'paid')      AS paid,
       ... two more ...
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p     ON p.id = oi.product_id
GROUP BY p.category;
```

references.solution.sql:
SELECT p.category,
       sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'pending')   AS pending,
       sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'paid')      AS paid,
       sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'shipped')   AS shipped,
       sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p     ON p.id = oi.product_id
GROUP BY p.category;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT p.category,
  sum(CASE WHEN o.status = 'pending' THEN oi.quantity * oi.price END),
  sum(CASE WHEN o.status = 'paid' THEN oi.quantity * oi.price END),
  sum(CASE WHEN o.status = 'shipped' THEN oi.quantity * oi.price END),
  sum(CASE WHEN o.status = 'cancelled' THEN oi.quantity * oi.price END)
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
GROUP BY p.category;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — signups by year, the CASE way

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. One row per `country`: `country`, `y2022`
(customers created in 2022), `y2023` (created in 2023). Use the
`count`/`sum`-with-CASE idiom for at least one of them — you need to be
able to *read* it in legacy code, so write it once. Counts, not NULLs:
a country with no 2022 signups must show 0. Any order. (12 rows;
signups span 2021–2023, so the two columns don't sum to the total.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 17_conditional_pivots ex2`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The year of a timestamp: `extract(year FROM created_at)` (lesson 18 makes
this official; that's the whole preview you need). Count-with-CASE:
`count(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 END)` — CASE without ELSE yields NULL, and
count skips NULLs. Or `sum(CASE ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.

## Hint 2
```sql
SELECT country,
       count(CASE WHEN extract(year FROM created_at) = 2022 THEN 1 END) AS y2022,
       count(CASE WHEN extract(year FROM created_at) = 2023 THEN 1 END) AS y2023
FROM customers
GROUP BY country;
```

(`count` of no matches is 0, so the "must show 0" requirement is free.)

## Exercise 3 — salary bands per department

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. HR wants a compensation grid: one row per
`department`, with a **count** of staff in each of three salary bands.

Columns, in this order: `department`, `under_60k` (salary below 60,000),
`mid` (60,000 up to but not including 100,000), `over_100k` (100,000 and
above). Five rows, any order.

Note what changes when the aggregate is `count` rather than `sum`: an empty
band shows **0**, not NULL, because `count` over zero rows is defined as
zero while every other aggregate returns NULL. That asymmetry is the reason
a `sum(...) FILTER (...)` pivot usually needs a `coalesce` and a
`count(*) FILTER (...)` pivot never does.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — each group's share of the whole

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The order-status breakdown with percentages: one
row per `status`, with the order count and that status's **share of all
orders** as a percentage rounded to 1 decimal.

Columns, in this order: `status`, `orders` (count), `pct`. Four rows, any
order. The four percentages should add to 100.

The denominator is the trick. You need the grand total *while* grouping,
and the tool is a window function layered on top of an aggregate:

```sql
round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 1) AS pct
```

`sum(count(*)) OVER ()` reads strangely and is exactly right: aggregation
happens first, producing four rows, and the window then sums across those
four. Windows are evaluated *after* grouping, so a window function may take
an aggregate as its argument — but not the other way round.

Run: `uv run dojo test 17_conditional_pivots ex4`

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
`GROUP BY status` first. The percentage's denominator is the total
across all groups, which an empty `OVER ()` window gives you.

## Hint 2
`round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 1) AS pct` - note the
`100.0` so the division is numeric rather than integer.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT status,
       count(*) AS orders,
       round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 1) AS pct
FROM orders
GROUP BY status;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT status, count(*) AS orders,
       round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 1) AS pct
FROM orders
GROUP BY status;

leaned on `date_trunc` twice without a proper introduction. Time to pay
the debt: truncation, extraction, interval arithmetic, and the
series-generation trick that finds what *didn't* happen.

## Concept

```sql
date_trunc('month', created_at)        -- 2023-07-19 14:02 -> 2023-07-01 00:00
extract(year  FROM created_at)         -- 2023 (numeric)
extract(dow   FROM created_at)         -- day of week, 0 = Sunday .. 6 = Saturday
extract(hour  FROM ts)                 -- 0..23
created_at + interval '7 days'         -- timestamp arithmetic
now() - interval '90 days'             -- (we never use now() in gates — determinism)
```

- **`date_trunc` groups; `extract` classifies.** Truncating to month keeps
  months of different years apart (2022-11 ≠ 2023-11); extracting month
  folds all Novembers together. Choosing wrong flips a report's meaning.
- Half-open ranges, always: `>= start AND < end` (you adopted this in
  lesson 12; it's doubly important with timestamps, where `BETWEEN`'s
  inclusive end bites at midnight).
- **`generate_series`** manufactures rows that don't exist in any table:

```sql
SELECT gs::date AS day
FROM generate_series('2023-10-15'::date, '2023-11-13'::date,
                     interval '1 day') AS gs;
```

  Joined (LEFT, lesson 09!) against real data, a series exposes the
  *holes* — days with no sales, hours with no events. Databases only
  store what happened; the series represents what could have.

One honest paragraph on types: `timestamptz` (our columns) stores an
instant in UTC and renders it in your session's time zone; `timestamp`
stores wall-clock digits with no zone attached. Cross-zone arithmetic
and DST make `timestamp` a foot-gun for instants — the rule in modern
PostgreSQL shops is **timestamptz unless you can argue otherwise** (a
birthday is a `date`; "9am local, every site" is a `time` + zone name).
Part 4 revisits this when you design schemas.

## Exercise 1 — orders by weekday

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Do we sell more on weekends? One row per day of
week: `dow` (0–6, integer — cast the extract: `extract(...)::int`),
`orders` (count). **Ordered by `dow`.** (7 rows.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 18_dates_times ex1`

## Exercise 2 — the days customer 4242 went quiet

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. The clickstream (`events`) spans about a month.
Customer 4242 shows up on most days — but not all. Return every date from
**2023-10-15 through 2023-11-13 inclusive** on which customer 4242
produced **zero events**. One column `day` (a `date`), **ordered
ascending**. Build the calendar with `generate_series`, LEFT JOIN the
customer's event days against it, keep the NULLs (lesson 09's anti-join,
third appearance).

Run: `uv run dojo test 18_dates_times ex2`

## Exercise 3 — extract classifies, date_trunc groups

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Is there a seasonal pattern? Count orders by
**calendar month number**, folding every year together: January 2022 and
January 2023 both land in month 1.

Columns: `month_no` (an integer 1–12 — cast the extract with `::int`),
`orders`. **Ordered by `month_no` ascending.** (12 rows.)

Compare this against lesson 12's ex5, which grouped by `date_trunc('month',
...)` and produced eleven *distinct* months. Same column, same table, two
completely different reports: truncation keeps periods apart, extraction
folds them together. Reaching for the wrong one produces a chart that looks
plausible and answers a question nobody asked.

Note also that this dataset spans thirteen months, so November and December
have one year of data where some other months have two — a seasonality
report over an incomplete number of years is comparing apples to two
apples.

Run: `uv run dojo test 18_dates_times ex3`

## Exercise 4 — weeks, and where they start

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The weekly trading report for October 2023: for
orders with `created_at` in October (half-open, as always), one row per
week with the order count and revenue.

Columns, in this order: `week` (`date_trunc('week', created_at)`),
`orders`, `revenue` (sum of `total`). **Ordered by `week` ascending.**

Count the rows before you run it. October 2023 has 31 days, so you might
expect four or five weeks — and you will get **six**, with the first and
last both partial. `date_trunc('week', ...)` follows ISO 8601: weeks start
on **Monday**, and October 1st 2023 was a Sunday, so it belongs to the week
beginning September 25th.

That is a real reporting hazard. A "weekly revenue" table whose first and
last rows are partial weeks will show a dip at both ends that nobody in the
business caused.

Run: `uv run dojo test 18_dates_times ex4`

## Challenge — peak purchase hours (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. The 3 hours of the day (0–23) with the
most `'purchase'` events. Columns: `hour` (int), `purchases`. Ordered by
`purchases` descending, then `hour` ascending, 3 rows.

Run: `uv run dojo test 18_dates_times challenge`

## Spaced review

`review1/`: orders per **first-week-of-signup**: how many orders were
placed within 7 days of the customer's own signup? One number — but
computed with the half-open interval pattern: `o.created_at >=
c.created_at AND o.created_at < c.created_at + interval '7 days'`.
Columns: just `first_week_orders`. (One row. If you get ~130,000 instead
of ~4,900, you forgot the lower bound — orders *before* signup snuck in.
Think about why that matters.)

# Reading - 18_dates_times

Time is the data type that has cost the industry the most money. Not because
the functions are hard, but because almost every intuition about calendars
is wrong somewhere, and the database will faithfully compute the wrong thing
without complaint.

## Notes

**`timestamptz` versus `timestamp`.** `timestamptz` stores an *instant* —
internally UTC — and renders it in the session's time zone. `timestamp`
stores wall-clock digits with no zone attached, which means it does not
identify a moment in time at all. The modern rule: **`timestamptz` unless
you can argue otherwise.** A birthday is a `date`. "9 a.m. local at every
site" is a `time` plus a zone name, resolved at read time. An event that
happened is a `timestamptz`. Storing instants as `timestamp` is the single
most common time-related schema mistake, and it surfaces as a one-hour bug
twice a year.

**`date_trunc` groups; `extract` classifies.** Truncating to month maps
every instant in November 2023 to `2023-11-01 00:00`, so 2022-11 and 2023-11
stay apart. Extracting the month gives `11` for both, folding all Novembers
together. The first is a time series; the second is seasonality. Choosing
wrong flips the meaning of the report while producing a perfectly plausible
chart.

**Weeks start on Monday.** `date_trunc('week', ...)` is ISO 8601, so a
Sunday belongs to the week that began the previous Monday. If your business
defines weeks as Sunday-start, `date_trunc` will silently disagree with
every dashboard you compare it against. The usual fix is arithmetic —
`date_trunc('week', ts + interval '1 day') - interval '1 day'` — and the
usual mistake is not noticing there was a question.

**Half-open ranges, permanently.** `>= start AND < end`. `BETWEEN` on
timestamps is a bug generator: `BETWEEN '2023-10-01' AND '2023-10-31'`
excludes all but the first instant of October 31st, because a bare date
means midnight. Half-open ranges also tile: consecutive periods meet exactly
once, with no gap and no overlap, which is what makes "the sum of the months
equals the year" true.

**`generate_series` manufactures the rows reality did not provide.** A
database stores what happened; a monitoring query needs to know what *did
not*. Generate the calendar, `LEFT JOIN` the facts, and the NULLs are the
answer:

```sql
SELECT gs::date AS day
FROM generate_series('2023-10-15'::date, '2023-11-13'::date,
                     interval '1 day') AS gs;
```

"Which shops reported no sales yesterday", "which sensors went quiet", "which
days had zero signups" are all the same query. The naive alternative —
querying what happened and eyeballing the gaps — cannot be automated, which
is why this pattern is worth more than its two lines suggest.

**Interval arithmetic is not commutative with calendars.** `+ interval '1
month'` on January 31st gives February 28th; adding a month twice is not the
same as adding two months in every case. `+ interval '1 day'` across a DST
boundary adds a calendar day for `timestamptz` and exactly 24 hours for
`timestamp` — a difference of one hour, twice a year, which is precisely the
kind of bug that is dismissed as "rounding" for six months. `age()` gives
you a symbolic interval ("1 year 2 mons"), while subtraction gives an exact
one; they answer different questions.

**Determinism.** No gate in this course calls `now()`, and no seeded row
depends on it. That is deliberate — a test whose expected output changes
with the wall clock is a test that fails on a Monday. When you need "the last
30 days" in production code, pass the reference instant in as a parameter
rather than reading the clock inside the query; it makes the query testable
and lets you re-run last week's report.

## ex1 — orders by weekday

`extract(dow ...)` returns 0 for Sunday through 6 for Saturday — and
`extract(isodow ...)` returns 1 for Monday through 7 for Sunday. Two
functions, two conventions, one off-by-one waiting to happen. The counts
here are flat because the generator does not model weekends; on real data
this is one of the first queries anyone runs.

## ex2 — the days customer 4242 went quiet

Calendar series, `LEFT JOIN`, keep the NULLs. This is the lesson's most
transferable pattern and the one worth being able to write from memory. Note
that it needs three lessons at once: `generate_series` for the expectation,
the outer join for the comparison, and lesson 05's `IS NULL` for the test.

## ex3 — extract classifies, date_trunc groups

The distinction, made concrete on the same column. Worth saying out loud
once: this report has twelve rows and the data covers thirteen months, so
November and December are drawn from a different number of years than the
rest. Seasonality over a non-integer number of years is a comparison nobody
should make without a footnote.

## ex4 — weeks, and where they start

Six weeks in a 31-day month, both ends partial, because ISO weeks start on
Monday. Two lessons in one: know your period boundaries, and know that the
first and last buckets of any period-grouped report are almost always
partial. Chart them unmarked and someone will ask why business collapsed at
the end of every month.

## challenge — peak purchase hours

`extract(hour ...)` classifying three million events. The hour is extracted
in the *session's* time zone, which for a `timestamptz` means the answer
changes if the session zone changes — a genuinely surprising property, and
the reason production reports pin the zone explicitly with `AT TIME ZONE`
rather than trusting whatever the client connected with.

## review1 — orders in the first week after signup

The half-open interval pattern with both bounds computed per row:
`o.created_at >= c.created_at AND o.created_at < c.created_at + interval '7
days'`. The prompt's warning is the real lesson — drop the lower bound and
you count every order the customer ever placed *before* signing up, which
is a nonsensical population that nonetheless produces a confident number
about 26 times too large.

## Further reading

- [Date/Time Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) — `date_trunc`, `extract`, `age`, `AT TIME ZONE`, and the interval arithmetic rules. The `date_trunc` week note is in here.
- [Date/Time Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-datetime.html) — the `timestamptz` versus `timestamp` argument, with the storage details that settle it.
- [Set Returning Functions — `generate_series`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-srf.html) — including the timestamp-stepping form used by the gap-days pattern.
- [Don't Do This — timestamp without time zone](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) — the short version of the argument, from the PostgreSQL wiki.

# Reading - 18_dates_times

Time is the data type that has cost the industry the most money. Not because
the functions are hard, but because almost every intuition about calendars
is wrong somewhere, and the database will faithfully compute the wrong thing
without complaint.

## Notes

**`timestamptz` versus `timestamp`.** `timestamptz` stores an *instant* —
internally UTC — and renders it in the session's time zone. `timestamp`
stores wall-clock digits with no zone attached, which means it does not
identify a moment in time at all. The modern rule: **`timestamptz` unless
you can argue otherwise.** A birthday is a `date`. "9 a.m. local at every
site" is a `time` plus a zone name, resolved at read time. An event that
happened is a `timestamptz`. Storing instants as `timestamp` is the single
most common time-related schema mistake, and it surfaces as a one-hour bug
twice a year.

**`date_trunc` groups; `extract` classifies.** Truncating to month maps
every instant in November 2023 to `2023-11-01 00:00`, so 2022-11 and 2023-11
stay apart. Extracting the month gives `11` for both, folding all Novembers
together. The first is a time series; the second is seasonality. Choosing
wrong flips the meaning of the report while producing a perfectly plausible
chart.

**Weeks start on Monday.** `date_trunc('week', ...)` is ISO 8601, so a
Sunday belongs to the week that began the previous Monday. If your business
defines weeks as Sunday-start, `date_trunc` will silently disagree with
every dashboard you compare it against. The usual fix is arithmetic —
`date_trunc('week', ts + interval '1 day') - interval '1 day'` — and the
usual mistake is not noticing there was a question.

**Half-open ranges, permanently.** `>= start AND < end`. `BETWEEN` on
timestamps is a bug generator: `BETWEEN '2023-10-01' AND '2023-10-31'`
excludes all but the first instant of October 31st, because a bare date
means midnight. Half-open ranges also tile: consecutive periods meet exactly
once, with no gap and no overlap, which is what makes "the sum of the months
equals the year" true.

**`generate_series` manufactures the rows reality did not provide.** A
database stores what happened; a monitoring query needs to know what *did
not*. Generate the calendar, `LEFT JOIN` the facts, and the NULLs are the
answer:

```sql
SELECT gs::date AS day
FROM generate_series('2023-10-15'::date, '2023-11-13'::date,
                     interval '1 day') AS gs;
```

"Which shops reported no sales yesterday", "which sensors went quiet", "which
days had zero signups" are all the same query. The naive alternative —
querying what happened and eyeballing the gaps — cannot be automated, which
is why this pattern is worth more than its two lines suggest.

**Interval arithmetic is not commutative with calendars.** `+ interval '1
month'` on January 31st gives February 28th; adding a month twice is not the
same as adding two months in every case. `+ interval '1 day'` across a DST
boundary adds a calendar day for `timestamptz` and exactly 24 hours for
`timestamp` — a difference of one hour, twice a year, which is precisely the
kind of bug that is dismissed as "rounding" for six months. `age()` gives
you a symbolic interval ("1 year 2 mons"), while subtraction gives an exact
one; they answer different questions.

**Determinism.** No gate in this course calls `now()`, and no seeded row
depends on it. That is deliberate — a test whose expected output changes
with the wall clock is a test that fails on a Monday. When you need "the last
30 days" in production code, pass the reference instant in as a parameter
rather than reading the clock inside the query; it makes the query testable
and lets you re-run last week's report.

## ex1 — orders by weekday

`extract(dow ...)` returns 0 for Sunday through 6 for Saturday — and
`extract(isodow ...)` returns 1 for Monday through 7 for Sunday. Two
functions, two conventions, one off-by-one waiting to happen. The counts
here are flat because the generator does not model weekends; on real data
this is one of the first queries anyone runs.

## ex2 — the days customer 4242 went quiet

Calendar series, `LEFT JOIN`, keep the NULLs. This is the lesson's most
transferable pattern and the one worth being able to write from memory. Note
that it needs three lessons at once: `generate_series` for the expectation,
the outer join for the comparison, and lesson 05's `IS NULL` for the test.

## ex3 — extract classifies, date_trunc groups

The distinction, made concrete on the same column. Worth saying out loud
once: this report has twelve rows and the data covers thirteen months, so
November and December are drawn from a different number of years than the
rest. Seasonality over a non-integer number of years is a comparison nobody
should make without a footnote.

## ex4 — weeks, and where they start

Six weeks in a 31-day month, both ends partial, because ISO weeks start on
Monday. Two lessons in one: know your period boundaries, and know that the
first and last buckets of any period-grouped report are almost always
partial. Chart them unmarked and someone will ask why business collapsed at
the end of every month.

## challenge — peak purchase hours

`extract(hour ...)` classifying three million events. The hour is extracted
in the *session's* time zone, which for a `timestamptz` means the answer
changes if the session zone changes — a genuinely surprising property, and
the reason production reports pin the zone explicitly with `AT TIME ZONE`
rather than trusting whatever the client connected with.

## review1 — orders in the first week after signup

The half-open interval pattern with both bounds computed per row:
`o.created_at >= c.created_at AND o.created_at < c.created_at + interval '7
days'`. The prompt's warning is the real lesson — drop the lower bound and
you count every order the customer ever placed *before* signing up, which
is a nonsensical population that nonetheless produces a confident number
about 26 times too large.

## Further reading

- [Date/Time Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) — `date_trunc`, `extract`, `age`, `AT TIME ZONE`, and the interval arithmetic rules. The `date_trunc` week note is in here.
- [Date/Time Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-datetime.html) — the `timestamptz` versus `timestamp` argument, with the storage details that settle it.
- [Set Returning Functions — `generate_series`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-srf.html) — including the timestamp-stepping form used by the gap-days pattern.
- [Don't Do This — timestamp without time zone](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) — the short version of the argument, from the PostgreSQL wiki.

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. The 3 hours of the day (0–23) with the

count descending with the hour tie-break, take 3.

```sql
SELECT extract(hour FROM ts)::int AS hour, count(*) AS purchases
FROM events
WHERE event_type = 'purchase'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY purchases DESC, hour
LIMIT 3;
```

```sql
WITH calendar AS (
```

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — extract classifies, date_trunc groups

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Is there a seasonal pattern? Count orders by
**calendar month number**, folding every year together: January 2022 and
January 2023 both land in month 1.

Columns: `month_no` (an integer 1–12 — cast the extract with `::int`),
`orders`. **Ordered by `month_no` ascending.** (12 rows.)

Compare this against lesson 12's ex5, which grouped by `date_trunc('month',
...)` and produced eleven *distinct* months. Same column, same table, two
completely different reports: truncation keeps periods apart, extraction
folds them together. Reaching for the wrong one produces a chart that looks
plausible and answers a question nobody asked.

Note also that this dataset spans thirteen months, so November and December
have one year of data where some other months have two — a seasonality
report over an incomplete number of years is comparing apples to two
apples.

Run: `uv run dojo test 18_dates_times ex3`

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — weeks, and where they start

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The weekly trading report for October 2023: for
orders with `created_at` in October (half-open, as always), one row per
week with the order count and revenue.

Columns, in this order: `week` (`date_trunc('week', created_at)`),
`orders`, `revenue` (sum of `total`). **Ordered by `week` ascending.**

Count the rows before you run it. October 2023 has 31 days, so you might
expect four or five weeks — and you will get **six**, with the first and
last both partial. `date_trunc('week', ...)` follows ISO 8601: weeks start
on **Monday**, and October 1st 2023 was a Sunday, so it belongs to the week
beginning September 25th.

That is a real reporting hazard. A "weekly revenue" table whose first and
last rows are partial weeks will show a dip at both ends that nobody in the
business caused.

lessons.briefing:
# 19 — Text and JSONB

Two column types carry *structure inside the value*: strings ("the
username is the part before the @") and JSONB documents
(`products.attributes` holds `{"color": ..., "size": ..., "tags":
[...]}`). This lesson is the read-side toolbox for both. In Part 5,
lessons 41–42 return here with indexes — today is about correctness.

## Concept

**Text surgery:**

```sql
split_part(email, '@', 1)        -- 'user4242@example.com' -> 'user4242'
position('@' IN email)           -- 1-based offset, 0 if absent
substring(email FROM 1 FOR 4)    -- 'user'
name ~ 'son$'                    -- regex match (case-sensitive; ~* insensitive)
regexp_replace(name, '\s+', ' ', 'g')
```

**JSONB navigation** (against `attributes`):

```sql
attributes ->  'tags'            -- extract as JSONB  (arrow keeps the type)
attributes ->> 'color'           -- extract as TEXT   (double-arrow casts out)
attributes @> '{"color": "red"}' -- containment: does the left side contain
                                 -- the right-side structure?
jsonb_array_elements_text(attributes -> 'tags')  -- one row per array element
```

The `->` vs `->>` distinction causes 90% of beginner JSONB bugs:
`attributes -> 'color' = 'red'` fails (JSONB vs text); either compare
with `->>`, or compare JSONB to JSONB: `-> 'color' = '"red"'::jsonb`
(note the inner quotes!).

`@>` (containment) is the idiomatic "does this document have this
shape" test — `{"tags": ["eco"]}` reads as "tags contains eco". It also
happens to be the operator GIN indexes accelerate (lesson 42 — remember
you wrote this query un-indexed today).

## Exercise 1 — usernames

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. For customers with `id <= 100`: their `id` and
the part of their email before the `@`, aliased `username`. Any order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 19_text_jsonb ex1`

## Exercise 2 — red XL hunting

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Products whose attributes say color `red` AND
size `xl`. Columns: `id`, `name`. Any order. Use `->>` twice (or one
`@>` with a two-key document — both pass; write the one you find
clearer, read the other in the hints). (512 rows.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 19_text_jsonb ex2`

## Exercise 3 — tagged eco

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Products whose `tags` array contains `'eco'`.
Columns: `id`, `name`. Any order. Use the containment operator `@>` —
this is its home turf. (2,079 rows.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 19_text_jsonb ex3`

## Exercise 4 — the first word

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Merchandising wants to group the catalogue by
brand, and the brand is the **first word** of the product name (`Nova
Kettle 812` is a `Nova`).

For products with `id <= 50`, return `id` and the first word of `name`
aliased **`brand`**. Any row order.

`split_part(text, delimiter, n)` returns the nth field, 1-based, and — this
is why it is the right tool — returns the empty string rather than NULL when
the field does not exist. Compare `substring(name FROM '^[^ ]+')`, which
does the same job with a regex and returns NULL on no match. Both are
defensible; knowing which one produces which answer on bad input is the
skill.

Run: `uv run dojo test 19_text_jsonb ex4`

## Exercise 5 — arrow versus double arrow

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Put the two JSONB extraction operators
side by side. For products with `id <= 20`, return three columns:

1. `id`
2. `attributes ->> 'color'` aliased **`color_text`**
3. `attributes -> 'tags'` aliased **`tags_json`**

Twenty rows, any order.

`->` returns **JSONB** and `->>` returns **text**. That single distinction
is behind most JSONB bugs: `attributes -> 'color' = 'red'` fails to compare
(JSONB against text), while `attributes ->> 'color' = 'red'` works, and
`attributes -> 'color' = '"red"'::jsonb` also works — note the quotes
*inside* the string, because a JSON string literal includes them.

The rule of thumb: use `->` while you are still navigating into the
document, and `->>` on the last step, when you want a value SQL can compare.

Run: `uv run dojo test 19_text_jsonb ex5`

## Exercise 6 — the colour census

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. How many products come in each colour? Group the
whole catalogue by the `color` key inside `attributes`.

Columns: `color` (text), `products` (count). Five rows, any order.

Extract with `->>` so you get text you can group on, then `GROUP BY` it
exactly as you would any other expression — this is lesson 07's
"grouping by an expression" with a JSONB accessor in the expression slot.

One thing to notice, because it matters in lesson 42: nothing about this
query can use an index today. `attributes ->> 'color'` is a function of a
column, so a plain index on `attributes` is useless to it, and the whole
10,000-row table must be read. Two fixes exist — an expression index on
`(attributes ->> 'color')` (lesson 40) and a GIN index on the document
(lesson 42) — and they help with different queries.

Run: `uv run dojo test 19_text_jsonb ex6`

## Challenge — the tag census (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. How many products carry each tag? Explode
every product's `tags` array into rows with
`jsonb_array_elements_text`, then group. Columns: `tag`, `products`
(count). Any order. (10 tags; each product has exactly 2.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 19_text_jsonb challenge`

## Spaced review

`review1/`: high-value purchases from the clickstream: events of type
`'purchase'` whose payload `value` exceeds 995. Columns: `id`, `value`
(as int). Any order. (`payload ->> 'value'` is text; cast before
comparing — text comparison would put '996' < '99'!)
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 19_text_jsonb

Text and JSONB are the two column types that carry structure *inside* the
value. Everything in this lesson is about reaching into that structure
correctly — and every performance consequence of doing so is deferred to
lessons 40 to 42, which is worth remembering while you write queries that
read entire tables today.

## Notes

**JSONB versus JSON.** `json` stores the exact text you inserted, including
whitespace, key order and duplicate keys. `jsonb` parses into a binary form:
keys are sorted, duplicates collapse to the last one, whitespace is gone,
and — the part that matters — it can be indexed and queried with operators.
Use `jsonb` unless you specifically need to preserve the original document
byte for byte.

**`->` versus `->>`.** `->` returns JSONB; `->>` returns text. Chain `->` to
navigate (`payload -> 'user' -> 'address'`) and finish with `->>` when you
want a value SQL can compare (`->> 'city'`). The classic bug is
`attributes -> 'color' = 'red'`, which fails because JSONB is not text; the
classic *silent* bug is comparing extracted text numerically without
casting, because `'996' < '99'` is true in text ordering. Always cast:
`(payload ->> 'value')::int`.

**Containment `@>` is the idiomatic shape test.** `attributes @> '{"color":
"red"}'` asks whether the left document contains the right one, at any
depth, including inside arrays: `@> '{"tags": ["eco"]}'` means "tags contains
eco". It reads well, it handles nesting, and — the reason it dominates real
JSONB code — it is the operator a GIN index accelerates (lesson 42). Get in
the habit of expressing JSONB predicates as containment where you can.

**Other operators worth knowing.** `?` tests whether a key exists;
`?|` and `?&` do "any of" and "all of" over an array of keys; `#>` and `#>>`
take a path array (`attributes #>> '{tags,0}'`); `jsonb_path_query` and the
`@@`/`@?` operators implement the SQL/JSON path language for anything more
complicated. `jsonb_array_elements_text(...)` turns an array into rows,
which is how you group by array element.

**Text: know which tool you are reaching for.** `split_part` for fixed
delimiters, `position` and `substring` for offsets, `~` and `~*` for regular
expressions, `regexp_replace` for rewriting, `format()` for building strings
safely. The difference that catches people is what each returns on a
non-match: `split_part` gives an empty string, `substring` with a regex
gives NULL, and `position` gives 0. Three different "not found" values in
one toolbox.

**Empty string is not NULL.** In PostgreSQL — unlike Oracle — `''` is a
real, non-NULL value. So `split_part` returning `''` will pass an
`IS NOT NULL` test and fail a "did we find anything" test written that way.
`nullif(split_part(...), '')` converts one into the other when you want NULL
semantics.

**`LIKE`, regex, and real search are three different things.** `LIKE
'%son%'` and `~ 'son'` both read every row: a B-tree cannot help a pattern
that does not anchor at the start. For substring search at scale you need a
trigram index (`pg_trgm`); for word-based search you need `tsvector` and GIN
(lesson 41). Knowing which of the three a requirement calls for — prefix
match, substring match, or linguistic search — is the actual decision.

**The design question JSONB always raises.** JSONB earns its place for
genuinely variable attributes: merchandising tags, third-party webhook
payloads, form submissions. It gets abused as schema avoidance — whole
orders stored as documents, queried through `->>` chains that no constraint
protects, no type checks, and no index helps. The smell test, which lesson
26 formalises: *if you know the keys in advance and query them constantly,
they are columns.* If they vary per row and you mostly store and fetch
whole, JSONB is honest. `products.attributes` in this database is a fair
use; `orders` as a document would not be.

## ex1 — usernames

`split_part(email, '@', 1)`. Trivial on generated data and a minefield on
real data, where an email column contains leading spaces, capitals,
plus-addressing and the occasional two `@` signs. Parsing user-entered text
is always more forgiving in the query than the data deserves.

## ex2 — red XL hunting

Two `->>` comparisons, or one `@>` with a two-key document. Both are
correct; only one of them can use a GIN index, which you will discover in
lesson 42. Writing it both ways now means the lesson-42 comparison lands on
a query you already understand.

## ex3 — tagged eco

Containment against an array. `@> '{"tags": ["eco"]}'` does not mean "tags
equals \[eco\]" — it means "tags contains eco among possibly other
elements", which is exactly the semantics a tag filter wants. This query
reads all 10,000 products today and will read almost none of them after
lesson 42.

## ex4 — the first word

A small function with a specific "not found" behaviour. The broader point:
deriving a value from text in the query means every consumer agrees on the
definition — but it also means no index can help unless you build an
expression index on the same expression (lesson 40).

## ex5 — arrow versus double arrow

The two operators, side by side, with their types visible. Once you have
seen `tags_json` come back as a JSON array and `color_text` as a bare
string, the rule "navigate with `->`, land with `->>`" stops needing to be
memorised.

## ex6 — the colour census

`GROUP BY` on a JSONB accessor — lesson 07's grouping-by-expression with a
new kind of expression. Note the honest performance footnote in the prompt:
this reads the whole table, and no index you can create with what you know
today changes that. Hold onto that; lesson 40 gives you the expression index
that does.

## challenge — the tag census

`jsonb_array_elements_text` is a *set-returning function*: one input row
becomes several output rows, which means the product row is duplicated once
per tag. That is a deliberate fan-out and it is safe here because you are
counting tags, not products. Put a `sum(price)` in that query instead and
you would double every product's price — the grain problem from lesson 08,
arriving from an unexpected direction.

## review1 — high-value purchases

The cast is the exercise. `payload ->> 'value'` is text, and comparing text
to `995` either errors or — worse, in some formulations — compares
lexicographically, where `'996' < '99'`. `(payload ->> 'value')::int > 995`
is the correct form, and it is also a function of a column, so remember it
when lesson 40 asks you for an expression to index.

## Further reading

- [JSON Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-json.html) — `json` versus `jsonb`, the containment semantics, and the indexing section that lesson 42 builds on.
- [JSON Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-json.html) — `->`, `->>`, `#>`, `@>`, `?`, `jsonb_array_elements_text`, and the SQL/JSON path language.
- [String Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-string.html) — `split_part`, `position`, `substring`, `format`, and the regex family.
- [Pattern Matching](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-matching.html) — `LIKE`, `SIMILAR TO`, POSIX regexes, and the note on which of them an index can serve.

```sql
attributes ->> 'color'           -- extract as TEXT   (double-arrow casts out)
attributes @> '{"color": "red"}' -- containment: does the left side contain
                                 -- the right-side structure?
jsonb_array_elements_text(attributes -> 'tags')  -- one row per array element
```

The `->` vs `->>` distinction causes 90% of beginner JSONB bugs:
`attributes -> 'color' = 'red'` fails (JSONB vs text); either compare
with `->>`, or compare JSONB to JSONB: `-> 'color' = '"red"'::jsonb`
(note the inner quotes!).

`@>` (containment) is the idiomatic "does this document have this
shape" test — `{"tags": ["eco"]}` reads as "tags contains eco". It also
happens to be the operator GIN indexes accelerate (lesson 42 — remember
you wrote this query un-indexed today).

## Exercise 1 — usernames

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. For customers with `id <= 100`: their `id` and
the part of their email before the `@`, aliased `username`. Any order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 19_text_jsonb ex1`

## Exercise 2 — red XL hunting

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Products whose attributes say color `red` AND
size `xl`. Columns: `id`, `name`. Any order. Use `->>` twice (or one
`@>` with a two-key document — both pass; write the one you find
clearer, read the other in the hints). (512 rows.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 19_text_jsonb ex2`

## Exercise 3 — tagged eco

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Products whose `tags` array contains `'eco'`.
Columns: `id`, `name`. Any order. Use the containment operator `@>` —
this is its home turf. (2,079 rows.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 19_text_jsonb ex3`

## Exercise 4 — the first word

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Merchandising wants to group the catalogue by
brand, and the brand is the **first word** of the product name (`Nova
Kettle 812` is a `Nova`).

For products with `id <= 50`, return `id` and the first word of `name`
aliased **`brand`**. Any row order.

`split_part(text, delimiter, n)` returns the nth field, 1-based, and — this
is why it is the right tool — returns the empty string rather than NULL when
the field does not exist. Compare `substring(name FROM '^[^ ]+')`, which
does the same job with a regex and returns NULL on no match. Both are
defensible; knowing which one produces which answer on bad input is the
skill.

Run: `uv run dojo test 19_text_jsonb ex4`

## Exercise 5 — arrow versus double arrow

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Put the two JSONB extraction operators
side by side. For products with `id <= 20`, return three columns:

1. `id`
2. `attributes ->> 'color'` aliased **`color_text`**
3. `attributes -> 'tags'` aliased **`tags_json`**

Twenty rows, any order.

`->` returns **JSONB** and `->>` returns **text**. That single distinction
is behind most JSONB bugs: `attributes -> 'color' = 'red'` fails to compare
(JSONB against text), while `attributes ->> 'color' = 'red'` works, and
`attributes -> 'color' = '"red"'::jsonb` also works — note the quotes
*inside* the string, because a JSON string literal includes them.

The rule of thumb: use `->` while you are still navigating into the
document, and `->>` on the last step, when you want a value SQL can compare.

Run: `uv run dojo test 19_text_jsonb ex5`

## Exercise 6 — the colour census

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. How many products come in each colour? Group the
whole catalogue by the `color` key inside `attributes`.

Columns: `color` (text), `products` (count). Five rows, any order.

Extract with `->>` so you get text you can group on, then `GROUP BY` it
exactly as you would any other expression — this is lesson 07's
"grouping by an expression" with a JSONB accessor in the expression slot.

One thing to notice, because it matters in lesson 42: nothing about this
query can use an index today. `attributes ->> 'color'` is a function of a
column, so a plain index on `attributes` is useless to it, and the whole
10,000-row table must be read. Two fixes exist — an expression index on
`(attributes ->> 'color')` (lesson 40) and a GIN index on the document
(lesson 42) — and they help with different queries.

Run: `uv run dojo test 19_text_jsonb ex6`

## Challenge — the tag census (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. How many products carry each tag? Explode
every product's `tags` array into rows with
`jsonb_array_elements_text`, then group. Columns: `tag`, `products`
(count). Any order. (10 tags; each product has exactly 2.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 19_text_jsonb challenge`

`review1/`: high-value purchases from the clickstream: events of type
`'purchase'` whose payload `value` exceeds 995. Columns: `id`, `value`
(as int). Any order. (`payload ->> 'value'` is text; cast before
comparing — text comparison would put '996' < '99'!)

## The teaching point

JSONB earns its keep for *genuinely* variable attributes — merchandising
tags, third-party payloads, form blobs. It gets abused as "schema
avoidance": entire orders stored as documents, then queried with `->>`
chains that no constraint protects and no type checks. The design smell
test (Part 4 formalizes it): if you know the keys in advance and query
them constantly, they're columns. If they vary by row and you mostly
store-and-fetch, JSONB is honest.
