# Reading - 19_text_jsonb

Text and JSONB are the two column types that carry structure *inside* the
value. Everything in this lesson is about reaching into that structure
correctly — and every performance consequence of doing so is deferred to
lessons 40 to 42, which is worth remembering while you write queries that
read entire tables today.

## Notes

**JSONB versus JSON.** `json` stores the exact text you inserted, including
whitespace, key order and duplicate keys. `jsonb` parses into a binary form:
keys are sorted, duplicates collapse to the last one, whitespace is gone,
and — the part that matters — it can be indexed and queried with operators.
Use `jsonb` unless you specifically need to preserve the original document
byte for byte.

**`->` versus `->>`.** `->` returns JSONB; `->>` returns text. Chain `->` to
navigate (`payload -> 'user' -> 'address'`) and finish with `->>` when you
want a value SQL can compare (`->> 'city'`). The classic bug is
`attributes -> 'color' = 'red'`, which fails because JSONB is not text; the
classic *silent* bug is comparing extracted text numerically without
casting, because `'996' < '99'` is true in text ordering. Always cast:
`(payload ->> 'value')::int`.

**Containment `@>` is the idiomatic shape test.** `attributes @> '{"color":
"red"}'` asks whether the left document contains the right one, at any
depth, including inside arrays: `@> '{"tags": ["eco"]}'` means "tags contains
eco". It reads well, it handles nesting, and — the reason it dominates real
JSONB code — it is the operator a GIN index accelerates (lesson 42). Get in
the habit of expressing JSONB predicates as containment where you can.

**Other operators worth knowing.** `?` tests whether a key exists;
`?|` and `?&` do "any of" and "all of" over an array of keys; `#>` and `#>>`
take a path array (`attributes #>> '{tags,0}'`); `jsonb_path_query` and the
`@@`/`@?` operators implement the SQL/JSON path language for anything more
complicated. `jsonb_array_elements_text(...)` turns an array into rows,
which is how you group by array element.

**Text: know which tool you are reaching for.** `split_part` for fixed
delimiters, `position` and `substring` for offsets, `~` and `~*` for regular
expressions, `regexp_replace` for rewriting, `format()` for building strings
safely. The difference that catches people is what each returns on a
non-match: `split_part` gives an empty string, `substring` with a regex
gives NULL, and `position` gives 0. Three different "not found" values in
one toolbox.

**Empty string is not NULL.** In PostgreSQL — unlike Oracle — `''` is a
real, non-NULL value. So `split_part` returning `''` will pass an
`IS NOT NULL` test and fail a "did we find anything" test written that way.
`nullif(split_part(...), '')` converts one into the other when you want NULL
semantics.

**`LIKE`, regex, and real search are three different things.** `LIKE
'%son%'` and `~ 'son'` both read every row: a B-tree cannot help a pattern
that does not anchor at the start. For substring search at scale you need a
trigram index (`pg_trgm`); for word-based search you need `tsvector` and GIN
(lesson 41). Knowing which of the three a requirement calls for — prefix
match, substring match, or linguistic search — is the actual decision.

**The design question JSONB always raises.** JSONB earns its place for
genuinely variable attributes: merchandising tags, third-party webhook
payloads, form submissions. It gets abused as schema avoidance — whole
orders stored as documents, queried through `->>` chains that no constraint
protects, no type checks, and no index helps. The smell test, which lesson
26 formalises: *if you know the keys in advance and query them constantly,
they are columns.* If they vary per row and you mostly store and fetch
whole, JSONB is honest. `products.attributes` in this database is a fair
use; `orders` as a document would not be.

## ex1 — usernames

`split_part(email, '@', 1)`. Trivial on generated data and a minefield on
real data, where an email column contains leading spaces, capitals,
plus-addressing and the occasional two `@` signs. Parsing user-entered text
is always more forgiving in the query than the data deserves.

## ex2 — red XL hunting

Two `->>` comparisons, or one `@>` with a two-key document. Both are
correct; only one of them can use a GIN index, which you will discover in
lesson 42. Writing it both ways now means the lesson-42 comparison lands on
a query you already understand.

## ex3 — tagged eco

Containment against an array. `@> '{"tags": ["eco"]}'` does not mean "tags
equals \[eco\]" — it means "tags contains eco among possibly other
elements", which is exactly the semantics a tag filter wants. This query
reads all 10,000 products today and will read almost none of them after
lesson 42.

## ex4 — the first word

A small function with a specific "not found" behaviour. The broader point:
deriving a value from text in the query means every consumer agrees on the
definition — but it also means no index can help unless you build an
expression index on the same expression (lesson 40).

## ex5 — arrow versus double arrow

The two operators, side by side, with their types visible. Once you have
seen `tags_json` come back as a JSON array and `color_text` as a bare
string, the rule "navigate with `->`, land with `->>`" stops needing to be
memorised.

## ex6 — the colour census

`GROUP BY` on a JSONB accessor — lesson 07's grouping-by-expression with a
new kind of expression. Note the honest performance footnote in the prompt:
this reads the whole table, and no index you can create with what you know
today changes that. Hold onto that; lesson 40 gives you the expression index
that does.

## challenge — the tag census

`jsonb_array_elements_text` is a *set-returning function*: one input row
becomes several output rows, which means the product row is duplicated once
per tag. That is a deliberate fan-out and it is safe here because you are
counting tags, not products. Put a `sum(price)` in that query instead and
you would double every product's price — the grain problem from lesson 08,
arriving from an unexpected direction.

## review1 — high-value purchases

The cast is the exercise. `payload ->> 'value'` is text, and comparing text
to `995` either errors or — worse, in some formulations — compares
lexicographically, where `'996' < '99'`. `(payload ->> 'value')::int > 995`
is the correct form, and it is also a function of a column, so remember it
when lesson 40 asks you for an expression to index.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — the tag census (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. How many products carry each tag? Explode
every product's `tags` array into rows with
`jsonb_array_elements_text`, then group. Columns: `tag`, `products`
(count). Any order. (10 tags; each product has exactly 2.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 19_text_jsonb challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
`jsonb_array_elements_text(attributes -> 'tags')` in the FROM clause
(cross joined — or as a LATERAL, same thing here) gives one row per
(product, tag). Then it's lesson 07: group and count.

## Hint 2
```sql
SELECT t.tag, count(*) AS products
FROM products p
CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_array_elements_text(p.attributes -> 'tags') AS t(tag)
GROUP BY t.tag;
```

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — the first word

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Merchandising wants to group the catalogue by
brand, and the brand is the **first word** of the product name (`Nova
Kettle 812` is a `Nova`).

For products with `id <= 50`, return `id` and the first word of `name`
aliased **`brand`**. Any row order.

`split_part(text, delimiter, n)` returns the nth field, 1-based, and — this
is why it is the right tool — returns the empty string rather than NULL when
the field does not exist. Compare `substring(name FROM '^[^ ]+')`, which
does the same job with a regex and returns NULL on no match. Both are
defensible; knowing which one produces which answer on bad input is the
skill.

Run: `uv run dojo test 19_text_jsonb ex4`

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — arrow versus double arrow

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Put the two JSONB extraction operators
side by side. For products with `id <= 20`, return three columns:

1. `id`
2. `attributes ->> 'color'` aliased **`color_text`**
3. `attributes -> 'tags'` aliased **`tags_json`**

Twenty rows, any order.

`->` returns **JSONB** and `->>` returns **text**. That single distinction
is behind most JSONB bugs: `attributes -> 'color' = 'red'` fails to compare
(JSONB against text), while `attributes ->> 'color' = 'red'` works, and
`attributes -> 'color' = '"red"'::jsonb` also works — note the quotes
*inside* the string, because a JSON string literal includes them.

The rule of thumb: use `->` while you are still navigating into the
document, and `->>` on the last step, when you want a value SQL can compare.

Run: `uv run dojo test 19_text_jsonb ex5`

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — the colour census

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. How many products come in each colour? Group the
whole catalogue by the `color` key inside `attributes`.

Columns: `color` (text), `products` (count). Five rows, any order.

Extract with `->>` so you get text you can group on, then `GROUP BY` it
exactly as you would any other expression — this is lesson 07's
"grouping by an expression" with a JSONB accessor in the expression slot.

One thing to notice, because it matters in lesson 42: nothing about this
query can use an index today. `attributes ->> 'color'` is a function of a
column, so a plain index on `attributes` is useless to it, and the whole
10,000-row table must be read. Two fixes exist — an expression index on
`(attributes ->> 'color')` (lesson 40) and a GIN index on the document
(lesson 42) — and they help with different queries.

# 20 — Querying capstone: the analytics sprint

Part 2's graduation project. Three asks from a product analytics sprint —
each one stacks CTEs, joins, windows, and date work. As in lesson 12, the
prompts are written as the requests actually arrive; the translation is
yours. Expect each of these to take several attempts. That's the design.

## Exercise 1 — daily active customers

> *"Standard DAU chart for the last week of data, please — how many
> distinct customers did anything on the site each day."*

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. From `events`: one row per day from
**2023-11-08 through 2023-11-14** (the last full week), columns `day`
(date) and `dau` (distinct `customer_id` count). **Ordered by `day`.**
(7 rows — every day has traffic, no series needed.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 20_querying_capstone ex1`

## Exercise 2 — signup cohorts that actually buy

> *"For each monthly signup cohort of 2023: how many customers signed up,
> and how many of them have ever placed an order. I want conversion at a
> glance."*

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Cohort = `date_trunc('month', customers.
created_at)`, restricted to 2023 signups (Jan 1 through Nov 14 — the
seed's end of time; 11 cohorts). Columns: `cohort`, `signups`, `buyers`
(customers of the cohort with ≥1 order — count them via EXISTS or a
LEFT-JOIN-DISTINCT, your call). **Ordered by `cohort`.**

Run: `uv run dojo test 20_querying_capstone ex2`

## Exercise 3 — top movers, September to October

> *"Which categories are heating up? Line-item revenue September vs
> October 2023, and the percent change, best movers first."*

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. For each product `category`: `sep_rev` (line
item revenue in Sep 2023), `oct_rev` (Oct 2023), `pct` = 100 × (oct −
sep) / sep **rounded to 1 decimal**. Filter by the *order's*
`created_at`; revenue = `quantity * price` from items, all order
statuses. **Ordered by `pct` descending, then `category`.** (6 rows.
FILTER makes the two-month pivot painless.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 20_querying_capstone ex3`

## Exercise 4 — "What does a week of traffic look like?"

> *"Break the last week down by event type — volume and reach. How many
> events of each kind, and how many different people did each one."*

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. From `events`, for `ts` in **2023-11-08 through
2023-11-14** (half-open: `>= '2023-11-08' AND < '2023-11-15'`), one row per
`event_type`.

Columns, in this order: `event_type`, `events` (count), `customers`
(distinct `customer_id`). **Ordered by `events` descending, then
`event_type` ascending.** (5 rows.)

"Volume and reach" is the whole ask, and the two numbers come apart:
`count(*)` and `count(DISTINCT customer_id)` measure different things, and a
funnel built on the wrong one exaggerates every step where people repeat
themselves.

Run: `uv run dojo test 20_querying_capstone ex4`

## Exercise 5 — "Who are our loyal customers?"

> *"One number I keep asking for and never getting: what share of our
> buyers are genuinely loyal — say, fifteen orders or more?"*

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Considering only customers who have placed at
least one order, produce **one row** with three columns:

1. `buyers` — how many customers have ever ordered
2. `loyal` — how many of those have **fifteen or more** orders
3. `loyal_pct` — `loyal` as a percentage of `buyers`, rounded to 1 decimal

Aggregate per customer in a CTE or derived table first, then aggregate
*that*. Aggregating an aggregate is the step people get stuck on, and it is
just a second `SELECT` around the first.

Note the population the request implies: customers who have never ordered
are excluded from both the numerator and the denominator. That is almost
certainly what was meant — but "what share of our *customers* are loyal" is
a different and equally reasonable question, and its answer is smaller by
the 5,003 people who have never bought anything.

Note the threshold too. "Fifteen or more" was the requester's number, not a
fact about the business — try 2, 10 and 20 in the lab and watch the
headline swing from 100% to under 2%. A metric with a hand-picked cutoff in
it is an argument, not a measurement.

Run: `uv run dojo test 20_querying_capstone ex5`

## Exercise 6 — "Are baskets getting bigger?"

> *"Average number of line items per order, by month, for this year. If
> that number is moving I want to know about it."*

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. For orders created in **2023** (half-open, Jan 1
to Jan 1), compute the average number of `order_items` rows per order, per
calendar month.

Columns, in this order: `month` (`date_trunc('month', o.created_at)`),
`avg_items` (average line count per order, rounded to **3** decimals).
**Ordered by `month` ascending.** (11 rows.)

The shape is two-stage and the stages must not be collapsed: count items
*per order* first, then average those counts *per month*. Try to do it in
one step — `count(*) / count(DISTINCT o.id)` over the joined rows — and you
get a number that is right only when every order has the same number of
lines. Averaging an average is one of the most common quietly-wrong things
in analytics.

Run: `uv run dojo test 20_querying_capstone ex6`

## Spaced review

`review1/`: purchases per day for the same last week (2023-11-08 through
2023-11-14): `day`, `purchases` (count of `'purchase'` events),
**ordered by day**.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 20_querying_capstone

Part 2 is over. Six exercises here, and none of them needed a construct you
had not already met — what they needed was decomposition: *define the
population, define the time grain, define the measure*. That is the skill
seniors interview for, and it survives every tool change.

## Notes

**Every metric hides a population.** "DAU" means distinct customers who did
*something* — but something on the site, or something that counts as
engagement? "Conversion" means bought — ever, or within the cohort window?
"Repeat rate" divides by buyers or by all customers, and the two numbers can
differ by a factor of two. None of these are SQL questions. All of them
determine which SQL is correct.

**Aggregating an aggregate needs two stages.** Average basket size is the
canonical example: count items per order, *then* average. Doing it in one
step — dividing total items by distinct orders — gives the right answer only
when the distribution is uniform, and quietly wrong ones otherwise. Whenever
a metric is "the average of a per-thing number", the query has two `GROUP
BY`s in it, one nested in the other.

**Volume and reach come apart.** `count(*)` and `count(DISTINCT
customer_id)` answer different questions, and every funnel, engagement
metric and "top pages" report has to pick one deliberately. A step where
people repeat themselves — page views, retries, add-to-cart — looks
dramatically bigger in volume than in reach.

**Percent change needs a guard.** `100 * (b - a) / a` errors when `a` is
zero and returns NULL when `a` is NULL. `nullif(a, 0)` turns the first into
the second. On a category league table with six well-populated rows this
never fires; on the same query segmented by country and week, it fires in
production on a Sunday.

**Cohort analysis is a join between two grains.** A cohort report has one
row per (cohort, measure) but is built from customer rows and order rows.
The safe construction is the one from lesson 14: aggregate each grain
separately, then join the small results — rather than joining first and
trying to un-duplicate afterwards.

**Say what the denominator is, in the column name.** `repeat_pct` is
ambiguous; `repeat_pct_of_buyers` is not. The cheapest defence against a
metric argument six months from now is a column name that already answered
it.

## ex1 — daily active customers

`count(DISTINCT customer_id)` per day over three million events. Note the
prompt's aside that no series is needed here because every day has traffic —
which is a fact about this dataset, not a property of the query. The same
query on a quieter table silently omits empty days, and lesson 18's
`generate_series` pattern is the fix.

## ex2 — signup cohorts that actually buy

Two populations at two grains: customers by signup month, and whether each
has ever ordered. `EXISTS` is the natural expression of "has ever" — it
short-circuits and cannot fan out — and it is why the `count(DISTINCT ...)`
version, while correct, is doing more work to say something less clearly.

## ex3 — top movers, September to October

`FILTER` turns a two-month comparison into a single pass, and the percent
change is the fragile part. Six categories all have September revenue, so
the division is safe; the habit of writing `nullif(sep_rev, 0)` anyway costs
nothing and removes the failure mode permanently.

## ex4 — "What does a week of traffic look like?"

Volume against reach, on the same rows. Look at the ratio per event type:
`view` has many more events than customers, `logout` far fewer. That ratio
*is* the engagement story, and it is invisible if a report shows only one of
the two columns.

## ex5 — "Who are our loyal customers?"

Aggregate, then aggregate again. Two definitions are buried in one sentence,
and both move the answer more than any amount of query tuning could. The
denominator excludes the 5,003 customers who have never ordered — defensible
here, and a different number from "share of all customers". And the
threshold was picked by the person asking: at two or more orders essentially
every buyer qualifies on this dataset, at fifteen about one in six does, at
twenty roughly one in ninety. A metric with a hand-chosen cutoff is an
argument dressed as a measurement, and the honest way to publish it is with
the cutoff in the column name.

This is also the exercise where a sanity check pays: the average customer
here has eleven orders, which is wildly unlike a real shop. Noticing that
your data does not look like the world is a skill worth more than most SQL —
a "repeat purchase rate" of 100% is not a triumph, it is a signal that
somebody generated the data.

## ex6 — "Are baskets getting bigger?"

The two-stage average, and the trap spelled out. Worth running the wrong
version once in the lab to see how close it looks — the collapsed
calculation produces a plausible number in the same range, which is exactly
why this error survives code review.

## review1 — purchases per day

The simplest query in the lesson, deliberately, as the spaced-review anchor
for the whole of Part 2. When it comes back, notice that you can now write
it without thinking — and that "without thinking" is what the last eight
lessons were for.

## Further reading

- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) — worth a final pass now that you have used `FILTER`, `DISTINCT` and ordered-set aggregates in anger.
- [`WITH` Queries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) — re-read the inlining notes; every query in this lesson is a CTE pipeline.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) — the reference you will keep open for the rest of your career.
- [Use The Index, Luke](https://use-the-index-luke.com/) — start reading it now. Everything you wrote in Part 2 reads whole tables, and Part 5 is about to explain what that costs and how to stop.

## Ten-pass spaced repetition

Use this ladder after completing **20 — Querying capstone: the analytics sprint**. Each pass changes the retrieval
task so repetition strengthens recall instead of becoming answer recognition.
Do the named exercise from a blank starting point whenever practical, and only
open its hints after recording your first attempt.

| Pass | When | Practice target | Retrieval task |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | now | `ex1` | Close the notes and state the central rule in one precise sentence. |
| 2 | 3 days | `ex2` | Rebuild the smallest valid example from memory, then explain each part. |
| 3 | 7 days | `ex3` | Predict the result or behavior before running anything; reconcile surprises. |
| 4 | 21 days | `ex4` | Solve from a blank file and name the first tempting mistake you avoided. |
| 5 | 60 days | `ex5` | Contrast this technique with its nearest alternative and choose between them. |
| 6 | 120 days | `ex6` | Add one realistic constraint and adapt the solution without consulting notes. |
| 7 | 240 days | `review1` | Debug a deliberately broken version; explain the evidence before the repair. |

# Reading - 20_querying_capstone

Part 2 is over. Six exercises here, and none of them needed a construct you
had not already met — what they needed was decomposition: *define the
population, define the time grain, define the measure*. That is the skill
seniors interview for, and it survives every tool change.

## Notes

**Every metric hides a population.** "DAU" means distinct customers who did
*something* — but something on the site, or something that counts as
engagement? "Conversion" means bought — ever, or within the cohort window?
"Repeat rate" divides by buyers or by all customers, and the two numbers can
differ by a factor of two. None of these are SQL questions. All of them
determine which SQL is correct.

**Aggregating an aggregate needs two stages.** Average basket size is the
canonical example: count items per order, *then* average. Doing it in one
step — dividing total items by distinct orders — gives the right answer only
when the distribution is uniform, and quietly wrong ones otherwise. Whenever
a metric is "the average of a per-thing number", the query has two `GROUP
BY`s in it, one nested in the other.

**Volume and reach come apart.** `count(*)` and `count(DISTINCT
customer_id)` answer different questions, and every funnel, engagement
metric and "top pages" report has to pick one deliberately. A step where
people repeat themselves — page views, retries, add-to-cart — looks
dramatically bigger in volume than in reach.

**Percent change needs a guard.** `100 * (b - a) / a` errors when `a` is
zero and returns NULL when `a` is NULL. `nullif(a, 0)` turns the first into
the second. On a category league table with six well-populated rows this
never fires; on the same query segmented by country and week, it fires in
production on a Sunday.

**Cohort analysis is a join between two grains.** A cohort report has one
row per (cohort, measure) but is built from customer rows and order rows.
The safe construction is the one from lesson 14: aggregate each grain
separately, then join the small results — rather than joining first and
trying to un-duplicate afterwards.

**Say what the denominator is, in the column name.** `repeat_pct` is
ambiguous; `repeat_pct_of_buyers` is not. The cheapest defence against a
metric argument six months from now is a column name that already answered
it.

## ex1 — daily active customers

`count(DISTINCT customer_id)` per day over three million events. Note the
prompt's aside that no series is needed here because every day has traffic —
which is a fact about this dataset, not a property of the query. The same
query on a quieter table silently omits empty days, and lesson 18's
`generate_series` pattern is the fix.

## ex2 — signup cohorts that actually buy

Two populations at two grains: customers by signup month, and whether each
has ever ordered. `EXISTS` is the natural expression of "has ever" — it
short-circuits and cannot fan out — and it is why the `count(DISTINCT ...)`
version, while correct, is doing more work to say something less clearly.

## ex3 — top movers, September to October

`FILTER` turns a two-month comparison into a single pass, and the percent
change is the fragile part. Six categories all have September revenue, so
the division is safe; the habit of writing `nullif(sep_rev, 0)` anyway costs
nothing and removes the failure mode permanently.

## ex4 — "What does a week of traffic look like?"

Volume against reach, on the same rows. Look at the ratio per event type:
`view` has many more events than customers, `logout` far fewer. That ratio
*is* the engagement story, and it is invisible if a report shows only one of
the two columns.

## ex5 — "Who are our loyal customers?"

Aggregate, then aggregate again. Two definitions are buried in one sentence,
and both move the answer more than any amount of query tuning could. The
denominator excludes the 5,003 customers who have never ordered — defensible
here, and a different number from "share of all customers". And the
threshold was picked by the person asking: at two or more orders essentially
every buyer qualifies on this dataset, at fifteen about one in six does, at
twenty roughly one in ninety. A metric with a hand-chosen cutoff is an
argument dressed as a measurement, and the honest way to publish it is with
the cutoff in the column name.

This is also the exercise where a sanity check pays: the average customer
here has eleven orders, which is wildly unlike a real shop. Noticing that
your data does not look like the world is a skill worth more than most SQL —
a "repeat purchase rate" of 100% is not a triumph, it is a signal that
somebody generated the data.

## ex6 — "Are baskets getting bigger?"

The two-stage average, and the trap spelled out. Worth running the wrong
version once in the lab to see how close it looks — the collapsed
calculation produces a plausible number in the same range, which is exactly
why this error survives code review.

## review1 — purchases per day

The simplest query in the lesson, deliberately, as the spaced-review anchor
for the whole of Part 2. When it comes back, notice that you can now write
it without thinking — and that "without thinking" is what the last eight
lessons were for.

## Further reading

- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) — worth a final pass now that you have used `FILTER`, `DISTINCT` and ordered-set aggregates in anger.
- [`WITH` Queries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) — re-read the inlining notes; every query in this lesson is a CTE pipeline.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) — the reference you will keep open for the rest of your career.
- [Use The Index, Luke](https://use-the-index-luke.com/) — start reading it now. Everything you wrote in Part 2 reads whole tables, and Part 5 is about to explain what that costs and how to stop.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — signup cohorts that actually buy

> *"For each monthly signup cohort of 2023: how many customers signed up,
> and how many of them have ever placed an order. I want conversion at a
> glance."*

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Cohort = `date_trunc('month', customers.
created_at)`, restricted to 2023 signups (Jan 1 through Nov 14 — the
seed's end of time; 11 cohorts). Columns: `cohort`, `signups`, `buyers`
(customers of the cohort with ≥1 order — count them via EXISTS or a
LEFT-JOIN-DISTINCT, your call). **Ordered by `cohort`.**

Run: `uv run dojo test 20_querying_capstone ex2`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
CTE over customers filtered to 2023: (cohort, id). Main query: group by
cohort; `signups` = count(*); `buyers` = count of members where an
EXISTS(orders for that customer) holds — a FILTER over a correlated
EXISTS works, as does joining a DISTINCT-customer_id orders CTE.

## Hint 2
```sql
WITH cohorts AS (
    SELECT id, date_trunc('month', created_at) AS cohort
    FROM customers
    WHERE created_at >= '2023-01-01'
)
SELECT cohort,
       count(*) AS signups,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE EXISTS (
           SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = cohorts.id
       )) AS buyers
FROM cohorts
GROUP BY cohort
ORDER BY cohort;
```

## Hint 1
CTE over customers filtered to 2023: (cohort, id). Main query: group by
cohort; `signups` = count(*); `buyers` = count of members where an
EXISTS(orders for that customer) holds — a FILTER over a correlated
EXISTS works, as does joining a DISTINCT-customer_id orders CTE.

## Hint 2
```sql
WITH cohorts AS (
    SELECT id, date_trunc('month', created_at) AS cohort
    FROM customers
    WHERE created_at >= '2023-01-01'
)
SELECT cohort,
       count(*) AS signups,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE EXISTS (
           SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = cohorts.id
       )) AS buyers
FROM cohorts
GROUP BY cohort
ORDER BY cohort;
```

## Exercise 3 — top movers, September to October

> *"Which categories are heating up? Line-item revenue September vs
> October 2023, and the percent change, best movers first."*

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. For each product `category`: `sep_rev` (line
item revenue in Sep 2023), `oct_rev` (Oct 2023), `pct` = 100 × (oct −
sep) / sep **rounded to 1 decimal**. Filter by the *order's*
`created_at`; revenue = `quantity * price` from items, all order
statuses. **Ordered by `pct` descending, then `category`.** (6 rows.
FILTER makes the two-month pivot painless.)

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Three-table join (orders for the date filter, items for revenue, products
for category), one GROUP BY category, two FILTERed sums (September /
October half-open ranges), then arithmetic on the two sums for `pct`.
Compute the sums in a CTE so the percent expression stays readable.

## Hint 2
```sql
WITH rev AS (
    SELECT p.category,
           sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) FILTER (
               WHERE o.created_at >= '2023-09-01'
                 AND o.created_at <  '2023-10-01') AS sep_rev,
           sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) FILTER (
               WHERE o.created_at >= '2023-10-01'
                 AND o.created_at <  '2023-11-01') AS oct_rev
    FROM orders o
    JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
    JOIN products p     ON p.id = oi.product_id
    GROUP BY p.category
)
SELECT category, sep_rev, oct_rev,
       round(100 * (oct_rev - sep_rev) / sep_rev, 1) AS pct
FROM rev
ORDER BY pct DESC, category;
```

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Three-table join (orders for the date filter, items for revenue, products
for category), one GROUP BY category, two FILTERed sums (September /
October half-open ranges), then arithmetic on the two sums for `pct`.
Compute the sums in a CTE so the percent expression stays readable.

## Hint 2
```sql
WITH rev AS (
    SELECT p.category,
           sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) FILTER (
               WHERE o.created_at >= '2023-09-01'
                 AND o.created_at <  '2023-10-01') AS sep_rev,
           sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) FILTER (
               WHERE o.created_at >= '2023-10-01'
                 AND o.created_at <  '2023-11-01') AS oct_rev
    FROM orders o
    JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
    JOIN products p     ON p.id = oi.product_id
    GROUP BY p.category
)
SELECT category, sep_rev, oct_rev,
       round(100 * (oct_rev - sep_rev) / sep_rev, 1) AS pct
FROM rev
ORDER BY pct DESC, category;
```

## Exercise 4 — "What does a week of traffic look like?"

> *"Break the last week down by event type — volume and reach. How many
> events of each kind, and how many different people did each one."*

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — "Who are our loyal customers?"

> *"One number I keep asking for and never getting: what share of our
> buyers are genuinely loyal — say, fifteen orders or more?"*

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Considering only customers who have placed at
least one order, produce **one row** with three columns:

1. `buyers` — how many customers have ever ordered
2. `loyal` — how many of those have **fifteen or more** orders
3. `loyal_pct` — `loyal` as a percentage of `buyers`, rounded to 1 decimal

Aggregate per customer in a CTE or derived table first, then aggregate
*that*. Aggregating an aggregate is the step people get stuck on, and it is
just a second `SELECT` around the first.

Note the population the request implies: customers who have never ordered
are excluded from both the numerator and the denominator. That is almost
certainly what was meant — but "what share of our *customers* are loyal" is
a different and equally reasonable question, and its answer is smaller by
the 5,003 people who have never bought anything.

Note the threshold too. "Fifteen or more" was the requester's number, not a
fact about the business — try 2, 10 and 20 in the lab and watch the
headline swing from 100% to under 2%. A metric with a hand-picked cutoff in
it is an argument, not a measurement.

Run: `uv run dojo test 20_querying_capstone ex5`

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The CTE has one row per buying customer with their order count. The
outer query counts those rows, twice - once unconditionally, once with a
FILTER.

## Hint 2
`round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE orders >= 15) / count(*), 1) AS loyal_pct`

references.solution.sql:
WITH per_customer AS (
    SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS orders
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT count(*)                              AS buyers,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE orders >= 15)  AS loyal,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE orders >= 15)
             / count(*), 1)                  AS loyal_pct
FROM per_customer;
references.expected.sql:
WITH per_customer AS (
    SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS orders
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT count(*) AS buyers,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE orders >= 15) AS loyal,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE orders >= 15) / count(*), 1) AS loyal_pct
FROM per_customer;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — "Are baskets getting bigger?"

> *"Average number of line items per order, by month, for this year. If
> that number is moving I want to know about it."*

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. For orders created in **2023** (half-open, Jan 1
to Jan 1), compute the average number of `order_items` rows per order, per
calendar month.

Columns, in this order: `month` (`date_trunc('month', o.created_at)`),
`avg_items` (average line count per order, rounded to **3** decimals).
**Ordered by `month` ascending.** (11 rows.)

The shape is two-stage and the stages must not be collapsed: count items
*per order* first, then average those counts *per month*. Try to do it in
one step — `count(*) / count(DISTINCT o.id)` over the joined rows — and you
get a number that is right only when every order has the same number of
lines. Averaging an average is one of the most common quietly-wrong things
in analytics.

Run: `uv run dojo test 20_querying_capstone ex6`

## Hint 1
CTE: join orders to order_items, `GROUP BY o.id` and the month, count
the lines. Outer: group that by month and average the counts.

## Hint 2
`round(avg(items), 3) AS avg_items` over the per-order CTE, grouped and

references.solution.sql:
WITH per_order AS (
    SELECT o.id,
           date_trunc('month', o.created_at) AS month,
           count(*) AS items
    FROM orders o
    JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
    WHERE o.created_at >= '2023-01-01'
      AND o.created_at <  '2024-01-01'
    GROUP BY o.id, date_trunc('month', o.created_at)
)
SELECT month,
       round(avg(items), 3) AS avg_items
FROM per_order
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;
references.expected.sql:

    SELECT o.id, date_trunc('month', o.created_at) AS month, count(*) AS items

    WHERE o.created_at >= '2023-01-01' AND o.created_at < '2024-01-01'
    GROUP BY o.id, 2
)

GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;

lessons.briefing:
# 21 — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE

Twenty lessons of reading; time to write. Part 3's rule of engagement:
**every graded run happens on a throwaway clone**, so the worst you can
do is fail a gate. Use that freedom — the fear of mutating data only goes
away through practicing mutation.

The gates change shape here too: there's no `expected.sql` anymore.
The test runs *your* statements, then interrogates the database state —
row counts, specific values, untouched neighbors. Read the gate before
you start; knowing what will be checked *is* the spec.

## Concept

```sql
-- multi-row insert
INSERT INTO products (id, name, category, price, description, attributes)
VALUES (20001, ..., '{"color": "black", ...}'),
       (20002, ...);

-- insert from a query (copy/transform existing rows)
INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, status, total, created_at)
SELECT id + 1000000, customer_id, 'pending', total, created_at
FROM orders WHERE ...;

-- update, optionally joining another table for its data
UPDATE order_items oi
SET price = p.price
FROM products p
WHERE p.id = oi.product_id AND ...;

-- delete, optionally joining (USING is DELETE's FROM)
DELETE FROM reviews r
USING products p
WHERE p.id = r.product_id AND p.category = '...';

-- any of them can hand back what they touched
UPDATE ... RETURNING id, price;
```

Three habits that separate professionals:

1. **Scope first.** Before any UPDATE/DELETE, run its WHERE as a SELECT
   and eyeball the count. The `dojo lab` clone is perfect for this.
2. **RETURNING beats a follow-up SELECT** — atomic, race-free, one round
   trip.
3. **Row counts are feedback.** `UPDATE 47` when you expected 3 is the
   database telling you your WHERE is wrong — *after* it's too late.
   Habit 1 exists because of this.

## Exercise 1 — merch drop (INSERT)

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. One multi-row INSERT adding three products:

| id | name | category | price | description | attributes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20001 | Dojo Tee | clothing | 25.00 | Official SQL Dojo t-shirt | `{"color": "black", "size": "l", "tags": ["new", "limited"]}` |
| 20002 | Dojo Mug | garden | 12.50 | Ceramic mug for plan-reading mornings | `{"color": "white", "size": "m", "tags": ["new", "bestseller"]}` |
| 20003 | Dojo Handbook | books | 16.50 | Print companion to the course | `{"color": "blue", "size": "s", "tags": ["new", "classic"]}` |

Run: `uv run dojo test 21_insert_update_delete ex1`

## Exercise 2 — targeted price cut (UPDATE)

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. The 300 never-ordered products aren't moving;
merchandising wants **10% off the never-ordered products in `garden`**
(only those!): set `price = round(price * 0.9, 2)`. The gate checks the
targets got exactly that price *and every other product is untouched* —
scope discipline is the graded skill.

Run: `uv run dojo test 21_insert_update_delete ex2`

## Exercise 3 — takedown (DELETE)

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Legal says the 1-star reviews of product 42
are a brigading attack: **delete every review of product 42 with rating
1** — and nothing else. The gate counts the collateral.

Run: `uv run dojo test 21_insert_update_delete ex3`

## Exercise 4 — UPDATE with a join (UPDATE ... FROM)

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Compliance is withdrawing from a market: **cancel
every `pending` order belonging to a customer in Japan (`'JP'`)** — set
their `status` to `'cancelled'`. Nothing else may change.

The condition lives in a *different table* from the rows you are updating,
which is what `UPDATE ... FROM` is for:

```sql
UPDATE orders o
SET status = 'cancelled'
FROM customers c
WHERE c.id = o.customer_id AND ...
```

`FROM` here is not a join in the `SELECT` sense — it names extra tables the
`WHERE` clause may reference, and the update applies to `orders` only. The
danger is the one you now expect: forget `c.id = o.customer_id` and every
pending order in the database matches, because the missing condition turns
it into a cross product. Rehearse the `WHERE` as a `SELECT` in the lab
first and read the count.

Run: `uv run dojo test 21_insert_update_delete ex4`

## Exercise 5 — DELETE with a join (DELETE ... USING)

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. A moderation sweep: **delete every 1-star review
of a `garden` product whose product `id` is below 100** — and nothing
else.

`DELETE` spells its extra-tables clause `USING` rather than `FROM` (because
`FROM` is already taken by `DELETE FROM`):

```sql
DELETE FROM reviews r
USING products p
WHERE p.id = r.product_id AND ...
```

Three conditions: the join key, the category, and the rating — plus the id
bound. Miss the join key and you delete every 1-star review in the
database. The gate counts the collateral, as it did in exercise 3.

Run: `uv run dojo test 21_insert_update_delete ex5`

## Exercise 6 — RETURNING what you changed

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Clearance: set the `price` of products **11, 22
and 33** to exactly **9.99**, and have the statement **hand back the rows
it changed** — `id`, `name`, `price` — using `RETURNING`.

One statement. The gate reads the result set your statement produced, so
the `RETURNING` clause is graded, not just the final state.

`RETURNING` is not a convenience. A follow-up `SELECT` after an `UPDATE`
is a second round trip against a database that may have changed underneath
you; `RETURNING` reports exactly the rows this statement touched, atomically,
in the same round trip. It works on `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` alike —
`DELETE ... RETURNING *` is how you archive rows you are about to destroy.

Run: `uv run dojo test 21_insert_update_delete ex6`

## Challenge — reorder flow (INSERT ... SELECT) (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Support wants a one-click "reorder":
recreate order **123** as new order **600001** — same customer, same
total, status `'pending'`, `created_at` timestamp `'2023-11-15'` — and
copy its line items as new rows with `id = old id + 1000000` and
`order_id = 600001` (same product, quantity, price). Two INSERT ...
SELECT statements in one file.

# Reading - 21_insert_update_delete

Twenty lessons of reading, and now you can change things. The difference is
not syntax — `UPDATE` is easier than a window function — it is that a
`SELECT` with a wrong `WHERE` wastes your afternoon and an `UPDATE` with a
wrong `WHERE` wastes everyone's quarter.

## Notes

**The `WHERE` clause is the same clause it always was.** Everything you
learned in lesson 02 applies unchanged: precedence, `NULL` handling,
`BETWEEN`'s inclusivity. What changed is the blast radius. `UPDATE
products SET price = ...` with no `WHERE` is not an error; it is 10,000
rows.

**The professional ritual, in order.**

1. Write the `WHERE` as a `SELECT` first and read the row count. If the
   count surprises you, stop.
2. Wrap the mutation in an explicit transaction (lesson 23).
3. Use `RETURNING` to see what actually changed.
4. Check the reported row count against your prediction *before* you commit.

Every step of that is free in a `dojo lab` clone and none of it is free in
production. Rehearsing it here is the point of Part 3.

**Row counts are the database talking to you.** `UPDATE 47` when you
expected 3 is a bug report delivered after the fact. That is precisely why
step 1 exists: the count you want to be surprised by is the one from the
`SELECT`, not the one from the `UPDATE`.

**`UPDATE ... FROM` and `DELETE ... USING`.** Both let the `WHERE` clause
reference other tables; the difference is only the keyword, and it exists
because `DELETE FROM` already spent the word `FROM`. Two things to know.
The join condition lives in the `WHERE` with everything else, so omitting it
silently produces a cross product and updates far more than you meant. And
if the extra table matches a target row more than once, PostgreSQL picks one
match arbitrarily and updates the row once — no error, non-deterministic
result. When the joined side can produce duplicates, aggregate it in a
subquery first.

**`INSERT ... SELECT` is how data gets copied and transformed.** It is also
the shape of most backfills: `INSERT INTO new_table SELECT ... FROM
old_table WHERE ...`. Backfilling a large table in one statement holds locks
and generates a single enormous transaction; production backfills run in
batches, with the batch boundary chosen so each transaction is short.

**`RETURNING` is atomic feedback.** `INSERT ... RETURNING id` gives you the
generated key without a second query and without a race. `DELETE ...
RETURNING *` gives you the rows you just destroyed, which is the cheapest
possible archive. `UPDATE ... RETURNING` lets you see exactly which rows a
conditional update actually caught. In application code it removes an entire
class of read-after-write bugs.

**What a mutation does *not* do.** It does not fire your application's
callbacks, invalidate your cache, or reindex your search engine. Anything
outside the database does not roll back with it — a fact that becomes the
central design problem in lesson 23's teaching point.

**MVCC, briefly.** An `UPDATE` in PostgreSQL does not overwrite a row; it
writes a new version and marks the old one dead. That is why updating every
row of a table doubles its size until `VACUUM` reclaims the space, and why
a long-running transaction can prevent that reclamation. Lesson 44 is
entirely about the consequences; for now, just know that "update" means
"insert plus tombstone" underneath.

## ex1 — merch drop (INSERT)

A multi-row `VALUES` list, including a JSONB literal written as a quoted
string and cast implicitly by the column's type. One statement inserting
three rows is not just tidier than three statements — it is one transaction,
one round trip, and one row count to check.

## ex2 — targeted price cut (UPDATE)

The graded skill is scope, not syntax. The gate snapshots the sum of every
*other* product's price before running your statement and compares
afterwards — which is exactly the check you should be running on yourself.
Note the `round(price * 0.9, 2)`: without the rounding you would store more
decimal places than the column's scale allows and PostgreSQL would round for
you, which is fine here and is not fine when the rounding rule matters.

## ex3 — takedown (DELETE)

`DELETE` has no undo outside a transaction. The gate counts the collateral
because that is the only number anyone cares about after an incident: not
"did the right rows go" but "did anything else".

Two conditions, and both are load-bearing: drop `product_id = 42` and you
delete every 1-star review in the database, drop `rating = 1` and you wipe
product 42's entire review history. Neither mistake raises an error, and
neither is visible in the row count unless you predicted it first. This is
the exercise where the rehearse-as-a-SELECT habit stops being advice and
starts being the job.

## ex4 — UPDATE with a join

The join condition in the `WHERE` is load-bearing in a way that has no
analogue in `SELECT`: omit it in a `SELECT` and you get a visibly absurd
number of rows, omit it here and you get a silent, committed cross product.
Rehearse it as a `SELECT` — the same `FROM ... WHERE` reads as a perfectly
ordinary join.

## ex5 — DELETE with a join

Same shape, different keyword. Worth noticing that this could also be
written with a subquery — `WHERE product_id IN (SELECT id FROM products
WHERE ...)` — and that the subquery version is harder to get catastrophically
wrong, because there is no join key to forget. When a `USING` clause is not
buying you anything, the subquery is the safer idiom.

## ex6 — RETURNING what you changed

The gate reads your statement's result set, so `RETURNING` is the exercise.
The habit worth forming: any mutation whose effect you would otherwise
verify with a follow-up `SELECT` should have a `RETURNING` clause instead.
It is fewer round trips, it is race-free, and it makes the statement
self-documenting about what it claims to touch.

## challenge — reorder flow (INSERT ... SELECT)

Two `INSERT ... SELECT` statements, and the second depends on the first —
which is a transaction waiting to be declared. Note the id arithmetic (`id +
1000000`) standing in for a sequence: real schemas would use `generated
always as identity` and let the database allocate, which lesson 24 covers.

## Further reading

- [`INSERT`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-insert.html) — `VALUES`, `INSERT ... SELECT`, `RETURNING`, and `ON CONFLICT` (lesson 22).
- [`UPDATE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-update.html) — the `FROM` clause and the explicit warning about non-deterministic results when the joined table matches more than once.
- [`DELETE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-delete.html) — `USING`, `RETURNING`, and the note on `TRUNCATE` as the faster alternative when you mean "all of them".
- [`RETURNING` data from modified rows](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/dml-returning.html) — short, and it will change how you write application code.

# 21 — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE

Twenty lessons of reading; time to write. Part 3's rule of engagement:
**every graded run happens on a throwaway clone**, so the worst you can
do is fail a gate. Use that freedom — the fear of mutating data only goes
away through practicing mutation.

The gates change shape here too: there's no `expected.sql` anymore.
The test runs *your* statements, then interrogates the database state —
row counts, specific values, untouched neighbors. Read the gate before
you start; knowing what will be checked *is* the spec.

## Concept

```sql
-- multi-row insert
INSERT INTO products (id, name, category, price, description, attributes)
VALUES (20001, ..., '{"color": "black", ...}'),
       (20002, ...);

-- insert from a query (copy/transform existing rows)
INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, status, total, created_at)
SELECT id + 1000000, customer_id, 'pending', total, created_at
FROM orders WHERE ...;

-- update, optionally joining another table for its data
UPDATE order_items oi
SET price = p.price
FROM products p
WHERE p.id = oi.product_id AND ...;

-- delete, optionally joining (USING is DELETE's FROM)
DELETE FROM reviews r
USING products p
WHERE p.id = r.product_id AND p.category = '...';

-- any of them can hand back what they touched
UPDATE ... RETURNING id, price;
```

Three habits that separate professionals:

1. **Scope first.** Before any UPDATE/DELETE, run its WHERE as a SELECT
   and eyeball the count. The `dojo lab` clone is perfect for this.
2. **RETURNING beats a follow-up SELECT** — atomic, race-free, one round
   trip.
3. **Row counts are feedback.** `UPDATE 47` when you expected 3 is the
   database telling you your WHERE is wrong — *after* it's too late.
   Habit 1 exists because of this.

## Exercise 1 — merch drop (INSERT)

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. One multi-row INSERT adding three products:

| id | name | category | price | description | attributes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20001 | Dojo Tee | clothing | 25.00 | Official SQL Dojo t-shirt | `{"color": "black", "size": "l", "tags": ["new", "limited"]}` |
| 20002 | Dojo Mug | garden | 12.50 | Ceramic mug for plan-reading mornings | `{"color": "white", "size": "m", "tags": ["new", "bestseller"]}` |
| 20003 | Dojo Handbook | books | 16.50 | Print companion to the course | `{"color": "blue", "size": "s", "tags": ["new", "classic"]}` |

Run: `uv run dojo test 21_insert_update_delete ex1`

## Exercise 2 — targeted price cut (UPDATE)

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. The 300 never-ordered products aren't moving;
merchandising wants **10% off the never-ordered products in `garden`**
(only those!): set `price = round(price * 0.9, 2)`. The gate checks the
targets got exactly that price *and every other product is untouched* —
scope discipline is the graded skill.

Run: `uv run dojo test 21_insert_update_delete ex2`

## Exercise 3 — takedown (DELETE)

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Legal says the 1-star reviews of product 42
are a brigading attack: **delete every review of product 42 with rating
1** — and nothing else. The gate counts the collateral.

Run: `uv run dojo test 21_insert_update_delete ex3`

## Exercise 4 — UPDATE with a join (UPDATE ... FROM)

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Compliance is withdrawing from a market: **cancel
every `pending` order belonging to a customer in Japan (`'JP'`)** — set
their `status` to `'cancelled'`. Nothing else may change.

The condition lives in a *different table* from the rows you are updating,
which is what `UPDATE ... FROM` is for:

```sql
UPDATE orders o
SET status = 'cancelled'
FROM customers c
WHERE c.id = o.customer_id AND ...
```

`FROM` here is not a join in the `SELECT` sense — it names extra tables the
`WHERE` clause may reference, and the update applies to `orders` only. The
danger is the one you now expect: forget `c.id = o.customer_id` and every
pending order in the database matches, because the missing condition turns
it into a cross product. Rehearse the `WHERE` as a `SELECT` in the lab
first and read the count.

Run: `uv run dojo test 21_insert_update_delete ex4`

## Exercise 5 — DELETE with a join (DELETE ... USING)

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. A moderation sweep: **delete every 1-star review
of a `garden` product whose product `id` is below 100** — and nothing
else.

`DELETE` spells its extra-tables clause `USING` rather than `FROM` (because
`FROM` is already taken by `DELETE FROM`):

```sql
DELETE FROM reviews r
USING products p
WHERE p.id = r.product_id AND ...
```

Three conditions: the join key, the category, and the rating — plus the id
bound. Miss the join key and you delete every 1-star review in the
database. The gate counts the collateral, as it did in exercise 3.

Run: `uv run dojo test 21_insert_update_delete ex5`

## Exercise 6 — RETURNING what you changed

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Clearance: set the `price` of products **11, 22
and 33** to exactly **9.99**, and have the statement **hand back the rows
it changed** — `id`, `name`, `price` — using `RETURNING`.

One statement. The gate reads the result set your statement produced, so
the `RETURNING` clause is graded, not just the final state.

`RETURNING` is not a convenience. A follow-up `SELECT` after an `UPDATE`
is a second round trip against a database that may have changed underneath
you; `RETURNING` reports exactly the rows this statement touched, atomically,
in the same round trip. It works on `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` alike —
`DELETE ... RETURNING *` is how you archive rows you are about to destroy.

Run: `uv run dojo test 21_insert_update_delete ex6`

## Challenge — reorder flow (INSERT ... SELECT) (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Support wants a one-click "reorder":
recreate order **123** as new order **600001** — same customer, same
total, status `'pending'`, `created_at` timestamp `'2023-11-15'` — and
copy its line items as new rows with `id = old id + 1000000` and
`order_id = 600001` (same product, quantity, price). Two INSERT ...
SELECT statements in one file.

Run: `uv run dojo test 21_insert_update_delete challenge`

## The gate

```python
"""Gates for 21_insert_update_delete. Quoted verbatim in README.md."""
import pytest

from dojo import grader
from dojo.lesson import Lesson

L = Lesson(__file__)


def test_ex1(lesson_db):
    ex = L.exercise("ex1")
    lesson_db.execute(ex.solution_sql)
    lesson_db.commit()
    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db,
        "SELECT count(*) FROM products WHERE id IN (20001, 20002, 20003)",
        3, "all three new products exist")
    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db, "SELECT name FROM products WHERE id = 20002",
        "Dojo Mug", "product 20002 is the mug")
    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db, "SELECT category FROM products WHERE id = 20003",
        "books", "product 20003 sits in books")
    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db,
        "SELECT sum(price) FROM products WHERE id IN (20001, 20002, 20003)",
        54, "prices add up (25.00 + 12.50 + 16.50)")


def test_ex2(lesson_db):
    target_where = """
        category = 'garden'
        AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.product_id = products.id)
    """
    expected_target = lesson_db.execute(
        f"SELECT sum(round(price * 0.9, 2)) FROM products WHERE {target_where}"
    ).fetchone()[0]
    untouched_before = lesson_db.execute(
        f"SELECT sum(price) FROM products WHERE NOT ({target_where})"
    ).fetchone()[0]

    ex = L.exercise("ex2")
    lesson_db.execute(ex.solution_sql)
    lesson_db.commit()

    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db,
        f"SELECT sum(price) FROM products WHERE {target_where}",
        expected_target, "never-ordered garden products got exactly 10% off, rounded")
    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db,
        f"SELECT sum(price) FROM products WHERE NOT ({target_where})",
        untouched_before, "every other product's price is untouched")


def test_ex3(lesson_db):
    doomed = lesson_db.execute(
        "SELECT count(*) FROM reviews WHERE product_id = 42 AND rating = 1"
    ).fetchone()[0]
    total = lesson_db.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM reviews").fetchone()[0]
    assert doomed > 0  # seed guarantees product 42 has 1-star reviews

    ex = L.exercise("ex3")
    lesson_db.execute(ex.solution_sql)
    lesson_db.commit()

    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db,
        "SELECT count(*) FROM reviews WHERE product_id = 42 AND rating = 1",
        0, "the 1-star reviews of product 42 are gone")
    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db, "SELECT count(*) FROM reviews",
        total - doomed, "exactly the doomed reviews were deleted - no more, no less")


def test_ex4(lesson_db):
    target = lesson_db.execute(
        "SELECT count(*) FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id "
        "WHERE c.country = 'JP' AND o.status = 'pending'").fetchone()[0]
    cancelled_before = lesson_db.execute(
        "SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled'").fetchone()[0]
    other_pending = lesson_db.execute(
        "SELECT count(*) FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id "
        "WHERE c.country <> 'JP' AND o.status = 'pending'").fetchone()[0]
    assert target > 0  # the seed guarantees Japanese pending orders exist

    ex = L.exercise("ex4")
    lesson_db.execute(ex.solution_sql)
    lesson_db.commit()

    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db,
        "SELECT count(*) FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id "
        "WHERE c.country = 'JP' AND o.status = 'pending'",
        0, "no pending Japanese orders remain")
    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db, "SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled'",
        cancelled_before + target,
        "exactly the Japanese pending orders became cancelled - no more, no less")
    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db,
        "SELECT count(*) FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id "
        "WHERE c.country <> 'JP' AND o.status = 'pending'",
        other_pending, "every other country's pending orders are untouched")


def test_ex5(lesson_db):
    doomed_sql = (
        "SELECT count(*) FROM reviews r JOIN products p ON p.id = r.product_id "
        "WHERE p.category = 'garden' AND p.id < 100 AND r.rating = 1")
    doomed = lesson_db.execute(doomed_sql).fetchone()[0]
    total = lesson_db.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM reviews").fetchone()[0]
    assert doomed > 0  # the seed guarantees such reviews exist

    ex = L.exercise("ex5")
    lesson_db.execute(ex.solution_sql)
    lesson_db.commit()

    grader.assert_scalar(lesson_db, doomed_sql, 0,
                         "the targeted 1-star garden reviews are gone")
    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db, "SELECT count(*) FROM reviews", total - doomed,
        "exactly the targeted reviews were deleted - no more, no less")


def test_ex6(lesson_db):
    ex = L.exercise("ex6")
    before = lesson_db.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM products").fetchone()[0]

    returned = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    lesson_db.commit()

    assert len(returned) == 3, (
        "RETURNING MISSING OR WRONG: the gate reads the result set your "
        f"statement produced and got {len(returned)} row(s), expected 3.\n"
        "  Add `RETURNING id, name, price` to your UPDATE."
    )
    assert all(len(r) == 3 for r in returned), (
        "RETURNING should hand back three columns: id, name, price."
    )
    assert {r[0] for r in returned} == {11, 22, 33}, (
        f"RETURNING gave ids {sorted(r[0] for r in returned)}, expected 11, 22, 33."
    )
    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db, "SELECT count(*) FROM products WHERE id IN (11, 22, 33) "
                   "AND price = 9.99",
        3, "all three products are now priced 9.99")
    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db, "SELECT count(*) FROM products", before,
        "an UPDATE must not change the number of rows")


@pytest.mark.challenge
def test_challenge(lesson_db):
    src = lesson_db.execute(
        "SELECT customer_id, total FROM orders WHERE id = 123").fetchone()
    src_items = lesson_db.execute(
        "SELECT product_id, quantity, price FROM order_items "
        "WHERE order_id = 123 ORDER BY product_id, id").fetchall()

    ex = L.exercise("challenge")
    lesson_db.execute(ex.solution_sql)
    lesson_db.commit()

    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db,
        "SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE id = 600001 AND status = 'pending' "
        "AND customer_id = %d AND total = %s" % (src[0], src[1]),
        1, "order 600001 mirrors order 123 (same customer and total, status pending)")
    new_items = lesson_db.execute(
        "SELECT product_id, quantity, price FROM order_items "
        "WHERE order_id = 600001 ORDER BY product_id, id").fetchall()
    grader.assert_rows_equal(new_items, src_items, ordered=True)
```

Note the ex2 gate's shape: it snapshots the expected state *before*
running your SQL, then compares after. State gates through the rest of
the course follow this pattern.

## The teaching point

`UPDATE`/`DELETE` without a rehearsed WHERE is how companies end up on
the news. The professional ritual: SELECT the scope, read the count,
wrap the mutation in a transaction (next two lessons), check RETURNING,
*then* commit. The dojo's clones make this rehearsal free; production
never does.

Next: **22_upsert** — insert-or-update without the race condition.

# Reading - 21_insert_update_delete

Twenty lessons of reading, and now you can change things. The difference is
not syntax — `UPDATE` is easier than a window function — it is that a
`SELECT` with a wrong `WHERE` wastes your afternoon and an `UPDATE` with a
wrong `WHERE` wastes everyone's quarter.

## Notes

**The `WHERE` clause is the same clause it always was.** Everything you
learned in lesson 02 applies unchanged: precedence, `NULL` handling,
`BETWEEN`'s inclusivity. What changed is the blast radius. `UPDATE
products SET price = ...` with no `WHERE` is not an error; it is 10,000
rows.

**The professional ritual, in order.**

1. Write the `WHERE` as a `SELECT` first and read the row count. If the
   count surprises you, stop.
2. Wrap the mutation in an explicit transaction (lesson 23).
3. Use `RETURNING` to see what actually changed.
4. Check the reported row count against your prediction *before* you commit.

Every step of that is free in a `dojo lab` clone and none of it is free in
production. Rehearsing it here is the point of Part 3.

**Row counts are the database talking to you.** `UPDATE 47` when you
expected 3 is a bug report delivered after the fact. That is precisely why
step 1 exists: the count you want to be surprised by is the one from the
`SELECT`, not the one from the `UPDATE`.

**`UPDATE ... FROM` and `DELETE ... USING`.** Both let the `WHERE` clause
reference other tables; the difference is only the keyword, and it exists
because `DELETE FROM` already spent the word `FROM`. Two things to know.
The join condition lives in the `WHERE` with everything else, so omitting it
silently produces a cross product and updates far more than you meant. And
if the extra table matches a target row more than once, PostgreSQL picks one
match arbitrarily and updates the row once — no error, non-deterministic
result. When the joined side can produce duplicates, aggregate it in a
subquery first.

**`INSERT ... SELECT` is how data gets copied and transformed.** It is also
the shape of most backfills: `INSERT INTO new_table SELECT ... FROM
old_table WHERE ...`. Backfilling a large table in one statement holds locks
and generates a single enormous transaction; production backfills run in
batches, with the batch boundary chosen so each transaction is short.

**`RETURNING` is atomic feedback.** `INSERT ... RETURNING id` gives you the
generated key without a second query and without a race. `DELETE ...
RETURNING *` gives you the rows you just destroyed, which is the cheapest
possible archive. `UPDATE ... RETURNING` lets you see exactly which rows a
conditional update actually caught. In application code it removes an entire
class of read-after-write bugs.

**What a mutation does *not* do.** It does not fire your application's
callbacks, invalidate your cache, or reindex your search engine. Anything
outside the database does not roll back with it — a fact that becomes the
central design problem in lesson 23's teaching point.

**MVCC, briefly.** An `UPDATE` in PostgreSQL does not overwrite a row; it
writes a new version and marks the old one dead. That is why updating every
row of a table doubles its size until `VACUUM` reclaims the space, and why
a long-running transaction can prevent that reclamation. Lesson 44 is
entirely about the consequences; for now, just know that "update" means
"insert plus tombstone" underneath.

## ex1 — merch drop (INSERT)

A multi-row `VALUES` list, including a JSONB literal written as a quoted
string and cast implicitly by the column's type. One statement inserting
three rows is not just tidier than three statements — it is one transaction,
one round trip, and one row count to check.

## ex2 — targeted price cut (UPDATE)

The graded skill is scope, not syntax. The gate snapshots the sum of every
*other* product's price before running your statement and compares
afterwards — which is exactly the check you should be running on yourself.
Note the `round(price * 0.9, 2)`: without the rounding you would store more
decimal places than the column's scale allows and PostgreSQL would round for
you, which is fine here and is not fine when the rounding rule matters.

## ex3 — takedown (DELETE)

`DELETE` has no undo outside a transaction. The gate counts the collateral
because that is the only number anyone cares about after an incident: not
"did the right rows go" but "did anything else".

Two conditions, and both are load-bearing: drop `product_id = 42` and you
delete every 1-star review in the database, drop `rating = 1` and you wipe
product 42's entire review history. Neither mistake raises an error, and
neither is visible in the row count unless you predicted it first. This is
the exercise where the rehearse-as-a-SELECT habit stops being advice and
starts being the job.

## ex4 — UPDATE with a join

The join condition in the `WHERE` is load-bearing in a way that has no
analogue in `SELECT`: omit it in a `SELECT` and you get a visibly absurd
number of rows, omit it here and you get a silent, committed cross product.
Rehearse it as a `SELECT` — the same `FROM ... WHERE` reads as a perfectly
ordinary join.

## ex5 — DELETE with a join

Same shape, different keyword. Worth noticing that this could also be
written with a subquery — `WHERE product_id IN (SELECT id FROM products
WHERE ...)` — and that the subquery version is harder to get catastrophically
wrong, because there is no join key to forget. When a `USING` clause is not
buying you anything, the subquery is the safer idiom.

## ex6 — RETURNING what you changed

The gate reads your statement's result set, so `RETURNING` is the exercise.
The habit worth forming: any mutation whose effect you would otherwise
verify with a follow-up `SELECT` should have a `RETURNING` clause instead.
It is fewer round trips, it is race-free, and it makes the statement
self-documenting about what it claims to touch.

## challenge — reorder flow (INSERT ... SELECT)

Two `INSERT ... SELECT` statements, and the second depends on the first —
which is a transaction waiting to be declared. Note the id arithmetic (`id +
1000000`) standing in for a sequence: real schemas would use `generated
always as identity` and let the database allocate, which lesson 24 covers.

## Further reading

- [`INSERT`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-insert.html) — `VALUES`, `INSERT ... SELECT`, `RETURNING`, and `ON CONFLICT` (lesson 22).
- [`UPDATE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-update.html) — the `FROM` clause and the explicit warning about non-deterministic results when the joined table matches more than once.
- [`DELETE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-delete.html) — `USING`, `RETURNING`, and the note on `TRUNCATE` as the faster alternative when you mean "all of them".
- [`RETURNING` data from modified rows](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/dml-returning.html) — short, and it will change how you write application code.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — UPDATE with a join (UPDATE ... FROM)

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Compliance is withdrawing from a market: **cancel
every `pending` order belonging to a customer in Japan (`'JP'`)** — set
their `status` to `'cancelled'`. Nothing else may change.

The condition lives in a *different table* from the rows you are updating,
which is what `UPDATE ... FROM` is for:

```sql
UPDATE orders o
SET status = 'cancelled'
FROM customers c
WHERE c.id = o.customer_id AND ...
```

`FROM` here is not a join in the `SELECT` sense — it names extra tables the
`WHERE` clause may reference, and the update applies to `orders` only. The
danger is the one you now expect: forget `c.id = o.customer_id` and every
pending order in the database matches, because the missing condition turns
it into a cross product. Rehearse the `WHERE` as a `SELECT` in the lab
first and read the count.

Run: `uv run dojo test 21_insert_update_delete ex4`

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — DELETE with a join (DELETE ... USING)

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. A moderation sweep: **delete every 1-star review
of a `garden` product whose product `id` is below 100** — and nothing
else.

`DELETE` spells its extra-tables clause `USING` rather than `FROM` (because
`FROM` is already taken by `DELETE FROM`):

```sql
DELETE FROM reviews r
USING products p
WHERE p.id = r.product_id AND ...
```

Three conditions: the join key, the category, and the rating — plus the id
bound. Miss the join key and you delete every 1-star review in the
database. The gate counts the collateral, as it did in exercise 3.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — RETURNING what you changed

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Clearance: set the `price` of products **11, 22
and 33** to exactly **9.99**, and have the statement **hand back the rows
it changed** — `id`, `name`, `price` — using `RETURNING`.

One statement. The gate reads the result set your statement produced, so
the `RETURNING` clause is graded, not just the final state.

`RETURNING` is not a convenience. A follow-up `SELECT` after an `UPDATE`
is a second round trip against a database that may have changed underneath
you; `RETURNING` reports exactly the rows this statement touched, atomically,
in the same round trip. It works on `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` alike —
`DELETE ... RETURNING *` is how you archive rows you are about to destroy.

Run: `uv run dojo test 21_insert_update_delete ex6`
