lessons.briefing:
# 22 — UPSERT: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT

"Insert this row — unless it exists, then update it instead." The naive
version is a SELECT-then-INSERT-or-UPDATE in application code, and it
harbors a race: two requests both SELECT, find nothing, both INSERT, one
crashes (or worse, both succeed and you have duplicates). PostgreSQL's
`ON CONFLICT` does the whole dance atomically — *if* there's a unique
constraint to conflict against. No constraint, no upsert: the constraint
**is** the mechanism.

This lesson gives you a playground via `setup.sql` (applied automatically
before each gate): an `inventory` table (`product_id` PRIMARY KEY,
`stock`, `updated_at`; products 1–100 stocked at 100) and a `price_watch`
table (products 10, 20, 30 with best-seen prices).

## Concept

```sql
INSERT INTO inventory (product_id, stock)
VALUES (50, 75)
ON CONFLICT (product_id)
DO UPDATE SET stock = EXCLUDED.stock;
```

- `ON CONFLICT (product_id)` names the **conflict target** — there must
  be a unique index/constraint on exactly that.
- `EXCLUDED` is the row that *tried* to be inserted. `SET stock =
  EXCLUDED.stock` means "take the new value"; `SET stock =
  inventory.stock + EXCLUDED.stock` would mean "add to the old".
- `DO NOTHING` swallows the conflict silently — for "register if absent".
- `DO UPDATE` takes a `WHERE` — update *only when* some condition on the
  old (`inventory.`) and new (`EXCLUDED.`) values holds.

**Idempotency** is the property worth designing for: run the statement
twice, second run is a no-op. `SET stock = EXCLUDED.stock` (overwrite) is
idempotent; `stock + EXCLUDED.stock` (accumulate) is not — retry a timed-
out request and inventory doubles. Every gate in this lesson **runs your
statement twice** and fails if the second run changes anything.

## Exercise 1 — the stocktake sync

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. The warehouse counted shelves: product **50 has
75 units**, product **150 has 40 units**. One statement: insert-or-
overwrite both rows into `inventory` (only `product_id` and `stock`;
`updated_at` keeps its default).

Run: `uv run dojo test 22_upsert ex1`

## Exercise 2 — register if absent

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Products **60** and **200** must have inventory
rows. If a row already exists (60 does, at stock 100), it must **not** be
touched; if absent (200), create it with stock 0. One statement.

Run: `uv run dojo test 22_upsert ex2`

## Exercise 3 — only update when it is an improvement

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. A second stocktake arrives, but this warehouse is
known to under-count: the rule is **only raise a stock figure, never lower
it**. Today's numbers are product **70 at 80**, product **80 at 120**,
product **250 at 5**.

One statement. Expected outcome:

- 70 currently holds 100 — 80 is lower, so the row must **not** change.
- 80 currently holds 100 — 120 is higher, so it becomes 120.
- 250 has no row at all — it is inserted with 5.

`DO UPDATE` accepts its own `WHERE`, evaluated per conflicting row, with
both the existing row (`inventory.`) and the proposed row (`EXCLUDED.`) in
scope:

```sql
ON CONFLICT (product_id) DO UPDATE
  SET stock = EXCLUDED.stock
  WHERE EXCLUDED.stock > inventory.stock
```

Convince yourself this is idempotent before you run it — the gate will run
your statement twice and compare.

Run: `uv run dojo test 22_upsert ex3`

## Exercise 4 — upserting a whole set at once

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The seasonal reset: every product with `id`
between **95 and 105 inclusive** should have an inventory row with stock
**50**, whether or not it has one today. (Products 95–100 already have
rows; 101–105 do not.)

One statement, and the rows come from a **query** rather than a `VALUES`
list: `INSERT INTO ... SELECT ... ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE ...`. The
conflict clause works identically — it is the *insert*, not the source of
the rows, that it attaches to.

This is how real syncs are written: read the source of truth, upsert the
lot, let the constraint sort out which rows were new. The alternative —
querying which ids exist, then splitting into an `INSERT` batch and an
`UPDATE` batch in application code — is more code, slower, and wrong under
concurrency.

Run: `uv run dojo test 22_upsert ex4`

## Challenge — conditional upsert (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. `price_watch` tracks the best (lowest)
price ever seen per product. Today's crawl: product 10 at **45.00**,
product 20 at **95.00**, product 40 at **60.00**. One statement that
inserts new products and updates existing ones **only if the new price
is lower**. (10 improves on 50 → updates; 95 is worse than 80 → row must
stay; 40 is new → inserts.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 22_upsert challenge`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 22_upsert

"Insert it, unless it is already there, in which case update it" sounds
like control flow and is actually a concurrency problem. `ON CONFLICT`
is how PostgreSQL lets you hand that problem to the machinery that is
already solving it.

## Notes

**Why the naive version is broken.** `SELECT` to check, then `INSERT` or
`UPDATE`, is a *check-then-act* race. Two connections can both find nothing,
both insert, and one gets a unique-violation — or, without a unique
constraint, both succeed and you have silently created a duplicate. No
amount of application-level care fixes this; the window between the check
and the act is real and cannot be closed from outside the database.

**The constraint is the mechanism.** `ON CONFLICT (product_id)` requires a
unique index or constraint on `product_id` — PostgreSQL uses the index's own
conflict detection, which is atomic by construction. No constraint, no
upsert. That is worth stating plainly because it reframes Part 4: the
constraints you are about to learn to design are not paperwork, they are the
things that make correct concurrent writes expressible at all.

**`EXCLUDED` is the row that tried.** Inside `DO UPDATE`, the existing row is
addressed by table name (`inventory.stock`) and the proposed row by
`EXCLUDED.stock`. `SET stock = EXCLUDED.stock` overwrites; `SET stock =
inventory.stock + EXCLUDED.stock` accumulates.

**Idempotency is a design decision, and usually the right one.** Run the
statement twice: overwrite is a no-op the second time, accumulate doubles
the value. Now recall that network requests time out and get retried, that
message queues deliver at-least-once, and that every deploy pipeline
eventually runs the same job twice. An accumulating upsert is a correctness
bug waiting for an infrastructure hiccup. When you genuinely need to
accumulate, carry an idempotency key — a per-event unique id whose
constraint absorbs the duplicate — rather than making the arithmetic
depend on how many times the statement ran. Every gate in this lesson runs
your statement twice for exactly this reason.

**`DO NOTHING` versus `DO UPDATE`.** `DO NOTHING` swallows the conflict
silently — right for "register this if absent", wrong when you wanted to
know. Note that `DO NOTHING` without a conflict target swallows *any*
constraint violation on that insert, not just the one you had in mind, which
is occasionally a nasty surprise.

**`DO UPDATE ... WHERE`.** The conditional upsert: update only when some
predicate over the old and new rows holds. "Keep the lowest price ever
seen", "only move a status forward", "ignore stale timestamps" are all this
shape, and all of them are also idempotent, which is not a coincidence — a
condition that is false once the update has been applied *is* what makes a
statement self-limiting.

**What it does not solve.** `ON CONFLICT` handles a conflict on **one**
arbiter index. It cannot express "update if this unique key matches, else
insert unless that other unique key matches". It also takes a row-level lock
on the conflicting row, so a busy upsert on the same key serialises — which
is correct, and worth knowing when it shows up as contention.

**`MERGE` exists too.** PostgreSQL 15 added the SQL-standard `MERGE`, which
is more general (multiple `WHEN` branches, `DELETE` actions) and, unlike `ON
CONFLICT`, does *not* have the same concurrency guarantee — it can raise a
serialisation failure under concurrent writes. For plain insert-or-update on
a unique key, `ON CONFLICT` remains the right tool.

## ex1 — the stocktake sync

Overwrite semantics, one existing row and one new one. The gate runs it
twice; if you wrote `stock = inventory.stock + EXCLUDED.stock` you will
watch idempotency fail in front of you, which is a better lesson than this
paragraph.

Notice what the single statement did *not* require you to know: which of the
two products already had a row. That is the entire value proposition. The
application does not query first, does not branch, and does not care — the
unique index answers the question at the moment of the write, which is the
only moment at which the answer is reliable.

## ex2 — register if absent

`DO NOTHING`. Note what the gate checks: that product 60 is *unchanged*, not
merely present. "Ensure a row exists" and "ensure a row has these values"
are different requirements and it is easy to write the second when you meant
the first.

## ex3 — only update when it is an improvement

The conditional upsert, and the cleanest illustration of why conditional
upserts tend to be idempotent for free: once the best value has been stored,
the condition that allowed the update is false. Monotonic rules — highest
seen, lowest seen, latest timestamp — are safe to retry by construction.

## ex4 — upserting a whole set at once

`INSERT ... SELECT ... ON CONFLICT`. This is the production shape: pull the
source of truth, upsert the whole batch, and let the unique index decide
which rows were new. One statement, one transaction, correct under
concurrency, and it does not care how the two sets overlap.

One caveat worth knowing before you use this on real data: if the *source*
query can produce two rows with the same key, the statement fails with
"cannot affect row a second time" — `ON CONFLICT` resolves conflicts against
the table, not within the incoming batch. Deduplicate the source first,
usually with `DISTINCT ON` (lesson 49).

## challenge — conditional upsert

`price_watch` keeps the lowest price ever seen, which is the monotonic rule
from ex3 pointing the other way. Three products, three different outcomes —
update, no-op, insert — from one statement. That is the whole argument for
upsert in one line: the branching happens inside the database, where the
uniqueness question is already being decided.

## Further reading

- [`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-insert.html) — the conflict target rules, `EXCLUDED`, and the notes on which index gets used as the arbiter.
- [`MERGE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-merge.html) — the SQL-standard alternative from PostgreSQL 15, with its concurrency caveat spelled out.
- [Unique Constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-constraints.html) — the constraint that makes upsert possible. Lesson 25 designs them.
- [Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/transaction-iso.html) — what "atomically" actually means here, and what else races look like. Lesson 23 next.

```python
"""Gates for 22_upsert. Quoted verbatim in README.md.

import pytest

from dojo import grader
from dojo.lesson import Lesson

L = Lesson(__file__)


def _snapshot(conn, table):
    return conn.execute(
        f"SELECT * FROM {table} ORDER BY product_id").fetchall()


def test_ex1(lesson_db):
    L.apply_setup(lesson_db)

        75, "existing product 50 overwritten to the stocktake value")

        lesson_db, "SELECT count(*) FROM inventory",
        101, "exactly one new row appeared")

    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db, "SELECT stock FROM inventory WHERE product_id = 60",
        100, "existing product 60 must NOT be touched by DO NOTHING")
    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db, "SELECT stock FROM inventory WHERE product_id = 200",
        0, "new product 200 registered with stock 0")
```

## The teaching point

Upsert is the canonical example of "push the race into the database":
the uniqueness fight is settled by the same machinery that enforces the
constraint, atomically, under any concurrency. Whenever application code
does check-then-act against the database, ask what happens when two
copies run at once — and whether a constraint plus ON CONFLICT (or its
cousins: advisory locks, SERIALIZABLE) should own the decision instead.
Part 4 is where you learn to *design* the constraints this depends on.

# Reading - 22_upsert

"Insert it, unless it is already there, in which case update it" sounds
like control flow and is actually a concurrency problem. `ON CONFLICT`
is how PostgreSQL lets you hand that problem to the machinery that is
already solving it.

## Notes

**Why the naive version is broken.** `SELECT` to check, then `INSERT` or
`UPDATE`, is a *check-then-act* race. Two connections can both find nothing,
both insert, and one gets a unique-violation — or, without a unique
constraint, both succeed and you have silently created a duplicate. No
amount of application-level care fixes this; the window between the check
and the act is real and cannot be closed from outside the database.

**The constraint is the mechanism.** `ON CONFLICT (product_id)` requires a
unique index or constraint on `product_id` — PostgreSQL uses the index's own
conflict detection, which is atomic by construction. No constraint, no
upsert. That is worth stating plainly because it reframes Part 4: the
constraints you are about to learn to design are not paperwork, they are the
things that make correct concurrent writes expressible at all.

**`EXCLUDED` is the row that tried.** Inside `DO UPDATE`, the existing row is
addressed by table name (`inventory.stock`) and the proposed row by
`EXCLUDED.stock`. `SET stock = EXCLUDED.stock` overwrites; `SET stock =
inventory.stock + EXCLUDED.stock` accumulates.

**Idempotency is a design decision, and usually the right one.** Run the
statement twice: overwrite is a no-op the second time, accumulate doubles
the value. Now recall that network requests time out and get retried, that
message queues deliver at-least-once, and that every deploy pipeline
eventually runs the same job twice. An accumulating upsert is a correctness
bug waiting for an infrastructure hiccup. When you genuinely need to
accumulate, carry an idempotency key — a per-event unique id whose
constraint absorbs the duplicate — rather than making the arithmetic
depend on how many times the statement ran. Every gate in this lesson runs
your statement twice for exactly this reason.

**`DO NOTHING` versus `DO UPDATE`.** `DO NOTHING` swallows the conflict
silently — right for "register this if absent", wrong when you wanted to
know. Note that `DO NOTHING` without a conflict target swallows *any*
constraint violation on that insert, not just the one you had in mind, which
is occasionally a nasty surprise.

**`DO UPDATE ... WHERE`.** The conditional upsert: update only when some
predicate over the old and new rows holds. "Keep the lowest price ever
seen", "only move a status forward", "ignore stale timestamps" are all this
shape, and all of them are also idempotent, which is not a coincidence — a
condition that is false once the update has been applied *is* what makes a
statement self-limiting.

**What it does not solve.** `ON CONFLICT` handles a conflict on **one**
arbiter index. It cannot express "update if this unique key matches, else
insert unless that other unique key matches". It also takes a row-level lock
on the conflicting row, so a busy upsert on the same key serialises — which
is correct, and worth knowing when it shows up as contention.

**`MERGE` exists too.** PostgreSQL 15 added the SQL-standard `MERGE`, which
is more general (multiple `WHEN` branches, `DELETE` actions) and, unlike `ON
CONFLICT`, does *not* have the same concurrency guarantee — it can raise a
serialisation failure under concurrent writes. For plain insert-or-update on
a unique key, `ON CONFLICT` remains the right tool.

## ex1 — the stocktake sync

Overwrite semantics, one existing row and one new one. The gate runs it
twice; if you wrote `stock = inventory.stock + EXCLUDED.stock` you will
watch idempotency fail in front of you, which is a better lesson than this
paragraph.

Notice what the single statement did *not* require you to know: which of the
two products already had a row. That is the entire value proposition. The
application does not query first, does not branch, and does not care — the
unique index answers the question at the moment of the write, which is the
only moment at which the answer is reliable.

## ex2 — register if absent

`DO NOTHING`. Note what the gate checks: that product 60 is *unchanged*, not
merely present. "Ensure a row exists" and "ensure a row has these values"
are different requirements and it is easy to write the second when you meant
the first.

## ex3 — only update when it is an improvement

The conditional upsert, and the cleanest illustration of why conditional
upserts tend to be idempotent for free: once the best value has been stored,
the condition that allowed the update is false. Monotonic rules — highest
seen, lowest seen, latest timestamp — are safe to retry by construction.

## ex4 — upserting a whole set at once

`INSERT ... SELECT ... ON CONFLICT`. This is the production shape: pull the
source of truth, upsert the whole batch, and let the unique index decide
which rows were new. One statement, one transaction, correct under
concurrency, and it does not care how the two sets overlap.

One caveat worth knowing before you use this on real data: if the *source*
query can produce two rows with the same key, the statement fails with
"cannot affect row a second time" — `ON CONFLICT` resolves conflicts against
the table, not within the incoming batch. Deduplicate the source first,
usually with `DISTINCT ON` (lesson 49).

## challenge — conditional upsert

`price_watch` keeps the lowest price ever seen, which is the monotonic rule
from ex3 pointing the other way. Three products, three different outcomes —
update, no-op, insert — from one statement. That is the whole argument for
upsert in one line: the branching happens inside the database, where the
uniqueness question is already being decided.

## Further reading

- [`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-insert.html) — the conflict target rules, `EXCLUDED`, and the notes on which index gets used as the arbiter.
- [`MERGE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-merge.html) — the SQL-standard alternative from PostgreSQL 15, with its concurrency caveat spelled out.
- [Unique Constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-constraints.html) — the constraint that makes upsert possible. Lesson 25 designs them.
- [Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/transaction-iso.html) — what "atomically" actually means here, and what else races look like. Lesson 23 next.

## Challenge — conditional upsert (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. `price_watch` tracks the best (lowest)
price ever seen per product. Today's crawl: product 10 at **45.00**,
product 20 at **95.00**, product 40 at **60.00**. One statement that
inserts new products and updates existing ones **only if the new price
is lower**. (10 improves on 50 → updates; 95 is worse than 80 → row must
stay; 40 is new → inserts.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 22_upsert challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
DO UPDATE ... WHERE: the update clause takes its own condition comparing
the incumbent (`price_watch.best_price`) with the challenger
(`EXCLUDED.best_price`).

## Hint 2
```sql
INSERT INTO price_watch (product_id, best_price)
VALUES (10, 45.00), (20, 95.00), (40, 60.00)
ON CONFLICT (product_id)
DO UPDATE SET best_price = EXCLUDED.best_price
WHERE EXCLUDED.best_price < price_watch.best_price;
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Same shape, but the conflict action is the one that does nothing at all.

## Hint 2
```sql
INSERT INTO inventory (product_id, stock)
VALUES (60, 0), (200, 0)
ON CONFLICT (product_id) DO NOTHING;
```

(Why insert 60 with stock 0 at all? Because you don't know it exists —
that's the point of the idiom. The DO NOTHING protects it.)

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — only update when it is an improvement

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. A second stocktake arrives, but this warehouse is
known to under-count: the rule is **only raise a stock figure, never lower
it**. Today's numbers are product **70 at 80**, product **80 at 120**,
product **250 at 5**.

One statement. Expected outcome:

- 70 currently holds 100 — 80 is lower, so the row must **not** change.
- 80 currently holds 100 — 120 is higher, so it becomes 120.
- 250 has no row at all — it is inserted with 5.

`DO UPDATE` accepts its own `WHERE`, evaluated per conflicting row, with
both the existing row (`inventory.`) and the proposed row (`EXCLUDED.`) in
scope:

```sql
ON CONFLICT (product_id) DO UPDATE
  SET stock = EXCLUDED.stock
  WHERE EXCLUDED.stock > inventory.stock
```

Convince yourself this is idempotent before you run it — the gate will run
your statement twice and compare.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — upserting a whole set at once

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The seasonal reset: every product with `id`
between **95 and 105 inclusive** should have an inventory row with stock
**50**, whether or not it has one today. (Products 95–100 already have
rows; 101–105 do not.)

One statement, and the rows come from a **query** rather than a `VALUES`
list: `INSERT INTO ... SELECT ... ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE ...`. The
conflict clause works identically — it is the *insert*, not the source of
the rows, that it attaches to.

This is how real syncs are written: read the source of truth, upsert the
lot, let the constraint sort out which rows were new. The alternative —
querying which ids exist, then splitting into an `INSERT` batch and an
`UPDATE` batch in application code — is more code, slower, and wrong under
concurrency.

lessons.briefing:
# 23 — Transactions

Move 250 from Alice to Bob: one UPDATE subtracts, another adds. Now
imagine the process dies *between* them — the money is simply gone, and
no log line will ever tell you where. The transaction is the database's
answer: a group of statements that becomes visible **all together or not
at all**.

`setup.sql` gives this lesson an `accounts` table: Alice 900, Bob 100,
Escrow 0, with a CHECK forbidding negative balances. The gates run your
script over an autocommit connection — meaning **your** `BEGIN` /
`COMMIT` / `ROLLBACK` statements are the only transaction control there
is, exactly like typing into psql.

## Concept

```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 250 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 250 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;
```

- Between `BEGIN` and `COMMIT`, your changes are invisible to everyone
  else and reversible by you. `ROLLBACK` abandons them entirely.
- **After any error inside a transaction, PostgreSQL refuses every
  further statement until you ROLLBACK** (`current transaction is
  aborted...`). Error handling isn't optional plumbing; it's part of the
  transaction's design.
- `SAVEPOINT name` / `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name` gives partial undo
  *inside* a transaction — how batch jobs skip one bad record without
  abandoning the batch. (The dojo's own constraint probes in Part 4 use
  savepoints — you'll see them from the other side.)
- A famous PostgreSQL superpower: **DDL is transactional**. A migration
  that creates a table, backfills it, and adds constraints can roll back
  as a unit. Not true in MySQL and Oracle; cherish it. (Part 4 builds on
  this.)

## Exercise 1 — the classic transfer

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Write the complete transaction transferring
**250.00 from Alice (id 1) to Bob (id 2)**: `BEGIN`, the two UPDATEs,
`COMMIT`. The gate verifies both balances and that the total across all
accounts is still 1000.

Run: `uv run dojo test 23_transactions ex1`

## Exercise 2 — survive a mid-flight crash

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Same transfer, 600.00 this time — but your
script must contain this exact line between the debit and the rest:

```sql
-- INJECT FAILURE HERE
```

The gate splits your script at that marker, runs the first half, then
**injects a crashing statement** (division by zero), and finally runs
your remainder. At that point the transaction is in the aborted state —
the only statement PostgreSQL will accept is `ROLLBACK`, so your
remainder must issue it. The gate then verifies Alice still has 900 and
Bob 100: the half-done debit evaporated with the rollback. That
evaporation is atomicity, demonstrated on your own script.

Shape of the file:

```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE ...;            -- the debit
-- INJECT FAILURE HERE
ROLLBACK;              -- your crash recovery
```

Run: `uv run dojo test 23_transactions ex2`

## Exercise 3 — changing your mind (ROLLBACK)

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Operations started moving **500.00 from Alice (id
1) into Escrow (id 3)** and then discovered the transfer was authorised
against the wrong account. Write the transaction that does the work and
then **abandons it**: `BEGIN`, both `UPDATE`s, `ROLLBACK`.

The gate checks that all three balances are exactly as `setup.sql` left
them — Alice 900, Bob 100, Escrow 0 — and that your script really did open
a transaction and roll it back.

`ROLLBACK` is not error handling here. It is a decision. Between `BEGIN`
and the end of the transaction, your changes are real to you and invisible
to everyone else, which means a transaction is a place to *try things* —
run the update, look at the result with a `SELECT`, and only then decide
whether the world should see it. That is the single most useful habit in
this lesson, and it costs nothing.

Run: `uv run dojo test 23_transactions ex3`

## Exercise 4 — recovering without giving up (SAVEPOINT)

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Exercise 2 met a failure and had no choice but to
throw the whole transaction away. A batch job cannot afford that: one bad
record must not cost you the other nine hundred. `SAVEPOINT` is the answer.

Write a transaction that:

1. moves **100.00 from Alice (id 1) to Escrow (id 3)**,
2. takes a `SAVEPOINT`,
3. contains the exact marker line `-- INJECT FAILURE HERE`,
4. **rolls back to the savepoint** — recovering the transaction rather than
   abandoning it,
5. then moves **50.00 from Alice to Bob (id 2)**,
6. and `COMMIT`s.

Final balances: Alice 750, Bob 150, Escrow 100.

The gate splits your file at the marker, runs the first half, injects a
division by zero, then runs your remainder. After the injected error the
transaction is in the aborted state — but `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT` is
accepted there, and it returns the transaction to a working state with the
work done *before* the savepoint still intact. That is the difference
between a batch job that skips a record and one that loses a night.

Shape of the file:

```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE ...;            -- the 100.00 into escrow
UPDATE ...;
SAVEPOINT batch;
-- INJECT FAILURE HERE
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT batch;
UPDATE ...;            -- the 50.00 to Bob
UPDATE ...;
COMMIT;
```

Run: `uv run dojo test 23_transactions ex4`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 23_transactions

A transaction is the database's promise that a group of statements becomes
visible all together or not at all. Everything else in this lesson — the
aborted state, savepoints, isolation levels — is a consequence of taking
that promise seriously under concurrency and failure.

## Notes

**ACID, in one line each.** *Atomicity*: all or nothing. *Consistency*: the
database's own rules (constraints, foreign keys) hold at every commit.
*Isolation*: concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-finished
work. *Durability*: once `COMMIT` returns, the change survives a crash.
PostgreSQL gives you all four; the interesting engineering is in what
"isolation" means precisely, and in what *your* code puts inside the
boundary.

**The aborted state is not a bug.** After any error inside a transaction,
PostgreSQL refuses every further statement with `current transaction is
aborted`. This is deliberate: continuing after a failed statement would let
you commit a half-applied change while believing everything worked. The only
statements accepted are `ROLLBACK` and `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT`. Error
handling is therefore part of the transaction's *design*, not plumbing to be
bolted on.

**Savepoints are partial undo.** `SAVEPOINT name` marks a point;
`ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name` discards everything after it *and* clears the
aborted state, leaving the transaction alive and the earlier work intact.
This is how a batch job skips one bad record without losing the batch, and
how psql's `ON_ERROR_ROLLBACK` works. It is not free — each savepoint
consumes a subtransaction id, and tens of thousands of them in one
transaction is a known performance cliff — but at batch granularity it is
exactly the right tool.

**DDL is transactional in PostgreSQL.** `CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE`,
`CREATE INDEX` (without `CONCURRENTLY`), even `DROP TABLE` — all roll back.
A migration that creates a table, backfills it, adds constraints and fails
halfway leaves *nothing* behind. MySQL and Oracle cannot do this, and
migration tooling in those ecosystems is shaped around the absence. Cherish
it; Part 4 leans on it heavily.

**Isolation levels, briefly.** PostgreSQL's default is `READ COMMITTED`:
each statement sees a snapshot taken at the moment that statement started.
So two statements in one transaction can see different data, and a
read-modify-write across two statements can lose an update. `REPEATABLE
READ` takes one snapshot for the whole transaction. `SERIALIZABLE` goes
further and guarantees the outcome equals *some* serial order of the
concurrent transactions — at the cost of transactions that fail with a
serialisation error and must be retried by the application. The practical
rule: if your logic reads a value, decides, then writes based on that
decision, `READ COMMITTED` is not enough on its own — use `SELECT ... FOR
UPDATE`, a unique constraint with `ON CONFLICT` (lesson 22), or
`SERIALIZABLE` with retry.

**Long transactions are expensive in a way that is not obvious.**
PostgreSQL's MVCC keeps old row versions alive as long as any transaction
might still need to see them. A transaction left open for an hour prevents
`VACUUM` from reclaiming *anything* newer than its snapshot, across the whole
database — bloating tables that transaction never touched. "Open a
transaction, then go and call an HTTP API" is the canonical way to cause
this. Lesson 44 is where it bites.

**The boundary is a design problem.** In application code transactions hide
inside a `with db.begin():` block, and the classic production bug is work
that escapes it in either direction: an HTTP call, a queue publish, a cache
invalidation *inside* the transaction (those do not roll back), or a commit
that lands while business invariants are still half-applied. Whenever you
touch transactional code, draw the boundary and ask two questions: what is
inside that cannot roll back, and what is outside that should be inside?
The outbox and saga patterns exist because the answers get hard at scale.

## ex1 — the classic transfer

Two updates, one atomic unit. The gate checks the sum as well as the
balances, because the invariant that actually matters is not "Alice has 650"
but "money is neither created nor destroyed". Write the invariant check
alongside the migration; it is the assertion that catches the bug you did
not think of.

## ex2 — survive a mid-flight crash

Atomicity demonstrated on your own script. The debit was really applied —
it was visible inside the transaction — and then it evaporated. Nothing in
the table, no log line, no compensating update. That is the guarantee you
are buying, and it is why "just be careful in application code" is not an
alternative.

## ex3 — changing your mind

`ROLLBACK` as a deliberate choice rather than an error path. The habit this
is really teaching: `BEGIN`, do the dangerous thing, `SELECT` to inspect the
result, and *then* decide. In psql this makes an `UPDATE` with a suspicious
`WHERE` completely safe to try. It is the professional ritual from lesson 21
with the safety catch actually engaged.

## ex4 — recovering without giving up

The difference between ex2 and ex4 is the difference between a job that dies
and a job that skips a record. Note precisely what survived: the escrow
transfer, which happened *before* the savepoint. Everything after it was
discarded, the transaction was restored to a usable state, and the later
work committed normally. Batch importers, migration scripts and
message-queue consumers are all built on this shape.

## Further reading

- [Transactions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-transactions.html) — the tutorial chapter, including savepoints. Short and worth reading start to finish.
- [Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/transaction-iso.html) — read-committed, repeatable-read and serializable, with the anomalies each one permits. The most important page in this lesson.
- [`SAVEPOINT`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-savepoint.html) — the reference page, plus `RELEASE SAVEPOINT` which you will want for long loops.
- [Explicit Locking](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/explicit-locking.html) — `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` and friends, for when read-then-write must not race.

## The gate

```python
"""Gates for 23_transactions. Quoted verbatim in README.md.

These gates run your script on a SEPARATE AUTOCOMMIT connection, so your
own BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK statements are fully in charge of transaction
boundaries - exactly like a psql session.
"""
import psycopg
import pytest

from dojo import db, grader
from dojo.lesson import Lesson

L = Lesson(__file__)

MARKER = "-- INJECT FAILURE HERE"


def test_ex1(lesson_db):
    L.apply_setup(lesson_db)
    ex = L.exercise("ex1")
    with db.connect(lesson_db.info.dbname, autocommit=True) as tx_conn:
        tx_conn.execute(ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_scalar(lesson_db, "SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1",
                         650, "Alice: 900 - 250")
    grader.assert_scalar(lesson_db, "SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 2",
                         350, "Bob: 100 + 250")
    grader.assert_scalar(lesson_db, "SELECT sum(balance) FROM accounts",
                         1000, "money is neither created nor destroyed")


def test_ex2(lesson_db):
    L.apply_setup(lesson_db)
    ex = L.exercise("ex2")
    script = ex.solution_sql
    assert MARKER in script, (
        "Your script must contain the literal marker line\n"
        f"    {MARKER}\n"
        "between the debit and your recovery handling - the gate injects a "
        "crash at that point to prove your transaction is atomic."
    )
    first_half, _, remainder = script.partition(MARKER)
    with db.connect(lesson_db.info.dbname, autocommit=True) as tx_conn:
        tx_conn.execute(first_half)
        with pytest.raises(psycopg.Error):
            tx_conn.execute("SELECT 1/0")  # the injected disaster
        try:
            tx_conn.execute(remainder)
        except psycopg.errors.InFailedSqlTransaction:
            raise AssertionError(
                "After the injected failure, the transaction is in a failed "
                "state: the ONLY statement PostgreSQL will accept is ROLLBACK. "
                "Your script's remainder must roll the transaction back."
            ) from None
    grader.assert_scalar(lesson_db, "SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1",
                         900, "Alice untouched - the half-done debit must vanish")
    grader.assert_scalar(lesson_db, "SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 2",
                         100, "Bob untouched")


def test_ex3(lesson_db):
    L.apply_setup(lesson_db)
    ex = L.exercise("ex3")
    script = ex.solution_sql
    lowered = script.lower()
    assert "begin" in lowered and "rollback" in lowered, (
        "This exercise is about ROLLBACK: your script must open a transaction "
        "with BEGIN, do the two UPDATEs, and abandon it with ROLLBACK."
    )
    assert "update" in lowered, (
        "Roll back some actual work - the script needs the two UPDATEs in it."
    )
    with db.connect(lesson_db.info.dbname, autocommit=True) as tx_conn:
        tx_conn.execute(script)
    grader.assert_scalar(lesson_db, "SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1",
                         900, "Alice untouched - the transaction was abandoned")
    grader.assert_scalar(lesson_db, "SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 3",
                         0, "Escrow untouched")
    grader.assert_scalar(lesson_db, "SELECT sum(balance) FROM accounts",
                         1000, "money is neither created nor destroyed")


def test_ex4(lesson_db):
    L.apply_setup(lesson_db)
    ex = L.exercise("ex4")
    script = ex.solution_sql
    assert MARKER in script, (
        "Your script must contain the literal marker line\n"
        f"    {MARKER}\n"
        "just after your SAVEPOINT - the gate injects a crash there."
    )
    assert "savepoint" in script.lower(), (
        "This exercise is about SAVEPOINT. Without one, the injected failure "
        "poisons the whole transaction and ROLLBACK is your only legal move."
```

# Reading - 23_transactions

A transaction is the database's promise that a group of statements becomes
visible all together or not at all. Everything else in this lesson — the
aborted state, savepoints, isolation levels — is a consequence of taking
that promise seriously under concurrency and failure.

## Notes

**ACID, in one line each.** *Atomicity*: all or nothing. *Consistency*: the
database's own rules (constraints, foreign keys) hold at every commit.
*Isolation*: concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-finished
work. *Durability*: once `COMMIT` returns, the change survives a crash.
PostgreSQL gives you all four; the interesting engineering is in what
"isolation" means precisely, and in what *your* code puts inside the
boundary.

**The aborted state is not a bug.** After any error inside a transaction,
PostgreSQL refuses every further statement with `current transaction is
aborted`. This is deliberate: continuing after a failed statement would let
you commit a half-applied change while believing everything worked. The only
statements accepted are `ROLLBACK` and `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT`. Error
handling is therefore part of the transaction's *design*, not plumbing to be
bolted on.

**Savepoints are partial undo.** `SAVEPOINT name` marks a point;
`ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name` discards everything after it *and* clears the
aborted state, leaving the transaction alive and the earlier work intact.
This is how a batch job skips one bad record without losing the batch, and
how psql's `ON_ERROR_ROLLBACK` works. It is not free — each savepoint
consumes a subtransaction id, and tens of thousands of them in one
transaction is a known performance cliff — but at batch granularity it is
exactly the right tool.

**DDL is transactional in PostgreSQL.** `CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE`,
`CREATE INDEX` (without `CONCURRENTLY`), even `DROP TABLE` — all roll back.
A migration that creates a table, backfills it, adds constraints and fails
halfway leaves *nothing* behind. MySQL and Oracle cannot do this, and
migration tooling in those ecosystems is shaped around the absence. Cherish
it; Part 4 leans on it heavily.

**Isolation levels, briefly.** PostgreSQL's default is `READ COMMITTED`:
each statement sees a snapshot taken at the moment that statement started.
So two statements in one transaction can see different data, and a
read-modify-write across two statements can lose an update. `REPEATABLE
READ` takes one snapshot for the whole transaction. `SERIALIZABLE` goes
further and guarantees the outcome equals *some* serial order of the
concurrent transactions — at the cost of transactions that fail with a
serialisation error and must be retried by the application. The practical
rule: if your logic reads a value, decides, then writes based on that
decision, `READ COMMITTED` is not enough on its own — use `SELECT ... FOR
UPDATE`, a unique constraint with `ON CONFLICT` (lesson 22), or
`SERIALIZABLE` with retry.

**Long transactions are expensive in a way that is not obvious.**
PostgreSQL's MVCC keeps old row versions alive as long as any transaction
might still need to see them. A transaction left open for an hour prevents
`VACUUM` from reclaiming *anything* newer than its snapshot, across the whole
database — bloating tables that transaction never touched. "Open a
transaction, then go and call an HTTP API" is the canonical way to cause
this. Lesson 44 is where it bites.

**The boundary is a design problem.** In application code transactions hide
inside a `with db.begin():` block, and the classic production bug is work
that escapes it in either direction: an HTTP call, a queue publish, a cache
invalidation *inside* the transaction (those do not roll back), or a commit
that lands while business invariants are still half-applied. Whenever you
touch transactional code, draw the boundary and ask two questions: what is
inside that cannot roll back, and what is outside that should be inside?
The outbox and saga patterns exist because the answers get hard at scale.

## ex1 — the classic transfer

Two updates, one atomic unit. The gate checks the sum as well as the
balances, because the invariant that actually matters is not "Alice has 650"
but "money is neither created nor destroyed". Write the invariant check
alongside the migration; it is the assertion that catches the bug you did
not think of.

## ex2 — survive a mid-flight crash

Atomicity demonstrated on your own script. The debit was really applied —
it was visible inside the transaction — and then it evaporated. Nothing in
the table, no log line, no compensating update. That is the guarantee you
are buying, and it is why "just be careful in application code" is not an
alternative.

## ex3 — changing your mind

`ROLLBACK` as a deliberate choice rather than an error path. The habit this
is really teaching: `BEGIN`, do the dangerous thing, `SELECT` to inspect the
result, and *then* decide. In psql this makes an `UPDATE` with a suspicious
`WHERE` completely safe to try. It is the professional ritual from lesson 21
with the safety catch actually engaged.

## ex4 — recovering without giving up

The difference between ex2 and ex4 is the difference between a job that dies
and a job that skips a record. Note precisely what survived: the escrow
transfer, which happened *before* the savepoint. Everything after it was
discarded, the transaction was restored to a usable state, and the later
work committed normally. Batch importers, migration scripts and
message-queue consumers are all built on this shape.

## Further reading

- [Transactions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-transactions.html) — the tutorial chapter, including savepoints. Short and worth reading start to finish.
- [Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/transaction-iso.html) — read-committed, repeatable-read and serializable, with the anomalies each one permits. The most important page in this lesson.
- [`SAVEPOINT`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-savepoint.html) — the reference page, plus `RELEASE SAVEPOINT` which you will want for long loops.
- [Explicit Locking](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/explicit-locking.html) — `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` and friends, for when read-then-write must not race.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — survive a mid-flight crash

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Same transfer, 600.00 this time — but your
script must contain this exact line between the debit and the rest:

```sql
-- INJECT FAILURE HERE
```

The gate splits your script at that marker, runs the first half, then
**injects a crashing statement** (division by zero), and finally runs
your remainder. At that point the transaction is in the aborted state —
the only statement PostgreSQL will accept is `ROLLBACK`, so your
remainder must issue it. The gate then verifies Alice still has 900 and
Bob 100: the half-done debit evaporated with the rollback. That
evaporation is atomicity, demonstrated on your own script.

Shape of the file:

```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE ...;            -- the debit
-- INJECT FAILURE HERE
ROLLBACK;              -- your crash recovery
```

Run: `uv run dojo test 23_transactions ex2`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The README's "shape of the file" block is nearly the whole answer: BEGIN,
the 600 debit from Alice, the marker line (copied exactly, including the
leading `--`), then ROLLBACK. The credit and COMMIT never get a chance
to exist - the injected crash sees to that.

## Hint 2
```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 600 WHERE id = 1;
-- INJECT FAILURE HERE
ROLLBACK;
```

Run it and read the gate's assertions as they pass: the debit really did
execute, and the rollback really did erase it.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — changing your mind (ROLLBACK)

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Operations started moving **500.00 from Alice (id
1) into Escrow (id 3)** and then discovered the transfer was authorised
against the wrong account. Write the transaction that does the work and
then **abandons it**: `BEGIN`, both `UPDATE`s, `ROLLBACK`.

The gate checks that all three balances are exactly as `setup.sql` left
them — Alice 900, Bob 100, Escrow 0 — and that your script really did open
a transaction and roll it back.

`ROLLBACK` is not error handling here. It is a decision. Between `BEGIN`
and the end of the transaction, your changes are real to you and invisible
to everyone else, which means a transaction is a place to *try things* —
run the update, look at the result with a `SELECT`, and only then decide
whether the world should see it. That is the single most useful habit in
this lesson, and it costs nothing.

Run: `uv run dojo test 23_transactions ex3`

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — recovering without giving up (SAVEPOINT)

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Exercise 2 met a failure and had no choice but to
throw the whole transaction away. A batch job cannot afford that: one bad
record must not cost you the other nine hundred. `SAVEPOINT` is the answer.

Write a transaction that:

1. moves **100.00 from Alice (id 1) to Escrow (id 3)**,
2. takes a `SAVEPOINT`,
3. contains the exact marker line `-- INJECT FAILURE HERE`,
4. **rolls back to the savepoint** — recovering the transaction rather than
   abandoning it,
5. then moves **50.00 from Alice to Bob (id 2)**,
6. and `COMMIT`s.

Final balances: Alice 750, Bob 150, Escrow 100.

The gate splits your file at the marker, runs the first half, injects a
division by zero, then runs your remainder. After the injected error the
transaction is in the aborted state — but `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT` is
accepted there, and it returns the transaction to a working state with the
work done *before* the savepoint still intact. That is the difference
between a batch job that skips a record and one that loses a night.

Shape of the file:

```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE ...;            -- the 100.00 into escrow
UPDATE ...;
SAVEPOINT batch;
-- INJECT FAILURE HERE
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT batch;
UPDATE ...;            -- the 50.00 to Bob
UPDATE ...;
COMMIT;
```

# 24 — DDL and choosing types

Part 4 flips your seat at the table: you've queried a schema for 24
lessons; now you get to *cause* one. `CREATE TABLE` is easy syntax — the
craft is in the type choices, and every choice is a promise to every
future query. The gates change again to match: they inspect the
**catalog** (PostgreSQL's own record of your schema, `pg_catalog`) and
then *probe* your tables with real INSERTs.

## Concept

```sql
CREATE TABLE coupons (
  code        text        PRIMARY KEY,
  percent_off numeric(5,2) NOT NULL,
  starts_on   date         NOT NULL,
  expires_on  date         NOT NULL,
  notes       text
);
```

The type decisions that come up weekly in real work:

- **text vs varchar(n)**: in PostgreSQL they're the same thing under the
  hood; `varchar(50)` adds only a length check you'll someday regret
  (name truncation bugs). House style in most PG shops: `text`, with a
  CHECK constraint if you truly need a limit.
- **numeric vs float for money**: `numeric` is exact decimal arithmetic;
  `float`/`double precision` is binary floating point — 0.1 has no exact
  binary representation, and money drifts. Exercise 2 makes you *watch*
  it drift. `numeric(10,2)` = 10 significant digits, 2 after the point.
- **timestamptz vs timestamp**: lesson 18's paragraph, now as a design
  rule — instants get `timestamptz`; calendar concepts (a coupon's
  validity date!) get `date`.
- **boolean** exists — use it instead of `'Y'`/`'N'` text flags you'll
  find in legacy schemas.
- **Arrays vs join tables**: PostgreSQL happily stores `text[]`. Fine
  for small, closed, order-insensitive lists nobody joins against
  (tags on `products.attributes` could be one). The moment you want
  "which products have tag X, with a FK guaranteeing X exists" — that's
  a join table (next lessons). When in doubt, normalize; arrays are the
  optimization, not the default.

## Exercise 1 — the coupons table

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Create `coupons` exactly as specced:

- `code` — text, primary key
- `percent_off` — `numeric(5,2)`, NOT NULL
- `starts_on`, `expires_on` — dates, NOT NULL
- `notes` — text, nullable

Run: `uv run dojo test 24_ddl_and_types ex1`

## Exercise 2 — watch float money break

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Two statements:

1. Create `ledger`: `id` int primary key, `amount_float` `double
   precision` NOT NULL, `amount_numeric` `numeric(10,2)` NOT NULL.
2. Insert **ten rows**, each with `0.1` in both amount columns (ids
   1–10; `generate_series` or ten VALUES tuples, your choice).

The gate then asserts `sum(amount_numeric) = 1.00` is **true** and
`sum(amount_float) = 1.0` is **false**. You are inserting the same ten
dimes into both columns; only one column can add them up correctly.
Run it, then try `SELECT sum(amount_float) FROM ledger;` in the lab and
look at the digits you'd have shipped to accounting.

Run: `uv run dojo test 24_ddl_and_types ex2`

## Exercise 3 — a table that refuses nonsense

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Create `subscriptions`:

- `id` — int, primary key
- `customer_id` — int, NOT NULL, references `customers(id)`
- `plan` — text, NOT NULL, and **only** `'free'`, `'pro'` or `'team'`
  are allowed (a `CHECK (plan IN (...))`)
- `is_active` — boolean, NOT NULL, **DEFAULT true**
- `started_at` — `timestamptz`, NOT NULL (an instant)
- `renews_on` — `date`, nullable (a calendar concept)

Four type decisions from the concept section, all in one table. `plan` is
a closed set of values, and the CHECK is how you say so without reaching
for an `enum` type — enums are real in PostgreSQL and genuinely awkward to
change, so a `text` column with a CHECK is the common house style. Note
also the deliberate split between `started_at` (an instant, so
`timestamptz`) and `renews_on` (a date on a calendar, so `date`).

The gate probes it: a row omitting `is_active` and `renews_on` must be
accepted and default to active, and `plan = 'enterprise'` must be
rejected.

Run: `uv run dojo test 24_ddl_and_types ex3`

## Exercise 4 — let the database do the arithmetic

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Create `invoices`:

- `id` — int, `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`, primary key
- `subtotal` — `numeric(10,2)`, NOT NULL
- `tax` — `numeric(10,2)`, NOT NULL
- `total` — `numeric(10,2)`, `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (subtotal + tax) STORED`

Two modern PostgreSQL features that remove a whole class of bugs.

`GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` is the standard-SQL way to say
"auto-assign this key" — it is the successor to `serial`, and unlike
`serial` it refuses an explicit value by default, so nobody can
accidentally insert an id that collides with the sequence.

A **generated column** is computed from other columns of the same row and
stored. `total` can never disagree with `subtotal + tax`, because there is
no way to write it — the gate proves this by trying, and expecting a
rejection. Compare that with the alternative everyone has shipped at some
point: a plain `total` column, kept in sync by application code, that
drifts the first time somebody updates `tax` through a different code
path.

Insert with just `(subtotal, tax)`; the other two columns take care of
themselves.

Run: `uv run dojo test 24_ddl_and_types ex4`

# Reading - 24_ddl_and_types

Part 4 changes your seat at the table. For twenty-four lessons the schema
was a fact of nature; now you cause it. Every type you choose is a promise
enforced on every future write by every future application, in every
language, forever — which makes type selection the cheapest correctness
work available to you.

## Notes

**`text` versus `varchar(n)`.** In PostgreSQL these are the same type with
the same storage and the same performance; `varchar(n)` merely adds a length
check. That check sounds prudent and is usually a future outage: names,
addresses and identifiers are longer than you think in some locale, and
changing the limit later requires an `ALTER TABLE`. House style in most
PostgreSQL shops is `text`, with a `CHECK (length(x) <= n)` when a limit is
genuinely part of the domain. (`char(n)` is worse still — it pads with
spaces. Do not use it.)

**`numeric` versus `float` for money.** `numeric` is exact decimal
arithmetic; `double precision` is IEEE 754 binary, and 0.1 has no exact
binary representation. Ten dimes stored as floats do not add to one dollar —
you will watch this happen in ex2. `numeric(10,2)` means ten significant
digits with two after the point. The rule is absolute: money, quantities that
must reconcile, and anything a human will audit go in `numeric`. Floats are
for measurements and scientific work where relative error is acceptable and
speed matters.

**`timestamptz` versus `timestamp` versus `date`.** An instant that happened
gets `timestamptz`. A calendar concept — a birthday, a coupon's validity
date, an invoice period — gets `date`, because it is not a moment in time at
all. `timestamp` without a zone is almost never what you want; lesson 18
argues it fully.

**Booleans are a type.** `'Y'`/`'N'` text flags, `0`/`1` integers and
`'true'`/`'false'` strings all exist in legacy schemas and all permit values
that mean nothing. A `boolean` column has three possible states (true,
false, NULL) and if you add `NOT NULL` it has two, which is what you meant.

**Closed sets: CHECK versus enum.** PostgreSQL has real `enum` types, and
they are compact and ordered — but adding a value requires `ALTER TYPE`, and
until PostgreSQL 12 you could not do that inside a transaction, and you
still cannot *remove* one. The common house style is `text` with a `CHECK
(col IN (...))`: readable, changeable with an ordinary migration, and just
as enforced. The third option — a lookup table with a foreign key — is right
when the set is data (categories, countries) rather than code.

**Identity columns.** `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` is standard SQL and the
modern replacement for `serial`. Two practical advantages: `ALWAYS` rejects
explicit inserts, so nobody can hand-place an id that later collides with the
sequence; and the sequence's ownership is properly recorded, so it is dropped
with the table. Use `GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY` only when a data
loader genuinely needs to supply ids.

**Generated columns.** `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expr) STORED` computes a value
from the same row's other columns and stores it. It cannot drift, because it
cannot be written. This is a *constraint* wearing a column's clothing:
anywhere your application maintains a derived field by hand, a generated
column removes the possibility of the two disagreeing. The limitation is
that the expression must be immutable and may only reference the current
row — no subqueries, no `now()`, no other tables.

**Arrays versus join tables.** PostgreSQL stores `text[]` happily, and it is
fine for a small, closed, order-insensitive list nobody joins against or
constrains. The moment you want "which products have tag X, guaranteed to be
a tag that exists", you want a join table with a foreign key. Arrays and
JSONB are the optimisation; normalisation is the default. Lesson 26 makes
the argument properly.

**Design for the constraint you cannot add later cheaply.** Every one of
these choices is easier now than after a billion rows exist. Lesson 28 is
about doing it afterwards anyway, safely, and it will make you appreciate
getting it right the first time.

## ex1 — the coupons table

Six columns, each a decision: `text` for the code, `numeric(5,2)` for a
percentage, `date` for calendar bounds, and one deliberately nullable column
so you can see the gate's probe insert omit it. Note `notes text` with no
`NOT NULL` — nullable *on purpose* is a legitimate design, and saying so
explicitly is what distinguishes it from nullable by accident.

## ex2 — watch float money break

The canonical schema-review catch, performed on your own table. Run `SELECT
sum(amount_float) FROM ledger` in the lab and look at the digits. Then
consider that this error compounds: every addition can introduce a new one,
and a ledger that has been summing floats for a year cannot be reconciled by
anyone. There is no rounding strategy that fixes it, because the wrong value
was stored, not merely displayed.

## ex3 — a table that refuses nonsense

Four type decisions plus a CHECK, and the gate proves each one bites.
Notice how much application code this table makes unnecessary: no plan
validation, no default-active logic, no "is this a date or a timestamp"
argument in code review. Every rule enforced here is enforced for the batch
script somebody runs at 2 a.m. too.

## ex4 — let the database do the arithmetic

Identity and generated columns are both answers to the same question: *what
can I stop trusting my application to get right?* A hand-maintained `total`
column is correct until the day someone updates `tax` through a code path
that forgot; a generated column is correct by construction. The gate's
rejection probe is the proof — there is literally no INSERT that can make
`total` disagree.

## Further reading

- [Data Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype.html) — the whole chapter is worth a skim once; the numeric and date/time sections are worth reading properly.
- [`CREATE TABLE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createtable.html) — identity columns, generated columns, and the exact syntax for inline constraints.
- [Generated Columns](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-generated-columns.html) — short page, and it lists the restrictions (immutable expressions, same row only).
- [Don't Do This](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) — the type section covers `char(n)`, `varchar(n)`, `money`, `timestamp`, and `serial`. Read it now that you have opinions.

- `plan` — text, NOT NULL, and **only** `'free'`, `'pro'` or `'team'`
  are allowed (a `CHECK (plan IN (...))`)
- `is_active` — boolean, NOT NULL, **DEFAULT true**
- `started_at` — `timestamptz`, NOT NULL (an instant)
- `renews_on` — `date`, nullable (a calendar concept)

Four type decisions from the concept section, all in one table. `plan` is
a closed set of values, and the CHECK is how you say so without reaching
for an `enum` type — enums are real in PostgreSQL and genuinely awkward to
change, so a `text` column with a CHECK is the common house style. Note
also the deliberate split between `started_at` (an instant, so
`timestamptz`) and `renews_on` (a date on a calendar, so `date`).

The gate probes it: a row omitting `is_active` and `renews_on` must be
accepted and default to active, and `plan = 'enterprise'` must be
rejected.

Run: `uv run dojo test 24_ddl_and_types ex3`

## Exercise 4 — let the database do the arithmetic

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Create `invoices`:

- `id` — int, `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`, primary key
- `subtotal` — `numeric(10,2)`, NOT NULL
- `tax` — `numeric(10,2)`, NOT NULL
- `total` — `numeric(10,2)`, `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (subtotal + tax) STORED`

Two modern PostgreSQL features that remove a whole class of bugs.

`GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` is the standard-SQL way to say
"auto-assign this key" — it is the successor to `serial`, and unlike
`serial` it refuses an explicit value by default, so nobody can
accidentally insert an id that collides with the sequence.

A **generated column** is computed from other columns of the same row and
stored. `total` can never disagree with `subtotal + tax`, because there is
no way to write it — the gate proves this by trying, and expecting a
rejection. Compare that with the alternative everyone has shipped at some
point: a plain `total` column, kept in sync by application code, that
drifts the first time somebody updates `tax` through a different code
path.

Insert with just `(subtotal, tax)`; the other two columns take care of
themselves.

Run: `uv run dojo test 24_ddl_and_types ex4`

## The teaching point

Types are the cheapest correctness tool you will ever get: a `numeric`
column *cannot* accumulate float error; a `date` *cannot* hold "n/a"; a
`boolean` *cannot* hold `'maybe'`. Every validation a type performs is
one your application code — all of it, in every language, forever —
doesn't have to. Schema review is mostly type review; the float-money
table is the canonical catch.

Next: **25_constraints** — promises the database enforces.

# Reading - 24_ddl_and_types

Part 4 changes your seat at the table. For twenty-four lessons the schema
was a fact of nature; now you cause it. Every type you choose is a promise
enforced on every future write by every future application, in every
language, forever — which makes type selection the cheapest correctness
work available to you.

## Notes

**`text` versus `varchar(n)`.** In PostgreSQL these are the same type with
the same storage and the same performance; `varchar(n)` merely adds a length
check. That check sounds prudent and is usually a future outage: names,
addresses and identifiers are longer than you think in some locale, and
changing the limit later requires an `ALTER TABLE`. House style in most
PostgreSQL shops is `text`, with a `CHECK (length(x) <= n)` when a limit is
genuinely part of the domain. (`char(n)` is worse still — it pads with
spaces. Do not use it.)

**`numeric` versus `float` for money.** `numeric` is exact decimal
arithmetic; `double precision` is IEEE 754 binary, and 0.1 has no exact
binary representation. Ten dimes stored as floats do not add to one dollar —
you will watch this happen in ex2. `numeric(10,2)` means ten significant
digits with two after the point. The rule is absolute: money, quantities that
must reconcile, and anything a human will audit go in `numeric`. Floats are
for measurements and scientific work where relative error is acceptable and
speed matters.

**`timestamptz` versus `timestamp` versus `date`.** An instant that happened
gets `timestamptz`. A calendar concept — a birthday, a coupon's validity
date, an invoice period — gets `date`, because it is not a moment in time at
all. `timestamp` without a zone is almost never what you want; lesson 18
argues it fully.

**Booleans are a type.** `'Y'`/`'N'` text flags, `0`/`1` integers and
`'true'`/`'false'` strings all exist in legacy schemas and all permit values
that mean nothing. A `boolean` column has three possible states (true,
false, NULL) and if you add `NOT NULL` it has two, which is what you meant.

**Closed sets: CHECK versus enum.** PostgreSQL has real `enum` types, and
they are compact and ordered — but adding a value requires `ALTER TYPE`, and
until PostgreSQL 12 you could not do that inside a transaction, and you
still cannot *remove* one. The common house style is `text` with a `CHECK
(col IN (...))`: readable, changeable with an ordinary migration, and just
as enforced. The third option — a lookup table with a foreign key — is right
when the set is data (categories, countries) rather than code.

**Identity columns.** `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` is standard SQL and the
modern replacement for `serial`. Two practical advantages: `ALWAYS` rejects
explicit inserts, so nobody can hand-place an id that later collides with the
sequence; and the sequence's ownership is properly recorded, so it is dropped
with the table. Use `GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY` only when a data
loader genuinely needs to supply ids.

**Generated columns.** `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expr) STORED` computes a value
from the same row's other columns and stores it. It cannot drift, because it
cannot be written. This is a *constraint* wearing a column's clothing:
anywhere your application maintains a derived field by hand, a generated
column removes the possibility of the two disagreeing. The limitation is
that the expression must be immutable and may only reference the current
row — no subqueries, no `now()`, no other tables.

**Arrays versus join tables.** PostgreSQL stores `text[]` happily, and it is
fine for a small, closed, order-insensitive list nobody joins against or
constrains. The moment you want "which products have tag X, guaranteed to be
a tag that exists", you want a join table with a foreign key. Arrays and
JSONB are the optimisation; normalisation is the default. Lesson 26 makes
the argument properly.

**Design for the constraint you cannot add later cheaply.** Every one of
these choices is easier now than after a billion rows exist. Lesson 28 is
about doing it afterwards anyway, safely, and it will make you appreciate
getting it right the first time.

## ex1 — the coupons table

Six columns, each a decision: `text` for the code, `numeric(5,2)` for a
percentage, `date` for calendar bounds, and one deliberately nullable column
so you can see the gate's probe insert omit it. Note `notes text` with no
`NOT NULL` — nullable *on purpose* is a legitimate design, and saying so
explicitly is what distinguishes it from nullable by accident.

## ex2 — watch float money break

The canonical schema-review catch, performed on your own table. Run `SELECT
sum(amount_float) FROM ledger` in the lab and look at the digits. Then
consider that this error compounds: every addition can introduce a new one,
and a ledger that has been summing floats for a year cannot be reconciled by
anyone. There is no rounding strategy that fixes it, because the wrong value
was stored, not merely displayed.

## ex3 — a table that refuses nonsense

Four type decisions plus a CHECK, and the gate proves each one bites.
Notice how much application code this table makes unnecessary: no plan
validation, no default-active logic, no "is this a date or a timestamp"
argument in code review. Every rule enforced here is enforced for the batch
script somebody runs at 2 a.m. too.

## ex4 — let the database do the arithmetic

Identity and generated columns are both answers to the same question: *what
can I stop trusting my application to get right?* A hand-maintained `total`
column is correct until the day someone updates `tax` through a code path
that forgot; a generated column is correct by construction. The gate's
rejection probe is the proof — there is literally no INSERT that can make
`total` disagree.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — a table that refuses nonsense

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Create `subscriptions`:

- `id` — int, primary key
- `customer_id` — int, NOT NULL, references `customers(id)`
- `plan` — text, NOT NULL, and **only** `'free'`, `'pro'` or `'team'`
  are allowed (a `CHECK (plan IN (...))`)
- `is_active` — boolean, NOT NULL, **DEFAULT true**
- `started_at` — `timestamptz`, NOT NULL (an instant)
- `renews_on` — `date`, nullable (a calendar concept)

Four type decisions from the concept section, all in one table. `plan` is
a closed set of values, and the CHECK is how you say so without reaching
for an `enum` type — enums are real in PostgreSQL and genuinely awkward to
change, so a `text` column with a CHECK is the common house style. Note
also the deliberate split between `started_at` (an instant, so
`timestamptz`) and `renews_on` (a date on a calendar, so `date`).

The gate probes it: a row omitting `is_active` and `renews_on` must be
accepted and default to active, and `plan = 'enterprise'` must be
rejected.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — let the database do the arithmetic

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Create `invoices`:

- `id` — int, `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`, primary key
- `subtotal` — `numeric(10,2)`, NOT NULL
- `tax` — `numeric(10,2)`, NOT NULL
- `total` — `numeric(10,2)`, `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (subtotal + tax) STORED`

Two modern PostgreSQL features that remove a whole class of bugs.

`GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` is the standard-SQL way to say
"auto-assign this key" — it is the successor to `serial`, and unlike
`serial` it refuses an explicit value by default, so nobody can
accidentally insert an id that collides with the sequence.

A **generated column** is computed from other columns of the same row and
stored. `total` can never disagree with `subtotal + tax`, because there is
no way to write it — the gate proves this by trying, and expecting a
rejection. Compare that with the alternative everyone has shipped at some
point: a plain `total` column, kept in sync by application code, that
drifts the first time somebody updates `tax` through a different code
path.

Insert with just `(subtotal, tax)`; the other two columns take care of
themselves.

```sql
);
```
