# Reading - 28_altering_live_schemas

Every schema you will ever change is already in production, already has
data, and already has traffic. `ALTER TABLE` is easy syntax; doing it
without an outage is the skill, and the whole skill reduces to one
question: *what does this statement lock, and for how long?*

## Notes

**The danger is lock duration, not lock strength.** Most `ALTER TABLE`
forms take an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock, which blocks every reader and
writer. That is fine when the statement is instant — a catalog update takes
microseconds. It is an outage when the statement also has to *scan or
rewrite* the table while holding the lock. So the safe patterns all share
one shape: **split the instant-but-locking step from the slow-but-concurrent
step.**

**Instant (catalog-only) operations:**

- `ADD COLUMN` (nullable, or with a **constant** default since PostgreSQL 11)
- `DROP COLUMN` — logical only; the bytes stay until each row is rewritten
- `RENAME COLUMN` / `RENAME TABLE`
- `ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID`
- `SET DEFAULT` / `DROP DEFAULT`

**Operations that scan or rewrite:**

- `SET NOT NULL` — scans the whole table to verify (though PostgreSQL 12+
  can skip the scan if an equivalent validated `CHECK` already proves it)
- `ADD CONSTRAINT` without `NOT VALID` — scans to verify
- `ALTER COLUMN TYPE` — usually a full rewrite plus index rebuilds
- `ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT <volatile expression>` — full rewrite

**The NOT NULL three-step.**

```sql
ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN c text;            -- 1. instant
UPDATE t SET c = ...;                       -- 2. no DDL lock, batchable
ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c SET NOT NULL;  -- 3. one scan, short lock
```

**The NOT VALID two-step.**

```sql
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_total_min
  CHECK (total >= 5) NOT VALID;             -- 1. polices new rows, instant
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_total_min;
                                            -- 2. audits old rows, weak lock
```

`NOT VALID` means "trust the past, police the future". `VALIDATE` then
checks the past under a lock that permits reads *and* writes. The classic
half-finished migration is step 1 without step 2 — the constraint exists,
the catalog looks right, and nobody ever confirmed the historical data. This
is exactly why lesson 25's gates test *behaviour* and not just the catalog.

**Two things production migrations add that these exercises do not.** First,
a `lock_timeout`: if your `ALTER` cannot get its lock in two seconds, it
should fail rather than queue — because while it queues, *every* subsequent
query on that table queues behind it, and a five-minute wait becomes a
five-minute outage even though your statement never ran. Second, batching:
a backfill `UPDATE` over ten million rows is one enormous transaction that
bloats the table and holds a snapshot open (lesson 44); real backfills loop
in chunks of a few thousand with a commit between them.

**`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`.** Building an index normally blocks writes
for the duration. `CONCURRENTLY` does two passes and blocks almost nothing —
at the cost of being slower, unable to run inside a transaction block, and
capable of leaving an `INVALID` index behind if it fails, which you must
drop and retry. On any table that matters, this is the only way to add an
index. Part 5 builds every index without it because the dojo's clones have
no concurrent traffic.

**Expand and contract.** The general pattern for a change that cannot be
atomic — renaming a column that applications read, splitting a table,
changing a type. *Expand*: add the new thing alongside the old, write to
both. *Migrate*: backfill, then switch readers over. *Contract*: stop
writing the old thing, then drop it. Each step is independently safe and
independently reversible, which is what makes the deploy boring. Lesson
26's ex4 was this pattern in miniature.

**DDL is transactional in PostgreSQL** (lesson 23), so a migration script
that fails halfway leaves nothing behind. This is a genuine superpower and
it changes how migrations are written — but note the exceptions: `CREATE
INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and `VACUUM` cannot run inside a transaction block.

## ex1 — the NOT NULL three-step

The three steps, plus a performance lesson hiding inside step 2: two
set-based `UPDATE`s beat a per-row correlated `CASE` by roughly a
thousand-fold, and the gate's runtime will tell you which you wrote. "Set
based, not row based" is the single most valuable instinct to bring from
application programming into SQL.

## ex2 — the NOT VALID two-step

The gate checks `pg_constraint.convalidated`, because a constraint that
exists but was never validated is the classic half-finished migration: it
looks correct in every schema dump and guarantees nothing about the rows
that were already there.

Worth being precise about what each half buys you. After step 1, every new
or updated row is checked — so the problem stops growing immediately, which
is often the urgent part. Step 2 is what lets you *reason* about the table:
until it runs, a query cannot assume the constraint holds, and neither can
you. Splitting an outage-shaped operation into an urgent instant half and a
patient concurrent half is the whole pattern of this lesson.

## ex3 — the column that costs nothing to add

One statement, and the thing to remember is the boundary: constant defaults
are instant, volatile ones rewrite the table. `DEFAULT false` and `DEFAULT
0` are safe on any table size; `DEFAULT now()` and `DEFAULT
gen_random_uuid()` are not, and PostgreSQL will not warn you before it
starts rewriting a hundred gigabytes.

## ex4 — DROP COLUMN does not free the space

The size assertion is the lesson. `DROP COLUMN` is a catalog change; the
data stays in every existing row until that row is rewritten. Two practical
consequences: dropping a column will not resolve a disk-space alert, and the
dropped column still counts against PostgreSQL's 1,600-column-per-table
limit until the table is rewritten. `VACUUM FULL` reclaims the space and
takes an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock for the duration; `pg_repack` does the same
job without the outage. Lesson 44 covers the vacuum side properly.

## Further reading

- [`ALTER TABLE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-altertable.html) — the reference page, including the "Notes" section that lists exactly which forms require a rewrite.
- [Explicit Locking — lock modes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/explicit-locking.html) — the conflict matrix. `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` against everything is the row that matters.
- [`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createindex.html) — the two-pass build, its restrictions, and what an `INVALID` index means.
- [Routine Vacuuming](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/routine-vacuuming.html) — why dropped columns and updated rows keep their space, and what reclaims it. Lesson 44.

# 28 — Altering live schemas

Every schema you'll ever meet is already in production, already has
data, and already has traffic. `ALTER TABLE` is easy; doing it **without
an outage** is the skill. The hidden danger is locking: many ALTERs take
an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock — every query on the table queues behind you,
and if your ALTER also has to *scan or rewrite* half a gigabyte while
holding that lock, the application is down and pretending otherwise.

The safe patterns all share one idea: **split the instant-but-locking
step from the slow-but-concurrent step.**

## Concept

Cheap and instant (brief lock, no scan — fine to run any time):

```sql
ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN loyalty_tier text;       -- nullable, no default scan*
ALTER TABLE customers RENAME COLUMN x TO y;
ALTER TABLE customers DROP COLUMN old_thing;              -- logical delete only
```

(*since PostgreSQL 11, even ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT is instant for
constant defaults — the default is stored once, not written per-row.)

**The NOT NULL three-step** — you can't just declare NOT NULL on a
populated nullable column without a full validating scan under lock.
Instead:

```sql
ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN c text;         -- 1. add nullable    (instant)
UPDATE t SET c = ... ;                   -- 2. backfill        (set-based, no DDL lock)
ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c SET NOT NULL;  -- 3. flip         (one scan, short)
```

**The NOT VALID two-step** — same trick for constraints:

```sql
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_total_min
  CHECK (total >= 5) NOT VALID;          -- 1. enforce for NEW rows (instant)
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_total_min;
                                         -- 2. scan old rows with a weak lock
```

`NOT VALID` means "trust the past, police the future"; `VALIDATE` then
audits the past without blocking writers. (In true production you'd add
lock timeouts and batch the backfill — Part 5's lesson 44 touches why;
the *shape* is what you're drilling here.)

## Exercise 1 — the NOT NULL three-step

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Give `customers` a `loyalty_tier` text column,
NOT NULL by the end, backfilled as: `'vip'` for customers with **more
than 20 orders** (there are exactly 250), `'member'` for everyone else.
Do it as the three-step. For the backfill, two set-based UPDATEs (set
everyone `'member'`, then upgrade the vips with an IN-subquery) beat a
per-row correlated CASE by roughly a thousand-fold — the gate will feel
the difference in runtime if you pick wrong.

Run: `uv run dojo test 28_altering_live_schemas ex1`

## Exercise 2 — the NOT VALID two-step

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Business rule: no order under 5.00. Add CHECK
constraint **named `orders_total_min`** (`total >= 5`) to `orders` using
NOT VALID, then VALIDATE it. The gate verifies the constraint exists,
**is validated** (it checks `pg_constraint.convalidated` — leaving it
NOT VALID forever is the classic half-finished migration), and rejects a
1.00 order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 28_altering_live_schemas ex2`

## Exercise 3 — the column that costs nothing to add

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Merchandising wants to hide discontinued
products without deleting them. Add a column to `products`:

```sql
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN is_archived boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false;
```

One statement — and the point of the exercise is *why one statement is
enough*. Before PostgreSQL 11, adding a `NOT NULL` column with a default
rewrote the entire table under an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock: every query
queued behind it, and on a large table that meant an outage. Since 11, a
**constant** default is stored once in the catalog and materialised lazily
as rows are read or updated, so the operation is instant regardless of
table size.

The word doing the work is *constant*. `DEFAULT false` is instant;
`DEFAULT random()` or `DEFAULT now()` is not, because each row would need a
different value — and PostgreSQL falls back to the full rewrite without
telling you. Knowing which side of that line your `ALTER` falls on is the
difference between a deploy and an incident.

The gate checks the column exists, is `NOT NULL`, that all 10,000 existing
rows read as `false`, and that a fresh insert defaults correctly.

Run: `uv run dojo test 28_altering_live_schemas ex3`

## Exercise 4 — DROP COLUMN does not free the space

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The `reviews.body` text is being moved to a
separate document store. Drop it:

```sql
ALTER TABLE reviews DROP COLUMN body;
```

One statement, instant, and it does **not** reclaim a single byte.
`DROP COLUMN` is a *logical* delete: PostgreSQL marks the attribute
dropped in the catalog and stops returning it, but the data stays inside
every existing row on disk. The space comes back only when each row is
next rewritten — by `VACUUM FULL`, by a `CLUSTER`, or gradually as rows
are updated.

The gate proves it: it measures `pg_relation_size('reviews')` before and
after your statement and asserts the two are **equal**.

That is not a flaw, it is the trade. An instant, non-blocking `ALTER` on a
million-row table is worth far more than the disk, and reclaiming space
requires an exclusive lock you would rather schedule than take by
surprise. The mistake to avoid is the one made in the other direction:
dropping a column to fix a disk-space alert, and being surprised when the
graph does not move.

Run: `uv run dojo test 28_altering_live_schemas ex4`

## The gate

```python
"""Gates for 28_altering_live_schemas. Quoted verbatim in README.md."""
from dojo import catalog, grader
from dojo.lesson import Lesson

L = Lesson(__file__)


def test_ex1(lesson_db):
    # measured, not hard-coded, so the gate holds at any DOJO_SCALE
    vips = lesson_db.execute(
        "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT customer_id FROM orders "
        "GROUP BY customer_id HAVING count(*) > 20) t").fetchone()[0]
    everyone = lesson_db.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM customers").fetchone()[0]

    ex = L.exercise("ex1")
    lesson_db.execute(ex.solution_sql)
    catalog.assert_table(lesson_db, "customers", {"loyalty_tier": "text"})
    catalog.assert_not_null(lesson_db, "customers", "loyalty_tier")
    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db,
        "SELECT count(*) FROM customers WHERE loyalty_tier = 'vip'",
        vips, "exactly the >20-order customers are vip")
    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db,
        "SELECT count(*) FROM customers WHERE loyalty_tier = 'member'",
        everyone - vips, "everyone else is member")


def test_ex2(lesson_db):
    ex = L.exercise("ex2")
    lesson_db.execute(ex.solution_sql)
    catalog.assert_check(lesson_db, "orders", "total")
    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db,
        "SELECT convalidated FROM pg_constraint "
        "WHERE conname = 'orders_total_min'",
        True, "the constraint was VALIDATEd, not left NOT VALID forever")
    catalog.rejects(
        lesson_db,
        "INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, status, total, created_at) "
        "VALUES (900001, 1, 'pending', 1.00, '2023-11-15')",
        why="new orders under the 5.00 minimum must be refused")


def test_ex3(lesson_db):
    rows = lesson_db.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM products").fetchone()[0]
    ex = L.exercise("ex3")
    lesson_db.execute(ex.solution_sql)
    catalog.assert_table(lesson_db, "products", {"is_archived": "boolean"})
    catalog.assert_not_null(lesson_db, "products", "is_archived")
    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db, "SELECT count(*) FROM products WHERE is_archived = false",
        rows, "every existing row reads as false without a rewrite")
    lesson_db.execute("SAVEPOINT default_probe")
    lesson_db.execute(
        "INSERT INTO products (id, name, category, price, description, attributes) "
        "VALUES (99001, 'Probe', 'books', 1.00, 'x', '{}'::jsonb)")
    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db, "SELECT is_archived FROM products WHERE id = 99001",
        False, "new rows get the default too")
    lesson_db.execute("ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT default_probe")


def test_ex4(lesson_db):
    size_before = lesson_db.execute(
        "SELECT pg_relation_size('reviews')").fetchone()[0]
    rows_before = lesson_db.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM reviews").fetchone()[0]
    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db,
        "SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.columns "
        "WHERE table_name = 'reviews' AND column_name = 'body'",
        1, "the body column is there to begin with")

    ex = L.exercise("ex4")
    lesson_db.execute(ex.solution_sql)
    lesson_db.commit()

    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db,
        "SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.columns "
        "WHERE table_name = 'reviews' AND column_name = 'body'",
        0, "the column is gone from the catalog")
    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db, "SELECT count(*) FROM reviews", rows_before,
        "and every row is still there - this was a catalog change, not a rewrite")
    grader.assert_scalar(
        lesson_db, "SELECT pg_relation_size('reviews')", size_before,
        "the table is exactly the same size on disk: DROP COLUMN is logical, "
        "and the bytes come back only when each row is next rewritten")
```

## The teaching point

Migration reviews in serious shops ask one question about every ALTER:
**what lock, for how long, scanning what?** The three-step and two-step
exist because the answers to "add NOT NULL column" and "add constraint"
are otherwise "exclusive, minutes, everything" — an outage disguised as
one line of DDL. You now know the disguise; Part 5 gives you the tools
to see the scan itself.

# Reading - 28_altering_live_schemas

Every schema you will ever change is already in production, already has
data, and already has traffic. `ALTER TABLE` is easy syntax; doing it
without an outage is the skill, and the whole skill reduces to one
question: *what does this statement lock, and for how long?*

## Notes

**The danger is lock duration, not lock strength.** Most `ALTER TABLE`
forms take an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock, which blocks every reader and
writer. That is fine when the statement is instant — a catalog update takes
microseconds. It is an outage when the statement also has to *scan or
rewrite* the table while holding the lock. So the safe patterns all share
one shape: **split the instant-but-locking step from the slow-but-concurrent
step.**

**Instant (catalog-only) operations:**

- `ADD COLUMN` (nullable, or with a **constant** default since PostgreSQL 11)
- `DROP COLUMN` — logical only; the bytes stay until each row is rewritten
- `RENAME COLUMN` / `RENAME TABLE`
- `ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID`
- `SET DEFAULT` / `DROP DEFAULT`

**Operations that scan or rewrite:**

- `SET NOT NULL` — scans the whole table to verify (though PostgreSQL 12+
  can skip the scan if an equivalent validated `CHECK` already proves it)
- `ADD CONSTRAINT` without `NOT VALID` — scans to verify
- `ALTER COLUMN TYPE` — usually a full rewrite plus index rebuilds
- `ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT <volatile expression>` — full rewrite

**The NOT NULL three-step.**

```sql
ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN c text;            -- 1. instant
UPDATE t SET c = ...;                       -- 2. no DDL lock, batchable
ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c SET NOT NULL;  -- 3. one scan, short lock
```

**The NOT VALID two-step.**

```sql
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT orders_total_min
  CHECK (total >= 5) NOT VALID;             -- 1. polices new rows, instant
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_total_min;
                                            -- 2. audits old rows, weak lock
```

`NOT VALID` means "trust the past, police the future". `VALIDATE` then
checks the past under a lock that permits reads *and* writes. The classic
half-finished migration is step 1 without step 2 — the constraint exists,
the catalog looks right, and nobody ever confirmed the historical data. This
is exactly why lesson 25's gates test *behaviour* and not just the catalog.

**Two things production migrations add that these exercises do not.** First,
a `lock_timeout`: if your `ALTER` cannot get its lock in two seconds, it
should fail rather than queue — because while it queues, *every* subsequent
query on that table queues behind it, and a five-minute wait becomes a
five-minute outage even though your statement never ran. Second, batching:
a backfill `UPDATE` over ten million rows is one enormous transaction that
bloats the table and holds a snapshot open (lesson 44); real backfills loop
in chunks of a few thousand with a commit between them.

**`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`.** Building an index normally blocks writes
for the duration. `CONCURRENTLY` does two passes and blocks almost nothing —
at the cost of being slower, unable to run inside a transaction block, and
capable of leaving an `INVALID` index behind if it fails, which you must
drop and retry. On any table that matters, this is the only way to add an
index. Part 5 builds every index without it because the dojo's clones have
no concurrent traffic.

**Expand and contract.** The general pattern for a change that cannot be
atomic — renaming a column that applications read, splitting a table,
changing a type. *Expand*: add the new thing alongside the old, write to
both. *Migrate*: backfill, then switch readers over. *Contract*: stop
writing the old thing, then drop it. Each step is independently safe and
independently reversible, which is what makes the deploy boring. Lesson
26's ex4 was this pattern in miniature.

**DDL is transactional in PostgreSQL** (lesson 23), so a migration script
that fails halfway leaves nothing behind. This is a genuine superpower and
it changes how migrations are written — but note the exceptions: `CREATE
INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and `VACUUM` cannot run inside a transaction block.

## ex1 — the NOT NULL three-step

The three steps, plus a performance lesson hiding inside step 2: two
set-based `UPDATE`s beat a per-row correlated `CASE` by roughly a
thousand-fold, and the gate's runtime will tell you which you wrote. "Set
based, not row based" is the single most valuable instinct to bring from
application programming into SQL.

## ex2 — the NOT VALID two-step

The gate checks `pg_constraint.convalidated`, because a constraint that
exists but was never validated is the classic half-finished migration: it
looks correct in every schema dump and guarantees nothing about the rows
that were already there.

Worth being precise about what each half buys you. After step 1, every new
or updated row is checked — so the problem stops growing immediately, which
is often the urgent part. Step 2 is what lets you *reason* about the table:
until it runs, a query cannot assume the constraint holds, and neither can
you. Splitting an outage-shaped operation into an urgent instant half and a
patient concurrent half is the whole pattern of this lesson.

## ex3 — the column that costs nothing to add

One statement, and the thing to remember is the boundary: constant defaults
are instant, volatile ones rewrite the table. `DEFAULT false` and `DEFAULT
0` are safe on any table size; `DEFAULT now()` and `DEFAULT
gen_random_uuid()` are not, and PostgreSQL will not warn you before it
starts rewriting a hundred gigabytes.

## ex4 — DROP COLUMN does not free the space

The size assertion is the lesson. `DROP COLUMN` is a catalog change; the
data stays in every existing row until that row is rewritten. Two practical
consequences: dropping a column will not resolve a disk-space alert, and the
dropped column still counts against PostgreSQL's 1,600-column-per-table
limit until the table is rewritten. `VACUUM FULL` reclaims the space and
takes an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock for the duration; `pg_repack` does the same
job without the outage. Lesson 44 covers the vacuum side properly.

## Further reading

- [`ALTER TABLE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-altertable.html) — the reference page, including the "Notes" section that lists exactly which forms require a rewrite.
- [Explicit Locking — lock modes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/explicit-locking.html) — the conflict matrix. `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` against everything is the row that matters.
- [`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createindex.html) — the two-pass build, its restrictions, and what an `INVALID` index means.
- [Routine Vacuuming](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/routine-vacuuming.html) — why dropped columns and updated rows keep their space, and what reclaims it. Lesson 44.

## Exercise 1 — the NOT NULL three-step

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Give `customers` a `loyalty_tier` text column,
NOT NULL by the end, backfilled as: `'vip'` for customers with **more
than 20 orders** (there are exactly 250), `'member'` for everyone else.
Do it as the three-step. For the backfill, two set-based UPDATEs (set
everyone `'member'`, then upgrade the vips with an IN-subquery) beat a
per-row correlated CASE by roughly a thousand-fold — the gate will feel
the difference in runtime if you pick wrong.

## Exercise 2 — the NOT VALID two-step

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Business rule: no order under 5.00. Add CHECK
constraint **named `orders_total_min`** (`total >= 5`) to `orders` using
NOT VALID, then VALIDATE it. The gate verifies the constraint exists,
**is validated** (it checks `pg_constraint.convalidated` — leaving it
NOT VALID forever is the classic half-finished migration), and rejects a
1.00 order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 28_altering_live_schemas ex2`

```sql
ALTER TABLE orders
```

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — the column that costs nothing to add

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Merchandising wants to hide discontinued
products without deleting them. Add a column to `products`:

```sql
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN is_archived boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false;
```

One statement — and the point of the exercise is *why one statement is
enough*. Before PostgreSQL 11, adding a `NOT NULL` column with a default
rewrote the entire table under an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock: every query
queued behind it, and on a large table that meant an outage. Since 11, a
**constant** default is stored once in the catalog and materialised lazily
as rows are read or updated, so the operation is instant regardless of
table size.

The word doing the work is *constant*. `DEFAULT false` is instant;
`DEFAULT random()` or `DEFAULT now()` is not, because each row would need a
different value — and PostgreSQL falls back to the full rewrite without
telling you. Knowing which side of that line your `ALTER` falls on is the
difference between a deploy and an incident.

The gate checks the column exists, is `NOT NULL`, that all 10,000 existing
rows read as `false`, and that a fresh insert defaults correctly.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — DROP COLUMN does not free the space

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The `reviews.body` text is being moved to a
separate document store. Drop it:

```sql
ALTER TABLE reviews DROP COLUMN body;
```

One statement, instant, and it does **not** reclaim a single byte.
`DROP COLUMN` is a *logical* delete: PostgreSQL marks the attribute
dropped in the catalog and stops returning it, but the data stays inside
every existing row on disk. The space comes back only when each row is
next rewritten — by `VACUUM FULL`, by a `CLUSTER`, or gradually as rows
are updated.

The gate proves it: it measures `pg_relation_size('reviews')` before and
after your statement and asserts the two are **equal**.

That is not a flaw, it is the trade. An instant, non-blocking `ALTER` on a
million-row table is worth far more than the disk, and reclaiming space
requires an exclusive lock you would rather schedule than take by
surprise. The mistake to avoid is the one made in the other direction:
dropping a column to fix a disk-space alert, and being surprised when the
graph does not move.

lessons.briefing:
# 29 — Design capstone: gift cards

The spec below is written the way specs actually arrive: in prose, with
the constraints implied rather than listed. Your job is to translate it
into tables, keys, constraints, and one view — everything Part 4 taught,
composed. The gate checks **properties**, not your exact DDL: several
correct designs pass, and yours only has to honor the named entry points.

> *"We're launching gift cards. Each card has a unique printed code and
> an initial balance — obviously never negative. Customers redeem a card
> against an order; a card can be used across multiple orders (partial
> redemption), and each redemption must say how much was used — a
> positive amount, naturally, tied to a real order in our system. Ops
> wants to look up any card and see how much is left on it."*

Required entry points (the gate queries these names):

- Table `gift_cards`: `id` (int, PK), `code` (text, NOT NULL, unique),
  `initial_balance` (numeric, CHECKed non-negative). Add whatever else
  seems right (an expiry date? issued_on? your call — ungraded).
- Table `gift_card_redemptions`: `id` (int, PK), `gift_card_id` (FK →
  `gift_cards`), `order_id` (FK → `orders`), `amount` (numeric, CHECKed
  positive).
- View `gift_card_balances`: `gift_card_id`, `remaining` = initial
  balance minus all redemptions — **including cards never redeemed**,
  which must show their full balance (there is a lesson-09/27 trap here;
  the gate springs it).

## Exercise 1 — the schema

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. The two tables, with every property the prose
implies. Before running the gate, attack your own schema in the lab the
way the gate will: negative card, orphan redemption, duplicate code,
zero-amount redemption.

Run: `uv run dojo test 29_design_capstone ex1`

## Exercise 2 — the balance view

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. The `gift_card_balances` view. The gate inserts
a card with two redemptions (expects the arithmetic) and a card with
none (expects the full balance — not NULL, not a missing row).

Run: `uv run dojo test 29_design_capstone ex2`

## Exercise 3 — the usage report

> *"While you're in there — Ops also wants to see how often each card gets
> used, not just what's left on it. Cards nobody has touched should show
> up as zero, obviously."*

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Create view **`gift_card_usage`** with three
columns:

- `gift_card_id`
- `redemptions` — how many redemption rows the card has (**0**, not NULL,
  for a card nobody has redeemed)
- `used` — the total amount redeemed (**0**, not NULL, for the same cards)

Your ex1 schema is created first automatically.

"Obviously" is the requester doing what requesters do. The trap is the same
one ex2 sprang, arriving twice in one view: a `LEFT JOIN` is needed so
untouched cards survive, `count(r.id)` rather than `count(*)` so they count
zero, and `coalesce(sum(...), 0)` because `sum` over no rows is NULL rather
than zero. Three lessons — 06, 09 and 27 — converging on one view.

Run: `uv run dojo test 29_design_capstone ex3`

## Exercise 4 — the batch they were printed in

> *"Last thing. The cards get printed in batches and we need to know which
> batch a card came from — sometimes a whole batch gets recalled. If we
> delete a batch record the cards themselves must survive; they're
> physically out there in people's wallets."*

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Two statements:

1. create `gift_card_batches` — `id` int primary key, `printed_on` date
   NOT NULL;
2. `ALTER TABLE gift_cards` to add a `batch_id` column referencing it,
   **`ON DELETE SET NULL`**.

Your ex1 schema is created first automatically.

The last sentence of the request is the spec for the delete policy, and it
rules out the other two options: `CASCADE` would destroy real gift cards
because a filing record was tidied away, and `RESTRICT` would make it
impossible to remove a batch record at all. `SET NULL` says "the card
outlives its paperwork", which is exactly what the requester described
without knowing there was a decision to make.

Note that `batch_id` must be **nullable** — both because `SET NULL`
requires it and because every card that already exists has no batch. That
is lesson 28's shape: add nullable, and never lock the table.

Run: `uv run dojo test 29_design_capstone ex4`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 29_design_capstone

Part 4 in one exercise: prose in, schema out. The spec never says "foreign
key", "CHECK" or "nullable" — it says "tied to a real order in our system",
"a positive amount, naturally", and "they're physically out there in
people's wallets". Translating those into constraints *is* schema design.

## Notes

**Read a spec for the words that imply a constraint.** "Unique printed
code" is `UNIQUE`. "Obviously never negative" is a `CHECK`. "Tied to a real
order in our system" is a foreign key. "A card can be used across multiple
orders" is a one-to-many relationship and therefore a separate table rather
than a column. Every one of those phrases was delivered as an aside, and
every one of them is load-bearing.

**The property the gate tests is the property that matters.** This lesson's
gates check *behaviour*, not DDL: several correct designs pass. That is how
schema review should work too — the question is never "did you write it the
way I would have" but "is this state representable, and should it be?".

**Attack your own schema before someone else does.** The checklist for any
new table: what is the identity of a row (primary key)? what must already
exist (foreign keys)? what values are impossible (CHECK)? what may be
absent, and does absence mean something (NOT NULL, and if nullable, why)?
what happens to children when a parent is deleted (ON DELETE)? Run the bad
inserts yourself in the lab — negative balance, orphan redemption, duplicate
code, zero-amount redemption — before the gate does.

**Derived values belong in a view, not a column.** The remaining balance is
`initial_balance` minus the sum of redemptions. Storing it as a column
creates a second source of truth that can drift; computing it in a view
cannot. The counter-argument is performance, and the answer to that is a
materialized view (lesson 46) or a generated column when the expression is
row-local (lesson 24) — both of which keep the derivation in one place.

**The NULL traps in a balance view are not incidental.** A card with no
redemptions must show its full balance, not NULL and not a missing row. That
requires a `LEFT JOIN` (lesson 09), `count(r.id)` rather than `count(*)`
(lesson 06), and `coalesce(sum(...), 0)` (lesson 04). Three lessons
converge, and getting any one of them wrong produces a view that is correct
for every card anyone tests and wrong for the ones nobody has used.

**Cross-row and cross-table rules need more than a CHECK.** "A card cannot
be redeemed for more than its balance" cannot be a `CHECK`, because a CHECK
sees only its own row. The options are a trigger, an `EXCLUDE` constraint
(for overlap-style rules), or accepting that the rule is enforced by the
application inside a transaction with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`. Knowing which
rules the database *can* enforce, and being explicit about the ones it
cannot, is a large part of designing a system that stays correct.

**Delete policies are domain decisions.** `CASCADE`, `RESTRICT` and `SET
NULL` are three different answers to "what does this deletion mean?", and
the right one comes from the product owner, not the engineer. The schema
just records the answer — but if nobody chooses, the default (`NO ACTION`)
gets chosen for you, and it is right more often than not.

## ex1 — the schema

Two tables, four implied constraints, and one deliberate open question:
`gift_card_redemptions` has no delete policy in the spec, so any is
defensible. Write down which you picked and why — the comment is worth more
than the choice.

Attack it yourself before the gate does. A negative `initial_balance`, a
redemption against card 99999, a second card with an existing code, a
redemption of 0.00: four `INSERT`s in the lab, and if any of them succeeds
you have found a rule the prose implied and your DDL did not. That is the
same exercise a reviewer performs on your migration, done by you first.

## ex2 — the balance view

The trap sprung deliberately. A card with no redemptions is the case that
never appears in a demo and always appears in production — on launch day
every card is unredeemed, so an `INNER JOIN` here produces an empty report
on precisely the day everyone is watching.

The general shape is worth naming: whenever a view reports "X, and its
related Y", ask what the row looks like when there is no Y. If the answer is
"it disappears", you have written an inner join into a question that was
about X.

## ex3 — the usage report

The same trap twice in one view — the count and the sum fail differently,
one giving 1 instead of 0 and the other giving NULL instead of 0. Both look
plausible in a spreadsheet, which is why the gate asserts them separately.

## ex4 — the batch they were printed in

A delete-policy decision handed to you in plain English, plus lesson 28's
add-a-nullable-column shape. Notice that the requirement "the cards must
survive" eliminated two of the three options without anyone naming a
foreign-key policy — which is what it looks like when a spec is complete
without being technical.

**Part 4 complete.** Next: **Part 5** stops asking whether your query is
correct and starts asking what it costs.

## Further reading

- [Constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-constraints.html) — one more pass, now with a design brief in hand.
- [`CREATE VIEW`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createview.html) — the derived-value half of this lesson.
- [Triggers](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/triggers.html) — where rules go when a CHECK cannot express them. Read the section on constraint triggers.
- [Using EXPLAIN](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/using-explain.html) — start here before lesson 30. Everything you have designed is about to be measured.

## The gate

```python
"""Gates for 29_design_capstone. Quoted verbatim in README.md.

Property-based gates: several correct designs pass. The required entry
points (table/column names below) are the contract; everything else -
extra columns, extra constraints, delete policies beyond the required
ones - is your call.

from dojo import catalog, grader
from dojo.lesson import Lesson

L = Lesson(__file__)


def test_ex1(lesson_db):
    ex = L.exercise("ex1")
    lesson_db.execute(ex.solution_sql)
    catalog.assert_table(lesson_db, "gift_cards", {
        "id": "int", "code": "text", "initial_balance": "numeric"})
    catalog.assert_pk(lesson_db, "gift_cards", ["id"])
    catalog.assert_unique(lesson_db, "gift_cards", ["code"])
    catalog.assert_not_null(lesson_db, "gift_cards", "code")
    catalog.assert_check(lesson_db, "gift_cards", "initial_balance")
    catalog.assert_table(lesson_db, "gift_card_redemptions", {
        "id": "int", "gift_card_id": "int", "order_id": "int",
        "amount": "numeric"})
    catalog.assert_pk(lesson_db, "gift_card_redemptions", ["id"])
    catalog.assert_fk(lesson_db, "gift_card_redemptions", ["gift_card_id"],
                      "gift_cards")
    catalog.assert_fk(lesson_db, "gift_card_redemptions", ["order_id"],
                      "orders")
    catalog.assert_check(lesson_db, "gift_card_redemptions", "amount")

    catalog.rejects(
        lesson_db,
        "INSERT INTO gift_cards (id, code, initial_balance) "
        "VALUES (1, 'GC-NEG', -100)",
        why="cards can't be born owing money")
    catalog.rejects(
        lesson_db,
        "INSERT INTO gift_card_redemptions (id, gift_card_id, order_id, amount) "
        "VALUES (1, 12345, 1, 10)",
        why="redemption against a card that doesn't exist")
    catalog.accepts(
        lesson_db,
        "INSERT INTO gift_cards (id, code, initial_balance) "
        "VALUES (1, 'GC-OK', 100)")
    lesson_db.execute("SAVEPOINT code_probe")
    lesson_db.execute(
        "INSERT INTO gift_cards (id, code, initial_balance) VALUES (2, 'GC-X', 50)")
```

Notice what the gate does *not* check: whether a card's redemptions can
exceed its balance. That invariant spans **multiple rows**, and CHECK
constraints see only one row at a time — enforcing it takes a trigger, a
serialized transaction pattern, or application logic with row locks
(`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`). Knowing which invariants the schema *can't*
hold — and saying so out loud in design review, and writing down where
the enforcement actually lives — is precisely the judgment this Part
was building toward.

# Reading - 29_design_capstone

Part 4 in one exercise: prose in, schema out. The spec never says "foreign
key", "CHECK" or "nullable" — it says "tied to a real order in our system",
"a positive amount, naturally", and "they're physically out there in
people's wallets". Translating those into constraints *is* schema design.

## Notes

**Read a spec for the words that imply a constraint.** "Unique printed
code" is `UNIQUE`. "Obviously never negative" is a `CHECK`. "Tied to a real
order in our system" is a foreign key. "A card can be used across multiple
orders" is a one-to-many relationship and therefore a separate table rather
than a column. Every one of those phrases was delivered as an aside, and
every one of them is load-bearing.

**The property the gate tests is the property that matters.** This lesson's
gates check *behaviour*, not DDL: several correct designs pass. That is how
schema review should work too — the question is never "did you write it the
way I would have" but "is this state representable, and should it be?".

**Attack your own schema before someone else does.** The checklist for any
new table: what is the identity of a row (primary key)? what must already
exist (foreign keys)? what values are impossible (CHECK)? what may be
absent, and does absence mean something (NOT NULL, and if nullable, why)?
what happens to children when a parent is deleted (ON DELETE)? Run the bad
inserts yourself in the lab — negative balance, orphan redemption, duplicate
code, zero-amount redemption — before the gate does.

**Derived values belong in a view, not a column.** The remaining balance is
`initial_balance` minus the sum of redemptions. Storing it as a column
creates a second source of truth that can drift; computing it in a view
cannot. The counter-argument is performance, and the answer to that is a
materialized view (lesson 46) or a generated column when the expression is
row-local (lesson 24) — both of which keep the derivation in one place.

**The NULL traps in a balance view are not incidental.** A card with no
redemptions must show its full balance, not NULL and not a missing row. That
requires a `LEFT JOIN` (lesson 09), `count(r.id)` rather than `count(*)`
(lesson 06), and `coalesce(sum(...), 0)` (lesson 04). Three lessons
converge, and getting any one of them wrong produces a view that is correct
for every card anyone tests and wrong for the ones nobody has used.

**Cross-row and cross-table rules need more than a CHECK.** "A card cannot
be redeemed for more than its balance" cannot be a `CHECK`, because a CHECK
sees only its own row. The options are a trigger, an `EXCLUDE` constraint
(for overlap-style rules), or accepting that the rule is enforced by the
application inside a transaction with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`. Knowing which
rules the database *can* enforce, and being explicit about the ones it
cannot, is a large part of designing a system that stays correct.

**Delete policies are domain decisions.** `CASCADE`, `RESTRICT` and `SET
NULL` are three different answers to "what does this deletion mean?", and
the right one comes from the product owner, not the engineer. The schema
just records the answer — but if nobody chooses, the default (`NO ACTION`)
gets chosen for you, and it is right more often than not.

## ex1 — the schema

Two tables, four implied constraints, and one deliberate open question:
`gift_card_redemptions` has no delete policy in the spec, so any is
defensible. Write down which you picked and why — the comment is worth more
than the choice.

Attack it yourself before the gate does. A negative `initial_balance`, a
redemption against card 99999, a second card with an existing code, a
redemption of 0.00: four `INSERT`s in the lab, and if any of them succeeds
you have found a rule the prose implied and your DDL did not. That is the
same exercise a reviewer performs on your migration, done by you first.

## ex2 — the balance view

The trap sprung deliberately. A card with no redemptions is the case that
never appears in a demo and always appears in production — on launch day
every card is unredeemed, so an `INNER JOIN` here produces an empty report
on precisely the day everyone is watching.

The general shape is worth naming: whenever a view reports "X, and its
related Y", ask what the row looks like when there is no Y. If the answer is
"it disappears", you have written an inner join into a question that was
about X.

## ex3 — the usage report

The same trap twice in one view — the count and the sum fail differently,
one giving 1 instead of 0 and the other giving NULL instead of 0. Both look
plausible in a spreadsheet, which is why the gate asserts them separately.

## ex4 — the batch they were printed in

A delete-policy decision handed to you in plain English, plus lesson 28's
add-a-nullable-column shape. Notice that the requirement "the cards must
survive" eliminated two of the three options without anyone naming a
foreign-key policy — which is what it looks like when a spec is complete
without being technical.

**Part 4 complete.** Next: **Part 5** stops asking whether your query is
correct and starts asking what it costs.

## Further reading

- [Constraints](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-constraints.html) — one more pass, now with a design brief in hand.
- [`CREATE VIEW`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createview.html) — the derived-value half of this lesson.
- [Triggers](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/triggers.html) — where rules go when a CHECK cannot express them. Read the section on constraint triggers.
- [Using EXPLAIN](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/using-explain.html) — start here before lesson 30. Everything you have designed is about to be measured.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — the schema

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. The two tables, with every property the prose
implies. Before running the gate, attack your own schema in the lab the
way the gate will: negative card, orphan redemption, duplicate code,
zero-amount redemption.

Run: `uv run dojo test 29_design_capstone ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
This is lesson 25's giftcards exercise scaled up: two CREATE TABLEs,
parents first. Walk the prose and convert each phrase: "unique printed
code" -> NOT NULL UNIQUE; "never negative" -> CHECK; "tied to a real
order" -> FK to orders; "positive amount" -> CHECK (amount > 0).

## Hint 2
```sql
CREATE TABLE gift_cards (
  id              int           PRIMARY KEY,
  code            text          NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  initial_balance numeric(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (initial_balance >= 0),
  issued_on       date          NOT NULL DEFAULT '2023-11-14'
);

CREATE TABLE gift_card_redemptions (
  id           int           PRIMARY KEY,
  gift_card_id int           NOT NULL REFERENCES gift_cards(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  order_id     int           NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
  amount       numeric(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (amount > 0)
);
```

(The CASCADE and issued_on are choices, not requirements - defend yours.)

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — the usage report

> *"While you're in there — Ops also wants to see how often each card gets
> used, not just what's left on it. Cards nobody has touched should show
> up as zero, obviously."*

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Create view **`gift_card_usage`** with three
columns:

- `gift_card_id`
- `redemptions` — how many redemption rows the card has (**0**, not NULL,
  for a card nobody has redeemed)
- `used` — the total amount redeemed (**0**, not NULL, for the same cards)

Your ex1 schema is created first automatically.

"Obviously" is the requester doing what requesters do. The trap is the same
one ex2 sprang, arriving twice in one view: a `LEFT JOIN` is needed so
untouched cards survive, `count(r.id)` rather than `count(*)` so they count
zero, and `coalesce(sum(...), 0)` because `sum` over no rows is NULL rather
than zero. Three lessons — 06, 09 and 27 — converging on one view.

Run: `uv run dojo test 29_design_capstone ex3`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
`LEFT JOIN` from `gift_cards`, `GROUP BY g.id`. Then the two traps:
`count(r.id)` not `count(*)`, and `coalesce(sum(r.amount), 0)`.

## Hint 2
```sql
CREATE VIEW gift_card_usage AS
SELECT g.id AS gift_card_id,
       count(r.id) AS redemptions,
       coalesce(sum(r.amount), 0) AS used
FROM gift_cards g
LEFT JOIN gift_card_redemptions r ON r.gift_card_id = g.id
GROUP BY g.id;
```

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — the batch they were printed in

> *"Last thing. The cards get printed in batches and we need to know which
> batch a card came from — sometimes a whole batch gets recalled. If we
> delete a batch record the cards themselves must survive; they're
> physically out there in people's wallets."*

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Two statements:

1. create `gift_card_batches` — `id` int primary key, `printed_on` date
   NOT NULL;
2. `ALTER TABLE gift_cards` to add a `batch_id` column referencing it,
   **`ON DELETE SET NULL`**.

Your ex1 schema is created first automatically.

The last sentence of the request is the spec for the delete policy, and it
rules out the other two options: `CASCADE` would destroy real gift cards
because a filing record was tidied away, and `RESTRICT` would make it
impossible to remove a batch record at all. `SET NULL` says "the card
outlives its paperwork", which is exactly what the requester described
without knowing there was a decision to make.

Note that `batch_id` must be **nullable** — both because `SET NULL`
requires it and because every card that already exists has no batch. That
is lesson 28's shape: add nullable, and never lock the table.

lessons.briefing:
# 30 — Reading EXPLAIN

Welcome to Part 5. Everything you've written so far was graded on *what*
it returned; from here on, the dojo also grades **how** the database got
it, and how fast. The instrument for all of it is `EXPLAIN` — and the
skill that separates "I added an index and prayed" from actual
performance work is *reading plans fluently*.

Two new commands become your daily drivers:

- `dojo plan <lesson> [ex]` — EXPLAIN your current `solution.sql`
  (applying your `indexes.sql` first), rendered as a tree. No gate.
- `dojo lab <lesson>` — your sandbox, now the place you run
  `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` by hand.

## Concept

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE total > 1999;             -- estimates only
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE total > 1999;     -- actually runs it
```

`EXPLAIN` shows the plan the optimizer chose with **estimated** costs and
row counts. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` executes the query and adds **actual** rows
and time per node. The estimated-vs-actual gap is diagnostic gold (lesson
36 is entirely about it).

A plan is a tree, executed leaves-first:

```
Sort  (rows=250, 91.2ms)
  Seq Scan on orders  (rows=250, 88.1ms)   <-- most expensive
        Filter: (total > 1999)
        Rows Removed by Filter: 499750
```

How to read any plan, in order of importance:

1. **Node types.** `Seq Scan` = read every row of the table. `Index
   Scan` = walk an index to the matching rows. There are ~a dozen more;
   Part 5 introduces them one per lesson.
2. **Actual rows per node** — the data volume flowing up the tree. A
   node that reads 500,000 rows to feed a node that outputs 11 is the
   waste you'll learn to eliminate.
3. **loops** — a node's figures are *per loop*; a nested inner side
   executing 500,000 times multiplies. (Lesson 37.)
4. **Buffers** (`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`) — pages touched: the
   physical-I/O truth behind the milliseconds.

# Reading - 30_reading_explain

`EXPLAIN` is the only feedback loop in this course that tells you *why* a
query is slow rather than *that* it is. Everything in Part 5 is a
consequence of learning to read it.

## Notes

**`EXPLAIN` versus `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`.** Plain `EXPLAIN` shows the plan and
the planner's *estimates* without running anything. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`
actually executes the query and adds measured row counts and timings. Use
ANALYZE by default — the gap between estimate and actual is the single most
diagnostic number in the output — but remember that it really runs the
query, so `EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE ...` deletes. Wrap those in a transaction
and roll back.

**Read a plan inside out and bottom up.** The tree is printed with the
final step at the top; execution flows from the leaves upward. Each node
consumes rows from its children and emits rows to its parent. The first
question to ask of any plan is "which leaf touches the most rows, and why
does it have to?".

**The numbers on a node line.** `cost=0.00..8543.00` is the planner's
arbitrary-unit estimate: startup cost before the first row, then total cost.
`rows=25000` is the estimated row count; `width=42` the estimated bytes per
row. With ANALYZE you also get `actual time=0.014..38.2 rows=24983 loops=1`.

**Estimate versus actual is the diagnosis.** When `rows=1` and `actual
rows=250000`, the planner chose its algorithm on a false premise and the
plan above that node is probably wrong too — that is lesson 36. Look for the
node where the ratio first explodes; everything above it is a consequence,
not a cause.

**`loops` matters more than it looks.** A node inside a nested loop runs
once per outer row, and `actual time` is reported **per loop**. A node
showing `actual time=0.05 rows=1 loops=250000` took twelve seconds, not
0.05 ms. Multiply before you conclude anything.

**Node types worth recognising immediately.**

- `Seq Scan` — read every row of the table. Correct for "most of the table",
  a red flag for "three rows".
- `Index Scan` — walk an index, then fetch each matching row from the heap.
- `Index Only Scan` — answer entirely from the index, no heap visit
  (lesson 34).
- `Bitmap Index Scan` + `Bitmap Heap Scan` — collect matching row locations,
  sort them, then read the heap in physical order. The planner's middle
  gear (lesson 38).
- `Nested Loop` / `Hash Join` / `Merge Join` — the three join algorithms
  (lesson 37).
- `Sort` — with `Sort Method: quicksort`, `top-N heapsort`, or `external
  merge Disk: ...`, the last of which means it spilled and `work_mem` is
  too small.
- `HashAggregate` / `GroupAggregate` — the two ways to group.

**`BUFFERS` is the underrated option.** `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` reports
how many 8 KB pages each node read, and whether they came from PostgreSQL's
cache (`shared hit`) or from the operating system (`shared read`). Timings
vary with cache state and machine load; buffer counts are stable, which
makes them the better metric for comparing two plans. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE,
BUFFERS, FORMAT JSON)` is what this course's own gates parse.

**A plan is a hypothesis about your data.** The planner does not know your
data; it knows a statistical summary of it (lesson 36). Every plan is the
cheapest route *given what it believes*, which is why the fix for a bad plan
is more often better statistics or a better index than a query rewrite.

## ex1 — name that node

A filter on an unindexed column has exactly one option: read everything. The
useful reflex to build is the reverse one — when you see `Seq Scan` on a
large table returning few rows, ask which index would have been used
instead, and why it does not exist.

## ex2 — read three facts from one plan

Estimated rows, actual rows, and total time. Those three numbers answer
"did the planner know what it was doing?" and "did it matter?" — which is
the whole of plan reading in two questions.

## ex3 — name the sort method

`top-N heapsort` is the planner recognising `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` and keeping
only ten rows in memory rather than sorting ten thousand. Note what it does
*not* save: every row is still read and compared. Removing the pass entirely
needs an index whose order already matches (lesson 35), and the difference
between "sorted cheaply" and "not sorted at all" is the difference between
40 ms and 0.1 ms.

## ex4 — name the join algorithm

`Hash Join` is the right choice here and the plan says so: no usable index
on `orders.customer_id`, and the query needs every row anyway. Watch what
the planner does with the same join once lesson 31 gives it an index and
lesson 37 changes the row counts — the SQL never changes, and the algorithm
does.

## Further reading

- [Using `EXPLAIN`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/using-explain.html) — the canonical walkthrough, with worked examples of every node type above. Read it once properly; it is the best-written chapter in the manual.
- [`EXPLAIN`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-explain.html) — the options: `ANALYZE`, `BUFFERS`, `VERBOSE`, `SETTINGS`, `FORMAT JSON`.
- [explain.depesz.com](https://explain.depesz.com/) — paste a plan, get the per-node exclusive time and the estimate/actual ratios highlighted. The fastest way to find the guilty node in a large plan.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Anatomy of an Index](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/anatomy) — what a B-tree actually is, which makes every plan node in Part 5 easier to reason about.

# 30 — Reading EXPLAIN

Welcome to Part 5. Everything you've written so far was graded on *what*
it returned; from here on, the dojo also grades **how** the database got
it, and how fast. The instrument for all of it is `EXPLAIN` — and the
skill that separates "I added an index and prayed" from actual
performance work is *reading plans fluently*.

Two new commands become your daily drivers:

- `dojo plan <lesson> [ex]` — EXPLAIN your current `solution.sql`
  (applying your `indexes.sql` first), rendered as a tree. No gate.
- `dojo lab <lesson>` — your sandbox, now the place you run
  `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` by hand.

## Concept

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE total > 1999;             -- estimates only
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE total > 1999;     -- actually runs it
```

`EXPLAIN` shows the plan the optimizer chose with **estimated** costs and
row counts. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` executes the query and adds **actual** rows
and time per node. The estimated-vs-actual gap is diagnostic gold (lesson
36 is entirely about it).

A plan is a tree, executed leaves-first:

```
Sort  (rows=250, 91.2ms)
  Seq Scan on orders  (rows=250, 88.1ms)   <-- most expensive
        Filter: (total > 1999)
        Rows Removed by Filter: 499750
```

How to read any plan, in order of importance:

1. **Node types.** `Seq Scan` = read every row of the table. `Index
   Scan` = walk an index to the matching rows. There are ~a dozen more;
   Part 5 introduces them one per lesson.
2. **Actual rows per node** — the data volume flowing up the tree. A
   node that reads 500,000 rows to feed a node that outputs 11 is the
   waste you'll learn to eliminate.
3. **loops** — a node's figures are *per loop*; a nested inner side
   executing 500,000 times multiplies. (Lesson 37.)
4. **Buffers** (`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`) — pages touched: the
   physical-I/O truth behind the milliseconds.

"Rows Removed by Filter: 499,750" is the single most valuable line for
index hunting: it means the executor *fetched and threw away* half a
million rows. An index's entire job is making that number small.

Professionals don't guess at performance, and they don't cargo-cult

# Reading - 30_reading_explain

`EXPLAIN` is the only feedback loop in this course that tells you *why* a
query is slow rather than *that* it is. Everything in Part 5 is a
consequence of learning to read it.

## Notes

**`EXPLAIN` versus `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`.** Plain `EXPLAIN` shows the plan and
the planner's *estimates* without running anything. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`
actually executes the query and adds measured row counts and timings. Use
ANALYZE by default — the gap between estimate and actual is the single most
diagnostic number in the output — but remember that it really runs the
query, so `EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE ...` deletes. Wrap those in a transaction
and roll back.

**Read a plan inside out and bottom up.** The tree is printed with the
final step at the top; execution flows from the leaves upward. Each node
consumes rows from its children and emits rows to its parent. The first
question to ask of any plan is "which leaf touches the most rows, and why
does it have to?".

**The numbers on a node line.** `cost=0.00..8543.00` is the planner's
arbitrary-unit estimate: startup cost before the first row, then total cost.
`rows=25000` is the estimated row count; `width=42` the estimated bytes per
row. With ANALYZE you also get `actual time=0.014..38.2 rows=24983 loops=1`.

**Estimate versus actual is the diagnosis.** When `rows=1` and `actual
rows=250000`, the planner chose its algorithm on a false premise and the
plan above that node is probably wrong too — that is lesson 36. Look for the
node where the ratio first explodes; everything above it is a consequence,
not a cause.

**`loops` matters more than it looks.** A node inside a nested loop runs
once per outer row, and `actual time` is reported **per loop**. A node
showing `actual time=0.05 rows=1 loops=250000` took twelve seconds, not
0.05 ms. Multiply before you conclude anything.

**Node types worth recognising immediately.**

- `Seq Scan` — read every row of the table. Correct for "most of the table",
  a red flag for "three rows".
- `Index Scan` — walk an index, then fetch each matching row from the heap.
- `Index Only Scan` — answer entirely from the index, no heap visit
  (lesson 34).
- `Bitmap Index Scan` + `Bitmap Heap Scan` — collect matching row locations,
  sort them, then read the heap in physical order. The planner's middle
  gear (lesson 38).
- `Nested Loop` / `Hash Join` / `Merge Join` — the three join algorithms
  (lesson 37).
- `Sort` — with `Sort Method: quicksort`, `top-N heapsort`, or `external
  merge Disk: ...`, the last of which means it spilled and `work_mem` is
  too small.
- `HashAggregate` / `GroupAggregate` — the two ways to group.

**`BUFFERS` is the underrated option.** `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` reports
how many 8 KB pages each node read, and whether they came from PostgreSQL's
cache (`shared hit`) or from the operating system (`shared read`). Timings
vary with cache state and machine load; buffer counts are stable, which
makes them the better metric for comparing two plans. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE,
BUFFERS, FORMAT JSON)` is what this course's own gates parse.

**A plan is a hypothesis about your data.** The planner does not know your
data; it knows a statistical summary of it (lesson 36). Every plan is the
cheapest route *given what it believes*, which is why the fix for a bad plan
is more often better statistics or a better index than a query rewrite.

## ex1 — name that node

A filter on an unindexed column has exactly one option: read everything. The
useful reflex to build is the reverse one — when you see `Seq Scan` on a
large table returning few rows, ask which index would have been used
instead, and why it does not exist.

## ex2 — read three facts from one plan

Estimated rows, actual rows, and total time. Those three numbers answer
"did the planner know what it was doing?" and "did it matter?" — which is
the whole of plan reading in two questions.

## ex3 — name the sort method

`top-N heapsort` is the planner recognising `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` and keeping
only ten rows in memory rather than sorting ten thousand. Note what it does
*not* save: every row is still read and compared. Removing the pass entirely
needs an index whose order already matches (lesson 35), and the difference
between "sorted cheaply" and "not sorted at all" is the difference between
40 ms and 0.1 ms.

## ex4 — name the join algorithm

`Hash Join` is the right choice here and the plan says so: no usable index
on `orders.customer_id`, and the query needs every row anyway. Watch what
the planner does with the same join once lesson 31 gives it an index and
lesson 37 changes the row counts — the SQL never changes, and the algorithm
does.

## Further reading

- [Using `EXPLAIN`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/using-explain.html) — the canonical walkthrough, with worked examples of every node type above. Read it once properly; it is the best-written chapter in the manual.
- [`EXPLAIN`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-explain.html) — the options: `ANALYZE`, `BUFFERS`, `VERBOSE`, `SETTINGS`, `FORMAT JSON`.
- [explain.depesz.com](https://explain.depesz.com/) — paste a plan, get the per-node exclusive time and the estimate/actual ratios highlighted. The fastest way to find the guilty node in a large plan.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Anatomy of an Index](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/anatomy) — what a B-tree actually is, which makes every plan node in Part 5 easier to reason about.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — name the sort method

Run this in the lab (`dojo lab 30_reading_explain`):

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT id, name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 10;
```

Look at the `Sort` node. Underneath the node line, PostgreSQL prints a
`Sort Method:` line naming the algorithm it actually used. Edit
`ex3/solution.sql` to return that method as a single text value — for
example `SELECT 'quicksort';` if that were the answer.

The answer is worth understanding rather than copying. PostgreSQL notices
`ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` and switches to an algorithm that keeps only the
best n rows in memory instead of sorting all 10,000 — a large constant
factor saved, but still a full pass over the table, because every row must
be examined to know it is not in the top ten. Lesson 35 removes the pass
entirely.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — name the join algorithm

In the lab, run:

```sql
EXPLAIN
SELECT c.country, sum(o.total)
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.country;
```

This is lesson 08's revenue-by-country query. Find the node that performs
the join and edit `ex4/solution.sql` to return its node type as a single
text value, spelled exactly as the plan spells it.

PostgreSQL has three join algorithms and it chose this one because it
needs every row of both tables and there is no index on
`orders.customer_id` to walk. It builds a hash table from the smaller
input and streams the larger one past it. Lesson 37 is about all three and
about what would make the planner change its mind.

# 31 — Your first index

Lesson 30's plans all said `Seq Scan`: to find customer 4242's eleven-ish
orders, PostgreSQL reads all 500,000 rows and throws away 499,989 of
them. It has no choice — with no index, the heap (the table's raw
storage) has no order, so *every* lookup is a full read. A B-tree index
is the fix: a sorted structure mapping `customer_id` values to row
locations, turning "read everything" into "descend a tree, fetch
eleven".

From this lesson on, you edit **two files** per exercise: `solution.sql`
usually ships with the query already written (the query isn't the
puzzle), and `indexes.sql`, which starts empty — the DDL is yours. And
the gate grows to three stages: right rows → right plan shape → **at
least 8x faster** than the naive baseline this machine measured for
itself on your first run (recalibrate anytime with `dojo
reset-baseline`).

## Concept

```sql
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_id_idx ON orders (customer_id);
```

- Naming convention: `<table>_<cols>_idx`. Postgres doesn't care;
  colleagues do.
- What you bought: lookups on `customer_id` go from O(all rows) to
  O(log n + matches). What you paid: ~11 MB of disk, and **every**
  INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on `orders` now maintains the tree. Indexes are
  never free; they're a bet that reads outnumber writes.
- What it does *not* buy: anything for other columns. An index on
  `customer_id` is useless for `WHERE total = ...` — exercise 2 makes
  you watch that failure so you never believe "the table is indexed"
  again. Tables aren't indexed; *columns* (really, *predicates*) are.

Use `dojo plan 31_first_index ex1` before and after writing the DDL —
watch the Seq Scan become an Index Scan (or Bitmap Heap Scan — both
count as victory; the gate only forbids the Seq Scan).

## Exercise 1 — index the lookup

`ex1/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id, status, total
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 4242;
```

Edit `ex1/indexes.sql`: create the index that serves it.

Run: `uv run dojo test 31_first_index ex1`

## Exercise 2 — watch the index NOT help

`ex2/indexes.sql` is **provided** — it contains exactly your ex1 index.
`ex2/solution.sql` needs the query (copy it in):

```sql
SELECT id, status, total
FROM orders
WHERE total = 123.45;
```

The gate asserts this plan **must contain a Seq Scan** — the
customer_id index is present and powerless, because `total` isn't in
it. No speed stage; the lesson is the shape.

Run: `uv run dojo test 31_first_index ex2`

## Exercise 3 — one product's reviews

`ex3/solution.sql` (provided) pulls one product's reviews out of a
million:

```sql
SELECT id, rating, created_at
FROM reviews
WHERE product_id = 42;
```

Edit `ex3/indexes.sql` with the index that makes it fast. Same move as
exercise 1 on a different table — and this is the shape you will meet more
than any other in real work: a foreign-key column, filtered by equality,
with no index because PostgreSQL does not create one for you.

The gate requires the plan to contain no `Seq Scan` and the query to run at
least 8× faster than the un-indexed baseline it measures on your machine.

Run: `uv run dojo test 31_first_index ex3`

## Exercise 4 — indexing a value, not a key

`ex4/solution.sql` (provided) finds the maximum-value orders:

```sql
SELECT id, customer_id, status
FROM orders
WHERE total > 1999.90;
```

Edit `ex4/indexes.sql`.

Nothing says an index has to be on a key or a foreign key — an index is
just a sorted copy of one or more columns plus a pointer back to the row,
and any column you filter on equality or range is a candidate. What makes
*this* one worth having is selectivity: `total > 1999.90` matches a
handful of rows out of half a million, so the index eliminates almost
everything. An index on `status`, which has four values across 500,000
rows, would eliminate almost nothing — lesson 39 comes back to why.

Run: `uv run dojo test 31_first_index ex4`

## Challenge — same move, bigger table (optional)

`challenge/solution.sql` (provided) hunts one customer's events in the
3-million-row clickstream:

```sql
SELECT id, ts
FROM events
WHERE customer_id = 31337;
```

Edit `challenge/indexes.sql`. Same 8x gate; note how much more an index
matters at 3M rows than 500k.

Run: `uv run dojo test 31_first_index challenge`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 31_first_index

An index is a sorted copy of some columns, plus a pointer back to each row.
That is the entire idea. Everything else in Part 5 is a consequence of it —
including every case where an index does not help.

## Notes

**Why sorted order is the whole trick.** Finding one value among 500,000
unsorted rows means looking at all of them. Finding it in a sorted structure
means a handful of comparisons: PostgreSQL's B-tree is a balanced tree with
a high branching factor, so even a million-row index is three or four levels
deep. Three page reads instead of a hundred thousand — that is where the
factor of a thousand comes from, and it is why the speedup grows with the
table rather than staying constant.

**An index scan is two steps.** Walk the tree to find matching entries, then
visit the heap to fetch each row (because the index holds only the indexed
columns and a pointer). The second step is random I/O, one page per matching
row, and it is why an index stops being worth it when the match is large:
reading 200,000 rows one random page at a time is *slower* than reading the
whole table sequentially. The planner knows this, which is why it sometimes
refuses to use an index you just built — and it is usually right. Lesson 38
covers the middle ground and lesson 34 covers avoiding the heap visit
entirely.

**PostgreSQL does not index foreign keys automatically.** Primary keys and
unique constraints get an index because they need one to enforce
uniqueness. Foreign-key *columns* get nothing. So `orders.customer_id`,
`order_items.order_id` and `reviews.product_id` — the three columns every
join in this course uses — are unindexed in the shipped schema, which is
both realistic and the reason lesson 33 has a war story. Two consequences:
joins scan, and deleting a parent row scans the child table looking for
references.

**Selectivity decides whether an index is worth building.** An index earns
its keep by *eliminating* rows. `total > 1999.90` matches a handful out of
500,000 — excellent. `status = 'paid'` matches half the table — the planner
will ignore the index and it is right to. The rule of thumb is that a plain
B-tree index stops paying somewhere around 5–10% selectivity, though the
real threshold depends on row width and physical clustering.

**Indexes are not free.** Each one is a separate structure that must be
updated on every `INSERT`, `UPDATE` (of an indexed column) and `DELETE`, it
consumes disk, and it competes for cache. A table with twelve indexes has
twelve write amplifications. The right number is "the ones your queries
actually use" — and `pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan` tells you which ones
those are, which is how you find the index somebody added in 2021 that has
never been read.

**Building an index locks writes** unless you use `CREATE INDEX
CONCURRENTLY` (lesson 28). On a live table, always concurrently.

## ex1 — index the lookup

One column, one index, and a speedup of two or three orders of magnitude.
Run `dojo plan 31_first_index ex1` before and after: the `Seq Scan` becomes
an `Index Scan`, and the estimated cost drops by roughly the same factor as
the measured time.

## ex2 — watch the index NOT help

The counter-example, and the reason the gate *requires* a `Seq Scan` here.
An index on `customer_id` cannot serve a filter on `total`; the index is
sorted by the wrong thing. Internalising "an index helps the column it is
on, and only that column" prevents most of the confusion in lessons 32
and 33.

## ex3 — one product's reviews

The single most common index in any real schema: a foreign-key column,
filtered by equality. Note that the *query* is unchanged from what you would
have written in Part 1; the index changes what the planner can do with it,
not what it means.

## ex4 — indexing a value, not a key

Selectivity in one exercise. `total > 1999.90` matches a handful; the index
is spectacular. Try `WHERE total > 100` in the lab with the same index and
watch the planner ignore it — matching 95% of the table means the index scan
would cost more than reading everything, and being *right* about that is one
of the planner's most useful behaviours.

## challenge — same move, bigger table

Three million rows, and the point is that the shape of the answer does not
change with the scale. The factor does: the bigger the haystack, the more an
index is worth, which is the opposite of most optimisations.

## Further reading

- [Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes.html) — the whole chapter; start with "Introduction" and "Index Types".
- [`CREATE INDEX`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createindex.html) — the syntax, including `CONCURRENTLY`, `INCLUDE`, and partial-index predicates.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Anatomy of an Index](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/anatomy) — the clearest explanation anywhere of what a B-tree is and why the leaf nodes are a doubly linked list.
- [Monitoring index usage](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/monitoring-stats.html) — `pg_stat_user_indexes`, for finding the indexes nobody has ever used.

# Reading - 31_first_index

An index is a sorted copy of some columns, plus a pointer back to each row.
That is the entire idea. Everything else in Part 5 is a consequence of it —
including every case where an index does not help.

## Notes

**Why sorted order is the whole trick.** Finding one value among 500,000
unsorted rows means looking at all of them. Finding it in a sorted structure
means a handful of comparisons: PostgreSQL's B-tree is a balanced tree with
a high branching factor, so even a million-row index is three or four levels
deep. Three page reads instead of a hundred thousand — that is where the
factor of a thousand comes from, and it is why the speedup grows with the
table rather than staying constant.

**An index scan is two steps.** Walk the tree to find matching entries, then
visit the heap to fetch each row (because the index holds only the indexed
columns and a pointer). The second step is random I/O, one page per matching
row, and it is why an index stops being worth it when the match is large:
reading 200,000 rows one random page at a time is *slower* than reading the
whole table sequentially. The planner knows this, which is why it sometimes
refuses to use an index you just built — and it is usually right. Lesson 38
covers the middle ground and lesson 34 covers avoiding the heap visit
entirely.

**PostgreSQL does not index foreign keys automatically.** Primary keys and
unique constraints get an index because they need one to enforce
uniqueness. Foreign-key *columns* get nothing. So `orders.customer_id`,
`order_items.order_id` and `reviews.product_id` — the three columns every
join in this course uses — are unindexed in the shipped schema, which is
both realistic and the reason lesson 33 has a war story. Two consequences:
joins scan, and deleting a parent row scans the child table looking for
references.

**Selectivity decides whether an index is worth building.** An index earns
its keep by *eliminating* rows. `total > 1999.90` matches a handful out of
500,000 — excellent. `status = 'paid'` matches half the table — the planner
will ignore the index and it is right to. The rule of thumb is that a plain
B-tree index stops paying somewhere around 5–10% selectivity, though the
real threshold depends on row width and physical clustering.

**Indexes are not free.** Each one is a separate structure that must be
updated on every `INSERT`, `UPDATE` (of an indexed column) and `DELETE`, it
consumes disk, and it competes for cache. A table with twelve indexes has
twelve write amplifications. The right number is "the ones your queries
actually use" — and `pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan` tells you which ones
those are, which is how you find the index somebody added in 2021 that has
never been read.

**Building an index locks writes** unless you use `CREATE INDEX
CONCURRENTLY` (lesson 28). On a live table, always concurrently.

## ex1 — index the lookup

One column, one index, and a speedup of two or three orders of magnitude.
Run `dojo plan 31_first_index ex1` before and after: the `Seq Scan` becomes
an `Index Scan`, and the estimated cost drops by roughly the same factor as
the measured time.

## ex2 — watch the index NOT help

The counter-example, and the reason the gate *requires* a `Seq Scan` here.
An index on `customer_id` cannot serve a filter on `total`; the index is
sorted by the wrong thing. Internalising "an index helps the column it is
on, and only that column" prevents most of the confusion in lessons 32
and 33.

## ex3 — one product's reviews

The single most common index in any real schema: a foreign-key column,
filtered by equality. Note that the *query* is unchanged from what you would
have written in Part 1; the index changes what the planner can do with it,
not what it means.

## ex4 — indexing a value, not a key

Selectivity in one exercise. `total > 1999.90` matches a handful; the index
is spectacular. Try `WHERE total > 100` in the lab with the same index and
watch the planner ignore it — matching 95% of the table means the index scan
would cost more than reading everything, and being *right* about that is one
of the planner's most useful behaviours.

## challenge — same move, bigger table

Three million rows, and the point is that the shape of the answer does not
change with the scale. The factor does: the bigger the haystack, the more an
index is worth, which is the opposite of most optimisations.

## Further reading

- [Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes.html) — the whole chapter; start with "Introduction" and "Index Types".
- [`CREATE INDEX`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createindex.html) — the syntax, including `CONCURRENTLY`, `INCLUDE`, and partial-index predicates.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Anatomy of an Index](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/anatomy) — the clearest explanation anywhere of what a B-tree is and why the leaf nodes are a doubly linked list.
- [Monitoring index usage](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/monitoring-stats.html) — `pg_stat_user_indexes`, for finding the indexes nobody has ever used.
