## Exercise 4 — indexing a value, not a key

`ex4/solution.sql` (provided) finds the maximum-value orders:

```sql
SELECT id, customer_id, status
FROM orders
WHERE total > 1999.90;
```

Edit `ex4/indexes.sql`.

Nothing says an index has to be on a key or a foreign key — an index is
just a sorted copy of one or more columns plus a pointer back to the row,
and any column you filter on equality or range is a candidate. What makes
*this* one worth having is selectivity: `total > 1999.90` matches a
handful of rows out of half a million, so the index eliminates almost
everything. An index on `status`, which has four values across 500,000
rows, would eliminate almost nothing — lesson 39 comes back to why.

lessons.briefing:
# 32 — Composite indexes

"Customer 4242's *paid* orders." Two predicates. A single-column index
on `customer_id` gets you to eleven rows fast and filters the rest —
decent. But an index on **(customer_id, status)** descends straight to
the exact rows: both predicates resolved inside the tree, zero rows
thrown away. Multi-column (composite) indexes are how real query
patterns get indexed — and their column *order* is the design decision
this lesson drills.

## Concept

```sql
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_status_idx ON orders (customer_id, status);
```

Think of a composite index as sorted by column 1, then column 2 within
equal column-1 values — a phone book sorted by (last name, first name).

The ordering rules that cover ~90% of real design:

1. **Equality columns first, range columns last.** For `WHERE a = ? AND
   b >= ?`, index `(a, b)`: the tree jumps to the `a` group, then reads
   the contiguous `b >= ?` run inside it. Index `(b, a)` instead and
   the range on `b` scatters your `a` matches across the whole scan.
2. **A range breaks the chain**: columns after the *first range column*
   in the index can't narrow the descent (they can still filter inside
   the index — helpful, but not the same thing).
3. The index also serves any **left prefix**: `(customer_id, status)`
   works for `WHERE customer_id = ?` alone. It does nothing for
   `WHERE status = ?` alone — that's next lesson's whole story.

## Exercise 1 — two equalities

`ex1/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id, total
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 4242
  AND status = 'paid';
```

Edit `ex1/indexes.sql`: one composite index serving both predicates.

Run: `uv run dojo test 32_composite_indexes ex1`

## Exercise 2 — equality then range

`ex2/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id, ts
FROM events
WHERE customer_id = 777
  AND ts >= '2023-11-01';
```

Edit `ex2/indexes.sql`. Rule 1 dictates the order — get it backwards
and the plan may still avoid a Seq Scan but the speed stage will notice
the wasted work on this 3M-row table.

Run: `uv run dojo test 32_composite_indexes ex2`

## Exercise 3 — two equalities on the line items

`ex3/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id, order_id, price
FROM order_items
WHERE product_id = 42 AND quantity = 3;
```

Edit `ex3/indexes.sql` with **one** composite index serving both
conditions.

Two equality conditions, so either column order works for *this* query —
`(product_id, quantity)` and `(quantity, product_id)` both find the rows.
They are not equally good, though: `quantity` has five distinct values
across a million rows, so leading with it means the tree narrows to
200,000 entries before the second column does any work. Lead with the
selective column.

Run: `uv run dojo test 32_composite_indexes ex3`

## Exercise 4 — equality first, range second

`ex4/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id, rating, created_at
FROM reviews
WHERE product_id = 42 AND rating >= 4;
```

Edit `ex4/indexes.sql` with one composite index.

Here the column order is **not** a matter of taste. A B-tree is sorted by
the first column, then the second within equal firsts, and so on — so once
you use a column for a *range*, everything after it is no longer in a
usable order. Equality columns first, range column last. Put `rating`
first and the index can only narrow to "rating 4 or 5", then scan 400,000
entries looking for the product.

This one rule explains most composite-index design in practice.

Run: `uv run dojo test 32_composite_indexes ex4`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 32_composite_indexes

A composite index is a sorted copy of *several* columns — sorted by the
first, then by the second within ties on the first, and so on. Every rule
about composite indexes falls straight out of that sentence, so it is worth
holding onto literally: think of a phone book sorted by (last name, first
name).

## Notes

**Column order is the design.** `(a, b)` and `(b, a)` are different indexes
with different capabilities. The phone book sorted by (last, first) answers
"everyone called Smith" and "Smith, John" instantly, and is useless for
"everyone called John".

**Equality columns first, range column last.** A B-tree can narrow on
consecutive leading columns as long as each one is pinned to a single value.
The moment a column is used for a range (`>=`, `<`, `BETWEEN`, `LIKE 'x%'`),
the entries after it are spread across the whole matched range and no later
column is in a usable order for filtering. So an index on `(product_id,
rating)` serves `product_id = 42 AND rating >= 4` beautifully, and
`(rating, product_id)` does not. Exactly one range column can be used, and
it must be last.

**Sort columns come after that.** If the query also has an `ORDER BY`, the
sort columns belong after the equality columns and — usually — instead of
the range. `WHERE customer_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at DESC` wants
`(customer_id, created_at)`. That is lesson 35.

**Lead with the selective column, all else equal.** When two conditions are
both equalities, either order finds the rows, but the more selective column
first means the tree narrows faster and fewer index pages are touched. The
exception, and it is a common one: if another query in your application
filters on the *less* selective column alone, leading with it may let one
index serve both queries. Index design is a portfolio decision, not a
per-query one.

**One good composite beats several single-column indexes.** PostgreSQL
*can* combine separate indexes via a bitmap AND (lesson 38), and it is much
worse than a composite: it scans both indexes fully, builds two bitmaps and
intersects them, where a composite index walks straight to the answer. Two
single-column indexes are a reasonable hedge when you do not know the query
mix; a composite is the answer when you do.

**Every prefix is free.** An index on `(a, b, c)` also serves queries on
`(a, b)` and on `(a)` alone — the same structure, stopping earlier. So
`(a, b, c)` makes a separate index on `(a)` redundant, and dropping the
redundant one saves write amplification and disk. This is the "left prefix
rule", and lesson 33 is entirely about the half of it that surprises people.

**Width has a cost.** Each extra column makes every index entry bigger,
which means fewer entries per page, more pages, more I/O, and a bigger
write penalty on every update. Adding a column "just in case" is not free —
though `INCLUDE` (lesson 34) is a cheaper way to carry payload columns that
are never searched.

## ex1 — two equalities

Both column orders work; one is better. Build the other one in the lab and
compare `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` — the row counts are identical and the
buffer counts are not, which is exactly the kind of difference that timing
alone can hide on a warm cache.

## ex2 — equality then range

The rule that matters most, felt directly. If you built it the other way
round first and watched the plan get slower, that is the lesson landing.

## ex3 — two equalities on the line items

A rep on a bigger table, with a large selectivity gap between the two
columns: `product_id` has 10,000 distinct values and `quantity` has five.
Leading with `quantity` still *works* — the gate would pass — and it does
several hundred times more index work to get there.

## ex4 — equality first, range second

The same rule as ex2, on different data, because this is the one to have in
your hands rather than in your notes. When you are asked to design an index
for a query, the algorithm is mechanical: list the equality columns, then
the range column, then the `ORDER BY` columns, and stop at the first range.

## Further reading

- [Multicolumn Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-multicolumn.html) — the official statement of the prefix rule, and the note on when PostgreSQL will use a non-leading column anyway (badly).
- [Combining Multiple Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-bitmap-scans.html) — what happens when you have two single-column indexes instead of one composite. Lesson 38.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Concatenated Keys](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause/the-equals-operator/concatenated-keys) — the phone-book explanation, with diagrams. Read this one.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Ranges](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause/searching-for-ranges) — why exactly one range column can be used, and why it must be last.

# 32 — Composite indexes

"Customer 4242's *paid* orders." Two predicates. A single-column index
on `customer_id` gets you to eleven rows fast and filters the rest —
decent. But an index on **(customer_id, status)** descends straight to
the exact rows: both predicates resolved inside the tree, zero rows
thrown away. Multi-column (composite) indexes are how real query
patterns get indexed — and their column *order* is the design decision
this lesson drills.

## Concept

```sql
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_status_idx ON orders (customer_id, status);
```

Think of a composite index as sorted by column 1, then column 2 within
equal column-1 values — a phone book sorted by (last name, first name).

The ordering rules that cover ~90% of real design:

1. **Equality columns first, range columns last.** For `WHERE a = ? AND
   b >= ?`, index `(a, b)`: the tree jumps to the `a` group, then reads
   the contiguous `b >= ?` run inside it. Index `(b, a)` instead and
   the range on `b` scatters your `a` matches across the whole scan.
2. **A range breaks the chain**: columns after the *first range column*
   in the index can't narrow the descent (they can still filter inside
   the index — helpful, but not the same thing).
3. The index also serves any **left prefix**: `(customer_id, status)`
   works for `WHERE customer_id = ?` alone. It does nothing for
   `WHERE status = ?` alone — that's next lesson's whole story.

## Exercise 1 — two equalities

`ex1/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id, total
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 4242
  AND status = 'paid';
```

Edit `ex1/indexes.sql`: one composite index serving both predicates.

Run: `uv run dojo test 32_composite_indexes ex1`

## Exercise 2 — equality then range

`ex2/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id, ts
FROM events
WHERE customer_id = 777
  AND ts >= '2023-11-01';
```

Edit `ex2/indexes.sql`. Rule 1 dictates the order — get it backwards
and the plan may still avoid a Seq Scan but the speed stage will notice
the wasted work on this 3M-row table.

Run: `uv run dojo test 32_composite_indexes ex2`

## Exercise 3 — two equalities on the line items

`ex3/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id, order_id, price
FROM order_items
WHERE product_id = 42 AND quantity = 3;
```

Edit `ex3/indexes.sql` with **one** composite index serving both
conditions.

Two equality conditions, so either column order works for *this* query —
`(product_id, quantity)` and `(quantity, product_id)` both find the rows.
They are not equally good, though: `quantity` has five distinct values
across a million rows, so leading with it means the tree narrows to
200,000 entries before the second column does any work. Lead with the
selective column.

Run: `uv run dojo test 32_composite_indexes ex3`

## Exercise 4 — equality first, range second

`ex4/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id, rating, created_at
FROM reviews
WHERE product_id = 42 AND rating >= 4;
```

Edit `ex4/indexes.sql` with one composite index.

Here the column order is **not** a matter of taste. A B-tree is sorted by
the first column, then the second within equal firsts, and so on — so once
you use a column for a *range*, everything after it is no longer in a
usable order. Equality columns first, range column last. Put `rating`
first and the index can only narrow to "rating 4 or 5", then scan 400,000
entries looking for the product.

This one rule explains most composite-index design in practice.

Run: `uv run dojo test 32_composite_indexes ex4`

## The teaching point

Composite-index design is *query-driven*, not table-driven: you index a
**pattern** (`by customer, filtered by status`) rather than columns in
isolation. The interview-and-review checklist: list the query's
equality predicates, then its range/sort columns — that's your column
order. And before adding a new index, check whether an existing one's
left prefix already covers you; index sprawl is a write-amplification
tax everyone forgets until the ingest pipeline slows.

# Reading - 32_composite_indexes

A composite index is a sorted copy of *several* columns — sorted by the
first, then by the second within ties on the first, and so on. Every rule
about composite indexes falls straight out of that sentence, so it is worth
holding onto literally: think of a phone book sorted by (last name, first
name).

## Notes

**Column order is the design.** `(a, b)` and `(b, a)` are different indexes
with different capabilities. The phone book sorted by (last, first) answers
"everyone called Smith" and "Smith, John" instantly, and is useless for
"everyone called John".

**Equality columns first, range column last.** A B-tree can narrow on
consecutive leading columns as long as each one is pinned to a single value.
The moment a column is used for a range (`>=`, `<`, `BETWEEN`, `LIKE 'x%'`),
the entries after it are spread across the whole matched range and no later
column is in a usable order for filtering. So an index on `(product_id,
rating)` serves `product_id = 42 AND rating >= 4` beautifully, and
`(rating, product_id)` does not. Exactly one range column can be used, and
it must be last.

**Sort columns come after that.** If the query also has an `ORDER BY`, the
sort columns belong after the equality columns and — usually — instead of
the range. `WHERE customer_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at DESC` wants
`(customer_id, created_at)`. That is lesson 35.

**Lead with the selective column, all else equal.** When two conditions are
both equalities, either order finds the rows, but the more selective column
first means the tree narrows faster and fewer index pages are touched. The
exception, and it is a common one: if another query in your application
filters on the *less* selective column alone, leading with it may let one
index serve both queries. Index design is a portfolio decision, not a
per-query one.

**One good composite beats several single-column indexes.** PostgreSQL
*can* combine separate indexes via a bitmap AND (lesson 38), and it is much
worse than a composite: it scans both indexes fully, builds two bitmaps and
intersects them, where a composite index walks straight to the answer. Two
single-column indexes are a reasonable hedge when you do not know the query
mix; a composite is the answer when you do.

**Every prefix is free.** An index on `(a, b, c)` also serves queries on
`(a, b)` and on `(a)` alone — the same structure, stopping earlier. So
`(a, b, c)` makes a separate index on `(a)` redundant, and dropping the
redundant one saves write amplification and disk. This is the "left prefix
rule", and lesson 33 is entirely about the half of it that surprises people.

**Width has a cost.** Each extra column makes every index entry bigger,
which means fewer entries per page, more pages, more I/O, and a bigger
write penalty on every update. Adding a column "just in case" is not free —
though `INCLUDE` (lesson 34) is a cheaper way to carry payload columns that
are never searched.

## ex1 — two equalities

Both column orders work; one is better. Build the other one in the lab and
compare `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` — the row counts are identical and the
buffer counts are not, which is exactly the kind of difference that timing
alone can hide on a warm cache.

## ex2 — equality then range

The rule that matters most, felt directly. If you built it the other way
round first and watched the plan get slower, that is the lesson landing.

## ex3 — two equalities on the line items

A rep on a bigger table, with a large selectivity gap between the two
columns: `product_id` has 10,000 distinct values and `quantity` has five.
Leading with `quantity` still *works* — the gate would pass — and it does
several hundred times more index work to get there.

## ex4 — equality first, range second

The same rule as ex2, on different data, because this is the one to have in
your hands rather than in your notes. When you are asked to design an index
for a query, the algorithm is mechanical: list the equality columns, then
the range column, then the `ORDER BY` columns, and stop at the first range.

## Further reading

## Exercise 1 — two equalities

`ex1/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id, total
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 4242
  AND status = 'paid';
```

Edit `ex1/indexes.sql`: one composite index serving both predicates.

Both predicates are equalities, so either order technically serves this
query - but `(customer_id, status)` also gives you the customer-alone
prefix for free (rule 3). Pick that.

`CREATE INDEX orders_customer_status_idx ON orders (customer_id, status);`

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — two equalities on the line items

`ex3/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id, order_id, price
FROM order_items
WHERE product_id = 42 AND quantity = 3;
```

Edit `ex3/indexes.sql` with **one** composite index serving both
conditions.

Two equality conditions, so either column order works for *this* query —
`(product_id, quantity)` and `(quantity, product_id)` both find the rows.
They are not equally good, though: `quantity` has five distinct values
across a million rows, so leading with it means the tree narrows to
200,000 entries before the second column does any work. Lead with the
selective column.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — equality first, range second

`ex4/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id, rating, created_at
FROM reviews
WHERE product_id = 42 AND rating >= 4;
```

Edit `ex4/indexes.sql` with one composite index.

Here the column order is **not** a matter of taste. A B-tree is sorted by
the first column, then the second within equal firsts, and so on — so once
you use a column for a *range*, everything after it is no longer in a
usable order. Equality columns first, range column last. Put `rating`
first and the index can only narrow to "rating 4 or 5", then scan 400,000
entries looking for the product.

This one rule explains most composite-index design in practice.

lessons.briefing:
# 33 — Left prefixes and the unindexed-FK trap

An index on `(a, b)` is sorted by `a` first — so for a query on `b`
alone it's as useful as a phone book when you only know someone's first
name. This "left prefix rule" sounds academic until you meet its most
expensive real-world incarnation: **foreign keys**.

Here's the trap. PostgreSQL auto-indexes primary keys (it must — the
index *is* the uniqueness enforcement). It does **not** auto-index
foreign key columns. `order_items.order_id` references `orders(id)` —
and in this database, like every fresh schema, it has no index. Every
"items of order X" lookup — the single most natural query in the schema
— seq-scans a million rows. So does every `DELETE FROM orders`
(checking for referencing children!). Entire consulting careers are
funded by this default.

## Concept

```sql
-- serves order_id-alone AND (order_id, product_id):
CREATE INDEX order_items_order_id_idx ON order_items (order_id);

-- (order_id, product_id) does NOT serve product_id alone:
--   the product_id values are scattered across all order_id groups
```

# Reading - 33_left_prefix

The left-prefix rule is the single most load-bearing fact about B-tree
indexes, and the one that costs the most time when it is not known: an index
on `(a, b)` helps a query on `a`, and does nothing useful for a query on `b`
alone.

## Notes

**Why it is true.** The index is sorted by `a` first, then by `b` within
equal `a`. Look up `a = 7` and the entries are contiguous — one descent of
the tree. Look up `b = 'purchase'` and the matching entries are scattered
through the whole index, once inside every distinct `a`. There is no
shortcut; the structure simply is not sorted the way that query needs.

**The phone book.** Sorted by (last name, first name). "Everyone called
Smith" — one page range. "Smith, John" — one entry. "Everyone called John" —
read the whole book. The rule is not a PostgreSQL quirk; it is what sorted
order means.

**Every prefix is free; no suffix is.** An index on `(a, b, c)` serves
`(a)`, `(a, b)` and `(a, b, c)`. It does not serve `(b)`, `(c)` or
`(b, c)`. So a separate index on `(a)` alongside `(a, b)` is redundant and
should be dropped — it costs write amplification and disk for nothing. Two
practical habits follow: audit for redundant prefixes when you inherit a
schema, and when you need both `(a, b)` and `(b, a)`, accept that you need
two indexes.

**PostgreSQL can misuse a non-leading column, and it is not a rescue.** The
planner may choose an index scan that filters on a trailing column while
scanning the *entire* index, when the index is much narrower than the table.
You will see this as an `Index Scan` with a huge `actual rows` on the index
and a small final count. It is not the prefix rule being broken; it is a
full scan of a smaller structure.

**Foreign keys are the reason this bites in production.** PostgreSQL does
not index foreign-key columns. So the join column your application uses
hundreds of times a second is unindexed until somebody notices — and worse,
`DELETE FROM parent` has to scan the entire child table for references,
which turns a one-row delete into a sequential scan of a million rows. Every
foreign key that is ever used in a join or a cascading delete wants an
index; that is close to all of them.

**Designing the order.** List the query's equality columns, then its range
column, then its `ORDER BY` columns. That ordering is the index. When
several queries compete, prefer the column order that lets one index serve
the most of them via prefixes — a `(customer_id, created_at)` index serves
"one customer's orders", "one customer's recent orders" and "one customer's
orders sorted by date", which is three query shapes for one index.

## ex1 — index the FK

The receipt query from lesson 08, made fast by the index PostgreSQL refused
to create for you. This is the most common missing index in the world.

## ex2 — the prefix rule, felt

The composite is pre-filled and the query filters the *trailing* column.
The gate insists on a `Seq Scan`, which is the plan being honest: the index
exists, it is on the right table, it contains the column, and it cannot
help. An index is not a general-purpose speed-up; it is a specific sorted
order.

## ex3 — the whole key

Both columns pinned to values, so the tree narrows on both in one descent.
Three million rows down to a handful. Note the column order argument in the
prompt — `customer_id` first is not arbitrary, it is the selective column,
and leading with `event_type` would narrow to 230,000 entries before doing
any real work.

## ex4 — half the key is still a key

The same index, a query on the leading column only, and it works. Having
seen both halves — ex2 fails, ex4 succeeds, same index — the rule should now
be something you can state without hedging: **leading columns, in order,
without gaps.**

## Further reading

- [Multicolumn Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-multicolumn.html) — the prefix rule as the manual states it, including when a non-leading column is used anyway.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Concatenated Keys](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause/the-equals-operator/concatenated-keys) — the definitive treatment, with the phone-book analogy and the redundant-index argument.
- [`ALTER TABLE ... ADD FOREIGN KEY`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-altertable.html) — and the manual's note that an index on the referencing column is *not* created automatically.
- [Index maintenance](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/monitoring-stats.html) — `pg_stat_user_indexes` for finding both the unused indexes and the redundant prefixes.

# 33 — Left prefixes and the unindexed-FK trap

An index on `(a, b)` is sorted by `a` first — so for a query on `b`
alone it's as useful as a phone book when you only know someone's first
name. This "left prefix rule" sounds academic until you meet its most
expensive real-world incarnation: **foreign keys**.

Here's the trap. PostgreSQL auto-indexes primary keys (it must — the
index *is* the uniqueness enforcement). It does **not** auto-index
foreign key columns. `order_items.order_id` references `orders(id)` —
and in this database, like every fresh schema, it has no index. Every
"items of order X" lookup — the single most natural query in the schema
— seq-scans a million rows. So does every `DELETE FROM orders`
(checking for referencing children!). Entire consulting careers are
funded by this default.

## Concept

```sql
-- serves order_id-alone AND (order_id, product_id):
CREATE INDEX order_items_order_id_idx ON order_items (order_id);

-- (order_id, product_id) does NOT serve product_id alone:
--   the product_id values are scattered across all order_id groups
```

Checklist form of the prefix rule for an index on `(a, b, c)`:

| predicate | served? |
|---|---|
| `a = ?` | yes |
| `a = ? AND b = ?` | yes |
| `a = ? AND b = ? AND c = ?` | yes |
| `b = ?` | **no** (not a left prefix) |
| `b = ? AND c = ?` | **no** |
| `a = ? AND c = ?` | partially (descends on `a`, filters `c` in-index) |

## The teaching point

Two habits from one lesson. First: **when you write a FK, decide about
its index in the same breath** — the answer is almost always yes (skip
only append-heavy tables whose parents are never deleted and never
joined from). Second: "column X is indexed" is not a sentence that
means anything — *predicates* are served or not, and only left prefixes
count. Reviewers who internalize this catch entire classes of
regression before deploy.

# Reading - 33_left_prefix

The left-prefix rule is the single most load-bearing fact about B-tree
indexes, and the one that costs the most time when it is not known: an index
on `(a, b)` helps a query on `a`, and does nothing useful for a query on `b`
alone.

## Notes

**Why it is true.** The index is sorted by `a` first, then by `b` within
equal `a`. Look up `a = 7` and the entries are contiguous — one descent of
the tree. Look up `b = 'purchase'` and the matching entries are scattered
through the whole index, once inside every distinct `a`. There is no
shortcut; the structure simply is not sorted the way that query needs.

**The phone book.** Sorted by (last name, first name). "Everyone called
Smith" — one page range. "Smith, John" — one entry. "Everyone called John" —
read the whole book. The rule is not a PostgreSQL quirk; it is what sorted
order means.

**Every prefix is free; no suffix is.** An index on `(a, b, c)` serves
`(a)`, `(a, b)` and `(a, b, c)`. It does not serve `(b)`, `(c)` or
`(b, c)`. So a separate index on `(a)` alongside `(a, b)` is redundant and
should be dropped — it costs write amplification and disk for nothing. Two
practical habits follow: audit for redundant prefixes when you inherit a
schema, and when you need both `(a, b)` and `(b, a)`, accept that you need
two indexes.

**PostgreSQL can misuse a non-leading column, and it is not a rescue.** The
planner may choose an index scan that filters on a trailing column while
scanning the *entire* index, when the index is much narrower than the table.
You will see this as an `Index Scan` with a huge `actual rows` on the index
and a small final count. It is not the prefix rule being broken; it is a
full scan of a smaller structure.

**Foreign keys are the reason this bites in production.** PostgreSQL does
not index foreign-key columns. So the join column your application uses
hundreds of times a second is unindexed until somebody notices — and worse,
`DELETE FROM parent` has to scan the entire child table for references,
which turns a one-row delete into a sequential scan of a million rows. Every
foreign key that is ever used in a join or a cascading delete wants an
index; that is close to all of them.

**Designing the order.** List the query's equality columns, then its range
column, then its `ORDER BY` columns. That ordering is the index. When
several queries compete, prefer the column order that lets one index serve
the most of them via prefixes — a `(customer_id, created_at)` index serves
"one customer's orders", "one customer's recent orders" and "one customer's
orders sorted by date", which is three query shapes for one index.

## ex1 — index the FK

The receipt query from lesson 08, made fast by the index PostgreSQL refused
to create for you. This is the most common missing index in the world.

## ex2 — the prefix rule, felt

The composite is pre-filled and the query filters the *trailing* column.
The gate insists on a `Seq Scan`, which is the plan being honest: the index
exists, it is on the right table, it contains the column, and it cannot
help. An index is not a general-purpose speed-up; it is a specific sorted
order.

## ex3 — the whole key

Both columns pinned to values, so the tree narrows on both in one descent.
Three million rows down to a handful. Note the column order argument in the
prompt — `customer_id` first is not arbitrary, it is the selective column,
and leading with `event_type` would narrow to 230,000 entries before doing
any real work.

## ex4 — half the key is still a key

The same index, a query on the leading column only, and it works. Having
seen both halves — ex2 fails, ex4 succeeds, same index — the rule should now
be something you can state without hedging: **leading columns, in order,
without gaps.**

## Further reading

- [Multicolumn Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-multicolumn.html) — the prefix rule as the manual states it, including when a non-leading column is used anyway.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Concatenated Keys](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause/the-equals-operator/concatenated-keys) — the definitive treatment, with the phone-book analogy and the redundant-index argument.
- [`ALTER TABLE ... ADD FOREIGN KEY`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-altertable.html) — and the manual's note that an index on the referencing column is *not* created automatically.
- [Index maintenance](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/monitoring-stats.html) — `pg_stat_user_indexes` for finding both the unused indexes and the redundant prefixes.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — half the key is still a key

`ex4/solution.sql` (provided) asks for **everything** one customer did:

```sql
SELECT id, event_type, ts
FROM events
WHERE customer_id = 4242;
```

Edit `ex4/indexes.sql` and build **the same two-column index as exercise
3** — `(customer_id, event_type)` — not a single-column one.

This is the half of the prefix rule that works, and it is worth proving to
yourself: a query on the *leading* column alone uses the composite index
happily, because the entries are sorted by `customer_id` first. Exercise 2
showed the other half — the trailing column alone gets nothing.

The practical consequence is that `(a, b)` makes a separate index on `(a)`
redundant. Every prefix of a composite index is free; every suffix costs a
second index.

lessons.briefing:
# 34 — Index-only scans

A normal Index Scan is a two-step dance: find the row in the index,
then fetch the full row from the heap (the table) — because the index
only holds its own columns, and because PostgreSQL must check the heap
to know if the row version is visible to your transaction (MVCC —
lesson 44 tells that story properly). But if the index *contains every
column the query touches*, step two can vanish: an **Index Only Scan**
answers from the index alone. For wide tables and hot queries, that's
the difference between touching megabytes and touching kilobytes.

## Concept

Two ways to get every needed column into the index:

```sql
-- 1. widen the key:
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_total_idx ON orders (customer_id, total);

-- 2. INCLUDE: carry payload columns without making them key columns
CREATE INDEX order_items_product_incl_idx
  ON order_items (product_id) INCLUDE (price);
```

`INCLUDE` columns ride along in the leaves but don't participate in
ordering or uniqueness — the honest way to say "I only need you for
covering, not for searching".

**The visibility map caveat** — this *will* bite you someday, so meet
it now: "answers from the index alone" is only legal for heap pages the
**visibility map** marks all-visible. That map is maintained by VACUUM.
On a freshly-bulk-updated table the map is stale, and your beautiful
Index Only Scan silently degrades into heap fetches (`Heap Fetches: N`
in EXPLAIN ANALYZE — nonzero means degraded). The dojo's gates VACUUM
the table after your `indexes.sql` so the demo is clean; production
gives no such courtesy, which is lesson 44's cliffhanger.

## Exercise 1 — cover by widening the key

`ex1/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT customer_id, total
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id BETWEEN 100 AND 200;
```

Edit `ex1/indexes.sql`. The gate demands an actual `Index Only Scan`
node — an ordinary Index Scan fails the shape stage. Which two columns
must the index hold?

Run: `uv run dojo test 34_index_only_scans ex1`

## Exercise 2 — cover with INCLUDE

`ex2/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT product_id, price
FROM order_items
WHERE product_id = 777;
```

Edit `ex2/indexes.sql` using the `INCLUDE` form — `price` is payload,
not a search key; say so in the DDL.

Run: `uv run dojo test 34_index_only_scans ex2`

## Exercise 3 — cover a range of reviews

`ex3/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT product_id, rating
FROM reviews
WHERE product_id BETWEEN 100 AND 200;
```

Edit `ex3/indexes.sql`. The gate requires an **`Index Only Scan`** in the
plan — not merely an `Index Scan`.

Two columns appear in the query: one is searched, one is output. Put both
in the index and PostgreSQL never has to visit the table at all — it
answers from the index pages alone. The range column leads because it is
the one being searched.

Roughly 20,000 rows match, which would normally be far too many for an
index scan to beat a sequential one — 20,000 random heap visits is worse
than reading the table. Removing the heap visits is what changes the
arithmetic, and it is why covering indexes matter most exactly where
ordinary indexes stop working.

Run: `uv run dojo test 34_index_only_scans ex3`

## Exercise 4 — payload with INCLUDE

`ex4/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT order_id, price
FROM order_items
WHERE order_id BETWEEN 1000 AND 1500;
```

Edit `ex4/indexes.sql` and cover it with **`INCLUDE`** rather than by
widening the key:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ... ON order_items (order_id) INCLUDE (price);
```

The gate requires an `Index Only Scan`.

`INCLUDE` columns are stored in the index's leaf pages only — not in the
internal nodes, and not part of the sort order. That makes them cheaper
than key columns (smaller internal nodes, shallower tree) and it means
they can be types a B-tree could not sort at all. The trade is that you
cannot search or order by them.

The rule: a column you **search or sort by** goes in the key; a column you
only **output** goes in `INCLUDE`.

Run: `uv run dojo test 34_index_only_scans ex4`

# Reading - 34_index_only_scans

An ordinary index scan is two steps: find the entries, then fetch each row
from the table. An index-only scan skips the second step entirely, because
everything the query asked for is already in the index. It is the single
biggest win available on a read-heavy workload, and it depends on a detail
of PostgreSQL's storage that surprises people.

## Notes

**Covering means the index contains every column the query touches** — in
the `SELECT` list, the `WHERE`, the `ORDER BY`, everywhere. One extra column
in the select list and the plan drops back to a plain `Index Scan` with a
heap visit per row. This is the strongest practical argument against
`SELECT *` that exists.

**Two ways to cover.** Widen the key — `(a, b)` — or use `INCLUDE` —
`(a) INCLUDE (b)`. `INCLUDE` columns live only in the leaf pages: they are
not part of the sort order, they do not appear in internal nodes (so the
tree stays shallow), and they may be types with no B-tree ordering at all.
The cost is that you cannot search or sort by them, and a unique index's
uniqueness applies only to the key columns — which is exactly the point when
you want `UNIQUE (email) INCLUDE (name)`.

**The visibility-map catch.** PostgreSQL's index entries do not record
whether a row version is visible to your transaction; only the heap does. So
an index-only scan still has to check visibility — unless the page is marked
*all-visible* in the table's **visibility map**, which `VACUUM` maintains.
Consequences that bite in production:

- A table that has just been heavily updated has few all-visible pages, so
  "index-only" scans do most of their heap fetches anyway.
- `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)` reports `Heap Fetches: n` under the node. `n` near
  zero means it really is index-only; a large `n` means you have the plan
  but not the benefit.
- The fix is usually to vacuum more aggressively on that table
  (`autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor`), not to change the index.

This course's template is vacuumed at seed time, so the visibility map is
warm and index-only scans behave.

**When covering is worth it.** Precisely when an ordinary index scan would
lose to a sequential scan: medium-selectivity queries where the heap visits
dominate. 20,000 random heap fetches cost more than reading the table
sequentially — remove them and the index wins again. Covering an index turns
a "too many rows for an index" query back into an index query.

**The cost.** A wider index is a bigger index: fewer entries per page, more
pages to read, more disk, and a larger write penalty on every update.
Covering four columns "just in case" is how an index becomes a second copy
of the table. Cover the query you actually run.

**A hint about ordering.** Index-only scans compose with lesson 35: an index
that covers *and* provides the `ORDER BY` order gives you a plan with no
heap visit and no sort node, which is about as good as PostgreSQL gets.

## ex1 — cover by widening the key

Search column first, output column second. Check `Heap Fetches:` in the
plan — it should be 0 or close to it, and that number is the difference
between an index-only scan that works and one that only looks like it does.

## ex2 — cover with INCLUDE

Same result, cheaper structure. The internal nodes of this index hold only
`customer_id`, so the tree is shallower than the ex1 version and the leaf
pages carry the payload. On a wide payload column the difference is
substantial.

## ex3 — cover a range of reviews

Twenty thousand matching rows — normally far past the point where an index
loses to a sequential scan. It wins here only because there are no heap
visits. That inversion is worth sitting with: covering does not make the
index faster, it removes the step that was making it slow.

## ex4 — payload with INCLUDE

The decision rule in one exercise: searched or sorted columns go in the key,
output-only columns go in `INCLUDE`. Try building it as `(order_id, price)`
instead and compare the index sizes with
`SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('...'))` — the difference is small
here and grows with the payload's width.

## Further reading

- [Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-index-only-scans.html) — the manual's own treatment, including the visibility-map explanation and `INCLUDE`.
- [Routine Vacuuming — the visibility map](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/routine-vacuuming.html) — why an under-vacuumed table cannot do index-only scans. Lesson 44.
- [`CREATE INDEX` — `INCLUDE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createindex.html) — the syntax and the restrictions on included columns.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Index-Only Scan](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/clustering/index-only-scan-covering-index) — the same idea from the "clustering data" angle, with the cost model spelled out.

table.

# Reading - 34_index_only_scans

An ordinary index scan is two steps: find the entries, then fetch each row
from the table. An index-only scan skips the second step entirely, because
everything the query asked for is already in the index. It is the single
biggest win available on a read-heavy workload, and it depends on a detail
of PostgreSQL's storage that surprises people.

## Notes

**Covering means the index contains every column the query touches** — in
the `SELECT` list, the `WHERE`, the `ORDER BY`, everywhere. One extra column
in the select list and the plan drops back to a plain `Index Scan` with a
heap visit per row. This is the strongest practical argument against
`SELECT *` that exists.

**Two ways to cover.** Widen the key — `(a, b)` — or use `INCLUDE` —
`(a) INCLUDE (b)`. `INCLUDE` columns live only in the leaf pages: they are
not part of the sort order, they do not appear in internal nodes (so the
tree stays shallow), and they may be types with no B-tree ordering at all.
The cost is that you cannot search or sort by them, and a unique index's
uniqueness applies only to the key columns — which is exactly the point when
you want `UNIQUE (email) INCLUDE (name)`.

**The visibility-map catch.** PostgreSQL's index entries do not record
whether a row version is visible to your transaction; only the heap does. So
an index-only scan still has to check visibility — unless the page is marked
*all-visible* in the table's **visibility map**, which `VACUUM` maintains.
Consequences that bite in production:

- A table that has just been heavily updated has few all-visible pages, so
  "index-only" scans do most of their heap fetches anyway.
- `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)` reports `Heap Fetches: n` under the node. `n` near
  zero means it really is index-only; a large `n` means you have the plan
  but not the benefit.
- The fix is usually to vacuum more aggressively on that table
  (`autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor`), not to change the index.

This course's template is vacuumed at seed time, so the visibility map is
warm and index-only scans behave.

**When covering is worth it.** Precisely when an ordinary index scan would
lose to a sequential scan: medium-selectivity queries where the heap visits
dominate. 20,000 random heap fetches cost more than reading the table
sequentially — remove them and the index wins again. Covering an index turns
a "too many rows for an index" query back into an index query.

**The cost.** A wider index is a bigger index: fewer entries per page, more
pages to read, more disk, and a larger write penalty on every update.
Covering four columns "just in case" is how an index becomes a second copy
of the table. Cover the query you actually run.

**A hint about ordering.** Index-only scans compose with lesson 35: an index
that covers *and* provides the `ORDER BY` order gives you a plan with no
heap visit and no sort node, which is about as good as PostgreSQL gets.

## ex1 — cover by widening the key

Search column first, output column second. Check `Heap Fetches:` in the
plan — it should be 0 or close to it, and that number is the difference
between an index-only scan that works and one that only looks like it does.

## ex2 — cover with INCLUDE

Same result, cheaper structure. The internal nodes of this index hold only
`customer_id`, so the tree is shallower than the ex1 version and the leaf
pages carry the payload. On a wide payload column the difference is
substantial.

## ex3 — cover a range of reviews

Twenty thousand matching rows — normally far past the point where an index
loses to a sequential scan. It wins here only because there are no heap
visits. That inversion is worth sitting with: covering does not make the
index faster, it removes the step that was making it slow.

## ex4 — payload with INCLUDE

The decision rule in one exercise: searched or sorted columns go in the key,
output-only columns go in `INCLUDE`. Try building it as `(order_id, price)`
instead and compare the index sizes with
`SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('...'))` — the difference is small
here and grows with the payload's width.

## Further reading

- [Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-index-only-scans.html) — the manual's own treatment, including the visibility-map explanation and `INCLUDE`.
- [Routine Vacuuming — the visibility map](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/routine-vacuuming.html) — why an under-vacuumed table cannot do index-only scans. Lesson 44.
- [`CREATE INDEX` — `INCLUDE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createindex.html) — the syntax and the restrictions on included columns.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Index-Only Scan](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/clustering/index-only-scan-covering-index) — the same idea from the "clustering data" angle, with the cost model spelled out.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — cover a range of reviews

`ex3/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT product_id, rating
FROM reviews
WHERE product_id BETWEEN 100 AND 200;
```

Edit `ex3/indexes.sql`. The gate requires an **`Index Only Scan`** in the
plan — not merely an `Index Scan`.

Two columns appear in the query: one is searched, one is output. Put both
in the index and PostgreSQL never has to visit the table at all — it
answers from the index pages alone. The range column leads because it is
the one being searched.

Roughly 20,000 rows match, which would normally be far too many for an
index scan to beat a sequential one — 20,000 random heap visits is worse
than reading the table. Removing the heap visits is what changes the
arithmetic, and it is why covering indexes matter most exactly where
ordinary indexes stop working.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — payload with INCLUDE

`ex4/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT order_id, price
FROM order_items
WHERE order_id BETWEEN 1000 AND 1500;
```

Edit `ex4/indexes.sql` and cover it with **`INCLUDE`** rather than by
widening the key:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ... ON order_items (order_id) INCLUDE (price);
```

The gate requires an `Index Only Scan`.

`INCLUDE` columns are stored in the index's leaf pages only — not in the
internal nodes, and not part of the sort order. That makes them cheaper
than key columns (smaller internal nodes, shallower tree) and it means
they can be types a B-tree could not sort at all. The trade is that you
cannot search or order by them.

The rule: a column you **search or sort by** goes in the key; a column you
only **output** goes in `INCLUDE`.

lessons.briefing:
# 35 — ORDER BY and indexes

A B-tree *is* an ordering — that's what the B stands for (balanced,
but the point stands). So far you've used indexes to find rows; they
can also hand rows back **already sorted**, deleting the Sort node
entirely. For top-N queries this is transformative: "newest 10 of 3
million" stops being "sort 3 million, keep 10" and becomes "read 10
index entries from the right-hand end".

## Concept

```sql
-- serves WHERE customer_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC:
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_created_idx ON orders (customer_id, created_at);
```

- An index on `(a, b)` delivers, for fixed `a`, rows ordered by `b` —
  in *either* direction: PostgreSQL walks B-trees backwards for DESC as
  happily as forwards. Explicit `DESC` in the DDL
  (`... (a, b DESC)`) matters only for **mixed** directions
  (`ORDER BY a ASC, b DESC`), which a uniform index can't provide by
  walking one way.
- The pattern to recognize: **equality predicates, then the ORDER BY
  columns, in the index, in that order.** Lesson 32's rule again, with
  "range" generalized to "range or sort".
- `LIMIT` is what makes this huge: an index satisfying the order means
  the executor can *stop after N rows*. Without it, even top-10 needs
  the full sort. Watch for node `Limit` above an Index Scan — that's
  the win-shape.

`dojo plan` both exercises before writing DDL — see the Sort node
you're about to delete.

## Exercise 1 — a customer's most recent orders

`ex1/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 4242
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

Edit `ex1/indexes.sql`. The gate forbids both Seq Scan **and Sort** —
the index must find *and* order. (The LIMIT matters: without it the
planner may happily grab one customer's handful of rows any old way
and sort them — cheaper than being clever. Give it a top-N and the
ordered index walk wins outright.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 35_order_by_and_indexes ex1`

## Exercise 2 — global top-N

`ex2/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id, ts
FROM events
ORDER BY ts DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

Edit `ex2/indexes.sql`. Ten rows from three million; the baseline
sorts everything. Your index should make this near-instant.

Run: `uv run dojo test 35_order_by_and_indexes ex2`

## Exercise 3 — one product's latest reviews

`ex3/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id, rating, created_at
FROM reviews
WHERE product_id = 42
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

Edit `ex3/indexes.sql`. The gate requires **no `Seq Scan` and no `Sort`**
in the plan.

Two clauses, one index. The equality column leads so the tree can narrow to
one product; the sort column follows so that, within that product, the
entries are already in `created_at` order. PostgreSQL then walks ten
entries and stops — it never sorts, and it never reads the eleventh row.

Getting the `Sort` node to disappear is a different and larger win than
making the scan fast: a sort must consume its entire input before it can
emit the first row, so it defeats `LIMIT` completely.

Run: `uv run dojo test 35_order_by_and_indexes ex3`

## Exercise 4 — the newest reviews, globally

`ex4/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id, product_id, created_at
FROM reviews
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

Edit `ex4/indexes.sql`. Again: no `Seq Scan`, no `Sort`.

No `WHERE` clause at all this time, so the index has exactly one job —
provide the order. A single-column index is enough, and PostgreSQL will
read it from one end and stop after twenty entries.

You do not actually need `DESC` in the index definition: a B-tree can be
walked in either direction, and the plan will say `Index Scan Backward`.
Direction only matters when *several* sort columns disagree —
`ORDER BY a ASC, b DESC` needs an index declared `(a ASC, b DESC)`, because
no single walk of `(a, b)` produces that order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 35_order_by_and_indexes ex4`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 35_order_by_and_indexes

A B-tree is not just a lookup structure, it is a *sorted* one — and that
second property is worth as much as the first. An index whose order matches
your `ORDER BY` does not merely find rows faster; it removes the sort
entirely, which is what makes `LIMIT` cheap.

## Notes

**A sort is a barrier.** It must consume its whole input before it can emit
the first row, so `ORDER BY x LIMIT 10` over a sorted-by-something-else
input reads everything, sorts it (or top-N heapsorts it), and then discards
all but ten. An index in the right order lets the plan *pipeline*: read the
first ten entries, stop. That is the difference between O(rows) and
O(limit), and it grows without bound as the table grows.

**The index order must match the query order, including direction.** A
B-tree can be walked forwards or backwards, so a single-column `ORDER BY`
works with either declaration — you will see `Index Scan Backward` in the
plan. Direction only matters when sort keys disagree with each other:
`ORDER BY a ASC, b DESC` requires an index declared `(a ASC, b DESC)`,
because neither walk of a plain `(a, b)` index produces that sequence.

**`NULLS FIRST`/`LAST` is part of the order too.** The default for `ASC` is
`NULLS LAST`, and an index declared with the other convention will not
satisfy the query. When a `Sort` node refuses to disappear despite an index
that looks right, this is a common culprit.

**Equality columns first, then sort columns.** `WHERE customer_id = 7 ORDER
BY created_at DESC` wants `(customer_id, created_at)`: the equality pins a
region of the index, and inside that region the entries are already ordered.
This is the most valuable composite-index shape there is, because it serves
"one customer's most recent N" — the query behind almost every activity feed
and audit log ever built.

**A range column ruins the ordering for everything after it.** `WHERE
created_at > x ORDER BY total` cannot be served in order by
`(created_at, total)`: within the matched range, `total` is not sorted. You
get the range scan or the ordering, not both. This is the same rule as
lesson 32's, seen from the sort side, and it is why some queries genuinely
need a sort.

**Ordered index scans and `DISTINCT`/`GROUP BY`.** The same property lets
PostgreSQL replace a `HashAggregate` with a pipelined `GroupAggregate`, and
a `Unique` node over a sorted input is nearly free. An index built for an
`ORDER BY` often speeds up unrelated grouping queries for this reason.

**Keyset pagination is where this pays off most.** Lesson 03 argued that
`OFFSET 100000` is linear in the page number. With an index matching the
sort, `WHERE (created_at, id) < (:last_created, :last_id) ORDER BY
created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 10` is a single descent into the tree and ten
entries — constant time, on page one and page ten thousand alike. That
combination is the practical payoff of this lesson.

## ex1 — a customer's most recent orders

The activity-feed shape. Check the plan: `Limit` directly over `Index Scan`,
with no `Sort` in between. When somebody says "the feed got slow as we
grew", this is usually the missing index.

## ex2 — global top-N

No `WHERE`, so the index exists purely to provide order. Twenty rows read
out of half a million, and the cost does not change as the table grows —
which is the property that makes a leaderboard safe to ship.

## ex3 — one product's latest reviews

Equality plus sort, the composite shape from the notes. Try the index the
other way round — `(created_at, product_id)` — and watch the `Sort`
disappear but the scan become enormous: the ordering is right and the
filtering is not.

## ex4 — the newest reviews, globally

The simplest case, and the one that demonstrates direction-independence: the
index is declared ascending and the query wants descending, and the plan
says `Index Scan Backward` with no sort. Worth seeing once so that you do
not add `DESC` to every index out of superstition.

## Further reading

- [Indexes and `ORDER BY`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-ordering.html) — direction, `NULLS FIRST`/`LAST`, and when an ordered scan beats a sort.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Indexing Order By](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/sorting-grouping/order-by) — including the pipelined-order-by argument that makes `LIMIT` cheap.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Paging Through Results](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/partial-results/fetch-next-page) — keyset pagination, now that you have the index that makes it work.
- [`CREATE INDEX`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createindex.html) — the `ASC`/`DESC`/`NULLS` clauses on index columns.

## The teaching point

"Latest N per X" powers every feed, inbox, and activity log in the
industry, and `(x, created_at)` composite indexes power every one that
scales. When someone reports "the first page is fast but sorting is
slow", check EXPLAIN for a Sort node under a Limit — it means the
database sorted everything to give back a page. The fix is never a
faster sort; it's an index that makes sorting unnecessary.

# Reading - 35_order_by_and_indexes

A B-tree is not just a lookup structure, it is a *sorted* one — and that
second property is worth as much as the first. An index whose order matches
your `ORDER BY` does not merely find rows faster; it removes the sort
entirely, which is what makes `LIMIT` cheap.

## Notes

**A sort is a barrier.** It must consume its whole input before it can emit
the first row, so `ORDER BY x LIMIT 10` over a sorted-by-something-else
input reads everything, sorts it (or top-N heapsorts it), and then discards
all but ten. An index in the right order lets the plan *pipeline*: read the
first ten entries, stop. That is the difference between O(rows) and
O(limit), and it grows without bound as the table grows.

**The index order must match the query order, including direction.** A
B-tree can be walked forwards or backwards, so a single-column `ORDER BY`
works with either declaration — you will see `Index Scan Backward` in the
plan. Direction only matters when sort keys disagree with each other:
`ORDER BY a ASC, b DESC` requires an index declared `(a ASC, b DESC)`,
because neither walk of a plain `(a, b)` index produces that sequence.

**`NULLS FIRST`/`LAST` is part of the order too.** The default for `ASC` is
`NULLS LAST`, and an index declared with the other convention will not
satisfy the query. When a `Sort` node refuses to disappear despite an index
that looks right, this is a common culprit.

**Equality columns first, then sort columns.** `WHERE customer_id = 7 ORDER
BY created_at DESC` wants `(customer_id, created_at)`: the equality pins a
region of the index, and inside that region the entries are already ordered.
This is the most valuable composite-index shape there is, because it serves
"one customer's most recent N" — the query behind almost every activity feed
and audit log ever built.

**A range column ruins the ordering for everything after it.** `WHERE
created_at > x ORDER BY total` cannot be served in order by
`(created_at, total)`: within the matched range, `total` is not sorted. You
get the range scan or the ordering, not both. This is the same rule as
lesson 32's, seen from the sort side, and it is why some queries genuinely
need a sort.

**Ordered index scans and `DISTINCT`/`GROUP BY`.** The same property lets
PostgreSQL replace a `HashAggregate` with a pipelined `GroupAggregate`, and
a `Unique` node over a sorted input is nearly free. An index built for an
`ORDER BY` often speeds up unrelated grouping queries for this reason.

**Keyset pagination is where this pays off most.** Lesson 03 argued that
`OFFSET 100000` is linear in the page number. With an index matching the
sort, `WHERE (created_at, id) < (:last_created, :last_id) ORDER BY
created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 10` is a single descent into the tree and ten
entries — constant time, on page one and page ten thousand alike. That
combination is the practical payoff of this lesson.

## ex1 — a customer's most recent orders

The activity-feed shape. Check the plan: `Limit` directly over `Index Scan`,
with no `Sort` in between. When somebody says "the feed got slow as we
grew", this is usually the missing index.

## ex2 — global top-N

No `WHERE`, so the index exists purely to provide order. Twenty rows read
out of half a million, and the cost does not change as the table grows —
which is the property that makes a leaderboard safe to ship.

## ex3 — one product's latest reviews

Equality plus sort, the composite shape from the notes. Try the index the
other way round — `(created_at, product_id)` — and watch the `Sort`
disappear but the scan become enormous: the ordering is right and the
filtering is not.

## ex4 — the newest reviews, globally

The simplest case, and the one that demonstrates direction-independence: the
index is declared ascending and the query wants descending, and the plan
says `Index Scan Backward` with no sort. Worth seeing once so that you do
not add `DESC` to every index out of superstition.

## Further reading

- [Indexes and `ORDER BY`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-ordering.html) — direction, `NULLS FIRST`/`LAST`, and when an ordered scan beats a sort.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Indexing Order By](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/sorting-grouping/order-by) — including the pipelined-order-by argument that makes `LIMIT` cheap.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Paging Through Results](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/partial-results/fetch-next-page) — keyset pagination, now that you have the index that makes it work.
- [`CREATE INDEX`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createindex.html) — the `ASC`/`DESC`/`NULLS` clauses on index columns.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — a customer's most recent orders

`ex1/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 4242
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

Edit `ex1/indexes.sql`. The gate forbids both Seq Scan **and Sort** —
the index must find *and* order. (The LIMIT matters: without it the
planner may happily grab one customer's handful of rows any old way
and sort them — cheaper than being clever. Give it a top-N and the
ordered index walk wins outright.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 35_order_by_and_indexes ex1`

`CREATE INDEX orders_customer_created_idx ON orders (customer_id, created_at);`

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — one product's latest reviews

`ex3/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id, rating, created_at
FROM reviews
WHERE product_id = 42
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

Edit `ex3/indexes.sql`. The gate requires **no `Seq Scan` and no `Sort`**
in the plan.

Two clauses, one index. The equality column leads so the tree can narrow to
one product; the sort column follows so that, within that product, the
entries are already in `created_at` order. PostgreSQL then walks ten
entries and stops — it never sorts, and it never reads the eleventh row.

Getting the `Sort` node to disappear is a different and larger win than
making the scan fast: a sort must consume its entire input before it can
emit the first row, so it defeats `LIMIT` completely.

## Exercise 4 — the newest reviews, globally

`ex4/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id, product_id, created_at
FROM reviews
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

Edit `ex4/indexes.sql`. Again: no `Seq Scan`, no `Sort`.

No `WHERE` clause at all this time, so the index has exactly one job —
provide the order. A single-column index is enough, and PostgreSQL will
read it from one end and stop after twenty entries.

You do not actually need `DESC` in the index definition: a B-tree can be
walked in either direction, and the plan will say `Index Scan Backward`.
Direction only matters when *several* sort columns disagree —
`ORDER BY a ASC, b DESC` needs an index declared `(a ASC, b DESC)`, because
no single walk of `(a, b)` produces that order.

lessons.briefing:
# 36 — Statistics and the planner

Lessons 31–35 made it look like indexes are always used when they fit.
They aren't — and when the planner "ignores your index", it's usually
being smarter than you, or working from stale information. The planner
chooses plans by **estimating row counts**, and those estimates come
from **statistics**: per-column histograms and most-common-value lists
that `ANALYZE` samples into `pg_stats`. Wrong stats → wrong estimates →
wrong plan. This lesson you get to cause, observe, and fix that.

`setup.sql` builds `hot_orders`: a full copy of `orders` with
autovacuum disabled and **no statistics whatsoever** — plus 500 rows of
a status the original table never had: `'refunded'`.

## Concept

```sql
ANALYZE hot_orders;                  -- resample statistics, table-level

SELECT * FROM pg_stats
WHERE tablename = 'hot_orders' AND attname = 'status';
-- most_common_vals: {paid, cancelled, shipped, pending, refunded}
-- most_common_freqs: {0.50, 0.166, ...}
```

- **Estimates drive everything.** `EXPLAIN` prints `rows=` per node
  *before* running; `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` prints both. A big gap between
  them is the diagnostic — the plan was chosen for a query shape that
  doesn't exist.
- Autovacuum normally re-ANALYZEs tables as they churn; bulk loads and
  freshly-created tables are the classic windows where stats lag (your
  ETL job creates a table, immediately queries it, and gets a comedy
  plan).
- **Selectivity decides index use.** `status = 'refunded'` matches 500
  of ~500k rows — index, obviously. A predicate matching nearly the
  whole table — an index would add tree-walking on top of reading
  everything anyway; a sequential read wins. The planner knowing the
  difference IS the statistics working. "Postgres isn't using my
  index" is very often "my predicate matches too much for an index to
  help".

## Exercise 1 — heal the stats

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. In the lab, first watch the sickness:
`EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM hot_orders WHERE status = 'refunded';` — with no
stats, the estimate is wildly off the actual 500. Your solution: the
one statement that fixes it. The gate checks `pg_stats` has rows for
`hot_orders` and that the estimate lands within an order of magnitude.

Run: `uv run dojo test 36_statistics_and_the_planner ex1`

## Exercise 2 — selectivity in action

`ex2/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id, total
FROM hot_orders
WHERE status = 'refunded';
```

Edit `ex2/indexes.sql`: index `status`. The gate then explains **two**
queries against your index: the rare `'refunded'` (must use the index)
and the everything-but-refunds sweep — `status IN ('paid', 'pending',
'shipped', 'cancelled')`, 99.9% of the table — which must **still Seq
Scan**. Same index, same column, opposite correct answers. (Try the
in-between in the lab: plain `status = 'paid'` at ~50% often gets a
*bitmap* scan — the planner's middle gear from upcoming lesson 38 —
because visiting every page anyway while skipping the filter on
non-matching rows can price out cheaper than a raw seq scan. The
spectrum is real, and the planner walks it for you.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 36_statistics_and_the_planner ex2`

# Reading - 36_statistics_and_the_planner

The planner does not know your data. It knows a statistical summary of it,
collected by `ANALYZE`, and every plan it produces is the cheapest route
*given what it believes*. Most bad plans are not bad decisions; they are
good decisions made on bad information.

## Notes

**What `ANALYZE` collects.** A random sample of rows per table, from which
PostgreSQL derives, per column: the fraction of NULLs, the number of
distinct values, a list of most-common values with their frequencies, a
histogram of the rest, and the physical/logical correlation. All of it lands
in `pg_statistic`, readable through the `pg_stats` view — go and look at it
for `orders.status`, because seeing the actual numbers demystifies the whole
subject.

**Selectivity drives everything.** From those summaries the planner
estimates how many rows each predicate will keep. That estimate decides
index versus sequential scan, which join algorithm to use, whether to hash
or sort, and how much memory to request. An estimate that is wrong by 1000×
does not produce a slightly worse plan; it produces a plan built for a
different query.

**Read the estimate/actual ratio first.** In `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, find the
lowest node where `rows=` and `actual rows=` diverge badly. Everything above
it is a consequence. That single habit resolves most "why is this slow"
questions faster than any amount of index guessing.

**Autovacuum runs `ANALYZE` for you — eventually.** The trigger is
proportional to table size, so a big table can absorb a large absolute
number of changes before it resamples. After a bulk load, a migration, or a
mass `UPDATE`, run `ANALYZE` yourself. It is cheap, it is safe, and a
freshly loaded table with no statistics is the most common cause of a
catastrophically bad plan in production.

**The per-column knob.** `ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN c SET STATISTICS n`
raises the sample detail for one column (default 100, max 10,000); the
global default lives in `default_statistics_target`. Raise it on skewed
columns where the most-common-values list is truncating something the
planner needs to know about.

**Correlated columns are the estimator's blind spot.** PostgreSQL assumes
predicates are independent, so `WHERE city = 'Paris' AND country = 'FR'`
gets estimated as the product of two selectivities — wildly too low, since
the two are perfectly dependent. `CREATE STATISTICS ... (dependencies,
ndistinct, mcv) ON a, b FROM t` teaches it otherwise. This is the fix for a
whole family of mysterious under-estimates.

**Correlation and the cost of an index scan.** `pg_stats.correlation` says
how closely a column's order matches the rows' physical order on disk. High
correlation (like `events.ts`, which is strictly increasing) makes an index
scan nearly sequential and therefore cheap; low correlation makes it random
I/O. This one number is why the same index is worth building on one column
and not on another — and it is the entire basis of BRIN (lesson 43).

**When the estimate is right and the plan is still bad**, the cost
*constants* may not match your hardware — `random_page_cost` defaults to 4.0,
which is sensible for spinning disks and much too high for SSDs, where
1.1 is typical. That single setting changes how willing the planner is to
use any index at all.

## ex1 — heal the stats

A table with no statistics at all, and a rare value the planner cannot
imagine. Watch the estimate before and after: this is what every freshly
restored database looks like until somebody analyses it.

## ex2 — selectivity in action

The same index, two queries, two different decisions — and the planner is
right both times. Refusing an index when the predicate matches most of the
table is a feature, and arguing with it (via `enable_seqscan = off`) is
almost always a way to make things slower while feeling productive.

## ex3 — buy the planner a better sample

A targeted knob rather than a global one. Note that the `ALTER` alone does
nothing: the target describes how the *next* `ANALYZE` should sample, so the
two statements are a pair. Forgetting the second one is the classic
half-applied tuning change.

## ex4 — a good estimate earns an index

The dependency, seen from the other side: with fresh statistics the planner
uses your index; without them it might not. Index tuning and statistics
tuning are the same activity, and an index that "does not work" is quite
often an index the planner has no reason to believe in.

## Further reading

- [Statistics Used by the Planner](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/planner-stats.html) — what `pg_stats` holds, and how each column is used.
- [Extended Statistics](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/planner-stats.html) — `CREATE STATISTICS` for correlated columns; the fix for multiplied-together selectivities.
- [Planner Cost Constants](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/runtime-config-query.html) — `random_page_cost`, `seq_page_cost`, `effective_cache_size`. Read the `random_page_cost` note about SSDs.
- [`ANALYZE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-analyze.html) — sampling behaviour and the per-column statistics target.
