# Reading - 40_expression_indexes

An index stores what you tell it to store. Usually that is a column; it can
just as easily be a function of a column — and that one generalisation
rescues an enormous number of queries that "cannot use an index".

## Notes

**The problem it solves.** `WHERE lower(email) = 'a@b.com'` cannot use an
index on `email`, because the index stores `email` and the query asks about
`lower(email)`. They are different values in a different order. An
expression index stores the computed values, sorted, and the query walks
straight to them.

**The expression must match.** PostgreSQL compares the query's expression
against the index's structurally. `lower(email)` matches `lower(email)`.
`upper(email)` does not. `length(name)` does not match `char_length(name)`
even though they are the same function under different names. When an
expression index goes unused, this is the first thing to check.

**Only immutable expressions may be indexed.** An `IMMUTABLE` function
always returns the same output for the same input, forever — which an index
requires, since the stored value must stay correct. `lower()` is immutable.
`now()` is volatile. `date_trunc('day', timestamptz)` is only *stable*,
because the result depends on the session time zone, so it cannot be
indexed — the workaround is `date_trunc('day', ts AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')`,
which pins the zone and becomes immutable. Casting a `timestamptz` to `date`
has the same problem for the same reason.

**Extra cost, in two places.** The expression is evaluated on every insert
and on every update of the underlying column, and again during `ANALYZE`.
An expensive function in an index is an expensive function on your write
path.

**Statistics come for free.** `ANALYZE` collects statistics on the
expression's values, not just the base column's. So an expression index also
teaches the planner how selective `lower(email) = ...` is — occasionally
worth creating for the estimates alone.

**Common real-world uses.** Case-insensitive lookup — `lower(email)`, and
note that a `UNIQUE` index on `lower(email)` enforces case-insensitive
uniqueness, which no plain constraint can. Extracting a key from JSONB.
Indexing a computed prefix — `left(code, 3)`. Full-text search, where
`to_tsvector('english', body)` is the expression (lesson 41). Functional
uniqueness, like `UNIQUE (lower(slug))`.

**The alternative: a generated column.** Since PostgreSQL 12 you can store
the computed value as a `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...) STORED` column (lesson
24) and index that normally. The trade-off: the generated column consumes
table space and is visible in `SELECT *`, but the query can reference it by
name instead of repeating the expression exactly — which removes the
matching problem entirely. On a team, that predictability is often worth
more than the disk.

## ex1 — the login lookup

The canonical case, and the one whose absence causes real login-latency
incidents. Note also the uniqueness angle: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON
customers (lower(email))` is how you stop `Bob@x.com` and `bob@x.com` both
registering.

## ex2 — index a computed prefix

Lesson 19's text surgery, made fast. The expression is doing real work per
row, so the index is buying you both the sorted order *and* the avoided
computation.

## ex3 — index a computed property

`length(name)` is not a column anybody designed, and indexing it is still
perfectly reasonable when a query needs it. Try `char_length(name) = 30` in
the lab afterwards — same rows, no index — and you will not forget the
exact-match rule.

## ex4 — index inside the JSON

The pattern that makes one JSONB key behave like a proper typed column,
cast and all. Compare it against lesson 42's GIN index: this one is narrow
and precise, serving equality and range on a single key; GIN is broad,
serving containment queries against any key without knowing them in advance.
Real schemas often have both.

## Further reading

- [Indexes on Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-expressional.html) — the syntax, the double parentheses, and the cost warning.
- [Function Volatility](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/xfunc-volatility.html) — `IMMUTABLE` versus `STABLE` versus `VOLATILE`, and why only the first can be indexed.
- [Generated Columns](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-generated-columns.html) — the store-it-instead alternative, with its own trade-offs.
- [JSON Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-json.html) — for ex4's extraction operators; lesson 42 indexes the same column a completely different way.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — index a computed property

`ex3/solution.sql` (provided) is a data-quality sweep:

```sql
SELECT id, name
FROM customers
WHERE length(name) = 30;
```

Edit `ex3/indexes.sql` with an index on the **expression**:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ... ON customers ((length(name)));
```

Note the double parentheses — one pair for the index's column list, one
around the expression. PostgreSQL requires them for anything that is not a
bare column name, and forgetting them is the most common syntax error in
this lesson.

The index stores the *computed* values, sorted. That is why the query's
expression must match the index's expression exactly: `length(name) = 30`
uses it, `char_length(name) = 30` does not, even though the two functions
are the same thing.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — index inside the JSON

`ex4/solution.sql` (provided) hunts a value buried in three million
clickstream payloads:

```sql
SELECT id, ts, customer_id
FROM events
WHERE (payload ->> 'value')::int = 999;
```

Edit `ex4/indexes.sql` with an expression index over exactly that
expression, cast included.

This is the pattern that makes a JSONB column behave like a column. The
extraction and the cast are both immutable, so PostgreSQL can precompute
and sort them — and the query goes from reading three million documents to
a handful of index entries.

It also has to match *exactly*. Index `(payload ->> 'value')` without the
cast and this query will not use it, because comparing text to an integer
is a different expression. Lesson 42's GIN index is the other approach:
this one is precise and narrow (one key, indexed as a proper type), GIN is
general and broad (any key, containment queries).

lessons.briefing:
# 41 — GIN and full-text search

"Find reviews that mention *excellent* and *battery*." The B-tree has
nothing to offer: `LIKE '%excellent%'` can't use one (no left anchor to
descend on — lesson 33's prefix rule at the character level), so it's
a sequential scan evaluating a substring match a million times. Worse,
LIKE doesn't even answer the real question — it matches `excellently`,
misses `Excellent.` vs case... Text search is a different *problem*,
and PostgreSQL ships a different index family for it: **GIN**
(Generalized Inverted Index) — for each word, the list of rows
containing it. Exactly how a book index works.

## Concept

```sql
SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'The battery life is excellent.');
-- 'batteri':2 'excel':5 'life':3            <- stemmed, stopwords dropped

SELECT to_tsvector('english', body) @@ to_tsquery('english', 'excellent & battery');
-- @@ means "document matches query"

CREATE INDEX reviews_body_fts_idx
  ON reviews USING gin (to_tsvector('english', body));
```

- `to_tsvector` normalizes a document: lowercase, **stemming**
  (`excellent` → `excel`, so *excellently* matches too), stopword
  removal, positions. `to_tsquery` does the same to your query and
  supports `&`, `|`, `!`, `<->` (phrase).
- The index is lesson 40's trick with a different access method:
  `USING gin` over the *expression* `to_tsvector('english', body)`.
  The query must spell the same expression, config name included.
- Ranking: `ts_rank(vector, query)` scores matches; order by it for
  "best first". The index finds; ranking still computes per *match* —
  cheap when matches are few.
- Heads-up: building GIN over a million review bodies takes ~a minute,
  and the first (un-indexed) baseline run of ex1 takes several seconds
  — the gate will feel slow once, then the baseline is cached.

## Exercise 1 — index the corpus

`ex1/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id
FROM reviews
WHERE to_tsvector('english', body) @@ to_tsquery('english', 'excellent & battery');
```

Edit `ex1/indexes.sql`: the GIN index from the concept block. Baseline:
a full-corpus tsvector evaluation. Yours: an inverted-index lookup.
This is the biggest single speedup in the course.

Run: `uv run dojo test 41_gin_fulltext ex1`

## Exercise 2 — rank the results

`ex2/solution.sql` (provided) — top five *durable* reviews:

```sql
SELECT id
FROM reviews
WHERE to_tsvector('english', body) @@ to_tsquery('english', 'durable')
ORDER BY ts_rank(to_tsvector('english', body),
                 to_tsquery('english', 'durable')) DESC, id
LIMIT 5;
```

Edit `ex2/indexes.sql` (same GIN index). Gate: correct rows + no Seq
Scan. Notice in `dojo plan`: the index finds the matches; the rank is
computed only for them.

Run: `uv run dojo test 41_gin_fulltext ex2`

## Exercise 3 — a query written by a human

`ex3/solution.sql` (provided) searches the same corpus, but the query
comes from a search box rather than from a developer:

```sql
SELECT id
FROM reviews
WHERE to_tsvector('english', body)
      @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'durable battery');
```

Edit `ex3/indexes.sql` with the same GIN index as exercise 1.

`to_tsquery` demands operator syntax — `'durable & battery'` — and raises a
syntax error on anything else, which makes it completely unsuitable for
user input. `plainto_tsquery` takes arbitrary text, normalises it, and ANDs
the terms together. It never raises on punctuation, quotes or stray
ampersands.

The three query-builders are worth knowing apart: `to_tsquery` for
developer-written expressions, `plainto_tsquery` for plain user text,
`websearch_to_tsquery` for search-engine syntax. Exercise 4 uses the
third.

Run: `uv run dojo test 41_gin_fulltext ex3`

## Exercise 4 — search-engine syntax

`ex4/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id
FROM reviews
WHERE to_tsvector('english', body)
      @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'excellent OR durable');
```

Edit `ex4/indexes.sql` — the same GIN index again.

`websearch_to_tsquery` understands the syntax people actually type into
search boxes: `"quoted phrases"`, `OR`, and `-excluded`. Everything else is
treated as literal text, so it can never raise a syntax error on user
input.

Three exercises, one index. That is the point worth taking away: the index
is over the *left* side of `@@` — the document — and it serves every query
you can express against it. You do not build an index per search term; you
build one index over the corpus.

Run: `uv run dojo test 41_gin_fulltext ex4`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 41_gin_fulltext

Full-text search is a different data structure, not a cleverer `LIKE`. A
B-tree indexes whole values in order; GIN indexes the *pieces* of a value,
and that inversion is what makes searching a million documents for a word
take milliseconds.

## Notes

**`tsvector` and `tsquery`.** `to_tsvector('english', body)` parses the text
into lexemes, strips stop words, applies the language's stemmer (so
"batteries", "battery" and "batteried" collapse to one lexeme) and records
positions. `to_tsquery` builds the search side with `&`, `|`, `!` and `<->`
(phrase). The `@@` operator asks whether the document matches the query.
Both sides must use the **same text-search configuration** — `'english'` in
one and the default in the other is a silent mismatch that ruins results and
the index.

**GIN is an inverted index.** For every lexeme, it stores the list of rows
containing it. Searching for a word is a direct lookup; combining words is
an intersection of lists. That is the same structure a search engine uses,
and it is why the cost scales with the number of *matches*, not with the
size of the corpus.

**GIN versus GiST for text.** GIN is larger, slower to build and update, and
substantially faster to query — the right default for a corpus that is read
far more than written. GiST is smaller and lossy (it can produce false
positives that must be rechecked), which makes it better for
frequently-updated data. For a review corpus, GIN.

**Index the expression, exactly.** The index is over
`to_tsvector('english', body)` — an expression index (lesson 40) — so the
query's left-hand side must match it character for character, configuration
name included. This is the single most common reason a full-text index goes
unused. The robust alternative is to store the vector in a generated column
(`GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', body)) STORED`) and index that
by name, which removes the matching problem entirely.

**Three query-builders, three input sources.** `to_tsquery` for expressions
you wrote — it raises on malformed input. `plainto_tsquery` for arbitrary
user text — it ANDs the words and never raises. `websearch_to_tsquery` for
search-box syntax with quotes, `OR` and `-term`. Passing raw user input to
`to_tsquery` is a reliable way to produce 500s.

**Ranking is not filtering.** `ts_rank` scores the matches; it does not find
them. The index serves the `WHERE`, then ranking runs over the surviving
rows, then `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` picks the top few. Ranking a million rows
would be slow — ranking the two hundred that matched is not.

**`gin_pending_list_limit` and write cost.** GIN buffers new entries in a
pending list and merges them in batches, which keeps inserts fast at the
cost of a slower first query after a burst of writes. `fastupdate` controls
it. Worth knowing when a GIN-indexed table has a spiky write pattern.

**When *not* to use full text.** For substring matching (`LIKE '%son%'`),
what you want is a trigram index from `pg_trgm`, not `tsvector` — full-text
search works on word boundaries and stems, so it will not find "son" inside
"Anderson". Knowing which of the two a requirement calls for is the actual
decision.

## ex1 — index the corpus

The index takes about a minute to build over a million documents, which is
itself informative: GIN build cost is real, and on a live table this is a
`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` job. Compare the plan before and after — the
`Seq Scan` was recomputing `to_tsvector` on every one of a million rows.

## ex2 — rank the results

Search then rank, in that order. `ts_rank` is a scoring function over the
matches, and the `LIMIT` applies after ranking — so the index does the
expensive part and the ranking touches only what survived.

## ex3 — a query written by a human

`plainto_tsquery` is the function to reach for whenever the text came from
outside your codebase. Try passing `'durable & battery'` through
`to_tsquery` and then through `plainto_tsquery` in the lab: the first
treats the ampersand as an operator, the second as a word to be ignored.
Neither is wrong; they have different jobs.

## ex4 — search-engine syntax

`websearch_to_tsquery` handles the syntax users already know from every
search box on the internet. Note that all three exercises share one index:
the index describes the *corpus*, and the query-builder is just a way of
phrasing a question about it.

## Further reading

- [Full Text Search](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/textsearch.html) — the whole chapter. Read the "Controlling Text Search" section for the three query-builders and `ts_rank`.
- [Text Search Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/textsearch-indexes.html) — GIN versus GiST, build cost, and the `fastupdate` behaviour.
- [GIN Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/gin.html) — what an inverted index actually stores, and the pending-list mechanism.
- [`pg_trgm`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/pgtrgm.html) — trigram indexes, for the substring and fuzzy-match cases that full-text search does not cover.

dedicated search engine. The honest answer: tsvector+GIN handles

typo-tolerance, faceting, and relevance tuning. The expensive mistake
is neither choice — it's shipping `LIKE '%term%'` to production and
calling it search. Now you never will.

# Reading - 41_gin_fulltext

Full-text search is a different data structure, not a cleverer `LIKE`. A
B-tree indexes whole values in order; GIN indexes the *pieces* of a value,
and that inversion is what makes searching a million documents for a word
take milliseconds.

## Notes

**`tsvector` and `tsquery`.** `to_tsvector('english', body)` parses the text
into lexemes, strips stop words, applies the language's stemmer (so
"batteries", "battery" and "batteried" collapse to one lexeme) and records
positions. `to_tsquery` builds the search side with `&`, `|`, `!` and `<->`
(phrase). The `@@` operator asks whether the document matches the query.
Both sides must use the **same text-search configuration** — `'english'` in
one and the default in the other is a silent mismatch that ruins results and
the index.

**GIN is an inverted index.** For every lexeme, it stores the list of rows
containing it. Searching for a word is a direct lookup; combining words is
an intersection of lists. That is the same structure a search engine uses,
and it is why the cost scales with the number of *matches*, not with the
size of the corpus.

**GIN versus GiST for text.** GIN is larger, slower to build and update, and
substantially faster to query — the right default for a corpus that is read
far more than written. GiST is smaller and lossy (it can produce false
positives that must be rechecked), which makes it better for
frequently-updated data. For a review corpus, GIN.

**Index the expression, exactly.** The index is over
`to_tsvector('english', body)` — an expression index (lesson 40) — so the
query's left-hand side must match it character for character, configuration
name included. This is the single most common reason a full-text index goes
unused. The robust alternative is to store the vector in a generated column
(`GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', body)) STORED`) and index that
by name, which removes the matching problem entirely.

**Three query-builders, three input sources.** `to_tsquery` for expressions
you wrote — it raises on malformed input. `plainto_tsquery` for arbitrary
user text — it ANDs the words and never raises. `websearch_to_tsquery` for
search-box syntax with quotes, `OR` and `-term`. Passing raw user input to
`to_tsquery` is a reliable way to produce 500s.

**Ranking is not filtering.** `ts_rank` scores the matches; it does not find
them. The index serves the `WHERE`, then ranking runs over the surviving
rows, then `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` picks the top few. Ranking a million rows
would be slow — ranking the two hundred that matched is not.

**`gin_pending_list_limit` and write cost.** GIN buffers new entries in a
pending list and merges them in batches, which keeps inserts fast at the
cost of a slower first query after a burst of writes. `fastupdate` controls
it. Worth knowing when a GIN-indexed table has a spiky write pattern.

**When *not* to use full text.** For substring matching (`LIKE '%son%'`),
what you want is a trigram index from `pg_trgm`, not `tsvector` — full-text
search works on word boundaries and stems, so it will not find "son" inside
"Anderson". Knowing which of the two a requirement calls for is the actual
decision.

## ex1 — index the corpus

The index takes about a minute to build over a million documents, which is
itself informative: GIN build cost is real, and on a live table this is a
`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` job. Compare the plan before and after — the
`Seq Scan` was recomputing `to_tsvector` on every one of a million rows.

## ex2 — rank the results

Search then rank, in that order. `ts_rank` is a scoring function over the
matches, and the `LIMIT` applies after ranking — so the index does the
expensive part and the ranking touches only what survived.

## ex3 — a query written by a human

`plainto_tsquery` is the function to reach for whenever the text came from
outside your codebase. Try passing `'durable & battery'` through
`to_tsquery` and then through `plainto_tsquery` in the lab: the first
treats the ampersand as an operator, the second as a word to be ignored.
Neither is wrong; they have different jobs.

## ex4 — search-engine syntax

`websearch_to_tsquery` handles the syntax users already know from every
search box on the internet. Note that all three exercises share one index:
the index describes the *corpus*, and the query-builder is just a way of
phrasing a question about it.

## Further reading

- [Full Text Search](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/textsearch.html) — the whole chapter. Read the "Controlling Text Search" section for the three query-builders and `ts_rank`.
- [Text Search Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/textsearch-indexes.html) — GIN versus GiST, build cost, and the `fastupdate` behaviour.
- [GIN Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/gin.html) — what an inverted index actually stores, and the pending-list mechanism.
- [`pg_trgm`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/pgtrgm.html) — trigram indexes, for the substring and fuzzy-match cases that full-text search does not cover.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — a query written by a human

`ex3/solution.sql` (provided) searches the same corpus, but the query
comes from a search box rather than from a developer:

```sql
SELECT id
FROM reviews
WHERE to_tsvector('english', body)
      @@ plainto_tsquery('english', 'durable battery');
```

Edit `ex3/indexes.sql` with the same GIN index as exercise 1.

`to_tsquery` demands operator syntax — `'durable & battery'` — and raises a
syntax error on anything else, which makes it completely unsuitable for
user input. `plainto_tsquery` takes arbitrary text, normalises it, and ANDs
the terms together. It never raises on punctuation, quotes or stray
ampersands.

The three query-builders are worth knowing apart: `to_tsquery` for
developer-written expressions, `plainto_tsquery` for plain user text,
`websearch_to_tsquery` for search-engine syntax. Exercise 4 uses the
third.

Run: `uv run dojo test 41_gin_fulltext ex3`

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — search-engine syntax

`ex4/solution.sql` (provided):

```sql
SELECT id
FROM reviews
WHERE to_tsvector('english', body)
      @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', 'excellent OR durable');
```

Edit `ex4/indexes.sql` — the same GIN index again.

`websearch_to_tsquery` understands the syntax people actually type into
search boxes: `"quoted phrases"`, `OR`, and `-excluded`. Everything else is
treated as literal text, so it can never raise a syntax error on user
input.

Three exercises, one index. That is the point worth taking away: the index
is over the *left* side of `@@` — the document — and it serves every query
you can express against it. You do not build an index per search term; you
build one index over the corpus.

lessons.briefing:
# 42 — GIN over JSONB

Lesson 19 left a debt: you queried `products.attributes` and
`events.payload` with `@>` containment, un-indexed — seq scans
evaluating JSONB predicates row by row. GIN pays it. The same inverted
index that mapped words → reviews can map **keys and values → rows**:
`"tags": "eco"` becomes an index entry exactly like a word did.

## Concept

```sql
CREATE INDEX products_attributes_idx
  ON products USING gin (attributes);

-- or, tuned for containment only:
CREATE INDEX events_payload_idx
  ON events USING gin (payload jsonb_path_ops);
```

- Plain `gin (col)` (the `jsonb_ops` default) indexes every key and
  every value separately; it supports `@>`, `?` (key exists), `?|`,
  `?&`.
- `jsonb_path_ops` indexes *hashed paths* (key-chain + value): only
  supports `@>` — but the index is substantially smaller and faster
  for it. Choosing it is you telling the database "containment is the
  only question I ask this column". For a 3-million-row clickstream,
  that trade is obviously right.
- What GIN doesn't accelerate: `payload ->> 'value' > 995`-style
  *range* predicates on extracted fields. For those, lesson 40 already
  gave you the answer — a B-tree **expression index** on
  `((payload ->> 'value')::int)`. Different question, different tree.
- Build cost is real: GIN on the events payloads takes on the order of
  a minute. Feel it once here, budget for it forever after.

## Exercise 1 — tag containment

`ex1/solution.sql` (provided) — every product tagged both `eco` and
`limited`:

```sql
SELECT id
FROM products
WHERE attributes @> '{"tags": ["eco", "limited"]}';
```

Edit `ex1/indexes.sql`: a GIN index on `attributes` (plain ops are
fine here — merchandising also asks `?`-style questions).

Run: `uv run dojo test 42_gin_jsonb ex1`

## Exercise 2 — needle in the clickstream

`ex2/solution.sql` (provided) — every event that touched product 4242's
page:

```sql
SELECT id
FROM events
WHERE payload @> '{"path": "/p/4242"}';
```

Edit `ex2/indexes.sql` — use `jsonb_path_ops`, and expect the build to
take a minute (3M payloads). ~300 rows out of 3,000,000: this is GIN's
home game.

Run: `uv run dojo test 42_gin_jsonb ex2`

## Exercise 3 — two keys at once

`ex3/solution.sql` (provided) finds a specific variant:

```sql
SELECT id, name
FROM products
WHERE attributes @> '{"color": "red", "size": "xl"}';
```

Edit `ex3/indexes.sql` with a GIN index on the whole `attributes` column.

One containment test, two keys, one index — and note what you did *not*
have to do: name the keys when creating the index. A GIN index over a JSONB
column indexes every key and value in every document, so it serves
containment queries for combinations nobody anticipated. That generality is
its entire selling point over lesson 40's expression index, which serves
exactly one expression and nothing else.

The price is size and write cost: a GIN index over a document column is
typically several times larger than a B-tree over one extracted key.

This gate checks your rows and that the index exists — it does **not**
demand a particular plan, and that is deliberate. `products` has only ten
thousand rows, and on a table that small a sequential scan is often the
cheapest plan even with a perfect index available. Insisting on an index
scan here would be asserting a fact about the table's size rather than about
your index. Exercise 4 makes the same point on three million rows, where the
planner has no such luxury.

Run: `uv run dojo test 42_gin_jsonb ex3`

## Exercise 4 — the smaller operator class

`ex4/solution.sql` (provided) searches three million clickstream
payloads:

```sql
SELECT id, ts
FROM events
WHERE payload @> '{"value": 999}';
```

Edit `ex4/indexes.sql` and build the GIN index with the
**`jsonb_path_ops`** operator class:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ... ON events USING gin (payload jsonb_path_ops);
```

The default operator class, `jsonb_ops`, indexes every key *and* every
value separately, which lets it serve key-existence operators (`?`, `?|`,
`?&`) as well as containment. `jsonb_path_ops` indexes only hashes of
complete paths — so it supports `@>` and nothing else, and in exchange it
is substantially smaller and often faster for the containment queries that
are most of what anyone actually runs.

Choosing an operator class is the most PostgreSQL-specific thing in Part 5,
and the principle generalises: an index is a data structure plus a set of
operators it can answer. Match both to your query.

Run: `uv run dojo test 42_gin_jsonb ex4`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 42_gin_jsonb

JSONB's containment operator and GIN were designed for each other. Together
they let a document column be queried at speed without giving up the
flexibility that made you choose a document column in the first place.

## Notes

**Why `@>` is the operator to build around.** `attributes @> '{"color":
"red"}'` asks whether the left document contains the right one — at any
depth, and inside arrays, so `@> '{"tags": ["eco"]}'` means "tags includes
eco". It is one operator that expresses most of what people want from a
document column, and it is the one GIN accelerates. Expressing JSONB
predicates as containment rather than as `->>` comparisons is the habit that
makes them indexable.

**A GIN index over JSONB indexes the contents, not the value.** For each
document it extracts keys and values and records which rows contain each
one. Querying is then an intersection of posting lists. Crucially, you did
not have to name the keys at index-creation time — which is what makes it
work for documents whose shape varies by row.

**Two operator classes.** `jsonb_ops` (the default) indexes every key and
every value separately, supporting `@>`, `?`, `?|`, `?&` and the path
operators. `jsonb_path_ops` indexes hashes of complete paths, supporting
only `@>` — and is typically several times smaller and faster for it. Use
`jsonb_path_ops` when containment is all you need, which is most of the
time.

**GIN versus an expression index.** Lesson 40's `CREATE INDEX ON events
((payload ->> 'value')::int)` is narrow and precise: one key, stored as a
proper type, serving equality *and ranges* and *ordering*. A GIN index is
broad: any key, containment only, no ranges, no ordering. They are
complementary, and real schemas frequently have both — a GIN index for the
open-ended queries and a B-tree on the two keys that are queried
constantly.

**GIN cannot do ranges or ordering.** `WHERE (payload ->> 'value')::int >
500` gets nothing from a GIN index no matter how it is written, because the
index stores an unordered inverted list. If you need ranges on a key, you
need a B-tree on the extracted expression.

**Cost.** A GIN index over a document column is large — often a significant
fraction of the table — and slower to update than a B-tree, because one row
change touches many posting lists. The pending-list mechanism
(`fastupdate`) softens the write cost and adds a first-query penalty after
a burst of inserts.

**The design question does not go away.** Indexing JSONB well makes it
*fast*; it does not make it *typed*. There is still no constraint stopping a
row from storing `"color": 5`, no foreign key on a tag, and no error when a
key is misspelled on write. Lesson 19's smell test stands: keys you know in
advance and query constantly are columns.

## ex1 — tag containment

Array containment, which is the case people most often assume they need a
separate table for. Note the query is unchanged from lesson 19 — the index
changed what it costs, not what it means.

## ex2 — needle in the clickstream

Three million documents, and the GIN index turns a full scan into a posting-
list lookup. Check the index's size with
`pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('...'))` and compare it against the table;
that ratio is the price of the generality.

## ex3 — two keys at once

One containment test, two keys, and — the part worth noticing — an index
that was built without knowing which keys would be queried. Try a
combination the exercise never mentions in the lab; it is fast too.

## ex4 — the smaller operator class

The operator-class decision, made explicitly. Build both versions in the lab
and compare `pg_relation_size` — `jsonb_path_ops` is usually a good deal
smaller. Then try a `?` key-existence query against it and watch it go
unused: you traded operators for size, deliberately.

## Further reading

- [JSON Types — `jsonb` Indexing](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-json.html) — the containment semantics and the two operator classes, with size comparisons.
- [JSON Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-json.html) — `@>`, `?`, `#>`, and the SQL/JSON path operators `@?` and `@@`.
- [GIN Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/gin.html) — the inverted-index internals, operator classes, and `fastupdate`.
- [Indexes on Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-expressional.html) — the complementary approach from lesson 40; most real schemas want both.

Edit `ex4/indexes.sql` and build the GIN index with the
**`jsonb_path_ops`** operator class:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ... ON events USING gin (payload jsonb_path_ops);
```

The default operator class, `jsonb_ops`, indexes every key *and* every
value separately, which lets it serve key-existence operators (`?`, `?|`,
`?&`) as well as containment. `jsonb_path_ops` indexes only hashes of
complete paths — so it supports `@>` and nothing else, and in exchange it
is substantially smaller and often faster for the containment queries that
are most of what anyone actually runs.

Choosing an operator class is the most PostgreSQL-specific thing in Part 5,
and the principle generalises: an index is a data structure plus a set of
operators it can answer. Match both to your query.

## The teaching point

The jsonb-column lifecycle in production: it starts as "flexible
extras", then one key becomes load-bearing, queries pile onto it, and
someone adds a GIN over the whole column — 10x bigger than needed and
slow to write. The craft is matching index to question: `@>` on the
whole document → GIN (path_ops if that's all); hot *scalar* field →
expression B-tree on the extraction; hot enough to constrain → promote
it to a real column (lesson 19's smell test, closing the loop). JSONB
is schema you haven't admitted to yet; index it like you mean it.

# Reading - 42_gin_jsonb

JSONB's containment operator and GIN were designed for each other. Together
they let a document column be queried at speed without giving up the
flexibility that made you choose a document column in the first place.

## Notes

**Why `@>` is the operator to build around.** `attributes @> '{"color":
"red"}'` asks whether the left document contains the right one — at any
depth, and inside arrays, so `@> '{"tags": ["eco"]}'` means "tags includes
eco". It is one operator that expresses most of what people want from a
document column, and it is the one GIN accelerates. Expressing JSONB
predicates as containment rather than as `->>` comparisons is the habit that
makes them indexable.

**A GIN index over JSONB indexes the contents, not the value.** For each
document it extracts keys and values and records which rows contain each
one. Querying is then an intersection of posting lists. Crucially, you did
not have to name the keys at index-creation time — which is what makes it
work for documents whose shape varies by row.

**Two operator classes.** `jsonb_ops` (the default) indexes every key and
every value separately, supporting `@>`, `?`, `?|`, `?&` and the path
operators. `jsonb_path_ops` indexes hashes of complete paths, supporting
only `@>` — and is typically several times smaller and faster for it. Use
`jsonb_path_ops` when containment is all you need, which is most of the
time.

**GIN versus an expression index.** Lesson 40's `CREATE INDEX ON events
((payload ->> 'value')::int)` is narrow and precise: one key, stored as a
proper type, serving equality *and ranges* and *ordering*. A GIN index is
broad: any key, containment only, no ranges, no ordering. They are
complementary, and real schemas frequently have both — a GIN index for the
open-ended queries and a B-tree on the two keys that are queried
constantly.

**GIN cannot do ranges or ordering.** `WHERE (payload ->> 'value')::int >
500` gets nothing from a GIN index no matter how it is written, because the
index stores an unordered inverted list. If you need ranges on a key, you
need a B-tree on the extracted expression.

**Cost.** A GIN index over a document column is large — often a significant
fraction of the table — and slower to update than a B-tree, because one row
change touches many posting lists. The pending-list mechanism
(`fastupdate`) softens the write cost and adds a first-query penalty after
a burst of inserts.

**The design question does not go away.** Indexing JSONB well makes it
*fast*; it does not make it *typed*. There is still no constraint stopping a
row from storing `"color": 5`, no foreign key on a tag, and no error when a
key is misspelled on write. Lesson 19's smell test stands: keys you know in
advance and query constantly are columns.

## ex1 — tag containment

Array containment, which is the case people most often assume they need a
separate table for. Note the query is unchanged from lesson 19 — the index
changed what it costs, not what it means.

## ex2 — needle in the clickstream

Three million documents, and the GIN index turns a full scan into a posting-
list lookup. Check the index's size with
`pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('...'))` and compare it against the table;
that ratio is the price of the generality.

## ex3 — two keys at once

One containment test, two keys, and — the part worth noticing — an index
that was built without knowing which keys would be queried. Try a
combination the exercise never mentions in the lab; it is fast too.

## ex4 — the smaller operator class

The operator-class decision, made explicitly. Build both versions in the lab
and compare `pg_relation_size` — `jsonb_path_ops` is usually a good deal
smaller. Then try a `?` key-existence query against it and watch it go
unused: you traded operators for size, deliberately.

## Further reading

- [JSON Types — `jsonb` Indexing](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-json.html) — the containment semantics and the two operator classes, with size comparisons.
- [JSON Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-json.html) — `@>`, `?`, `#>`, and the SQL/JSON path operators `@?` and `@@`.
- [GIN Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/gin.html) — the inverted-index internals, operator classes, and `fastupdate`.
- [Indexes on Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-expressional.html) — the complementary approach from lesson 40; most real schemas want both.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — two keys at once

`ex3/solution.sql` (provided) finds a specific variant:

```sql
SELECT id, name
FROM products
WHERE attributes @> '{"color": "red", "size": "xl"}';
```

Edit `ex3/indexes.sql` with a GIN index on the whole `attributes` column.

One containment test, two keys, one index — and note what you did *not*
have to do: name the keys when creating the index. A GIN index over a JSONB
column indexes every key and value in every document, so it serves
containment queries for combinations nobody anticipated. That generality is
its entire selling point over lesson 40's expression index, which serves
exactly one expression and nothing else.

The price is size and write cost: a GIN index over a document column is
typically several times larger than a B-tree over one extracted key.

This gate checks your rows and that the index exists — it does **not**
demand a particular plan, and that is deliberate. `products` has only ten
thousand rows, and on a table that small a sequential scan is often the
cheapest plan even with a perfect index available. Insisting on an index
scan here would be asserting a fact about the table's size rather than about
your index. Exercise 4 makes the same point on three million rows, where the
planner has no such luxury.

## Exercise 4 — the smaller operator class

`ex4/solution.sql` (provided) searches three million clickstream
payloads:

```sql
SELECT id, ts
FROM events
WHERE payload @> '{"value": 999}';
```

Edit `ex4/indexes.sql` and build the GIN index with the
**`jsonb_path_ops`** operator class:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ... ON events USING gin (payload jsonb_path_ops);
```

The default operator class, `jsonb_ops`, indexes every key *and* every
value separately, which lets it serve key-existence operators (`?`, `?|`,
`?&`) as well as containment. `jsonb_path_ops` indexes only hashes of
complete paths — so it supports `@>` and nothing else, and in exchange it
is substantially smaller and often faster for the containment queries that
are most of what anyone actually runs.

Choosing an operator class is the most PostgreSQL-specific thing in Part 5,
and the principle generalises: an index is a data structure plus a set of
operators it can answer. Match both to your query.

lessons.briefing:
# 43 — BRIN (and a wave at GiST)

`events.ts` has a property no other column here has: it's **physically
correlated** with row order — the seed appends events in time order,
one per second, so page 1 holds the oldest timestamps and the last
page the newest. A B-tree on it works fine... and stores an entry for
every one of 3 million rows to do it. **BRIN** (Block Range INdex)
exploits the correlation instead: per *range of pages*, store just the
min and max `ts`. A time-range query skips every page range whose
min/max can't overlap. The index is a rounding error in size.

## Concept

```sql
CREATE INDEX events_ts_brin_idx ON events USING brin (ts);
```

- BRIN only works when value order ≈ physical order (check
  `pg_stats.correlation` — near 1.0 is BRIN country). Append-only
  logs, event streams, IoT: perfect. A column like `orders.total`
  (values scattered everywhere): useless — every page range spans the
  whole domain and nothing prunes.
- The plan shape is bitmap-flavored (lesson 38): `Bitmap Heap Scan`
  over a `Bitmap Index Scan` on the BRIN, with lossy blocks rechecked.
  More rechecking than a B-tree; unbeatable size-per-usefulness.
- **GiST**, the other specialist family, gets an honest wave rather
  than an exercise: it generalizes trees to *overlapping* regions —
  geometric shapes, ranges (`tstzrange` — "no double-booking"
  exclusion constraints!), nearest-neighbor `ORDER BY point <-> ?`.
  PostGIS runs on it. File it under "know it exists"; reach for it
  when your predicate is *contains / overlaps / nearest*, not equals.

## Exercise 1 — BRIN the clickstream

`ex1/solution.sql` (provided) — one hour of traffic:

```sql
SELECT count(*)
FROM events
WHERE ts >= '2023-11-14 00:00+00'
  AND ts < '2023-11-14 01:00+00';
```

Edit `ex1/indexes.sql`: the BRIN index. The gate wants no Seq Scan and
8x — which a 48 KB index will deliver over 3 million rows, because the
data cooperates.

Run: `uv run dojo test 43_gist_brin ex1`

## Exercise 2 — weigh both trees

`ex2/indexes.sql`: create **both** a B-tree and the BRIN on
`events.ts`, named exactly `events_ts_btree_idx` and
`events_ts_brin_idx`. `ex2/solution.sql` then answers with a query
(copy it in):

```sql
SELECT pg_relation_size('events_ts_btree_idx') >
       50 * pg_relation_size('events_ts_brin_idx');
```

Expected answer: `true` — the B-tree is not 2x or 10x but *hundreds* of
times larger. Check the actual sizes in the lab with
`pg_size_pretty()`; the number is worth having seen once.

Run: `uv run dojo test 43_gist_brin ex2`

## Exercise 3 — tune the block range

`ex3/solution.sql` (provided) takes a two-hour slice of the clickstream:

```sql
SELECT count(*)
FROM events
WHERE ts >= '2023-11-13 08:00+00'
  AND ts < '2023-11-13 10:00+00';
```

Edit `ex3/indexes.sql` and build a BRIN index with a **smaller block
range**:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ... ON events USING brin (ts) WITH (pages_per_range = 32);
```

The default is 128 pages per summarised range. Fewer pages per range means
more, finer summaries: a bigger index (still tiny — kilobytes, not
gigabytes) that can exclude more of the table for a narrow query. More
pages per range means a smaller index that is coarser and re-reads more
data.

This is the whole BRIN tuning knob, and the trade-off is unusually easy to
reason about: narrow queries want small ranges, wide queries do not care.

Run: `uv run dojo test 43_gist_brin ex3`

## Exercise 4 — the rows your BRIN cannot see

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. This one is about operating a BRIN, not building
one.

The gate builds `events_ts_brin_new_idx` for you, then inserts **30,000 new
events behind the index's back**. Your job is the one statement that makes
those rows visible to it.

Here is the trap. A BRIN stores one summary per block range, and PostgreSQL
does **not** summarise a range the moment rows land in it — that would mean
touching the index on every insert, which is precisely the cost BRIN exists
to avoid. New pages stay unsummarised until `VACUUM` runs, or until somebody
calls the function that does it explicitly. Until then the index cannot
exclude them, so every query has to read them all.

That is why a BRIN on a freshly loaded table often looks like it "isn't
working": it is working exactly as designed, on the ranges it knows about.
The fixes are to summarise after a bulk load, or to create the index `WITH
(autosummarize = on)` so vacuum does it as it goes.

Your statement must return the number of ranges it summarised — the
function does that for you.

**A note on the exercise this replaced.** An earlier draft asked you to BRIN
`events.id` to show that BRIN cares about physical correlation rather than
about time. That is true — but `events.id` is the table's **primary key**,
so it already has a B-tree, and no BRIN can beat one. The point stands and
is worth testing yourself: `events.customer_id` is scattered across every
block range, so a BRIN on it can never exclude anything.
`pg_stats.correlation` is the number that tells you in advance, and checking
it before building a BRIN is the whole design process.

Run: `uv run dojo test 43_gist_brin ex4`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 43_gist_brin

B-trees are not the only index type, and the two in this lesson exist for
cases a B-tree serves badly: data with a shape (GiST) and data with an
order it already has on disk (BRIN).

## Notes

**BRIN summarises block ranges.** For every group of pages — 128 by default
— it stores the minimum and maximum value found there. Nothing else. To
answer a range query it walks that tiny summary, discards every range whose
min/max cannot overlap, and scans only the surviving pages. The index for a
three-million-row table is measured in **kilobytes**, against hundreds of
megabytes for a B-tree on the same column.

**It only works on correlated data.** If the values in each block range are
tightly clustered, most ranges can be excluded. If they are scattered — like
`customer_id` in a clickstream — every range's min/max spans the whole value
space, nothing is excluded, and the index does nothing while still costing
you maintenance. `pg_stats.correlation` (close to 1 or -1) is the number to
check before building one, and it is the entire design decision.

**The archetype.** Append-only, time-ordered tables: logs, events, metrics,
audit trails. Rows arrive in timestamp order and are never moved, so
physical order and timestamp order agree permanently. `events.ts` in this
database is strictly increasing with `id`, which is why both columns are
BRIN-friendly.

**BRIN is lossy by design.** It never identifies rows, only candidate pages,
so every BRIN plan is a `Bitmap Heap Scan` that rechecks each row. That is
fine when the ranges exclude 99% of the table and useless when they exclude
nothing.

**Tuning.** `pages_per_range` trades index size against precision — smaller
ranges give finer exclusion at slightly more space. New data is not
summarised until `VACUUM` runs or you call `brin_summarize_new_values()`,
so a BRIN index on a freshly loaded table can appear not to work.
`autosummarize = on` handles this automatically.

**Where B-trees still win.** Point lookups. A BRIN cannot find one row; it
can only narrow to a few thousand pages. If you need `WHERE ts = x` to
return one row instantly, that is a B-tree.

**GiST is a different idea entirely.** Where a B-tree indexes a total order,
GiST is a framework for indexing things that have *shape* — geometric
objects, ranges, full-text vectors, `pg_trgm` similarity. Its operators are
overlap (`&&`), containment (`@>`), and distance (`<->`), not less-than. Two
consequences worth knowing even without a geometric column: `EXCLUDE USING
gist (room WITH =, daterange(...) WITH &&)` is how you enforce
non-overlapping bookings (lesson 25), and `ORDER BY point <-> :target LIMIT
10` is a k-nearest-neighbour search executed *as an index scan* rather than
as a sort.

**The general lesson.** An index is a data structure plus a set of operators
it can answer. B-tree: ordered values, equality and range. Hash: equality
only. GIN: contents of a composite value, containment and membership. GiST:
shape, overlap and distance. BRIN: physical clustering, ranges over huge
tables. Choosing an index type is choosing which of those matches your
query.

## ex1 — BRIN the clickstream

A kilobyte-scale index over three million rows, answering a half-day range.
Compare `pg_relation_size` of this index with a B-tree on the same column —
the ratio is usually four or five orders of magnitude, and that is what
makes BRIN viable on tables where a B-tree would be unaffordable.

## ex2 — weigh both trees

Both indexes on the same column, so you can see the trade directly: the
B-tree is faster and enormous, the BRIN is slower and free. On a
hundred-billion-row event table, "free" wins.

## ex3 — tune the block range

`pages_per_range = 32` gives four times the summary detail for a two-hour
query. On a wider query it would make no measurable difference — which is
the honest version of most tuning knobs: they matter at one end of the
workload and not the other.

## ex4 — the rows your BRIN cannot see

The operational half of BRIN, and the reason people report that it "doesn't
work" after a bulk load. Summarisation is deliberately lazy: covering a
range the instant a row lands in it would mean touching the index on every
insert, which is the cost BRIN exists to avoid. So new pages sit
unsummarised — invisible to range exclusion — until `VACUUM` reaches them or
you call `brin_summarize_new_values()` yourself.

Two habits follow. Summarise (or vacuum) after any bulk load into a
BRIN-indexed table. And prefer `WITH (autosummarize = on)` when the table
grows continuously, so autovacuum keeps up without anyone remembering to.

The exercise this replaced is still worth doing in the lab, and the reason
it was replaced is instructive. It asked for a BRIN on `events.id` to show
that BRIN cares about *physical correlation* rather than about time — which
is true, except that `events.id` is the primary key and already has a
B-tree, so the comparison was rigged from the start. Run it on
`events.customer_id` instead: check `pg_stats.correlation` for `ts`, `id`
and `customer_id`, and you will see the rule before you run a single query.

## Further reading

- [BRIN Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/brin.html) — how block-range summaries work, `pages_per_range`, `autosummarize`, and the operator classes.
- [GiST Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/gist.html) — the extensible framework, its operators, and the k-nearest-neighbour support.
- [Range Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/rangetypes.html) — the `EXCLUDE USING gist` non-overlap constraint, in full.
- [Index Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-types.html) — the one-page summary of B-tree, hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN and BRIN, and what each can answer.

# 43 — BRIN (and a wave at GiST)

`events.ts` has a property no other column here has: it's **physically
correlated** with row order — the seed appends events in time order,
one per second, so page 1 holds the oldest timestamps and the last
page the newest. A B-tree on it works fine... and stores an entry for
every one of 3 million rows to do it. **BRIN** (Block Range INdex)
exploits the correlation instead: per *range of pages*, store just the
min and max `ts`. A time-range query skips every page range whose
min/max can't overlap. The index is a rounding error in size.

## Concept

```sql
CREATE INDEX events_ts_brin_idx ON events USING brin (ts);
```

- BRIN only works when value order ≈ physical order (check
  `pg_stats.correlation` — near 1.0 is BRIN country). Append-only
  logs, event streams, IoT: perfect. A column like `orders.total`
  (values scattered everywhere): useless — every page range spans the
  whole domain and nothing prunes.
- The plan shape is bitmap-flavored (lesson 38): `Bitmap Heap Scan`
  over a `Bitmap Index Scan` on the BRIN, with lossy blocks rechecked.
  More rechecking than a B-tree; unbeatable size-per-usefulness.
- **GiST**, the other specialist family, gets an honest wave rather
  than an exercise: it generalizes trees to *overlapping* regions —
  geometric shapes, ranges (`tstzrange` — "no double-booking"
  exclusion constraints!), nearest-neighbor `ORDER BY point <-> ?`.
  PostGIS runs on it. File it under "know it exists"; reach for it
  when your predicate is *contains / overlaps / nearest*, not equals.

## Exercise 1 — BRIN the clickstream

`ex1/solution.sql` (provided) — one hour of traffic:

```sql
SELECT count(*)
FROM events
WHERE ts >= '2023-11-14 00:00+00'
  AND ts < '2023-11-14 01:00+00';
```

Edit `ex1/indexes.sql`: the BRIN index. The gate wants no Seq Scan and
8x — which a 48 KB index will deliver over 3 million rows, because the
data cooperates.

Run: `uv run dojo test 43_gist_brin ex1`

## Exercise 2 — weigh both trees

`ex2/indexes.sql`: create **both** a B-tree and the BRIN on
`events.ts`, named exactly `events_ts_btree_idx` and
`events_ts_brin_idx`. `ex2/solution.sql` then answers with a query
(copy it in):

```sql
SELECT pg_relation_size('events_ts_btree_idx') >
       50 * pg_relation_size('events_ts_brin_idx');
```

Expected answer: `true` — the B-tree is not 2x or 10x but *hundreds* of
times larger. Check the actual sizes in the lab with
`pg_size_pretty()`; the number is worth having seen once.

Run: `uv run dojo test 43_gist_brin ex2`

## Exercise 3 — tune the block range

`ex3/solution.sql` (provided) takes a two-hour slice of the clickstream:

```sql
SELECT count(*)
FROM events
WHERE ts >= '2023-11-13 08:00+00'
  AND ts < '2023-11-13 10:00+00';
```

Edit `ex3/indexes.sql` and build a BRIN index with a **smaller block
range**:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ... ON events USING brin (ts) WITH (pages_per_range = 32);
```

The default is 128 pages per summarised range. Fewer pages per range means
more, finer summaries: a bigger index (still tiny — kilobytes, not
gigabytes) that can exclude more of the table for a narrow query. More
pages per range means a smaller index that is coarser and re-reads more
data.

This is the whole BRIN tuning knob, and the trade-off is unusually easy to
reason about: narrow queries want small ranges, wide queries do not care.

Run: `uv run dojo test 43_gist_brin ex3`

## Exercise 4 — the rows your BRIN cannot see

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. This one is about operating a BRIN, not building
one.

The gate builds `events_ts_brin_new_idx` for you, then inserts **30,000 new
events behind the index's back**. Your job is the one statement that makes
those rows visible to it.

Here is the trap. A BRIN stores one summary per block range, and PostgreSQL
does **not** summarise a range the moment rows land in it — that would mean
touching the index on every insert, which is precisely the cost BRIN exists
to avoid. New pages stay unsummarised until `VACUUM` runs, or until somebody
calls the function that does it explicitly. Until then the index cannot
exclude them, so every query has to read them all.

That is why a BRIN on a freshly loaded table often looks like it "isn't
working": it is working exactly as designed, on the ranges it knows about.
The fixes are to summarise after a bulk load, or to create the index `WITH
(autosummarize = on)` so vacuum does it as it goes.

Your statement must return the number of ranges it summarised — the
function does that for you.

**A note on the exercise this replaced.** An earlier draft asked you to BRIN
`events.id` to show that BRIN cares about physical correlation rather than
about time. That is true — but `events.id` is the table's **primary key**,
so it already has a B-tree, and no BRIN can beat one. The point stands and
is worth testing yourself: `events.customer_id` is scattered across every
block range, so a BRIN on it can never exclude anything.
`pg_stats.correlation` is the number that tells you in advance, and checking
it before building a BRIN is the whole design process.

Run: `uv run dojo test 43_gist_brin ex4`

## The gate

```python
"""Gates for 43_gist_brin. Quoted verbatim in README.md.

Part 5's three-stage gate: correct rows -> right plan shape -> fast enough
against this machine's own cached baseline (data/baseline.json).
"""
import pytest

from dojo import db, grader, timing
from dojo.lesson import Lesson
from dojo.plan import explain

L = Lesson(__file__)


def test_ex1(lesson_db):
    ex = L.exercise("ex1")
    expected = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.expected_sql)
    baseline = timing.cached_baseline(lesson_db, f"{L.slug}::test_ex1",
                                      ex.expected_sql)
    ex.apply_indexes(lesson_db)
    actual = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_rows_equal(actual, expected)
    p = explain(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_plan(p, must_not_have=['Seq Scan'])
    measured = timing.measure_execution_ms(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_faster_than_baseline(measured, baseline, ratio=5)


def test_ex2(lesson_db):
    """Size comparison: indexes must exist BEFORE the probe can run."""
    ex = L.exercise("ex2")
    ex.apply_indexes(lesson_db)
    expected = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.expected_sql)
    actual = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_rows_equal(actual, expected)


def test_ex3(lesson_db):
    ex = L.exercise("ex3")
    expected = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.expected_sql)
    baseline = timing.cached_baseline(lesson_db, f"{L.slug}::test_ex3",
                                      ex.expected_sql)
    ex.apply_indexes(lesson_db)
    actual = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_rows_equal(actual, expected)
    p = explain(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_plan(p, must_not_have=['Seq Scan'])
    measured = timing.measure_execution_ms(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_faster_than_baseline(measured, baseline, ratio=8)


def test_ex4(lesson_db):
    """Rows that arrive after a BRIN is built are invisible to it until
    somebody summarises them. The gate builds the index, inserts behind its
    back, and asks the learner to close the gap."""
    ex = L.exercise("ex4")
    lesson_db.execute(
        "CREATE INDEX events_ts_brin_new_idx ON events USING brin (ts) "
        "WITH (pages_per_range = 4)")
    lesson_db.execute(
        "INSERT INTO events (id, customer_id, event_type, payload, ts) "
        "SELECT 90000000 + i, 1, 'view', '{}'::jsonb, "
        "       '2023-12-01'::timestamptz + i * interval '1 second' "
        "FROM generate_series(1, 30000) AS i")
    lesson_db.commit()

    returned = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    lesson_db.commit()

    assert returned and len(returned[0]) == 1, (
        "Your statement should return one value: the number of block ranges "
        "it summarised."
    )
    summarised = returned[0][0]
    assert isinstance(summarised, int) and summarised >= 20, (
        f"ONLY {summarised!r} RANGE(S) SUMMARISED: 30,000 rows were inserted "
        "after the index was built, which leaves many block ranges uncovered.\n"
        "  There is a function that summarises them; the index is named "
        "'events_ts_brin_new_idx'."
    )
    left = lesson_db.execute(
        "SELECT brin_summarize_new_values('events_ts_brin_new_idx')"
    ).fetchone()[0]
    assert left == 0, (
        f"{left} range(s) still unsummarised after your statement ran - it "
        "should have covered all of them."
    )
```

## The teaching point

BRIN is the index you retrofit onto the table everyone was afraid of:
the 2-billion-row events archive where a B-tree would take 50 GB you
don't have. It costs almost nothing to try (`CREATE INDEX ... USING
brin` builds fast, too). The prerequisite check is one query away —
`SELECT correlation FROM pg_stats WHERE tablename = '...' AND attname
= '...'` — and "is the data physically ordered by this column?" is a
question worth asking about every big time-series table you ever meet.

Next: **44_mvcc_vacuum_bloat** — where dead rows go, and who cleans up.

# Reading - 43_gist_brin

B-trees are not the only index type, and the two in this lesson exist for
cases a B-tree serves badly: data with a shape (GiST) and data with an
order it already has on disk (BRIN).

## Notes

**BRIN summarises block ranges.** For every group of pages — 128 by default
— it stores the minimum and maximum value found there. Nothing else. To
answer a range query it walks that tiny summary, discards every range whose
min/max cannot overlap, and scans only the surviving pages. The index for a
three-million-row table is measured in **kilobytes**, against hundreds of
megabytes for a B-tree on the same column.

**It only works on correlated data.** If the values in each block range are
tightly clustered, most ranges can be excluded. If they are scattered — like
`customer_id` in a clickstream — every range's min/max spans the whole value
space, nothing is excluded, and the index does nothing while still costing
you maintenance. `pg_stats.correlation` (close to 1 or -1) is the number to
check before building one, and it is the entire design decision.

**The archetype.** Append-only, time-ordered tables: logs, events, metrics,
audit trails. Rows arrive in timestamp order and are never moved, so
physical order and timestamp order agree permanently. `events.ts` in this
database is strictly increasing with `id`, which is why both columns are
BRIN-friendly.

**BRIN is lossy by design.** It never identifies rows, only candidate pages,
so every BRIN plan is a `Bitmap Heap Scan` that rechecks each row. That is
fine when the ranges exclude 99% of the table and useless when they exclude
nothing.

**Tuning.** `pages_per_range` trades index size against precision — smaller
ranges give finer exclusion at slightly more space. New data is not
summarised until `VACUUM` runs or you call `brin_summarize_new_values()`,
so a BRIN index on a freshly loaded table can appear not to work.
`autosummarize = on` handles this automatically.

**Where B-trees still win.** Point lookups. A BRIN cannot find one row; it
can only narrow to a few thousand pages. If you need `WHERE ts = x` to
return one row instantly, that is a B-tree.

**GiST is a different idea entirely.** Where a B-tree indexes a total order,
GiST is a framework for indexing things that have *shape* — geometric
objects, ranges, full-text vectors, `pg_trgm` similarity. Its operators are
overlap (`&&`), containment (`@>`), and distance (`<->`), not less-than. Two
consequences worth knowing even without a geometric column: `EXCLUDE USING
gist (room WITH =, daterange(...) WITH &&)` is how you enforce
non-overlapping bookings (lesson 25), and `ORDER BY point <-> :target LIMIT
10` is a k-nearest-neighbour search executed *as an index scan* rather than
as a sort.

**The general lesson.** An index is a data structure plus a set of operators
it can answer. B-tree: ordered values, equality and range. Hash: equality
only. GIN: contents of a composite value, containment and membership. GiST:
shape, overlap and distance. BRIN: physical clustering, ranges over huge
tables. Choosing an index type is choosing which of those matches your
query.

## ex1 — BRIN the clickstream

A kilobyte-scale index over three million rows, answering a half-day range.
Compare `pg_relation_size` of this index with a B-tree on the same column —
the ratio is usually four or five orders of magnitude, and that is what
makes BRIN viable on tables where a B-tree would be unaffordable.

## ex2 — weigh both trees

Both indexes on the same column, so you can see the trade directly: the
B-tree is faster and enormous, the BRIN is slower and free. On a
hundred-billion-row event table, "free" wins.

## ex3 — tune the block range

`pages_per_range = 32` gives four times the summary detail for a two-hour
query. On a wider query it would make no measurable difference — which is
the honest version of most tuning knobs: they matter at one end of the
workload and not the other.

## ex4 — the rows your BRIN cannot see

The operational half of BRIN, and the reason people report that it "doesn't
work" after a bulk load. Summarisation is deliberately lazy: covering a
range the instant a row lands in it would mean touching the index on every
insert, which is the cost BRIN exists to avoid. So new pages sit
unsummarised — invisible to range exclusion — until `VACUUM` reaches them or
you call `brin_summarize_new_values()` yourself.

Two habits follow. Summarise (or vacuum) after any bulk load into a
BRIN-indexed table. And prefer `WITH (autosummarize = on)` when the table
grows continuously, so autovacuum keeps up without anyone remembering to.

The exercise this replaced is still worth doing in the lab, and the reason
it was replaced is instructive. It asked for a BRIN on `events.id` to show
that BRIN cares about *physical correlation* rather than about time — which
is true, except that `events.id` is the primary key and already has a
B-tree, so the comparison was rigged from the start. Run it on
`events.customer_id` instead: check `pg_stats.correlation` for `ts`, `id`
and `customer_id`, and you will see the rule before you run a single query.

## Further reading

- [BRIN Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/brin.html) — how block-range summaries work, `pages_per_range`, `autosummarize`, and the operator classes.
- [GiST Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/gist.html) — the extensible framework, its operators, and the k-nearest-neighbour support.
- [Range Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/rangetypes.html) — the `EXCLUDE USING gist` non-overlap constraint, in full.
- [Index Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-types.html) — the one-page summary of B-tree, hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN and BRIN, and what each can answer.

## Exercise 3 — tune the block range

`ex3/solution.sql` (provided) takes a two-hour slice of the clickstream:

```sql
SELECT count(*)
FROM events
WHERE ts >= '2023-11-13 08:00+00'
  AND ts < '2023-11-13 10:00+00';
```

Edit `ex3/indexes.sql` and build a BRIN index with a **smaller block
range**:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ... ON events USING brin (ts) WITH (pages_per_range = 32);
```

The default is 128 pages per summarised range. Fewer pages per range means
more, finer summaries: a bigger index (still tiny — kilobytes, not
gigabytes) that can exclude more of the table for a narrow query. More
pages per range means a smaller index that is coarser and re-reads more
data.

This is the whole BRIN tuning knob, and the trade-off is unusually easy to
reason about: narrow queries want small ranges, wide queries do not care.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — the rows your BRIN cannot see

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. This one is about operating a BRIN, not building
one.

The gate builds `events_ts_brin_new_idx` for you, then inserts **30,000 new
events behind the index's back**. Your job is the one statement that makes
those rows visible to it.

Here is the trap. A BRIN stores one summary per block range, and PostgreSQL
does **not** summarise a range the moment rows land in it — that would mean
touching the index on every insert, which is precisely the cost BRIN exists
to avoid. New pages stay unsummarised until `VACUUM` runs, or until somebody
calls the function that does it explicitly. Until then the index cannot
exclude them, so every query has to read them all.

That is why a BRIN on a freshly loaded table often looks like it "isn't
working": it is working exactly as designed, on the ranges it knows about.
The fixes are to summarise after a bulk load, or to create the index `WITH
(autosummarize = on)` so vacuum does it as it goes.

Your statement must return the number of ranges it summarised — the
function does that for you.

**A note on the exercise this replaced.** An earlier draft asked you to BRIN
`events.id` to show that BRIN cares about physical correlation rather than
about time. That is true — but `events.id` is the table's **primary key**,
so it already has a B-tree, and no BRIN can beat one. The point stands and
is worth testing yourself: `events.customer_id` is scattered across every
block range, so a BRIN on it can never exclude anything.
`pg_stats.correlation` is the number that tells you in advance, and checking
it before building a BRIN is the whole design process.

lessons.briefing:
# 44 — MVCC, VACUUM, and bloat

Here is the secret that explains half of PostgreSQL's personality:
**UPDATE doesn't update and DELETE doesn't delete.** Under MVCC
(multi-version concurrency control), an UPDATE writes a *new* row
version and leaves the old one in place, invisible to new
transactions but still physically there — because a concurrent
transaction that started earlier may still need to see it. Readers
never block writers this way. The price: **dead tuples** — expired
versions nobody can see — accumulate until `VACUUM` reclaims them.
Unreclaimed, they are **bloat**: tables and indexes physically larger
than their live data, scans touching pages full of ghosts.

`setup.sql` gives you `bloat_orders` (100,000 rows, autovacuum off so
the janitor won't preempt your homework). The gate then UPDATEs every
row — instantly creating 100,000 dead tuples — and hands the mess to
your solution.

## Concept

```sql
SELECT n_live_tup, n_dead_tup, last_vacuum, last_autovacuum
FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'bloat_orders';

VACUUM bloat_orders;        -- reclaim dead tuples for reuse
VACUUM FULL bloat_orders;   -- rewrite the table compactly (EXCLUSIVE LOCK!)
```

- Plain `VACUUM`: marks dead space reusable, updates the visibility
  map (lesson 34's dependency!), never blocks reads/writes — but
  mostly does **not** shrink the file; space is recycled internally.
- `VACUUM FULL`: rewrites the whole table into a new compact file.
  Takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the duration — on a big
  production table that's an outage. It's the fire extinguisher, not
  the sprinkler system.
- **Autovacuum** is the sprinkler system: it watches dead-tuple
  counters and vacuums (and re-ANALYZEs — lesson 36's other shoe)
  automatically. Real tuning means making autovacuum keep *up* (more
  workers, lower thresholds on hot tables), not vacuuming by hand.
- Two prose-only pressure-relief valves worth knowing: **HOT updates**
  (an update that changes no indexed column can reuse space on the
  same page cheaply) and **fillfactor** (leave headroom per page so
  HOT has room to work). File under "why update-heavy tables get
  fillfactor 80".

## Exercise 1 — reclaim

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`: after the gate's mass UPDATE, make ≥90% of
the dead tuples go away. (One statement. Not the FULL one — no lock
justification here.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 44_mvcc_vacuum_bloat ex1`

## Exercise 2 — shrink

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`: this gate measures the table's **file size**
before and after your solution and requires a real shrink. Plain
VACUUM won't move that number — see the concept section for what will,
and note the lock you'd be paying in production.

Run: `uv run dojo test 44_mvcc_vacuum_bloat ex2`

## Exercise 3 — reclaim and resample in one pass

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. After the gate's mass `UPDATE`, `bloat_orders`
has ~100,000 dead tuples **and** statistics that describe the table as it
was before. Fix both with **one statement**.

`VACUUM` reclaims dead tuples. `ANALYZE` resamples statistics. `VACUUM
ANALYZE` does both in a single pass over the table, which is why it is the
standard thing to run after a bulk change — a mass update leaves you with
two problems, and running only the first one leaves the planner working
from a description of a table that no longer exists (lesson 36).

The gate checks that the dead tuples are gone *and* that fresh statistics
exist.

Run: `uv run dojo test 44_mvcc_vacuum_bloat ex3`

## Exercise 4 — indexes bloat too

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The mass `UPDATE` did not only bloat the table.
Every update wrote a new row version, and every new row version needed new
entries in every index — so `bloat_orders`'s indexes have roughly doubled
too, and a plain `VACUUM` does not compact them.

Write the **one statement** that rebuilds the table's indexes compactly.
The gate measures `pg_indexes_size('bloat_orders')` before and after and
requires a real shrink.

Two things worth knowing before you use it on something that matters. The
plain form takes an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock on the table for the whole
rebuild — an outage on a large index. `REINDEX ... CONCURRENTLY` (from
PostgreSQL 12) builds the replacement alongside the original and swaps it,
blocking almost nothing, at the cost of taking longer and being unable to
run inside a transaction block.

Run: `uv run dojo test 44_mvcc_vacuum_bloat ex4`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 44_mvcc_vacuum_bloat

PostgreSQL never overwrites a row. An `UPDATE` writes a new version and
marks the old one dead; a `DELETE` only marks. Everything in this lesson —
bloat, vacuum, long-transaction pathologies, wraparound — follows from that
one implementation choice, and so does the reason readers never block
writers.

## Notes

**MVCC in one paragraph.** Every row version carries the transaction ids
that created and deleted it. Every transaction takes a *snapshot* and sees
only the versions visible to it. So a reader never waits for a writer and a
writer never waits for a reader — the great practical virtue of the design —
and in exchange the table accumulates versions nobody can see any more.

**Dead tuples are the cost.** Update every row of a 100,000-row table and
you now have 200,000 row versions, half of them dead. The table has doubled
on disk, sequential scans read twice as much, and the cache holds half as
much useful data.

**`VACUUM` marks space reusable; it does not give it back.** Plain `VACUUM`
scans for dead tuples and records their space as free *within* the table, so
future inserts reuse it. The file on disk stays the same size. That is
normally exactly right: the table has reached its working size and shrinking
it would just mean growing it again.

**`VACUUM FULL` rewrites the table compactly and returns the space** — under
an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock for the entire rewrite, and needing enough free
disk for a second copy. It is an outage on a large table. `pg_repack` does
the same job online and is what production systems use.

**Autovacuum is doing this already,** triggered when dead tuples exceed a
fraction of the table (`autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor`, 20% by default).
Because it is proportional, a very large table can accumulate an enormous
absolute number of dead rows before autovacuum bothers — which is why big
tables often get per-table settings.

**`VACUUM` does three other jobs.** It updates the **visibility map**, which
is what makes index-only scans possible (lesson 34). It updates the **free
space map**. And it freezes old transaction ids to prevent **wraparound** —
a genuine emergency in which PostgreSQL will refuse writes to protect data.
An unvacuumable table is a countdown.

**The long-transaction pathology.** `VACUUM` may only remove versions no
running transaction could still need. One transaction left open for hours
pins the horizon and prevents cleanup *across the entire database*, including
tables it never touched. "Open a transaction, then wait on an HTTP call" is
the classic cause. `SELECT max(now() - xact_start) FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state <> 'idle'` is the query that finds it.

**Indexes bloat too, and differently.** Every new row version needs new
index entries. `VACUUM` marks index entries reusable but does not compact
the B-tree, so index bloat outlives table bloat. `REINDEX` rebuilds
compactly; `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY` does it without the outage.

**Where to look.** `pg_stat_user_tables` gives `n_dead_tup`, `last_vacuum`
and `last_autovacuum`. `pg_relation_size` and `pg_indexes_size` give the
sizes. Together they answer "is this table bloated, and is anything
cleaning it up?" — the two questions behind most mysterious slowdowns on
otherwise healthy systems.

## ex1 — reclaim

One word. Watch `n_dead_tup` fall to zero while `pg_relation_size` does not
move — that gap between "reclaimed" and "returned" is the whole distinction
between `VACUUM` and `VACUUM FULL`.

## ex2 — shrink

The file really shrinks, and the cost is the lock. Notice that the gate
could not have been written any other way: nothing except a full rewrite
moves that number, which is exactly why the operation needs scheduling
rather than improvising.

## ex3 — reclaim and resample in one pass

After a mass update you have two problems, and running only the first leaves
the planner reasoning about a table that no longer exists. `VACUUM ANALYZE`
is the habit to build for the end of any bulk load or migration.

## ex4 — indexes bloat too

The part people forget. Table bloat is visible in `pg_relation_size` and
gets fixed by autovacuum's ordinary work; index bloat is visible only in
`pg_indexes_size` and does not. On a table with a high update rate, a
periodic `REINDEX CONCURRENTLY` is routine maintenance, not an emergency
measure.

## Further reading

- [Routine Vacuuming](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/routine-vacuuming.html) — dead tuples, the visibility map, freezing, and transaction-id wraparound. The most operationally important chapter in the manual.
- [Concurrency Control (MVCC)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/mvcc.html) — why readers never block writers, and what a snapshot is.
- [`VACUUM`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-vacuum.html) and [`REINDEX`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-reindex.html) — the options, including `CONCURRENTLY` and what it does not lock.
- [Monitoring Statistics](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/monitoring-stats.html) — `pg_stat_user_tables`, for `n_dead_tup` and the last-vacuum timestamps.
