lessons.briefing:
# 48 — LATERAL joins

> **Part 7 — Advanced patterns (bonus).** You have finished the course. These
> three lessons cover patterns that don't fit the beginner-to-performance arc
> but that you will reach for constantly in real reporting work. No new gate
> machinery — just correctness gates, like Parts 1–2.

You already know how to get *one* aggregate per group (`GROUP BY`, lesson 07)
and how to rank rows *within* a group (window functions, lesson 15). But some
questions want neither: they want, for each group, a **whole small result
set** — "the three most expensive products in every category", "each
department's two top earners". A subquery could compute that for one category;
the trick is running it once *per* category and gluing the pieces together.

That is what `LATERAL` does. A normal subquery in `FROM` is self-contained —
it cannot see the other tables in the same `FROM`. A `LATERAL` subquery *can*:
it is evaluated once for each row produced on its left, with that row's columns
in scope. It turns a subquery into a per-row function call.

## Concept

```sql
SELECT c.category, t.name, t.price
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products) c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT name, price
    FROM products p
    WHERE p.category = c.category   -- references c — only legal because LATERAL
    ORDER BY price DESC, id
    LIMIT 3
) t;
```

Read it left to right: produce each distinct `category`; for **each** one, run
the parenthesised subquery with `c.category` bound to that value; the subquery
returns up to three rows; emit them. Without `LATERAL`, the `WHERE p.category =
c.category` reference to `c` is an error — the subquery would have no idea what
`c` is.

Things worth internalising:

- `CROSS JOIN LATERAL (…)` is the common form. `JOIN LATERAL (…) ON true` is
  the same thing. A set-returning function in `FROM` (like
  `jsonb_array_elements`) is *implicitly* lateral — it can already see earlier
  tables — so you rarely write the keyword there.
- The killer feature is a **`LIMIT` that runs per group**. Window functions
  rank rows but still hand you the whole partition; `LATERAL … LIMIT n` stops
  at `n` rows per driving row, which is both what you asked for and cheaper.
- If the lateral subquery returns no rows for some driving row, `CROSS JOIN`
  drops that driving row (like an inner join). Use `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (…) ON
  true` to keep it with NULLs.
- Order the subquery deterministically (`ORDER BY price DESC, id`) so "top n"
  is well defined when prices tie.

## Exercise 1 — top three products per category

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. For every product `category`, return the three most
expensive products in it: columns `category`, `name`, `price`. Six categories
× three = **18 rows**, any order. (Break price ties by `id` so exactly three
come back per category.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 48_lateral_joins ex1`

## Exercise 2 — each department's two top earners

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. For every `department` in `staff`, return the two
highest-paid people: columns `department`, `name`, `salary`. Five departments
× two = **10 rows**, any order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 48_lateral_joins ex2`

## Exercise 3 — each customer's two most recent orders

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. For every customer with `id <= 20`, return their
two most recent orders.

Columns, in this order: `customer_id`, `id` (the order's), `created_at`.
Any row order. (Customers 1–20 all have orders, so expect 40 rows.)

The shape is the same as exercise 1 with a different "top N per group", and
it is worth noticing what `LATERAL` buys here that `row_number()` does not:
the inner query runs **per customer** and stops after two rows, so with an
index on `(customer_id, created_at DESC)` it reads exactly forty index
entries. The window-function version numbers *every* order of all twenty
customers and then throws away all but two per group.

For small N over many groups, that difference is the whole reason `LATERAL`
exists.

Run: `uv run dojo test 48_lateral_joins ex3`

## Exercise 4 — LATERAL as an unpivot

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Turn each product's JSONB attributes into rows.
For products with `id <= 5`, produce one row per (product, attribute) pair
for the two scalar attributes `color` and `size`.

Columns, in this order: `id`, `attr` (the literal text `'color'` or
`'size'`), `value` (the extracted text). **10 rows** (5 products × 2
attributes), any order.

The idiom is lesson 17's unpivot:

```sql
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (VALUES ('color', attributes ->> 'color'),
                           ('size',  attributes ->> 'size')) AS v(attr, value)
```

An ordinary subquery in `FROM` cannot mention `attributes`, because
`FROM` items are evaluated independently. `LATERAL` lifts exactly that
restriction: it means "this `FROM` item may see the rows to its left".
Once you read it that way, `LATERAL` stops being a special join type and
becomes the obvious answer to *for each row, compute something*.

Run: `uv run dojo test 48_lateral_joins ex4`

## Challenge — average price of each category's five priciest (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. For every `category`, return `category` and
`avg_top5`: the average `price` of that category's five most expensive
products, rounded to 2 decimals. **6 rows**, any order.

Difficulty note: the ordering matters *before* the aggregate — you must pick
the five rows first, then average them. A single `AVG(...) GROUP BY category`
averages the entire category and is wrong. Nest a subquery inside the LATERAL.

Run: `uv run dojo test 48_lateral_joins challenge`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 48_lateral_joins

`LATERAL` means one thing: *this `FROM` item may reference the items to its
left*. Every use of it — top-N per group, per-row computation, unpivoting,
calling a set-returning function with a row's value — is that one rule
applied.

## Notes

**Why the restriction exists at all.** Items in a `FROM` clause are
conceptually evaluated independently and then joined, so a plain subquery in
`FROM` cannot see the other tables' columns. That is what makes join
reordering legal. `LATERAL` opts one item out of that rule: it is evaluated
once per row of what precedes it, like a correlated subquery that can return
many rows and many columns.

**`CROSS JOIN LATERAL` versus `LEFT JOIN LATERAL`.** With `CROSS JOIN
LATERAL`, an outer row whose subquery returns nothing **disappears** — it is
an inner join. `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (...) ON true` keeps it, NULL-extended.
For "top N per group", the difference is whether groups with no rows appear
at all, and it is lesson 09's mistake wearing a new costume.

**Top-N per group: three tools, and they are not interchangeable.**

- `row_number()` in a CTE (lesson 15): numbers *every* row, then discards.
  One pass, no index required, cost proportional to the whole table.
- `DISTINCT ON` (lesson 49): the N = 1 case, in three lines. Requires a sort
  by the partition key.
- `LATERAL`: runs a small query per group and stops at N. With a matching
  index, cost is proportional to *groups × N* rather than to the table.

For 6 categories × 5 rows, `LATERAL` reads 30 index entries where the window
version reads 10,000 rows. For a query that needs a rank *value* anyway, or
where there is no index to exploit, the window function wins. Knowing which
situation you are in is the point.

**Aggregates per row.** `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT count(*), sum(total)
FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) AS s ON true` computes several
aggregates for each customer in one subquery — where three scalar subqueries
in the SELECT list (lesson 13) would run three separate correlated queries.
Same answer, one traversal.

**Set-returning functions.** `FROM t, unnest(t.arr)` and
`FROM t, jsonb_array_elements(t.doc)` are implicitly lateral — PostgreSQL
allows the reference without the keyword when the item is a function call.
Writing `CROSS JOIN LATERAL` explicitly is clearer about what is happening.

**Reading a lateral plan.** It appears as a `Nested Loop` with the lateral
subquery on the inner side and `loops=` equal to the outer row count. That
is the cost model in one number, and it is also the warning: `LATERAL` over
a million outer rows with an unindexed inner query is a million small
queries.

## ex1 — top three products per category

Six outer rows, three inner rows each. The plan's `loops=6` is the whole
story — this is a correlated subquery that is allowed to return a table.

## ex2 — each department's two top earners

The same shape on a different pair of columns, which is the point of a rep.
Notice that the query reads almost exactly like the English sentence that
describes it: for each department, the two highest-paid people.

## ex3 — each customer's two most recent orders

Twenty groups, two rows each, and the version of this query that scales:
with an index on `(customer_id, created_at DESC)` the inner query is an
index scan that stops after two entries. Compare the plan against the
`row_number()` version from lesson 15 — same rows, very different work.

## ex4 — LATERAL as an unpivot

The lesson-17 idiom, and the clearest demonstration of the underlying rule:
the `VALUES` list references `p.attributes`, which is only legal because of
`LATERAL`. Once `LATERAL` reads as "may see the row to its left", this stops
looking like a trick.

## challenge — average price of each category's five priciest

An aggregate over a lateral subquery: the inner query produces five rows per
category, the outer one averages them. This is the composition that makes
`LATERAL` genuinely more expressive than `DISTINCT ON` — you can do
arbitrary work with the per-group rows, not just pick one.

## Further reading

- [`LATERAL` Subqueries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the "Table Expressions" chapter's `LATERAL` section, including the implicit-lateral rule for function calls.
- [`SELECT` — `FROM` clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — where `LATERAL` may appear and how it interacts with join types.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) — the other top-N-per-group tool, for the comparison in the notes.
- [Set Returning Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-srf.html) — `unnest`, `generate_series`, `jsonb_array_elements`: the functions most often used laterally.

# 48 — LATERAL joins

> **Part 7 — Advanced patterns (bonus).** You have finished the course. These
> three lessons cover patterns that don't fit the beginner-to-performance arc
> but that you will reach for constantly in real reporting work. No new gate
> machinery — just correctness gates, like Parts 1–2.

You already know how to get *one* aggregate per group (`GROUP BY`, lesson 07)
and how to rank rows *within* a group (window functions, lesson 15). But some
questions want neither: they want, for each group, a **whole small result
set** — "the three most expensive products in every category", "each
department's two top earners". A subquery could compute that for one category;
the trick is running it once *per* category and gluing the pieces together.

That is what `LATERAL` does. A normal subquery in `FROM` is self-contained —
it cannot see the other tables in the same `FROM`. A `LATERAL` subquery *can*:
it is evaluated once for each row produced on its left, with that row's columns
in scope. It turns a subquery into a per-row function call.

## Concept

```sql
SELECT c.category, t.name, t.price
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products) c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT name, price
    FROM products p
    WHERE p.category = c.category   -- references c — only legal because LATERAL
    ORDER BY price DESC, id
    LIMIT 3
) t;
```

Read it left to right: produce each distinct `category`; for **each** one, run
the parenthesised subquery with `c.category` bound to that value; the subquery
returns up to three rows; emit them. Without `LATERAL`, the `WHERE p.category =
c.category` reference to `c` is an error — the subquery would have no idea what
`c` is.

Things worth internalising:

- `CROSS JOIN LATERAL (…)` is the common form. `JOIN LATERAL (…) ON true` is
  the same thing. A set-returning function in `FROM` (like
  `jsonb_array_elements`) is *implicitly* lateral — it can already see earlier
  tables — so you rarely write the keyword there.
- The killer feature is a **`LIMIT` that runs per group**. Window functions
  rank rows but still hand you the whole partition; `LATERAL … LIMIT n` stops
  at `n` rows per driving row, which is both what you asked for and cheaper.
- If the lateral subquery returns no rows for some driving row, `CROSS JOIN`
  drops that driving row (like an inner join). Use `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (…) ON
  true` to keep it with NULLs.
- Order the subquery deterministically (`ORDER BY price DESC, id`) so "top n"
  is well defined when prices tie.

## Exercise 1 — top three products per category

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. For every product `category`, return the three most
expensive products in it: columns `category`, `name`, `price`. Six categories
× three = **18 rows**, any order. (Break price ties by `id` so exactly three
come back per category.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 48_lateral_joins ex1`

## Exercise 2 — each department's two top earners

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. For every `department` in `staff`, return the two
highest-paid people: columns `department`, `name`, `salary`. Five departments
× two = **10 rows**, any order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 48_lateral_joins ex2`

## Exercise 3 — each customer's two most recent orders

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. For every customer with `id <= 20`, return their
two most recent orders.

Columns, in this order: `customer_id`, `id` (the order's), `created_at`.
Any row order. (Customers 1–20 all have orders, so expect 40 rows.)

The shape is the same as exercise 1 with a different "top N per group", and
it is worth noticing what `LATERAL` buys here that `row_number()` does not:
the inner query runs **per customer** and stops after two rows, so with an
index on `(customer_id, created_at DESC)` it reads exactly forty index
entries. The window-function version numbers *every* order of all twenty
customers and then throws away all but two per group.

For small N over many groups, that difference is the whole reason `LATERAL`
exists.

Run: `uv run dojo test 48_lateral_joins ex3`

## Exercise 4 — LATERAL as an unpivot

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Turn each product's JSONB attributes into rows.
For products with `id <= 5`, produce one row per (product, attribute) pair
for the two scalar attributes `color` and `size`.

Columns, in this order: `id`, `attr` (the literal text `'color'` or
`'size'`), `value` (the extracted text). **10 rows** (5 products × 2
attributes), any order.

The idiom is lesson 17's unpivot:

```sql
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (VALUES ('color', attributes ->> 'color'),
                           ('size',  attributes ->> 'size')) AS v(attr, value)
```

An ordinary subquery in `FROM` cannot mention `attributes`, because
`FROM` items are evaluated independently. `LATERAL` lifts exactly that
restriction: it means "this `FROM` item may see the rows to its left".
Once you read it that way, `LATERAL` stops being a special join type and
becomes the obvious answer to *for each row, compute something*.

Run: `uv run dojo test 48_lateral_joins ex4`

## Challenge — average price of each category's five priciest (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. For every `category`, return `category` and
`avg_top5`: the average `price` of that category's five most expensive
products, rounded to 2 decimals. **6 rows**, any order.

Difficulty note: the ordering matters *before* the aggregate — you must pick
the five rows first, then average them. A single `AVG(...) GROUP BY category`
averages the entire category and is wrong. Nest a subquery inside the LATERAL.

Run: `uv run dojo test 48_lateral_joins challenge`

## The teaching point

The moment a requirement contains the words "top N per" or "the most recent
few per", reach for `LATERAL`. It is the clean answer to the top-N-per-group
problem that window functions solve awkwardly (rank, then filter in an outer
query) and correlated subqueries solve unreadably. It also composes: the
lateral subquery can join, aggregate, and limit — a whole query per driving
row. Query planners handle it well, especially when the inner table has an
index on the correlation column (a Part 5 idea: an index on
`products(category, price)` turns each lateral probe into a cheap index scan).

# Reading - 48_lateral_joins

`LATERAL` means one thing: *this `FROM` item may reference the items to its
left*. Every use of it — top-N per group, per-row computation, unpivoting,
calling a set-returning function with a row's value — is that one rule
applied.

## Notes

**Why the restriction exists at all.** Items in a `FROM` clause are
conceptually evaluated independently and then joined, so a plain subquery in
`FROM` cannot see the other tables' columns. That is what makes join
reordering legal. `LATERAL` opts one item out of that rule: it is evaluated
once per row of what precedes it, like a correlated subquery that can return
many rows and many columns.

**`CROSS JOIN LATERAL` versus `LEFT JOIN LATERAL`.** With `CROSS JOIN
LATERAL`, an outer row whose subquery returns nothing **disappears** — it is
an inner join. `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (...) ON true` keeps it, NULL-extended.
For "top N per group", the difference is whether groups with no rows appear
at all, and it is lesson 09's mistake wearing a new costume.

**Top-N per group: three tools, and they are not interchangeable.**

- `row_number()` in a CTE (lesson 15): numbers *every* row, then discards.
  One pass, no index required, cost proportional to the whole table.
- `DISTINCT ON` (lesson 49): the N = 1 case, in three lines. Requires a sort
  by the partition key.
- `LATERAL`: runs a small query per group and stops at N. With a matching
  index, cost is proportional to *groups × N* rather than to the table.

For 6 categories × 5 rows, `LATERAL` reads 30 index entries where the window
version reads 10,000 rows. For a query that needs a rank *value* anyway, or
where there is no index to exploit, the window function wins. Knowing which
situation you are in is the point.

**Aggregates per row.** `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT count(*), sum(total)
FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) AS s ON true` computes several
aggregates for each customer in one subquery — where three scalar subqueries
in the SELECT list (lesson 13) would run three separate correlated queries.
Same answer, one traversal.

**Set-returning functions.** `FROM t, unnest(t.arr)` and
`FROM t, jsonb_array_elements(t.doc)` are implicitly lateral — PostgreSQL
allows the reference without the keyword when the item is a function call.
Writing `CROSS JOIN LATERAL` explicitly is clearer about what is happening.

**Reading a lateral plan.** It appears as a `Nested Loop` with the lateral
subquery on the inner side and `loops=` equal to the outer row count. That
is the cost model in one number, and it is also the warning: `LATERAL` over
a million outer rows with an unindexed inner query is a million small
queries.

## ex1 — top three products per category

Six outer rows, three inner rows each. The plan's `loops=6` is the whole
story — this is a correlated subquery that is allowed to return a table.

## ex2 — each department's two top earners

The same shape on a different pair of columns, which is the point of a rep.
Notice that the query reads almost exactly like the English sentence that
describes it: for each department, the two highest-paid people.

## ex3 — each customer's two most recent orders

Twenty groups, two rows each, and the version of this query that scales:
with an index on `(customer_id, created_at DESC)` the inner query is an
index scan that stops after two entries. Compare the plan against the
`row_number()` version from lesson 15 — same rows, very different work.

## ex4 — LATERAL as an unpivot

The lesson-17 idiom, and the clearest demonstration of the underlying rule:
the `VALUES` list references `p.attributes`, which is only legal because of
`LATERAL`. Once `LATERAL` reads as "may see the row to its left", this stops
looking like a trick.

## challenge — average price of each category's five priciest

An aggregate over a lateral subquery: the inner query produces five rows per
category, the outer one averages them. This is the composition that makes
`LATERAL` genuinely more expressive than `DISTINCT ON` — you can do
arbitrary work with the per-group rows, not just pick one.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — average price of each category's five priciest (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. For every `category`, return `category` and
`avg_top5`: the average `price` of that category's five most expensive
products, rounded to 2 decimals. **6 rows**, any order.

Difficulty note: the ordering matters *before* the aggregate — you must pick
the five rows first, then average them. A single `AVG(...) GROUP BY category`
averages the entire category and is wrong. Nest a subquery inside the LATERAL.

Run: `uv run dojo test 48_lateral_joins challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two things have to happen per category and in this order: first pick the five
most expensive products, *then* average their prices. You cannot do that with
one flat `AVG(...) ... GROUP BY category` — an aggregate over the whole
category averages all ~1,600 rows, not just the top five. You need a per-group
`LIMIT` before the average, which means a lateral subquery.

## Hint 2
Nest two subqueries inside the LATERAL: the inner one selects the five
highest prices for the current category (`ORDER BY price DESC, id LIMIT 5`),
and the outer one averages them.

```sql
... CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT avg(price) FROM (
        SELECT price FROM products p
        WHERE p.category = c.category
        ORDER BY price DESC, id LIMIT 5
    ) x
) t
```

## Hint 3
Wrap it up: `SELECT c.category, round(t.avg_top5, 2)` and give the inner
`avg(price)` the alias `avg_top5`. Round to 2 decimals so the numbers line up
with the gate.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Two things have to happen per category and in this order: first pick the five
most expensive products, *then* average their prices. You cannot do that with
one flat `AVG(...) ... GROUP BY category` — an aggregate over the whole
category averages all ~1,600 rows, not just the top five. You need a per-group
`LIMIT` before the average, which means a lateral subquery.

## Hint 2
Nest two subqueries inside the LATERAL: the inner one selects the five
highest prices for the current category (`ORDER BY price DESC, id LIMIT 5`),
and the outer one averages them.

```sql
... CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT avg(price) FROM (
        SELECT price FROM products p
        WHERE p.category = c.category
        ORDER BY price DESC, id LIMIT 5
    ) x
) t
```

## Hint 3
Wrap it up: `SELECT c.category, round(t.avg_top5, 2)` and give the inner
`avg(price)` the alias `avg_top5`. Round to 2 decimals so the numbers line up
with the gate.

references.solution.sql:
-- 48_lateral_joins/challenge reference
SELECT c.category, round(t.avg_top5, 2) AS avg_top5
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products) AS c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT avg(price) AS avg_top5
    FROM (
        SELECT price
        FROM products p
        WHERE p.category = c.category
        ORDER BY price DESC, id
        LIMIT 5
    ) AS top5
) AS t;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Same shape as exercise 1, on a different table: the two highest-paid people
*in each department*. The per-group `LIMIT 2` is the tell that you want a
lateral subquery.

## Hint 2
Drive the query from the distinct departments and join each to a lateral
subquery filtered to that department, ordered by salary descending, limited
to two rows.

## Hint 3
```sql
SELECT d.department, t.name, t.salary
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT department FROM staff) d
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT name, salary FROM staff s
    WHERE s.department = d.department
    ORDER BY salary DESC, id
    LIMIT 2
) t;
```

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — each customer's two most recent orders

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. For every customer with `id <= 20`, return their
two most recent orders.

Columns, in this order: `customer_id`, `id` (the order's), `created_at`.
Any row order. (Customers 1–20 all have orders, so expect 40 rows.)

The shape is the same as exercise 1 with a different "top N per group", and
it is worth noticing what `LATERAL` buys here that `row_number()` does not:
the inner query runs **per customer** and stops after two rows, so with an
index on `(customer_id, created_at DESC)` it reads exactly forty index
entries. The window-function version numbers *every* order of all twenty
customers and then throws away all but two per group.

For small N over many groups, that difference is the whole reason `LATERAL`
exists.

Run: `uv run dojo test 48_lateral_joins ex3`

## Exercise 4 — LATERAL as an unpivot

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Turn each product's JSONB attributes into rows.
For products with `id <= 5`, produce one row per (product, attribute) pair
for the two scalar attributes `color` and `size`.

Columns, in this order: `id`, `attr` (the literal text `'color'` or
`'size'`), `value` (the extracted text). **10 rows** (5 products × 2
attributes), any order.

The idiom is lesson 17's unpivot:

```sql
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (VALUES ('color', attributes ->> 'color'),
                           ('size',  attributes ->> 'size')) AS v(attr, value)
```

An ordinary subquery in `FROM` cannot mention `attributes`, because
`FROM` items are evaluated independently. `LATERAL` lifts exactly that
restriction: it means "this `FROM` item may see the rows to its left".
Once you read it that way, `LATERAL` stops being a special join type and
becomes the obvious answer to *for each row, compute something*.

lessons.briefing:
# 49 — DISTINCT ON

You have already solved "one row per group" three different ways: a correlated
subquery (lesson 13), and `row_number() ... = 1` filtered in a CTE (lesson 15).
Both work everywhere. But Postgres ships a shortcut that is shorter than either
and, for this exact job, usually faster: `DISTINCT ON`.

`DISTINCT ON (expr)` keeps the **first row of each distinct value of `expr`**,
and "first" is decided by the query's `ORDER BY`. That is the whole idea — and
also the whole footgun. If your `ORDER BY` doesn't start with the `DISTINCT ON`
expression, Postgres rejects it; if it does, whatever you sort by *next*
decides which row survives each group.

## Concept

```sql
-- the newest order for each customer
SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id)
       customer_id, id, created_at
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer_id, created_at DESC;
```

`ORDER BY customer_id` groups the scan; within each customer, `created_at
DESC` puts the newest order first; `DISTINCT ON (customer_id)` keeps that first
row and discards the rest of the customer's orders. Change `DESC` to `ASC` and
you get each customer's *first* order instead — the selection rule lives
entirely in the `ORDER BY`.

Details that bite:

- **The `ORDER BY` must lead with the `DISTINCT ON` column(s).** `DISTINCT ON
  (category) ... ORDER BY price` is a syntax error. `... ORDER BY category,
  price` is correct.
- Add a **tie-break** (`, id`) when the sort key can repeat within a group, or
  which row you keep is arbitrary and can change between runs.
- The result comes out sorted by the `DISTINCT ON` columns. If you want it
  presented in some *other* order, wrap it in a subquery and sort outside
  (that's the challenge).
- `DISTINCT ON` is PostgreSQL-specific. The portable equivalent is the
  `row_number() = 1` idiom; reach for that if the query must run on another
  database.

## Exercise 1 — the cheapest product in each category

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. One row per `category`: the product with the lowest
`price`. Columns `category`, `name`, `price`. **6 rows**, any order. (Break
price ties by `id`.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 49_distinct_on ex1`

## Exercise 2 — each department's newest hire

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. One row per `department`: the most recently hired
person. Columns `department`, `name`, `hired_on`. **5 rows**, any order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 49_distinct_on ex2`

## Exercise 3 — each customer's first order

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. For every customer with `id <= 30`, their
**earliest** order.

Columns, in this order: `customer_id`, `id` (the order's), `created_at`.
Any row order. (30 rows.)

Same construct, opposite direction. The rule that makes `DISTINCT ON` work
is unchanged: the `ORDER BY` must **start with** the `DISTINCT ON`
expressions, and whatever comes after them decides which row survives per
group. Here that means `ORDER BY customer_id, created_at ASC, id ASC` —
earliest first, with `id` as a deterministic tie-break.

Get the leading columns wrong and PostgreSQL raises an error rather than
guessing, which is one of the friendlier things about this feature.

Run: `uv run dojo test 49_distinct_on ex3`

## Exercise 4 — the best review of each product

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. For each product with `id <= 20`, the
**highest-rated** review of that product.

Columns, in this order: `product_id`, `id` (the review's), `rating`. Any
row order. (20 rows.)

Ties matter here in a way they did not before: ratings are integers from 1
to 5 over a thousand-odd reviews per product, so a product will have many
5-star reviews and the "best" one is genuinely ambiguous. Break the tie on
`id` ascending so the answer is deterministic.

That is worth generalising. `DISTINCT ON` always returns exactly one row per
group, so *something* decides which — and if you do not say what, PostgreSQL
picks whichever row the sort happened to place first, which can differ
between runs. A `DISTINCT ON` query without a tie-break is a query with a
bug that has not surfaced yet.

Run: `uv run dojo test 49_distinct_on ex4`

## Challenge — priciest per category, ranked (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. The most expensive product in each `category` —
columns `category`, `name`, `price` — but the result must be **ordered by
`price` descending** (most expensive category leader first). **6 rows, this
ordering is graded.**

Difficulty note: `DISTINCT ON (category)` forces the query's own `ORDER BY` to
begin with `category`, which fights the presentation order you need. You will
have to select in one query and sort in another.

Run: `uv run dojo test 49_distinct_on challenge`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 49_distinct_on

`DISTINCT ON` is a PostgreSQL extension that solves one problem completely:
**one row per group, chosen by an ordering**. It is not standard SQL, and
for the problem it solves it is shorter and usually faster than anything
that is.

## Notes

**How it reads.** `SELECT DISTINCT ON (expr) ...` keeps the **first** row of
each group of rows sharing the same `expr`, where "first" is decided by the
query's `ORDER BY`. So the shape is always: group key in `DISTINCT ON`,
group key first in `ORDER BY`, then the criterion that decides the winner,
then a tie-break.

**The `ORDER BY` must lead with the `DISTINCT ON` expressions.** PostgreSQL
enforces this and raises an error otherwise, which is a kindness — the
alternative would be silently returning an arbitrary row. Note that this
also means you cannot directly sort the *result* by something else; wrap it
in a subquery or CTE and sort outside, which is what the challenge asks for.

**Always give it a tie-break.** `DISTINCT ON` returns exactly one row per
group, so something decides which — and with no tie-break that something is
whatever the sort happened to produce, which may differ between runs and
between PostgreSQL versions. Add a unique column at the end of the `ORDER
BY` and the answer becomes deterministic.

**Compared with the alternatives.** `row_number() ... WHERE rn = 1` is the
portable version and takes six lines instead of three. `LATERAL` (lesson 48)
generalises to N > 1 and to arbitrary per-group work. `DISTINCT ON` handles
exactly N = 1, in the fewest characters, and with a matching index —
`(group_key, order_key)` — it can be executed as a single ordered index scan
with a `Unique` node on top, which is about as cheap as this question gets.

**The index that makes it fast.** `(customer_id, created_at DESC)` gives the
planner the exact order the query asks for, so there is no `Sort` node and
the `Unique` node just skips duplicates as they stream past. Without such an
index PostgreSQL sorts the whole input first — correct, but the cost of a
sort rather than of a scan.

**Where it shows up.** Latest status per entity, current price per product,
most recent login per user, newest row per key in a change log, the winning
bid per auction. Any question of the form "the *something*-est row per
group" is this construct.

**Portability.** It is PostgreSQL-only. If the query has to run on other
engines too, `row_number()` is the version to write. If it does not, the
brevity is worth having.

## ex1 — the cheapest product in each category

Three lines for a question that took a correlated subquery in lesson 03 and
a windowed CTE in lesson 15. Note the tie-break on `id` in the prompt — the
cheapest product in a category is not unique, and the query has to say what
to do about that.

## ex2 — each department's newest hire

The same shape with a descending criterion. Building the habit of reading
the `ORDER BY` as "group, then winner, then tie-break" makes these
write-once queries.

## ex3 — each customer's first order

Ascending instead of descending, and nothing else changes. Worth pausing on
how small the edit is compared with the equivalent change in a
window-function version, where the direction lives inside an `OVER` clause
that also has to keep its partition in sync.

## ex4 — the best review of each product

The tie-break earns its keep here: with only five possible ratings and
hundreds of reviews per product, the "best" review is massively ambiguous,
and without `id` at the end of the `ORDER BY` you get a different answer on
a different day. That is the failure mode `DISTINCT ON` makes easy to write
and easy to miss.

## challenge — priciest per category, ranked

The restriction from the notes, met head-on: the `ORDER BY` belongs to the
`DISTINCT ON` and cannot also order the output. Wrap it and sort outside.
This is the standard workaround and worth having in your hands.

## Further reading

- [`SELECT` — `DISTINCT ON`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — the reference text, including the warning about unpredictable results without a full `ORDER BY`.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) — `row_number()`, the portable equivalent.
- [`LATERAL` Subqueries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the generalisation to N > 1. Lesson 48.
- [Use The Index, Luke — Top-N Queries](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/partial-results/top-n-queries) — the index shape that makes all three approaches fast.

# 49 — DISTINCT ON

You have already solved "one row per group" three different ways: a correlated
subquery (lesson 13), and `row_number() ... = 1` filtered in a CTE (lesson 15).
Both work everywhere. But Postgres ships a shortcut that is shorter than either
and, for this exact job, usually faster: `DISTINCT ON`.

`DISTINCT ON (expr)` keeps the **first row of each distinct value of `expr`**,
and "first" is decided by the query's `ORDER BY`. That is the whole idea — and
also the whole footgun. If your `ORDER BY` doesn't start with the `DISTINCT ON`
expression, Postgres rejects it; if it does, whatever you sort by *next*
decides which row survives each group.

## Concept

```sql
-- the newest order for each customer
SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id)
       customer_id, id, created_at
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer_id, created_at DESC;
```

`ORDER BY customer_id` groups the scan; within each customer, `created_at
DESC` puts the newest order first; `DISTINCT ON (customer_id)` keeps that first
row and discards the rest of the customer's orders. Change `DESC` to `ASC` and
you get each customer's *first* order instead — the selection rule lives
entirely in the `ORDER BY`.

Details that bite:

- **The `ORDER BY` must lead with the `DISTINCT ON` column(s).** `DISTINCT ON
  (category) ... ORDER BY price` is a syntax error. `... ORDER BY category,
  price` is correct.
- Add a **tie-break** (`, id`) when the sort key can repeat within a group, or
  which row you keep is arbitrary and can change between runs.
- The result comes out sorted by the `DISTINCT ON` columns. If you want it
  presented in some *other* order, wrap it in a subquery and sort outside
  (that's the challenge).
- `DISTINCT ON` is PostgreSQL-specific. The portable equivalent is the
  `row_number() = 1` idiom; reach for that if the query must run on another
  database.

## Exercise 1 — the cheapest product in each category

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. One row per `category`: the product with the lowest
`price`. Columns `category`, `name`, `price`. **6 rows**, any order. (Break
price ties by `id`.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 49_distinct_on ex1`

## Exercise 2 — each department's newest hire

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. One row per `department`: the most recently hired
person. Columns `department`, `name`, `hired_on`. **5 rows**, any order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 49_distinct_on ex2`

## Exercise 3 — each customer's first order

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. For every customer with `id <= 30`, their
**earliest** order.

Columns, in this order: `customer_id`, `id` (the order's), `created_at`.
Any row order. (30 rows.)

Same construct, opposite direction. The rule that makes `DISTINCT ON` work
is unchanged: the `ORDER BY` must **start with** the `DISTINCT ON`
expressions, and whatever comes after them decides which row survives per
group. Here that means `ORDER BY customer_id, created_at ASC, id ASC` —
earliest first, with `id` as a deterministic tie-break.

Get the leading columns wrong and PostgreSQL raises an error rather than
guessing, which is one of the friendlier things about this feature.

Run: `uv run dojo test 49_distinct_on ex3`

## Exercise 4 — the best review of each product

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. For each product with `id <= 20`, the
**highest-rated** review of that product.

Columns, in this order: `product_id`, `id` (the review's), `rating`. Any
row order. (20 rows.)

Ties matter here in a way they did not before: ratings are integers from 1
to 5 over a thousand-odd reviews per product, so a product will have many
5-star reviews and the "best" one is genuinely ambiguous. Break the tie on
`id` ascending so the answer is deterministic.

That is worth generalising. `DISTINCT ON` always returns exactly one row per
group, so *something* decides which — and if you do not say what, PostgreSQL
picks whichever row the sort happened to place first, which can differ
between runs. A `DISTINCT ON` query without a tie-break is a query with a
bug that has not surfaced yet.

Run: `uv run dojo test 49_distinct_on ex4`

## Challenge — priciest per category, ranked (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. The most expensive product in each `category` —
columns `category`, `name`, `price` — but the result must be **ordered by
`price` descending** (most expensive category leader first). **6 rows, this
ordering is graded.**

Difficulty note: `DISTINCT ON (category)` forces the query's own `ORDER BY` to
begin with `category`, which fights the presentation order you need. You will
have to select in one query and sort in another.

Run: `uv run dojo test 49_distinct_on challenge`

`test_ex1`/`test_ex2` compare as a set; `test_challenge` passes `ordered=True`,
so the rows must come back in the required price-descending order.

## The teaching point

`DISTINCT ON` is the tersest way to express "the latest / earliest / best row
per key", and you will see it constantly in Postgres codebases: newest price
per product, latest status per ticket, most recent login per user. The reason
it stays readable where a window function sprawls is that it collapses "rank,
then keep rank 1" into a single clause. Just remember the rule that makes it
work and the rule that trips everyone: the `ORDER BY` is both the grouping
mechanism and the selection mechanism, and it must lead with the `DISTINCT ON`
expression.

# Reading - 49_distinct_on

`DISTINCT ON` is a PostgreSQL extension that solves one problem completely:
**one row per group, chosen by an ordering**. It is not standard SQL, and
for the problem it solves it is shorter and usually faster than anything
that is.

## Notes

**How it reads.** `SELECT DISTINCT ON (expr) ...` keeps the **first** row of
each group of rows sharing the same `expr`, where "first" is decided by the
query's `ORDER BY`. So the shape is always: group key in `DISTINCT ON`,
group key first in `ORDER BY`, then the criterion that decides the winner,
then a tie-break.

**The `ORDER BY` must lead with the `DISTINCT ON` expressions.** PostgreSQL
enforces this and raises an error otherwise, which is a kindness — the
alternative would be silently returning an arbitrary row. Note that this
also means you cannot directly sort the *result* by something else; wrap it
in a subquery or CTE and sort outside, which is what the challenge asks for.

**Always give it a tie-break.** `DISTINCT ON` returns exactly one row per
group, so something decides which — and with no tie-break that something is
whatever the sort happened to produce, which may differ between runs and
between PostgreSQL versions. Add a unique column at the end of the `ORDER
BY` and the answer becomes deterministic.

**Compared with the alternatives.** `row_number() ... WHERE rn = 1` is the
portable version and takes six lines instead of three. `LATERAL` (lesson 48)
generalises to N > 1 and to arbitrary per-group work. `DISTINCT ON` handles
exactly N = 1, in the fewest characters, and with a matching index —
`(group_key, order_key)` — it can be executed as a single ordered index scan
with a `Unique` node on top, which is about as cheap as this question gets.

**The index that makes it fast.** `(customer_id, created_at DESC)` gives the
planner the exact order the query asks for, so there is no `Sort` node and
the `Unique` node just skips duplicates as they stream past. Without such an
index PostgreSQL sorts the whole input first — correct, but the cost of a
sort rather than of a scan.

**Where it shows up.** Latest status per entity, current price per product,
most recent login per user, newest row per key in a change log, the winning
bid per auction. Any question of the form "the *something*-est row per
group" is this construct.

**Portability.** It is PostgreSQL-only. If the query has to run on other
engines too, `row_number()` is the version to write. If it does not, the
brevity is worth having.

## ex1 — the cheapest product in each category

Three lines for a question that took a correlated subquery in lesson 03 and
a windowed CTE in lesson 15. Note the tie-break on `id` in the prompt — the
cheapest product in a category is not unique, and the query has to say what
to do about that.

## ex2 — each department's newest hire

The same shape with a descending criterion. Building the habit of reading
the `ORDER BY` as "group, then winner, then tie-break" makes these
write-once queries.

## ex3 — each customer's first order

Ascending instead of descending, and nothing else changes. Worth pausing on
how small the edit is compared with the equivalent change in a
window-function version, where the direction lives inside an `OVER` clause
that also has to keep its partition in sync.

## ex4 — the best review of each product

The tie-break earns its keep here: with only five possible ratings and
hundreds of reviews per product, the "best" review is massively ambiguous,
and without `id` at the end of the `ORDER BY` you get a different answer on

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — priciest per category, ranked (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. The most expensive product in each `category` —
columns `category`, `name`, `price` — but the result must be **ordered by
`price` descending** (most expensive category leader first). **6 rows, this
ordering is graded.**

Difficulty note: `DISTINCT ON (category)` forces the query's own `ORDER BY` to
begin with `category`, which fights the presentation order you need. You will
have to select in one query and sort in another.

Run: `uv run dojo test 49_distinct_on challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Getting the most expensive product per category is easy with `DISTINCT ON
(category) ... ORDER BY category, price DESC`. The twist is the *output* order:
the gate wants the six rows sorted by `price` descending, but `DISTINCT ON`
forces the query's `ORDER BY` to start with `category`. Those two orderings
conflict.

## Hint 2
You can't do both sorts in one `ORDER BY`. Do the `DISTINCT ON` in an inner
query (ordered by `category, price DESC, id`), then re-sort the result in an
outer query:

```sql
SELECT category, name, price
FROM ( SELECT DISTINCT ON (category) ... ORDER BY category, price DESC, id ) x
ORDER BY ...;
```

## Hint 3
The outer `ORDER BY price DESC` gives the required presentation order. The
inner query's `ORDER BY` is only there to drive the `DISTINCT ON` selection —
it does not survive to the final output, which is exactly why you need the
outer sort.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Getting the most expensive product per category is easy with `DISTINCT ON
(category) ... ORDER BY category, price DESC`. The twist is the *output* order:
the gate wants the six rows sorted by `price` descending, but `DISTINCT ON`
forces the query's `ORDER BY` to start with `category`. Those two orderings
conflict.

## Hint 2
You can't do both sorts in one `ORDER BY`. Do the `DISTINCT ON` in an inner
query (ordered by `category, price DESC, id`), then re-sort the result in an
outer query:

```sql
SELECT category, name, price
FROM ( SELECT DISTINCT ON (category) ... ORDER BY category, price DESC, id ) x
ORDER BY ...;
```

## Hint 3
The outer `ORDER BY price DESC` gives the required presentation order. The
inner query's `ORDER BY` is only there to drive the `DISTINCT ON` selection —
it does not survive to the final output, which is exactly why you need the
outer sort.

FROM (
    SELECT DISTINCT ON (category) category, name, price
    FROM products
    ORDER BY category, price DESC, id
) best
ORDER BY price DESC;

## Hint 1
One row per department again — this time the *most recently hired* person.
Same tool, `DISTINCT ON (department)`; only the sort direction changes.

## Hint 2
Most recent means the largest `hired_on`, so sort it descending. The
`DISTINCT ON` expression still has to be the first thing in `ORDER BY`:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT ON (department) department, name, hired_on
FROM staff
ORDER BY department, hired_on DESC ...;
```

## Hint 3
`ORDER BY department, hired_on DESC, id` — department first (required),
`hired_on DESC` so the newest hire is the first row kept, `id` as a tie-break.

SELECT DISTINCT ON (department)
       department, name, hired_on
FROM staff
ORDER BY department, hired_on DESC, id;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — each customer's first order

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. For every customer with `id <= 30`, their
**earliest** order.

Columns, in this order: `customer_id`, `id` (the order's), `created_at`.
Any row order. (30 rows.)

Same construct, opposite direction. The rule that makes `DISTINCT ON` work
is unchanged: the `ORDER BY` must **start with** the `DISTINCT ON`
expressions, and whatever comes after them decides which row survives per
group. Here that means `ORDER BY customer_id, created_at ASC, id ASC` —
earliest first, with `id` as a deterministic tie-break.

Get the leading columns wrong and PostgreSQL raises an error rather than
guessing, which is one of the friendlier things about this feature.

Run: `uv run dojo test 49_distinct_on ex3`

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — the best review of each product

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. For each product with `id <= 20`, the
**highest-rated** review of that product.

Columns, in this order: `product_id`, `id` (the review's), `rating`. Any
row order. (20 rows.)

Ties matter here in a way they did not before: ratings are integers from 1
to 5 over a thousand-odd reviews per product, so a product will have many
5-star reviews and the "best" one is genuinely ambiguous. Break the tie on
`id` ascending so the answer is deterministic.

That is worth generalising. `DISTINCT ON` always returns exactly one row per
group, so *something* decides which — and if you do not say what, PostgreSQL
picks whichever row the sort happened to place first, which can differ
between runs. A `DISTINCT ON` query without a tie-break is a query with a
bug that has not surfaced yet.

lessons.briefing:
# 50 — GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP, and CUBE

Back in lesson 07 a `GROUP BY status` gave you four rows — one per status. But
real reports almost always want the four rows **and** the total underneath
them. In lesson 17 you faked multi-level summaries with `CASE`/`FILTER`
pivots. This lesson is the real tool: `GROUP BY` extensions that compute
several grouping levels — subtotals, grand totals, cross-tabs — in a single
pass over the data.

The mechanism is one query that is grouped *more than one way at once*. Where a
plain `GROUP BY (a, b)` produces exactly the (a, b) combinations, `GROUPING
SETS`, `ROLLUP`, and `CUBE` produce a *union of several groupings* and stack
the results.

## Concept

Three spellings, from most explicit to most convenient:

```sql
-- list the groupings yourself: by category, by status, and the grand total
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((category), (status), ())

-- ROLLUP (a, b) = the hierarchy: (a,b), then (a), then ()  — subtotals + total
GROUP BY ROLLUP (category, status)

-- CUBE (a, b) = every combination: (a,b), (a), (b), ()      — the full cross-tab
GROUP BY CUBE (category, status)
```

- `()` is the **grand total** — "group by nothing", one row over everything.
- A rolled-up / subtotal row carries `NULL` in the column it aggregated over.
  That NULL is indistinguishable from a real NULL in the data — so Postgres
  gives you **`GROUPING(col)`**, which returns `1` when the row is a subtotal
  over `col` and `0` when `col` holds a genuine value. Use it to label or
  filter subtotal rows.
- `ROLLUP (a, b)` is a *hierarchy* (it does **not** produce a `(b)`-only
  subtotal); `CUBE (a, b)` is *every* subset. Pick the one whose rows you
  actually want — or spell them out with `GROUPING SETS`.

Paste the concept queries into `uv run dojo lab 50_grouping_sets` and watch the
NULL-bearing subtotal rows appear.

## Exercise 1 — revenue per status, with a grand total

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Sum `orders.total` per `status`, and add one more row
for the total across all orders. Columns `status`, `revenue`. **5 rows** (four
statuses + the grand total, whose `status` is NULL), any order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 50_grouping_sets ex1`

## Exercise 2 — category totals and status totals in one query

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. In a single query, produce revenue broken down three
ways: by product `category`, by order `status`, and overall. Revenue is
`sum(quantity * price)` over `order_items` (join `products` for the category
and `orders` for the status). Columns `category`, `status`, `revenue`. **11
rows** (6 categories + 4 statuses + 1 grand total; the unused dimension is NULL
in each row), any order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 50_grouping_sets ex2`

## Exercise 3 — every combination, with CUBE

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Over the same three-table join as exercise 2,
produce **every** breakdown of revenue by category and status at once:
each (category, status) pair, each category's subtotal, each status's
subtotal, and the grand total.

Columns, in this order: `category`, `status`, `revenue` (sum of
`quantity * price`). Any row order.

`CUBE (a, b)` is shorthand for `GROUPING SETS ((a, b), (a), (b), ())` —
every subset of the listed columns. With six categories and four statuses
that is 24 + 6 + 4 + 1 = **35 rows**, and the subtotal rows carry NULL in
the columns they are not grouped by.

`ROLLUP (a, b)` is the other shorthand and means something different: only
the *hierarchical* subsets — `(a, b)`, `(a)`, `()`. Use `ROLLUP` when the
columns nest (year → month → day, country → city); use `CUBE` when they are
independent dimensions you want crossed.

Run: `uv run dojo test 50_grouping_sets ex3`

## Exercise 4 — two independent breakdowns in one pass

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Management wants a single result containing
three different views of `orders` revenue: **by month**, **by status**, and
**overall** — but *not* the month × status cross-tab, which would be 52
noisy rows nobody asked for.

Columns, in this order: `month` (`date_trunc('month', created_at)`),
`status`, `revenue` (sum of `total`). Any row order. (13 months + 4
statuses + 1 grand total = **18 rows**.)

This is the case `GROUPING SETS` exists for and neither `ROLLUP` nor `CUBE`
can express: you are listing exactly the aggregations you want, and they
are not a hierarchy or a full cross product.

Write it as `GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((...), (...), ())`. The empty
parentheses are the grand total — one group containing every row.

Note what you have avoided: three separate queries, three scans of half a
million rows, and three results that could disagree with each other if the
data changed between them.

Run: `uv run dojo test 50_grouping_sets ex4`

## Challenge — a category × status hierarchy, labelled (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Use `ROLLUP (category, status)` over the same
join to produce every (category, status) revenue, a subtotal per category, and
the grand total. Add a fourth column `is_subtotal` = `GROUPING(status)` so a
consumer can tell subtotal rows from detail rows. Columns `category`,
`status`, `revenue`, `is_subtotal`. **31 rows**, any order.

Difficulty note: notice `ROLLUP` gives you per-category subtotals but *no*
per-status subtotal — that asymmetry is the lesson. `GROUPING(status)` is `1`
on the category-subtotal and grand-total rows, `0` on detail rows.

Run: `uv run dojo test 50_grouping_sets challenge`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 50_grouping_sets

`GROUPING SETS` lets one query produce several different `GROUP BY`
results at once, in one pass over the data. It is the difference between a
report built from four queries that might disagree and a report built from
one that cannot.

## Notes

**The mental model.** `GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((a, b), (a), ())` is
`UNION ALL` of three grouped queries — by `(a, b)`, by `(a)`, and by nothing
at all — except that PostgreSQL computes them together, sharing the scan and
often sharing the sort. The output columns are the union of all the grouping
columns; a row produced by a set that does not include a column carries NULL
there.

**`ROLLUP` and `CUBE` are shorthands, and they mean different things.**
`ROLLUP (a, b, c)` gives the *hierarchical* subsets — `(a,b,c)`, `(a,b)`,
`(a)`, `()` — which is what you want for nested dimensions: year → month →
day, country → region → city. `CUBE (a, b, c)` gives *every* subset, all
eight of them, which is what you want for independent dimensions you intend
to cross. Choosing the wrong one produces either missing subtotals or a
result three times larger than the question.

**The NULL ambiguity, and `GROUPING()`.** A subtotal row has NULL in the
columns it is not grouped by — but a real group can also have NULL there, if
the data has NULLs. The two are indistinguishable by looking. `GROUPING(col)`
returns 1 when `col` was *not* part of that row's grouping set and 0 when it
was, which disambiguates them exactly:

```sql
CASE WHEN grouping(category) = 1 THEN 'ALL CATEGORIES' ELSE category END
```

Any report that ships subtotals to humans wants labels built this way,
because "NULL" in a category column is not a word anyone should have to
interpret.

**Ordering the output.** The rows come back in whatever order the
implementation produces; a report almost always wants subtotals positioned
deliberately. Sort by `grouping(...)` first, then by the column — that puts
detail rows before their subtotal, or after it, on purpose.

**Why it beats `UNION ALL` of separate queries.** One scan instead of N.
One consistent snapshot, so the parts cannot disagree with the whole. And
one query to maintain when the revenue definition changes — which it will.

**Where the work actually happens.** `EXPLAIN` shows a `GroupAggregate` or
`HashAggregate` with a `Group Key` and several `Sort Key`/`Group Key` lines,
or a `MixedAggregate` node. PostgreSQL will reuse a single sorted input for
several grouping sets when it can, which is the source of most of the
saving; a set list that requires many incompatible sorts is more expensive
than it looks.

**The relationship to pivoting.** Lesson 17 turned rows into columns for
one dimension. `GROUPING SETS` produces the *long-form* version of a
cross-tab with all its margins, which is exactly the shape a BI tool or a
dataframe wants to receive. Long form with margins from SQL, rotation in the
presentation layer, is the combination that scales.

## ex1 — revenue per status, with a grand total

The minimal grouping set: `((status), ())`. Note the grand-total row's NULL
status — and that you have to *know* it means "all statuses" rather than
"orders with no status", which is exactly the ambiguity `GROUPING()` exists
to remove.

## ex2 — category totals and status totals in one query

Two independent breakdowns plus the overall, in one pass. Written as three
queries and stitched together, this is three scans of half a million rows
and three chances for the numbers to disagree.

## ex3 — every combination, with CUBE

Thirty-five rows from one clause. Worth checking a property while you are
here: the sum of the category subtotals, the sum of the status subtotals,
and the grand total should all be the same number. When they are not, the
join grain is wrong (lesson 08), and a `CUBE` result is an unusually good
place to notice.

## ex4 — two independent breakdowns in one pass

The case neither shorthand can express, which is why the general form
exists. Notice that the month × status cross-tab is deliberately *absent* —
`GROUPING SETS` lets you ask for exactly the aggregations somebody wants
rather than the full lattice they did not.

## challenge — a category × status hierarchy, labelled

`ROLLUP` plus `GROUPING()` to label the subtotal rows. This is what a
finished report looks like: hierarchical subtotals, a grand total, and
labels a human can read without a footnote explaining what NULL means.

**Course complete.** You have written every query in this course yourself,
against a real database, with an automated gate that showed you its evidence
every time it disagreed with you. That is the loop; it works on any database
and any language, and it is yours now.

## Further reading

- [`GROUPING SETS`, `CUBE`, `ROLLUP`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) — the "Table Expressions" chapter's section, with the equivalence to `UNION ALL` spelled out.
- [`GROUPING()`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) — the grouping operations table, for disambiguating subtotal NULLs.
- [`SELECT` — `GROUP BY`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — the full grammar, including how grouping sets combine when you list several.
- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) — a last pass over `FILTER`, `DISTINCT`, ordered-set aggregates and `string_agg`, all of which compose with grouping sets.

pivots. This lesson is the real tool: `GROUP BY` extensions that compute
several grouping levels — subtotals, grand totals, cross-tabs — in a single
pass over the data.

The mechanism is one query that is grouped *more than one way at once*. Where a
plain `GROUP BY (a, b)` produces exactly the (a, b) combinations, `GROUPING
SETS`, `ROLLUP`, and `CUBE` produce a *union of several groupings* and stack
the results.

## Concept

Three spellings, from most explicit to most convenient:

```sql
-- list the groupings yourself: by category, by status, and the grand total
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((category), (status), ())

-- ROLLUP (a, b) = the hierarchy: (a,b), then (a), then ()  — subtotals + total
GROUP BY ROLLUP (category, status)

-- CUBE (a, b) = every combination: (a,b), (a), (b), ()      — the full cross-tab
GROUP BY CUBE (category, status)
```

- `()` is the **grand total** — "group by nothing", one row over everything.
- A rolled-up / subtotal row carries `NULL` in the column it aggregated over.
  That NULL is indistinguishable from a real NULL in the data — so Postgres
  gives you **`GROUPING(col)`**, which returns `1` when the row is a subtotal
  over `col` and `0` when `col` holds a genuine value. Use it to label or
  filter subtotal rows.
- `ROLLUP (a, b)` is a *hierarchy* (it does **not** produce a `(b)`-only
  subtotal); `CUBE (a, b)` is *every* subset. Pick the one whose rows you
  actually want — or spell them out with `GROUPING SETS`.

Paste the concept queries into `uv run dojo lab 50_grouping_sets` and watch the
NULL-bearing subtotal rows appear.

## Exercise 1 — revenue per status, with a grand total

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Sum `orders.total` per `status`, and add one more row
for the total across all orders. Columns `status`, `revenue`. **5 rows** (four
statuses + the grand total, whose `status` is NULL), any order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 50_grouping_sets ex1`

## Exercise 2 — category totals and status totals in one query

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. In a single query, produce revenue broken down three
ways: by product `category`, by order `status`, and overall. Revenue is
`sum(quantity * price)` over `order_items` (join `products` for the category
and `orders` for the status). Columns `category`, `status`, `revenue`. **11
rows** (6 categories + 4 statuses + 1 grand total; the unused dimension is NULL
in each row), any order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 50_grouping_sets ex2`

## Exercise 3 — every combination, with CUBE

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Over the same three-table join as exercise 2,
produce **every** breakdown of revenue by category and status at once:
each (category, status) pair, each category's subtotal, each status's
subtotal, and the grand total.

Columns, in this order: `category`, `status`, `revenue` (sum of
`quantity * price`). Any row order.

`CUBE (a, b)` is shorthand for `GROUPING SETS ((a, b), (a), (b), ())` —
every subset of the listed columns. With six categories and four statuses
that is 24 + 6 + 4 + 1 = **35 rows**, and the subtotal rows carry NULL in
the columns they are not grouped by.

`ROLLUP (a, b)` is the other shorthand and means something different: only
the *hierarchical* subsets — `(a, b)`, `(a)`, `()`. Use `ROLLUP` when the
columns nest (year → month → day, country → city); use `CUBE` when they are
independent dimensions you want crossed.

Run: `uv run dojo test 50_grouping_sets ex3`

## Exercise 4 — two independent breakdowns in one pass

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Management wants a single result containing
three different views of `orders` revenue: **by month**, **by status**, and
**overall** — but *not* the month × status cross-tab, which would be 52
noisy rows nobody asked for.

Columns, in this order: `month` (`date_trunc('month', created_at)`),
`status`, `revenue` (sum of `total`). Any row order. (13 months + 4
statuses + 1 grand total = **18 rows**.)

This is the case `GROUPING SETS` exists for and neither `ROLLUP` nor `CUBE`
can express: you are listing exactly the aggregations you want, and they
are not a hierarchy or a full cross product.

Write it as `GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((...), (...), ())`. The empty
parentheses are the grand total — one group containing every row.

Note what you have avoided: three separate queries, three scans of half a
million rows, and three results that could disagree with each other if the
data changed between them.

Run: `uv run dojo test 50_grouping_sets ex4`

## Challenge — a category × status hierarchy, labelled (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Use `ROLLUP (category, status)` over the same
join to produce every (category, status) revenue, a subtotal per category, and
the grand total. Add a fourth column `is_subtotal` = `GROUPING(status)` so a
consumer can tell subtotal rows from detail rows. Columns `category`,
`status`, `revenue`, `is_subtotal`. **31 rows**, any order.

Difficulty note: notice `ROLLUP` gives you per-category subtotals but *no*
per-status subtotal — that asymmetry is the lesson. `GROUPING(status)` is `1`
on the category-subtotal and grand-total rows, `0` on detail rows.

Run: `uv run dojo test 50_grouping_sets challenge`

## The teaching point

Every "summary with subtotals" a stakeholder has ever asked for — sales by
region with regional and national totals, a P&L with line items rolling up to
categories — is a `ROLLUP` or `GROUPING SETS` away, computed in one scan
instead of one query per level `UNION`-ed together. The database does the
stacking; you just declare which levels you want. And when the NULLs get
confusing, `GROUPING()` is the flashlight.

# Reading - 50_grouping_sets

`GROUPING SETS` lets one query produce several different `GROUP BY`
results at once, in one pass over the data. It is the difference between a
report built from four queries that might disagree and a report built from
one that cannot.

## Notes

**The mental model.** `GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((a, b), (a), ())` is
`UNION ALL` of three grouped queries — by `(a, b)`, by `(a)`, and by nothing
at all — except that PostgreSQL computes them together, sharing the scan and
often sharing the sort. The output columns are the union of all the grouping
columns; a row produced by a set that does not include a column carries NULL
there.

**`ROLLUP` and `CUBE` are shorthands, and they mean different things.**
`ROLLUP (a, b, c)` gives the *hierarchical* subsets — `(a,b,c)`, `(a,b)`,
`(a)`, `()` — which is what you want for nested dimensions: year → month →
day, country → region → city. `CUBE (a, b, c)` gives *every* subset, all
eight of them, which is what you want for independent dimensions you intend
to cross. Choosing the wrong one produces either missing subtotals or a
result three times larger than the question.

**The NULL ambiguity, and `GROUPING()`.** A subtotal row has NULL in the
columns it is not grouped by — but a real group can also have NULL there, if
the data has NULLs. The two are indistinguishable by looking. `GROUPING(col)`
returns 1 when `col` was *not* part of that row's grouping set and 0 when it
was, which disambiguates them exactly:

```sql
CASE WHEN grouping(category) = 1 THEN 'ALL CATEGORIES' ELSE category END
```

Any report that ships subtotals to humans wants labels built this way,
because "NULL" in a category column is not a word anyone should have to
interpret.

**Ordering the output.** The rows come back in whatever order the
implementation produces; a report almost always wants subtotals positioned
deliberately. Sort by `grouping(...)` first, then by the column — that puts
detail rows before their subtotal, or after it, on purpose.

**Why it beats `UNION ALL` of separate queries.** One scan instead of N.
One consistent snapshot, so the parts cannot disagree with the whole. And
one query to maintain when the revenue definition changes — which it will.

**Where the work actually happens.** `EXPLAIN` shows a `GroupAggregate` or
`HashAggregate` with a `Group Key` and several `Sort Key`/`Group Key` lines,
or a `MixedAggregate` node. PostgreSQL will reuse a single sorted input for
several grouping sets when it can, which is the source of most of the
saving; a set list that requires many incompatible sorts is more expensive
than it looks.

**The relationship to pivoting.** Lesson 17 turned rows into columns for
one dimension. `GROUPING SETS` produces the *long-form* version of a
cross-tab with all its margins, which is exactly the shape a BI tool or a
dataframe wants to receive. Long form with margins from SQL, rotation in the
presentation layer, is the combination that scales.

## ex1 — revenue per status, with a grand total

The minimal grouping set: `((status), ())`. Note the grand-total row's NULL
status — and that you have to *know* it means "all statuses" rather than
"orders with no status", which is exactly the ambiguity `GROUPING()` exists
to remove.

## ex2 — category totals and status totals in one query

Two independent breakdowns plus the overall, in one pass. Written as three
queries and stitched together, this is three scans of half a million rows
and three chances for the numbers to disagree.

## ex3 — every combination, with CUBE

Thirty-five rows from one clause. Worth checking a property while you are
here: the sum of the category subtotals, the sum of the status subtotals,
and the grand total should all be the same number. When they are not, the
join grain is wrong (lesson 08), and a `CUBE` result is an unusually good
place to notice.

## ex4 — two independent breakdowns in one pass

The case neither shorthand can express, which is why the general form
exists. Notice that the month × status cross-tab is deliberately *absent* —
`GROUPING SETS` lets you ask for exactly the aggregations somebody wants
rather than the full lattice they did not.

## challenge — a category × status hierarchy, labelled

`ROLLUP` plus `GROUPING()` to label the subtotal rows. This is what a
finished report looks like: hierarchical subtotals, a grand total, and
labels a human can read without a footnote explaining what NULL means.

against a real database, with an automated gate that showed you its evidence
every time it disagreed with you. That is the loop; it works on any database
and any language, and it is yours now.

- [`SELECT` — `GROUP BY`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) — the full grammar, including how grouping sets combine when you list several.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — a category × status hierarchy, labelled (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Use `ROLLUP (category, status)` over the same
join to produce every (category, status) revenue, a subtotal per category, and
the grand total. Add a fourth column `is_subtotal` = `GROUPING(status)` so a
consumer can tell subtotal rows from detail rows. Columns `category`,
`status`, `revenue`, `is_subtotal`. **31 rows**, any order.

Difficulty note: notice `ROLLUP` gives you per-category subtotals but *no*
per-status subtotal — that asymmetry is the lesson. `GROUPING(status)` is `1`
on the category-subtotal and grand-total rows, `0` on detail rows.

Run: `uv run dojo test 50_grouping_sets challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
`ROLLUP (category, status)` builds a hierarchy: every (category, status) pair,
then a subtotal per category, then one grand total — 6×4 + 6 + 1 = 31 rows.
Notice what it does *not* give you: a subtotal per status on its own (that
would need `CUBE` or an explicit `GROUPING SETS`). The point of this exercise
is to see the difference.

## Hint 2
The subtotal and grand-total rows carry `NULL` in the rolled-up column, which
looks identical to a real NULL. `GROUPING(status)` disambiguates: it returns
`1` when the row is aggregated *over* status (a subtotal), `0` when `status` is
a genuine value.

```sql
SELECT p.category, o.status, sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) AS revenue,
       GROUPING(o.status) AS is_subtotal
FROM ...
GROUP BY ROLLUP (p.category, o.status);
```

## Hint 3
Use the same three-table join as exercise 2. The `is_subtotal` column is
literally `GROUPING(o.status)` — return it as-is (0 or 1). Don't filter
anything out; the gate expects all 31 rows.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
`ROLLUP (category, status)` builds a hierarchy: every (category, status) pair,
then a subtotal per category, then one grand total — 6×4 + 6 + 1 = 31 rows.
Notice what it does *not* give you: a subtotal per status on its own (that
would need `CUBE` or an explicit `GROUPING SETS`). The point of this exercise
is to see the difference.

## Hint 2
The subtotal and grand-total rows carry `NULL` in the rolled-up column, which
looks identical to a real NULL. `GROUPING(status)` disambiguates: it returns
`1` when the row is aggregated *over* status (a subtotal), `0` when `status` is
a genuine value.

```sql
SELECT p.category, o.status, sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) AS revenue,
       GROUPING(o.status) AS is_subtotal
FROM ...
GROUP BY ROLLUP (p.category, o.status);
```

## Hint 3
Use the same three-table join as exercise 2. The `is_subtotal` column is
literally `GROUPING(o.status)` — return it as-is (0 or 1). Don't filter
anything out; the gate expects all 31 rows.

SELECT p.category, o.status,
       sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) AS revenue,
       GROUPING(o.status) AS is_subtotal
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
JOIN orders   o ON o.id = oi.order_id
GROUP BY ROLLUP (p.category, o.status);

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
This is three different reports in one result: revenue by category, revenue by
status, and the grand total. `GROUPING SETS` lets you list exactly the
groupings you want — no more, no less — instead of running three queries and
`UNION`-ing them.

## Hint 2
First get the join right — line-item revenue needs the product (for category)
and the order (for status):

```sql
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
JOIN orders   o ON o.id = oi.order_id
```

Then list the three groupings: `GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((p.category),
(o.status), ())`. The empty `()` is the grand total.

## Hint 3
Revenue is `sum(oi.quantity * oi.price)`. Select `p.category, o.status,
sum(...)`. Category rows come back with `status` NULL, status rows with
`category` NULL, and the `()` set produces one row with both NULL. Eleven rows
total; you don't have to order them.

references.solution.sql:
-- 50_grouping_sets/ex2 reference
SELECT p.category, o.status, sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) AS revenue
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
JOIN orders   o ON o.id = oi.order_id
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((p.category), (o.status), ());

GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((p.category), (o.status), ());

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — every combination, with CUBE

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Over the same three-table join as exercise 2,
produce **every** breakdown of revenue by category and status at once:
each (category, status) pair, each category's subtotal, each status's
subtotal, and the grand total.

Columns, in this order: `category`, `status`, `revenue` (sum of
`quantity * price`). Any row order.

`CUBE (a, b)` is shorthand for `GROUPING SETS ((a, b), (a), (b), ())` —
every subset of the listed columns. With six categories and four statuses
that is 24 + 6 + 4 + 1 = **35 rows**, and the subtotal rows carry NULL in
the columns they are not grouped by.

`ROLLUP (a, b)` is the other shorthand and means something different: only
the *hierarchical* subsets — `(a, b)`, `(a)`, `()`. Use `ROLLUP` when the
columns nest (year → month → day, country → city); use `CUBE` when they are
independent dimensions you want crossed.

## Exercise 4 — two independent breakdowns in one pass

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Management wants a single result containing
three different views of `orders` revenue: **by month**, **by status**, and
**overall** — but *not* the month × status cross-tab, which would be 52
noisy rows nobody asked for.

Columns, in this order: `month` (`date_trunc('month', created_at)`),
`status`, `revenue` (sum of `total`). Any row order. (13 months + 4
statuses + 1 grand total = **18 rows**.)

This is the case `GROUPING SETS` exists for and neither `ROLLUP` nor `CUBE`
can express: you are listing exactly the aggregations you want, and they
are not a hierarchy or a full cross product.

Write it as `GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((...), (...), ())`. The empty
parentheses are the grand total — one group containing every row.

Note what you have avoided: three separate queries, three scans of half a
million rows, and three results that could disagree with each other if the
data changed between them.
