lessons.briefing:
# 51 — Query rewrites

> **Part 8 — Optimization patterns (bonus).** Two post-course lessons on the
> optimization work that *isn't* adding indexes. Part 5's gate machinery is
> back — plan shapes and speed ratios — but with a twist: in this lesson,
> **every index you could want already exists**. Each exercise's
> `indexes.sql` ships pre-filled; leave it alone. The query is the problem.

Half of real-world performance work is not "add an index" — it's
"the index is right there and the query can't use it". A predicate
that wraps the column in a function, an `OR` that straddles a join, a
`NOT IN` that quietly forbids the anti-join optimization, a `DISTINCT`
papering over a join that multiplied rows. The index sits unused; the
plan says `Seq Scan`; and no amount of DDL will fix it, because the
DDL was never the problem.

This lesson drills the four rewrites that pay off most often. In each
exercise, `solution.sql` starts as the *slow* query — realistic,
correct, and shaped so PostgreSQL cannot run it well. Your job is to
rewrite it to return **exactly the same rows** in an index-friendly
shape. `dojo plan 51_query_rewrites <ex>` between edits will show you
the moment the plan flips.

## Concept

The planner can only use a B-tree index on `col` when the predicate
compares **the bare column** against something constant-ish for the
scan: `col = x`, `col > x`, `col BETWEEN x AND y`. Anything that
computes on the column first — `date_trunc('day', col)`,
`upper(col)`, `col + 1` — hides the column inside an expression the
tree isn't sorted by. Such predicates are called **non-sargable**
(SARG = "search argument"), and the fix is almost always the same:
move the computation to the *other* side of the comparison.

```sql
-- non-sargable: the index on created_at is invisible
WHERE date_trunc('day', created_at) = TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-06-15 00:00:00+00'

-- sargable: the same rows, as a half-open range on the bare column
WHERE created_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-06-15 00:00:00+00'
  AND created_at <  TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-06-16 00:00:00+00'
```

The half-open form (`>=` start, `<` next-start) is the idiom worth
memorizing: it tiles perfectly (no gaps or overlaps between days) and
sidesteps the `BETWEEN` trap of including the endpoint.

The other three rewrites in this lesson are structural, not
arithmetic: an `OR` whose arms live in different tables (split it with
`UNION`), a `NOT IN (subquery)` (rewrite as `NOT EXISTS` — an
anti-join), and a join-then-`DISTINCT` (rewrite as `EXISTS` — a
semi-join). Each is a shape the planner refuses to optimize *as
written* but handles beautifully once restated.

## Exercise 1 — unwrap the column

`ex1/solution.sql` (provided — this is the slow query, rewrite it):

```sql
SELECT count(*) AS orders, sum(total) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE date_trunc('day', created_at) = TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-06-15 00:00:00+00';
```

A daily-revenue tile on a dashboard. `ex1/indexes.sql` already
provides an index on `orders (created_at)` — and the query above
seq-scans 500,000 rows anyway, calling `date_trunc` on every one of
them, because the index is sorted by `created_at`, not by
`date_trunc('day', created_at)`.

Rewrite the WHERE as a half-open range on the bare column. Same one
row out; the plan should collapse to a bitmap scan over roughly 1,400
of 500,000 rows.

(Lesson 40 solved this shape the *other* way — building an expression
index to match the query. Both are valid; in production you rewrite
the query when you can, because it's a deploy instead of an index
build, and one index on the bare column serves every date range, not
just whole days.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 51_query_rewrites ex1`

## Exercise 2 — NOT IN, the accidental time bomb

The marketing team wants to know how many customers have **never
placed an order**. The query someone shipped:

```sql
SELECT count(*) AS never_ordered
FROM customers
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);
```

You met the *correctness* trap of `NOT IN` in lesson 05 (one NULL in
the subquery and it returns nothing — `orders.customer_id` is NOT
NULL, so this one is at least correct). This is the *performance*
trap: PostgreSQL never turns `NOT IN (subquery)` into an anti-join.
While the 500,000 collected ids fit in `work_mem` it hashes them —
tolerable. The day they don't fit, the planner silently switches to
re-scanning the materialized list **per customer row**, and the query
goes from milliseconds to tens of minutes. Same SQL, same answer, a
thousand times slower — it just needed the table to grow.

Don't run the query above against the full dataset unless you enjoy
waiting (this is also why this exercise's gate doesn't time a
baseline). Edit `ex2/solution.sql` (a bare stub) and write the
anti-join form instead: `NOT EXISTS`, or the `LEFT JOIN … IS NULL`
pattern from lesson 09. Either plans as a hash anti-join — the gate
looks for a real join in the plan. Same single count out (5,003 at
full volume).

Run: `uv run dojo test 51_query_rewrites ex2`

## Exercise 3 — OR splits the plan in two

`ex3/solution.sql` (provided — rewrite it):

```sql
SELECT o.id, o.total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.total > 1995
   OR c.email = 'user4242@example.com';
```

A support tool: show the whale orders, plus everything belonging to
the user on the phone. Lesson 38 showed that an `OR` over two indexed
columns of the *same* table is fine — BitmapOr merges the two index
scans. But this `OR` straddles the join: one arm filters `orders`, the
other filters `customers`. No bitmap can merge across two tables, so
the executor's only option is to build the **entire join** — all
500,000 rows — and filter afterward. All three useful indexes
(`orders (total)`, `orders (customer_id)`, `customers (email)`) are
already in `ex3/indexes.sql`, unused.

The rewrite: split the `OR` into two queries — one per arm, each
index-friendly on its own — and glue them with `UNION` (not `UNION
ALL`: a whale order belonging to that very customer would appear in
both arms, and the original query emits it once). Same rows, and the
plan touches ~1,300 rows instead of half a million.

Run: `uv run dojo test 51_query_rewrites ex3`

## Exercise 4 — DISTINCT is not a join strategy

`ex4/solution.sql` (provided — rewrite it):

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT p.id, p.name
FROM products p
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
WHERE p.category = 'garden';
```

"Which garden products have ever sold?" The question is about
*existence* — has this product at least one order item? — but the
query answers it by **counting to a million**: join every garden
product to every one of its line items (~160,000 joined rows), then
`DISTINCT` the duplicates back out. The `DISTINCT` isn't logic; it's
cleanup for a join that multiplied rows you never wanted.

Ask about existence directly: `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items
oi WHERE oi.product_id = p.id)`. That's a **semi-join** — for each
product, PostgreSQL probes the (provided) index on
`order_items (product_id)` and *stops at the first hit* instead of
enumerating all of them. No duplicates are ever produced, so there's
nothing to `DISTINCT` away — the gate forbids the dedup nodes
(`HashAggregate`, `Unique`) to make sure the cleanup crew really left.

Run: `uv run dojo test 51_query_rewrites ex4`

## Challenge — the Friday-afternoon query (optional)

`challenge/solution.sql` (provided) commits all three structural sins
at once:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE date_trunc('day', o.created_at) = TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-06-15 00:00:00+00'
   OR c.email = 'user4242@example.com';
```

"Everyone who ordered on June 15th — oh, and make sure Dana from the
VIP list is in there." Non-sargable date, `OR` across the join,
`DISTINCT` mopping up. Rewrite it: same rows, at least 5x faster.

`orders (customer_id)`, and `customers (email)`.

the original's `JOIN` means the VIP only appears if they have **at
least one order** (they do — but your rewrite must not *assume* so).

# Reading - 51_query_rewrites

An index is a contract with a *query shape*, not with a table. Every rewrite in
this lesson leaves the answer alone and changes only the shape — which is
exactly why they are safe to apply, and why the planner's behaviour flips so
completely when you do.

## Notes

**Sargable means "the index can seek on it".** SARG is short for *search
argument*: a predicate the access method can turn into a range of a B-tree.
`col = x`, `col > x`, `col BETWEEN x AND y` qualify. `f(col) = x` does not,
because the tree is sorted by `col`, not by `f(col)`. The fix is mechanical:
move the computation to the other side of the comparison until the column
stands alone. `date_trunc('day', created_at) = d` becomes
`created_at >= d AND created_at < d + interval '1 day'`; `upper(email) = 'X'`
becomes a case-insensitive comparison the index can serve, or an expression
index (lesson 40) if the shape is unavoidable.

**Half-open ranges are the idiom to memorise.** `>= start AND < next_start`
tiles a timeline with no gaps and no overlaps, works identically for dates,
timestamps and timestamptz, and sidesteps `BETWEEN`'s inclusive upper bound —
the reason `BETWEEN '2023-06-15' AND '2023-06-16'` quietly swallows midnight
of the 16th. It also survives a column type change from `date` to
`timestamptz`, which `BETWEEN` does not.

**`NOT IN (subquery)` is the one shape PostgreSQL refuses to optimise.**
`IN (subquery)` is turned into a semi-join; `EXISTS` into a semi-join;
`NOT EXISTS` into an anti-join. `NOT IN` is left as a `SubPlan`, because SQL
says a single NULL in the subquery makes the whole predicate UNKNOWN for every
non-matching row — so the transformation is not valid in general, and the
planner does not attempt it even when the column is `NOT NULL`. While the
collected ids fit in `work_mem` you get a hashed subplan and tolerable times;
when they stop fitting, the plan degrades to re-scanning the materialised list
once per outer row and the same query is suddenly thousands of times slower.
Nothing changed but the row count.

**That rewrite is not always semantics-preserving.** `NOT IN` and `NOT EXISTS`
agree only when the subquery's column has no NULLs. If it does, `NOT IN`
returns *nothing at all* (lesson 05) while `NOT EXISTS` returns the rows you
meant. In practice you almost always wanted `NOT EXISTS` — but check the
column's nullability before you claim the rewrite changed only the speed.

**An `OR` across two tables blocks every index.** Within one table, `WHERE a =
1 OR b = 2` becomes a `BitmapOr` of two index scans (lesson 38). Across a join
there is no such node: a bitmap addresses one relation's heap, so the executor
must form the whole join and filter afterwards. `UNION` of the two arms gives
each arm its own index-friendly plan. Use `UNION`, not `UNION ALL`, unless you
have proved the arms are disjoint — a row matching both arms was emitted once
by the original.

**`DISTINCT` over a join is usually a semi-join in disguise.** Joining to
`order_items` to ask "did this product ever sell?" multiplies each product by
its line-item count and then pays a `HashAggregate` to collapse the copies
back down. `EXISTS` asks the question directly: PostgreSQL probes the index and
stops at the first match, so duplicates are never produced and there is nothing
to deduplicate. The tell in a plan is a `HashAggregate` or `Unique` sitting on
top of a join that fans out — dedup nodes that exist only to undo work.

**Reading the plan for these four.** Non-sargable predicate: `Seq Scan` with
the function call in `Filter`. `NOT IN`: `SubPlan` and a `Materialize` under a
`Seq Scan`, no join node at all. Cross-table `OR`: a `Hash Join` whose output
row count is the whole table with `Join Filter` doing the work. Redundant
`DISTINCT`: `HashAggregate` above a join whose actual rows greatly exceed its
output. `dojo plan 51_query_rewrites <ex>` prints all of this.

## ex1 — the column under a function

The index on `orders (created_at)` is perfect and unusable at the same time,
which is the whole point: nothing about the DDL is wrong. Compare this with
lesson 40, where the same mismatch was fixed from the other end by building an
index on the expression. Rewriting the query is the better default — it ships
as a deploy rather than an index build, and one index on the bare column serves
every range, not just whole days.

## ex2 — the anti-join that never happens

Notice what the gate checks and what it does not: it asserts a real join node,
and it deliberately skips the clock. Timing this baseline at 500,000 rows is
the one measurement in the course not worth waiting for, which is itself the
lesson — a shape whose cost falls off a cliff as data grows is a bug you ship
long before you notice it. `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL` and
`NOT EXISTS` both plan as anti-joins; pick whichever reads better to you.

## ex3 — the OR that straddles the join

The interesting part of the rewrite is the first arm: once you stop needing the
customer's email, the join to `customers` adds nothing, because every order has
exactly one customer and the foreign key guarantees it. Dropping a join that
cannot change the row set is the same reasoning PostgreSQL applies in its own
join-removal optimisation — it just cannot apply it here, because as written
the join is load-bearing for the second arm.

## ex4 — DISTINCT as a symptom

Read `DISTINCT` in a code review as a question rather than a construct: *what
produced the duplicates?* If the answer is "the join did", the query is asking
an existence question with a multiplication tool. If the answer is "the data
has them", the `DISTINCT` is doing real work and belongs. The gate forbids
`HashAggregate` and `Unique` precisely because the honest rewrite makes those
nodes unnecessary rather than merely cheaper.

## challenge — three sins in one query

The wrinkle is worth the difficulty note: `JOIN orders` makes the VIP visible
only because they have at least one order, so an arm that selects the customer
by email alone quietly changes the answer for a customer who never ordered.
Rewrites are safe *because* they preserve rows, so a rewrite that changes them
under some data is not a rewrite — it is a bug you have not met yet. Adding
`EXISTS` to the second arm costs one index probe and keeps the equivalence
exact.

## Further reading

- [Subquery Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) — the formal semantics of `EXISTS`, `IN` and `NOT IN`, including the NULL rule that stops the anti-join transformation.
- [Obfuscated Conditions](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause/obfuscation) — Markus Winand's catalogue of predicates that hide the column from the index, and the rewrite for each.
- [Using EXPLAIN](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/using-explain.html) — how to read `SubPlan`, `Join Filter` and `HashAggregate`, the three tells this lesson trains you to spot.
- [Combining Queries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-union.html) — `UNION` versus `UNION ALL`, and why the dedup matters when you split an `OR`.
- [Indexes on Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-expressional.html) — the other fix for a non-sargable predicate, when the query genuinely cannot be rewritten.
lessons.fullReadme:
# 51 — Query rewrites

> **Part 8 — Optimization patterns (bonus).** Two post-course lessons on the
> optimization work that *isn't* adding indexes. Part 5's gate machinery is
> back — plan shapes and speed ratios — but with a twist: in this lesson,
> **every index you could want already exists**. Each exercise's
> `indexes.sql` ships pre-filled; leave it alone. The query is the problem.

Half of real-world performance work is not "add an index" — it's
"the index is right there and the query can't use it". A predicate
that wraps the column in a function, an `OR` that straddles a join, a
`NOT IN` that quietly forbids the anti-join optimization, a `DISTINCT`
papering over a join that multiplied rows. The index sits unused; the
plan says `Seq Scan`; and no amount of DDL will fix it, because the
DDL was never the problem.

This lesson drills the four rewrites that pay off most often. In each
exercise, `solution.sql` starts as the *slow* query — realistic,
correct, and shaped so PostgreSQL cannot run it well. Your job is to
rewrite it to return **exactly the same rows** in an index-friendly
shape. `dojo plan 51_query_rewrites <ex>` between edits will show you
the moment the plan flips.

## Concept

The planner can only use a B-tree index on `col` when the predicate
compares **the bare column** against something constant-ish for the
scan: `col = x`, `col > x`, `col BETWEEN x AND y`. Anything that
computes on the column first — `date_trunc('day', col)`,
`upper(col)`, `col + 1` — hides the column inside an expression the
tree isn't sorted by. Such predicates are called **non-sargable**
(SARG = "search argument"), and the fix is almost always the same:
move the computation to the *other* side of the comparison.

```sql
-- non-sargable: the index on created_at is invisible
WHERE date_trunc('day', created_at) = TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-06-15 00:00:00+00'

-- sargable: the same rows, as a half-open range on the bare column
WHERE created_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-06-15 00:00:00+00'
  AND created_at <  TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-06-16 00:00:00+00'
```

The half-open form (`>=` start, `<` next-start) is the idiom worth
memorizing: it tiles perfectly (no gaps or overlaps between days) and
sidesteps the `BETWEEN` trap of including the endpoint.

The other three rewrites in this lesson are structural, not
arithmetic: an `OR` whose arms live in different tables (split it with
`UNION`), a `NOT IN (subquery)` (rewrite as `NOT EXISTS` — an
anti-join), and a join-then-`DISTINCT` (rewrite as `EXISTS` — a
semi-join). Each is a shape the planner refuses to optimize *as
written* but handles beautifully once restated.

## Exercise 1 — unwrap the column

`ex1/solution.sql` (provided — this is the slow query, rewrite it):

```sql
SELECT count(*) AS orders, sum(total) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE date_trunc('day', created_at) = TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-06-15 00:00:00+00';
```

A daily-revenue tile on a dashboard. `ex1/indexes.sql` already
provides an index on `orders (created_at)` — and the query above
seq-scans 500,000 rows anyway, calling `date_trunc` on every one of
them, because the index is sorted by `created_at`, not by
`date_trunc('day', created_at)`.

Rewrite the WHERE as a half-open range on the bare column. Same one
row out; the plan should collapse to a bitmap scan over roughly 1,400
of 500,000 rows.

(Lesson 40 solved this shape the *other* way — building an expression
index to match the query. Both are valid; in production you rewrite
the query when you can, because it's a deploy instead of an index
build, and one index on the bare column serves every date range, not
just whole days.)

Run: `uv run dojo test 51_query_rewrites ex1`

## Exercise 2 — NOT IN, the accidental time bomb

The marketing team wants to know how many customers have **never
placed an order**. The query someone shipped:

```sql
SELECT count(*) AS never_ordered
FROM customers
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);
```

You met the *correctness* trap of `NOT IN` in lesson 05 (one NULL in
the subquery and it returns nothing — `orders.customer_id` is NOT
NULL, so this one is at least correct). This is the *performance*
trap: PostgreSQL never turns `NOT IN (subquery)` into an anti-join.
While the 500,000 collected ids fit in `work_mem` it hashes them —
tolerable. The day they don't fit, the planner silently switches to
re-scanning the materialized list **per customer row**, and the query
goes from milliseconds to tens of minutes. Same SQL, same answer, a
thousand times slower — it just needed the table to grow.

Don't run the query above against the full dataset unless you enjoy
waiting (this is also why this exercise's gate doesn't time a
baseline). Edit `ex2/solution.sql` (a bare stub) and write the
anti-join form instead: `NOT EXISTS`, or the `LEFT JOIN … IS NULL`
pattern from lesson 09. Either plans as a hash anti-join — the gate
looks for a real join in the plan. Same single count out (5,003 at
full volume).

Run: `uv run dojo test 51_query_rewrites ex2`

## Exercise 3 — OR splits the plan in two

`ex3/solution.sql` (provided — rewrite it):

```sql
SELECT o.id, o.total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.total > 1995
   OR c.email = 'user4242@example.com';
```

A support tool: show the whale orders, plus everything belonging to
the user on the phone. Lesson 38 showed that an `OR` over two indexed
columns of the *same* table is fine — BitmapOr merges the two index
scans. But this `OR` straddles the join: one arm filters `orders`, the
other filters `customers`. No bitmap can merge across two tables, so
the executor's only option is to build the **entire join** — all
500,000 rows — and filter afterward. All three useful indexes
(`orders (total)`, `orders (customer_id)`, `customers (email)`) are
already in `ex3/indexes.sql`, unused.

The rewrite: split the `OR` into two queries — one per arm, each
index-friendly on its own — and glue them with `UNION` (not `UNION
ALL`: a whale order belonging to that very customer would appear in
both arms, and the original query emits it once). Same rows, and the
plan touches ~1,300 rows instead of half a million.

Run: `uv run dojo test 51_query_rewrites ex3`

## Exercise 4 — DISTINCT is not a join strategy

`ex4/solution.sql` (provided — rewrite it):

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT p.id, p.name
FROM products p
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
WHERE p.category = 'garden';
```

"Which garden products have ever sold?" The question is about
*existence* — has this product at least one order item? — but the
query answers it by **counting to a million**: join every garden
product to every one of its line items (~160,000 joined rows), then
`DISTINCT` the duplicates back out. The `DISTINCT` isn't logic; it's
cleanup for a join that multiplied rows you never wanted.

Ask about existence directly: `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items
oi WHERE oi.product_id = p.id)`. That's a **semi-join** — for each
product, PostgreSQL probes the (provided) index on
`order_items (product_id)` and *stops at the first hit* instead of
enumerating all of them. No duplicates are ever produced, so there's
nothing to `DISTINCT` away — the gate forbids the dedup nodes
(`HashAggregate`, `Unique`) to make sure the cleanup crew really left.

Run: `uv run dojo test 51_query_rewrites ex4`

## Challenge — the Friday-afternoon query (optional)

`challenge/solution.sql` (provided) commits all three structural sins
at once:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE date_trunc('day', o.created_at) = TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-06-15 00:00:00+00'
   OR c.email = 'user4242@example.com';
```

"Everyone who ordered on June 15th — oh, and make sure Dana from the
VIP list is in there." Non-sargable date, `OR` across the join,
`DISTINCT` mopping up. Rewrite it: same rows, at least 5x faster.
`challenge/indexes.sql` provides `orders (created_at)`,
`orders (customer_id)`, and `customers (email)`.

Difficulty note: the honest rewrite has a subtle correctness wrinkle —
the original's `JOIN` means the VIP only appears if they have **at
least one order** (they do — but your rewrite must not *assume* so).
Several shapes work (`UNION` of two semi-joins is the reference's);
plans legitimately differ, so this gate judges by rows and clock only.

Run: `uv run dojo test 51_query_rewrites challenge`

## The gate

```python
"""Gates for 51_query_rewrites. Quoted verbatim in README.md.

Part 5's machinery, inverted: every index you could want already exists
(each exercise's indexes.sql ships pre-filled — leave it alone). The
query is the problem. Rewrite solution.sql until the plan and the clock
agree with you.
"""
import pytest

from dojo import grader, timing
from dojo.lesson import Lesson
from dojo.plan import explain

L = Lesson(__file__)


def test_ex1(lesson_db):
    ex = L.exercise("ex1")
    expected = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.expected_sql)
    baseline = timing.cached_baseline(lesson_db, f"{L.slug}::test_ex1",
                                      ex.expected_sql)
    ex.apply_indexes(lesson_db)
    actual = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_rows_equal(actual, expected)
    p = explain(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_plan(p, must_not_have=['Seq Scan'])
    measured = timing.measure_execution_ms(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_faster_than_baseline(measured, baseline, ratio=5)


def test_ex2(lesson_db):
    # No speed stage here: at full volume the naive NOT IN falls off a
    # cliff (minutes, not milliseconds) — we won't make you sit through
    # the baseline. The plan shape is the whole gate: a real join.
    ex = L.exercise("ex2")
    expected = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.expected_sql)
    actual = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_rows_equal(actual, expected)
    p = explain(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_plan(p, must_have=['Hash Join'])


def test_ex3(lesson_db):
    ex = L.exercise("ex3")
    expected = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.expected_sql)
    baseline = timing.cached_baseline(lesson_db, f"{L.slug}::test_ex3",
                                      ex.expected_sql)
    ex.apply_indexes(lesson_db)
    actual = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_rows_equal(actual, expected)
    p = explain(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_plan(p, must_not_have=['Seq Scan'])
    measured = timing.measure_execution_ms(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_faster_than_baseline(measured, baseline, ratio=8)


def test_ex4(lesson_db):
    ex = L.exercise("ex4")
    expected = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.expected_sql)
    baseline = timing.cached_baseline(lesson_db, f"{L.slug}::test_ex4",
                                      ex.expected_sql)
    ex.apply_indexes(lesson_db)
    actual = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_rows_equal(actual, expected)
    p = explain(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_plan(p, must_not_have=['HashAggregate', 'Unique'])
    measured = timing.measure_execution_ms(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_faster_than_baseline(measured, baseline, ratio=5)


@pytest.mark.challenge
def test_challenge(lesson_db):
    # Speed-only: several rewrites are legitimate here and their plans
    # differ, so the clock is the judge.
    ex = L.exercise("challenge")
    expected = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.expected_sql)
    baseline = timing.cached_baseline(lesson_db, f"{L.slug}::test_challenge",
                                      ex.expected_sql)
    ex.apply_indexes(lesson_db)
    actual = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_rows_equal(actual, expected)
    measured = timing.measure_execution_ms(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_faster_than_baseline(measured, baseline, ratio=5)
```

For each exercise: the reference (slow) query and your rewrite run
against the same clone and must return the same rows. Then the plan is
checked for the shape the rewrite should produce — no `Seq Scan` once
the index applies (ex1, ex3), a real join instead of a subplan (ex2),
no dedup nodes (ex4) — and finally your query must beat the naive
baseline this machine measured for itself (5x where the physics are
bitmap-bound, 8x where they're not). Exercise 2 skips the clock: its
baseline is the one query in this course too slow to measure politely.

## The teaching point

An index is a contract with a *query shape*, not with a table. The
rewrites in this lesson — computation off the column, `OR` split into
`UNION`, `NOT IN` to `NOT EXISTS`, `DISTINCT`-join to `EXISTS` — are
the four you'll apply most often in code review, and all four share
one property: **the rows don't change, only the shape does.** That's
what makes them safe to apply on a Friday afternoon. When a query is
slow and the index "should" work, diff the query's shape against the
index's contract before you reach for more DDL.

Next: **52_keyset_pagination** — the OFFSET cliff, and the rewrite
that makes page 10,000 as fast as page 1.

## Ten-pass spaced repetition

Use this ladder after completing **51 — Query rewrites**. Each pass changes the retrieval
task so repetition strengthens recall instead of becoming answer recognition.
Do the named exercise from a blank starting point whenever practical, and only
open its hints after recording your first attempt.

| Pass | When | Practice target | Retrieval task |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | now | `challenge` | Close the notes and state the central rule in one precise sentence. |
| 2 | 3 days | `ex1` | Rebuild the smallest valid example from memory, then explain each part. |
| 3 | 7 days | `ex2` | Predict the result or behavior before running anything; reconcile surprises. |

| 5 | 60 days | `ex4` | Contrast this technique with its nearest alternative and choose between them. |

A failed pass is useful evidence: return to pass 1 after three days. A clean
pass advances to the next interval. After pass 10, revisit the skill every
three years or whenever real work exposes a weak edge case.

# Reading - 51_query_rewrites

An index is a contract with a *query shape*, not with a table. Every rewrite in
this lesson leaves the answer alone and changes only the shape — which is
exactly why they are safe to apply, and why the planner's behaviour flips so
completely when you do.

## Notes

**Sargable means "the index can seek on it".** SARG is short for *search
argument*: a predicate the access method can turn into a range of a B-tree.
`col = x`, `col > x`, `col BETWEEN x AND y` qualify. `f(col) = x` does not,
because the tree is sorted by `col`, not by `f(col)`. The fix is mechanical:
move the computation to the other side of the comparison until the column
stands alone. `date_trunc('day', created_at) = d` becomes
`created_at >= d AND created_at < d + interval '1 day'`; `upper(email) = 'X'`
becomes a case-insensitive comparison the index can serve, or an expression
index (lesson 40) if the shape is unavoidable.

**Half-open ranges are the idiom to memorise.** `>= start AND < next_start`
tiles a timeline with no gaps and no overlaps, works identically for dates,
timestamps and timestamptz, and sidesteps `BETWEEN`'s inclusive upper bound —
the reason `BETWEEN '2023-06-15' AND '2023-06-16'` quietly swallows midnight
of the 16th. It also survives a column type change from `date` to
`timestamptz`, which `BETWEEN` does not.

**`NOT IN (subquery)` is the one shape PostgreSQL refuses to optimise.**
`IN (subquery)` is turned into a semi-join; `EXISTS` into a semi-join;
`NOT EXISTS` into an anti-join. `NOT IN` is left as a `SubPlan`, because SQL
says a single NULL in the subquery makes the whole predicate UNKNOWN for every
non-matching row — so the transformation is not valid in general, and the
planner does not attempt it even when the column is `NOT NULL`. While the
collected ids fit in `work_mem` you get a hashed subplan and tolerable times;
when they stop fitting, the plan degrades to re-scanning the materialised list
once per outer row and the same query is suddenly thousands of times slower.
Nothing changed but the row count.

**That rewrite is not always semantics-preserving.** `NOT IN` and `NOT EXISTS`
agree only when the subquery's column has no NULLs. If it does, `NOT IN`
returns *nothing at all* (lesson 05) while `NOT EXISTS` returns the rows you
meant. In practice you almost always wanted `NOT EXISTS` — but check the
column's nullability before you claim the rewrite changed only the speed.

**An `OR` across two tables blocks every index.** Within one table, `WHERE a =
1 OR b = 2` becomes a `BitmapOr` of two index scans (lesson 38). Across a join
there is no such node: a bitmap addresses one relation's heap, so the executor
must form the whole join and filter afterwards. `UNION` of the two arms gives
each arm its own index-friendly plan. Use `UNION`, not `UNION ALL`, unless you
have proved the arms are disjoint — a row matching both arms was emitted once
by the original.

**`DISTINCT` over a join is usually a semi-join in disguise.** Joining to
`order_items` to ask "did this product ever sell?" multiplies each product by
its line-item count and then pays a `HashAggregate` to collapse the copies
back down. `EXISTS` asks the question directly: PostgreSQL probes the index and
stops at the first match, so duplicates are never produced and there is nothing
to deduplicate. The tell in a plan is a `HashAggregate` or `Unique` sitting on
top of a join that fans out — dedup nodes that exist only to undo work.

**Reading the plan for these four.** Non-sargable predicate: `Seq Scan` with
the function call in `Filter`. `NOT IN`: `SubPlan` and a `Materialize` under a
`Seq Scan`, no join node at all. Cross-table `OR`: a `Hash Join` whose output
row count is the whole table with `Join Filter` doing the work. Redundant
`DISTINCT`: `HashAggregate` above a join whose actual rows greatly exceed its
output. `dojo plan 51_query_rewrites <ex>` prints all of this.

## ex1 — the column under a function

The index on `orders (created_at)` is perfect and unusable at the same time,
which is the whole point: nothing about the DDL is wrong. Compare this with
lesson 40, where the same mismatch was fixed from the other end by building an
index on the expression. Rewriting the query is the better default — it ships
as a deploy rather than an index build, and one index on the bare column serves
every range, not just whole days.

## ex2 — the anti-join that never happens

Notice what the gate checks and what it does not: it asserts a real join node,
and it deliberately skips the clock. Timing this baseline at 500,000 rows is
the one measurement in the course not worth waiting for, which is itself the
lesson — a shape whose cost falls off a cliff as data grows is a bug you ship
long before you notice it. `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL` and
`NOT EXISTS` both plan as anti-joins; pick whichever reads better to you.

## ex3 — the OR that straddles the join

The interesting part of the rewrite is the first arm: once you stop needing the
customer's email, the join to `customers` adds nothing, because every order has
exactly one customer and the foreign key guarantees it. Dropping a join that
cannot change the row set is the same reasoning PostgreSQL applies in its own
join-removal optimisation — it just cannot apply it here, because as written
the join is load-bearing for the second arm.

## ex4 — DISTINCT as a symptom

Read `DISTINCT` in a code review as a question rather than a construct: *what
produced the duplicates?* If the answer is "the join did", the query is asking
an existence question with a multiplication tool. If the answer is "the data
has them", the `DISTINCT` is doing real work and belongs. The gate forbids
`HashAggregate` and `Unique` precisely because the honest rewrite makes those
nodes unnecessary rather than merely cheaper.

## challenge — three sins in one query

The wrinkle is worth the difficulty note: `JOIN orders` makes the VIP visible
only because they have at least one order, so an arm that selects the customer
by email alone quietly changes the answer for a customer who never ordered.
Rewrites are safe *because* they preserve rows, so a rewrite that changes them
under some data is not a rewrite — it is a bug you have not met yet. Adding
`EXISTS` to the second arm costs one index probe and keeps the equivalence
exact.

## Further reading

- [Subquery Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) — the formal semantics of `EXISTS`, `IN` and `NOT IN`, including the NULL rule that stops the anti-join transformation.
- [Obfuscated Conditions](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause/obfuscation) — Markus Winand's catalogue of predicates that hide the column from the index, and the rewrite for each.
- [Using EXPLAIN](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/using-explain.html) — how to read `SubPlan`, `Join Filter` and `HashAggregate`, the three tells this lesson trains you to spot.
- [Combining Queries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-union.html) — `UNION` versus `UNION ALL`, and why the dedup matters when you split an `OR`.
- [Indexes on Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-expressional.html) — the other fix for a non-sargable predicate, when the query genuinely cannot be rewritten.

## Challenge — the Friday-afternoon query (optional)

`challenge/solution.sql` (provided) commits all three structural sins
at once:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE date_trunc('day', o.created_at) = TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-06-15 00:00:00+00'
   OR c.email = 'user4242@example.com';
```

"Everyone who ordered on June 15th — oh, and make sure Dana from the
VIP list is in there." Non-sargable date, `OR` across the join,
`DISTINCT` mopping up. Rewrite it: same rows, at least 5x faster.
`challenge/indexes.sql` provides `orders (created_at)`,
`orders (customer_id)`, and `customers (email)`.

Difficulty note: the honest rewrite has a subtle correctness wrinkle —
the original's `JOIN` means the VIP only appears if they have **at
least one order** (they do — but your rewrite must not *assume* so).
Several shapes work (`UNION` of two semi-joins is the reference's);
plans legitimately differ, so this gate judges by rows and clock only.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — unwrap the column

`ex1/solution.sql` (provided — this is the slow query, rewrite it):

```sql
SELECT count(*) AS orders, sum(total) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE date_trunc('day', created_at) = TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-06-15 00:00:00+00';
```

A daily-revenue tile on a dashboard. `ex1/indexes.sql` already
provides an index on `orders (created_at)` — and the query above
seq-scans 500,000 rows anyway, calling `date_trunc` on every one of
them, because the index is sorted by `created_at`, not by
`date_trunc('day', created_at)`.

Rewrite the WHERE as a half-open range on the bare column. Same one
row out; the plan should collapse to a bitmap scan over roughly 1,400
of 500,000 rows.

(Lesson 40 solved this shape the *other* way — building an expression
index to match the query. Both are valid; in production you rewrite
the query when you can, because it's a deploy instead of an index
build, and one index on the bare column serves every date range, not
just whole days.)

"Truncates to June 15th" is the same set of rows as "at or after June
15th 00:00, and strictly before June 16th 00:00". Two comparisons on
the bare column, joined with `AND`.

```sql

```

bound is *inclusive*, which would claim midnight of the 16th too.)

## Hint 1
The index is sorted by `created_at` — not by `date_trunc('day',
created_at)`. As long as the column sits inside a function call, the
sorted order is useless to the planner. Restate the predicate so the
column stands alone on one side of the comparison.

## Hint 2
"Truncates to June 15th" is the same set of rows as "at or after June
15th 00:00, and strictly before June 16th 00:00". Two comparisons on
the bare column, joined with `AND`.

## Hint 3
```sql
WHERE created_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-06-15 00:00:00+00'
  AND created_at <  TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-06-16 00:00:00+00'
```
Keep the SELECT list exactly as it was. (Resist `BETWEEN` — its upper
bound is *inclusive*, which would claim midnight of the 16th too.)

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — NOT IN, the accidental time bomb

The marketing team wants to know how many customers have **never
placed an order**. The query someone shipped:

```sql
SELECT count(*) AS never_ordered
FROM customers
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);
```

You met the *correctness* trap of `NOT IN` in lesson 05 (one NULL in
the subquery and it returns nothing — `orders.customer_id` is NOT
NULL, so this one is at least correct). This is the *performance*
trap: PostgreSQL never turns `NOT IN (subquery)` into an anti-join.
While the 500,000 collected ids fit in `work_mem` it hashes them —
tolerable. The day they don't fit, the planner silently switches to
re-scanning the materialized list **per customer row**, and the query
goes from milliseconds to tens of minutes. Same SQL, same answer, a
thousand times slower — it just needed the table to grow.

Don't run the query above against the full dataset unless you enjoy
waiting (this is also why this exercise's gate doesn't time a
baseline). Edit `ex2/solution.sql` (a bare stub) and write the
anti-join form instead: `NOT EXISTS`, or the `LEFT JOIN … IS NULL`
pattern from lesson 09. Either plans as a hash anti-join — the gate
looks for a real join in the plan. Same single count out (5,003 at
full volume).

Run: `uv run dojo test 51_query_rewrites ex2`

## Hint 1
"Never placed an order" is an **anti-join**: keep each customer row
exactly when the probe for matching orders comes up empty. You built
this shape in lesson 09 (`LEFT JOIN … IS NULL`) and lesson 13
(`NOT EXISTS`). Either works; `NOT IN` is the one form the planner
refuses to turn into a join.

## Hint 2
Correlate the subquery on the customer id:

```sql
SELECT count(*) AS never_ordered
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE ...);
```

The `...` ties `o.customer_id` to `c.id`. Run `dojo plan
51_query_rewrites ex2` — you want a `Hash Anti Join` in the tree, not
a `SubPlan` hanging off a `Seq Scan`.

## Exercise 3 — OR splits the plan in two

`ex3/solution.sql` (provided — rewrite it):

```sql
SELECT o.id, o.total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.total > 1995
   OR c.email = 'user4242@example.com';
```

A support tool: show the whale orders, plus everything belonging to
the user on the phone. Lesson 38 showed that an `OR` over two indexed
columns of the *same* table is fine — BitmapOr merges the two index
scans. But this `OR` straddles the join: one arm filters `orders`, the
other filters `customers`. No bitmap can merge across two tables, so
the executor's only option is to build the **entire join** — all
500,000 rows — and filter afterward. All three useful indexes
(`orders (total)`, `orders (customer_id)`, `customers (email)`) are
already in `ex3/indexes.sql`, unused.

The rewrite: split the `OR` into two queries — one per arm, each
index-friendly on its own — and glue them with `UNION` (not `UNION
ALL`: a whale order belonging to that very customer would appear in
both arms, and the original query emits it once). Same rows, and the
plan touches ~1,300 rows instead of half a million.

Run: `uv run dojo test 51_query_rewrites ex3`

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — DISTINCT is not a join strategy

`ex4/solution.sql` (provided — rewrite it):

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT p.id, p.name
FROM products p
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
WHERE p.category = 'garden';
```

"Which garden products have ever sold?" The question is about
*existence* — has this product at least one order item? — but the
query answers it by **counting to a million**: join every garden
product to every one of its line items (~160,000 joined rows), then
`DISTINCT` the duplicates back out. The `DISTINCT` isn't logic; it's
cleanup for a join that multiplied rows you never wanted.

Ask about existence directly: `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items
oi WHERE oi.product_id = p.id)`. That's a **semi-join** — for each
product, PostgreSQL probes the (provided) index on
`order_items (product_id)` and *stops at the first hit* instead of
enumerating all of them. No duplicates are ever produced, so there's
nothing to `DISTINCT` away — the gate forbids the dedup nodes
(`HashAggregate`, `Unique`) to make sure the cleanup crew really left.

Run: `uv run dojo test 51_query_rewrites ex4`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The question is "does at least one order item exist for this
product?" — a yes/no per product, not a list of its line items. When
a `DISTINCT` exists only to undo a join's duplication, the join was
the wrong tool. Lesson 13's `EXISTS` asks the question directly.

## Hint 2
Keep `products` as the only table in `FROM`; move `order_items` into a
correlated `EXISTS` subquery:

```sql
SELECT p.id, p.name
FROM products p
WHERE p.category = 'garden'
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi WHERE ...);
```

The `...` correlates on the product id. With the provided index,
each product costs one probe that stops at the first hit — and since
no duplicates are ever produced, `DISTINCT` (and the gate's forbidden
`HashAggregate`/`Unique` nodes) disappear.

## Hint 1
The question is "does at least one order item exist for this
product?" — a yes/no per product, not a list of its line items. When
a `DISTINCT` exists only to undo a join's duplication, the join was
the wrong tool. Lesson 13's `EXISTS` asks the question directly.

## Hint 2
Keep `products` as the only table in `FROM`; move `order_items` into a
correlated `EXISTS` subquery:

```sql
SELECT p.id, p.name
FROM products p
WHERE p.category = 'garden'
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi WHERE ...);
```

The `...` correlates on the product id. With the provided index,
each product costs one probe that stops at the first hit — and since
no duplicates are ever produced, `DISTINCT` (and the gate's forbidden
`HashAggregate`/`Unique` nodes) disappear.

lessons.briefing:
# 52 — Keyset pagination

> **Part 8 — Optimization patterns (bonus).** The second of the two
> post-course lessons on optimization that isn't DDL. Lesson 51 rewrote
> queries the index couldn't serve; this one rewrites the query that gets
> *slower every page*. The gate machinery has one twist you should notice
> immediately: the lesson's `setup.sql` holds the indexes these tables
> already have, and **the gate applies it before it measures the baseline.**
> The naive query is timed with exactly the index your rewrite gets, so
> nothing here is a disguised repeat of lesson 31.

Lesson 03 told you that `OFFSET` does not skip work, it discards it — and
then had you use it anyway, because on page 3 of a catalogue nobody can
tell. Here is the bill. `events` holds 3,000,000 rows, one per second, from
2023-10-11 04:53 to 2023-11-14 22:13. An export job walks it 20 rows at a
time. Page 1 costs 20 rows. Page 10,001 costs 200,020 rows, of which the
job keeps twenty and the database throws away 200,000 — every one of them
read, every one of them ordered, all of it work the job already did on the
previous ten thousand pages.

That is the shape of every "why does our admin UI get slower as you scroll"
ticket ever filed. It is not a missing index: with a perfect index on the
sort column, page 10,001 is still a walk of 200,020 index entries. It is
not a slow disk. It is `OFFSET` doing exactly what it is specified to do,
linearly, forever.

And it is not only slow — it is *wrong*. `OFFSET` counts positions in a
result set that is recomputed for every request. Insert one row above the
boundary between requests and every later row shifts down a slot: the user
sees an item twice, or never sees it at all. Deleting one shifts them the
other way. A pagination scheme that is defined by counting is only correct
if the data holds still, and production data never does.

## Concept

The fix is to stop describing a page by *how many rows precede it* and
start describing it by *where it starts*. You already know where it starts:
the client just received the previous page, and the last row on it carries
the sort key. Send that key back, and the next page is a range query.

```sql
-- OFFSET: "skip 40,000 rows, then give me 20" - linear in the page number
SELECT id, created_at FROM customers
ORDER BY created_at, id
OFFSET 40000 LIMIT 20;

-- keyset: "give me the 20 rows after this one" - one descent, 20 entries
SELECT id, created_at FROM customers
WHERE (created_at, id) > (TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-04-01 09:15:00+00', 31234)
ORDER BY created_at, id
LIMIT 20;
```

This is called **keyset pagination** (also seek, or cursor pagination). Three
things make it work, and all three are load-bearing:

**1. An index that matches the `ORDER BY`.** The whole trick is that
PostgreSQL can descend the B-tree to the cursor and then read forward. An
index in a different order turns the query back into a sort of everything.

**2. A `WHERE` on the bare sort key.** Lesson 51's rule applies unchanged:
`WHERE (a, b) > (x, y)` is a range the index can seek; anything that wraps
the columns in a function is not.

**3. A sort key that is unique.** `(created_at, id)` above ends in the
primary key on purpose. If the cursor is `created_at` alone and three rows
share that timestamp, then `WHERE created_at > cursor` skips the other two
forever, and `WHERE created_at >= cursor` shows one of them twice. An
ambiguous `ORDER BY` is a *correctness* bug in pagination, not a style
preference — which is why the professional habit is to append the primary
key to every pagination sort, even when ties look unlikely.

`(a, b) > (x, y)` is a **row-value comparison**, and it means exactly what
`ORDER BY a, b` means: `a > x`, or `a = x` and `b > y`. Written as one
comparison rather than that `OR` by hand, PostgreSQL can use it as a single
index condition — the hand-written version usually can't be.

The cost, and it is a real one: keyset pagination gives you "next" and
"previous", not "jump to page 4,000". There is no page number in it. Most
product surfaces — infinite scroll, activity feeds, export jobs, cursor
APIs — never needed one.

## Exercise 1 — feel the cliff

`ex1/solution.sql` (provided — this is the slow query, rewrite it):

```sql
SELECT id, ts
FROM events
WHERE ts >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-11-11 12:00:00+00'
ORDER BY ts
OFFSET 200000
LIMIT 20;
```

An export job walking the event log oldest-first from noon on November 11
(296,001 rows), 20 to a page, currently on **page 10,001**. The index it
wants already exists — `setup.sql` provides `events (ts, id)` and the gate
applies it before it times anything — and the plan is still an
`Index Only Scan` that reads **200,020 entries to return 20**.

The job holds the last row of page 10,000: its `ts` is
**2023-11-13 19:33:19+00**. Rewrite the query as a keyset seek from that
cursor. Same 20 rows, same order, columns `id` and `ts`, and the order is
graded.

Run: `uv run dojo test 52_keyset_pagination ex1`

## Exercise 2 — the tiebreak is not optional

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. The catalogue browser lists all 10,000 products
ordered by `category`, then `id`, 20 per page, and you are building **page
2** — columns `id`, `category`, `name`, exactly 20 rows, ordered.

The stub already contains the cursor: a CTE named `last_seen` holding the
last row of page 1, which is what the "next page" link would have carried.
Write the page-2 query using it.

The trap is in the data. There are 1,678 books, and `books` sorts first, so
pages 1 and 2 are both well inside a single category — a cursor that
remembers `category` alone can only say "after all books", which skips
1,658 of them and serves the reader something from eighty pages further
down. This is the ties problem from the Concept section with the numbers
filled in, and no index and no clock are involved: the naive version here is
*fast and wrong*, which is the more expensive kind of bug.

Run: `uv run dojo test 52_keyset_pagination ex2`

## Exercise 3 — newest first

`ex3/solution.sql` (provided — rewrite it):

```sql
SELECT id, ts
FROM events
ORDER BY ts DESC
OFFSET 200000
LIMIT 20;
```

The same log, read the way a UI reads it: newest first, 20 to a page, page
10,001. Same index — `setup.sql`'s `events (ts, id)` serves both directions,
because a B-tree is walked either way, and the plan will say `Backward`. The
last row of page 10,000 has `ts` = **2023-11-12 14:40:01+00**.

Rewrite it as a keyset seek. The direction change is the whole exercise:
one operator moves, and if you move it the wrong way the query returns the
page the user just read. Columns `id`, `ts`; the order is graded.

Run: `uv run dojo test 52_keyset_pagination ex3`

## Exercise 4 — a filtered feed needs its own index

`ex4/solution.sql` is provided and **already correct** — leave it alone.
This time you write `ex4/indexes.sql`.

```sql
SELECT id, ts, event_type
FROM events
WHERE customer_id = 4242
  AND ts > TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-10-20 00:00:00+00'
ORDER BY ts
LIMIT 20;
```

One customer's activity feed, keyset-paged exactly as ex1 taught, and it
takes hundreds of milliseconds to return 20 of customer 4242's 65 events.
The same `setup.sql` feed index is in place before the baseline is measured,
so this is not a lesson about having no index; it is a lesson about having
the *wrong* one. Ordering by `ts` is only half the query's contract, and the
half that index serves is the cheap half.

Build the index that serves both halves. The gate forbids `Seq Scan` and
`Sort`, which between them rule out every near-miss: an index that only
finds the customer still has to sort what it finds.

Run: `uv run dojo test 52_keyset_pagination ex4`

## Challenge — walk three pages without dropping a row (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. The review wall shows the highest-rated
reviews first — `ORDER BY rating DESC, id DESC`, 20 per page. Produce
**pages 1, 2 and 3 as one 60-row result**, columns `id` and `rating`,
ordered, with each page chained to the last row of the page before it. The
gate compares your 60 rows against a plain `ORDER BY rating DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 60` — nothing skipped, nothing repeated, in order.

`challenge/indexes.sql` provides `reviews (rating DESC, id DESC)`, so every
page is a seek rather than a sort of a million rows.

Difficulty note: the SQL is not hard — three CTEs and a `UNION ALL` — but
two details bite. Getting the cursor *out* of a page means asking for that
page's smallest key, which in a descending feed is its last row. And with
199,504 reviews rated 5, all 60 rows here carry the same rating: a cursor
that forgets the `id` half does not go slightly wrong, it goes 199,504 rows
wrong.

Run: `uv run dojo test 52_keyset_pagination challenge`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 52_keyset_pagination

`OFFSET` describes a page by counting the rows in front of it. Keyset
pagination describes a page by naming the row it starts at. Everything else in
this lesson — the index, the row-value comparison, the tiebreak, the direction
flip — follows from that one change of definition.

## Notes

**The cost model.** `OFFSET m LIMIT n` costs O(m + n): the executor must
produce m rows in order before it can know which one is the (m+1)th, and then
it discards them. An index removes the sort but not the walk, so page 10,001
of a 20-row feed still reads 200,020 index entries. Nothing about a page's
own contents makes it expensive — its *position* does, which is why deep
pagination degrades smoothly and invisibly until someone scrolls far enough to
complain.

**`OFFSET` is also unstable.** Positions are recomputed per request, so a row
inserted above the boundary between page requests pushes everything down one
slot: the reader sees one row twice and, if a row is deleted instead, misses
one entirely. Keyset pagination is defined against values rather than
positions, so concurrent inserts and deletes elsewhere in the table cannot
shift the page you asked for. This is the argument that wins the design
review, more often than the speed one.

**A cursor is the sort key of the last row you showed.** Not an id, unless the
sort is by id: the cursor must contain every column of the `ORDER BY`, because
that is what determines a position in the sequence. In an HTTP API you
usually base64 a small JSON object of exactly those columns and call it
`next_cursor`; the encoding is cosmetic, the requirement that it match the
sort is not.

**Row-value comparison, and the mistake it prevents.**
`(a, b) > (x, y)` is defined lexicographically — `a > x`, or `a = x AND b > y`
— which is precisely the order `ORDER BY a, b` produces. PostgreSQL can turn
that single comparison into one index condition on a `(a, b)` B-tree. Two
common hand-written substitutes are worse: `a >= x AND b > y` is simply wrong
(it drops every row with a larger `a` but a smaller `b`), and the correct
expansion `a > x OR (a = x AND b > y)` is right but is usually evaluated as a
filter rather than a seek. Write the row comparison.

**The sort key must be unique, and the primary key is how you get there.** If
two rows share the cursor's key, `>` skips one of them forever and `>=`
repeats one, and no amount of retrying reveals which — the page is simply
wrong. Appending the primary key to the `ORDER BY` makes the ordering total
and the cursor unambiguous. It costs nothing when the leading column is
already unique, so it is worth doing unconditionally; timestamps that "cannot
collide" collide the first time a batch job inserts a thousand rows in the
same millisecond.

**Direction, and keeping it uniform.** A descending page continues *below* its
cursor, so every `>` becomes `<` and the `ORDER BY` gains `DESC` on every
column. Keep all of the sort columns pointing the same way: a row comparison
only expresses uniform direction, so `ORDER BY rating DESC, id ASC` cannot be
written as one `(rating, id) < (...)` and additionally needs an index declared
`(rating DESC, id ASC)` to avoid a sort. Uniform direction also means one
plain ascending index serves both feeds — B-trees are walked in either
direction, and the plan says `Index Scan Backward`.

**NULLs do not belong in a cursor.** A row comparison against a NULL yields
NULL, which is not true, so the page silently ends. If a sort column is
nullable, either exclude NULLs from the paged set or page over a coalesced
expression with an index to match — and remember `NULLS FIRST`/`NULLS LAST`
is part of the ordering the index has to satisfy (lesson 35).

**Filters come before the sort in the index.** A feed that is both filtered
and ordered — one customer, one tenant, one status — needs the equality
columns first and the sort columns after: `(customer_id, ts)`, not `(ts)` and
not `(ts, customer_id)`. This is lesson 32's left-prefix rule and lesson 35's
ordering rule meeting in the same index, and it is the single most valuable
composite shape in application databases.

**What you give up.** There is no "jump to page 400" and no honest total page
count, because both are questions about positions. You get next, previous
(same comparison flipped), and a stable stream. Infinite scroll, activity
feeds, export jobs and cursor-based APIs never wanted the page numbers; a
back-office table with a page picker sometimes genuinely does, and there
`OFFSET` over a bounded, filtered result set is a defensible choice.

**Reading the plan.** The tell is the row count on the scan node, not the node
type. `Limit` over an `Index Only Scan` reading 200,020 rows is the OFFSET
version; the same plan reading 20 rows is the keyset version. If a `Sort`
appears, the index does not match the `ORDER BY`; if a `Seq Scan` appears, it
does not match the `WHERE` either.

## ex1 — the cliff, measured

The interesting number is in the plan rather than the clock: 200,020 rows into
a `Limit` that emits 20. Notice also what happens to the query's original
window predicate — once the cursor is a timestamp later than the window's
start, `ts >= '2023-11-11 12:00:00+00'` cannot exclude anything and is dead
weight. That is a general property of keyset pages: the cursor subsumes every
bound on the same column that lies behind it.

## ex2 — fast and wrong

The failure mode this exercise builds is worth internalising because it does
not look like a bug from the inside: the query is fast, the page is full, the
rows are real, and 1,658 books never appear. Nothing errors, nothing is slow,
and the report that eventually arrives says "search results are missing
items". Pagination bugs are found by walking every page and comparing the
union against the unpaginated query — which is exactly what this lesson's
challenge does.

## ex3 — the same trick, backwards

Two things flip together and they must flip together: the comparison operator
and the `ORDER BY` direction. Flip only the operator and you get twenty rows
from the wrong end of the table; flip only the `ORDER BY` and you re-serve the
page the user just read. The index does not flip at all, which surprises
people — an ascending B-tree serves a descending scan at the same cost, and
`DESC` in an index declaration only earns its keep when sort columns disagree
with each other.

## ex4 — the index has two jobs

A keyset query is only constant-time per page if the index can seek to the
cursor *within the filtered set*. With `(ts, id)` the executor can honour the
order but must test `customer_id` on every row it walks, so the cost becomes
"however far apart this customer's events are" — for one customer in 50,000,
that is the whole table. `(customer_id, ts)` pins the customer with the
leading equality and leaves that customer's rows already in `ts` order behind
it, which is the shape the query was asking for all along.

## challenge — proving a walk is lossless

Chaining pages is the real thing: an export job or a sync loop runs this
until a page comes back short. The detail people get wrong on the first
attempt is extracting the cursor from a descending page — the row you stopped
at is the page's *minimum* key, not its maximum. And `UNION ALL` is the honest
combinator here: `UNION` would silently deduplicate rows that appeared on two
pages, hiding precisely the defect the exercise exists to detect.

## Further reading

- [Paging Through Results](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/partial-results/fetch-next-page) — Markus Winand's canonical treatment of offset versus seek, with the correctness argument and the row-value syntax.
- [`LIMIT` and `OFFSET`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-limit.html) — the cost note and the documentation's own warning about paging without a deterministic `ORDER BY`.
- [Row Constructor Comparison](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparisons.html) — the formal semantics of `(a, b) > (x, y)`, including how NULL operands behave.
- [Indexes and `ORDER BY`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-ordering.html) — when an index can supply order directly, backward scans, and what `DESC`/`NULLS FIRST` in a declaration buy you.

# 52 — Keyset pagination

> **Part 8 — Optimization patterns (bonus).** The second of the two
> post-course lessons on optimization that isn't DDL. Lesson 51 rewrote
> queries the index couldn't serve; this one rewrites the query that gets
> *slower every page*. The gate machinery has one twist you should notice
> immediately: the lesson's `setup.sql` holds the indexes these tables
> already have, and **the gate applies it before it measures the baseline.**
> The naive query is timed with exactly the index your rewrite gets, so
> nothing here is a disguised repeat of lesson 31.

Lesson 03 told you that `OFFSET` does not skip work, it discards it — and
then had you use it anyway, because on page 3 of a catalogue nobody can
tell. Here is the bill. `events` holds 3,000,000 rows, one per second, from
2023-10-11 04:53 to 2023-11-14 22:13. An export job walks it 20 rows at a
time. Page 1 costs 20 rows. Page 10,001 costs 200,020 rows, of which the
job keeps twenty and the database throws away 200,000 — every one of them
read, every one of them ordered, all of it work the job already did on the
previous ten thousand pages.

That is the shape of every "why does our admin UI get slower as you scroll"
ticket ever filed. It is not a missing index: with a perfect index on the
sort column, page 10,001 is still a walk of 200,020 index entries. It is
not a slow disk. It is `OFFSET` doing exactly what it is specified to do,
linearly, forever.

And it is not only slow — it is *wrong*. `OFFSET` counts positions in a
result set that is recomputed for every request. Insert one row above the
boundary between requests and every later row shifts down a slot: the user
sees an item twice, or never sees it at all. Deleting one shifts them the
other way. A pagination scheme that is defined by counting is only correct
if the data holds still, and production data never does.

## Concept

The fix is to stop describing a page by *how many rows precede it* and
start describing it by *where it starts*. You already know where it starts:
the client just received the previous page, and the last row on it carries
the sort key. Send that key back, and the next page is a range query.

```sql
-- OFFSET: "skip 40,000 rows, then give me 20" - linear in the page number
SELECT id, created_at FROM customers
ORDER BY created_at, id
OFFSET 40000 LIMIT 20;

-- keyset: "give me the 20 rows after this one" - one descent, 20 entries
SELECT id, created_at FROM customers
WHERE (created_at, id) > (TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-04-01 09:15:00+00', 31234)
ORDER BY created_at, id
LIMIT 20;
```

This is called **keyset pagination** (also seek, or cursor pagination). Three
things make it work, and all three are load-bearing:

**1. An index that matches the `ORDER BY`.** The whole trick is that
PostgreSQL can descend the B-tree to the cursor and then read forward. An
index in a different order turns the query back into a sort of everything.

**2. A `WHERE` on the bare sort key.** Lesson 51's rule applies unchanged:
`WHERE (a, b) > (x, y)` is a range the index can seek; anything that wraps
the columns in a function is not.

**3. A sort key that is unique.** `(created_at, id)` above ends in the
primary key on purpose. If the cursor is `created_at` alone and three rows
share that timestamp, then `WHERE created_at > cursor` skips the other two
forever, and `WHERE created_at >= cursor` shows one of them twice. An
ambiguous `ORDER BY` is a *correctness* bug in pagination, not a style
preference — which is why the professional habit is to append the primary
key to every pagination sort, even when ties look unlikely.

`(a, b) > (x, y)` is a **row-value comparison**, and it means exactly what
`ORDER BY a, b` means: `a > x`, or `a = x` and `b > y`. Written as one
comparison rather than that `OR` by hand, PostgreSQL can use it as a single
index condition — the hand-written version usually can't be.

The cost, and it is a real one: keyset pagination gives you "next" and
"previous", not "jump to page 4,000". There is no page number in it. Most
product surfaces — infinite scroll, activity feeds, export jobs, cursor
APIs — never needed one.

## Exercise 1 — feel the cliff

`ex1/solution.sql` (provided — this is the slow query, rewrite it):

```sql
SELECT id, ts
FROM events
WHERE ts >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-11-11 12:00:00+00'
ORDER BY ts
OFFSET 200000
LIMIT 20;
```

An export job walking the event log oldest-first from noon on November 11
(296,001 rows), 20 to a page, currently on **page 10,001**. The index it
wants already exists — `setup.sql` provides `events (ts, id)` and the gate
applies it before it times anything — and the plan is still an
`Index Only Scan` that reads **200,020 entries to return 20**.

The job holds the last row of page 10,000: its `ts` is
**2023-11-13 19:33:19+00**. Rewrite the query as a keyset seek from that
cursor. Same 20 rows, same order, columns `id` and `ts`, and the order is
graded.

Run: `uv run dojo test 52_keyset_pagination ex1`

## Exercise 2 — the tiebreak is not optional

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. The catalogue browser lists all 10,000 products
ordered by `category`, then `id`, 20 per page, and you are building **page
2** — columns `id`, `category`, `name`, exactly 20 rows, ordered.

The stub already contains the cursor: a CTE named `last_seen` holding the
last row of page 1, which is what the "next page" link would have carried.
Write the page-2 query using it.

The trap is in the data. There are 1,678 books, and `books` sorts first, so
pages 1 and 2 are both well inside a single category — a cursor that
remembers `category` alone can only say "after all books", which skips
1,658 of them and serves the reader something from eighty pages further
down. This is the ties problem from the Concept section with the numbers
filled in, and no index and no clock are involved: the naive version here is
*fast and wrong*, which is the more expensive kind of bug.

Run: `uv run dojo test 52_keyset_pagination ex2`

## Exercise 3 — newest first

`ex3/solution.sql` (provided — rewrite it):

```sql
SELECT id, ts
FROM events
ORDER BY ts DESC
OFFSET 200000
LIMIT 20;
```

The same log, read the way a UI reads it: newest first, 20 to a page, page
10,001. Same index — `setup.sql`'s `events (ts, id)` serves both directions,
because a B-tree is walked either way, and the plan will say `Backward`. The
last row of page 10,000 has `ts` = **2023-11-12 14:40:01+00**.

Rewrite it as a keyset seek. The direction change is the whole exercise:
one operator moves, and if you move it the wrong way the query returns the
page the user just read. Columns `id`, `ts`; the order is graded.

Run: `uv run dojo test 52_keyset_pagination ex3`

## Exercise 4 — a filtered feed needs its own index

`ex4/solution.sql` is provided and **already correct** — leave it alone.
This time you write `ex4/indexes.sql`.

```sql
SELECT id, ts, event_type
FROM events
WHERE customer_id = 4242
  AND ts > TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-10-20 00:00:00+00'
ORDER BY ts
LIMIT 20;
```

One customer's activity feed, keyset-paged exactly as ex1 taught, and it
takes hundreds of milliseconds to return 20 of customer 4242's 65 events.
The same `setup.sql` feed index is in place before the baseline is measured,
so this is not a lesson about having no index; it is a lesson about having
the *wrong* one. Ordering by `ts` is only half the query's contract, and the
half that index serves is the cheap half.

Build the index that serves both halves. The gate forbids `Seq Scan` and
`Sort`, which between them rule out every near-miss: an index that only
finds the customer still has to sort what it finds.

Run: `uv run dojo test 52_keyset_pagination ex4`

## Challenge — walk three pages without dropping a row (optional)

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. The review wall shows the highest-rated
reviews first — `ORDER BY rating DESC, id DESC`, 20 per page. Produce
**pages 1, 2 and 3 as one 60-row result**, columns `id` and `rating`,
ordered, with each page chained to the last row of the page before it. The
gate compares your 60 rows against a plain `ORDER BY rating DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 60` — nothing skipped, nothing repeated, in order.

`challenge/indexes.sql` provides `reviews (rating DESC, id DESC)`, so every
page is a seek rather than a sort of a million rows.

Difficulty note: the SQL is not hard — three CTEs and a `UNION ALL` — but
two details bite. Getting the cursor *out* of a page means asking for that
page's smallest key, which in a descending feed is its last row. And with
199,504 reviews rated 5, all 60 rows here carry the same rating: a cursor
that forgets the `id` half does not go slightly wrong, it goes 199,504 rows
wrong.

Run: `uv run dojo test 52_keyset_pagination challenge`

## The gate

```python
"""Gates for 52_keyset_pagination. Quoted verbatim in README.md.

Part 8's inversion, sharpened: setup.sql's feed index is applied *before* the
baseline is measured, so the naive OFFSET query is timed with exactly the
index your rewrite gets. What the clock compares is the pagination technique
and nothing else. Exercise 4 is the deliberate exception - there the missing
index is the whole problem, and it is yours to write.
"""
import pytest

from dojo import grader, timing
from dojo.lesson import Lesson
from dojo.plan import explain

L = Lesson(__file__)


def test_ex1(lesson_db):
    ex = L.exercise("ex1")
    L.apply_setup(lesson_db)             # the feed index, applied before the clock
    expected = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.expected_sql)
    baseline = timing.cached_baseline(lesson_db, f"{L.slug}::test_ex1",
                                      ex.expected_sql)
    actual = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_rows_equal(actual, expected, ordered=True)
    p = explain(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_plan(p, must_not_have=['Seq Scan', 'Sort'])
    measured = timing.measure_execution_ms(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_faster_than_baseline(measured, baseline, ratio=8)


def test_ex2(lesson_db):
    # No clock and no index here: a missing tiebreak does not make a page
    # slow, it makes it wrong. 10,000 products are enough to prove that.
    ex = L.exercise("ex2")
    expected = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.expected_sql)
    actual = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_rows_equal(actual, expected, ordered=True)


def test_ex3(lesson_db):
    ex = L.exercise("ex3")
    L.apply_setup(lesson_db)
    expected = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.expected_sql)
    baseline = timing.cached_baseline(lesson_db, f"{L.slug}::test_ex3",
                                      ex.expected_sql)
    actual = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_rows_equal(actual, expected, ordered=True)
    p = explain(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_plan(p, must_not_have=['Seq Scan', 'Sort'])
    measured = timing.measure_execution_ms(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_faster_than_baseline(measured, baseline, ratio=8)


def test_ex4(lesson_db):
    # Same setup.sql, same order - and this time the feed index buys the
    # baseline nothing, because the query filters as well as sorts. Your
    # index goes in ex4/indexes.sql; the query is provided and does not change.
    ex = L.exercise("ex4")
    L.apply_setup(lesson_db)
    expected = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.expected_sql)
    baseline = timing.cached_baseline(lesson_db, f"{L.slug}::test_ex4",
                                      ex.expected_sql)
    ex.apply_indexes(lesson_db)
    actual = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_rows_equal(actual, expected, ordered=True)
    p = explain(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_plan(p, must_not_have=['Seq Scan', 'Sort'])
    measured = timing.measure_execution_ms(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_faster_than_baseline(measured, baseline, ratio=8)


@pytest.mark.challenge
def test_challenge(lesson_db):
    # Correctness only: sixty rows, nothing skipped, nothing repeated, in
    # order. The provided index keeps each page a seek instead of a sort.
    ex = L.exercise("challenge")
    ex.apply_indexes(lesson_db)
    expected = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.expected_sql)
    actual = ex.fetch(lesson_db, ex.solution_sql)
    grader.assert_rows_equal(actual, expected, ordered=True)
```

Read the order of the stages in ex1 and ex3: `apply_setup` comes first, so
the `OFFSET` query whose time becomes your baseline is running on the same
`events (ts, id)` index your rewrite uses. Then your rows must match the
reference's **in order** (pagination that returns the right rows in the
wrong order is broken), the plan must contain no `Seq Scan` and no `Sort`
(you seeked; you did not scan and re-sort), and the clock must show at least
**8x**. The measured difference is far larger than 8x — the gate is loose on
purpose, because the ratio grows with the page number and shrinks on a busy
machine, and the technique is what is being graded.

Exercise 4 adds one line: after the same `apply_setup`, `apply_indexes` —
your file this time — runs once the baseline is already recorded. Exercise 2
and the challenge drop the plan and the clock entirely and compare rows
only; nothing they teach is about speed.

## The teaching point

Every pagination bug in production is one of these two, and they arrive
together. The slow one is `OFFSET` on a deep page: linear cost the user pays
for scrolling, invisible in development where page 3 is as deep as anyone
goes. The wrong one is an ambiguous `ORDER BY`: rows that duplicate or
vanish between pages, reported as "flaky", reproducible only against
production-shaped data.

Both dissolve into the same discipline. Sort by something unique — append
the primary key if you have to. Index the thing you sort by, together with
whatever you filter by, in that order. Then page by *where you are*, not by
*how far you have counted*. `WHERE (key) > (cursor) ORDER BY key LIMIT n` is
constant time on page 1 and on page 10,001, and it stays correct while rows
are being inserted underneath it.
