# Reading - 54_interview_drills

Six drills, six shapes, and a clock. What follows is the theory behind each
one — why interviewers reach for it, what they are watching for while you
type, and the specific mistake that costs the offer.

## Notes

**The shapes are the syllabus.** A hands-on SQL screen is not a test of how
much SQL you know; it is a test of whether four or five specific query
shapes are automatic. Top-N per group, running total and period-over-period,
latest-row-per-key, a cohort aggregate, and a report that has to include the
rows where nothing happened. If you can produce each of those from memory,
you have covered the overwhelming majority of what gets asked, and your
attention is free for the part that is actually specific to the question.

**Aggregate first, window second.** Four of the six drills here have the same
skeleton: collapse to the grain the question is about, then use a window
function to compare each of those rows to its neighbours. Monthly revenue
then `lag`. Customer revenue then `row_number`. Getting the grain right is
the whole game — if you find yourself windowing over raw `orders` rows when
the question is about months, you have skipped a layer and the query will
fight you.

**You cannot filter a window function in the same SELECT that computes it.**
Window functions are evaluated after `WHERE` and `GROUP BY` and before
`ORDER BY` and `LIMIT`, so `WHERE rn <= 3` has to live one level out — in
the query that selects from the CTE or subquery where `rn` was computed.
Every top-N-per-group query is two layers for this reason and no other, and
being able to say *why* is worth more than being able to type it.

**Determinism is a requirement, not a nicety.** `row_number()` over a tie
picks arbitrarily, which means the same query can return different rows on
different runs — a bug that survives code review because it passes every
time you run it and fails on the day the data shifts. Add a unique column to
the `ORDER BY` inside the window, and repeat the same ordering in the outer
`ORDER BY`. Every drill in this lesson names its tie-break; in a real
interview, naming it yourself unprompted is the move.

**A report needs the rows where nothing happened.** This is the one people
have never thought about until it bites: months with no hires, days with no
orders, categories with no sales. Those rows are not in the table, so no
`GROUP BY` can produce them. You manufacture the axis with `generate_series`
and `LEFT JOIN` the data onto it — and then remember `count(col)` rather
than `count(*)`, or your empty months report one instead of zero.

**On the clock.** Time-boxes here are deliberately tight-ish. If one runs
out, take the hint and note that you took it; the value of the drill is the
diagnostic, not the pass. A drill you solved on Hint 2 today is exactly the
drill to redo cold in a week — which is what the review ladder is for, and
why this lesson ships a review variant.

## ex1 — top three customers per country

The single most-asked hands-on question, in one variant or another. Two
layers: a `GROUP BY` down to one row per customer with their revenue, then
`row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY revenue DESC, id)` and
`WHERE rn <= 3` outside it.

What the interviewer is actually watching for is whether you ask what
"spent the most" means before you write it. Does it include cancelled
orders? Here it does not — that is why the prompt says so, and in the room
it is the question you should have asked. The second thing they watch for is
the tie-break: without `, id` in the window's `ORDER BY`, two customers on
identical revenue come back in whatever order the planner produced, and
"whatever the planner produced" is not an answer.

The follow-up to be ready for is "what if I wanted everyone tied for third,
not exactly three?" — that is `rank()` instead of `row_number()`, and being
able to switch between them on request is the point of Q23 in lesson 53's
question bank.

## ex2 — monthly revenue and the change from last month

Aggregate to the grain, then look sideways. `date_trunc('month',
created_at)` with `sum(total)` gives one row per month; `lag(revenue) OVER
(ORDER BY month)` gives that row the previous month's number, and the
subtraction is the answer. This is the query that makes people finally
understand what window functions are *for*: a `GROUP BY` has thrown away the
neighbouring rows by the time you want them, and a self-join on
"month - 1 month" is a mess by comparison.

Leave the first month's `change` as NULL. It is genuinely unknown — there is
no prior month in the data — and `coalesce(..., 0)` there would assert that
revenue was flat, which is a different claim and a false one. Interviewers
notice; "I left it NULL because we have no November 2022 baseline" is a
better sentence than any zero.

The natural follow-up is the percentage version, `round(100.0 * (revenue -
prev) / prev, 1)`, and it comes with two traps worth having ready: integer
division if you write `100` instead of `100.0`, and a division by zero if any
month could have zero revenue — `nullif(prev, 0)` is the guard.

## ex3 — the latest order per customer

Deduplication down to one row per key, asked here as "their most recent
order" but just as often as "remove the duplicates, keep the newest". Rank
inside the partition with `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER
BY created_at DESC, id DESC)` and keep `rn = 1`.

Have the second answer ready, because in a PostgreSQL interview it lands
well: `SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id) ... ORDER BY customer_id,
created_at DESC, id DESC` does it in one pass and reads beautifully, at the
cost of being PostgreSQL-only. Lesson 49 is the whole story. The
`ORDER BY` in a `DISTINCT ON` query is not optional decoration — it is what
decides which row survives, which is why the leading column must be the
`DISTINCT ON` key.

The trap here is subtle and worth saying out loud: the tie-break. Two orders
at the same `created_at` and no `id DESC` means an arbitrary winner, and
because collisions are rare it will pass every test you write and then
misbehave in production exactly once a quarter.

## ex4 — do first-time buyers come back?

A cohort aggregate, and the drill in this lesson most likely to eat your
time-box. Three layers: find each customer's first order, label them with
its month, then ask whether they ordered again inside thirty days of *that
customer's own* first order.

The elegant version uses `min(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id)`,
which attaches the first-order timestamp to **every** one of that customer's
order rows without collapsing them — so the comparison `created_at >
first_at AND created_at <= first_at + INTERVAL '30 days'` can be evaluated
row by row, then folded up with `bool_or`. That is the window-versus-GROUP-BY
distinction doing real work: a `GROUP BY` would have thrown away the
individual orders you need to test.

Two mistakes to avoid deliberately. Strict `>` on the first comparison, or
the first order matches its own window and every cohort reports 100%
retention — a number so clean it should make you suspicious immediately. And
a fixed calendar window (`first day of the cohort month + 30 days`) is a
*different* metric from a per-customer window; both are legitimate, they
answer different questions, and an interviewer will absolutely ask which one
you implemented.

Do notice the shape of the answer: the November and December 2022 cohorts
are enormous and everything after is tiny. That is an artefact of a synthetic
dataset where the order history starts all at once, not a business insight —
a good reminder to look at cohort sizes before you draw conclusions from
cohort rates.

## ex5 — the report that includes its empty months

The rows you need are not in the database. Four months of 2019 have no sales
hires, so `GROUP BY date_trunc('month', hired_on)` can only ever return
eight rows, and no amount of clever aggregation will produce the other four.
You have to build the axis and attach the data to it — `generate_series`
gives you the twelve months, and a `LEFT JOIN` hangs the hires off it.

Then the two traps, and they are both callbacks. `count(*)` counts the
NULL-extended row and prints **1** for the empty months, because a
NULL-extended row is still a row — `count(s.id)` gives the 0 you want.
And putting `s.department = 'sales'` in the `WHERE` clause instead of the
`ON` clause deletes every NULL-extended row and silently converts your
`LEFT JOIN` back into an inner one, which is lesson 09's entire subject
turning up in an interview eleven lessons later.

There is a second correct shape: aggregate the hires first in a CTE, then
`LEFT JOIN` that onto the calendar and `coalesce(hires, 0)`. It is easier to
reason about, harder to get the join condition wrong, and a perfectly good
thing to say you prefer.

## challenge — the country scorecard

This is the take-home in miniature, and its difficulty is not SQL — it is
holding six definitions straight while you write. `revenue` excludes
cancelled orders, `orders` counts them, `buyers` counts customers rather
than orders, `avg_order_value` averages only the non-cancelled ones. Every
one of those is a place where a plausible query produces a wrong number that
nobody catches, which is precisely why the exercise looks like this.

The structural move is decomposition: one aggregate per country for the
measures, one ranked aggregate per (country, customer) for the top customer,
joined at the end on `country`. Trying to produce the top customer's *name*
inside the same `GROUP BY c.country` is the trap — a name is not an
aggregate of the group, and the moment you notice that, the second CTE
writes itself. `FILTER (WHERE ...)` is what lets the differently-filtered
measures share one pass over the data instead of becoming four subqueries.

Write `100.0`, not `100`. `100 * 4 / 24` is integer division and evaluates
to 16, not 16.7, and the report ships with every cancel rate rounded to a
whole number. It is a one-character bug and it is one of the most common
real-world defects in reporting SQL.

For the follow-up: if this scorecard had to run every fifteen minutes on a
table a hundred times this size, what would you change? The answers are a
materialized view refreshed on a schedule (lesson 46), an index on
`orders.customer_id` so the join stops being a full scan (lesson 33), or
pre-aggregating to a daily summary table and reading that. Having one of
those ready turns a query exercise into an architecture conversation, which
is the conversation more senior candidates get to have.

## review1 — best seller per category

Top-N-per-group with N = 1, which is the version most likely to appear on a
whiteboard because it fits on one. The measure is units — `sum(quantity)`
from `order_items` — not revenue and not the number of orders, and reading
the measure correctly is half of what is being tested.

When it comes round on the review ladder, write it both ways: `row_number()`
with `rn = 1`, and `DISTINCT ON (category)`. Then say which you would ship
and why. Two correct answers plus a stated preference is what fluency sounds
like from the other side of the table, and it takes about ninety seconds
longer than one answer.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL — Window Functions Tutorial](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) — the gentlest correct explanation of partitions and frames, and where windows sit relative to `WHERE`. Behind ex1, ex2 and ex4.
- [PostgreSQL — SELECT: DISTINCT ON](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html#SQL-DISTINCT) — the exact semantics of which row survives, and why the `ORDER BY` is load-bearing. The other answer to ex3.
- [PostgreSQL — Set Returning Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-srf.html) — `generate_series` over dates and timestamps, the tool that manufactures the missing rows in ex5.
- [PostgreSQL — Aggregate Expressions and FILTER](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html#SYNTAX-AGGREGATES) — how `FILTER` restricts one aggregate to a subset of the group, which is what makes the challenge one pass instead of four.
- [Modern SQL — Window functions](https://modern-sql.com/feature/over) — the same material with the standard's history and other engines' quirks, useful when the interviewer's background is not PostgreSQL.

| `cancel_rate` | `round(100.0 * <cancelled orders> / <all orders>, 1)` |
| `top_customer` | `name` of the customer with the highest non-cancelled spend in that country; ties broken by lower customer `id` |

**Ordered by `revenue` descending.** (12 rows.)

floor every rate to a whole number, and it is the kind of silent wrongness
this exercise exists to make you feel once. The reference query takes about
fifteen seconds against the full dataset, so budget for that in your timer
rather than assuming your query hung.

most likely to be handed on a whiteboard.

## The teaching point

Nobody writes a top-N-per-group query from first principles in an interview.
They write it from memory, because they have written it thirty times, and
the mental effort goes into the parts that are actually specific to the
question — what "revenue" excludes, what happens on a tie, whether the
report needs its empty rows. That is the whole reason this lesson exists as
drills with a clock rather than as more exercises: the shapes have to be
automatic so that your attention is free for the requirements.

The other half of it is the requirements themselves. Look back at the
challenge's definition table — `revenue` excludes cancelled orders, `orders`
counts them, `buyers` counts customers and not orders. In a real interview
that table does not exist; the interviewer says one paragraph and expects you
to ask. The candidates who do well are not the ones who type fastest, they
are the ones who spend the first ninety seconds making the ambiguity go
away, and then write a query that is right the first time.

these shapes come back on the 3 → 7 → 21 → 60-day ladder. Book them into the
week before your interview and they will be warm when you need them.

# Reading - 54_interview_drills

Six drills, six shapes, and a clock. What follows is the theory behind each
one — why interviewers reach for it, what they are watching for while you
type, and the specific mistake that costs the offer.

## Notes

**The shapes are the syllabus.** A hands-on SQL screen is not a test of how
much SQL you know; it is a test of whether four or five specific query
shapes are automatic. Top-N per group, running total and period-over-period,
latest-row-per-key, a cohort aggregate, and a report that has to include the
rows where nothing happened. If you can produce each of those from memory,
you have covered the overwhelming majority of what gets asked, and your
attention is free for the part that is actually specific to the question.

**Aggregate first, window second.** Four of the six drills here have the same
skeleton: collapse to the grain the question is about, then use a window
function to compare each of those rows to its neighbours. Monthly revenue
then `lag`. Customer revenue then `row_number`. Getting the grain right is
the whole game — if you find yourself windowing over raw `orders` rows when
the question is about months, you have skipped a layer and the query will
fight you.

**You cannot filter a window function in the same SELECT that computes it.**
Window functions are evaluated after `WHERE` and `GROUP BY` and before
`ORDER BY` and `LIMIT`, so `WHERE rn <= 3` has to live one level out — in
the query that selects from the CTE or subquery where `rn` was computed.
Every top-N-per-group query is two layers for this reason and no other, and
being able to say *why* is worth more than being able to type it.

**Determinism is a requirement, not a nicety.** `row_number()` over a tie
picks arbitrarily, which means the same query can return different rows on
different runs — a bug that survives code review because it passes every
time you run it and fails on the day the data shifts. Add a unique column to
the `ORDER BY` inside the window, and repeat the same ordering in the outer
`ORDER BY`. Every drill in this lesson names its tie-break; in a real
interview, naming it yourself unprompted is the move.

**A report needs the rows where nothing happened.** This is the one people
have never thought about until it bites: months with no hires, days with no
orders, categories with no sales. Those rows are not in the table, so no
`GROUP BY` can produce them. You manufacture the axis with `generate_series`
and `LEFT JOIN` the data onto it — and then remember `count(col)` rather
than `count(*)`, or your empty months report one instead of zero.

**On the clock.** Time-boxes here are deliberately tight-ish. If one runs
out, take the hint and note that you took it; the value of the drill is the
diagnostic, not the pass. A drill you solved on Hint 2 today is exactly the
drill to redo cold in a week — which is what the review ladder is for, and
why this lesson ships a review variant.

## ex1 — top three customers per country

The single most-asked hands-on question, in one variant or another. Two
layers: a `GROUP BY` down to one row per customer with their revenue, then
`row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY revenue DESC, id)` and
`WHERE rn <= 3` outside it.

What the interviewer is actually watching for is whether you ask what
"spent the most" means before you write it. Does it include cancelled
orders? Here it does not — that is why the prompt says so, and in the room
it is the question you should have asked. The second thing they watch for is
the tie-break: without `, id` in the window's `ORDER BY`, two customers on
identical revenue come back in whatever order the planner produced, and
"whatever the planner produced" is not an answer.

The follow-up to be ready for is "what if I wanted everyone tied for third,
not exactly three?" — that is `rank()` instead of `row_number()`, and being
able to switch between them on request is the point of Q23 in lesson 53's
question bank.

## ex2 — monthly revenue and the change from last month

Aggregate to the grain, then look sideways. `date_trunc('month',
created_at)` with `sum(total)` gives one row per month; `lag(revenue) OVER
(ORDER BY month)` gives that row the previous month's number, and the
subtraction is the answer. This is the query that makes people finally
understand what window functions are *for*: a `GROUP BY` has thrown away the
neighbouring rows by the time you want them, and a self-join on
"month - 1 month" is a mess by comparison.

Leave the first month's `change` as NULL. It is genuinely unknown — there is
no prior month in the data — and `coalesce(..., 0)` there would assert that
revenue was flat, which is a different claim and a false one. Interviewers
notice; "I left it NULL because we have no November 2022 baseline" is a
better sentence than any zero.

The natural follow-up is the percentage version, `round(100.0 * (revenue -
prev) / prev, 1)`, and it comes with two traps worth having ready: integer
division if you write `100` instead of `100.0`, and a division by zero if any
month could have zero revenue — `nullif(prev, 0)` is the guard.

## ex3 — the latest order per customer

Deduplication down to one row per key, asked here as "their most recent
order" but just as often as "remove the duplicates, keep the newest". Rank
inside the partition with `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER
BY created_at DESC, id DESC)` and keep `rn = 1`.

Have the second answer ready, because in a PostgreSQL interview it lands
well: `SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id) ... ORDER BY customer_id,
created_at DESC, id DESC` does it in one pass and reads beautifully, at the
cost of being PostgreSQL-only. Lesson 49 is the whole story. The
`ORDER BY` in a `DISTINCT ON` query is not optional decoration — it is what
decides which row survives, which is why the leading column must be the
`DISTINCT ON` key.

The trap here is subtle and worth saying out loud: the tie-break. Two orders
at the same `created_at` and no `id DESC` means an arbitrary winner, and
because collisions are rare it will pass every test you write and then
misbehave in production exactly once a quarter.

## ex4 — do first-time buyers come back?

A cohort aggregate, and the drill in this lesson most likely to eat your
time-box. Three layers: find each customer's first order, label them with
its month, then ask whether they ordered again inside thirty days of *that
customer's own* first order.

The elegant version uses `min(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id)`,
which attaches the first-order timestamp to **every** one of that customer's
order rows without collapsing them — so the comparison `created_at >
first_at AND created_at <= first_at + INTERVAL '30 days'` can be evaluated
row by row, then folded up with `bool_or`. That is the window-versus-GROUP-BY
distinction doing real work: a `GROUP BY` would have thrown away the
individual orders you need to test.

Two mistakes to avoid deliberately. Strict `>` on the first comparison, or
the first order matches its own window and every cohort reports 100%
retention — a number so clean it should make you suspicious immediately. And
a fixed calendar window (`first day of the cohort month + 30 days`) is a
*different* metric from a per-customer window; both are legitimate, they
answer different questions, and an interviewer will absolutely ask which one
you implemented.

Do notice the shape of the answer: the November and December 2022 cohorts
are enormous and everything after is tiny. That is an artefact of a synthetic
dataset where the order history starts all at once, not a business insight —
a good reminder to look at cohort sizes before you draw conclusions from
cohort rates.

## ex5 — the report that includes its empty months

The rows you need are not in the database. Four months of 2019 have no sales
hires, so `GROUP BY date_trunc('month', hired_on)` can only ever return
eight rows, and no amount of clever aggregation will produce the other four.
You have to build the axis and attach the data to it — `generate_series`
gives you the twelve months, and a `LEFT JOIN` hangs the hires off it.

Then the two traps, and they are both callbacks. `count(*)` counts the
NULL-extended row and prints **1** for the empty months, because a
NULL-extended row is still a row — `count(s.id)` gives the 0 you want.
And putting `s.department = 'sales'` in the `WHERE` clause instead of the
`ON` clause deletes every NULL-extended row and silently converts your
`LEFT JOIN` back into an inner one, which is lesson 09's entire subject
turning up in an interview eleven lessons later.

There is a second correct shape: aggregate the hires first in a CTE, then
`LEFT JOIN` that onto the calendar and `coalesce(hires, 0)`. It is easier to
reason about, harder to get the join condition wrong, and a perfectly good
thing to say you prefer.

## challenge — the country scorecard

This is the take-home in miniature, and its difficulty is not SQL — it is
holding six definitions straight while you write. `revenue` excludes
cancelled orders, `orders` counts them, `buyers` counts customers rather
than orders, `avg_order_value` averages only the non-cancelled ones. Every
one of those is a place where a plausible query produces a wrong number that
nobody catches, which is precisely why the exercise looks like this.

The structural move is decomposition: one aggregate per country for the
measures, one ranked aggregate per (country, customer) for the top customer,
joined at the end on `country`. Trying to produce the top customer's *name*
inside the same `GROUP BY c.country` is the trap — a name is not an
aggregate of the group, and the moment you notice that, the second CTE
writes itself. `FILTER (WHERE ...)` is what lets the differently-filtered
measures share one pass over the data instead of becoming four subqueries.

Write `100.0`, not `100`. `100 * 4 / 24` is integer division and evaluates
to 16, not 16.7, and the report ships with every cancel rate rounded to a
whole number. It is a one-character bug and it is one of the most common
real-world defects in reporting SQL.

For the follow-up: if this scorecard had to run every fifteen minutes on a
table a hundred times this size, what would you change? The answers are a
materialized view refreshed on a schedule (lesson 46), an index on
`orders.customer_id` so the join stops being a full scan (lesson 33), or
pre-aggregating to a daily summary table and reading that. Having one of
those ready turns a query exercise into an architecture conversation, which
is the conversation more senior candidates get to have.

## review1 — best seller per category

Top-N-per-group with N = 1, which is the version most likely to appear on a
whiteboard because it fits on one. The measure is units — `sum(quantity)`
from `order_items` — not revenue and not the number of orders, and reading
the measure correctly is half of what is being tested.

When it comes round on the review ladder, write it both ways: `row_number()`
with `rn = 1`, and `DISTINCT ON (category)`. Then say which you would ship
and why. Two correct answers plus a stated preference is what fluency sounds
like from the other side of the table, and it takes about ninety seconds
longer than one answer.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL — Window Functions Tutorial](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) — the gentlest correct explanation of partitions and frames, and where windows sit relative to `WHERE`. Behind ex1, ex2 and ex4.
- [PostgreSQL — SELECT: DISTINCT ON](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html#SQL-DISTINCT) — the exact semantics of which row survives, and why the `ORDER BY` is load-bearing. The other answer to ex3.
- [PostgreSQL — Set Returning Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-srf.html) — `generate_series` over dates and timestamps, the tool that manufactures the missing rows in ex5.
- [PostgreSQL — Aggregate Expressions and FILTER](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html#SYNTAX-AGGREGATES) — how `FILTER` restricts one aggregate to a subset of the group, which is what makes the challenge one pass instead of four.
- [Modern SQL — Window functions](https://modern-sql.com/feature/over) — the same material with the standard's history and other engines' quirks, useful when the interviewer's background is not PostgreSQL.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — the take-home, in 45 minutes (optional, hard)

> *"Build me a one-page country scorecard. Per country: revenue, how many
> orders, how many customers actually bought, average order value, what
> percentage of orders got cancelled, and the name of our single biggest
> customer there. Sort it so the biggest market is at the top."*

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. This is a realistic 45-minute composite: no
single construct in it is new, and the difficulty is entirely in holding six
definitions straight at once. Read the definitions twice — they deliberately
do not all filter the same way.

Columns, in this order:

| column | definition |
|---|---|
| `country` | the customer's country |
| `revenue` | `sum(o.total)` over that country's **non-cancelled** orders |
| `orders` | count of **all** that country's orders, cancelled included |
| `buyers` | number of distinct customers with at least one order |
| `avg_order_value` | `round(avg(o.total), 2)` over the **non-cancelled** orders |
| `cancel_rate` | `round(100.0 * <cancelled orders> / <all orders>, 1)` |
| `top_customer` | `name` of the customer with the highest non-cancelled spend in that country; ties broken by lower customer `id` |

**Ordered by `revenue` descending.** (12 rows.)

Write `100.0` and not `100` in the cancel rate — integer division would
floor every rate to a whole number, and it is the kind of silent wrongness
this exercise exists to make you feel once. The reference query takes about
fifteen seconds against the full dataset, so budget for that in your timer
rather than assuming your query hung.

Run: `uv run dojo test 54_interview_drills challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Do not try to write it as one `SELECT`. Sketch the report as two independent
results -- the per-country measures, and the per-country top customer --
then join them on `country` at the end. That decomposition is most of what
is being assessed.

## Hint 2
Measures: one `GROUP BY c.country` over `customers` joined to `orders`,
using `FILTER (WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled')` on the money columns while
`count(*)` stays over every order. Top customer: group by
`(country, customer)`, rank with `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY country
ORDER BY sum(o.total) DESC, c.id)`, keep `rn = 1`.

## Hint 3
Three things that decide whether the numbers are right. `100.0`, not `100`,
or integer division floors your cancel rate to a whole number. `avg(total)
FILTER (...)` averages only the non-cancelled orders while `count(*)` counts
all of them -- read the spec once more and check which measure excludes
what. And `count(DISTINCT o.customer_id)` counts buyers, whereas `count(*)`
counts orders; mixing them up is the single most common way this report goes
out wrong.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Do not try to write it as one `SELECT`. Sketch the report as two independent
results -- the per-country measures, and the per-country top customer --
then join them on `country` at the end. That decomposition is most of what
is being assessed.

## Hint 2
Measures: one `GROUP BY c.country` over `customers` joined to `orders`,
using `FILTER (WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled')` on the money columns while
`count(*)` stays over every order. Top customer: group by
`(country, customer)`, rank with `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY country
ORDER BY sum(o.total) DESC, c.id)`, keep `rn = 1`.

## Hint 3
Three things that decide whether the numbers are right. `100.0`, not `100`,
or integer division floors your cancel rate to a whole number. `avg(total)
FILTER (...)` averages only the non-cancelled orders while `count(*)` counts
all of them -- read the spec once more and check which measure excludes
what. And `count(DISTINCT o.customer_id)` counts buyers, whereas `count(*)`
counts orders; mixing them up is the single most common way this report goes
out wrong.

references.solution.sql:
WITH stats AS (
  SELECT c.country,
         sum(o.total) FILTER (WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled') AS revenue,
         count(*) AS orders,
         count(DISTINCT o.customer_id) AS buyers,
         round(avg(o.total) FILTER (WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'), 2)
             AS avg_order_value,
         round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'cancelled')
               / count(*), 1) AS cancel_rate
  FROM customers c
  JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
  GROUP BY c.country),
best AS (
  SELECT c.country, c.id, c.name, sum(o.total) AS spent
  FROM customers c
  JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
  WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
  GROUP BY c.country, c.id, c.name)
SELECT s.country, s.revenue, s.orders, s.buyers, s.avg_order_value,
       s.cancel_rate, t.name AS top_customer
FROM stats s
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT b.name
  FROM best b
  WHERE b.country = s.country
  ORDER BY b.spent DESC, b.id
  LIMIT 1) t
ORDER BY s.revenue DESC;
references.expected.sql:
WITH per_country AS (
  SELECT c.country,
         sum(o.total) FILTER (WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled')           AS revenue,
         count(*)                                                      AS orders,
         count(DISTINCT o.customer_id)                                 AS buyers,
         round(avg(o.total) FILTER (WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'), 2) AS avg_order_value,
         round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'cancelled')
               / count(*), 1)                                          AS cancel_rate
  FROM customers c
  JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
  GROUP BY c.country),
spend AS (
  SELECT c.country, c.name,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY c.country
                            ORDER BY sum(o.total) DESC, c.id) AS rn
  FROM customers c
  JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status <> 'cancelled'
  GROUP BY c.country, c.id, c.name)
SELECT p.country, p.revenue, p.orders, p.buyers, p.avg_order_value,
       p.cancel_rate, s.name AS top_customer
FROM per_country p
JOIN spend s ON s.country = p.country AND s.rn = 1
ORDER BY p.revenue DESC;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — "Top three customers per country" · ⏱ 10 minutes

> *"We're planning regional account reviews. For each country, give me the
> three customers who've spent the most with us. I want the country, the
> customer, and what they spent."*

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Spend means `sum(orders.total)` over that
customer's orders **excluding cancelled ones**. Columns, in this order:
`country`, `id`, `name`, `revenue`. Ties on revenue are broken by lower
customer `id` first, and exactly three rows per country.

**Ordered by `country` ascending, then `revenue` descending, then `id`
ascending.** (36 rows — twelve countries, three each.)

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two questions stacked: "what did each customer spend?" and "who are the top
three inside each country?". The first collapses rows, the second ranks
inside groups. Do them in that order, in two layers.

## Hint 2
CTE one: `customers` joined to non-cancelled `orders`, `GROUP BY c.country,
c.id, c.name`, `sum(o.total) AS revenue`. CTE two: add `row_number() OVER
(PARTITION BY country ORDER BY revenue DESC, id)`. Then `WHERE rn <= 3`.

## Hint 3
Two details the gate will hold you to. The cancelled filter belongs with the
join or in `WHERE` -- it is what "revenue" means here. And the `, id`
tie-break must appear in *both* the `OVER (... ORDER BY ...)` and the final
`ORDER BY`, or two customers on identical revenue will come back in an order
the planner chose and you did not.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Two questions stacked: "what did each customer spend?" and "who are the top
three inside each country?". The first collapses rows, the second ranks
inside groups. Do them in that order, in two layers.

## Hint 2
CTE one: `customers` joined to non-cancelled `orders`, `GROUP BY c.country,
c.id, c.name`, `sum(o.total) AS revenue`. CTE two: add `row_number() OVER
(PARTITION BY country ORDER BY revenue DESC, id)`. Then `WHERE rn <= 3`.

## Hint 3
Two details the gate will hold you to. The cancelled filter belongs with the
join or in `WHERE` -- it is what "revenue" means here. And the `, id`
tie-break must appear in *both* the `OVER (... ORDER BY ...)` and the final
`ORDER BY`, or two customers on identical revenue will come back in an order
the planner chose and you did not.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT country, id, name, revenue
FROM (
  SELECT c.country, c.id, c.name, sum(o.total) AS revenue,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY c.country
                            ORDER BY sum(o.total) DESC, c.id) AS rn
  FROM customers c
  JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
  WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
  GROUP BY c.country, c.id, c.name
) ranked
WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY country, revenue DESC, id;
references.expected.sql:
WITH spend AS (
  SELECT c.country, c.id, c.name, sum(o.total) AS revenue
  FROM customers c
  JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status <> 'cancelled'
  GROUP BY c.country, c.id, c.name),
ranked AS (
  SELECT country, id, name, revenue,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY country
                            ORDER BY revenue DESC, id) AS rn
  FROM spend)
SELECT country, id, name, revenue
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY country, revenue DESC, id;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
"Latest row per key" is one of the three or four queries you will be asked
for by name. Number the rows inside each customer, newest first, and keep
number one.

## Hint 2
`row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY o.customer_id ORDER BY o.created_at DESC,
o.id DESC)` in a CTE, then `WHERE rn = 1` outside it. The country filter
joins `customers` and belongs in the CTE, not after the ranking.

## Hint 3
Know the second answer too, because interviewers like it: `SELECT DISTINCT
ON (customer_id) ... ORDER BY customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC` does
the same job in one pass -- PostgreSQL-specific, taught in lesson 49. Both
need the same tie-break; without `id DESC` a customer with two orders at the
same instant returns an arbitrary one.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT ON (o.customer_id)
       o.customer_id, o.id, o.created_at, o.total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.country = 'JP'
ORDER BY o.customer_id, o.created_at DESC, o.id DESC;
references.expected.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id, o.id, o.created_at, o.total,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY o.customer_id
                            ORDER BY o.created_at DESC, o.id DESC) AS rn
  FROM orders o
  JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
  WHERE c.country = 'JP')
SELECT customer_id, id, created_at, total
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY customer_id;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — "Do first-time buyers come back?" · ⏱ 15 minutes

> *"Group customers by the month they placed their first ever order. For
> each of those cohorts, tell me how big it was and how many of them came
> back and ordered again within thirty days."*

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. A customer's cohort is
`date_trunc('month', <their earliest order's created_at>)`. They count as
returning if they placed **another** order strictly after their first one
and no later than **first order + 30 days**.

Columns, in this order: `cohort_month`, `cohort_size`, `repeat_30d`.

**Ordered by `cohort_month` ascending.** (11 rows.)

Two things decide whether this is right, and interviewers watch for both.
The comparison against the first order must be strict (`>`), or the first
order counts as its own repeat and every cohort is 100% retained. And the
30-day window is measured from **each customer's own first order**, not from
the start of the month — a per-customer window, which is why this is harder
than it sounds.

Run: `uv run dojo test 54_interview_drills ex4`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Three layers. Which month did each customer's *first* order fall in? Did
that customer order again inside 30 days of that first order? Then count
customers per cohort month.

## Hint 2
`min(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS first_at` keeps every
order row *and* tells each one when the customer started -- which a
`GROUP BY` version would have thrown away. Collapse to one row per customer
with `bool_or(created_at > first_at AND created_at <= first_at + INTERVAL
'30 days')`.

## Hint 3
Two traps. `>` not `>=` on the first comparison, or the first order counts
as its own repeat and every cohort is 100% retained. And count with
`count(*) FILTER (WHERE repeated)` rather than a second query -- the
interviewer wants the cohort size and the retained count on the same row so
the ratio is readable.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Three layers. Which month did each customer's *first* order fall in? Did
that customer order again inside 30 days of that first order? Then count
customers per cohort month.

## Hint 2
`min(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS first_at` keeps every
order row *and* tells each one when the customer started -- which a
`GROUP BY` version would have thrown away. Collapse to one row per customer
with `bool_or(created_at > first_at AND created_at <= first_at + INTERVAL
'30 days')`.

## Hint 3
Two traps. `>` not `>=` on the first comparison, or the first order counts
as its own repeat and every cohort is 100% retained. And count with
`count(*) FILTER (WHERE repeated)` rather than a second query -- the
interviewer wants the cohort size and the retained count on the same row so
the ratio is readable.

references.solution.sql:
WITH firsts AS (
  SELECT customer_id, min(created_at) AS first_at
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id),
repeats AS (
  SELECT f.customer_id, date_trunc('month', f.first_at) AS cohort_month,
         count(o.id) AS later_orders
  FROM firsts f
  LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = f.customer_id
                    AND o.created_at > f.first_at
                    AND o.created_at <= f.first_at + INTERVAL '30 days'
  GROUP BY f.customer_id, 2)
SELECT cohort_month, count(*) AS cohort_size,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE later_orders > 0) AS repeat_30d
FROM repeats
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
WITH marked AS (
  SELECT customer_id, created_at,
         min(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS first_at
  FROM orders),
per_customer AS (
  SELECT customer_id, date_trunc('month', first_at) AS cohort_month,
         bool_or(created_at > first_at
                 AND created_at <= first_at + INTERVAL '30 days') AS repeated
  FROM marked
  GROUP BY customer_id, 2)
SELECT cohort_month, count(*) AS cohort_size,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE repeated) AS repeat_30d
FROM per_customer
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

that month — **zero included**. Columns, in this order: `month` (the first
day of the month, as a `date`) and `hires`.

## Hint 2

Two ways to get it wrong. `count(*)` counts the NULL-extended row and prints

references.solution.sql:
WITH hired AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', hired_on)::date AS month, count(*) AS hires
  FROM staff
  WHERE department = 'sales'
    AND hired_on >= DATE '2019-01-01'
    AND hired_on < DATE '2020-01-01'
  GROUP BY 1)
SELECT cal.month::date AS month, coalesce(h.hires, 0) AS hires
FROM generate_series(DATE '2019-01-01', DATE '2019-12-01',
                     INTERVAL '1 month') AS cal(month)
LEFT JOIN hired h ON h.month = cal.month::date
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT g.month::date AS month, count(s.id) AS hires
FROM generate_series(DATE '2019-01-01', DATE '2019-12-01',
                     INTERVAL '1 month') AS g(month)
LEFT JOIN staff s ON s.department = 'sales'
                 AND date_trunc('month', s.hired_on)::date = g.month::date
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

## Spaced review

`review1/`: each category's single best-selling product by units sold —
columns `category`, `id`, `name`, `units` (the sum of
`order_items.quantity`), ties broken by lower product `id`, ordered by
`category` ascending. Top-N-per-group with N = 1, which is the form you are
most likely to be handed on a whiteboard.
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
"Best-selling" is units, not revenue and not order count, so the measure
comes from `order_items.quantity`. One row per product first, then one
winner per category.

## Hint 2
Aggregate `sum(oi.quantity)` grouped by category and product, then
`row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY units DESC, id)` and keep
`rn = 1`.

## Hint 3
`DISTINCT ON (category) ... ORDER BY category, units DESC, id` is the
shorter PostgreSQL answer and worth writing once for comparison. Whichever
you pick, the `, id` tie-break is not optional: several products sell within
a unit or two of each other here, and without it the winner changes between
runs.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
"Best-selling" is units, not revenue and not order count, so the measure
comes from `order_items.quantity`. One row per product first, then one
winner per category.

## Hint 2
Aggregate `sum(oi.quantity)` grouped by category and product, then
`row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY units DESC, id)` and keep
`rn = 1`.

## Hint 3
`DISTINCT ON (category) ... ORDER BY category, units DESC, id` is the
shorter PostgreSQL answer and worth writing once for comparison. Whichever
you pick, the `, id` tie-break is not optional: several products sell within
a unit or two of each other here, and without it the winner changes between
runs.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT ON (category) category, id, name, units
FROM (
  SELECT p.category, p.id, p.name, sum(oi.quantity) AS units
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
  GROUP BY p.category, p.id, p.name
) totals
ORDER BY category, units DESC, id;
references.expected.sql:
WITH units AS (
  SELECT p.category, p.id, p.name, sum(oi.quantity) AS units
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
  GROUP BY p.category, p.id, p.name),
ranked AS (
  SELECT category, id, name, units,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY category
                            ORDER BY units DESC, id) AS rn
  FROM units)
SELECT category, id, name, units
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY category;

# 55 - Drills: the SELECT list

These eight problems drill the SELECT list - lesson 01 - and nothing else:
which columns come back, in which order, what you can compute on the way out,
and what `DISTINCT` really de-duplicates. If any of them feels like guessing,
redo 01 before you continue.

## Exercise 1 - columns, in the order asked for

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. The catalog export wants every product, but not in
the order the table happens to store them. Return exactly three columns, in
this order: `category`, `id`, `price`. Every product row, any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 55_drills_select_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - a column that is not in the table

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Payroll's importer needs a currency marker on every
row, and `staff` does not have one. Return four columns, in this order: `id`,
`name`, `salary`, and a fourth column whose value is the text `USD` on every
row. All staff, any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 55_drills_select_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - dividing a salary

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. The benefits team quotes pay monthly. Return three
columns, in this order: `id`, `salary`, and `salary` divided by 12. Do not
round it - hand back whatever the division gives you. All staff, any row
order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 55_drills_select_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - the values a column actually takes

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Before writing a bulk-discount rule, ops wants to
know which order quantities ever occur. Return one column - the distinct
values of `order_items.quantity` - with no duplicates. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 55_drills_select_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - distinct pairs, NULL included

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. The org-chart tool wants every combination of
department and manager that occurs in `staff`. Return two columns, in this
order: `department` and `manager_id`, with duplicate pairs removed. One
member of staff has no manager; that pair belongs in the output too. Any row
order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 55_drills_select_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - two derived columns from one

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Finance wants a VAT worksheet. Return four columns,
in this order: `id`, `price`, the VAT amount at 20 percent (`price * 0.2`),
and the gross price (`price * 1.2`). Do not round either figure. Every
product, any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 55_drills_select_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - the division that throws away the remainder

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. A colleague reports that "half the ratings come out
as zero" in a report that halves `reviews.rating`. Return the distinct
combinations of three columns, in this order: `rating`, `rating / 2`, and
`rating / 2.0`. Duplicates removed; any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 55_drills_select_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - bucketing with modulo

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Merchandising wants to know which 100-dollar price
bands each category actually occupies. Return the distinct combinations of
two columns, in this order: `category`, and the band computed as
`price - price % 100`. Duplicates removed; any row order.

The band for a 137.53 product is `100.00`; for a 54.46 product it is `0.00`.

Run: `uv run dojo test 55_drills_select_1 ex8`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 55_drills_select_1

Eight problems on the clause everyone thinks is trivial. The trivial part is
the syntax; the part that bites is arithmetic types and what `DISTINCT`
applies to.

## Notes

Two ideas unite this set. The first is that **the SELECT list is a per-row
expression list**, not a list of columns: a literal, an arithmetic
expression, or a function call is as legal there as a bare column name, and
the result is computed once per surviving row. The second is that **`DISTINCT`
de-duplicates the whole output row, after those expressions have been
evaluated** - never one named column. That ordering is the source of most
surprises in this set: an expression that collapses many inputs to one value
(integer division, a modulo bucket) makes `DISTINCT` return far fewer rows
than the underlying column has values, and adding one more column to the list
can undo the de-duplication entirely.

The third thing worth internalising is that **arithmetic in SQL is typed**.
`numeric / numeric` keeps decimals; `integer / integer` throws the remainder
away without a warning, because the result type of `int / int` is `int`. That
single rule accounts for an enormous number of "the report says zero" bugs,
and it is why `quantity / 2` and `quantity / 2.0` are different questions.

## ex1 - columns, in the order asked for

This tests whether you read the required output shape before you started
typing. The classic mistake is writing the columns in table order out of
habit and never noticing, because the query runs perfectly and returns
plausible rows. The model answer simply lists the three names in the sequence
the prompt gave, which is also why every prompt in this course spells the
order out: a correctness gate compares tuples by position, exactly like the
CSV consumer downstream of your real query would.

## ex2 - a column that is not in the table

The point is that the SELECT list holds expressions, and a literal is the
simplest expression there is. The classic mistake is reaching for double
quotes, which in SQL name an identifier rather than a string, producing a
confusing "column USD does not exist" error. The model answer puts `'USD'`
straight into the list; PostgreSQL types it as text and repeats it on every
row, which is exactly how flat exports get their constant marker columns.

## ex3 - dividing a salary

This tests numeric division and the discipline of returning exactly what was
asked for. The classic mistake is helpfully rounding to two decimals because
money "should" have two decimals - which silently changes every value in the
column. The model answer divides and stops. Worth noticing in the output: the
quotient carries far more decimal places than the input, because `numeric`
division picks a result scale generous enough not to lose information.

## ex4 - the values a column actually takes

This tests `DISTINCT` in its simplest form and, quietly, your willingness to
run a query that reads the whole of `order_items` to return a handful of
values. The classic
mistake is adding the primary key to the SELECT list "for context", which
makes every row unique again and returns the whole table. The model answer
asks only for the column whose value set you want. `GROUP BY quantity` with
no aggregate is the same question phrased differently, and PostgreSQL plans
both nearly identically.

## ex5 - distinct pairs, NULL included

This tests that `DISTINCT` de-duplicates the entire selected row, and that
NULL is a value it can group. The classic mistake is assuming a NULL will be
dropped, or adding `WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL` defensively and losing the
one row the org chart most needs. The model answer selects both columns under
one `DISTINCT`. Note the asymmetry that trips people later: `DISTINCT` calls
two NULLs the same, while `=` calls them unknown.

## ex6 - two derived columns from one

This tests computing more than one derived column in a single pass, which is
what report queries actually look like. The classic mistake is computing the
gross as `price + price * 0.2` and assuming it must equal `price * 1.2` - it
does here, but only because both sides land on the same numeric scale, and
that is a coincidence you should not rely on. The model answer writes the two
multiplications side by side and lets the SELECT list do the work once.

## ex7 - the division that throws away the remainder

This tests the single most expensive type rule for beginners: `integer /
integer` is integer division, so `1 / 2` is `0` and no warning is issued. The
classic mistake is writing the average of an integer column as a division by
an integer literal and shipping a report full of zeros. The model answer puts
both forms side by side so the difference is visible in one glance. Note also
that `DISTINCT` runs after the expressions, which is why the whole reviews
table collapses to five rows.

## ex8 - bucketing with modulo

This is the whole set in one query: an arithmetic expression that collapses
many inputs into a few outputs, with `DISTINCT` applied after it. The classic
mistake is leaving `price` in the SELECT list alongside the band, which makes
every row unique again and returns the entire catalog. The model answer
computes `price - price % 100` and de-duplicates the pairs. `%` on `numeric`
is exact here, which is precisely why this bucketing trick is safe on money
and would not be on a floating-point column.

## Further reading

- [SELECT Lists](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-select-lists.html) - what may appear between SELECT and FROM, and how output column names are decided.
- [DISTINCT Clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-select-lists.html#QUERIES-DISTINCT) - the exact rule: duplicate elimination happens on the whole result row.
- [Numeric Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-numeric.html) - why integer division truncates and what precision `numeric` promises.
- [Mathematical Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-math.html) - the `%` operator and friends, including their behaviour on `numeric`.

Every gate here runs the reference query and yours against the same clone and
compares the rows as an unordered multiset: the values and the column order
must match, the row order does not. Column *names* are never checked, so an
alias is for the human reading your query, not for the gate.

## The teaching point

The SELECT list is the only clause that can invent data. Everything else in a
query narrows, joins, or sorts rows that already exist; the SELECT list is
where a price becomes a price-with-tax and a salary becomes a monthly figure.
Getting fluent here is what stops you from pulling raw columns into
application code and recomputing the same arithmetic in three services.

# Reading - 55_drills_select_1

Eight problems on the clause everyone thinks is trivial. The trivial part is
the syntax; the part that bites is arithmetic types and what `DISTINCT`
applies to.

## Notes

Two ideas unite this set. The first is that **the SELECT list is a per-row
expression list**, not a list of columns: a literal, an arithmetic
expression, or a function call is as legal there as a bare column name, and
the result is computed once per surviving row. The second is that **`DISTINCT`
de-duplicates the whole output row, after those expressions have been
evaluated** - never one named column. That ordering is the source of most
surprises in this set: an expression that collapses many inputs to one value
(integer division, a modulo bucket) makes `DISTINCT` return far fewer rows
than the underlying column has values, and adding one more column to the list
can undo the de-duplication entirely.

The third thing worth internalising is that **arithmetic in SQL is typed**.
`numeric / numeric` keeps decimals; `integer / integer` throws the remainder
away without a warning, because the result type of `int / int` is `int`. That
single rule accounts for an enormous number of "the report says zero" bugs,
and it is why `quantity / 2` and `quantity / 2.0` are different questions.

## ex1 - columns, in the order asked for

This tests whether you read the required output shape before you started
typing. The classic mistake is writing the columns in table order out of
habit and never noticing, because the query runs perfectly and returns
plausible rows. The model answer simply lists the three names in the sequence
the prompt gave, which is also why every prompt in this course spells the
order out: a correctness gate compares tuples by position, exactly like the
CSV consumer downstream of your real query would.

## ex2 - a column that is not in the table

The point is that the SELECT list holds expressions, and a literal is the
simplest expression there is. The classic mistake is reaching for double
quotes, which in SQL name an identifier rather than a string, producing a
confusing "column USD does not exist" error. The model answer puts `'USD'`
straight into the list; PostgreSQL types it as text and repeats it on every
row, which is exactly how flat exports get their constant marker columns.

## ex3 - dividing a salary

This tests numeric division and the discipline of returning exactly what was
asked for. The classic mistake is helpfully rounding to two decimals because
money "should" have two decimals - which silently changes every value in the
column. The model answer divides and stops. Worth noticing in the output: the
quotient carries far more decimal places than the input, because `numeric`
division picks a result scale generous enough not to lose information.

## ex4 - the values a column actually takes

This tests `DISTINCT` in its simplest form and, quietly, your willingness to
run a query that reads the whole of `order_items` to return a handful of
values. The classic
mistake is adding the primary key to the SELECT list "for context", which
makes every row unique again and returns the whole table. The model answer
asks only for the column whose value set you want. `GROUP BY quantity` with
no aggregate is the same question phrased differently, and PostgreSQL plans
both nearly identically.

## ex5 - distinct pairs, NULL included

This tests that `DISTINCT` de-duplicates the entire selected row, and that
NULL is a value it can group. The classic mistake is assuming a NULL will be
dropped, or adding `WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL` defensively and losing the
one row the org chart most needs. The model answer selects both columns under
one `DISTINCT`. Note the asymmetry that trips people later: `DISTINCT` calls
two NULLs the same, while `=` calls them unknown.

## ex6 - two derived columns from one

This tests computing more than one derived column in a single pass, which is
what report queries actually look like. The classic mistake is computing the
gross as `price + price * 0.2` and assuming it must equal `price * 1.2` - it
does here, but only because both sides land on the same numeric scale, and
that is a coincidence you should not rely on. The model answer writes the two
multiplications side by side and lets the SELECT list do the work once.

## ex7 - the division that throws away the remainder

This tests the single most expensive type rule for beginners: `integer /
integer` is integer division, so `1 / 2` is `0` and no warning is issued. The
classic mistake is writing the average of an integer column as a division by
an integer literal and shipping a report full of zeros. The model answer puts
both forms side by side so the difference is visible in one glance. Note also
that `DISTINCT` runs after the expressions, which is why the whole reviews
table collapses to five rows.

## ex8 - bucketing with modulo

This is the whole set in one query: an arithmetic expression that collapses
many inputs into a few outputs, with `DISTINCT` applied after it. The classic
mistake is leaving `price` in the SELECT list alongside the band, which makes
every row unique again and returns the entire catalog. The model answer
computes `price - price % 100` and de-duplicates the pairs. `%` on `numeric`
is exact here, which is precisely why this bucketing trick is safe on money
and would not be on a floating-point column.

## Further reading

- [SELECT Lists](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-select-lists.html) - what may appear between SELECT and FROM, and how output column names are decided.
- [DISTINCT Clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-select-lists.html#QUERIES-DISTINCT) - the exact rule: duplicate elimination happens on the whole result row.
- [Numeric Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-numeric.html) - why integer division truncates and what precision `numeric` promises.
- [Mathematical Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-math.html) - the `%` operator and friends, including their behaviour on `numeric`.

A SELECT list item does not have to reference a column. A constant is a
perfectly good expression, and it is evaluated once per row.

Single quotes make a string literal in SQL: `'USD'`. Double quotes mean
something else entirely (an identifier), so `"USD"` will fail with a
column-does-not-exist error.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
A SELECT list item does not have to reference a column. A constant is a
perfectly good expression, and it is evaluated once per row.

## Hint 2
Single quotes make a string literal in SQL: `'USD'`. Double quotes mean
something else entirely (an identifier), so `"USD"` will fail with a
column-does-not-exist error.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT s.id, s.name, s.salary, 'USD'::text AS currency
FROM staff AS s;
references.expected.sql: SELECT id, name, salary, 'USD' FROM staff;

## Exercise 3 - dividing a salary

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. The benefits team quotes pay monthly. Return three
columns, in this order: `id`, `salary`, and `salary` divided by 12. Do not
round it - hand back whatever the division gives you. All staff, any row
order.

One arithmetic operator applied to one column. The interesting part is

quotient, and rounding would change the values the gate compares.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
`rating` is an `integer`. What type is `2`? What type is `2.0`? The result
type of a division is decided by its operands, and it decides whether the
remainder survives.

## Hint 2
Write the divisor exactly as the prompt gives it in each column - `2` in
one, `2.0` in the other. Then wrap the three-column list in `DISTINCT`; the
expressions are evaluated first, so only a few rows survive.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT r.rating,
       r.rating / 2 AS halved_int,
       r.rating / 2.0 AS halved_numeric
FROM reviews AS r
GROUP BY r.rating;
references.expected.sql: SELECT DISTINCT rating, rating / 2, rating / 2.0 FROM reviews;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 - bucketing with modulo

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Merchandising wants to know which 100-dollar price
bands each category actually occupies. Return the distinct combinations of
two columns, in this order: `category`, and the band computed as
`price - price % 100`. Duplicates removed; any row order.

The band for a 137.53 product is `100.00`; for a 54.46 product it is `0.00`.

Run: `uv run dojo test 55_drills_select_1 ex8`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
`%` is the modulo operator and it works on `numeric`, not just integers.
Subtracting the remainder from the value is the classic way to round *down*
to a multiple of something.

## Hint 2
Compute the band as an expression inside the SELECT list, then let
`DISTINCT` de-duplicate the pairs. Do not compute it in a `WHERE` clause -
there is nothing to filter here.

## Hint 3
The two ideas stack in one direction only: expressions are evaluated for
every row first, and `DISTINCT` de-duplicates what comes out. So the answer
has at most one row per (category, band) pair even though thousands of
products feed each one. If you get thousands of rows back, check whether an
extra column - `id`, or `price` itself - crept into your SELECT list.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
`%` is the modulo operator and it works on `numeric`, not just integers.
Subtracting the remainder from the value is the classic way to round *down*
to a multiple of something.

## Hint 2
Compute the band as an expression inside the SELECT list, then let
`DISTINCT` de-duplicate the pairs. Do not compute it in a `WHERE` clause -
there is nothing to filter here.

## Hint 3
The two ideas stack in one direction only: expressions are evaluated for
every row first, and `DISTINCT` de-duplicates what comes out. So the answer
has at most one row per (category, band) pair even though thousands of
products feed each one. If you get thousands of rows back, check whether an
extra column - `id`, or `price` itself - crept into your SELECT list.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT band.category, band.floor_price
FROM (
  SELECT p.category,
         p.price - p.price % 100 AS floor_price
  FROM products AS p
) AS band
GROUP BY band.category, band.floor_price;
references.expected.sql: SELECT DISTINCT category, price - price % 100 FROM products;

lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 56_drills_select_2

More projection, with the emphasis on expressions that build on each other
and on `DISTINCT` applied to columns that barely repeat.

## Notes

This set drills the same clause as 55 but pushes on two edges. The first is
**operator precedence inside the SELECT list**: SQL arithmetic follows the
ordinary rules, so `price + price * 0.05` is a five percent markup while
`(price + price) * 0.05` is a tenth of the price, and the two are only one
pair of brackets apart. If a computed column is ever wrong by a suspiciously
round factor, precedence is the first thing to check.

The second edge is **`DISTINCT` over near-unique data**. De-duplication is
cheap to write and expensive to run: PostgreSQL has to sort or hash every
row of the input to prove which ones repeat. When the columns you selected
include anything close to a key, nothing is removed and you have paid for a
sort that changed nothing. The habit worth building is to ask, before typing
`DISTINCT`, *which* duplicates you expect and where they come from - if you
cannot answer, the keyword is probably hiding a modelling mistake rather than
fixing one.

## ex1 - a four-column export

A warm-up that tests reading discipline: four columns, none of them in table
order. The classic mistake is `SELECT *`, which returns the right data in the
wrong shape and would fail the gate on column count alone. The model answer
names the four columns in the requested sequence. Naming columns explicitly
is also the production habit: a `SELECT *` silently changes shape the day
somebody adds a column to the table.

## ex2 - reordering a wide table

This tests projection on a table where the natural column order and the
requested one differ, and where the temptation to de-duplicate is strongest.
The classic mistake here is a reflexive `DISTINCT`, which cannot remove
anything because `id` is unique and costs a full sort or hash of the table.
The model answer projects the three columns and stops; the useful reflex is
asking what duplicates you expect before you ask for them to be removed.

## ex3 - prices in cents

This tests that scaling a `numeric` keeps its scale, which matters the moment
a real payments API rejects `29040.00` where it wanted `29040`. The classic
mistake is adding a cast the prompt did not ask for and changing every value
in the column. The model answer multiplies and stops. In production the cast
belongs there - but deliberately, as `(price * 100)::bigint`, once you have
decided what should happen to fractional cents.

## ex4 - which products have ever sold

This tests `DISTINCT` as a set-extraction tool over a large child table, and
it is the first half of an anti-join. The classic mistake is joining to
`products` because the word "product" appears in the prompt, which adds work
and risks duplicating rows. The model answer reads one column of one table.
Keep the result in mind: it is smaller than the product catalog, and the
missing ids are exactly the never-ordered stock the outer-join lessons hunt.

## ex5 - the rating combinations that occur

This tests multi-column `DISTINCT` on a genuinely large input, where the
answer is neither tiny nor the whole table. The classic mistake is selecting
`id` alongside the pair, which makes every review row unique and defeats the
de-duplication entirely. The model answer names exactly the two columns whose
combinations are wanted. Notice the result size: it is close to the number of
products times five, which tells you nearly every product has collected every
rating.

## ex6 - a coupon that can go negative

This tests the discipline of returning what was asked rather than what seems
sensible, and it previews why real discount logic needs `greatest(price - 5,
0)` or a `CASE`. The classic mistake is filtering out the cheap products so
the column looks tidy, which quietly deletes exactly the rows the analysis
was about. The model answer subtracts and returns everything. Flat discounts
on a catalog with a wide price range always produce this shape.

## ex7 - brackets change the answer

This tests operator precedence, the arithmetic bug that survives review
because both versions run and both return plausible money. The classic
mistake is trusting a computed column because it "looks about right" - a
markup that is twice what it should be still looks like a price. The model
answer writes both forms verbatim so the difference is visible per row.
Precedence in SQL is the ordinary one; the danger is that nothing warns you.

## ex8 - the payroll worksheet

This is the shape a real report query has: a handful of raw columns and a
handful computed from them, all in one pass so that every consumer agrees on
the definitions. The classic mistake is losing track of position in a
seven-item list - most often by repeating the bonus in the package column, so
the total package silently excludes the salary. The model answer writes each
expression as specified and keeps the seven positions straight, which is most
of the work in production reporting.

## Further reading

- [SELECT Lists](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-select-lists.html) - column labels, `AS`, and the rules for what a select item may be.
- [Operator Precedence](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-syntax-lexical.html#SQL-PRECEDENCE) - the table that settles every argument about brackets in an expression.
- [Value Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html) - the full grammar of what can be computed per row, and in what order.
- [Data Type Formatting Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-formatting.html) - when a computed column needs to be formatted rather than merely calculated.

# Reading - 56_drills_select_2

More projection, with the emphasis on expressions that build on each other
and on `DISTINCT` applied to columns that barely repeat.

## Notes

This set drills the same clause as 55 but pushes on two edges. The first is
**operator precedence inside the SELECT list**: SQL arithmetic follows the
ordinary rules, so `price + price * 0.05` is a five percent markup while
`(price + price) * 0.05` is a tenth of the price, and the two are only one
pair of brackets apart. If a computed column is ever wrong by a suspiciously
round factor, precedence is the first thing to check.

The second edge is **`DISTINCT` over near-unique data**. De-duplication is
cheap to write and expensive to run: PostgreSQL has to sort or hash every
row of the input to prove which ones repeat. When the columns you selected
include anything close to a key, nothing is removed and you have paid for a
sort that changed nothing. The habit worth building is to ask, before typing
`DISTINCT`, *which* duplicates you expect and where they come from - if you
cannot answer, the keyword is probably hiding a modelling mistake rather than
fixing one.

## ex1 - a four-column export

A warm-up that tests reading discipline: four columns, none of them in table
order. The classic mistake is `SELECT *`, which returns the right data in the
wrong shape and would fail the gate on column count alone. The model answer
names the four columns in the requested sequence. Naming columns explicitly
is also the production habit: a `SELECT *` silently changes shape the day
somebody adds a column to the table.

## ex2 - reordering a wide table

This tests projection on a table where the natural column order and the
requested one differ, and where the temptation to de-duplicate is strongest.
The classic mistake here is a reflexive `DISTINCT`, which cannot remove
anything because `id` is unique and costs a full sort or hash of the table.
The model answer projects the three columns and stops; the useful reflex is
asking what duplicates you expect before you ask for them to be removed.

## ex3 - prices in cents

This tests that scaling a `numeric` keeps its scale, which matters the moment
a real payments API rejects `29040.00` where it wanted `29040`. The classic
mistake is adding a cast the prompt did not ask for and changing every value
in the column. The model answer multiplies and stops. In production the cast
belongs there - but deliberately, as `(price * 100)::bigint`, once you have
decided what should happen to fractional cents.

## ex4 - which products have ever sold

This tests `DISTINCT` as a set-extraction tool over a large child table, and
it is the first half of an anti-join. The classic mistake is joining to
`products` because the word "product" appears in the prompt, which adds work
and risks duplicating rows. The model answer reads one column of one table.
Keep the result in mind: it is smaller than the product catalog, and the
missing ids are exactly the never-ordered stock the outer-join lessons hunt.

## ex5 - the rating combinations that occur

This tests multi-column `DISTINCT` on a genuinely large input, where the
answer is neither tiny nor the whole table. The classic mistake is selecting
`id` alongside the pair, which makes every review row unique and defeats the
de-duplication entirely. The model answer names exactly the two columns whose
combinations are wanted. Notice the result size: it is close to the number of
products times five, which tells you nearly every product has collected every
rating.

## ex6 - a coupon that can go negative

This tests the discipline of returning what was asked rather than what seems
sensible, and it previews why real discount logic needs `greatest(price - 5,
0)` or a `CASE`. The classic mistake is filtering out the cheap products so
the column looks tidy, which quietly deletes exactly the rows the analysis
was about. The model answer subtracts and returns everything. Flat discounts
on a catalog with a wide price range always produce this shape.

## ex7 - brackets change the answer

This tests operator precedence, the arithmetic bug that survives review
because both versions run and both return plausible money. The classic
mistake is trusting a computed column because it "looks about right" - a
markup that is twice what it should be still looks like a price. The model
answer writes both forms verbatim so the difference is visible per row.
Precedence in SQL is the ordinary one; the danger is that nothing warns you.

## ex8 - the payroll worksheet

This is the shape a real report query has: a handful of raw columns and a
handful computed from them, all in one pass so that every consumer agrees on
the definitions. The classic mistake is losing track of position in a
seven-item list - most often by repeating the bonus in the package column, so
the total package silently excludes the salary. The model answer writes each
expression as specified and keeps the seven positions straight, which is most
of the work in production reporting.

## Further reading

- [SELECT Lists](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-select-lists.html) - column labels, `AS`, and the rules for what a select item may be.
- [Operator Precedence](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-syntax-lexical.html#SQL-PRECEDENCE) - the table that settles every argument about brackets in an expression.
- [Value Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html) - the full grammar of what can be computed per row, and in what order.
- [Data Type Formatting Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-formatting.html) - when a computed column needs to be formatted rather than merely calculated.

## Exercise 7 - brackets change the answer

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. A five percent markup was implemented twice, once
with brackets in the wrong place, and finance wants both figures side by side.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
`*` binds tighter than `+`, exactly as in arithmetic. The bracketed
version therefore doubles the price before it takes five percent.

## Hint 2
Do not simplify either expression. `(price + price) * 0.05` is the same
as `price * 0.1`, but writing it that way loses the point of the exercise -
and the two forms do not always land on the same `numeric` scale.
