# 57 - Drills: comparisons, IN, BETWEEN

Eight problems on the value-set half of `WHERE` - lesson 02. Comparisons,
`IN`, `NOT IN`, `BETWEEN`, and the ways each of them quietly includes or
excludes an endpoint. Redo 02 first if the difference between `<` and `<=`
has ever cost you a row.

## Exercise 1 - one comparison

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. The clearance shelf takes anything under five
dollars. Return every product whose `price` is **strictly less than 5**.
Three columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `price`. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 57_drills_where_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - equality on text

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. The engineering director wants her roster. Return
every member of `staff` whose `department` is exactly `engineering`. Four
columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `department`, `salary`. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 57_drills_where_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - comparing dates

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. The ten-year-service awards need candidates. Return
every member of `staff` hired **before 1 January 2015** - `hired_on` strictly
earlier than that date. Three columns, in this order: `id`, `name`,
`hired_on`. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 57_drills_where_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - a short list of values

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The customer-facing teams are being surveyed
together. Return every member of `staff` whose `department` is either `sales`
or `support`. Three columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `department`. Use
`IN` for the test. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 57_drills_where_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - everything outside a list

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Strategy wants the long tail: every customer whose
`country` is **not** one of our five largest markets - `US`, `GB`, `DE`, `FR`
or `CA`. Three columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `country`. Any row
order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 57_drills_where_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - an inclusive range

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Pricing is studying the products clustered around
the catalog's average price. Return every product whose `price` is between
249 and 251, **inclusive on both ends**, using `BETWEEN`. Four columns, in
this order: `id`, `name`, `category`, `price`. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 57_drills_where_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - a list and a range together

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Compensation review is looking at the technical
middle of the company. Return every member of `staff` whose `department` is
`engineering` or `ops`, **and** whose `salary` is between 90000 and 100000
inclusive. Four columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `department`, `salary`.
Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 57_drills_where_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - excluding the middle

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. The two ends of the toy and book ranges are being
re-photographed: the very cheap and the very expensive, nothing in between.
Return every product whose `category` is `toys` or `books`, and whose `price`
is **not** between 50 and 450 (that exclusion is inclusive of both bounds, so
a product at exactly 50.00 is excluded). Four columns, in this order: `id`,
`name`, `category`, `price`. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 57_drills_where_1 ex8`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 57_drills_where_1

Eight narrowing problems. Nothing here is syntactically hard; every one of
them is a chance to be precise about which rows survive.

## Notes

This set drills the predicates that test a value against a set or a range,
and the skill being trained is **endpoint discipline**. `BETWEEN x AND y` is
inclusive on both ends - it means `>= x AND <= y` - which is convenient for
integers and prices and a genuine hazard for timestamps, where the bare date
`'2023-01-31'` means midnight and therefore excludes almost the whole day.
The professional habit for time ranges is half-open: `>= start AND < next`.

`IN` is `OR` in a smaller box: `status IN ('paid','shipped')` is exactly
`status = 'paid' OR status = 'shipped'`, with the parenthesisation already
correct, which is a quiet argument for preferring it. `NOT IN` is its
opposite only while no NULL is involved - the moment a NULL appears in the
list or in the column, `NOT IN` returns no rows at all rather than the rows
you expected. Nothing in this set has a nullable column on the left, so the
trap stays disarmed; lesson 05 arms it.

One more habit: a comparison against a `date` column and a comparison against
a `timestamptz` column look identical and behave differently. `staff.hired_on`
is a plain `date`, so `< '2015-01-01'` is exactly what it appears to be.

## ex1 - one comparison

This tests strict versus inclusive comparison, the smallest possible version
of the endpoint question that runs through the whole set. The classic mistake
is `<=`, which silently adds the boundary rows and is invisible unless you
count. The model answer uses `<` because "under" is exclusive in English and
the prompt said "strictly". When a spec says "under", "up to", or "through",
ask which endpoints are included before you write the operator.

## ex2 - equality on text

This tests exact text equality, and the restraint not to reach for pattern
matching when a plain `=` is correct. The classic mistake is capitalising the
literal, which returns zero rows and no error. The model answer compares the
column to the exact stored value. A single-value `IN` list is the same
predicate written differently, which is worth seeing once: `IN` really is
just `=` with room for more values.

## ex3 - comparing dates

This tests date comparison and, again, the boundary. The classic mistake is
`<=` on a date boundary, which is how "hired before 2015" turns into "hired
before 2015, plus everyone hired on the first working day of it". The model
answer keeps the comparison strict. Note that `hired_on` is a plain `date`,
so no time component can hide behind the literal - the same predicate on a
`timestamptz` column would need much more care.

## ex4 - a short list of values

This tests `IN` as shorthand for a chain of equalities. The classic mistake
is writing `department = 'sales' OR 'support'`, which is not a syntax error
in every dialect and means something else entirely where it parses. The model
answer lists both values inside one `IN`. The real argument for `IN` is not
brevity but safety: it has no precedence for you to get wrong, which is the
whole subject of the next drill set.

## ex5 - everything outside a list

This tests `NOT IN` and plants a flag for later. The classic mistake is
chaining `<>` with `OR` - `country <> 'US' OR country <> 'GB'` is true for
every row on earth, because no country can be both. The model answer negates
the whole membership test at once. Remember the caveat: `NOT IN` against a
list or subquery containing a NULL returns nothing, silently, and that bug
has shipped in production more than once.

## ex6 - an inclusive range

This tests `BETWEEN` and its inclusivity. The classic mistake is writing the
bounds backwards, which returns zero rows without complaint because `BETWEEN`
is defined as `>= first AND <= second` with no reordering. The model answer
puts the low bound first. Write the expanded form once and keep it in mind:
that expansion is exactly why `BETWEEN` on timestamps is a trap and
`BETWEEN` on prices is not.

## ex7 - a list and a range together

This tests combining a set predicate with a range predicate, and it is the
first place in the set where precedence could bite. The classic mistake is
expanding `IN` to an unbracketed `OR`, which produces every engineer
regardless of salary plus the ops people in band. The model answer keeps the
`IN` intact so no brackets are needed. The planner will apply whichever
condition it estimates is cheaper first, and neither ordering changes the
answer.

## ex8 - excluding the middle

The hard version: a membership test and a negated range in one predicate.
This tests whether you can turn `NOT BETWEEN` into its `OR` form without
losing an endpoint, since both comparisons become strict under negation. The
classic mistake is writing `price < 50 OR price > 450` without brackets, so
`AND` grabs only the first half and the result fills with cheap products from
every category. The model answer keeps `NOT BETWEEN` whole, which has no
precedence to get wrong.

## Further reading

- [Comparison Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html) - the definitions of `BETWEEN`, `IN`, and `IS DISTINCT FROM`, endpoints included.
- [Subquery Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) - what `IN` and `NOT IN` mean once the right-hand side is a subquery, and why NULLs matter there.
- [The WHERE Clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-WHERE) - where filtering sits in the logical evaluation order of a query.
- [Date/Time Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-datetime.html) - why a bare date literal compared against a timestamp means midnight.

# 57 - Drills: comparisons, IN, BETWEEN

Eight problems on the value-set half of `WHERE` - lesson 02. Comparisons,
`IN`, `NOT IN`, `BETWEEN`, and the ways each of them quietly includes or
excludes an endpoint. Redo 02 first if the difference between `<` and `<=`
has ever cost you a row.

## Exercise 1 - one comparison

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. The clearance shelf takes anything under five
dollars. Return every product whose `price` is **strictly less than 5**.
Three columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `price`. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 57_drills_where_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - equality on text

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. The engineering director wants her roster. Return
every member of `staff` whose `department` is exactly `engineering`. Four
columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `department`, `salary`. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 57_drills_where_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - comparing dates

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. The ten-year-service awards need candidates. Return
every member of `staff` hired **before 1 January 2015** - `hired_on` strictly
earlier than that date. Three columns, in this order: `id`, `name`,
`hired_on`. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 57_drills_where_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - a short list of values

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The customer-facing teams are being surveyed
together. Return every member of `staff` whose `department` is either `sales`
or `support`. Three columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `department`. Use
`IN` for the test. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 57_drills_where_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - everything outside a list

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Strategy wants the long tail: every customer whose
`country` is **not** one of our five largest markets - `US`, `GB`, `DE`, `FR`
or `CA`. Three columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `country`. Any row
order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 57_drills_where_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - an inclusive range

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Pricing is studying the products clustered around
the catalog's average price. Return every product whose `price` is between
249 and 251, **inclusive on both ends**, using `BETWEEN`. Four columns, in
this order: `id`, `name`, `category`, `price`. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 57_drills_where_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - a list and a range together

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Compensation review is looking at the technical
middle of the company. Return every member of `staff` whose `department` is
`engineering` or `ops`, **and** whose `salary` is between 90000 and 100000
inclusive. Four columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `department`, `salary`.
Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 57_drills_where_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - excluding the middle

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. The two ends of the toy and book ranges are being
re-photographed: the very cheap and the very expensive, nothing in between.
Return every product whose `category` is `toys` or `books`, and whose `price`
is **not** between 50 and 450 (that exclusion is inclusive of both bounds, so
a product at exactly 50.00 is excluded). Four columns, in this order: `id`,
`name`, `category`, `price`. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 57_drills_where_1 ex8`

## The teaching point

A wrong `WHERE` clause does not raise an error. It returns a confident,
plausible, wrong answer, and the only defence is knowing exactly which rows
each operator lets through. Say the row count you expect out loud before you
run the query: being wrong is the information, and the size of the error
usually names the bug.

# Reading - 57_drills_where_1

Eight narrowing problems. Nothing here is syntactically hard; every one of
them is a chance to be precise about which rows survive.

## Notes

This set drills the predicates that test a value against a set or a range,
and the skill being trained is **endpoint discipline**. `BETWEEN x AND y` is
inclusive on both ends - it means `>= x AND <= y` - which is convenient for
integers and prices and a genuine hazard for timestamps, where the bare date
`'2023-01-31'` means midnight and therefore excludes almost the whole day.
The professional habit for time ranges is half-open: `>= start AND < next`.

`IN` is `OR` in a smaller box: `status IN ('paid','shipped')` is exactly
`status = 'paid' OR status = 'shipped'`, with the parenthesisation already
correct, which is a quiet argument for preferring it. `NOT IN` is its
opposite only while no NULL is involved - the moment a NULL appears in the
list or in the column, `NOT IN` returns no rows at all rather than the rows
you expected. Nothing in this set has a nullable column on the left, so the
trap stays disarmed; lesson 05 arms it.

One more habit: a comparison against a `date` column and a comparison against
a `timestamptz` column look identical and behave differently. `staff.hired_on`
is a plain `date`, so `< '2015-01-01'` is exactly what it appears to be.

## ex1 - one comparison

This tests strict versus inclusive comparison, the smallest possible version
of the endpoint question that runs through the whole set. The classic mistake
is `<=`, which silently adds the boundary rows and is invisible unless you
count. The model answer uses `<` because "under" is exclusive in English and
the prompt said "strictly". When a spec says "under", "up to", or "through",
ask which endpoints are included before you write the operator.

## ex2 - equality on text

This tests exact text equality, and the restraint not to reach for pattern
matching when a plain `=` is correct. The classic mistake is capitalising the
literal, which returns zero rows and no error. The model answer compares the
column to the exact stored value. A single-value `IN` list is the same
predicate written differently, which is worth seeing once: `IN` really is
just `=` with room for more values.

## ex3 - comparing dates

This tests date comparison and, again, the boundary. The classic mistake is
`<=` on a date boundary, which is how "hired before 2015" turns into "hired
before 2015, plus everyone hired on the first working day of it". The model
answer keeps the comparison strict. Note that `hired_on` is a plain `date`,
so no time component can hide behind the literal - the same predicate on a
`timestamptz` column would need much more care.

## ex4 - a short list of values

This tests `IN` as shorthand for a chain of equalities. The classic mistake
is writing `department = 'sales' OR 'support'`, which is not a syntax error
in every dialect and means something else entirely where it parses. The model
answer lists both values inside one `IN`. The real argument for `IN` is not
brevity but safety: it has no precedence for you to get wrong, which is the
whole subject of the next drill set.

## ex5 - everything outside a list

This tests `NOT IN` and plants a flag for later. The classic mistake is
chaining `<>` with `OR` - `country <> 'US' OR country <> 'GB'` is true for
every row on earth, because no country can be both. The model answer negates
the whole membership test at once. Remember the caveat: `NOT IN` against a
list or subquery containing a NULL returns nothing, silently, and that bug
has shipped in production more than once.

## ex6 - an inclusive range

This tests `BETWEEN` and its inclusivity. The classic mistake is writing the
bounds backwards, which returns zero rows without complaint because `BETWEEN`
is defined as `>= first AND <= second` with no reordering. The model answer
puts the low bound first. Write the expanded form once and keep it in mind:
that expansion is exactly why `BETWEEN` on timestamps is a trap and
`BETWEEN` on prices is not.

## ex7 - a list and a range together

This tests combining a set predicate with a range predicate, and it is the
first place in the set where precedence could bite. The classic mistake is
expanding `IN` to an unbracketed `OR`, which produces every engineer
regardless of salary plus the ops people in band. The model answer keeps the
`IN` intact so no brackets are needed. The planner will apply whichever
condition it estimates is cheaper first, and neither ordering changes the
answer.

## ex8 - excluding the middle

The hard version: a membership test and a negated range in one predicate.
This tests whether you can turn `NOT BETWEEN` into its `OR` form without
losing an endpoint, since both comparisons become strict under negation. The
classic mistake is writing `price < 50 OR price > 450` without brackets, so
`AND` grabs only the first half and the result fills with cheap products from
every category. The model answer keeps `NOT BETWEEN` whole, which has no
precedence to get wrong.

## Further reading

- [Comparison Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html) - the definitions of `BETWEEN`, `IN`, and `IS DISTINCT FROM`, endpoints included.
- [Subquery Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) - what `IN` and `NOT IN` mean once the right-hand side is a subquery, and why NULLs matter there.
- [The WHERE Clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-WHERE) - where filtering sits in the logical evaluation order of a query.
- [Date/Time Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-datetime.html) - why a bare date literal compared against a timestamp means midnight.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
A date literal is written as a quoted string; PostgreSQL will compare it
to a `date` column without complaint, and you can be explicit with
`DATE '2015-01-01'` or `'2015-01-01'::date`.

## Hint 2
"Before 1 January 2015" excludes 1 January 2015 itself. Strict `<` is
right; `<=` would let anyone hired on New Year's Day in.

references.expected.sql: SELECT id, name, hired_on FROM staff WHERE hired_on < DATE '2015-01-01';

## Exercise 4 - a short list of values

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The customer-facing teams are being surveyed
together. Return every member of `staff` whose `department` is either `sales`
or `support`. Three columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `department`. Use
`IN` for the test. Any row order.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two acceptable values for one column. `IN` takes a comma-separated list
of literals in brackets.

## Hint 2
```sql
WHERE department IN (<value>, <value>)
```

The long-hand version is an `OR` of two equalities - worth writing once so
you can see they are the same predicate.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT s.id, s.name, s.department, s.salary
FROM staff AS s
WHERE (s.department = 'engineering' OR s.department = 'ops')

SELECT id, name, department, salary
FROM staff

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 - excluding the middle

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. The two ends of the toy and book ranges are being
re-photographed: the very cheap and the very expensive, nothing in between.
Return every product whose `category` is `toys` or `books`, and whose `price`
is **not** between 50 and 450 (that exclusion is inclusive of both bounds, so
a product at exactly 50.00 is excluded). Four columns, in this order: `id`,
`name`, `category`, `price`. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 57_drills_where_1 ex8`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
There is a negated form of the range predicate, and it is spelled exactly
how you would guess.

## Hint 2
`price NOT BETWEEN 50 AND 450` is `NOT (price >= 50 AND price <= 450)`,
which by De Morgan is `price < 50 OR price > 450`. Note that both endpoints
flip to strict comparisons.

## Hint 3
If you write the `OR` form by hand, bracket it. Without brackets, `AND`
binds tighter than `OR` and the category test attaches to only one half of
the range, letting in every cheap product in the catalog. Compare your row
count against the `NOT BETWEEN` version - they must agree exactly.

## Hint 1
There is a negated form of the range predicate, and it is spelled exactly
how you would guess.

## Hint 2
`price NOT BETWEEN 50 AND 450` is `NOT (price >= 50 AND price <= 450)`,
which by De Morgan is `price < 50 OR price > 450`. Note that both endpoints
flip to strict comparisons.

## Hint 3
If you write the `OR` form by hand, bracket it. Without brackets, `AND`
binds tighter than `OR` and the category test attaches to only one half of
the range, letting in every cheap product in the catalog. Compare your row
count against the `NOT BETWEEN` version - they must agree exactly.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT p.id, p.name, p.category, p.price
FROM products AS p
WHERE p.category IN ('toys', 'books')
  AND (p.price < 50 OR p.price > 450);
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, name, category, price
FROM products
WHERE category IN ('toys', 'books')
  AND price NOT BETWEEN 50 AND 450;

lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 58_drills_where_2

Boolean composition, drilled. Every problem here is one bracket away from a
different question, which is the entire point.

## Notes

The rule that generates this whole set: **`AND` binds tighter than `OR`**, so
`a OR b AND c` parses as `a OR (b AND c)`. It matches arithmetic - `AND` is
the `*`, `OR` is the `+` - it is standard across every SQL dialect, and it is
responsible for an enormous number of production bugs, because the wrong
reading is usually *more* rows rather than an error.

The second tool is **De Morgan's laws**, which tell you what happens when you
push a `NOT` inside brackets: `NOT (a OR b)` becomes `NOT a AND NOT b`, and
`NOT (a AND b)` becomes `NOT a OR NOT b`. The conjunction and the disjunction
swap places. Getting this backwards produces a predicate that is true for
almost every row - the classic `country <> 'US' OR country <> 'GB'`, which no
row on earth can fail.

Both rules are safe here for a reason worth naming: every column these drills
filter on is declared `NOT NULL`. In three-valued logic `NOT unknown` is
still `unknown`, and a row whose predicate is unknown is discarded exactly
like a false one, silently. That is lesson 05's subject, and these drills are
the before picture.

## ex1 - two conditions, both required

The baseline: a conjunction of two independent tests. This exists so the
later problems have something to contrast against. The classic mistake at
this level is reaching for `OR` because the prompt used the word "and" only
once - read the requirement as "both of these are true of the row". The model
answer joins the two comparisons with `AND`; swapping their order is
identical in meaning and in plan.

## ex2 - two conditions, either will do

This tests disjunction, and the fact that `OR` is not a union of two result
sets - a row satisfying both branches still appears once. The classic mistake
is worrying about duplicates and adding `DISTINCT`, which cannot help and
costs a sort. The model answer uses a plain `OR`. The reference solution
writes the same predicate through De Morgan's laws, which is worth reading
once as a preview of ex6.

## ex3 - negating one test

This tests negation in its simplest form and flags the hazard that makes it
interesting later. The classic mistake is assuming `<> 'sales'` means
"everything else" on any column - it means that only when the column cannot
be NULL, since an unknown comparison is discarded like a false one. The model
answer negates the equality directly. Try the same shape on a nullable column
in lesson 05 and watch rows disappear.

## ex4 - the bracket that changes the question

The precedence trap, walked into deliberately. This tests whether you bracket
a disjunction before joining it to anything with `AND`. The classic mistake
returns every shipped order at any price, because the unbracketed form parses
as `shipped OR (cancelled AND cheap)`. The model answer brackets the `OR`.
The reference uses `IN`, which is the same predicate with no precedence left
to get wrong - usually the better production answer.

## ex5 - one category, two extremes

The mirror image of ex4: here the `OR` is on the numeric side. This tests the
same precedence rule from the other direction, which is worth drilling
separately because the unbracketed failure looks different - you get
expensive products from categories you never asked about. The model answer
brackets the two price comparisons. The reference reaches for `NOT BETWEEN`,
which expresses "outside this range" with no brackets at all.

## ex6 - pushing NOT inside brackets

This tests De Morgan's laws in the direction people get wrong. The classic
mistake is `<> 'sales' OR <> 'support'`, a predicate that is true for every
row ever stored, and which therefore looks like the filter simply did not
run. The model answer negates the whole disjunction; the reference shows the
distributed form with the connective correctly flipped to `AND`. When a
negated filter returns the whole table, this is almost always why.

## ex7 - two branches, each with two conditions

This tests composing a disjunction of conjunctions, the shape almost every
real eligibility rule takes. The classic mistake is factoring the categories
out - `category IN ('toys','books') AND (price > 450 OR price < 30)` - which
looks tidier and is a different question, since it admits cheap toys and
expensive books. The model answer keeps each rule intact. Note that the
brackets here are for the human, not the parser.

## ex8 - negating a compound predicate

The hard version, and a fair interview question: a negation over a
disjunction where one branch is itself a range. This tests both De Morgan
steps at once, since the `OR` becomes an `AND` and the `BETWEEN` splits into
two strict comparisons that must then be re-bracketed. The classic mistake is
distributing the `NOT` over only the first branch. The model answer negates
the whole thing in place, which is both correct and easier to review.

## Further reading

- [Logical Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-logical.html) - the truth tables for `AND`, `OR` and `NOT`, including the unknown column.
- [Operator Precedence](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-syntax-lexical.html#SQL-PRECEDENCE) - the authoritative table; `AND` above `OR` is the row that matters here.
- [The WHERE Clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-WHERE) - a reminder that only rows whose condition is *true* survive - not merely not-false.
- [Comparison Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html) - the operators being combined, and what each one returns for a NULL input.

# Reading - 58_drills_where_2

Boolean composition, drilled. Every problem here is one bracket away from a
different question, which is the entire point.

## Notes

The rule that generates this whole set: **`AND` binds tighter than `OR`**, so
`a OR b AND c` parses as `a OR (b AND c)`. It matches arithmetic - `AND` is
the `*`, `OR` is the `+` - it is standard across every SQL dialect, and it is
responsible for an enormous number of production bugs, because the wrong
reading is usually *more* rows rather than an error.

The second tool is **De Morgan's laws**, which tell you what happens when you
push a `NOT` inside brackets: `NOT (a OR b)` becomes `NOT a AND NOT b`, and
`NOT (a AND b)` becomes `NOT a OR NOT b`. The conjunction and the disjunction
swap places. Getting this backwards produces a predicate that is true for
almost every row - the classic `country <> 'US' OR country <> 'GB'`, which no
row on earth can fail.

Both rules are safe here for a reason worth naming: every column these drills
filter on is declared `NOT NULL`. In three-valued logic `NOT unknown` is
still `unknown`, and a row whose predicate is unknown is discarded exactly
like a false one, silently. That is lesson 05's subject, and these drills are
the before picture.

## ex1 - two conditions, both required

The baseline: a conjunction of two independent tests. This exists so the
later problems have something to contrast against. The classic mistake at
this level is reaching for `OR` because the prompt used the word "and" only
once - read the requirement as "both of these are true of the row". The model
answer joins the two comparisons with `AND`; swapping their order is
identical in meaning and in plan.

## ex2 - two conditions, either will do

This tests disjunction, and the fact that `OR` is not a union of two result
sets - a row satisfying both branches still appears once. The classic mistake
is worrying about duplicates and adding `DISTINCT`, which cannot help and
costs a sort. The model answer uses a plain `OR`. The reference solution
writes the same predicate through De Morgan's laws, which is worth reading
once as a preview of ex6.

## ex3 - negating one test

This tests negation in its simplest form and flags the hazard that makes it
interesting later. The classic mistake is assuming `<> 'sales'` means
"everything else" on any column - it means that only when the column cannot
be NULL, since an unknown comparison is discarded like a false one. The model
answer negates the equality directly. Try the same shape on a nullable column
in lesson 05 and watch rows disappear.

## ex4 - the bracket that changes the question

The precedence trap, walked into deliberately. This tests whether you bracket
a disjunction before joining it to anything with `AND`. The classic mistake
returns every shipped order at any price, because the unbracketed form parses
as `shipped OR (cancelled AND cheap)`. The model answer brackets the `OR`.
The reference uses `IN`, which is the same predicate with no precedence left
to get wrong - usually the better production answer.

## ex5 - one category, two extremes

The mirror image of ex4: here the `OR` is on the numeric side. This tests the
same precedence rule from the other direction, which is worth drilling
separately because the unbracketed failure looks different - you get
expensive products from categories you never asked about. The model answer
brackets the two price comparisons. The reference reaches for `NOT BETWEEN`,
which expresses "outside this range" with no brackets at all.

## ex6 - pushing NOT inside brackets

This tests De Morgan's laws in the direction people get wrong. The classic
mistake is `<> 'sales' OR <> 'support'`, a predicate that is true for every
row ever stored, and which therefore looks like the filter simply did not
run. The model answer negates the whole disjunction; the reference shows the
distributed form with the connective correctly flipped to `AND`. When a
negated filter returns the whole table, this is almost always why.

## ex7 - two branches, each with two conditions

This tests composing a disjunction of conjunctions, the shape almost every
real eligibility rule takes. The classic mistake is factoring the categories
out - `category IN ('toys','books') AND (price > 450 OR price < 30)` - which
looks tidier and is a different question, since it admits cheap toys and
expensive books. The model answer keeps each rule intact. Note that the
brackets here are for the human, not the parser.

## ex8 - negating a compound predicate

The hard version, and a fair interview question: a negation over a
disjunction where one branch is itself a range. This tests both De Morgan
steps at once, since the `OR` becomes an `AND` and the `BETWEEN` splits into
two strict comparisons that must then be re-bracketed. The classic mistake is
distributing the `NOT` over only the first branch. The model answer negates
the whole thing in place, which is both correct and easier to review.

## Further reading

- [Logical Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-logical.html) - the truth tables for `AND`, `OR` and `NOT`, including the unknown column.
- [Operator Precedence](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-syntax-lexical.html#SQL-PRECEDENCE) - the authoritative table; `AND` above `OR` is the row that matters here.
- [The WHERE Clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-WHERE) - a reminder that only rows whose condition is *true* survive - not merely not-false.
- [Comparison Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html) - the operators being combined, and what each one returns for a NULL input.

Three spellings work here: `NOT (...)`, `<>`, and `NOT IN (...)`. Pick
one.

NULL row, because `NULL <> 'sales'` is unknown, not true.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The category test applies to both price branches, so the price branches
have to be bracketed together.

## Hint 2
If you drop the brackets you get `(electronics AND cheap) OR expensive`,
which hands you the most expensive product in every category. That is the
symptom to recognise.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT p.id, p.name, p.category, p.price
FROM products AS p
WHERE p.category = 'electronics'
  AND p.price NOT BETWEEN 10 AND 490;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, name, category, price
FROM products
WHERE category = 'electronics'
  AND (price < 10 OR price > 490);

## Exercise 6 - pushing NOT inside brackets

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. The back-office teams are everyone who is not
customer-facing. Return every member of `staff` whose `department` is neither
`sales` nor `support`. Three columns, in this order: `id`, `name`,
`department`. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 58_drills_where_2 ex6`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
"Neither A nor B" is the negation of "A or B". Write it that way first,
then try pushing the `NOT` inside the brackets and see what the connective
becomes.

## Hint 2
De Morgan: `NOT (a OR b)` is `NOT a AND NOT b`. The `OR` turns into an
`AND`. Writing `dept <> 'sales' OR dept <> 'support'` instead returns every
row in the table, because no department can be both.

## Hint 1
Write the inner predicate first and get it running on its own. Only then
wrap it in `NOT (...)` - and confirm the two row counts add up to the whole
catalog.

## Hint 2
Pushing the `NOT` in twice: `NOT (a OR b)` is `NOT a AND NOT b`, then
`NOT (price BETWEEN 100 AND 400)` becomes `price < 100 OR price > 400` with
both comparisons strict.

## Hint 3
The distributed form needs brackets around the price disjunction, or
`AND` will bind tighter than the `OR` and let in every cheap book. Run both
forms and compare the counts: if they differ, the brackets are the reason.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT p.id, p.name, p.category, p.price
FROM products AS p
WHERE p.category NOT IN ('books', 'food')
  AND (p.price < 100 OR p.price > 400);

# 59 - Drills: patterns and mixed predicates

The third `WHERE` set - lesson 02's pattern-matching half, plus the mixed
predicates that combine a pattern with a range or a list. `%` and `_` are the
whole vocabulary; knowing which of them you need is the whole skill. Redo 02
and 57 first if `LIKE` and `ILIKE` still feel interchangeable.

## Exercise 1 - an anchored prefix

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. The Nova line is being discontinued. Every product
name is built as `<line> <item> <id>`, so the Nova products are the ones whose
`name` starts with `Nova ` (note the trailing space). Return three columns, in
this order: `id`, `name`, `category`. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 59_drills_where_3 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - a suffix

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. The warehouse audits one tenth of the catalog by
checking every product whose `name` ends with the digit `7`. Return two
columns, in this order: `id`, `name`. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 59_drills_where_3 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - counting characters with underscore

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Support is investigating a batch of accounts created
in one run. Every email has the shape `user<id>@example.com`, and the batch is
the customers whose id has **exactly three digits and starts with a 2**.
Match that with `LIKE` and underscores - not with a numeric comparison on
`id`. Return two columns, in this order: `id`, `email`. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 59_drills_where_3 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - case-insensitive containment

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. A supplier recall covers every blanket in the
catalog, and nobody trusts the capitalisation in the source spreadsheet.
Return every product whose `name` contains `blanket`,
matched **case-insensitively**. Three columns, in this order: `id`, `name`,
`price`. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 59_drills_where_3 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - excluding a pattern

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. The toy department is re-listing everything except
the dolls. Return every product whose `category` is `toys` and whose `name`
does **not** contain `Doll` (matched case-sensitively). Two columns, in this
order: `id`, `name`. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 59_drills_where_3 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - a pattern and a range

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. The Frost line's mid-price stock is going into a
bundle. Return every product whose `name` starts with `Frost ` and whose
`price` is between 100 and 200 inclusive. Three columns, in this order: `id`,
`name`, `price`. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 59_drills_where_3 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - two patterns and a threshold

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. The premium electronics promo covers routers and
tablets only, above 400 dollars. Return every product whose `name` contains
`Router` **or** contains `Tablet`, **and** whose `price` is over 400. Four
columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `category`, `price`. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 59_drills_where_3 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - a fixed-width pattern and an exclusion

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. The very first cohort of signups is being surveyed,
minus our two biggest markets. Return every customer whose `email` matches
`user<two digits>@example.com` - exactly two digits - **and** whose `country`
is neither `US` nor `GB`. Three columns, in this order: `id`, `email`,
`country`. Any row order.

lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 59_drills_where_3

Pattern matching, drilled against text that has real structure - product
names that end in their own id, emails built from a template - because that
is where `LIKE` genuinely belongs.

## Notes

`LIKE` has exactly two metacharacters. **`%` matches any run of characters,
including none; `_` matches exactly one.** Everything else in the pattern is
a literal. `ILIKE` is the case-insensitive variant, and it is a PostgreSQL
extension rather than standard SQL. `NOT LIKE` negates the whole match.

Two consequences worth holding on to. The first is about **anchoring**: a
pattern that begins with a literal (`'Nova %'`) can use an ordinary B-tree
index on that column, while a pattern that begins with `%` cannot, ever - a
leading wildcard forces a full scan no matter what you index. That is why
`LIKE 'user1__@example.com'` is a reasonable production predicate and
`LIKE '%son%'` over a large table is a design smell.

The second is about **precision**: `_` is the tool people forget, and it is
what turns a vague pattern into an exact one. `'user1%@example.com'` matches
customer 1, 10, and 1000; `'user1__@example.com'` matches exactly the
three-digit ids beginning with 1. When the text has a fixed shape, use `_`
and get the shape enforced for free.

## ex1 - an anchored prefix

This tests a left-anchored `LIKE`, the one shape that an ordinary index can
still help with. The classic mistake is dropping the trailing space, which
widens the match to anything merely beginning with those four letters. The
model answer spells the literal out including the space. The reference uses
`left(name, 5)` instead, which is the same test written as a function and is
what an expression index would key on (lesson 40).

## ex2 - a suffix

This tests a right-anchored pattern and quietly makes the indexing point. The
classic mistake is `LIKE '7%'`, which matches names *starting* with 7 - here
that is nothing at all, so you get an empty result and no clue why. The model
answer puts the wildcard first. Because every product name ends in its own
id, this predicate is really "ids ending in 7", which is why it returns a
clean tenth of the catalog.

## ex3 - counting characters with underscore

This tests `_`, the metacharacter everyone forgets, and the difference
between "some characters" and "exactly this many". The classic mistake is
`'user2%@example.com'`, which matches every id beginning with 2 regardless of
length. The model answer uses two underscores to pin the length. The
reference does the same job with a POSIX regex, where `.` is the
single-character wildcard and `%` has no meaning at all.

## ex4 - case-insensitive containment

This tests `ILIKE` against data whose capitalisation you cannot rely on. The
classic mistake is plain `LIKE` with a lower-case literal, which returns zero
rows and looks like missing data rather than a bug. The model answer uses
`ILIKE`. The reference lower-cases the column instead, which is the portable
form and, not coincidentally, the expression you would build an index on if
this predicate ever had to be fast.

## ex5 - excluding a pattern

This tests `NOT LIKE` combined with an ordinary equality. The classic mistake
is negating the wrong half - `category <> 'toys' AND name NOT LIKE '%Doll%'`
reads almost identically and answers a completely different question. The
model answer negates only the pattern. The reference replaces it with
`position(... IN ...) = 0`, which is the function form and makes the "does
not occur anywhere" meaning explicit.

## ex6 - a pattern and a range

This tests combining a pattern with a range, which is the commonest real
`WHERE` clause in existence. The classic mistake is an off-by-one at the
range boundary while all the attention goes to the pattern. The model answer
uses `LIKE` for the text and `BETWEEN` for the number. The reference swaps in
`starts_with` and the expanded comparisons, so you can see that all three
spellings describe the same set of rows.

## ex7 - two patterns and a threshold

This tests precedence again, now with patterns on the `OR` side. The classic
mistake is omitting the brackets, which yields every router in the catalog
regardless of price. The model answer brackets the two `LIKE` tests before
joining the price threshold with `AND`. The reference collapses the
disjunction into one regular expression, which removes the brackets by
removing the `OR` - a trade of familiarity for safety.

## ex8 - a fixed-width pattern and an exclusion

The composite: a fixed-width pattern joined to a negated membership test.
This tests `_` for exact length and `NOT IN` for exclusion in one predicate,
which is a fair interview question because both halves have a well-known
failure mode. The classic mistake is the `<> A OR <> B` exclusion, which
quietly disables the filter. The model answer pins the length with two
underscores and negates the whole country list at once.

## Further reading

- [Pattern Matching](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-matching.html) - `LIKE`, `SIMILAR TO` and POSIX regular expressions, with the escape rules for each.
- [String Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-string.html) - `starts_with`, `position`, `left` and `right` - the function forms of several patterns here.
- [Indexes and ORDER BY / operator classes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-opclass.html) - why a `LIKE` pattern anchored on the left can use an index and a leading `%` cannot.
- [Full Text Search](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/textsearch-intro.html) - what to reach for when you catch yourself writing `%word%` against prose.

# Reading - 59_drills_where_3

Pattern matching, drilled against text that has real structure - product
names that end in their own id, emails built from a template - because that
is where `LIKE` genuinely belongs.

## Notes

`LIKE` has exactly two metacharacters. **`%` matches any run of characters,
including none; `_` matches exactly one.** Everything else in the pattern is
a literal. `ILIKE` is the case-insensitive variant, and it is a PostgreSQL
extension rather than standard SQL. `NOT LIKE` negates the whole match.

Two consequences worth holding on to. The first is about **anchoring**: a
pattern that begins with a literal (`'Nova %'`) can use an ordinary B-tree
index on that column, while a pattern that begins with `%` cannot, ever - a
leading wildcard forces a full scan no matter what you index. That is why
`LIKE 'user1__@example.com'` is a reasonable production predicate and
`LIKE '%son%'` over a large table is a design smell.

The second is about **precision**: `_` is the tool people forget, and it is
what turns a vague pattern into an exact one. `'user1%@example.com'` matches
customer 1, 10, and 1000; `'user1__@example.com'` matches exactly the
three-digit ids beginning with 1. When the text has a fixed shape, use `_`
and get the shape enforced for free.

## ex1 - an anchored prefix

This tests a left-anchored `LIKE`, the one shape that an ordinary index can
still help with. The classic mistake is dropping the trailing space, which
widens the match to anything merely beginning with those four letters. The
model answer spells the literal out including the space. The reference uses
`left(name, 5)` instead, which is the same test written as a function and is
what an expression index would key on (lesson 40).

## ex2 - a suffix

This tests a right-anchored pattern and quietly makes the indexing point. The
classic mistake is `LIKE '7%'`, which matches names *starting* with 7 - here
that is nothing at all, so you get an empty result and no clue why. The model
answer puts the wildcard first. Because every product name ends in its own
id, this predicate is really "ids ending in 7", which is why it returns a
clean tenth of the catalog.

## ex3 - counting characters with underscore

This tests `_`, the metacharacter everyone forgets, and the difference
between "some characters" and "exactly this many". The classic mistake is
`'user2%@example.com'`, which matches every id beginning with 2 regardless of
length. The model answer uses two underscores to pin the length. The
reference does the same job with a POSIX regex, where `.` is the
single-character wildcard and `%` has no meaning at all.

## ex4 - case-insensitive containment

This tests `ILIKE` against data whose capitalisation you cannot rely on. The
classic mistake is plain `LIKE` with a lower-case literal, which returns zero
rows and looks like missing data rather than a bug. The model answer uses
`ILIKE`. The reference lower-cases the column instead, which is the portable
form and, not coincidentally, the expression you would build an index on if
this predicate ever had to be fast.

## ex5 - excluding a pattern

This tests `NOT LIKE` combined with an ordinary equality. The classic mistake
is negating the wrong half - `category <> 'toys' AND name NOT LIKE '%Doll%'`
reads almost identically and answers a completely different question. The
model answer negates only the pattern. The reference replaces it with
`position(... IN ...) = 0`, which is the function form and makes the "does
not occur anywhere" meaning explicit.

## ex6 - a pattern and a range

This tests combining a pattern with a range, which is the commonest real
`WHERE` clause in existence. The classic mistake is an off-by-one at the
range boundary while all the attention goes to the pattern. The model answer
uses `LIKE` for the text and `BETWEEN` for the number. The reference swaps in
`starts_with` and the expanded comparisons, so you can see that all three
spellings describe the same set of rows.

## ex7 - two patterns and a threshold

This tests precedence again, now with patterns on the `OR` side. The classic
mistake is omitting the brackets, which yields every router in the catalog
regardless of price. The model answer brackets the two `LIKE` tests before
joining the price threshold with `AND`. The reference collapses the
disjunction into one regular expression, which removes the brackets by
removing the `OR` - a trade of familiarity for safety.

## ex8 - a fixed-width pattern and an exclusion

The composite: a fixed-width pattern joined to a negated membership test.
This tests `_` for exact length and `NOT IN` for exclusion in one predicate,
which is a fair interview question because both halves have a well-known
failure mode. The classic mistake is the `<> A OR <> B` exclusion, which
quietly disables the filter. The model answer pins the length with two
underscores and negates the whole country list at once.

## Further reading

- [Pattern Matching](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-matching.html) - `LIKE`, `SIMILAR TO` and POSIX regular expressions, with the escape rules for each.
- [String Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-string.html) - `starts_with`, `position`, `left` and `right` - the function forms of several patterns here.
- [Indexes and ORDER BY / operator classes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-opclass.html) - why a `LIKE` pattern anchored on the left can use an index and a leading `%` cannot.
- [Full Text Search](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/textsearch-intro.html) - what to reach for when you catch yourself writing `%word%` against prose.

## Exercise 3 - counting characters with underscore

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Support is investigating a batch of accounts created
in one run. Every email has the shape `user<id>@example.com`, and the batch is
the customers whose id has **exactly three digits and starts with a 2**.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two patterns joined by `OR`, then a numeric test joined by `AND`. That
combination always needs brackets.

## Hint 2
Without them, `AND` binds tighter and you get `Router-anything` at any
price plus expensive tablets - a superset that looks plausible until you
count it.

## Hint 3
A regular expression can express the two alternatives in one predicate:
the `~` operator matches a POSIX regex, and `(A|B)` means "either". Getting
the bracketed `LIKE` version working first is still the better route -
reach for the regex only once you can see the two are the same set.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Two patterns joined by `OR`, then a numeric test joined by `AND`. That
combination always needs brackets.

## Hint 2
Without them, `AND` binds tighter and you get `Router-anything` at any
price plus expensive tablets - a superset that looks plausible until you
count it.

## Hint 3
A regular expression can express the two alternatives in one predicate:
the `~` operator matches a POSIX regex, and `(A|B)` means "either". Getting
the bracketed `LIKE` version working first is still the better route -
reach for the regex only once you can see the two are the same set.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT p.id, p.name, p.category, p.price
FROM products AS p
WHERE p.name ~ '(Router|Tablet)'
  AND p.price > 400;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, name, category, price
FROM products
WHERE (name LIKE '%Router%' OR name LIKE '%Tablet%')
  AND price > 400;

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 - a fixed-width pattern and an exclusion

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. The very first cohort of signups is being surveyed,
minus our two biggest markets. Return every customer whose `email` matches
`user<two digits>@example.com` - exactly two digits - **and** whose `country`
is neither `US` nor `GB`. Three columns, in this order: `id`, `email`,
`country`. Any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 59_drills_where_3 ex8`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two underscores, not a `%`. The whole point of the cohort is that the id
is two digits long.

## Hint 2
The country exclusion is `NOT IN` (or its De Morgan twin, `<> 'US' AND <>
'GB'`). Writing it as `<> 'US' OR <> 'GB'` returns every customer, since no
country can be both.

## Hint 3
Build it in two steps and check each: run the pattern alone and confirm
the ids you get are all two-digit; then add the country exclusion and
confirm the count only goes down. If adding a filter makes a result grow,
an `OR` has escaped its brackets.

lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 60_drills_order_limit_1

Ordering, drilled. The syntax is five minutes; the discipline of making an
order *total* is the part that takes practice.

## Notes

`ORDER BY` takes a list of keys, each with its own direction, and applies
them left to right: the second key only decides between rows the first key
tied. `ASC` is the default and `DESC` reverses only the key it is attached
to - `ORDER BY a, b DESC` sorts `a` ascending and `b` descending, which is
not what a hurried reader assumes.

The rule that matters most in this set is **totality**. If your sort keys do
not uniquely determine an order, the rows that tie come back in whatever
sequence the executor produced them, and that sequence is an implementation
detail: it can change between runs, between plans, and between PostgreSQL
versions. Adding a unique column - here, always the primary key - as the last
key makes the order total and the query reproducible. That is why every
prompt in this set names its tie-break, and it is what an interviewer is
listening for when they ask "what if two rows have the same revenue?".

`LIMIT` then takes the first N rows *of that order*. PostgreSQL does not
sort everything and throw the rest away - for a small N it uses a top-N heap
sort, which is why `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 10` over a very large table is fast
and `ORDER BY ...` without the limit is not.

## ex1 - the longest-serving staff

This tests the basic shape - sort ascending, take the first N - and the habit
of appending a unique tie-break. The classic mistake is omitting `id`, which
usually passes and occasionally does not, which is the worst possible
failure mode. The model answer sorts by date then by key. `FETCH FIRST 10
ROWS ONLY` in the reference is the SQL-standard spelling of `LIMIT 10`; both
plan identically in PostgreSQL.

## ex2 - sorting text

This tests text ordering and the lesson hiding inside it: a string sort is
not a numeric sort. The classic mistake is reading the output as broken
because `1372` precedes `141`, and then "fixing" it with a cast the prompt
did not ask for. The model answer sorts the text as text. Text collation is also
locale-dependent, which is why the same query can order differently on a
database initialised with a different `LC_COLLATE`.

## ex3 - grouped alphabetically by country

This tests multi-key ordering and the left-to-right precedence of sort keys.
The classic mistake is writing the keys in the order the columns appear in
the SELECT list rather than the order the report needs. The model answer
follows the prompt exactly. The reference sorts by output position - `ORDER
BY 3, 2, 1` - which is legal, occasionally handy, and a maintenance hazard
the moment somebody edits the SELECT list.

## ex4 - the newest reviews

This tests per-key sort direction, the detail that catches people who assume
`DESC` applies to everything after it. The classic mistake is exactly that -
one `DESC` at the end of a two-key list, producing the oldest reviews with a
descending id tie-break. The model answer marks both keys. Note how cheap
this is despite the table size: a top-N sort keeps only ten rows in memory
while it scans.

## ex5 - the second page

This tests `OFFSET` as pagination and the off-by-one everybody makes once.
The classic mistake is `OFFSET 26`, which quietly drops the first row of page
two. The model answer skips exactly one page's worth. Worth knowing for later:
`OFFSET` gets slower the deeper you page, because the server still produces
and discards every skipped row - lesson 52 replaces it with keyset
pagination.

## ex6 - newest hire in each department

This tests mixed sort directions across three keys. The classic mistake is
reading "newest first in each department" as a per-group top-N and reaching
for window functions - the prompt asks only for a listing, and `ORDER BY`
plus `LIMIT` is the whole answer. The model answer marks each key's direction
independently. Recognising which of the two problems you have been handed is
a real interview skill.

## ex7 - sorting by an expression

This tests sorting by a computed value and the necessity of a tie-break when
the sort key has few distinct values. The classic mistake is omitting `id`
and getting a different twenty rows on a different run, because a hundred
products share each cents value. The model answer sorts by the expression and
breaks ties on the key. An index on `(price % 1)` would make this cheap -
that is lesson 40's expression index.

## ex8 - three keys, mixed, on a large table

This tests a three-key sort with a direction change in the middle, over a
table big enough that guessing does not work. The classic mistake is letting
one `DESC` leak onto the following keys, which reverses the date order inside
each country. The model answer states each direction explicitly - including
the `ASC`s, which are redundant to the parser and valuable to the reader.
Being explicit is free and it removes the ambiguity from review.

## Further reading

- [Sorting Rows](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-order.html) - the ORDER BY clause: multiple keys, per-key direction, and NULL placement.
- [LIMIT and OFFSET](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-limit.html) - the documentation's own warning that LIMIT without ORDER BY returns an unpredictable subset.
- [Collation Support](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/collation.html) - why sorting text is a locale question, not an ASCII one.
- [Use The Index, Luke - Sorting and Grouping](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/sorting-grouping) - the same clause seen from the index's point of view; you will re-read this in Part 5.

# Reading - 60_drills_order_limit_1

Ordering, drilled. The syntax is five minutes; the discipline of making an
order *total* is the part that takes practice.

## Notes

`ORDER BY` takes a list of keys, each with its own direction, and applies
them left to right: the second key only decides between rows the first key
tied. `ASC` is the default and `DESC` reverses only the key it is attached
to - `ORDER BY a, b DESC` sorts `a` ascending and `b` descending, which is
not what a hurried reader assumes.

The rule that matters most in this set is **totality**. If your sort keys do
not uniquely determine an order, the rows that tie come back in whatever
sequence the executor produced them, and that sequence is an implementation
detail: it can change between runs, between plans, and between PostgreSQL
versions. Adding a unique column - here, always the primary key - as the last
key makes the order total and the query reproducible. That is why every
prompt in this set names its tie-break, and it is what an interviewer is
listening for when they ask "what if two rows have the same revenue?".

`LIMIT` then takes the first N rows *of that order*. PostgreSQL does not
sort everything and throw the rest away - for a small N it uses a top-N heap
sort, which is why `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 10` over a very large table is fast
and `ORDER BY ...` without the limit is not.

## ex1 - the longest-serving staff

This tests the basic shape - sort ascending, take the first N - and the habit
of appending a unique tie-break. The classic mistake is omitting `id`, which
usually passes and occasionally does not, which is the worst possible
failure mode. The model answer sorts by date then by key. `FETCH FIRST 10
ROWS ONLY` in the reference is the SQL-standard spelling of `LIMIT 10`; both
plan identically in PostgreSQL.

## ex2 - sorting text

This tests text ordering and the lesson hiding inside it: a string sort is
not a numeric sort. The classic mistake is reading the output as broken
because `1372` precedes `141`, and then "fixing" it with a cast the prompt
did not ask for. The model answer sorts the text as text. Text collation is also
locale-dependent, which is why the same query can order differently on a
database initialised with a different `LC_COLLATE`.

## ex3 - grouped alphabetically by country

This tests multi-key ordering and the left-to-right precedence of sort keys.
The classic mistake is writing the keys in the order the columns appear in
the SELECT list rather than the order the report needs. The model answer
follows the prompt exactly. The reference sorts by output position - `ORDER
BY 3, 2, 1` - which is legal, occasionally handy, and a maintenance hazard
the moment somebody edits the SELECT list.

## ex4 - the newest reviews

This tests per-key sort direction, the detail that catches people who assume
`DESC` applies to everything after it. The classic mistake is exactly that -
one `DESC` at the end of a two-key list, producing the oldest reviews with a
descending id tie-break. The model answer marks both keys. Note how cheap
this is despite the table size: a top-N sort keeps only ten rows in memory
while it scans.

## ex5 - the second page

This tests `OFFSET` as pagination and the off-by-one everybody makes once.
The classic mistake is `OFFSET 26`, which quietly drops the first row of page
two. The model answer skips exactly one page's worth. Worth knowing for later:
`OFFSET` gets slower the deeper you page, because the server still produces
and discards every skipped row - lesson 52 replaces it with keyset
pagination.

## ex6 - newest hire in each department

This tests mixed sort directions across three keys. The classic mistake is
reading "newest first in each department" as a per-group top-N and reaching
for window functions - the prompt asks only for a listing, and `ORDER BY`
plus `LIMIT` is the whole answer. The model answer marks each key's direction
independently. Recognising which of the two problems you have been handed is
a real interview skill.

## ex7 - sorting by an expression

This tests sorting by a computed value and the necessity of a tie-break when
the sort key has few distinct values. The classic mistake is omitting `id`
and getting a different twenty rows on a different run, because a hundred
products share each cents value. The model answer sorts by the expression and
breaks ties on the key. An index on `(price % 1)` would make this cheap -
that is lesson 40's expression index.

## ex8 - three keys, mixed, on a large table

This tests a three-key sort with a direction change in the middle, over a
table big enough that guessing does not work. The classic mistake is letting
one `DESC` leak onto the following keys, which reverses the date order inside
each country. The model answer states each direction explicitly - including
the `ASC`s, which are redundant to the parser and valuable to the reader.
Being explicit is free and it removes the ambiguity from review.

## Further reading

- [Sorting Rows](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-order.html) - the ORDER BY clause: multiple keys, per-key direction, and NULL placement.
- [LIMIT and OFFSET](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-limit.html) - the documentation's own warning that LIMIT without ORDER BY returns an unpredictable subset.
- [Collation Support](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/collation.html) - why sorting text is a locale question, not an ASCII one.
- [Use The Index, Luke - Sorting and Grouping](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/sorting-grouping) - the same clause seen from the index's point of view; you will re-read this in Part 5.

longest-serving** members of `staff` - the earliest `hired_on` first. Three

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Earliest first is the default direction. The second key exists only to
settle ties on the first.

## Hint 2
```sql
ORDER BY hired_on ASC, id ASC
LIMIT 10
```

Without the `id` key, two people hired on the same day could come back in
either order, and the gate compares positions.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT s.id, s.name, s.hired_on
FROM staff AS s
ORDER BY s.hired_on, s.id
FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, name, hired_on
FROM staff
ORDER BY hired_on ASC, id ASC
LIMIT 10;

## Hint 1

Look hard at the ten names you get back. Every product name ends in its

SELECT ranked.id, ranked.name, ranked.category
FROM (

) AS ranked
ORDER BY ranked.name, ranked.id;

SELECT id, name, category
FROM products
ORDER BY name ASC, id ASC
LIMIT 10;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Most recent first means descending on the timestamp. Both keys are
descending here - say so on both.

## Hint 2
`ORDER BY created_at, id DESC` sorts the timestamp *ascending*: `DESC`
attaches to one key only, never to the whole list.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT r.id, r.product_id, r.rating, r.created_at
FROM reviews AS r
ORDER BY r.created_at DESC, r.id DESC
OFFSET 0
LIMIT 10;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, product_id, rating, created_at
FROM reviews
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 10;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 - the second page

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. The premium catalog is paginated twenty-five
products to a page, most expensive first. Return **page two** - that is, skip
the first twenty-five rows of the ordering and return the next twenty-five.
Three columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `price`.

**Ordered by `price` descending, then `id` ascending.** Twenty-five rows.

Run: `uv run dojo test 60_drills_order_limit_1 ex5`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
One clause skips rows and another caps them. Both apply after the sort.

## Hint 2
Page two of a twenty-five-row page means `OFFSET 25`, not `OFFSET 26` -
the offset counts rows to discard, not the row number to start at.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
`ORDER BY` accepts any expression, not just a column name. The expression
does not have to appear in the SELECT list.

## Hint 2
`price % 1` is the remainder after dividing by one - the cents. Expect
heavy ties at `0.99`, which is exactly why the prompt gives you an `id`
tie-break.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT q.id, q.name, q.price
FROM (
  SELECT p.id, p.name, p.price, p.price % 1 AS cents
  FROM products AS p
) AS q
ORDER BY q.cents DESC, q.id
LIMIT 20;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY price % 1 DESC, id ASC
LIMIT 20;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 - three keys, mixed, on a large table

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. The retention team reads the customer list from the
last country alphabetically backwards, oldest signups first inside each
country. Return the first thirty rows. Four columns, in this order: `id`,
`name`, `country`, `created_at`.

**Ordered by `country` descending, then `created_at` ascending, then `id`
ascending.** Thirty rows.

Run: `uv run dojo test 60_drills_order_limit_1 ex8`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Read the direction of each key separately. Only the first one is
descending.

## Hint 2
All thirty rows will come from the alphabetically last country, because
the first key dominates and that country has far more than thirty
customers.

## Hint 3
Build it up one key at a time and look at the output after each: sort by
country alone and confirm the last country is on top, then add
`created_at ASC` and confirm the dates now climb inside that country, then
add `id`. Debugging a three-key sort by staring at the finished query is
much harder than watching it assemble.

lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 61_drills_order_limit_2

Ordering again, at the edges: NULL placement, deep pagination, and sort keys
that never appear in the output.

## Notes

Three things this set drills that lesson 03 introduced and nobody practises
enough.

**NULL placement is a choice.** PostgreSQL's default is `NULLS LAST` for
ascending and `NULLS FIRST` for descending - which is consistent (NULL sorts
as if it were larger than everything) and is still not what most reports
want. `ORDER BY manager_id DESC NULLS LAST` overrides it. Because the default
flips with the direction, changing a sort from ascending to descending
silently moves your NULL rows from the bottom of the report to the top.

**A sort key does not have to be selected.** `ORDER BY price DESC` is legal
in a query that returns only `id` and `name`. That is genuinely useful, and
it is also the one place a reader of your output cannot check your work - so
say in the prompt, the ticket, or a comment what the rows are ordered by.
(The exception arrives with `SELECT DISTINCT` and set operations, where the
sort key *must* appear in the select list, because the rows being sorted are
no longer the rows you read.)

**`OFFSET` is a scan, not a seek.** The server produces every row you skip
and throws it away, so page 500 costs five hundred pages of work. It is fine
for the first few pages of a UI and wrong for a batch export; lesson 52
replaces it with keyset pagination.

## ex1 - category listing, priciest first

A warm-up that tests mixed directions across three keys where the SELECT list
order and the sort key order deliberately do not line up. The classic mistake
is assuming the two lists are the same and sorting by `id` second because it
is the second column. The model answer names the keys the prompt named. The
reference uses ordinal positions to make the mismatch visible - readable
here, fragile in a codebase.

## ex2 - the five highest paid

This tests the canonical top-N shape and the distinction between "the top
five" and "everyone above a threshold". The classic mistake is the threshold,
which produces four rows one week and nine the next. The model answer sorts
and limits. Interviewers ask the follow-up on purpose: with `LIMIT 5` a tie
at fifth place is broken arbitrarily unless you say how, which is what the
`id` key is for.

## ex3 - deciding where the NULL goes

This tests NULL placement and the fact that its default flips with the sort
direction. The classic mistake is assuming NULLs always sort last, which is
true for `ASC` and false for `DESC`, so reversing a report quietly moves the
NULL rows across it. The model answer states `NULLS LAST` explicitly. The
reference sorts on the boolean `manager_id IS NULL` first, which is the
portable trick for dialects without the modifier.

## ex4 - page three of the directory

This tests offset arithmetic - page N with size S skips `(N - 1) * S` rows -
and the tie-break that makes paging reproducible at all. The classic mistake
is an under-specified sort: with ties in `name` and no `id` key, the same row
can appear on both page two and page three, or on neither. The model answer
makes the order total first and pages second. Duplicate rows across pages are
almost always this bug.

## ex5 - the latest cancellations

This tests the interaction of `WHERE`, `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT`, and the
logical order in which they apply. The classic mistake is imagining `LIMIT`
runs first - "the ten newest orders, of which the cancelled ones" - which
would return anywhere from zero to ten rows. The model answer filters, then
orders, then limits. Reading the clauses as a pipeline in that sequence
settles most beginner confusion about what `LIMIT` sees.

## ex6 - sorting by a column you did not select

This tests that sort keys are independent of the select list, which surprises
people who think of `ORDER BY` as operating on the output. The classic
mistake is adding `price` to the SELECT list to "make it sortable" and
failing the gate on column count. The model answer sorts by a column it never
returns. One caveat for later: under `SELECT DISTINCT` or a `UNION` the sort
key *must* be in the select list, because the rows being ordered are no
longer the table's rows.

## ex7 - NULLs plus a second key

This tests attaching a NULL modifier to one key of several, and keeping the
remaining directions straight. The classic mistake is putting `NULLS LAST` at
the end of the whole list, where it modifies the tie-break instead of the
column that actually has NULLs. The model answer attaches it to
`manager_id`. Writing a modifier that matches the current default is not
noise: it is the only thing that keeps the report stable when the direction
changes.

## ex8 - deep into a three-key listing

The composite: a total three-key order with a direction change, consumed a
page at a time. This tests whether pagination and multi-key sorting can be
held in your head at once, which is exactly what a "give me the next page of
this report" ticket asks for. The classic mistake is an incomplete sort, so
rows shuffle between pages and the export gains duplicates. The model answer
makes the order total, then offsets.

## Further reading

- [Sorting Rows](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-order.html) - the ORDER BY clause including NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST and the defaults per direction.
- [LIMIT and OFFSET](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-limit.html) - why deep OFFSET is expensive and why LIMIT needs a deterministic order.
- [SELECT reference page](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) - the formal grammar: which expressions ORDER BY may name, and the DISTINCT restriction.
- [Use The Index, Luke - Paging Through Results](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/partial-results) - offset versus keyset pagination, with the plans that explain the difference.

# Reading - 61_drills_order_limit_2

Ordering again, at the edges: NULL placement, deep pagination, and sort keys
that never appear in the output.

## Notes

Three things this set drills that lesson 03 introduced and nobody practises
enough.

**NULL placement is a choice.** PostgreSQL's default is `NULLS LAST` for
ascending and `NULLS FIRST` for descending - which is consistent (NULL sorts
as if it were larger than everything) and is still not what most reports
want. `ORDER BY manager_id DESC NULLS LAST` overrides it. Because the default
flips with the direction, changing a sort from ascending to descending
silently moves your NULL rows from the bottom of the report to the top.

**A sort key does not have to be selected.** `ORDER BY price DESC` is legal
in a query that returns only `id` and `name`. That is genuinely useful, and
it is also the one place a reader of your output cannot check your work - so
say in the prompt, the ticket, or a comment what the rows are ordered by.
(The exception arrives with `SELECT DISTINCT` and set operations, where the
sort key *must* appear in the select list, because the rows being sorted are
no longer the rows you read.)

**`OFFSET` is a scan, not a seek.** The server produces every row you skip
and throws it away, so page 500 costs five hundred pages of work. It is fine
for the first few pages of a UI and wrong for a batch export; lesson 52
replaces it with keyset pagination.

## ex1 - category listing, priciest first

A warm-up that tests mixed directions across three keys where the SELECT list
order and the sort key order deliberately do not line up. The classic mistake
is assuming the two lists are the same and sorting by `id` second because it
is the second column. The model answer names the keys the prompt named. The
reference uses ordinal positions to make the mismatch visible - readable
here, fragile in a codebase.

## ex2 - the five highest paid

This tests the canonical top-N shape and the distinction between "the top
five" and "everyone above a threshold". The classic mistake is the threshold,
which produces four rows one week and nine the next. The model answer sorts
and limits. Interviewers ask the follow-up on purpose: with `LIMIT 5` a tie
at fifth place is broken arbitrarily unless you say how, which is what the
`id` key is for.

## ex3 - deciding where the NULL goes

This tests NULL placement and the fact that its default flips with the sort
direction. The classic mistake is assuming NULLs always sort last, which is
true for `ASC` and false for `DESC`, so reversing a report quietly moves the
NULL rows across it. The model answer states `NULLS LAST` explicitly. The
reference sorts on the boolean `manager_id IS NULL` first, which is the
portable trick for dialects without the modifier.

## ex4 - page three of the directory

This tests offset arithmetic - page N with size S skips `(N - 1) * S` rows -
and the tie-break that makes paging reproducible at all. The classic mistake
is an under-specified sort: with ties in `name` and no `id` key, the same row
can appear on both page two and page three, or on neither. The model answer
makes the order total first and pages second. Duplicate rows across pages are
almost always this bug.

## ex5 - the latest cancellations

This tests the interaction of `WHERE`, `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT`, and the
logical order in which they apply. The classic mistake is imagining `LIMIT`
runs first - "the ten newest orders, of which the cancelled ones" - which
would return anywhere from zero to ten rows. The model answer filters, then
orders, then limits. Reading the clauses as a pipeline in that sequence
settles most beginner confusion about what `LIMIT` sees.

## ex6 - sorting by a column you did not select

This tests that sort keys are independent of the select list, which surprises
people who think of `ORDER BY` as operating on the output. The classic
mistake is adding `price` to the SELECT list to "make it sortable" and
failing the gate on column count. The model answer sorts by a column it never
returns. One caveat for later: under `SELECT DISTINCT` or a `UNION` the sort
key *must* be in the select list, because the rows being ordered are no
longer the table's rows.

## ex7 - NULLs plus a second key

This tests attaching a NULL modifier to one key of several, and keeping the
remaining directions straight. The classic mistake is putting `NULLS LAST` at
the end of the whole list, where it modifies the tie-break instead of the
column that actually has NULLs. The model answer attaches it to
`manager_id`. Writing a modifier that matches the current default is not
noise: it is the only thing that keeps the report stable when the direction
changes.

## ex8 - deep into a three-key listing

The composite: a total three-key order with a direction change, consumed a
page at a time. This tests whether pagination and multi-key sorting can be
held in your head at once, which is exactly what a "give me the next page of
this report" ticket asks for. The classic mistake is an incomplete sort, so
rows shuffle between pages and the export gains duplicates. The model answer
makes the order total, then offsets.

## Further reading

- [Sorting Rows](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-order.html) - the ORDER BY clause including NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST and the defaults per direction.
- [LIMIT and OFFSET](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-limit.html) - why deep OFFSET is expensive and why LIMIT needs a deterministic order.
- [SELECT reference page](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) - the formal grammar: which expressions ORDER BY may name, and the DISTINCT restriction.
- [Use The Index, Luke - Paging Through Results](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/partial-results) - offset versus keyset pagination, with the plans that explain the difference.
