exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Three keys, and the NULL modifier belongs to the first one only.

## Hint 2
`NULLS LAST` is already the default for `ASC` here, so the modifier
changes nothing today. Write it anyway: it documents the intent, and it
survives someone flipping the direction later.

## Hint 3
Assemble it left to right and check after each key. Sort by `manager_id`
alone and confirm the NULL row is last; add `salary DESC` and confirm the
pay now falls inside each manager's block; add `id`. If the twenty rows
change between two identical runs, a tie-break is missing.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT s.id, s.name, s.manager_id, s.salary
FROM staff AS s
ORDER BY (s.manager_id IS NULL) ASC, s.manager_id ASC, s.salary DESC, s.id ASC
LIMIT 20;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, name, manager_id, salary
FROM staff
ORDER BY manager_id ASC NULLS LAST, salary DESC, id ASC
LIMIT 20;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 - deep into a three-key listing

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. The lifecycle team reads customers country by
country alphabetically, newest signups first inside each country, and has
already worked through the first hundred rows. Return the next twenty-five.
Four columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `country`, `created_at`.

**Ordered by `country` ascending, then `created_at` descending, then `id`
ascending; skip 100 rows and return 25.**

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Everything in this problem has appeared already: three keys with mixed
directions, plus an offset and a limit.

## Hint 2
Get the ordering right with no `OFFSET` at all and eyeball the first few
rows; only then add the paging. Debugging a sort through a hundred skipped
rows is needlessly hard.

## Hint 3
The skipped rows are still produced and discarded by the server, so this
query does about as much work as returning 125 rows. That is fine at 100 and
is the reason batch exports use a key range instead of an offset.

# 62 - Drills: numbers, rounding, and casts

Eight problems on the numeric half of lesson 04: `round` with a positive and
a negative scale, `trunc`, `floor`, `ceil`, casts, and the division that
throws the remainder away. Redo 04's concept section if the second argument
of `round` is unfamiliar.

## Exercise 1 - to the nearest dollar

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. The shelf-edge labels have no room for cents. Return
three columns, in this order: `id`, `price`, and `price` rounded to the
nearest whole number. Every product, any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 62_drills_expressions_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - monthly pay, to the cent

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. The offer letters quote a monthly figure to two
decimal places. Return three columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, and
`salary / 12` rounded to **2** decimal places. All staff, any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 62_drills_expressions_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - rounding left of the point

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. A price-distribution chart needs two coarser views
of every price. Return four columns, in this order: `id`, `price`, `price`
rounded to the nearest **ten**, and `price` rounded to the nearest
**hundred**. Every product, any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 62_drills_expressions_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - cutting versus casting

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Two different exporters disagree about how to drop
the cents, and pricing wants both answers side by side. Return four columns,
in this order: `id`, `price`, `trunc(price)`, and `price::int`. Every
product, any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 62_drills_expressions_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - down and up

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Warehouse packing needs the dollar floor and the
dollar ceiling of every price. Return four columns, in this order: `id`,
`price`, `floor(price)`, and `ceil(price)`. Every product, any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 62_drills_expressions_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - how far from the band

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Compensation bands are thousands of dollars wide,
and HR wants to see how far each salary sits from its band. Return four
columns, in this order: `id`, `salary`, `salary` rounded to the nearest
**thousand**, and the difference `salary - round(salary, -3)`. That
difference is negative for anyone below their band's midpoint - leave it
negative. All staff, any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 62_drills_expressions_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - rounded and raw, side by side

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. A twenty-percent-off sale is being reviewed and
finance wants to see what rounding actually changes. Return four columns, in
this order: `id`, `price`, `round(price * 0.8, 2)`, and the unrounded
`price * 0.8`. Write both expressions exactly as given. Every product, any
row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 62_drills_expressions_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - three ways to divide by three

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. A three-for-the-price-of-one calculator produced
different numbers in three services, and the whole point of this exercise is
to see why. Return five columns, in this order: `id`, `price`, `price::int`,
`price::int / 3`, and `round(price / 3, 2)`. Write each expression exactly as
given. Every product, any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 62_drills_expressions_1 ex8`

# Reading - 62_drills_expressions_1

Numeric expressions, drilled. Each of these is one function call wide; the
difficulty is knowing exactly which rounding rule you just applied.

## Notes

Four functions do almost all of the work here and they are not
interchangeable. **`round(x)`** goes to the nearest integer, with halves away
from zero on `numeric`. **`trunc(x)`** cuts the fractional part off, which is
the same as `floor` for positive numbers and the opposite of it for negative
ones. **`floor(x)`** goes down, **`ceil(x)`** goes up, both regardless of
sign. Confusing `trunc` with `floor` costs nothing on a price list and
everything on a ledger that contains refunds.

**`round(x, n)` takes a second argument**, and it may be negative. `round(x,
2)` gives cents; `round(x, -3)` rounds to the nearest thousand. The negative
form is the one people never learn and then reimplement badly as `round(x /
1000) * 1000`.

**A cast is not a truncation.** `price::int` rounds to nearest - it does not
chop - which surprises everyone arriving from C or Java. And once a value has
become an `integer`, `/` becomes integer division: `290::int / 3` is `96`,
not `96.8`. That single conversion is behind most "the percentages are all
zero" reports.

## ex1 - to the nearest dollar

The baseline: rounding to the nearest integer, so the later problems have
something to contrast with. The classic mistake is reaching for a cast or for
`trunc`, both of which look right on a sample of cheap products and diverge
on anything ending above .50. The model answer calls `round` with no second
argument. `round(x, 0)` is the same call written explicitly, which is worth
seeing before ex3 makes the second argument do real work.

## ex2 - monthly pay, to the cent

This tests the two-argument form of `round` and the order of operations
around it. The classic mistake is rounding the input instead of the output,
which both fails to shorten the result and quietly changes it. The model
answer divides, then rounds once. Rounding once at the end is the general
rule: every intermediate rounding is an error you have chosen to introduce
and then propagate.

## ex3 - rounding left of the point

This tests the negative-scale form of `round`, which most people never meet
and then reimplement as `round(x / 100) * 100`. The classic mistake is
assuming a negative argument truncates - it does not, it still rounds to
nearest, which is why a 54.46 product lands on 100 and not on 0. The model
answer passes `-1` and `-2` directly. Histogram buckets usually want `floor`
semantics instead; know which you asked for.

## ex4 - cutting versus casting

This tests the difference between truncation and a rounding cast, and it is
the single most useful fact in this lesson. The classic mistake is assuming
`::int` chops like C's `(int)` does, so an exporter that "drops the cents"
silently rounds half the catalog upwards. The model answer returns both so
the divergence is visible per row. The reference substitutes `floor`, which
equals `trunc` here only because every price is positive.

## ex5 - down and up

This tests directional rounding, the pair you want whenever a business rule
says "always round up" (shipping units) or "always round down" (loyalty
points). The classic mistake is using `round` for either, which is right on
average and wrong on every individual row that matters. The model answer
calls each function directly; `ceiling` in the reference is a documented
alias for `ceil`, and `trunc` matches `floor` here because prices are
positive.

## ex6 - how far from the band

This tests composing an expression out of one you have already written, and
the discipline of not tidying away a sign. The classic mistake is `abs`,
which destroys exactly the fact HR is looking for. The model answer subtracts
the rounded band from the raw salary. Note that `round` to the nearest
thousand can move a value in either direction, which is why roughly half the
drifts come back negative.

## ex7 - rounded and raw, side by side

This tests where the precision in a `numeric` calculation actually goes, and
it is the reason a discount total computed per line can differ by cents from
one computed on the invoice. The classic mistake is assuming the two columns
must be identical because "money has two decimals" - the type does not
enforce that, the multiplication grows the scale, and only `round` shortens
it. The model answer shows both so the third digit is visible.

## ex8 - three ways to divide by three

The composite, and a fair interview question: it combines the rounding cast
from ex4 with integer division and with a `numeric` division rounded at the
end. This tests whether you can predict the type of every intermediate value,
because each type change silently rewrites the arithmetic. The classic
mistake is casting early "to keep it tidy" and losing both the fraction and
the remainder. The model answer computes each column exactly as specified so
the three answers can be compared row by row.

## Further reading

- [Mathematical Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-math.html) - round, trunc, floor, ceil and the exact rounding rule each one applies.
- [Numeric Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-numeric.html) - why `numeric` is exact, what scale a division produces, and when integer division bites.
- [Type Conversion](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/typeconv.html) - how PostgreSQL resolves the types in a mixed expression before evaluating it.
- [CREATE CAST / cast syntax](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createcast.html) - the machinery behind `::`, and a reminder that numeric-to-integer casts round.

# Reading - 62_drills_expressions_1

Numeric expressions, drilled. Each of these is one function call wide; the
difficulty is knowing exactly which rounding rule you just applied.

## Notes

Four functions do almost all of the work here and they are not
interchangeable. **`round(x)`** goes to the nearest integer, with halves away
from zero on `numeric`. **`trunc(x)`** cuts the fractional part off, which is
the same as `floor` for positive numbers and the opposite of it for negative
ones. **`floor(x)`** goes down, **`ceil(x)`** goes up, both regardless of
sign. Confusing `trunc` with `floor` costs nothing on a price list and
everything on a ledger that contains refunds.

**`round(x, n)` takes a second argument**, and it may be negative. `round(x,
2)` gives cents; `round(x, -3)` rounds to the nearest thousand. The negative
form is the one people never learn and then reimplement badly as `round(x /
1000) * 1000`.

**A cast is not a truncation.** `price::int` rounds to nearest - it does not
chop - which surprises everyone arriving from C or Java. And once a value has
become an `integer`, `/` becomes integer division: `290::int / 3` is `96`,
not `96.8`. That single conversion is behind most "the percentages are all
zero" reports.

## ex1 - to the nearest dollar

The baseline: rounding to the nearest integer, so the later problems have
something to contrast with. The classic mistake is reaching for a cast or for
`trunc`, both of which look right on a sample of cheap products and diverge
on anything ending above .50. The model answer calls `round` with no second
argument. `round(x, 0)` is the same call written explicitly, which is worth
seeing before ex3 makes the second argument do real work.

## ex2 - monthly pay, to the cent

This tests the two-argument form of `round` and the order of operations
around it. The classic mistake is rounding the input instead of the output,
which both fails to shorten the result and quietly changes it. The model
answer divides, then rounds once. Rounding once at the end is the general
rule: every intermediate rounding is an error you have chosen to introduce
and then propagate.

## ex3 - rounding left of the point

This tests the negative-scale form of `round`, which most people never meet
and then reimplement as `round(x / 100) * 100`. The classic mistake is
assuming a negative argument truncates - it does not, it still rounds to
nearest, which is why a 54.46 product lands on 100 and not on 0. The model
answer passes `-1` and `-2` directly. Histogram buckets usually want `floor`
semantics instead; know which you asked for.

## ex4 - cutting versus casting

This tests the difference between truncation and a rounding cast, and it is
the single most useful fact in this lesson. The classic mistake is assuming
`::int` chops like C's `(int)` does, so an exporter that "drops the cents"
silently rounds half the catalog upwards. The model answer returns both so
the divergence is visible per row. The reference substitutes `floor`, which
equals `trunc` here only because every price is positive.

## ex5 - down and up

This tests directional rounding, the pair you want whenever a business rule
says "always round up" (shipping units) or "always round down" (loyalty
points). The classic mistake is using `round` for either, which is right on
average and wrong on every individual row that matters. The model answer
calls each function directly; `ceiling` in the reference is a documented
alias for `ceil`, and `trunc` matches `floor` here because prices are
positive.

## ex6 - how far from the band

This tests composing an expression out of one you have already written, and
the discipline of not tidying away a sign. The classic mistake is `abs`,
which destroys exactly the fact HR is looking for. The model answer subtracts
the rounded band from the raw salary. Note that `round` to the nearest
thousand can move a value in either direction, which is why roughly half the
drifts come back negative.

## ex7 - rounded and raw, side by side

This tests where the precision in a `numeric` calculation actually goes, and
it is the reason a discount total computed per line can differ by cents from
one computed on the invoice. The classic mistake is assuming the two columns
must be identical because "money has two decimals" - the type does not
enforce that, the multiplication grows the scale, and only `round` shortens
it. The model answer shows both so the third digit is visible.

## ex8 - three ways to divide by three

The composite, and a fair interview question: it combines the rounding cast
from ex4 with integer division and with a `numeric` division rounded at the
end. This tests whether you can predict the type of every intermediate value,
because each type change silently rewrites the arithmetic. The classic
mistake is casting early "to keep it tidy" and losing both the fraction and
the remainder. The model answer computes each column exactly as specified so
the three answers can be compared row by row.

## Further reading

- [Mathematical Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-math.html) - round, trunc, floor, ceil and the exact rounding rule each one applies.
- [Numeric Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-numeric.html) - why `numeric` is exact, what scale a division produces, and when integer division bites.
- [Type Conversion](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/typeconv.html) - how PostgreSQL resolves the types in a mixed expression before evaluating it.
- [CREATE CAST / cast syntax](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-createcast.html) - the machinery behind `::`, and a reminder that numeric-to-integer casts round.

`numeric` multiplication adds the scales of its operands, so a
two-decimal price times a one-decimal factor gives a three-decimal result -
the third digit is what column four shows you and column three removes.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 - three ways to divide by three

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. A three-for-the-price-of-one calculator produced
different numbers in three services, and the whole point of this exercise is
to see why. Return five columns, in this order: `id`, `price`, `price::int`,
`price::int / 3`, and `round(price / 3, 2)`. Write each expression exactly as
given. Every product, any row order.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Column three converts the price to an `integer`. Ask yourself what that
makes the `/` in column four.

## Hint 2
`integer / integer` is integer division in SQL: the remainder is
discarded and no warning is issued. Column five divides the original
`numeric` instead, so it keeps its decimals until `round` shortens them.

## Hint 3
Three separate rules are stacked here and each one changes the answer:
the cast rounds rather than truncates, the division that follows it drops
the remainder, and the `numeric` division does neither. Get columns one to
three running, then add four and five one at a time and read every value on
a single row before moving on.

# Reading - 63_drills_expressions_2

Text expressions, drilled on data with real structure: names that follow a
template, emails built from an id, product names that carry their own key.

## Notes

The functions in this set divide into three jobs. **Case folding** (`lower`,
`upper`) normalises text so comparisons and slugs behave; it is also
locale-dependent, which is why "the same string in upper case" is a harder
question in Turkish than the ASCII intuition suggests. **Extraction**
(`left`, `right`, `substring`, `split_part`) pulls a piece out; `split_part`
is the one worth memorising, because it takes a delimiter and a
one-based index and returns the empty string rather than NULL when the part
does not exist. **Assembly** (`||`, `concat`, `lpad`) puts the pieces back
together.

Two traps recur. The first is **NULL propagation through `||`**: if any
operand is NULL the whole concatenation is NULL, silently blanking a row that
looked fine in testing. `concat()` differs - it treats NULL as an empty
string - and `coalesce` is how you choose deliberately rather than by
accident.

The second is **`coalesce` and types**. Every argument must be reconcilable
to one type, so `coalesce(manager_id, 'ROOT')` fails: an `integer` and a text
literal have no common type. Casting the column first - `coalesce(manager_id
::text, 'ROOT')` - is the fix, and it forces you to decide what the column
means once it leaves the database.

## ex1 - case folding

The baseline, and the expression a case-insensitive index would be built on
(lesson 40). The classic mistake is confusing case folding with
case-insensitive *comparison*: `lower(name)` changes the data you return,
while `ILIKE` changes how a comparison behaves and leaves the data alone. The
model answer folds the column. Worth remembering that case folding follows
the database collation, so it is not a pure ASCII operation.

## ex2 - a placeholder for the missing manager

This tests `coalesce` together with the type-unification rule that governs
every conditional expression in SQL. The classic mistake is supplying a text
fallback for an integer column and reading the resulting error as a bug in
`coalesce`. The model answer casts the column to `text` before offering the
literal. Doing the cast explicitly is also a design moment: you have just
decided how this column is represented once it leaves the database.

## ex3 - both ends of a string

This tests the two fixed-width extractors and their symmetry. The classic
mistake is reaching for `substring` with hand-computed offsets for the tail,
which is where an off-by-one lives; `right(name, 4)` has no arithmetic to get
wrong. The model answer uses `left` and `right`. The reference does it the
hard way with `substring` and `length` so you can see the offset arithmetic
that `right` is saving you.

## ex4 - splitting a name

This tests `split_part` and its one-based index, and it deliberately runs
against names that do not all have exactly two parts. The classic mistake is
treating field 1 and field 2 as "first name" and "surname" and building a
product feature on it - a title, a middle name or a suffix breaks that
assumption immediately. The model answer returns the split as it is. Naive
name parsing is a genuine source of production embarrassment.

## ex5 - a URL slug

This tests function composition, the first two-step expression in the set.
The classic mistake is arguing the argument order of `replace` - the string
comes first, then what to find, then what to put there - and quietly
producing a slug with the hyphens and spaces swapped. The model answer folds
the case and then replaces. Real slug generation also has to strip
punctuation and collapse runs of separators, which is where regular
expressions earn their place.

## ex6 - pulling the id back out of an email

This tests chaining two extractions, which is what parsing structured text
actually looks like. The classic mistake is running `replace(email, 'user',
'')` over the whole address instead of the local part, which happens to work
on this domain and breaks the moment a domain contains those four letters.
The model answer isolates the local part first and only then strips the
prefix: narrow the string before you edit it.

## ex7 - a corporate email address

This tests assembling four pieces into one string, which is the everyday
shape of display-text work. The classic mistake is a missing or doubled
separator - the result is a valid string, so nothing complains and only
reading the output catches it. The model answer folds each part before
joining. Note the reference's `concat`, which takes any number of arguments
and, unlike `||`, treats a NULL argument as an empty string.

## ex8 - the warehouse SKU

The composite: case folding, fixed-width extraction, a cast, zero padding and
two separators in one expression. This tests whether you can hold a format
specification in your head and reproduce it exactly, which is the whole job
when a downstream system parses your output by position. The classic mistake
is padding before the cast, or padding to the wrong width. The model answer
builds each field independently and joins them last.

## Further reading

- [String Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-string.html) - the whole toolbox: `||`, `concat`, `left`, `right`, `split_part`, `replace`, `lpad`.
- [Conditional Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-conditional.html) - `coalesce`, `nullif` and `greatest`, and the type-unification rule that governs them.
- [Type Conversion](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/typeconv.html) - how PostgreSQL picks a common type for the arms of a conditional expression.
- [Character Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-character.html) - why `text` is the sensible default and what `char(n)` padding would do to these results.

that string handling has no type checker: a missing separator produces a
perfectly valid string that is wrong, so the only defence is looking at the
output.

# Reading - 63_drills_expressions_2

Text expressions, drilled on data with real structure: names that follow a
template, emails built from an id, product names that carry their own key.

## Notes

The functions in this set divide into three jobs. **Case folding** (`lower`,
`upper`) normalises text so comparisons and slugs behave; it is also
locale-dependent, which is why "the same string in upper case" is a harder
question in Turkish than the ASCII intuition suggests. **Extraction**
(`left`, `right`, `substring`, `split_part`) pulls a piece out; `split_part`
is the one worth memorising, because it takes a delimiter and a
one-based index and returns the empty string rather than NULL when the part
does not exist. **Assembly** (`||`, `concat`, `lpad`) puts the pieces back
together.

Two traps recur. The first is **NULL propagation through `||`**: if any
operand is NULL the whole concatenation is NULL, silently blanking a row that
looked fine in testing. `concat()` differs - it treats NULL as an empty
string - and `coalesce` is how you choose deliberately rather than by
accident.

The second is **`coalesce` and types**. Every argument must be reconcilable
to one type, so `coalesce(manager_id, 'ROOT')` fails: an `integer` and a text
literal have no common type. Casting the column first - `coalesce(manager_id
::text, 'ROOT')` - is the fix, and it forces you to decide what the column
means once it leaves the database.

## ex1 - case folding

The baseline, and the expression a case-insensitive index would be built on
(lesson 40). The classic mistake is confusing case folding with
case-insensitive *comparison*: `lower(name)` changes the data you return,
while `ILIKE` changes how a comparison behaves and leaves the data alone. The
model answer folds the column. Worth remembering that case folding follows
the database collation, so it is not a pure ASCII operation.

## ex2 - a placeholder for the missing manager

This tests `coalesce` together with the type-unification rule that governs
every conditional expression in SQL. The classic mistake is supplying a text
fallback for an integer column and reading the resulting error as a bug in
`coalesce`. The model answer casts the column to `text` before offering the
literal. Doing the cast explicitly is also a design moment: you have just
decided how this column is represented once it leaves the database.

## ex3 - both ends of a string

This tests the two fixed-width extractors and their symmetry. The classic
mistake is reaching for `substring` with hand-computed offsets for the tail,
which is where an off-by-one lives; `right(name, 4)` has no arithmetic to get
wrong. The model answer uses `left` and `right`. The reference does it the
hard way with `substring` and `length` so you can see the offset arithmetic
that `right` is saving you.

## ex4 - splitting a name

This tests `split_part` and its one-based index, and it deliberately runs
against names that do not all have exactly two parts. The classic mistake is
treating field 1 and field 2 as "first name" and "surname" and building a
product feature on it - a title, a middle name or a suffix breaks that
assumption immediately. The model answer returns the split as it is. Naive
name parsing is a genuine source of production embarrassment.

## ex5 - a URL slug

This tests function composition, the first two-step expression in the set.
The classic mistake is arguing the argument order of `replace` - the string
comes first, then what to find, then what to put there - and quietly
producing a slug with the hyphens and spaces swapped. The model answer folds
the case and then replaces. Real slug generation also has to strip
punctuation and collapse runs of separators, which is where regular
expressions earn their place.

## ex6 - pulling the id back out of an email

This tests chaining two extractions, which is what parsing structured text
actually looks like. The classic mistake is running `replace(email, 'user',
'')` over the whole address instead of the local part, which happens to work
on this domain and breaks the moment a domain contains those four letters.
The model answer isolates the local part first and only then strips the
prefix: narrow the string before you edit it.

## ex7 - a corporate email address

This tests assembling four pieces into one string, which is the everyday
shape of display-text work. The classic mistake is a missing or doubled
separator - the result is a valid string, so nothing complains and only
reading the output catches it. The model answer folds each part before
joining. Note the reference's `concat`, which takes any number of arguments
and, unlike `||`, treats a NULL argument as an empty string.

## ex8 - the warehouse SKU

The composite: case folding, fixed-width extraction, a cast, zero padding and
two separators in one expression. This tests whether you can hold a format
specification in your head and reproduce it exactly, which is the whole job
when a downstream system parses your output by position. The classic mistake
is padding before the cast, or padding to the wrong width. The model answer
builds each field independently and joins them last.

## Further reading

- [String Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-string.html) - the whole toolbox: `||`, `concat`, `left`, `right`, `split_part`, `replace`, `lpad`.
- [Conditional Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-conditional.html) - `coalesce`, `nullif` and `greatest`, and the type-unification rule that governs them.
- [Type Conversion](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/typeconv.html) - how PostgreSQL picks a common type for the arms of a conditional expression.
- [Character Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-character.html) - why `text` is the sensible default and what `char(n)` padding would do to these results.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
`split_part(string, delimiter, n)` returns the nth field. The index is
one-based, not zero-based.

## Hint 2
The delimiter is a single space in quotes. If every second column comes
back empty you probably passed `0` as the index, or split on the wrong
character.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT q.id, q.name, q.part1, q.part2
FROM (
  SELECT s.id, s.name,
         split_part(s.name, ' ', 1) AS part1,
         split_part(s.name, ' ', 2) AS part2
  FROM staff AS s
) AS q;
references.expected.sql: SELECT id, name, split_part(name, ' ', 1), split_part(name, ' ', 2) FROM staff;

## Hint 1
Three ideas you have already used: split the name, fold the case, glue
the pieces with `||`.

## Hint 2
The two literal pieces are `'.'` and `'@corp.example'`. Every operand of
`||` must be text - all of these already are, so no cast is needed here.

## Hint 3
Build it outwards from the middle. Get the two `split_part` calls
returning the right words, wrap each in `lower`, then add the separator, and
only then the domain. Checking the output at each step costs one run and
saves you from hunting a missing dot in a finished expression.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT q.id, q.name,
       concat(lower(q.p1), '.', lower(q.p2), '@corp.example') AS work_email
FROM (
  SELECT s.id, s.name,
         split_part(s.name, ' ', 1) AS p1,
         split_part(s.name, ' ', 2) AS p2
  FROM staff AS s
) AS q;

references.solution.sql:
SELECT q.id,
       concat(q.cat3, '-', q.padded, '-', q.slug) AS sku
FROM (
  SELECT p.id,
         upper(left(p.category, 3))            AS cat3,
         lpad(cast(p.id AS text), 6, '0')      AS padded,
         replace(lower(p.name), ' ', '_')      AS slug
  FROM products AS p
) AS q;

lessons.briefing:
# 64 - Drills: CASE

Eight problems on lesson 04's workhorse: `CASE`, SQL's per-row if/else.
Branch order, the missing `ELSE`, both syntactic forms, and what happens when
one `CASE` lives inside another. Redo 04's concept section if "stops at the
first true WHEN" is not already reflex.

## Exercise 1 - two branches

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Merchandising splits the catalog in two: a product
priced at 400 or more is `premium`, everything else is `standard`. Return
three columns, in this order: `id`, `price`, and the label. Every product,
any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 64_drills_case_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - the simple form

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Facilities splits staff by desk type: `sales` and
`support` are `field`, everyone else is `office`. Write it with the **simple**
`CASE` form - `CASE department WHEN ... THEN ... END` - rather than the
searched form. Return three columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, and the
desk type. All staff, any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 64_drills_case_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - no ELSE on purpose

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. The content team only has editorial groupings for
two categories: `books` are `media` and `electronics` are `tech`. Every other
category must come back as **NULL** - do not invent a label for it, and do
not write an `ELSE`.

Return three columns, in this order: `id`, `category`, and the grouping.
Every product, any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 64_drills_case_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - branch order decides everything

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Compensation bands, checked from the top down: over
100000 is `senior`, over 60000 is `mid`, anything else is `junior`. Both
thresholds are strict. Return three columns, in this order: `id`, `salary`,
and the band. All staff, any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 64_drills_case_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - a CASE that returns a number

# Reading - 64_drills_case_1

Conditional expressions, drilled. `CASE` is easy to write and easy to get
subtly wrong, and every problem here targets one of the specific ways.

## Notes

`CASE` comes in two forms. The **searched** form takes a full condition per
branch - `CASE WHEN price < 50 THEN ... END` - and is what you want almost
always. The **simple** form compares one expression against a list of
values, as in `CASE department WHEN 'sales' THEN ... END`; it reads
beautifully for an enumeration and cannot express a range or a compound test
at all.

Three rules govern the rest. **Evaluation stops at the first true branch**,
so a ladder is implicitly nested: the second `WHEN` already knows the first
was false, which is why `WHEN price < 50` followed by `WHEN price < 200`
means "50 up to 200" without you writing the lower bound. Reverse those two
branches and the second becomes unreachable - the query still runs, and every
mid-priced product is silently labelled as budget.

**Without an `ELSE`, unmatched rows get NULL.** Not an error, not a default
string - NULL, which then propagates through any `||` it meets and disappears
from any `= 'x'` comparison downstream. Omit the `ELSE` when you mean NULL,
and write it when you do not.

**All branches must share one type.** The `THEN` values and the `ELSE` are
unified into a single result type by the same rules that govern `coalesce`,
so a ladder mixing `'unknown'` with a numeric price will not compile until
you decide which one it is.

## ex1 - two branches

The baseline: a two-branch conditional with an explicit `ELSE`, so every row
gets a label. This tests the syntax and the boundary at once. The classic
mistake is forgetting `END`, which produces a syntax error pointing at the
wrong place. The model answer covers both cases explicitly. The reference
inverts the condition and swaps the arms, which is the same rule written from
the other side - both are fine, and neither leaves a row unlabelled.

## ex2 - the simple form

This tests the simple `CASE` form, which reads well for an enumeration and is
worth recognising in other people's SQL. The classic mistake is mixing the
two forms - writing `CASE department WHEN department = 'sales'`, which
compares the department to a boolean and fails. The model answer keeps the
expression in the header and bare values in the branches. The reference shows
the searched form with `IN`, which is what you would usually write once more
than two values are involved.

## ex3 - no ELSE on purpose

This tests the default behaviour of an unmatched `CASE`, which is the source
of an entire family of production bugs. The classic mistake is the opposite
one: omitting `ELSE` by accident in a ladder that was supposed to be
exhaustive, so unclassified rows silently become NULL and then vanish from
every downstream `WHERE label = 'x'`. The model answer omits `ELSE`
deliberately, which is the only reason it is correct.

## ex4 - branch order decides everything

This tests first-match evaluation, the property that makes ladders concise
and makes a misordered ladder silently wrong. The classic mistake is sorting
the branches from lowest threshold upwards, which makes every branch after
the first unreachable without any warning at all. The model answer descends.
The reference ascends with the comparisons flipped, which is the same rule
written the other way round - and shows that only the *combination* of order
and operator is correct or not.

## ex5 - a CASE that returns a number

This tests a `CASE` used as a value rather than a label, and the type
unification across its arms. The classic mistake is treating `CASE` as a
statement and trying to "do nothing" in the else branch - there is no doing
nothing in an expression, so the untouched rows must explicitly return
`price`. The model answer supplies both arms as numeric expressions.
Conditional pricing like this is exactly what lesson 17 generalises into
pivots.

## ex6 - a CASE over a NULL

This tests `IS NULL` inside a `CASE` and the cast that concatenation demands.
The classic mistake is `WHEN manager_id = NULL`, which is never true, so the
CEO falls through to the `ELSE`, concatenates against a NULL, and comes back
as NULL rather than as `CEO`. The model answer tests with `IS NULL`. The
reference exploits that same NULL propagation deliberately - the
concatenation is NULL exactly for the CEO, so `coalesce` supplies the label.

## ex7 - two ladders in one row

This tests holding two independent conditional rules in one select list, and
choosing the right `CASE` shape for each: a threshold ladder for the numeric
one, an enumeration for the categorical one. The classic mistake is a missing
`END`, which makes the parser blame the next column entirely. The model
answer keeps the two expressions separate and complete. Reaching for a
five-branch ladder where a lookup table belongs is a design question worth
asking in real work.

## ex8 - a CASE inside a CASE

The hard version: a two-dimensional rule expressed as a conditional. This
tests whether you can see that a nested `CASE` and a flat four-branch ladder
are the same rule, and that the flat form's correctness depends entirely on
branch order. The classic mistake in the flat form is putting the
category-only branch first, which makes the expensive-electronics branch
unreachable. The model answer nests, so each dimension is handled where it
belongs and no ordering is load-bearing.

## Further reading

- [Conditional Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-conditional.html) - the definitive description of both CASE forms, plus COALESCE, NULLIF and GREATEST.
- [Type Conversion - UNION, CASE and Related Constructs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/typeconv-union-case.html) - the exact rule for unifying the types of every CASE branch.
- [Expression Evaluation Rules](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html#SYNTAX-EXPRESS-EVAL) - why CASE is one of the few places where PostgreSQL guarantees evaluation order.
- [Comparison Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html) - what each WHEN condition returns when its input is NULL, and why that is not a true branch.

# Reading - 64_drills_case_1

Conditional expressions, drilled. `CASE` is easy to write and easy to get
subtly wrong, and every problem here targets one of the specific ways.

## Notes

`CASE` comes in two forms. The **searched** form takes a full condition per
branch - `CASE WHEN price < 50 THEN ... END` - and is what you want almost
always. The **simple** form compares one expression against a list of
values, as in `CASE department WHEN 'sales' THEN ... END`; it reads
beautifully for an enumeration and cannot express a range or a compound test
at all.

Three rules govern the rest. **Evaluation stops at the first true branch**,
so a ladder is implicitly nested: the second `WHEN` already knows the first
was false, which is why `WHEN price < 50` followed by `WHEN price < 200`
means "50 up to 200" without you writing the lower bound. Reverse those two
branches and the second becomes unreachable - the query still runs, and every
mid-priced product is silently labelled as budget.

**Without an `ELSE`, unmatched rows get NULL.** Not an error, not a default
string - NULL, which then propagates through any `||` it meets and disappears
from any `= 'x'` comparison downstream. Omit the `ELSE` when you mean NULL,
and write it when you do not.

**All branches must share one type.** The `THEN` values and the `ELSE` are
unified into a single result type by the same rules that govern `coalesce`,
so a ladder mixing `'unknown'` with a numeric price will not compile until
you decide which one it is.

## ex1 - two branches

The baseline: a two-branch conditional with an explicit `ELSE`, so every row
gets a label. This tests the syntax and the boundary at once. The classic
mistake is forgetting `END`, which produces a syntax error pointing at the
wrong place. The model answer covers both cases explicitly. The reference
inverts the condition and swaps the arms, which is the same rule written from
the other side - both are fine, and neither leaves a row unlabelled.

## ex2 - the simple form

This tests the simple `CASE` form, which reads well for an enumeration and is
worth recognising in other people's SQL. The classic mistake is mixing the
two forms - writing `CASE department WHEN department = 'sales'`, which
compares the department to a boolean and fails. The model answer keeps the
expression in the header and bare values in the branches. The reference shows
the searched form with `IN`, which is what you would usually write once more
than two values are involved.

## ex3 - no ELSE on purpose

This tests the default behaviour of an unmatched `CASE`, which is the source
of an entire family of production bugs. The classic mistake is the opposite
one: omitting `ELSE` by accident in a ladder that was supposed to be
exhaustive, so unclassified rows silently become NULL and then vanish from
every downstream `WHERE label = 'x'`. The model answer omits `ELSE`
deliberately, which is the only reason it is correct.

## ex4 - branch order decides everything

This tests first-match evaluation, the property that makes ladders concise
and makes a misordered ladder silently wrong. The classic mistake is sorting
the branches from lowest threshold upwards, which makes every branch after
the first unreachable without any warning at all. The model answer descends.
The reference ascends with the comparisons flipped, which is the same rule
written the other way round - and shows that only the *combination* of order
and operator is correct or not.

## ex5 - a CASE that returns a number

This tests a `CASE` used as a value rather than a label, and the type
unification across its arms. The classic mistake is treating `CASE` as a
statement and trying to "do nothing" in the else branch - there is no doing
nothing in an expression, so the untouched rows must explicitly return
`price`. The model answer supplies both arms as numeric expressions.
Conditional pricing like this is exactly what lesson 17 generalises into
pivots.

## ex6 - a CASE over a NULL

This tests `IS NULL` inside a `CASE` and the cast that concatenation demands.
The classic mistake is `WHEN manager_id = NULL`, which is never true, so the
CEO falls through to the `ELSE`, concatenates against a NULL, and comes back
as NULL rather than as `CEO`. The model answer tests with `IS NULL`. The
reference exploits that same NULL propagation deliberately - the
concatenation is NULL exactly for the CEO, so `coalesce` supplies the label.

## ex7 - two ladders in one row

This tests holding two independent conditional rules in one select list, and
choosing the right `CASE` shape for each: a threshold ladder for the numeric
one, an enumeration for the categorical one. The classic mistake is a missing
`END`, which makes the parser blame the next column entirely. The model
answer keeps the two expressions separate and complete. Reaching for a
five-branch ladder where a lookup table belongs is a design question worth
asking in real work.

## ex8 - a CASE inside a CASE

The hard version: a two-dimensional rule expressed as a conditional. This
tests whether you can see that a nested `CASE` and a flat four-branch ladder
are the same rule, and that the flat form's correctness depends entirely on
branch order. The classic mistake in the flat form is putting the
category-only branch first, which makes the expensive-electronics branch
unreachable. The model answer nests, so each dimension is handled where it
belongs and no ordering is load-bearing.

## Further reading

- [Conditional Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-conditional.html) - the definitive description of both CASE forms, plus COALESCE, NULLIF and GREATEST.
- [Type Conversion - UNION, CASE and Related Constructs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/typeconv-union-case.html) - the exact rule for unifying the types of every CASE branch.
- [Expression Evaluation Rules](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html#SYNTAX-EXPRESS-EVAL) - why CASE is one of the few places where PostgreSQL guarantees evaluation order.
- [Comparison Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html) - what each WHEN condition returns when its input is NULL, and why that is not a true branch.

CASE WHEN <condition> THEN 'premium' ELSE 'standard' END

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Evaluation stops at the first true branch, so the second `WHEN` already
knows the first was false. You do not need to write the upper bound.

## Hint 2
Put the branches in the order the prompt gives them. If you test
`> 60000` first, nobody can ever reach `senior` - the query still runs and
everybody senior is labelled `mid`.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT s.id, s.salary,
       CASE WHEN s.salary <= 60000 THEN 'junior'
            WHEN s.salary <= 100000 THEN 'mid'
            ELSE 'senior'
       END AS band
FROM staff AS s;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, salary,
       CASE WHEN salary > 100000 THEN 'senior'
            WHEN salary > 60000 THEN 'mid'
            ELSE 'junior'
       END
FROM staff;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The test is `IS NULL`, not `= NULL`. Comparing anything to NULL with `=`
yields unknown, which is never a true branch.

## Hint 2
The `ELSE` arm concatenates a literal with a number, so the number needs
to become text. Watch the trailing space in `'reports to '` - the gate
compares strings exactly.

references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, name,
       CASE WHEN manager_id IS NULL THEN 'CEO'
            ELSE 'reports to ' || manager_id::text
       END
FROM staff;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 - two ladders in one row

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. The pricing dashboard wants two independent
classifications on every product row. Return five columns, in this order:

| position | value |
|---|---|
| 1 | `id` |
| 2 | `category` |
| 3 | `price` |
| 4 | price band: `A` under 100, `B` under 200, `C` under 300, `D` under 400, `E` otherwise |
| 5 | department: `hard` for `electronics` and `garden`, `soft` for `clothing` and `toys`, `consumable` for `books` and `food` |

All thresholds in column 4 are strict. Every product, any row order.

Run: `uv run dojo test 64_drills_case_1 ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two `CASE` expressions side by side in the select list, each closed with
its own `END` and separated by a comma. They do not interact.

## Hint 2
Column 4 is a ladder and relies on first-match evaluation, so each
branch needs only its upper bound. Column 5 is an enumeration, so `IN`
lists or the simple `CASE` form both read well.

## Hint 3
Get column 4 right on its own first - five branches is where a missing
comma or a missing `END` hides best - then add column 5. Check one product
from each category and one from each band before you run the gate.

## Hint 1
Two `CASE` expressions side by side in the select list, each closed with
its own `END` and separated by a comma. They do not interact.

Column 4 is a ladder and relies on first-match evaluation, so each

SELECT p.id, p.category, p.price,
       CASE WHEN p.price >= 400 THEN 'E'

            WHEN p.price >= 100 THEN 'B'

lessons.briefing:
# 65 - Drills: NULL logic, set 1

These eight problems drill three-valued logic - lesson 05, with a little of
04's `coalesce` and `concat` - on the one column in this database that is
naturally NULL, `staff.manager_id`, plus a few NULLs you will manufacture
yourself. If any of them feels like guessing, reread 05 before you continue:
NULL is the one topic where a wrong mental model produces queries that run
happily and answer the wrong question.

## Exercise 1 - is there a manager or not

For every staff member with `id` of 20 or less, return the columns `id`,
`name`, `manager_id`, and a fourth column `has_manager` holding the boolean
result of testing whether `manager_id` is not null.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 65_drills_null_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - coalesce, and the type trap inside it

For every staff member in the `ops` department, return `id`, `name`, and a
column `manager` containing the `manager_id` rendered as text, or the string
`'none'` where there is no manager.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 65_drills_null_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - the pipe operator versus concat

For every staff member with `id` of 12 or less, return three columns: `id`,
then `piped` built as `name || ' -> ' || manager_id`, then `joined` built as
`concat(name, ' -> ', manager_id)`.

One of those two columns is NULL for the CEO and the other is not. Write
both exactly as described and see which.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 65_drills_null_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - where NULLs sort

Return `id`, `name` and `manager_id` for every staff member, sorted by
`manager_id` **descending with NULLs last**, and then by `id` ascending.

**Ordered exactly as described** - this gate compares row order.

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 65_drills_null_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - aggregating nothing at all

`orders.status` never contains the value `'refunded'`, so this query has no
rows to work with. Return one row with four columns computed over
`orders` restricted to `status = 'refunded'`: `n` = `count(*)`,
`revenue` = `sum(total)`, `revenue_or_zero` = the same sum with NULL
replaced by `0`, and `newest` = `max(created_at)`.

Ordering does not matter - it is a single row.

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 65_drills_null_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - DISTINCT thinks NULLs are equal

Return the distinct values of `manager_id` in `staff` - one column, named
`manager_id`.

**Ordered by `manager_id` ascending**, leaving PostgreSQL's default NULL
placement alone.

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 65_drills_null_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - NOT IN, and the empty answer

Return `id` and `name` for every staff member who is **not** the manager of
anybody in the `ops` department.

Build the excluded set from the `manager_id` values of `ops` staff. That set
contains a NULL, and a naive `NOT IN` against it returns no rows at all - the
whole point of this drill is to write the version that does not.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 65_drills_null_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - the rows a WHERE clause throws away

Return `id`, `name`, `manager_id` and `salary` for every staff row where the
condition

```
manager_id > 5 AND salary > 100000
```

is **not true** - that is, every row a `WHERE` clause carrying that condition
would reject, including the rows where it evaluates to unknown rather than
false.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 65_drills_null_1 ex8`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 65_drills_null_1

Eight drills on the only value in SQL that is not equal to itself. Read this
after you have attempted them, pass or fail.

## Notes

The unifying rule of this set: NULL is not a value, it is the absence of one,
so every operator you hand it returns "unknown" rather than an answer. That
single fact explains all eight problems. Comparisons (`=`, `<>`, `>`) return
NULL instead of true or false; `WHERE` keeps only rows where the predicate is
literally TRUE, so unknown rows disappear silently; arithmetic and `||`
propagate NULL through the whole expression; and `NOT IN` against a list
containing NULL can never return true. The tools that survive contact with
NULL are the ones that were designed for it: `IS NULL`, `IS DISTINCT FROM`,
`IS NOT TRUE`, `coalesce`, `nullif`, and `concat`. Learn which of your
everyday operators are NULL-blind and you stop being surprised.

## ex1 - is there a manager or not

The point of putting `manager_id IS NOT NULL` in the SELECT list is to see
that it returns a real boolean - true or false, never NULL - while
`manager_id = something` would return NULL for the CEO's row. The classic
mistake is `manager_id <> NULL`, which yields NULL for every row including
rows that clearly have a manager, so a filter built on it returns nothing at
all. Model answer: test with `IS NOT NULL`, which is the only comparison in
SQL guaranteed to answer true or false.

## ex2 - coalesce, and the type trap inside it

This drills the substitution habit and the type rule that comes with it.
`coalesce` is variadic and strictly typed: every argument is resolved to a
single common type, so mixing an integer column with a text default is an
error rather than a silent cast. The classic mistake is reaching for
`coalesce(manager_id, 'none')` and reading the resulting message as a bug in
your logic instead of a missing `::text`. Model answer: cast the column to
text first, then substitute, because a display placeholder is a display
concern.

## ex3 - the pipe operator versus concat

Two ways to build the same string, one of which quietly deletes the row's
whole label when a single input is missing. `||` is strict (NULL in, NULL
out) because it is an ordinary operator; `concat()` is a function that
documents itself as ignoring NULL arguments, so the CEO gets `Name -> ` with
a dangling arrow rather than nothing at all. The classic mistake is building
a display name with `||` and then wondering why a handful of rows in a report
are blank. Model answer: use `||` when a missing part should invalidate the
whole string, `concat` when it should not.

## ex4 - where NULLs sort

Sorting is the one place where SQL does give NULL a defined position: it
sorts as though it were larger than everything, which means the default
placement flips when you add `DESC`. That asymmetry is the trap. The classic
mistake is writing `ORDER BY manager_id DESC` for a "biggest first" report
and getting the row with no value at the top, above the actual maximum -
which looks like a data bug and is not one. Model answer: whenever a sort key
is nullable, write `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST` explicitly and stop thinking
about the default.

## ex5 - aggregating nothing at all

A bare aggregate query always returns exactly one row, even when its input is
empty - and that row is mostly NULLs, because `sum`, `avg`, `min` and `max`
have nothing to report. `count` is the exception and answers 0. The classic
mistake is a dashboard that prints an empty cell instead of a zero, or worse,
arithmetic like `sum(total) * 1.2` that turns the whole KPI row NULL. Model
answer: `coalesce` on the outside of the aggregate, because the substitution
belongs to the result, not to the rows that were never there.

## ex6 - DISTINCT thinks NULLs are equal

Deduplication uses a different notion of sameness than `=` does. Two NULLs
are never equal under a comparison, yet `DISTINCT` and `GROUP BY` collapse
them into a single output row, because both are defined in terms of "not
distinct from" rather than "equals". The classic mistake is assuming NULL
rows vanish from a `DISTINCT` list the way they vanish from a `WHERE` clause;
they do not, they arrive as one anonymous entry at the end. Model answer:
`SELECT DISTINCT`, and remember that `GROUP BY` would give you the identical
result set.

## ex7 - NOT IN, and the empty answer

This is the single most expensive NULL bug in professional SQL, because the
symptom is an empty result rather than an error. `NOT IN` is defined as a
chain of `<>` comparisons joined by AND, so one NULL in the list makes every
row's predicate unknown, and unknown rows are dropped. The classic mistake is
to conclude "there are no such staff" and ship it. Model answer: exclude the
NULLs from the subquery explicitly, or use `NOT EXISTS`, which is immune
because it tests whether a matching row exists rather than comparing values.

## ex8 - the rows a WHERE clause throws away

Splitting a table into "kept" and "rejected" halves is a routine reporting
job - reconciliation, audit trails, "why is this row missing" queries - and
with a nullable column in the predicate the naive complement loses rows from
both halves at once. `NOT (unknown)` is `unknown`, so the CEO row fails both
the filter and its negation. The classic mistake is trusting that the two
queries partition the table; count them and they will not add up. Model
answer: `IS NOT TRUE` collapses false and unknown into one honest bucket.

## Further reading

- [Comparison Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html) - `IS NULL`, `IS DISTINCT FROM`, and the `IS TRUE`/`IS NOT TRUE` family in one short page.
- [Conditional Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-conditional.html) - `COALESCE`, `NULLIF`, `CASE`, `GREATEST`/`LEAST` and how each treats NULL.
- [String Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-string.html) - the reference that spells out why `||` returns NULL and `concat()` does not.
- [`SELECT` - the `ORDER BY` clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html#SQL-ORDERBY) - `NULLS FIRST` / `NULLS LAST` and the defaults that flip with `DESC`.

# 65 - Drills: NULL logic, set 1

These eight problems drill three-valued logic - lesson 05, with a little of
04's `coalesce` and `concat` - on the one column in this database that is
naturally NULL, `staff.manager_id`, plus a few NULLs you will manufacture
yourself. If any of them feels like guessing, reread 05 before you continue:
NULL is the one topic where a wrong mental model produces queries that run
happily and answer the wrong question.

## Exercise 1 - is there a manager or not

For every staff member with `id` of 20 or less, return the columns `id`,
`name`, `manager_id`, and a fourth column `has_manager` holding the boolean
result of testing whether `manager_id` is not null.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 65_drills_null_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - coalesce, and the type trap inside it

For every staff member in the `ops` department, return `id`, `name`, and a
column `manager` containing the `manager_id` rendered as text, or the string
`'none'` where there is no manager.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 65_drills_null_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - the pipe operator versus concat

For every staff member with `id` of 12 or less, return three columns: `id`,
then `piped` built as `name || ' -> ' || manager_id`, then `joined` built as
`concat(name, ' -> ', manager_id)`.

One of those two columns is NULL for the CEO and the other is not. Write
both exactly as described and see which.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 65_drills_null_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - where NULLs sort

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 65_drills_null_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - aggregating nothing at all

rows to work with. Return one row with four columns computed over

replaced by `0`, and `newest` = `max(created_at)`.

## Exercise 6 - DISTINCT thinks NULLs are equal

`manager_id`.

placement alone.

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 65_drills_null_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - NOT IN, and the empty answer

anybody in the `ops` department.

contains a NULL, and a naive `NOT IN` against it returns no rows at all - the
whole point of this drill is to write the version that does not.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 65_drills_null_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - the rows a WHERE clause throws away

Return `id`, `name`, `manager_id` and `salary` for every staff row where the
condition

```
manager_id > 5 AND salary > 100000
```

is **not true** - that is, every row a `WHERE` clause carrying that condition
would reject, including the rows where it evaluates to unknown rather than
false.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 65_drills_null_1 ex8`

# Reading - 65_drills_null_1

Eight drills on the only value in SQL that is not equal to itself. Read this
after you have attempted them, pass or fail.

## Notes

The unifying rule of this set: NULL is not a value, it is the absence of one,
so every operator you hand it returns "unknown" rather than an answer. That
single fact explains all eight problems. Comparisons (`=`, `<>`, `>`) return
NULL instead of true or false; `WHERE` keeps only rows where the predicate is
literally TRUE, so unknown rows disappear silently; arithmetic and `||`
propagate NULL through the whole expression; and `NOT IN` against a list
containing NULL can never return true. The tools that survive contact with
NULL are the ones that were designed for it: `IS NULL`, `IS DISTINCT FROM`,
`IS NOT TRUE`, `coalesce`, `nullif`, and `concat`. Learn which of your
everyday operators are NULL-blind and you stop being surprised.

## ex1 - is there a manager or not

The point of putting `manager_id IS NOT NULL` in the SELECT list is to see
that it returns a real boolean - true or false, never NULL - while
`manager_id = something` would return NULL for the CEO's row. The classic
mistake is `manager_id <> NULL`, which yields NULL for every row including
rows that clearly have a manager, so a filter built on it returns nothing at
all. Model answer: test with `IS NOT NULL`, which is the only comparison in
SQL guaranteed to answer true or false.

## ex2 - coalesce, and the type trap inside it

This drills the substitution habit and the type rule that comes with it.
`coalesce` is variadic and strictly typed: every argument is resolved to a
single common type, so mixing an integer column with a text default is an
error rather than a silent cast. The classic mistake is reaching for
`coalesce(manager_id, 'none')` and reading the resulting message as a bug in
your logic instead of a missing `::text`. Model answer: cast the column to
text first, then substitute, because a display placeholder is a display
concern.

## ex3 - the pipe operator versus concat

Two ways to build the same string, one of which quietly deletes the row's
whole label when a single input is missing. `||` is strict (NULL in, NULL
out) because it is an ordinary operator; `concat()` is a function that
documents itself as ignoring NULL arguments, so the CEO gets `Name -> ` with
a dangling arrow rather than nothing at all. The classic mistake is building
a display name with `||` and then wondering why a handful of rows in a report
are blank. Model answer: use `||` when a missing part should invalidate the
whole string, `concat` when it should not.

## ex4 - where NULLs sort

Sorting is the one place where SQL does give NULL a defined position: it
sorts as though it were larger than everything, which means the default
placement flips when you add `DESC`. That asymmetry is the trap. The classic
mistake is writing `ORDER BY manager_id DESC` for a "biggest first" report
and getting the row with no value at the top, above the actual maximum -
which looks like a data bug and is not one. Model answer: whenever a sort key
is nullable, write `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST` explicitly and stop thinking
about the default.

## ex5 - aggregating nothing at all

A bare aggregate query always returns exactly one row, even when its input is
empty - and that row is mostly NULLs, because `sum`, `avg`, `min` and `max`
have nothing to report. `count` is the exception and answers 0. The classic
mistake is a dashboard that prints an empty cell instead of a zero, or worse,
arithmetic like `sum(total) * 1.2` that turns the whole KPI row NULL. Model
answer: `coalesce` on the outside of the aggregate, because the substitution
belongs to the result, not to the rows that were never there.

## ex6 - DISTINCT thinks NULLs are equal

Deduplication uses a different notion of sameness than `=` does. Two NULLs
are never equal under a comparison, yet `DISTINCT` and `GROUP BY` collapse
them into a single output row, because both are defined in terms of "not
distinct from" rather than "equals". The classic mistake is assuming NULL
rows vanish from a `DISTINCT` list the way they vanish from a `WHERE` clause;
they do not, they arrive as one anonymous entry at the end. Model answer:
`SELECT DISTINCT`, and remember that `GROUP BY` would give you the identical
result set.

## ex7 - NOT IN, and the empty answer

This is the single most expensive NULL bug in professional SQL, because the
symptom is an empty result rather than an error. `NOT IN` is defined as a
chain of `<>` comparisons joined by AND, so one NULL in the list makes every
row's predicate unknown, and unknown rows are dropped. The classic mistake is
to conclude "there are no such staff" and ship it. Model answer: exclude the
NULLs from the subquery explicitly, or use `NOT EXISTS`, which is immune
because it tests whether a matching row exists rather than comparing values.

## ex8 - the rows a WHERE clause throws away

Splitting a table into "kept" and "rejected" halves is a routine reporting
job - reconciliation, audit trails, "why is this row missing" queries - and
with a nullable column in the predicate the naive complement loses rows from
both halves at once. `NOT (unknown)` is `unknown`, so the CEO row fails both
the filter and its negation. The classic mistake is trusting that the two
queries partition the table; count them and they will not add up. Model
answer: `IS NOT TRUE` collapses false and unknown into one honest bucket.

## Further reading

- [Comparison Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html) - `IS NULL`, `IS DISTINCT FROM`, and the `IS TRUE`/`IS NOT TRUE` family in one short page.
- [Conditional Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-conditional.html) - `COALESCE`, `NULLIF`, `CASE`, `GREATEST`/`LEAST` and how each treats NULL.
- [String Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-string.html) - the reference that spells out why `||` returns NULL and `concat()` does not.
- [`SELECT` - the `ORDER BY` clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html#SQL-ORDERBY) - `NULLS FIRST` / `NULLS LAST` and the defaults that flip with `DESC`.

## Exercise 1 - is there a manager or not

For every staff member with `id` of 20 or less, return the columns `id`,
`name`, `manager_id`, and a fourth column `has_manager` holding the boolean
result of testing whether `manager_id` is not null.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 65_drills_null_1 ex1`

## Hint 1

`IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL` are not only filters. They are ordinary boolean expressions and can sit in the SELECT list like any other computation.

`SELECT id, name, manager_id, <the test> AS has_manager FROM staff WHERE ... ORDER BY id;` - the test is the same three words you would put in a WHERE clause.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL` are not only filters. They are ordinary boolean expressions and can sit in the SELECT list like any other computation.

## Hint 2

`SELECT id, name, manager_id, <the test> AS has_manager FROM staff WHERE ... ORDER BY id;` - the test is the same three words you would put in a WHERE clause.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT id, name, manager_id, NOT (manager_id IS NULL) AS has_manager
FROM staff
WHERE id <= 20
ORDER BY id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, name, manager_id, manager_id IS NOT NULL AS has_manager
FROM staff
WHERE id <= 20
ORDER BY id;

## Exercise 3 - the pipe operator versus concat

For every staff member with `id` of 12 or less, return three columns: `id`,
then `piped` built as `name || ' -> ' || manager_id`, then `joined` built as

both exactly as described and see which.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The `||` operator is strict: give any operand a NULL and the whole expression is NULL. `concat()` is not strict - it skips NULL arguments and carries on.

## Hint 2

Write the two columns literally as the prompt spells them, then look at row 1. The difference you see is the entire lesson.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT id,
       CASE WHEN manager_id IS NULL THEN NULL
            ELSE name || ' -> ' || manager_id END AS piped,
       name || ' -> ' || coalesce(manager_id::text, '') AS joined
FROM staff
WHERE id <= 12
ORDER BY id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id,
       name || ' -> ' || manager_id AS piped,
       concat(name, ' -> ', manager_id) AS joined
FROM staff
WHERE id <= 12
ORDER BY id;

## Exercise 4 - where NULLs sort

Return `id`, `name` and `manager_id` for every staff member, sorted by

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

PostgreSQL treats NULL as larger than every non-NULL value when sorting. Under `ASC` that puts NULLs last; under `DESC` it puts them first.

## Hint 2

The default is not what this prompt wants, so say so explicitly: `ORDER BY manager_id DESC NULLS LAST, id`.

## Hint 1

An aggregate over zero rows still produces one row. `count` answers 0 there; every other aggregate answers NULL, because there is nothing to add up or compare.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS n,
       sum(total) AS revenue,
       CASE WHEN sum(total) IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE sum(total) END AS revenue_or_zero,
       max(created_at) AS newest
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'refunded';
references.expected.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS n,
       sum(total) AS revenue,
       coalesce(sum(total), 0) AS revenue_or_zero,
       max(created_at) AS newest
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'refunded';

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 - NOT IN, and the empty answer

Return `id` and `name` for every staff member who is **not** the manager of
anybody in the `ops` department.

Build the excluded set from the `manager_id` values of `ops` staff. That set
contains a NULL, and a naive `NOT IN` against it returns no rows at all - the
whole point of this drill is to write the version that does not.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 65_drills_null_1 ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`x NOT IN (a, b, NULL)` expands to `x <> a AND x <> b AND x <> NULL`. That last conjunct is never true, so the whole expression is never true - it is either false or unknown, and both are rejected.

## Hint 2

Two ways out, and both are worth writing once: filter the NULLs out of the subquery with `WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL`, or switch to `NOT EXISTS`, which asks about row existence instead of value equality.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT s.id, s.name
FROM staff s
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM staff o

## Exercise 8 - the rows a WHERE clause throws away

Return `id`, `name`, `manager_id` and `salary` for every staff row where the
condition

```
manager_id > 5 AND salary > 100000
```

is **not true** - that is, every row a `WHERE` clause carrying that condition
would reject, including the rows where it evaluates to unknown rather than
false.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 65_drills_null_1 ex8`

## Hint 1

The complement of a filter is not `NOT (filter)`. A three-valued predicate has three outcomes, and `NOT` maps unknown to unknown - so the rows that were dropped for being unknown get dropped again.

## Hint 2

PostgreSQL gives you the exact test you need: `(<predicate>) IS NOT TRUE`. Alternatively, take the `NOT` version and OR in the rows whose NULL made the predicate unknown.

lessons.briefing:
# 66 - Drills: NULL logic, set 2

Set 1 kept NULLs inside a single row. These eight take them into aggregates,
`GROUP BY` and outer joins - lesson 05 crossed with 06, 07 and 09 - which is
where a missing value stops being a display problem and starts changing your
totals. Every problem here has a number in it that comes out differently
depending on whether you counted the NULLs or skipped them.

## Exercise 1 - count(*) is not count(column)

For each `staff` department, return `department`, `headcount` = the number of
staff rows in it, and `with_manager` = the number of those rows whose
`manager_id` is present.

**Ordered by `department` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 66_drills_null_2 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - a NULL group nobody asked for

Group `orders` by `nullif(status, 'cancelled')` - an expression that turns
the cancelled orders into a NULL group and leaves the rest alone. Return
`live_status` (that expression), `orders` = the number of rows in the group,
and `revenue` = `sum(total)`.

**Ordered by `live_status` ascending with NULLs first.**

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 66_drills_null_2 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - NULL-safe equality

Return `id`, `name` and `manager_id` for every staff member whose
`manager_id` is **not distinct from** the `manager_id` of staff member 1 -
that is, matches it under a comparison where NULL equals NULL.

Get the value to compare against with a scalar subquery on `staff`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 66_drills_null_2 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - dividing by a count that might be zero

For each `staff` department return `department`, `headcount` = `count(*)`,
`principals` = the number of staff earning 190000 or more, and
`staff_per_principal` = `headcount` divided by `principals`, computed as
numeric and rounded to 2 decimal places.

Several departments have no principals at all. That row's ratio must come
back as NULL rather than raising a division-by-zero error.

**Ordered by `department` ascending.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 66_drills_null_2 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - counting what did not match

For each product category, how many of its products have never appeared in
any `order_items` row? Return `category` and `never_ordered`.

Write this as an outer join from `products` to `order_items` and keep the
rows where the join found nothing.

**Ordered by `category` ascending.**

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 66_drills_null_2 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - sum of nothing, defaulted to zero

For every staff member earning less than 100000, return `id`, `name`,
`reports` = the number of people who report directly to them (0 when nobody
does), and `report_payroll` = the total salary of those direct reports,
reported as `0` rather than NULL when there are none.

Most of these people manage nobody, so most rows are the interesting case.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 66_drills_null_2 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - HAVING on the gap between two counts

Which departments contain at least one staff member with no manager? Return
`department`, `headcount` = `count(*)`, and `rootless` = how many of them
have a NULL `manager_id` - keeping only the departments where `rootless` is
at least 1.

Express the HAVING condition as a comparison between two counts rather than
by filtering rows in `WHERE`.

**Ordered by `department` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 66_drills_null_2 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - average of nothing versus average of zeros

For every product in the `books` category, return `id`, `name`,
`recent_5star` = the number of 5-star reviews it received on or after
2023-11-01, `avg_recent` = the average of those ratings rounded to 2, and
`avg_zero_filled` = the average of `coalesce(rating, 0)` over the same outer
join, also rounded to 2.

Join with `LEFT JOIN reviews` and put both the rating test and the date test
in the `ON` clause, so that products with no qualifying review still appear.
Most books have none, and those rows are where the two averages disagree.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 66_drills_null_2 ex8`
