# Reading - 66_drills_null_2

Eight drills on what NULL does once you start grouping, counting and joining.
Read after you have attempted them.

## Notes

Three rules unite this set. First, aggregates ignore NULL inputs: `count(col)`
counts non-NULL values while `count(*)` counts rows, and `avg` divides by the
number of non-NULL values rather than by the number of rows - so the same
column can produce two defensible averages. Second, grouping does the
opposite of comparison: `GROUP BY` gathers all the NULLs into one group
rather than discarding them, which means a NULL group can appear in a report
that never mentioned NULL. Third, outer joins manufacture NULLs on purpose,
and the aggregate you write on top of the join decides whether an unmatched
row reads as zero, as NULL, or as one - which is exactly the difference
between `count(*)`, `count(right.col)` and `coalesce(sum(...), 0)`.

## ex1 - count(*) is not count(column)

The cheapest NULL audit in SQL: put `count(*)` and `count(col)` side by side
and the gap between them is the number of missing values. Only the department
containing the CEO shows a gap here, which is what makes the result readable
at a glance. The classic mistake is the reverse - using `count(col)` when you
meant to count rows, and quietly under-reporting a group. Model answer: count
rows with `count(*)`, count values with `count(col)`, and never let the choice
be accidental.

## ex2 - a NULL group nobody asked for

Grouping keeps what filtering throws away. A NULL grouping key does not
disappear - it becomes a group of its own, labelled with nothing, and a
reader who does not know the query cannot tell whether that row means
"cancelled", "unknown" or "not applicable". The classic mistake is shipping a
report with a blank row in the category column and no legend. Model answer:
`nullif` makes the NULL deliberately, so you can see grouping treat NULLs as
one value even though comparison never would.

## ex3 - NULL-safe equality

`IS DISTINCT FROM` and its negation are the operators you want whenever a
comparison must treat two missing values as a match: deduplication, change
detection between an old and a new row, and merge logic all depend on it.
The classic mistake is writing `a = b OR (a IS NULL AND b IS NULL)` by hand,
which works but has to be repeated for every column and is easy to get wrong
under `NOT`. Model answer: one operator, one comparison, and the subquery
supplies the NULL that makes the point.

## ex4 - dividing by a count that might be zero

Every rate you will ever compute has a denominator that can be zero on some
slice of the data, usually the slice nobody tested. `nullif(x, 0)` converts
the crash into a missing value, which is the honest answer: the ratio is not
zero, it is undefined. The classic mistake is `coalesce(..., 0)` around the
whole ratio, which reports "zero staff per principal" for a department that
has no principals at all. Model answer: guard the divisor, keep the NULL, and
let the presentation layer decide how to draw it.

## ex5 - counting what did not match

The anti-join reads NULL as evidence: the right-hand columns are NULL for
exactly the rows that found no partner, so `WHERE oi.id IS NULL` after a
LEFT JOIN means "no match existed". The classic mistake is testing a nullable
column instead of the key - if the right table allowed NULLs in the column
you test, you would also catch rows that did match. Model answer: outer join,
test the key for NULL, then aggregate. `NOT EXISTS` expresses the same idea
without the join and is usually the clearer of the two.

## ex6 - sum of nothing, defaulted to zero

This is the pair of behaviours that outer-joined aggregates hinge on:
`count` of a right-hand column answers 0 for an unmatched group, but every
other aggregate answers NULL, because zero values were summed rather than
zero being one of them. Both `coalesce(sum(x), 0)` and `sum(coalesce(x, 0))`
happen to work here, which is worth noticing rather than memorising - the
first defaults the result, the second defaults the inputs, and they diverge
the moment a matched row can itself carry a NULL. The classic mistake is
`count(*)`, which counts the NULL-extended row and reports 1 report for
somebody who has none.

## ex7 - HAVING on the gap between two counts

A group-level test for missing data, written without touching `WHERE`. The
distinction matters because the two counts in the SELECT list have to be
computed over the whole department; pre-filtering the rows would leave you
with `headcount` equal to `rootless` in every surviving group. The classic
mistake is exactly that - moving the NULL test into `WHERE`, getting a
plausible-looking result, and not noticing that the first column is now
meaningless. Model answer: filter groups with `HAVING`, and let `FILTER`
carry the conditional counting inside the group.

## ex8 - average of nothing versus average of zeros

Two averages over the same join, differing only in where the `coalesce`
sits, and they answer different questions: "how good were the recent 5-star
reviews" versus "how good were the reviews, counting a silent product as
zero". Neither is wrong; publishing the wrong one is. The classic mistake is
the second form appearing by accident, usually because somebody wrapped
everything in `coalesce` to make the blanks in a spreadsheet go away, and the
resulting chart says a well-reviewed book scored 0. Note also that the
filters live in `ON` - in `WHERE` they would discard the very rows this drill
is about.

## Further reading

- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - read the sentence about NULL inputs at the top of the table, then the `FILTER` syntax notes.
- [`GROUP BY` and `HAVING`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) - grouping semantics, including how grouping treats values that are not distinct from each other.
- [Joins Between Tables](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-join.html) - the tutorial's outer-join section, where the NULL-extended row is introduced with a worked example.
- [Comparison Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html) - `IS DISTINCT FROM` and `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`, the NULL-safe equality pair used in exercise 3.

# Reading - 66_drills_null_2

Eight drills on what NULL does once you start grouping, counting and joining.
Read after you have attempted them.

## Notes

Three rules unite this set. First, aggregates ignore NULL inputs: `count(col)`
counts non-NULL values while `count(*)` counts rows, and `avg` divides by the
number of non-NULL values rather than by the number of rows - so the same
column can produce two defensible averages. Second, grouping does the
opposite of comparison: `GROUP BY` gathers all the NULLs into one group
rather than discarding them, which means a NULL group can appear in a report
that never mentioned NULL. Third, outer joins manufacture NULLs on purpose,
and the aggregate you write on top of the join decides whether an unmatched
row reads as zero, as NULL, or as one - which is exactly the difference
between `count(*)`, `count(right.col)` and `coalesce(sum(...), 0)`.

## ex1 - count(*) is not count(column)

The cheapest NULL audit in SQL: put `count(*)` and `count(col)` side by side
and the gap between them is the number of missing values. Only the department
containing the CEO shows a gap here, which is what makes the result readable
at a glance. The classic mistake is the reverse - using `count(col)` when you
meant to count rows, and quietly under-reporting a group. Model answer: count
rows with `count(*)`, count values with `count(col)`, and never let the choice
be accidental.

## ex2 - a NULL group nobody asked for

Grouping keeps what filtering throws away. A NULL grouping key does not
disappear - it becomes a group of its own, labelled with nothing, and a
reader who does not know the query cannot tell whether that row means
"cancelled", "unknown" or "not applicable". The classic mistake is shipping a
report with a blank row in the category column and no legend. Model answer:
`nullif` makes the NULL deliberately, so you can see grouping treat NULLs as
one value even though comparison never would.

## ex3 - NULL-safe equality

`IS DISTINCT FROM` and its negation are the operators you want whenever a
comparison must treat two missing values as a match: deduplication, change
detection between an old and a new row, and merge logic all depend on it.
The classic mistake is writing `a = b OR (a IS NULL AND b IS NULL)` by hand,
which works but has to be repeated for every column and is easy to get wrong
under `NOT`. Model answer: one operator, one comparison, and the subquery
supplies the NULL that makes the point.

## ex4 - dividing by a count that might be zero

Every rate you will ever compute has a denominator that can be zero on some
slice of the data, usually the slice nobody tested. `nullif(x, 0)` converts
the crash into a missing value, which is the honest answer: the ratio is not
zero, it is undefined. The classic mistake is `coalesce(..., 0)` around the
whole ratio, which reports "zero staff per principal" for a department that
has no principals at all. Model answer: guard the divisor, keep the NULL, and
let the presentation layer decide how to draw it.

## ex5 - counting what did not match

The anti-join reads NULL as evidence: the right-hand columns are NULL for
exactly the rows that found no partner, so `WHERE oi.id IS NULL` after a
LEFT JOIN means "no match existed". The classic mistake is testing a nullable
column instead of the key - if the right table allowed NULLs in the column
you test, you would also catch rows that did match. Model answer: outer join,
test the key for NULL, then aggregate. `NOT EXISTS` expresses the same idea
without the join and is usually the clearer of the two.

## ex6 - sum of nothing, defaulted to zero

This is the pair of behaviours that outer-joined aggregates hinge on:
`count` of a right-hand column answers 0 for an unmatched group, but every
other aggregate answers NULL, because zero values were summed rather than
zero being one of them. Both `coalesce(sum(x), 0)` and `sum(coalesce(x, 0))`
happen to work here, which is worth noticing rather than memorising - the
first defaults the result, the second defaults the inputs, and they diverge
the moment a matched row can itself carry a NULL. The classic mistake is
`count(*)`, which counts the NULL-extended row and reports 1 report for
somebody who has none.

## ex7 - HAVING on the gap between two counts

A group-level test for missing data, written without touching `WHERE`. The
distinction matters because the two counts in the SELECT list have to be
computed over the whole department; pre-filtering the rows would leave you
with `headcount` equal to `rootless` in every surviving group. The classic
mistake is exactly that - moving the NULL test into `WHERE`, getting a
plausible-looking result, and not noticing that the first column is now
meaningless. Model answer: filter groups with `HAVING`, and let `FILTER`
carry the conditional counting inside the group.

## ex8 - average of nothing versus average of zeros

Two averages over the same join, differing only in where the `coalesce`
sits, and they answer different questions: "how good were the recent 5-star
reviews" versus "how good were the reviews, counting a silent product as
zero". Neither is wrong; publishing the wrong one is. The classic mistake is
the second form appearing by accident, usually because somebody wrapped
everything in `coalesce` to make the blanks in a spreadsheet go away, and the
resulting chart says a well-reviewed book scored 0. Note also that the
filters live in `ON` - in `WHERE` they would discard the very rows this drill
is about.

## Exercise 1 - count(*) is not count(column)

For each `staff` department, return `department`, `headcount` = the number of
staff rows in it, and `with_manager` = the number of those rows whose
`manager_id` is present.

**Ordered by `department` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 66_drills_null_2 ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`count(*)` counts rows. `count(<expression>)` counts the rows where that expression is not NULL. Exactly one department in this company differs between the two.

## Hint 2

Group by `department` and put two counts in the SELECT list: one counting
rows, one counting the values of the column that can be NULL. Both are
`count`, and only the argument differs.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`count(*)` counts rows. `count(<expression>)` counts the rows where that expression is not NULL. Exactly one department in this company differs between the two.

## Hint 2

Group by `department` and put two counts in the SELECT list: one counting
rows, one counting the values of the column that can be NULL. Both are
`count`, and only the argument differs.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT department,
       count(*) AS headcount,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL) AS with_manager
FROM staff
GROUP BY department
ORDER BY department;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT department, count(*) AS headcount, count(manager_id) AS with_manager
FROM staff
GROUP BY department
ORDER BY department;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Plain `=` cannot do this: staff member 1 has no manager, so `manager_id = (that subquery)` is NULL for every row and the filter keeps nothing.

## Hint 2

`a IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b` is the NULL-safe equality operator - true when both sides are equal and also true when both sides are NULL.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT id, name, manager_id
FROM staff
WHERE NOT (manager_id IS DISTINCT FROM (SELECT manager_id FROM staff WHERE id = 1))
ORDER BY id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, name, manager_id
FROM staff
WHERE manager_id IS NOT DISTINCT FROM (SELECT manager_id FROM staff WHERE id = 1)
ORDER BY id;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 - dividing by a count that might be zero

For each `staff` department return `department`, `headcount` = `count(*)`,
`principals` = the number of staff earning 190000 or more, and
`staff_per_principal` = `headcount` divided by `principals`, computed as
numeric and rounded to 2 decimal places.

Several departments have no principals at all. That row's ratio must come
back as NULL rather than raising a division-by-zero error.

**Ordered by `department` ascending.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 66_drills_null_2 ex4`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`nullif(denominator, 0)` turns a zero divisor into NULL, and dividing by NULL gives NULL instead of an error. This is the standard guard for any rate or ratio.

## Hint 2

Both counts can be written with `FILTER (WHERE ...)`. Cast the numerator to numeric before dividing, or integer division will truncate the answer to whole numbers.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`nullif(denominator, 0)` turns a zero divisor into NULL, and dividing by NULL gives NULL instead of an error. This is the standard guard for any rate or ratio.

## Hint 2

Both counts can be written with `FILTER (WHERE ...)`. Cast the numerator to numeric before dividing, or integer division will truncate the answer to whole numbers.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT department,
       count(*) AS headcount,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE salary >= 190000) AS principals,
       CASE WHEN count(*) FILTER (WHERE salary >= 190000) = 0 THEN NULL
            ELSE round(count(*)::numeric
                       / count(*) FILTER (WHERE salary >= 190000), 2)
       END AS staff_per_principal
FROM staff
GROUP BY department
ORDER BY department;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT department,
       count(*) AS headcount,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE salary >= 190000) AS principals,
       round(count(*)::numeric
             / nullif(count(*) FILTER (WHERE salary >= 190000), 0), 2) AS staff_per_principal
FROM staff
GROUP BY department
ORDER BY department;

references.solution.sql:
SELECT p.category, count(*) AS never_ordered
FROM products p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.product_id = p.id)

ORDER BY p.category;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT p.category, count(*) AS never_ordered
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
WHERE oi.id IS NULL
GROUP BY p.category
ORDER BY p.category;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Join `staff` to itself with a LEFT JOIN so that people who manage nobody survive the join, then group by the manager's id.

## Hint 2

For an unmatched row the right-hand side is entirely NULL, so `count(r.id)` is 0 while `sum(r.salary)` is NULL. Only one of those two needs a `coalesce`.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT s.id, s.name,
       count(r.id) AS reports,
       sum(coalesce(r.salary, 0)) AS report_payroll
FROM staff s
LEFT JOIN staff r ON r.manager_id = s.id
WHERE s.salary < 100000
GROUP BY s.id, s.name
ORDER BY s.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT s.id, s.name,
       count(r.id) AS reports,
       coalesce(sum(r.salary), 0) AS report_payroll
FROM staff s
LEFT JOIN staff r ON r.manager_id = s.id
WHERE s.salary < 100000
GROUP BY s.id, s.name
ORDER BY s.id;

## Exercise 8 - average of nothing versus average of zeros

For every product in the `books` category, return `id`, `name`,
`recent_5star` = the number of 5-star reviews it received on or after
2023-11-01, `avg_recent` = the average of those ratings rounded to 2, and
`avg_zero_filled` = the average of `coalesce(rating, 0)` over the same outer
join, also rounded to 2.

Join with `LEFT JOIN reviews` and put both the rating test and the date test
in the `ON` clause, so that products with no qualifying review still appear.
Most books have none, and those rows are where the two averages disagree.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 66_drills_null_2 ex8`

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The conditions on `reviews` belong in `ON`, not in `WHERE`. Moving them to `WHERE` deletes the unmatched rows and turns your outer join back into an inner one.

## Hint 2

`avg(r.rating)` skips NULL inputs entirely, so a product with no match has nothing to average and returns NULL. `avg(coalesce(r.rating, 0))` feeds it a zero instead, which is a value, so the average is 0.00.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT p.id, p.name,
       count(r.id) AS recent_5star,
       round(sum(r.rating)::numeric / nullif(count(r.id), 0), 2) AS avg_recent,
       round(sum(coalesce(r.rating, 0))::numeric / count(*), 2) AS avg_zero_filled
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN reviews r
       ON r.product_id = p.id
      AND r.rating = 5
      AND r.created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01'
WHERE p.category = 'books'
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY p.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT p.id, p.name,
       count(r.id) AS recent_5star,
       round(avg(r.rating), 2) AS avg_recent,
       round(avg(coalesce(r.rating, 0)), 2) AS avg_zero_filled
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN reviews r
       ON r.product_id = p.id
      AND r.rating = 5
      AND r.created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01'
WHERE p.category = 'books'
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY p.id;

lessons.briefing:
# 67 - Drills: aggregates, set 1

Eight problems on lesson 06's five workhorses - `count`, `sum`, `min`, `max`,
`avg` - plus `DISTINCT` and `FILTER`. Every one of them returns a single row,
because that is what a bare aggregate query does, and the whole set is about
being precise on what exactly is being counted. If the difference between
`count(*)` and `count(col)` is not automatic yet, reread 06 first.

## Exercise 1 - the shape of one category

One row describing the `garden` products: `products` = how many there are,
`cheapest` = the lowest price, `dearest` = the highest price, and
`avg_price` = the average price rounded to 2 decimal places, in that column
order.

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 67_drills_aggregates_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - how many rows, how many things

Over the 1-star rows of `reviews`, return one row with `one_star` = how many
such reviews exist and `products_hit` = how many distinct products they are
spread across, in that column order.

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 67_drills_aggregates_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - summing a computed column

Over the rows of `order_items` whose `product_id` is 100 or less, return
`lines` = the number of item rows, `units` = the total `quantity`, and
`revenue` = the sum of `quantity * price` rounded to 2, in that column order.

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 67_drills_aggregates_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - min and max on timestamps

One row describing the time span covered by `orders`: `first_order` =
`min(created_at)`, `last_order` = `max(created_at)`, and `span_days` = the
number of whole days between them, computed by casting both to `date` and
subtracting.

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 67_drills_aggregates_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - several slices, one row

One row over all of `products`: `products` = the total number of rows,
`cheap` = how many cost less than 50, `dear` = how many cost more than 450,
and `avg_electronics` = the average price of the electronics products,
rounded to 2 - in that column order.

Use `FILTER (WHERE ...)` rather than four separate queries.

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 67_drills_aggregates_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - distinct counts skip the NULLs

One row about `staff`: `staff` = the number of rows, `managers` = the number
of distinct `manager_id` values, `departments` = the number of distinct
departments, and `payroll` = the sum of all salaries, in that column order.

Note that `managers` counts values, not rows - so the CEO's missing manager
does not become an entry.

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 67_drills_aggregates_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - a percentage that is not zero

One row of order KPIs: `paid_pct` = paid orders as a percentage of all
orders, rounded to 2 decimal places; `avg_paid` = the average `total` of paid
orders rounded to 2; `avg_other` = the average `total` of every order that is
not paid, rounded to 2 - in that column order.

Write the percentage as `100.0 * <paid count> / <total count>`, with the
decimal point, and rounded to 2.

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 67_drills_aggregates_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - an average of counts

How many item lines does an order carry, on average, when orders with no
items count as zero? Restrict to orders whose `id` is 5000 or less.

Return one row: `avg_items` = the average number of lines per order rounded
to 4 decimal places, `max_items` = the largest number of lines on any of
those orders, and `empty_orders` = how many of them have no items at all.

Count the lines per order first, in a subquery, then aggregate that result.
An outer join is what keeps the empty orders in the picture.

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 67_drills_aggregates_1 ex8`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 67_drills_aggregates_1

Eight single-row drills on the standard aggregates. Read after attempting
them, pass or fail.

## Notes

An aggregate query with no `GROUP BY` collapses its whole input to one row,
and the interesting decisions are all about what goes into that collapse.
Three of them recur through this set. What is being counted: rows
(`count(*)`), non-NULL values (`count(col)`), or distinct values
(`count(DISTINCT col)`), each a different number over the same column.
Which rows participate: a `WHERE` clause restricts the whole query, while
`FILTER (WHERE ...)` restricts one aggregate, which is how several different
slices land in one row. And what type comes out: `count` gives bigint, `sum`
and `avg` over numeric give numeric, and `avg` over an integer column gives
numeric too - so `100.0 * a / b` and `100 * a / b` are different queries, and
only one of them is right.

## ex1 - the shape of one category

The standard four-number summary, and the query you should be able to type
without thinking. Worth noticing: `price` is `NOT NULL`, so `count(*)` and
`count(price)` agree here - which is precisely why they cannot teach you
anything on this table, and why the next drills use columns where they
differ. The classic mistake is rounding with a single-argument `round`, which
takes the average to a whole number. Model answer: filter once in `WHERE`,
aggregate four times, round only for display.

## ex2 - how many rows, how many things

`count(*)` and `count(DISTINCT col)` answer questions that sound the same in
English and are not: the number of complaints versus the number of products
complained about. The gap between them is the average number of complaints
per affected product, which is usually the number somebody actually wanted.
The classic mistake is quoting the row count as though it were a count of
things. Model answer: one query, two counts, and a `WHERE` clause shared by
both.

## ex3 - summing a computed column

The most common arithmetic error in reporting SQL is aggregating before
multiplying. `sum(a * b)` adds up the per-row products; `sum(a) * sum(b)`
multiplies two unrelated totals and produces a number with no meaning, but
one that looks plausible enough to survive review. The classic mistake is
exactly that swap, usually introduced while "simplifying" a query. Model
answer: compute the per-row value inside the aggregate, because the line
value is a property of the line.

## ex4 - min and max on timestamps

Knowing the time span of a fact table is the first thing to establish before
writing any date-filtered report, and it is two aggregates. The subtlety is
the arithmetic: `date - date` yields an integer count of days, while
`timestamptz - timestamptz` yields an interval such as `364 days 21:56:03`,
which cannot be compared with a plain number. The classic mistake is mixing
the two and then trying to round an interval. Model answer: cast to `date`
first when you want whole days.

## ex5 - several slices, one row

`FILTER` is what makes single-row dashboards possible: one pass over the
table, four different populations, no subqueries and no self-joins. Before it
existed people wrote `sum(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`, which still
works and is worth being able to read. The classic mistake is putting the
slice condition in `WHERE` instead, which silently restricts every other
column in the row too. Model answer: `WHERE` for the population the whole
query is about, `FILTER` for the population one number is about.

## ex6 - distinct counts skip the NULLs

The asymmetry drilled here is worth memorising: `SELECT DISTINCT manager_id`
returns a NULL row, while `count(DISTINCT manager_id)` does not count it, so
the length of the first is one more than the value of the second. Both are
correct; they answer "how many different entries are there" and "how many
different managers are there". The classic mistake is deriving one from the
other and being off by one, which in a small company is invisible and in a
report is wrong.

## ex7 - a percentage that is not zero

The integer-division trap is the reason this drill exists: `100 * a / b`
evaluates left to right, so with bigint counts you get an integer percentage,
and `a / b * 100` gives you a flat zero. Writing `100.0` promotes the
expression to numeric before the division happens. The classic mistake
survives code review because a percentage of 16 instead of 16.66 looks like a
rounding choice. Model answer: one decimal point in the constant, and
`FILTER` for the numerator so the denominator still sees every row.

## ex8 - an average of counts

"Average per entity" always means two levels of aggregation, and the second
level is where the zeros are decided. With an inner join, orders with no
items never reach the outer average and the answer comes out too high; with
`count(*)` instead of `count(oi.id)`, the NULL-extended row counts as one
item and the answer comes out too high again, differently. The classic
mistake is dividing two grand totals instead - `count(items) / count(orders)`
- which happens to be right here but breaks the moment the prompt asks for a
median or a maximum. Model answer: aggregate per order, then aggregate the
aggregates.

## Further reading

- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - the full table, with the return type of each aggregate and the note that they all ignore NULL inputs.
- [Aggregate Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html#SYNTAX-AGGREGATES) - where `DISTINCT`, `ORDER BY` and `FILTER` may appear inside an aggregate call.
- [`FILTER` explained](https://modern-sql.com/feature/filter) - Markus Winand on why `FILTER` replaced `sum(CASE ...)`, with portability notes.
- [Numeric Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-numeric.html) - integer division, and why `numeric` is the money type in this schema.

rounded to 2 - in that column order.

Use `FILTER (WHERE ...)` rather than four separate queries.

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 67_drills_aggregates_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - distinct counts skip the NULLs

One row about `staff`: `staff` = the number of rows, `managers` = the number
of distinct `manager_id` values, `departments` = the number of distinct
departments, and `payroll` = the sum of all salaries, in that column order.

Note that `managers` counts values, not rows - so the CEO's missing manager
does not become an entry.

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 67_drills_aggregates_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - a percentage that is not zero

One row of order KPIs: `paid_pct` = paid orders as a percentage of all
orders, rounded to 2 decimal places; `avg_paid` = the average `total` of paid
orders rounded to 2; `avg_other` = the average `total` of every order that is
not paid, rounded to 2 - in that column order.

Write the percentage as `100.0 * <paid count> / <total count>`, with the
decimal point, and rounded to 2.

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 67_drills_aggregates_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - an average of counts

How many item lines does an order carry, on average, when orders with no
items count as zero? Restrict to orders whose `id` is 5000 or less.

Return one row: `avg_items` = the average number of lines per order rounded
to 4 decimal places, `max_items` = the largest number of lines on any of
those orders, and `empty_orders` = how many of them have no items at all.

Count the lines per order first, in a subquery, then aggregate that result.
An outer join is what keeps the empty orders in the picture.

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 67_drills_aggregates_1 ex8`

# Reading - 67_drills_aggregates_1

Eight single-row drills on the standard aggregates. Read after attempting
them, pass or fail.

## Notes

An aggregate query with no `GROUP BY` collapses its whole input to one row,
and the interesting decisions are all about what goes into that collapse.
Three of them recur through this set. What is being counted: rows
(`count(*)`), non-NULL values (`count(col)`), or distinct values
(`count(DISTINCT col)`), each a different number over the same column.
Which rows participate: a `WHERE` clause restricts the whole query, while
`FILTER (WHERE ...)` restricts one aggregate, which is how several different
slices land in one row. And what type comes out: `count` gives bigint, `sum`
and `avg` over numeric give numeric, and `avg` over an integer column gives
numeric too - so `100.0 * a / b` and `100 * a / b` are different queries, and
only one of them is right.

## ex1 - the shape of one category

The standard four-number summary, and the query you should be able to type
without thinking. Worth noticing: `price` is `NOT NULL`, so `count(*)` and
`count(price)` agree here - which is precisely why they cannot teach you
anything on this table, and why the next drills use columns where they
differ. The classic mistake is rounding with a single-argument `round`, which
takes the average to a whole number. Model answer: filter once in `WHERE`,
aggregate four times, round only for display.

## ex2 - how many rows, how many things

`count(*)` and `count(DISTINCT col)` answer questions that sound the same in
English and are not: the number of complaints versus the number of products
complained about. The gap between them is the average number of complaints
per affected product, which is usually the number somebody actually wanted.
The classic mistake is quoting the row count as though it were a count of
things. Model answer: one query, two counts, and a `WHERE` clause shared by
both.

## ex3 - summing a computed column

The most common arithmetic error in reporting SQL is aggregating before
multiplying. `sum(a * b)` adds up the per-row products; `sum(a) * sum(b)`
multiplies two unrelated totals and produces a number with no meaning, but
one that looks plausible enough to survive review. The classic mistake is
exactly that swap, usually introduced while "simplifying" a query. Model
answer: compute the per-row value inside the aggregate, because the line
value is a property of the line.

## ex4 - min and max on timestamps

Knowing the time span of a fact table is the first thing to establish before
writing any date-filtered report, and it is two aggregates. The subtlety is
the arithmetic: `date - date` yields an integer count of days, while
`timestamptz - timestamptz` yields an interval such as `364 days 21:56:03`,
which cannot be compared with a plain number. The classic mistake is mixing
the two and then trying to round an interval. Model answer: cast to `date`
first when you want whole days.

## ex5 - several slices, one row

`FILTER` is what makes single-row dashboards possible: one pass over the
table, four different populations, no subqueries and no self-joins. Before it
existed people wrote `sum(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`, which still
works and is worth being able to read. The classic mistake is putting the
slice condition in `WHERE` instead, which silently restricts every other
column in the row too. Model answer: `WHERE` for the population the whole
query is about, `FILTER` for the population one number is about.

## ex6 - distinct counts skip the NULLs

The asymmetry drilled here is worth memorising: `SELECT DISTINCT manager_id`
returns a NULL row, while `count(DISTINCT manager_id)` does not count it, so
the length of the first is one more than the value of the second. Both are
correct; they answer "how many different entries are there" and "how many
different managers are there". The classic mistake is deriving one from the
other and being off by one, which in a small company is invisible and in a
report is wrong.

## ex7 - a percentage that is not zero

The integer-division trap is the reason this drill exists: `100 * a / b`
evaluates left to right, so with bigint counts you get an integer percentage,
and `a / b * 100` gives you a flat zero. Writing `100.0` promotes the
expression to numeric before the division happens. The classic mistake
survives code review because a percentage of 16 instead of 16.66 looks like a
rounding choice. Model answer: one decimal point in the constant, and
`FILTER` for the numerator so the denominator still sees every row.

## ex8 - an average of counts

"Average per entity" always means two levels of aggregation, and the second
level is where the zeros are decided. With an inner join, orders with no
items never reach the outer average and the answer comes out too high; with
`count(*)` instead of `count(oi.id)`, the NULL-extended row counts as one
item and the answer comes out too high again, differently. The classic
mistake is dividing two grand totals instead - `count(items) / count(orders)`
- which happens to be right here but breaks the moment the prompt asks for a
median or a maximum. Model answer: aggregate per order, then aggregate the
aggregates.

## Further reading

- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - the full table, with the return type of each aggregate and the note that they all ignore NULL inputs.
- [Aggregate Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html#SYNTAX-AGGREGATES) - where `DISTINCT`, `ORDER BY` and `FILTER` may appear inside an aggregate call.
- [`FILTER` explained](https://modern-sql.com/feature/filter) - Markus Winand on why `FILTER` replaced `sum(CASE ...)`, with portability notes.
- [Numeric Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-numeric.html) - integer division, and why `numeric` is the money type in this schema.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 - the shape of one category

One row describing the `garden` products: `products` = how many there are,
`cheapest` = the lowest price, `dearest` = the highest price, and
`avg_price` = the average price rounded to 2 decimal places, in that column
order.

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 67_drills_aggregates_1 ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One `WHERE` clause restricts every aggregate in the row, so the category filter goes there rather than inside each function.

## Hint 2

`round(avg(price), 2)` - the two-argument `round` only exists for numeric, which is what `price` and its average already are.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Revenue is the sum of the line values, and a line's value is its quantity times its unit price. Multiply first, then sum.

## Hint 2

`sum(quantity * price)` and `sum(quantity) * sum(price)` are different numbers and only one of them is money. Write the first.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT count(id) AS lines,
       sum(quantity) AS units,
       round(sum(price * quantity), 2) AS revenue
FROM order_items
WHERE product_id <= 100;

SELECT count(*) AS lines,
       sum(quantity) AS units,
       round(sum(quantity * price), 2) AS revenue

WHERE product_id <= 100;

       max(created_at) AS last_order,
       (max(created_at)::date - min(created_at)::date)::int AS span_days

## Exercise 5 - several slices, one row

One row over all of `products`: `products` = the total number of rows,
`cheap` = how many cost less than 50, `dear` = how many cost more than 450,
and `avg_electronics` = the average price of the electronics products,
rounded to 2 - in that column order.

Use `FILTER (WHERE ...)` rather than four separate queries.

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 67_drills_aggregates_1 ex5`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`FILTER` attaches to a single aggregate call and restricts only that one: `count(*) FILTER (WHERE price < 50)`. The rest of the row still sees every product.

## Hint 2

It works on any aggregate, not just `count` - `avg(price) FILTER (WHERE category = 'electronics')` averages only the matching rows.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`FILTER` attaches to a single aggregate call and restricts only that one: `count(*) FILTER (WHERE price < 50)`. The rest of the row still sees every product.

## Hint 2

It works on any aggregate, not just `count` - `avg(price) FILTER (WHERE category = 'electronics')` averages only the matching rows.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS products,
       sum(CASE WHEN price < 50 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cheap,
       sum(CASE WHEN price > 450 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS dear,
       round(avg(CASE WHEN category = 'electronics' THEN price END), 2) AS avg_electronics
FROM products;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS products,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE price < 50) AS cheap,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE price > 450) AS dear,
       round(avg(price) FILTER (WHERE category = 'electronics'), 2) AS avg_electronics
FROM products;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 - distinct counts skip the NULLs

One row about `staff`: `staff` = the number of rows, `managers` = the number
of distinct `manager_id` values, `departments` = the number of distinct
departments, and `payroll` = the sum of all salaries, in that column order.

Note that `managers` counts values, not rows - so the CEO's missing manager
does not become an entry.

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 67_drills_aggregates_1 ex6`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`count(DISTINCT col)` counts distinct non-NULL values. `SELECT DISTINCT col` would return a row for NULL as well - the two disagree by exactly one here.

## Hint 2

All four numbers come from one pass over the same table, so this is a single `SELECT` with no subqueries and no `GROUP BY`.

## Hint 1

`count(DISTINCT col)` counts distinct non-NULL values. `SELECT DISTINCT col` would return a row for NULL as well - the two disagree by exactly one here.

## Hint 2

All four numbers come from one pass over the same table, so this is a single `SELECT` with no subqueries and no `GROUP BY`.

SELECT count(*) AS staff,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT manager_id FROM staff
                              WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL) m) AS managers,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT department FROM staff) d) AS departments,
       sum(salary) AS payroll
FROM staff;

SELECT count(*) AS staff,
       count(DISTINCT manager_id) AS managers,

## Hint 1

references.solution.sql:
SELECT round(100.0 * sum(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / count(*), 2) AS paid_pct,
       round(avg(total) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid'), 2) AS avg_paid,
       round(avg(CASE WHEN status <> 'paid' THEN total END), 2) AS avg_other
FROM orders;

FROM orders;

How many item lines does an order carry, on average, when orders with no

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Aggregates do not nest: `avg(count(*))` is an error. The count has to finish in an inner query before the average can start on its output.

## Hint 2

Inner query: one row per order with `count(oi.id)` as the line count, using a LEFT JOIN so item-less orders survive with a count of 0. Outer query: the three aggregates over those rows.

references.solution.sql:
WITH per_order AS (
  SELECT o.id, count(oi.id) AS items
  FROM orders o
  LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
  WHERE o.id <= 5000
  GROUP BY o.id)
SELECT round(avg(items), 4) AS avg_items,
       max(items) AS max_items,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE items = 0) AS empty_orders
FROM per_order;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT round(avg(items), 4) AS avg_items,
       max(items) AS max_items,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE items = 0) AS empty_orders
FROM (SELECT o.id, count(oi.id) AS items
      FROM orders o
      LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
      WHERE o.id <= 5000
      GROUP BY o.id) t;

# 68 - Drills: aggregates, set 2

Set 1 drilled which rows go into an aggregate. These eight drill the
arithmetic that happens once they are in there - weighted averages, averages
that fill blanks with zero, shares of a total, and aggregates computed on top
of other aggregates. Source lesson is 06; the last two also lean on the
subquery habit from 13.

## Exercise 1 - one product's reviews

One row summarising the reviews of product 42: `reviews` = how many there
are, `avg_rating` = the average rating rounded to 2 decimal places, `worst` =
the lowest rating, `best` = the highest, in that column order.

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 68_drills_aggregates_2 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - the shape of the customer table

One row about `customers`: `customers` = the number of rows, `countries` =
the number of distinct countries, `first_signup` = the earliest
`created_at`, `last_signup` = the latest, in that column order.

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 68_drills_aggregates_2 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - units, revenue, and the average line

Over the `order_items` rows belonging to orders with `order_id` of 2000 or
less: `units` = the total quantity, `revenue` = the sum of
`quantity * price` rounded to 2, and `avg_line` = the average of
`quantity * price` rounded to 2, in that column order.

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 68_drills_aggregates_2 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - zero-filled average versus filtered average

Two averages of the same column over `orders`, which are not the same number:

- `avg_zero_filled` = the average of `total` across **all** orders, with
  non-paid orders contributing 0. Write it as
  `avg(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN total ELSE 0 END)`, rounded to 2.
- `avg_paid_only` = the average of `total` over only the paid orders,
  rounded to 2.
- `paid_orders` = how many paid orders there are.

Return them in that column order, in one row.

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 68_drills_aggregates_2 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - weighted versus unweighted

Over the `order_items` rows with `product_id` of 500 or less, return
`weighted_unit_price` = `sum(quantity * price) / sum(quantity)` rounded to 4
decimal places, `plain_avg_price` = `avg(price)` rounded to 4, and `units` =
the total quantity, in that column order.

The first two numbers are both "the average price" and they are not equal.

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 68_drills_aggregates_2 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - distinct counting with a filter on top

One row over `orders`: `orders` = the row count, `customers` = how many
distinct customers appear, `cancellers` = how many distinct customers appear
among the cancelled orders, and `months` = how many distinct values
`date_trunc('month', created_at)` takes - in that column order.

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 68_drills_aggregates_2 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - a share of the total, in one pass

Over the `order_items` rows with `product_id` of 200 or less, return
`revenue` = the sum of `quantity * price` rounded to 2, `single_unit_revenue`
= the same sum restricted to lines with `quantity = 1`, rounded to 2, and
`single_unit_pct` = the second as a percentage of the first, rounded to 2 -
in that column order.

Write the percentage with `100.0` so the division is not integer division.

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 68_drills_aggregates_2 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - the aggregate of an aggregate

How lopsided is review coverage within the `food` category? Count the reviews
per product first (only products that have at least one review can appear),
then describe that distribution in one row: `products_reviewed` = how many
products it covers, `max_reviews` = the largest count, `min_reviews` = the
smallest, `avg_reviews` = the average count rounded to 2 - in that column
order.

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 68_drills_aggregates_2 ex8`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 68_drills_aggregates_2

Eight drills on aggregate arithmetic. Read them after your attempt - several
of these have a right answer and a plausible wrong one that differ by a rule
rather than by a typo.

## Notes

Once the rows are chosen, an aggregate is just arithmetic, and the arithmetic
has an order of operations that most reporting bugs violate. Multiply before
you sum (`sum(a * b)`), because the product is a property of the row. Divide
after you sum (`sum(a) / sum(b)`) when you want a weighted average, because
the weights live in the denominator - and note that this is a different
number from `avg(a / b)`, which weights every row equally. Decide explicitly
whether missing rows should count as zero: `avg(x) FILTER (WHERE cond)`
averages the matching rows, `avg(CASE WHEN cond THEN x ELSE 0 END)` averages
all of them with zeros filled in, and the two answers can differ by a factor
of two. And when a question needs an aggregate of an aggregate - the average
of a count, the maximum of a sum - the inner one has to finish in a subquery
or CTE first, because aggregates cannot nest.

## ex1 - one product's reviews

A warm-up, but with one real point in it: `avg` over an integer column
returns numeric rather than truncating, which is why `avg(rating)` can be
3.04 even though no rating ever is. The classic mistake is computing an
average as `sum(rating) / count(*)` without a cast, which in integer
arithmetic floors the result to 3 and looks almost right. Model answer: use
`avg`, and round only because the prompt asked for two decimals.

## ex2 - the shape of the customer table

This is the query to run first whenever you meet an unfamiliar table: how
many rows, how many distinct values in the column you plan to group by, and
what period it covers. Those three numbers tell you whether a `GROUP BY
country` will return a readable dozen rows or fifty thousand. The classic
mistake is skipping it and discovering the cardinality from a report that
scrolls for a minute. Model answer: one pass, four aggregates, no subqueries.

## ex3 - units, revenue, and the average line

Two averages hide in every line-item table and they answer different
questions: the average value of a line, and the average price of a unit. This
drill asks for the first, which weights every line equally regardless of how
many units it moved. The classic mistake is treating them as interchangeable
in a summary table, so that two numbers which should agree do not, and nobody
can say why. Model answer: `avg(quantity * price)`, and say in the column
name what the row unit is.

## ex4 - zero-filled average versus filtered average

The most consequential one-character difference in reporting SQL: an `ELSE 0`
that should have been an `ELSE NULL`. Both queries are legitimate - "average
revenue per order including the ones that did not pay" is a real metric - but
they differ by roughly the paid share of the table, and only one of them can
be labelled "average paid order value". The classic mistake is copying a
`sum(CASE ... ELSE 0 END)` idiom, which is correct for sums, straight into an
`avg`, where the zeros are extra rows in the denominator. Model answer:
`FILTER` when you want the population restricted, `ELSE 0` only when you
really want the zeros counted.

## ex5 - weighted versus unweighted

The distinction between a weighted and an unweighted average is the one that
turns up in every price, rate and score aggregation, and the difference is
which unit the average is "per". `avg(price)` is the average price per line
of paperwork; `sum(qty * price) / sum(qty)` is the average price per unit
sold. The classic mistake is quoting the first as though it were the second,
which biases the answer towards products that sell one at a time. Model
answer: sum the numerator, sum the denominator, divide once.

## ex6 - distinct counting with a filter on top

Three flavours of counting in one row, and each is a different question about
the same half-million orders: how many transactions, how many people, how
many people in one segment, how many periods. The one that surprises people
is the last - counting distinct values of an expression is how you measure
coverage without grouping. The classic mistake is `count(DISTINCT *)`, which
does not exist, or assuming `FILTER` has to come before `DISTINCT`. Model
answer: DISTINCT inside, FILTER outside.

## ex7 - a share of the total, in one pass

"X as a percentage of the total" is the single most requested column in
reporting, and inside one aggregate query it needs no subquery at all: the
filtered aggregate is the numerator, the unfiltered one is the denominator.
The classic mistakes are two - integer division flooring the result to zero,
and rounding the inputs before dividing, which introduces error that then
gets multiplied by a hundred. Model answer: `100.0 *` filtered `/`
unfiltered, `round` once at the end.

## ex8 - the aggregate of an aggregate

Distribution questions - biggest, smallest, average per entity - are always
two-stage, and the stage boundary is the thing to see: the inner query
decides what one row means (one product), the outer query summarises those
rows. Because the join filters to `food` before grouping, `count(*)` in the
outer query counts food products with reviews, not all food products; a
product with zero reviews cannot appear in an inner-joined result at all,
which is a limitation worth naming rather than papering over. The classic
mistake is nesting the aggregates directly and reading the error message as a
syntax problem instead of a levels problem.

## Further reading

- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - return types matter here: `avg` over integers gives numeric, `sum` over numeric stays numeric.
- [Subquery Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) - the reference for the scalar subqueries used in the last two drills.
- [`WITH` queries (CTEs)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) - the readable way to stage an inner aggregate before aggregating it again.
- [Numeric Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-numeric.html) - integer division, numeric precision, and why money is `numeric` in this schema.

# Reading - 68_drills_aggregates_2

Eight drills on aggregate arithmetic. Read them after your attempt - several
of these have a right answer and a plausible wrong one that differ by a rule
rather than by a typo.

## Notes

Once the rows are chosen, an aggregate is just arithmetic, and the arithmetic
has an order of operations that most reporting bugs violate. Multiply before
you sum (`sum(a * b)`), because the product is a property of the row. Divide
after you sum (`sum(a) / sum(b)`) when you want a weighted average, because
the weights live in the denominator - and note that this is a different
number from `avg(a / b)`, which weights every row equally. Decide explicitly
whether missing rows should count as zero: `avg(x) FILTER (WHERE cond)`
averages the matching rows, `avg(CASE WHEN cond THEN x ELSE 0 END)` averages
all of them with zeros filled in, and the two answers can differ by a factor
of two. And when a question needs an aggregate of an aggregate - the average
of a count, the maximum of a sum - the inner one has to finish in a subquery
or CTE first, because aggregates cannot nest.

## ex1 - one product's reviews

A warm-up, but with one real point in it: `avg` over an integer column
returns numeric rather than truncating, which is why `avg(rating)` can be
3.04 even though no rating ever is. The classic mistake is computing an
average as `sum(rating) / count(*)` without a cast, which in integer
arithmetic floors the result to 3 and looks almost right. Model answer: use
`avg`, and round only because the prompt asked for two decimals.

## ex2 - the shape of the customer table

This is the query to run first whenever you meet an unfamiliar table: how
many rows, how many distinct values in the column you plan to group by, and
what period it covers. Those three numbers tell you whether a `GROUP BY
country` will return a readable dozen rows or fifty thousand. The classic
mistake is skipping it and discovering the cardinality from a report that
scrolls for a minute. Model answer: one pass, four aggregates, no subqueries.

## ex3 - units, revenue, and the average line

Two averages hide in every line-item table and they answer different
questions: the average value of a line, and the average price of a unit. This
drill asks for the first, which weights every line equally regardless of how
many units it moved. The classic mistake is treating them as interchangeable
in a summary table, so that two numbers which should agree do not, and nobody
can say why. Model answer: `avg(quantity * price)`, and say in the column
name what the row unit is.

## ex4 - zero-filled average versus filtered average

The most consequential one-character difference in reporting SQL: an `ELSE 0`
that should have been an `ELSE NULL`. Both queries are legitimate - "average
revenue per order including the ones that did not pay" is a real metric - but
they differ by roughly the paid share of the table, and only one of them can
be labelled "average paid order value". The classic mistake is copying a
`sum(CASE ... ELSE 0 END)` idiom, which is correct for sums, straight into an
`avg`, where the zeros are extra rows in the denominator. Model answer:
`FILTER` when you want the population restricted, `ELSE 0` only when you
really want the zeros counted.

## ex5 - weighted versus unweighted

The distinction between a weighted and an unweighted average is the one that
turns up in every price, rate and score aggregation, and the difference is
which unit the average is "per". `avg(price)` is the average price per line
of paperwork; `sum(qty * price) / sum(qty)` is the average price per unit
sold. The classic mistake is quoting the first as though it were the second,
which biases the answer towards products that sell one at a time. Model
answer: sum the numerator, sum the denominator, divide once.

## ex6 - distinct counting with a filter on top

Three flavours of counting in one row, and each is a different question about
the same half-million orders: how many transactions, how many people, how
many people in one segment, how many periods. The one that surprises people
is the last - counting distinct values of an expression is how you measure
coverage without grouping. The classic mistake is `count(DISTINCT *)`, which
does not exist, or assuming `FILTER` has to come before `DISTINCT`. Model
answer: DISTINCT inside, FILTER outside.

## ex7 - a share of the total, in one pass

"X as a percentage of the total" is the single most requested column in
reporting, and inside one aggregate query it needs no subquery at all: the
filtered aggregate is the numerator, the unfiltered one is the denominator.
The classic mistakes are two - integer division flooring the result to zero,
and rounding the inputs before dividing, which introduces error that then
gets multiplied by a hundred. Model answer: `100.0 *` filtered `/`
unfiltered, `round` once at the end.

## ex8 - the aggregate of an aggregate

Distribution questions - biggest, smallest, average per entity - are always
two-stage, and the stage boundary is the thing to see: the inner query
decides what one row means (one product), the outer query summarises those
rows. Because the join filters to `food` before grouping, `count(*)` in the
outer query counts food products with reviews, not all food products; a
product with zero reviews cannot appear in an inner-joined result at all,
which is a limitation worth naming rather than papering over. The classic
mistake is nesting the aggregates directly and reading the error message as a
syntax problem instead of a levels problem.

## Further reading

- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - return types matter here: `avg` over integers gives numeric, `sum` over numeric stays numeric.
- [Subquery Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) - the reference for the scalar subqueries used in the last two drills.
- [`WITH` queries (CTEs)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) - the readable way to stage an inner aggregate before aggregating it again.
- [Numeric Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-numeric.html) - integer division, numeric precision, and why money is `numeric` in this schema.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 - one product's reviews

One row summarising the reviews of product 42: `reviews` = how many there
are, `avg_rating` = the average rating rounded to 2 decimal places, `worst` =
the lowest rating, `best` = the highest, in that column order.

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 68_drills_aggregates_2 ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`rating` is an integer column, so its average is not an integer - `avg` returns numeric and `round(x, 2)` works on it directly.

## Hint 2

One `WHERE product_id = 42` restricts all four aggregates; none of them needs a FILTER.

SELECT count(rating) AS reviews,

       min(rating) AS worst,
       max(rating) AS best
FROM reviews
WHERE product_id = 42;

SELECT count(*) AS reviews,
       round(avg(rating), 2) AS avg_rating,

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The per-row expression `quantity * price` is the line value. Both the sum and the average are taken over that expression, not over the columns separately.

## Hint 2

`avg(quantity * price)` is the average line value. `sum(quantity * price) / sum(quantity)` would be something else entirely - the average price per unit, which is drilled in exercise 5.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT sum(quantity) AS units,
       round(sum(quantity * price), 2) AS revenue,
       round(sum(quantity * price) / count(*), 2) AS avg_line
FROM order_items
WHERE order_id <= 2000;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 - zero-filled average versus filtered average

Two averages of the same column over `orders`, which are not the same number:

- `avg_zero_filled` = the average of `total` across **all** orders, with
  non-paid orders contributing 0. Write it as
  `avg(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN total ELSE 0 END)`, rounded to 2.
- `avg_paid_only` = the average of `total` over only the paid orders,
  rounded to 2.
- `paid_orders` = how many paid orders there are.

Return them in that column order, in one row.

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 68_drills_aggregates_2 ex4`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The difference is the denominator. One average divides by every order; the other divides only by the paid ones, because `avg` ignores NULL inputs and `FILTER` removes rows from that aggregate entirely.

## Hint 2

`CASE WHEN cond THEN total ELSE 0 END` feeds a zero into the average. `CASE WHEN cond THEN total END` - with no ELSE - feeds a NULL, which `avg` skips, making it equivalent to the FILTER form.

FROM orders;

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`DISTINCT` and `FILTER` can appear on the same aggregate call: `count(DISTINCT col) FILTER (WHERE ...)`. The DISTINCT goes inside the parentheses, the FILTER after them.

You can count distinct values of an expression, not just of a column - `count(DISTINCT date_trunc('month', created_at))` is how you ask how many months the table spans.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`DISTINCT` and `FILTER` can appear on the same aggregate call: `count(DISTINCT col) FILTER (WHERE ...)`. The DISTINCT goes inside the parentheses, the FILTER after them.

## Hint 2

You can count distinct values of an expression, not just of a column - `count(DISTINCT date_trunc('month', created_at))` is how you ask how many months the table spans.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS orders,
       count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers,
       count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN status = 'cancelled' THEN customer_id END) AS cancellers,
       count(DISTINCT date_trunc('month', created_at)) AS months
FROM orders;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS orders,
       count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers,
       count(DISTINCT customer_id) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled') AS cancellers,
       count(DISTINCT date_trunc('month', created_at)) AS months
FROM orders;

SELECT round(sum(quantity * price), 2) AS revenue,
       round(sum(CASE WHEN quantity = 1 THEN quantity * price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS single_unit_revenue,

FROM order_items

             / sum(quantity * price), 2) AS single_unit_pct
FROM order_items
WHERE product_id <= 200;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

You cannot write `max(count(*))`. The inner aggregate must be computed by a subquery or CTE whose rows are then aggregated by the outer query.

## Hint 2

Stage it: the inner query joins `reviews` to `products`, keeps the food
category, and groups by the product to produce one row per product with its
review count. The outer query then runs its four aggregates over those rows.

references.solution.sql:
WITH per_product AS (
  SELECT r.product_id, count(*) AS reviews
  FROM reviews r
  JOIN products p ON p.id = r.product_id
  WHERE p.category = 'food'
  GROUP BY r.product_id)
SELECT count(*) AS products_reviewed,
       max(reviews) AS max_reviews,
       min(reviews) AS min_reviews,
       round(avg(reviews), 2) AS avg_reviews
FROM per_product;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS products_reviewed,
       max(reviews) AS max_reviews,
       min(reviews) AS min_reviews,
       round(avg(reviews), 2) AS avg_reviews
FROM (SELECT r.product_id, count(*) AS reviews
      FROM reviews r
      JOIN products p ON p.id = r.product_id
      WHERE p.category = 'food'
      GROUP BY r.product_id) t;

# 69 - Drills: aggregates, set 3

The last aggregates set, and the one closest to the work: KPI rows built
entirely out of `FILTER`, counting that stays honest about NULLs, and two
finishers that aggregate across a join. Source lesson is 06 throughout, with
08 and 09 supplying the joins in exercises 7 and 8.

## Exercise 1 - the order KPI row

One row of order KPIs, in this column order: `paid_revenue` = the sum of
`total` over paid orders rounded to 2, `cancelled_revenue` = the same for
cancelled orders rounded to 2, `pending_orders` = how many orders are
pending, and `orders` = how many orders there are altogether.

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 69_drills_aggregates_3 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - the staff KPI row

One row about `staff`, in this column order: `payroll` = the sum of salaries
rounded to 2, `avg_salary` = the average salary rounded to 2, `top_salary` =
the highest salary, `first_hire` = the earliest `hired_on`, and `rootless` =
how many staff have no manager.

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 69_drills_aggregates_3 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - a histogram in a single row

Turn the rating distribution of `reviews` sideways. Return one row with six
columns in this order: `r1`, `r2`, `r3`, `r4`, `r5` - the number of reviews
with each rating from 1 to 5 - and `total` = the number of reviews
altogether.

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 69_drills_aggregates_3 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - extremes and how many values there are

One row about product prices: `cheapest` = the minimum price, `dearest` = the
maximum, `distinct_prices` = how many different price values exist, and
`spread` = `max(price) - min(price)` rounded to 2 - in that column order.

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 69_drills_aggregates_3 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - counting people, not orders

One row about the customers behind the orders, in this column order:
`buyers` = how many distinct customers appear in `orders`, `paid_buyers` =
how many distinct customers have at least one paid order, `cancel_buyers` =
how many have at least one cancelled order, and `whale_buyers` = how many
have at least one order with a `total` above 1900.

The three filtered counts overlap - a customer can be in all of them.

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 69_drills_aggregates_3 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - ratios between aggregates

One row of derived ratios over `orders`, in this column order: `orders` =
the row count, `buyers` = the number of distinct customers,
`orders_per_buyer` = orders divided by buyers as numeric rounded to 3, and
`revenue_per_buyer` = `sum(total)` divided by buyers rounded to 2.

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 69_drills_aggregates_3 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - review health for one category

Join `reviews` to `products` and describe the electronics category in one
row, in this column order: `reviews` = how many reviews electronics products
have, `products_covered` = how many distinct products those reviews touch,
`avg_rating` = the average rating rounded to 2, and `negative_pct` = the
percentage of those reviews rated 2 or lower, rounded to 2.

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 69_drills_aggregates_3 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - customers who never bought

Describe the Japanese customer base in one row, counting the customers who
have never ordered anything. Outer-join `customers` to `orders` and return,
in this column order: `customers` = the number of distinct JP customers,
`buyers` = how many of them have at least one order, `orders` = the total
number of orders they placed, `revenue` = the sum of those totals rounded to
2 (0 if there were none), and `orders_per_customer` = orders divided by
customers as numeric, rounded to 4.

The join must be a LEFT JOIN and the country filter belongs to `customers`.

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 69_drills_aggregates_3 ex8`

# Reading - 69_drills_aggregates_3

Eight drills on conditional aggregation and counting things that may not be
there. Read after your attempt.

## Notes

A KPI row is a single `SELECT` in which every column is an aggregate over a
different slice of the same scan, and `FILTER (WHERE ...)` is what makes that
possible: the query reads the table once and each number decides for itself
which rows it wants. Two things keep such a row honest. First, be explicit
about which counting question each column asks - rows, non-NULL values, or
distinct values - because on a joined result all three differ, and
`count(DISTINCT c.id)` is often the only one that means "customers". Second,
remember that an aggregate over no matching rows returns NULL rather than
zero for everything except `count`, so any figure that must read as 0 needs
`coalesce` on the outside. Ratios need the same care they always did: promote
to numeric before dividing, and round once, at the end.

## ex1 - the order KPI row

This is the shape of nine out of ten summary queries in a real reporting
codebase: one table, one scan, several `FILTER`ed aggregates, and a grand
total that must not be filtered. The classic mistake is putting the first
condition in `WHERE` because it feels natural, which quietly turns the final
`count(*)` into a count of paid orders. Model answer: `WHERE` describes the
report's population, `FILTER` describes one column's population, and here the
report's population is everything.

## ex2 - the staff KPI row

Five aggregates over five different ideas - a total, a central tendency, an
extreme, a boundary date, and a data-quality count - which is roughly the
anatomy of every "state of the table" query. The last column is the one worth
practising both ways, because `count(*) - count(col)` is the idiom that tells
you how many values are missing without a FILTER, and it generalises to any
column you suspect of being sparse.

## ex3 - a histogram in a single row

This is a pivot done by hand, and it is the honest way to do one in
PostgreSQL: the set of output columns is fixed at write time, so the values
must be known in advance - here, ratings 1 to 5. That is the essential
limitation of pivoting in SQL, and the reason lesson 17 spends its time on it
rather than on syntax. The classic mistake is expecting a `GROUP BY` to
produce columns; it produces rows, and turning rows into columns is a
different operation. The self-check in Hint 2 is the habit worth keeping.

## ex4 - extremes and how many values there are

Two aggregates can be combined arithmetically in the SELECT list because both
have already collapsed to scalars - this is the same reason `sum(a) /
sum(b)` works and `sum(a) / b` does not. The third column is the interesting
one: comparing distinct values against row count is how you find out whether
a column behaves like an identifier, a category, or a measurement. The
classic mistake is `count(DISTINCT *)`, which is not valid syntax; DISTINCT
inside an aggregate applies to one expression.

## ex5 - counting people, not orders

Counting people rather than events is the difference between "we processed
half a million orders" and "we served forty-five thousand customers", and
`count(DISTINCT customer_id)` with a `FILTER` is the whole technique. The
classic mistake is assuming the segments partition the customer base and
building a pie chart out of overlapping counts. Model answer: distinct
counting per segment, and a sentence in the report saying the segments
overlap.

## ex6 - ratios between aggregates

Per-entity ratios are the most-quoted numbers in any business review and the
easiest to compute wrongly, because the numerator and the denominator count
different things: rows over distinct values. The type rule bites here too -
`count(*) / count(DISTINCT ...)` is integer division and returns 11 where the
truth is 11.121. The classic mistake is rounding an already-truncated
integer and believing the trailing zeros. Model answer: cast once, divide
once, round once.

## ex7 - review health for one category

The first drill in this set where `count(*)` and `count(DISTINCT ...)` count
genuinely different things: after a join, one row is one review, so the row
count is reviews and the distinct count is products. Getting that wrong turns
"1,666 products" into "166,000 products" and nobody notices, because both
numbers are plausible. The classic mistake is filtering on the joined table
in the `ON` clause here - harmless for an inner join, but a habit that
becomes a bug the moment somebody changes it to a LEFT JOIN.

## ex8 - customers who never bought

Every counting rule in this lesson meets at once here. On a left-joined
result `count(*)` counts join rows (orders, plus one phantom per customer
with none), `count(o.id)` counts real orders, `count(DISTINCT c.id)` counts
customers, and `count(DISTINCT o.customer_id)` counts buyers - four different
numbers from one result set. The classic mistake is moving the country filter
into the `ON` clause, which keeps every customer in the world in the result
and inflates the denominator. Model answer: filter the preserved side in
`WHERE`, count each thing with the aggregate that means it, and `coalesce`
the sum so an empty segment reads as 0 rather than blank.

## Further reading

- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - the whole table, plus the note that every aggregate but `count` returns NULL over an empty input.
- [`FILTER` explained](https://modern-sql.com/feature/filter) - conditional aggregation before and after the FILTER clause existed.
- [Joins Between Tables](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-join.html) - the outer-join semantics that exercise 8 aggregates over.
- [Date/Time Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) - `min`/`max` on timestamps and dates, used in the staff KPI row.

One row about the customers behind the orders, in this column order:
`buyers` = how many distinct customers appear in `orders`, `paid_buyers` =
how many distinct customers have at least one paid order, `cancel_buyers` =
how many have at least one cancelled order, and `whale_buyers` = how many
have at least one order with a `total` above 1900.

The three filtered counts overlap - a customer can be in all of them.

One row of derived ratios over `orders`, in this column order: `orders` =
the row count, `buyers` = the number of distinct customers,
`orders_per_buyer` = orders divided by buyers as numeric rounded to 3, and
`revenue_per_buyer` = `sum(total)` divided by buyers rounded to 2.

have, `products_covered` = how many distinct products those reviews touch,
`avg_rating` = the average rating rounded to 2, and `negative_pct` = the
percentage of those reviews rated 2 or lower, rounded to 2.

Describe the Japanese customer base in one row, counting the customers who
have never ordered anything. Outer-join `customers` to `orders` and return,

`buyers` = how many of them have at least one order, `orders` = the total
