# Reading - 76_drills_outer_joins_1

Outer joins, and the small number of ways they go wrong. Every problem in
this set is one of them.

## Notes

**An outer join is a promise about the left side.** `A LEFT JOIN B` says:
every row of `A` appears in the output at least once. Where a matching `B`
row exists you get the pair; where none exists you get the `A` row with every
`B` column set to NULL. That invented row is called a NULL-extension, and
almost every bug in this set is a query that destroys one somewhere.

**`count(*)` counts rows; `count(col)` counts values.** A NULL-extended row
is a row, so `count(*)` in a group with no matches returns 1. `count(b.id)`
skips NULLs and returns 0. This is the single most common outer-join defect
in production reporting, and it is invisible until somebody notices that
nobody has zero of anything.

**`sum` over nothing is NULL, not zero.** Counts recover on their own;
sums, averages, mins and maxes do not. `coalesce(sum(x), 0)` is the fix, and
you have to decide consciously whether zero is even the honest answer - for a
sum it usually is, for an average it usually is not.

**A restriction on the right table belongs in `ON`.** `WHERE b.something =
'x'` is evaluated after the join, and it is false for every NULL-extended
row, so it silently deletes them and turns your outer join into an inner one.
Putting the same predicate in the `ON` clause makes it part of what counts as
a match instead, and the unmatched left rows survive. A restriction on the
*left* table is unaffected either way, which is why the rule is easy to
half-learn.

**`RIGHT` is `LEFT` with the tables swapped.** There is no third semantics to
memorise: decide which table must survive, then put it on the surviving side
of the keyword. Most codebases write everything as `LEFT` for consistency,
which is a fine convention as long as you can read the other one.

**Outer-ness has to survive every hop.** In a three-table chain, one inner
join anywhere downstream throws away the rows the outer join was protecting.
And once a second one-to-many join enters the query, counts start
double-counting: `count(DISTINCT ...)` is the repair for a count, and
pre-aggregating each branch is the repair for everything else.

## ex1 - the customers who never bought anything

The most-used outer join there is: a dimension, its facts, and a requirement
that the dimension come back whole. An inner join answers a different
question - "customers who have ordered" - and answers it correctly, which is
why the bug survives review.

The classic mistake is `count(*)`. The customers with no orders are exactly
the rows you added the `LEFT JOIN` to keep, and `count(*)` reports 1 for each
of them, so the report says every Spanish customer has ordered at least once.

The model answer left-joins orders onto customers, groups by the customer,
and counts `o.id` - a column that is NULL precisely when the NULL-extension
happened. The reference solution takes the other good route: aggregate orders
per customer first, then left-join that summary and `coalesce` the miss.

## ex2 - counts and sums behave differently

Roughly one order in seven in this dataset has no line items at all, so this
is the same shape as ex1 with one extra wrinkle: two measures that fail in
two different ways.

The classic mistake is `coalesce`ing neither, or both, without thinking.
`count(oi.id)` is already 0 for an empty group; wrapping it in `coalesce`
does nothing and suggests you have not worked out why. `sum(oi.quantity)`
over an empty group is NULL - SQL's aggregate functions ignore NULL inputs,
and the sum of no numbers is undefined rather than zero - so that one does
need the wrapper.

The model answer left-joins the lines, groups by the order, and treats the
two measures differently on purpose.

## ex3 - the raw shape, before any grouping

Strip the aggregation away and you can see what a `LEFT JOIN` actually
produces: one output row per matching pair, plus one NULL-extended row for
each left row that matched nothing. Being able to picture this is what makes
the aggregated versions obvious rather than magical.

The classic mistake is expecting NULLs where there are matches. A customer
with eleven orders contributes eleven rows and no NULLs; only the customers
with zero orders get the invented row. The second mistake is the ordering:
Postgres sorts NULLs **last** in ascending order by default, so producing
them first takes an explicit `NULLS FIRST`.

The model answer is a plain `LEFT JOIN` with both customer predicates in
`WHERE`, which is safe because they restrict the left table. The reference
solution spells the semantics out literally - an inner join `UNION ALL` the
unmatched rows with NULLs supplied by hand - which is exactly what a `LEFT
JOIN` means and worth reading once.

## ex4 - the same thing, mirrored

`RIGHT JOIN` keeps every row of the table on its right. That is the whole
definition. The exercise forces the direction so that the mirror gets
practised rather than avoided, because you will read code that uses it.

The classic mistake here is not the keyword, it is the predicates. `rating =
5` and the date restriction describe which reviews count as a match, so they
belong in the `ON` clause; move either into `WHERE` and every product without
a recent 5-star review is deleted from the report - the exact thing the outer
join was there to prevent.

The model answer puts all three conditions on the reviews side into `ON`,
keeps the two product predicates in `WHERE` (they restrict the surviving
table, so they are safe there), and counts `r.id`.

## ex5 - inner and outer in the same query

Two joins, two different jobs. `customers` is present only to supply the
country filter, and every order has a customer, so that join can and should
be inner. `order_items` is present to be counted, and an order with no
`quantity = 5` line still belongs in the report, so that one must be outer.

The classic mistake is a blanket policy - making everything a `LEFT JOIN`
"to be safe", or making everything inner out of habit. Mixing them in one
`FROM` is completely normal; the question to ask at each join is "can this
side legitimately have nothing, and do I still want the row if it does?"

The model answer inner-joins the customer, left-joins the lines with
`quantity = 5` in the `ON`, and counts `oi.id`.

## ex6 - print the bug next to the fix

This one is deliberately artificial: both columns come from the same grouped
outer join and differ only in what is being counted. Seeing `1` and `0` on
the same row is the fastest way to make the distinction permanent.

The classic mistake is assuming `count(*)` and `count(col)` are
interchangeable because on inner joins they usually are. They diverge exactly
where outer joins matter, which is exactly where you are least likely to be
checking.

The model answer groups the left join and writes both counts; note that the
`total > 1900` restriction has to be in the `ON` clause, or there would be no
unmatched customers left to demonstrate anything.

## ex7 - outer-ness has to survive two hops

A customer with no orders has no order lines either, so the second join has
nothing to match. Write it as an inner join and those customers vanish from
the answer - the `LEFT JOIN` in the first hop bought you nothing, because the
second hop threw the rows away again.

The classic mistake after fixing that is the order count. Once `order_items`
is in the `FROM`, a three-line order contributes three rows, so `count(o.id)`
counts lines and labels them orders. `count(DISTINCT o.id)` is what survives
the fan-out; `sum(oi.quantity)` is already at line grain and is correct as it
stands, but still needs `coalesce` for the customers with nothing.

The model answer chains two `LEFT JOIN`s and mixes `count(DISTINCT ...)` with
a coalesced `sum`. The reference pre-aggregates orders and lines per customer
in a subquery and joins the summary, which is the shape that scales to five
measures without any of this reasoning.

## ex8 - two branches, both outer

Order lines and reviews are independent branches hanging off the same
product. Join both and the rows multiply: a product with 20 qualifying lines
and 2 qualifying reviews produces 40 rows, and both plain counts report 40.
The result is not a little wrong, it is wrong by the size of the other
branch.

The classic mistake is trusting the number because it is plausible. Forty
lines for a popular toy looks fine; the only way to catch it is to know the
shape of your `FROM` and count the join paths.

The model answer uses `count(DISTINCT oi.id)` and `count(DISTINCT r.id)`,
which works because each branch carries its own primary key, and keeps every
non-product predicate in an `ON` clause so that products with nothing to
report still appear with zeros. The reference solution pre-aggregates each
branch into its own subquery and left-joins both - slower to type, immune to
the whole class of bug, and the answer you should give when an interviewer
asks how you would add a third measure.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL - Joined Tables](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-JOIN) - the formal definition of `LEFT`, `RIGHT` and `FULL` joins, including the sentence about the `ON` condition being applied before NULL-extension. The source of truth for ex4 and ex5.
- [PostgreSQL - Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - `count(*)` versus `count(expression)`, and the note that aggregates other than `count` return NULL over an empty input. Behind ex1, ex2 and ex6.
- [PostgreSQL - COALESCE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-conditional.html#FUNCTIONS-COALESCE-NVL-IFNULL) - the standard way to give a missing measure a defined value, and its type-resolution rules.
- [PostgreSQL - ORDER BY and NULLS FIRST/LAST](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-order.html) - why NULLs sort last by default in ascending order, which is the ordering trap in ex3.
- [Modern SQL - outer joins and the ON clause](https://modern-sql.com/feature/left-join) - a compact tour of what moves between `ON` and `WHERE`, with the same examples in other engines.

# Reading - 76_drills_outer_joins_1

Outer joins, and the small number of ways they go wrong. Every problem in
this set is one of them.

## Notes

**An outer join is a promise about the left side.** `A LEFT JOIN B` says:
every row of `A` appears in the output at least once. Where a matching `B`
row exists you get the pair; where none exists you get the `A` row with every
`B` column set to NULL. That invented row is called a NULL-extension, and
almost every bug in this set is a query that destroys one somewhere.

**`count(*)` counts rows; `count(col)` counts values.** A NULL-extended row
is a row, so `count(*)` in a group with no matches returns 1. `count(b.id)`
skips NULLs and returns 0. This is the single most common outer-join defect
in production reporting, and it is invisible until somebody notices that
nobody has zero of anything.

**`sum` over nothing is NULL, not zero.** Counts recover on their own;
sums, averages, mins and maxes do not. `coalesce(sum(x), 0)` is the fix, and
you have to decide consciously whether zero is even the honest answer - for a
sum it usually is, for an average it usually is not.

**A restriction on the right table belongs in `ON`.** `WHERE b.something =
'x'` is evaluated after the join, and it is false for every NULL-extended
row, so it silently deletes them and turns your outer join into an inner one.
Putting the same predicate in the `ON` clause makes it part of what counts as
a match instead, and the unmatched left rows survive. A restriction on the
*left* table is unaffected either way, which is why the rule is easy to
half-learn.

**`RIGHT` is `LEFT` with the tables swapped.** There is no third semantics to
memorise: decide which table must survive, then put it on the surviving side
of the keyword. Most codebases write everything as `LEFT` for consistency,
which is a fine convention as long as you can read the other one.

**Outer-ness has to survive every hop.** In a three-table chain, one inner
join anywhere downstream throws away the rows the outer join was protecting.
And once a second one-to-many join enters the query, counts start
double-counting: `count(DISTINCT ...)` is the repair for a count, and
pre-aggregating each branch is the repair for everything else.

## ex1 - the customers who never bought anything

The most-used outer join there is: a dimension, its facts, and a requirement
that the dimension come back whole. An inner join answers a different
question - "customers who have ordered" - and answers it correctly, which is
why the bug survives review.

The classic mistake is `count(*)`. The customers with no orders are exactly
the rows you added the `LEFT JOIN` to keep, and `count(*)` reports 1 for each
of them, so the report says every Spanish customer has ordered at least once.

The model answer left-joins orders onto customers, groups by the customer,
and counts `o.id` - a column that is NULL precisely when the NULL-extension
happened. The reference solution takes the other good route: aggregate orders
per customer first, then left-join that summary and `coalesce` the miss.

## ex2 - counts and sums behave differently

Roughly one order in seven in this dataset has no line items at all, so this
is the same shape as ex1 with one extra wrinkle: two measures that fail in
two different ways.

The classic mistake is `coalesce`ing neither, or both, without thinking.
`count(oi.id)` is already 0 for an empty group; wrapping it in `coalesce`
does nothing and suggests you have not worked out why. `sum(oi.quantity)`
over an empty group is NULL - SQL's aggregate functions ignore NULL inputs,
and the sum of no numbers is undefined rather than zero - so that one does
need the wrapper.

The model answer left-joins the lines, groups by the order, and treats the
two measures differently on purpose.

## ex3 - the raw shape, before any grouping

Strip the aggregation away and you can see what a `LEFT JOIN` actually
produces: one output row per matching pair, plus one NULL-extended row for
each left row that matched nothing. Being able to picture this is what makes
the aggregated versions obvious rather than magical.

The classic mistake is expecting NULLs where there are matches. A customer
with eleven orders contributes eleven rows and no NULLs; only the customers
with zero orders get the invented row. The second mistake is the ordering:
Postgres sorts NULLs **last** in ascending order by default, so producing
them first takes an explicit `NULLS FIRST`.

The model answer is a plain `LEFT JOIN` with both customer predicates in
`WHERE`, which is safe because they restrict the left table. The reference
solution spells the semantics out literally - an inner join `UNION ALL` the
unmatched rows with NULLs supplied by hand - which is exactly what a `LEFT
JOIN` means and worth reading once.

## ex4 - the same thing, mirrored

`RIGHT JOIN` keeps every row of the table on its right. That is the whole
definition. The exercise forces the direction so that the mirror gets
practised rather than avoided, because you will read code that uses it.

The classic mistake here is not the keyword, it is the predicates. `rating =
5` and the date restriction describe which reviews count as a match, so they
belong in the `ON` clause; move either into `WHERE` and every product without
a recent 5-star review is deleted from the report - the exact thing the outer
join was there to prevent.

The model answer puts all three conditions on the reviews side into `ON`,
keeps the two product predicates in `WHERE` (they restrict the surviving
table, so they are safe there), and counts `r.id`.

## ex5 - inner and outer in the same query

Two joins, two different jobs. `customers` is present only to supply the
country filter, and every order has a customer, so that join can and should
be inner. `order_items` is present to be counted, and an order with no
`quantity = 5` line still belongs in the report, so that one must be outer.

The classic mistake is a blanket policy - making everything a `LEFT JOIN`
"to be safe", or making everything inner out of habit. Mixing them in one
`FROM` is completely normal; the question to ask at each join is "can this
side legitimately have nothing, and do I still want the row if it does?"

The model answer inner-joins the customer, left-joins the lines with
`quantity = 5` in the `ON`, and counts `oi.id`.

## ex6 - print the bug next to the fix

This one is deliberately artificial: both columns come from the same grouped
outer join and differ only in what is being counted. Seeing `1` and `0` on
the same row is the fastest way to make the distinction permanent.

The classic mistake is assuming `count(*)` and `count(col)` are
interchangeable because on inner joins they usually are. They diverge exactly
where outer joins matter, which is exactly where you are least likely to be
checking.

The model answer groups the left join and writes both counts; note that the
`total > 1900` restriction has to be in the `ON` clause, or there would be no
unmatched customers left to demonstrate anything.

## ex7 - outer-ness has to survive two hops

A customer with no orders has no order lines either, so the second join has
nothing to match. Write it as an inner join and those customers vanish from
the answer - the `LEFT JOIN` in the first hop bought you nothing, because the
second hop threw the rows away again.

The classic mistake after fixing that is the order count. Once `order_items`
is in the `FROM`, a three-line order contributes three rows, so `count(o.id)`
counts lines and labels them orders. `count(DISTINCT o.id)` is what survives
the fan-out; `sum(oi.quantity)` is already at line grain and is correct as it
stands, but still needs `coalesce` for the customers with nothing.

The model answer chains two `LEFT JOIN`s and mixes `count(DISTINCT ...)` with
a coalesced `sum`. The reference pre-aggregates orders and lines per customer
in a subquery and joins the summary, which is the shape that scales to five
measures without any of this reasoning.

## ex8 - two branches, both outer

Order lines and reviews are independent branches hanging off the same
product. Join both and the rows multiply: a product with 20 qualifying lines
and 2 qualifying reviews produces 40 rows, and both plain counts report 40.
The result is not a little wrong, it is wrong by the size of the other
branch.

The classic mistake is trusting the number because it is plausible. Forty
lines for a popular toy looks fine; the only way to catch it is to know the
shape of your `FROM` and count the join paths.

The model answer uses `count(DISTINCT oi.id)` and `count(DISTINCT r.id)`,
which works because each branch carries its own primary key, and keeps every
non-product predicate in an `ON` clause so that products with nothing to
report still appear with zeros. The reference solution pre-aggregates each
branch into its own subquery and left-joins both - slower to type, immune to
the whole class of bug, and the answer you should give when an interviewer
asks how you would add a third measure.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL - Joined Tables](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-JOIN) - the formal definition of `LEFT`, `RIGHT` and `FULL` joins, including the sentence about the `ON` condition being applied before NULL-extension. The source of truth for ex4 and ex5.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1

Every customer in country `ES`, with how many orders they have placed -
including the ones who have placed none. Columns, in this order: `id`,
`name`, `orders`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 76_drills_outer_joins_1 ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
An inner join can only ever return customers who have at least one order. The prompt wants every Spanish customer, including the ones who have never bought anything, so the join has to keep the left side whole.

## Hint 2
`FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id`, then group by the customer. Now think hard about which count you write: a customer with no orders still produces one row, so one of `count(*)` and `count(o.id)` reports 1 and the other reports 0.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
An inner join can only ever return customers who have at least one order. The prompt wants every Spanish customer, including the ones who have never bought anything, so the join has to keep the left side whole.

## Hint 2
`FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id`, then group by the customer. Now think hard about which count you write: a customer with no orders still produces one row, so one of `count(*)` and `count(o.id)` reports 1 and the other reports 0.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name, coalesce(t.n, 0) AS orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS n
           FROM orders
           GROUP BY customer_id) t ON t.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.country = 'ES'
ORDER BY c.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name, count(o.id) AS orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.country = 'ES'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY c.id;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
No aggregation this time - you are looking at the raw shape a LEFT JOIN produces. One row per matching order, and for a customer with no orders at all, exactly one row with the right-hand columns filled in with NULL.

## Hint 2
`FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id` with both customer predicates in `WHERE`. The ordering asks for the NULL-extended row first within each customer, which is what `ORDER BY c.id, o.id NULLS FIRST` gives you - Postgres sorts NULLs last by default for ascending order.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name, o.id, o.total
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.country = 'ES' AND c.created_at >= '2023-10-01'
UNION ALL
SELECT c.id, c.name, NULL::int, NULL::numeric
FROM customers c
WHERE c.country = 'ES' AND c.created_at >= '2023-10-01'
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)
ORDER BY 1, 3 NULLS FIRST;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name, o.id AS order_id, o.total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.country = 'ES' AND c.created_at >= '2023-10-01'
ORDER BY c.id, o.id NULLS FIRST;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4

Same idea from the other side. Every `garden` product priced above 480, with
the number of **5-star reviews it received on or after 2023-11-10** - zero
included. Write this one with `reviews` as the left table and `products` as
the right table, so the join keyword you need is `RIGHT JOIN`. Columns, in
this order: `id`, `name`, `late_five_star`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 76_drills_outer_joins_1 ex4`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
A RIGHT JOIN keeps every row of the table written on the right of the keyword, exactly as a LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the one on the left. Same operation, mirrored - so decide which table must survive before you decide which keyword to type.

## Hint 2
`FROM reviews r RIGHT JOIN products p ON ...` keeps all products. The rating and date restrictions describe **which reviews count as a match**, not which products you want, so they belong in the `ON` clause; move either of them to `WHERE` and every product with no recent 5-star review disappears.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
A RIGHT JOIN keeps every row of the table written on the right of the keyword, exactly as a LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the one on the left. Same operation, mirrored - so decide which table must survive before you decide which keyword to type.

## Hint 2
`FROM reviews r RIGHT JOIN products p ON ...` keeps all products. The rating and date restrictions describe **which reviews count as a match**, not which products you want, so they belong in the `ON` clause; move either of them to `WHERE` and every product with no recent 5-star review disappears.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT p.id, p.name, count(r.id)
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN reviews r ON r.product_id = p.id
     AND r.rating = 5
     AND r.created_at >= DATE '2023-11-10'
WHERE p.category = 'garden' AND p.price > 480
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY p.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT p.id, p.name, count(r.id) AS late_five_star
FROM reviews r
RIGHT JOIN products p ON p.id = r.product_id
      AND r.rating = 5
      AND r.created_at >= '2023-11-10'
WHERE p.category = 'garden' AND p.price > 480
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY p.id;

## Hint 1
Two joins with two different jobs in one query. The customer is there only to supply a filter, so an order without a customer is impossible and that join can be inner. The lines are there to be counted, and an order with none of them still belongs in the report.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Two joins with two different jobs in one query. The customer is there only to supply a filter, so an order without a customer is impossible and that join can be inner. The lines are there to be counted, and an order with none of them still belongs in the report.

## Hint 2
`FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON ... LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id AND oi.quantity = 5`. Mixing inner and outer joins in one `FROM` is normal; what matters is that `quantity = 5` sits in the `ON` of the outer join, because in `WHERE` it would throw away every order that has no such line.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT o.id, o.total, coalesce(b.n, 0)
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT order_id, count(*) AS n
           FROM order_items
           WHERE quantity = 5
           GROUP BY order_id) b ON b.order_id = o.id
WHERE c.country = 'MX' AND o.created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01'
ORDER BY o.id;

WHERE c.country = 'MX' AND o.created_at >= '2023-11-01'

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
This one asks you to print the bug next to the fix. Both columns come out of the same grouped LEFT JOIN; they differ only in what you count.

## Hint 2
`count(*)` counts rows in the group, and a NULL-extended row is still a row - so a customer with no qualifying order gets 1. `count(o.id)` counts non-NULL values of that column, so the same customer gets 0. references.solution.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name,
       greatest(count(o.id), 1) AS rows_returned,
       count(o.id) AS big_orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.total > 1900
WHERE c.country = 'CA' AND c.created_at >= DATE '2023-09-01'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY c.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name, count(*) AS rows_returned, count(o.id) AS big_orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.total > 1900
WHERE c.country = 'CA' AND c.created_at >= '2023-09-01'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY c.id;

## Exercise 7

Every customer in country `BR` who signed up on or after `2023-06-01`, with
how many orders they have placed and how many units they have bought in
total across all those orders' lines. Customers with no orders report `0`
and `0`. Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `orders`, `units`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Three tables, and the outer-ness has to survive both hops. A customer with no orders has no order lines either, so the moment the second join is an inner one those customers disappear again - even though the first join kept them.

## Hint 2
`customers LEFT JOIN orders LEFT JOIN order_items`, grouped by the customer. Then the counting problem: after the second join a three-line order contributes three rows, so a plain `count(o.id)` counts lines and calls them orders.

## Hint 3
`count(DISTINCT o.id)` is what survives the fan-out for the order count; `sum(oi.quantity)` is already at line grain so it needs no `DISTINCT`, but it does need `coalesce` to turn the NULL of an empty group into 0.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Three tables, and the outer-ness has to survive both hops. A customer with no orders has no order lines either, so the moment the second join is an inner one those customers disappear again - even though the first join kept them.

## Hint 2
`customers LEFT JOIN orders LEFT JOIN order_items`, grouped by the customer. Then the counting problem: after the second join a three-line order contributes three rows, so a plain `count(o.id)` counts lines and calls them orders.

## Hint 3
`count(DISTINCT o.id)` is what survives the fan-out for the order count; `sum(oi.quantity)` is already at line grain so it needs no `DISTINCT`, but it does need `coalesce` to turn the NULL of an empty group into 0.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name, coalesce(s.orders, 0), coalesce(s.units, 0)
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN (SELECT o.customer_id,
                  count(DISTINCT o.id) AS orders,
                  coalesce(sum(oi.quantity), 0) AS units
           FROM orders o
           JOIN customers c2 ON c2.id = o.customer_id
                AND c2.country = 'BR'
                AND c2.created_at >= DATE '2023-06-01'
           LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
           GROUP BY o.customer_id) s ON s.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.country = 'BR' AND c.created_at >= DATE '2023-06-01'
ORDER BY c.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name,
       count(DISTINCT o.id) AS orders,
       coalesce(sum(oi.quantity), 0) AS units
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
WHERE c.country = 'BR' AND c.created_at >= '2023-06-01'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY c.id;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8

For every `toys` product priced above 495: how many order lines sold it in a
quantity of exactly 5, and how many 1-star reviews it received on or after
`2023-11-01`. Both counts are `0` where there is nothing to count, and no
product may be dropped. Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `big_lines`,
`recent_one_star`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 76_drills_outer_joins_1 ex8`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two independent branches hang off each product: its order lines and its reviews. Picture one product with 20 qualifying lines and 2 qualifying reviews, and work out how many rows the joined result has for that product before you write any aggregate.

## Hint 2
It has 40 - every line paired with every review. A plain `count(oi.id)` therefore reports 40 lines and 40 reviews, both wrong by exactly the size of the other branch.

## Hint 3
`count(DISTINCT ...)` on each side collapses the duplication, because both branches carry their own primary key. Keep both joins outer and keep the rating and date restrictions in the `ON` clause, or products with no recent complaint drop out of the report.

SELECT p.id, p.name, coalesce(b.n, 0), coalesce(w.n, 0)
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN (SELECT product_id, count(*) AS n
           FROM order_items
           WHERE quantity = 5
           GROUP BY product_id) b ON b.product_id = p.id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT product_id, count(*) AS n
           FROM reviews
           WHERE rating = 1 AND created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01'
           GROUP BY product_id) w ON w.product_id = p.id
WHERE p.category = 'toys' AND p.price > 495
ORDER BY p.id;

# Reading - 77_drills_outer_joins_2

One rule, applied eight times: a predicate in `ON` decides what counts as a
match, a predicate in `WHERE` decides which rows you keep. For outer joins
those are different questions.

## Notes

**The evaluation order is the whole explanation.** Postgres evaluates the
`ON` condition first and pairs up whatever it can; then it manufactures a
NULL-extended row for every left row that found no partner; only then does
`WHERE` run. So a `WHERE` test on a right-hand column is applied to rows
where that column is NULL by construction - and `NULL = 'cancelled'` is not
true, so the row is dropped. Your outer join quietly became an inner join.

**Say what the predicate is about.** "Only cancelled orders count as a match"
belongs in `ON`. "Only customers who have a cancelled order" belongs in
`WHERE`. Both sentences are reasonable requirements and they have different
answers; the reason this is worth drilling is that the SQL for them differs
by four characters and reads almost identically.

**`FILTER` is the third option, and usually the best one.** When you want
several differently-restricted measures over the same group, moving the
restriction into the aggregate - `count(*) FILTER (WHERE ...)` - keeps one
join, one pass, and no risk of dropping rows. `CASE WHEN ... THEN` inside an
aggregate is the portable spelling of the same idea.

**You can outer-join to a joined result.** `LEFT JOIN (a JOIN b ON ...) ON
...` treats the pair as one unit: the NULL row appears when *the combination*
matched nothing. Chaining two joins one after another asks a different
question and gets a different answer. A subquery does the same job and is
easier to read.

**`FULL JOIN` means either side can be missing.** Everything you know about
`LEFT` applies twice, which has one specific consequence: the join key itself
can be NULL, so the key column in your `SELECT` list has to be rebuilt with
`coalesce(a.k, b.k)`. Forgetting that is the signature full-join bug.

**Aggregate before you outer-join when the right side is one-to-many and you
only care whether it exists.** Reducing it to one row per key first turns the
join one-to-one, which makes `count(*)` count what you think it counts and
`IS NULL` mean what you think it means.

## ex1 - the restriction that belongs in ON

The report is about Australian customers, all of them, and "cancelled" only
describes which of their orders should be counted. That is a statement about
matching, so it goes in the `ON` clause and the customers with nothing to
count survive with zero.

The classic mistake is `WHERE o.status = 'cancelled'`, which reads perfectly
and deletes every customer the outer join was protecting - including all the
ones with a clean record, which is precisely the population a churn or
quality report exists to show.

The model answer puts the status test in `ON` and counts `o.id`. The
reference gets there differently, by summarising cancelled orders per
customer first and left-joining the summary, which sidesteps the question
entirely - a good habit when a report grows past two measures.

## ex2 - the restriction that belongs in WHERE

Now the requirement really is "customers who have at least one cancelled
order", and that is a statement about which customers you keep. An inner join
says it directly and needs no ceremony.

The classic mistake here is the mirror image of ex1: reflexively writing
`LEFT JOIN` because the previous problem needed one. It is not wrong - the
reference solution shows that `LEFT JOIN` with the status test in `WHERE`
gives exactly this answer - but it is misleading code, because a reader has
to work out that the outer join is decorative.

The model answer is a plain inner join with both predicates in `WHERE`. Run
it next to ex1 and compare the row counts: the difference is the population
that only ex1 can see.

## ex3 - three subsets, one join

Once a report needs several measures over different slices of the same group,
joining once per slice stops scaling and joining with a `WHERE` stops being
correct. `FILTER` restricts an individual aggregate to part of the group and
leaves the group itself alone.

The classic mistake is forgetting that the revenue column needs `coalesce`
while the counts do not. `count(...)` over an empty subset is 0; `sum(...)`
over an empty subset is NULL. The two behave differently on purpose - zero
things counted is genuinely zero, whereas the sum of no numbers is genuinely
undefined - and a report that prints NULL where the business expects 0.00 is
a bug report waiting to happen.

The model answer uses one `LEFT JOIN` and three aggregates, two of them
filtered. The reference writes the same thing with `CASE` expressions inside
the aggregates, which is what you use on engines without `FILTER`.

## ex4 - outer-joining to a joined result

"An order with no line for an expensive product" is a condition about the
combination of `order_items` and `products`, not about either one alone. Join
them first, then outer-join the pair.

The classic mistake is `LEFT JOIN order_items ... LEFT JOIN products ... AND
p.price > 400`. That gives an order with three cheap lines three rows with
NULL product names, instead of the one row the prompt asks for - the
NULL-extension happened at the wrong level. The other classic mistake is
making the second join inner, which deletes every order whose lines are all
cheap.

The model answer wraps the inner join in parentheses and outer-joins the
whole thing; the reference builds the expensive lines in a subquery and
outer-joins that. They are the same query with different punctuation, and the
subquery version is the one to write when somebody else has to read it.

## ex5 - one table, two joins, doubled counts

Attaching `orders` twice under two aliases is a legitimate way to ask for two
disjoint subsets, and it comes with an immediate cost: a customer with 5 paid
and 2 cancelled orders produces 10 rows, so both plain counts report 10. The
number is wrong by exactly the size of the *other* subset, which makes it
plausible enough to ship.

The classic mistake is trusting the totals. The tell is that both columns
show the same value on every row - a strong hint that you are counting the
cross product rather than either branch.

The model answer repairs it with `count(DISTINCT p.id)` and `count(DISTINCT
x.id)`. The reference avoids the situation altogether with a single join and
two `FILTER`ed counts, which is faster, shorter and the answer to give when
an interviewer asks how you would add a third status.

## ex6 - reduce the right side before joining it

There are far more order lines than there are products, so joining them
directly produces one row per line, in which `count(*)` counts lines. The
question is about products, so the right side has to be collapsed to one row
per product before it touches `products`.

The classic mistake is `LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id ...
WHERE oi.id IS NULL` combined with a `count(*)`: the `WHERE` version answers
"how many never-ordered products" but cannot also report the category total
in the same pass, and people then write two queries and join them by hand.

The model answer left-joins `SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM order_items`,
which makes the join one-to-one, so `count(*)` counts products and
`s.product_id IS NULL` marks the unsold ones. The reference does the same
with `GROUP BY` instead of `DISTINCT` and computes the second number by
subtraction - `count(*) - count(s.product_id)` - which is the same
`count(*)`-versus-`count(col)` distinction from the previous drill set, used
deliberately this time.

## ex7 - NULL-extension meets FILTER

Two chained outer joins, each carrying a restriction in its `ON` clause, and
a `FILTER` on top. The interesting case is a product whose only quantity-5
line sits on an October order: the line survives the first join, the order is
NULL-extended by the second, and `o.status <> 'cancelled'` evaluates to NULL.

The classic mistake is expecting that row to land in `good_units` because
"it wasn't cancelled". `FILTER` keeps rows where the condition is **true**,
and NULL is not true, so the row contributes to neither bucket - which is the
right answer, because an order outside the window should not be counted at
all. Three-valued logic doing exactly what you want, for once.

The model answer chains the two outer joins, splits with `FILTER`, and
`coalesce`s both sums. The reference computes the whole sales side in one
pre-filtered subquery and left-joins it, which makes the window explicit
instead of implicit - usually the clearer choice when the window is a
business rule rather than a technicality.

## ex8 - the full outer join

Some products sold in the last two days without being praised; others were
praised without selling. Neither one-sided join can produce both groups, and
`UNION`ing two left joins duplicates the overlap. `FULL JOIN` is the operator
built for this.

The classic mistake is selecting `s.product_id` as the key. On a praise-only
row that column is NULL, so the report shows a NULL product id next to a real
review count. `coalesce(s.product_id, r.product_id)` is not optional
decoration - in a full join, the key belongs to whichever side turned up.

The second classic mistake is labelling the buckets by testing the measures
(`WHERE units IS NULL`) rather than the keys. That conflates "this side had
no row" with "this side had a row whose value was NULL", and preserving that
distinction is most of the reason full joins exist.

The model answer aggregates both sides to one row per product, full-joins the
summaries, rebuilds the key with `coalesce`, and labels with a `CASE` over
the two key columns. The reference reaches the same result by building the
union of the two key sets first and left-joining both summaries onto it -
more verbose, completely portable, and the version to fall back on when a
full join's NULL bookkeeping starts to hurt.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL - Joined Tables](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-JOIN) - the paragraph stating that the `ON` condition is applied before NULL-extension and `WHERE` after it. This is the whole lesson in one sentence.
- [PostgreSQL - Aggregate Expressions and FILTER](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html#SYNTAX-AGGREGATES) - the exact semantics of `FILTER (WHERE ...)`, including that only rows where the condition is true are fed to the aggregate. Behind ex3, ex5 and ex7.
- [PostgreSQL - Comparison Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html) - three-valued logic, and why a comparison against a NULL-extended column is neither true nor false. The mechanism behind the ex7 surprise.
- [PostgreSQL - Subqueries in FROM](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-SUBQUERIES) - pre-aggregating a one-to-many side so the outer join becomes one-to-one, used in ex4, ex6 and ex8.
- [Modern SQL - FULL OUTER JOIN](https://modern-sql.com/feature/full-outer-join) - what full joins are for, the `coalesce` on the key, and how to emulate them where they are missing.

# Reading - 77_drills_outer_joins_2

One rule, applied eight times: a predicate in `ON` decides what counts as a
match, a predicate in `WHERE` decides which rows you keep. For outer joins
those are different questions.

## Notes

**The evaluation order is the whole explanation.** Postgres evaluates the
`ON` condition first and pairs up whatever it can; then it manufactures a
NULL-extended row for every left row that found no partner; only then does
`WHERE` run. So a `WHERE` test on a right-hand column is applied to rows
where that column is NULL by construction - and `NULL = 'cancelled'` is not
true, so the row is dropped. Your outer join quietly became an inner join.

**Say what the predicate is about.** "Only cancelled orders count as a match"
belongs in `ON`. "Only customers who have a cancelled order" belongs in
`WHERE`. Both sentences are reasonable requirements and they have different
answers; the reason this is worth drilling is that the SQL for them differs
by four characters and reads almost identically.

**`FILTER` is the third option, and usually the best one.** When you want
several differently-restricted measures over the same group, moving the
restriction into the aggregate - `count(*) FILTER (WHERE ...)` - keeps one
join, one pass, and no risk of dropping rows. `CASE WHEN ... THEN` inside an
aggregate is the portable spelling of the same idea.

**You can outer-join to a joined result.** `LEFT JOIN (a JOIN b ON ...) ON
...` treats the pair as one unit: the NULL row appears when *the combination*
matched nothing. Chaining two joins one after another asks a different
question and gets a different answer. A subquery does the same job and is
easier to read.

**`FULL JOIN` means either side can be missing.** Everything you know about
`LEFT` applies twice, which has one specific consequence: the join key itself
can be NULL, so the key column in your `SELECT` list has to be rebuilt with
`coalesce(a.k, b.k)`. Forgetting that is the signature full-join bug.

**Aggregate before you outer-join when the right side is one-to-many and you
only care whether it exists.** Reducing it to one row per key first turns the
join one-to-one, which makes `count(*)` count what you think it counts and
`IS NULL` mean what you think it means.

## ex1 - the restriction that belongs in ON

The report is about Australian customers, all of them, and "cancelled" only
describes which of their orders should be counted. That is a statement about
matching, so it goes in the `ON` clause and the customers with nothing to
count survive with zero.

The classic mistake is `WHERE o.status = 'cancelled'`, which reads perfectly
and deletes every customer the outer join was protecting - including all the
ones with a clean record, which is precisely the population a churn or
quality report exists to show.

The model answer puts the status test in `ON` and counts `o.id`. The
reference gets there differently, by summarising cancelled orders per
customer first and left-joining the summary, which sidesteps the question
entirely - a good habit when a report grows past two measures.

## ex2 - the restriction that belongs in WHERE

Now the requirement really is "customers who have at least one cancelled
order", and that is a statement about which customers you keep. An inner join
says it directly and needs no ceremony.

The classic mistake here is the mirror image of ex1: reflexively writing
`LEFT JOIN` because the previous problem needed one. It is not wrong - the
reference solution shows that `LEFT JOIN` with the status test in `WHERE`
gives exactly this answer - but it is misleading code, because a reader has
to work out that the outer join is decorative.

The model answer is a plain inner join with both predicates in `WHERE`. Run
it next to ex1 and compare the row counts: the difference is the population
that only ex1 can see.

## ex3 - three subsets, one join

Once a report needs several measures over different slices of the same group,
joining once per slice stops scaling and joining with a `WHERE` stops being
correct. `FILTER` restricts an individual aggregate to part of the group and
leaves the group itself alone.

The classic mistake is forgetting that the revenue column needs `coalesce`
while the counts do not. `count(...)` over an empty subset is 0; `sum(...)`
over an empty subset is NULL. The two behave differently on purpose - zero
things counted is genuinely zero, whereas the sum of no numbers is genuinely
undefined - and a report that prints NULL where the business expects 0.00 is
a bug report waiting to happen.

The model answer uses one `LEFT JOIN` and three aggregates, two of them
filtered. The reference writes the same thing with `CASE` expressions inside
the aggregates, which is what you use on engines without `FILTER`.

## ex4 - outer-joining to a joined result

"An order with no line for an expensive product" is a condition about the
combination of `order_items` and `products`, not about either one alone. Join
them first, then outer-join the pair.

The classic mistake is `LEFT JOIN order_items ... LEFT JOIN products ... AND
p.price > 400`. That gives an order with three cheap lines three rows with
NULL product names, instead of the one row the prompt asks for - the
NULL-extension happened at the wrong level. The other classic mistake is
making the second join inner, which deletes every order whose lines are all
cheap.

The model answer wraps the inner join in parentheses and outer-joins the
whole thing; the reference builds the expensive lines in a subquery and
outer-joins that. They are the same query with different punctuation, and the
subquery version is the one to write when somebody else has to read it.

## ex5 - one table, two joins, doubled counts

Attaching `orders` twice under two aliases is a legitimate way to ask for two
disjoint subsets, and it comes with an immediate cost: a customer with 5 paid
and 2 cancelled orders produces 10 rows, so both plain counts report 10. The
number is wrong by exactly the size of the *other* subset, which makes it
plausible enough to ship.

The classic mistake is trusting the totals. The tell is that both columns
show the same value on every row - a strong hint that you are counting the
cross product rather than either branch.

The model answer repairs it with `count(DISTINCT p.id)` and `count(DISTINCT
x.id)`. The reference avoids the situation altogether with a single join and
two `FILTER`ed counts, which is faster, shorter and the answer to give when
an interviewer asks how you would add a third status.

## ex6 - reduce the right side before joining it

There are far more order lines than there are products, so joining them
directly produces one row per line, in which `count(*)` counts lines. The
question is about products, so the right side has to be collapsed to one row
per product before it touches `products`.

The classic mistake is `LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id ...
WHERE oi.id IS NULL` combined with a `count(*)`: the `WHERE` version answers
"how many never-ordered products" but cannot also report the category total
in the same pass, and people then write two queries and join them by hand.

The model answer left-joins `SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM order_items`,
which makes the join one-to-one, so `count(*)` counts products and
`s.product_id IS NULL` marks the unsold ones. The reference does the same
with `GROUP BY` instead of `DISTINCT` and computes the second number by
subtraction - `count(*) - count(s.product_id)` - which is the same
`count(*)`-versus-`count(col)` distinction from the previous drill set, used
deliberately this time.

## ex7 - NULL-extension meets FILTER

Two chained outer joins, each carrying a restriction in its `ON` clause, and
a `FILTER` on top. The interesting case is a product whose only quantity-5
line sits on an October order: the line survives the first join, the order is
NULL-extended by the second, and `o.status <> 'cancelled'` evaluates to NULL.

The classic mistake is expecting that row to land in `good_units` because
"it wasn't cancelled". `FILTER` keeps rows where the condition is **true**,
and NULL is not true, so the row contributes to neither bucket - which is the
right answer, because an order outside the window should not be counted at
all. Three-valued logic doing exactly what you want, for once.

The model answer chains the two outer joins, splits with `FILTER`, and
`coalesce`s both sums. The reference computes the whole sales side in one
pre-filtered subquery and left-joins it, which makes the window explicit
instead of implicit - usually the clearer choice when the window is a
business rule rather than a technicality.

## ex8 - the full outer join

Some products sold in the last two days without being praised; others were
praised without selling. Neither one-sided join can produce both groups, and
`UNION`ing two left joins duplicates the overlap. `FULL JOIN` is the operator
built for this.

The classic mistake is selecting `s.product_id` as the key. On a praise-only
row that column is NULL, so the report shows a NULL product id next to a real
review count. `coalesce(s.product_id, r.product_id)` is not optional
decoration - in a full join, the key belongs to whichever side turned up.

The second classic mistake is labelling the buckets by testing the measures
(`WHERE units IS NULL`) rather than the keys. That conflates "this side had
no row" with "this side had a row whose value was NULL", and preserving that
distinction is most of the reason full joins exist.

The model answer aggregates both sides to one row per product, full-joins the
summaries, rebuilds the key with `coalesce`, and labels with a `CASE` over
the two key columns. The reference reaches the same result by building the
union of the two key sets first and left-joining both summaries onto it -
more verbose, completely portable, and the version to fall back on when a
full join's NULL bookkeeping starts to hurt.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL - Joined Tables](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-JOIN) - the paragraph stating that the `ON` condition is applied before NULL-extension and `WHERE` after it. This is the whole lesson in one sentence.
- [PostgreSQL - Aggregate Expressions and FILTER](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html#SYNTAX-AGGREGATES) - the exact semantics of `FILTER (WHERE ...)`, including that only rows where the condition is true are fed to the aggregate. Behind ex3, ex5 and ex7.
- [PostgreSQL - Comparison Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html) - three-valued logic, and why a comparison against a NULL-extended column is neither true nor false. The mechanism behind the ex7 surprise.
- [PostgreSQL - Subqueries in FROM](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-SUBQUERIES) - pre-aggregating a one-to-many side so the outer join becomes one-to-one, used in ex4, ex6 and ex8.
- [Modern SQL - FULL OUTER JOIN](https://modern-sql.com/feature/full-outer-join) - what full joins are for, the `coalesce` on the key, and how to emulate them where they are missing.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1

Every customer in country `AU`, with how many of their orders were
**cancelled**. Customers with no cancelled orders - and customers with no
orders at all - must appear with `0`. Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`,
`cancelled`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 77_drills_outer_joins_2 ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Every Australian customer has to appear, including the ones with no cancelled orders and the ones with no orders at all. So `cancelled` is a restriction on what counts as a match, not a restriction on which customers you want.

## Hint 2
`LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'cancelled'`. Put that status test in `WHERE` instead and every customer who should have scored 0 disappears, because the NULL-extended row fails it.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Every Australian customer has to appear, including the ones with no cancelled orders and the ones with no orders at all. So `cancelled` is a restriction on what counts as a match, not a restriction on which customers you want.

## Hint 2
`LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'cancelled'`. Put that status test in `WHERE` instead and every customer who should have scored 0 disappears, because the NULL-extended row fails it.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name, coalesce(x.n, 0) AS cancelled
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS n
           FROM orders
           WHERE status = 'cancelled'
           GROUP BY customer_id) x ON x.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.country = 'AU'
ORDER BY c.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name, count(o.id) AS cancelled
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'cancelled'
WHERE c.country = 'AU'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY c.id;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Three measures over three different subsets of the same group, and the join may only happen once. Nothing may move into `WHERE` - the customers with no orders still need a row of zeros.

## Hint 2
`FILTER (WHERE ...)` restricts one aggregate to part of its group: `count(o.id) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'cancelled')`. The revenue column needs one more thing than the counts do, because a sum over an empty subset is NULL rather than 0.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name,
       count(o.id) AS orders,
       count(CASE WHEN o.status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 END) AS cancelled,
       coalesce(sum(CASE WHEN o.status <> 'cancelled' THEN o.total END), 0) AS revenue
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.country = 'AU'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY c.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name,
       count(o.id) AS orders,
       count(o.id) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled,
       coalesce(sum(o.total) FILTER (WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'), 0) AS revenue
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.country = 'AU'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY c.id;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4

For every order belonging to a customer with `id <= 3`: the order's `id`,
its `status`, and the `name` of each line's product **where that product is
priced above 400**. An order with no such line appears exactly once, with
NULL in the product column. Columns, in this order: `id`, `status`,
`product`.

**Ordered by the order's `id` ascending, then `product` ascending with NULLs
first.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 77_drills_outer_joins_2 ex4`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The thing you want to outer-join to is not a table, it is the result of joining two tables. An order qualifies for a NULL row when that combined result has nothing for it - which is a different condition from either table having nothing.

## Hint 2
Two shapes work. Wrap the inner join in parentheses and outer-join the whole thing: `LEFT JOIN (order_items oi JOIN products p ON ...) ON oi.order_id = o.id`. Or build the expensive lines in a subquery first and `LEFT JOIN` that. What does not work is joining the two tables one after another and hoping - a cheap line would give you a row you did not want.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The thing you want to outer-join to is not a table, it is the result of joining two tables. An order qualifies for a NULL row when that combined result has nothing for it - which is a different condition from either table having nothing.

## Hint 2
Two shapes work. Wrap the inner join in parentheses and outer-join the whole thing: `LEFT JOIN (order_items oi JOIN products p ON ...) ON oi.order_id = o.id`. Or build the expensive lines in a subquery first and `LEFT JOIN` that. What does not work is joining the two tables one after another and hoping - a cheap line would give you a row you did not want.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT o.id, o.status, x.name AS product
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN (SELECT oi.order_id, p.name
           FROM order_items oi
           JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
           WHERE p.price > 400) x ON x.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.customer_id <= 3
ORDER BY o.id, x.name NULLS FIRST;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT o.id, o.status, p.name AS product
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN (order_items oi JOIN products p
           ON p.id = oi.product_id AND p.price > 400)
       ON oi.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.customer_id <= 3
ORDER BY o.id, p.name NULLS FIRST;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Two counts over two disjoint subsets of the same customer's orders. There are two natural shapes - one join with two filtered aggregates, or two separate outer joins - and only one of them is safe by default.

## Hint 2
If you attach `orders` twice, a customer with 5 paid and 2 cancelled orders gets 10 rows, and every plain count reports 10. The repair for a count is `count(DISTINCT ...)`; the way to avoid the problem entirely is a single `LEFT JOIN` with `FILTER (WHERE ...)` on each aggregate.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name,
       count(o.id) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'paid') AS paid,
       count(o.id) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.country = 'IN' AND c.created_at >= DATE '2023-08-01'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY c.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name,
       count(DISTINCT p.id) AS paid,
       count(DISTINCT x.id) AS cancelled
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders p ON p.customer_id = c.id AND p.status = 'paid'
LEFT JOIN orders x ON x.customer_id = c.id AND x.status = 'cancelled'
WHERE c.country = 'IN' AND c.created_at >= '2023-08-01'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY c.id;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
You need two numbers per category, and one of them is about products that have no order lines at all. Joining `products` straight to `order_items` would give you one row per order line and a count of lines, not of products.

## Hint 2
Reduce the right side to one row per product **before** you join it - `SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM order_items` is enough. Then the outer join is one-to-one, `count(*)` counts products, and `s.product_id IS NULL` marks the ones that never sold.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT p.category,
       count(*) AS products,
       count(*) - count(s.product_id) AS never_ordered
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN (SELECT product_id FROM order_items GROUP BY product_id) s
       ON s.product_id = p.id
GROUP BY p.category
ORDER BY p.category;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT p.category,
       count(*) AS products,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE s.product_id IS NULL) AS never_ordered
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM order_items) s
       ON s.product_id = p.id
GROUP BY p.category
ORDER BY p.category;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7

For every `toys` product priced above 490, look only at order lines with
`quantity = 5` that belong to orders **created on or after 2023-11-01**, and
split their units two ways: `good_units` from orders that are not cancelled,
`lost_units` from orders that are. Every one of those products appears, with
`0` where there is nothing to count. Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`,
`good_units`, `lost_units`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 77_drills_outer_joins_2 ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Every restriction in this prompt is about which sales count, not about which products you want, so none of them may reach `WHERE` except the two on `products` itself.

## Hint 2
Chain two outer joins, one carrying `oi.quantity = 5` and one carrying the order date, then split the total with `FILTER (WHERE o.status ...)`.

## Hint 3
Think about what happens to a product whose only quantity-5 line belongs to an October order: the line survives the first join, the order is NULL-extended by the second, and `o.status <> 'cancelled'` is then NULL - which is not true, so `FILTER` excludes it from both buckets. That is the behaviour the prompt describes, and the `coalesce` turns the resulting empty sums into zeros.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Every restriction in this prompt is about which sales count, not about which products you want, so none of them may reach `WHERE` except the two on `products` itself.

## Hint 2
Chain two outer joins, one carrying `oi.quantity = 5` and one carrying the order date, then split the total with `FILTER (WHERE o.status ...)`.

## Hint 3
Think about what happens to a product whose only quantity-5 line belongs to an October order: the line survives the first join, the order is NULL-extended by the second, and `o.status <> 'cancelled'` is then NULL - which is not true, so `FILTER` excludes it from both buckets. That is the behaviour the prompt describes, and the `coalesce` turns the resulting empty sums into zeros.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT p.id, p.name,
       coalesce(s.good, 0) AS good_units,
       coalesce(s.lost, 0) AS lost_units
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN (SELECT oi.product_id,
                  sum(oi.quantity) FILTER (WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled') AS good,
                  sum(oi.quantity) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'cancelled') AS lost
           FROM order_items oi
           JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
           WHERE oi.quantity = 5
             AND o.created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01'
           GROUP BY oi.product_id) s ON s.product_id = p.id
WHERE p.category = 'toys' AND p.price > 490
ORDER BY p.id;
references.expected.sql:

       coalesce(sum(oi.quantity) FILTER (WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'), 0) AS good_units,
       coalesce(sum(oi.quantity) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'cancelled'), 0) AS lost_units
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id AND oi.quantity = 5
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id AND o.created_at >= '2023-11-01'
WHERE p.category = 'toys' AND p.price > 490
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY p.id;

## Hint 1
Neither side contains all the products you need: some sold without being praised, some were praised without selling. A `LEFT JOIN` in either direction loses one of those groups.

## Hint 2
Aggregate each side to one row per product first, then `FULL JOIN` the two summaries on `product_id`. In a full join **either** side can be NULL, so the key column itself has to be rebuilt with `coalesce` - reading `s.product_id` alone would give NULL for every praise-only row.

## Hint 3
The label is a plain `CASE` over which side survived: test `s.product_id IS NOT NULL` and `r.product_id IS NOT NULL`. Do not test `units IS NULL` instead - that conflates 'no row on this side' with 'a row whose measure happened to be NULL', which is a distinction full joins exist to preserve.

references.solution.sql:
WITH s AS (
    SELECT oi.product_id, sum(oi.quantity) AS units
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
    WHERE o.created_at >= DATE '2023-11-13'
    GROUP BY oi.product_id
), r AS (
    SELECT product_id, count(*) AS praises
    FROM reviews
    WHERE rating = 5 AND created_at >= DATE '2023-11-13'
    GROUP BY product_id
), ids AS (
    SELECT product_id FROM s
    UNION
    SELECT product_id FROM r
)
SELECT i.product_id,
       coalesce(s.units, 0) AS units,
       coalesce(r.praises, 0) AS praises,
       CASE WHEN s.product_id IS NOT NULL AND r.product_id IS NOT NULL THEN 'both'
            WHEN s.product_id IS NOT NULL THEN 'sales only'
            ELSE 'praise only' END AS bucket
FROM ids i
LEFT JOIN s ON s.product_id = i.product_id
LEFT JOIN r ON r.product_id = i.product_id
ORDER BY i.product_id;

SELECT coalesce(s.product_id, r.product_id) AS product_id,
       coalesce(s.units, 0) AS units,
       coalesce(r.praises, 0) AS praises,
       CASE WHEN s.product_id IS NOT NULL AND r.product_id IS NOT NULL THEN 'both'
            WHEN s.product_id IS NOT NULL THEN 'sales only'
            ELSE 'praise only' END AS bucket
FROM (SELECT oi.product_id, sum(oi.quantity) AS units
      FROM order_items oi
      JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
      WHERE o.created_at >= '2023-11-13'
      GROUP BY oi.product_id) s
FULL JOIN (SELECT product_id, count(*) AS praises
           FROM reviews
           WHERE rating = 5 AND created_at >= '2023-11-13'
           GROUP BY product_id) r ON r.product_id = s.product_id
ORDER BY 1;

lessons.briefing:
# 78 - Drills: anti-joins and semi-joins

Eight problems about presence and absence: customers who have never done a
thing, products nobody bought this month, orders where *every* line agrees.
This set draws on lessons 09 (the `LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL` anti-join) and 13
(`EXISTS` / `NOT EXISTS`, and why `NOT IN` is a trap). Exercise 4 will bite
you if you skipped the NULL lesson - that is intentional.

## Exercise 1

Customers in country `IN` who have **never placed a paid order**. Having
cancelled, pending or shipped orders is fine; having no orders at all is also
fine. Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 78_drills_anti_semi_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2

Customers in country `IN` who have bought at least one product in the `books`
category - each customer appearing exactly once, however many books they
have bought. Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 78_drills_anti_semi_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3

`garden` products priced above 480 that were **never sold in a quantity of 5
on an order created on or after 2023-11-01**. Both halves of that description
have to hold at once for a sale to disqualify a product. Columns, in this

# Reading - 78_drills_anti_semi_1

Semi-joins and anti-joins: filtering one table by whether a matching row
exists somewhere else, without letting that somewhere else into your result.

## Notes

**A semi-join filters; it does not multiply.** "Customers who have bought a
book" is a question about `customers`, and the answer has exactly one row per
customer. A plain join answers a different question - it returns one row per
*book line* - and people patch it with `DISTINCT`. That works, but it means
building a large intermediate result and then throwing most of it away.
`EXISTS` stops at the first match and never produces the duplicates in the
first place.

**An anti-join is the same thing negated,** and it has three spellings in
PostgreSQL: `NOT EXISTS (correlated subquery)`, `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key
IS NULL`, and `NOT IN (subquery)`. The first two are equivalent and safe. The
third is not.

**`NOT IN` with a NULL in the list can never be true.** `x NOT IN (a, b,
NULL)` expands to `x <> a AND x <> b AND x <> NULL`, and the last conjunct is
unknown rather than false - so the whole expression is unknown for every row,
and `WHERE` keeps nothing. It fails silently: no error, no warning, just an
empty result that looks like "there are none". Whenever the subquery selects
a nullable column, use `NOT EXISTS` instead, or add `WHERE col IS NOT NULL`
inside the subquery.

**`EXISTS` is not fooled by NULLs** because it never compares values across
the boundary - it asks whether the correlated subquery produced any row at
all, and a row that fails to match simply is not produced. This is the reason
to reach for it by default rather than as a repair.

**Two conditions of opposite sign need two subqueries.** "Has ordered but
never bought electronics" cannot be a join plus a filter, because the
customer's book order would satisfy the filter on its own. One `EXISTS` and
one `NOT EXISTS`, each correlated, each independent.

**SQL has no `FOR ALL`, so you write it as a double negative.** "Every line
has quantity 5" becomes "no line has a quantity other than 5" - plus a
separate check that there is at least one line, because "no line disagrees"
is vacuously true for an order with nothing in it. That vacuous-truth footnote
is the part interviewers actually probe.

**Anti-joins and outer joins are the same operation seen twice.** The
`LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL` spelling literally keeps the NULL-extended rows the
previous two drill sets were about, and throws away the matches. If you can
see that, you understand both.

## ex1 - the absence of a particular kind of row

"Never placed a paid order" is not "has no orders" - a customer with three
cancelled orders qualifies, and so does a customer with none. The condition
lives entirely inside the absence.

The classic mistake is `LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE
o.status <> 'paid' ...`, which finds customers who have *some* non-paid
order, a completely different set. If the status test is going to live in a
join at all, it has to be in the `ON` clause, and then the surviving
condition is `o.id IS NULL`.

The model answer is `NOT EXISTS` with both the correlation and the status
inside the subquery; the reference shows the anti-join spelling, with
`o.status = 'paid'` in the `ON` and `o.id IS NULL` in the `WHERE`.

## ex2 - the semi-join, and why DISTINCT is a patch

An Indian customer who has bought forty books is still one customer. Joining
`customers` to `orders` to `order_items` to `products` produces forty rows
for them, and `DISTINCT` collapses those back to one - correct, but the
duplicates were created only to be destroyed.

The classic mistake is forgetting the dedup entirely and reporting a customer
list with repeats. The subtler one is deduping with `GROUP BY c.id, c.name`,
which works and quietly tells a reader that you meant to aggregate something.

The model answer is a single `EXISTS` whose subquery does the whole
three-table walk. The planner turns it into a hash semi-join, which stops
scanning a customer's lines as soon as one matches.

## ex3 - the absence is described by two tables

A sale disqualifies a product only if it was quantity 5 **and** the order
fell in the window. Both halves belong inside the `NOT EXISTS`; pulling
either one out into the outer `WHERE` changes the meaning completely, because
then you are testing a property of the product rather than of the sale.

The classic mistake is the anti-join written carelessly: `LEFT JOIN
order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id AND oi.quantity = 5 LEFT JOIN orders o
ON o.id = oi.order_id WHERE o.created_at >= '2023-11-01' AND ...`. Once the
date test is in `WHERE`, the NULL-extended rows you were about to detect are
already gone.

The model answer correlates a two-table `NOT EXISTS`; the reference builds
the disqualified product ids as one `DISTINCT` subquery, left-joins that, and
keeps the misses - which is the shape to use when the same exclusion list is
needed twice.

## ex4 - the NOT IN trap, on purpose

`SELECT ... FROM staff s WHERE s.id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM staff)` is
the sentence in English, it is what everybody writes, and it returns zero
rows. `staff.manager_id` is NULL for the CEO, and `NOT IN` against a list
containing NULL is unknown for every candidate row.

The classic mistake is not the query, it is the diagnosis: an empty result
reads as "there are no such rows", which is a plausible answer, so people
accept it. That is what makes this the most dangerous construct in the
language - it does not fail, it lies.

The model answer is `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM staff r WHERE r.manager_id =
s.id)`. It is immune because it never compares a value to NULL across the
boundary; a row whose `manager_id` is NULL simply does not match, and not
matching is exactly what the subquery is looking for. The reference uses the
`LEFT JOIN ... WHERE r.id IS NULL` self anti-join, equally safe. If you are
attached to `NOT IN`, the repair is `WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL` inside the
subquery - and having to remember that is the argument for not using it.

## ex5 - one presence, one absence

Two requirements pointing in opposite directions about the same customer.
Neither can be a join with a filter: a customer who bought a novel and a
laptop has an order row where `category <> 'electronics'`, so any
filter-based attempt lets them through.

The classic mistake is dropping the `EXISTS` half. Customers who have never
ordered anything have certainly never ordered electronics, so `NOT EXISTS`
alone returns them too - and they are not the people the report is about.
Whenever an anti-join answers a business question, ask whether "did nothing
at all" should count.

The model answer is `EXISTS (orders)` and `NOT EXISTS (orders -> lines ->
products with category 'electronics')`, both correlated on the customer, both
in the outer `WHERE`. The reference does it with joins: an inner join to the
distinct set of customers who ordered, and a left anti-join against the
distinct set who bought electronics.

## ex6 - same table, both signs

Both conditions read `reviews`, in the same window, differing only in the
rating. That is precisely why they cannot share a join: a single joined row
can testify that *this* review is a five, but it can say nothing at all about
whether some other review is a one.

The classic mistake is `WHERE r.rating = 5 AND r.rating <> 1`, which is just
`rating = 5` with extra words. Any condition of the form "no row of this kind
exists" needs its own subquery; conditions about a single row can share one.

The model answer pairs `EXISTS (... rating = 5 ...)` with `NOT EXISTS (...
rating = 1 ...)`, each carrying the date window. The reference joins the
distinct set of well-reviewed products and left-anti-joins the badly-reviewed
one, which makes the two populations visible as sets and is easier to extend
to a third rating.

## ex7 - churn is an anti-join with a calendar

Active in October, silent afterwards. Two windows over the same table, one
`EXISTS` and one `NOT EXISTS`, and the only real subtlety is the boundaries:
use half-open ranges so that an order at exactly midnight on 1 November
belongs to exactly one window.

The classic mistake is `BETWEEN '2023-10-01' AND '2023-11-01'`, which is
inclusive at both ends and puts that midnight order in both windows - so a
customer who ordered only then counts as both active and churned. With
`timestamptz` columns, half-open is the only boundary convention that never
needs a special case.

The model answer uses the two correlated subqueries. The reference shows the
set-operation route - October customer ids `EXCEPT` November customer ids -
which deduplicates for free and is often the clearest way to express a churn
or diff report.

## ex8 - "every" is "not any, of the opposite"

There is no `FOR ALL` in SQL, so "every line has quantity 5" has to be
rewritten as "no line has a quantity other than 5". That rewrite is
mechanical once you have seen it, and it is asked in interviews constantly.

The classic mistake is the vacuous case. `NOT EXISTS (line with quantity <>
5)` is true for an order with no lines at all - nothing disagrees, because
nothing is there - so those orders sail into the result. The second condition,
`EXISTS (any line)`, is what the prompt means by "at least one line", and
being the person who notices that unprompted is worth a lot.

A subtler version of the same mistake is `NOT EXISTS (line with quantity <>
5)` where `quantity` could be NULL: `NULL <> 5` is unknown, so a NULL line
would not disagree either. It cannot happen here - `order_items.quantity` is
`NOT NULL` - but the reasoning is the same one that makes `NOT IN` dangerous,
and it is worth carrying.

The model answer uses the two subqueries. The reference takes the aggregate
route: group the lines by order and keep the groups where the count of
offending lines is zero, which handles "at least one line" automatically
because a group cannot exist without a row in it.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL - Subquery Expressions: EXISTS, IN, NOT IN](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) - the definitive statement that `NOT IN` yields NULL when the subquery produces a NULL, and the note recommending `NOT EXISTS` instead. Read the `NOT IN` paragraph twice; it is ex4 in one sentence.
- [PostgreSQL - Comparison Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html) - three-valued logic, `IS DISTINCT FROM`, and why `x <> NULL` is unknown rather than true.
- [PostgreSQL - Joined Tables](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-JOIN) - the outer-join semantics that make the `LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL` anti-join work, and why the extra predicate has to be in `ON`.
- [PostgreSQL - Combining Queries: UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-union.html) - the set-operation spelling of an anti-join, used in the ex7 reference, and its automatic deduplication.
- [Use The Index, Luke - Semi-joins and anti-joins](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause/searching-for-ranges) - how these shapes are executed and indexed, which is why `EXISTS` costs no more than a join despite reading like a loop.
