# Reading - 78_drills_anti_semi_1

Semi-joins and anti-joins: filtering one table by whether a matching row
exists somewhere else, without letting that somewhere else into your result.

## Notes

**A semi-join filters; it does not multiply.** "Customers who have bought a
book" is a question about `customers`, and the answer has exactly one row per
customer. A plain join answers a different question - it returns one row per
*book line* - and people patch it with `DISTINCT`. That works, but it means
building a large intermediate result and then throwing most of it away.
`EXISTS` stops at the first match and never produces the duplicates in the
first place.

**An anti-join is the same thing negated,** and it has three spellings in
PostgreSQL: `NOT EXISTS (correlated subquery)`, `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key
IS NULL`, and `NOT IN (subquery)`. The first two are equivalent and safe. The
third is not.

**`NOT IN` with a NULL in the list can never be true.** `x NOT IN (a, b,
NULL)` expands to `x <> a AND x <> b AND x <> NULL`, and the last conjunct is
unknown rather than false - so the whole expression is unknown for every row,
and `WHERE` keeps nothing. It fails silently: no error, no warning, just an
empty result that looks like "there are none". Whenever the subquery selects
a nullable column, use `NOT EXISTS` instead, or add `WHERE col IS NOT NULL`
inside the subquery.

**`EXISTS` is not fooled by NULLs** because it never compares values across
the boundary - it asks whether the correlated subquery produced any row at
all, and a row that fails to match simply is not produced. This is the reason
to reach for it by default rather than as a repair.

**Two conditions of opposite sign need two subqueries.** "Has ordered but
never bought electronics" cannot be a join plus a filter, because the
customer's book order would satisfy the filter on its own. One `EXISTS` and
one `NOT EXISTS`, each correlated, each independent.

**SQL has no `FOR ALL`, so you write it as a double negative.** "Every line
has quantity 5" becomes "no line has a quantity other than 5" - plus a
separate check that there is at least one line, because "no line disagrees"
is vacuously true for an order with nothing in it. That vacuous-truth footnote
is the part interviewers actually probe.

**Anti-joins and outer joins are the same operation seen twice.** The
`LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL` spelling literally keeps the NULL-extended rows the
previous two drill sets were about, and throws away the matches. If you can
see that, you understand both.

## ex1 - the absence of a particular kind of row

"Never placed a paid order" is not "has no orders" - a customer with three
cancelled orders qualifies, and so does a customer with none. The condition
lives entirely inside the absence.

The classic mistake is `LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE
o.status <> 'paid' ...`, which finds customers who have *some* non-paid
order, a completely different set. If the status test is going to live in a
join at all, it has to be in the `ON` clause, and then the surviving
condition is `o.id IS NULL`.

The model answer is `NOT EXISTS` with both the correlation and the status
inside the subquery; the reference shows the anti-join spelling, with
`o.status = 'paid'` in the `ON` and `o.id IS NULL` in the `WHERE`.

## ex2 - the semi-join, and why DISTINCT is a patch

An Indian customer who has bought forty books is still one customer. Joining
`customers` to `orders` to `order_items` to `products` produces forty rows
for them, and `DISTINCT` collapses those back to one - correct, but the
duplicates were created only to be destroyed.

The classic mistake is forgetting the dedup entirely and reporting a customer
list with repeats. The subtler one is deduping with `GROUP BY c.id, c.name`,
which works and quietly tells a reader that you meant to aggregate something.

The model answer is a single `EXISTS` whose subquery does the whole
three-table walk. The planner turns it into a hash semi-join, which stops
scanning a customer's lines as soon as one matches.

## ex3 - the absence is described by two tables

A sale disqualifies a product only if it was quantity 5 **and** the order
fell in the window. Both halves belong inside the `NOT EXISTS`; pulling
either one out into the outer `WHERE` changes the meaning completely, because
then you are testing a property of the product rather than of the sale.

The classic mistake is the anti-join written carelessly: `LEFT JOIN
order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id AND oi.quantity = 5 LEFT JOIN orders o
ON o.id = oi.order_id WHERE o.created_at >= '2023-11-01' AND ...`. Once the
date test is in `WHERE`, the NULL-extended rows you were about to detect are
already gone.

The model answer correlates a two-table `NOT EXISTS`; the reference builds
the disqualified product ids as one `DISTINCT` subquery, left-joins that, and
keeps the misses - which is the shape to use when the same exclusion list is
needed twice.

## ex4 - the NOT IN trap, on purpose

`SELECT ... FROM staff s WHERE s.id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM staff)` is
the sentence in English, it is what everybody writes, and it returns zero
rows. `staff.manager_id` is NULL for the CEO, and `NOT IN` against a list
containing NULL is unknown for every candidate row.

The classic mistake is not the query, it is the diagnosis: an empty result
reads as "there are no such rows", which is a plausible answer, so people
accept it. That is what makes this the most dangerous construct in the
language - it does not fail, it lies.

The model answer is `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM staff r WHERE r.manager_id =
s.id)`. It is immune because it never compares a value to NULL across the
boundary; a row whose `manager_id` is NULL simply does not match, and not
matching is exactly what the subquery is looking for. The reference uses the
`LEFT JOIN ... WHERE r.id IS NULL` self anti-join, equally safe. If you are
attached to `NOT IN`, the repair is `WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL` inside the
subquery - and having to remember that is the argument for not using it.

## ex5 - one presence, one absence

Two requirements pointing in opposite directions about the same customer.
Neither can be a join with a filter: a customer who bought a novel and a
laptop has an order row where `category <> 'electronics'`, so any
filter-based attempt lets them through.

The classic mistake is dropping the `EXISTS` half. Customers who have never
ordered anything have certainly never ordered electronics, so `NOT EXISTS`
alone returns them too - and they are not the people the report is about.
Whenever an anti-join answers a business question, ask whether "did nothing
at all" should count.

The model answer is `EXISTS (orders)` and `NOT EXISTS (orders -> lines ->
products with category 'electronics')`, both correlated on the customer, both
in the outer `WHERE`. The reference does it with joins: an inner join to the
distinct set of customers who ordered, and a left anti-join against the
distinct set who bought electronics.

## ex6 - same table, both signs

Both conditions read `reviews`, in the same window, differing only in the
rating. That is precisely why they cannot share a join: a single joined row
can testify that *this* review is a five, but it can say nothing at all about
whether some other review is a one.

The classic mistake is `WHERE r.rating = 5 AND r.rating <> 1`, which is just
`rating = 5` with extra words. Any condition of the form "no row of this kind
exists" needs its own subquery; conditions about a single row can share one.

The model answer pairs `EXISTS (... rating = 5 ...)` with `NOT EXISTS (...
rating = 1 ...)`, each carrying the date window. The reference joins the
distinct set of well-reviewed products and left-anti-joins the badly-reviewed
one, which makes the two populations visible as sets and is easier to extend
to a third rating.

## ex7 - churn is an anti-join with a calendar

Active in October, silent afterwards. Two windows over the same table, one
`EXISTS` and one `NOT EXISTS`, and the only real subtlety is the boundaries:
use half-open ranges so that an order at exactly midnight on 1 November
belongs to exactly one window.

The classic mistake is `BETWEEN '2023-10-01' AND '2023-11-01'`, which is
inclusive at both ends and puts that midnight order in both windows - so a
customer who ordered only then counts as both active and churned. With
`timestamptz` columns, half-open is the only boundary convention that never
needs a special case.

The model answer uses the two correlated subqueries. The reference shows the
set-operation route - October customer ids `EXCEPT` November customer ids -
which deduplicates for free and is often the clearest way to express a churn
or diff report.

## ex8 - "every" is "not any, of the opposite"

There is no `FOR ALL` in SQL, so "every line has quantity 5" has to be
rewritten as "no line has a quantity other than 5". That rewrite is
mechanical once you have seen it, and it is asked in interviews constantly.

The classic mistake is the vacuous case. `NOT EXISTS (line with quantity <>
5)` is true for an order with no lines at all - nothing disagrees, because
nothing is there - so those orders sail into the result. The second condition,
`EXISTS (any line)`, is what the prompt means by "at least one line", and
being the person who notices that unprompted is worth a lot.

A subtler version of the same mistake is `NOT EXISTS (line with quantity <>
5)` where `quantity` could be NULL: `NULL <> 5` is unknown, so a NULL line
would not disagree either. It cannot happen here - `order_items.quantity` is
`NOT NULL` - but the reasoning is the same one that makes `NOT IN` dangerous,
and it is worth carrying.

The model answer uses the two subqueries. The reference takes the aggregate
route: group the lines by order and keep the groups where the count of
offending lines is zero, which handles "at least one line" automatically
because a group cannot exist without a row in it.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL - Subquery Expressions: EXISTS, IN, NOT IN](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) - the definitive statement that `NOT IN` yields NULL when the subquery produces a NULL, and the note recommending `NOT EXISTS` instead. Read the `NOT IN` paragraph twice; it is ex4 in one sentence.
- [PostgreSQL - Comparison Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html) - three-valued logic, `IS DISTINCT FROM`, and why `x <> NULL` is unknown rather than true.
- [PostgreSQL - Joined Tables](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-JOIN) - the outer-join semantics that make the `LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL` anti-join work, and why the extra predicate has to be in `ON`.
- [PostgreSQL - Combining Queries: UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-union.html) - the set-operation spelling of an anti-join, used in the ex7 reference, and its automatic deduplication.
- [Use The Index, Luke - Semi-joins and anti-joins](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause/searching-for-ranges) - how these shapes are executed and indexed, which is why `EXISTS` costs no more than a join despite reading like a loop.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
You are looking for an absence: no paid order anywhere in this customer's history. Customers with cancelled or pending orders still qualify, and so do customers with no orders at all.

## Hint 2
Two spellings do this. `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid')`, or a `LEFT JOIN` carrying `o.status = 'paid'` in its `ON` clause followed by `WHERE o.id IS NULL`. Note where the status test has to sit in the second one.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'
WHERE c.country = 'IN' AND o.id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE c.country = 'IN'
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
                  WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid')
ORDER BY c.id;

This is the opposite of an anti-join: you want the customers for whom a matching row **does** exist, and you want each of them once no matter how many books they have bought.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
This is the opposite of an anti-join: you want the customers for whom a matching row **does** exist, and you want each of them once no matter how many books they have bought.

## Hint 2
`EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ... JOIN products p ... WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND p.category = 'books')` stops at the first match and cannot duplicate. A plain join through the three tables works too, but a customer with forty book lines then appears forty times unless you dedupe.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE c.country = 'IN' AND p.category = 'books'
ORDER BY c.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE c.country = 'IN'
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1
              FROM orders o
              JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
              JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
              WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND p.category = 'books')
ORDER BY c.id;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3

`garden` products priced above 480 that were **never sold in a quantity of 5
on an order created on or after 2023-11-01**. Both halves of that description
have to hold at once for a sale to disqualify a product. Columns, in this
order: `id`, `name`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 78_drills_anti_semi_1 ex3`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The thing that must not exist is described by two tables at once: a line with quantity 5 **and** an order created in the window. Both conditions belong inside the absence, not outside it.

## Hint 2
`NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi JOIN orders o ON ... WHERE oi.product_id = p.id AND ...)`. If you prefer the outer-join spelling, build the set of disqualified product ids as a subquery first, `LEFT JOIN` it, and keep the rows where it came back NULL.

## Hint 1
The thing that must not exist is described by two tables at once: a line with quantity 5 **and** an order created in the window. Both conditions belong inside the absence, not outside it.

`NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi JOIN orders o ON ... WHERE oi.product_id = p.id AND ...)`. If you prefer the outer-join spelling, build the set of disqualified product ids as a subquery first, `LEFT JOIN` it, and keep the rows where it came back NULL.

SELECT p.id, p.name
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT oi.product_id
           FROM order_items oi
           JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
           WHERE oi.quantity = 5
             AND o.created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01') x ON x.product_id = p.id
WHERE p.category = 'garden' AND p.price > 480
  AND x.product_id IS NULL
ORDER BY p.id;

SELECT p.id, p.name

                  WHERE oi.product_id = p.id

ORDER BY p.id;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Two conditions of opposite sign about the same customer: something must exist, and something else must not. Neither one can be expressed by joining and filtering, because a customer with both a book order and a laptop order would pass on the strength of the book row alone.

## Hint 2
One `EXISTS` for the orders and one `NOT EXISTS` for the electronics purchases, both correlated on `o.customer_id = c.id`, both in the `WHERE` clause of the outer query.

## Hint 3
The reason the `EXISTS` half is needed at all: a customer with no orders whatsoever has bought no electronics either, so the `NOT EXISTS` alone would sweep all of them in. The prompt asks for people who shop with us, just never for electronics.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM orders) b ON b.customer_id = c.id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT o.customer_id
           FROM orders o
           JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
           JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
           WHERE p.category = 'electronics') e ON e.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.country = 'JP' AND e.customer_id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE c.country = 'JP'
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1
                  FROM orders o
                  JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
                  JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
                  WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND p.category = 'electronics')
ORDER BY c.id;

## Hint 1
Both conditions read the same table, in the same window, with different ratings - and one of them is a presence while the other is an absence. They cannot share a single join.

`EXISTS (... rating = 5 ...)` and `NOT EXISTS (... rating = 1 ...)`, each correlated on `r.product_id = p.id` and each carrying the date window. A single join with `rating = 5 AND rating <> 1` is a different and much weaker claim: it only says one particular review is a five, not that no review is a one.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Both conditions read the same table, in the same window, with different ratings - and one of them is a presence while the other is an absence. They cannot share a single join.

## Hint 2
`EXISTS (... rating = 5 ...)` and `NOT EXISTS (... rating = 1 ...)`, each correlated on `r.product_id = p.id` and each carrying the date window. A single join with `rating = 5 AND rating <> 1` is a different and much weaker claim: it only says one particular review is a five, not that no review is a one.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT p.id, p.name
FROM products p
JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM reviews
      WHERE rating = 5 AND created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01') good
  ON good.product_id = p.id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM reviews
           WHERE rating = 1 AND created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01') bad
  ON bad.product_id = p.id
WHERE p.category = 'books' AND bad.product_id IS NULL
ORDER BY p.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT p.id, p.name
FROM products p
WHERE p.category = 'books'
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM reviews r
              WHERE r.product_id = p.id AND r.rating = 5
                AND r.created_at >= '2023-11-01')
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM reviews r
                  WHERE r.product_id = p.id AND r.rating = 1
                    AND r.created_at >= '2023-11-01')
ORDER BY p.id;

## Exercise 7

Churn. Customers in country `US` who placed at least one order in **October
2023** (`>= '2023-10-01'` and `< '2023-11-01'`) and **no order at all** on or
after `2023-11-01`. Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

There is a second good spelling worth knowing: the October customer ids `EXCEPT` the November customer ids, joined back to `customers` for the names. `EXCEPT` deduplicates on its own, which is exactly what a one-row-per-customer answer wants.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders
      WHERE created_at >= DATE '2023-10-01'
        AND created_at <  DATE '2023-11-01'
      EXCEPT
      SELECT customer_id FROM orders
      WHERE created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01') x ON x.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.country = 'US'
ORDER BY c.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE c.country = 'US'
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
              WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
                AND o.created_at >= '2023-10-01'
                AND o.created_at <  '2023-11-01')
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
                  WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
                    AND o.created_at >= '2023-11-01')
ORDER BY c.id;

# 79 - Drills: self-joins and hierarchies

Eight problems on one table joined to itself: employee and manager, teammate
and teammate, and the shapes that fall out of an inequality in an `ON`
clause. This set drills lesson 10, and everything here runs against `staff`,
by far the smallest table in the dataset - so these are fast to iterate on
and there is nowhere to hide.

## Exercise 1

Everyone in the `support` department, with the name of the person they report
to. Columns, in this order: the employee's `id`, `name`, `salary`, and
`manager` (the manager's name).

**Ordered by the employee's `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 79_drills_self_joins_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2

Teammate pairs in the `engineering` department - two people who report to the
same manager. Each pair appears exactly once, with the lower `id` first, and
nobody is paired with themselves. Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`,
`id2`, `name2`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending, then `id2` ascending.**

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 79_drills_self_joins_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3

Every row of `staff`, with the name of their manager and how far their own
salary sits above or below their manager's. The one person who has no
manager still appears, with NULL in both of those columns. Columns, in this
order: `id`, `name`, `manager`, `gap` (the employee's salary minus the
manager's).

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 79_drills_self_joins_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4

Everyone whose department differs from their manager's. Columns, in this
order: the employee's `id`, `name`, `department`, then `manager` (the
manager's name) and `manager_department`.

**Ordered by the employee's `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 79_drills_self_joins_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5

For every person in the `sales` department, how many people **in the same
department** earn strictly more than they do. The top earner must appear with
`0`. Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `richer_colleagues`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 79_drills_self_joins_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6

Every manager with **at least 5 direct reports**: their own id, name and
department, how many direct reports they have, and the average salary of
those reports rounded to 2 decimal places. Columns, in this order: `id`,
`name`, `department`, `reports`, `avg_report_salary`.

**Ordered by `reports` descending, then `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 79_drills_self_joins_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7

Pairs of people who report to the same manager where the second was hired
**at least 1825 days** (five years) after the first. Columns, in this order:
`id`, `name` (the earlier hire), `id2`, `name2` (the later hire), and
`days_apart` - a plain integer count of days.

**Ordered by `id` ascending, then `id2` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 79_drills_self_joins_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8

Every person who manages at least one other person: their id, their name, how
many direct reports they have, and the name of their **highest-paid** direct
report - ties broken by the lower staff `id`. Columns, in this order: `id`,
`name`, `reports`, `top_report`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 79_drills_self_joins_1 ex8`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 79_drills_self_joins_1

One table, two aliases. Everything in this set follows from taking that
sentence literally.

## Notes

**A self-join is not a special kind of join.** `staff e JOIN staff m ON m.id
= e.manager_id` is the ordinary join you already know; the only new thing is
that both inputs happen to be the same table, so both need aliases and every
column reference needs a prefix. Postgres will refuse an unqualified `name`
here, and that error message is doing you a favour.

**The `ON` clause does not have to be an equality.** `t.salary > s.salary`,
`b.hired_on - a.hired_on >= 1825`, `a.id < b.id` are all legal join
conditions, and each of them produces a genuinely different shape: a ranking,
a gap analysis, a deduplicated pair list. Most of the leverage in self-joins
comes from remembering this.

**Pair queries are symmetric until you break them.** Joining a table to
itself on a shared attribute pairs every row with itself and every real pair
twice. `a.id < b.id` kills both problems in one condition - strictly less
than, not `<>`, because `<>` only removes the self-pairs and leaves the
mirror images. When the pair is already ordered by something else (a hire
date, a salary), the inequality that expresses that ordering does the same
job.

**NULL join keys never match, and that is usually what you want.**
`b.manager_id = a.manager_id` cannot pair the CEO with anybody, because the
CEO's `manager_id` is NULL and `NULL = NULL` is unknown. In a teammate query
that is exactly right. In an "everyone with their manager" query it is a bug,
and the fix is `LEFT JOIN`.

**A hierarchy is a self-join per level.** One join gets you the manager, two
get the manager's manager, three get the level above that. This dataset's
tree is four levels deep, so three chained self-joins reach the top from the
bottom. When the depth is unknown or unbounded, that approach runs out and
you need a recursive CTE - lesson 14, and drill set 89.

**An aggregate cannot produce a name.** "How many reports" is an aggregate of
the group; "the name of the best-paid report" is a property of one particular
row in it. The moment a report needs both, you need two constructs: a
`GROUP BY` for the number and a correlated subquery, `DISTINCT ON`, or a
window function for the row.

## ex1 - the plain employee-manager join

The shape everything else is built on. `staff` appears twice, once as the
employee and once as the manager, joined on `m.id = e.manager_id`.

The classic mistake is getting the direction backwards - `e.id =
m.manager_id` joins each manager to their reports instead, which is a valid
query answering a different question and produces plausible-looking rubbish.
Say the join out loud: "the manager row whose id equals this employee's
manager_id."

The model answer aliases both copies and prefixes every column; the reference
writes the same join starting from the manager side, to make the point that
join order is irrelevant to the result.

## ex2 - pairs, once each

Joining `staff` to itself on `manager_id` pairs everyone in a team with
everyone in that team, themselves included, in both directions. For a team of
four that is 16 rows where you wanted 6.

The classic mistake is `a.id <> b.id`, which removes the four self-pairs and
leaves 12 - every real pair still appears twice, mirrored. `a.id < b.id`
removes both classes at once and additionally guarantees the "lower id first"
the prompt asks for, which is why it is the idiom rather than one of several
options.

The model answer puts the inequality in the `ON` clause. The reference uses
the old comma-join spelling with everything in `WHERE`; the two are identical
to the planner, and seeing them side by side is a reminder that `ON` and
`WHERE` are interchangeable for inner joins - and only for inner joins.

## ex3 - the CEO problem

There is exactly one row in `staff` with a NULL `manager_id`, and an inner
self-join drops it silently. An answer one row short of the whole table is
the kind of error that survives review because nobody counts.

The classic mistake, after switching to `LEFT JOIN`, is special-casing the
gap column with a `CASE`. There is no need: `e.salary - NULL` is NULL, so the
arithmetic already produces the right answer. SQL's NULL propagation is
annoying in `WHERE` clauses and helpful in `SELECT` lists.

The model answer is a single `LEFT JOIN`. The reference uses two correlated
scalar subqueries instead, which return NULL when they find no row - the same
result by a different mechanism, and the shape to reach for when you want one
column from a lookup table without touching the join tree.

## ex4 - comparing two copies of the same column

Nothing structurally new; the value is in becoming comfortable with
`e.department <> m.department`, a comparison between two aliases of one
column. Read it as a sentence about two people and it stops looking strange.

The classic mistake is forgetting that `<>` is unknown when either side is
NULL. It does not bite here because the inner join has already excluded the
only NULL-manager row, but change that join to `LEFT` and the CEO's row
would quietly vanish again - this time in the `WHERE` clause rather than the
join. The reference uses `IS DISTINCT FROM`, which is the NULL-safe version
and treats NULL as an ordinary value.

The model answer joins employee to manager and compares the two department
columns directly. The rows it finds are the seams of the org chart, where a
department boundary is crossed.

## ex5 - an inequality join is a ranking

"How many colleagues earn more than me" is a count over a self-join whose
condition is `t.salary > s.salary`. Every person is joined to exactly the set
of people who out-earn them, and the size of that set is the answer.

The classic mistake is an inner join, which deletes the best-paid person in
the department - the one whose set is empty, and the one everybody actually
wants to see. The fix is `LEFT JOIN` plus `count(t.id)`, which is the same
`count(*)`-versus-`count(col)` distinction the outer-join drills were about,
turning up in a self-join.

The model answer does exactly that. The reference uses a correlated scalar
subquery, which cannot have the empty-set problem at all, because it returns
one row per person by construction. Worth knowing that this whole shape is
what `rank()` computes in one pass - lesson 15 - and that the self-join
version is what people wrote before window functions existed.

## ex6 - grouping a self-join

The grain is the manager; the rows being aggregated are their reports. So:
self-join, group by the manager's own columns, aggregate the report columns.

The classic mistake is putting the `>= 5` test in `WHERE`. It is a statement
about the size of the group, which does not exist until after grouping, so it
belongs in `HAVING`. The second mistake is grouping by `m.id` alone and then
selecting `m.name` - Postgres actually allows this, because `staff.id` is the
primary key and functionally determines the rest of the row, but it is not
portable and it hides the intent.

The model answer groups the join and filters with `HAVING`. Note what the
inner join does for free: managers with no reports produce no rows and are
absent from the answer without any extra condition, which here is exactly
right.

## ex7 - the inequality does the deduplication

Same teammate join as ex2, but the pair is ordered by hire date rather than
by id, so `a.id < b.id` would be wrong - it would throw away every pair where
the earlier hire happens to have the higher id.

The classic mistake is adding it anyway out of habit. Look at the result: the
last row of the reference answer pairs a higher-id person with a lower-id
one - an older-hire-with-higher-id pair that `a.id < b.id` would have
deleted. When a
condition already forces an order on the pair, it *is* the deduplication.

The other thing worth noticing is the arithmetic. Subtracting two `date`
values in PostgreSQL yields an integer number of days - not an interval, and
not a timestamp difference. That is why the prompt can ask for a plain
`days_apart` and why `1825` on the right-hand side of the comparison works
without a cast.

## ex8 - a count and a name in one row

The number of reports is an aggregate. The best-paid report's name is not -
it belongs to one specific row of the group, and no aggregate function can
extract it. Recognising that split is the whole exercise; once you have, both
halves are easy.

The classic mistake is `max(e.salary)` and `e.name` in the same `SELECT`,
which Postgres rejects, followed by `max(e.name)`, which it accepts and which
returns the alphabetically last name in the team. That second version is the
dangerous one: it runs, it looks right, and it is wrong on most rows.

The model answer counts with a `GROUP BY` and fetches the name with a
correlated subquery ordered by `salary DESC, id LIMIT 1`. The reference uses
`DISTINCT ON (manager_id)` with the same ordering - the compact PostgreSQL
idiom for "one row per key, the best one" (lesson 49) - joined back to the
counts. Either way the tie-break belongs in the ordering, not in your hopes:
without `, id` two reports on identical salaries would resolve differently
from run to run.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL - Table Aliases](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-TABLE-ALIASES) - the section that explicitly covers joining a table to itself, and why the aliases are mandatory rather than stylistic.
- [PostgreSQL - Joined Tables](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-JOIN) - that the `ON` condition is any boolean expression, which is what licenses the inequality joins in ex5 and ex7.
- [PostgreSQL - Date/Time Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) - the operator table showing `date - date` returning an integer number of days. Behind ex7.
- [PostgreSQL - SELECT: DISTINCT ON](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html#SQL-DISTINCT) - one row per group chosen by an `ORDER BY`, the reference solution's answer to ex8.
- [PostgreSQL - WITH Queries (recursive)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) - where self-joins stop being enough: unbounded hierarchy depth, and the `WITH RECURSIVE` form that replaces them.

# 79 - Drills: self-joins and hierarchies

Eight problems on one table joined to itself: employee and manager, teammate
and teammate, and the shapes that fall out of an inequality in an `ON`
clause. This set drills lesson 10, and everything here runs against `staff`,
by far the smallest table in the dataset - so these are fast to iterate on
and there is nowhere to hide.

## Exercise 1

Everyone in the `support` department, with the name of the person they report
to. Columns, in this order: the employee's `id`, `name`, `salary`, and
`manager` (the manager's name).

**Ordered by the employee's `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 79_drills_self_joins_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2

Teammate pairs in the `engineering` department - two people who report to the
same manager. Each pair appears exactly once, with the lower `id` first, and
nobody is paired with themselves. Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`,
`id2`, `name2`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending, then `id2` ascending.**

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 79_drills_self_joins_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3

Every row of `staff`, with the name of their manager and how far their own
salary sits above or below their manager's. The one person who has no
manager still appears, with NULL in both of those columns. Columns, in this
order: `id`, `name`, `manager`, `gap` (the employee's salary minus the
manager's).

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 79_drills_self_joins_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4

Everyone whose department differs from their manager's. Columns, in this
order: the employee's `id`, `name`, `department`, then `manager` (the
manager's name) and `manager_department`.

**Ordered by the employee's `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 79_drills_self_joins_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5

For every person in the `sales` department, how many people **in the same
department** earn strictly more than they do. The top earner must appear with
`0`. Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `richer_colleagues`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 79_drills_self_joins_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6

Every manager with **at least 5 direct reports**: their own id, name and
department, how many direct reports they have, and the average salary of
those reports rounded to 2 decimal places. Columns, in this order: `id`,
`name`, `department`, `reports`, `avg_report_salary`.

**Ordered by `reports` descending, then `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 79_drills_self_joins_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7

Pairs of people who report to the same manager where the second was hired
**at least 1825 days** (five years) after the first. Columns, in this order:
`id`, `name` (the earlier hire), `id2`, `name2` (the later hire), and
`days_apart` - a plain integer count of days.

**Ordered by `id` ascending, then `id2` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 79_drills_self_joins_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8

Every person who manages at least one other person: their id, their name, how
many direct reports they have, and the name of their **highest-paid** direct
report - ties broken by the lower staff `id`. Columns, in this order: `id`,
`name`, `reports`, `top_report`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 79_drills_self_joins_1 ex8`

# Reading - 79_drills_self_joins_1

One table, two aliases. Everything in this set follows from taking that
sentence literally.

## Notes

**A self-join is not a special kind of join.** `staff e JOIN staff m ON m.id
= e.manager_id` is the ordinary join you already know; the only new thing is
that both inputs happen to be the same table, so both need aliases and every
column reference needs a prefix. Postgres will refuse an unqualified `name`
here, and that error message is doing you a favour.

**The `ON` clause does not have to be an equality.** `t.salary > s.salary`,
`b.hired_on - a.hired_on >= 1825`, `a.id < b.id` are all legal join
conditions, and each of them produces a genuinely different shape: a ranking,
a gap analysis, a deduplicated pair list. Most of the leverage in self-joins
comes from remembering this.

**Pair queries are symmetric until you break them.** Joining a table to
itself on a shared attribute pairs every row with itself and every real pair
twice. `a.id < b.id` kills both problems in one condition - strictly less
than, not `<>`, because `<>` only removes the self-pairs and leaves the
mirror images. When the pair is already ordered by something else (a hire
date, a salary), the inequality that expresses that ordering does the same
job.

**NULL join keys never match, and that is usually what you want.**
`b.manager_id = a.manager_id` cannot pair the CEO with anybody, because the
CEO's `manager_id` is NULL and `NULL = NULL` is unknown. In a teammate query
that is exactly right. In an "everyone with their manager" query it is a bug,
and the fix is `LEFT JOIN`.

**A hierarchy is a self-join per level.** One join gets you the manager, two
get the manager's manager, three get the level above that. This dataset's
tree is four levels deep, so three chained self-joins reach the top from the
bottom. When the depth is unknown or unbounded, that approach runs out and
you need a recursive CTE - lesson 14, and drill set 89.

**An aggregate cannot produce a name.** "How many reports" is an aggregate of
the group; "the name of the best-paid report" is a property of one particular
row in it. The moment a report needs both, you need two constructs: a
`GROUP BY` for the number and a correlated subquery, `DISTINCT ON`, or a
window function for the row.

## ex1 - the plain employee-manager join

The shape everything else is built on. `staff` appears twice, once as the
employee and once as the manager, joined on `m.id = e.manager_id`.

The classic mistake is getting the direction backwards - `e.id =
m.manager_id` joins each manager to their reports instead, which is a valid
query answering a different question and produces plausible-looking rubbish.
Say the join out loud: "the manager row whose id equals this employee's
manager_id."

The model answer aliases both copies and prefixes every column; the reference
writes the same join starting from the manager side, to make the point that
join order is irrelevant to the result.

## ex2 - pairs, once each

Joining `staff` to itself on `manager_id` pairs everyone in a team with
everyone in that team, themselves included, in both directions. For a team of
four that is 16 rows where you wanted 6.

The classic mistake is `a.id <> b.id`, which removes the four self-pairs and
leaves 12 - every real pair still appears twice, mirrored. `a.id < b.id`
removes both classes at once and additionally guarantees the "lower id first"
the prompt asks for, which is why it is the idiom rather than one of several
options.

The model answer puts the inequality in the `ON` clause. The reference uses
the old comma-join spelling with everything in `WHERE`; the two are identical
to the planner, and seeing them side by side is a reminder that `ON` and
`WHERE` are interchangeable for inner joins - and only for inner joins.

## ex3 - the CEO problem

There is exactly one row in `staff` with a NULL `manager_id`, and an inner
self-join drops it silently. An answer one row short of the whole table is
the kind of error that survives review because nobody counts.

The classic mistake, after switching to `LEFT JOIN`, is special-casing the
gap column with a `CASE`. There is no need: `e.salary - NULL` is NULL, so the
arithmetic already produces the right answer. SQL's NULL propagation is
annoying in `WHERE` clauses and helpful in `SELECT` lists.

The model answer is a single `LEFT JOIN`. The reference uses two correlated
scalar subqueries instead, which return NULL when they find no row - the same
result by a different mechanism, and the shape to reach for when you want one
column from a lookup table without touching the join tree.

## ex4 - comparing two copies of the same column

Nothing structurally new; the value is in becoming comfortable with
`e.department <> m.department`, a comparison between two aliases of one
column. Read it as a sentence about two people and it stops looking strange.

The classic mistake is forgetting that `<>` is unknown when either side is
NULL. It does not bite here because the inner join has already excluded the
only NULL-manager row, but change that join to `LEFT` and the CEO's row
would quietly vanish again - this time in the `WHERE` clause rather than the
join. The reference uses `IS DISTINCT FROM`, which is the NULL-safe version
and treats NULL as an ordinary value.

The model answer joins employee to manager and compares the two department
columns directly. The rows it finds are the seams of the org chart, where a
department boundary is crossed.

## ex5 - an inequality join is a ranking

"How many colleagues earn more than me" is a count over a self-join whose
condition is `t.salary > s.salary`. Every person is joined to exactly the set
of people who out-earn them, and the size of that set is the answer.

The classic mistake is an inner join, which deletes the best-paid person in
the department - the one whose set is empty, and the one everybody actually
wants to see. The fix is `LEFT JOIN` plus `count(t.id)`, which is the same
`count(*)`-versus-`count(col)` distinction the outer-join drills were about,
turning up in a self-join.

The model answer does exactly that. The reference uses a correlated scalar
subquery, which cannot have the empty-set problem at all, because it returns
one row per person by construction. Worth knowing that this whole shape is
what `rank()` computes in one pass - lesson 15 - and that the self-join
version is what people wrote before window functions existed.

## ex6 - grouping a self-join

The grain is the manager; the rows being aggregated are their reports. So:
self-join, group by the manager's own columns, aggregate the report columns.

The classic mistake is putting the `>= 5` test in `WHERE`. It is a statement
about the size of the group, which does not exist until after grouping, so it
belongs in `HAVING`. The second mistake is grouping by `m.id` alone and then
selecting `m.name` - Postgres actually allows this, because `staff.id` is the
primary key and functionally determines the rest of the row, but it is not
portable and it hides the intent.

The model answer groups the join and filters with `HAVING`. Note what the
inner join does for free: managers with no reports produce no rows and are
absent from the answer without any extra condition, which here is exactly
right.

## ex7 - the inequality does the deduplication

Same teammate join as ex2, but the pair is ordered by hire date rather than
by id, so `a.id < b.id` would be wrong - it would throw away every pair where
the earlier hire happens to have the higher id.

The classic mistake is adding it anyway out of habit. Look at the result: the
last row of the reference answer pairs a higher-id person with a lower-id
one - an older-hire-with-higher-id pair that `a.id < b.id` would have
deleted. When a
condition already forces an order on the pair, it *is* the deduplication.

The other thing worth noticing is the arithmetic. Subtracting two `date`
values in PostgreSQL yields an integer number of days - not an interval, and
not a timestamp difference. That is why the prompt can ask for a plain
`days_apart` and why `1825` on the right-hand side of the comparison works
without a cast.

## ex8 - a count and a name in one row

The number of reports is an aggregate. The best-paid report's name is not -
it belongs to one specific row of the group, and no aggregate function can
extract it. Recognising that split is the whole exercise; once you have, both
halves are easy.

The classic mistake is `max(e.salary)` and `e.name` in the same `SELECT`,
which Postgres rejects, followed by `max(e.name)`, which it accepts and which
returns the alphabetically last name in the team. That second version is the
dangerous one: it runs, it looks right, and it is wrong on most rows.

The model answer counts with a `GROUP BY` and fetches the name with a
correlated subquery ordered by `salary DESC, id LIMIT 1`. The reference uses
`DISTINCT ON (manager_id)` with the same ordering - the compact PostgreSQL
idiom for "one row per key, the best one" (lesson 49) - joined back to the
counts. Either way the tie-break belongs in the ordering, not in your hopes:
without `, id` two reports on identical salaries would resolve differently
from run to run.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL - Table Aliases](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-TABLE-ALIASES) - the section that explicitly covers joining a table to itself, and why the aliases are mandatory rather than stylistic.
- [PostgreSQL - Joined Tables](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-JOIN) - that the `ON` condition is any boolean expression, which is what licenses the inequality joins in ex5 and ex7.
- [PostgreSQL - Date/Time Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) - the operator table showing `date - date` returning an integer number of days. Behind ex7.
- [PostgreSQL - SELECT: DISTINCT ON](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html#SQL-DISTINCT) - one row per group chosen by an `ORDER BY`, the reference solution's answer to ex8.
- [PostgreSQL - WITH Queries (recursive)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) - where self-joins stop being enough: unbounded hierarchy depth, and the `WITH RECURSIVE` form that replaces them.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The employee and the manager are both rows of `staff`. One table, two roles - so the table has to appear twice in the `FROM`, under two different aliases.

## Hint 2
`FROM staff e JOIN staff m ON m.id = e.manager_id`. Every column in the `SELECT` list has to say which copy it came from; `name` on its own is ambiguous and Postgres will say so.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT e.id, e.name, e.salary, m.name
FROM staff m
JOIN staff e ON e.manager_id = m.id
WHERE e.department = 'support'
ORDER BY e.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT e.id, e.name, e.salary, m.name AS manager
FROM staff e
JOIN staff m ON m.id = e.manager_id
WHERE e.department = 'support'
ORDER BY e.id;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Two people are teammates when they report to the same manager. Join `staff` to itself on `manager_id`, and think about what that join gives you before you filter anything.

## Hint 2
It gives you each person paired with themselves, and each real pair twice, once in each direction. `a.id < b.id` removes both problems at once - it is strictly less than, not `<>`. Note also that the join condition can never match the CEO, because `NULL = NULL` is not true.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT a.id, a.name, b.id, b.name
FROM staff a, staff b
WHERE a.manager_id = b.manager_id
  AND a.id < b.id
  AND a.department = 'engineering'
ORDER BY a.id, b.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT a.id, a.name, b.id AS id2, b.name AS name2
FROM staff a
JOIN staff b ON b.manager_id = a.manager_id AND a.id < b.id
WHERE a.department = 'engineering'
ORDER BY a.id, b.id;

SELECT e.id, e.name,
       (SELECT m.name FROM staff m WHERE m.id = e.manager_id) AS manager,
       e.salary - (SELECT m.salary FROM staff m WHERE m.id = e.manager_id) AS gap

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The comparison you need is between two columns of the same name in two copies of the same table. That is only confusing until you have aliased both copies.

## Hint 2
`JOIN staff m ON m.id = e.manager_id WHERE e.department <> m.department`. Because departments are inherited down this tree, the answer is small and the rows it finds are exactly the boundary of the org chart - worth looking at once you have it.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT e.id, e.name, e.department, m.name, m.department
FROM staff m
JOIN staff e ON e.manager_id = m.id
WHERE e.department IS DISTINCT FROM m.department
ORDER BY e.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT e.id, e.name, e.department, m.name AS manager,
       m.department AS manager_department
FROM staff e
JOIN staff m ON m.id = e.manager_id
WHERE e.department <> m.department
ORDER BY e.id;

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5

For every person in the `sales` department, how many people **in the same
department** earn strictly more than they do. The top earner must appear with
`0`. Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `richer_colleagues`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 79_drills_self_joins_1 ex5`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
For each person you need a count of other people who satisfy a condition relative to **that** person. A self-join whose `ON` clause is an inequality rather than an equality does exactly this.

## Hint 2
`LEFT JOIN staff t ON t.department = s.department AND t.salary > s.salary`, then group by `s.id`. The join must be outer and the count must be `count(t.id)`, or the best-paid person in the department - the one whose answer is 0 - disappears from the report.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
For each person you need a count of other people who satisfy a condition relative to **that** person. A self-join whose `ON` clause is an inequality rather than an equality does exactly this.

## Hint 2
`LEFT JOIN staff t ON t.department = s.department AND t.salary > s.salary`, then group by `s.id`. The join must be outer and the count must be `count(t.id)`, or the best-paid person in the department - the one whose answer is 0 - disappears from the report.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT s.id, s.name,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM staff t
        WHERE t.department = s.department AND t.salary > s.salary) AS richer_colleagues
FROM staff s
WHERE s.department = 'sales'
ORDER BY s.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT s.id, s.name, count(t.id) AS richer_colleagues
FROM staff s
LEFT JOIN staff t ON t.department = s.department AND t.salary > s.salary
WHERE s.department = 'sales'
GROUP BY s.id, s.name
ORDER BY s.id;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The grain of the answer is the manager, but the rows being counted and averaged are the reports. Both come from `staff`, so this is a self-join followed by a `GROUP BY` on the manager's own columns.

## Hint 2
`FROM staff m JOIN staff e ON e.manager_id = m.id GROUP BY m.id, m.name, m.department`. The `>= 5` restriction is about the size of the group, so it is a `HAVING`, not a `WHERE` - and note that people with no reports never appear at all, which is what an inner join is for here.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT m.id, m.name, m.department, r.reports, r.avg_report_salary
FROM staff m
JOIN (SELECT manager_id,
             count(*) AS reports,
             round(avg(salary), 2) AS avg_report_salary
      FROM staff
      WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL
      GROUP BY manager_id) r ON r.manager_id = m.id
WHERE r.reports >= 5
ORDER BY r.reports DESC, m.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT m.id, m.name, m.department,
       count(*) AS reports,
       round(avg(e.salary), 2) AS avg_report_salary
FROM staff m
JOIN staff e ON e.manager_id = m.id
GROUP BY m.id, m.name, m.department
HAVING count(*) >= 5
ORDER BY count(*) DESC, m.id;

## Hint 2

references.solution.sql:
SELECT a.id, a.name, b.id, b.name, b.hired_on - a.hired_on
FROM staff a
JOIN staff b ON b.manager_id = a.manager_id
WHERE b.hired_on >= a.hired_on + 1825
ORDER BY a.id, b.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT a.id, a.name, b.id AS id2, b.name AS name2,
       (b.hired_on - a.hired_on) AS days_apart
FROM staff a
JOIN staff b ON b.manager_id = a.manager_id
            AND b.hired_on - a.hired_on >= 1825
ORDER BY a.id, b.id;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8

Every person who manages at least one other person: their id, their name, how
many direct reports they have, and the name of their **highest-paid** direct
report - ties broken by the lower staff `id`. Columns, in this order: `id`,
`name`, `reports`, `top_report`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 79_drills_self_joins_1 ex8`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two things per manager: a number that is an aggregate of the group, and a name that is not. A name cannot be produced by `count` or `avg`, so it has to come from somewhere the `GROUP BY` cannot reach.

## Hint 2
Count the reports with a self-join and a `GROUP BY` on the manager. For the name, either a correlated subquery that orders that manager's reports and takes the first, or a separate ranked query joined back on `manager_id`.

## Hint 3
The tie-break is load-bearing: `ORDER BY salary DESC, id` inside whichever construct you choose, so that two reports on identical salaries always resolve the same way. `DISTINCT ON (manager_id)` with that same ordering is the compact PostgreSQL spelling of "one row per manager, the best one".

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Two things per manager: a number that is an aggregate of the group, and a name that is not. A name cannot be produced by `count` or `avg`, so it has to come from somewhere the `GROUP BY` cannot reach.

## Hint 2
Count the reports with a self-join and a `GROUP BY` on the manager. For the name, either a correlated subquery that orders that manager's reports and takes the first, or a separate ranked query joined back on `manager_id`.

## Hint 3
The tie-break is load-bearing: `ORDER BY salary DESC, id` inside whichever construct you choose, so that two reports on identical salaries always resolve the same way. `DISTINCT ON (manager_id)` with that same ordering is the compact PostgreSQL spelling of "one row per manager, the best one".

references.solution.sql:
WITH cnt AS (
    SELECT manager_id, count(*) AS reports
    FROM staff
    WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL
    GROUP BY manager_id
), best AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT ON (manager_id) manager_id, name
    FROM staff
    WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL
    ORDER BY manager_id, salary DESC, id
)
SELECT m.id, m.name, cnt.reports, best.name
FROM staff m
JOIN cnt ON cnt.manager_id = m.id
JOIN best ON best.manager_id = m.id
ORDER BY m.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT m.id, m.name, count(e.id) AS reports,
       (SELECT e2.name FROM staff e2
        WHERE e2.manager_id = m.id
        ORDER BY e2.salary DESC, e2.id
        LIMIT 1) AS top_report
FROM staff m
JOIN staff e ON e.manager_id = m.id
GROUP BY m.id, m.name
ORDER BY m.id;

# 80 - Drills: set operations

Eight problems on `UNION`, `INTERSECT` and `EXCEPT`: what each one does to
duplicates, what `ALL` changes, where the `ORDER BY` goes, and the operator
precedence that silently answers a different question. This set drills lesson
11. Every answer here is a set of ids or pairs, so the row counts themselves
are part of the feedback.

## Exercise 1

One list of customer ids: everybody in country `MX`, together with everybody
who signed up before `2022-01-01`. Anyone who qualifies on both counts
appears **once**. Column: `id`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 80_drills_set_ops_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2

The same two lists, stacked **without** removing duplicates - so a customer
who satisfies both conditions appears twice. Column: `id`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 80_drills_set_ops_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3

Product ids that were **both** sold in a quantity of 5 on an order created on
or after `2023-11-01` **and** given a 1-star review created on or after
`2023-11-01`. Each product id appears once. Column: `product_id`.

**Ordered by `product_id` ascending.**

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 80_drills_set_ops_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4

Product ids that appear in `reviews` but **never** in `order_items`. Each
appears once. Column: `product_id`.

**Ordered by `product_id` ascending.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 80_drills_set_ops_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5

Two columns this time. Take every `(customer_id, status)` pair that occurs on
an order created in **October 2023** (`>= '2023-10-01'` and `< '2023-11-01'`)
and remove every pair that also occurs on an order created **on or after
2023-11-01**. A pair is removed only when **both** values match. Columns, in
this order: `customer_id`, `status`.

**Ordered by `customer_id` ascending, then `status` ascending.**

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 80_drills_set_ops_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6

Multiplicity matters here. Restricting both sides to customers with `id <=
2000`: take the `customer_id` of every order created in **October 2023**
(`>= '2023-10-01'` and `< '2023-11-01'`) - one entry per order, duplicates
kept - and subtract the `customer_id` of every order created **on or after
2023-11-01**, again one entry per order. A customer with four October orders
and one November order must appear three times. Column: `customer_id`.

**Ordered by `customer_id` ascending.**

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 80_drills_set_ops_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7

Combine the customer ids of everybody in country `JP` with the `customer_id`
of every order whose `total` is above 1995, remove duplicates, and return the
**10 smallest ids**. Column: `id`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 80_drills_set_ops_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8

Product ids that are in category `toys` **and** satisfy at least one of the
following: they received a 1-star review created on or after `2023-11-01`, or
they were sold in a quantity of 5 on an order created on or after
`2023-11-01`. Each id appears once. Column: `product_id`.

**Ordered by `product_id` ascending.**

Write this one with set operators and read your own query back carefully
before you run it - the obvious spelling parses as something else.

# Reading - 80_drills_set_ops_1

`UNION`, `INTERSECT`, `EXCEPT`: three operators, one duplicate rule, and one
precedence rule that catches everybody once.

## Notes

**Set operators work on whole rows, not on columns.** Both branches must
produce the same number of columns with compatible types, and two rows are
"the same" only when every column matches. That is why a two-column `EXCEPT`
removes a `(customer, status)` pair rather than a customer - a distinction
worth stating out loud before you write one.

**Bare means distinct; `ALL` means keep everything.** `UNION`, `INTERSECT`
and `EXCEPT` all deduplicate by default, which is genuinely convenient and
genuinely expensive: the database has to sort or hash the entire result to
find the duplicates. `UNION ALL` just concatenates. If you know the branches
are disjoint, `UNION ALL` is free correctness plus free speed.

**`EXCEPT ALL` is multiset subtraction.** For each value it keeps
`max(0, left_count - right_count)` copies. Plain `EXCEPT` collapses each
value to one and then deletes it entirely if it appears on the right even
once. These are different questions: "which orders have no counterpart" versus
"which customers appear only on the left".

**Set operators are anti-joins and semi-joins in disguise.** `A EXCEPT B` is
an anti-join, `A INTERSECT B` is a semi-join, and both dedupe on the way out.
Which spelling to use is a readability decision, not a correctness one - with
one exception: `EXCEPT` compares whole rows, so where a `NOT EXISTS` would
need three correlated conditions, `EXCEPT` needs none.

**`ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` belong to the whole statement.** Written after the
last branch, they apply to the combined result, not to that branch - and the
column names available to sort by come from the **first** branch. If a query
needs a sort or limit inside one branch, that branch has to be parenthesised
or moved into a subquery.

**`INTERSECT` binds tighter than `UNION` and `EXCEPT`.** `A UNION B INTERSECT
C` means `A UNION (B INTERSECT C)`. This is the arithmetic precedence rule
applied to sets, it is in the standard, and it produces a query that runs
happily and answers something you did not ask. Parenthesise whenever you mix
operators, even when you are sure.

## ex1 - UNION deduplicates

Two overlapping populations, one list. `UNION` concatenates and then removes
duplicate rows, so a Mexican customer who also signed up early appears once.

The classic mistake is `SELECT DISTINCT ... UNION SELECT DISTINCT ...`, which
is harmless but shows the deduplication was not understood; `UNION` already
does it across the combined result, and per-branch `DISTINCT` cannot achieve
that. The other mistake is putting an `ORDER BY` on the first branch, which is
a syntax error in this position for good reason - there is nothing meaningful
it could order.

The model answer is a two-branch `UNION` with one trailing `ORDER BY`. The
reference collapses the whole thing into a single scan with `OR` and
`DISTINCT`, which is what the planner effectively does anyway when both
branches read the same table, and is the version to prefer in that case.

## ex2 - UNION ALL keeps them

Same data, one keyword different, and the row count grows by exactly the size
of the overlap. Running ex1 and ex2 back to back is the cheapest possible
demonstration of what `UNION` costs and what it buys.

The classic mistake is defaulting to `UNION` everywhere. On disjoint branches
- which is most real cases, since people usually union things that cannot
overlap - the deduplication pass is pure waste, and on large results it is the
dominant cost of the query.

The model answer uses `UNION ALL`. The reference wraps the union in a
subquery and sorts outside it, which is worth seeing once: it makes explicit
that the `ORDER BY` was never part of either branch.

## ex3 - INTERSECT is a semi-join

Two sets computed by completely different routes - one through orders and
lines, one through reviews - and you want their overlap. `INTERSECT` compares
the two result sets directly, so neither branch needs to know anything about
the other.

The classic mistake is joining the two branches on `product_id` instead. That
works, but a product with three bulk lines and two complaints then produces
six rows, and you are back to needing `DISTINCT`. `INTERSECT` deduplicates on
both sides as part of its definition.

The model answer is a straight `INTERSECT`. The reference asks the same
question of `products` with two `EXISTS` subqueries - usually faster when the
driving table is small and indexed, and the more natural shape when you also
need columns like the product's name, which a set operator cannot give you
without another join.

## ex4 - EXCEPT is an anti-join

Everything reviewed, minus everything sold. The answer is the products that
exist and have opinions attached but have never appeared on an order - and
`EXCEPT` finds them with no join at all.

The classic mistake is `NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_items)`, which
would be safe here only because that column is `NOT NULL`. Relying on that is
a habit that eventually meets a nullable column and returns silently empty -
lesson 05, and drill set 78 ex4.

The model answer is a two-line `EXCEPT`. The reference uses `NOT EXISTS` with
an explicit `DISTINCT`, which is what you would write if you also needed the
review count or the product name in the same query.

## ex5 - set operators compare whole rows

Two columns per branch, and the removal rule is "both match". A customer with
a `paid` order in October and a `cancelled` order in November keeps their
`(customer, 'paid')` pair, because that exact pair does not appear on the
right.

The classic mistake is reading the query as if it removed customers. It does
not: it removes pairs. Expressing the same thing with `NOT EXISTS` makes the
danger obvious, because you have to write both correlated conditions by hand
and it is easy to write only one.

The model answer is a two-column `EXCEPT`. The reference is the `NOT EXISTS`
version with both conditions spelled out, and comparing the two is the point
- the set operator is shorter precisely because the whole-row comparison is
built in.

## ex6 - EXCEPT ALL counts copies

`EXCEPT ALL` is the operator people forget exists, and it answers a question
plain `EXCEPT` cannot: how many October orders are left over after pairing
each one off against a November order from the same customer.

The classic mistake is expecting `EXCEPT` to do this and being surprised that
active customers disappear entirely. `EXCEPT` is about membership; `EXCEPT
ALL` is about counts. Say which one the business question is asking for
before you choose.

The model answer is a four-line `EXCEPT ALL`. The reference implements the
same semantics by hand - count each side, subtract, and expand the difference
back into rows with `generate_series` - which is worth reading once because it
makes the `max(0, left - right)` rule concrete.

## ex7 - the ORDER BY belongs to the whole thing

A single `ORDER BY id LIMIT 10` after the last branch sorts and truncates the
combined, deduplicated result. Attach either to a branch and you get the ten
smallest of that branch, unioned with all of the other - a different answer
that is easy to produce by accident.

The classic mistake is `ORDER BY customer_id`. The output column names come
from the first branch, so after `SELECT id ... UNION SELECT customer_id ...`
the column is called `id` and nothing else will resolve. Postgres will tell
you so, which is the good outcome; the bad outcome is when both branches
happen to have the same column names and you sort by the wrong one without
noticing.

The model answer relies on the trailing clauses applying to the whole
statement. The reference wraps the union in a subquery - more typing, no
ambiguity, and the version to write when somebody else maintains the query.

## ex8 - precedence, the one that gets everybody

`A UNION B INTERSECT C` is parsed as `A UNION (B INTERSECT C)`, exactly as
`1 + 2 * 3` is `1 + (2 * 3)`. The query runs, returns a plausible number of
rows, and answers "products with a recent complaint, plus toys that had a
recent bulk sale" instead of "toys with either".

The classic mistake is trusting left-to-right reading. Set operators are not
evaluated in written order, and the failure is invisible: no error, no
warning, just a result set that is too big and looks fine. The habit worth
building is to parenthesise every mixed expression, even when the precedence
happens to be on your side.

The model answer parenthesises the `UNION` and intersects the whole thing
with the toys. The reference sidesteps set operators entirely - a `WHERE` on
`products` with two `EXISTS` subqueries joined by `OR` - which is both faster
here and immune to the precedence question. When a set expression starts
needing parentheses to be readable, that is usually the signal to rewrite it
as predicates on one driving table.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL - Combining Queries (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-union.html) - the duplicate rules, the `ALL` variants, and the sentence stating that `INTERSECT` binds more tightly than the other two. Behind every exercise here, and ex8 in particular.
- [PostgreSQL - SELECT: UNION / INTERSECT / EXCEPT clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html#SQL-UNION) - the exact `max(0, m - n)` definition of `EXCEPT ALL` and its `INTERSECT ALL` counterpart. Behind ex6.
- [PostgreSQL - SELECT: ORDER BY and LIMIT with set operations](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html#SQL-ORDERBY) - why the sort applies to the whole statement and why the column names come from the first branch. Behind ex7.
- [PostgreSQL - Subquery Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) - the `EXISTS` / `NOT EXISTS` spellings that the reference solutions use as the alternative to `INTERSECT` and `EXCEPT`.
- [Modern SQL - UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT](https://modern-sql.com/feature/intersect-except) - support and quirks across engines, useful because `EXCEPT` is spelled `MINUS` in some of them.

# Reading - 80_drills_set_ops_1

`UNION`, `INTERSECT`, `EXCEPT`: three operators, one duplicate rule, and one
precedence rule that catches everybody once.

## Notes

**Set operators work on whole rows, not on columns.** Both branches must
produce the same number of columns with compatible types, and two rows are
"the same" only when every column matches. That is why a two-column `EXCEPT`
removes a `(customer, status)` pair rather than a customer - a distinction
worth stating out loud before you write one.

**Bare means distinct; `ALL` means keep everything.** `UNION`, `INTERSECT`
and `EXCEPT` all deduplicate by default, which is genuinely convenient and
genuinely expensive: the database has to sort or hash the entire result to
find the duplicates. `UNION ALL` just concatenates. If you know the branches
are disjoint, `UNION ALL` is free correctness plus free speed.

**`EXCEPT ALL` is multiset subtraction.** For each value it keeps
`max(0, left_count - right_count)` copies. Plain `EXCEPT` collapses each
value to one and then deletes it entirely if it appears on the right even
once. These are different questions: "which orders have no counterpart" versus
"which customers appear only on the left".

**Set operators are anti-joins and semi-joins in disguise.** `A EXCEPT B` is
an anti-join, `A INTERSECT B` is a semi-join, and both dedupe on the way out.
Which spelling to use is a readability decision, not a correctness one - with
one exception: `EXCEPT` compares whole rows, so where a `NOT EXISTS` would
need three correlated conditions, `EXCEPT` needs none.

**`ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` belong to the whole statement.** Written after the
last branch, they apply to the combined result, not to that branch - and the
column names available to sort by come from the **first** branch. If a query
needs a sort or limit inside one branch, that branch has to be parenthesised
or moved into a subquery.

**`INTERSECT` binds tighter than `UNION` and `EXCEPT`.** `A UNION B INTERSECT
C` means `A UNION (B INTERSECT C)`. This is the arithmetic precedence rule
applied to sets, it is in the standard, and it produces a query that runs
happily and answers something you did not ask. Parenthesise whenever you mix
operators, even when you are sure.

## ex1 - UNION deduplicates

Two overlapping populations, one list. `UNION` concatenates and then removes
duplicate rows, so a Mexican customer who also signed up early appears once.

The classic mistake is `SELECT DISTINCT ... UNION SELECT DISTINCT ...`, which
is harmless but shows the deduplication was not understood; `UNION` already
does it across the combined result, and per-branch `DISTINCT` cannot achieve
that. The other mistake is putting an `ORDER BY` on the first branch, which is
a syntax error in this position for good reason - there is nothing meaningful
it could order.

The model answer is a two-branch `UNION` with one trailing `ORDER BY`. The
reference collapses the whole thing into a single scan with `OR` and
`DISTINCT`, which is what the planner effectively does anyway when both
branches read the same table, and is the version to prefer in that case.

## ex2 - UNION ALL keeps them

Same data, one keyword different, and the row count grows by exactly the size
of the overlap. Running ex1 and ex2 back to back is the cheapest possible
demonstration of what `UNION` costs and what it buys.

The classic mistake is defaulting to `UNION` everywhere. On disjoint branches
- which is most real cases, since people usually union things that cannot
overlap - the deduplication pass is pure waste, and on large results it is the
dominant cost of the query.

The model answer uses `UNION ALL`. The reference wraps the union in a
subquery and sorts outside it, which is worth seeing once: it makes explicit
that the `ORDER BY` was never part of either branch.

## ex3 - INTERSECT is a semi-join

Two sets computed by completely different routes - one through orders and
lines, one through reviews - and you want their overlap. `INTERSECT` compares
the two result sets directly, so neither branch needs to know anything about
the other.

The classic mistake is joining the two branches on `product_id` instead. That
works, but a product with three bulk lines and two complaints then produces
six rows, and you are back to needing `DISTINCT`. `INTERSECT` deduplicates on
both sides as part of its definition.

The model answer is a straight `INTERSECT`. The reference asks the same
question of `products` with two `EXISTS` subqueries - usually faster when the
driving table is small and indexed, and the more natural shape when you also
need columns like the product's name, which a set operator cannot give you
without another join.

## ex4 - EXCEPT is an anti-join

Everything reviewed, minus everything sold. The answer is the products that
exist and have opinions attached but have never appeared on an order - and
`EXCEPT` finds them with no join at all.

The classic mistake is `NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM order_items)`, which
would be safe here only because that column is `NOT NULL`. Relying on that is
a habit that eventually meets a nullable column and returns silently empty -
lesson 05, and drill set 78 ex4.

The model answer is a two-line `EXCEPT`. The reference uses `NOT EXISTS` with
an explicit `DISTINCT`, which is what you would write if you also needed the
review count or the product name in the same query.

## ex5 - set operators compare whole rows

Two columns per branch, and the removal rule is "both match". A customer with
a `paid` order in October and a `cancelled` order in November keeps their
`(customer, 'paid')` pair, because that exact pair does not appear on the
right.

The classic mistake is reading the query as if it removed customers. It does
not: it removes pairs. Expressing the same thing with `NOT EXISTS` makes the
danger obvious, because you have to write both correlated conditions by hand
and it is easy to write only one.

The model answer is a two-column `EXCEPT`. The reference is the `NOT EXISTS`
version with both conditions spelled out, and comparing the two is the point
- the set operator is shorter precisely because the whole-row comparison is
built in.

## ex6 - EXCEPT ALL counts copies

`EXCEPT ALL` is the operator people forget exists, and it answers a question
plain `EXCEPT` cannot: how many October orders are left over after pairing
each one off against a November order from the same customer.

The classic mistake is expecting `EXCEPT` to do this and being surprised that
active customers disappear entirely. `EXCEPT` is about membership; `EXCEPT
ALL` is about counts. Say which one the business question is asking for
before you choose.

The model answer is a four-line `EXCEPT ALL`. The reference implements the
same semantics by hand - count each side, subtract, and expand the difference
back into rows with `generate_series` - which is worth reading once because it
makes the `max(0, left - right)` rule concrete.

## ex7 - the ORDER BY belongs to the whole thing

A single `ORDER BY id LIMIT 10` after the last branch sorts and truncates the
combined, deduplicated result. Attach either to a branch and you get the ten
smallest of that branch, unioned with all of the other - a different answer
that is easy to produce by accident.

The classic mistake is `ORDER BY customer_id`. The output column names come
from the first branch, so after `SELECT id ... UNION SELECT customer_id ...`
the column is called `id` and nothing else will resolve. Postgres will tell
you so, which is the good outcome; the bad outcome is when both branches
happen to have the same column names and you sort by the wrong one without
noticing.

The model answer relies on the trailing clauses applying to the whole
statement. The reference wraps the union in a subquery - more typing, no
ambiguity, and the version to write when somebody else maintains the query.

## ex8 - precedence, the one that gets everybody

`A UNION B INTERSECT C` is parsed as `A UNION (B INTERSECT C)`, exactly as
`1 + 2 * 3` is `1 + (2 * 3)`. The query runs, returns a plausible number of
rows, and answers "products with a recent complaint, plus toys that had a
recent bulk sale" instead of "toys with either".

The classic mistake is trusting left-to-right reading. Set operators are not
evaluated in written order, and the failure is invisible: no error, no
warning, just a result set that is too big and looks fine. The habit worth
building is to parenthesise every mixed expression, even when the precedence
happens to be on your side.

The model answer parenthesises the `UNION` and intersects the whole thing
with the toys. The reference sidesteps set operators entirely - a `WHERE` on
`products` with two `EXISTS` subqueries joined by `OR` - which is both faster
here and immune to the precedence question. When a set expression starts
needing parentheses to be readable, that is usually the signal to rewrite it
as predicates on one driving table.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL - Combining Queries (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-union.html) - the duplicate rules, the `ALL` variants, and the sentence stating that `INTERSECT` binds more tightly than the other two. Behind every exercise here, and ex8 in particular.
- [PostgreSQL - SELECT: UNION / INTERSECT / EXCEPT clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html#SQL-UNION) - the exact `max(0, m - n)` definition of `EXCEPT ALL` and its `INTERSECT ALL` counterpart. Behind ex6.
- [PostgreSQL - SELECT: ORDER BY and LIMIT with set operations](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html#SQL-ORDERBY) - why the sort applies to the whole statement and why the column names come from the first branch. Behind ex7.
- [PostgreSQL - Subquery Expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) - the `EXISTS` / `NOT EXISTS` spellings that the reference solutions use as the alternative to `INTERSECT` and `EXCEPT`.
- [Modern SQL - UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT](https://modern-sql.com/feature/intersect-except) - support and quirks across engines, useful because `EXCEPT` is spelled `MINUS` in some of them.
