## Exercise 1

One list of customer ids: everybody in country `MX`, together with everybody
who signed up before `2022-01-01`. Anyone who qualifies on both counts
appears **once**. Column: `id`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 80_drills_set_ops_1 ex1`

Two lists of customer ids, combined into one, with anybody who qualifies on both counts appearing only once.

`SELECT ... UNION SELECT ...` and a single `ORDER BY id` at the very end - the ordering applies to the combined result, not to either branch. Plain `UNION` removes duplicates for you; you do not need `DISTINCT` as well.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Two independently computed sets of product ids, and you want the ones that appear in both. There is an operator for precisely that.

## Hint 2
`INTERSECT`. Both branches may produce a product id many times over - a product can have several bulk lines and several complaints - but `INTERSECT` (without `ALL`) deduplicates, so no `DISTINCT` is needed on either side.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT p.id AS product_id
FROM products p
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1
              FROM order_items oi
              JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
              WHERE oi.product_id = p.id
                AND oi.quantity = 5
                AND o.created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01')
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM reviews r
              WHERE r.product_id = p.id AND r.rating = 1
                AND r.created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01')
ORDER BY p.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT oi.product_id
FROM order_items oi
JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
WHERE oi.quantity = 5 AND o.created_at >= '2023-11-01'
INTERSECT
SELECT r.product_id
FROM reviews r
WHERE r.rating = 1 AND r.created_at >= '2023-11-01'
ORDER BY 1;

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Everything that has been reviewed, minus everything that has ever been sold. Set subtraction, in one operator.

## Hint 2
`SELECT product_id FROM reviews EXCEPT SELECT product_id FROM order_items`. Notice what this is: an anti-join written as arithmetic on sets. `EXCEPT` also deduplicates, so a product reviewed forty times and never sold still comes back once.

## Hint 1
Everything that has been reviewed, minus everything that has ever been sold. Set subtraction, in one operator.

## Hint 2
`SELECT product_id FROM reviews EXCEPT SELECT product_id FROM order_items`. Notice what this is: an anti-join written as arithmetic on sets. `EXCEPT` also deduplicates, so a product reviewed forty times and never sold still comes back once.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT r.product_id
FROM reviews r
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi
                  WHERE oi.product_id = r.product_id)
ORDER BY 1;

EXCEPT
SELECT product_id FROM order_items
ORDER BY 1;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Set operations are not restricted to one column. Two branches match if they have the same number of columns and compatible types, and the whole row is what gets compared.

## Hint 2
`SELECT customer_id, status FROM orders WHERE <october> EXCEPT SELECT customer_id, status FROM orders WHERE <november>`. A pair is removed only if **both** columns match - a customer who ordered `paid` in October and `cancelled` in November keeps their October pair.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT o.customer_id, o.status
FROM orders o
WHERE o.created_at >= DATE '2023-10-01'
  AND o.created_at <  DATE '2023-11-01'
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders n
                  WHERE n.customer_id = o.customer_id
                    AND n.status = o.status
                    AND n.created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01')
ORDER BY 1, 2;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT customer_id, status FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2023-10-01' AND created_at < '2023-11-01'
EXCEPT
SELECT customer_id, status FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2023-11-01'
ORDER BY 1, 2;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
This one is about multiplicity, not membership. A customer with four October orders and one November order should still appear - three times.

## Hint 2
`EXCEPT ALL` does multiset subtraction: for each value it keeps `max(0, count in the left branch - count in the right branch)` copies. Plain `EXCEPT` would collapse each customer to one row and then remove them entirely if they appear on the right even once.

references.solution.sql:
WITH a AS (
    SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS n
    FROM orders
    WHERE customer_id <= 2000
      AND created_at >= DATE '2023-10-01'
      AND created_at <  DATE '2023-11-01'
    GROUP BY customer_id
), b AS (
    SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS n
    FROM orders
    WHERE customer_id <= 2000
      AND created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01'
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT a.customer_id
FROM a
LEFT JOIN b ON b.customer_id = a.customer_id
CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series(1, (a.n - coalesce(b.n, 0))::int) g
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT customer_id FROM orders
WHERE customer_id <= 2000
  AND created_at >= '2023-10-01' AND created_at < '2023-11-01'
EXCEPT ALL
SELECT customer_id FROM orders
WHERE customer_id <= 2000
  AND created_at >= '2023-11-01'
ORDER BY 1;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7

Combine the customer ids of everybody in country `JP` with the `customer_id`
of every order whose `total` is above 1995, remove duplicates, and return the
**10 smallest ids**. Column: `id`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 80_drills_set_ops_1 ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Combine the two id lists first, deduplicate, and only then take the smallest ten. Sorting or limiting either branch on its own would give a different - and wrong - answer.

## Hint 2
A single `ORDER BY` and a single `LIMIT` written after the last branch apply to the whole set operation, not to that branch. If you want to be certain of that, wrap the `UNION` in a subquery and sort the subquery; the two are equivalent and the second is harder to misread.

## Hint 3
The name you sort by comes from the **first** branch: after `SELECT id ... UNION SELECT customer_id ...` the output column is called `id`, so `ORDER BY id` works and `ORDER BY customer_id` does not.

## Hint 1
Combine the two id lists first, deduplicate, and only then take the smallest ten. Sorting or limiting either branch on its own would give a different - and wrong - answer.

## Hint 2
A single `ORDER BY` and a single `LIMIT` written after the last branch apply to the whole set operation, not to that branch. If you want to be certain of that, wrap the `UNION` in a subquery and sort the subquery; the two are equivalent and the second is harder to misread.

## Hint 3
The name you sort by comes from the **first** branch: after `SELECT id ... UNION SELECT customer_id ...` the output column is called `id`, so `ORDER BY id` works and `ORDER BY customer_id` does not.

lessons.briefing:
# 81 - Drills: multi-join reports 1

Eight report queries: a dimension from one table, measures from another,
filters from a third. This set draws on lessons 08 and 12 and asks the
questions a stakeholder actually asks - per status, per category, per month,
per country. The SQL is never exotic; the difficulty is choosing the grain
and getting each measure's definition right.

## Exercise 1

Orders placed in **September 2023** (`>= '2023-09-01'` and `< '2023-10-01'`)
by customers in country `GB`, summarised per status. Columns, in this order:
`status`, `orders` (how many), `revenue` (the sum of `orders.total`).

**Ordered by `status` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 81_drills_multi_join_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2

The ten best-selling products of **October 2023** (`>= '2023-10-01'` and
`< '2023-11-01'`) by units sold. Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`,
`units` (the sum of `order_items.quantity`). Ties on units are broken by the
lower product `id`.

**Ordered by `units` descending, then `id` ascending.** Exactly 10 rows.

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 81_drills_multi_join_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3

Revenue per month per category, for orders created on or after
`2023-10-01`. Columns, in this order: `month` - use
`date_trunc('month', o.created_at)` - then `category`, then `revenue` (the
sum of `quantity * price` taken from the order line).

**Ordered by `month` ascending, then `category` ascending.**

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 81_drills_multi_join_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4

A per-country summary over the whole dataset. Columns, in this order:
`country`, `buyers` (how many distinct customers of that country have
ordered), `orders` (how many orders they placed, **cancelled ones
included**), `revenue` (the sum of `orders.total` over the **non-cancelled**
orders only, `0` if there are none).

**Ordered by `revenue` descending, then `country` ascending.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 81_drills_multi_join_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5

For orders created on or after `2023-11-01`, per status: the average number
of order lines per order and the average number of units per order, each
rounded to 2 decimal places. Orders with no lines count as `0` lines and `0`
units and must be included. Columns, in this order: `status`, `avg_lines`,
`avg_units`.

**Ordered by `status` ascending.**

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 81_drills_multi_join_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6

For orders created on or after `2023-11-01`, per category: revenue (the sum
of `quantity * price` from the order line) and that category's share of the
window's **total** revenue as a percentage rounded to 2 decimal places.
Columns, in this order: `category`, `revenue`, `pct`.

**Ordered by `revenue` descending, then `category` ascending.**

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 81_drills_multi_join_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7

For orders created on or after `2023-11-01`, the single best category per
customer country by revenue (`quantity * price` from the order line) - one
row per country, ties broken by the alphabetically first category. Columns,
in this order: `country`, `category`, `revenue`.

**Ordered by `country` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 81_drills_multi_join_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8

A category scorecard over orders created on or after `2023-10-01`. Columns,
in this order: `category`, `units` (sum of quantities), `revenue` (sum of
`quantity * price`), `orders` (how many **distinct** orders contained the
category), `buyers` (how many **distinct** customers bought it), and
`avg_line_revenue` - the average of `quantity * price` across the lines,
rounded to 2 decimal places. Keep only the categories whose (unrounded)
average line revenue is **above 750**.

**Ordered by `revenue` descending, then `category` ascending.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 81_drills_multi_join_1 ex8`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 81_drills_multi_join_1

Report SQL. The joins are easy; choosing the grain and pinning down each
measure's definition is the job.

## Notes

**Decide the grain before you type.** "One row per status", "one row per
month per category", "one row per country" - that sentence determines the
`GROUP BY` and everything else follows. Most report bugs are grain bugs:
the query groups at a finer level than the question, or aggregates across a
join that has already multiplied the rows.

**The join grain is usually the order line.** Once `order_items` is in the
`FROM`, one order with three lines is three rows. Sums over line columns are
correct at that grain; anything counting orders or customers must use
`count(DISTINCT ...)`, and anything summing an order-level column (like
`orders.total`) is now wrong by a factor of the line count.

**Every measure has a definition, and they rarely agree.** In one report,
revenue excludes cancelled orders, the order count includes them, and the
buyer count counts customers rather than orders. `FILTER (WHERE ...)` is what
lets differently-defined measures share one pass; without it people write
three subqueries and join them.

**You cannot nest aggregates, so two levels means two queries.** "Average
number of lines per order" is `avg` of a `count`, which Postgres rejects
outright. Collapse to one row per order in a subquery or CTE, then aggregate
those rows. The rejection is a feature - it forces you to say which grain the
average is over.

**A row-level percentage needs a number from outside the row.** Either an
uncorrelated scalar subquery that recomputes the total, or a window function
over the already-aggregated result. `sum(x) OVER ()` after a `GROUP BY` totals
the groups, which is exactly what a share-of-total column wants.

**Top-N-per-group is always two layers.** Aggregate to (group, candidate,
measure), then rank within the group and keep the winners. `max()` gives you
the number but not the row it came from, and joining back on the number
breaks on ties.

**Half-open date ranges, always.** `>= start AND < next_start`. `BETWEEN` on
a `timestamptz` includes both endpoints, so a midnight row lands in two
buckets - a bug that shows up as a total that is very slightly too big and
that nobody ever finds.

## ex1 - the smallest possible report

Two tables, one grouping column, two measures. `customers` contributes
nothing to the output; it is there so the country filter has something to
filter.

The classic mistake is `BETWEEN '2023-09-01' AND '2023-09-30'`, which drops
everything after midnight on the 30th - most of a day of orders. Half-open
ranges have no such edge case and never need you to know how long the month
was.

The model answer joins, filters, and groups by `o.status`; the reference is
the same query written from the other table, to make the point that join
order changes nothing.

## ex2 - aggregate, then rank, then cut

`LIMIT` applies to the grouped rows, so the query has to aggregate all of
October before it can know which ten products win. That is not a wasteful
plan, it is the only correct one.

The classic mistake is the missing tie-break. Several products in this window
sit on identical unit totals, and `ORDER BY units DESC` alone lets the
planner return them in any order - so the tenth row changes between runs and
the query is not reproducible. `ORDER BY units DESC, p.id` fixes it, and
naming the tie-break unprompted is a habit worth having.

The model answer groups the three-table join by product and limits. The
reference aggregates `order_items` down to one row per product first and
joins `products` afterwards, which is the cheaper shape when the product
table is wide.

## ex3 - grouping by a computed column

The month does not exist as a column; it is `date_trunc('month',
o.created_at)`, and grouping by an expression is exactly as legal as grouping
by a column.

The classic mistake is `GROUP BY month`, referring to the `SELECT` alias.
Postgres does allow that as an extension, but it does not allow it once the
alias collides with a real column name, and it is not portable - writing the
expression again, or using the output position `GROUP BY 1, 2`, always works.

The model answer groups by the two expressions and sorts by the same. Note
that `date_trunc` on a `timestamptz` returns a `timestamptz`, so the month
column is a timestamp at midnight, not a date - worth knowing before you
compare it to something.

## ex4 - three measures, three definitions

This is the exercise that teaches the habit. `buyers` counts customers,
`orders` counts orders including cancelled ones, `revenue` sums only the
non-cancelled ones. Three different scopes, one join, no `WHERE` on the
status.

The classic mistake is a `WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'`, which fixes the
revenue and quietly corrupts the order count. The second is `count(c.id)` for
the buyers, which counts orders again because the join has already repeated
each customer once per order.

The model answer uses `count(DISTINCT o.customer_id)`, a plain `count(*)`,
and a `FILTER`ed `sum` with a `coalesce`. The reference writes the filtered
sum as a `CASE` inside the aggregate - the portable spelling, and the one to
recognise in older code.

## ex5 - two levels of aggregation

"Average lines per order" is an average of a count. `avg(count(*))` is a
syntax error, and the error is telling you that two different grains are
involved: one row per order for the count, one row per status for the
average.

The classic mistake is skipping the first level - grouping the joined rows by
status and dividing line count by order count by hand. That gives the same
number here, but it stops working the moment the outer aggregate is anything
other than a mean, and it hides the intermediate result that makes the query
readable.

The second mistake is an inner join to `order_items`. Around one order in
seven has no lines at all; dropping them raises both averages, because the
zeros that should pull the mean down are simply absent. The `coalesce` on the
units matters for the same reason - `avg` skips NULLs, so a NULL there would
silently reduce the denominator too.

## ex6 - a share of a total

Each row needs the grand total, which no single group can compute. Two
answers, both worth having: an uncorrelated scalar subquery that recomputes
the window's revenue once, or `sum(revenue) OVER ()` applied to the already
grouped rows.

The classic mistake in the general case is integer division - `100 * x / y`
where both are integers floors to a whole number. It does not bite here,
because `numeric * numeric` stays numeric, but the ordering of the operations
still does: divide first and you round a fraction below 1 to zero before the
multiplication can rescue it. Multiply, then divide, then round.

The model answer uses the scalar subquery; the reference uses the window
function over a subquery that has already grouped. The window version is the
one to prefer when the total is expensive, because it reuses the rows you
already have instead of rescanning.

## ex7 - the best one per group

Two layers. Layer one: revenue for every (country, category) pair. Layer two:
within each country, keep the row with the highest revenue.

The classic mistake is `max(revenue) GROUP BY country`, which gives the
winning number but not the winning category - and joining the aggregate back
to the detail on `(country, revenue)` produces two rows whenever two
categories tie exactly. Ranking keeps the row itself, which is what the report
needs.

The model answer uses `DISTINCT ON (country)` with `ORDER BY country, revenue
DESC, category` - the PostgreSQL idiom for "first row per key". The reference
uses `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY ...)` filtered to
`rn = 1`, which is portable and is the version to write in an interview
unless someone has said the word PostgreSQL. Either way the tie-break lives
inside the ranking, and the same tie-break has to be repeated in the final
`ORDER BY` if the output order matters.

## ex8 - the scorecard

Six columns, and the whole exercise is holding their definitions apart while
the join grain works against you. Units and revenue are sums over lines, so
the line grain suits them. Orders and buyers are counts of things that repeat
across lines, so they need `DISTINCT`. The average is over lines again.

The classic mistake is `count(o.id)` for the orders: a three-line order
contributes three, and the report claims three times the traffic. It is
plausible, it is never questioned, and it is the single most common defect in
hand-written analytics SQL.

The second is putting the final restriction in `WHERE`. It is a statement
about an aggregate of the group, which does not exist until the grouping has
happened, so it belongs in `HAVING` - where you must repeat the whole
expression, because `HAVING` cannot see `SELECT` aliases either. The
reference sidesteps that by computing the average in a subquery and filtering
it from outside, which is often the more readable arrangement once the
expression gets long.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL - GROUP BY and HAVING](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-GROUP) - what may appear in a `SELECT` list alongside aggregates, and why `HAVING` exists separately from `WHERE`. Behind ex1, ex4 and ex8.
- [PostgreSQL - Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - `count(DISTINCT ...)`, and the note that aggregate calls cannot be nested, which is the rule ex5 is built on.
- [PostgreSQL - Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) - `sum(x) OVER ()` for a grand total and `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)` for top-N-per-group. Behind ex6 and ex7.
- [PostgreSQL - SELECT: DISTINCT ON](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html#SQL-DISTINCT) - the shorter PostgreSQL-only route to "the best row per key" used in ex7.
- [PostgreSQL - Date/Time Functions: date_trunc](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html#FUNCTIONS-DATETIME-TRUNC) - how `date_trunc` behaves on `timestamptz`, including the time-zone question that decides which month a midnight order belongs to.

# 81 - Drills: multi-join reports 1

Eight report queries: a dimension from one table, measures from another,
filters from a third. This set draws on lessons 08 and 12 and asks the
questions a stakeholder actually asks - per status, per category, per month,
per country. The SQL is never exotic; the difficulty is choosing the grain
and getting each measure's definition right.

## Exercise 1

Orders placed in **September 2023** (`>= '2023-09-01'` and `< '2023-10-01'`)
by customers in country `GB`, summarised per status. Columns, in this order:
`status`, `orders` (how many), `revenue` (the sum of `orders.total`).

**Ordered by `status` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 81_drills_multi_join_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2

The ten best-selling products of **October 2023** (`>= '2023-10-01'` and
`< '2023-11-01'`) by units sold. Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`,
`units` (the sum of `order_items.quantity`). Ties on units are broken by the
lower product `id`.

**Ordered by `units` descending, then `id` ascending.** Exactly 10 rows.

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 81_drills_multi_join_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3

Revenue per month per category, for orders created on or after
`2023-10-01`. Columns, in this order: `month` - use
`date_trunc('month', o.created_at)` - then `category`, then `revenue` (the
sum of `quantity * price` taken from the order line).

**Ordered by `month` ascending, then `category` ascending.**

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 81_drills_multi_join_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4

A per-country summary over the whole dataset. Columns, in this order:
`country`, `buyers` (how many distinct customers of that country have
ordered), `orders` (how many orders they placed, **cancelled ones
included**), `revenue` (the sum of `orders.total` over the **non-cancelled**
orders only, `0` if there are none).

**Ordered by `revenue` descending, then `country` ascending.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 81_drills_multi_join_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5

For orders created on or after `2023-11-01`, per status: the average number
of order lines per order and the average number of units per order, each
rounded to 2 decimal places. Orders with no lines count as `0` lines and `0`
units and must be included. Columns, in this order: `status`, `avg_lines`,
`avg_units`.

**Ordered by `status` ascending.**

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 81_drills_multi_join_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6

For orders created on or after `2023-11-01`, per category: revenue (the sum
of `quantity * price` from the order line) and that category's share of the
window's **total** revenue as a percentage rounded to 2 decimal places.
Columns, in this order: `category`, `revenue`, `pct`.

**Ordered by `revenue` descending, then `category` ascending.**

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 81_drills_multi_join_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7

For orders created on or after `2023-11-01`, the single best category per
customer country by revenue (`quantity * price` from the order line) - one
row per country, ties broken by the alphabetically first category. Columns,
in this order: `country`, `category`, `revenue`.

**Ordered by `country` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 81_drills_multi_join_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8

A category scorecard over orders created on or after `2023-10-01`. Columns,
in this order: `category`, `units` (sum of quantities), `revenue` (sum of
`quantity * price`), `orders` (how many **distinct** orders contained the
category), `buyers` (how many **distinct** customers bought it), and
`avg_line_revenue` - the average of `quantity * price` across the lines,
rounded to 2 decimal places. Keep only the categories whose (unrounded)
average line revenue is **above 750**.

**Ordered by `revenue` descending, then `category` ascending.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 81_drills_multi_join_1 ex8`

# Reading - 81_drills_multi_join_1

Report SQL. The joins are easy; choosing the grain and pinning down each
measure's definition is the job.

## Notes

**Decide the grain before you type.** "One row per status", "one row per
month per category", "one row per country" - that sentence determines the
`GROUP BY` and everything else follows. Most report bugs are grain bugs:
the query groups at a finer level than the question, or aggregates across a
join that has already multiplied the rows.

**The join grain is usually the order line.** Once `order_items` is in the
`FROM`, one order with three lines is three rows. Sums over line columns are
correct at that grain; anything counting orders or customers must use
`count(DISTINCT ...)`, and anything summing an order-level column (like
`orders.total`) is now wrong by a factor of the line count.

**Every measure has a definition, and they rarely agree.** In one report,
revenue excludes cancelled orders, the order count includes them, and the
buyer count counts customers rather than orders. `FILTER (WHERE ...)` is what
lets differently-defined measures share one pass; without it people write
three subqueries and join them.

**You cannot nest aggregates, so two levels means two queries.** "Average
number of lines per order" is `avg` of a `count`, which Postgres rejects
outright. Collapse to one row per order in a subquery or CTE, then aggregate
those rows. The rejection is a feature - it forces you to say which grain the
average is over.

**A row-level percentage needs a number from outside the row.** Either an
uncorrelated scalar subquery that recomputes the total, or a window function
over the already-aggregated result. `sum(x) OVER ()` after a `GROUP BY` totals
the groups, which is exactly what a share-of-total column wants.

**Top-N-per-group is always two layers.** Aggregate to (group, candidate,
measure), then rank within the group and keep the winners. `max()` gives you
the number but not the row it came from, and joining back on the number
breaks on ties.

**Half-open date ranges, always.** `>= start AND < next_start`. `BETWEEN` on
a `timestamptz` includes both endpoints, so a midnight row lands in two
buckets - a bug that shows up as a total that is very slightly too big and
that nobody ever finds.

## ex1 - the smallest possible report

Two tables, one grouping column, two measures. `customers` contributes
nothing to the output; it is there so the country filter has something to
filter.

The classic mistake is `BETWEEN '2023-09-01' AND '2023-09-30'`, which drops
everything after midnight on the 30th - most of a day of orders. Half-open
ranges have no such edge case and never need you to know how long the month
was.

The model answer joins, filters, and groups by `o.status`; the reference is
the same query written from the other table, to make the point that join
order changes nothing.

## ex2 - aggregate, then rank, then cut

`LIMIT` applies to the grouped rows, so the query has to aggregate all of
October before it can know which ten products win. That is not a wasteful
plan, it is the only correct one.

The classic mistake is the missing tie-break. Several products in this window
sit on identical unit totals, and `ORDER BY units DESC` alone lets the
planner return them in any order - so the tenth row changes between runs and
the query is not reproducible. `ORDER BY units DESC, p.id` fixes it, and
naming the tie-break unprompted is a habit worth having.

The model answer groups the three-table join by product and limits. The
reference aggregates `order_items` down to one row per product first and
joins `products` afterwards, which is the cheaper shape when the product
table is wide.

## ex3 - grouping by a computed column

The month does not exist as a column; it is `date_trunc('month',
o.created_at)`, and grouping by an expression is exactly as legal as grouping
by a column.

The classic mistake is `GROUP BY month`, referring to the `SELECT` alias.
Postgres does allow that as an extension, but it does not allow it once the
alias collides with a real column name, and it is not portable - writing the
expression again, or using the output position `GROUP BY 1, 2`, always works.

The model answer groups by the two expressions and sorts by the same. Note
that `date_trunc` on a `timestamptz` returns a `timestamptz`, so the month
column is a timestamp at midnight, not a date - worth knowing before you
compare it to something.

## ex4 - three measures, three definitions

This is the exercise that teaches the habit. `buyers` counts customers,
`orders` counts orders including cancelled ones, `revenue` sums only the
non-cancelled ones. Three different scopes, one join, no `WHERE` on the
status.

The classic mistake is a `WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'`, which fixes the
revenue and quietly corrupts the order count. The second is `count(c.id)` for
the buyers, which counts orders again because the join has already repeated
each customer once per order.

The model answer uses `count(DISTINCT o.customer_id)`, a plain `count(*)`,
and a `FILTER`ed `sum` with a `coalesce`. The reference writes the filtered
sum as a `CASE` inside the aggregate - the portable spelling, and the one to
recognise in older code.

## ex5 - two levels of aggregation

"Average lines per order" is an average of a count. `avg(count(*))` is a
syntax error, and the error is telling you that two different grains are
involved: one row per order for the count, one row per status for the
average.

The classic mistake is skipping the first level - grouping the joined rows by
status and dividing line count by order count by hand. That gives the same
number here, but it stops working the moment the outer aggregate is anything
other than a mean, and it hides the intermediate result that makes the query
readable.

The second mistake is an inner join to `order_items`. Around one order in
seven has no lines at all; dropping them raises both averages, because the
zeros that should pull the mean down are simply absent. The `coalesce` on the
units matters for the same reason - `avg` skips NULLs, so a NULL there would
silently reduce the denominator too.

## ex6 - a share of a total

Each row needs the grand total, which no single group can compute. Two
answers, both worth having: an uncorrelated scalar subquery that recomputes
the window's revenue once, or `sum(revenue) OVER ()` applied to the already
grouped rows.

The classic mistake in the general case is integer division - `100 * x / y`
where both are integers floors to a whole number. It does not bite here,
because `numeric * numeric` stays numeric, but the ordering of the operations
still does: divide first and you round a fraction below 1 to zero before the
multiplication can rescue it. Multiply, then divide, then round.

The model answer uses the scalar subquery; the reference uses the window
function over a subquery that has already grouped. The window version is the
one to prefer when the total is expensive, because it reuses the rows you
already have instead of rescanning.

## ex7 - the best one per group

Two layers. Layer one: revenue for every (country, category) pair. Layer two:
within each country, keep the row with the highest revenue.

The classic mistake is `max(revenue) GROUP BY country`, which gives the
winning number but not the winning category - and joining the aggregate back
to the detail on `(country, revenue)` produces two rows whenever two
categories tie exactly. Ranking keeps the row itself, which is what the report
needs.

The model answer uses `DISTINCT ON (country)` with `ORDER BY country, revenue
DESC, category` - the PostgreSQL idiom for "first row per key". The reference
uses `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY ...)` filtered to
`rn = 1`, which is portable and is the version to write in an interview
unless someone has said the word PostgreSQL. Either way the tie-break lives
inside the ranking, and the same tie-break has to be repeated in the final
`ORDER BY` if the output order matters.

## ex8 - the scorecard

Six columns, and the whole exercise is holding their definitions apart while
the join grain works against you. Units and revenue are sums over lines, so
the line grain suits them. Orders and buyers are counts of things that repeat
across lines, so they need `DISTINCT`. The average is over lines again.

The classic mistake is `count(o.id)` for the orders: a three-line order
contributes three, and the report claims three times the traffic. It is
plausible, it is never questioned, and it is the single most common defect in
hand-written analytics SQL.

The second is putting the final restriction in `WHERE`. It is a statement
about an aggregate of the group, which does not exist until the grouping has
happened, so it belongs in `HAVING` - where you must repeat the whole
expression, because `HAVING` cannot see `SELECT` aliases either. The
reference sidesteps that by computing the average in a subquery and filtering
it from outside, which is often the more readable arrangement once the
expression gets long.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL - GROUP BY and HAVING](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-GROUP) - what may appear in a `SELECT` list alongside aggregates, and why `HAVING` exists separately from `WHERE`. Behind ex1, ex4 and ex8.
- [PostgreSQL - Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - `count(DISTINCT ...)`, and the note that aggregate calls cannot be nested, which is the rule ex5 is built on.
- [PostgreSQL - Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) - `sum(x) OVER ()` for a grand total and `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)` for top-N-per-group. Behind ex6 and ex7.
- [PostgreSQL - SELECT: DISTINCT ON](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html#SQL-DISTINCT) - the shorter PostgreSQL-only route to "the best row per key" used in ex7.
- [PostgreSQL - Date/Time Functions: date_trunc](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html#FUNCTIONS-DATETIME-TRUNC) - how `date_trunc` behaves on `timestamptz`, including the time-zone question that decides which month a midnight order belongs to.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
One row per status, so `orders.status` is the grouping column. `customers` is in the query for one reason only - to supply the country filter.

## Hint 2
Join the two tables, filter on the country and the half-open date range, then `GROUP BY o.status`. Half-open (`>= '2023-09-01' AND < '2023-10-01'`) is what keeps a midnight order out of two months at once.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT o.status, count(o.id), sum(o.total)
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.country = 'GB'
  AND o.created_at >= DATE '2023-09-01'
  AND o.created_at <  DATE '2023-10-01'
GROUP BY o.status
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT o.status, count(*) AS orders, sum(o.total) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.country = 'GB'
  AND o.created_at >= '2023-09-01'
  AND o.created_at <  '2023-10-01'
GROUP BY o.status
ORDER BY o.status;

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Aggregate first, sort second, cut third. The `LIMIT` applies to the grouped result, not to the rows going into it.

Join the three tables, `GROUP BY p.id, p.name`, then `ORDER BY units DESC, p.id LIMIT 10`. The tie-break on `p.id` is not decoration - without it, two products on identical unit counts can swap places between runs and the tenth row becomes a coin toss.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Aggregate first, sort second, cut third. The `LIMIT` applies to the grouped result, not to the rows going into it.

## Hint 2
Join the three tables, `GROUP BY p.id, p.name`, then `ORDER BY units DESC, p.id LIMIT 10`. The tie-break on `p.id` is not decoration - without it, two products on identical unit counts can swap places between runs and the tenth row becomes a coin toss.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT p.id, p.name, t.units
FROM (SELECT oi.product_id, sum(oi.quantity) AS units
      FROM order_items oi
      JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
      WHERE o.created_at >= DATE '2023-10-01'
        AND o.created_at <  DATE '2023-11-01'
      GROUP BY oi.product_id) t
JOIN products p ON p.id = t.product_id
ORDER BY t.units DESC, p.id
LIMIT 10;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT p.id, p.name, sum(oi.quantity) AS units
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.created_at >= '2023-10-01'
  AND o.created_at <  '2023-11-01'
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY units DESC, p.id
LIMIT 10;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Three measures with three different definitions over the same group: one counts customers, one counts orders, one sums a subset of the orders. Only one join, and no `WHERE` on the status.

## Hint 2
`count(DISTINCT o.customer_id)` for the buyers - a country with 200 orders from 30 people has 30 buyers. `count(*)` for the orders, cancelled ones included. And `sum(o.total) FILTER (WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled')` for the revenue, so the exclusion applies to that measure alone.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT c.country,
       count(DISTINCT c.id) AS buyers,
       count(o.id) AS orders,
       coalesce(sum(CASE WHEN o.status <> 'cancelled' THEN o.total END), 0) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.country
ORDER BY 4 DESC, 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.country,
       count(DISTINCT o.customer_id) AS buyers,
       count(*) AS orders,
       coalesce(sum(o.total) FILTER (WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'), 0) AS revenue
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.country
ORDER BY revenue DESC, c.country;

For orders created on or after `2023-11-01`, per status: the average number
of order lines per order and the average number of units per order, each
rounded to 2 decimal places. Orders with no lines count as `0` lines and `0`

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
"Average lines per order" is an average of a count, and you cannot nest aggregates. So there are two levels here: collapse to one row per order first, then average those rows within each status.

## Hint 2
Inner query: `GROUP BY o.id, o.status` producing `lines` and `units` per order. Outer query: `GROUP BY status` averaging them. The inner join to `order_items` has to be outer, or orders with no lines vanish and the averages come out too high.

## Hint 3
Getting the two levels right is the whole exercise, and the tell that you have fused them is `avg(count(*))`, which Postgres rejects. The empty orders also need `coalesce` on the units, so that they contribute a genuine 0 to the average rather than a NULL that `avg` would skip.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
"Average lines per order" is an average of a count, and you cannot nest aggregates. So there are two levels here: collapse to one row per order first, then average those rows within each status.

## Hint 2
Inner query: `GROUP BY o.id, o.status` producing `lines` and `units` per order. Outer query: `GROUP BY status` averaging them. The inner join to `order_items` has to be outer, or orders with no lines vanish and the averages come out too high.

## Hint 3
Getting the two levels right is the whole exercise, and the tell that you have fused them is `avg(count(*))`, which Postgres rejects. The empty orders also need `coalesce` on the units, so that they contribute a genuine 0 to the average rather than a NULL that `avg` would skip.

references.solution.sql:
WITH per_order AS (
    SELECT o.id, o.status,
           coalesce(s.lines, 0) AS lines,
           coalesce(s.units, 0) AS units
    FROM orders o
    LEFT JOIN (SELECT oi.order_id,
                      count(*) AS lines,
                      sum(oi.quantity) AS units
               FROM order_items oi
               JOIN orders o2 ON o2.id = oi.order_id
                    AND o2.created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01'
               GROUP BY oi.order_id) s ON s.order_id = o.id
    WHERE o.created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01'
)
SELECT status, round(avg(lines), 2), round(avg(units), 2)
FROM per_order
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY status;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT t.status,
       round(avg(t.lines), 2) AS avg_lines,
       round(avg(t.units), 2) AS avg_units
FROM (SELECT o.id, o.status,
             count(oi.id) AS lines,
             coalesce(sum(oi.quantity), 0) AS units
      FROM orders o
      LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
      WHERE o.created_at >= '2023-11-01'
      GROUP BY o.id, o.status) t
GROUP BY t.status
ORDER BY t.status;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6

For orders created on or after `2023-11-01`, per category: revenue (the sum
of `quantity * price` from the order line) and that category's share of the
window's **total** revenue as a percentage rounded to 2 decimal places.
Columns, in this order: `category`, `revenue`, `pct`.

**Ordered by `revenue` descending, then `category` ascending.**

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 81_drills_multi_join_1 ex6`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Each row needs a number the row itself cannot produce: the total across every category. That total has to be computed somewhere else and brought in.

## Hint 2
Two good routes. A scalar subquery in the `SELECT` list that recomputes the window's total revenue - it is uncorrelated, so it runs once. Or aggregate to one row per category first and then use `sum(revenue) OVER ()`, which totals the whole result set.

## Hint 3
Both operands are `numeric`, so `100 * x / total` does exact decimal arithmetic and there is no integer-division trap here - but keep the multiplication before the division, or you will round a fraction to zero on the way.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Each row needs a number the row itself cannot produce: the total across every category. That total has to be computed somewhere else and brought in.

## Hint 2
Two good routes. A scalar subquery in the `SELECT` list that recomputes the window's total revenue - it is uncorrelated, so it runs once. Or aggregate to one row per category first and then use `sum(revenue) OVER ()`, which totals the whole result set.

## Hint 3
Both operands are `numeric`, so `100 * x / total` does exact decimal arithmetic and there is no integer-division trap here - but keep the multiplication before the division, or you will round a fraction to zero on the way.

SELECT category, revenue,
       round(100 * revenue / sum(revenue) OVER (), 2) AS pct
FROM (SELECT p.category, sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) AS revenue
      FROM orders o
      JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
      JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
      WHERE o.created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01'
      GROUP BY p.category) t
ORDER BY revenue DESC, category;

## Hint 1

references.solution.sql:
SELECT country, category, revenue
FROM (SELECT c.country, p.category,
             sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) AS revenue,
             row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY c.country
                                ORDER BY sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) DESC,
                                         p.category) AS rn
      FROM customers c
      JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
      JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
      JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
      WHERE o.created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01'
      GROUP BY c.country, p.category) x
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY country;

WITH t AS (

    JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
    WHERE o.created_at >= '2023-11-01'
    GROUP BY c.country, p.category
)

FROM t

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Six columns, four different kinds of measure, one grouping column. Work out for each one whether it is a sum over lines, a count of distinct parents, or an average - the join grain is the line, and orders and customers repeat across lines.

## Hint 2
`count(o.id)` would count lines and call them orders; a three-line order must contribute one. `count(DISTINCT o.id)` and `count(DISTINCT o.customer_id)` are what survive the fan-out.

## Hint 3
The final restriction is on an aggregate of the group, so it belongs in `HAVING` - and note that you may repeat the whole aggregate expression there, or filter on it from an enclosing query, but you may not refer to the `SELECT` alias.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT category, units, revenue, orders, buyers, avg_line_revenue
FROM (SELECT p.category,
             sum(oi.quantity) AS units,
             sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) AS revenue,
             count(DISTINCT o.id) AS orders,
             count(DISTINCT o.customer_id) AS buyers,
             round(avg(oi.quantity * oi.price), 2) AS avg_line_revenue,
             avg(oi.quantity * oi.price) AS raw_avg
      FROM order_items oi
      JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
      JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
      WHERE o.created_at >= DATE '2023-10-01'
      GROUP BY p.category) t
WHERE raw_avg > 750
ORDER BY revenue DESC, category;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT p.category,
       sum(oi.quantity) AS units,
       sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) AS revenue,
       count(DISTINCT o.id) AS orders,
       count(DISTINCT o.customer_id) AS buyers,
       round(avg(oi.quantity * oi.price), 2) AS avg_line_revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.created_at >= '2023-10-01'
GROUP BY p.category
HAVING avg(oi.quantity * oi.price) > 750
ORDER BY revenue DESC, p.category;

# 82 - Drills: multi-join reports 2

Eight more report queries, this time with two independent branches hanging
off the same table - sales on one side, reviews on the other. This set draws
on lessons 08 and 12 and is mostly one lesson repeated in different costumes:
when a report needs measures from two one-to-many relationships, you
summarise each branch before you join them.

## Exercise 1

Per category, over reviews created on or after `2023-08-01`: how many
distinct products received a review in that window, how many reviews there
were, and the average rating rounded to 2 decimal places. Columns, in this
order: `category`, `products`, `reviews`, `avg_rating`.

**Ordered by `category` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 82_drills_multi_join_2 ex1`

## Exercise 2

For `books` products only, per rating: how many reviews carry that rating and
how many **distinct** products received it. Columns, in this order: `rating`,
`reviews`, `products`.

**Ordered by `rating` ascending.**

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 82_drills_multi_join_2 ex2`

## Exercise 3

For each month from `2023-01-01` up to (but not including) `2023-12-01`: how
many customers signed up that month and how many orders were placed that
month. The two counts are unrelated to each other - an order in March has
nothing to do with a signup in March. Columns, in this order: `month` (use
`date_trunc('month', created_at)`), `new_customers`, `orders`.

**Ordered by `month` ascending.**

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 82_drills_multi_join_2 ex3`

## Exercise 4

Per category, over the whole dataset: `units` (the sum of
`order_items.quantity`), `revenue` (the sum of `quantity * price` from the
order line), and `avg_rating` - the average of **every** review of every
product in that category, rounded to 2 decimal places. Columns, in this
order: `category`, `units`, `revenue`, `avg_rating`.

**Ordered by `category` ascending.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 82_drills_multi_join_2 ex4`

## Exercise 5

For orders created on or after `2023-11-01`, one row per `(category,
status)` pair: how many **distinct** orders contained that category with that
status, and the revenue (`quantity * price` from the order line). Columns, in
this order: `category`, `status`, `orders`, `revenue`.

**Ordered by `category` ascending, then `status` ascending.**

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 82_drills_multi_join_2 ex5`

## Exercise 6

For every `electronics` product priced above 495: `units` (total quantity
ever sold, `0` if it has never been sold), `reviews` (how many it has, `0` if
none), and `avg_rating` rounded to 2 decimal places - which stays **NULL** if
the product has no reviews. Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `units`,
`reviews`, `avg_rating`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 82_drills_multi_join_2 ex6`

## Exercise 7

Customers who bought products from **at least 3 different categories** on
orders created on or after `2023-11-01`. Columns, in this order: `id`,
`name`, `categories` (how many distinct categories).

**Ordered by `categories` descending, then `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 82_drills_multi_join_2 ex7`

## Exercise 8

A country scorecard for orders created on or after `2023-11-01`. Per customer
country: `revenue` (the sum of `quantity * price` from the order line),
`units` (the sum of quantities), `orders` (how many **distinct** orders), and
`top_product` - the `name` of the product with the most units sold in that
country, ties broken by the lower product `id`. Columns, in this order:
`country`, `revenue`, `units`, `orders`, `top_product`.

**Ordered by `revenue` descending, then `country` ascending.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 82_drills_multi_join_2 ex8`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 82_drills_multi_join_2

Reports whose measures come from two different one-to-many relationships.
There is one right structural move, and this set makes you perform it six
different ways.

## Notes

**Two branches multiply.** `products` has many order lines and many reviews.
Put both in one `FROM` and you get the cross product per product: 40 lines
times 100 reviews is 4,000 rows where you wanted 140. Counts can be repaired
with `count(DISTINCT ...)` because each branch carries a primary key. Sums
cannot be repaired at all.

**Averages hide the damage.** This is what makes fan-out genuinely dangerous
rather than merely annoying. When every review of a product is duplicated the
same number of times, the *average* rating is unchanged - so a report showing
a plausible 3.01 average next to a revenue figure a hundred times too large
looks internally consistent. The average is not evidence that the join is
sound.

**Summarise, then join.** One CTE per branch, each grouped to the reporting
key, joined at the end. It is more typing, it is immune to the whole class of
bug, and it extends to a fourth measure without any new reasoning. When
somebody asks how you would add "returns" to the report, this is the answer
that costs nothing.

**Not every pair of tables has a join key.** Signups per month and orders per
month share only a time axis. There is no meaningful `customers JOIN orders`
for that question - a customer who signed up in March may have ordered in
July. Aggregate each side to the axis and join on the axis.

**Zero and NULL are different answers.** Units sold and review counts become
`0` when there is nothing, because zero sales is a real quantity. An average
rating over no reviews stays NULL, because the average of nothing is not
zero - `coalesce`ing it would assert that nobody liked a product nobody
rated.

**`count(DISTINCT ...)` in `HAVING` is normal.** When the measure being
filtered is itself the distinct count, you write the expression twice: once
in `SELECT` and once in `HAVING`, because `HAVING` cannot see output aliases.
Reducing to distinct pairs in a subquery first turns it back into a plain
`count(*)` and is usually cheaper.

## ex1 - counting two things at two grains

The join is one-to-many from products to reviews, so after it the review is
the grain. `count(*)` counts reviews, which is one of the columns you want;
the other column wants products, and each product now appears once per review.

The classic mistake is `count(p.id)`, which counts non-NULL product ids -
that is, reviews again. The distinction between `count(x)` and
`count(DISTINCT x)` is invisible until the join grain is finer than the thing
being counted, which is most of the time in report SQL.

The model answer uses `count(DISTINCT p.id)` and `count(r.id)`; the reference
counts the same things from the reviews side, to make the point that which
table you write first has no effect on the grain.

## ex2 - the dimension is a measure column

Nothing multiplies here, because the grouping column is `rating` and the
grain is still the review. `products` is present only to restrict the
population to one category.

The classic mistake is expecting `reviews` and `products` to be near each
other in size. They are not: every book product receives ratings of all five
values, so the distinct product count per rating is close to the total number
of book products while the review count is twenty times larger. Reading that
shape correctly is a good check that you understand what you grouped.

The model answer joins and filters; the reference uses `IN (SELECT id FROM
products WHERE category = 'books')`, which is the semi-join spelling and
avoids widening the row before aggregating it.

## ex3 - two aggregates with no join key

Signups and orders have no row-level relationship. There is no join between
`customers` and `orders` that answers this question - trying one produces a
number that means "orders placed by customers who signed up in this month",
which is a cohort metric and a different report.

The classic mistake is exactly that: joining on `customer_id` and grouping by
one of the two timestamps. It runs, it produces eleven rows, and it answers
something nobody asked.

The model answer aggregates each table to one row per month and joins on
`month`. It uses an inner join because both tables have rows in every month
of the range; if either could be empty for a month, this would need a `FULL
JOIN` and a `coalesce` on the key. The reference tags rows from both tables
into one stream with `UNION ALL` and separates them again with `FILTER`,
which is a neat trick when the two sources share a shape.

## ex4 - the fan-out, at full strength

Sales and reviews both hang off `products`. Joined together, each sales line
is repeated once per review - about a hundred times here - so `units` and
`revenue` come out roughly a hundred times too large while `avg_rating`
remains exactly correct.

The classic mistake is `sum(DISTINCT oi.quantity)`, offered as the fix by
analogy with `count(DISTINCT ...)`. It is not a fix: it adds up the distinct
*values*, so two lines of 3 units become 3 and a product that sold quantities
1 through 5 reports 15 regardless of how many lines there were. There is no
aggregate that recovers a true sum from a multiplied join.

The model answer builds one CTE per branch, each grouped by category, and
joins the two six-row summaries. The reference does the sales side as a
two-stage rollup - per product, then per category - which is the shape you
end up with when the per-product numbers are also needed elsewhere.

## ex5 - two dimensions, one fan-out

The grouping columns come from two different tables and the measures from the
line between them. Revenue is at line grain and is correct as a plain sum;
the order count is not, because an order with three books contributes three
rows to the `('books', 'paid')` group.

The classic mistake is `count(*)`, which counts qualifying lines and labels
them orders. The number is always at least as large as the truth and looks
entirely reasonable, which is why nobody catches it.

The model answer uses `count(DISTINCT o.id)`. The reference collapses to one
row per `(order, category)` first and then counts rows, which is the same
idea done structurally: once the grain matches the thing you are counting,
`count(*)` is correct again and no `DISTINCT` is needed.

## ex6 - the same problem, one grain finer

Per product rather than per category, so the two branches must be summarised
per product before they touch `products`. After that both joins are
one-to-one and nothing can multiply.

The classic mistake is `coalesce(avg_rating, 0)`. Units and review counts
become zero because a product that never sold really did sell zero. An
average over no ratings is undefined, and turning it into 0 puts an unreviewed
product at the bottom of every ranking - a report that invents unanimous
one-star hatred out of silence.

The model answer left-joins two pre-aggregated subqueries and coalesces
exactly two of the three measures. The reference pushes the product filter
down into both subqueries so they aggregate a few thousand rows instead of a
million - worth noticing, because the naive version does the whole table's
work to answer a question about fourteen products.

## ex7 - the measure is the filter

`count(DISTINCT p.category)` appears twice: once as the output column, once
in `HAVING`. That repetition is not a smell, it is the rule - `HAVING` runs
before the `SELECT` list is evaluated, so it cannot see the alias.

The classic mistake is `WHERE count(...) >= 3`, which Postgres rejects
because aggregates do not exist at `WHERE` time. The second is `count(DISTINCT
p.id) >= 3` - distinct *products*, not categories - which passes silently and
answers a much easier question.

The model answer groups the four-table join and filters with `HAVING`. The
reference reduces to `SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, category` first, which
makes each pair one row and turns the whole thing into a plain `count(*)`.
That shape is faster and, more importantly, it is self-documenting: the
intermediate result is literally the list of customer-category pairs.

## ex8 - four aggregates and one row-valued answer

Revenue, units and order count are aggregates of the country group.
`top_product` is not - it is a name belonging to one specific row, and no
aggregate function can produce it. That split is the whole design of the
query.

The classic mistake is `max(p.name)`, which Postgres happily accepts and
which returns the alphabetically last product name in the country. It is
wrong on nearly every row and the report gives no sign of it.

The model answer builds the joined line rows once in a CTE and aggregates
that CTE twice: by country for the totals, and by country and product for the
ranking, from which `DISTINCT ON (country)` takes the winner. The reference
does the ranking with `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY
sum(q) DESC, product_id)` - note the aggregate inside the window's `ORDER BY`,
which is legal because window functions are evaluated after grouping, and is
the trick that lets you rank groups without an extra subquery level. Either
way, the `product_id` tie-break is what makes the answer the same on every
run.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL - Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - `count(DISTINCT ...)` versus `count(...)`, and the exact meaning of `sum(DISTINCT ...)` that makes it the wrong repair in ex4.
- [PostgreSQL - WITH Queries (CTEs)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) - the mechanism behind "summarise each branch, then join the summaries", used in ex3, ex4, ex7 and ex8.
- [PostgreSQL - GROUP BY and HAVING](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-GROUP) - why `HAVING` cannot see `SELECT` aliases and why aggregates are illegal in `WHERE`. Behind ex7.
- [PostgreSQL - Window Function Calls](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html#SYNTAX-WINDOW-FUNCTIONS) - that window functions run after grouping, which is what allows `row_number() OVER (ORDER BY sum(q) DESC)` in the ex8 reference.
- [PostgreSQL - COALESCE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-conditional.html#FUNCTIONS-COALESCE-NVL-IFNULL) - the function at the centre of the zero-versus-NULL decision in ex6.

on lessons 08 and 12 and is mostly one lesson repeated in different costumes:
when a report needs measures from two one-to-many relationships, you
summarise each branch before you join them.

Per category, over reviews created on or after `2023-08-01`: how many
distinct products received a review in that window, how many reviews there
were, and the average rating rounded to 2 decimal places. Columns, in this
order: `category`, `products`, `reviews`, `avg_rating`.

**Ordered by `category` ascending.**

For `books` products only, per rating: how many reviews carry that rating and
how many **distinct** products received it. Columns, in this order: `rating`,
`reviews`, `products`.

For each month from `2023-01-01` up to (but not including) `2023-12-01`: how
many customers signed up that month and how many orders were placed that
month. The two counts are unrelated to each other - an order in March has
nothing to do with a signup in March. Columns, in this order: `month` (use
`date_trunc('month', created_at)`), `new_customers`, `orders`.

**Ordered by `month` ascending.**

`order_items.quantity`), `revenue` (the sum of `quantity * price` from the

product in that category, rounded to 2 decimal places. Columns, in this
order: `category`, `units`, `revenue`, `avg_rating`.

**Ordered by `category` ascending.**

For orders created on or after `2023-11-01`, one row per `(category,
status)` pair: how many **distinct** orders contained that category with that

this order: `category`, `status`, `orders`, `revenue`.

**Ordered by `category` ascending, then `status` ascending.**

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 82_drills_multi_join_2 ex5`

For every `electronics` product priced above 495: `units` (total quantity
ever sold, `0` if it has never been sold), `reviews` (how many it has, `0` if

Customers who bought products from **at least 3 different categories** on

# Reading - 82_drills_multi_join_2

Reports whose measures come from two different one-to-many relationships.
There is one right structural move, and this set makes you perform it six
different ways.

## Notes

**Two branches multiply.** `products` has many order lines and many reviews.
Put both in one `FROM` and you get the cross product per product: 40 lines
times 100 reviews is 4,000 rows where you wanted 140. Counts can be repaired
with `count(DISTINCT ...)` because each branch carries a primary key. Sums
cannot be repaired at all.

**Averages hide the damage.** This is what makes fan-out genuinely dangerous
rather than merely annoying. When every review of a product is duplicated the
same number of times, the *average* rating is unchanged - so a report showing
a plausible 3.01 average next to a revenue figure a hundred times too large
looks internally consistent. The average is not evidence that the join is
sound.

**Summarise, then join.** One CTE per branch, each grouped to the reporting
key, joined at the end. It is more typing, it is immune to the whole class of
bug, and it extends to a fourth measure without any new reasoning. When
somebody asks how you would add "returns" to the report, this is the answer
that costs nothing.

**Not every pair of tables has a join key.** Signups per month and orders per
month share only a time axis. There is no meaningful `customers JOIN orders`
for that question - a customer who signed up in March may have ordered in
July. Aggregate each side to the axis and join on the axis.

**Zero and NULL are different answers.** Units sold and review counts become
`0` when there is nothing, because zero sales is a real quantity. An average
rating over no reviews stays NULL, because the average of nothing is not
zero - `coalesce`ing it would assert that nobody liked a product nobody
rated.

**`count(DISTINCT ...)` in `HAVING` is normal.** When the measure being
filtered is itself the distinct count, you write the expression twice: once
in `SELECT` and once in `HAVING`, because `HAVING` cannot see output aliases.
Reducing to distinct pairs in a subquery first turns it back into a plain
`count(*)` and is usually cheaper.

## ex1 - counting two things at two grains

The join is one-to-many from products to reviews, so after it the review is
the grain. `count(*)` counts reviews, which is one of the columns you want;
the other column wants products, and each product now appears once per review.

The classic mistake is `count(p.id)`, which counts non-NULL product ids -
that is, reviews again. The distinction between `count(x)` and
`count(DISTINCT x)` is invisible until the join grain is finer than the thing
being counted, which is most of the time in report SQL.

The model answer uses `count(DISTINCT p.id)` and `count(r.id)`; the reference
counts the same things from the reviews side, to make the point that which
table you write first has no effect on the grain.

## ex2 - the dimension is a measure column

Nothing multiplies here, because the grouping column is `rating` and the
grain is still the review. `products` is present only to restrict the
population to one category.

The classic mistake is expecting `reviews` and `products` to be near each
other in size. They are not: every book product receives ratings of all five
values, so the distinct product count per rating is close to the total number
of book products while the review count is twenty times larger. Reading that
shape correctly is a good check that you understand what you grouped.

The model answer joins and filters; the reference uses `IN (SELECT id FROM
products WHERE category = 'books')`, which is the semi-join spelling and
avoids widening the row before aggregating it.

## ex3 - two aggregates with no join key

Signups and orders have no row-level relationship. There is no join between
`customers` and `orders` that answers this question - trying one produces a
number that means "orders placed by customers who signed up in this month",
which is a cohort metric and a different report.

The classic mistake is exactly that: joining on `customer_id` and grouping by
one of the two timestamps. It runs, it produces eleven rows, and it answers
something nobody asked.

The model answer aggregates each table to one row per month and joins on
`month`. It uses an inner join because both tables have rows in every month
of the range; if either could be empty for a month, this would need a `FULL
JOIN` and a `coalesce` on the key. The reference tags rows from both tables
into one stream with `UNION ALL` and separates them again with `FILTER`,
which is a neat trick when the two sources share a shape.

## ex4 - the fan-out, at full strength

Sales and reviews both hang off `products`. Joined together, each sales line
is repeated once per review - about a hundred times here - so `units` and
`revenue` come out roughly a hundred times too large while `avg_rating`
remains exactly correct.

The classic mistake is `sum(DISTINCT oi.quantity)`, offered as the fix by
analogy with `count(DISTINCT ...)`. It is not a fix: it adds up the distinct
*values*, so two lines of 3 units become 3 and a product that sold quantities
1 through 5 reports 15 regardless of how many lines there were. There is no
aggregate that recovers a true sum from a multiplied join.

The model answer builds one CTE per branch, each grouped by category, and
joins the two six-row summaries. The reference does the sales side as a
two-stage rollup - per product, then per category - which is the shape you
end up with when the per-product numbers are also needed elsewhere.

## ex5 - two dimensions, one fan-out

The grouping columns come from two different tables and the measures from the
line between them. Revenue is at line grain and is correct as a plain sum;
the order count is not, because an order with three books contributes three
rows to the `('books', 'paid')` group.

The classic mistake is `count(*)`, which counts qualifying lines and labels
them orders. The number is always at least as large as the truth and looks
entirely reasonable, which is why nobody catches it.

The model answer uses `count(DISTINCT o.id)`. The reference collapses to one
row per `(order, category)` first and then counts rows, which is the same
idea done structurally: once the grain matches the thing you are counting,
`count(*)` is correct again and no `DISTINCT` is needed.

## ex6 - the same problem, one grain finer

Per product rather than per category, so the two branches must be summarised
per product before they touch `products`. After that both joins are
one-to-one and nothing can multiply.

The classic mistake is `coalesce(avg_rating, 0)`. Units and review counts
become zero because a product that never sold really did sell zero. An
average over no ratings is undefined, and turning it into 0 puts an unreviewed
product at the bottom of every ranking - a report that invents unanimous
one-star hatred out of silence.

The model answer left-joins two pre-aggregated subqueries and coalesces
exactly two of the three measures. The reference pushes the product filter
down into both subqueries so they aggregate a few thousand rows instead of a
million - worth noticing, because the naive version does the whole table's
work to answer a question about fourteen products.

## ex7 - the measure is the filter

`count(DISTINCT p.category)` appears twice: once as the output column, once
in `HAVING`. That repetition is not a smell, it is the rule - `HAVING` runs
before the `SELECT` list is evaluated, so it cannot see the alias.

The classic mistake is `WHERE count(...) >= 3`, which Postgres rejects
because aggregates do not exist at `WHERE` time. The second is `count(DISTINCT
p.id) >= 3` - distinct *products*, not categories - which passes silently and
answers a much easier question.

The model answer groups the four-table join and filters with `HAVING`. The
reference reduces to `SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, category` first, which
makes each pair one row and turns the whole thing into a plain `count(*)`.
That shape is faster and, more importantly, it is self-documenting: the
intermediate result is literally the list of customer-category pairs.

## ex8 - four aggregates and one row-valued answer

Revenue, units and order count are aggregates of the country group.
`top_product` is not - it is a name belonging to one specific row, and no
aggregate function can produce it. That split is the whole design of the
query.

The classic mistake is `max(p.name)`, which Postgres happily accepts and
which returns the alphabetically last product name in the country. It is
wrong on nearly every row and the report gives no sign of it.

The model answer builds the joined line rows once in a CTE and aggregates
that CTE twice: by country for the totals, and by country and product for the
ranking, from which `DISTINCT ON (country)` takes the winner. The reference
does the ranking with `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY
sum(q) DESC, product_id)` - note the aggregate inside the window's `ORDER BY`,
which is legal because window functions are evaluated after grouping, and is
the trick that lets you rank groups without an extra subquery level. Either
way, the `product_id` tie-break is what makes the answer the same on every
run.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL - Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - `count(DISTINCT ...)` versus `count(...)`, and the exact meaning of `sum(DISTINCT ...)` that makes it the wrong repair in ex4.
- [PostgreSQL - WITH Queries (CTEs)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) - the mechanism behind "summarise each branch, then join the summaries", used in ex3, ex4, ex7 and ex8.
- [PostgreSQL - GROUP BY and HAVING](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-GROUP) - why `HAVING` cannot see `SELECT` aliases and why aggregates are illegal in `WHERE`. Behind ex7.
- [PostgreSQL - Window Function Calls](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html#SYNTAX-WINDOW-FUNCTIONS) - that window functions run after grouping, which is what allows `row_number() OVER (ORDER BY sum(q) DESC)` in the ex8 reference.
- [PostgreSQL - COALESCE](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-conditional.html#FUNCTIONS-COALESCE-NVL-IFNULL) - the function at the centre of the zero-versus-NULL decision in ex6.

## Exercise 1

Per category, over reviews created on or after `2023-08-01`: how many
distinct products received a review in that window, how many reviews there
were, and the average rating rounded to 2 decimal places. Columns, in this
order: `category`, `products`, `reviews`, `avg_rating`.

**Ordered by `category` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 82_drills_multi_join_2 ex1`

## Hint 1
One row per category. The join grain is the review, so anything counting products has to say so explicitly.

## Hint 2
`count(*)` here counts reviews, which is what the second column wants. The first column wants products, and after the join each product appears once per review it has - `count(DISTINCT p.id)` is what collapses that back.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
One row per category. The join grain is the review, so anything counting products has to say so explicitly.

## Hint 2
`count(*)` here counts reviews, which is what the second column wants. The first column wants products, and after the join each product appears once per review it has - `count(DISTINCT p.id)` is what collapses that back.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT p.category,
       count(DISTINCT r.product_id),
       count(*),
       round(avg(r.rating), 2)
FROM reviews r
JOIN products p ON p.id = r.product_id
WHERE r.created_at >= DATE '2023-08-01'
GROUP BY p.category
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT p.category,
       count(DISTINCT p.id) AS products,
       count(r.id) AS reviews,
       round(avg(r.rating), 2) AS avg_rating
FROM products p
JOIN reviews r ON r.product_id = p.id
WHERE r.created_at >= '2023-08-01'
GROUP BY p.category
ORDER BY p.category;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Two completely independent counts over two unrelated tables that happen to share a time axis. There is no join key between customers and orders that would give you this - a customer's signup month has nothing to do with the month their orders land in.

## Hint 2
Aggregate each table to one row per month in its own CTE, then join the two summaries on `month`. Both tables have rows in every month of the range, so an inner join is safe here; if they did not, this would need a `FULL JOIN`.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT month,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE src = 'c') AS new_customers,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE src = 'o') AS orders
FROM (
    SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month, 'c' AS src
    FROM customers
    WHERE created_at >= DATE '2023-01-01' AND created_at < DATE '2023-12-01'
    UNION ALL
    SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at), 'o'
    FROM orders
    WHERE created_at >= DATE '2023-01-01' AND created_at < DATE '2023-12-01'
) t
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;
references.expected.sql:
WITH c AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month, count(*) AS new_customers
    FROM customers
    WHERE created_at >= '2023-01-01' AND created_at < '2023-12-01'
    GROUP BY 1
), o AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month, count(*) AS orders
    FROM orders
    WHERE created_at >= '2023-01-01' AND created_at < '2023-12-01'
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT c.month, c.new_customers, o.orders
FROM c
JOIN o ON o.month = c.month
ORDER BY c.month;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Sales and reviews are two independent one-to-many branches off `products`. Put both in the same `FROM` and every sales line is repeated once per review of that product.

## Hint 2
Roughly a hundred times, in this dataset. `count(DISTINCT ...)` could rescue a count, but `sum(oi.quantity)` cannot be rescued at all - there is no way back from a multiplied sum.

## Hint 3
Aggregate each branch separately - one CTE per branch, both grouped by category - and join the two summaries on `category`. Notice that the average rating is unaffected by the fan-out even when the sums are destroyed by it, which is exactly why the bug is so hard to spot.

references.solution.sql:
WITH per_product AS (
    SELECT product_id,
           sum(quantity) AS units,
           sum(quantity * price) AS revenue
    FROM order_items
    GROUP BY product_id
), sales AS (
    SELECT p.category, sum(pp.units) AS units, sum(pp.revenue) AS revenue
    FROM per_product pp
    JOIN products p ON p.id = pp.product_id
    GROUP BY p.category
), rated AS (
    SELECT p.category, round(avg(r.rating), 2) AS avg_rating
    FROM reviews r
    JOIN products p ON p.id = r.product_id
    GROUP BY p.category
)
SELECT s.category, s.units, s.revenue, rd.avg_rating
FROM sales s
JOIN rated rd ON rd.category = s.category
ORDER BY s.category;
references.expected.sql:
WITH sales AS (
    SELECT p.category,
           sum(oi.quantity) AS units,
           sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) AS revenue
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
    GROUP BY p.category
), rated AS (
    SELECT p.category, round(avg(r.rating), 2) AS avg_rating
    FROM reviews r
    JOIN products p ON p.id = r.product_id
    GROUP BY p.category
)
SELECT s.category, s.units, s.revenue, rd.avg_rating
FROM sales s
JOIN rated rd ON rd.category = s.category
ORDER BY s.category;

## Hint 1
Two grouping columns from two different tables - the category from `products` and the status from `orders` - with the measures coming from the line in between.

Join the three tables, filter the window, `GROUP BY p.category, o.status`. The revenue is a sum at line grain and is fine, but the order count is not: an order with three lines in the same category contributes three rows, so `count(DISTINCT o.id)` is what the report means.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Two grouping columns from two different tables - the category from `products` and the status from `orders` - with the measures coming from the line in between.

## Hint 2
Join the three tables, filter the window, `GROUP BY p.category, o.status`. The revenue is a sum at line grain and is fine, but the order count is not: an order with three lines in the same category contributes three rows, so `count(DISTINCT o.id)` is what the report means.

references.solution.sql:
WITH per_order_category AS (
    SELECT o.id AS order_id, o.status, p.category,
           sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) AS revenue
    FROM orders o
    JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
    JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
    WHERE o.created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01'
    GROUP BY o.id, o.status, p.category
)
SELECT category, status, count(*) AS orders, sum(revenue) AS revenue
FROM per_order_category
GROUP BY category, status
ORDER BY category, status;

JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.created_at >= '2023-11-01'
GROUP BY p.category, o.status
ORDER BY p.category, o.status;

## Hint 1
Same two branches as ex4, but the report is per product rather than per category - so joining both branches directly to `products` multiplies the rows all over again.

## Hint 2
Summarise each branch to one row per product in its own subquery, then `LEFT JOIN` both onto the product slice. Because each subquery now has at most one row per product, the joins are one-to-one and nothing multiplies.
