The three NULL cases are all different on purpose. Units and review count become `0` because a product that sold nothing genuinely sold zero. references.solution.sql:
WITH sel AS (
    SELECT id, name FROM products
    WHERE category = 'electronics' AND price > 495
)
SELECT sel.id, sel.name,
       coalesce(s.units, 0) AS units,
       coalesce(r.reviews, 0) AS reviews,
       r.avg_rating
FROM sel
LEFT JOIN (SELECT oi.product_id, sum(oi.quantity) AS units
           FROM order_items oi
           WHERE oi.product_id IN (SELECT id FROM sel)
           GROUP BY oi.product_id) s ON s.product_id = sel.id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT rv.product_id, count(*) AS reviews,
                  round(avg(rv.rating), 2) AS avg_rating
           FROM reviews rv
           WHERE rv.product_id IN (SELECT id FROM sel)
           GROUP BY rv.product_id) r ON r.product_id = sel.id
ORDER BY sel.id;

       coalesce(s.units, 0) AS units,
       coalesce(r.reviews, 0) AS reviews,
       r.avg_rating

           FROM order_items
           GROUP BY product_id) s ON s.product_id = p.id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT product_id, count(*) AS reviews, round(avg(rating), 2) AS avg_rating
           FROM reviews
           GROUP BY product_id) r ON r.product_id = p.id
WHERE p.category = 'electronics' AND p.price > 495
ORDER BY p.id;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The measure is a count of **distinct** categories, and it is also the thing being filtered on. A customer who bought four books has bought in one category, not four.

## Hint 2
`count(DISTINCT p.category)` in the `SELECT` list and the same expression again in `HAVING` - the restriction is on an aggregate of the group, so `WHERE` cannot see it and `HAVING` cannot see the `SELECT` alias either.

## Hint 3
The other route is to reduce first: a `SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, category` subquery gives one row per pair, after which a plain `count(*)` per customer is the answer. That shape is usually cheaper and always easier to explain.

references.solution.sql:
WITH pairs AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT o.customer_id, p.category
    FROM orders o
    JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
    JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
    WHERE o.created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01'
), counted AS (
    SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS categories
    FROM pairs
    GROUP BY customer_id
    HAVING count(*) >= 3
)
SELECT c.id, c.name, counted.categories
FROM counted
JOIN customers c ON c.id = counted.customer_id
ORDER BY counted.categories DESC, c.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name, count(DISTINCT p.category) AS categories
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.created_at >= '2023-11-01'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
HAVING count(DISTINCT p.category) >= 3
ORDER BY categories DESC, c.id;

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8

A country scorecard for orders created on or after `2023-11-01`. Per customer
country: `revenue` (the sum of `quantity * price` from the order line),
`units` (the sum of quantities), `orders` (how many **distinct** orders), and
`top_product` - the `name` of the product with the most units sold in that
country, ties broken by the lower product `id`. Columns, in this order:
`country`, `revenue`, `units`, `orders`, `top_product`.

**Ordered by `revenue` descending, then `country` ascending.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 82_drills_multi_join_2 ex8`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Four measures at country grain plus one value that is not an aggregate at all - a product name. Those two things cannot come out of the same `GROUP BY`, so plan for two summaries joined at the end.

## Hint 2
Build the joined line-level rows once, in a CTE. Aggregate that CTE by country for the totals. Aggregate it again by country and product for the ranking, then keep the top row per country.

## Hint 3
`count(DISTINCT order_id)` for the order count, because the line grain repeats each order. `DISTINCT ON (country)` with `ORDER BY country, units DESC, product_id`, or `row_number()` partitioned the same way, for the best seller. The `product_id` tie-break is required by the prompt and is what makes the answer reproducible.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Four measures at country grain plus one value that is not an aggregate at all - a product name. Those two things cannot come out of the same `GROUP BY`, so plan for two summaries joined at the end.

## Hint 2
Build the joined line-level rows once, in a CTE. Aggregate that CTE by country for the totals. Aggregate it again by country and product for the ranking, then keep the top row per country.

## Hint 3
`count(DISTINCT order_id)` for the order count, because the line grain repeats each order. `DISTINCT ON (country)` with `ORDER BY country, units DESC, product_id`, or `row_number()` partitioned the same way, for the best seller. The `product_id` tie-break is required by the prompt and is what makes the answer reproducible.

references.solution.sql:
WITH lines AS (
    SELECT c.country, p.id AS product_id, p.name AS product_name,
           oi.quantity AS q, oi.quantity * oi.price AS rev, o.id AS order_id
    FROM customers c
    JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
    JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
    JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
    WHERE o.created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01'
), ranked AS (
    SELECT country, product_name,
           row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY country
                              ORDER BY sum(q) DESC, product_id) AS rn
    FROM lines
    GROUP BY country, product_id, product_name
)
SELECT t.country, t.revenue, t.units, t.orders, ranked.product_name AS top_product
FROM (SELECT country, sum(rev) AS revenue, sum(q) AS units,
             count(DISTINCT order_id) AS orders
      FROM lines
      GROUP BY country) t
JOIN ranked ON ranked.country = t.country AND ranked.rn = 1
ORDER BY t.revenue DESC, t.country;

WITH lines AS (
    SELECT c.country,
           p.id AS product_id,
           p.name AS product_name,
           oi.quantity AS q,
           oi.quantity * oi.price AS rev,
           o.id AS order_id
    FROM customers c
    JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
    JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
    JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
    WHERE o.created_at >= '2023-11-01'
), totals AS (
    SELECT country,
           sum(rev) AS revenue,
           sum(q) AS units,
           count(DISTINCT order_id) AS orders
    FROM lines
    GROUP BY country
), best AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT ON (country) country, product_name
    FROM (SELECT country, product_id, product_name, sum(q) AS units
          FROM lines
          GROUP BY country, product_id, product_name) z
    ORDER BY country, units DESC, product_id
)
SELECT t.country, t.revenue, t.units, t.orders, b.product_name AS top_product
FROM totals t
JOIN best b ON b.country = t.country
ORDER BY t.revenue DESC, t.country;

lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 83_drills_subqueries_1

Where a subquery may stand, what it returns there, and the one question that
decides everything: does it need to know about the outer row?

## Notes

**A subquery is just a query used as a value, a list, or a table.** In
`WHERE x > (SELECT ...)` it must return one row and one column - a scalar. In
`WHERE x IN (SELECT ...)` it returns one column and any number of rows. In
`FROM (SELECT ...) t` it returns a whole table and needs an alias. In the
`SELECT` list it must again be scalar, producing one value per output row.

**Correlated or not is the load-bearing distinction.** If the subquery
mentions a column from the outer query, it is correlated: conceptually it is
re-evaluated for every outer row, and its answer differs from row to row. If
it does not, it is computed once and reused. Everything else about subqueries
- cost, when they are legal, whether they can be rewritten as a join -
follows from that.

**Correlated does not have to mean slow, but it can.** Postgres flattens
correlated `EXISTS` and `IN` into semi-joins and anti-joins, so those cost
about what a join costs. A correlated scalar aggregate in the `SELECT` list is
different: it runs as a subplan per row, and against an unindexed column that
is a full scan per row. Exercise 2 is deliberately the slow spelling so you
can feel it; the fast spelling is the pre-aggregated `LEFT JOIN` in the
reference.

**A subquery does not inherit the outer `WHERE`.** `WHERE category = 'toys'
AND price > (SELECT avg(price) FROM products)` compares toys against the
average of *everything*. If the threshold is meant to be category-specific,
the subquery needs its own filter. This is the single most common
misunderstanding about scalar subqueries.

**`IN` and `NOT IN` are not symmetric in safety.** `IN` behaves sensibly
whatever the list contains. `NOT IN` yields unknown for every row if the list
contains a single NULL, so the query returns nothing at all. It is safe only
when the subquery's column is `NOT NULL` - and knowing that requires checking
the schema, which is why `NOT EXISTS` is the better default.

**A derived table turns `HAVING` into `WHERE`.** Aggregate in a subquery,
name it, and its aggregates become ordinary columns at the next level up.
That is not just a stylistic choice: it lets you filter, sort, join, or
aggregate the aggregates, which `HAVING` alone cannot do.

**Averaging aggregates is two levels, always.** "The average customer's
revenue" is not `avg(orders.total)`. One is the mean of a per-customer sum,
the other the mean of a single order. Both are one line of SQL and they differ
by an order of magnitude.

## ex1 - the uncorrelated scalar

One number, computed once, compared against every row. The subquery mentions
nothing from the outer query, so Postgres evaluates it a single time and
substitutes the result.

The classic mistake is omitting the category filter inside the subquery.
`(SELECT avg(price) FROM products)` is the average across all six categories,
which is a legitimate number and not the one the prompt asked for; the query
runs and returns a plausible number of rows.

The model answer repeats the filter in both places. The reference lifts the
threshold into a one-row CTE and cross-joins it, which makes the "computed
once" explicit and is worth reaching for when the same threshold is needed
twice.

## ex2 - the correlated scalar, in the SELECT list

Two subqueries, both mentioning `c.id`, each producing one value per
customer. This is the shape people write first because it reads exactly like
the requirement, and it is also the shape that scales worst.

The classic mistake is expecting the count to be NULL for a customer with no
orders. `count(*)` over zero rows is 0, so a scalar subquery returning a count
returns 0; `max(total)` over zero rows is NULL. The two behave differently and
the prompt asks for both behaviours on purpose.

The model answer uses the two correlated subqueries. The reference
pre-aggregates the orders into one row per customer and left-joins that,
which computes both measures in one pass instead of two per customer. On this
dataset the difference is roughly a factor of ten, and `orders.customer_id`
has no index - an observation that leads straight into Part 5.

## ex3 - IN with a list

The subquery returns a column of product ids. `IN` asks whether the outer
row's id appears in it, and does not care how many times.

The classic mistake is reaching for a join instead and forgetting that a
product with three qualifying lines then appears three times. `IN` is a
semi-join: it filters the outer rows and never multiplies them.

The model answer uses `IN` with an uncorrelated subquery. The reference uses
a correlated `EXISTS`, which Postgres plans almost identically; the practical
difference is that `EXISTS` can stop at the first match and `IN` may need the
whole list, and that `EXISTS` extends naturally to conditions involving more
than one column.

## ex4 - NOT IN, and when it is safe

Here `NOT IN` is correct, because `reviews.product_id` is declared `NOT NULL`
and the list therefore cannot contain a NULL. That is a real fact about this
schema, and it is the only thing standing between this query and the silent
empty result you met in drill set 78.

The classic mistake is generalising from this exercise. "It worked last time"
is how `NOT IN` gets used against a nullable column, and the failure mode is
zero rows with no error - a result that reads as a legitimate answer.

The model answer uses `NOT IN`; the reference uses `NOT EXISTS`. Both are
correct here; only one of them stays correct when somebody makes the column
nullable next quarter.

## ex5 - the correlated threshold

Every row is compared against a different number: the average of that
person's own team. Correlation is not an optimisation detail here, it is the
requirement - an uncorrelated `(SELECT avg(salary) FROM staff)` would answer
a different question.

The classic mistake is forgetting the CEO. Their `manager_id` is NULL, so the
subquery's `t.manager_id = s.manager_id` matches no rows, `avg` over no rows
is NULL, and `salary > NULL` is unknown - so they are excluded anyway, but by
accident rather than by intent. Saying so explicitly is what the prompt asks
for and what an interviewer listens for.

The model answer is the correlated subquery. The reference computes
`avg(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY manager_id)` in one pass and filters it one
level out - the window-function answer to every "compare each row to its
group" question, and the one to give when the table is large.

## ex6 - the derived table

Aggregate first, filter second. Inside the subquery, `count(*)` is an
aggregate; outside it, `orders` is just a column, and a plain `WHERE` works
on it.

The classic mistake is `WHERE count(*) >= 15` in the original query, which
Postgres rejects because aggregates do not exist at `WHERE` time. The
`HAVING` version is the direct fix and is exactly as correct - the reference
shows it - but the derived table generalises: you can join it, sort by a
computed column, or aggregate it again, none of which `HAVING` gives you.

The model answer wraps the aggregate in a subquery and filters outside. Note
that the ordering has to name the columns as they exist at the level where the
`ORDER BY` runs; in the `HAVING` version you sort by `sum(total)` again,
because the alias is not visible there either.

## ex7 - averaging an aggregate

"The average customer's revenue" requires per-customer revenue to exist
first. That is one subquery to build it and a second aggregate over the
result - two levels, unavoidably.

The classic mistake is `avg(total)` straight from `orders`, which is the
average *order*, around a thousand here rather than around nine thousand.
The query runs, the threshold is nine times too small, and the result set is
far too large - but nothing about it looks wrong unless you know the numbers.

The model answer repeats the per-customer aggregation twice, once for the
rows and once inside the threshold. The reference names it once as a CTE and
uses it in both places, which is shorter, self-documenting, and makes it
obvious that both sides are the same computation.

## ex8 - three subqueries doing three different jobs

The company-wide average is an uncorrelated scalar. The department filter is
on the group's average, so it belongs in `HAVING`. And the top earner's name
is not an aggregate at all - it is a value from one particular row of the
group.

The classic mistake is `max(s.name)`, which Postgres accepts and which
returns the alphabetically last name in the department. It is wrong on most
rows, it never errors, and it is the most common way this shape of report goes
quietly bad.

The model answer puts a correlated subquery in the `SELECT` list of a grouped
query - legal because it references only the grouping column, which is fixed
within the group - ordered by `salary DESC, id` with `LIMIT 1`. The reference
computes the aggregates and the top earners as two separate CTEs and joins
them, using `DISTINCT ON (department)` for the winner. The tie-break on `id`
is required in both: without it, two people on identical salaries would make
the query return different names on different runs.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL - Scalar Subqueries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html#SQL-SYNTAX-SCALAR-SUBQUERIES) - the rules for a subquery used as a value, including that it must return at most one row and yields NULL when it returns none. Behind ex1, ex2, ex5 and ex8.
- [PostgreSQL - Subquery Expressions: IN, NOT IN, EXISTS](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) - the semantics of each, and the explicit warning about `NOT IN` with NULLs. Behind ex3 and ex4.
- [PostgreSQL - Subqueries in FROM](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-SUBQUERIES) - derived tables, why they need an alias, and how they turn aggregates into ordinary columns. Behind ex6 and ex7.
- [PostgreSQL - GROUP BY and HAVING](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-GROUP) - why the restriction in ex8 belongs in `HAVING`, and what a grouped query's `SELECT` list may legally contain.
- [PostgreSQL - Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) - the one-pass alternative to a correlated per-group aggregate, used in the ex5 reference.

Use this ladder after completing **83 - Drills: subqueries 1**. Each pass changes the retrieval
task so repetition strengthens recall instead of becoming answer recognition.
Do the named exercise from a blank starting point whenever practical, and only
open its hints after recording your first attempt.

| Pass | When | Practice target | Retrieval task |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | now | `ex1` | Close the notes and state the central rule in one precise sentence. |

# Reading - 83_drills_subqueries_1

Where a subquery may stand, what it returns there, and the one question that
decides everything: does it need to know about the outer row?

## Notes

**A subquery is just a query used as a value, a list, or a table.** In
`WHERE x > (SELECT ...)` it must return one row and one column - a scalar. In
`WHERE x IN (SELECT ...)` it returns one column and any number of rows. In
`FROM (SELECT ...) t` it returns a whole table and needs an alias. In the
`SELECT` list it must again be scalar, producing one value per output row.

**Correlated or not is the load-bearing distinction.** If the subquery
mentions a column from the outer query, it is correlated: conceptually it is
re-evaluated for every outer row, and its answer differs from row to row. If
it does not, it is computed once and reused. Everything else about subqueries
- cost, when they are legal, whether they can be rewritten as a join -
follows from that.

**Correlated does not have to mean slow, but it can.** Postgres flattens
correlated `EXISTS` and `IN` into semi-joins and anti-joins, so those cost
about what a join costs. A correlated scalar aggregate in the `SELECT` list is
different: it runs as a subplan per row, and against an unindexed column that
is a full scan per row. Exercise 2 is deliberately the slow spelling so you
can feel it; the fast spelling is the pre-aggregated `LEFT JOIN` in the
reference.

**A subquery does not inherit the outer `WHERE`.** `WHERE category = 'toys'
AND price > (SELECT avg(price) FROM products)` compares toys against the
average of *everything*. If the threshold is meant to be category-specific,
the subquery needs its own filter. This is the single most common
misunderstanding about scalar subqueries.

**`IN` and `NOT IN` are not symmetric in safety.** `IN` behaves sensibly
whatever the list contains. `NOT IN` yields unknown for every row if the list
contains a single NULL, so the query returns nothing at all. It is safe only
when the subquery's column is `NOT NULL` - and knowing that requires checking
the schema, which is why `NOT EXISTS` is the better default.

**A derived table turns `HAVING` into `WHERE`.** Aggregate in a subquery,
name it, and its aggregates become ordinary columns at the next level up.
That is not just a stylistic choice: it lets you filter, sort, join, or
aggregate the aggregates, which `HAVING` alone cannot do.

**Averaging aggregates is two levels, always.** "The average customer's
revenue" is not `avg(orders.total)`. One is the mean of a per-customer sum,
the other the mean of a single order. Both are one line of SQL and they differ
by an order of magnitude.

## ex1 - the uncorrelated scalar

One number, computed once, compared against every row. The subquery mentions
nothing from the outer query, so Postgres evaluates it a single time and
substitutes the result.

The classic mistake is omitting the category filter inside the subquery.
`(SELECT avg(price) FROM products)` is the average across all six categories,
which is a legitimate number and not the one the prompt asked for; the query
runs and returns a plausible number of rows.

The model answer repeats the filter in both places. The reference lifts the
threshold into a one-row CTE and cross-joins it, which makes the "computed
once" explicit and is worth reaching for when the same threshold is needed
twice.

## ex2 - the correlated scalar, in the SELECT list

Two subqueries, both mentioning `c.id`, each producing one value per
customer. This is the shape people write first because it reads exactly like
the requirement, and it is also the shape that scales worst.

The classic mistake is expecting the count to be NULL for a customer with no
orders. `count(*)` over zero rows is 0, so a scalar subquery returning a count
returns 0; `max(total)` over zero rows is NULL. The two behave differently and
the prompt asks for both behaviours on purpose.

The model answer uses the two correlated subqueries. The reference
pre-aggregates the orders into one row per customer and left-joins that,
which computes both measures in one pass instead of two per customer. On this
dataset the difference is roughly a factor of ten, and `orders.customer_id`
has no index - an observation that leads straight into Part 5.

## ex3 - IN with a list

The subquery returns a column of product ids. `IN` asks whether the outer
row's id appears in it, and does not care how many times.

The classic mistake is reaching for a join instead and forgetting that a
product with three qualifying lines then appears three times. `IN` is a
semi-join: it filters the outer rows and never multiplies them.

The model answer uses `IN` with an uncorrelated subquery. The reference uses
a correlated `EXISTS`, which Postgres plans almost identically; the practical
difference is that `EXISTS` can stop at the first match and `IN` may need the
whole list, and that `EXISTS` extends naturally to conditions involving more
than one column.

## ex4 - NOT IN, and when it is safe

Here `NOT IN` is correct, because `reviews.product_id` is declared `NOT NULL`
and the list therefore cannot contain a NULL. That is a real fact about this
schema, and it is the only thing standing between this query and the silent
empty result you met in drill set 78.

The classic mistake is generalising from this exercise. "It worked last time"
is how `NOT IN` gets used against a nullable column, and the failure mode is
zero rows with no error - a result that reads as a legitimate answer.

The model answer uses `NOT IN`; the reference uses `NOT EXISTS`. Both are
correct here; only one of them stays correct when somebody makes the column
nullable next quarter.

## ex5 - the correlated threshold

Every row is compared against a different number: the average of that
person's own team. Correlation is not an optimisation detail here, it is the
requirement - an uncorrelated `(SELECT avg(salary) FROM staff)` would answer
a different question.

The classic mistake is forgetting the CEO. Their `manager_id` is NULL, so the
subquery's `t.manager_id = s.manager_id` matches no rows, `avg` over no rows
is NULL, and `salary > NULL` is unknown - so they are excluded anyway, but by
accident rather than by intent. Saying so explicitly is what the prompt asks
for and what an interviewer listens for.

The model answer is the correlated subquery. The reference computes
`avg(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY manager_id)` in one pass and filters it one
level out - the window-function answer to every "compare each row to its
group" question, and the one to give when the table is large.

## ex6 - the derived table

Aggregate first, filter second. Inside the subquery, `count(*)` is an
aggregate; outside it, `orders` is just a column, and a plain `WHERE` works
on it.

The classic mistake is `WHERE count(*) >= 15` in the original query, which
Postgres rejects because aggregates do not exist at `WHERE` time. The
`HAVING` version is the direct fix and is exactly as correct - the reference
shows it - but the derived table generalises: you can join it, sort by a
computed column, or aggregate it again, none of which `HAVING` gives you.

The model answer wraps the aggregate in a subquery and filters outside. Note
that the ordering has to name the columns as they exist at the level where the
`ORDER BY` runs; in the `HAVING` version you sort by `sum(total)` again,
because the alias is not visible there either.

## ex7 - averaging an aggregate

"The average customer's revenue" requires per-customer revenue to exist
first. That is one subquery to build it and a second aggregate over the
result - two levels, unavoidably.

The classic mistake is `avg(total)` straight from `orders`, which is the
average *order*, around a thousand here rather than around nine thousand.
The query runs, the threshold is nine times too small, and the result set is
far too large - but nothing about it looks wrong unless you know the numbers.

The model answer repeats the per-customer aggregation twice, once for the
rows and once inside the threshold. The reference names it once as a CTE and
uses it in both places, which is shorter, self-documenting, and makes it
obvious that both sides are the same computation.

## ex8 - three subqueries doing three different jobs

The company-wide average is an uncorrelated scalar. The department filter is
on the group's average, so it belongs in `HAVING`. And the top earner's name
is not an aggregate at all - it is a value from one particular row of the
group.

The classic mistake is `max(s.name)`, which Postgres accepts and which
returns the alphabetically last name in the department. It is wrong on most
rows, it never errors, and it is the most common way this shape of report goes
quietly bad.

The model answer puts a correlated subquery in the `SELECT` list of a grouped
query - legal because it references only the grouping column, which is fixed
within the group - ordered by `salary DESC, id` with `LIMIT 1`. The reference
computes the aggregates and the top earners as two separate CTEs and joins
them, using `DISTINCT ON (department)` for the winner. The tie-break on `id`
is required in both: without it, two people on identical salaries would make
the query return different names on different runs.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL - Scalar Subqueries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html#SQL-SYNTAX-SCALAR-SUBQUERIES) - the rules for a subquery used as a value, including that it must return at most one row and yields NULL when it returns none. Behind ex1, ex2, ex5 and ex8.
- [PostgreSQL - Subquery Expressions: IN, NOT IN, EXISTS](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) - the semantics of each, and the explicit warning about `NOT IN` with NULLs. Behind ex3 and ex4.
- [PostgreSQL - Subqueries in FROM](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-SUBQUERIES) - derived tables, why they need an alias, and how they turn aggregates into ordinary columns. Behind ex6 and ex7.
- [PostgreSQL - GROUP BY and HAVING](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-GROUP) - why the restriction in ex8 belongs in `HAVING`, and what a grouped query's `SELECT` list may legally contain.
- [PostgreSQL - Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) - the one-pass alternative to a correlated per-group aggregate, used in the ex5 reference.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1

`toys` products priced above the average price **of toys**. Columns, in this
order: `id`, `name`, `price`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 83_drills_subqueries_1 ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The threshold is a single number that has to be computed from the same table you are filtering, and it is the same number for every row - so it can be worked out once, before any comparison happens.

## Hint 2
A scalar subquery is a parenthesised `SELECT` returning exactly one row and one column, and it can appear anywhere a value can: `WHERE price > (SELECT avg(price) FROM products WHERE category = 'toys')`. Note that the subquery needs its own category filter - it does not inherit the outer query's `WHERE`.

WITH t AS (
    SELECT avg(price) AS avg_price FROM products WHERE category = 'toys'
)
SELECT p.id, p.name, p.price
FROM products p, t
WHERE p.category = 'toys' AND p.price > t.avg_price
ORDER BY p.id;

FROM products

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
A subquery can also appear in the `SELECT` list, where it produces one value per output row. Each of these two needs to know which customer the current row is about.

## Hint 2
`(SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)` - the reference to `c.id` from inside the subquery is what makes it correlated, and it is re-evaluated for every customer. references.solution.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name, coalesce(s.n, 0) AS orders, s.biggest
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS n, max(total) AS biggest
           FROM orders
           WHERE customer_id <= 12
           GROUP BY customer_id) s ON s.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.id <= 12
ORDER BY c.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) AS orders,
       (SELECT max(o.total) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) AS biggest
FROM customers c
WHERE c.id <= 12
ORDER BY c.id;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The subquery here returns a whole column of values rather than a single one, and you want the products whose id appears somewhere in it.

## Hint 2
`WHERE p.id IN (SELECT oi.product_id FROM ... )`. The subquery is uncorrelated - it does not mention `p` at all - so it is one list computed once. It may contain a product id many times over and `IN` will not care, and it cannot duplicate the outer rows the way a join would.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT p.id, p.name
FROM products p
WHERE p.category = 'garden'
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1
              FROM order_items oi
              JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
              WHERE oi.product_id = p.id
                AND oi.quantity = 5
                AND o.created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01')
ORDER BY p.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT p.id, p.name
FROM products p
WHERE p.category = 'garden'
  AND p.id IN (SELECT oi.product_id
               FROM order_items oi
               JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
               WHERE oi.quantity = 5
                 AND o.created_at >= '2023-11-01')
ORDER BY p.id;

references.solution.sql:
SELECT id, name, salary
FROM (SELECT s.id, s.name, s.salary,
             avg(s.salary) OVER (PARTITION BY s.manager_id) AS team_avg
      FROM staff s
      WHERE s.manager_id IS NOT NULL) t
WHERE salary > team_avg
ORDER BY id;

SELECT s.id, s.name, s.salary
FROM staff s
WHERE s.manager_id IS NOT NULL
  AND s.salary > (SELECT avg(t.salary) FROM staff t

ORDER BY s.id;

## Hint 1
A subquery can also stand where a table stands. Aggregate the orders into one row per customer first, give that result a name, and then filter it as if it were a table.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
A subquery can also stand where a table stands. Aggregate the orders into one row per customer first, give that result a name, and then filter it as if it were a table.

## Hint 2
`FROM (SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS orders, sum(total) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE status <> 'cancelled' GROUP BY customer_id) t` - and now `WHERE t.orders >= 15` is a plain `WHERE`, because at this level `orders` is just a column. The `HAVING` version of the same query is equally correct; write both and decide which you find easier to read.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS orders, sum(total) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING count(*) >= 15
ORDER BY sum(total) DESC, customer_id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT t.customer_id, t.orders, t.revenue
FROM (SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS orders, sum(total) AS revenue
      FROM orders
      WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
      GROUP BY customer_id) t
WHERE t.orders >= 15
ORDER BY t.revenue DESC, t.customer_id;

## Exercise 7

Customers whose non-cancelled revenue is **more than twice the average
customer's** non-cancelled revenue. The average is over customers, not over
orders: build one revenue figure per customer, then average those. Columns,
in this order: `customer_id`, `revenue`.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The comparison is between one customer's revenue and the **average customer's** revenue - which is not the average of the `orders` table. You have to build the per-customer totals before you can average them.

## Hint 2
Two levels of subquery. An inner one that groups orders into one row per customer, and then an average taken over **those rows**. Note that `avg(total)` straight from `orders` is a different and much smaller number - the average order, not the average customer.

## Hint 3
The cutoff is the same for every row, so it can be a scalar subquery in the `WHERE` clause or a one-row CTE cross-joined in. Either way it is computed once, and the aggregation over `orders` happens twice - a CTE makes that reuse explicit.

WITH agg AS (
    SELECT department, count(*) AS staff, avg(salary) AS avg_salary
    FROM staff
    GROUP BY department
), top AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT ON (department) department, name
    FROM staff
    ORDER BY department, salary DESC, id
)
SELECT agg.department, agg.staff, top.name AS top_earner
FROM agg
JOIN top ON top.department = agg.department
WHERE agg.avg_salary > (SELECT avg(salary) FROM staff)
ORDER BY agg.department;

SELECT s.department,
       count(*) AS staff,
       (SELECT t.name FROM staff t

        LIMIT 1) AS top_earner
FROM staff s
GROUP BY s.department
HAVING avg(s.salary) > (SELECT avg(salary) FROM staff)
ORDER BY s.department;

# 84 - Drills: subqueries 2

Eight problems on the subquery forms that come after the basics: `ANY` and
`ALL`, row-constructor `IN`, a subquery inside `HAVING`, correlated counting,
and a derived table that supplies the value a correlated subquery correlates
on. This set drills lesson 13. Several of these have a fast spelling and a
catastrophically slow one that returns the same rows - the reading says which
is which.

## Exercise 1

Members of `staff` who earn more than **every** `engineering` employee whose
salary is below 60000. Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `department`,
`salary`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

`toys` products priced above **at least one** `electronics` product priced
above 490. Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `price`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 84_drills_subqueries_2 ex2`

Per category: the average product price rounded to 2 decimal places, and how
many of that category's products are priced above that (unrounded) average.

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 84_drills_subqueries_2 ex3`

For every member of the `engineering` department: their id, name, `hired_on`
date, and the **salary of the person hired immediately before them within the

counting as earlier when two people share a date. The earliest hire in the

## Exercise 5

Among customers with `id <= 10000`, counting only **non-cancelled** orders:

**Ordered by `orders` descending, then `customer_id` ascending.**

Orders created in **October 2023** (`>= '2023-10-01'` and `< '2023-11-01'`)

after 2023-11-01**. Both values must match. Columns, in this order: `id`,
`customer_id`, `status`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 84_drills_subqueries_2 ex6`

## Exercise 7

For every `books` product priced above 495: its id, name, price, and how many
**other `books` products are strictly cheaper** than it. Columns, in this
order: `id`, `name`, `price`, `cheaper_books`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 84_drills_subqueries_2 ex7`

## Exercise 8

The most typical person in each department: the one whose salary is nearest
to their department's average, with the lower staff `id` winning a tie.
Columns, in this order: `department`, `most_typical` (their name),
`typical_salary` (their salary), `avg_salary` (the department average rounded
to 2 decimal places).

**Ordered by `department` ascending.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 84_drills_subqueries_2 ex8`

# Reading - 84_drills_subqueries_2

The second half of the subquery toolkit: quantified comparisons, row
constructors, aggregates of aggregates, and the question of which side of a
correlation you drive from.

## Notes

**`ANY` and `ALL` are quantified comparisons.** `x > ANY (subquery)` is true
if the comparison holds for at least one row; `x > ALL (subquery)` if it holds
for every row. `= ANY` is exactly what `IN` means, and `<> ALL` is exactly
what `NOT IN` means - which is also the cleanest explanation of why `NOT IN`
breaks on NULLs.

**The empty-set cases differ, and they matter.** `> ALL` of nothing is
**true** - there is no counterexample. `> ANY` of nothing is **false** - there
is no witness. Rewriting them as `> (SELECT max(...))` and `> (SELECT
min(...))` changes that: both become a comparison against NULL, which is
unknown, so both return no rows. On a non-empty list the two spellings agree
exactly; decide which behaviour you want before you rely on either.

**A row constructor compares several columns at once.** `(a, b) IN (SELECT x,
y FROM ...)` matches only when both columns agree, and `(a, b) < (c, d)`
compares left to right like a compound sort key. Both are standard SQL and
both save you from writing conjunctions by hand - where the risk is writing
only half of one.

**You cannot nest aggregates, so an aggregate of aggregates is two queries.**
`avg(count(*))` is rejected. Group once in a subquery or CTE to produce the
counts as rows, then aggregate those rows. The same shape answers "more than
the average customer", "above the median department", and every other
comparison against a population of groups.

**Correlate from the small side.** A correlated subquery is re-executed once
per row of the query it sits in. Correlating a per-category aggregate from a
scan of the whole products table runs it once per product; correlating it
from a six-row derived table of categories runs it six times, for the same
answer.
When a correlated query is slow, the fix is usually not to remove the
correlation but to move it.

**`EXISTS` and `IN` are cheap; correlated aggregates are not.** Postgres
flattens semi-joins and anti-joins into hash joins. A correlated `count`,
`avg`, or `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1` in the `SELECT` list runs as a subplan per
row, and against an unindexed column each execution is a full scan. That is
not a reason to avoid them - on a small driving set they are the clearest
thing to write - it is a reason to know how many times they will run.

**"Nearest" is a sort, not a filter.** There is no operator for "closest to";
you order by the absolute difference and take the first row. The tie-break
belongs in the same `ORDER BY`, or the answer changes between runs.

## ex1 - ALL, and the empty-list footnote

`salary > ALL (list)` reads as "beats everybody on that list". The natural
rewrite is `> (SELECT max(...))`, and on this data the two agree exactly.

The classic mistake is assuming they always agree. They part company on an
empty list: `> ALL` of nothing is true, because a universal claim over an
empty set has no counterexample, while `max` of nothing is NULL and every
comparison against NULL is unknown. A filter that quietly returns everybody
in one version and nobody in the other is worth ten seconds of thought.

The model answer uses `> ALL`; the reference spells out the same logic as
`NOT EXISTS (someone on the list this person fails to beat)`, which is what
`ALL` compiles to and which behaves identically in the empty case.

## ex2 - ANY is the other quantifier

`> ANY` needs only one witness, so it is equivalent to `> (SELECT min(...))`.
Reading `ANY` as "at least one" and `ALL` as "every" out loud is enough to
stop confusing them.

The classic mistake is reading `> ANY` as "greater than any of them", which
in English sounds like *all* of them. The SQL keyword means the opposite of
what the English idiom suggests, which is exactly why `SOME` exists as a
synonym - `> SOME (...)` reads correctly and means the same thing.

The model answer uses `> ANY`; the reference compares against the minimum. On
a non-empty list they are interchangeable, and the `min` version is the one
most readers will parse faster.

## ex3 - correlate from the small side

Six averages, six counts. The interesting decision is which side of the
correlation drives: the six-row derived table of category averages, or the
full scan of the products table.

The classic mistake is the one-liner: `FROM products p WHERE p.price >
(SELECT avg(price) FROM products p2 WHERE p2.category = p.category) GROUP BY
p.category`. It is correct, it is the sentence translated directly into SQL,
and it re-executes an aggregate over the whole table once per product. At
full volume it takes minutes; the version driven from the six-row side takes
a fraction of a second.

The model answer builds the averages in a derived table and correlates a
`count` from those six rows. The reference joins the averages back to
`products` and uses `count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.price > a.avg_price)`, which is
one pass and no correlation at all. Both are fine; the version that
correlates from the whole table is the one to recognise and reject.

## ex4 - the previous row, without a window function

For each person, one value from the nearest earlier row in the same
department. A correlated subquery ordered `hired_on DESC` with `LIMIT 1`
picks it out.

The classic mistake is `t.hired_on < s.hired_on`, which is wrong when two
people were hired on the same date: neither is "before" the other, so both
skip past their true neighbour. `(t.hired_on, t.id) < (s.hired_on, s.id)`
compares the pair left to right and gives a strict total order, which is the
same thing the `ORDER BY hired_on, id` in the window version does.

The reference uses `lag(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY
hired_on, id)` - one pass instead of one scan per person - with the
`engineering` filter applied **one level out**. That placement matters:
window functions run after `WHERE`, so filtering in the same query would
change which rows the window can see. Here it happens not to matter, because
the partition is the department, but the habit of separating the two is what
keeps window queries correct.

## ex5 - an aggregate of aggregates

The threshold is the average number of orders per customer, which requires
per-customer counts to exist before anything can be averaged. `avg(count(*))`
is rejected by Postgres, and the rejection is the hint.

The classic mistake is comparing against something that is not the average
customer - `avg(total)`, or a count over the whole table divided by nothing
in particular. Being able to say precisely which population an average is over
is most of what separates a correct report from a plausible one.

The model answer nests a derived table inside the `HAVING` clause's scalar
subquery. The reference names the per-customer counts once as a CTE and uses
it twice, which is the same computation with the duplication made visible -
and the version that survives somebody adding a third condition.

## ex6 - matching on a pair

`(o.customer_id, o.status) IN (SELECT n.customer_id, n.status FROM ...)` is a
single membership test over two columns. A customer who ordered in both
windows with different statuses does not match, and the row constructor says
that without any conjunctions.

The classic mistake is the hand-written `EXISTS` with only one of the two
equality conditions. It runs, it returns more rows, and nothing about the
result announces that half the requirement is missing. The row-constructor
form cannot be half-written.

The model answer uses the row constructor; the reference writes both
conditions out inside `EXISTS`. Comparing them is the point - the second is
more flexible (it can express inequalities and extra conditions) and is
exactly where the omission bug lives.

## ex7 - a correlated count is a rank

"How many books are cheaper than this one" is a correlated aggregate, and it
is also what `rank()` computes. Doing it by hand is worth practising because
it makes the window-function version obvious later.

The classic mistake is leaving the category filter out of the subquery. The
outer `WHERE p.category = 'books'` does not reach inside; without repeating
it, the count is over every product in the table rather than every book, and
each number comes out several times too large.

The model answer uses the correlated `count` - cheap here because the outer
set is a handful of rows. The reference uses a self-join with
`LEFT JOIN products c ON c.category = 'books' AND c.price < p.price` and a
`GROUP BY`; the join must
be outer, or the cheapest qualifying book - the one whose answer is 0 - would
disappear from the result entirely.

## ex8 - a derived table feeding a correlated subquery

Two dependent steps. The department average has to exist before "nearest to
it" means anything, and the value being correlated on is itself computed.
That is the structural idea worth taking away: a derived table can supply the
correlation value, not just the rows.

The classic mistake is treating "nearest" as a filter and searching for an
operator that does not exist. It is a sort: `ORDER BY abs(salary -
avg_salary)` and `LIMIT 1`. The second mistake is omitting `, s.id` from that
ordering, which leaves two equally typical people to be resolved by the
planner - a query that passes today and returns a different name after the
next `VACUUM`.

The model answer runs two correlated subqueries, one per output column, which
is honest but does the same search twice. The reference does it once with
`DISTINCT ON (department)` over a join to the averages, returning the name and
the salary together - the shape to reach for whenever "the best row per group"
needs more than one column from that row.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL - Subquery Expressions: ANY/SOME and ALL](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) - the definitions, the note that `= ANY` is `IN` and `<> ALL` is `NOT IN`, and the empty-subquery results that ex1 turns on.
- [PostgreSQL - Row Constructor Comparison](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html#ROW-WISE-COMPARISON) - how `(a, b) < (c, d)` and `(a, b) IN (...)` are evaluated, used in ex4 and ex6.
- [PostgreSQL - Subqueries in FROM](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-SUBQUERIES) - derived tables, which are what make an aggregate of aggregates expressible in ex3, ex5 and ex8.
- [PostgreSQL - Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) - `lag` and `rank`, the one-pass alternatives to the correlated subqueries in ex4 and ex7, including where they sit relative to `WHERE`.
- [PostgreSQL - SELECT: DISTINCT ON](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html#SQL-DISTINCT) - the single-pass "best row per group" used in the ex8 reference.

# 84 - Drills: subqueries 2

Eight problems on the subquery forms that come after the basics: `ANY` and
`ALL`, row-constructor `IN`, a subquery inside `HAVING`, correlated counting,
and a derived table that supplies the value a correlated subquery correlates
on. This set drills lesson 13. Several of these have a fast spelling and a
catastrophically slow one that returns the same rows - the reading says which
is which.

## Exercise 1

Members of `staff` who earn more than **every** `engineering` employee whose
salary is below 60000. Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `department`,
`salary`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 84_drills_subqueries_2 ex1`

## Exercise 2

`toys` products priced above **at least one** `electronics` product priced
above 490. Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `price`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 84_drills_subqueries_2 ex2`

## Exercise 3

Per category: the average product price rounded to 2 decimal places, and how
many of that category's products are priced above that (unrounded) average.
Columns, in this order: `category`, `avg_price`, `above_average`.

**Ordered by `category` ascending.**

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 84_drills_subqueries_2 ex3`

## Exercise 4

For every member of the `engineering` department: their id, name, `hired_on`
date, and the **salary of the person hired immediately before them within the
same department**. Order of hire is `hired_on`, with the lower staff `id`
counting as earlier when two people share a date. The earliest hire in the
department reports NULL. Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `hired_on`,
`previous_hire_salary`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 84_drills_subqueries_2 ex4`

## Exercise 5

Among customers with `id <= 10000`, counting only **non-cancelled** orders:
the customers who have placed more orders than the average customer in that
same population. Columns, in this order: `customer_id`, `orders`.

**Ordered by `orders` descending, then `customer_id` ascending.**

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 84_drills_subqueries_2 ex5`

## Exercise 6

Orders created in **October 2023** (`>= '2023-10-01'` and `< '2023-11-01'`)
whose `(customer_id, status)` pair also occurs on some order created **on or
after 2023-11-01**. Both values must match. Columns, in this order: `id`,
`customer_id`, `status`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 84_drills_subqueries_2 ex6`

## Exercise 7

For every `books` product priced above 495: its id, name, price, and how many
**other `books` products are strictly cheaper** than it. Columns, in this
order: `id`, `name`, `price`, `cheaper_books`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 84_drills_subqueries_2 ex7`

## Exercise 8

The most typical person in each department: the one whose salary is nearest
to their department's average, with the lower staff `id` winning a tie.
Columns, in this order: `department`, `most_typical` (their name),
`typical_salary` (their salary), `avg_salary` (the department average rounded
to 2 decimal places).

**Ordered by `department` ascending.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 84_drills_subqueries_2 ex8`

# Reading - 84_drills_subqueries_2

The second half of the subquery toolkit: quantified comparisons, row
constructors, aggregates of aggregates, and the question of which side of a
correlation you drive from.

## Notes

**`ANY` and `ALL` are quantified comparisons.** `x > ANY (subquery)` is true
if the comparison holds for at least one row; `x > ALL (subquery)` if it holds
for every row. `= ANY` is exactly what `IN` means, and `<> ALL` is exactly
what `NOT IN` means - which is also the cleanest explanation of why `NOT IN`
breaks on NULLs.

**The empty-set cases differ, and they matter.** `> ALL` of nothing is
**true** - there is no counterexample. `> ANY` of nothing is **false** - there
is no witness. Rewriting them as `> (SELECT max(...))` and `> (SELECT
min(...))` changes that: both become a comparison against NULL, which is
unknown, so both return no rows. On a non-empty list the two spellings agree
exactly; decide which behaviour you want before you rely on either.

**A row constructor compares several columns at once.** `(a, b) IN (SELECT x,
y FROM ...)` matches only when both columns agree, and `(a, b) < (c, d)`
compares left to right like a compound sort key. Both are standard SQL and
both save you from writing conjunctions by hand - where the risk is writing
only half of one.

**You cannot nest aggregates, so an aggregate of aggregates is two queries.**
`avg(count(*))` is rejected. Group once in a subquery or CTE to produce the
counts as rows, then aggregate those rows. The same shape answers "more than
the average customer", "above the median department", and every other
comparison against a population of groups.

**Correlate from the small side.** A correlated subquery is re-executed once
per row of the query it sits in. Correlating a per-category aggregate from a
scan of the whole products table runs it once per product; correlating it
from a six-row derived table of categories runs it six times, for the same
answer.
When a correlated query is slow, the fix is usually not to remove the
correlation but to move it.

**`EXISTS` and `IN` are cheap; correlated aggregates are not.** Postgres
flattens semi-joins and anti-joins into hash joins. A correlated `count`,
`avg`, or `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1` in the `SELECT` list runs as a subplan per
row, and against an unindexed column each execution is a full scan. That is
not a reason to avoid them - on a small driving set they are the clearest
thing to write - it is a reason to know how many times they will run.

**"Nearest" is a sort, not a filter.** There is no operator for "closest to";
you order by the absolute difference and take the first row. The tie-break
belongs in the same `ORDER BY`, or the answer changes between runs.

## ex1 - ALL, and the empty-list footnote

`salary > ALL (list)` reads as "beats everybody on that list". The natural
rewrite is `> (SELECT max(...))`, and on this data the two agree exactly.

The classic mistake is assuming they always agree. They part company on an
empty list: `> ALL` of nothing is true, because a universal claim over an
empty set has no counterexample, while `max` of nothing is NULL and every
comparison against NULL is unknown. A filter that quietly returns everybody
in one version and nobody in the other is worth ten seconds of thought.

The model answer uses `> ALL`; the reference spells out the same logic as
`NOT EXISTS (someone on the list this person fails to beat)`, which is what
`ALL` compiles to and which behaves identically in the empty case.

## ex2 - ANY is the other quantifier

`> ANY` needs only one witness, so it is equivalent to `> (SELECT min(...))`.
Reading `ANY` as "at least one" and `ALL` as "every" out loud is enough to
stop confusing them.

The classic mistake is reading `> ANY` as "greater than any of them", which
in English sounds like *all* of them. The SQL keyword means the opposite of
what the English idiom suggests, which is exactly why `SOME` exists as a
synonym - `> SOME (...)` reads correctly and means the same thing.

The model answer uses `> ANY`; the reference compares against the minimum. On
a non-empty list they are interchangeable, and the `min` version is the one
most readers will parse faster.

## ex3 - correlate from the small side

Six averages, six counts. The interesting decision is which side of the
correlation drives: the six-row derived table of category averages, or the
full scan of the products table.

The classic mistake is the one-liner: `FROM products p WHERE p.price >
(SELECT avg(price) FROM products p2 WHERE p2.category = p.category) GROUP BY
p.category`. It is correct, it is the sentence translated directly into SQL,
and it re-executes an aggregate over the whole table once per product. At
full volume it takes minutes; the version driven from the six-row side takes
a fraction of a second.

The model answer builds the averages in a derived table and correlates a
`count` from those six rows. The reference joins the averages back to
`products` and uses `count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.price > a.avg_price)`, which is
one pass and no correlation at all. Both are fine; the version that
correlates from the whole table is the one to recognise and reject.

## ex4 - the previous row, without a window function

For each person, one value from the nearest earlier row in the same
department. A correlated subquery ordered `hired_on DESC` with `LIMIT 1`
picks it out.

The classic mistake is `t.hired_on < s.hired_on`, which is wrong when two
people were hired on the same date: neither is "before" the other, so both
skip past their true neighbour. `(t.hired_on, t.id) < (s.hired_on, s.id)`
compares the pair left to right and gives a strict total order, which is the
same thing the `ORDER BY hired_on, id` in the window version does.

The reference uses `lag(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY
hired_on, id)` - one pass instead of one scan per person - with the
`engineering` filter applied **one level out**. That placement matters:
window functions run after `WHERE`, so filtering in the same query would
change which rows the window can see. Here it happens not to matter, because
the partition is the department, but the habit of separating the two is what
keeps window queries correct.

## ex5 - an aggregate of aggregates

The threshold is the average number of orders per customer, which requires
per-customer counts to exist before anything can be averaged. `avg(count(*))`
is rejected by Postgres, and the rejection is the hint.

The classic mistake is comparing against something that is not the average
customer - `avg(total)`, or a count over the whole table divided by nothing
in particular. Being able to say precisely which population an average is over
is most of what separates a correct report from a plausible one.

The model answer nests a derived table inside the `HAVING` clause's scalar
subquery. The reference names the per-customer counts once as a CTE and uses
it twice, which is the same computation with the duplication made visible -
and the version that survives somebody adding a third condition.

## ex6 - matching on a pair

`(o.customer_id, o.status) IN (SELECT n.customer_id, n.status FROM ...)` is a
single membership test over two columns. A customer who ordered in both
windows with different statuses does not match, and the row constructor says
that without any conjunctions.

The classic mistake is the hand-written `EXISTS` with only one of the two
equality conditions. It runs, it returns more rows, and nothing about the
result announces that half the requirement is missing. The row-constructor
form cannot be half-written.

The model answer uses the row constructor; the reference writes both
conditions out inside `EXISTS`. Comparing them is the point - the second is
more flexible (it can express inequalities and extra conditions) and is
exactly where the omission bug lives.

## ex7 - a correlated count is a rank

"How many books are cheaper than this one" is a correlated aggregate, and it
is also what `rank()` computes. Doing it by hand is worth practising because
it makes the window-function version obvious later.

The classic mistake is leaving the category filter out of the subquery. The
outer `WHERE p.category = 'books'` does not reach inside; without repeating
it, the count is over every product in the table rather than every book, and
each number comes out several times too large.

The model answer uses the correlated `count` - cheap here because the outer
set is a handful of rows. The reference uses a self-join with
`LEFT JOIN products c ON c.category = 'books' AND c.price < p.price` and a
`GROUP BY`; the join must
be outer, or the cheapest qualifying book - the one whose answer is 0 - would
disappear from the result entirely.

## ex8 - a derived table feeding a correlated subquery

Two dependent steps. The department average has to exist before "nearest to
it" means anything, and the value being correlated on is itself computed.
That is the structural idea worth taking away: a derived table can supply the
correlation value, not just the rows.

The classic mistake is treating "nearest" as a filter and searching for an
operator that does not exist. It is a sort: `ORDER BY abs(salary -
avg_salary)` and `LIMIT 1`. The second mistake is omitting `, s.id` from that
ordering, which leaves two equally typical people to be resolved by the
planner - a query that passes today and returns a different name after the
next `VACUUM`.

The model answer runs two correlated subqueries, one per output column, which
is honest but does the same search twice. The reference does it once with
`DISTINCT ON (department)` over a join to the averages, returning the name and
the salary together - the shape to reach for whenever "the best row per group"
needs more than one column from that row.

## Further reading

- [PostgreSQL - Subquery Expressions: ANY/SOME and ALL](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) - the definitions, the note that `= ANY` is `IN` and `<> ALL` is `NOT IN`, and the empty-subquery results that ex1 turns on.
- [PostgreSQL - Row Constructor Comparison](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html#ROW-WISE-COMPARISON) - how `(a, b) < (c, d)` and `(a, b) IN (...)` are evaluated, used in ex4 and ex6.
- [PostgreSQL - Subqueries in FROM](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-SUBQUERIES) - derived tables, which are what make an aggregate of aggregates expressible in ex3, ex5 and ex8.
- [PostgreSQL - Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) - `lag` and `rank`, the one-pass alternatives to the correlated subqueries in ex4 and ex7, including where they sit relative to `WHERE`.
- [PostgreSQL - SELECT: DISTINCT ON](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html#SQL-DISTINCT) - the single-pass "best row per group" used in the ex8 reference.

## Exercise 1

Members of `staff` who earn more than **every** `engineering` employee whose
salary is below 60000. Columns, in this order: `id`, `name`, `department`,
`salary`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The subquery returns a whole column of salaries, and the person has to beat every single one of them.

## Hint 2
`salary > ALL (SELECT salary FROM staff WHERE department = 'engineering' AND salary < 60000)` says exactly that. Read it as "there is nobody in that list this person fails to beat", which is also how you would write it with `NOT EXISTS`.

## Hint 3
`> ALL` is very nearly `> (SELECT max(...))`, and that spelling is usually clearer - but the two disagree when the list is empty. `> ALL` of nothing is true (there is no counterexample); `> NULL` is unknown, so the `max` version returns no rows at all. Know which behaviour you want before you pick.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The subquery returns a whole column of salaries, and the person has to beat every single one of them.

## Hint 2
`salary > ALL (SELECT salary FROM staff WHERE department = 'engineering' AND salary < 60000)` says exactly that. Read it as "there is nobody in that list this person fails to beat", which is also how you would write it with `NOT EXISTS`.

## Hint 3
`> ALL` is very nearly `> (SELECT max(...))`, and that spelling is usually clearer - but the two disagree when the list is empty. `> ALL` of nothing is true (there is no counterexample); `> NULL` is unknown, so the `max` version returns no rows at all. Know which behaviour you want before you pick.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT s.id, s.name, s.department, s.salary
FROM staff s
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM staff t
                  WHERE t.department = 'engineering'
                    AND t.salary < 60000
                    AND t.salary >= s.salary)
ORDER BY s.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, name, department, salary
FROM staff
WHERE salary > ALL (SELECT salary FROM staff
                    WHERE department = 'engineering' AND salary < 60000)
ORDER BY id;

## Hint 1
The mirror of the previous problem: the product only has to beat **one** member of the list, not all of them.

`price > ANY (SELECT ...)`, which is the same as comparing against the minimum of the list. `SOME` is a synonym for `ANY` if you ever meet it. Note that `= ANY (...)` is precisely what `IN (...)` means.

SELECT p.id, p.name, p.price
FROM products p
WHERE p.category = 'toys'
  AND p.price > (SELECT min(price) FROM products

ORDER BY p.id;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Two steps that have to happen in order: each category's average price, and then a count of that category's products above it. Six averages, six counts.

## Hint 2
Compute the averages once, in a derived table or CTE grouped by category. Selecting from that gives you six rows, and a correlated subquery over `products` can then reference `d.avg_price` as an ordinary column.

## Hint 3
The tempting one-liner - `FROM products p WHERE p.price > (SELECT avg(price) FROM products p2 WHERE p2.category = p.category)` grouped by category - gives the same answer and re-runs that aggregate once per product, for every product in the table. Correlating from the six-row side instead of the whole-table side is the whole trick.

references.solution.sql:
WITH avgs AS (
    SELECT category, avg(price) AS avg_price
    FROM products
    GROUP BY category
)
SELECT a.category,
       round(a.avg_price, 2) AS avg_price,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.price > a.avg_price) AS above_average
FROM avgs a
JOIN products p ON p.category = a.category
GROUP BY a.category, a.avg_price
ORDER BY a.category;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT d.category,
       round(d.avg_price, 2) AS avg_price,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM products p
        WHERE p.category = d.category AND p.price > d.avg_price) AS above_average
FROM (SELECT category, avg(price) AS avg_price
      FROM products
      GROUP BY category) d
ORDER BY d.category;

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
For each person you want one value from a different row of the same table - the one immediately before them in hire order within their department. The very first hire has nobody before them and reports NULL.

## Hint 2
A correlated subquery ordered `hired_on DESC` with `LIMIT 1` picks the nearest earlier row. Use a row comparison, `(t.hired_on, t.id) < (s.hired_on, s.id)`, so that two people hired on the same day are still strictly ordered - Postgres compares row constructors left to right, like a compound sort key.

## Hint 3
The other answer is `lag(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY hired_on, id)`, computed for the whole table and then filtered down to engineering **one level out** - a window function is evaluated after `WHERE`, so filtering in the same query would change which rows the window can see.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
For each person you want one value from a different row of the same table - the one immediately before them in hire order within their department. The very first hire has nobody before them and reports NULL.

## Hint 2
A correlated subquery ordered `hired_on DESC` with `LIMIT 1` picks the nearest earlier row. Use a row comparison, `(t.hired_on, t.id) < (s.hired_on, s.id)`, so that two people hired on the same day are still strictly ordered - Postgres compares row constructors left to right, like a compound sort key.

## Hint 3
The other answer is `lag(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY hired_on, id)`, computed for the whole table and then filtered down to engineering **one level out** - a window function is evaluated after `WHERE`, so filtering in the same query would change which rows the window can see.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT id, name, hired_on, previous_hire_salary
FROM (SELECT s.id, s.name, s.hired_on, s.department,
             lag(s.salary) OVER (PARTITION BY s.department
                                 ORDER BY s.hired_on, s.id) AS previous_hire_salary
      FROM staff s) t
WHERE t.department = 'engineering'
ORDER BY t.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT s.id, s.name, s.hired_on,
       (SELECT t.salary FROM staff t
        WHERE t.department = s.department
          AND (t.hired_on, t.id) < (s.hired_on, s.id)
        ORDER BY t.hired_on DESC, t.id DESC
        LIMIT 1) AS previous_hire_salary
FROM staff s
WHERE s.department = 'engineering'
ORDER BY s.id;

## Exercise 5

Among customers with `id <= 10000`, counting only **non-cancelled** orders:
the customers who have placed more orders than the average customer in that
same population. Columns, in this order: `customer_id`, `orders`.

**Ordered by `orders` descending, then `customer_id` ascending.**

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The threshold is the average number of orders **per customer**, which means the per-customer counts have to exist before the average can be taken. Two levels of aggregation, one inside the other.

## Hint 2
`HAVING count(*) > (SELECT avg(n) FROM (SELECT count(*) AS n FROM orders WHERE ... GROUP BY customer_id) t)`. The inner derived table is what turns a set of groups into a set of rows that can themselves be averaged - you cannot write `avg(count(*))`.

## Hint 3
A CTE says the same thing more legibly: name the per-customer counts once, then select from it and compare against an average taken over it. Both spellings compute the aggregation twice; the CTE just makes it obvious that the two are the same computation.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The threshold is the average number of orders **per customer**, which means the per-customer counts have to exist before the average can be taken. Two levels of aggregation, one inside the other.

## Hint 2
`HAVING count(*) > (SELECT avg(n) FROM (SELECT count(*) AS n FROM orders WHERE ... GROUP BY customer_id) t)`. The inner derived table is what turns a set of groups into a set of rows that can themselves be averaged - you cannot write `avg(count(*))`.

## Hint 3
A CTE says the same thing more legibly: name the per-customer counts once, then select from it and compare against an average taken over it. Both spellings compute the aggregation twice; the CTE just makes it obvious that the two are the same computation.

references.solution.sql:
WITH per_customer AS (
    SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS orders
    FROM orders
    WHERE customer_id <= 10000 AND status <> 'cancelled'
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT pc.customer_id, pc.orders
FROM per_customer pc
WHERE pc.orders > (SELECT avg(orders) FROM per_customer)
ORDER BY pc.orders DESC, pc.customer_id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS orders
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id <= 10000 AND status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING count(*) > (SELECT avg(t.n)
                   FROM (SELECT count(*) AS n
                         FROM orders
                         WHERE customer_id <= 10000 AND status <> 'cancelled'
                         GROUP BY customer_id) t)
ORDER BY orders DESC, customer_id;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
The membership test is on a **pair** of values, not on one. A customer who ordered in both windows but with different statuses does not qualify.

## Hint 2
`IN` accepts a row constructor on the left and a two-column subquery on the right: `(o.customer_id, o.status) IN (SELECT n.customer_id, n.status FROM ...)`. The equivalent `EXISTS` spells both equality conditions out by hand, which is more typing and much harder to get half-right by accident.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, o.status
FROM orders o
WHERE o.created_at >= DATE '2023-10-01'
  AND o.created_at <  DATE '2023-11-01'
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders n
              WHERE n.customer_id = o.customer_id
                AND n.status = o.status
                AND n.created_at >= DATE '2023-11-01')
ORDER BY o.id;

SELECT o.id, o.customer_id, o.status
FROM orders o
WHERE o.created_at >= '2023-10-01'
  AND o.created_at <  '2023-11-01'
  AND (o.customer_id, o.status) IN (SELECT n.customer_id, n.status
                                    FROM orders n
                                    WHERE n.created_at >= '2023-11-01')
ORDER BY o.id;

`(SELECT count(*) FROM products c WHERE c.category = 'books' AND c.price < p.price)` in the `SELECT` list. Note that the subquery has to repeat the category restriction: the outer `WHERE` does not reach inside it.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT p.id, p.name, p.price, count(c.id) AS cheaper_books
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN products c ON c.category = 'books' AND c.price < p.price
WHERE p.category = 'books' AND p.price > 495
GROUP BY p.id, p.name, p.price
ORDER BY p.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT p.id, p.name, p.price,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM products c
        WHERE c.category = 'books' AND c.price < p.price) AS cheaper_books
FROM products p
WHERE p.category = 'books' AND p.price > 495
ORDER BY p.id;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8

The most typical person in each department: the one whose salary is nearest
to their department's average, with the lower staff `id` winning a tie.
Columns, in this order: `department`, `most_typical` (their name),
`typical_salary` (their salary), `avg_salary` (the department average rounded
to 2 decimal places).

**Ordered by `department` ascending.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 84_drills_subqueries_2 ex8`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Two things have to happen in order: work out each department's average salary, then find the person in that department whose salary is nearest to it. The second step needs the first step's answer as an input.

## Hint 2
Put the averages in a derived table or CTE - one row per department - and select from that. A correlated subquery over `staff` can then reference the average as an ordinary column while ordering by `abs(s.salary - d.avg_salary)`.

## Hint 3
"Nearest" is a sort, not a filter: order by the absolute difference and take `LIMIT 1`, with `s.id` as the tie-break so two equally typical people always resolve the same way. `DISTINCT ON (department)` with that same `ORDER BY` does the whole thing in one pass and returns the name and the salary together, instead of needing a separate subquery for each column.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Two things have to happen in order: work out each department's average salary, then find the person in that department whose salary is nearest to it. The second step needs the first step's answer as an input.

## Hint 2
Put the averages in a derived table or CTE - one row per department - and select from that. A correlated subquery over `staff` can then reference the average as an ordinary column while ordering by `abs(s.salary - d.avg_salary)`.

## Hint 3
"Nearest" is a sort, not a filter: order by the absolute difference and take `LIMIT 1`, with `s.id` as the tie-break so two equally typical people always resolve the same way. `DISTINCT ON (department)` with that same `ORDER BY` does the whole thing in one pass and returns the name and the salary together, instead of needing a separate subquery for each column.

references.solution.sql:
WITH avgs AS (
    SELECT department, avg(salary) AS avg_salary
    FROM staff
    GROUP BY department
)
SELECT DISTINCT ON (s.department)
       s.department, s.name, s.salary, round(a.avg_salary, 2) AS avg_salary
FROM staff s
JOIN avgs a ON a.department = s.department
ORDER BY s.department, abs(s.salary - a.avg_salary), s.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT d.department,
       (SELECT s.name FROM staff s
        WHERE s.department = d.department
        ORDER BY abs(s.salary - d.avg_salary), s.id
        LIMIT 1) AS most_typical,
       (SELECT s.salary FROM staff s
        WHERE s.department = d.department
        ORDER BY abs(s.salary - d.avg_salary), s.id
        LIMIT 1) AS typical_salary,
       round(d.avg_salary, 2) AS avg_salary
FROM (SELECT department, avg(salary) AS avg_salary
      FROM staff
      GROUP BY department) d
ORDER BY d.department;
