# Reading - 93_drills_windows_4

Eight drills on bucketing with `ntile`, on percentages of a partition, and on
windows computed over joined rows. Read after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

`ntile(b)` sorts the partition and cuts it into `b` groups as equal as
possible. Two properties are worth internalising. It divides by **row count**,
not by value - a decile of customers always holds a tenth of the customers,
however lopsided their order counts are, which is exactly why decile reports
are useful for comparing populations and useless for finding natural
breakpoints in a distribution. And when the row count does not divide evenly,
the remainder goes to the **earliest** buckets: twelve rows into five buckets
gives 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, not 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, and not some arbitrary spread. That
rule is what makes `ntile` reproducible and also what makes it impossible to
imitate with a naive `row_number() * b / count(*)` expression, which
distributes the remainder differently. Because the buckets are defined
positionally, the window's `ORDER BY` must be fully deterministic or the
boundaries move between runs. The other half of the set is the share-of-
partition idiom - a value divided by `sum(value) OVER (PARTITION BY ...)` -
which works identically whether the rows came from one table or from a
three-way join, because a window function sees whatever rows the `FROM` and
`WHERE` clauses produced and does not care where they came from.

## ex1 - salary quartiles inside each department

`ntile` with a partition gives every department its own four buckets, so
"quartile 1" means top quarter *of that department* and the salary ranges
differ from department to department. This is the right shape for a fairness
review and the wrong shape for "who are the best paid people in the company",
which needs an unpartitioned window. The classic mistake is omitting the `id`
tie-break: two colleagues on identical salaries would then be assigned to
buckets in whatever order the sort produced.

## ex2 - what each company-wide quartile looks like

Grouping by a bucket requires computing the bucket first, in a CTE or derived
table, for the same reason ranking requires it - the window has not run when
`GROUP BY` does. With 500 staff and 4 buckets the split is exactly 125 each,
which makes this the one exercise in the set where the remainder rule does not
show itself. Reading `min_salary` and `max_salary` down the four rows shows
the shape of the pay distribution far better than a single average does.

## ex3 - each line's share of its order

A window over joined rows, which is the whole point: `PARTITION BY
oi.order_id` groups the rows the join produced, and the join to `products`
adds a column without disturbing them. Because an order can contain the same
product twice, the ordering has to use the order item's own `id` to be
deterministic. The percentages inside an order sum to 100, and the reference's
join to a derived per-order aggregate shows what the window is saving you: a
second pass over `order_items`.

## ex4 - twelve countries into five buckets

The `countries` column reads 3, 3, 2, 2, 2 - the remainder of 12 divided by 5
lands in the first two buckets. Knowing this is not trivia: it means the top
bucket of an `ntile` is never smaller than the bottom one, so "top decile"
comparisons are always at least fair to the bottom. It also means `ntile` on a
small result set is a blunt instrument; with twelve rows, bucket boundaries
say very little about the data and a great deal about the arithmetic.

## ex5 - category mix within each price band

Grouping by two keys and partitioning by one of them, with the twist that the
key is an expression - so `floor(price / 100) * 100` has to be written
identically in `GROUP BY` and in `PARTITION BY`, or the two will not match and
the shares will be wrong in ways that are hard to see. This is the strongest
argument for the reference's spelling, which names the band in a CTE and
computes the band totals by grouping that. The `100.0` guards against integer
division, as always.

## ex6 - customer deciles by order count

The standard customer-value report: equal-sized slices of the population,
described by the metric that ordered them plus whatever else is interesting.
Note that `min_orders` and `max_orders` come out very close together across
neighbouring deciles, because order counts per customer cluster tightly around
eleven - which is itself the finding. The revenue column is deliberately not
what the deciles were built on, so it shows how well "orders placed" predicts
"money spent".

## ex7 - the two biggest countries of every month

Three ideas at once: aggregate over a join, a share-of-partition window, and a
top-N-per-partition filter needing its own query level. The `sum(revenue)
OVER (PARTITION BY month)` is computed before the `rn <= 2` filter, which is
essential - if you filtered first, the percentages would be shares of the two
surviving rows and would sum to 100 rather than to the roughly 30% they
actually represent. The reference computes the month totals in a separate CTE
and joins, which makes that ordering explicit.

## ex8 - how much revenue lives in the top quartile

A concentration report, and a good place to notice what is *not* in it: the
300 products that have never been ordered have no row in `order_items`, so
they are absent from the CTE and are never assigned a quartile. If the
question were "of all products", the CTE would need a `LEFT JOIN` from
`products` and a `coalesce(sum(...), 0)`. The top quartile turns out to hold
well under half the revenue, because prices and quantities here are uniform
random rather than the power law that real catalogues follow - on real data
this same query is how you discover the 80/20.

## Further reading

- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) - `ntile`, `percent_rank`, `cume_dist` and the rest of the built-in window functions.
- [Window Function Processing](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-WINDOW) - when windows run relative to `GROUP BY` and `WHERE`.
- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - the aggregates that double as window functions.
- [Mathematical Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-math.html) - `floor`, `round` and the integer-division rules behind the `100.0` in the share columns.

# Reading - 93_drills_windows_4

Eight drills on bucketing with `ntile`, on percentages of a partition, and on
windows computed over joined rows. Read after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

`ntile(b)` sorts the partition and cuts it into `b` groups as equal as
possible. Two properties are worth internalising. It divides by **row count**,
not by value - a decile of customers always holds a tenth of the customers,
however lopsided their order counts are, which is exactly why decile reports
are useful for comparing populations and useless for finding natural
breakpoints in a distribution. And when the row count does not divide evenly,
the remainder goes to the **earliest** buckets: twelve rows into five buckets
gives 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, not 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, and not some arbitrary spread. That
rule is what makes `ntile` reproducible and also what makes it impossible to
imitate with a naive `row_number() * b / count(*)` expression, which
distributes the remainder differently. Because the buckets are defined
positionally, the window's `ORDER BY` must be fully deterministic or the
boundaries move between runs. The other half of the set is the share-of-
partition idiom - a value divided by `sum(value) OVER (PARTITION BY ...)` -
which works identically whether the rows came from one table or from a
three-way join, because a window function sees whatever rows the `FROM` and
`WHERE` clauses produced and does not care where they came from.

## ex1 - salary quartiles inside each department

`ntile` with a partition gives every department its own four buckets, so
"quartile 1" means top quarter *of that department* and the salary ranges
differ from department to department. This is the right shape for a fairness
review and the wrong shape for "who are the best paid people in the company",
which needs an unpartitioned window. The classic mistake is omitting the `id`
tie-break: two colleagues on identical salaries would then be assigned to
buckets in whatever order the sort produced.

## ex2 - what each company-wide quartile looks like

Grouping by a bucket requires computing the bucket first, in a CTE or derived
table, for the same reason ranking requires it - the window has not run when
`GROUP BY` does. With 500 staff and 4 buckets the split is exactly 125 each,
which makes this the one exercise in the set where the remainder rule does not
show itself. Reading `min_salary` and `max_salary` down the four rows shows
the shape of the pay distribution far better than a single average does.

## ex3 - each line's share of its order

A window over joined rows, which is the whole point: `PARTITION BY
oi.order_id` groups the rows the join produced, and the join to `products`
adds a column without disturbing them. Because an order can contain the same
product twice, the ordering has to use the order item's own `id` to be
deterministic. The percentages inside an order sum to 100, and the reference's
join to a derived per-order aggregate shows what the window is saving you: a
second pass over `order_items`.

## ex4 - twelve countries into five buckets

The `countries` column reads 3, 3, 2, 2, 2 - the remainder of 12 divided by 5
lands in the first two buckets. Knowing this is not trivia: it means the top
bucket of an `ntile` is never smaller than the bottom one, so "top decile"
comparisons are always at least fair to the bottom. It also means `ntile` on a
small result set is a blunt instrument; with twelve rows, bucket boundaries
say very little about the data and a great deal about the arithmetic.

## ex5 - category mix within each price band

Grouping by two keys and partitioning by one of them, with the twist that the
key is an expression - so `floor(price / 100) * 100` has to be written
identically in `GROUP BY` and in `PARTITION BY`, or the two will not match and
the shares will be wrong in ways that are hard to see. This is the strongest
argument for the reference's spelling, which names the band in a CTE and
computes the band totals by grouping that. The `100.0` guards against integer
division, as always.

## ex6 - customer deciles by order count

The standard customer-value report: equal-sized slices of the population,
described by the metric that ordered them plus whatever else is interesting.
Note that `min_orders` and `max_orders` come out very close together across
neighbouring deciles, because order counts per customer cluster tightly around
eleven - which is itself the finding. The revenue column is deliberately not
what the deciles were built on, so it shows how well "orders placed" predicts
"money spent".

## ex7 - the two biggest countries of every month

Three ideas at once: aggregate over a join, a share-of-partition window, and a
top-N-per-partition filter needing its own query level. The `sum(revenue)
OVER (PARTITION BY month)` is computed before the `rn <= 2` filter, which is
essential - if you filtered first, the percentages would be shares of the two
surviving rows and would sum to 100 rather than to the roughly 30% they
actually represent. The reference computes the month totals in a separate CTE
and joins, which makes that ordering explicit.

## ex8 - how much revenue lives in the top quartile

A concentration report, and a good place to notice what is *not* in it: the
300 products that have never been ordered have no row in `order_items`, so
they are absent from the CTE and are never assigned a quartile. If the
question were "of all products", the CTE would need a `LEFT JOIN` from
`products` and a `coalesce(sum(...), 0)`. The top quartile turns out to hold
well under half the revenue, because prices and quantities here are uniform
random rather than the power law that real catalogues follow - on real data
this same query is how you discover the 80/20.

## Further reading

- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) - `ntile`, `percent_rank`, `cume_dist` and the rest of the built-in window functions.
- [Window Function Processing](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-WINDOW) - when windows run relative to `GROUP BY` and `WHERE`.
- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - the aggregates that double as window functions.
- [Mathematical Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-math.html) - `floor`, `round` and the integer-division rules behind the `100.0` in the share columns.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT id, name, department, salary, quartile
FROM (SELECT id, name, department, salary, ntile(4) OVER w AS quartile
      FROM staff
      WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC, id)) t
ORDER BY department, quartile, id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, name, department, salary,
       ntile(4) OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS quartile
FROM staff
ORDER BY department, quartile, id;

SELECT quartile,
       count(*) AS staff,
       round(min(salary), 2) AS min_salary,
       round(max(salary), 2) AS max_salary

      FROM staff) t

## Exercise 3 - each line's share of its order

Every order item belonging to orders 1 to 300, joined to `products` for the
name, and shown next to its order's total. Columns, in this order: `id` (the
order item's), `order_id`, `name`, `line_total` = `round(quantity * price, 2)`,
`order_total` = the same sum over the whole order rounded to 2, and
`pct_of_order` = `round(100 * <line> / <order total>, 2)`.

The window partitions by `order_id` and runs over the joined rows.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The join to `products` only adds a name. The window works on the rows the join produced, exactly as it would on a single table.

## Hint 2

`sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) OVER (PARTITION BY oi.order_id)` gives the order's total on every one of its lines, and dividing the line by it gives the share.

## Hint 3

An order can hold the same product twice, so order the output by `oi.order_id, oi.id` - `product_id` is not a unique key within an order.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT oi.id, oi.order_id, p.name,
       round(oi.quantity * oi.price, 2) AS line_total,
       round(t.order_total, 2) AS order_total,
       round(100 * (oi.quantity * oi.price) / t.order_total, 2) AS pct_of_order
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
JOIN (SELECT order_id, sum(quantity * price) AS order_total
      FROM order_items
      WHERE order_id <= 300
      GROUP BY order_id) t ON t.order_id = oi.order_id
WHERE oi.order_id <= 300
ORDER BY oi.order_id, oi.id;

       round(oi.quantity * oi.price, 2) AS line_total,
       round(sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) OVER (PARTITION BY oi.order_id), 2)
         AS order_total,
       round(100 * (oi.quantity * oi.price)

## Hint 1

Two levels: count customers per country, bucket the twelve resulting rows, then describe the buckets.

`ntile(5) OVER (ORDER BY customers DESC, country)` over the per-country CTE. When you see the `countries` column, notice which buckets got the two spare rows - `ntile` always front-loads the remainder.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT bucket,
       count(*) AS countries,
       min(customers) AS min_customers,
       max(customers) AS max_customers
FROM (SELECT country, customers,
             ntile(5) OVER (ORDER BY customers DESC, country) AS bucket
      FROM (SELECT country, count(*) AS customers
            FROM customers
            GROUP BY country) c) b
GROUP BY bucket
ORDER BY bucket;
references.expected.sql:
WITH per_country AS (
    SELECT country, count(*) AS customers
    FROM customers
    GROUP BY country
), bucketed AS (
    SELECT country, customers,
           ntile(5) OVER (ORDER BY customers DESC, country) AS bucket
    FROM per_country
)
SELECT bucket,
       count(*) AS countries,
       min(customers) AS min_customers,
       max(customers) AS max_customers
FROM bucketed
GROUP BY bucket
ORDER BY bucket;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Group by band and category; partition by band alone. The band expression therefore appears twice.

## Hint 2

`GROUP BY floor(price / 100) * 100, category` and then `sum(count(*)) OVER (PARTITION BY floor(price / 100) * 100)`. The two expressions must be written identically or PostgreSQL will treat them as different keys.

references.solution.sql:
WITH per_pair AS (
    SELECT floor(price / 100) * 100 AS band, category, count(*) AS products
    FROM products
    GROUP BY 1, 2
), per_band AS (
    SELECT band, sum(products) AS products
    FROM per_pair
    GROUP BY band
)
SELECT p.band, p.category, p.products,
       round(100.0 * p.products / b.products, 2) AS pct_of_band
FROM per_pair p
JOIN per_band b ON b.band = p.band
ORDER BY p.band, p.category;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT floor(price / 100) * 100 AS band,
       category,
       count(*) AS products,
       round(100.0 * count(*)
             / sum(count(*)) OVER (PARTITION BY floor(price / 100) * 100), 2)
         AS pct_of_band
FROM products
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY band, category;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Aggregate revenue by month and country first. Everything after that is two windows over the same twelve-ish rows per month.

## Hint 2

`sum(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY month)` for the denominator and `row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY month ORDER BY revenue DESC, country)` to pick the top two - both in the same CTE, filtered one level up.

## Hint 3

The share must be computed before the `rn <= 2` filter. Filtering first would make the two percentages add up to 100 instead of to the roughly third of the month they really are.

references.solution.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('month', o.created_at) AS month,
           c.country,
           sum(o.total) AS revenue
    FROM orders o
    JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
    GROUP BY 1, 2
), per_month AS (
    SELECT month, sum(revenue) AS month_revenue
    FROM monthly
    GROUP BY month
), ranked AS (
    SELECT m.month, m.country, m.revenue, p.month_revenue,
           rank() OVER (PARTITION BY m.month
                        ORDER BY m.revenue DESC, m.country) AS rn
    FROM monthly m
    JOIN per_month p ON p.month = m.month
)
SELECT month, country,
       round(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       round(100 * revenue / month_revenue, 2) AS pct_of_month,
       rn
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 2
ORDER BY month, rn;
references.expected.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('month', o.created_at) AS month,
           c.country,
           sum(o.total) AS revenue
    FROM orders o
    JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
    GROUP BY 1, 2
), ranked AS (
    SELECT month, country, revenue,
           sum(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY month) AS month_revenue,
           row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY month
                              ORDER BY revenue DESC, country) AS rn
    FROM monthly
)
SELECT month, country,
       round(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       round(100 * revenue / month_revenue, 2) AS pct_of_month,
       rn
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 2
ORDER BY month, rn;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 - how much revenue lives in the top quartile

Total each product's revenue as `sum(quantity * price)` over `order_items`,
split the products into four quartiles by revenue (highest first,
`product_id` ascending as the tie-break), and report each quartile. Columns,
in this order: `quartile`, `products`, `revenue` rounded to 2, `pct_of_total`
= `round(100 * <quartile revenue> / <all revenue>, 2)`.

Products that were never ordered do not appear in `order_items` and so are
not bucketed at all.

**Ordered by `quartile` ascending.**

## Hint 1

Revenue per product first, from `order_items` alone - no join to `products` is needed for any of the output columns.

## Hint 2

`ntile(4) OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC, product_id)` in a second CTE, then group by the quartile and use `sum(sum(revenue)) OVER ()` for the grand total.

## Hint 3

Products never ordered have no `order_items` rows, so they never enter the CTE and are not bucketed. That is what the prompt intends - do not add a `LEFT JOIN` from `products`.

references.solution.sql:
WITH product_revenue AS (
    SELECT product_id, sum(quantity * price) AS revenue
    FROM order_items
    GROUP BY product_id
), quartiles AS (
    SELECT product_id, revenue,
           ntile(4) OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC, product_id) AS quartile
    FROM product_revenue
), per_quartile AS (
    SELECT quartile, count(*) AS products, sum(revenue) AS revenue
    FROM quartiles
    GROUP BY quartile
), total AS (
    SELECT sum(revenue) AS revenue FROM per_quartile
)
SELECT q.quartile, q.products,
       round(q.revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       round(100 * q.revenue / t.revenue, 2) AS pct_of_total
FROM per_quartile q
CROSS JOIN total t
ORDER BY q.quartile;

WITH product_revenue AS (
    SELECT product_id, sum(quantity * price) AS revenue
    FROM order_items
    GROUP BY product_id

# 94 - Drills: window frames

Eight problems from lesson 16 on the third part of an `OVER` clause: the
frame. `PARTITION BY` says which rows are in play and `ORDER BY` puts them in
a line; the frame says how far along that line the aggregate may look from
each row. Get it explicit and moving averages, trailing sums and
"still-to-come" totals all fall out of the same syntax.

## Exercise 1 - a centred three-month average

Monthly revenue smoothed by averaging each month with its immediate
neighbours. Columns, in this order: `month` = `date_trunc('month',
created_at)`, `revenue` = `sum(total)` rounded to 2, `ma3` =
`round(avg(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1
FOLLOWING), 2)`.

The first and last months average over two values, not three.

**Ordered by `month` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 94_drills_frames_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - a trailing three-month sum

Monthly order counts with a rolling total of this month and the two before.
Columns, in this order: `month`, `orders`, `trailing3` = `sum(orders) OVER
(ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`.

**Ordered by `month` ascending.**

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 94_drills_frames_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - the default frame, written out

Monthly revenue with a running total and a high-water mark, both using an
explicit `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`. Columns, in this
order: `month`, `revenue` rounded to 2, `running_revenue` rounded to 2,
`best_so_far` = the largest single month's revenue up to and including this
one, rounded to 2.

The reference omits the frame entirely and gets the same answer - the reading
explains exactly when that is safe.

**Ordered by `month` ascending.**

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 94_drills_frames_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - looking forward instead of back

Monthly revenue with the revenue that is still ahead. Columns, in this order:
`month`, `revenue` rounded to 2, `revenue_from_here` = `sum(revenue)` over
`ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING` rounded to 2, and
`months_from_here` = `count(*)` over the same frame.

The first row's `revenue_from_here` is the whole year; the last row's is its
own revenue.

**Ordered by `month` ascending.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 94_drills_frames_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - a moving average inside each partition

Weekly revenue per order status, each with a four-week trailing average of its
own status. Columns, in this order: `week` = `date_trunc('week', created_at)`,
`status`, `revenue` rounded to 2, `ma4` = `round(avg(revenue) OVER (PARTITION
BY status ORDER BY week ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2)`.

**Ordered by `status` ascending, then `week` ascending.**

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 94_drills_frames_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - ROWS against RANGE

Every review of product 77, with two cumulative sums of `rating` that differ
only in their frame mode. Columns, in this order: `id`, `rating`, `sum_rows` =
`sum(rating) OVER (ORDER BY rating, id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND
CURRENT ROW)`, `sum_range` = `sum(rating) OVER (ORDER BY rating RANGE BETWEEN
UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`.

Write both exactly as given. Rows sharing a rating get distinct `sum_rows` and
an identical `sum_range`.

**Ordered by `rating` ascending, then `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 94_drills_frames_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - days that beat their own trend

Take the orders created on or after 2023-09-16, total them by day, attach a
seven-day trailing average (`ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`), and
return only the days whose own revenue exceeded that average. Columns, in this
order: `day` = `date_trunc('day', created_at)`, `revenue` rounded to 2, `ma7`
rounded to 2.

Compare the raw values; round only in the output.

**Ordered by `day` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 94_drills_frames_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - a moving-average crossover

Weekly revenue with a short and a long trailing average and the signal they
generate. Columns, in this order: `week`, `revenue` rounded to 2, `ma4` = the
four-week trailing average rounded to 2, `ma12` = the twelve-week trailing
average rounded to 2, and `signal` = the text `'above'` when the raw `ma4`
exceeds the raw `ma12`, otherwise `'below'`.

Compare the unrounded averages.

**Ordered by `week` ascending.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 94_drills_frames_1 ex8`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 94_drills_frames_1

Eight drills on window frames and the moving statistics they produce. Read
after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

A frame is the third and least-used part of an `OVER` clause, and it is where
moving averages live. The syntax is `ROWS|RANGE|GROUPS BETWEEN <start> AND
<end>`, with the bounds drawn from `UNBOUNDED PRECEDING`, `n PRECEDING`,
`CURRENT ROW`, `n FOLLOWING` and `UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`. `ROWS` counts
positions: `2 PRECEDING` means two rows back, whatever their values. `RANGE`
counts values: with an ordered numeric or date column, `INTERVAL '6 days'
PRECEDING` means every row whose ordering value is within six days, however
many rows that is - and with no offset, `RANGE` treats all rows sharing an
ordering value as one indivisible peer group. That peer-group behaviour is the
default frame when a window has an `ORDER BY`, which is why exercise 6 exists
and why a running total over a non-unique ordering surprises people. Two
practical habits follow. Say `ROWS` explicitly whenever you mean "the previous
n rows", because the default is `RANGE` and it is not the same thing. And
remember that a `ROWS n PRECEDING` frame silently means "the previous n
**rows**", not "the previous n **days**" - on a series with a missing day, a
seven-row average quietly reaches eight days back. Where gaps are possible,
generate the calendar first (set 89) or use a `RANGE` frame with an interval
offset.

## ex1 - a centred three-month average

A frame with a `FOLLOWING` bound is the same machinery pointed both ways, and
it produces a smoother that does not lag behind the signal - which is the
right choice for looking at history and the wrong one for anything that has to
run in real time, because the future half of the frame does not exist yet. The
edges are the detail worth noticing: the first and last rows have no
neighbour on one side, so they average two values, and their `ma3` is
therefore noisier than the middle of the series. No `NULL`s appear, because
the frame is simply smaller.

## ex2 - a trailing three-month sum

`ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` is the shape of every "last N
periods" metric there is, and the count is inclusive of the current row - `2
PRECEDING` plus `CURRENT ROW` is three rows, not four. The classic
off-by-one is asking for a three-month total and writing `3 PRECEDING`. The
first two rows again sum over fewer rows rather than returning `NULL`; if you
need them blanked out, that is a `CASE` on the row number, not a frame.

## ex3 - the default frame, written out

The explicit frame and the reference's bare `OVER (ORDER BY month)` give
identical results here because `month` is unique - each row is its own peer
group, so `RANGE` and `ROWS` agree. Writing it out anyway is the safer habit,
because the day the ordering stops being unique the bare version changes
meaning silently. Note also that `max()` over a growing frame is a high-water
mark, which is a running maximum and not the same as the partition maximum you
would get with no `ORDER BY` at all.

## ex4 - looking forward instead of back

`CURRENT ROW AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING` is a reverse running total, useful for
burn-down and backlog reports: at every point it says how much is left. The
reference computes the same column as "the grand total minus everything
strictly before this row", which needs a `coalesce` because the frame
`UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING` is empty for the first row and `sum`
over an empty frame is `NULL`. That `NULL` is worth remembering - it is the
same reason a `lag()` on the first row is `NULL`.

## ex5 - a moving average inside each partition

Partition, order and frame together, which is the full `OVER` clause. Each
status gets its own 53-week series and its own moving average, and the frames
never cross a partition boundary - the first three weeks of each status
average over fewer rows, independently. The reference's correlated subquery
has to repeat the `n.status = w.status` correlation to reproduce that, which
is exactly the partition, spelled by hand.

## ex6 - ROWS against RANGE

Ninety-odd reviews across five ratings. `sum_rows` climbs one review at a
time; `sum_range` jumps in five steps, because every review sharing a rating is
a peer of every other and `RANGE` includes the current row's entire peer
group. Neither is a bug. `sum_range` is the answer to "the total for all
ratings at or below mine" and `sum_rows` is the answer to "the total up to my
position in this ordering" - and if your `ORDER BY` is unique you never have
to choose, which is why the distinction stays hidden for years and then
produces one very confusing report.

## ex7 - days that beat their own trend

A moving average used as a baseline rather than as output: compute it, compare
each day against it, keep the winners. The filter has to live one level up
because a window result cannot appear in `WHERE`, and the comparison uses the
raw average rather than the rounded one so that a day a hundredth above the
line is not thrown away by presentation. This query is the skeleton of every
anomaly-detection dashboard; swapping the seven-row frame for a longer one, or
comparing against a multiple of the average, is the whole of the tuning.

## ex8 - a moving-average crossover

Two frames of different lengths over the same series, with a `CASE` reading
the pair. The short average reacts quickly and the long one slowly, so
`signal` flips when the recent trend crosses the established one - the
classic technical-analysis indicator, here applied to weekly revenue. Two
things to note. Both averages are trailing, so this could be computed live.
And the first eleven weeks are not really comparable, because `ma12` is
averaging fewer than twelve weeks and is therefore closer to `ma4` than it
would otherwise be - a warm-up period every rolling indicator has and most
dashboards forget to hide.

## Further reading

- [Window Function Calls](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html#SYNTAX-WINDOW-FUNCTIONS) - the complete frame grammar, `ROWS` against `RANGE` against `GROUPS`, and `EXCLUDE`.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) - the introduction and the default frame.
- [Window Function Processing](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-WINDOW) - peer groups and why the default frame includes them.
- [Date/Time Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) - interval arithmetic, needed for `RANGE` frames measured in days or weeks.

# Reading - 94_drills_frames_1

Eight drills on window frames and the moving statistics they produce. Read
after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

A frame is the third and least-used part of an `OVER` clause, and it is where
moving averages live. The syntax is `ROWS|RANGE|GROUPS BETWEEN <start> AND
<end>`, with the bounds drawn from `UNBOUNDED PRECEDING`, `n PRECEDING`,
`CURRENT ROW`, `n FOLLOWING` and `UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING`. `ROWS` counts
positions: `2 PRECEDING` means two rows back, whatever their values. `RANGE`
counts values: with an ordered numeric or date column, `INTERVAL '6 days'
PRECEDING` means every row whose ordering value is within six days, however
many rows that is - and with no offset, `RANGE` treats all rows sharing an
ordering value as one indivisible peer group. That peer-group behaviour is the
default frame when a window has an `ORDER BY`, which is why exercise 6 exists
and why a running total over a non-unique ordering surprises people. Two
practical habits follow. Say `ROWS` explicitly whenever you mean "the previous
n rows", because the default is `RANGE` and it is not the same thing. And
remember that a `ROWS n PRECEDING` frame silently means "the previous n
**rows**", not "the previous n **days**" - on a series with a missing day, a
seven-row average quietly reaches eight days back. Where gaps are possible,
generate the calendar first (set 89) or use a `RANGE` frame with an interval
offset.

## ex1 - a centred three-month average

A frame with a `FOLLOWING` bound is the same machinery pointed both ways, and
it produces a smoother that does not lag behind the signal - which is the
right choice for looking at history and the wrong one for anything that has to
run in real time, because the future half of the frame does not exist yet. The
edges are the detail worth noticing: the first and last rows have no
neighbour on one side, so they average two values, and their `ma3` is
therefore noisier than the middle of the series. No `NULL`s appear, because
the frame is simply smaller.

## ex2 - a trailing three-month sum

`ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` is the shape of every "last N
periods" metric there is, and the count is inclusive of the current row - `2
PRECEDING` plus `CURRENT ROW` is three rows, not four. The classic
off-by-one is asking for a three-month total and writing `3 PRECEDING`. The
first two rows again sum over fewer rows rather than returning `NULL`; if you
need them blanked out, that is a `CASE` on the row number, not a frame.

## ex3 - the default frame, written out

The explicit frame and the reference's bare `OVER (ORDER BY month)` give
identical results here because `month` is unique - each row is its own peer
group, so `RANGE` and `ROWS` agree. Writing it out anyway is the safer habit,
because the day the ordering stops being unique the bare version changes
meaning silently. Note also that `max()` over a growing frame is a high-water
mark, which is a running maximum and not the same as the partition maximum you
would get with no `ORDER BY` at all.

## ex4 - looking forward instead of back

`CURRENT ROW AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING` is a reverse running total, useful for
burn-down and backlog reports: at every point it says how much is left. The
reference computes the same column as "the grand total minus everything
strictly before this row", which needs a `coalesce` because the frame
`UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING` is empty for the first row and `sum`
over an empty frame is `NULL`. That `NULL` is worth remembering - it is the
same reason a `lag()` on the first row is `NULL`.

## ex5 - a moving average inside each partition

Partition, order and frame together, which is the full `OVER` clause. Each
status gets its own 53-week series and its own moving average, and the frames
never cross a partition boundary - the first three weeks of each status
average over fewer rows, independently. The reference's correlated subquery
has to repeat the `n.status = w.status` correlation to reproduce that, which
is exactly the partition, spelled by hand.

## ex6 - ROWS against RANGE

Ninety-odd reviews across five ratings. `sum_rows` climbs one review at a
time; `sum_range` jumps in five steps, because every review sharing a rating is
a peer of every other and `RANGE` includes the current row's entire peer
group. Neither is a bug. `sum_range` is the answer to "the total for all
ratings at or below mine" and `sum_rows` is the answer to "the total up to my
position in this ordering" - and if your `ORDER BY` is unique you never have
to choose, which is why the distinction stays hidden for years and then
produces one very confusing report.

## ex7 - days that beat their own trend

A moving average used as a baseline rather than as output: compute it, compare
each day against it, keep the winners. The filter has to live one level up
because a window result cannot appear in `WHERE`, and the comparison uses the
raw average rather than the rounded one so that a day a hundredth above the
line is not thrown away by presentation. This query is the skeleton of every
anomaly-detection dashboard; swapping the seven-row frame for a longer one, or
comparing against a multiple of the average, is the whole of the tuning.

## ex8 - a moving-average crossover

Two frames of different lengths over the same series, with a `CASE` reading
the pair. The short average reacts quickly and the long one slowly, so
`signal` flips when the recent trend crosses the established one - the
classic technical-analysis indicator, here applied to weekly revenue. Two
things to note. Both averages are trailing, so this could be computed live.
And the first eleven weeks are not really comparable, because `ma12` is
averaging fewer than twelve weeks and is therefore closer to `ma4` than it
would otherwise be - a warm-up period every rolling indicator has and most
dashboards forget to hide.

## Further reading

- [Window Function Calls](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html#SYNTAX-WINDOW-FUNCTIONS) - the complete frame grammar, `ROWS` against `RANGE` against `GROUPS`, and `EXCLUDE`.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) - the introduction and the default frame.
- [Window Function Processing](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-WINDOW) - peer groups and why the default frame includes them.
- [Date/Time Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) - interval arithmetic, needed for `RANGE` frames measured in days or weeks.

## Exercise 1 - a centred three-month average

Monthly revenue smoothed by averaging each month with its immediate
neighbours. Columns, in this order: `month` = `date_trunc('month',
created_at)`, `revenue` = `sum(total)` rounded to 2, `ma3` =
`round(avg(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1
FOLLOWING), 2)`.

The first and last months average over two values, not three.

**Ordered by `month` ascending.**

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The window has to look one row back and one row forward from wherever it is standing.

## Hint 2

`avg(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING)`. Nothing special is needed at the edges - the frame simply contains fewer rows there.

references.solution.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month, sum(total) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT m.month,
       round(m.revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       round((SELECT avg(n.revenue) FROM monthly n
              WHERE n.month BETWEEN m.month - INTERVAL '1 month'
                                AND m.month + INTERVAL '1 month'), 2) AS ma3
FROM monthly m
ORDER BY m.month;
references.expected.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month, sum(total) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month,
       round(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       round(avg(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month
                                ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING), 2)
         AS ma3
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

"This month and the two before" is three rows, and the frame bound counts only the ones before.

## Hint 2

`sum(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)` - `2 PRECEDING` plus the current row makes three.

references.solution.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month, count(*) AS orders
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT m.month, m.orders,
       (SELECT sum(n.orders) FROM monthly n
        WHERE n.month BETWEEN m.month - INTERVAL '2 months'
                          AND m.month) AS trailing3
FROM monthly m
ORDER BY m.month;
references.expected.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month, count(*) AS orders
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT month, orders,
       sum(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month
                         ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS trailing3
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 - the default frame, written out

Monthly revenue with a running total and a high-water mark, both using an
explicit `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW`. Columns, in this
order: `month`, `revenue` rounded to 2, `running_revenue` rounded to 2,
`best_so_far` = the largest single month's revenue up to and including this
one, rounded to 2.

The reference omits the frame entirely and gets the same answer - the reading
explains exactly when that is safe.

**Ordered by `month` ascending.**

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 94_drills_frames_1 ex3`

references.solution.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month, sum(total) AS revenue
    FROM orders

)

       round(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       round(sum(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 2) AS running_revenue,
       round(max(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 2) AS best_so_far
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

All three parts of an `OVER` clause at once: which rows belong together, in what order, and how far back to look.

## Hint 2

`avg(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY status ORDER BY week ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`. Frames never reach across a partition boundary, so each status warms up independently.

references.solution.sql:
WITH weekly AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('week', created_at) AS week, status, sum(total) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY 1, 2
)
SELECT w.week, w.status,
       round(w.revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       round((SELECT avg(n.revenue) FROM weekly n
              WHERE n.status = w.status
                AND n.week BETWEEN w.week - INTERVAL '3 weeks'
                               AND w.week), 2) AS ma4
FROM weekly w
ORDER BY w.status, w.week;
references.expected.sql:
WITH weekly AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('week', created_at) AS week, status, sum(total) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY 1, 2
)
SELECT week, status,
       round(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       round(avg(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY status ORDER BY week
                                ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2)
         AS ma4
FROM weekly
ORDER BY status, week;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 - ROWS against RANGE

Every review of product 77, with two cumulative sums of `rating` that differ
only in their frame mode. Columns, in this order: `id`, `rating`, `sum_rows` =
`sum(rating) OVER (ORDER BY rating, id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND
CURRENT ROW)`, `sum_range` = `sum(rating) OVER (ORDER BY rating RANGE BETWEEN
UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`.

Write both exactly as given. Rows sharing a rating get distinct `sum_rows` and
an identical `sum_range`.

**Ordered by `rating` ascending, then `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 94_drills_frames_1 ex6`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write both columns exactly as given and read the output before trying to explain it. The two frames differ by one keyword.

## Hint 2

`ROWS` counts positions, so with a unique ordering each row's frame ends exactly at that row. `RANGE` counts ordering *values*, so every review with the same rating is a peer and they all see the same frame.

## Hint 3

The `ROWS` window orders by `rating, id` deliberately - a `ROWS` frame over a non-unique ordering would depend on the physical order of tied rows, which PostgreSQL does not promise.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write both columns exactly as given and read the output before trying to explain it. The two frames differ by one keyword.

## Hint 2

`ROWS` counts positions, so with a unique ordering each row's frame ends exactly at that row. `RANGE` counts ordering *values*, so every review with the same rating is a peer and they all see the same frame.

## Hint 3

The `ROWS` window orders by `rating, id` deliberately - a `ROWS` frame over a non-unique ordering would depend on the physical order of tied rows, which PostgreSQL does not promise.

references.solution.sql:
WITH mine AS (
    SELECT id, rating FROM reviews WHERE product_id = 77
)
SELECT m.id, m.rating,
       (SELECT sum(t.rating) FROM mine t
        WHERE (t.rating, t.id) <= (m.rating, m.id)) AS sum_rows,
       (SELECT sum(t.rating) FROM mine t
        WHERE t.rating <= m.rating) AS sum_range
FROM mine m
ORDER BY m.rating, m.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, rating,
       sum(rating) OVER (ORDER BY rating, id
                         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING
                                  AND CURRENT ROW) AS sum_rows,
       sum(rating) OVER (ORDER BY rating
                         RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING
                                   AND CURRENT ROW) AS sum_range
FROM reviews
WHERE product_id = 77
ORDER BY rating, id;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three steps: daily totals, a trailing average attached to each day, then keep only the days that beat their own average.

## Hint 2

`avg(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)` in a CTE - six preceding rows plus the current one is seven days.

references.solution.sql:
WITH daily AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at) AS day, sum(total) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE created_at >= '2023-09-16'
    GROUP BY 1
), smoothed AS (
    SELECT d.day, d.revenue,
           (SELECT avg(n.revenue) FROM daily n
            WHERE n.day BETWEEN d.day - INTERVAL '6 days' AND d.day) AS ma7
    FROM daily d
)
SELECT day, round(revenue, 2) AS revenue, round(ma7, 2) AS ma7
FROM smoothed
WHERE revenue > ma7
ORDER BY day;

           avg(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day
                              ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS ma7
    FROM daily
)

FROM smoothed
WHERE revenue > ma7
ORDER BY day;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two trailing averages over the same weekly series, differing only in how far back their frames reach.

## Hint 2

`ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` gives four weeks; `ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` gives twelve. Compute both in one CTE.

## Hint 3

The `CASE` compares the unrounded `ma4` and `ma12` from that CTE - comparing the rounded columns would flip the signal on weeks where the two are within a hundredth of each other.

references.solution.sql:
WITH weekly AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('week', created_at) AS week, sum(total) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY 1
), averages AS (
    SELECT w.week, w.revenue,
           (SELECT avg(n.revenue) FROM weekly n
            WHERE n.week BETWEEN w.week - INTERVAL '3 weeks' AND w.week) AS ma4,
           (SELECT avg(n.revenue) FROM weekly n
            WHERE n.week BETWEEN w.week - INTERVAL '11 weeks' AND w.week) AS ma12
    FROM weekly w
)
SELECT week,
       round(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       round(ma4, 2) AS ma4,
       round(ma12, 2) AS ma12,
       CASE WHEN ma4 > ma12 THEN 'above' ELSE 'below' END AS signal
FROM averages
ORDER BY week;
references.expected.sql:
WITH weekly AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('week', created_at) AS week, sum(total) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY 1
), averages AS (
    SELECT week, revenue,
           avg(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY week
                              ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS ma4,
           avg(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY week
                              ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS ma12
    FROM weekly
)
SELECT week,
       round(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
       round(ma4, 2) AS ma4,
       round(ma12, 2) AS ma12,
       CASE WHEN ma4 > ma12 THEN 'above' ELSE 'below' END AS signal
FROM averages
ORDER BY week;

# 95 - Drills: LAG and LEAD, set 1

Eight problems on looking sideways: `lag()` and `lead()` from lesson 16 -
previous row, next row, offsets, and the deltas and gaps built from them.
Every problem here is "this row compared to a neighbouring row"; if the NULL
at the edge of a series or the ORDER BY inside `OVER` still feels wobbly,
reread 16 before starting.

## Exercise 1 - yesterday's number beside today's

Paid orders per day for September 2023 (half-open range, as always). For
each day return `day` = `date_trunc('day', created_at)`, `orders` = how many
paid orders that day, and `prev_day` = the previous day's count via LAG
(NULL on September 1st).

**Ordered by `day` ascending.** (30 rows.)

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 95_drills_lag_lead_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - the next hire

For the engineering department, list every staff member with the date the
department's **next** hire arrived. Return `id`, `name`, `hired_on`, and
`next_hire` = the `hired_on` of the next engineer by hire date via LEAD,
breaking hire-date ties by `id` - NULL for the newest hire.

**Ordered by `hired_on` ascending, then `id` ascending.** (112 rows.)

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 95_drills_lag_lead_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - the same weekday last week

Daily revenue from shipped orders for August 2023: `day` =
`date_trunc('day', created_at)`, `revenue` = the sum of `total` that day,
and `week_ago` = the revenue from **seven rows earlier** via LAG's offset
argument (NULL for the first seven days).

**Ordered by `day` ascending.** (31 rows.)

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 95_drills_lag_lead_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - the gap between two orders

How long does customer 42 wait between orders? For every order of customer
42 return `id`, `created_at`, and `since_prev` = this order's `created_at`
minus the previous order's (an interval, NULL for the first order), taking
orders in `created_at` order with `id` as the tie-break.

**Ordered by `created_at` ascending, then `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 95_drills_lag_lead_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - a LAG that restarts per group

Among products priced 495.00 or more, walk each category's price ladder.
Return `category`, `id`, `price`, and `prev_in_cat` = the price of the
previous product **within the same category** by (`price`, `id`) order -
NULL for the cheapest of each category.

**Ordered by `category` ascending, then `price` ascending, then `id`
ascending.** (About a hundred rows.)

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 95_drills_lag_lead_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - rating swings

Product 42's reviews, in arrival order: did opinion move? Return `id`,
`created_at`, `rating`, `prev_rating` = the previous review's rating, and
`shift` = `rating - prev_rating` (both NULL for the first review). Order
rows - and the window - by `created_at` with `id` as tie-break.

**Ordered by `created_at` ascending, then `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 95_drills_lag_lead_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - the longest silence

For each of the customers with `id <= 5`: the longest stretch between two
consecutive events of theirs in the clickstream. Return `customer_id` and
`longest_gap` = the largest `ts`-to-`ts` gap between that customer's
consecutive events (an interval).

**Ordered by `customer_id` ascending.** (5 rows.)

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 95_drills_lag_lead_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - local minima

The dip days of July 2023: days whose total order revenue was lower than
**both** the day before and the day after. Build daily revenue for July
(all statuses), attach both neighbours, and keep only the local minima.
Return `day` and `revenue`.

**Ordered by `day` ascending.** (July 1st and 31st can never qualify -
think about why before reading the hints.)

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 95_drills_lag_lead_1 ex8`

# Reading - 95_drills_lag_lead_1

Eight drills on reading a neighbouring row without a self-join. Read after
your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

`lag()` and `lead()` are positional: they fetch a value from N rows away in
the order the OVER clause declares, and nothing else. Three consequences run
through this whole set. First, the ORDER BY inside the OVER is part of the
answer's meaning - an unstated tie-break makes the result random, which is
why every window here carries one. Second, the edges produce NULL, and
almost always the NULL is the truthful answer; the optional third argument
that substitutes a default is for the rare case where a made-up number is
better than an honest blank. Third, windows are computed after WHERE and
GROUP BY, so "aggregate first, then window over the small result" is the
shape of every exercise from ex1 on, and "filter on the window's value in
an outer query" is the shape of ex8. LAG sees the previous *row*, not the
previous *day* - if a day were missing from the daily CTE, `lag(..., 1)`
would silently reach one day further back. This dataset has orders every
day, but production data does not; lesson 101 fixes that with a generated
calendar.

## ex1 - yesterday's number beside today's

What it tests: the two-step rhythm - GROUP BY to one row per day in a CTE,
then LAG over the days. The classic mistake is trying to write
`lag(count(*))` and an ORDER BY into one query level and fighting the
planner's evaluation order; it works here by accident of syntax but reads
backwards. The model answer aggregates first because a window over 500,000
raw orders answers a different question than a window over 30 daily rows.

## ex2 - the next hire

What it tests: LEAD is LAG mirrored, and the edge NULL moves to the other
end of the series. The classic mistake is leaving the tie-break out of
`OVER (ORDER BY hired_on)` - two engineers hired the same day would then
swap `next_hire` values from run to run and the gate would fail
intermittently. The model answer orders the window and the output by the
same (`hired_on`, `id`) pair, which is the habit worth automating.

## ex3 - the same weekday last week

What it tests: the offset argument. `lag(revenue, 7)` compares Tuesday to
Tuesday, which is what a week-over-week report means; `lag(revenue)` would
compare Tuesday to Monday and look plausible while being wrong. The classic
mistake is patching the seven leading NULLs with the default argument -
`lag(revenue, 7, 0)` - which invents a zero-revenue week and makes the
first real week look like infinite growth. The model answer leaves NULL
meaning "no such week".

## ex4 - the gap between two orders

What it tests: LAG on a timestamp and interval arithmetic in one step -
`created_at - lag(created_at) OVER (...)` is the whole idea. The classic
mistake before window functions was a self-join on `o2.created_at <
o1.created_at` with a `max()` underneath, quadratic and hard to read. The
model reasoning: the subtraction happens per row, the NULL for the first
order propagates through the arithmetic exactly as lesson 05 promised, and
no join ever enters the picture.

## ex5 - a LAG that restarts per group

What it tests: PARTITION BY as the reset switch. Without it, the window
runs across category boundaries and the first toy inherits a price from the
last garden tool. The classic mistake is partitioning correctly but
ordering only by `price` - equal prices then make `prev_in_cat`
nondeterministic. The model answer puts (`price`, `id`) in the window and
the same keys plus `category` in the outer ORDER BY, so both the values and
the row order are fully pinned down.

## ex6 - rating swings

What it tests: deriving two columns from one LAG. Writing the OVER clause
twice is fine - PostgreSQL computes identical windows once - but the CTE
formulation (window inside, arithmetic outside) is easier to extend when a
third derived column shows up. The classic mistake is ordering the window
by `id` alone on the theory that ids follow time; review ids are assigned
in insert order, not review-date order, so the trajectory would be
scrambled. Order by the timestamp the question is about.

## ex7 - the longest silence

What it tests: window output as aggregate input - the two-layer pattern
that answers most "extreme gap" interview questions. The layers cannot be
merged: `max(ts - lag(ts) OVER (...))` in one SELECT is rejected because
aggregates cannot take window results in the same level. The classic
mistake is forgetting PARTITION BY, which measures a phantom gap from one
customer's last event to the next customer's first. The model answer also
leans on `max()` ignoring the NULL that each customer's first event
carries.

## ex8 - local minima

What it tests: LAG and LEAD on the same row, then filtering on window
output from an outer query - windows are evaluated after WHERE, so the
comparison must live one level up. The classic mistake is expecting July
1st or 31st to appear: `revenue < NULL` is NULL, NULL is not true, and the
edge days drop out - correct behaviour, since a day with one neighbour
cannot be a local minimum. The model answer reads as a pipeline: daily
CTE, neighbour CTE, one WHERE.

## Further reading

- [Window Functions tutorial](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) - the mental model: partitions, frames, and when each function sees what.
- [Window Function Calls](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html#SYNTAX-WINDOW-FUNCTIONS) - full syntax of OVER, including ordering and the rules for what may appear where.
- [General-Purpose Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) - `lag`, `lead`, offsets and defaults, and their edge behaviour.
- [Use The Index, Luke - on pagination and offsets](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/partial-results/window-functions) - window functions from the performance side.

# Reading - 95_drills_lag_lead_1

Eight drills on reading a neighbouring row without a self-join. Read after
your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

`lag()` and `lead()` are positional: they fetch a value from N rows away in
the order the OVER clause declares, and nothing else. Three consequences run
through this whole set. First, the ORDER BY inside the OVER is part of the
answer's meaning - an unstated tie-break makes the result random, which is
why every window here carries one. Second, the edges produce NULL, and
almost always the NULL is the truthful answer; the optional third argument
that substitutes a default is for the rare case where a made-up number is
better than an honest blank. Third, windows are computed after WHERE and
GROUP BY, so "aggregate first, then window over the small result" is the
shape of every exercise from ex1 on, and "filter on the window's value in
an outer query" is the shape of ex8. LAG sees the previous *row*, not the
previous *day* - if a day were missing from the daily CTE, `lag(..., 1)`
would silently reach one day further back. This dataset has orders every
day, but production data does not; lesson 101 fixes that with a generated
calendar.

## ex1 - yesterday's number beside today's

What it tests: the two-step rhythm - GROUP BY to one row per day in a CTE,
then LAG over the days. The classic mistake is trying to write
`lag(count(*))` and an ORDER BY into one query level and fighting the
planner's evaluation order; it works here by accident of syntax but reads
backwards. The model answer aggregates first because a window over 500,000
raw orders answers a different question than a window over 30 daily rows.

## ex2 - the next hire

What it tests: LEAD is LAG mirrored, and the edge NULL moves to the other
end of the series. The classic mistake is leaving the tie-break out of
`OVER (ORDER BY hired_on)` - two engineers hired the same day would then
swap `next_hire` values from run to run and the gate would fail
intermittently. The model answer orders the window and the output by the
same (`hired_on`, `id`) pair, which is the habit worth automating.

## ex3 - the same weekday last week

What it tests: the offset argument. `lag(revenue, 7)` compares Tuesday to
Tuesday, which is what a week-over-week report means; `lag(revenue)` would
compare Tuesday to Monday and look plausible while being wrong. The classic
mistake is patching the seven leading NULLs with the default argument -
`lag(revenue, 7, 0)` - which invents a zero-revenue week and makes the
first real week look like infinite growth. The model answer leaves NULL
meaning "no such week".

## ex4 - the gap between two orders

What it tests: LAG on a timestamp and interval arithmetic in one step -
`created_at - lag(created_at) OVER (...)` is the whole idea. The classic
mistake before window functions was a self-join on `o2.created_at <
o1.created_at` with a `max()` underneath, quadratic and hard to read. The
model reasoning: the subtraction happens per row, the NULL for the first
order propagates through the arithmetic exactly as lesson 05 promised, and
no join ever enters the picture.

## ex5 - a LAG that restarts per group

What it tests: PARTITION BY as the reset switch. Without it, the window
runs across category boundaries and the first toy inherits a price from the
last garden tool. The classic mistake is partitioning correctly but
ordering only by `price` - equal prices then make `prev_in_cat`
nondeterministic. The model answer puts (`price`, `id`) in the window and
the same keys plus `category` in the outer ORDER BY, so both the values and
the row order are fully pinned down.

## ex6 - rating swings

What it tests: deriving two columns from one LAG. Writing the OVER clause
twice is fine - PostgreSQL computes identical windows once - but the CTE
formulation (window inside, arithmetic outside) is easier to extend when a
third derived column shows up. The classic mistake is ordering the window
by `id` alone on the theory that ids follow time; review ids are assigned
in insert order, not review-date order, so the trajectory would be
scrambled. Order by the timestamp the question is about.

## ex7 - the longest silence

What it tests: window output as aggregate input - the two-layer pattern
that answers most "extreme gap" interview questions. The layers cannot be
merged: `max(ts - lag(ts) OVER (...))` in one SELECT is rejected because
aggregates cannot take window results in the same level. The classic
mistake is forgetting PARTITION BY, which measures a phantom gap from one
customer's last event to the next customer's first. The model answer also
leans on `max()` ignoring the NULL that each customer's first event
carries.

## ex8 - local minima

What it tests: LAG and LEAD on the same row, then filtering on window
output from an outer query - windows are evaluated after WHERE, so the
comparison must live one level up. The classic mistake is expecting July
1st or 31st to appear: `revenue < NULL` is NULL, NULL is not true, and the
edge days drop out - correct behaviour, since a day with one neighbour
cannot be a local minimum. The model answer reads as a pipeline: daily
CTE, neighbour CTE, one WHERE.

## Further reading

- [Window Functions tutorial](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) - the mental model: partitions, frames, and when each function sees what.
- [Window Function Calls](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html#SYNTAX-WINDOW-FUNCTIONS) - full syntax of OVER, including ordering and the rules for what may appear where.
- [General-Purpose Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) - `lag`, `lead`, offsets and defaults, and their edge behaviour.
- [Use The Index, Luke - on pagination and offsets](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/partial-results/window-functions) - window functions from the performance side.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 - yesterday's number beside today's

Paid orders per day for September 2023 (half-open range, as always). For
each day return `day` = `date_trunc('day', created_at)`, `orders` = how many
paid orders that day, and `prev_day` = the previous day's count via LAG
(NULL on September 1st).

**Ordered by `day` ascending.** (30 rows.)

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 95_drills_lag_lead_1 ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two steps: first collapse the month into one row per day (a GROUP BY in a CTE), then attach each row's predecessor with a window function. LAG cannot run until the daily rows exist.

## Hint 2

`lag(orders) OVER (ORDER BY day)` on the CTE's output. The first day of the month has no predecessor, so its `prev_day` is NULL - leave it that way.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two steps: first collapse the month into one row per day (a GROUP BY in a CTE), then attach each row's predecessor with a window function. LAG cannot run until the daily rows exist.

## Hint 2

`lag(orders) OVER (ORDER BY day)` on the CTE's output. The first day of the month has no predecessor, so its `prev_day` is NULL - leave it that way.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT day, orders, lag(orders) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS prev_day
FROM (SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at) AS day, count(id) AS orders
      FROM orders
      WHERE status = 'paid'
        AND created_at >= '2023-09-01'
        AND created_at < '2023-10-01'
      GROUP BY date_trunc('day', created_at)) d
ORDER BY day;
references.expected.sql:
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at) AS day, count(*) AS orders
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'paid'
    AND created_at >= '2023-09-01' AND created_at < '2023-10-01'
  GROUP BY 1)
SELECT day, orders, lag(orders) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS prev_day
FROM daily
ORDER BY day;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

LAG takes an optional second argument: how many rows back to look. One row back is yesterday; the same weekday last week is seven rows back.

## Hint 2

`lag(revenue, 7) OVER (ORDER BY day)` on a CTE of daily shipped revenue. The first seven days have no row seven back, so `week_ago` is NULL for them - that is correct, not a bug to patch.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT day, revenue, lag(revenue, 7) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS week_ago
FROM (SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at) AS day, sum(total) AS revenue
      FROM orders
      WHERE status = 'shipped'
        AND created_at >= '2023-08-01'
        AND created_at < '2023-09-01'
      GROUP BY date_trunc('day', created_at)) d
ORDER BY day;
references.expected.sql:
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at) AS day, sum(total) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'shipped'
    AND created_at >= '2023-08-01' AND created_at < '2023-09-01'
  GROUP BY 1)
SELECT day, revenue, lag(revenue, 7) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS week_ago
FROM daily
ORDER BY day;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 - the gap between two orders

How long does customer 42 wait between orders? For every order of customer
42 return `id`, `created_at`, and `since_prev` = this order's `created_at`
minus the previous order's (an interval, NULL for the first order), taking
orders in `created_at` order with `id` as the tie-break.

**Ordered by `created_at` ascending, then `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 95_drills_lag_lead_1 ex4`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The gap between an order and the one before it is a subtraction: this row's timestamp minus the previous row's timestamp. LAG fetches the previous timestamp; no self-join needed.

## Hint 2

`created_at - lag(created_at) OVER (ORDER BY created_at, id)` produces an interval directly. The first order has no predecessor, so the subtraction is `timestamp - NULL` and yields NULL - lesson 05's rule working in your favour.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The gap between an order and the one before it is a subtraction: this row's timestamp minus the previous row's timestamp. LAG fetches the previous timestamp; no self-join needed.

## Hint 2

`created_at - lag(created_at) OVER (ORDER BY created_at, id)` produces an interval directly. The first order has no predecessor, so the subtraction is `timestamp - NULL` and yields NULL - lesson 05's rule working in your favour.

references.solution.sql:
WITH seq AS (
  SELECT id, created_at,
         lag(created_at) OVER (ORDER BY created_at, id) AS prev_at
  FROM orders
  WHERE customer_id = 42)
SELECT id, created_at, created_at - prev_at AS since_prev
FROM seq
ORDER BY created_at, id;

       created_at - lag(created_at) OVER (ORDER BY created_at, id) AS since_prev

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two derived columns, one LAG: the previous row's rating, and this row's rating minus it. You may write `lag(rating) OVER (...)` twice with identical OVER clauses, or window once in a CTE and subtract outside.

## Hint 2

The window's ORDER BY is `created_at, id` - arrival order with a tie-break - and the outer ORDER BY repeats it. The first review has `prev_rating` NULL and therefore `shift` NULL too.

references.solution.sql:
WITH seq AS (
  SELECT id, created_at, rating,
         lag(rating) OVER (ORDER BY created_at, id) AS prev_rating
  FROM reviews
  WHERE product_id = 42)
SELECT id, created_at, rating, prev_rating, rating - prev_rating AS shift
FROM seq
ORDER BY created_at, id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, created_at, rating,
       lag(rating) OVER (ORDER BY created_at, id) AS prev_rating,
       rating - lag(rating) OVER (ORDER BY created_at, id) AS shift
FROM reviews
WHERE product_id = 42
ORDER BY created_at, id;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 - the longest silence

For each of the customers with `id <= 5`: the longest stretch between two
consecutive events of theirs in the clickstream. Return `customer_id` and
`longest_gap` = the largest `ts`-to-`ts` gap between that customer's
consecutive events (an interval).

**Ordered by `customer_id` ascending.** (5 rows.)

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 95_drills_lag_lead_1 ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two layers: first turn each customer's event stream into a stream of gaps (LAG partitioned by customer), then take the biggest gap per customer (GROUP BY with max). Neither layer can do the whole job alone.

## Hint 2

In a CTE: `ts - lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ts) AS gap`, filtered to `customer_id <= 5`. The partition matters - without it, one customer's first event measures a "gap" from a different customer's last event.

## Hint 3

The outer query is plain lesson 07 material: `SELECT customer_id, max(gap) FROM gaps GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id`. Each customer's first event carries a NULL gap; `max()` ignores NULLs, so nothing special is needed for it.

## Hint 1

Two layers: first turn each customer's event stream into a stream of gaps (LAG partitioned by customer), then take the biggest gap per customer (GROUP BY with max). Neither layer can do the whole job alone.

## Hint 2

In a CTE: `ts - lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ts) AS gap`, filtered to `customer_id <= 5`. The partition matters - without it, one customer's first event measures a "gap" from a different customer's last event.

## Hint 3

The outer query is plain lesson 07 material: `SELECT customer_id, max(gap) FROM gaps GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id`. Each customer's first event carries a NULL gap; `max()` ignores NULLs, so nothing special is needed for it.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT customer_id, max(gap) AS longest_gap
FROM (SELECT customer_id,
             ts - lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY id) AS gap
      FROM events
      WHERE customer_id IN (1, 2, 3, 4, 5)) g
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY customer_id;
references.expected.sql:
WITH gaps AS (
  SELECT customer_id,
         ts - lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ts) AS gap
  FROM events
  WHERE customer_id <= 5)
SELECT customer_id, max(gap) AS longest_gap
FROM gaps
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY customer_id;

             lag(revenue)  OVER (ORDER BY day) AS prev,
