exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The same join as ex4, with the roles of the two dimensions swapped: the
rating becomes the grouping key and the category becomes the column list.

## Hint 2

`GROUP BY r.rating`, then six `count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.category = '...')`
columns in alphabetical order. Five rows out, because there are five ratings.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT r.rating,
       count(CASE WHEN p.category = 'books' THEN 1 END) AS books,
       count(CASE WHEN p.category = 'clothing' THEN 1 END) AS clothing,
       count(CASE WHEN p.category = 'electronics' THEN 1 END) AS electronics,
       count(CASE WHEN p.category = 'food' THEN 1 END) AS food,
       count(CASE WHEN p.category = 'garden' THEN 1 END) AS garden,
       count(CASE WHEN p.category = 'toys' THEN 1 END) AS toys
FROM products p
JOIN reviews r ON r.product_id = p.id
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT r.rating,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.category = 'books') AS books,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.category = 'clothing') AS clothing,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.category = 'electronics') AS electronics,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.category = 'food') AS food,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.category = 'garden') AS garden,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.category = 'toys') AS toys
FROM reviews r
JOIN products p ON p.id = r.product_id
GROUP BY r.rating
ORDER BY r.rating;

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 - new against returning

One row per month of `orders`. Return `month` =
`date_trunc('month', created_at)`, `orders` = the orders created that month,
`new_customers` = how many distinct customers placed their **first ever**
order that month, and `returning_customers` = how many distinct customers
ordered that month whose first ever order was in an earlier month.

A customer counts once per month, in exactly one of the two columns.

**Ordered by `month` ascending.** (13 rows.)

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 98_drills_pivots_2 ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

"First ever order" is a per-customer aggregate, and it does not depend on the
month being reported - so compute it once, for every customer, before you
start grouping by month.

## Hint 2

A CTE of `customer_id, min(created_at)` joined back to `orders` gives every
order both its own month and its customer's first month. The two columns are
then filtered counts comparing those two values.

## Hint 3

Count *customers*, not rows: `count(DISTINCT o.customer_id) FILTER (...)`.
Truncate both sides to the month before comparing, or a customer whose first
order was on the 3rd will look like a returning customer on the 20th of the
same month.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

"First ever order" is a per-customer aggregate, and it does not depend on the
month being reported - so compute it once, for every customer, before you
start grouping by month.

## Hint 2

A CTE of `customer_id, min(created_at)` joined back to `orders` gives every
order both its own month and its customer's first month. The two columns are
then filtered counts comparing those two values.

## Hint 3

Count *customers*, not rows: `count(DISTINCT o.customer_id) FILTER (...)`.
Truncate both sides to the month before comparing, or a customer whose first
order was on the 3rd will look like a returning customer on the 20th of the
same month.

references.solution.sql:
WITH firsts AS (
  SELECT customer_id, date_trunc('month', min(created_at)) AS first_month
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id),
tagged AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id,
         date_trunc('month', o.created_at) AS month,
         f.first_month
  FROM orders o
  JOIN firsts f ON f.customer_id = o.customer_id)
SELECT month,
       count(*) AS orders,
       count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN month = first_month THEN customer_id END) AS new_customers,
       count(DISTINCT CASE WHEN month > first_month THEN customer_id END) AS returning_customers
FROM tagged
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;
references.expected.sql:
WITH firsts AS (
  SELECT customer_id, min(created_at) AS first_order
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id)
SELECT date_trunc('month', o.created_at) AS month,
       count(*) AS orders,
       count(DISTINCT o.customer_id)
         FILTER (WHERE date_trunc('month', o.created_at)
                     = date_trunc('month', f.first_order)) AS new_customers,
       count(DISTINCT o.customer_id)
         FILTER (WHERE date_trunc('month', o.created_at)
                     > date_trunc('month', f.first_order)) AS returning_customers
FROM orders o
JOIN firsts f ON f.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY date_trunc('month', o.created_at)
ORDER BY month;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Four stages, each one a CTE: pivot to the grid, un-pivot it so the status
names become values, number the rows inside each month by their count, keep
number one.

## Hint 2

The ranking cannot happen while the statuses are columns - `row_number()
OVER (PARTITION BY month ORDER BY orders DESC)` needs one row per status.
That is the reason the un-pivot is in the query at all.

## Hint 3

Break the tie with `status ASC` inside the window's `ORDER BY` so exactly one
row survives per month, then filter `rn = 1` from the level above (a window

references.solution.sql:
WITH grid AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month,
         count(CASE WHEN status = 'pending' THEN 1 END) AS pending,
         count(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 END) AS paid,
         count(CASE WHEN status = 'shipped' THEN 1 END) AS shipped,
         count(CASE WHEN status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 END) AS cancelled
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY 1),
tall AS (
  SELECT month, 'pending' AS status, pending AS orders FROM grid
  UNION ALL
  SELECT month, 'paid', paid FROM grid
  UNION ALL
  SELECT month, 'shipped', shipped FROM grid
  UNION ALL
  SELECT month, 'cancelled', cancelled FROM grid)
SELECT DISTINCT ON (month) month, status, orders
FROM tall
ORDER BY month, orders DESC, status;
references.expected.sql:
WITH grid AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'pending') AS pending,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid') AS paid,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'shipped') AS shipped,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY date_trunc('month', created_at)),
tall AS (
  SELECT g.month, v.status, v.orders
  FROM grid g
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL (VALUES ('pending', g.pending),
                             ('paid', g.paid),
                             ('shipped', g.shipped),
                             ('cancelled', g.cancelled)) AS v(status, orders)),
ranked AS (
  SELECT month, status, orders,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY month
                            ORDER BY orders DESC, status ASC) AS rn
  FROM tall)
SELECT month, status, orders
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY month;

# 99 - Drills: dates and times, set 1

Eight problems on lesson 18: truncating a timestamp to a bucket, pulling a
field out of it, subtracting two of them, and expressing a period as a
half-open range. Every date bug you will ever ship is one of those four done
carelessly, so this set is deliberately unglamorous. Reread 18 if
`date_trunc` and `extract` still blur into each other.

One convention throughout: a period is written `>= start AND < end`. Never
`BETWEEN` on a timestamp - `BETWEEN '2023-06-01' AND '2023-06-30'` silently
excludes almost all of the 30th, because a bare date means midnight.

## Exercise 1 - three views of one timestamp

For the orders with `id <= 20` return `id`, `created_at`, `order_date` =
`created_at` cast to `date`, and `hour_bucket` =
`date_trunc('hour', created_at)`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (20 rows.)

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 99_drills_dates_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - a month label

For the staff with `id <= 20` return `id`, `name`, `hired_on`, and
`hire_month` = the hire date formatted as `YYYY-MM` text, for example
`2019-04`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (20 rows.)

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 99_drills_dates_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - the quarterly numbers

One row per quarter of `orders`: `quarter` =
`date_trunc('quarter', created_at)`, `orders` = how many were created in it,
and `revenue` = the sum of `total` rounded to 2.

**Ordered by `quarter` ascending.** (5 rows - the data spans a little over
four quarters.)

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 99_drills_dates_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - a month, day by day, with weekday names

For the orders created in June 2023, one row per calendar day: `day` =
`created_at` cast to `date`, `dow_name` = the English weekday name with no
padding (`Monday`, not `Monday   `), and `orders` = how many orders that
day.

Use a half-open range for June.

**Ordered by `day` ascending.** (30 rows.)

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 99_drills_dates_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - tenure in days and years

For every member of the `engineering` department return `id`, `name`,
`hired_on`, `tenure_days` = the number of days from `hired_on` to
2023-11-14, and `tenure_years` = that day count divided by 365.0 and rounded
to 1.

Subtracting one `date` from another gives an integer number of days - no
cast, no `interval`.

**Ordered by `hired_on` ascending, then `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 99_drills_dates_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - the same span as an interval

For every member of the `sales` department return `id`, `name`, `hired_on`,
`tenure` = `age(DATE '2023-11-14', hired_on)`, and `full_years` = the whole
years of that interval as an `int`.

`age()` gives you years, months and days rather than a day count; the years
field is what a HR report calls a work anniversary.

**Ordered by `hired_on` ascending, then `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 99_drills_dates_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - how long has this customer been with us

Among the customers with `customer_id <= 200` in `orders`, keep those whose
ordering history spans 300 days or more, and return `customer_id`,
`first_order` = their earliest `created_at` as a `date`, `last_order` = the
latest as a `date`, and `span_days` = the difference between those two
dates.

**Ordered by `span_days` descending, then `customer_id` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 99_drills_dates_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - the 30-day follow-up

For every order of customer 42 return `id`, `created_at`, and `within_30d` =
how many *other* orders that same customer placed strictly after this one
and strictly within 30 days of it (`created_at + interval '30 days'` is the
exclusive upper bound).

**Ordered by `created_at` ascending, then `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 99_drills_dates_1 ex8`

# Reading - 99_drills_dates_1

Eight drills on the four operations that make up all date handling:
truncate, extract, subtract, and bound a range. Read after your attempt,
pass or fail.

## Notes

`date_trunc` and `extract` look similar and are opposites. `date_trunc`
keeps the type - a timestamp goes in, a timestamp comes out, snapped down to
the start of the bucket - which is why it can be sorted, compared and
grouped and still mean an instant in time. `extract` throws the type away
and returns a bare number, so `extract(month FROM created_at) = 6` folds
every June of every year together, which is sometimes what you want and is
usually a bug in a trend report. Subtraction is a third thing again:
`date - date` is an integer count of days, `timestamp - timestamp` is an
`interval`, and `age(a, b)` is an interval measured in calendar units rather
than elapsed time, so it knows that a month can be 28 or 31 days. And the
range convention is not pedantry: `created_at < DATE '2023-07-01'` includes
every instant of June 30th including 23:59:59.999, while `BETWEEN` with an
end date of June 30th stops at midnight and quietly drops a day of data.

## ex1 - three views of one timestamp

What this tested: that a timestamp has a type and casting changes it. The
cast to `date` discards the time of day and gives you a `date` value;
`date_trunc('hour', ...)` keeps a full timestamp and merely zeroes the
smaller fields. The classic mistake is treating them as interchangeable -
they group identically but they do not display, sort against a timestamp, or
subtract identically. The model answer shows both beside the original so the
difference is visible in one glance.

## ex2 - a month label

What this tested: `to_char`, the formatter, as distinct from `date_trunc`,
the bucketer. Both answer "which month", but one returns text you can print
and the other returns a timestamp you can compute with. The classic mistake
is grouping a report by the `to_char` string: `'2023-09'` sorts fine, but
`'Sep 2023'` sorts alphabetically and puts April first. Format at the end,
group on the real thing.

## ex3 - the quarterly numbers

What this tested: that `date_trunc` takes any bucket name, quarter included,
and that the grouping key can be the truncated timestamp itself. Five rows
is right for a year of data that starts in mid-November: the first and last
quarters are partial. The classic mistake is `extract(quarter FROM ...)`,
which returns 1 to 4 and merges the 2022 and 2023 fourth quarters into one
misleading row.

## ex4 - a month, day by day, with weekday names

What this tested: a half-open month range, plus the padding trap in
`to_char`. The `Day` pattern is blank-padded to nine characters, so
`'Monday   '` is not `'Monday'` and a comparison against the short string
fails silently; `trim()` or the `FM` prefix removes it. The classic mistake
is `BETWEEN '2023-06-01' AND '2023-06-30'`, which loses everything after
midnight on the 30th - about one day in thirty of the data.

## ex5 - tenure in days and years

What this tested: date subtraction and integer division. `DATE '2023-11-14'
- hired_on` is an `int`, so dividing by `365` would floor the result to
whole years; dividing by `365.0` promotes the expression to `numeric` and
keeps the fraction, which is why the prompt spells out the constant. The
classic mistake is `now() - hired_on`, which gives a different answer every
day and cannot be tested; the model answer anchors on a fixed date.

## ex6 - the same span as an interval

What this tested: `age()` against plain subtraction. `age()` walks the
calendar - "4 years 2 mons 11 days" - while subtraction counts elapsed days,
and the two disagree about February in a way that matters for anniversaries
and contract terms. The classic mistake is `extract(year FROM ...)` on the
*date* rather than on the interval, which returns the hire year instead of
the tenure. The model answer extracts from `age(...)`, and casts to `int`
because `extract` returns `numeric`.

## ex7 - how long has this customer been with us

What this tested: aggregates that produce dates, and a `HAVING` clause over
a derived quantity. `min()` and `max()` work on timestamps exactly as they
do on numbers, and the span is the difference of the two casts. The classic
mistake is putting the 300-day condition in `WHERE`, where the aggregates do
not yet exist; the reference sidesteps the repetition by computing the
aggregates in a CTE and filtering with an ordinary `WHERE` outside it.

## ex8 - the 30-day follow-up

What this tested: a range condition inside a join - the pattern behind
"repeat purchase within 30 days", "second incident within a quarter", and
every cohort follow-up metric. The interval arithmetic happens per row:
`o.created_at + interval '30 days'` is a moving bound, not a constant. The
classic mistake is an inner join, which drops the orders that had no
follow-up instead of reporting a zero for them; a `LEFT JOIN` with
`count(o2.id)` keeps them, as does the reference's correlated subquery.

## Further reading

- [Date/Time Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) - `date_trunc`, `extract`, `age`, and the arithmetic table showing which combination yields what type.
- [Date/Time Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-datetime.html) - `date`, `timestamp`, `timestamptz` and `interval`, and how literals are parsed.
- [Data Type Formatting Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-formatting.html) - `to_char` patterns, including the `FM` prefix that suppresses padding.
- [`BETWEEN` and range predicates](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html) - why an inclusive upper bound is the wrong tool for a timestamp.

## Ten-pass spaced repetition

Use this ladder after completing **99 - Drills: dates and times, set 1**. Each pass changes the retrieval
task so repetition strengthens recall instead of becoming answer recognition.
Do the named exercise from a blank starting point whenever practical, and only
open its hints after recording your first attempt.

| Pass | When | Practice target | Retrieval task |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | now | `ex1` | Close the notes and state the central rule in one precise sentence. |
| 2 | 3 days | `ex2` | Rebuild the smallest valid example from memory, then explain each part. |
| 3 | 7 days | `ex3` | Predict the result or behavior before running anything; reconcile surprises. |
| 4 | 21 days | `ex4` | Solve from a blank file and name the first tempting mistake you avoided. |
| 5 | 60 days | `ex5` | Contrast this technique with its nearest alternative and choose between them. |
| 6 | 120 days | `ex6` | Add one realistic constraint and adapt the solution without consulting notes. |
| 7 | 240 days | `ex7` | Debug a deliberately broken version; explain the evidence before the repair. |
| 8 | 1 year | `ex8` | Teach the idea aloud in two minutes, including one boundary case. |
| 9 | 18 months | `ex1` | Transfer the pattern to a new domain and verify the result with the gate. |
| 10 | 3 years | `ex2` | Complete a cold, timed solution and write the rule you want to retain long-term. |

A failed pass is useful evidence: return to pass 1 after three days. A clean
pass advances to the next interval. After pass 10, revisit the skill every
three years or whenever real work exposes a weak edge case.

# Reading - 99_drills_dates_1

Eight drills on the four operations that make up all date handling:
truncate, extract, subtract, and bound a range. Read after your attempt,
pass or fail.

## Notes

`date_trunc` and `extract` look similar and are opposites. `date_trunc`
keeps the type - a timestamp goes in, a timestamp comes out, snapped down to
the start of the bucket - which is why it can be sorted, compared and
grouped and still mean an instant in time. `extract` throws the type away
and returns a bare number, so `extract(month FROM created_at) = 6` folds
every June of every year together, which is sometimes what you want and is
usually a bug in a trend report. Subtraction is a third thing again:
`date - date` is an integer count of days, `timestamp - timestamp` is an
`interval`, and `age(a, b)` is an interval measured in calendar units rather
than elapsed time, so it knows that a month can be 28 or 31 days. And the
range convention is not pedantry: `created_at < DATE '2023-07-01'` includes
every instant of June 30th including 23:59:59.999, while `BETWEEN` with an
end date of June 30th stops at midnight and quietly drops a day of data.

## ex1 - three views of one timestamp

What this tested: that a timestamp has a type and casting changes it. The
cast to `date` discards the time of day and gives you a `date` value;
`date_trunc('hour', ...)` keeps a full timestamp and merely zeroes the
smaller fields. The classic mistake is treating them as interchangeable -
they group identically but they do not display, sort against a timestamp, or
subtract identically. The model answer shows both beside the original so the
difference is visible in one glance.

## ex2 - a month label

What this tested: `to_char`, the formatter, as distinct from `date_trunc`,
the bucketer. Both answer "which month", but one returns text you can print
and the other returns a timestamp you can compute with. The classic mistake
is grouping a report by the `to_char` string: `'2023-09'` sorts fine, but
`'Sep 2023'` sorts alphabetically and puts April first. Format at the end,
group on the real thing.

## ex3 - the quarterly numbers

What this tested: that `date_trunc` takes any bucket name, quarter included,
and that the grouping key can be the truncated timestamp itself. Five rows
is right for a year of data that starts in mid-November: the first and last
quarters are partial. The classic mistake is `extract(quarter FROM ...)`,
which returns 1 to 4 and merges the 2022 and 2023 fourth quarters into one
misleading row.

## ex4 - a month, day by day, with weekday names

What this tested: a half-open month range, plus the padding trap in
`to_char`. The `Day` pattern is blank-padded to nine characters, so
`'Monday   '` is not `'Monday'` and a comparison against the short string
fails silently; `trim()` or the `FM` prefix removes it. The classic mistake
is `BETWEEN '2023-06-01' AND '2023-06-30'`, which loses everything after
midnight on the 30th - about one day in thirty of the data.

## ex5 - tenure in days and years

What this tested: date subtraction and integer division. `DATE '2023-11-14'
- hired_on` is an `int`, so dividing by `365` would floor the result to
whole years; dividing by `365.0` promotes the expression to `numeric` and
keeps the fraction, which is why the prompt spells out the constant. The
classic mistake is `now() - hired_on`, which gives a different answer every
day and cannot be tested; the model answer anchors on a fixed date.

## ex6 - the same span as an interval

What this tested: `age()` against plain subtraction. `age()` walks the
calendar - "4 years 2 mons 11 days" - while subtraction counts elapsed days,
and the two disagree about February in a way that matters for anniversaries
and contract terms. The classic mistake is `extract(year FROM ...)` on the
*date* rather than on the interval, which returns the hire year instead of
the tenure. The model answer extracts from `age(...)`, and casts to `int`
because `extract` returns `numeric`.

## ex7 - how long has this customer been with us

What this tested: aggregates that produce dates, and a `HAVING` clause over
a derived quantity. `min()` and `max()` work on timestamps exactly as they
do on numbers, and the span is the difference of the two casts. The classic
mistake is putting the 300-day condition in `WHERE`, where the aggregates do
not yet exist; the reference sidesteps the repetition by computing the
aggregates in a CTE and filtering with an ordinary `WHERE` outside it.

## ex8 - the 30-day follow-up

What this tested: a range condition inside a join - the pattern behind
"repeat purchase within 30 days", "second incident within a quarter", and
every cohort follow-up metric. The interval arithmetic happens per row:
`o.created_at + interval '30 days'` is a moving bound, not a constant. The
classic mistake is an inner join, which drops the orders that had no
follow-up instead of reporting a zero for them; a `LEFT JOIN` with
`count(o2.id)` keeps them, as does the reference's correlated subquery.

## Further reading

- [Date/Time Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) - `date_trunc`, `extract`, `age`, and the arithmetic table showing which combination yields what type.
- [Date/Time Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-datetime.html) - `date`, `timestamp`, `timestamptz` and `interval`, and how literals are parsed.
- [Data Type Formatting Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-formatting.html) - `to_char` patterns, including the `FM` prefix that suppresses padding.
- [`BETWEEN` and range predicates](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-comparison.html) - why an inclusive upper bound is the wrong tool for a timestamp.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two different reductions of the same value: one changes the type to `date`,
the other keeps the timestamp and zeroes the minutes and seconds.

## Hint 2

`created_at::date` (or `cast(created_at AS date)`) and
`date_trunc('hour', created_at)`. Nothing is grouped here - one row per
order.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT id,
       created_at,
       cast(created_at AS date) AS order_date,
       date_trunc('hour', created_at) AS hour_bucket
FROM orders
WHERE id <= 20
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id,
       created_at,
       created_at::date AS order_date,
       date_trunc('hour', created_at) AS hour_bucket
FROM orders
WHERE id <= 20
ORDER BY id;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A half-open June, one group per calendar day, and a formatted weekday name
alongside it. Both non-aggregated columns have to appear in the `GROUP BY`.

## Hint 2

`to_char(created_at, 'Day')` pads the name to nine characters - wrap it in
`trim()`, or use the `FM` prefix (`'FMDay'`) which suppresses the padding.
The range is `>= DATE '2023-06-01' AND < DATE '2023-07-01'`.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at)::date AS day,
       to_char(created_at, 'FMDay') AS dow_name,
       count(*) AS orders
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= DATE '2023-06-01'
  AND created_at < DATE '2023-07-01'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT created_at::date AS day,
       trim(to_char(created_at, 'Day')) AS dow_name,
       count(*) AS orders
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= DATE '2023-06-01'
  AND created_at < DATE '2023-07-01'
GROUP BY created_at::date, trim(to_char(created_at, 'Day'))
ORDER BY day;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 - tenure in days and years

For every member of the `engineering` department return `id`, `name`,
`hired_on`, `tenure_days` = the number of days from `hired_on` to
2023-11-14, and `tenure_years` = that day count divided by 365.0 and rounded
to 1.

Subtracting one `date` from another gives an integer number of days - no
cast, no `interval`.

**Ordered by `hired_on` ascending, then `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 99_drills_dates_1 ex5`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Subtracting a `date` from a `date` gives a plain integer count of days. The
second column is that integer turned into years.

## Hint 2

`DATE '2023-11-14' - hired_on` is the day count. Divide by `365.0`, not by
`365` - integer division would throw the fraction away before `round` ever
sees it.

## Hint 1

Subtracting a `date` from a `date` gives a plain integer count of days. The
second column is that integer turned into years.

## Hint 2

`DATE '2023-11-14' - hired_on` is the day count. Divide by `365.0`, not by
`365` - integer division would throw the fraction away before `round` ever
sees it.

SELECT id, name, hired_on,
       (DATE '2023-11-14' - hired_on) AS tenure_days,
       round((DATE '2023-11-14' - hired_on)::numeric / 365, 1) AS tenure_years
FROM staff
WHERE department = 'engineering'
ORDER BY 3, 1;

## Exercise 7 - how long has this customer been with us

Among the customers with `customer_id <= 200` in `orders`, keep those whose
ordering history spans 300 days or more, and return `customer_id`,
`first_order` = their earliest `created_at` as a `date`, `last_order` = the
latest as a `date`, and `span_days` = the difference between those two
dates.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two aggregates per customer and a filter on the distance between them. The
filter is about the group, not about individual orders.

`min(created_at)::date` and `max(created_at)::date`, then their difference.

expression three times.

`WHERE customer_id <= 200` still belongs in `WHERE`: it restricts which rows
are aggregated, which is a different job from restricting which groups
survive. Sort by `span_days` descending with `customer_id` as the tie-break.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two aggregates per customer and a filter on the distance between them. The
filter is about the group, not about individual orders.

## Hint 2

`min(created_at)::date` and `max(created_at)::date`, then their difference.
The 300-day condition belongs in `HAVING` - or compute the aggregates in a
CTE and use an ordinary `WHERE` on the outside, which avoids writing the
expression three times.

## Hint 3

`WHERE customer_id <= 200` still belongs in `WHERE`: it restricts which rows
are aggregated, which is a different job from restricting which groups
survive. Sort by `span_days` descending with `customer_id` as the tie-break.

references.solution.sql:
WITH spans AS (
  SELECT customer_id,
         min(created_at)::date AS first_order,
         max(created_at)::date AS last_order
  FROM orders
  WHERE customer_id <= 200
  GROUP BY customer_id)
SELECT customer_id, first_order, last_order,
       last_order - first_order AS span_days
FROM spans
WHERE last_order - first_order >= 300
ORDER BY 4 DESC, 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT customer_id,
       min(created_at)::date AS first_order,
       max(created_at)::date AS last_order,
       max(created_at)::date - min(created_at)::date AS span_days
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id <= 200
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING max(created_at)::date - min(created_at)::date >= 300
ORDER BY span_days DESC, customer_id;

## Hint 1

Each order needs a count of the customer's *other* orders inside a window
that moves with it - the bound is `this row's created_at + interval '30
days'`, not a fixed date.

## Hint 2

Either join `orders` to itself on the customer plus the two range conditions

references.solution.sql:
SELECT o.id, o.created_at,
       (SELECT count(*)
        FROM orders x
        WHERE x.customer_id = o.customer_id
          AND x.created_at > o.created_at
          AND x.created_at < o.created_at + interval '30 days') AS within_30d
FROM orders o
WHERE o.customer_id = 42
ORDER BY 2, 1;

SELECT o.id, o.created_at, count(o2.id) AS within_30d
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN orders o2
       ON o2.customer_id = o.customer_id
      AND o2.created_at > o.created_at
      AND o2.created_at < o.created_at + interval '30 days'
WHERE o.customer_id = 42
GROUP BY o.id, o.created_at
ORDER BY o.created_at, o.id;

# Reading - 100_drills_dates_2

Eight drills on the parts of date handling that only show up in real
reports: epochs, formatting, custom buckets, intervals as numbers, and gap
rules. Read after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

Three ideas carry this set. First, a timestamp is a number underneath -
`extract(epoch FROM ts)` exposes it, and once you have a number you can do
arithmetic that the calendar functions do not offer, which is how any bucket
size is built: divide the epoch by the bucket in seconds, floor it, multiply
back. Second, `to_char` is a presentation layer and should be the last thing
that happens to a value; the one exception is `'YYYY-MM'`, which sorts
identically to the timestamps it came from and is therefore safe as a
grouping key - `'Mon YYYY'` is not. Third, an `interval` is not a number:
comparing two intervals works, but turning one into "months" requires
deciding what a month is, which is precisely why `age()` exists and why
`extract(year ...) * 12 + extract(month ...)` is the standard incantation.
The gap rule in ex8 is the shape of every sessionization job in the
industry, and it is nothing more than `lag()` plus a comparison against an
interval literal.

## ex1 - the timestamp as a number

What this tested: that `extract(epoch FROM ...)` is the bridge between
timestamps and arithmetic. It returns `numeric` in modern PostgreSQL, hence
the cast to `bigint`; APIs and log formats speak in these numbers, so the
conversion has to be reflexive. The classic mistake is assuming the epoch
depends on the session time zone - it does not, because it is measured from
a fixed instant, which is exactly what makes it useful for comparison.

## ex2 - two formats side by side

What this tested: `to_char` patterns, and the padding trap once more.
`HH24` is the 24-hour clock - `HH` is 12-hour and will make midnight and
noon indistinguishable - and `Day` is blank-padded to nine characters unless
you use the `FM` prefix or `trim()`. The model answer builds both columns
from the same timestamp so you can see that formatting never changes the
underlying value, only its rendering.

## ex3 - grouping by a formatted month

What this tested: when a text key is acceptable. `'2023-09' < '2023-10'` as
text agrees with the timestamps' order, so grouping and sorting by the
formatted string is safe and produces a report that needs no post-processing.
The classic mistake is any other format: `'Sep 2023'` sorts April first, and
`'09/2023'` sorts January of every year together. When in doubt, group by
`date_trunc` and format in the outer query, as the reference does.

## ex4 - a bucket `date_trunc` does not offer

What this tested: building your own bucket. `date_trunc` supports minute,
hour, day and friends, but not "every 15 minutes", so you truncate to the
enclosing hour and add back whole quarter-hours: `floor(extract(minute FROM
ts) / 15)` steps of `interval '15 minutes'`. The reference shows the other
standard trick, flooring the epoch to a multiple of 900 seconds and
converting back with `to_timestamp`. The classic mistake is grouping by the
un-floored minute and hoping the report aggregates itself later.

## ex5 - an interval turned into a number

What this tested: that arithmetic on intervals needs a policy. `age()` gives
years, months and days, and "months of tenure" is defined as twelve times
the years plus the months - the leftover days are deliberately discarded,
because that is what "whole months" means. The classic mistake is
`extract(month FROM age(...))` alone, which returns a number from 0 to 11
and makes a four-year veteran look like a new hire.

## ex6 - one week, exactly

What this tested: the half-open range, one more time, on a boundary where
getting it wrong is invisible. Seven days means `>= Monday AND < the
following Monday`; `BETWEEN '2023-03-13' AND '2023-03-19'` looks like the
same week and loses almost all of Sunday. The model answer states the end as
the exclusive bound, and the reference writes it as `start + interval '7
days'` so the length of the period appears in the query text.

## ex7 - how long until the first order

What this tested: an aggregate under an outer join, where the NULLs are the
interesting part. A customer with no orders must survive the join and report
NULL twice - and the subtraction propagates that NULL automatically, so no
special case is needed. The classic mistake is an inner join or a
`coalesce(..., 0)` on `days_to_first`, both of which claim that a customer
who never ordered ordered on the day they signed up.

## ex8 - sessions from a gap rule

What this tested: the sessionization idiom. Take the previous event's
timestamp per customer with `lag()`, compare the gap against an interval
literal, and count the rows that begin a new session - a NULL gap (the
customer's first event) counts as a start too, which is why the predicate
has two branches. The classic mistake is forgetting `PARTITION BY
customer_id`, which measures a gap across the boundary between two
customers' histories and merges their sessions. Note that the session
*count* needs no numbering; assigning session ids would be a running `sum()`
over the same flag.

## Further reading

- [Date/Time Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) - `extract`, `age`, `to_timestamp`, and interval arithmetic.
- [Data Type Formatting Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-formatting.html) - every `to_char` pattern, including `HH24`, `FM` and the padding rules.
- [Date/Time Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-datetime.html) - what an `interval` stores, and why months and days are kept separately from seconds.
- [Window Functions reference](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) - `lag()`, used here to turn a list of events into a list of gaps.

# Reading - 100_drills_dates_2

Eight drills on the parts of date handling that only show up in real
reports: epochs, formatting, custom buckets, intervals as numbers, and gap
rules. Read after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

Three ideas carry this set. First, a timestamp is a number underneath -
`extract(epoch FROM ts)` exposes it, and once you have a number you can do
arithmetic that the calendar functions do not offer, which is how any bucket
size is built: divide the epoch by the bucket in seconds, floor it, multiply
back. Second, `to_char` is a presentation layer and should be the last thing
that happens to a value; the one exception is `'YYYY-MM'`, which sorts
identically to the timestamps it came from and is therefore safe as a
grouping key - `'Mon YYYY'` is not. Third, an `interval` is not a number:
comparing two intervals works, but turning one into "months" requires
deciding what a month is, which is precisely why `age()` exists and why
`extract(year ...) * 12 + extract(month ...)` is the standard incantation.
The gap rule in ex8 is the shape of every sessionization job in the
industry, and it is nothing more than `lag()` plus a comparison against an
interval literal.

## ex1 - the timestamp as a number

What this tested: that `extract(epoch FROM ...)` is the bridge between
timestamps and arithmetic. It returns `numeric` in modern PostgreSQL, hence
the cast to `bigint`; APIs and log formats speak in these numbers, so the
conversion has to be reflexive. The classic mistake is assuming the epoch
depends on the session time zone - it does not, because it is measured from
a fixed instant, which is exactly what makes it useful for comparison.

## ex2 - two formats side by side

What this tested: `to_char` patterns, and the padding trap once more.
`HH24` is the 24-hour clock - `HH` is 12-hour and will make midnight and
noon indistinguishable - and `Day` is blank-padded to nine characters unless
you use the `FM` prefix or `trim()`. The model answer builds both columns
from the same timestamp so you can see that formatting never changes the
underlying value, only its rendering.

## ex3 - grouping by a formatted month

What this tested: when a text key is acceptable. `'2023-09' < '2023-10'` as
text agrees with the timestamps' order, so grouping and sorting by the
formatted string is safe and produces a report that needs no post-processing.
The classic mistake is any other format: `'Sep 2023'` sorts April first, and
`'09/2023'` sorts January of every year together. When in doubt, group by
`date_trunc` and format in the outer query, as the reference does.

## ex4 - a bucket `date_trunc` does not offer

What this tested: building your own bucket. `date_trunc` supports minute,
hour, day and friends, but not "every 15 minutes", so you truncate to the
enclosing hour and add back whole quarter-hours: `floor(extract(minute FROM
ts) / 15)` steps of `interval '15 minutes'`. The reference shows the other
standard trick, flooring the epoch to a multiple of 900 seconds and
converting back with `to_timestamp`. The classic mistake is grouping by the
un-floored minute and hoping the report aggregates itself later.

## ex5 - an interval turned into a number

What this tested: that arithmetic on intervals needs a policy. `age()` gives
years, months and days, and "months of tenure" is defined as twelve times
the years plus the months - the leftover days are deliberately discarded,
because that is what "whole months" means. The classic mistake is
`extract(month FROM age(...))` alone, which returns a number from 0 to 11
and makes a four-year veteran look like a new hire.

## ex6 - one week, exactly

What this tested: the half-open range, one more time, on a boundary where
getting it wrong is invisible. Seven days means `>= Monday AND < the
following Monday`; `BETWEEN '2023-03-13' AND '2023-03-19'` looks like the
same week and loses almost all of Sunday. The model answer states the end as
the exclusive bound, and the reference writes it as `start + interval '7
days'` so the length of the period appears in the query text.

## ex7 - how long until the first order

What this tested: an aggregate under an outer join, where the NULLs are the
interesting part. A customer with no orders must survive the join and report
NULL twice - and the subtraction propagates that NULL automatically, so no
special case is needed. The classic mistake is an inner join or a
`coalesce(..., 0)` on `days_to_first`, both of which claim that a customer
who never ordered ordered on the day they signed up.

## ex8 - sessions from a gap rule

What this tested: the sessionization idiom. Take the previous event's
timestamp per customer with `lag()`, compare the gap against an interval
literal, and count the rows that begin a new session - a NULL gap (the
customer's first event) counts as a start too, which is why the predicate
has two branches. The classic mistake is forgetting `PARTITION BY
customer_id`, which measures a gap across the boundary between two
customers' histories and merges their sessions. Note that the session
*count* needs no numbering; assigning session ids would be a running `sum()`
over the same flag.

## Further reading

- [Date/Time Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) - `extract`, `age`, `to_timestamp`, and interval arithmetic.
- [Data Type Formatting Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-formatting.html) - every `to_char` pattern, including `HH24`, `FM` and the padding rules.
- [Date/Time Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-datetime.html) - what an `interval` stores, and why months and days are kept separately from seconds.
- [Window Functions reference](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) - `lag()`, used here to turn a list of events into a list of gaps.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

There is a field name that gives you the whole timestamp as a count of
seconds rather than one of its calendar parts.

## Hint 2

`extract(epoch FROM created_at)` returns `numeric`; cast it to `bigint` so
the column is a whole number of seconds.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT id, created_at,
       cast(date_part('epoch', created_at) AS bigint) AS epoch_seconds
FROM orders
WHERE id <= 15
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, created_at,
       extract(epoch FROM created_at)::bigint AS epoch_seconds
FROM orders
WHERE id <= 15
ORDER BY id;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 - two formats side by side

For the orders with `id <= 15` return `id`, `stamp` = `created_at` formatted
as `YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI`, and `day_name` = the unpadded English weekday name
of that order.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (15 rows.)

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 100_drills_dates_2 ex2`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two `to_char` calls over the same column. One renders the whole timestamp,
the other only the weekday name.

## Hint 2

`'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI'` for the stamp - `HH24`, not `HH`, or afternoon looks
like morning. For the name, `'FMDay'` (or `trim()` around `'Day'`) drops the
blank padding.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two `to_char` calls over the same column. One renders the whole timestamp,
the other only the weekday name.

## Hint 2

`'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI'` for the stamp - `HH24`, not `HH`, or afternoon looks
like morning. For the name, `'FMDay'` (or `trim()` around `'Day'`) drops the
blank padding.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT id,
       to_char(created_at, 'YYYY-MM-DD') || ' ' || to_char(created_at, 'HH24:MI') AS stamp,
       trim(to_char(created_at, 'Day')) AS day_name
FROM orders
WHERE id <= 15
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id,
       to_char(created_at, 'YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI') AS stamp,
       to_char(created_at, 'FMDay') AS day_name
FROM orders
WHERE id <= 15
ORDER BY id;

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`date_trunc` has no 15-minute bucket, so build one: the start of the hour

`date_trunc('hour', ts) + (floor(extract(minute FROM ts) / 15))::int *
interval '15 minutes'`. The alternative is to floor the epoch seconds to a
multiple of 900 and convert back with `to_timestamp`.

Group by the whole bucket expression (or by its ordinal), not by the minute
- and remember the cast before multiplying an interval, because `extract`
returns `numeric`.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`date_trunc` has no 15-minute bucket, so build one: the start of the hour
plus however many whole quarter-hours have passed inside it.

## Hint 2

`date_trunc('hour', ts) + (floor(extract(minute FROM ts) / 15))::int *
interval '15 minutes'`. The alternative is to floor the epoch seconds to a
multiple of 900 and convert back with `to_timestamp`.

## Hint 3

Group by the whole bucket expression (or by its ordinal), not by the minute
- and remember the cast before multiplying an interval, because `extract`
returns `numeric`.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT to_timestamp(floor(extract(epoch FROM ts) / 900) * 900) AS bucket,
       count(*) AS events
FROM events
WHERE id <= 20000
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT date_trunc('hour', ts)
         + (floor(extract(minute FROM ts) / 15))::int * interval '15 minutes' AS bucket,
       count(*) AS events
FROM events
WHERE id <= 20000
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY bucket;

## Exercise 5 - an interval turned into a number

For every member of the `support` department return `id`, `name`,
`hired_on`, and `tenure_months` = whole months of tenure at 2023-11-14,
computed from `age()` as `years * 12 + months`, as an `int`.

**Ordered by `tenure_months` descending, then `id` ascending.**

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`age()` returns years, months and days. Whole months of tenure means the
years converted to months plus the months field - the days are dropped on
purpose.

## Hint 2

`extract(year FROM age(...)) * 12 + extract(month FROM age(...))`, cast to
`int`. Writing `age()` twice is fine; a `LATERAL` subquery naming it once is
tidier.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`age()` returns years, months and days. Whole months of tenure means the
years converted to months plus the months field - the days are dropped on
purpose.

## Hint 2

`extract(year FROM age(...)) * 12 + extract(month FROM age(...))`, cast to
`int`. Writing `age()` twice is fine; a `LATERAL` subquery naming it once is
tidier.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT s.id, s.name, s.hired_on,
       (extract(year FROM a.tenure) * 12 + extract(month FROM a.tenure))::int AS tenure_months
FROM staff s
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT age(DATE '2023-11-14', s.hired_on) AS tenure) a
WHERE s.department = 'support'
ORDER BY 4 DESC, 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, name, hired_on,
       extract(year FROM age(DATE '2023-11-14', hired_on))::int * 12
         + extract(month FROM age(DATE '2023-11-14', hired_on))::int AS tenure_months
FROM staff
WHERE department = 'support'
ORDER BY tenure_months DESC, id;

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One row per customer, whether or not that customer ever ordered - so the
join direction is fixed, and the earliest order is an aggregate over the
right-hand side.

## Hint 2

`LEFT JOIN orders` and `min(o.created_at)`, grouped by the customer; or
reduce `orders` to one row per customer in a CTE and left-join that. Both
give NULL for the customers with no orders.

## Hint 3

Do not patch the NULLs. `NULL - date` is NULL, which is the honest answer
for `days_to_first` when there is no first order; a `coalesce(..., 0)` would
claim they ordered on the day they signed up.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

One row per customer, whether or not that customer ever ordered - so the
join direction is fixed, and the earliest order is an aggregate over the
right-hand side.

## Hint 2

`LEFT JOIN orders` and `min(o.created_at)`, grouped by the customer; or
reduce `orders` to one row per customer in a CTE and left-join that. Both
give NULL for the customers with no orders.

## Hint 3

Do not patch the NULLs. `NULL - date` is NULL, which is the honest answer
for `days_to_first` when there is no first order; a `coalesce(..., 0)` would
claim they ordered on the day they signed up.

references.solution.sql:
WITH firsts AS (
  SELECT customer_id, min(created_at)::date AS first_order
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id)
SELECT c.id AS customer_id,
       c.created_at::date AS signed_up,
       f.first_order,
       f.first_order - c.created_at::date AS days_to_first
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN firsts f ON f.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.id <= 100
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.id AS customer_id,
       c.created_at::date AS signed_up,
       min(o.created_at)::date AS first_order,
       min(o.created_at)::date - c.created_at::date AS days_to_first
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.id <= 100
GROUP BY c.id, c.created_at
ORDER BY c.id;

## Exercise 8 - sessions from a gap rule

For the customers with `customer_id <= 5` in `events`, split their activity
into sessions: a new session starts at a customer's first event, and again
whenever more than 30 minutes have passed since their previous event.
Return `customer_id`, `events` = their total number of events, and
`sessions` = how many sessions that rule produces.

**Ordered by `customer_id` ascending.** (5 rows.)

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A session boundary is a property of one row: either it is the customer's
first event, or the gap since their previous event is too large. Count the
boundaries and you have counted the sessions.

## Hint 2

`lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ts, id)` in a CTE, then a
conditional count in the outer query. The partition is what stops a gap from
being measured across two different customers.

## Hint 3

The first event of each customer has a NULL previous timestamp, and
`NULL > interval '30 minutes'` is NULL rather than true - so the predicate
needs an explicit `prev_ts IS NULL OR ...` branch or the count comes out one
short for everybody.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A session boundary is a property of one row: either it is the customer's
first event, or the gap since their previous event is too large. Count the
boundaries and you have counted the sessions.

## Hint 2

`lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ts, id)` in a CTE, then a
conditional count in the outer query. The partition is what stops a gap from
being measured across two different customers.

## Hint 3

The first event of each customer has a NULL previous timestamp, and
`NULL > interval '30 minutes'` is NULL rather than true - so the predicate
needs an explicit `prev_ts IS NULL OR ...` branch or the count comes out one
short for everybody.

references.solution.sql:
WITH gaps AS (
  SELECT customer_id,
         ts - lag(ts) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ts, id) AS gap
  FROM events
  WHERE customer_id <= 5)
SELECT customer_id,
       count(*) AS events,
       sum(CASE WHEN gap IS NULL OR gap > interval '30 minutes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS sessions
FROM gaps
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

# 101 - Drills: generated calendars, set 1

Eight problems on the one thing `GROUP BY` cannot do: report a period that
has no rows. Grouping invents nothing - a day with no orders simply does not
appear - so when a report must show every day, hour or bucket, the periods
have to come from somewhere else. That somewhere is `generate_series`, and
the pattern is always the same: generate the spine, `LEFT JOIN` the data to
it, and count the data's key so the empty periods come back as zero. Lesson
18 introduced it; this set makes it automatic.

## Exercise 1 - a month of days

Return a single column `day` containing every date in January 2023, from
2023-01-01 to 2023-01-31.

**Ordered by `day` ascending.** (31 rows.)

`month_name` = its three-letter English abbreviation (`Jan`, `Feb`, ...).

**Ordered by `month_start` ascending.** (12 rows.)

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 101_drills_series_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - every day of March, orders or not

For every date in March 2023 return `day` and `orders` = how many orders
were created that day, with 0 for any day that had none.

Generate the days; do not take them from `orders`.

**Ordered by `day` ascending.** (31 rows.)

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 101_drills_series_1 ex3`

For 2023-05-10, return `hour` = the hour of day as an `int` from 0 to 23,

lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 101_drills_series_1

Eight drills on generating the rows your data does not contain. Read after
your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

Every "zero rows for Tuesday" bug has the same cause and the same fix.
`GROUP BY` builds groups out of rows that exist, so a period with no data
produces no group, and the gap in the report is indistinguishable from a
gap in the chart's x-axis. `generate_series` manufactures the periods
independently of the data - it takes a start, a stop (inclusive) and a step,
and works for integers, numerics and timestamps alike - and the calendar
then becomes the left side of a `LEFT JOIN`. Two details make or break the
pattern. Count the *data's* key, `count(o.id)`, not `count(*)`: after an
outer join every calendar row has at least one row, so `count(*)` reports 1
for the empty days. And put the data-side restrictions in the join condition
or in a pre-aggregated CTE, never in the outer `WHERE`, because a `WHERE`
clause that mentions the right-hand table turns your outer join back into an
inner one and deletes the very rows you generated. Pre-aggregating is also
the faster shape: reduce the big table to one row per bucket first, then
join a few dozen calendar rows to a few dozen aggregate rows.

## ex1 - a month of days

What this tested: the bare mechanics. `generate_series(DATE '2023-01-01',
DATE '2023-01-31', interval '1 day')` yields timestamps, so the cast to
`date` is part of the answer, and the stop value is *inclusive* - unlike
almost every range convention in this course, which is worth remembering
before you write `- interval '1 day'` out of habit. It may be called in the
SELECT list or in `FROM`; the `FROM` form is the one that composes.

## ex2 - the twelve month starts

What this tested: that the step can be any interval, months included, and
that month steps are calendar-aware rather than 30-day approximations. The
reference builds the same list from `generate_series(0, 11)` plus month
arithmetic, which is the version to reach for when the periods are not
evenly spaced. The classic mistake is `'Mon'` versus `'MON'` versus `'mon'` -
`to_char` copies the case of the pattern into the output.

## ex3 - every day of March, orders or not

What this tested: the calendar `LEFT JOIN`, in its simplest form. Two things
have to be right at once: the join must be from the calendar to the data,
and the count must be of a column from the data side. `count(*)` would
return 1 for every empty day, which is the single most common bug in this
whole pattern - and a plausible-looking one, because 1 is not obviously
wrong. March happens to have orders every day, which is exactly why this is
a drill and not a discovery.

## ex4 - all twenty-four hours

What this tested: that the spine does not have to be dates. Twenty-four
integers make a perfectly good calendar, joined against the extracted hour;
the reference generates 24 timestamps an hour apart instead and joins on
`date_trunc('hour', ...)`, which generalises better when the report spans
more than one day. The classic mistake is filtering the day in the outer
`WHERE` after an outer join, which silently drops the hours with no orders.

## ex5 - the weeks nobody was hired

What this tested: the anti-join against a generated spine - "which periods
are missing" rather than "how many in each period". `NOT EXISTS` over the
week's half-open range says it directly; the reference's `LEFT JOIN ...
WHERE s.id IS NULL` says the same thing and is the form you will meet more
often. The classic mistake is `hired_on BETWEEN week_start AND week_start +
7`, which makes each week eight days long and lets a Monday hire suppress
two weeks at once.

## ex6 - a histogram with empty bars

What this tested: a numeric series. Buckets are the same problem as days -
an empty bar must still be drawn - and `generate_series(0, 450, 50)` gives
you the bar labels regardless of what the data contains. Compare it with the
`floor(price / 50) * 50` grouping you have written before: that version is
shorter and cannot produce an empty bucket, which makes it right for
exploration and wrong for a chart with a fixed axis.

## ex7 - a running total over a calendar

What this tested: the composition of two patterns. The calendar guarantees
28 rows, and the window function then accumulates over them - which is
precisely why the calendar matters: a running total computed over only the
days that had orders would still be correct at each point but would draw a
misleading line, jumping from the 3rd to the 6th as if nothing happened
between. The model answer aggregates per day first, then sums over the
ordered days with the default running frame.

## ex8 - a dense grid, two dimensions

What this tested: that a spine can have more than one axis. Cross-joining
three departments with twelve months produces the 36 cells the report needs,
and the `LEFT JOIN` fills the ones that have data - the same shape as a
pivot table's skeleton, built explicitly. The classic mistake is joining
`staff` to the months and grouping by department, which produces only the
department-months that actually contain a hire and leaves the report with
ragged rows.

## Further reading

- [Set Returning Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-srf.html) - `generate_series` for numbers and timestamps, and the inclusive stop value.
- [Table Expressions - joins](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) - what `LEFT JOIN` does with unmatched rows, and why a `WHERE` on the right side undoes it.
- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - `count(*)` against `count(expression)`, the distinction that makes the zero-fill work.
- [Window Function Calls](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html#SYNTAX-WINDOW-FUNCTIONS) - the default frame used by the running total in ex7.

# Reading - 101_drills_series_1

Eight drills on generating the rows your data does not contain. Read after
your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

Every "zero rows for Tuesday" bug has the same cause and the same fix.
`GROUP BY` builds groups out of rows that exist, so a period with no data
produces no group, and the gap in the report is indistinguishable from a
gap in the chart's x-axis. `generate_series` manufactures the periods
independently of the data - it takes a start, a stop (inclusive) and a step,
and works for integers, numerics and timestamps alike - and the calendar
then becomes the left side of a `LEFT JOIN`. Two details make or break the
pattern. Count the *data's* key, `count(o.id)`, not `count(*)`: after an
outer join every calendar row has at least one row, so `count(*)` reports 1
for the empty days. And put the data-side restrictions in the join condition
or in a pre-aggregated CTE, never in the outer `WHERE`, because a `WHERE`
clause that mentions the right-hand table turns your outer join back into an
inner one and deletes the very rows you generated. Pre-aggregating is also
the faster shape: reduce the big table to one row per bucket first, then
join a few dozen calendar rows to a few dozen aggregate rows.

## ex1 - a month of days

What this tested: the bare mechanics. `generate_series(DATE '2023-01-01',
DATE '2023-01-31', interval '1 day')` yields timestamps, so the cast to
`date` is part of the answer, and the stop value is *inclusive* - unlike
almost every range convention in this course, which is worth remembering
before you write `- interval '1 day'` out of habit. It may be called in the
SELECT list or in `FROM`; the `FROM` form is the one that composes.

## ex2 - the twelve month starts

What this tested: that the step can be any interval, months included, and
that month steps are calendar-aware rather than 30-day approximations. The
reference builds the same list from `generate_series(0, 11)` plus month
arithmetic, which is the version to reach for when the periods are not
evenly spaced. The classic mistake is `'Mon'` versus `'MON'` versus `'mon'` -
`to_char` copies the case of the pattern into the output.

## ex3 - every day of March, orders or not

What this tested: the calendar `LEFT JOIN`, in its simplest form. Two things
have to be right at once: the join must be from the calendar to the data,
and the count must be of a column from the data side. `count(*)` would
return 1 for every empty day, which is the single most common bug in this
whole pattern - and a plausible-looking one, because 1 is not obviously
wrong. March happens to have orders every day, which is exactly why this is
a drill and not a discovery.

## ex4 - all twenty-four hours

What this tested: that the spine does not have to be dates. Twenty-four
integers make a perfectly good calendar, joined against the extracted hour;
the reference generates 24 timestamps an hour apart instead and joins on
`date_trunc('hour', ...)`, which generalises better when the report spans
more than one day. The classic mistake is filtering the day in the outer
`WHERE` after an outer join, which silently drops the hours with no orders.

## ex5 - the weeks nobody was hired

What this tested: the anti-join against a generated spine - "which periods
are missing" rather than "how many in each period". `NOT EXISTS` over the
week's half-open range says it directly; the reference's `LEFT JOIN ...
WHERE s.id IS NULL` says the same thing and is the form you will meet more
often. The classic mistake is `hired_on BETWEEN week_start AND week_start +
7`, which makes each week eight days long and lets a Monday hire suppress
two weeks at once.

## ex6 - a histogram with empty bars

What this tested: a numeric series. Buckets are the same problem as days -
an empty bar must still be drawn - and `generate_series(0, 450, 50)` gives
you the bar labels regardless of what the data contains. Compare it with the
`floor(price / 50) * 50` grouping you have written before: that version is
shorter and cannot produce an empty bucket, which makes it right for
exploration and wrong for a chart with a fixed axis.

## ex7 - a running total over a calendar

What this tested: the composition of two patterns. The calendar guarantees
28 rows, and the window function then accumulates over them - which is
precisely why the calendar matters: a running total computed over only the
days that had orders would still be correct at each point but would draw a
misleading line, jumping from the 3rd to the 6th as if nothing happened
between. The model answer aggregates per day first, then sums over the
ordered days with the default running frame.

## ex8 - a dense grid, two dimensions

What this tested: that a spine can have more than one axis. Cross-joining
three departments with twelve months produces the 36 cells the report needs,
and the `LEFT JOIN` fills the ones that have data - the same shape as a
pivot table's skeleton, built explicitly. The classic mistake is joining
`staff` to the months and grouping by department, which produces only the
department-months that actually contain a hire and leaves the report with
ragged rows.

## Further reading

- [Set Returning Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-srf.html) - `generate_series` for numbers and timestamps, and the inclusive stop value.
- [Table Expressions - joins](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html) - what `LEFT JOIN` does with unmatched rows, and why a `WHERE` on the right side undoes it.
- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - `count(*)` against `count(expression)`, the distinction that makes the zero-fill work.
- [Window Function Calls](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html#SYNTAX-WINDOW-FUNCTIONS) - the default frame used by the running total in ex7.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Nothing is read from a table here - the rows are manufactured. The function
takes a start, an inclusive stop, and a step.

## Hint 2

`generate_series(DATE '2023-01-01', DATE '2023-01-31', interval '1 day')`
returns timestamps; cast each one to `date`. Put it in `FROM` with an alias,
or call it directly in the SELECT list.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT generate_series(DATE '2023-01-01', DATE '2023-01-31', interval '1 day')::date AS day
ORDER BY day;

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The step does not have to be a day. A month step is calendar-aware, so it
lands on the 1st of every month without any arithmetic on your part.

## Hint 2

`generate_series(DATE '2023-01-01', DATE '2023-12-01', interval '1 month')`,
then `to_char(..., 'Mon')` for the label - the pattern's capitalisation is
copied into the output, so `'Mon'` gives `Jan` and `'MON'` gives `JAN`.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The days come from `generate_series`, the counts come from `orders`, and the
calendar is the left side of the join so that every generated day survives.

## Hint 2

`LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.created_at::date = c.day`, then `count(o.id)`.
Counting `o.id` rather than `*` is what turns a day with no orders into a 0
instead of a 1.

## Hint 3

The faster shape - and the one that scales - is to aggregate `orders` into
one row per day inside a CTE first, then left-join those few rows to the
calendar and `coalesce` the missing counts to 0.

references.solution.sql:
WITH calendar AS (
  SELECT g::date AS day
  FROM generate_series(DATE '2023-03-01', DATE '2023-03-31', interval '1 day') AS g),
daily AS (
  SELECT created_at::date AS day, count(*) AS orders
  FROM orders
  WHERE created_at >= DATE '2023-03-01'
    AND created_at < DATE '2023-04-01'
  GROUP BY 1)
SELECT c.day, coalesce(d.orders, 0) AS orders
FROM calendar c
LEFT JOIN daily d ON d.day = c.day
ORDER BY c.day;
references.expected.sql:
WITH calendar AS (
  SELECT g::date AS day
  FROM generate_series(DATE '2023-03-01', DATE '2023-03-31', interval '1 day') AS g)
SELECT c.day, count(o.id) AS orders
FROM calendar c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.created_at::date = c.day
GROUP BY c.day
ORDER BY c.day;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A spine does not have to be made of dates: twenty-four integers are a
perfectly good axis, joined against the hour extracted from each order.

## Hint 2

`generate_series(0, 23)` on one side; on the other, the orders of
2023-05-10 grouped by `extract(hour FROM created_at)::int`. Keep the day
restriction on the orders side of the join, never in the outer `WHERE`.

## Hint 3

If you prefer timestamps, generate the 24 hourly slots of that day and join
on `date_trunc('hour', created_at) = slot`, then report
`extract(hour FROM slot)::int`. Either way the empty hours must survive.

references.solution.sql:
WITH slots AS (
  SELECT g AS slot
  FROM generate_series(TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-05-10 00:00', TIMESTAMPTZ '2023-05-10 23:00',
                       interval '1 hour') AS g)
SELECT extract(hour FROM s.slot)::int AS hour,
       count(o.id) AS orders
FROM slots s
LEFT JOIN orders o ON date_trunc('hour', o.created_at) = s.slot
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
WITH hours AS (
  SELECT generate_series(0, 23) AS hour),
by_hour AS (
  SELECT extract(hour FROM created_at)::int AS hour, count(*) AS orders
  FROM orders
  WHERE created_at >= DATE '2023-05-10'
    AND created_at < DATE '2023-05-11'
  GROUP BY 1)
SELECT h.hour, coalesce(b.orders, 0) AS orders
FROM hours h
LEFT JOIN by_hour b ON b.hour = h.hour
ORDER BY h.hour;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 - the weeks nobody was hired

Generate the 52 weeks that start on Mondays from 2023-01-02 to 2023-12-25,
and return `week_start` for the weeks in which no member of `staff` was
hired - that is, no `hired_on` falls in `[week_start, week_start + 7)`.

**Ordered by `week_start` ascending.**

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 101_drills_series_1 ex5`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This is an anti-join against a generated spine: keep the weeks for which the
data has nothing to say.

## Hint 2

`NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM staff s WHERE s.hired_on >= w.week_start AND
s.hired_on < w.week_start + 7)`, or the `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE s.id IS NULL`
spelling of the same idea.

## Hint 3

Keep the window half-open. `BETWEEN week_start AND week_start + 7` covers
eight days and lets one Monday hire knock out two weeks. Adding an integer
to a `date` adds days, so `w.week_start + 7` is the following Monday.

## Hint 1

This is an anti-join against a generated spine: keep the weeks for which the
data has nothing to say.

## Hint 2

`NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM staff s WHERE s.hired_on >= w.week_start AND
s.hired_on < w.week_start + 7)`, or the `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE s.id IS NULL`
spelling of the same idea.

## Hint 3

Keep the window half-open. `BETWEEN week_start AND week_start + 7` covers
eight days and lets one Monday hire knock out two weeks. Adding an integer
to a `date` adds days, so `w.week_start + 7` is the following Monday.

references.solution.sql:
WITH weeks AS (
  SELECT g::date AS week_start
  FROM generate_series(DATE '2023-01-02', DATE '2023-12-25', interval '1 week') AS g)
SELECT w.week_start
FROM weeks w
LEFT JOIN staff s
       ON s.hired_on >= w.week_start
      AND s.hired_on < w.week_start + 7
WHERE s.id IS NULL
ORDER BY w.week_start;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The same pattern as the calendars, with numbers instead of dates: the bar
labels are generated, and the products are joined onto them.

## Hint 2

`generate_series(0, 450, 50)` gives the ten bucket starts. Join each product
to its bucket with a half-open range, `price >= bucket_start AND price <
bucket_start + 50`, and count the product key so an empty bucket reports 0.

references.solution.sql:
WITH buckets AS (
  SELECT generate_series(0, 450, 50) AS bucket_start),
hist AS (
  SELECT (floor(price / 50) * 50)::int AS bucket_start, count(*) AS products
  FROM products
  GROUP BY 1)
SELECT b.bucket_start, coalesce(h.products, 0) AS products
FROM buckets b
LEFT JOIN hist h ON h.bucket_start = b.bucket_start
ORDER BY b.bucket_start;
references.expected.sql:
WITH buckets AS (
  SELECT generate_series(0, 450, 50) AS bucket_start)
SELECT b.bucket_start, count(p.id) AS products
FROM buckets b
LEFT JOIN products p ON p.price >= b.bucket_start
                    AND p.price < b.bucket_start + 50
GROUP BY b.bucket_start
ORDER BY b.bucket_start;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two patterns stacked: build the zero-filled daily counts exactly as in ex3,
then accumulate over them. The calendar has to exist before the running
total, or the line would skip the empty days.

## Hint 2

Put the daily counts in a CTE, then `sum(orders) OVER (ORDER BY day)` in the
outer query - an ordered window with no frame clause already means "from the
start up to this row".

## Hint 3

If you prefer to be explicit, `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT
ROW` says the same thing and is worth writing out at least once so the
default stops being magic.

references.solution.sql:
WITH calendar AS (
  SELECT g::date AS day
  FROM generate_series(DATE '2023-02-01', DATE '2023-02-28', interval '1 day') AS g),
counted AS (
  SELECT created_at::date AS day, count(*) AS orders
  FROM orders
  WHERE created_at >= DATE '2023-02-01'
    AND created_at < DATE '2023-03-01'
  GROUP BY 1),
daily AS (
  SELECT c.day, coalesce(n.orders, 0) AS orders
  FROM calendar c
  LEFT JOIN counted n ON n.day = c.day)
SELECT day, orders,
       sum(orders) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS running_orders
FROM daily
ORDER BY day;
references.expected.sql:
WITH calendar AS (
  SELECT g::date AS day
  FROM generate_series(DATE '2023-02-01', DATE '2023-02-28', interval '1 day') AS g),
daily AS (
  SELECT c.day, count(o.id) AS orders
  FROM calendar c
  LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.created_at::date = c.day
  GROUP BY c.day)
SELECT day, orders,
       sum(orders) OVER (ORDER BY day
                         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_orders
FROM daily
ORDER BY day;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 - a dense grid, two dimensions

For each of the three departments `engineering`, `sales`, `support` and each
month of 2023, return `department`, `month_start`, and `hires` = how many
staff of that department were hired in that month, 0 when none were.

Every combination must appear, so the spine is the departments crossed with
the months.

**Ordered by `department` ascending, then `month_start` ascending.** (36
rows.)

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 101_drills_series_1 ex8`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The report has 36 cells and the data will not supply all of them, so both
axes have to be generated: three departments crossed with twelve months.

## Hint 2

A `VALUES` list makes the department axis; `generate_series` with a one-month
step makes the other. `CROSS JOIN` them, then `LEFT JOIN staff` on the
department *and* the month range.

## Hint 3

Every condition about `staff` belongs in the join condition (or in a
pre-aggregated CTE), never in the outer `WHERE` - one `WHERE s.department =
...` would turn the outer join into an inner one and the empty cells would
vanish. Count `s.id`, not `*`.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The report has 36 cells and the data will not supply all of them, so both
axes have to be generated: three departments crossed with twelve months.

## Hint 2

A `VALUES` list makes the department axis; `generate_series` with a one-month
step makes the other. `CROSS JOIN` them, then `LEFT JOIN staff` on the
department *and* the month range.

## Hint 3

Every condition about `staff` belongs in the join condition (or in a
pre-aggregated CTE), never in the outer `WHERE` - one `WHERE s.department =
...` would turn the outer join into an inner one and the empty cells would
vanish. Count `s.id`, not `*`.

references.solution.sql:
WITH months AS (
  SELECT g::date AS month_start
  FROM generate_series(DATE '2023-01-01', DATE '2023-12-01', interval '1 month') AS g),
depts AS (
  SELECT d.department
  FROM (VALUES ('engineering'), ('sales'), ('support')) AS d(department)),
hires AS (
  SELECT department, date_trunc('month', hired_on)::date AS month_start, count(*) AS hires
  FROM staff
  WHERE hired_on >= DATE '2023-01-01'
    AND hired_on < DATE '2024-01-01'
    AND department IN ('engineering', 'sales', 'support')
  GROUP BY 1, 2)
SELECT d.department, m.month_start, coalesce(h.hires, 0) AS hires
FROM depts d
CROSS JOIN months m
LEFT JOIN hires h ON h.department = d.department
                 AND h.month_start = m.month_start
ORDER BY 1, 2;

WITH months AS (
  SELECT g::date AS month_start
  FROM generate_series(DATE '2023-01-01', DATE '2023-12-01', interval '1 month') AS g),
depts AS (

  FROM (VALUES ('engineering'), ('sales'), ('support')) AS d(department))
SELECT d.department, m.month_start, count(s.id) AS hires
FROM depts d
CROSS JOIN months m
LEFT JOIN staff s ON s.department = d.department
                 AND s.hired_on >= m.month_start
                 AND s.hired_on < m.month_start + interval '1 month'
