lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 102_drills_text_1

Eight drills on the string functions you reach for daily. Read after your
attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

The text functions divide into four jobs, and knowing which job you are
doing usually picks the function for you. Measuring and locating -
`length`, `position` - give you numbers, and every one of them is 1-based,
which is the single most common off-by-one in SQL for anyone arriving from a
0-based language. Slicing - `left`, `right`, `substring`, `split_part` -
takes those numbers and returns parts. Assembling - `||`, `concat`,
`format`, `string_agg` - goes the other way, and the important difference is
NULL handling: `'a' || NULL` is NULL, while `concat('a', NULL)` is `'a'`, so
the operator is honest and the function is convenient. Formatting -
`to_char`, `lpad`, `rpad` - is about the shape of the output rather than its
content, and belongs at the very end of a pipeline, never in a grouping key.
One quiet trap runs through all four: `length` counts characters, not bytes,
and on a UTF-8 database that is the number you want but not the number a
`varchar(n)` limit or a byte-oriented API is talking about.

## ex1 - measure and shout

What this tested: the two most basic operations, and the fact that
`length()` and `char_length()` are the same function in PostgreSQL. Neither
is `octet_length`, which counts bytes and differs for any non-ASCII text -
a distinction that costs nothing to know now and saves an afternoon later.
`upper()` is locale-aware, so it is not merely an ASCII arithmetic trick.

## ex2 - tidy and pad

What this tested: `initcap`, which capitalises the first letter of every
word and lower-cases the rest - so `initcap(lower(x))` and `initcap(x)` are
the same thing, and `initcap` is not a safe way to normalise names like
`McDonald`. `rpad(name, 30, '.')` both pads *and truncates* to exactly 30
characters, which is what "fixed width" means and is the classic surprise:
a longer value comes back cut, not overflowing.

## ex3 - find the marker

What this tested: `position(substring IN string)`, which returns a 1-based
index and 0 when the substring is absent - not NULL, which matters when you
subtract from it. The domain length is `length(email) - at_pos`, and it is
worth checking that arithmetic on one example rather than trusting it:
off-by-one here is invisible until somebody reads the output.

## ex4 - one line per product

What this tested: `format()`, the printf of SQL, against manual `||`
concatenation. `format` reads better when there are several pieces and does
not vanish when one of them is NULL, and `%s` casts each argument to text
automatically - which is why the numeric price needs no explicit cast. The
classic mistake with `||` is forgetting that any NULL operand annihilates
the whole expression.

## ex5 - a list in a cell

What this tested: `string_agg`, the aggregate that concatenates instead of
counting - and the fact that it takes its own `ORDER BY` inside the call.
Without that ordering the result is whatever order the rows happened to
arrive in, which makes the output unstable between runs and untestable. The
classic mistake is trying to sort it with the query's outer `ORDER BY`,
which sorts the groups, not the values inside them.

## ex6 - money as text

What this tested: `to_char` on a number, and its habit of reserving a space
for the sign. The `9` pattern right-aligns and pads, so the raw result
begins with blanks; the `FM` prefix ("fill mode") suppresses them, and
`trim()` does the same job after the fact. The classic mistake is comparing
such a string against an expected literal without noticing the leading
space - the values look identical in a terminal.

## ex7 - mask the address

What this tested: composing locate, slice and repeat into one expression -
the shape of every redaction, every "show last four digits", every partial
disclosure. Keeping the length identical is the constraint that makes it
interesting: `repeat('*', at_pos - 2)` is exactly the number of hidden
characters, and getting the `- 2` right requires actually counting on one
example. The reference does it with `overlay`, which replaces a slice in
place and states the intent more directly.

## ex8 - the commonest first word

What this tested: a derived grouping key, plus top-N. `split_part(name, '
', 1)` gives the adjective, the `GROUP BY` counts them, and the tie-break on
the word itself makes the "top five" reproducible when several adjectives
tie - which they will, since the generator draws from a small vocabulary.
The classic mistake is grouping by the alias while ordering by the count and
omitting the second sort key, so the report shuffles between runs.

## Further reading

- [String Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-string.html) - `length`, `position`, `overlay`, `repeat`, `initcap`, `format` and the rest, with their exact signatures.
- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - `string_agg` and `array_agg`, including the `ORDER BY` allowed inside an aggregate call.
- [Data Type Formatting Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-formatting.html) - `to_char` for numbers, the `9` and `0` patterns, and the `FM` prefix.
- [Character Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-character.html) - `text` against `varchar(n)` and `char(n)`, and why the padded type is a trap.

# Reading - 102_drills_text_1

Eight drills on the string functions you reach for daily. Read after your
attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

The text functions divide into four jobs, and knowing which job you are
doing usually picks the function for you. Measuring and locating -
`length`, `position` - give you numbers, and every one of them is 1-based,
which is the single most common off-by-one in SQL for anyone arriving from a
0-based language. Slicing - `left`, `right`, `substring`, `split_part` -
takes those numbers and returns parts. Assembling - `||`, `concat`,
`format`, `string_agg` - goes the other way, and the important difference is
NULL handling: `'a' || NULL` is NULL, while `concat('a', NULL)` is `'a'`, so
the operator is honest and the function is convenient. Formatting -
`to_char`, `lpad`, `rpad` - is about the shape of the output rather than its
content, and belongs at the very end of a pipeline, never in a grouping key.
One quiet trap runs through all four: `length` counts characters, not bytes,
and on a UTF-8 database that is the number you want but not the number a
`varchar(n)` limit or a byte-oriented API is talking about.

## ex1 - measure and shout

What this tested: the two most basic operations, and the fact that
`length()` and `char_length()` are the same function in PostgreSQL. Neither
is `octet_length`, which counts bytes and differs for any non-ASCII text -
a distinction that costs nothing to know now and saves an afternoon later.
`upper()` is locale-aware, so it is not merely an ASCII arithmetic trick.

## ex2 - tidy and pad

What this tested: `initcap`, which capitalises the first letter of every
word and lower-cases the rest - so `initcap(lower(x))` and `initcap(x)` are
the same thing, and `initcap` is not a safe way to normalise names like
`McDonald`. `rpad(name, 30, '.')` both pads *and truncates* to exactly 30
characters, which is what "fixed width" means and is the classic surprise:
a longer value comes back cut, not overflowing.

## ex3 - find the marker

What this tested: `position(substring IN string)`, which returns a 1-based
index and 0 when the substring is absent - not NULL, which matters when you
subtract from it. The domain length is `length(email) - at_pos`, and it is
worth checking that arithmetic on one example rather than trusting it:
off-by-one here is invisible until somebody reads the output.

## ex4 - one line per product

What this tested: `format()`, the printf of SQL, against manual `||`
concatenation. `format` reads better when there are several pieces and does
not vanish when one of them is NULL, and `%s` casts each argument to text
automatically - which is why the numeric price needs no explicit cast. The
classic mistake with `||` is forgetting that any NULL operand annihilates
the whole expression.

## ex5 - a list in a cell

What this tested: `string_agg`, the aggregate that concatenates instead of
counting - and the fact that it takes its own `ORDER BY` inside the call.
Without that ordering the result is whatever order the rows happened to
arrive in, which makes the output unstable between runs and untestable. The
classic mistake is trying to sort it with the query's outer `ORDER BY`,
which sorts the groups, not the values inside them.

## ex6 - money as text

What this tested: `to_char` on a number, and its habit of reserving a space
for the sign. The `9` pattern right-aligns and pads, so the raw result
begins with blanks; the `FM` prefix ("fill mode") suppresses them, and
`trim()` does the same job after the fact. The classic mistake is comparing
such a string against an expected literal without noticing the leading
space - the values look identical in a terminal.

## ex7 - mask the address

What this tested: composing locate, slice and repeat into one expression -
the shape of every redaction, every "show last four digits", every partial
disclosure. Keeping the length identical is the constraint that makes it
interesting: `repeat('*', at_pos - 2)` is exactly the number of hidden
characters, and getting the `- 2` right requires actually counting on one
example. The reference does it with `overlay`, which replaces a slice in
place and states the intent more directly.

## ex8 - the commonest first word

What this tested: a derived grouping key, plus top-N. `split_part(name, '
', 1)` gives the adjective, the `GROUP BY` counts them, and the tie-break on
the word itself makes the "top five" reproducible when several adjectives
tie - which they will, since the generator draws from a small vocabulary.
The classic mistake is grouping by the alias while ordering by the count and
omitting the second sort key, so the report shuffles between runs.

## Further reading

- [String Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-string.html) - `length`, `position`, `overlay`, `repeat`, `initcap`, `format` and the rest, with their exact signatures.
- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - `string_agg` and `array_agg`, including the `ORDER BY` allowed inside an aggregate call.
- [Data Type Formatting Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-formatting.html) - `to_char` for numbers, the `9` and `0` patterns, and the `FM` prefix.
- [Character Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-character.html) - `text` against `varchar(n)` and `char(n)`, and why the padded type is a trap.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

One function title-cases a string; another pads it on the right to a fixed
width with a chosen character.

## Hint 2

`initcap(...)` lower-cases everything it does not capitalise, and
`rpad(name, 30, '.')` fills - or truncates - to exactly 30 characters.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT id, name,
       initcap(name) AS pretty,
       substr(name || repeat('.', 30), 1, 30) AS padded
FROM staff
WHERE id <= 20
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, name,
       initcap(lower(name)) AS pretty,
       rpad(name, 30, '.') AS padded
FROM staff
WHERE id <= 20
ORDER BY id;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

One text column assembled from three values plus fixed punctuation. Mind the
spaces and the parentheses - the gate compares the strings literally.

## Hint 2

`format('%s (%s) costs %s', name, category, price)` casts each argument to
text for you; `concat(...)` or the `||` operator work too, but `||` yields
NULL if any operand is NULL.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT id,
       concat(name, ' (', category, ') costs ', price) AS label
FROM products
WHERE id <= 15
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id,
       format('%s (%s) costs %s', name, category, price) AS label
FROM products
WHERE id <= 15
ORDER BY id;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 - a list in a cell

Among the products with `id <= 60`, return one row per `category`:
`category`, `products` = how many of them it has, and `names` = their names
joined into one string with `, ` between them, **in ascending `id` order**.

**Ordered by `category` ascending.**

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 102_drills_text_1 ex5`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An aggregate that concatenates instead of counting. Like every aggregate it
runs per group, and like no other it cares about the order of its input.

## Hint 2

`string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY id)` - the `ORDER BY` goes *inside* the
aggregate call. The query's own `ORDER BY` sorts the six output rows and has
no influence on the order inside each string.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three pieces: the first character, a run of stars as long as the hidden
part, and everything from the `@` onwards. Locate the `@` first; everything
else is arithmetic around that position.

## Hint 2

`repeat('*', position('@' IN email) - 2)` is the star run - count it on
`user1@example.com` to convince yourself of the `- 2`. Then glue the pieces
with `||`, or replace the slice in place with `overlay`.

## Hint 3

`substring(email FROM position('@' IN email))` returns the `@` and
everything after it, so the three pieces reassemble to the original length.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT id, email,
       overlay(email PLACING repeat('*', position('@' IN email) - 2)
                     FROM 2 FOR position('@' IN email) - 2) AS masked
FROM customers
WHERE id <= 30
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, email,
       left(email, 1)
         || repeat('*', position('@' IN email) - 2)
         || substring(email FROM position('@' IN email)) AS masked
FROM customers
WHERE id <= 30
ORDER BY id;

lessons.briefing:
# 103 - Drills: regular expressions, set 1

Eight problems on PostgreSQL's POSIX regular expressions - the `~` family of
operators plus `substring`, `regexp_replace`, `regexp_match` and
`regexp_split_to_array`. Lesson 19 introduced pattern matching on this
dataset; here you test, extract, rewrite and split with patterns rather than
with positions.

Two rules of the road. `~` is case-sensitive and `~*` is not; `!~` is the
negation. And a pattern is anchored only where you say so - `'[0-9]+'`
matches a digit *anywhere* in the string, which is usually not the question
you meant to ask.

## Exercise 1 - does it match

For the customers with `id <= 20` return `id`, `email`, and `two_digit_id` =
a boolean, true when the address begins with `user` followed by exactly two
digits and then the `@`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (20 rows.)

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 103_drills_regex_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - the pattern as a filter

Return `id` and `email` for every customer whose whole address matches
`user` + exactly two digits + `@example.com` - anchored at both ends, with
the dot treated as a literal dot.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (90 rows.)

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 103_drills_regex_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - pull out the number

Product names end in a number. For the products with `id <= 20` return `id`,
`name`, and `trailing_number` = that trailing run of digits, as text.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (20 rows.)

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 103_drills_regex_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - take the number off

# Reading - 103_drills_regex_1

Eight drills on POSIX regular expressions inside SQL: testing, filtering,
extracting, rewriting and splitting. Read after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

PostgreSQL offers three pattern languages and it is worth knowing why. `LIKE`
is simple and indexable with the right operator class; `SIMILAR TO` is a
regrettable SQL-standard hybrid that nobody should reach for; POSIX regular
expressions - `~`, `~*`, `!~`, `substring(x FROM pattern)`,
`regexp_replace`, `regexp_match`, `regexp_split_to_array` - are the real
tool. Three habits keep them honest. Anchor deliberately: without `^` and
`$` a pattern matches anywhere, so `'[0-9]{2}'` is true for a
three-digit string too. Escape the characters that mean something - a bare
`.` matches any character, which makes `'user@example.com'` match
`'userXexample!com'` as well. And remember that a regular expression cannot
use an ordinary B-tree index, so a `WHERE name ~ '...'` on a large table is
a sequential scan; when the pattern is a plain prefix, `LIKE 'abc%'` can use
an index and the regex cannot.

## ex1 - does it match

What this tested: that `~` is an operator returning a boolean, so it belongs
in a SELECT list as comfortably as in a `WHERE`. Seeing the true and false
values side by side with the data is the fastest way to debug a pattern -
much faster than filtering and wondering why nothing came back. The classic
mistake is omitting the `^`, which would let a match start anywhere in the
address.

## ex2 - the pattern as a filter

What this tested: full anchoring, and escaping the dot. `^...$` pins the
pattern to the whole string; `\.` (or a bracketed `[.]`) makes the dot
literal rather than "any character". Ninety rows is the check: exactly the
customers with two-digit ids, from 10 to 99. The classic mistake -
forgetting the escape - passes this dataset silently, because every address
really does contain a dot there, and only breaks on data you have not seen.

## ex3 - pull out the number

What this tested: `substring(string FROM pattern)`, which returns the
matching text rather than a boolean - and returns NULL when there is no
match, which is the behaviour that makes it usable in a SELECT list. The
`$` anchor is what makes it the *trailing* number; without it the pattern
would still find the same digits here, but only because there is nothing
earlier to find.

## ex4 - take the number off

What this tested: `regexp_replace`, and the fact that the space is part of
what has to go. Matching `'\s*[0-9]+$'` consumes the separator too, which is
tidier than replacing the digits and then trimming - though the reference
shows the trim version, because in real data you rarely know which
whitespace is there. Note that `regexp_replace` without the `'g'` flag
replaces the first match only, which is correct here and wrong in ex6.

## ex5 - a case-insensitive census

What this tested: `~*` inside a `FILTER` clause - a conditional aggregate
whose condition happens to be a pattern. The alternative,
`lower(name) ~ '^[aeiou]'`, is equally correct and is the one that can use a
functional index. The classic mistake is `~ '^[aeiouAEIOU]'`, which works
until somebody adds an accented character and quietly stops.

## ex6 - strip the punctuation

What this tested: the `'g'` flag. Without it `regexp_replace` removes only
the first offending character, so `Dr. Barbara Collins PhD` loses its dot
and keeps everything else - a bug that looks like a success on most rows.
The character class is negated: `[^A-Za-z ]` is "anything that is not a
letter or a space", and `[^[:alpha:] ]` is the locale-aware spelling of the
same idea.

## ex7 - three captures at once

What this tested: capture groups. `regexp_match` returns a `text[]` of the
groups - not of the whole match - so `[1]`, `[2]`, `[3]` are the three
pieces, and the array is NULL when the pattern does not match at all, which
propagates cleanly. The classic mistake is expecting element 0 to hold the
full match, as in most programming languages; PostgreSQL arrays start at 1
and `regexp_match` returns only the groups. The reference uses
`regexp_replace` with backreferences instead, which is the trick to reach
for when you want the pieces reassembled rather than separated.

## ex8 - the names that do not fit

What this tested: negation plus splitting - the shape of a data-quality
audit. `!~` finds the rows a well-formed pattern rejects, and
`regexp_split_to_array` then measures how far off they are; `array_length`
of the result is the number of pieces. The classic mistake is `NOT name ~
'...'` written as `name ~ 'NOT...'` or, more subtly, an unanchored pattern,
which would accept `Dr. Barbara Collins PhD` because two plain words do
appear somewhere inside it.

## Further reading

- [Pattern Matching](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-matching.html) - `LIKE`, `SIMILAR TO` and the POSIX regular expressions, with the full metacharacter table.
- [POSIX regular expression details](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-matching.html#POSIX-SYNTAX-DETAILS) - greediness, bracket expressions and the character classes such as `[:alpha:]`.
- [String Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-string.html) - `substring`, `regexp_replace`, `regexp_match`, `regexp_split_to_array` and their flag arguments.
- [Indexes on expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-expressional.html) - how `lower(col)` can be indexed when a case-insensitive pattern cannot.

# Reading - 103_drills_regex_1

Eight drills on POSIX regular expressions inside SQL: testing, filtering,
extracting, rewriting and splitting. Read after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

PostgreSQL offers three pattern languages and it is worth knowing why. `LIKE`
is simple and indexable with the right operator class; `SIMILAR TO` is a
regrettable SQL-standard hybrid that nobody should reach for; POSIX regular
expressions - `~`, `~*`, `!~`, `substring(x FROM pattern)`,
`regexp_replace`, `regexp_match`, `regexp_split_to_array` - are the real
tool. Three habits keep them honest. Anchor deliberately: without `^` and
`$` a pattern matches anywhere, so `'[0-9]{2}'` is true for a
three-digit string too. Escape the characters that mean something - a bare
`.` matches any character, which makes `'user@example.com'` match
`'userXexample!com'` as well. And remember that a regular expression cannot
use an ordinary B-tree index, so a `WHERE name ~ '...'` on a large table is
a sequential scan; when the pattern is a plain prefix, `LIKE 'abc%'` can use
an index and the regex cannot.

## ex1 - does it match

What this tested: that `~` is an operator returning a boolean, so it belongs
in a SELECT list as comfortably as in a `WHERE`. Seeing the true and false
values side by side with the data is the fastest way to debug a pattern -
much faster than filtering and wondering why nothing came back. The classic
mistake is omitting the `^`, which would let a match start anywhere in the
address.

## ex2 - the pattern as a filter

What this tested: full anchoring, and escaping the dot. `^...$` pins the
pattern to the whole string; `\.` (or a bracketed `[.]`) makes the dot
literal rather than "any character". Ninety rows is the check: exactly the
customers with two-digit ids, from 10 to 99. The classic mistake -
forgetting the escape - passes this dataset silently, because every address
really does contain a dot there, and only breaks on data you have not seen.

## ex3 - pull out the number

What this tested: `substring(string FROM pattern)`, which returns the
matching text rather than a boolean - and returns NULL when there is no
match, which is the behaviour that makes it usable in a SELECT list. The
`$` anchor is what makes it the *trailing* number; without it the pattern
would still find the same digits here, but only because there is nothing
earlier to find.

## ex4 - take the number off

What this tested: `regexp_replace`, and the fact that the space is part of
what has to go. Matching `'\s*[0-9]+$'` consumes the separator too, which is
tidier than replacing the digits and then trimming - though the reference
shows the trim version, because in real data you rarely know which
whitespace is there. Note that `regexp_replace` without the `'g'` flag
replaces the first match only, which is correct here and wrong in ex6.

## ex5 - a case-insensitive census

What this tested: `~*` inside a `FILTER` clause - a conditional aggregate
whose condition happens to be a pattern. The alternative,
`lower(name) ~ '^[aeiou]'`, is equally correct and is the one that can use a
functional index. The classic mistake is `~ '^[aeiouAEIOU]'`, which works
until somebody adds an accented character and quietly stops.

## ex6 - strip the punctuation

What this tested: the `'g'` flag. Without it `regexp_replace` removes only
the first offending character, so `Dr. Barbara Collins PhD` loses its dot
and keeps everything else - a bug that looks like a success on most rows.
The character class is negated: `[^A-Za-z ]` is "anything that is not a
letter or a space", and `[^[:alpha:] ]` is the locale-aware spelling of the
same idea.

## ex7 - three captures at once

What this tested: capture groups. `regexp_match` returns a `text[]` of the
groups - not of the whole match - so `[1]`, `[2]`, `[3]` are the three
pieces, and the array is NULL when the pattern does not match at all, which
propagates cleanly. The classic mistake is expecting element 0 to hold the
full match, as in most programming languages; PostgreSQL arrays start at 1
and `regexp_match` returns only the groups. The reference uses
`regexp_replace` with backreferences instead, which is the trick to reach
for when you want the pieces reassembled rather than separated.

## ex8 - the names that do not fit

What this tested: negation plus splitting - the shape of a data-quality
audit. `!~` finds the rows a well-formed pattern rejects, and
`regexp_split_to_array` then measures how far off they are; `array_length`
of the result is the number of pieces. The classic mistake is `NOT name ~
'...'` written as `name ~ 'NOT...'` or, more subtly, an unanchored pattern,
which would accept `Dr. Barbara Collins PhD` because two plain words do
appear somewhere inside it.

## Further reading

- [Pattern Matching](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-matching.html) - `LIKE`, `SIMILAR TO` and the POSIX regular expressions, with the full metacharacter table.
- [POSIX regular expression details](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-matching.html#POSIX-SYNTAX-DETAILS) - greediness, bracket expressions and the character classes such as `[:alpha:]`.
- [String Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-string.html) - `substring`, `regexp_replace`, `regexp_match`, `regexp_split_to_array` and their flag arguments.
- [Indexes on expressions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/indexes-expressional.html) - how `lower(col)` can be indexed when a case-insensitive pattern cannot.

## Exercise 1 - does it match

For the customers with `id <= 20` return `id`, `email`, and `two_digit_id` =
a boolean, true when the address begins with `user` followed by exactly two

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The match operator returns a boolean, so it can be a column. The pattern has
to be anchored at the start and has to say "exactly two digits".

## Hint 2

`email ~ '^user[0-9]{2}@'`. The `{2}` is the repetition count; `^` pins the
match to the beginning, and the `@` after the digits stops a three-digit id
from matching.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The match operator returns a boolean, so it can be a column. The pattern has
to be anchored at the start and has to say "exactly two digits".

## Hint 2

`email ~ '^user[0-9]{2}@'`. The `{2}` is the repetition count; `^` pins the
match to the beginning, and the `@` after the digits stops a three-digit id
from matching.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT id, email,
       email ~ '^user[[:digit:]][[:digit:]]@' AS two_digit_id
FROM customers
WHERE id <= 20
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, email,
       email ~ '^user[0-9]{2}@' AS two_digit_id
FROM customers
WHERE id <= 20
ORDER BY id;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 - the pattern as a filter

Return `id` and `email` for every customer whose whole address matches
`user` + exactly two digits + `@example.com` - anchored at both ends, with
the dot treated as a literal dot.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (90 rows.)

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 103_drills_regex_1 ex2`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Same pattern as ex1, now in `WHERE` and anchored at both ends so the whole
address has to match, not just its beginning.

## Hint 2

`^user[0-9]{2}@example\.com$`. The backslash makes the dot a literal dot -
without it the pattern also accepts `example!com`. A bracketed `[.]` says
the same thing without the escape.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Replace the part you do not want with the empty string. Remember the space
in front of the number - it has to disappear too, or every result ends in a
blank.

## Hint 2

`regexp_replace(name, '\s*[0-9]+$', '')` swallows the separator along with
the digits. Replacing only the digits and then calling `btrim()` is the
equally valid two-step version.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT id, name,
       btrim(regexp_replace(name, '[0-9]+$', '')) AS base_name
FROM products
WHERE id <= 20
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, name,
       regexp_replace(name, '\s*[0-9]+$', '') AS base_name
FROM products
WHERE id <= 20
ORDER BY id;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Delete everything that is not a letter or a space - so the character class
is a negated one, and the replacement is the empty string.

## Hint 2

`regexp_replace(name, '[^A-Za-z ]', '', 'g')`. The `'g'` flag is the whole
exercise: without it only the first punctuation character is removed, which
looks like it worked on most rows.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT id, name,
       regexp_replace(name, '[^[:alpha:] ]+', '', 'g') AS letters_only
FROM staff
WHERE id <= 30
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, name,
       regexp_replace(name, '[^A-Za-z ]', '', 'g') AS letters_only
FROM staff
WHERE id <= 30
ORDER BY id;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 - three captures at once

For the products with `id <= 20` return `id`, `adjective` = the first word,
`noun` = the second word, and `tag` = the trailing number as an `int`,
extracted with a single anchored pattern of three capture groups.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (20 rows.)

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 103_drills_regex_1 ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One pattern, three parenthesised groups, anchored at both ends so the whole
name has to fit the shape `word word number`.

## Hint 2

`regexp_match(name, '^(\S+) (\S+) ([0-9]+)$')` returns a `text[]` holding
the captures. Subscript it: `[1]`, `[2]`, `[3]` - PostgreSQL arrays are
1-based and the array holds only the groups, not the whole match.

## Hint 3

The third capture is text, so cast it to `int` for the `tag` column. The
other way round is `regexp_replace` with the backreferences `\1`, `\2`,
`\3` as the replacement string.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

One pattern, three parenthesised groups, anchored at both ends so the whole
name has to fit the shape `word word number`.

## Hint 2

`regexp_match(name, '^(\S+) (\S+) ([0-9]+)$')` returns a `text[]` holding
the captures. Subscript it: `[1]`, `[2]`, `[3]` - PostgreSQL arrays are
1-based and the array holds only the groups, not the whole match.

## Hint 3

The third capture is text, so cast it to `int` for the `tag` column. The
other way round is `regexp_replace` with the backreferences `\1`, `\2`,
`\3` as the replacement string.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT id,
       regexp_replace(name, '^(\S+) (\S+) ([0-9]+)$', '\1') AS adjective,
       regexp_replace(name, '^(\S+) (\S+) ([0-9]+)$', '\2') AS noun,
       regexp_replace(name, '^(\S+) (\S+) ([0-9]+)$', '\3')::int AS tag
FROM products
WHERE id <= 20
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id,
       (regexp_match(name, '^(\S+) (\S+) ([0-9]+)$'))[1] AS adjective,
       (regexp_match(name, '^(\S+) (\S+) ([0-9]+)$'))[2] AS noun,
       ((regexp_match(name, '^(\S+) (\S+) ([0-9]+)$'))[3])::int AS tag
FROM products
WHERE id <= 20
ORDER BY id;

lessons.briefing:
# 104 - Drills: jsonb, set 1

Eight problems on the `attributes` document every product carries - a small
`jsonb` object with a `color`, a `size`, and a `tags` array of two labels.
Lesson 19 introduced `->`, `->>` and containment; this set adds the path
operators, key and element existence, the functions that expand a document
into rows, and the ones that build a document back up.

Keep the two arrow operators straight: `->` returns `jsonb` (so it can be
chained), `->>` returns `text` (so it can be compared to a string, cast, or
grouped). Nearly every jsonb bug is one of them where the other belonged.

## Exercise 1 - two fields, two shapes

For the products with `id <= 20` return `id`, `size` = the `size` attribute
as text, and `tag_count` = the number of elements in the `tags` array, as an
`int`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (20 rows.)

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 104_drills_jsonb_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - a census on a document field

Return one row per distinct `size`: `size` (as text) and `products` = how
many products carry it.

**Ordered by `size` ascending.** (4 rows.)

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 104_drills_jsonb_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - reaching in by path

For the products with `id <= 20` return `id`, `first_tag` = the first
element of `tags` as **text**, and `tags` = the whole `tags` array as
**jsonb**.

Use the path operators `#>` and `#>>` for at least one of the two columns.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (20 rows.)

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 104_drills_jsonb_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - does the array contain it

Return `id` and `name` for every product with `id <= 200` whose `tags` array
contains the label `premium`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 104_drills_jsonb_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - the document as rows

For the products with `id <= 10`, expand the attributes into one row per
key, **excluding** the `tags` array. Return `id`, `key`, and `value`, both
as text.

**Ordered by `id` ascending, then `key` ascending.** (20 rows.)

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 104_drills_jsonb_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - build a document

For the products with `id <= 10` return `id` and `doc` = a `jsonb` object
with exactly three keys: `name` (the product name), `price` (the price as a
JSON number), and `color` (the colour attribute as a JSON string).

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (10 rows.)

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 104_drills_jsonb_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - a JSON array per group

Among the products with `id <= 30`, return one row per `category`:
`category`, `products` = how many there are, and `names` = a `jsonb` array
of their names **in ascending `id` order**.

**Ordered by `category` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 104_drills_jsonb_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - a pivot over a document field

Return one row per `color`: `color` (as text), `products` = how many
products have it, `on_sale` = how many of those also carry the `sale` tag,
and `pct_sale` = `round(100.0 * on_sale / products, 1)`.

**Ordered by `color` ascending.** (5 rows.)

lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 104_drills_jsonb_1

Eight drills on reading, expanding and building `jsonb` documents. Read
after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

`jsonb` is a parsed, binary representation: keys are deduplicated and
reordered, whitespace is gone, and lookups are fast - unlike `json`, which
stores the original text and reparses it every time you touch it. Store
`jsonb` unless you need the source bytes back verbatim. The access operators
come in pairs, and the rule is mechanical: the single-arrow forms `->` and
`#>` return `jsonb`, so they chain and can be compared to other documents;
the double-arrow forms `->>` and `#>>` return `text`, so they end a chain
and are what you compare to strings, cast to numbers, or group by. Two
different questions hide behind similar-looking operators, too: `?` asks
whether a *key* exists in an object or a *string element* exists in an
array, while `@>` asks whether one document contains another, which is the
one a GIN index supports best. And when a document has to become rows, the
expanders (`jsonb_each`, `jsonb_each_text`, `jsonb_array_elements`,
`jsonb_array_elements_text`) are set-returning functions, so they belong in
`FROM`, usually behind a `LATERAL`.

## ex1 - two fields, two shapes

What this tested: the arrow pair and one array function. `attributes ->>
'size'` yields text; had you written `->` the column would be a JSON string
including its quotes, which prints almost identically and compares
differently - a bug that survives a casual eyeball. `jsonb_array_length`
saves you from expanding the array just to count it.

## ex2 - a census on a document field

What this tested: grouping by a document field, which is exactly like
grouping by any other expression once `->>` has produced text. The classic
mistake is `GROUP BY attributes -> 'size'`, which groups the JSON values -
it happens to give the same four groups here, but the labels come back
quoted and the type is wrong for anything downstream. Four sizes is the
check.

## ex3 - reaching in by path

What this tested: `#>` and `#>>`, which take an array of path steps and walk
them - `'{tags,0}'` means "the `tags` key, then element 0". They matter as
soon as documents nest, because `a -> 'b' -> 'c' ->> 'd'` becomes a path in
one operator. Array indexing is 0-based here, unlike SQL arrays, which are
1-based: the two conventions sit side by side in the same query and the
mismatch is a genuine source of bugs.

## ex4 - does the array contain it

What this tested: `?` on an array, which tests for a string *element*, not
for a key - the same operator does both jobs depending on what is to its
left. The reference uses containment, `attributes @> '{"tags":["premium"]}'`,
which is the form a GIN index on the whole column accelerates; `?` is
supported by the default GIN operator class too, but only when applied to
the indexed column itself, not to an expression of it. The classic mistake
is `attributes ->> 'tags' LIKE '%premium%'`, which treats a document as a
string and will happily match a tag called `premium-refurbished`.

## ex5 - the document as rows

What this tested: expanding an object into key/value rows, and the `-`
operator that removes a key from a document before you do. Both are worth
knowing: `jsonb_each_text` is the generic way to inspect documents whose
shape you do not know in advance, and `attributes - 'tags'` is the tidiest
way to say "everything except". The classic mistake is calling a
set-returning function in the SELECT list; it works in PostgreSQL, but
`CROSS JOIN LATERAL` in `FROM` is what other people can read.

## ex6 - build a document

What this tested: construction rather than extraction. `jsonb_build_object`
takes alternating keys and values and infers each value's JSON type - the
numeric price becomes a JSON number, not a string, which is the detail the
gate checks. The reference builds the same object with `to_jsonb` over a
one-row subquery, which is the trick for turning a whole record into a
document without naming every key twice.

## ex7 - a JSON array per group

What this tested: `jsonb_agg`, an ordinary aggregate that happens to produce
a document - and, like `string_agg`, one that takes its own `ORDER BY`
inside the call. Without it the array's element order is whatever the
aggregation produced, which is unstable between runs and therefore untestable.
Aggregating into JSON is how a report hands a nested result to an
application in one round trip instead of N.

## ex8 - a pivot over a document field

What this tested: everything at once - a document field as the grouping key,
an existence test inside a `FILTER`, and a ratio over two aggregates. Note
that `count(*) FILTER (WHERE attributes -> 'tags' ? 'sale')` reads a
document twice per row and cannot use an index for the filter, which is
fine at ten thousand rows and would not be at ten million; that is the point
at which the tag would be promoted to a real column or an expression index.
The classic mistake remains integer division - keep the `100.0`.

## Further reading

- [JSON Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-json.html) - `json` against `jsonb`, and what jsonb normalises away.
- [JSON Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-json.html) - the full operator table (`->`, `->>`, `#>`, `#>>`, `?`, `@>`, `-`) and the expanders and builders.
- [jsonb Indexing](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-json.html#JSON-INDEXING) - which operators a GIN index can serve, and the `jsonb_path_ops` opclass.
- [Set Returning Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-srf.html) - why `jsonb_each` and friends belong in `FROM`.

# 104 - Drills: jsonb, set 1

Eight problems on the `attributes` document every product carries - a small
`jsonb` object with a `color`, a `size`, and a `tags` array of two labels.
Lesson 19 introduced `->`, `->>` and containment; this set adds the path
operators, key and element existence, the functions that expand a document
into rows, and the ones that build a document back up.

Keep the two arrow operators straight: `->` returns `jsonb` (so it can be
chained), `->>` returns `text` (so it can be compared to a string, cast, or
grouped). Nearly every jsonb bug is one of them where the other belonged.

# Reading - 104_drills_jsonb_1

Eight drills on reading, expanding and building `jsonb` documents. Read
after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

`jsonb` is a parsed, binary representation: keys are deduplicated and
reordered, whitespace is gone, and lookups are fast - unlike `json`, which
stores the original text and reparses it every time you touch it. Store
`jsonb` unless you need the source bytes back verbatim. The access operators
come in pairs, and the rule is mechanical: the single-arrow forms `->` and
`#>` return `jsonb`, so they chain and can be compared to other documents;
the double-arrow forms `->>` and `#>>` return `text`, so they end a chain
and are what you compare to strings, cast to numbers, or group by. Two
different questions hide behind similar-looking operators, too: `?` asks
whether a *key* exists in an object or a *string element* exists in an
array, while `@>` asks whether one document contains another, which is the
one a GIN index supports best. And when a document has to become rows, the
expanders (`jsonb_each`, `jsonb_each_text`, `jsonb_array_elements`,
`jsonb_array_elements_text`) are set-returning functions, so they belong in
`FROM`, usually behind a `LATERAL`.

## ex1 - two fields, two shapes

What this tested: the arrow pair and one array function. `attributes ->>
'size'` yields text; had you written `->` the column would be a JSON string
including its quotes, which prints almost identically and compares
differently - a bug that survives a casual eyeball. `jsonb_array_length`
saves you from expanding the array just to count it.

## ex2 - a census on a document field

What this tested: grouping by a document field, which is exactly like
grouping by any other expression once `->>` has produced text. The classic
mistake is `GROUP BY attributes -> 'size'`, which groups the JSON values -
it happens to give the same four groups here, but the labels come back
quoted and the type is wrong for anything downstream. Four sizes is the
check.

## ex3 - reaching in by path

What this tested: `#>` and `#>>`, which take an array of path steps and walk
them - `'{tags,0}'` means "the `tags` key, then element 0". They matter as
soon as documents nest, because `a -> 'b' -> 'c' ->> 'd'` becomes a path in
one operator. Array indexing is 0-based here, unlike SQL arrays, which are
1-based: the two conventions sit side by side in the same query and the
mismatch is a genuine source of bugs.

## ex4 - does the array contain it

What this tested: `?` on an array, which tests for a string *element*, not
for a key - the same operator does both jobs depending on what is to its
left. The reference uses containment, `attributes @> '{"tags":["premium"]}'`,
which is the form a GIN index on the whole column accelerates; `?` is
supported by the default GIN operator class too, but only when applied to
the indexed column itself, not to an expression of it. The classic mistake
is `attributes ->> 'tags' LIKE '%premium%'`, which treats a document as a
string and will happily match a tag called `premium-refurbished`.

## ex5 - the document as rows

What this tested: expanding an object into key/value rows, and the `-`
operator that removes a key from a document before you do. Both are worth
knowing: `jsonb_each_text` is the generic way to inspect documents whose
shape you do not know in advance, and `attributes - 'tags'` is the tidiest
way to say "everything except". The classic mistake is calling a
set-returning function in the SELECT list; it works in PostgreSQL, but
`CROSS JOIN LATERAL` in `FROM` is what other people can read.

## ex6 - build a document

What this tested: construction rather than extraction. `jsonb_build_object`
takes alternating keys and values and infers each value's JSON type - the
numeric price becomes a JSON number, not a string, which is the detail the
gate checks. The reference builds the same object with `to_jsonb` over a
one-row subquery, which is the trick for turning a whole record into a
document without naming every key twice.

## ex7 - a JSON array per group

What this tested: `jsonb_agg`, an ordinary aggregate that happens to produce
a document - and, like `string_agg`, one that takes its own `ORDER BY`
inside the call. Without it the array's element order is whatever the
aggregation produced, which is unstable between runs and therefore untestable.
Aggregating into JSON is how a report hands a nested result to an
application in one round trip instead of N.

## ex8 - a pivot over a document field

What this tested: everything at once - a document field as the grouping key,
an existence test inside a `FILTER`, and a ratio over two aggregates. Note
that `count(*) FILTER (WHERE attributes -> 'tags' ? 'sale')` reads a
document twice per row and cannot use an index for the filter, which is
fine at ten thousand rows and would not be at ten million; that is the point
at which the tag would be promoted to a real column or an expression index.
The classic mistake remains integer division - keep the `100.0`.

## Further reading

- [JSON Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-json.html) - `json` against `jsonb`, and what jsonb normalises away.
- [JSON Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-json.html) - the full operator table (`->`, `->>`, `#>`, `#>>`, `?`, `@>`, `-`) and the expanders and builders.
- [jsonb Indexing](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-json.html#JSON-INDEXING) - which operators a GIN index can serve, and the `jsonb_path_ops` opclass.
- [Set Returning Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-srf.html) - why `jsonb_each` and friends belong in `FROM`.

## Hint 1

Two steps into the document: the `tags` key, then its first element. The
path operators take both steps in one go.

## Hint 2

`attributes #>> '{tags,0}'` returns the first tag as text; `attributes #>
'{tags}'` returns the array as `jsonb`. Array elements are numbered from 0,
not from 1.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT id,
       attributes->'tags'->>0 AS first_tag,
       attributes->'tags' AS tags
FROM products
WHERE id <= 20
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id,
       attributes #>> '{tags,0}' AS first_tag,
       attributes #> '{tags}' AS tags
FROM products
WHERE id <= 20
ORDER BY id;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

This one builds a document rather than reading one. The function takes the
keys and values as alternating arguments.

## Hint 2

`jsonb_build_object('name', name, 'price', price, 'color',
attributes->>'color')`. Pass `price` as the numeric column, not as text, so
it lands in the document as a JSON number.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT p.id, to_jsonb(t) AS doc
FROM products p
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT p.name AS name, p.price AS price,
         p.attributes->>'color' AS color) t
WHERE p.id <= 10
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id,
       jsonb_build_object('name', name, 'price', price,
                          'color', attributes->>'color') AS doc
FROM products
WHERE id <= 10
ORDER BY id;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 - a JSON array per group

Among the products with `id <= 30`, return one row per `category`:
`category`, `products` = how many there are, and `names` = a `jsonb` array
of their names **in ascending `id` order**.

**Ordered by `category` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 104_drills_jsonb_1 ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An aggregate that returns a JSON array instead of a number. Like every
aggregate it runs once per group.

## Hint 2

`jsonb_agg(name ORDER BY id)` - the `ORDER BY` sits inside the aggregate
call and fixes the order of the elements. The query's own `ORDER BY` only
sorts the output rows.

## Hint 3

`to_jsonb(array_agg(name ORDER BY id))` produces the identical array by
building a SQL array first; either is fine, and both need the inner
ordering to be reproducible.

## Hint 1

An aggregate that returns a JSON array instead of a number. Like every
aggregate it runs once per group.

## Hint 2

`jsonb_agg(name ORDER BY id)` - the `ORDER BY` sits inside the aggregate
call and fixes the order of the elements. The query's own `ORDER BY` only
sorts the output rows.

## Hint 3

`to_jsonb(array_agg(name ORDER BY id))` produces the identical array by
building a SQL array first; either is fine, and both need the inner
ordering to be reproducible.

SELECT category,
       count(id) AS products,
       to_jsonb(array_agg(name ORDER BY id)) AS names
FROM products
WHERE id <= 30
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT category,
       count(*) AS products,
       jsonb_agg(name ORDER BY id) AS names
FROM products
WHERE id <= 30
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY category;

# 105 - Drills: JSONB, set 2

Eight problems that take lesson 19's JSONB toolbox to the `events` stream:
every event carries a `payload` like `{"path": "/p/1234", "value": 618}`, and
every product still carries its `attributes` document. If `->` versus `->>`,
containment with `@>`, or `jsonb_array_elements_text` feel shaky, reread
lesson 19 before starting - this set assumes all three.

## Exercise 1 - the path out of the payload

For the events with `id <= 15`, return `id` and `path` = the payload's `path`
key, as text.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (15 rows.)

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 105_drills_jsonb_2 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - the number inside the path

Every path has the shape `/p/<product id>`. For the events with `id <= 25`,
return `id` and `product_id` = the id embedded in the path, **as an
integer**, not text.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (25 rows.)

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 105_drills_jsonb_2 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - payloads pinned at the ceiling

The payload's `value` runs from 0 to 1000. How many events hit exactly 1000?
Return one row, one column `hits`. Write the condition as a containment test
(`@>`) - the extract-and-cast version is in the hints, and it is worth having
written both at least once.

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 105_drills_jsonb_2 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - the average value per event type

For each `event_type`, return `event_type` and `avg_value` = the average of
the payload's `value`, rounded to 1 decimal place. Remember what `->>`
returns: text averages badly.

**Ordered by `event_type` ascending.** (5 rows.)

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 105_drills_jsonb_2 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - the garden tag report

For `garden` products only: explode the `tags` array and return one row per
`tag` with `products` = how many garden products carry it and `avg_price` =
their average price rounded to 2 decimal places.

**Ordered by `tag` ascending.** (10 rows - every tag shows up in garden.)

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 105_drills_jsonb_2 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - the value histogram

Bucket every event by its payload `value` into bands of 100: `band` =
`(value as int) / 100` with integer division (0-99 is band 0, 100-199 is
band 1, ... and the exact value 1000 sits alone in band 10). Per band:
`band`, `events` = how many events landed there, `customers` = how many
distinct customers produced them.

**Ordered by `band` ascending.** (11 rows.)

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 105_drills_jsonb_2 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - the ten busiest product pages

Every `view` event's path names a product page. Return the ten most-viewed
products: `product_id` (parsed out of the path), `name` (from `products`),
and `views` = how many view events landed there.

**Ordered by `views` descending, then `product_id` ascending, limited to
ten rows** - view counts sit close together, so the tie-break decides who
makes the list.

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 105_drills_jsonb_2 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - which tags travel together

Every product carries exactly two distinct tags - one unordered pair per
product. Count the pairs across the catalogue: `tag_a`, `tag_b` (with
`tag_a` alphabetically before `tag_b`), and `products` = how many products
carry exactly that pair.

**Ordered by `products` descending, then `tag_a`, then `tag_b`.** (45 rows -
every pair of the ten tags occurs.)

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 105_drills_jsonb_2 ex8`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 105_drills_jsonb_2

Eight drills applying lesson 19's JSONB operators to the clickstream and the
catalogue. Read after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

Three operations cover almost all read-side JSONB work, and this set uses
each where it is strongest. Extraction (`->` to stay in JSONB, `->>` to step
out to text) feeds SQL that wants a scalar; containment (`@>`) asks whether a
document has a shape, and is the operator a GIN index accelerates in lesson
42; expansion (`jsonb_array_elements_text`) turns an array into rows so the
relational machinery - GROUP BY, JOIN, window functions - can take over. The
recurring trap is the type at each boundary: `->>` always hands you text, so
every number needs a cast before it is compared, averaged, or joined on, and
every JSONB-to-JSONB comparison needs the JSON quoting rules respected. When
a query on a document column goes wrong, check the boundary first.

## ex1

A warm-up on the extraction boundary: `path` had to come out as text, which
is `->>`. What it was really testing is whether you reach for the right
arrow without thinking. The classic mistake is `-> 'path'`, which returns a
JSONB string - it renders with quotation marks and compares unequal to every
text value. The model answer is one `->>` and nothing else; the reference
spells it `jsonb_extract_path_text` to show the functional form exists.

## ex2

This one chains two toolboxes: JSONB extraction hands you `/p/1234` and the
string functions take over. The classic mistake is stopping at
`split_part(...)` and returning text - the gate compares typed values, and
`'1234'` is not `1234`. The model reasoning: split on `/`, remember
`split_part` counts fields 1-based with an empty first field (the path
starts with the delimiter), so the id is field 3, then cast.

## ex3

Containment as a predicate. `payload @> '{"value": 1000}'` reads "the
payload contains a value key equal to 1000" and matches numbers as numbers -
no cast, no text comparison. The classic mistake is quoting the number
(`{"value": "1000"}`), which matches nothing because JSON strings and JSON
numbers never compare equal. The reference shows the extract-and-cast
version; both are correct, and lesson 42 explains why the containment form
becomes the fast one once a GIN index exists.

## ex4

An ordinary grouped average with a type boundary in the middle. What it
tested: extracting the measure (`->> 'value'`), casting it, and aggregating
- in that order. The classic mistake is `avg(payload ->> 'value')`, which
errors because text has no average, or casting after aggregating, which
never parses. The model answer groups by `event_type` and averages the cast
value; the round-to-one-decimal is presentation, applied last.

## ex5

Expansion followed by aggregation: once `jsonb_array_elements_text` has
turned each two-tag array into two rows, the query is lesson 07's grouped
report. The subtle point being tested is that a set-returning function in
FROM already sees the table's columns - implicit LATERAL - so no keyword is
needed. The classic mistake is trying to GROUP BY the array itself, which
groups by the pair rather than by each tag. The reference exploits this
dataset's fixed shape (exactly two elements) with a UNION ALL of `->> 0` and
`->> 1` - correct here, brittle anywhere arrays vary in length.

## ex6

A histogram whose bucket key is arithmetic on an extracted document value:
cast first, integer-divide second, group by the whole expression. What it
tested: lesson 07's group-by-a-computed-value with a JSONB accessor and a
cast folded into the expression, plus two measures at different grains
(events and distinct customers) sharing one pass. The classic mistake is
dividing before casting - text has no division - or grouping by a rounded
float instead of integer division, which produces band edges that drift.
The model reasoning: make the bucket function total and cheap, then the
histogram is just GROUP BY it.

## ex7

The join key is computed. Parsing `product_id` out of the path and joining
it to `products` tests whether you will put an expression in a join
condition - beginners often materialise a temp-table-like CTE first, which
the reference does deliberately to show it reads well too. The classic
mistake is forgetting the cast, joining text to int, and reading an operator
error. Second lesson inside: view counts per product are tightly clustered,
so the ten-row cut needs the `product_id` tie-break to be a well-defined
set - the same determinism rule every top-N in this course has drilled.

## ex8

The senior version of expansion: a self-pairing. Expanding the same array
twice produces every ordered combination per product, and `a.tag < b.tag`
keeps exactly one representative of each unordered pair - the standard
dedupe-a-cross-product trick, the same one lesson 79's teammate-pairs drill
used on rows. The classic mistake is `!=` instead of `<`, which double
counts every pair. The reference solves it without any expansion at all -
`least`/`greatest` of the two elements - which works only because every
array here has exactly two distinct elements, and knowing when a shortcut's
precondition holds is the actual skill being tested.

## Further reading

- [JSON Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-json.html) - the jsonb type, and section 8.14.3 on containment semantics.
- [JSON Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-json.html) - `->`, `->>`, `@>`, `jsonb_array_elements_text`, and friends.
- [String Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-string.html) - `split_part`, `substring`, `substr` for path surgery.
- [GIN Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/gin-intro.html) - why the containment operator is the one to prefer once lesson 42's indexes exist.

# 105 - Drills: JSONB, set 2

Eight problems that take lesson 19's JSONB toolbox to the `events` stream:
every event carries a `payload` like `{"path": "/p/1234", "value": 618}`, and
every product still carries its `attributes` document. If `->` versus `->>`,
containment with `@>`, or `jsonb_array_elements_text` feel shaky, reread
lesson 19 before starting - this set assumes all three.

## Exercise 1 - the path out of the payload

For the events with `id <= 15`, return `id` and `path` = the payload's `path`
key, as text.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (15 rows.)

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 105_drills_jsonb_2 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - the number inside the path

Every path has the shape `/p/<product id>`. For the events with `id <= 25`,
return `id` and `product_id` = the id embedded in the path, **as an
integer**, not text.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (25 rows.)

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 105_drills_jsonb_2 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - payloads pinned at the ceiling

The payload's `value` runs from 0 to 1000. How many events hit exactly 1000?
Return one row, one column `hits`. Write the condition as a containment test
(`@>`) - the extract-and-cast version is in the hints, and it is worth having
written both at least once.

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 105_drills_jsonb_2 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - the average value per event type

For each `event_type`, return `event_type` and `avg_value` = the average of
the payload's `value`, rounded to 1 decimal place. Remember what `->>`
returns: text averages badly.

**Ordered by `event_type` ascending.** (5 rows.)

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 105_drills_jsonb_2 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - the garden tag report

For `garden` products only: explode the `tags` array and return one row per
`tag` with `products` = how many garden products carry it and `avg_price` =
their average price rounded to 2 decimal places.

**Ordered by `tag` ascending.** (10 rows - every tag shows up in garden.)

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 105_drills_jsonb_2 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - the value histogram

Bucket every event by its payload `value` into bands of 100: `band` =

band 1, ... and the exact value 1000 sits alone in band 10). Per band:

distinct customers produced them.

**Ordered by `band` ascending.** (11 rows.)

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 105_drills_jsonb_2 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - the ten busiest product pages

Every `view` event's path names a product page. Return the ten most-viewed
products: `product_id` (parsed out of the path), `name` (from `products`),
and `views` = how many view events landed there.

**Ordered by `views` descending, then `product_id` ascending, limited to
ten rows** - view counts sit close together, so the tie-break decides who
makes the list.

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 105_drills_jsonb_2 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - which tags travel together

Every product carries exactly two distinct tags - one unordered pair per
product. Count the pairs across the catalogue: `tag_a`, `tag_b` (with
`tag_a` alphabetically before `tag_b`), and `products` = how many products
carry exactly that pair.

**Ordered by `products` descending, then `tag_a`, then `tag_b`.** (45 rows -
every pair of the ten tags occurs.)

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 105_drills_jsonb_2 ex8`

# Reading - 105_drills_jsonb_2

Eight drills applying lesson 19's JSONB operators to the clickstream and the
catalogue. Read after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

Three operations cover almost all read-side JSONB work, and this set uses
each where it is strongest. Extraction (`->` to stay in JSONB, `->>` to step
out to text) feeds SQL that wants a scalar; containment (`@>`) asks whether a
document has a shape, and is the operator a GIN index accelerates in lesson
42; expansion (`jsonb_array_elements_text`) turns an array into rows so the
relational machinery - GROUP BY, JOIN, window functions - can take over. The
recurring trap is the type at each boundary: `->>` always hands you text, so
every number needs a cast before it is compared, averaged, or joined on, and
every JSONB-to-JSONB comparison needs the JSON quoting rules respected. When
a query on a document column goes wrong, check the boundary first.

## ex1

A warm-up on the extraction boundary: `path` had to come out as text, which
is `->>`. What it was really testing is whether you reach for the right
arrow without thinking. The classic mistake is `-> 'path'`, which returns a
JSONB string - it renders with quotation marks and compares unequal to every
text value. The model answer is one `->>` and nothing else; the reference
spells it `jsonb_extract_path_text` to show the functional form exists.

## ex2

This one chains two toolboxes: JSONB extraction hands you `/p/1234` and the
string functions take over. The classic mistake is stopping at
`split_part(...)` and returning text - the gate compares typed values, and
`'1234'` is not `1234`. The model reasoning: split on `/`, remember
`split_part` counts fields 1-based with an empty first field (the path
starts with the delimiter), so the id is field 3, then cast.

## ex3

Containment as a predicate. `payload @> '{"value": 1000}'` reads "the
payload contains a value key equal to 1000" and matches numbers as numbers -
no cast, no text comparison. The classic mistake is quoting the number
(`{"value": "1000"}`), which matches nothing because JSON strings and JSON
numbers never compare equal. The reference shows the extract-and-cast
version; both are correct, and lesson 42 explains why the containment form
becomes the fast one once a GIN index exists.

## ex4

An ordinary grouped average with a type boundary in the middle. What it
tested: extracting the measure (`->> 'value'`), casting it, and aggregating
- in that order. The classic mistake is `avg(payload ->> 'value')`, which
errors because text has no average, or casting after aggregating, which
never parses. The model answer groups by `event_type` and averages the cast
value; the round-to-one-decimal is presentation, applied last.

## ex5

Expansion followed by aggregation: once `jsonb_array_elements_text` has
turned each two-tag array into two rows, the query is lesson 07's grouped
report. The subtle point being tested is that a set-returning function in
FROM already sees the table's columns - implicit LATERAL - so no keyword is
needed. The classic mistake is trying to GROUP BY the array itself, which
groups by the pair rather than by each tag. The reference exploits this
dataset's fixed shape (exactly two elements) with a UNION ALL of `->> 0` and
`->> 1` - correct here, brittle anywhere arrays vary in length.

## ex6

A histogram whose bucket key is arithmetic on an extracted document value:
cast first, integer-divide second, group by the whole expression. What it
tested: lesson 07's group-by-a-computed-value with a JSONB accessor and a
cast folded into the expression, plus two measures at different grains
(events and distinct customers) sharing one pass. The classic mistake is
dividing before casting - text has no division - or grouping by a rounded
float instead of integer division, which produces band edges that drift.
The model reasoning: make the bucket function total and cheap, then the
histogram is just GROUP BY it.

## ex7

The join key is computed. Parsing `product_id` out of the path and joining
it to `products` tests whether you will put an expression in a join
condition - beginners often materialise a temp-table-like CTE first, which
the reference does deliberately to show it reads well too. The classic
mistake is forgetting the cast, joining text to int, and reading an operator
error. Second lesson inside: view counts per product are tightly clustered,
so the ten-row cut needs the `product_id` tie-break to be a well-defined
set - the same determinism rule every top-N in this course has drilled.

## ex8

The senior version of expansion: a self-pairing. Expanding the same array
twice produces every ordered combination per product, and `a.tag < b.tag`
keeps exactly one representative of each unordered pair - the standard
dedupe-a-cross-product trick, the same one lesson 79's teammate-pairs drill
used on rows. The classic mistake is `!=` instead of `<`, which double
counts every pair. The reference solves it without any expansion at all -
`least`/`greatest` of the two elements - which works only because every
array here has exactly two distinct elements, and knowing when a shortcut's
precondition holds is the actual skill being tested.

## Further reading

- [JSON Types](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/datatype-json.html) - the jsonb type, and section 8.14.3 on containment semantics.
- [JSON Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-json.html) - `->`, `->>`, `@>`, `jsonb_array_elements_text`, and friends.
- [String Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-string.html) - `split_part`, `substring`, `substr` for path surgery.
- [GIN Indexes](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/gin-intro.html) - why the containment operator is the one to prefer once lesson 42's indexes exist.

## Hint 1

The payload is a JSONB document and you want one key out of it as plain text - this is the double-arrow operator from lesson 19.

SELECT id, jsonb_extract_path_text(payload, 'path') AS path
FROM events
WHERE id <= 15
ORDER BY id;

SELECT id, payload ->> 'path' AS path
FROM events
WHERE id <= 15
ORDER BY id;

the payload's `value`, rounded to 1 decimal place. Remember what `->>`
returns: text averages badly.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A plain GROUP BY report (lesson 07) - except the measure lives inside a JSONB document and comes out of the double-arrow as text, which avg() refuses to touch.

## Hint 2

Cast before you aggregate: avg((payload ->> 'value')::int). The inner parentheses matter - the cast applies to the extracted text, not to the payload column.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A plain GROUP BY report (lesson 07) - except the measure lives inside a JSONB document and comes out of the double-arrow as text, which avg() refuses to touch.

## Hint 2

Cast before you aggregate: avg((payload ->> 'value')::int). The inner parentheses matter - the cast applies to the extracted text, not to the payload column.

references.solution.sql:
WITH vals AS (
  SELECT event_type, (payload ->> 'value')::int AS v
  FROM events)
SELECT event_type, round(avg(v), 1) AS avg_value
FROM vals
GROUP BY event_type
ORDER BY event_type;

       round(avg((payload ->> 'value')::int), 1) AS avg_value

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

You cannot group by an array element until each element is its own row. Lesson 19's challenge used the function that does exactly that.

## Hint 2

Put jsonb_array_elements_text(attributes -> 'tags') in the FROM clause next to products - a set-returning function there may reference the table's columns - then it is an ordinary GROUP BY over the exploded rows, with the category filter unchanged.

references.solution.sql:
WITH exploded AS (
  SELECT attributes -> 'tags' ->> 0 AS tag, price
  FROM products WHERE category = 'garden'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT attributes -> 'tags' ->> 1, price
  FROM products WHERE category = 'garden')
SELECT tag, count(*) AS products, round(avg(price), 2) AS avg_price
FROM exploded
GROUP BY tag
ORDER BY tag;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT t.tag,
       count(*) AS products,
       round(avg(p.price), 2) AS avg_price
FROM products p,
     jsonb_array_elements_text(p.attributes -> 'tags') AS t(tag)
WHERE p.category = 'garden'
GROUP BY t.tag
ORDER BY t.tag;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A histogram over a number that lives inside a document: extract the value, cast it, and integer-divide by 100 so 0-99 become band 0, 100-199 become band 1, and so on.

## Hint 2

GROUP BY (payload ->> 'value')::int / 100 - the whole expression, spelled the same in SELECT. Two measures per band: count(*) and count(DISTINCT customer_id). Band 10 exists and is tiny: only the exact value 1000 lands there.

references.solution.sql:
WITH v AS (
  SELECT (payload ->> 'value')::int / 100 AS band, customer_id
  FROM events)
SELECT band,
       count(*) AS events,
       count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers
FROM v
GROUP BY band
ORDER BY band;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT (payload ->> 'value')::int / 100 AS band,
       count(*) AS events,
       count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers
FROM events
GROUP BY (payload ->> 'value')::int / 100
ORDER BY band;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 - the ten busiest product pages

Every `view` event's path names a product page. Return the ten most-viewed
products: `product_id` (parsed out of the path), `name` (from `products`),
and `views` = how many view events landed there.

**Ordered by `views` descending, then `product_id` ascending, limited to
ten rows** - view counts sit close together, so the tie-break decides who
makes the list.

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 105_drills_jsonb_2 ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three earlier ideas chained: pull the product id out of the path (this set's ex2), join it to products (lesson 08), and count per product (lesson 07). Nothing new - the work is keeping the cast in the join condition straight.

## Hint 2

The join condition is p.id = split_part(e.payload ->> 'path', '/', 3)::int, with WHERE event_type = 'view' narrowing the stream first. Group by the extracted id and the name.

## Hint 3

View counts per product sit close together, so two products can tie - which is why the prompt pins the order to views DESC, product_id ASC before the LIMIT 10. Leave the tie-break out and "the" top ten is not a well-defined set.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three earlier ideas chained: pull the product id out of the path (this set's ex2), join it to products (lesson 08), and count per product (lesson 07). Nothing new - the work is keeping the cast in the join condition straight.

## Hint 2

The join condition is p.id = split_part(e.payload ->> 'path', '/', 3)::int, with WHERE event_type = 'view' narrowing the stream first. Group by the extracted id and the name.

## Hint 3

View counts per product sit close together, so two products can tie - which is why the prompt pins the order to views DESC, product_id ASC before the LIMIT 10. Leave the tie-break out and "the" top ten is not a well-defined set.

references.solution.sql:
WITH v AS (
  SELECT substr(payload ->> 'path', 4)::int AS pid
  FROM events
  WHERE event_type = 'view')
SELECT v.pid AS product_id, p.name, count(*) AS views
FROM v
JOIN products p ON p.id = v.pid
GROUP BY v.pid, p.name
ORDER BY views DESC, product_id ASC
LIMIT 10;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT split_part(e.payload ->> 'path', '/', 3)::int AS product_id,
       p.name,
       count(*) AS views
FROM events e
JOIN products p ON p.id = split_part(e.payload ->> 'path', '/', 3)::int
WHERE e.event_type = 'view'
GROUP BY 1, p.name
ORDER BY views DESC, product_id ASC
LIMIT 10;

## Hint 1

A pair is two elements of the same array, so the array has to be expanded twice - two set-returning calls over the same tags array, side by side in the FROM clause.

Two expansions give you every ordered combination, including (x, x) and both (x, y) and (y, x). One comparison in the WHERE clause collapses all of that to each unordered pair exactly once.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT least(attributes -> 'tags' ->> 0, attributes -> 'tags' ->> 1)    AS tag_a,
       greatest(attributes -> 'tags' ->> 0, attributes -> 'tags' ->> 1) AS tag_b,
       count(*) AS products
FROM products
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY products DESC, tag_a, tag_b;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT a.tag AS tag_a,
       b.tag AS tag_b,
       count(*) AS products
FROM products p,
     jsonb_array_elements_text(p.attributes -> 'tags') AS a(tag),
     jsonb_array_elements_text(p.attributes -> 'tags') AS b(tag)
WHERE a.tag < b.tag
GROUP BY a.tag, b.tag
ORDER BY products DESC, tag_a, tag_b;

# 106 - Drills: LATERAL joins, set 1

Eight problems on lesson 48: a subquery in FROM that can see the rows to its
left, runs once per driving row, and - the killer feature - carries a LIMIT
that applies per group instead of per query. If `CROSS JOIN LATERAL` versus
`LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true` is not yet automatic, reread lesson 48 first.

## Exercise 1 - the three newest hires per department

For every `staff` department, return its three most recently hired people:
`department`, `name`, `hired_on`. Break `hired_on` ties by `id` ascending.

**Ordered by `department` ascending, then `hired_on` descending, then `id`
ascending.** (15 rows.)

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 106_drills_lateral_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - each customer's priciest order

For every customer with `id <= 15`, their single most expensive order:
`customer_id`, `order_id`, `total`. Break `total` ties by the order's `id`
ascending. A customer with no orders should not appear - the plain `CROSS
JOIN LATERAL` gives you that for free.

**Ordered by `customer_id` ascending.**

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 106_drills_lateral_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - the latest review, keeping the reviewless

For every product with `id <= 12`: `id`, `name`, and the product's most
recent review as `review_id` and `rating` (ties on `created_at` broken by
the review's `id`, higher id wins). Products with no reviews must still
appear, with NULLs in the review columns.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (12 rows.)

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 106_drills_lateral_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - the top-three payroll

For every department: `department` and `top3_payroll` = the sum of its three
highest salaries (ties broken by `id`). Pick the three first, then sum -
that ordering of steps is the whole exercise.

**Ordered by `department` ascending.** (5 rows.)

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 106_drills_lateral_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - the three freshest reviews of each rating

For each of the five ratings (drive the lateral from `SELECT DISTINCT
rating`, not a hand-typed list), the three most recent reviews carrying it:
`rating`, `review_id`, `created_at`. Break `created_at` ties by the
review's `id`, higher id wins.

**Ordered by `rating` ascending, then `created_at` descending, then
`review_id` descending.** (15 rows.)

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 106_drills_lateral_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - the last three events of each early customer

For every customer with `id <= 5`, their three most recent events from the
three-million-row stream: `customer_id`, `event_type`, `ts`. (Event
timestamps never tie - they increase strictly with `id`.)

**Ordered by `customer_id` ascending, then `ts` descending.** (15 rows.)

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 106_drills_lateral_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - the quarter's bestsellers, per category

For every product category, the three products with the most units sold in
orders created on or after `2023-10-01`: `category`, `product_id`, `name`,
`units` = the sum of `order_items.quantity`. Break `units` ties by
`product_id` ascending. The lateral subquery has to join, group, sort, and
limit - a whole report per driving row.

**Ordered by `category` ascending, then `units` descending, then
`product_id` ascending.** (18 rows.)

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 106_drills_lateral_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - the whales' latest moves

Find the five customers with the highest non-cancelled revenue (sum of
`total` over their non-cancelled orders; break revenue ties by
`customer_id`). For each, return `customer_id`, `revenue`, and their most
recent non-cancelled order as `last_order_id` and `last_created_at` (ties
broken by order `id`, higher wins).

**Ordered by `revenue` descending, then `customer_id` ascending.** (5 rows.)

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 106_drills_lateral_1 ex8`
