# Reading - 106_drills_lateral_1

Eight drills on per-row subqueries. Read after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

Every problem in this set is the same sentence with different nouns: *for
each X, the top N Y by Z*. Once you hear that sentence, the query writes
itself - a driving set on the left, a `LATERAL` subquery on the right that
filters to the current driving row, sorts by Z with a tie-break, and stops
at `LIMIT N`. The two decisions that remain are the join flavour (`CROSS
JOIN LATERAL` drops driving rows with no matches, `LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON
true` keeps them) and the tie-break, which is not optional: a top-N whose
sort key can repeat is nondeterministic without one. The window-function
formulation (`row_number() ... WHERE rn <= N`) always works too and is what
the references here mostly use - it ranks everything and then discards,
where the lateral stops early per group. Same rows, different work.

## ex1

Direct application of the lesson-48 pattern with a derived driving set.
What it tested: building the left side with `SELECT DISTINCT department`
rather than hard-coding five names, and remembering the tie-break on
`hired_on`. The classic mistake is `ORDER BY hired_on` alone inside the
lateral - two same-day hires make "the three newest" ambiguous and the gate
notices. The model answer sorts `hired_on DESC, id ASC` inside and repeats
the full ordering outside.

## ex2

The LIMIT 1 lookup, and a semantics question disguised as syntax: should a
customer with no orders appear? The prompt says no, and `CROSS JOIN
LATERAL` encodes exactly that - it behaves like an inner join. The classic
mistake is not thinking about the question at all, which happens to pass
here and then silently loses rows in the next report where it should not.
The reference solves it with `DISTINCT ON (customer_id) ... ORDER BY
customer_id, total DESC, id` - lesson 49's shortcut for the same shape.

## ex3

Ex2's mirror image: the empty lookup must survive. What it tested: `LEFT
JOIN LATERAL (...) ON true`, including the slightly odd mandatory `ON
true`. The classic mistake is writing `CROSS JOIN LATERAL` and losing any
reviewless product, or filtering on a review column in the outer WHERE,
which turns the outer join back into an inner one - lesson 09's oldest
trap, resurfacing here. The model reasoning: requirements about *keeping*
rows always decide the join type before anything else is written.

## ex4

Pick-then-aggregate. The trap is that `sum()` and `LIMIT` in one query
level run in the wrong order - aggregates happen before the limit, so a
one-level query sums the whole department and then "limits" a single row.
The nesting inside the lateral (inner query picks three rows, outer sums
them) is what sequences the steps. The classic mistake is exactly that
one-level version; it returns each department's full payroll and fails
loudly. Same lesson as 48's challenge, drilled on a different aggregate.

## ex5

A repeat of the pattern with the driving set built from the fact table
itself (`SELECT DISTINCT rating`). The point being tested is small but
real: a million reviews at one-second timestamp granularity collide
constantly, so the `id` tie-break is what makes "the three freshest" a
fixed set. The classic mistake is assuming a timestamp column will not
tie; only `events.ts` in this dataset carries that guarantee, and knowing
which columns do is part of knowing the data.

## ex6

The efficiency argument made concrete. Per customer, the lateral reads a
handful of events and stops; the window version scans and ranks every event
of every driving customer before throwing almost all of it away. On a
3,000,000-row stream that difference is the reason this pattern exists (and
in Part 5 an index on `(customer_id, ts)` turns each lateral probe into a
few index reads). What it tested: nothing new - recognising that the same
five-line shape scales from `staff` to `events` unchanged.

## ex7

The lateral subquery as a full report: join, filter, group, sort, limit,
all per driving row. What it tested: composing a three-table aggregate
inside the lateral without losing the correlation (`p.category =
c.category`). The classic mistake is putting the category correlation in
the outer query's WHERE - it is out of scope there - or grouping outside
the lateral, which computes a global top three instead of three per
category. The reference is the honest window version; both must agree row
for row, which is worth verifying by eye once.

## ex8

Two stacked patterns: an aggregate-sort-limit CTE builds the driving set
(the five whales), then a per-row lookup fetches each whale's latest
non-cancelled order. What it tested: consistency of the business rule
across both halves - the status filter has to appear in the revenue
aggregate *and* in the lateral, or a cancelled order can surface as
somebody's "last order" while contributing nothing to their revenue. That
is the kind of quiet contradiction stakeholders find months later. The
reference computes the same thing with `DISTINCT ON` joined to the top-five
CTE.

## Further reading

- [Table Expressions - LATERAL Subqueries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-LATERAL) - the formal scoping rules for what a lateral item may reference.
- [SELECT](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) - the LATERAL clause in the reference grammar, and LIMIT interaction with ORDER BY.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) - the rank-then-filter alternative every exercise here could be rewritten with.
- [PostgreSQL Wiki - Loose indexscan](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Loose_indexscan) - the skip-scan family of tricks for per-group firsts, and why indexes make lateral probes cheap.

# 106 - Drills: LATERAL joins, set 1

Eight problems on lesson 48: a subquery in FROM that can see the rows to its
left, runs once per driving row, and - the killer feature - carries a LIMIT
that applies per group instead of per query. If `CROSS JOIN LATERAL` versus
`LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true` is not yet automatic, reread lesson 48 first.

## Exercise 1 - the three newest hires per department

For every `staff` department, return its three most recently hired people:
`department`, `name`, `hired_on`. Break `hired_on` ties by `id` ascending.

**Ordered by `department` ascending, then `hired_on` descending, then `id`
ascending.** (15 rows.)

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 106_drills_lateral_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - each customer's priciest order

For every customer with `id <= 15`, their single most expensive order:
`customer_id`, `order_id`, `total`. Break `total` ties by the order's `id`
ascending. A customer with no orders should not appear - the plain `CROSS
JOIN LATERAL` gives you that for free.

**Ordered by `customer_id` ascending.**

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 106_drills_lateral_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - the latest review, keeping the reviewless

For every product with `id <= 12`: `id`, `name`, and the product's most
recent review as `review_id` and `rating` (ties on `created_at` broken by
the review's `id`, higher id wins). Products with no reviews must still
appear, with NULLs in the review columns.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (12 rows.)

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 106_drills_lateral_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - the top-three payroll

For every department: `department` and `top3_payroll` = the sum of its three
highest salaries (ties broken by `id`). Pick the three first, then sum -
that ordering of steps is the whole exercise.

**Ordered by `department` ascending.** (5 rows.)

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 106_drills_lateral_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - the three freshest reviews of each rating

For each of the five ratings (drive the lateral from `SELECT DISTINCT
rating`, not a hand-typed list), the three most recent reviews carrying it:
`rating`, `review_id`, `created_at`. Break `created_at` ties by the
review's `id`, higher id wins.

**Ordered by `rating` ascending, then `created_at` descending, then
`review_id` descending.** (15 rows.)

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 106_drills_lateral_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - the last three events of each early customer

For every customer with `id <= 5`, their three most recent events from the
three-million-row stream: `customer_id`, `event_type`, `ts`. (Event
timestamps never tie - they increase strictly with `id`.)

**Ordered by `customer_id` ascending, then `ts` descending.** (15 rows.)

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 106_drills_lateral_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - the quarter's bestsellers, per category

For every product category, the three products with the most units sold in
orders created on or after `2023-10-01`: `category`, `product_id`, `name`,
`units` = the sum of `order_items.quantity`. Break `units` ties by
`product_id` ascending. The lateral subquery has to join, group, sort, and
limit - a whole report per driving row.

**Ordered by `category` ascending, then `units` descending, then
`product_id` ascending.** (18 rows.)

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 106_drills_lateral_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - the whales' latest moves

Find the five customers with the highest non-cancelled revenue (sum of
`total` over their non-cancelled orders; break revenue ties by
`customer_id`). For each, return `customer_id`, `revenue`, and their most
recent non-cancelled order as `last_order_id` and `last_created_at` (ties
broken by order `id`, higher wins).

**Ordered by `revenue` descending, then `customer_id` ascending.** (5 rows.)

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 106_drills_lateral_1 ex8`

# Reading - 106_drills_lateral_1

Eight drills on per-row subqueries. Read after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

Every problem in this set is the same sentence with different nouns: *for
each X, the top N Y by Z*. Once you hear that sentence, the query writes
itself - a driving set on the left, a `LATERAL` subquery on the right that
filters to the current driving row, sorts by Z with a tie-break, and stops
at `LIMIT N`. The two decisions that remain are the join flavour (`CROSS
JOIN LATERAL` drops driving rows with no matches, `LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON
true` keeps them) and the tie-break, which is not optional: a top-N whose
sort key can repeat is nondeterministic without one. The window-function
formulation (`row_number() ... WHERE rn <= N`) always works too and is what
the references here mostly use - it ranks everything and then discards,
where the lateral stops early per group. Same rows, different work.

## ex1

Direct application of the lesson-48 pattern with a derived driving set.
What it tested: building the left side with `SELECT DISTINCT department`
rather than hard-coding five names, and remembering the tie-break on
`hired_on`. The classic mistake is `ORDER BY hired_on` alone inside the
lateral - two same-day hires make "the three newest" ambiguous and the gate
notices. The model answer sorts `hired_on DESC, id ASC` inside and repeats
the full ordering outside.

## ex2

The LIMIT 1 lookup, and a semantics question disguised as syntax: should a
customer with no orders appear? The prompt says no, and `CROSS JOIN
LATERAL` encodes exactly that - it behaves like an inner join. The classic
mistake is not thinking about the question at all, which happens to pass
here and then silently loses rows in the next report where it should not.
The reference solves it with `DISTINCT ON (customer_id) ... ORDER BY
customer_id, total DESC, id` - lesson 49's shortcut for the same shape.

## ex3

Ex2's mirror image: the empty lookup must survive. What it tested: `LEFT
JOIN LATERAL (...) ON true`, including the slightly odd mandatory `ON
true`. The classic mistake is writing `CROSS JOIN LATERAL` and losing any
reviewless product, or filtering on a review column in the outer WHERE,
which turns the outer join back into an inner one - lesson 09's oldest
trap, resurfacing here. The model reasoning: requirements about *keeping*
rows always decide the join type before anything else is written.

## ex4

Pick-then-aggregate. The trap is that `sum()` and `LIMIT` in one query
level run in the wrong order - aggregates happen before the limit, so a
one-level query sums the whole department and then "limits" a single row.
The nesting inside the lateral (inner query picks three rows, outer sums
them) is what sequences the steps. The classic mistake is exactly that
one-level version; it returns each department's full payroll and fails
loudly. Same lesson as 48's challenge, drilled on a different aggregate.

## ex5

A repeat of the pattern with the driving set built from the fact table
itself (`SELECT DISTINCT rating`). The point being tested is small but
real: a million reviews at one-second timestamp granularity collide
constantly, so the `id` tie-break is what makes "the three freshest" a
fixed set. The classic mistake is assuming a timestamp column will not
tie; only `events.ts` in this dataset carries that guarantee, and knowing
which columns do is part of knowing the data.

## ex6

The efficiency argument made concrete. Per customer, the lateral reads a
handful of events and stops; the window version scans and ranks every event
of every driving customer before throwing almost all of it away. On a
3,000,000-row stream that difference is the reason this pattern exists (and
in Part 5 an index on `(customer_id, ts)` turns each lateral probe into a
few index reads). What it tested: nothing new - recognising that the same
five-line shape scales from `staff` to `events` unchanged.

## ex7

The lateral subquery as a full report: join, filter, group, sort, limit,
all per driving row. What it tested: composing a three-table aggregate
inside the lateral without losing the correlation (`p.category =
c.category`). The classic mistake is putting the category correlation in
the outer query's WHERE - it is out of scope there - or grouping outside
the lateral, which computes a global top three instead of three per
category. The reference is the honest window version; both must agree row
for row, which is worth verifying by eye once.

## ex8

Two stacked patterns: an aggregate-sort-limit CTE builds the driving set
(the five whales), then a per-row lookup fetches each whale's latest
non-cancelled order. What it tested: consistency of the business rule
across both halves - the status filter has to appear in the revenue
aggregate *and* in the lateral, or a cancelled order can surface as
somebody's "last order" while contributing nothing to their revenue. That
is the kind of quiet contradiction stakeholders find months later. The
reference computes the same thing with `DISTINCT ON` joined to the top-five
CTE.

## Further reading

- [Table Expressions - LATERAL Subqueries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-LATERAL) - the formal scoping rules for what a lateral item may reference.
- [SELECT](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html) - the LATERAL clause in the reference grammar, and LIMIT interaction with ORDER BY.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) - the rank-then-filter alternative every exercise here could be rewritten with.
- [PostgreSQL Wiki - Loose indexscan](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Loose_indexscan) - the skip-scan family of tricks for per-group firsts, and why indexes make lateral probes cheap.

## Exercise 1 - the three newest hires per department

For every `staff` department, return its three most recently hired people:
`department`, `name`, `hired_on`. Break `hired_on` ties by `id` ascending.

**Ordered by `department` ascending, then `hired_on` descending, then `id`
ascending.** (15 rows.)

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 106_drills_lateral_1 ex1`

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

"The three newest per department" is top-N-per-group - lesson 48's home turf. The driving rows are the five distinct departments; the lateral subquery runs once for each.

## Hint 2

SELECT DISTINCT department as the left side, then CROSS JOIN LATERAL a subquery that filters staff to d.department, sorts by hired_on DESC with id as tie-break, and stops at LIMIT 3.

references.solution.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT department, name, hired_on, id,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY department
                            ORDER BY hired_on DESC, id) AS rn
  FROM staff)
SELECT department, name, hired_on
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY department, hired_on DESC, id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT d.department, t.name, t.hired_on
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT department FROM staff) d
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT s.name, s.hired_on, s.id
  FROM staff s
  WHERE s.department = d.department
  ORDER BY s.hired_on DESC, s.id ASC
  LIMIT 3) t
ORDER BY d.department, t.hired_on DESC, t.id;

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The order matters before the aggregate: pick each department's three biggest salaries first, then sum those three. A plain sum() GROUP BY department adds up everybody.

## Hint 2

Nest inside the LATERAL: an inner subquery does ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 3 for the current department, and an outer SELECT sum(...) collapses those three rows to one. The lateral returns a single row per department.

## Hint 3

Shape: CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT sum(salary) FROM (SELECT salary FROM staff WHERE department = d.department ORDER BY salary DESC, id LIMIT 3) top) t. An aggregate directly next to a LIMIT in the same query level would aggregate first and limit after - the nesting is what sequences pick-then-sum.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The order matters before the aggregate: pick each department's three biggest salaries first, then sum those three. A plain sum() GROUP BY department adds up everybody.

## Hint 2

Nest inside the LATERAL: an inner subquery does ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 3 for the current department, and an outer SELECT sum(...) collapses those three rows to one. The lateral returns a single row per department.

## Hint 3

Shape: CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT sum(salary) FROM (SELECT salary FROM staff WHERE department = d.department ORDER BY salary DESC, id LIMIT 3) top) t. An aggregate directly next to a LIMIT in the same query level would aggregate first and limit after - the nesting is what sequences pick-then-sum.

references.solution.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT department, salary,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY department
                            ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS rn
  FROM staff)
SELECT department, sum(salary) AS top3_payroll
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 3
GROUP BY department
ORDER BY department;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT d.department, t.top3_payroll
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT department FROM staff) d
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT sum(top.salary) AS top3_payroll
  FROM (SELECT s.salary
        FROM staff s
        WHERE s.department = d.department
        ORDER BY s.salary DESC, s.id ASC
        LIMIT 3) top) t
ORDER BY d.department;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Identical shape to ex2 with LIMIT 3 instead of 1, on a table six times the size of orders. This is where the per-group LIMIT stops being style and starts being the reason LATERAL exists: it never ranks the whole stream.

## Hint 2

Inside the LATERAL: WHERE e.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY e.ts DESC LIMIT 3. Event timestamps are unique (they increase strictly with id), so no extra tie-break is needed.

references.solution.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT customer_id, event_type, ts,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                            ORDER BY ts DESC) AS rn
  FROM events
  WHERE customer_id <= 5)
SELECT customer_id, event_type, ts
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY customer_id, ts DESC;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.id AS customer_id, t.event_type, t.ts
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT e.event_type, e.ts
  FROM events e
  WHERE e.customer_id = c.id
  ORDER BY e.ts DESC
  LIMIT 3) t
WHERE c.id <= 5
ORDER BY c.id, t.ts DESC;

## Exercise 7 - the quarter's bestsellers, per category

For every product category, the three products with the most units sold in
orders created on or after `2023-10-01`: `category`, `product_id`, `name`,
`units` = the sum of `order_items.quantity`. Break `units` ties by
`product_id` ascending. The lateral subquery has to join, group, sort, and
limit - a whole report per driving row.

`product_id` ascending.** (18 rows.)

The lateral subquery is a whole query, not just a lookup: it may join, filter, group, and only then sort and limit. Here it computes units per product for one category and keeps the best three.

Inside the LATERAL, join products to order_items to orders, filter WHERE p.category = c.category AND o.created_at >= '2023-10-01', GROUP BY p.id, p.name, ORDER BY the summed units DESC with p.id as tie-break, LIMIT 3.

The window alternative computes units for every product in every category and ranks them all before discarding the losers - correct, and what the reference does. With a per-category LIMIT the lateral only ever keeps three per driving row; compare both shapes and notice they must agree row for row.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The lateral subquery is a whole query, not just a lookup: it may join, filter, group, and only then sort and limit. Here it computes units per product for one category and keeps the best three.

## Hint 2

Inside the LATERAL, join products to order_items to orders, filter WHERE p.category = c.category AND o.created_at >= '2023-10-01', GROUP BY p.id, p.name, ORDER BY the summed units DESC with p.id as tie-break, LIMIT 3.

## Hint 3

The window alternative computes units for every product in every category and ranks them all before discarding the losers - correct, and what the reference does. With a per-category LIMIT the lateral only ever keeps three per driving row; compare both shapes and notice they must agree row for row.

references.solution.sql:
WITH sold AS (
  SELECT p.category, p.id, p.name, sum(oi.quantity) AS units
  FROM products p
  JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
  JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
  WHERE o.created_at >= '2023-10-01'
  GROUP BY p.category, p.id, p.name),
ranked AS (
  SELECT category, id, name, units,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY category
                            ORDER BY units DESC, id) AS rn
  FROM sold)
SELECT category, id AS product_id, name, units
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY category, units DESC, product_id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.category, t.product_id, t.name, t.units
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products) c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT p.id AS product_id, p.name, sum(oi.quantity) AS units
  FROM products p
  JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
  JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
  WHERE p.category = c.category
    AND o.created_at >= '2023-10-01'
  GROUP BY p.id, p.name
  ORDER BY units DESC, p.id ASC
  LIMIT 3) t
ORDER BY c.category, t.units DESC, t.product_id;

## Hint 1

Two problems stacked: first build the driving set (top five spenders - an aggregate, sorted and limited, in a CTE), then run a per-row lookup against it.

## Hint 2

The CTE groups non-cancelled orders by customer, sums total, and keeps the top five by revenue with customer_id as tie-break. The LATERAL then fetches that customer's newest non-cancelled order: ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 1.

## Hint 3

Keep the status filter in both places. Dropping it from the lateral quietly lets a cancelled order be somebody's "last order", and the two halves of the report would disagree about which orders exist.

references.solution.sql:
WITH per_customer AS (
  SELECT customer_id, sum(total) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
  GROUP BY customer_id),
top5 AS (
  SELECT customer_id, revenue
  FROM per_customer
  ORDER BY revenue DESC, customer_id
  LIMIT 5),
latest AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id)
         customer_id, id AS last_order_id, created_at AS last_created_at
  FROM orders
  WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
  ORDER BY customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC)
SELECT t.customer_id, t.revenue, l.last_order_id, l.last_created_at
FROM top5 t
JOIN latest l USING (customer_id)
ORDER BY t.revenue DESC, t.customer_id;

  SELECT customer_id, sum(total) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
  GROUP BY customer_id
  ORDER BY revenue DESC, customer_id
  LIMIT 5)
SELECT s.customer_id, s.revenue, t.last_order_id, t.last_created_at
FROM spenders s
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT o.id AS last_order_id, o.created_at AS last_created_at
  FROM orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = s.customer_id
    AND o.status <> 'cancelled'
  ORDER BY o.created_at DESC, o.id DESC
  LIMIT 1) t
ORDER BY s.revenue DESC, s.customer_id;

# 107 - Drills: DISTINCT ON, set 1

Eight problems on lesson 49: `DISTINCT ON (expr)` keeps the first row per
group, "first" is whatever the `ORDER BY` says after its mandatory leading
match with the `DISTINCT ON` expression, and a missing tie-break is a bug
that has not surfaced yet. If any of that sentence is news, reread 49.

## Exercise 1 - the order that started each pile

One row per order `status`: the **oldest** order carrying it. Columns
`status`, `order_id`, `created_at`. Break `created_at` ties by `id`,
lower id wins.

**Ordered by `status` ascending.** (4 rows.)

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 107_drills_distinct_on_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - the latest order that still counts

For every customer with `id <= 25`: their most recent **non-cancelled**
order. Columns `customer_id`, `order_id`, `status`, `created_at`. Ties on
`created_at` broken by order `id`, higher wins. A customer whose orders are
all cancelled (or who has none) does not appear.

**Ordered by `customer_id` ascending.**

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 107_drills_distinct_on_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - the stream's last word, per type

For each of the five `event_type` values, the most recent event: columns
`event_type`, `event_id`, `ts`.

**Ordered by `event_type` ascending.** (5 rows.)

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 107_drills_distinct_on_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - the cheapest of each size

Among `clothing` products, the cheapest product of each `size` in
`attributes`. Columns `size`, `id`, `name`, `price`. Break price ties by
`id` ascending. The group key is a JSONB expression - `DISTINCT ON` does
not care.

**Ordered by `size` ascending.** (4 rows.)

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 107_drills_distinct_on_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - the order that opened each month

For each calendar month of 2023, the **first** order created in it. Columns
`month` (`date_trunc('month', created_at)`), `order_id`, `created_at`. Ties
broken by order `id` ascending.

**Ordered by `month` ascending.** (11 rows - the data ends mid-November.)

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 107_drills_distinct_on_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - every manager's newest hire

For every staff member who manages at least one person: `manager_id`, the
manager's `name` as `manager`, and their most recently hired direct report
as `newest_report` with that report's `hired_on`. Ties on `hired_on` broken
by the report's `id`, higher wins. You will need the self-join from lesson
10 to put the manager's name on the row.

**Ordered by `manager_id` ascending.**

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 107_drills_distinct_on_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - which country won each month?

For each calendar month of 2023: the customer country with the highest
non-cancelled order revenue (`sum(total)`, join `customers` for the
country; revenue ties broken by `country` ascending). Columns `month`
(`date_trunc('month', created_at)`), `country`, `revenue`. Aggregate
first (revenue per month per country), then pick per month - and note the
required output order below, which is **not** the order `DISTINCT ON`
will hand you.

**Ordered by `revenue` descending, then `month` ascending.** (11 rows.)

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 107_drills_distinct_on_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - when did we last see them?

For every customer with `id <= 10`: `id`, `name`, and their most recent
event as `last_event_type` and `last_ts` - keeping customers with **no
events at all**, with NULLs in both event columns.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.** (10 rows.)

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 107_drills_distinct_on_1 ex8`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 107_drills_distinct_on_1

Eight drills on one-row-per-group picks. Read after your attempt, pass or
fail.

## Notes

`DISTINCT ON` is a selection rule wearing an `ORDER BY`'s clothes: the sort
must lead with the group expression, and everything after that decides which
row of each group survives. That gives the construct exactly three failure
modes, and this set walks into all of them on purpose. Forget the leading
match and PostgreSQL refuses the query outright (the friendly failure).
Forget the tie-break and the query runs, returns plausible rows, and returns
*different* plausible rows after the next VACUUM (the dangerous failure).
Want the output presented in an order that is not the group key, and you
must wrap the pick in a subquery and sort outside (the workaround, drilled
in ex7). Every problem here also has a `row_number() = 1` spelling - the
references use it throughout - which is portable SQL and the form to reach
for the moment a colleague on MySQL has to read your query.

## ex1

The lesson-49 pattern verbatim on a new axis, pointed backwards: `ASC`
picks each status's oldest order. What it tested: the leading `ORDER BY`
rule and a deliberate tie-break, because half a million orders at
one-second granularity make same-second collisions inside a status a
certainty. The classic mistake is `ORDER BY created_at` alone - a syntax
error here, since the sort must start with `status`. The model answer
reads: group by status, oldest first, lower id settles dead heats.

## ex2

A pre-filter changes what "latest" means. The status condition must run
before the pick - `WHERE` does exactly that - so the survivor is each
customer's latest order *among the non-cancelled ones*. The classic mistake
is picking first and filtering after (an outer query's WHERE): that erases
customers whose most recent order was cancelled instead of falling back to
their previous one, which is a different report with quieter numbers. Where
a filter sits relative to a pick is a correctness decision, not style.

## ex3

Scale test with training wheels: `events.ts` is unique by construction, so
the tie-break can be skipped without harm - once you can say *why*. What it
was really testing is whether you know when determinism comes for free. The
classic mistake is assuming that property holds for every timestamp column;
`orders.created_at` and `customers.created_at` both collide. The model
answer sorts `event_type, ts DESC` and would add `, id DESC` on any column
without a uniqueness guarantee.

## ex4

`DISTINCT ON` over an expression. The parser wants the leading `ORDER BY`
item to match the `DISTINCT ON` expression, so `attributes ->> 'size'`
appears twice, verbatim. The classic mistake is writing the alias (`ORDER
BY size, ...` works, but only because PostgreSQL resolves the alias to the
same expression - rely on the verbatim form when in doubt). What it tested:
that the group key can be computed - a JSONB extraction, a `date_trunc`, an
arithmetic bucket - without changing the construct at all.

## ex5

Same idea pointed backwards in time: `ASC` instead of `DESC` flips "latest
per group" into "first per group", and nothing else moves. What it tested:
the selection rule lives entirely in the sort direction, plus a computed
group key (`date_trunc`). The classic mistake is an off-by-one on the year
filter - a closed `<= '2023-12-31'` drops nothing here but is the wrong
habit; the half-open `>= 2023-01-01 AND < 2024-01-01` form from lesson 18
is the one that survives timestamps.

## ex6

Composition with a self-join. The pick runs over the joined row set, so
`DISTINCT ON (s.manager_id)` sees reports already paired with their
manager's name - one construct, no second pass. What it tested: qualifying
every column once two copies of `staff` are in play, and realising the CEO
needs no special handling (a NULL `manager_id` never joins, so the row
never exists to be picked from). The classic mistake is grouping by the
manager's *name* - two managers can share one.

## ex7

The presentation-order conflict, which is the single most common real-world
stumble with this construct. The pick needs `ORDER BY month, revenue DESC,
country`; the stakeholder wants `revenue DESC, month`. One query cannot
serve both masters, so the pick becomes a subquery and the outer query
sorts the eleven survivors. The classic mistake is trying to bolt the
presentation sort onto the `DISTINCT ON` query and fighting the parser. The
model reasoning: aggregate, pick, present - three stages, each with its own
ordering needs, only the last one visible to the reader.

## ex8

Keeping the empty groups. `DISTINCT ON` alone answers "last event per
customer *who has events*"; the prompt demands all ten customers, so the
pick is built first and a `LEFT JOIN` attaches it - lesson 09's
join-then-keep logic wrapped around lesson 49's pick. The classic mistake
is `LEFT JOIN events` followed by `DISTINCT ON` with the customer filter in
the wrong place, or any filter on the events side in the outer `WHERE`,
which silently turns the join inner. The reference shows the third
spelling, `LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... LIMIT 1`, and choosing between the three
by index availability is a Part 5 conversation.

## Further reading

- [SELECT - DISTINCT Clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html#SQL-DISTINCT) - the formal rules for DISTINCT ON and its ORDER BY interaction.
- [Table Expressions - LATERAL Subqueries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-LATERAL) - the equivalent per-row-lookup spelling used in ex8's reference.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) - row_number(), the portable one-row-per-group idiom every reference here uses.
- [PostgreSQL Wiki - Don't do this](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) - a catalogue of adjacent footguns, including ambiguous picks that "work" until they don't.

## Ten-pass spaced repetition

Use this ladder after completing **107 - Drills: DISTINCT ON, set 1**. Each pass changes the retrieval
task so repetition strengthens recall instead of becoming answer recognition.
Do the named exercise from a blank starting point whenever practical, and only
open its hints after recording your first attempt.

| Pass | When | Practice target | Retrieval task |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | now | `ex1` | Close the notes and state the central rule in one precise sentence. |
| 2 | 3 days | `ex2` | Rebuild the smallest valid example from memory, then explain each part. |
| 3 | 7 days | `ex3` | Predict the result or behavior before running anything; reconcile surprises. |

| 5 | 60 days | `ex5` | Contrast this technique with its nearest alternative and choose between them. |
| 6 | 120 days | `ex6` | Add one realistic constraint and adapt the solution without consulting notes. |
| 7 | 240 days | `ex7` | Debug a deliberately broken version; explain the evidence before the repair. |
| 8 | 1 year | `ex8` | Teach the idea aloud in two minutes, including one boundary case. |
| 9 | 18 months | `ex1` | Transfer the pattern to a new domain and verify the result with the gate. |
| 10 | 3 years | `ex2` | Complete a cold, timed solution and write the rule you want to retain long-term. |

A failed pass is useful evidence: return to pass 1 after three days. A clean
pass advances to the next interval. After pass 10, revisit the skill every
three years or whenever real work exposes a weak edge case.

# Reading - 107_drills_distinct_on_1

Eight drills on one-row-per-group picks. Read after your attempt, pass or
fail.

## Notes

`DISTINCT ON` is a selection rule wearing an `ORDER BY`'s clothes: the sort
must lead with the group expression, and everything after that decides which
row of each group survives. That gives the construct exactly three failure
modes, and this set walks into all of them on purpose. Forget the leading
match and PostgreSQL refuses the query outright (the friendly failure).
Forget the tie-break and the query runs, returns plausible rows, and returns
*different* plausible rows after the next VACUUM (the dangerous failure).
Want the output presented in an order that is not the group key, and you
must wrap the pick in a subquery and sort outside (the workaround, drilled
in ex7). Every problem here also has a `row_number() = 1` spelling - the
references use it throughout - which is portable SQL and the form to reach
for the moment a colleague on MySQL has to read your query.

## ex1

The lesson-49 pattern verbatim on a new axis, pointed backwards: `ASC`
picks each status's oldest order. What it tested: the leading `ORDER BY`
rule and a deliberate tie-break, because half a million orders at
one-second granularity make same-second collisions inside a status a
certainty. The classic mistake is `ORDER BY created_at` alone - a syntax
error here, since the sort must start with `status`. The model answer
reads: group by status, oldest first, lower id settles dead heats.

## ex2

A pre-filter changes what "latest" means. The status condition must run
before the pick - `WHERE` does exactly that - so the survivor is each
customer's latest order *among the non-cancelled ones*. The classic mistake
is picking first and filtering after (an outer query's WHERE): that erases
customers whose most recent order was cancelled instead of falling back to
their previous one, which is a different report with quieter numbers. Where
a filter sits relative to a pick is a correctness decision, not style.

## ex3

Scale test with training wheels: `events.ts` is unique by construction, so
the tie-break can be skipped without harm - once you can say *why*. What it
was really testing is whether you know when determinism comes for free. The
classic mistake is assuming that property holds for every timestamp column;
`orders.created_at` and `customers.created_at` both collide. The model
answer sorts `event_type, ts DESC` and would add `, id DESC` on any column
without a uniqueness guarantee.

## ex4

`DISTINCT ON` over an expression. The parser wants the leading `ORDER BY`
item to match the `DISTINCT ON` expression, so `attributes ->> 'size'`
appears twice, verbatim. The classic mistake is writing the alias (`ORDER
BY size, ...` works, but only because PostgreSQL resolves the alias to the
same expression - rely on the verbatim form when in doubt). What it tested:
that the group key can be computed - a JSONB extraction, a `date_trunc`, an
arithmetic bucket - without changing the construct at all.

## ex5

Same idea pointed backwards in time: `ASC` instead of `DESC` flips "latest
per group" into "first per group", and nothing else moves. What it tested:
the selection rule lives entirely in the sort direction, plus a computed
group key (`date_trunc`). The classic mistake is an off-by-one on the year
filter - a closed `<= '2023-12-31'` drops nothing here but is the wrong
habit; the half-open `>= 2023-01-01 AND < 2024-01-01` form from lesson 18
is the one that survives timestamps.

## ex6

Composition with a self-join. The pick runs over the joined row set, so
`DISTINCT ON (s.manager_id)` sees reports already paired with their
manager's name - one construct, no second pass. What it tested: qualifying
every column once two copies of `staff` are in play, and realising the CEO
needs no special handling (a NULL `manager_id` never joins, so the row
never exists to be picked from). The classic mistake is grouping by the
manager's *name* - two managers can share one.

## ex7

The presentation-order conflict, which is the single most common real-world
stumble with this construct. The pick needs `ORDER BY month, revenue DESC,
country`; the stakeholder wants `revenue DESC, month`. One query cannot
serve both masters, so the pick becomes a subquery and the outer query
sorts the eleven survivors. The classic mistake is trying to bolt the
presentation sort onto the `DISTINCT ON` query and fighting the parser. The
model reasoning: aggregate, pick, present - three stages, each with its own
ordering needs, only the last one visible to the reader.

## ex8

Keeping the empty groups. `DISTINCT ON` alone answers "last event per
customer *who has events*"; the prompt demands all ten customers, so the
pick is built first and a `LEFT JOIN` attaches it - lesson 09's
join-then-keep logic wrapped around lesson 49's pick. The classic mistake
is `LEFT JOIN events` followed by `DISTINCT ON` with the customer filter in
the wrong place, or any filter on the events side in the outer `WHERE`,
which silently turns the join inner. The reference shows the third
spelling, `LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... LIMIT 1`, and choosing between the three
by index availability is a Part 5 conversation.

## Further reading

- [SELECT - DISTINCT Clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html#SQL-DISTINCT) - the formal rules for DISTINCT ON and its ORDER BY interaction.
- [Table Expressions - LATERAL Subqueries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-LATERAL) - the equivalent per-row-lookup spelling used in ex8's reference.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) - row_number(), the portable one-row-per-group idiom every reference here uses.
- [PostgreSQL Wiki - Don't do this](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) - a catalogue of adjacent footguns, including ambiguous picks that "work" until they don't.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

One row per status, and "which row" is decided by a sort - that is DISTINCT ON in one sentence (lesson 49). The ORDER BY must lead with the status.

## Hint 2

DISTINCT ON (status) ... ORDER BY status, created_at ASC, id ASC. Ascending picks the oldest order of each status; the id settles any same-second tie deterministically.

references.solution.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT status, id, created_at,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY status
                            ORDER BY created_at ASC, id ASC) AS rn
  FROM orders)
SELECT status, id AS order_id, created_at
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY status;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT ON (status)
       status, id AS order_id, created_at
FROM orders
ORDER BY status, created_at ASC, id ASC;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Same construct as ex1 with a row filter in front: WHERE runs before DISTINCT ON picks survivors, so cancelled orders must be gone before "latest" is decided.

## Hint 2

DISTINCT ON (customer_id) with WHERE customer_id <= 25 AND status <> 'cancelled', then ORDER BY customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC. Filtering after the pick (in an outer query) would return nothing at all for a customer whose latest order happened to be cancelled - a different report.

references.solution.sql:
WITH live AS (
  SELECT customer_id, id, status, created_at,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                            ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC) AS rn
  FROM orders
  WHERE customer_id <= 25
    AND status <> 'cancelled')
SELECT customer_id, id AS order_id, status, created_at
FROM live
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY customer_id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id)
       customer_id, id AS order_id, status, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id <= 25
  AND status <> 'cancelled'
ORDER BY customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

DISTINCT ON takes any expression, not just a column - here the group key lives inside a JSONB document (lesson 19's double-arrow).

## Hint 2

DISTINCT ON (attributes ->> 'size') with ORDER BY attributes ->> 'size', price ASC, id ASC. The leading ORDER BY expression must match the DISTINCT ON expression exactly, character for character as far as the parser cares.

references.solution.sql:
WITH sized AS (
  SELECT attributes ->> 'size' AS size, id, name, price,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY attributes ->> 'size'
                            ORDER BY price ASC, id ASC) AS rn
  FROM products
  WHERE category = 'clothing')
SELECT size, id, name, price
FROM sized
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY size;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT ON (attributes ->> 'size')
       attributes ->> 'size' AS size, id, name, price
FROM products
WHERE category = 'clothing'
ORDER BY attributes ->> 'size', price ASC, id ASC;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The group key is computed - date_trunc('month', ...) - and the selection rule runs the other way from every "latest" exercise: earliest first.

## Hint 2

DISTINCT ON (date_trunc('month', created_at)) ... ORDER BY date_trunc('month', created_at), created_at ASC, id ASC, with the 2023 window in WHERE. ASC picks the first order of the month; id breaks a same-second photo finish.

references.solution.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month, id, created_at,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY date_trunc('month', created_at)
                            ORDER BY created_at ASC, id ASC) AS rn
  FROM orders
  WHERE created_at >= '2023-01-01' AND created_at < '2024-01-01')
SELECT month, id AS order_id, created_at
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY month;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT ON (date_trunc('month', created_at))
       date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month,
       id AS order_id, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2023-01-01' AND created_at < '2024-01-01'
ORDER BY date_trunc('month', created_at), created_at ASC, id ASC;

## Exercise 6 - every manager's newest hire

For every staff member who manages at least one person: `manager_id`, the
manager's `name` as `manager`, and their most recently hired direct report
as `newest_report` with that report's `hired_on`. Ties on `hired_on` broken
by the report's `id`, higher wins. You will need the self-join from lesson
10 to put the manager's name on the row.

**Ordered by `manager_id` ascending.**

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 107_drills_distinct_on_1 ex6`

WITH ranked AS (

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two stages before the presentation: aggregate revenue per (month, country), then keep each month's best country. DISTINCT ON works on a CTE's output exactly as on a table.

## Hint 2

Stage one groups the non-cancelled 2023 join by month and country. Stage two is DISTINCT ON (month) ... ORDER BY month, revenue DESC, country ASC.

## Hint 3

The required output order (revenue DESC) fights DISTINCT ON, whose own ORDER BY must lead with month - so the pick and the presentation cannot share one ORDER BY. Wrap the DISTINCT ON stage and sort outside it. That wrap is the whole point of the exercise.

references.solution.sql:
WITH rev AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', o.created_at) AS month,
         c.country,
         sum(o.total) AS revenue
  FROM orders o
  JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
  WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
    AND o.created_at >= '2023-01-01' AND o.created_at < '2024-01-01'
  GROUP BY date_trunc('month', o.created_at), c.country),
ranked AS (
  SELECT month, country, revenue,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY month
                            ORDER BY revenue DESC, country ASC) AS rn
  FROM rev)
SELECT month, country, revenue
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY revenue DESC, month ASC;
references.expected.sql:
WITH rev AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', o.created_at) AS month,
         c.country,
         sum(o.total) AS revenue
  FROM orders o
  JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
  WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
    AND o.created_at >= '2023-01-01' AND o.created_at < '2024-01-01'
  GROUP BY date_trunc('month', o.created_at), c.country),
winners AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (month)
         month, country, revenue
  FROM rev
  ORDER BY month, revenue DESC, country ASC)
SELECT month, country, revenue
FROM winners
ORDER BY revenue DESC, month ASC;

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two requirements pull apart: one row per customer from the stream (DISTINCT ON), and keep customers who never appear in the stream (an outer join, lesson 09). Neither construct alone does both.

## Hint 2

Build the one-per-customer picks as a subquery - DISTINCT ON (customer_id) ... ORDER BY customer_id, ts DESC - and LEFT JOIN customers to it. Filtering c.id <= 10 belongs to the customers side, so it can sit in the outer WHERE without killing the outer join.

The order of operations matters: the subquery picks each customer's last event first, then the LEFT JOIN attaches it (or NULLs). A LEFT JOIN to raw events followed by DISTINCT ON would also work but drags three million rows through the join to keep one each. Lesson 48's LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two requirements pull apart: one row per customer from the stream (DISTINCT ON), and keep customers who never appear in the stream (an outer join, lesson 09). Neither construct alone does both.

## Hint 2

Build the one-per-customer picks as a subquery - DISTINCT ON (customer_id) ... ORDER BY customer_id, ts DESC - and LEFT JOIN customers to it. Filtering c.id <= 10 belongs to the customers side, so it can sit in the outer WHERE without killing the outer join.

## Hint 3

The order of operations matters: the subquery picks each customer's last event first, then the LEFT JOIN attaches it (or NULLs). A LEFT JOIN to raw events followed by DISTINCT ON would also work but drags three million rows through the join to keep one each. Lesson 48's LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... LIMIT 1 is the third spelling - the reference uses it.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name, t.event_type AS last_event_type, t.ts AS last_ts
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT e.event_type, e.ts
  FROM events e
  WHERE e.customer_id = c.id
  ORDER BY e.ts DESC
  LIMIT 1) t ON true
WHERE c.id <= 10
ORDER BY c.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name, e.event_type AS last_event_type, e.ts AS last_ts
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id)
         customer_id, event_type, ts
  FROM events
  ORDER BY customer_id, ts DESC) e
  ON e.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.id <= 10
ORDER BY c.id;

# 108 - Drills: GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP, CUBE, set 1

Eight problems on lesson 50: one query grouped several ways at once, subtotal
rows wearing NULLs, and `GROUPING()` to tell a synthetic NULL from a real
one. If ROLLUP-versus-CUBE-versus-spell-it-out is not yet a reflex, reread
lesson 50 before starting.

## Exercise 1 - headcount, with the bottom line

Headcount per `staff` department plus one all-staff total row in the same
result: `department`, `headcount`. The total row's `department` is NULL.

**Ordered by `department` ascending** (the NULL total row sorts last). (6
rows.)

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 108_drills_grouping_sets_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - signups by country and year, rolled up

For customers in `US`, `GB`, and `DE`: signups per (country, signup year),
a subtotal per country, and a grand total. Columns `country`, `yr` =
`extract(year FROM created_at)::int`, `signups`. Use the hierarchy
shorthand, not a hand-written list of groupings.

**Ordered by `country` ascending, then `yr` ascending** (NULL subtotals
after their details). (13 rows: 9 detail + 3 country subtotals + 1 total.)

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 108_drills_grouping_sets_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - a total row that says so

Orders per status plus a total row - but the total must be labelled: column
`status_label` reads `'all statuses'` on the total row and the plain status
elsewhere, column `orders` is the count. Use `GROUPING()`, not a NULL test,
to build the label.

**Ordered by `status_label` ascending.** (5 rows; `'all statuses'` happens
to sort first.)

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 108_drills_grouping_sets_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - first half of 2023, months under quarters

Revenue (`sum(total)`) for orders created in the first half of 2023
(half-open: `>= '2023-01-01' AND < '2023-07-01'`), broken down by month,
subtotalled by quarter, and totalled overall. Columns `qtr`
(`date_trunc('quarter', created_at)`), `month` (`date_trunc('month',
created_at)`), `revenue`.

**Ordered by `qtr` ascending, then `month` ascending.** (9 rows: 6 months
+ 2 quarter subtotals + 1 grand total.)

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 108_drills_grouping_sets_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - two breakdowns, no total

For reviews created on or after `2023-06-01` (join `products` for the
category): review counts **by category** and **by rating** in one result -
and *no* grand-total row. Columns `category`, `rating`, `reviews`; the
dimension a row is not grouped by is NULL.

**Ordered by `category` ascending, then `rating` ascending.** (11 rows: 6
categories then 5 ratings.)

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 108_drills_grouping_sets_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - keep only the margins

Over orders by customers in `FR` and `CA` (join `customers`): run `GROUP BY
CUBE (country, status)` and keep **only the marginal rows** - per-country
subtotals and per-status subtotals - discarding the detail rows and the
grand total, using `GROUPING()` in `HAVING`. Columns `country`, `status`,
`orders`.

**Ordered by `country` ascending, then `status` ascending.** (6 rows: 2
countries + 4 statuses.)

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 108_drills_grouping_sets_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - units and revenue by category and size

For `toys` and `food` products, over all their order lines: `units` =
`sum(quantity)` and `revenue` = `sum(quantity * price)` from `order_items`,
by (category, size), subtotalled per category, and totalled overall. The
size lives at `attributes ->> 'size'`. Columns `category`, `size`, `units`,
`revenue`.

**Ordered by `category` ascending, then `size` ascending.** (11 rows: 2x4
detail + 2 subtotals + 1 total.)

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 108_drills_grouping_sets_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - two NULLs walk into a report

Headcount per manager over `staff`, with a grand total - except the CEO's
`manager_id` is genuinely NULL, so the total row's synthetic NULL needs
disambiguating. Return `manager_label`: the manager id as text, `'NOBODY'`
for the staff with no manager, `'ALL'` for the grand-total row; and
`headcount`. One row per manager, plus the `'NOBODY'` row, plus `'ALL'`.

**Ordered by `headcount` descending, then `manager_label` ascending.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 108_drills_grouping_sets_1 ex8`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 108_drills_grouping_sets_1

Eight drills on multi-level aggregation. Read after your attempt, pass or
fail.

## Notes

All three constructs are shorthand for the same thing: a *union of
groupings* computed in one pass. `GROUPING SETS` lists the groupings
explicitly; `ROLLUP (a, b)` expands to the hierarchy `(a,b), (a), ()`;
`CUBE (a, b)` expands to every subset. Choosing between them is choosing
which rows you owe the reader - and nothing else, which is why every
exercise here can also be written as a UNION ALL of ordinary GROUP BYs (the
references do exactly that, at the price of scanning the data once per
grouping). The one genuinely new concept is the subtotal NULL: rolled-up
columns read NULL, that NULL is indistinguishable from a real one in the
data, and `GROUPING(col)` - 1 if the row aggregated `col` away, 0 otherwise
- is the only honest way to tell them apart. Ex8 is this set's reason to
exist; the rest build up to it.

## ex1

The smallest possible rollup, drilled for shape recognition: `ROLLUP
(department)` is `GROUPING SETS ((department), ())`. What it tested:
knowing the grand total costs one clause, not a second query or a UNION.
The classic mistake is computing the total in application code and having
it disagree with the details after the next data change - the single-pass
version cannot disagree with itself. Ascending sort parks the NULL row
last, which is a default worth memorising: ASC means NULLS LAST.

## ex2

ROLLUP as hierarchy. Country contains year, so the three useful levels are
detail, per-country, overall - and `ROLLUP (country, yr)` produces exactly
those, while `CUBE` would add per-year-across-countries rows nobody asked
for. What it tested: matching the construct to the shape of the question,
and grouping by an expression (`extract(...)::int`) spelled identically in
SELECT and GROUP BY. The classic mistake is column order - `ROLLUP (yr,
country)` subtotals by year, a different report.

## ex3

`GROUPING()` for presentation. The label must come from the grouping
machinery, not from `coalesce(status, 'all statuses')` - a NULL test gives
the same answer *today*, but only because `status` happens to be NOT NULL,
and it trains exactly the habit that breaks in ex8. What it tested: putting
`GROUPING(status)` inside a CASE in the SELECT list. The model reasoning:
the question "is this a subtotal row" is metadata, and GROUPING is the only
place that metadata survives.

## ex4

The reporting classic: months under quarters under everything, one scan of
the period. What it tested: a two-level `ROLLUP` over two computed
expressions, plus lesson 18's half-open window discipline on the way in.
The classic mistake is grouping by month alone and computing quarters in
your head - or worse, in a spreadsheet stapled to the query's output. Note
how ordering by `qtr, month` interleaves each quarter's subtotal directly
after its months; that adjacency is why rollup output is pleasant to read
raw.

## ex5

The case the shorthands cannot express: two independent breakdowns and no
total. `ROLLUP` always ends in `()`; `CUBE` adds the cross too; only
`GROUPING SETS ((a), (b))` says precisely this. What it tested: knowing
that the empty set `()` is a choice, not a default. The classic mistake is
using CUBE and filtering the unwanted rows afterwards - it works (ex6 makes
you do it deliberately), but scanning to compute rows you then discard is
the tool telling you it was the wrong tool.

## ex6

The inverse of ex5: produce all four CUBE levels, keep two, and let
`GROUPING()` do the keeping *in HAVING* - proof that GROUPING is an
ordinary expression usable wherever groups are visible. The arithmetic
trick `GROUPING(a) + GROUPING(b) = 1` reads "exactly one dimension rolled
up", i.e. the margins. The classic mistake is filtering with `country IS
NULL OR status IS NULL`, which here happens to work but conflates data
NULLs with subtotal NULLs - the exact confusion this lesson exists to
unlearn. The reference asks for the margins directly with GROUPING SETS.

## ex7

A rollup where the second level is a JSONB extraction. Nothing about the
grouping machinery changes; what changes is the bookkeeping - the
expression must be spelled identically in SELECT and in ROLLUP, and two
measures (units, revenue) ride along untouched. What it tested: composing
lesson 19's accessors with lesson 50's grouping without flinching, and
predicting the row inventory (4 sizes x 2 categories + 2 + 1) before
running - the fastest correctness check a multi-level report has.

## ex8

The disambiguation problem in its pure form. `staff.manager_id` is really
NULL for the CEO, so the rollup's total row and the CEO's row *both* show
NULL - and only `GROUPING(manager_id)` can separate "aggregated away" from
"absent in the data". The CASE must test GROUPING first: the total row also
passes `IS NULL`, so branch order is load-bearing. The classic mistake is
`COALESCE(manager_id::text, 'NOBODY')` over the rollup, which cheerfully
labels the grand total NOBODY and hands the CEO 501 direct reports. The
reference sidesteps with UNION ALL - defensible, two scans, and a reminder
that the single-pass version is the one that needed the new concept.

## Further reading

- [GROUPING SETS, CUBE, and ROLLUP](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-GROUPING-SETS) - the expansion rules, and how duplicate grouping sets behave.
- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html#FUNCTIONS-GROUPING-TABLE) - GROUPING() and its bitmask form for multiple arguments.
- [SELECT - GROUP BY Clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html#SQL-GROUPBY) - the reference grammar, including grouping by expressions.
- [Sorting Rows](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-order.html) - NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST, and why ascending subtotals land after their details by default.

# Reading - 108_drills_grouping_sets_1

Eight drills on multi-level aggregation. Read after your attempt, pass or
fail.

## Notes

All three constructs are shorthand for the same thing: a *union of
groupings* computed in one pass. `GROUPING SETS` lists the groupings
explicitly; `ROLLUP (a, b)` expands to the hierarchy `(a,b), (a), ()`;
`CUBE (a, b)` expands to every subset. Choosing between them is choosing
which rows you owe the reader - and nothing else, which is why every
exercise here can also be written as a UNION ALL of ordinary GROUP BYs (the
references do exactly that, at the price of scanning the data once per
grouping). The one genuinely new concept is the subtotal NULL: rolled-up
columns read NULL, that NULL is indistinguishable from a real one in the
data, and `GROUPING(col)` - 1 if the row aggregated `col` away, 0 otherwise
- is the only honest way to tell them apart. Ex8 is this set's reason to
exist; the rest build up to it.

## ex1

The smallest possible rollup, drilled for shape recognition: `ROLLUP
(department)` is `GROUPING SETS ((department), ())`. What it tested:
knowing the grand total costs one clause, not a second query or a UNION.
The classic mistake is computing the total in application code and having
it disagree with the details after the next data change - the single-pass
version cannot disagree with itself. Ascending sort parks the NULL row
last, which is a default worth memorising: ASC means NULLS LAST.

## ex2

ROLLUP as hierarchy. Country contains year, so the three useful levels are
detail, per-country, overall - and `ROLLUP (country, yr)` produces exactly
those, while `CUBE` would add per-year-across-countries rows nobody asked
for. What it tested: matching the construct to the shape of the question,
and grouping by an expression (`extract(...)::int`) spelled identically in
SELECT and GROUP BY. The classic mistake is column order - `ROLLUP (yr,
country)` subtotals by year, a different report.

## ex3

`GROUPING()` for presentation. The label must come from the grouping
machinery, not from `coalesce(status, 'all statuses')` - a NULL test gives
the same answer *today*, but only because `status` happens to be NOT NULL,
and it trains exactly the habit that breaks in ex8. What it tested: putting
`GROUPING(status)` inside a CASE in the SELECT list. The model reasoning:
the question "is this a subtotal row" is metadata, and GROUPING is the only
place that metadata survives.

## ex4

The reporting classic: months under quarters under everything, one scan of
the period. What it tested: a two-level `ROLLUP` over two computed
expressions, plus lesson 18's half-open window discipline on the way in.
The classic mistake is grouping by month alone and computing quarters in
your head - or worse, in a spreadsheet stapled to the query's output. Note
how ordering by `qtr, month` interleaves each quarter's subtotal directly
after its months; that adjacency is why rollup output is pleasant to read
raw.

## ex5

The case the shorthands cannot express: two independent breakdowns and no
total. `ROLLUP` always ends in `()`; `CUBE` adds the cross too; only
`GROUPING SETS ((a), (b))` says precisely this. What it tested: knowing
that the empty set `()` is a choice, not a default. The classic mistake is
using CUBE and filtering the unwanted rows afterwards - it works (ex6 makes
you do it deliberately), but scanning to compute rows you then discard is
the tool telling you it was the wrong tool.

## ex6

The inverse of ex5: produce all four CUBE levels, keep two, and let
`GROUPING()` do the keeping *in HAVING* - proof that GROUPING is an
ordinary expression usable wherever groups are visible. The arithmetic
trick `GROUPING(a) + GROUPING(b) = 1` reads "exactly one dimension rolled
up", i.e. the margins. The classic mistake is filtering with `country IS
NULL OR status IS NULL`, which here happens to work but conflates data
NULLs with subtotal NULLs - the exact confusion this lesson exists to
unlearn. The reference asks for the margins directly with GROUPING SETS.

## ex7

A rollup where the second level is a JSONB extraction. Nothing about the
grouping machinery changes; what changes is the bookkeeping - the
expression must be spelled identically in SELECT and in ROLLUP, and two
measures (units, revenue) ride along untouched. What it tested: composing
lesson 19's accessors with lesson 50's grouping without flinching, and
predicting the row inventory (4 sizes x 2 categories + 2 + 1) before
running - the fastest correctness check a multi-level report has.

## ex8

The disambiguation problem in its pure form. `staff.manager_id` is really
NULL for the CEO, so the rollup's total row and the CEO's row *both* show
NULL - and only `GROUPING(manager_id)` can separate "aggregated away" from
"absent in the data". The CASE must test GROUPING first: the total row also
passes `IS NULL`, so branch order is load-bearing. The classic mistake is
`COALESCE(manager_id::text, 'NOBODY')` over the rollup, which cheerfully
labels the grand total NOBODY and hands the CEO 501 direct reports. The
reference sidesteps with UNION ALL - defensible, two scans, and a reminder
that the single-pass version is the one that needed the new concept.

## Further reading

- [GROUPING SETS, CUBE, and ROLLUP](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-GROUPING-SETS) - the expansion rules, and how duplicate grouping sets behave.
- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html#FUNCTIONS-GROUPING-TABLE) - GROUPING() and its bitmask form for multiple arguments.
- [SELECT - GROUP BY Clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html#SQL-GROUPBY) - the reference grammar, including grouping by expressions.
- [Sorting Rows](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-order.html) - NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST, and why ascending subtotals land after their details by default.

## Exercise 1 - headcount, with the bottom line

Headcount per `staff` department plus one all-staff total row in the same
result: `department`, `headcount`. The total row's `department` is NULL.

**Ordered by `department` ascending** (the NULL total row sorts last). (6
rows.)

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 108_drills_grouping_sets_1 ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Five department rows plus one all-staff row from a single scan - lesson 50's one-level hierarchy. The extra row carries NULL in the rolled-up column.

## Hint 2

GROUP BY ROLLUP (department) produces the per-department groups and the grand total in one go. ORDER BY department puts the NULL total row last, because ascending sorts place NULLs last by default.

SELECT country, extract(year FROM created_at)::int AS yr, count(*) AS signups

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The total row should say 'all statuses', not NULL - and the honest way to detect the total row is GROUPING(), not a NULL test (lesson 50).

## Hint 2

CASE WHEN GROUPING(status) = 1 THEN 'all statuses' ELSE status END, over GROUP BY ROLLUP (status). GROUPING(status) returns 1 exactly on rows where status was rolled away.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT status AS status_label, count(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY status
UNION ALL
SELECT 'all statuses', count(*)
FROM orders
ORDER BY 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(status) = 1 THEN 'all statuses'
            ELSE status END AS status_label,
       count(*) AS orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY ROLLUP (status)
ORDER BY status_label;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 - first half of 2023, months under quarters

Revenue (`sum(total)`) for orders created in the first half of 2023
(half-open: `>= '2023-01-01' AND < '2023-07-01'`), broken down by month,
subtotalled by quarter, and totalled overall. Columns `qtr`
(`date_trunc('quarter', created_at)`), `month` (`date_trunc('month',
created_at)`), `revenue`.

**Ordered by `qtr` ascending, then `month` ascending.** (9 rows: 6 months
+ 2 quarter subtotals + 1 grand total.)

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 108_drills_grouping_sets_1 ex4`

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

CUBE produces four grouping levels; the report wants only the two one-dimensional ones. GROUPING() is how a HAVING clause can tell the levels apart.

## Hint 2

GROUPING(col) is 1 when the row aggregates that column away. A marginal row rolls up exactly one of the two dimensions, so the two GROUPING() values sum to 1.

## Hint 3

HAVING GROUPING(c.country) + GROUPING(o.status) = 1 keeps the country rows and the status rows, discarding the 8 detail rows and the grand total. (The reference gets the same rows by asking for them directly with GROUPING SETS - once you can write both, you understand both.)

references.solution.sql:
SELECT c.country, o.status, count(*) AS orders
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.country IN ('FR', 'CA')
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((c.country), (o.status))
ORDER BY c.country, o.status;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.country, o.status, count(*) AS orders
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.country IN ('FR', 'CA')
GROUP BY CUBE (c.country, o.status)
HAVING GROUPING(c.country) + GROUPING(o.status) = 1
ORDER BY c.country, o.status;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 - units and revenue by category and size

For `toys` and `food` products, over all their order lines: `units` =
`sum(quantity)` and `revenue` = `sum(quantity * price)` from `order_items`,
by (category, size), subtotalled per category, and totalled overall. The
size lives at `attributes ->> 'size'`. Columns `category`, `size`, `units`,
`revenue`.

**Ordered by `category` ascending, then `size` ascending.** (11 rows: 2x4
detail + 2 subtotals + 1 total.)

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 108_drills_grouping_sets_1 ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A rollup whose second level is not a column but a JSONB extraction - the grouping machinery does not care, as long as SELECT and ROLLUP spell the expression identically.

## Hint 2

GROUP BY ROLLUP (p.category, p.attributes ->> 'size') over the order_items-to-products join, filtered to the two categories. Two measures ride along unchanged: sum(quantity) and sum(quantity * price).

## Hint 3

Expected shape: four size rows per category, one subtotal per category (size NULL), one grand total (both NULL) - eleven rows. If you see size subtotals per se (category NULL, size set), you wrote CUBE, which answers a question nobody asked.

## Hint 1

A rollup whose second level is not a column but a JSONB extraction - the grouping machinery does not care, as long as SELECT and ROLLUP spell the expression identically.

## Hint 2

GROUP BY ROLLUP (p.category, p.attributes ->> 'size') over the order_items-to-products join, filtered to the two categories. Two measures ride along unchanged: sum(quantity) and sum(quantity * price).

## Hint 3

Expected shape: four size rows per category, one subtotal per category (size NULL), one grand total (both NULL) - eleven rows. If you see size subtotals per se (category NULL, size set), you wrote CUBE, which answers a question nobody asked.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT p.category,
       p.attributes ->> 'size' AS size,
       sum(oi.quantity) AS units,
       sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) AS revenue
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE p.category IN ('toys', 'food')
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS
  ((p.category, p.attributes ->> 'size'),
   (p.category),
   ())
ORDER BY 1, 2;

## Hint 1

Two different NULLs collide here: the CEO's genuinely NULL manager_id, and the synthetic NULL ROLLUP writes on the total row. A NULL test cannot tell them apart. GROUPING() exists for exactly this.

## Hint 2

GROUPING(manager_id) is 1 only on the rolled-up total row - the CEO's row, whose NULL came from the data, reports 0. Branch on GROUPING first, then on IS NULL.

## Hint 3

CASE WHEN GROUPING(manager_id) = 1 THEN 'ALL' WHEN manager_id IS NULL THEN 'NOBODY' ELSE manager_id::text END - order of the branches matters, since the total row also passes the IS NULL test. Everyone reports to somebody except the CEO, so NOBODY carries exactly one head.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT COALESCE(manager_id::text, 'NOBODY') AS manager_label,
       count(*) AS headcount
FROM staff
GROUP BY manager_id
UNION ALL
SELECT 'ALL', count(*)
FROM staff
ORDER BY 2 DESC, 1;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT CASE WHEN GROUPING(manager_id) = 1 THEN 'ALL'
            WHEN manager_id IS NULL THEN 'NOBODY'
            ELSE manager_id::text END AS manager_label,
       count(*) AS headcount
FROM staff
GROUP BY ROLLUP (manager_id)
ORDER BY headcount DESC, manager_label;

# 109 - Drills: report requests, set 1

Eight requests, written the way they actually arrive - a sentence from a
manager, not a spec. Translating prose into an exact query is the drilled
skill; the machinery is lessons 06-08, 12, 16-18 and 20. The output contract
under each quote is exact, because the gate compares literal rows.

## Exercise 1 - the Monday number

> "Quick one before the exec call: October, paid orders only - how many
> orders, how much revenue, and what was the average order worth?"

One row, three columns: `orders`, `revenue` = `sum(total)`, `aov` =
`round(avg(total), 2)`. October 2023, `status = 'paid'`, half-open dates.

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 109_drills_reports_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - the same month, split by week

> "Nice. Now split October by week so I can see the shape."

Columns `week` (`date_trunc('week', created_at)`), `orders`, `revenue` =
`sum(total)`; paid October orders as in ex1. **Ordered by `week`
ascending.** (6 rows - PostgreSQL weeks start Monday, so the first and last
rows are partial weeks.)

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 109_drills_reports_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - who is paying the bills this quarter

> "Top eight countries by real revenue since the quarter started, with the
> order counts. Real - leave the cancellations out."

Orders created on or after `2023-10-01`, `status <> 'cancelled'`, joined to
`customers` for `country`. Columns `country`, `orders`, `revenue` =
`sum(total)`. **Ordered by `revenue` descending, then `country` ascending,
limited to 8 rows.**

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 109_drills_reports_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - are cancellations eating us?

> "For each month this year: how many orders, how many got cancelled, and
> the cancellation rate. I want to see if it is drifting."

2023 orders. Columns `month` (`date_trunc('month', created_at)`), `orders`,
`cancelled`, `cancel_pct` = `round(100.0 * cancelled / orders, 1)`.
**Ordered by `month` ascending.** (11 rows - the data ends mid-November.)

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 109_drills_reports_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - how fast do signups start buying?

> "Of the people who did buy something: how long after signing up did their
> first order come, on average? By signup year, please."

For every customer with at least one order: their wait =
`min(order created_at)::date - signup created_at::date` in days. Columns
`signup_year` (`extract(year FROM customers.created_at)::int`), `buyers`,
`avg_days` = the average wait rounded to 1 decimal. **Ordered by
`signup_year` ascending.** (3 rows: 2021-2023.)

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 109_drills_reports_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - weekends versus weekdays, by category

> "Marketing swears weekends behave differently. Line-item revenue per
> category, weekday money and weekend money side by side - skip cancelled
> orders."

Over `order_items` joined to `orders` and `products`, `status <>
'cancelled'`: columns `category`, `weekday_rev`, `weekend_rev` - each a
`sum(quantity * price)` filtered by `extract(isodow FROM o.created_at)`
(`>= 6` is the weekend). **Ordered by `category` ascending.** (6 rows.)

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 109_drills_reports_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - the growth column

> "Paid orders per month for 2023, with the percent change on the previous
> month, and just tell me up or down - I read arrows faster than numbers."

Columns `month`, `orders` (paid, 2023), `change_pct` = `round(100.0 *
(orders - prev) / prev, 1)` where `prev` is the previous month's count, and
`trend` = `'up'` / `'down'` / `'flat'` comparing `orders` to `prev`.
January has no previous month: its `change_pct` and `trend` are NULL.
**Ordered by `month` ascending.** (11 rows.)

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 109_drills_reports_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - the whales that stopped calling

> "Our biggest customers who have gone quiet: top ten by lifetime real
> revenue among the ones with no order since September. Names on them,
> and when we last saw them."

Non-cancelled orders only, in both the revenue and the "last seen" sense: a
customer qualifies when their **latest non-cancelled order** is before
`2023-09-01`. Columns `customer_id`, `name`, `revenue` = `sum(total)`,
`last_order_at` = `max(created_at)`. **Ordered by `revenue` descending,
then `customer_id` ascending, limited to 10 rows.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 109_drills_reports_1 ex8`
