# Reading - 109_drills_reports_1

Eight requests translated from manager-speak. Read after your attempt, pass
or fail.

## Notes

The hard part of report work is rarely the SQL - it is the translation
table between prose and clauses. "Real revenue" is a status filter;
"October" is a half-open timestamp range; "rate" is a filtered count over a
total count with 100.0 doing the decimal work; "gone quiet since" is a
condition on max(), which only HAVING can see; "on average, how long until"
is a two-stage pipeline because the thing being averaged must be computed
per customer first. Every exercise here is one of those translations plus
machinery you already drilled. The habit worth building: before typing,
write the population in one sentence (whose rows count?), the grain (one
row per what?), and the measure - then check the finished query against all
three. Most wrong reports fail the population test, not the arithmetic.

## ex1

Three aggregates, one filtered scan, no grouping. What it tested: turning
"October, paid" into a half-open range plus a status equality without
over-thinking it. The classic mistake is `BETWEEN '2023-10-01' AND
'2023-10-31'`, which silently drops all of October 31st past midnight -
lesson 18's oldest lesson. The model answer filters once and lets count,
sum, and avg share the pass.

## ex2

The same population at week grain. What it tested: knowing
date_trunc('week', ...) starts weeks on Monday, so October's first "week"
begins September 25th and the month's edges land in partial buckets. The
classic mistake is assuming week one starts October 1st and treating the
low first bar as a sales dip. Deliver edge-bucket caveats with the chart,
not after the panicked reply-all.

## ex3

A join for the dimension, a filter for the population, an ordered LIMIT
for the "top". What it tested: assembling the standard revenue-by-X shape
quickly and pinning the tie-break (country ASC) so eighth place is
deterministic. The classic mistake is grouping by the customer instead of
the country, or forgetting that "since the quarter started" needs no upper
bound - the data ends when it ends.

## ex4

A rate per bucket: total count and conditional count over the same groups.
What it tested: count(*) FILTER (WHERE ...) - lesson 06 - plus the 100.0
multiplier that keeps the division out of integer arithmetic. The classic
mistake is computing cancelled counts in one query and totals in another
and dividing in a spreadsheet; the single-pass version cannot drift out of
sync with itself.

## ex5

The two-grain pipeline in its purest form: the wait (first order minus
signup) exists per customer, so it must be computed per customer before it
can be averaged per year. What it tested: min() at one grain feeding avg()
at another, date subtraction yielding integer days, and the population
sentence - "of the people who did buy" - which the inner join implements
for free. The classic mistake is joining and averaging in one grouped pass
over order rows, which weights frequent buyers' waits more heavily; the
reference's DISTINCT ON firsts makes the per-customer stage explicit.

## ex6

A two-column pivot with the pivot condition on a *different table* than
the measure: the day-of-week comes from the order, the money from the
line. What it tested: lesson 17's FILTER pivot after a three-table join,
and extract(isodow ...) where Saturday is 6 - isodow, not dow, whose
Sunday-is-zero convention has ruined many weekend reports. The classic
mistake is pivoting on the line's own attributes and wondering why the
weekend column looks random.

## ex7

lag() over a pre-aggregated CTE, then two derived columns comparing the
same pair of numbers. What it tested: lesson 16's frame-free lag, NULL
propagation doing the January edge case for free in the percentage, and an
explicit CASE for the label. The classic mistake is dividing by the
current month instead of the previous one - growth is measured against
where you were - or forgetting that the trend CASE needs its NULL branch
first, before the comparisons.

## ex8

"Gone quiet" is a property of the group, not of any row: their *latest*
order predates the cutoff. What it tested: HAVING on max(created_at) while
sum() rides the same grouped pass, and the difference between that and a
WHERE on created_at - which computes September-era revenue and hides
customers who ordered since, a different and wronger report. The model
reasoning: row filters change the money; group filters change only who
qualifies. Chose the wrong one and both numbers lie.

## Further reading

- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - FILTER syntax and every aggregate used in this set.
- [Date/Time Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) - date_trunc grains, extract(isodow), interval arithmetic.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) - lag() and friends for month-over-month shapes.
- [SELECT - HAVING](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html#SQL-HAVING) - conditions on groups versus conditions on rows, in the reference grammar.

## Ten-pass spaced repetition

Use this ladder after completing **109 - Drills: report requests, set 1**. Each pass changes the retrieval
task so repetition strengthens recall instead of becoming answer recognition.
Do the named exercise from a blank starting point whenever practical, and only
open its hints after recording your first attempt.

| Pass | When | Practice target | Retrieval task |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | now | `ex1` | Close the notes and state the central rule in one precise sentence. |
| 2 | 3 days | `ex2` | Rebuild the smallest valid example from memory, then explain each part. |
| 3 | 7 days | `ex3` | Predict the result or behavior before running anything; reconcile surprises. |
| 4 | 21 days | `ex4` | Solve from a blank file and name the first tempting mistake you avoided. |
| 5 | 60 days | `ex5` | Contrast this technique with its nearest alternative and choose between them. |
| 6 | 120 days | `ex6` | Add one realistic constraint and adapt the solution without consulting notes. |
| 7 | 240 days | `ex7` | Debug a deliberately broken version; explain the evidence before the repair. |
| 8 | 1 year | `ex8` | Teach the idea aloud in two minutes, including one boundary case. |
| 9 | 18 months | `ex1` | Transfer the pattern to a new domain and verify the result with the gate. |
| 10 | 3 years | `ex2` | Complete a cold, timed solution and write the rule you want to retain long-term. |

A failed pass is useful evidence: return to pass 1 after three days. A clean
pass advances to the next interval. After pass 10, revisit the skill every
three years or whenever real work exposes a weak edge case.

# Reading - 109_drills_reports_1

Eight requests translated from manager-speak. Read after your attempt, pass
or fail.

## Notes

The hard part of report work is rarely the SQL - it is the translation
table between prose and clauses. "Real revenue" is a status filter;
"October" is a half-open timestamp range; "rate" is a filtered count over a
total count with 100.0 doing the decimal work; "gone quiet since" is a
condition on max(), which only HAVING can see; "on average, how long until"
is a two-stage pipeline because the thing being averaged must be computed
per customer first. Every exercise here is one of those translations plus
machinery you already drilled. The habit worth building: before typing,
write the population in one sentence (whose rows count?), the grain (one
row per what?), and the measure - then check the finished query against all
three. Most wrong reports fail the population test, not the arithmetic.

## ex1

Three aggregates, one filtered scan, no grouping. What it tested: turning
"October, paid" into a half-open range plus a status equality without
over-thinking it. The classic mistake is `BETWEEN '2023-10-01' AND
'2023-10-31'`, which silently drops all of October 31st past midnight -
lesson 18's oldest lesson. The model answer filters once and lets count,
sum, and avg share the pass.

## ex2

The same population at week grain. What it tested: knowing
date_trunc('week', ...) starts weeks on Monday, so October's first "week"
begins September 25th and the month's edges land in partial buckets. The
classic mistake is assuming week one starts October 1st and treating the
low first bar as a sales dip. Deliver edge-bucket caveats with the chart,
not after the panicked reply-all.

## ex3

A join for the dimension, a filter for the population, an ordered LIMIT
for the "top". What it tested: assembling the standard revenue-by-X shape
quickly and pinning the tie-break (country ASC) so eighth place is
deterministic. The classic mistake is grouping by the customer instead of
the country, or forgetting that "since the quarter started" needs no upper
bound - the data ends when it ends.

## ex4

A rate per bucket: total count and conditional count over the same groups.
What it tested: count(*) FILTER (WHERE ...) - lesson 06 - plus the 100.0
multiplier that keeps the division out of integer arithmetic. The classic
mistake is computing cancelled counts in one query and totals in another
and dividing in a spreadsheet; the single-pass version cannot drift out of
sync with itself.

## ex5

The two-grain pipeline in its purest form: the wait (first order minus
signup) exists per customer, so it must be computed per customer before it
can be averaged per year. What it tested: min() at one grain feeding avg()
at another, date subtraction yielding integer days, and the population
sentence - "of the people who did buy" - which the inner join implements
for free. The classic mistake is joining and averaging in one grouped pass
over order rows, which weights frequent buyers' waits more heavily; the
reference's DISTINCT ON firsts makes the per-customer stage explicit.

## ex6

A two-column pivot with the pivot condition on a *different table* than
the measure: the day-of-week comes from the order, the money from the
line. What it tested: lesson 17's FILTER pivot after a three-table join,
and extract(isodow ...) where Saturday is 6 - isodow, not dow, whose
Sunday-is-zero convention has ruined many weekend reports. The classic
mistake is pivoting on the line's own attributes and wondering why the
weekend column looks random.

## ex7

lag() over a pre-aggregated CTE, then two derived columns comparing the
same pair of numbers. What it tested: lesson 16's frame-free lag, NULL
propagation doing the January edge case for free in the percentage, and an
explicit CASE for the label. The classic mistake is dividing by the
current month instead of the previous one - growth is measured against
where you were - or forgetting that the trend CASE needs its NULL branch
first, before the comparisons.

## ex8

"Gone quiet" is a property of the group, not of any row: their *latest*
order predates the cutoff. What it tested: HAVING on max(created_at) while
sum() rides the same grouped pass, and the difference between that and a
WHERE on created_at - which computes September-era revenue and hides
customers who ordered since, a different and wronger report. The model
reasoning: row filters change the money; group filters change only who
qualifies. Chose the wrong one and both numbers lie.

## Further reading

- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - FILTER syntax and every aggregate used in this set.
- [Date/Time Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) - date_trunc grains, extract(isodow), interval arithmetic.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) - lag() and friends for month-over-month shapes.
- [SELECT - HAVING](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html#SQL-HAVING) - conditions on groups versus conditions on rows, in the reference grammar.

## Exercise 1 - the Monday number

> "Quick one before the exec call: October, paid orders only - how many
> orders, how much revenue, and what was the average order worth?"

One row, three columns: `orders`, `revenue` = `sum(total)`, `aov` =
`round(avg(total), 2)`. October 2023, `status = 'paid'`, half-open dates.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

"Last month" is October 2023, "how much did we make" is paid orders only, and all three numbers come from one filtered aggregate - no grouping at all.

## Hint 2

WHERE status = 'paid' AND created_at >= '2023-10-01' AND created_at < '2023-11-01', then count(*), sum(total), and round(avg(total), 2) in one SELECT. Half-open date ranges, as always with timestamps.

references.solution.sql:
WITH oct_paid AS (
  SELECT total
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'paid'
    AND created_at >= '2023-10-01' AND created_at < '2023-11-01')
SELECT count(*) AS orders,
       sum(total) AS revenue,
       round(sum(total) / count(*), 2) AS aov
FROM oct_paid;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS orders,
       sum(total) AS revenue,
       round(avg(total), 2) AS aov
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
  AND created_at >= '2023-10-01' AND created_at < '2023-11-01';

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 - the same month, split by week

> "Nice. Now split October by week so I can see the shape."

Columns `week` (`date_trunc('week', created_at)`), `orders`, `revenue` =
`sum(total)`; paid October orders as in ex1. **Ordered by `week`
ascending.** (6 rows - PostgreSQL weeks start Monday, so the first and last
rows are partial weeks.)

references.solution.sql:
WITH oct_paid AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('week', created_at) AS week, total
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'paid'
    AND created_at >= '2023-10-01' AND created_at < '2023-11-01')
SELECT week, count(*) AS orders, sum(total) AS revenue
FROM oct_paid
GROUP BY week
ORDER BY week;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

"This quarter so far" is everything from October 1 onward - the data simply ends mid-November. "Real revenue" translates to excluding cancelled orders; the country lives one join away.

## Hint 2

Join orders to customers, filter status <> 'cancelled' AND created_at >= '2023-10-01', group by country, ORDER BY revenue DESC with country as tie-break, LIMIT 8.

references.solution.sql:
WITH per_country AS (
  SELECT c.country, count(*) AS orders, sum(o.total) AS revenue
  FROM orders o
  JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
  WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
    AND o.created_at >= '2023-10-01'
  GROUP BY c.country),
ranked AS (
  SELECT country, orders, revenue,
         row_number() OVER (ORDER BY revenue DESC, country) AS rn
  FROM per_country)
SELECT country, orders, revenue
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 8
ORDER BY revenue DESC, country;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.country, count(*) AS orders, sum(o.total) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
  AND o.created_at >= '2023-10-01'
GROUP BY c.country
ORDER BY revenue DESC, country ASC
LIMIT 8;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Total and conditional count over the same monthly groups: count(*) plus a FILTER clause (lesson 06), and the rate is one divided by the other.

## Hint 2

count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled') gives the numerator. Multiply by 100.0 - the decimal point matters, integer division would floor every rate to zero - and round to 1.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month,
       count(*) AS orders,
       sum(CASE WHEN status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled,
       round(100.0 * sum(CASE WHEN status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / count(*), 1) AS cancel_pct
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2023-01-01' AND created_at < '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY date_trunc('month', created_at)
ORDER BY month;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month,
       count(*) AS orders,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled') / count(*), 1) AS cancel_pct
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2023-01-01' AND created_at < '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY date_trunc('month', created_at)
ORDER BY month;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 - how fast do signups start buying?

> "Of the people who did buy something: how long after signing up did their
> first order come, on average? By signup year, please."

For every customer with at least one order: their wait =
`min(order created_at)::date - signup created_at::date` in days. Columns
`signup_year` (`extract(year FROM customers.created_at)::int`), `buyers`,
`avg_days` = the average wait rounded to 1 decimal. **Ordered by
`signup_year` ascending.** (3 rows: 2021-2023.)

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 109_drills_reports_1 ex5`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two aggregations at different grains: first, each buyer's earliest order (per customer); then the average of those waits (per signup year). Collapsing them into one pass computes something else.

## Hint 2

Stage one: join customers to orders, GROUP BY customer, keep min(o.created_at) and the signup date. The wait in days is min(...)::date - c.created_at::date - date minus date is already an integer.

## Hint 3

Stage two groups stage one by signup year: count(*) is the buyers, round(avg(days), 1) the average wait. Customers who never ordered fall out at the join, which is what "among customers who bought" means - state that population note when you deliver numbers like these.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two aggregations at different grains: first, each buyer's earliest order (per customer); then the average of those waits (per signup year). Collapsing them into one pass computes something else.

## Hint 2

Stage one: join customers to orders, GROUP BY customer, keep min(o.created_at) and the signup date. The wait in days is min(...)::date - c.created_at::date - date minus date is already an integer.

## Hint 3

Stage two groups stage one by signup year: count(*) is the buyers, round(avg(days), 1) the average wait. Customers who never ordered fall out at the join, which is what "among customers who bought" means - state that population note when you deliver numbers like these.

references.solution.sql:
WITH first_orders AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id)
         customer_id, created_at AS first_at
  FROM orders
  ORDER BY customer_id, created_at ASC, id ASC)
SELECT extract(year FROM c.created_at)::int AS signup_year,
       count(*) AS buyers,
       round(avg(f.first_at::date - c.created_at::date), 1) AS avg_days
FROM first_orders f
JOIN customers c ON c.id = f.customer_id
GROUP BY extract(year FROM c.created_at)::int
ORDER BY signup_year;
references.expected.sql:
WITH firsts AS (
  SELECT c.id,
         extract(year FROM c.created_at)::int AS signup_year,
         min(o.created_at)::date - c.created_at::date AS days_to_first
  FROM customers c
  JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
  GROUP BY c.id, c.created_at)
SELECT signup_year,
       count(*) AS buyers,
       round(avg(days_to_first), 1) AS avg_days
FROM firsts
GROUP BY signup_year
ORDER BY signup_year;

## Hint 1

A two-column pivot (lesson 17): one row per category, weekday money in one column, weekend money in the other. The day-of-week test is lesson 18's extract(isodow ...), where Saturday is 6.

## Hint 2

Two filtered sums over the three-table join: sum(quantity * price) FILTER (WHERE extract(isodow FROM o.created_at) >= 6) for weekends, < 6 for weekdays, non-cancelled orders only. references.solution.sql:
SELECT p.category,
       sum(CASE WHEN extract(isodow FROM o.created_at) < 6
                THEN oi.quantity * oi.price ELSE 0 END) AS weekday_rev,
       sum(CASE WHEN extract(isodow FROM o.created_at) >= 6
                THEN oi.quantity * oi.price ELSE 0 END) AS weekend_rev
FROM order_items oi
JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY p.category
ORDER BY p.category;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT p.category,
       sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) FILTER (WHERE extract(isodow FROM o.created_at) < 6)  AS weekday_rev,
       sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) FILTER (WHERE extract(isodow FROM o.created_at) >= 6) AS weekend_rev
FROM order_items oi
JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY p.category
ORDER BY p.category;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Monthly paid order counts first (a CTE), then each month against the one before - lesson 16's lag(). The percentage and the label both compare the same two numbers.

## Hint 2

lag(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month) is last month's count. change_pct is 100.0 * (orders - prev) / prev rounded to 1; January has no prev, so both computed columns are NULL there - division by NULL is NULL, no special casing needed for the pct.

## Hint 3

Naming the lag once in an intermediate CTE (SELECT ..., lag(...) AS prev) keeps the final SELECT readable and the CASE honest: WHEN prev IS NULL THEN NULL first, then the up/down/flat branches. Writing lag() four times inline also works - the reference and expected answers do one each.

references.solution.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month, count(*) AS orders
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'paid'
    AND created_at >= '2023-01-01' AND created_at < '2024-01-01'
  GROUP BY 1),
lagged AS (
  SELECT month, orders,
         lag(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev
  FROM monthly)
SELECT month,
       orders,
       round(100.0 * (orders - prev) / prev, 1) AS change_pct,
       CASE WHEN prev IS NULL THEN NULL
            WHEN orders > prev THEN 'up'
            WHEN orders < prev THEN 'down'
            ELSE 'flat' END AS trend
FROM lagged
ORDER BY month;
references.expected.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month, count(*) AS orders
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'paid'
    AND created_at >= '2023-01-01' AND created_at < '2024-01-01'
  GROUP BY date_trunc('month', created_at))
SELECT month,
       orders,
       round(100.0 * (orders - lag(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month))
             / lag(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month), 1) AS change_pct,
       CASE WHEN lag(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month) IS NULL THEN NULL
            WHEN orders > lag(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month) THEN 'up'
            WHEN orders < lag(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month) THEN 'down'
            ELSE 'flat' END AS trend
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 - the whales that stopped calling

> "Our biggest customers who have gone quiet: top ten by lifetime real
> revenue among the ones with no order since September. Names on them,
> and when we last saw them."

Non-cancelled orders only, in both the revenue and the "last seen" sense: a
customer qualifies when their **latest non-cancelled order** is before
`2023-09-01`. Columns `customer_id`, `name`, `revenue` = `sum(total)`,
`last_order_at` = `max(created_at)`. **Ordered by `revenue` descending,
then `customer_id` ascending, limited to 10 rows.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 109_drills_reports_1 ex8`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

"Has not ordered since" is a property of a customer's whole order history - their latest order predates the cutoff - so it is a condition on max(created_at), which only HAVING (or a post-aggregation WHERE) can see.

## Hint 2

Group non-cancelled orders by customer; keep groups with HAVING max(created_at) < '2023-09-01'. The revenue sum and the last-order timestamp come from the same grouped pass.

## Hint 3

Do not filter created_at < '2023-09-01' in WHERE - that computes revenue as of September and hides any customer who ordered after the cutoff only partially. The row filter changes both the population and the money; the group filter changes only the population. Rank by revenue, tie-break customer_id, LIMIT 10.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

"Has not ordered since" is a property of a customer's whole order history - their latest order predates the cutoff - so it is a condition on max(created_at), which only HAVING (or a post-aggregation WHERE) can see.

## Hint 2

Group non-cancelled orders by customer; keep groups with HAVING max(created_at) < '2023-09-01'. The revenue sum and the last-order timestamp come from the same grouped pass.

## Hint 3

Do not filter created_at < '2023-09-01' in WHERE - that computes revenue as of September and hides any customer who ordered after the cutoff only partially. The row filter changes both the population and the money; the group filter changes only the population. Rank by revenue, tie-break customer_id, LIMIT 10.

references.solution.sql:
WITH lifetime AS (
  SELECT customer_id,
         sum(total) AS revenue,
         max(created_at) AS last_order_at
  FROM orders
  WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
  GROUP BY customer_id)
SELECT l.customer_id, c.name, l.revenue, l.last_order_at
FROM lifetime l
JOIN customers c ON c.id = l.customer_id
WHERE l.last_order_at < '2023-09-01'
ORDER BY l.revenue DESC, l.customer_id ASC
LIMIT 10;

SELECT o.customer_id,
       c.name,
       sum(o.total) AS revenue,
       max(o.created_at) AS last_order_at
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY o.customer_id, c.name
HAVING max(o.created_at) < '2023-09-01'
ORDER BY revenue DESC, customer_id ASC
LIMIT 10;

# Reading - 110_drills_reports_2

Eight report requests, heavy on cohorts and two-stage aggregation. Read
after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

Almost every request in this set hides the same structural decision: *which
grain do I aggregate at first?* Cohort questions (ex5, ex7) are
per-customer facts rolled up to per-cohort summaries; the distribution
question (ex6) is a per-customer measure histogrammed; the two-ratio
table (ex8) hinges entirely on order-grain versus customer-grain
denominators; even the hall of shame (ex3) is per-product facts filtered
and ranked. Collapse the two
grains into one pass and you get numbers that look plausible and are wrong
- the averaged average, the order counted as a buyer. The other recurring
skill is population honesty: every one of these reports silently excludes
somebody (never-buyers, customers absent from the stream, cohorts without a
full 30-day runway), and the analyst's job is to know exactly who and say
so when handing over the number.

## ex1

A warm-up that is really about restraint: no filter, because the requester
wants cancelled orders *in* the comparison. What it tested: reading intent
before typing WHERE. The classic mistake is reflexively excluding
cancellations because other revenue reports do - here that deletes the most
interesting row. The model answer is a four-row GROUP BY with a rounded
average, nothing more.

## ex2

date_trunc at quarter grain over the full two-year customer table. What it
tested: picking the grain the requester named rather than the one you
usually type, and remembering partial edge buckets. The classic mistake is
labelling quarters by extract(quarter ...) alone, which merges 2022-Q4 with
2023-Q4; date_trunc keeps the year in the key. The first and last quarters
are partial - a chart without that footnote invites a false "growth"
story at the edges.

## ex3

Threshold-then-rank. The HAVING floor (100 reviews or more) is what makes
"worst" mean something - without it a product with one angry review tops
the list. What it tested: HAVING on a count, plus a subtle ordering rule:
sort on the *unrounded* average and tie-break by id, because two products
sharing a rounded 2.71 still differ in truth, and sorting the display value
makes the bottom-ten roster shuffle between runs. Rank on the real number,
display the rounded one.

## ex4

A relative time window: the report anchors on max(ts), not on a date
somebody typed. What it tested: lesson 18's interval arithmetic driving a
lesson 17 FILTER pivot, and the half-open upper bound (last_day + 1 day)
that keeps all of the final day. The classic mistake is WHERE ts >= now()
- interval '3 days' - this dataset's clock stopped in November 2023, and
any report anchored on the wall clock instead of the data returns nothing
and gets blamed on the database.

## ex5

A per-customer deadline. "Within 30 days" means within 30 days *of their
own signup* - the comparison c.created_at + interval '30 days' rides along
per row, which is what makes this a cohort query rather than a date-range
query. The classic mistake is one shared cutoff date, which flatters early
cohorts and starves late ones. The model reasoning: a customer converts
fast iff their first order beats their personal deadline, so min(created_at)
per customer answers it in one pass - and the November cohort has not had
its full 30 days yet, which an honest report says out loud.

## ex6

The aggregate of an aggregate, drilled before on orders (lesson 68) and
here on a 3,000,000-row stream. What it tested: count(DISTINCT ...) at the
inner grain, a histogram at the outer grain, and knowing the population is
"customers who appear in events at all". The classic mistake is joining
customers in and reporting a zero-types row - defensible, but a different
question than the one asked, and the kind of silent scope change that makes
two dashboards disagree.

## ex7

Buyers versus heavy buyers. The inner join to orders quietly implements
"bought at all", and the heaviness test lives at the customer grain (order
count >= 12), then rolls up to the cohort. What it tested: FILTER over a
grouped CTE, denominator discipline - the rate divides heavy by *buyers*,
not by signups - and threshold awareness: the typical buyer here places
about ten orders, so a bar of two would read ~100% and measure nothing.
The classic mistake is counting orders instead of customers somewhere in
the pipeline; the rate then exceeds 100% and, worse, sometimes does not,
so it survives review.

## ex8

Two ratios that differ only in their denominator, which is the entire
point: AOV divides revenue by orders, ARPU divides the same revenue by
distinct buyers, and the gap between them is repeat purchasing made
visible (arpu / aov is literally orders per buyer). What it tested:
running count(*), count(DISTINCT customer_id), and sum(total) through one
grouped pass and dividing carefully at the end. The classic mistake is
using the wrong denominator in one of the two - the report still renders,
the two columns just quietly answer the same question twice, which is
exactly the confusion the requester complained about.

## Further reading

- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - FILTER, count(DISTINCT ...), and their interaction.
- [Date/Time Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) - date_trunc, interval arithmetic, and extract.
- [WITH Queries (CTEs)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) - staging multi-grain pipelines readably.
- [Use The Index, Luke - Dates](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause/obfuscation/dates) - why half-open ranges on raw columns beat function-wrapped filters.

# Reading - 110_drills_reports_2

Eight report requests, heavy on cohorts and two-stage aggregation. Read
after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

Almost every request in this set hides the same structural decision: *which
grain do I aggregate at first?* Cohort questions (ex5, ex7) are
per-customer facts rolled up to per-cohort summaries; the distribution
question (ex6) is a per-customer measure histogrammed; the two-ratio
table (ex8) hinges entirely on order-grain versus customer-grain
denominators; even the hall of shame (ex3) is per-product facts filtered
and ranked. Collapse the two
grains into one pass and you get numbers that look plausible and are wrong
- the averaged average, the order counted as a buyer. The other recurring
skill is population honesty: every one of these reports silently excludes
somebody (never-buyers, customers absent from the stream, cohorts without a
full 30-day runway), and the analyst's job is to know exactly who and say
so when handing over the number.

## ex1

A warm-up that is really about restraint: no filter, because the requester
wants cancelled orders *in* the comparison. What it tested: reading intent
before typing WHERE. The classic mistake is reflexively excluding
cancellations because other revenue reports do - here that deletes the most
interesting row. The model answer is a four-row GROUP BY with a rounded
average, nothing more.

## ex2

date_trunc at quarter grain over the full two-year customer table. What it
tested: picking the grain the requester named rather than the one you
usually type, and remembering partial edge buckets. The classic mistake is
labelling quarters by extract(quarter ...) alone, which merges 2022-Q4 with
2023-Q4; date_trunc keeps the year in the key. The first and last quarters
are partial - a chart without that footnote invites a false "growth"
story at the edges.

## ex3

Threshold-then-rank. The HAVING floor (100 reviews or more) is what makes
"worst" mean something - without it a product with one angry review tops
the list. What it tested: HAVING on a count, plus a subtle ordering rule:
sort on the *unrounded* average and tie-break by id, because two products
sharing a rounded 2.71 still differ in truth, and sorting the display value
makes the bottom-ten roster shuffle between runs. Rank on the real number,
display the rounded one.

## ex4

A relative time window: the report anchors on max(ts), not on a date
somebody typed. What it tested: lesson 18's interval arithmetic driving a
lesson 17 FILTER pivot, and the half-open upper bound (last_day + 1 day)
that keeps all of the final day. The classic mistake is WHERE ts >= now()
- interval '3 days' - this dataset's clock stopped in November 2023, and
any report anchored on the wall clock instead of the data returns nothing
and gets blamed on the database.

## ex5

A per-customer deadline. "Within 30 days" means within 30 days *of their
own signup* - the comparison c.created_at + interval '30 days' rides along
per row, which is what makes this a cohort query rather than a date-range
query. The classic mistake is one shared cutoff date, which flatters early
cohorts and starves late ones. The model reasoning: a customer converts
fast iff their first order beats their personal deadline, so min(created_at)
per customer answers it in one pass - and the November cohort has not had
its full 30 days yet, which an honest report says out loud.

## ex6

The aggregate of an aggregate, drilled before on orders (lesson 68) and
here on a 3,000,000-row stream. What it tested: count(DISTINCT ...) at the
inner grain, a histogram at the outer grain, and knowing the population is
"customers who appear in events at all". The classic mistake is joining
customers in and reporting a zero-types row - defensible, but a different
question than the one asked, and the kind of silent scope change that makes
two dashboards disagree.

## ex7

Buyers versus heavy buyers. The inner join to orders quietly implements
"bought at all", and the heaviness test lives at the customer grain (order
count >= 12), then rolls up to the cohort. What it tested: FILTER over a
grouped CTE, denominator discipline - the rate divides heavy by *buyers*,
not by signups - and threshold awareness: the typical buyer here places
about ten orders, so a bar of two would read ~100% and measure nothing.
The classic mistake is counting orders instead of customers somewhere in
the pipeline; the rate then exceeds 100% and, worse, sometimes does not,
so it survives review.

## ex8

Two ratios that differ only in their denominator, which is the entire
point: AOV divides revenue by orders, ARPU divides the same revenue by
distinct buyers, and the gap between them is repeat purchasing made
visible (arpu / aov is literally orders per buyer). What it tested:
running count(*), count(DISTINCT customer_id), and sum(total) through one
grouped pass and dividing carefully at the end. The classic mistake is
using the wrong denominator in one of the two - the report still renders,
the two columns just quietly answer the same question twice, which is
exactly the confusion the requester complained about.

## Further reading

- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - FILTER, count(DISTINCT ...), and their interaction.
- [Date/Time Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) - date_trunc, interval arithmetic, and extract.
- [WITH Queries (CTEs)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html) - staging multi-grain pipelines readably.
- [Use The Index, Luke - Dates](https://use-the-index-luke.com/sql/where-clause/obfuscation/dates) - why half-open ranges on raw columns beat function-wrapped filters.

## Hint 1

One grouped pass over orders: a count and an average per status. Lesson 07 shape, nothing hidden.

references.solution.sql:
WITH grouped AS (
  SELECT status, count(*) AS orders, sum(total) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY status)
SELECT status, orders, round(revenue / orders, 2) AS avg_total
FROM grouped
ORDER BY status;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT status,
       count(*) AS orders,
       round(avg(total), 2) AS avg_total
FROM orders
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY status;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Aggregate reviews per product, keep only products with enough of them (a HAVING threshold), and take the bottom of the list. The join to products is only there for the name.

## Hint 2

HAVING count(*) >= 100 guards against a one-review product "winning" with a single 1-star. Sort ascending on the average.

## Hint 3

Sort on the unrounded average - ORDER BY avg(rating), not the rounded output column - and tie-break by id. Two products can share a rounded 2.71 while their true averages differ; sorting the display value shuffles them arbitrarily.

references.solution.sql:
WITH scored AS (
  SELECT product_id,
         count(*) AS reviews,
         avg(rating) AS raw_avg
  FROM reviews
  GROUP BY product_id
  HAVING count(*) >= 100)
SELECT p.id, p.name, s.reviews, round(s.raw_avg, 2) AS avg_rating
FROM scored s
JOIN products p ON p.id = s.product_id
ORDER BY s.raw_avg ASC, p.id ASC
LIMIT 10;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT p.id, p.name,
       count(*) AS reviews,
       round(avg(r.rating), 2) AS avg_rating
FROM products p
JOIN reviews r ON r.product_id = p.id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
HAVING count(*) >= 100
ORDER BY avg(r.rating) ASC, p.id ASC
LIMIT 10;

## Hint 2

## Hint 3

references.solution.sql:
WITH bounds AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('day', max(ts)) AS last_day
  FROM events),
windowed AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('day', ts) AS day, event_type
  FROM events, bounds
  WHERE ts >= last_day - interval '2 days'
    AND ts <  last_day + interval '1 day')
SELECT day,
       sum(CASE WHEN event_type = 'view'        THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS views,
       sum(CASE WHEN event_type = 'click'       THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS clicks,
       sum(CASE WHEN event_type = 'add_to_cart' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS carts,
       sum(CASE WHEN event_type = 'purchase'    THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS purchases,
       sum(CASE WHEN event_type = 'logout'      THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS logouts
FROM windowed
GROUP BY day
ORDER BY day;
references.expected.sql:
WITH bounds AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('day', max(ts)) AS last_day
  FROM events)
SELECT date_trunc('day', e.ts) AS day,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE e.event_type = 'view')        AS views,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE e.event_type = 'click')       AS clicks,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE e.event_type = 'add_to_cart') AS carts,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE e.event_type = 'purchase')    AS purchases,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE e.event_type = 'logout')      AS logouts
FROM events e, bounds b
WHERE e.ts >= b.last_day - interval '2 days'
  AND e.ts <  b.last_day + interval '1 day'
GROUP BY date_trunc('day', e.ts)
ORDER BY day;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 - do new signups convert fast?

> "For each signup month this year: how many people signed up, and how many
> ordered within their first 30 days. Percentage too."

2023 signup cohorts (`date_trunc('month', customers.created_at)`). A fast
buyer has an order with `o.created_at < c.created_at + interval '30
days'`. Columns `cohort`, `signups`, `fast_buyers`, `fast_pct` =
`round(100.0 * fast_buyers / signups, 1)`. **Ordered by `cohort`
ascending.** (11 rows.)

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Per 2023 signup month: everybody, and the subset who ordered within 30 days of their own signup. The deadline is per-customer - c.created_at + interval '30 days' - not a fixed date.

## Hint 2

Build the fast-buyer set once (join customers to orders, keep o.created_at < c.created_at + interval '30 days', DISTINCT customer), LEFT JOIN it back to the cohort population, and count both columns per cohort. count(f.id) skips the NULLs of the non-converters - lesson 66's counting trick doing real work.

## Hint 3

Equivalent and tidier: a customer converted fast if and only if their FIRST order beat the deadline, so min(created_at) per customer in a CTE also answers it - the reference does that. Note the last cohorts have not had a full 30 days of runway; a real report would say so.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Per 2023 signup month: everybody, and the subset who ordered within 30 days of their own signup. The deadline is per-customer - c.created_at + interval '30 days' - not a fixed date.

## Hint 2

Build the fast-buyer set once (join customers to orders, keep o.created_at < c.created_at + interval '30 days', DISTINCT customer), LEFT JOIN it back to the cohort population, and count both columns per cohort. count(f.id) skips the NULLs of the non-converters - lesson 66's counting trick doing real work.

## Hint 3

Equivalent and tidier: a customer converted fast if and only if their FIRST order beat the deadline, so min(created_at) per customer in a CTE also answers it - the reference does that. Note the last cohorts have not had a full 30 days of runway; a real report would say so.

references.solution.sql:
WITH firsts AS (
  SELECT customer_id, min(created_at) AS first_order
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id)
SELECT date_trunc('month', c.created_at) AS cohort,
       count(*) AS signups,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE f.first_order < c.created_at + interval '30 days') AS fast_buyers,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE f.first_order < c.created_at + interval '30 days')
             / count(*), 1) AS fast_pct
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN firsts f ON f.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.created_at >= '2023-01-01'
GROUP BY date_trunc('month', c.created_at)
ORDER BY cohort;
references.expected.sql:
WITH cohort_customers AS (
  SELECT id, created_at, date_trunc('month', created_at) AS cohort
  FROM customers
  WHERE created_at >= '2023-01-01'),
fast AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT cc.id
  FROM cohort_customers cc
  JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = cc.id
  WHERE o.created_at < cc.created_at + interval '30 days')
SELECT cc.cohort,
       count(*) AS signups,
       count(f.id) AS fast_buyers,
       round(100.0 * count(f.id) / count(*), 1) AS fast_pct
FROM cohort_customers cc
LEFT JOIN fast f ON f.id = cc.id
GROUP BY cc.cohort
ORDER BY cc.cohort;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Cohort = signup quarter, population = 2023 signups who bought at all, and "heavy" is a property of a customer's order count - so aggregate per customer before aggregating per cohort.

## Hint 2

Stage one: join 2023 customers to their orders, GROUP BY customer, keep the count. An inner join is the "bought at all" filter for free.

## Hint 3

Stage two groups stage one by cohort: buyers = count(*), heavy = count(*) FILTER (WHERE orders >= 12), and the rate is 100.0 * heavy / buyers rounded to 1. If your rate sits near 100 percent, your threshold is testing "ordered at all" - the typical buyer here places about ten orders, which is why the bar sits above it.

references.solution.sql:
WITH counts AS (
  SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS orders
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id)
SELECT date_trunc('quarter', c.created_at) AS cohort,
       count(*) AS buyers,
       sum(CASE WHEN n.orders >= 12 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS heavy,
       round(100.0 * sum(CASE WHEN n.orders >= 12 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / count(*), 1) AS heavy_pct
FROM customers c
JOIN counts n ON n.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.created_at >= '2023-01-01'
GROUP BY date_trunc('quarter', c.created_at)
ORDER BY cohort;
references.expected.sql:
WITH per_customer AS (
  SELECT c.id,
         date_trunc('quarter', c.created_at) AS cohort,
         count(o.id) AS orders
  FROM customers c
  JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
  WHERE c.created_at >= '2023-01-01'
  GROUP BY c.id, date_trunc('quarter', c.created_at))
SELECT cohort,
       count(*) AS buyers,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE orders >= 12) AS heavy,
       round(100.0 * count(*) FILTER (WHERE orders >= 12) / count(*), 1) AS heavy_pct
FROM per_customer
GROUP BY cohort
ORDER BY cohort;

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two ratios, two denominators: the average order divides revenue by ORDERS, revenue per buyer divides the same revenue by DISTINCT customers. Everything comes from one grouped pass over non-cancelled 2023 orders.

## Hint 2

aov = round(sum(total) / count(*), 2) - or round(avg(total), 2), same number - and arpu = round(sum(total) / count(DISTINCT customer_id), 2). arpu can never be below aov, because a buyer places at least one order.

## Hint 3

Sanity check worth knowing: arpu / aov = orders per buyer. If your arpu comes out BELOW your aov, one of the denominators is counting the wrong thing - usually orders where buyers belong.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two ratios, two denominators: the average order divides revenue by ORDERS, revenue per buyer divides the same revenue by DISTINCT customers. Everything comes from one grouped pass over non-cancelled 2023 orders.

## Hint 2

aov = round(sum(total) / count(*), 2) - or round(avg(total), 2), same number - and arpu = round(sum(total) / count(DISTINCT customer_id), 2). arpu can never be below aov, because a buyer places at least one order.

## Hint 3

Sanity check worth knowing: arpu / aov = orders per buyer. If your arpu comes out BELOW your aov, one of the denominators is counting the wrong thing - usually orders where buyers belong.

references.solution.sql:
WITH m AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month, customer_id, total
  FROM orders
  WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
    AND created_at >= '2023-01-01' AND created_at < '2024-01-01')
SELECT month,
       count(*) AS orders,
       count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS buyers,
       round(avg(total), 2) AS aov,
       round(sum(total) / count(DISTINCT customer_id), 2) AS arpu
FROM m
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;

       count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS buyers,
       round(sum(total) / count(*), 2) AS aov,

FROM orders
WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
  AND created_at >= '2023-01-01' AND created_at < '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY date_trunc('month', created_at)
ORDER BY month;

# 111 - Drills: report requests, set 3

The last reports set, and the hardest translations: relative time windows,
window functions inside business asks, and one genuine interview classic at
the end. The quotes are the request; the contract below each is what the
gate grades.

## Exercise 1 - what did yesterday look like?

> "Morning digest: yesterday's traffic in one line - events, distinct
> visitors, purchases."

"Yesterday" is the last complete day of the stream: with `last_day =
date_trunc('day', max(ts))`, the window is `ts >= last_day - interval '1
day' AND ts < last_day`. One row: `events`, `actives` (distinct
`customer_id`), `purchases` (events of type `'purchase'`).

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 111_drills_reports_3 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - books versus electronics, head to head

> "Settle an argument: October, real money only - did books or electronics
> earn more?"

One row, two columns: `books_rev` and `electronics_rev`, each the
`sum(quantity * price)` of that category's order lines for orders created
in October 2023 with `status <> 'cancelled'`.

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 111_drills_reports_3 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - a price ladder for the toy aisle

> "Bucket the toys for the gift guide: under 100, 100 to 300, 300 plus.
> How many in each shelf and the average price - cheap shelf first."

Columns `band` (exactly the labels `'under 100'`, `'100 to 299.99'`,
`'300 and up'`), `products`, `avg_price` = `round(avg(price), 2)`.
**Ordered cheapest band first** - sort by `min(price)` per band, not
alphabetically. (3 rows.)

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 111_drills_reports_3 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - who is underpaid around here?

> "HR review: everyone sitting 20 percent or more below their own
> department's average salary, worst-off first."

Columns `id`, `name`, `department`, `salary`, `dept_avg` =
`round(avg, 2)`, `below_pct` = `round(100.0 * (avg - salary) / avg, 1)`.
Qualify on the **unrounded** average (`salary <= 0.8 * dept_avg`).
**Ordered by the unrounded gap ratio descending, then `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 111_drills_reports_3 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - does one product carry each category?

> "For every category: its single biggest earner, and how much of the
> category's revenue that one product represents."

Non-cancelled line revenue (`quantity * price`) per product, then per
category: the top product (revenue ties broken by product `id`). Columns
`category`, `product_id`, `name`, `revenue`, `cat_share_pct` =
`round(100.0 * revenue / category revenue, 1)`. **Ordered by `category`
ascending.** (6 rows.)

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 111_drills_reports_3 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - how long between orders, typically?

> "One number: on average, how many days pass between a customer's
> consecutive orders?"

Gaps are per customer (`lag` over their orders by `created_at`, ties by
`id`), measured in whole days between `::date` values; first orders have
no gap and do not count. One row: `avg_gap_days` = the average gap rounded
to 1 decimal.

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 111_drills_reports_3 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - revenue per buyer, where it means something

> "Rank countries by revenue per buyer - real revenue - but only where we
> have at least a hundred buyers, I do not want boutique noise."

Non-cancelled orders joined to customers. Columns `country`, `buyers`
(distinct customers), `revenue` = `sum(total)`, `per_buyer` =
`round(revenue / buyers, 2)`; keep countries with `buyers >= 100`.
**Ordered by `per_buyer` descending, then `country` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 111_drills_reports_3 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - the golden basket

> "Which category pairs actually get bought together? Same order, two
> different categories - count the orders, best pairs first."

Columns `cat_a`, `cat_b` (alphabetical within the pair: `cat_a < cat_b`),
`orders` = the number of **distinct orders** containing at least one line
from each. An order with three books lines and two toys lines is one
books-toys order. **Ordered by `orders` descending, then `cat_a`, then
`cat_b`.** (15 rows.)

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 111_drills_reports_3 ex8`

# Reading - 111_drills_reports_3

The hardest of the three report sets. Read after your attempt, pass or
fail.

## Notes

Two disciplines separate this set from the previous two. First, *relative
anchors*: reports that say "yesterday" or "the cheapest shelf first" cannot
hard-code what they mean - they derive it from the data (`max(ts)`,
`min(price)`) so the query stays true as the data moves. Second, *decision
math versus display math*: several exercises round a number for the reader
while filtering or sorting on its unrounded value, and keeping those two
uses separate is the difference between a report that is stable and one
whose bottom edge flickers. The finale is a genuine interview staple - the
co-occurrence (basket) query - whose two traps, double-counted pairs and
join-row inflation, are both worth failing once here where it is cheap.

## ex1

A relative time window with a one-row answer. What it tested: anchoring
"yesterday" on `date_trunc('day', max(ts))` and taking the day *before* it,
because the stream's final day is partial and would understate everything.
The classic mistake is anchoring on `now()` - this dataset's clock stopped
in 2023, and a wall-clock anchor returns zeros that get blamed on the
database rather than the query. Three aggregates share the filtered pass.

## ex2

A two-cell pivot over a three-table join. What it tested: keeping each
filter at its own grain - month on the order, category on the product,
money on the line - and lesson 17's FILTER doing the split. The classic
mistake is joining and then summing `oi.price` alone (forgetting quantity),
or filtering the month on the line's implicit date, which does not exist -
line items have no timestamp, and noticing that *is* the exercise.

## ex3

CASE buckets with a semantic sort. Alphabetical band order is nonsense to a
reader, and the fix - `ORDER BY min(price)` - sorts groups by an aggregate
that never appears in the output, which many people do not know is legal.
What it tested: exact label discipline (the gate compares strings) and that
ordering trick. The classic mistake is a second CASE in ORDER BY that
drifts out of sync with the first when a band edge changes; deriving the
order from the data cannot drift.

## ex4

A window average as a per-row benchmark, then a filter on it - which
forces the CTE wrap, because WHERE cannot see window results (lesson 15's
rule resurfacing under HR's clothing). What it tested: that wrap, plus
qualifying and sorting on unrounded values while displaying rounded ones.
The classic mistake is filtering `below_pct >= 20` after rounding: someone
at 19.96 rounds to 20.0 and appears - or disappears - depending on which
value you compared. Decide on the truth, display the summary.

## ex5

One per-product revenue CTE asked two questions: who is biggest per
category, and how big is the category. The pick is lesson 49's DISTINCT ON
(or `row_number() = 1`); the denominator is either a second grouped pass
joined back or a window `sum() OVER (PARTITION BY category)` riding the
same scan - the reference does both jobs in one window pass. The classic
mistake is computing the share against *overall* revenue instead of the
category's, which makes every flagship look tiny and the report pointless.

## ex6

Consecutive-row arithmetic at scale: lag() partitioned per customer,
date-cast subtraction, then an average over the gaps - two stages, since
window output cannot feed an aggregate in the same query. The elegant
check hidden in the reference: gaps telescope, so the global average gap
is `sum(last - first) / sum(n - 1)` over multi-order customers, no window
at all. If the two spellings disagree, the window version's partition
leaked across customers. Knowing a second derivation of your own number is
the cheapest audit there is.

## ex7

A ratio with a distinct-count denominator and a volume floor. What it
tested: `count(DISTINCT customer_id)` doing double duty in the SELECT and
the HAVING, and understanding *why* the floor exists - a three-buyer
country can top any per-buyer ranking on luck alone, and the requester
preemptively declined that conversation. The classic mistake is dividing
by `count(*)` (orders, not buyers), which deflates exactly the countries
with loyal repeat customers - the opposite of the question.

## ex8

The basket query. Two independent dedupes must both happen: each unordered
category pair counted once per order (`p1.category < p2.category`), and
each order counted once per pair no matter how many line combinations
produce it (`count(DISTINCT order_id)`). Miss the first and every pair
appears twice, mirrored; miss the second and multi-line orders inflate
their pairs quadratically - both bugs produce plausible-looking leader
boards, which is what makes this an interview favourite. The reference
reduces first (DISTINCT order-category pairs in a CTE) and then counts
plainly - the shape that scales, and the one to remember.

## Further reading

- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) - partitioned lag() and running benchmarks.
- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - FILTER, distinct aggregates, and aggregates in ORDER BY.
- [Date/Time Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) - date_trunc anchoring and interval arithmetic.
- [Self-Joins (PostgreSQL wiki examples)](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/SQL_scripts) - co-occurrence and pairing patterns over a single table.

## Ten-pass spaced repetition

Use this ladder after completing **111 - Drills: report requests, set 3**. Each pass changes the retrieval
task so repetition strengthens recall instead of becoming answer recognition.
Do the named exercise from a blank starting point whenever practical, and only
open its hints after recording your first attempt.

| Pass | When | Practice target | Retrieval task |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | now | `ex1` | Close the notes and state the central rule in one precise sentence. |
| 2 | 3 days | `ex2` | Rebuild the smallest valid example from memory, then explain each part. |
| 3 | 7 days | `ex3` | Predict the result or behavior before running anything; reconcile surprises. |
| 4 | 21 days | `ex4` | Solve from a blank file and name the first tempting mistake you avoided. |
| 5 | 60 days | `ex5` | Contrast this technique with its nearest alternative and choose between them. |
| 6 | 120 days | `ex6` | Add one realistic constraint and adapt the solution without consulting notes. |
| 7 | 240 days | `ex7` | Debug a deliberately broken version; explain the evidence before the repair. |
| 8 | 1 year | `ex8` | Teach the idea aloud in two minutes, including one boundary case. |
| 9 | 18 months | `ex1` | Transfer the pattern to a new domain and verify the result with the gate. |
| 10 | 3 years | `ex2` | Complete a cold, timed solution and write the rule you want to retain long-term. |

A failed pass is useful evidence: return to pass 1 after three days. A clean

# Reading - 111_drills_reports_3

The hardest of the three report sets. Read after your attempt, pass or
fail.

## Notes

Two disciplines separate this set from the previous two. First, *relative
anchors*: reports that say "yesterday" or "the cheapest shelf first" cannot
hard-code what they mean - they derive it from the data (`max(ts)`,
`min(price)`) so the query stays true as the data moves. Second, *decision
math versus display math*: several exercises round a number for the reader
while filtering or sorting on its unrounded value, and keeping those two
uses separate is the difference between a report that is stable and one
whose bottom edge flickers. The finale is a genuine interview staple - the
co-occurrence (basket) query - whose two traps, double-counted pairs and
join-row inflation, are both worth failing once here where it is cheap.

## ex1

A relative time window with a one-row answer. What it tested: anchoring
"yesterday" on `date_trunc('day', max(ts))` and taking the day *before* it,
because the stream's final day is partial and would understate everything.
The classic mistake is anchoring on `now()` - this dataset's clock stopped
in 2023, and a wall-clock anchor returns zeros that get blamed on the
database rather than the query. Three aggregates share the filtered pass.

## ex2

A two-cell pivot over a three-table join. What it tested: keeping each
filter at its own grain - month on the order, category on the product,
money on the line - and lesson 17's FILTER doing the split. The classic
mistake is joining and then summing `oi.price` alone (forgetting quantity),
or filtering the month on the line's implicit date, which does not exist -
line items have no timestamp, and noticing that *is* the exercise.

## ex3

CASE buckets with a semantic sort. Alphabetical band order is nonsense to a
reader, and the fix - `ORDER BY min(price)` - sorts groups by an aggregate
that never appears in the output, which many people do not know is legal.
What it tested: exact label discipline (the gate compares strings) and that
ordering trick. The classic mistake is a second CASE in ORDER BY that
drifts out of sync with the first when a band edge changes; deriving the
order from the data cannot drift.

## ex4

A window average as a per-row benchmark, then a filter on it - which
forces the CTE wrap, because WHERE cannot see window results (lesson 15's
rule resurfacing under HR's clothing). What it tested: that wrap, plus
qualifying and sorting on unrounded values while displaying rounded ones.
The classic mistake is filtering `below_pct >= 20` after rounding: someone
at 19.96 rounds to 20.0 and appears - or disappears - depending on which
value you compared. Decide on the truth, display the summary.

## ex5

One per-product revenue CTE asked two questions: who is biggest per
category, and how big is the category. The pick is lesson 49's DISTINCT ON
(or `row_number() = 1`); the denominator is either a second grouped pass
joined back or a window `sum() OVER (PARTITION BY category)` riding the
same scan - the reference does both jobs in one window pass. The classic
mistake is computing the share against *overall* revenue instead of the
category's, which makes every flagship look tiny and the report pointless.

## ex6

Consecutive-row arithmetic at scale: lag() partitioned per customer,
date-cast subtraction, then an average over the gaps - two stages, since
window output cannot feed an aggregate in the same query. The elegant
check hidden in the reference: gaps telescope, so the global average gap
is `sum(last - first) / sum(n - 1)` over multi-order customers, no window
at all. If the two spellings disagree, the window version's partition
leaked across customers. Knowing a second derivation of your own number is
the cheapest audit there is.

## ex7

A ratio with a distinct-count denominator and a volume floor. What it
tested: `count(DISTINCT customer_id)` doing double duty in the SELECT and
the HAVING, and understanding *why* the floor exists - a three-buyer
country can top any per-buyer ranking on luck alone, and the requester
preemptively declined that conversation. The classic mistake is dividing
by `count(*)` (orders, not buyers), which deflates exactly the countries
with loyal repeat customers - the opposite of the question.

## ex8

The basket query. Two independent dedupes must both happen: each unordered
category pair counted once per order (`p1.category < p2.category`), and
each order counted once per pair no matter how many line combinations
produce it (`count(DISTINCT order_id)`). Miss the first and every pair
appears twice, mirrored; miss the second and multi-line orders inflate
their pairs quadratically - both bugs produce plausible-looking leader
boards, which is what makes this an interview favourite. The reference
reduces first (DISTINCT order-category pairs in a CTE) and then counts
plainly - the shape that scales, and the one to remember.

## Further reading

- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) - partitioned lag() and running benchmarks.
- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - FILTER, distinct aggregates, and aggregates in ORDER BY.
- [Date/Time Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-datetime.html) - date_trunc anchoring and interval arithmetic.
- [Self-Joins (PostgreSQL wiki examples)](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/SQL_scripts) - co-occurrence and pairing patterns over a single table.

## Exercise 1 - what did yesterday look like?

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

"Yesterday" relative to a stream that stopped in 2023 means the last complete day of data: the day before the day max(ts) falls on. Anchor on the data, never on the wall clock.

## Hint 2

last_day = date_trunc('day', max(ts)); the window is ts >= last_day - interval '1 day' AND ts < last_day. Then count(*), count(DISTINCT customer_id), and a FILTER count of purchases in one pass.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS events,
       count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS actives,
       sum(CASE WHEN event_type = 'purchase' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS purchases
FROM events
WHERE ts >= (SELECT date_trunc('day', max(ts)) - interval '1 day' FROM events)
  AND ts <  (SELECT date_trunc('day', max(ts)) FROM events);
references.expected.sql:
WITH bounds AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('day', max(ts)) AS last_day
  FROM events)
SELECT count(*) AS events,
       count(DISTINCT e.customer_id) AS actives,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE e.event_type = 'purchase') AS purchases
FROM events e, bounds b
WHERE e.ts >= b.last_day - interval '1 day'
  AND e.ts <  b.last_day;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

One row, two columns - a two-cell pivot (lesson 17). The revenue is line-item money (quantity * price), the month filter lives on the order, the category on the product.

## Hint 2

Two filtered sums over the three-table join: sum(quantity * price) FILTER (WHERE category = 'books') and the electronics twin, October half-open, cancelled orders out.

references.solution.sql:
WITH rev AS (
  SELECT p.category, sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) AS revenue
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
  JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
  WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
    AND o.created_at >= '2023-10-01' AND o.created_at < '2023-11-01'
    AND p.category IN ('books', 'electronics')
  GROUP BY p.category)
SELECT max(revenue) FILTER (WHERE category = 'books')       AS books_rev,
       max(revenue) FILTER (WHERE category = 'electronics') AS electronics_rev
FROM rev;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) FILTER (WHERE p.category = 'books')       AS books_rev,
       sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) FILTER (WHERE p.category = 'electronics') AS electronics_rev
FROM order_items oi
JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
  AND o.created_at >= '2023-10-01' AND o.created_at < '2023-11-01'
  AND p.category IN ('books', 'electronics');

## Exercise 3 - a price ladder for the toy aisle

> "Bucket the toys for the gift guide: under 100, 100 to 300, 300 plus.
> How many in each shelf and the average price - cheap shelf first."

Columns `band` (exactly the labels `'under 100'`, `'100 to 299.99'`,
`'300 and up'`), `products`, `avg_price` = `round(avg(price), 2)`.
**Ordered cheapest band first** - sort by `min(price)` per band, not
alphabetically. (3 rows.)

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

CASE buckets (lesson 64) as the grouping key, over toys only. The interesting part is the ordering: alphabetical order would put '100 to 299.99' before 'under 100', which reads like a shuffled ladder.

## Hint 2

Group by the CASE expression, then ORDER BY min(price) - each band's cheapest product sorts the bands into their natural ladder without a second CASE. (Ordering by an aggregate you never SELECT is legal and underused; a CASE-based sort key works too.)

## Hint 1

CASE buckets (lesson 64) as the grouping key, over toys only. The interesting part is the ordering: alphabetical order would put '100 to 299.99' before 'under 100', which reads like a shuffled ladder.

## Hint 2

Group by the CASE expression, then ORDER BY min(price) - each band's cheapest product sorts the bands into their natural ladder without a second CASE. (Ordering by an aggregate you never SELECT is legal and underused; a CASE-based sort key works too.)

references.solution.sql:
WITH banded AS (
  SELECT CASE WHEN price < 100 THEN 'under 100'
              WHEN price < 300 THEN '100 to 299.99'
              ELSE '300 and up' END AS band,
         price
  FROM products
  WHERE category = 'toys')
SELECT band, count(*) AS products, round(avg(price), 2) AS avg_price
FROM banded
GROUP BY band
ORDER BY CASE band WHEN 'under 100' THEN 1
                   WHEN '100 to 299.99' THEN 2
                   ELSE 3 END;

SELECT CASE WHEN price < 100 THEN 'under 100'
            WHEN price < 300 THEN '100 to 299.99'
            ELSE '300 and up' END AS band,
       count(*) AS products,
       round(avg(price), 2) AS avg_price
FROM products
WHERE category = 'toys'
GROUP BY CASE WHEN price < 100 THEN 'under 100'
              WHEN price < 300 THEN '100 to 299.99'
              ELSE '300 and up' END
ORDER BY min(price);

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Each row needs its own department's average sitting next to it - a window average (lesson 15), or equivalently a grouped CTE joined back. "20 percent or more below" compares salary against 0.8 times that average.

## Hint 2

avg(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) puts the benchmark on every row, but a window result cannot be referenced in the same query's WHERE - wrap it in a CTE and filter outside.

## Hint 3

Filter with salary <= 0.8 * dept_avg (the unrounded average), and sort by the unrounded gap ratio descending with id as tie-break. Rounding first and then filtering on the rounded value shifts people across the 20.0 boundary - display math and decision math are different math.

references.solution.sql:
WITH davg AS (
  SELECT department, avg(salary) AS dept_avg
  FROM staff
  GROUP BY department)
SELECT s.id, s.name, s.department, s.salary,
       round(d.dept_avg, 2) AS dept_avg,
       round(100.0 * (d.dept_avg - s.salary) / d.dept_avg, 1) AS below_pct
FROM staff s
JOIN davg d USING (department)
WHERE s.salary <= 0.8 * d.dept_avg
ORDER BY (d.dept_avg - s.salary) / d.dept_avg DESC, s.id ASC;
references.expected.sql:
WITH scored AS (
  SELECT id, name, department, salary,
         avg(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS dept_avg
  FROM staff)
SELECT id, name, department, salary,
       round(dept_avg, 2) AS dept_avg,
       round(100.0 * (dept_avg - salary) / dept_avg, 1) AS below_pct
FROM scored
WHERE salary <= 0.8 * dept_avg
ORDER BY (dept_avg - salary) / dept_avg DESC, id ASC;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three facts per category - its total revenue, its best product, and that product's revenue - all derived from one per-product revenue table. Build that table once in a CTE and ask it both questions.

## Hint 2

From the per-product CTE: DISTINCT ON (category) ... ORDER BY category, revenue DESC, id picks the flagship; a second grouped pass (or a window sum) gets the category total.

## Hint 3

The share divides the flagship's revenue by the category total - 100.0 * revenue / cat_rev, rounded to 1. The window formulation carries both row_number() and sum() OVER the same partition, answering everything in one pass; the two-CTE join is the same report spelled longhand.

references.solution.sql:
WITH prod_rev AS (
  SELECT p.category, p.id, p.name, sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) AS revenue
  FROM products p
  JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
  JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
  WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
  GROUP BY p.category, p.id, p.name),
w AS (
  SELECT category, id, name, revenue,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY category
                            ORDER BY revenue DESC, id ASC) AS rn,
         sum(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY category) AS cat_rev
  FROM prod_rev)
SELECT category, id AS product_id, name, revenue,
       round(100.0 * revenue / cat_rev, 1) AS cat_share_pct
FROM w
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY category;
references.expected.sql:
WITH prod_rev AS (
  SELECT p.category, p.id, p.name, sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) AS revenue
  FROM products p
  JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
  JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
  WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
  GROUP BY p.category, p.id, p.name),
tot AS (
  SELECT category, sum(revenue) AS cat_rev
  FROM prod_rev
  GROUP BY category),
best AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (category)
         category, id, name, revenue
  FROM prod_rev
  ORDER BY category, revenue DESC, id ASC)
SELECT b.category, b.id AS product_id, b.name, b.revenue,
       round(100.0 * b.revenue / t.cat_rev, 1) AS cat_share_pct
FROM best b
JOIN tot t USING (category)
ORDER BY b.category;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 - how long between orders, typically?

> "One number: on average, how many days pass between a customer's
> consecutive orders?"

Gaps are per customer (`lag` over their orders by `created_at`, ties by
`id`), measured in whole days between `::date` values; first orders have
no gap and do not count. One row: `avg_gap_days` = the average gap rounded
to 1 decimal.

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 111_drills_reports_3 ex6`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A gap exists between consecutive orders of the same customer - lag() partitioned by customer (lesson 16), ordered by time. Averaging the gaps is a second stage, because window results cannot feed an aggregate in the same query.

## Hint 2

gap_days = created_at::date - (lag(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at, id))::date. Each customer's first order has no predecessor - its NULL gap must not count, and avg() skips NULLs, so it does not.

## Hint 3

Sanity-check with algebra: a customer's gaps telescope, so the sum of everyone's gaps is sum(last order date - first order date) and the gap count is sum(orders - 1) over customers with 2+ orders. The reference computes the average that way - no window at all. If your number disagrees with it, your window probably crossed customers.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A gap exists between consecutive orders of the same customer - lag() partitioned by customer (lesson 16), ordered by time. Averaging the gaps is a second stage, because window results cannot feed an aggregate in the same query.

## Hint 2

gap_days = created_at::date - (lag(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at, id))::date. Each customer's first order has no predecessor - its NULL gap must not count, and avg() skips NULLs, so it does not.

## Hint 3

Sanity-check with algebra: a customer's gaps telescope, so the sum of everyone's gaps is sum(last order date - first order date) and the gap count is sum(orders - 1) over customers with 2+ orders. The reference computes the average that way - no window at all. If your number disagrees with it, your window probably crossed customers.

references.solution.sql:
WITH per_c AS (
  SELECT customer_id,
         count(*) AS n,
         max(created_at)::date AS last_day,
         min(created_at)::date AS first_day
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
  HAVING count(*) >= 2)
SELECT round(sum(last_day - first_day)::numeric / sum(n - 1), 1) AS avg_gap_days
FROM per_c;
references.expected.sql:
WITH gaps AS (
  SELECT created_at::date
         - (lag(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                                  ORDER BY created_at, id))::date AS gap_days
  FROM orders)
SELECT round(avg(gap_days), 1) AS avg_gap_days
FROM gaps
WHERE gap_days IS NOT NULL;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Revenue per buyer needs a distinct-customer denominator - an order count would flatter countries full of repeat buyers. The volume floor is a HAVING condition on that same distinct count.

## Hint 2

count(DISTINCT o.customer_id) is both the buyers column and the HAVING guard (>= 100). per_buyer = round(sum(total) / that count, 2), non-cancelled only, ranked descending with the country as tie-break.

references.solution.sql:
WITH per_customer AS (
  SELECT c.country, o.customer_id, sum(o.total) AS spent
  FROM orders o
  JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
  WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
  GROUP BY c.country, o.customer_id)
SELECT country,
       count(*) AS buyers,
       sum(spent) AS revenue,
       round(sum(spent) / count(*), 2) AS per_buyer
FROM per_customer
GROUP BY country
HAVING count(*) >= 100
ORDER BY per_buyer DESC, country ASC;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.country,
       count(DISTINCT o.customer_id) AS buyers,
       sum(o.total) AS revenue,
       round(sum(o.total) / count(DISTINCT o.customer_id), 2) AS per_buyer
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY c.country
HAVING count(DISTINCT o.customer_id) >= 100
ORDER BY per_buyer DESC, country ASC;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

"Bought together" means two lines of the same order landing in two different categories - a self-join of order_items on order_id, with each side joined to products for its category.

## Hint 2

The pair must be unordered and counted once: category-a < category-b (the same dedupe trick as tag pairs and teammate pairs). And an order with three books and two toys is still ONE books-toys basket - count DISTINCT order_id, not join rows.

## Hint 3

The cleaner shape reduces first: a CTE of DISTINCT (order_id, category) pairs, self-joined with a.category < b.category, then a plain count(*) - the distinct work happens once instead of inside the aggregate. Fifteen possible pairs, all present; ordered by orders DESC with the pair as tie-break.

references.solution.sql:
WITH oc AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT oi.order_id, p.category
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id)
SELECT a.category AS cat_a,
       b.category AS cat_b,
       count(*) AS orders
FROM oc a
JOIN oc b ON b.order_id = a.order_id
         AND a.category < b.category
GROUP BY a.category, b.category
ORDER BY orders DESC, cat_a ASC, cat_b ASC;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT p1.category AS cat_a,
       p2.category AS cat_b,
       count(DISTINCT oi1.order_id) AS orders
FROM order_items oi1
JOIN order_items oi2 ON oi2.order_id = oi1.order_id
JOIN products p1 ON p1.id = oi1.product_id
JOIN products p2 ON p2.id = oi2.product_id
WHERE p1.category < p2.category
GROUP BY p1.category, p2.category
ORDER BY orders DESC, cat_a ASC, cat_b ASC;
