# 112 - Drills: mixed gauntlet, set 1

The first of three cumulative gauntlets: every exercise welds two or three
topics from anywhere in the course - JSONB with joins, anti-joins with
business rules, window frames with verdicts. Nothing here is new; the drill
is recognising which tools the sentence needs and composing them cleanly.

## Exercise 1 - clothing revenue by colour

Line-item revenue (`sum(quantity * price)` over `order_items`) for
`clothing` products, grouped by the product's `color` attribute. Columns
`color`, `revenue`.

**Ordered by `color` ascending.** (5 rows.)

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 112_drills_mixed_1 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - the weekly rhythm

Orders per ISO day of week, with a weekend flag. Columns `dow` =
`extract(isodow FROM created_at)::int` (Monday is 1), `orders`,
`is_weekend` = boolean, true for days 6 and 7.

**Ordered by `dow` ascending.** (7 rows.)

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 112_drills_mixed_1 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - German signups that never stuck

Customers in `DE` who signed up on or after `2023-01-01` and have **no
non-cancelled order** - never ordered at all, or every order cancelled.
Columns `id`, `name`, `created_at`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 112_drills_mixed_1 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - the person in the middle

For every `staff` department: the person on the **middle rung** of its
salary ladder. Rank each department's staff by `salary DESC, id ASC`; with
`n` people, the middle is position `(n + 1) / 2` using integer division
(so 5 people give position 3, 4 people give position 2). Columns
`department`, `name`, `salary`.

**Ordered by `department` ascending.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 112_drills_mixed_1 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - who lapsed in November?

One row, one column `lapsed`: how many customers placed at least one order
in October 2023 but none in November 2023. (Half-open month ranges; the
data ends November 14, which counts as November.)

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 112_drills_mixed_1 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - price versus reputation

Per category: `avg_price` = `round(avg(products.price), 2)` and
`avg_rating` = `round(avg(reviews.rating), 2)` across all reviews of that
category's products. Columns `category`, `avg_price`, `avg_rating`. The
two averages live at different grains - aggregate each on its own, then
join; one big join-then-average pass computes a subtly different (and
wrong) `avg_price`.

**Ordered by `category` ascending.** (6 rows.)

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 112_drills_mixed_1 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - beating your own average

Monthly `electronics` line revenue for 2023, each month judged against the
average of **up to three prior months** (the current month excluded from
its own benchmark). Columns `month`, `revenue`, `prior3_avg` = the frame
average rounded to 2 (NULL for January, which has no prior months), `flag`
= `'above'` / `'below'` comparing the unrounded values (NULL for January).

**Ordered by `month` ascending.** (11 rows.)

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 112_drills_mixed_1 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - the whales' favourite aisles

The five customers with the highest non-cancelled revenue (`sum(total)`,
ties by `customer_id`), each with their favourite category: the one where
they bought the most units (`sum(quantity)` over non-cancelled orders,
ties broken by `category` ascending). Columns `customer_id`, `revenue`,
`fav_category`.

**Ordered by `revenue` descending, then `customer_id` ascending.** (5
rows.)

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 112_drills_mixed_1 ex8`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 112_drills_mixed_1

The first gauntlet: every problem welds topics from across the course. Read
after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

Composed queries fail differently from simple ones: each ingredient works,
and the weld leaks. A status filter that lives in the wrong half of an
anti-join, a business rule applied to revenue but not to the favourite, a
window frame that includes the row it is supposed to judge - none of these
error out, all of them return confident numbers. The discipline this set
drills is stating each rule once in prose ("non-cancelled, everywhere
money or votes are counted") and then checking every clause of the
finished query against that sentence. Where two grains meet (ex6),
aggregate each side before joining; where a pick depends on an aggregate
(ex8), sequence the stages explicitly. Composition is mostly sequencing.

## ex1

JSONB meets the fact table: the grouping key is an extraction, the measure
is two joins away from it. What it tested: putting `->> 'color'` in GROUP
BY without staging it, and keeping the category filter on products where
it belongs. The classic mistake is grouping by the JSONB value `->
'color'` instead of the text `->> 'color'` - it works, but the output
carries quoted JSON strings and the gate notices the difference.

## ex2

A derived flag over a grouped expression. What it tested: `extract(isodow
...)` (Monday-first, so the weekend is 6 and 7) and the rule that SELECT
may build new expressions out of grouped ones - `dow >= 6` needs no
aggregate because `dow` is the group key. The classic mistake is
`extract(dow ...)`, whose Sunday-is-zero convention shifts the whole week
and flags Friday-Saturday as the weekend.

## ex3

An anti-join with a condition *inside* it. "No non-cancelled order" places
`status <> 'cancelled'` in the NOT EXISTS subquery; moving it outside
changes the question to "customers we cannot join a live order to after
filtering", which quietly drops the all-cancelled customers the request
most wants to see. What it tested: that placement decision, twice welded
to plain date and country filters. The reference is the LEFT JOIN ... IS
NULL spelling with the same condition riding the ON clause - same rule,
same placement question, different syntax.

## ex4

Rank-and-pick-the-middle: a position that depends on the group's size
needs two windows over the same partition - `row_number()` for where each
row sits and `count(*) OVER` for how long the ladder is - and then a
filter comparing them, which forces the CTE wrap because WHERE cannot see
window output. What it tested: that two-window composition, integer
division doing the middle-of-an-even-group tie-policy, and `row_number()`
(not `rank()`, whose gaps after salary ties would leave some departments
with no row at the computed position at all). The reference's lateral
`OFFSET (n+1)/2 - 1 LIMIT 1` is the same arithmetic walking instead of
numbering.

## ex5

A set difference wrapped in a count. What it tested: EXCEPT's built-in
deduplication doing exactly what "customers who..." needs, and half-open
month windows on both sides. The classic mistake appears in the anti-join
spelling: forgetting the DISTINCT on the October side and counting
*orders* whose customer skipped November, which inflates the answer by
every repeat buyer. EXCEPT never has that bug, which is a fine reason to
reach for it.

## ex6

The two-grain trap. Price is a per-product fact; rating is a per-review
fact; joining first and averaging after weights each product's price by
its review count - a number that looks right and means nothing. What it
tested: aggregating each measure at its own grain in its own CTE and
joining the two six-row summaries. This is the single most common silent
bug in analytics SQL; the fix - aggregate first, join after - is worth
saying aloud until it is reflex.

## ex7

A window frame with an exclusion. `ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND 1
PRECEDING` is the whole exercise: the benchmark must not include the month
it judges, and the frame edge is where that rule lives. What it tested:
frame arithmetic (empty frame for January gives NULL for free; partial
frames average what exists), plus comparing on unrounded values while
displaying rounded ones. The reference builds the same average by hand
from three lag() columns - reading it once makes the frame version feel
less like syntax and more like a sentence.

## ex8

The full three-stage weld: aggregate-sort-limit to find the whales, a
per-driving-row grouped pick for the favourite, and one business rule
(non-cancelled) that must hold in *both* stages. What it tested: lesson
48's lateral carrying a GROUP BY inside it, deterministic tie-breaks at
both levels, and rule consistency - a cancelled order's items must not
vote for the favourite of a customer whose revenue already excludes them.
Senior interviews love this shape precisely because the weld, not the SQL,
is where candidates leak.

## Further reading

- [Window Function Calls - Frames](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html#SYNTAX-WINDOW-FUNCTIONS) - ROWS BETWEEN and frame-edge semantics.
- [Combining Queries (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-union.html) - set-operation deduplication rules.
- [Table Expressions - LATERAL Subqueries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-LATERAL) - grouped subqueries per driving row.
- [JSON Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-json.html) - the extraction operators and their return types.

# Reading - 112_drills_mixed_1

The first gauntlet: every problem welds topics from across the course. Read
after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

Composed queries fail differently from simple ones: each ingredient works,
and the weld leaks. A status filter that lives in the wrong half of an
anti-join, a business rule applied to revenue but not to the favourite, a
window frame that includes the row it is supposed to judge - none of these
error out, all of them return confident numbers. The discipline this set
drills is stating each rule once in prose ("non-cancelled, everywhere
money or votes are counted") and then checking every clause of the
finished query against that sentence. Where two grains meet (ex6),
aggregate each side before joining; where a pick depends on an aggregate
(ex8), sequence the stages explicitly. Composition is mostly sequencing.

## ex1

JSONB meets the fact table: the grouping key is an extraction, the measure
is two joins away from it. What it tested: putting `->> 'color'` in GROUP
BY without staging it, and keeping the category filter on products where
it belongs. The classic mistake is grouping by the JSONB value `->
'color'` instead of the text `->> 'color'` - it works, but the output
carries quoted JSON strings and the gate notices the difference.

## ex2

A derived flag over a grouped expression. What it tested: `extract(isodow
...)` (Monday-first, so the weekend is 6 and 7) and the rule that SELECT
may build new expressions out of grouped ones - `dow >= 6` needs no
aggregate because `dow` is the group key. The classic mistake is
`extract(dow ...)`, whose Sunday-is-zero convention shifts the whole week
and flags Friday-Saturday as the weekend.

## ex3

An anti-join with a condition *inside* it. "No non-cancelled order" places
`status <> 'cancelled'` in the NOT EXISTS subquery; moving it outside
changes the question to "customers we cannot join a live order to after
filtering", which quietly drops the all-cancelled customers the request
most wants to see. What it tested: that placement decision, twice welded
to plain date and country filters. The reference is the LEFT JOIN ... IS
NULL spelling with the same condition riding the ON clause - same rule,
same placement question, different syntax.

## ex4

Rank-and-pick-the-middle: a position that depends on the group's size
needs two windows over the same partition - `row_number()` for where each
row sits and `count(*) OVER` for how long the ladder is - and then a
filter comparing them, which forces the CTE wrap because WHERE cannot see
window output. What it tested: that two-window composition, integer
division doing the middle-of-an-even-group tie-policy, and `row_number()`
(not `rank()`, whose gaps after salary ties would leave some departments
with no row at the computed position at all). The reference's lateral
`OFFSET (n+1)/2 - 1 LIMIT 1` is the same arithmetic walking instead of
numbering.

## ex5

A set difference wrapped in a count. What it tested: EXCEPT's built-in
deduplication doing exactly what "customers who..." needs, and half-open
month windows on both sides. The classic mistake appears in the anti-join
spelling: forgetting the DISTINCT on the October side and counting
*orders* whose customer skipped November, which inflates the answer by
every repeat buyer. EXCEPT never has that bug, which is a fine reason to
reach for it.

## ex6

The two-grain trap. Price is a per-product fact; rating is a per-review
fact; joining first and averaging after weights each product's price by
its review count - a number that looks right and means nothing. What it
tested: aggregating each measure at its own grain in its own CTE and
joining the two six-row summaries. This is the single most common silent
bug in analytics SQL; the fix - aggregate first, join after - is worth
saying aloud until it is reflex.

## ex7

A window frame with an exclusion. `ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND 1
PRECEDING` is the whole exercise: the benchmark must not include the month
it judges, and the frame edge is where that rule lives. What it tested:
frame arithmetic (empty frame for January gives NULL for free; partial
frames average what exists), plus comparing on unrounded values while
displaying rounded ones. The reference builds the same average by hand
from three lag() columns - reading it once makes the frame version feel
less like syntax and more like a sentence.

## ex8

The full three-stage weld: aggregate-sort-limit to find the whales, a
per-driving-row grouped pick for the favourite, and one business rule
(non-cancelled) that must hold in *both* stages. What it tested: lesson
48's lateral carrying a GROUP BY inside it, deterministic tie-breaks at
both levels, and rule consistency - a cancelled order's items must not
vote for the favourite of a customer whose revenue already excludes them.
Senior interviews love this shape precisely because the weld, not the SQL,
is where candidates leak.

## Further reading

- [Window Function Calls - Frames](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-expressions.html#SYNTAX-WINDOW-FUNCTIONS) - ROWS BETWEEN and frame-edge semantics.
- [Combining Queries (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-union.html) - set-operation deduplication rules.
- [Table Expressions - LATERAL Subqueries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-LATERAL) - grouped subqueries per driving row.
- [JSON Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-json.html) - the extraction operators and their return types.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 - clothing revenue by colour

Line-item revenue (`sum(quantity * price)` over `order_items`) for
`clothing` products, grouped by the product's `color` attribute. Columns
`color`, `revenue`.

**Ordered by `color` ascending.** (5 rows.)

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 112_drills_mixed_1 ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two topics: a JSONB extraction as the grouping key (lesson 19) over a join to the money table (lesson 08). The colour lives on the product; the money lives on the line.

## Hint 2

Join order_items to products, filter category = 'clothing', GROUP BY attributes ->> 'color', sum quantity * price. Five colours, alphabetical.

## Hint 1

Two topics: a JSONB extraction as the grouping key (lesson 19) over a join to the money table (lesson 08). The colour lives on the product; the money lives on the line.

## Hint 2

Join order_items to products, filter category = 'clothing', GROUP BY attributes ->> 'color', sum quantity * price. Five colours, alphabetical.

references.solution.sql:
WITH clothing AS (
  SELECT id, attributes ->> 'color' AS color
  FROM products
  WHERE category = 'clothing')
SELECT c.color, sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) AS revenue
FROM order_items oi
JOIN clothing c ON c.id = oi.product_id
GROUP BY c.color
ORDER BY c.color;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT p.attributes ->> 'color' AS color,
       sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) AS revenue
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE p.category = 'clothing'
GROUP BY p.attributes ->> 'color'
ORDER BY color;

## Hint 1

Dates plus a derived boolean: group by the ISO day of week (lesson 18 - Monday is 1, Sunday is 7), and compute the weekend flag from the same expression.

## Hint 2

GROUP BY extract(isodow FROM created_at)::int; the flag is that expression >= 6, which is legal in SELECT because it is built from the grouped expression. Seven rows, Monday first.

references.solution.sql:
WITH d AS (
  SELECT extract(isodow FROM created_at)::int AS dow
  FROM orders)
SELECT dow,
       count(*) AS orders,
       CASE WHEN dow IN (6, 7) THEN true ELSE false END AS is_weekend
FROM d
GROUP BY dow
ORDER BY dow;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT extract(isodow FROM created_at)::int AS dow,
       count(*) AS orders,
       extract(isodow FROM created_at)::int >= 6 AS is_weekend
FROM orders
GROUP BY extract(isodow FROM created_at)::int
ORDER BY dow;

## Hint 1

Three topics welded: a date filter on signups, a country filter, and an anti-join (lesson 13) whose condition is not "no orders" but "no orders that survived".

## Hint 2

NOT EXISTS with the status condition INSIDE the subquery: no order of theirs with status <> 'cancelled'. A customer whose only orders were cancelled must appear - putting the status test outside the anti-join silently changes who counts.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name, c.created_at
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
 AND o.status <> 'cancelled'
WHERE c.country = 'DE'
  AND c.created_at >= '2023-01-01'
  AND o.id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.id, c.name, c.created_at
FROM customers c
WHERE c.country = 'DE'
  AND c.created_at >= '2023-01-01'
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM orders o
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
      AND o.status <> 'cancelled')
ORDER BY c.id;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two windows over the same partition: a row number down the salary ladder, and the partition's size. The middle rung is position (n + 1) / 2 with integer division - which needs both numbers on every row.

## Hint 2

row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC, id) and count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY department) in one CTE, then WHERE rn = (n + 1) / 2 outside - window results are invisible to the same query's WHERE.

## Hint 3

Check the arithmetic against tiny cases: n = 5 gives position 3 (the true middle), n = 4 gives position 2 (the upper of the middle pair) - integer division makes that choice for you, and the prompt adopts it. The id tie-break keeps "the" middle person stable when salaries repeat.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT d.department, t.name, t.salary
FROM (SELECT department, count(*) AS n
      FROM staff
      GROUP BY department) d
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT s.name, s.salary
  FROM staff s
  WHERE s.department = d.department
  ORDER BY s.salary DESC, s.id ASC
  OFFSET (d.n + 1) / 2 - 1
  LIMIT 1) t
ORDER BY d.department;
references.expected.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT department, name, salary, id,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY department
                            ORDER BY salary DESC, id ASC) AS rn,
         count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS n
  FROM staff)
SELECT department, name, salary
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = (n + 1) / 2
ORDER BY department;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

"Ordered in October but not in November" is a set difference (lesson 11) between two customer-id sets, wrapped in a count. Dates are half-open ranges, as always.

## Hint 2

(October customer ids) EXCEPT (November customer ids), then count the survivors in an outer query. EXCEPT deduplicates both sides for free; the anti-join spelling (NOT EXISTS against November) needs an explicit DISTINCT - the reference shows it.

references.solution.sql:
WITH october AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT customer_id
  FROM orders
  WHERE created_at >= '2023-10-01' AND created_at < '2023-11-01')
SELECT count(*) AS lapsed
FROM october o
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM orders n
  WHERE n.customer_id = o.customer_id
    AND n.created_at >= '2023-11-01' AND n.created_at < '2023-12-01');
references.expected.sql:
SELECT count(*) AS lapsed
FROM (
  SELECT customer_id
  FROM orders
  WHERE created_at >= '2023-10-01' AND created_at < '2023-11-01'
  EXCEPT
  SELECT customer_id
  FROM orders
  WHERE created_at >= '2023-11-01' AND created_at < '2023-12-01') x;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 - price versus reputation

Per category: `avg_price` = `round(avg(products.price), 2)` and
`avg_rating` = `round(avg(reviews.rating), 2)` across all reviews of that
category's products. Columns `category`, `avg_price`, `avg_rating`. The
two averages live at different grains - aggregate each on its own, then
join; one big join-then-average pass computes a subtly different (and
wrong) `avg_price`.

**Ordered by `category` ascending.** (6 rows.)

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 112_drills_mixed_1 ex6`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two averages living at different grains: price is per product, rating is per review. Averaging both over one big join quietly weights product prices by how many reviews each product has.

## Hint 2

Aggregate each measure in its own CTE - products grouped by category, reviews joined to products grouped by category - then join the two six-row results. This is lesson 14's answer to every fan-out bug.

## Hint 3

If you want to see the bug you avoided: join products to reviews first and take avg(p.price) - it drifts from the true per-product average wherever review counts are uneven. Aggregate first, join after, whenever two fact tables meet one dimension.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two averages living at different grains: price is per product, rating is per review. Averaging both over one big join quietly weights product prices by how many reviews each product has.

## Hint 2

Aggregate each measure in its own CTE - products grouped by category, reviews joined to products grouped by category - then join the two six-row results. This is lesson 14's answer to every fan-out bug.

## Hint 3

If you want to see the bug you avoided: join products to reviews first and take avg(p.price) - it drifts from the true per-product average wherever review counts are uneven. Aggregate first, join after, whenever two fact tables meet one dimension.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT c.category,
       (SELECT round(avg(price), 2)
        FROM products
        WHERE category = c.category) AS avg_price,
       (SELECT round(avg(r.rating), 2)
        FROM reviews r
        JOIN products p2 ON p2.id = r.product_id
        WHERE p2.category = c.category) AS avg_rating
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products) c
ORDER BY c.category;

WITH price AS (
  SELECT category, round(avg(price), 2) AS avg_price
  FROM products
  GROUP BY category),
rating AS (
  SELECT p.category, round(avg(r.rating), 2) AS avg_rating
  FROM reviews r
  JOIN products p ON p.id = r.product_id
  GROUP BY p.category)

FROM price
JOIN rating USING (category)
ORDER BY category;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three topics: a three-table join aggregated to months, a window average over a FRAME that excludes the current row, and a CASE verdict. The benchmark is the average of up to three PRIOR months - the current month must not smooth itself.

## Hint 2

avg(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING). Ending the frame at 1 PRECEDING is the whole exercise; CURRENT ROW would include this month in its own benchmark.

## Hint 3

January has an empty frame - avg over nothing is NULL - so its prior3_avg and flag are both NULL, no special casing needed. February and March compare against fewer than three months, which the frame handles by averaging what exists. Compare on the unrounded average, display the rounded one.

references.solution.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('month', o.created_at) AS month,
         sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) AS revenue
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
  JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
  WHERE p.category = 'electronics'
    AND o.created_at >= '2023-01-01' AND o.created_at < '2024-01-01'
  GROUP BY date_trunc('month', o.created_at)),
lagged AS (
  SELECT month, revenue,
         lag(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS r1,
         lag(revenue, 2) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS r2,
         lag(revenue, 3) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS r3
  FROM monthly),
manual AS (
  SELECT month, revenue,
         (coalesce(r1, 0) + coalesce(r2, 0) + coalesce(r3, 0))
         / NULLIF((CASE WHEN r1 IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END)
                + (CASE WHEN r2 IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END)
                + (CASE WHEN r3 IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END), 0) AS prior3
  FROM lagged)
SELECT month,
       revenue,
       round(prior3, 2) AS prior3_avg,
       CASE WHEN prior3 IS NULL THEN NULL
            WHEN revenue > prior3 THEN 'above'
            ELSE 'below' END AS flag
FROM manual
ORDER BY month;

         sum(oi.quantity * oi.price) AS revenue

  JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
  WHERE p.category = 'electronics'
    AND o.created_at >= '2023-01-01' AND o.created_at < '2024-01-01'
  GROUP BY date_trunc('month', o.created_at)),
w AS (
  SELECT month, revenue,
         avg(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month
                            ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) AS prior3

       round(prior3, 2) AS prior3_avg,
       CASE WHEN prior3 IS NULL THEN NULL
            WHEN revenue > prior3 THEN 'above'
            ELSE 'below' END AS flag
FROM w
ORDER BY month;

references.solution.sql:
WITH spend AS (
  SELECT customer_id, sum(total) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
  GROUP BY customer_id),
top5 AS (
  SELECT customer_id, revenue
  FROM spend
  ORDER BY revenue DESC, customer_id ASC
  LIMIT 5),
units AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id, p.category, sum(oi.quantity) AS units
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
  JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
  WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
    AND o.customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM top5)
  GROUP BY o.customer_id, p.category),
fav AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id)
         customer_id, category AS fav_category
  FROM units
  ORDER BY customer_id, units DESC, category ASC)
SELECT t.customer_id, t.revenue, f.fav_category
FROM top5 t
JOIN fav f USING (customer_id)
ORDER BY t.revenue DESC, t.customer_id ASC;
references.expected.sql:
WITH spend AS (
  SELECT customer_id, sum(total) AS revenue
  FROM orders
  WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
  GROUP BY customer_id
  ORDER BY revenue DESC, customer_id ASC
  LIMIT 5)
SELECT s.customer_id, s.revenue, f.fav_category
FROM spend s
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT p.category AS fav_category
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
  JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
  WHERE o.customer_id = s.customer_id
    AND o.status <> 'cancelled'
  GROUP BY p.category
  ORDER BY sum(oi.quantity) DESC, p.category ASC
  LIMIT 1) f
ORDER BY s.revenue DESC, s.customer_id ASC;

# 113 - Drills: mixed gauntlet, set 2

Second gauntlet. The welds get less obvious: semi-joins hiding inside
conditional aggregates, set operations over JSONB tests, grouping sets fed
by a staged join. Say what each clause is for before you type it.

## Exercise 1 - the name census

The five most common first initials among customer names: `initial` =
the first character of `name`, `customers` = how many names start with it.

**Ordered by `customers` descending, then `initial` ascending, limited to 5
rows.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 113_drills_mixed_2 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - how stale is the pending pile?

As of the dataset's last day (`DATE '2023-11-14'`): one row with
`pending_orders` = how many orders are `pending`, and `avg_age_days` = the
average age in whole days (`DATE '2023-11-14' - created_at::date`),
rounded to 1 decimal.

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 113_drills_mixed_2 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - who actually bought off product 7's page?

Every `purchase` event whose payload `path` is exactly `'/p/7'`: columns
`id`, `customer_id`, `value` = the payload's `value` **as an integer**.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 113_drills_mixed_2 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - the management premium

Per department: `mgr_avg` = the average salary of people who manage at
least one person, `ic_avg` = the average salary of everyone else - both
rounded to 2. "Manages someone" means their `id` appears as another row's
`manager_id`. A department with nobody on one side shows NULL there.
Columns `department`, `mgr_avg`, `ic_avg`.

**Ordered by `department` ascending.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 113_drills_mixed_2 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - the freshest opinion per category

For each product category, its most recent review: columns `category`,
`review_id`, `rating`, `created_at`. Ties on `created_at` broken by the
review's `id`, higher wins. The category lives one join away from the
review.

**Ordered by `category` ascending.** (6 rows.)

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 113_drills_mixed_2 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - eco or sale, not both

Products tagged `'eco'` or tagged `'sale'` but **not both**: columns `id`,
`name`. Tag tests are containment against `attributes -> 'tags'`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 113_drills_mixed_2 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - are the baskets growing?

For every customer with `id <= 10` who has at least two orders: compare
their **first** order's `total` with their **last** order's (first and
last by `created_at`, ties by order `id` - lowest wins for first, highest
for last). Columns `customer_id`, `orders`, `first_total`, `last_total`,
`direction` = `'up'` / `'down'` / `'flat'` comparing last against first.

**Ordered by `customer_id` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 113_drills_mixed_2 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - the exec one-pager

Over **paid and shipped** orders only, line revenue (`quantity * price`)
three ways in one result: by product `category`, by order `status`, and
one grand-total row - no cross-tab. Add `pct_of_total` =
`round(100.0 * revenue / grand total, 1)` on every row (the grand-total
row reads 100.0). Columns `category`, `status`, `revenue`,
`pct_of_total`; the dimension a row is not grouped by is NULL.

**Ordered by `category` ascending, then `status` ascending** (NULLs last,
so the grand total lands at the bottom). (9 rows: 6 categories + 2
statuses + 1 total.)

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 113_drills_mixed_2 ex8`
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - 113_drills_mixed_2

Second gauntlet. Read after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

A theme runs through this set: *predicates that are not columns*. Whether a
staff member is a manager, whether a product carries a tag, whether an
order is a customer's first or last - none of these live in a field; each
is computed by a semi-join, a containment test, or a window over the
group.
The skill being drilled is noticing that the sentence's adjective ("the
managers", "the eco ones", "consecutive") is really a subquery, and then
deciding where that subquery belongs: inside a FILTER, inside an ON clause,
or staged in a CTE. The set closes with the report-engineering pattern that
makes multi-level summaries trustworthy - stage the filtered join once,
derive every number from that one staging CTE, and let the grand total
divide by itself as a built-in audit.

## ex1

String surgery as a group key, then count-sort-limit. What it tested:
left()/substr() (lesson 63 territory) composed with lesson 07's counting
and lesson 03's deterministic top-N - initials collide constantly, so the
tie-break earns its place. The classic mistake is sorting only by count
and shipping a five-row list that reorders itself between runs.

## ex2

Date arithmetic inside an aggregate. `DATE '2023-11-14' -
created_at::date` is an integer day count, so avg() consumes it directly;
skip the cast and the subtraction yields an interval, whose average then
needs different handling. What it tested: choosing the snapshot
deliberately (the dataset's last day - a report anchored on now() against
frozen data reads as years of backlog) and rounding once, at the end.

## ex3

Precision filtering on a document column. The path test is exact string
equality - `'/p/7'` - not a LIKE, which would also catch `/p/70` through
`/p/799`; the classic mistake here is exactly that pattern-match reflex.
What it tested: two JSONB reads with different jobs in one query (a filter
on `path`, a typed extraction of `value`), and the reference shows the
containment spelling `payload @> '{"path": "/p/7"}'` - the form lesson
42's GIN index would accelerate.

## ex4

A semi-join dressed as an adjective. "Managers" is `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM
staff r WHERE r.manager_id = s.id)` - the same table on both sides, lesson
10's self-referencing shape inside lesson 13's EXISTS, driving two FILTER
averages. What it tested: conditional aggregation over a computed
predicate, and reading NULL as "average of nobody" rather than an error.
The reference materialises the manager-id set in a CTE first - same
question, and safe from the NOT IN NULL trap only because it filters NULLs
explicitly.

## ex5

A pick across a join: the group key (category) is on products, the sort
keys are on reviews, and DISTINCT ON happily runs over the joined shape.
What it tested: lesson 49 composed with lesson 08, plus tie-break honesty
at scale - a million reviews at one-second granularity produce same-second
neighbours, so `r.id DESC` decides. The classic mistake is picking the
newest review first and joining after, which picks per *product* and then
keeps an arbitrary one per category.

## ex6

Symmetric difference, two ways. The set-operation spelling - (eco EXCEPT
sale) UNION (sale EXCEPT eco) - says the requirement almost verbatim; the
boolean spelling - the two containment tests compared with `<>` - is XOR
in one WHERE clause. What it tested: recognising "one but not both" as a
named shape rather than hand-rolling OR/AND/NOT logic, which is where the
classic mistake lives (forgetting to exclude the both-tags products, or
excluding them from only one side).

## ex7

Two opposite picks over the same partition, then a verdict. First and
last are the same one-per-group problem pointed in opposite directions -
two DISTINCT ON passes, or one pass numbering each customer's orders both
ways and harvesting the ends with max(total) FILTER (WHERE rn = 1). What
it tested: that double-pick composition, the population guard (a
single-order customer has no trajectory - HAVING count(*) >= 2 removes
them, and forgetting it returns rows whose first and last are the same
order, reading 'flat' with a straight face), and full tie-breaks at both
ends so the verdict is reproducible. The comparison itself is a plain
CASE - the work is everything before it.

## ex8

Report engineering. Everything derives from one staged CTE - the filtered
three-table join - so the grouped rows, the grand total, and the
percentages cannot disagree about which orders count. GROUPING SETS
((category), (status), ()) produces exactly the three views with no
cross-tab noise, and the share column needs the grand total beside every
row, which a one-row CTE cross-joined after grouping provides cleanly.
What it tested: all of that sequencing, plus the built-in audit - the ()
row's pct is 100.0 by construction, and if it is not, the base and the
total drifted apart somewhere.

## Further reading

- [GROUPING SETS, CUBE, and ROLLUP](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-GROUPING-SETS) - multi-level aggregation in one pass.
- [Combining Queries (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-union.html) - set semantics for the symmetric difference.
- [Row and Array Comparisons - EXISTS](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) - semi-join predicates and the NOT IN NULL hazard.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) - lag() and the ordering discipline consecutive-row logic depends on.

# 113 - Drills: mixed gauntlet, set 2

Second gauntlet. The welds get less obvious: semi-joins hiding inside
conditional aggregates, set operations over JSONB tests, grouping sets fed
by a staged join. Say what each clause is for before you type it.

## Exercise 1 - the name census

The five most common first initials among customer names: `initial` =
the first character of `name`, `customers` = how many names start with it.

**Ordered by `customers` descending, then `initial` ascending, limited to 5
rows.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 113_drills_mixed_2 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - how stale is the pending pile?

As of the dataset's last day (`DATE '2023-11-14'`): one row with
`pending_orders` = how many orders are `pending`, and `avg_age_days` = the
average age in whole days (`DATE '2023-11-14' - created_at::date`),
rounded to 1 decimal.

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 113_drills_mixed_2 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - who actually bought off product 7's page?

Every `purchase` event whose payload `path` is exactly `'/p/7'`: columns
`id`, `customer_id`, `value` = the payload's `value` **as an integer**.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 113_drills_mixed_2 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - the management premium

Per department: `mgr_avg` = the average salary of people who manage at
least one person, `ic_avg` = the average salary of everyone else - both
rounded to 2. "Manages someone" means their `id` appears as another row's
`manager_id`. A department with nobody on one side shows NULL there.
Columns `department`, `mgr_avg`, `ic_avg`.

**Ordered by `department` ascending.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 113_drills_mixed_2 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - the freshest opinion per category

For each product category, its most recent review: columns `category`,
`review_id`, `rating`, `created_at`. Ties on `created_at` broken by the
review's `id`, higher wins. The category lives one join away from the
review.

**Ordered by `category` ascending.** (6 rows.)

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 113_drills_mixed_2 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - eco or sale, not both

Products tagged `'eco'` or tagged `'sale'` but **not both**: columns `id`,
`name`. Tag tests are containment against `attributes -> 'tags'`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 113_drills_mixed_2 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - are the baskets growing?

For every customer with `id <= 10` who has at least two orders: compare
their **first** order's `total` with their **last** order's (first and
last by `created_at`, ties by order `id` - lowest wins for first, highest
for last). Columns `customer_id`, `orders`, `first_total`, `last_total`,
`direction` = `'up'` / `'down'` / `'flat'` comparing last against first.

**Ordered by `customer_id` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 113_drills_mixed_2 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - the exec one-pager

Over **paid and shipped** orders only, line revenue (`quantity * price`)
three ways in one result: by product `category`, by order `status`, and
one grand-total row - no cross-tab. Add `pct_of_total` =
`round(100.0 * revenue / grand total, 1)` on every row (the grand-total
row reads 100.0). Columns `category`, `status`, `revenue`,
`pct_of_total`; the dimension a row is not grouped by is NULL.

**Ordered by `category` ascending, then `status` ascending** (NULLs last,
so the grand total lands at the bottom). (9 rows: 6 categories + 2
statuses + 1 total.)

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 113_drills_mixed_2 ex8`

# Reading - 113_drills_mixed_2

Second gauntlet. Read after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

A theme runs through this set: *predicates that are not columns*. Whether a
staff member is a manager, whether a product carries a tag, whether an
order is a customer's first or last - none of these live in a field; each
is computed by a semi-join, a containment test, or a window over the
group.
The skill being drilled is noticing that the sentence's adjective ("the
managers", "the eco ones", "consecutive") is really a subquery, and then
deciding where that subquery belongs: inside a FILTER, inside an ON clause,
or staged in a CTE. The set closes with the report-engineering pattern that
makes multi-level summaries trustworthy - stage the filtered join once,
derive every number from that one staging CTE, and let the grand total
divide by itself as a built-in audit.

## ex1

String surgery as a group key, then count-sort-limit. What it tested:
left()/substr() (lesson 63 territory) composed with lesson 07's counting
and lesson 03's deterministic top-N - initials collide constantly, so the
tie-break earns its place. The classic mistake is sorting only by count
and shipping a five-row list that reorders itself between runs.

## ex2

Date arithmetic inside an aggregate. `DATE '2023-11-14' -
created_at::date` is an integer day count, so avg() consumes it directly;
skip the cast and the subtraction yields an interval, whose average then
needs different handling. What it tested: choosing the snapshot
deliberately (the dataset's last day - a report anchored on now() against
frozen data reads as years of backlog) and rounding once, at the end.

## ex3

Precision filtering on a document column. The path test is exact string
equality - `'/p/7'` - not a LIKE, which would also catch `/p/70` through
`/p/799`; the classic mistake here is exactly that pattern-match reflex.
What it tested: two JSONB reads with different jobs in one query (a filter
on `path`, a typed extraction of `value`), and the reference shows the
containment spelling `payload @> '{"path": "/p/7"}'` - the form lesson
42's GIN index would accelerate.

## ex4

A semi-join dressed as an adjective. "Managers" is `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM
staff r WHERE r.manager_id = s.id)` - the same table on both sides, lesson
10's self-referencing shape inside lesson 13's EXISTS, driving two FILTER
averages. What it tested: conditional aggregation over a computed
predicate, and reading NULL as "average of nobody" rather than an error.
The reference materialises the manager-id set in a CTE first - same
question, and safe from the NOT IN NULL trap only because it filters NULLs
explicitly.

## ex5

A pick across a join: the group key (category) is on products, the sort
keys are on reviews, and DISTINCT ON happily runs over the joined shape.
What it tested: lesson 49 composed with lesson 08, plus tie-break honesty
at scale - a million reviews at one-second granularity produce same-second
neighbours, so `r.id DESC` decides. The classic mistake is picking the
newest review first and joining after, which picks per *product* and then
keeps an arbitrary one per category.

## ex6

Symmetric difference, two ways. The set-operation spelling - (eco EXCEPT
sale) UNION (sale EXCEPT eco) - says the requirement almost verbatim; the
boolean spelling - the two containment tests compared with `<>` - is XOR
in one WHERE clause. What it tested: recognising "one but not both" as a
named shape rather than hand-rolling OR/AND/NOT logic, which is where the
classic mistake lives (forgetting to exclude the both-tags products, or
excluding them from only one side).

## ex7

Two opposite picks over the same partition, then a verdict. First and
last are the same one-per-group problem pointed in opposite directions -
two DISTINCT ON passes, or one pass numbering each customer's orders both
ways and harvesting the ends with max(total) FILTER (WHERE rn = 1). What
it tested: that double-pick composition, the population guard (a
single-order customer has no trajectory - HAVING count(*) >= 2 removes
them, and forgetting it returns rows whose first and last are the same
order, reading 'flat' with a straight face), and full tie-breaks at both
ends so the verdict is reproducible. The comparison itself is a plain
CASE - the work is everything before it.

## ex8

Report engineering. Everything derives from one staged CTE - the filtered
three-table join - so the grouped rows, the grand total, and the
percentages cannot disagree about which orders count. GROUPING SETS
((category), (status), ()) produces exactly the three views with no
cross-tab noise, and the share column needs the grand total beside every
row, which a one-row CTE cross-joined after grouping provides cleanly.
What it tested: all of that sequencing, plus the built-in audit - the ()
row's pct is 100.0 by construction, and if it is not, the base and the
total drifted apart somewhere.

## Further reading

- [GROUPING SETS, CUBE, and ROLLUP](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-table-expressions.html#QUERIES-GROUPING-SETS) - multi-level aggregation in one pass.
- [Combining Queries (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT)](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-union.html) - set semantics for the symmetric difference.
- [Row and Array Comparisons - EXISTS](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-subquery.html) - semi-join predicates and the NOT IN NULL hazard.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-window.html) - lag() and the ordering discipline consecutive-row logic depends on.

## Exercise 1 - the name census

The five most common first initials among customer names: `initial` =
the first character of `name`, `customers` = how many names start with it.

**Ordered by `customers` descending, then `initial` ascending, limited to 5
rows.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 113_drills_mixed_2 ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Text surgery as a grouping key (lesson 04 meets lesson 07): one character off the front of the name, then an ordinary count-sort-limit.

## Hint 2

GROUP BY left(name, 1), ORDER BY the count descending with the initial as tie-break, LIMIT 5. Adjacent letters tie easily at this scale - the tie-break is not decoration.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Text surgery as a grouping key (lesson 04 meets lesson 07): one character off the front of the name, then an ordinary count-sort-limit.

## Hint 2

GROUP BY left(name, 1), ORDER BY the count descending with the initial as tie-break, LIMIT 5. Adjacent letters tie easily at this scale - the tie-break is not decoration.

references.solution.sql:
WITH initials AS (
  SELECT substr(name, 1, 1) AS initial
  FROM customers)
SELECT initial, count(*) AS customers
FROM initials
GROUP BY initial
ORDER BY customers DESC, initial ASC
LIMIT 5;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT left(name, 1) AS initial, count(*) AS customers
FROM customers
GROUP BY left(name, 1)
ORDER BY customers DESC, initial ASC
LIMIT 5;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two JSONB reads in one WHERE: an equality on the extracted path (or a containment test - either works) plus the event-type filter, then a cast on the way out for the value column.

## Hint 2

payload ->> 'path' = '/p/7' AND event_type = 'purchase'; select (payload ->> 'value')::int so the column is a number, not text. Product 7's page is exactly the string '/p/7' - no pattern matching needed.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT id, customer_id, (payload ->> 'value')::int AS value
FROM events
WHERE event_type = 'purchase'
  AND payload @> '{"path": "/p/7"}'
ORDER BY id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT id, customer_id, (payload ->> 'value')::int AS value
FROM events
WHERE event_type = 'purchase'
  AND payload ->> 'path' = '/p/7'
ORDER BY id;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 - the management premium

Per department: `mgr_avg` = the average salary of people who manage at
least one person, `ic_avg` = the average salary of everyone else - both
rounded to 2. "Manages someone" means their `id` appears as another row's
`manager_id`. A department with nobody on one side shows NULL there.
Columns `department`, `mgr_avg`, `ic_avg`.

**Ordered by `department` ascending.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 113_drills_mixed_2 ex4`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

"Is a manager" is not a column - it is a semi-join against the same table (lesson 10 meets lesson 13): someone whose id appears in another row's manager_id. The two averages are conditional aggregates over that test.

## Hint 2

avg(salary) FILTER (WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM staff r WHERE r.manager_id = s.id)) for managers; NOT EXISTS for the rest. A department with nobody on one side returns NULL for that column - the average of nothing - which is honest and expected.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

"Is a manager" is not a column - it is a semi-join against the same table (lesson 10 meets lesson 13): someone whose id appears in another row's manager_id. The two averages are conditional aggregates over that test.

## Hint 2

avg(salary) FILTER (WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM staff r WHERE r.manager_id = s.id)) for managers; NOT EXISTS for the rest. A department with nobody on one side returns NULL for that column - the average of nothing - which is honest and expected.

references.solution.sql:
WITH managers AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT manager_id AS id
  FROM staff
  WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL)
SELECT s.department,
       round(avg(s.salary) FILTER (WHERE s.id IN (SELECT id FROM managers)), 2) AS mgr_avg,
       round(avg(s.salary) FILTER (WHERE s.id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM managers)), 2) AS ic_avg
FROM staff s
GROUP BY s.department
ORDER BY s.department;

         SELECT 1 FROM staff r WHERE r.manager_id = s.id)), 2) AS ic_avg
FROM staff s
GROUP BY s.department
ORDER BY s.department;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A one-per-group pick (lesson 49) where the group key lives on the OTHER side of a join: the review's category comes from products. Join first, then pick.

## Hint 2

DISTINCT ON (p.category) over reviews joined to products, ORDER BY p.category, r.created_at DESC, r.id DESC - the higher review id settles same-second ties, and one million reviews make those ties real.

references.solution.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT p.category, r.id, r.rating, r.created_at,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY p.category
                            ORDER BY r.created_at DESC, r.id DESC) AS rn
  FROM reviews r
  JOIN products p ON p.id = r.product_id)
SELECT category, id AS review_id, rating, created_at
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY category;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT ON (p.category)
       p.category, r.id AS review_id, r.rating, r.created_at
FROM reviews r
JOIN products p ON p.id = r.product_id
ORDER BY p.category, r.created_at DESC, r.id DESC;

## Hint 1

"One of the two tags but not both" is a symmetric difference - two set operations (lesson 11) over two containment tests (lesson 19), or one boolean trick.

## Hint 2

(eco EXCEPT sale) UNION (sale EXCEPT eco). Each containment test is attributes -> 'tags' @> '["eco"]' and its sale twin.

## Hint 3

The boolean spelling in the reference - WHERE (has_eco) <> (has_sale) - works because XOR is exactly "the two booleans differ". Both shapes must return identical rows; if yours differs, check whether you excluded the eco-AND-sale products or only one direction of them.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT id, name
FROM products
WHERE (attributes -> 'tags' @> '["eco"]') <> (attributes -> 'tags' @> '["sale"]')
ORDER BY id;

ORDER BY id;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 - are the baskets growing?

For every customer with `id <= 10` who has at least two orders: compare
their **first** order's `total` with their **last** order's (first and
last by `created_at`, ties by order `id` - lowest wins for first, highest
for last). Columns `customer_id`, `orders`, `first_total`, `last_total`,
`direction` = `'up'` / `'down'` / `'flat'` comparing last against first.

**Ordered by `customer_id` ascending.**

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 113_drills_mixed_2 ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Each customer's first and last order are two one-per-group picks over the SAME rows with opposite sort directions, and the verdict is a CASE comparing what the two picks carried. Single-order customers have nothing to compare - filter them out by count.

## Hint 2

One shape: two DISTINCT ON CTEs (ORDER BY customer_id, created_at ASC / DESC, with id tie-breaks) plus a counts CTE with HAVING count(*) >= 2, joined on customer_id.

## Hint 3

The single-pass shape: number each customer's orders twice - row_number() ascending and descending - plus count(*) OVER, then aggregate with max(total) FILTER (WHERE rn = 1) for each end. Both spellings must agree exactly; if 'flat' never appears in either, that is correct - identical first and last totals are merely possible, not guaranteed.

The single-pass shape: number each customer's orders twice - row_number() ascending and descending - plus count(*) OVER, then aggregate with max(total) FILTER (WHERE rn = 1) for each end. Both spellings must agree exactly; if 'flat' never appears in either, that is correct - identical first and last totals are merely possible, not guaranteed.

references.solution.sql:
WITH firsts AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id)
         customer_id, total AS first_total
  FROM orders
  WHERE customer_id <= 10
  ORDER BY customer_id, created_at ASC, id ASC),
lasts AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id)
         customer_id, total AS last_total
  FROM orders
  WHERE customer_id <= 10
  ORDER BY customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC),
counts AS (
  SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS orders
  FROM orders
  WHERE customer_id <= 10
  GROUP BY customer_id
  HAVING count(*) >= 2)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.orders, f.first_total, l.last_total,
       CASE WHEN l.last_total > f.first_total THEN 'up'
            WHEN l.last_total < f.first_total THEN 'down'
            ELSE 'flat' END AS direction
FROM counts c
JOIN firsts f USING (customer_id)
JOIN lasts l USING (customer_id)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
references.expected.sql:
WITH seq AS (
  SELECT customer_id, total,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                            ORDER BY created_at ASC, id ASC) AS rn_first,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                            ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC) AS rn_last,
         count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS orders
  FROM orders
  WHERE customer_id <= 10)
SELECT customer_id,
       orders,
       max(total) FILTER (WHERE rn_first = 1) AS first_total,
       max(total) FILTER (WHERE rn_last = 1) AS last_total,
       CASE WHEN max(total) FILTER (WHERE rn_last = 1)
               > max(total) FILTER (WHERE rn_first = 1) THEN 'up'
            WHEN max(total) FILTER (WHERE rn_last = 1)
               < max(total) FILTER (WHERE rn_first = 1) THEN 'down'
            ELSE 'flat' END AS direction
FROM seq
WHERE orders >= 2
GROUP BY customer_id, orders
ORDER BY customer_id;

## Hint 1

Three topics: a filtered three-table join staged in a CTE, GROUPING SETS over it (by category, by status, and overall - no cross-tab), and a share-of-total column that needs the grand total available on every row.

## Hint 2

Stage the joined, filtered line revenue once in a base CTE; both the grouping-sets pass and the grand total read from it, so the two cannot disagree. GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((category), (status), ()) gives exactly the nine rows.

## Hint 3

The pct needs the grand total NEXT TO each grouped row: compute it in its own one-row CTE and CROSS JOIN it after the grouping (dividing inside the grouped query forces awkward aggregates-of-constants). The () row divides by itself - its pct is 100.0, a free sanity check.

references.solution.sql:
WITH base AS (
  SELECT p.category, o.status, oi.quantity * oi.price AS line_rev
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
  JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
  WHERE o.status IN ('paid', 'shipped')),
g AS (
  SELECT category, NULL::text AS status, sum(line_rev) AS revenue
  FROM base
  GROUP BY category
  UNION ALL
  SELECT NULL::text, status, sum(line_rev)
  FROM base
  GROUP BY status
  UNION ALL
  SELECT NULL::text, NULL::text, sum(line_rev)
  FROM base)
SELECT category, status, revenue,
       round(100.0 * revenue / (SELECT sum(line_rev) FROM base), 1) AS pct_of_total
FROM g
ORDER BY category, status;
references.expected.sql:
WITH base AS (
  SELECT p.category, o.status, oi.quantity * oi.price AS line_rev
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
  JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
  WHERE o.status IN ('paid', 'shipped')),
tot AS (
  SELECT sum(line_rev) AS grand
  FROM base),
g AS (
  SELECT category, status, sum(line_rev) AS revenue
  FROM base
  GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((category), (status), ()))
SELECT g.category, g.status, g.revenue,
       round(100.0 * g.revenue / t.grand, 1) AS pct_of_total
FROM g
CROSS JOIN tot t
ORDER BY g.category, g.status;

# 114 - Drills: mixed gauntlet, set 3

The final problem set of the course. Every exercise welds two or three
topics; the last two are the kind of question a senior interview saves for
the end. Take them cold, then read `reading.md` even if you passed.

## Exercise 1 - who costs what

Per department: `payroll` = `sum(salary)` and `payroll_pct` =
`round(100.0 * payroll / total payroll, 1)`. Columns `department`,
`payroll`, `payroll_pct`.

**Ordered by `department` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 114_drills_mixed_3 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - the weekly bestseller board

For each week (`date_trunc('week', orders.created_at)`) touching October
2023 orders (half-open month filter on the order date): the product with
the most units sold (`sum(order_items.quantity)`, ties by `product_id`
ascending). Columns `week`, `product_id`, `name`, `units`.

**Ordered by `week` ascending.** (6 rows - Monday weeks, partial at the
edges.)

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 114_drills_mixed_3 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - premium gear nobody got excited about

`electronics` products priced above 480 whose page (`path = '/p/<id>'`)
never recorded a `view` event with payload `value >= 999`. Columns `id`,
`name`, `price`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 114_drills_mixed_3 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - where cancellations beat shipments

Per customer country: `paid`, `shipped`, `cancelled` order counts - but
only countries where `cancelled > shipped`. Columns `country`, `paid`,
`shipped`, `cancelled`.

**Ordered by `country` ascending.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 114_drills_mixed_3 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - the CEO's lieutenants, weighed

For each **direct report of the CEO** (the one staff row with NULL
`manager_id`): `name`, and `subtree` = how many people their whole subtree
contains, **including themselves**. Columns `name`, `subtree`.

**Ordered by `subtree` descending, then `name` ascending.**

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 114_drills_mixed_3 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - every tag's flagship

For each of the ten tags: the most expensive product carrying it (price
ties by `id` ascending). Columns `tag`, `product_id`, `name`, `price`. A
product may legitimately win both of its tags.

**Ordered by `tag` ascending.** (10 rows.)

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 114_drills_mixed_3 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - the streak counter

One row, one column `streak_customers`: how many customers have placed
orders in **three or more consecutive calendar months** at least once
(months of `created_at`, consecutive meaning m, m+1, m+2 all present in
that customer's set of order months).

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 114_drills_mixed_3 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - page conversion, end to end

For the ten most-viewed product pages in the whole stream: `product_id`
(parsed from the payload path), `name`, `category`, `views`, `purchases`
(both event counts for that page), and `conv_pct` = `round(100.0 *
purchases / views, 1)` (NULL-safe: guard the division with
`NULLIF(views, 0)`).

**Ordered by `views` descending, then `product_id` ascending, limited to
10 rows.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 114_drills_mixed_3 ex8`

# Reading - 114_drills_mixed_3

The last set in the course. Read after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

If the earlier gauntlets drilled welding, this one drills *sequencing under
pressure*: every exercise has an order of operations that matters more than
any single clause. Aggregate before you pick a winner (ex2), reduce the big
table before you anti-join it (ex3), carry bookkeeping through a recursion
(ex5), collapse to the right grain before hunting patterns (ex7). The
interview observation behind the set: senior candidates are not
distinguished by knowing more syntax - they are distinguished by naming the
stages out loud before writing any of them, and by adding the two
characters of tie-break or NULLIF that make an answer *stay* correct. Every
query here has at least one such two-character decision.

## ex1

Share-of-total over a grouped result: a window `sum() OVER ()` riding the
five grouped rows, or a scalar subquery for the denominator. What it
tested: knowing a window can run *after* grouping, over the groups
themselves. The classic mistake is `100 * salary / sum(salary)` inside the
grouped pass - mixing grains mid-aggregate - or integer division eating
the decimals before round() sees them.

## ex2

Aggregate, then pick, then decorate. Units per (week, product) must exist
before "best per week" means anything, and the name join is presentation,
attached last. What it tested: the three-stage sequencing plus edge-bucket
honesty (Monday-truncated weeks overlap the month's edges). The classic
mistake is DISTINCT ON over raw joined lines - picking the biggest single
line, not the biggest weekly total - which returns confident nonsense.

## ex3

An anti-join against a computed slice of a 3,000,000-row stream. Both
spellings are correct; the reduce-first one (DISTINCT hot product ids in a
CTE, then LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL) scans events once instead of potentially
per product, which is the habit that survives contact with production. The
two traps: comparing the payload value as text (where '99' >= '999' is
false but '9990' would love a word) and pattern-matching the path (`LIKE
'/p/7%'` catches forty pages). Exact equality on a built string, cast
before comparing.

## ex4

A pivot compared against itself. HAVING cannot see output aliases, so the
comparison repeats both FILTER aggregates - or you stage the pivot in a
CTE and write a plain WHERE over named columns, which is the reference's
choice and the more maintainable one when the pivot grows. What it tested:
that alias-visibility rule under combination pressure, and reading the
result honestly - cancelled-versus-shipped is a noisy near-tie in this
data, so the qualifying list is short and unstable across reseeds, which
is exactly what the numbers say it should be.

## ex5

Recursion with an anchor column. The seed rows are the CEO's direct
reports; their id and name ride every recursive step unchanged, so the
final GROUP BY can attribute each descendant to the right lieutenant. What
it tested: lesson 14's recursive CTE plus the technique of carrying
constant bookkeeping through the walk - and two details people miss:
grouping by anchor *id* (names can collide), and counting the lieutenant
themselves, which the seed row does automatically.

## ex6

Expansion then pick: the tag rows do not exist until
jsonb_array_elements_text manufactures them, and then DISTINCT ON (tag)
with a full tie-break is lesson 49 verbatim. What it tested: composing the
two without staging confusion, and accepting a correct oddity - a product
carries two tags and may win both. The classic mistake is trying to pick
per product first and then per tag, which loses any tag whose flagship was
out-priced within its own product's other tag.

## ex7

Gaps and islands. Reduce to DISTINCT (customer, month) first - order
counts per month are noise here - then the anchor trick: month minus
(row_number months) is constant exactly along a consecutive run, so
consecutive months form a group and HAVING count(*) >= 3 finds the
streaks. What it tested: the single most-asked hard interview pattern in
analytics SQL. The reference's triple self-join (m, m+1, m+2 all present)
is easier to believe and stops scaling the moment the question says
"five"; the islands version changes one digit. Know both, deploy the
second.

## ex8

The end-to-end weld: parse (split_part + cast), pivot (two FILTER counts
in one grouped pass), decorate (join products), rank deterministically,
and guard the division. Each piece appeared alone earlier in the course;
what it tested is doing all five without leaking - the one real trap being
the two-CTE formulation, where purchases must arrive via LEFT JOIN +
COALESCE or a viewed-but-never-bought page silently vanishes instead of
reporting the 0.0 conversion that was the whole point of measuring. The
NULLIF guard costs nothing today and saves the report the day a page has
purchases attributed but no views.

## Further reading

- [WITH Queries - Recursive Queries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html#QUERIES-WITH-RECURSIVE) - the recursion contract and termination.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) - row_number() as the engine of both picks and islands.
- [JSON Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-json.html) - extraction and set-returning expansion.
- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - FILTER counts and their NULL behaviour.
- [PostgreSQL Wiki - Don't do this](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) - a checklist of the quiet mistakes this course spent 115 lessons unlearning.

# 114 - Drills: mixed gauntlet, set 3

The final problem set of the course. Every exercise welds two or three
topics; the last two are the kind of question a senior interview saves for
the end. Take them cold, then read `reading.md` even if you passed.

## Exercise 1 - who costs what

Per department: `payroll` = `sum(salary)` and `payroll_pct` =
`round(100.0 * payroll / total payroll, 1)`. Columns `department`,
`payroll`, `payroll_pct`.

**Ordered by `department` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 114_drills_mixed_3 ex1`

## Exercise 2 - the weekly bestseller board

For each week (`date_trunc('week', orders.created_at)`) touching October
2023 orders (half-open month filter on the order date): the product with
the most units sold (`sum(order_items.quantity)`, ties by `product_id`
ascending). Columns `week`, `product_id`, `name`, `units`.

**Ordered by `week` ascending.** (6 rows - Monday weeks, partial at the
edges.)

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 114_drills_mixed_3 ex2`

## Exercise 3 - premium gear nobody got excited about

`electronics` products priced above 480 whose page (`path = '/p/<id>'`)
never recorded a `view` event with payload `value >= 999`. Columns `id`,
`name`, `price`.

**Ordered by `id` ascending.**

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 114_drills_mixed_3 ex3`

## Exercise 4 - where cancellations beat shipments

Per customer country: `paid`, `shipped`, `cancelled` order counts - but
only countries where `cancelled > shipped`. Columns `country`, `paid`,
`shipped`, `cancelled`.

**Ordered by `country` ascending.**

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 114_drills_mixed_3 ex4`

## Exercise 5 - the CEO's lieutenants, weighed

For each **direct report of the CEO** (the one staff row with NULL
`manager_id`): `name`, and `subtree` = how many people their whole subtree
contains, **including themselves**. Columns `name`, `subtree`.

**Ordered by `subtree` descending, then `name` ascending.**

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 114_drills_mixed_3 ex5`

## Exercise 6 - every tag's flagship

For each of the ten tags: the most expensive product carrying it (price
ties by `id` ascending). Columns `tag`, `product_id`, `name`, `price`. A
product may legitimately win both of its tags.

**Ordered by `tag` ascending.** (10 rows.)

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 114_drills_mixed_3 ex6`

## Exercise 7 - the streak counter

One row, one column `streak_customers`: how many customers have placed
orders in **three or more consecutive calendar months** at least once
(months of `created_at`, consecutive meaning m, m+1, m+2 all present in
that customer's set of order months).

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 114_drills_mixed_3 ex7`

## Exercise 8 - page conversion, end to end

For the ten most-viewed product pages in the whole stream: `product_id`
(parsed from the payload path), `name`, `category`, `views`, `purchases`
(both event counts for that page), and `conv_pct` = `round(100.0 *
purchases / views, 1)` (NULL-safe: guard the division with
`NULLIF(views, 0)`).

**Ordered by `views` descending, then `product_id` ascending, limited to
10 rows.**

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 114_drills_mixed_3 ex8`

# Reading - 114_drills_mixed_3

The last set in the course. Read after your attempt, pass or fail.

## Notes

If the earlier gauntlets drilled welding, this one drills *sequencing under
pressure*: every exercise has an order of operations that matters more than
any single clause. Aggregate before you pick a winner (ex2), reduce the big
table before you anti-join it (ex3), carry bookkeeping through a recursion
(ex5), collapse to the right grain before hunting patterns (ex7). The
interview observation behind the set: senior candidates are not
distinguished by knowing more syntax - they are distinguished by naming the
stages out loud before writing any of them, and by adding the two
characters of tie-break or NULLIF that make an answer *stay* correct. Every
query here has at least one such two-character decision.

## ex1

Share-of-total over a grouped result: a window `sum() OVER ()` riding the
five grouped rows, or a scalar subquery for the denominator. What it
tested: knowing a window can run *after* grouping, over the groups
themselves. The classic mistake is `100 * salary / sum(salary)` inside the
grouped pass - mixing grains mid-aggregate - or integer division eating
the decimals before round() sees them.

## ex2

Aggregate, then pick, then decorate. Units per (week, product) must exist
before "best per week" means anything, and the name join is presentation,
attached last. What it tested: the three-stage sequencing plus edge-bucket
honesty (Monday-truncated weeks overlap the month's edges). The classic
mistake is DISTINCT ON over raw joined lines - picking the biggest single
line, not the biggest weekly total - which returns confident nonsense.

## ex3

An anti-join against a computed slice of a 3,000,000-row stream. Both
spellings are correct; the reduce-first one (DISTINCT hot product ids in a
CTE, then LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL) scans events once instead of potentially
per product, which is the habit that survives contact with production. The
two traps: comparing the payload value as text (where '99' >= '999' is
false but '9990' would love a word) and pattern-matching the path (`LIKE
'/p/7%'` catches forty pages). Exact equality on a built string, cast
before comparing.

## ex4

A pivot compared against itself. HAVING cannot see output aliases, so the
comparison repeats both FILTER aggregates - or you stage the pivot in a
CTE and write a plain WHERE over named columns, which is the reference's
choice and the more maintainable one when the pivot grows. What it tested:
that alias-visibility rule under combination pressure, and reading the
result honestly - cancelled-versus-shipped is a noisy near-tie in this
data, so the qualifying list is short and unstable across reseeds, which
is exactly what the numbers say it should be.

## ex5

Recursion with an anchor column. The seed rows are the CEO's direct
reports; their id and name ride every recursive step unchanged, so the
final GROUP BY can attribute each descendant to the right lieutenant. What
it tested: lesson 14's recursive CTE plus the technique of carrying
constant bookkeeping through the walk - and two details people miss:
grouping by anchor *id* (names can collide), and counting the lieutenant
themselves, which the seed row does automatically.

## ex6

Expansion then pick: the tag rows do not exist until
jsonb_array_elements_text manufactures them, and then DISTINCT ON (tag)
with a full tie-break is lesson 49 verbatim. What it tested: composing the
two without staging confusion, and accepting a correct oddity - a product
carries two tags and may win both. The classic mistake is trying to pick
per product first and then per tag, which loses any tag whose flagship was
out-priced within its own product's other tag.

## ex7

Gaps and islands. Reduce to DISTINCT (customer, month) first - order
counts per month are noise here - then the anchor trick: month minus
(row_number months) is constant exactly along a consecutive run, so
consecutive months form a group and HAVING count(*) >= 3 finds the
streaks. What it tested: the single most-asked hard interview pattern in
analytics SQL. The reference's triple self-join (m, m+1, m+2 all present)
is easier to believe and stops scaling the moment the question says
"five"; the islands version changes one digit. Know both, deploy the
second.

## ex8

The end-to-end weld: parse (split_part + cast), pivot (two FILTER counts
in one grouped pass), decorate (join products), rank deterministically,
and guard the division. Each piece appeared alone earlier in the course;
what it tested is doing all five without leaking - the one real trap being
the two-CTE formulation, where purchases must arrive via LEFT JOIN +
COALESCE or a viewed-but-never-bought page silently vanishes instead of
reporting the 0.0 conversion that was the whole point of measuring. The
NULLIF guard costs nothing today and saves the report the day a page has
purchases attributed but no views.

## Further reading

- [WITH Queries - Recursive Queries](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/queries-with.html#QUERIES-WITH-RECURSIVE) - the recursion contract and termination.
- [Window Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/tutorial-window.html) - row_number() as the engine of both picks and islands.
- [JSON Functions and Operators](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-json.html) - extraction and set-returning expansion.
- [Aggregate Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-aggregate.html) - FILTER counts and their NULL behaviour.
- [PostgreSQL Wiki - Don't do this](https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Don%27t_Do_This) - a checklist of the quiet mistakes this course spent 115 lessons unlearning.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 - who costs what

Per department: `payroll` = `sum(salary)` and `payroll_pct` =
`round(100.0 * payroll / total payroll, 1)`. Columns `department`,
`payroll`, `payroll_pct`.

**Ordered by `department` ascending.**

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 114_drills_mixed_3 ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Group first, then a share-of-total: the total can come from a window sum over the grouped rows or from a scalar subquery. Two topics, one line each.

## Hint 2

Group staff by department with sum(salary), then 100.0 * payroll / sum(payroll) OVER () rounded to 1 - a window over a grouped result is the concise spelling.

## Hint 1

Group first, then a share-of-total: the total can come from a window sum over the grouped rows or from a scalar subquery. Two topics, one line each.

## Hint 2

Group staff by department with sum(salary), then 100.0 * payroll / sum(payroll) OVER () rounded to 1 - a window over a grouped result is the concise spelling.

references.solution.sql:
SELECT department,
       sum(salary) AS payroll,
       round(100.0 * sum(salary) / (SELECT sum(salary) FROM staff), 1) AS payroll_pct
FROM staff
GROUP BY department
ORDER BY department;

FROM d
ORDER BY department;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three stages: aggregate units per (week, product) over the joined October window, pick the best product per week, and fetch the name. Aggregation must come before the pick - you cannot pick a winner from unaggregated lines.

## Hint 2

date_trunc('week', o.created_at) buckets by Monday-started weeks - October 2023 spans six of them, edges partial. The pick is DISTINCT ON (week) ... ORDER BY week, units DESC, product_id, or the row_number() = 1 twin.

references.solution.sql:
WITH wk AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('week', o.created_at) AS week,
         oi.product_id,
         sum(oi.quantity) AS units
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
  WHERE o.created_at >= '2023-10-01' AND o.created_at < '2023-11-01'
  GROUP BY date_trunc('week', o.created_at), oi.product_id),
ranked AS (
  SELECT week, product_id, units,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY week
                            ORDER BY units DESC, product_id ASC) AS rn
  FROM wk)
SELECT r.week, r.product_id, p.name, r.units
FROM ranked r
JOIN products p ON p.id = r.product_id
WHERE r.rn = 1
ORDER BY r.week;
references.expected.sql:
WITH wk AS (
  SELECT date_trunc('week', o.created_at) AS week,
         oi.product_id,
         sum(oi.quantity) AS units
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id
  WHERE o.created_at >= '2023-10-01' AND o.created_at < '2023-11-01'
  GROUP BY date_trunc('week', o.created_at), oi.product_id)
SELECT DISTINCT ON (week)
       week, w.product_id, p.name, w.units
FROM wk w
JOIN products p ON p.id = w.product_id
ORDER BY week, w.units DESC, w.product_id ASC;

## Hint 1

An anti-join whose inner side is a JSONB slice of the event stream: views with a payload value of 999 or more, matched to the product by its page path.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

An anti-join whose inner side is a JSONB slice of the event stream: views with a payload value of 999 or more, matched to the product by its page path.

## Hint 2

Either correlate (NOT EXISTS with payload ->> 'path' = '/p/' || p.id) or reduce first: a CTE of DISTINCT hot-viewed product ids parsed from the path, then products LEFT JOIN it and keep the NULLs.

## Hint 3

The reduce-first shape scans three million events once instead of once per product - with 69 candidate products either survives, but the habit of shrinking the big side before an anti-join is what keeps this pattern alive on real data. Both value tests need the ::int cast; text comparison would let '99' beat '999'.

references.solution.sql:
WITH hot AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT split_part(payload ->> 'path', '/', 3)::int AS pid
  FROM events
  WHERE event_type = 'view'
    AND (payload ->> 'value')::int >= 999)
SELECT p.id, p.name, p.price
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN hot h ON h.pid = p.id
WHERE p.category = 'electronics'
  AND p.price > 480
  AND h.pid IS NULL
ORDER BY p.id;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT p.id, p.name, p.price
FROM products p
WHERE p.category = 'electronics'
  AND p.price > 480
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM events e
    WHERE e.event_type = 'view'
      AND e.payload ->> 'path' = '/p/' || p.id
      AND (e.payload ->> 'value')::int >= 999)
ORDER BY p.id;
