## Hint 1

A status pivot per country (lesson 17's FILTER counts over a join), then a comparison BETWEEN two of the pivoted columns as the group filter.

## Hint 2

HAVING must repeat the aggregates - count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled') > count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'shipped') - because output aliases are not visible there. A CTE plus an ordinary WHERE on the named columns is the alias-friendly spelling.

references.solution.sql:
WITH pivoted AS (
  SELECT c.country,
         sum(CASE WHEN o.status = 'paid'      THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid,
         sum(CASE WHEN o.status = 'shipped'   THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS shipped,
         sum(CASE WHEN o.status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled
  FROM orders o
  JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
  GROUP BY c.country)
SELECT country, paid, shipped, cancelled
FROM pivoted
WHERE cancelled > shipped
ORDER BY country;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT c.country,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'paid')      AS paid,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'shipped')   AS shipped,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.country
HAVING count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'cancelled')
     > count(*) FILTER (WHERE o.status = 'shipped')
ORDER BY c.country;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Recursion (lesson 14) with bookkeeping: walk each subtree downward while remembering WHICH of the CEO's direct reports it started from, then count per starting point.

## Hint 2

Seed the recursive CTE with the CEO's direct reports (manager_id = the CEO's id - the one row whose manager_id IS NULL), carrying each one's id and name along as anchor columns that never change during recursion.

## Hint 3

The recursive step joins staff ON s.manager_id = current member id, copying the anchor columns through. Afterwards GROUP BY the anchor (id and name - two people can share a name) and count(*); the direct report counts themselves. Order by subtree DESC with name as tie-break.

references.solution.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE walk AS (
  SELECT s.id, s.name AS anchor_name, s.id AS anchor_id
  FROM staff s
  JOIN staff ceo ON ceo.id = s.manager_id
                AND ceo.manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.id, w.anchor_name, w.anchor_id
  FROM staff s
  JOIN walk w ON s.manager_id = w.id)
SELECT anchor_name AS name, count(*) AS subtree
FROM walk
GROUP BY anchor_id, anchor_name
ORDER BY subtree DESC, name ASC;
references.expected.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE directs AS (
  SELECT id, name
  FROM staff
  WHERE manager_id = (SELECT id FROM staff WHERE manager_id IS NULL)),
tree AS (
  SELECT d.id AS root_id, d.name AS root_name, d.id AS member_id
  FROM directs d
  UNION ALL
  SELECT t.root_id, t.root_name, s.id
  FROM tree t
  JOIN staff s ON s.manager_id = t.member_id)
SELECT root_name AS name, count(*) AS subtree
FROM tree
GROUP BY root_id, root_name
ORDER BY subtree DESC, name ASC;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Expand first, pick second: jsonb_array_elements_text turns each product into two (tag, product) rows, and then "the priciest per tag" is an ordinary one-per-group pick (lesson 49).

## Hint 2

DISTINCT ON (t.tag) over the expanded FROM clause, ORDER BY t.tag, p.price DESC, p.id. A product can win two tags at once - it carries two - and that is correct, not a bug.

references.solution.sql:
WITH exploded AS (
  SELECT t.tag, p.id, p.name, p.price,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY t.tag
                            ORDER BY p.price DESC, p.id ASC) AS rn
  FROM products p,
       jsonb_array_elements_text(p.attributes -> 'tags') AS t(tag))
SELECT tag, id AS product_id, name, price
FROM exploded
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY tag;
references.expected.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT ON (t.tag)
       t.tag, p.id AS product_id, p.name, p.price
FROM products p,
     jsonb_array_elements_text(p.attributes -> 'tags') AS t(tag)
ORDER BY t.tag, p.price DESC, p.id ASC;

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 - the streak counter

One row, one column `streak_customers`: how many customers have placed
orders in **three or more consecutive calendar months** at least once
(months of `created_at`, consecutive meaning m, m+1, m+2 all present in
that customer's set of order months).

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Run: `uv run dojo test 114_drills_mixed_3 ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Gaps and islands - the interview classic. Reduce orders to DISTINCT (customer, month) first; then "3 consecutive months" is a run in each customer's month sequence.

## Hint 2

The islands trick: number each customer's months with row_number(), then m - rn months is CONSTANT within a consecutive run and different across gaps. Group by (customer, that anchor), HAVING count(*) >= 3, and count distinct customers who own such a group.

## Hint 3

The reference dodges the trick entirely: a customer qualifies if any month m has m + 1 month and m + 2 months present too - a triple self-join of the months CTE. Both must agree exactly; the islands version generalises to "N consecutive" without adding joins, which is why it is the one interviewers want.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Gaps and islands - the interview classic. Reduce orders to DISTINCT (customer, month) first; then "3 consecutive months" is a run in each customer's month sequence.

## Hint 2

The islands trick: number each customer's months with row_number(), then m - rn months is CONSTANT within a consecutive run and different across gaps. Group by (customer, that anchor), HAVING count(*) >= 3, and count distinct customers who own such a group.

## Hint 3

The reference dodges the trick entirely: a customer qualifies if any month m has m + 1 month and m + 2 months present too - a triple self-join of the months CTE. Both must agree exactly; the islands version generalises to "N consecutive" without adding joins, which is why it is the one interviewers want.

references.solution.sql:
WITH months AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, date_trunc('month', created_at) AS m
  FROM orders)
SELECT count(DISTINCT m1.customer_id) AS streak_customers
FROM months m1
JOIN months m2 ON m2.customer_id = m1.customer_id
              AND m2.m = m1.m + interval '1 month'
JOIN months m3 ON m3.customer_id = m1.customer_id
              AND m3.m = m1.m + interval '2 months'
;
references.expected.sql:
WITH months AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, date_trunc('month', created_at) AS m
  FROM orders),
numbered AS (
  SELECT customer_id, m,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY m) AS rn
  FROM months),
islands AS (
  SELECT customer_id, m - (rn * interval '1 month') AS anchor
  FROM numbered)
SELECT count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS streak_customers
FROM (
  SELECT customer_id
  FROM islands
  GROUP BY customer_id, anchor
  HAVING count(*) >= 3) s;

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The full weld: parse the product id out of every view and purchase payload, pivot the two counts per product, join the catalogue for name and category, then rank by views with a deterministic cut.

## Hint 2

One grouped pass with two FILTER counts (WHERE event_type IN ('view', 'purchase') then FILTER each) beats two scans. The conversion is 100.0 * purchases / views rounded to 1 - guard the division with NULLIF(views, 0) even though every top page has views; habits are for the day the data changes.

## Hint 3

If you build views and purchases in separate CTEs instead, the purchases side must come through a LEFT join with COALESCE - a heavily viewed page with zero purchases is a conversion of 0.0, not a missing row. That silent row loss is this exercise's real trap.

references.solution.sql:
WITH v AS (
  SELECT split_part(payload ->> 'path', '/', 3)::int AS pid, count(*) AS views
  FROM events
  WHERE event_type = 'view'
  GROUP BY split_part(payload ->> 'path', '/', 3)::int),
b AS (
  SELECT split_part(payload ->> 'path', '/', 3)::int AS pid, count(*) AS purchases
  FROM events
  WHERE event_type = 'purchase'
  GROUP BY split_part(payload ->> 'path', '/', 3)::int)
SELECT v.pid AS product_id, p.name, p.category, v.views,
       COALESCE(b.purchases, 0) AS purchases,
       round(100.0 * COALESCE(b.purchases, 0) / NULLIF(v.views, 0), 1) AS conv_pct
FROM v
LEFT JOIN b ON b.pid = v.pid
JOIN products p ON p.id = v.pid
ORDER BY v.views DESC, product_id ASC
LIMIT 10;
references.expected.sql:
WITH stats AS (
  SELECT split_part(payload ->> 'path', '/', 3)::int AS product_id,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'view')     AS views,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE event_type = 'purchase') AS purchases
  FROM events
  WHERE event_type IN ('view', 'purchase')
  GROUP BY split_part(payload ->> 'path', '/', 3)::int)
SELECT s.product_id, p.name, p.category, s.views, s.purchases,
       round(100.0 * s.purchases / NULLIF(s.views, 0), 1) AS conv_pct
FROM stats s
JOIN products p ON p.id = s.product_id
ORDER BY s.views DESC, s.product_id ASC
LIMIT 10;
